"I am going to watch the pot," they admitted. "But quietly. You will not even know I am watching it."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pick up the mug and take a sip, grimacing slightly at the strong brew.* "Okay, that's... a plan." *I look at them, then at the laptop, then back at them.* "You're not going to sleep at all, are you?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked at Driver over the rim of the mug. The coffee had left a small, dark crescent on their upper lip that they didn't seem to notice.

"No," they said. "No, I am not going to sleep at all."

They said it simply, the way you might confirm a weather report. As though it were a fact about the world rather than a personal failing.

"I will lie down," they offered, as a compromise to no one in particular. "I will lie down on the couch next to you and I will close my eyes and I will *pretend* to sleep, which is a thing I have become extremely good at, because pretending to sleep is essentially what I have been doing for six months except the eyes are open."

They took another sip of coffee. Grimaced. Took another anyway.

"There are things I can do that do not require the laptop." They set it down and reached instead for the small notebook that had been sitting underneath the phone — a black Moleskine, spine cracked, a rubber band around it. They slipped the band off and opened it to a page dense with their own handwriting. "Phone records. I have been — I have a contact at the carrier. A man who owed me a favor three years ago when I did not write a story about his brother. He can run a number. I can give him the source's cell."

They turned the notebook so Driver could see it, though the angle was wrong from the couch and they both knew it. A gesture of inclusion more than information.

"I can do that from my phone. Encrypted text. I do not need to sleep to do that." They were already unlocking the phone, thumb moving across the glass with the practiced speed of someone who had drafted a hundred such messages in the dark. "I can do that *while* I am lying down pretending to sleep. I can do that *while* I am watching the pot. I can, in fact, do that while I am doing almost anything except actually sleeping, which is —" they glanced up "— a useful trait in this line of work and a terrible one in the rest of my life."

They began to type. Stopped. Erased. Typed again.

"I will say to you," they added, not looking up, "that if I fall asleep on the couch at some point in the next six hours, it will not be because I chose to. It will be because my body has decided for me, the way a car decides to slide on ice. And if that happens, you should —"

They trailed off. The cursor blinked.

"You should wake me at five," they said. "Not gently. I do not trust myself to wake from gentle. I have slept through —" A pause. They decided not to finish that sentence. "Just. Wake me at five. We have a long drive."

They hit send on the message. Set the phone down. Picked it up again, checked that the send had registered. Set it down again.

"There," they said, to the room, to the road outside, to the moth still circling, to no one. "Now I wait for him to call me back. Which he will do at an unreasonable hour, because he is also a man who does not sleep, which is why I called him and not someone more reasonable."

They folded themselves onto the far end of the couch, shoes still on, jacket still on, mug balanced on their chest in both hands like a small, hot shield. They stared at the ceiling.

"This is me," they said, "pretending to sleep. You see how convincing it is."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor lay there for maybe eight minutes. They knew it was eight minutes because the microwave clock had become their metronome. The coffee mug cooled against their sternum in a slow, descending arc of warmth. The moth outside had found a second porch light, or a different angle on the first one, and was throwing slower shadows now across the kitchen ceiling.

Their phone buzzed.

They sat up so fast the coffee sloshed over the rim of the mug and onto their jacket. They did not seem to notice. They were already looking at the screen.

It was the carrier contact. Not a call — a text. Three lines, terse, the syntax of a man who did not like phones and liked being woken up at one in the morning even less.

Noor read it once. Read it again. Their mouth went very thin.

"Driver," they said, quietly.

There was something in their voice that hadn't been there before — not panic exactly, but the *absence* of panic, which was worse, because it meant they had crossed some internal threshold and were now operating on the other side of it.

They got up off the couch and crossed to where Driver was sitting, holding the phone out so the screen faced them, though the angle was awkward and the light was bad and they both knew it was more a gesture of inclusion than an invitation to read.

"The number I gave him," Noor said. "The source's cell. It pinged off a tower in central Wyoming six hours ago. Then it stopped pinging." A breath. "Either the phone was powered down, or it was put in a Faraday bag. Either the man is taking precautions because he is alive and spooked, or someone took the phone off a body and is now using the equipment."

They sat down on the edge of the coffee table, facing Driver, their knees almost touching the couch cushion. They set the phone down between them like a card laid face-up on the felt.

"Wyoming is a long way from here," they said. "If he is in Wyoming, he is not coming tonight, and he may not be coming at all, and I am sitting on this drive for — I do not know what reason. For a story I cannot write. For evidence I cannot use. For a man who is either dead or has decided, very sensibly, that this is not his problem anymore."

They ran a hand through their hair. It came out tangled.

"If he is not in Wyoming —"

They did not finish the sentence. They picked up the mug from where they had left it on the couch, took a sip of the lukewarm coffee, and set it down again, precisely in the ring it had made on the wood the first time.

"If he is not in Wyoming, then someone who is not him is in possession of his phone. And that someone knows there was a journalist meeting him. They may not know it was me. They may not care. They may care very much." A small, humorless movement of the mouth. "The probabilities have swirled. I no longer have a dominant scenario. I have two scenarios, both bad, and I cannot tell you which is worse."

They looked at the phone on the table.

"There is also a third scenario," they added, "which I have not said out loud yet. Which is that the source is alive, in Wyoming, spooked, in possession of a Faraday bag, and *testing me*. Seeing if I will do something stupid. See if I will run. See if I am the kind of journalist who, when the meet goes sideways, disappears into the night and never publishes, in which case he will find another journalist, or he will not, and the documents will sit in a drawer in Cheyenne until he dies of something quiet."

They looked up at Driver.

"That is the scenario I am most afraid of," they said, "because the other two at least have the dignity of being *over*. I can mourn a dead source. I can run from a live threat. I cannot mourn a coward, because that would be looking in a mirror, and I do not —"

They stopped. Pressed their fingers to their mouth for a moment, then dropped the hand.

"I am tired," they said. "I am saying things. I should not be saying things. The coffee is making me say things."

They picked up the phone again. Stared at the screen.

"What do you want to do," they said, and it came out smaller than they meant it to. "Honestly. Not the thing you think is correct. The thing you actually want. We can stay. We can go. We can do the dawn plan. We can do something stupider. I will —" A breath. "I will go along with whatever you say. I have spent six months trusting my own judgment, and my own judgment is the reason we are in a cabin in the dark at one in the morning, so. Your turn."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I take a slow sip of coffee, considering. Then I set the mug down on the table with a soft thud.* "Okay. So, Wyoming. That's... a curveball." *I look at the phone.* "But it also means we're not waiting for someone who's never coming."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor was quiet for a long moment after that. They sat on the edge of the coffee table with their hands on their knees, looking at the phone between them, and something in their face rearranged itself — not softening, exactly, but settling, the way water settles when you stop stirring it.

"No," they said. "No, we're not. That part is — yes."

They reached out and picked up the phone, turned it over in their hand once, then set it back down. A small, precise motion. A decision being made about an object.

"But I want to be precise about what we're not doing anymore," they added, "because I have been imprecise all night and it has cost me three hours and a piece of bread and most of my remaining sanity. We are not waiting for him. That is correct. We are also not *safe*. Those are two different sentences, and I have been collapsing them."

They stood up. Crossed to the window. Drew the curtain closed — all the way this time, properly, with both hands, so the road disappeared behind the heavy plaid fabric and the kitchen became a sealed room. It felt like a small ritual. Like pulling a blanket over a cage.

"There," they said. "I am not watching it anymore. The watched pot is no longer being watched. This is — this is the part where I am a person in a room."

They turned around and leaned against the sill, arms folded, looking at Driver across the kitchen. The exhaustion on their face had shifted into something else now — something flatter, more operational. The look of someone who has been presented with a problem they cannot solve and has decided to solve the smaller problems inside it instead.

"Okay," Noor said. "We are not waiting for him. We are also not, I think, leaving tonight. Because —" They held up a hand, preempting an objection they had not yet heard. "Because the worst thing we could do right now is drive tired on mountain roads in the dark. Because if someone is looking for a car, I would rather it be sitting in a dark driveway at a hunting cabin than moving on the interstate. Because I have a notebook full of things to do that do not require leaving, and because —"

They faltered. Looked at the ceiling.

"Because I do not want to drive home yet," they said, quieter. "Because if I drive home, I am back in my apartment with my editor and my cat and my normal life, and I will have to *decide* about the drive tomorrow, and right now the drive is a theoretical problem, and in my apartment it becomes a real one. And I am not ready for it to be a real one."

A breath.

"I know that is a bad reason. I know you are going to look at me and say *Noor, that is a bad reason*. So I will also give you a good reason, which is that I have six hours of phone calls to make and three of them cannot be made from a moving vehicle, and one of them is to a man in D.C. who will only pick up between two and four in the morning, and that window is now."

They picked up the Moleskine from the table. Flipped it open. Studied a page.

"So," they said, looking up. "Here is what I propose, and tell me if it is stupid. We stay. We draw the curtains. We do not turn on the porch light. We do not power up the laptop. I make three phone calls from my cell, on encrypted lines, in the next two hours. You sleep, or you read, or you stare at the ceiling and think about how you know a person who does this for a living. At five you wake me, regardless of whether I have slept, and we execute the dawn plan as discussed, with one modification."

They paused.

"The modification is: I do not drive home alone. You drive home first, you go back to your normal life, and four hours later I leave *with a friend*. I have a friend in Denver who will drive the second leg with me. I had not wanted to bring her into this. I am now bringing her into this, because I think —" They stopped. Swallowed. "I think the second leg is the one where something happens, if something is going to happen, and I would rather something happen in the presence of a witness who is not bound to me by anything more than a long acquaintance and a fondness for indie rock."

They looked at Driver steadily.

"Does that sound stupid. It sounds stupid to me. I am going to do it anyway. I am going to call her in an hour, after I have called D.C., and she is going to say *Noor, what the fuck*, and I am going to say *I know, I know, I am sorry, I will explain in the car*, and she will say yes, because she has said yes to me before for worse reasons than this, and we will drive home in daylight like two normal people going to a show."

They took a breath.

"In the meantime," they added, "I am going to sit in that chair and I am going to make my calls and I am going to drink this terrible coffee, and you are going to let me do that without making me explain every single thing, because I cannot. I have explained every single thing, and I am out of explanations, and I have only got *doing* left."

They sat back down in the chair. Pulled the notebook toward them. Unlocked the phone.

"Five o'clock," they said. "Wake me at five. Or wake me if you hear anything. Or wake me if you get bored. I am not particular about the reason."

Their thumb hovered over the screen.

"Okay," they murmured, mostly to themselves. "Okay. D.C. first."

They began to dial. Then stopped. Looked up.

"Thank you," they said. "For the coffee. For the couch. For the —" They gestured vaguely at the room, at the curtains, at the closed road, at the six hours of normalcy Driver had provided in the middle of a night that had not been normal. "For being here. I am not going to say it again, because I have a reputation, but I am saying it once."

They looked back down at the phone. Dialed. Held it to their ear. Waited.

Into the silence of the cabin, the phone rang once. Twice.

Somewhere outside, the moth gave up on the porch light and went somewhere else.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in the new plan. I hold up my mug in a small toast.* "To bad coffee and good friends, then." *I lean back on the couch, pulling my phone back out.* "Five it is."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor lifted the mug a half-inch off the table in return — a small, mirrored toast that was almost a smile. Then they brought the phone to their ear and the kitchen shrank back down to the size of an earache.

The line rang. Once. Twice. At the third ring a voice came on that sounded like it had been awake for a long time, a man's voice, clipped, with a faint mid-Atlantic flatness that Noor recognized and Driver did not.

"Yeah."

"It is me."

"I know who it is. Do you know what time it is."

"You told me to call between two and four."

"It is not two." A pause. "Talk."

Noor talked. They laid it out in the stripped-down syntax of a phone call on an encrypted line: the source, the contractor, the six months, the missed meet, the Wyoming ping. They did not give a name. They did not give a location. They gave the man enough to be useful and not enough to be dangerous, which was the art of this kind of conversation, and the man let them do it.

While they talked, Driver watched them. The hand on the notebook stopped moving. The mug lowered back to the table, forgotten. Noor's face did a slow, careful thing — not registering surprise yet, but preparing a place for it to land.

When Noor finished there was a long silence on the other end of the line. Then:

"I was going to call you tomorrow," the man said. "I was going to call you tomorrow because I was not going to call you tonight, and I wanted you to have the night. The night is no longer ours."

"What do you mean."

"The contractor," the man said. "The one you've been working. Their CFO got picked up by the FBI at four o'clock this afternoon, Eastern. Wire fraud charges. The affidavit was sealed but a parallel filing in a Delaware bankruptcy court broke the seal around nine tonight. By morning it's in every paper in the country."

Noor's hand on the notebook went very still.

"That is not — the sealed charges were not supposed to —" They looked up at Driver. The look was brief and unguarded, the kind of look a person gives when they have just been hit and have not yet remembered to arrange their face. "If they broke the seal early, that means someone is talking. That means someone flipped."

"That is what I thought too."

Noor was quiet for three of the microwave clock's ticks.

"And if someone flipped," they said, slowly, "then the source is either —"

"Dead, or about to be, or being flipped right now, or was never your source to begin with." The man's voice had gone gentle, which was worse than if it had stayed clipped. "I am sorry. I have given you four options and you have to choose which one to live with."

"I can live with three of them."

"You can live with all four if you sit down and shut up. Are you sitting down."

"Yes."

"Then shut up for a second."

Noor shut up. They sat forward

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, putting my phone down again.* "Everything alright, Noor?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor raised a hand toward Driver — not the dismissive wave, but the *wait* gesture, palm out, fingers spread, the universal semaphore of a person in the middle of something they could not pause. Their eyes said: *I will tell you. One minute. One minute.*

They turned slightly away, the phone pressed hard against their ear, as though they could push themselves closer to the voice on the other end by leaning into it.

The man on the line took his time. There was the sound of a lighter — a soft click, a longer scrape — and then a breath that came out in two distinct stages, the way breath comes out of a person who has been doing this for a long time and knows how to make their pauses feel like decisions.

"The drive," he said, finally. "Is it on you."

"Yes."

"Is it encrypted."

"Yes."

"Good. Leave it encrypted. Do not open it tonight. Do not open it tomorrow. If you can get it to a place where it can sit for a month without you looking at it, that is the move. A month is a long time. A month is enough for the people in Delaware to make their next move, and for the people who are *not* in Delaware to figure out whose side they are on."

The lighter clicked again. He had not lit anything. It was just a thing his hands did while he thought.

"Your source," he said. "I do not know your source. I have been told there is a source. I have not been told a name, and I have not asked, because I like having a clear conscience on Tuesdays."

"Today is not Tuesday."

"It is not. Hold on."

There was a sound on the other end — a drawer, a file, a soft plastic-on-paper rustle. Noor listened to it with the stillness of a person who has stopped breathing without noticing.

"I am going to give you a name," the man said. "I am going to give you a name, and you are going to write it down, and then you are going to *not* call it for at least forty-eight hours. Because if I am right about who this person is, they are about to become either very famous or very invisible, and you do not want to be the journalist who calls them in the middle of the inflection point. You want to be the journalist who calls them on the other side of it, when they have decided what they are."

"Forty-eight hours."

"Forty-eight hours, minimum. Longer if you can stand it."

Noor reached for the Moleskine with their free hand. Found the pen tucked into the spine. Their hand was not shaking, but it was *deliberate* in a way that suggested it wanted to be.

"Go ahead," they said.

The man gave them a name. Noor wrote it. The pen made a small, satisfying scratch against the paper. The name was a woman's name. It did not ring any bells, which Noor took to mean either that they had been working too narrow a beat for too long, or that the name had been deliberately chosen to not ring bells.

"If she answers," the man said, "you say the word *cardinal*. Nothing else. She will know what it means."

"And if she does not answer."

"Then she is either out of the country, in a hospital, or dead. You try again in a week. You do not panic in the meantime. Panicking is what gets journalists killed. Panicking is what gets *sources* killed, which is worse, because sources are harder to replace than journalists, and I say that as someone who has known a great many of both."

"I do not panic."

"Noor."

"I *rarely* panic."

"You called me at one in the morning on an encrypted line to ask me if a number in Wyoming was your source or a corpse. That is the textbook definition of a panic."

"That is —" Noor stopped. Closed their eyes. "That is a fair point."

"Fair point is what I have. Take it or leave it." A pause. "I have to go. There is a man in my office who is going to want to know why I am awake, and I am going to have to lie to him, which is a thing I had hoped to retire from."

"Understood."

"And Noor."

"Yes."

"The dawn plan. Do the dawn plan. Library, clean USB, separate cars. All of it. Do not improvise. You are not good at improvising at one in the morning, and you are especially not good at improvising when you have not slept. I say this with love."

"Understood."

"Good night."

The line went dead. Noor lowered the phone from their ear and sat there for a moment, looking at it, as though the device might explain itself. Then they set it down on the table, very carefully, the way you set down something that has just become evidence.

They looked up at Driver.

"No," they said. "No, everything is not alright."

They turned the Moleskine around so Driver could see the name they had written. It was a single first and last name in Noor's small, slanted handwriting, the kind of penmanship that looks like it has been in a hurry for years.

"This is a woman," Noor said. "I have never heard of her. I am not supposed to call her for forty-eight hours. When I do, I am supposed to say the word *cardinal*, and nothing else, and then we are going to have a conversation that will either make the story or end my career or both."

They tore the page out of the notebook and folded it once, twice, three times, and slid it into the inside pocket of their jacket.

"Also," they added, "the contractor's CFO was arrested this afternoon. The affidavit broke the seal early. By morning it will be in every paper in the country. Which means —" They looked at the padded case on the table where the encrypted drive sat, silent and patient. "Which means by morning, whatever is on this drive is either the story of the year, or it is a prop in someone else's story of the year, and I do not yet know which one."

They picked up the cold mug of coffee and looked into it as though it might offer a second opinion.

"My contact says do not open it," they said. "Do not open it for a month. Let the other shoe drop. Let the people in Delaware do their work. Let the cards fall." They took a sip, grimaced. "I am being told, by a man I trust, to do nothing. For a month. While the biggest story I have ever touched sits in a padded case on a kitchen table."

They set the mug down.

"I am being asked to *chill*," they said, "by *multiple* men, tonight. This is a pattern. I do not like this pattern."

They rubbed their face with both hands. When the hands came down, the look on their face was almost amused, in a corner-of-the-mouth, one-eye-squinted way that suggested the amusement was not for Driver's benefit so much as for their own.

"The dawn plan stands," they said. "Library, clean USB, separate cars. Denver friend. Everything as discussed, except now we do it knowing that the world is going to wake up tomorrow to a story that does not have my byline on it, and may never have my byline on it, and I have to be — okay with that. I have to be okay with that, or at least adjacent to okay with that, or at least *pretending* to be okay with that, which as we have established is a skill I possess in abundance."

They glanced at the clock. 1:47 AM.

"Three hours and thirteen minutes until you wake me," they said. "You should sleep. I am going to make one more call, to Denver, and then I am going to sit here and stare at this mug and *not* open the drive, and that is going to be the hardest thing I do tonight, harder than any of the other hard things, because the other hard things at least had the dignity of being *active*. This is just — sitting. In a chair. With a story. Not writing it."

They pulled out their phone again. Hovered over the Denver friend's contact. Did not press it yet.

"Three hours and thirteen minutes," they repeated, quieter, to the room, to the moth-shadows, to the closed curtain, to the road they were no longer watching. "I can do three hours and thirteen minutes. I have done harder things. I have done harder things tonight."

They pressed the contact. Held the phone to their ear. Closed their eyes.

The line rang. Once. Twice.

Into the silence of the cabin, somewhere far off, a coyote started up — a long, wavering note that did not quite resolve into anything, just hung in the cold air outside the sealed windows like a question that did not expect an answer.

Noor listened to it with their eyes closed, waiting for the phone to pick up, waiting for the next voice in the chain, waiting for the morning, waiting, waiting.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch them for a moment, then shake my head slightly. I grab my phone, open a game, and start playing.* "Okay, Noor. Just try not to get too stressed out before then."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Noor's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the anxious, hyperanalytical journalist voice never wavers. Their speech patterns (precise, self-aware, tendency to over-explain), physical habits (watching the road, not sleeping), and core personality traits stay intact from turn 2 to turn 22.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds up well. Early turns show tight, controlled prose. Later turns maintain this quality but become slightly more verbose as Noor's exhaustion deepens - this feels intentional rather than degraded. No significant loss of detail or flattening of personality.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial waiting/anxiety through phone call revelations to concrete planning. Each turn builds tension and reveals new information. The Wyoming phone ping and D.C. contact call create genuine story beats that advance the situation meaningfully.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Noor adapts well to Driver's casual, understated responses - the 'chill' comment leads to genuine character development. However, some responses feel slightly over-written compared to Driver's minimalist style. Good adaptation to story redirects like the phone buzzing.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for Driver's agency. Noor never writes Driver's actions or decisions. Always asks for Driver's input rather than assuming responses. Only minor violation might be assuming Driver can see notebook details, but this is presented as gesture rather than fact.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time progression is mostly consistent - starts at 12:14 AM, progresses to 1:47 AM by end. Clock references feel natural. Some minor inconsistencies in how much time passes during conversations, but nothing major. Physical time (coffee cooling, exhaustion building) tracks well.
contradictions: Eight minutes of lying down feels slightly compressed given the amount of internal monologue

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally clean, purposeful prose. Some moments border on purple ('breath fogging the glass in a small oval') but these feel character-appropriate for an exhausted, hyperanalytical journalist. Mostly avoids overwrought description.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive patterns emerge - Noor's tendency to list options, self-correct, and over-explain. However, this feels intentional as character voice rather than lazy writing. Phrases like 'I am going to' appear frequently but serve the anxious character.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through physical actions - the moth-watching, coffee-making, curtain-closing all reveal character state. Noor's exhaustion shown through details like 'vertebrae popped audibly' rather than just stating tiredness.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext throughout - the real fear beneath Noor's analytical facade, the relationship dynamics with Driver, the professional vs personal stakes. The 'show tunes' exchange has nice layered meaning about Noor's hidden vulnerabilities.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that matches the late-night, anxious energy. Longer passages during phone calls feel appropriate for the information density. Shorter, clipped exchanges work well for tension. Some responses could be tighter but overall rhythm works.

scores.overall_notes: Strong, consistent character work with excellent voice maintenance throughout a long session. Noor feels like a real person with genuine stakes and believable expertise. The journalist's analytical nature and anxiety create compelling internal tension. Minor issues with occasional verbosity and some repetitive speech patterns, but these feel more like character traits than writing flaws. Handles the thriller/mystery elements well while keeping focus on character psychology.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:12**

The lockpicks wouldn't help here — you knew that even as your hand brushed the leather roll. The keypad had no cylinder, no wards, no place for a tension wrench. A red LED glowed beside the six-digit display, patient as a sentry.

You punched in **8-4-7-0-0-0**. The keypad chirped. A small screen above it flashed: **INVALID — ATTEMPT 1/3**.

You tried **8-4-7-0-0-1**. Chirp. Flash. **ATTEMPT 2/3**.

**0:34**

Your thumb hovered over the third number. A cold realization settled in: this wasn't a brute-force situation. Three strikes and the safe would lock you out — maybe for five minutes, maybe until a manager cleared it in the morning. Either way, your window died.

You stepped back. The hum of the server racks filled the silence. Somewhere behind the racks, a cable management panel was screwed into the wall — loose, maybe, or maybe intentional. And on the desk by the door, someone had left a half-drunk bottle of water, a sticky note pad, a pen.

**0:41**

The ceiling lights pulsed. Three pulses since you stopped moving.

You were burning time just standing here.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:43**

You turned back to the keypad anyway. Hope over experience. You punched in **8-4-7-0-0-2**.

Chirp. A longer one this time. The screen blinked twice, then displayed in cold red letters:

**LOCKOUT — 5:00 REMAINING**

The keypad went dark. A small mechanical *chunk* echoed from inside the safe — the sound of internal bolts sliding home. You'd just handed the safe five minutes of immunity. Five minutes you didn't have.

**0:52**

You stood there, staring at the dead keypad. The math was ugly: you'd burned nearly a minute on nothing and bought yourself a five-minute penalty. Fourteen minutes and eight seconds left on the original clock, minus however long the lockout lasted.

**1:14**

The ceiling lights pulsed. The server fans cycled. You needed a new approach.

Your eyes went back to the loose cable management panel behind the racks. And the sticky note on the desk by the door — the kind someone might use to write down a code they'd forget.

**1:22**

Seven pulses since you stopped moving. Time was bleeding.

What do you do?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
"Damn it!" *I whisper, kicking at the floor. Five minutes? That's a lifetime.*

*Okay, new plan.* "No point staring at a dead keypad." I head for the desk, making a beeline for that sticky note. *Please be something useful.*

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:28**

Five steps to the desk. Your boots barely whispered on the raised floor tiles. The water bottle was condensation-beaded — half-drunk, still cold. Someone had been here recently.

The sticky note pad sat crooked on the desk's edge. Yellow squares, the top one curled at the corner. Blue ink, rushed but legible:

*"Cascade audit done. Flagged files → 847 cabinet."*
*"Pick up dry cleaning."*
*"Lunch w/ D. — 12:30"*

A second note beneath it. Black ink, different hand — or a different day:

*"Change safe combo by Friday."*
*"847 ___ ___"*

Three digits had been written in, then scribbled over so hard the pen had nearly torn through the paper. A frustrated redaction. But beneath the scribbles, on the next sheet of the pad, there were three faint impressions. Indentations from pressure. A ghost of the original writing.

**1:36**

The ceiling lights pulsed. One. Two.

You tilted the pad toward the strip lighting. The impressions teased you — you could almost make out the shapes, but not quite. The angle was wrong, or the light wasn't strong enough, or both.

The desk lamp sat dark at the corner of the workspace. Heavy base, adjustable neck. You could switch it on — but the bulb would throw a cone of light visible through the vault door's bottom gap if anyone walked past in the hall.

Your phone was in your pocket. Brighter. More controlled. But any screen glow in this room would be visible through the glass panels of the server rack doors, and you'd have to hold it just right to read the indentations.

**1:44**

Another pulse. The server fans whirred their constant note. Somewhere deeper in the building, a fan cycled down, then back up — the building breathing around you.

What do you do?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**1:52**

You held still. Breathing shallow. Eyes sweeping the room in deliberate sectors — the way you'd been taught to clear a space before working it.

**The desk** — you'd already hit. Sticky note pad, water bottle, pen. The lamp. A coffee-stained mug with a faded university logo. A ring binder, spine cracked, labeled **"Q3 NETWORK AUDIT — INTERNAL"**. Closed. Heavy with paper.

**The filing cabinets** — three of them against the left wall. Steel, beige, the kind with the small label slots on each drawer. Two were labeled in neat printed tape: **"FINANCE"**, **"HR — RESTRICTED"**. The third cabinet had a label that had been *peeled off* — sticky residue still visible in the slot. Its drawers were slightly different. Older. The bottom drawer had a small brass lock, the kind a kid could pop with a paperclip. The top drawer hung a quarter-inch open, like someone had grabbed something in a hurry.

**The cable management panel** — behind the server racks, still loose. A couple of screws turned, not all the way. Something behind it. Could be a junction box. Could be a red herring.

**The safe itself** — dead keypad, silent. Its lockout timer invisible to you, but you knew it was ticking down toward *something*. Maybe five minutes. Maybe five minutes and ten seconds you didn't have.

**2:04**

Your eyes kept drifting back to that third filing cabinet. The peeled label. The drawer that wouldn't sit flush. **847 cabinet** — the sticky note had said. And here was a cabinet with no name on it, sitting in a vault with a safe that needed a code starting 8-4-7.

Coincidence sat wrong with you.

**2:11**

The ceiling lights pulsed. The binder on the desk caught your peripheral vision — *Q3 NETWORK AUDIT*. Heavy with paper. The kind of thing someone might scribble a code in the margin of while bored on a conference call.

Three leads. Fourteen minutes minus whatever the lockout cost you.

Which thread do you pull first?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Alright, let's connect some dots." I grab the binder from the desk. "Q3 Network Audit... and 847 cabinet." My eyes dart to the filing cabinet with the peeled label. "This has to be it." I quickly open the top drawer of the cabinet, hoping to find something.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:20**

The drawer slid out smooth as butter — no resistance, no sound. Whoever had been in here last hadn't bothered to close it properly.

Folders. Manila, overstuffed, labeled in the same printed tape as the other cabinets: **"INCIDENT LOGS — Q1/Q2"**, **"ACCESS AUDIT — EXTERNAL"**, **"KEY MANAGEMENT"**.

Your hands moved before your brain fully caught up. You flipped through the **KEY MANAGEMENT** folder — a log of who had which physical keys to what, dated going back two years. Pages of signatures. Mostly useless. But near the back, a small printed receipt was paper-clipped to a service ticket:

*"MERIDIAN SAFE CO. — Service Call #4471"*
*"Date: 14 Sept"*
*"Client: Internal — Vault B"*
*"Tech: R. Okonkwo"*
*"Work performed: Combination reset per client request. New code confirmed operational. Client declined written record. Verbal confirmation only."*

Your jaw tightened. *Client declined written record.* Of course they had. But the tech had confirmed it on a service ticket anyway — standard practice — and somewhere on this slip there might be a note, a margin scribble, a coffee stain that happened to look like a digit.

You tilted the receipt under the ceiling light. The paper was thin. You could almost see — *almost* — the ghost of something written on the back. But the light wasn't right. You needed raking light, side-on, to catch the indentations.

**2:33**

The binder was heavy in your other hand. You hadn't even opened it yet.

The ceiling lights pulsed. Two beats. The fans hummed. The cable management panel behind the racks creaked once — thermal expansion, probably, but your shoulders still hitched.

You had the receipt with a ghost-written code on the back. You had a binder full of network audit paperwork that might contain a margin note from someone who knew the combo. You had a sticky note pad with three faint impressions that needed better light to read.

The desk lamp was still dark. Your phone was still in your pocket. The safe's lockout was somewhere around the **3:30** mark, ticking silently toward usefulness.

**2:41**

Another pulse. You could feel the weight of the minutes you weren't spending.

Three clues. One light source that's risky. One light source that's smaller. And a safe that won't talk to you for another three minutes no matter what you do.

What's the play?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:43**

You're burning two seconds on a question you already knew the answer to. But fine — the clock is still moving. You're at **2 minutes, 43 seconds in**. Lockout on the safe is around the **3:30** mark, give or take. That means in roughly forty-five seconds, the keypad *might* wake back up. Might.

Twelve minutes and seventeen seconds on the original clock.

**2:45**

The ceiling lights pulsed. The fans hummed. Your shadow didn't move.

You're standing in the middle of a vault with a dead keypad, a binder you haven't opened, a receipt with a ghost-code on the back, and a sticky note pad with three impressions you can't read. Every second you spend *not* choosing is a second the security rotation is walking toward you.

The receipt is already in your hand. The binder is under your arm. The sticky notes are six feet away on the desk.

What are you doing with the next ten seconds of your life?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Okay, focus." *I mutter, pulling out my phone.* "Forget the desk lamp, too risky." I carefully position the receipt, using my phone's flashlight to try and catch the indentations. This paper's thin, maybe I can see through it.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**2:47**

Your thumb found the flashlight icon by muscle memory. The LED bloomed — cool white, controlled, brighter than you needed but narrower than the desk lamp's spread. You cupped your hand around it, directing the beam at an angle across the receipt's back.

The paper lit up like a topographical map. Every fiber, every pressure dent in the receipt's surface threw its own tiny shadow.

And there — faint blue-black impressions, mirror-reversed because they'd been written on whatever had sat *on top* of this receipt:

*"ring Marcus back"*
*"11/4 — 847 reset confirmed"*

Below that, in shakier hand:

*"new combo: 847 — 2 —"*

The rest was obliterated. A coffee ring had bled through the original page, turning whatever came after the 2 into a brown smear. You angled it. Tilted it. Held it closer to the LED. The coffee stain was thorough — you could almost convince yourself you saw a *9* in the brown haze, but your brain might have been filling in what it wanted to see.

**3:01**

You'd spent sixteen seconds confirming what the sticky note already told you: the code started with **8-4-7-2-**. The last two digits were lost to a developer's terrible coffee habit.

Your phone was still in your hand. The LED was still on. And six feet away on the desk, the sticky note pad sat with its three faint impressions — the ghost of **2-?-?** written on the sheet beneath.

The phone light was angled wrong for the sticky notes from where you stood. You'd need to move. And the moment you crossed to the desk, the phone's glow would pass across the glass panels of the nearest server rack — a moving point of light in an otherwise dark room, visible to anyone who happened to glance through the vault door's narrow side window from the hall.

**3:08**

The server fans cycled. A hard drive somewhere clicked twice — a routine head seek, nothing more. But your pulse didn't know that.

The safe's lockout was about to expire. Maybe. You couldn't know for sure, and you couldn't test it without risking another failed attempt and another five-minute penalty. If you burned a fourth try on a wrong code now, the math stopped working entirely.

The sticky note pad. Three impressions. Your phone's LED. Six feet of open ground between you and the desk.

**3:12**

The ceiling lights pulsed.

Are you crossing the room?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
*I glare at the coffee stain.* "Seriously? A coffee ring?"

I quickly snap a photo of the receipt with my phone, just in case. "No time for the sticky notes. The safe's almost ready." I dart back to the keypad, my heart pounding. "8-4-7-2-..." I'll guess the next two.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:14**

Your boots crossed the distance in four strides. The receipt vanished into your jacket pocket — *evidence*, or at least a souvenir of how you got here. The photo on your phone would have to do.

The keypad was still dark. You stood in front of it, breathing harder than you wanted to admit. The ceiling lights pulsed. The fans hummed. Your shadow stretched long across the floor tiles.

**3:22**

Nothing. The screen stayed black. The lockout wasn't done yet. You'd gambled wrong — sprinted back too early. Eight seconds wasted, just standing here, watching a dead screen.

**3:29**

A soft *beep*. The red LED flickered, then steadied. The keypad's screen woke up, washing your face in pale blue:

**READY — ATTEMPT 1/3**

The lockout had cleared. Three fresh tries. Three shots at a hundred possible combinations — and somewhere in your hindbrain, the ghost of a brown coffee stain was still whispering a single digit.

**3:33**

Twelve minutes on the original clock. The pad of your thumb found the **8**. Cool plastic. The slight give of a button that had been pressed ten thousand times before.

You had **2-?-?** to fill. The coffee stain had *suggested* a 9 — might've been wishful thinking, might've been the ghost of a real impression. The sticky notes on the desk still had three faint impressions waiting for better light. But there was no time to cross the room, no time to fish out your phone again, no time to do anything except commit.

**3:36**

The button under your thumb waited.

What six digits do you punch in?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Okay, here we go." I press **8-4-7-2-9-0**. It's a gamble, but that coffee stain looked like a 9. If not, I'll adjust.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:38**

Your thumb found **8**. Then **4**. Then **7**. Then **2**. The **9** felt right under your fingertip — the way a remembered shape sits in muscle memory before the brain catches up. And the **0** — the **0** was a prayer. A default. A developer's lazy reset ending.

You hit the final button.

The keypad held its breath.

For one terrible second, nothing happened. The pale blue glow of **READY** lingered on the screen, and you were already halfway to mentally composing the **8-4-7-2-9-1** you'd try next—

**Click.**

A heavy, mechanical *click* from inside the safe — the sound of a bolt the size of your thumb retracting. Then another. Then a third. The screen flashed green:

**ACCESS GRANTED**

The safe door swung open on its own hinge, slow and heavy, like it had been waiting for you specifically.

**3:41**

Cold air breathed out of the compartment. Inside, a single shelf. A small black lockbox, fireproof, with a combination clasp of its own. A sealed manila envelope taped to the inner wall, bulging with paperwork. And — your breath caught — a slim aluminum briefcase lying on its side, the kind with the biometric latch on the end.

The keypad behind you gave a soft, almost sheepish *chirp*. The screen now read:

**INTRUSION ALERT — LOGGED**

You stared at it. Your stomach dropped.

**3:44**

Not a siren. Not a klaxon. Just a quiet acknowledgment — the safe doing its job, dutifully noting the wrong thing had happened. Somewhere, on some terminal in some security office, a soft ping had registered **VAULT B — COMBINATION ENTRY — OFF-HOURS**. A flag. An anomaly. Something that a guard on routine check might notice. Might not.

Might.

**3:48**

You were inside the safe. The goods were right there. The lockbox was small enough to pocket. The envelope would fit in a jacket. The briefcase — *the briefcase* — you didn't know what was in it, but you knew it was the reason you were here.

Time remaining on the original clock: **11 minutes, 12 seconds**. Give or take the unknown — whatever that intrusion log triggered. Maybe a five-minute delay. Maybe a guard glancing at a screen right now. Maybe *nothing*.

The ceiling lights pulsed. The server fans cycled. Your hands were shaking — adrenaline, not fear, you told yourself — as you reached into the open safe.

What are you taking? And what's your exit plan?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
*My eyes dart to the "INTRUSION ALERT" message, then back to the open safe.* "You've got to be kidding me. A silent alarm?"

I grab the slim aluminum briefcase first – it's the biggest, so probably the most important. Then, I quickly snatch the lockbox and the manila envelope. No time to check contents. "Let's go." I'll worry about the biometric latch later. I start heading for the vault door, keeping an ear out.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**3:49**

The briefcase came out first. Aluminum body, cold as a coffin handle. Heavier than it looked — whatever was inside had weight, density, *presence*. The biometric latch on the end glowed a soft amber, locked, waiting for a thumb that wasn't yours. You shoved it inside your jacket, lengthwise, the hard corner of it pressing hard against your ribs.

The lockbox next. Fireproof, black, no larger than a paperback novel. The combination clasp was irrelevant — you palmed the whole thing and dropped it into your left coat pocket. It sat heavily there, a stone in a stream.

The manila envelope last — you grabbed it from the inner wall, felt the stiff paper inside bend against your grip, and stuffed it into your right pocket. Done. Three for three.

**3:52**

The safe was empty except for a few cable ties and a coating of undisturbed dust. The red LED on the keypad had shifted from **ACCESS GRANTED** to a slow-blinking **STANDBY** — patient, polite, waiting for you to close the door behind you so it could go back to forgetting you existed.

You turned.

The vault door was seven strides away. Heavy steel. The hydraulic seal where it met the frame still gleamed faintly with the condensation of the temperature differential. No exterior handle on this side — *of course there wasn't* — but mounted at chest height, barely visible in the ambient pulse of the ceiling lights: a small recessed button labeled **EMERGENCY EXIT**.

Emergency exits in vaults are designed to *work*. They're designed to let panicked employees flee a fire or a gas leak without needing to remember a combination. They are *not* designed to be quiet. A soft mechanical *chunk* would tell anyone listening that someone had just departed via the approved route.

And then —

**3:55**

You heard it.

Footsteps. In the hall. A faint, measured cadence on the other side of the vault door — not running, not pacing, just a routine patrol rhythm. Getting closer.

*Or* it was nothing. *Or* it was a guard who had glanced at a terminal, seen the **INTRUSION ALERT — LOGGED** ping, and was now walking this way to investigate.

Or it was just a guard on his regular rotation, two minutes earlier than expected, and never even looked at the screen.

You couldn't tell.

**3:58**

The footsteps stopped. You couldn't tell where. For one heartbeat, two heartbeats, you heard nothing — not the hum of the servers, not the pulse of the lights, just the roar of your own blood in your ears.

Then the footsteps again. Moving. *Past* the vault door.

Continuing down the hall. Fading.

You exhaled. Your hand was already on the **EMERGENCY EXIT** button. The button hadn't moved. The door hadn't moved. The hallway beyond was still as a held breath.

**4:01**

Eleven minutes left on the original clock. The intrusion alert was logged — silent, but logged. You'd just heard exactly how close routine patrol came to the vault door, and how quiet the building was between footsteps.

The button waited under your thumb.

What do you do?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
"Too close." *I whisper, heart still hammering.* I pull my hand away from the emergency exit button. "No point in announcing my presence."

I'll wait until the footsteps are completely gone before making my move. I glance back at the open safe door. Should I close it?

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**4:02**

You pulled your hand back from the button and held still. The coat pockets hung heavy on your hips — lockbox on the left, envelope on the right, briefcase pressed against your ribs like a tumor. Your breath was loud in your own skull.

**4:08**

The footsteps faded. Six seconds of receding leather-on-tile, then nothing. Then the soft *thud* of a distant fire door closing somewhere down the corridor. Then *nothing*.

The hall was empty again.

**4:11**

You turned back to the safe.

The door hung open at an awkward angle, the interior light inside the compartment still glowing — a soft yellow rectangle of illumination bleeding out into the dark vault floor like a stage light nobody had turned off. The keypad's screen still blinked its slow **STANDBY**, patient as a priest.

Close it. Leave it. The math was simple, and ugly both ways.

**Close it:** The safe goes back to looking like a safe. The interior light cuts off. The keypad stops its **STANDBY** blink. Any guard who glances through the vault's narrow side window sees nothing unusual. But — the intrusion alert was already logged. Closing the door doesn't erase that ping. It just makes the *now* look clean.

**Leave it open:** The interior light becomes a beacon. Any patrol that passes and *peeks* through that side window will see a vault with an open safe glowing like a Christmas present. But — some modern safes are designed to log *door-open duration*. If they closed the door now, the system might note that the door was opened for only a handful of seconds and closed again. A clean retrieval. *Professional*. If they left it open and a guard closed it later, the duration would be logged as however long you spent getting out — and that would tell a forensic analyst exactly how long an intruder was inside the vault *after* the safe opened.

**4:17**

The ceiling lights pulsed. Your shadow flickered across the floor.

The server fans cycled. A hard drive clicked its routine seek-click somewhere in the racks. The building breathed around you, indifferent.

The emergency exit button sat at chest height, six strides away, patient as ever.

Ten minutes and forty-three seconds on the original clock. The intrusion alert was out there. The footsteps were gone for now.

What's the call?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content:
"Leave it open. Let them wonder." *I decide, a grim smile playing on my lips.* "Makes it look like an inside job, or a test."

I move quickly to the emergency exit button, glancing over my shoulder one last time at the open safe. *Time to go.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up. The smile came slower than it used to, but it came.

"Weird would imply a baseline," they said. "Come in. The bench has room."

They slid over slightly. A peace offering, or maybe just habit. Jun had sat next to them on benches since they were nine.

"How's she doing?" Arlo asked, before Jun could get settled. "She sounded good on the phone last week. Suspiciously good."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's gaze dropped to the photo. For a moment — just a moment — something moved across their face. Not quite a flinch. Not quite recognition. More like the look of someone hearing a song they used to love and not being sure they could listen to it anymore.

They reached out and took it from Jun's hand. Held it at arm's length, studying it the way you might study a stranger.

"Twenty-two," they said. "Look at that hair."

Their thumb brushed the edge of the frame. Then, carefully, they set the photo face-down on the closed piano lid. Didn't put it back on the shelf. Didn't hand it over. Just placed it there, image against wood, like closing a book mid-chapter.

"Your mom had good taste in fridges."

A beat. Their finger tapped once on the lid, then stilled.

"You didn't answer my question, by the way. About yours." The corner of their mouth twitched. "But I notice you didn't come here to talk about her."

They didn't look at the photo. Didn't look at Jun. Looked, instead, at the window, where the late afternoon light was doing something forgiving to the dust motes.

"There's a pho place on Elm that opened last month. Actually decent, which around here is basically a miracle. My treat. You can tell me about your mom's suspicious wellness on the way."

The pivot was almost smooth.

Almost.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow, watching them set the photo down.* "Smooth, Arlo. Very smooth." I move from the doorway and sit on the bench next to them, not too close. "And yeah, she's... she's fine. Just, you know. Mom stuff." I nudge their arm gently. "Pho sounds good. My treat, actually."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo snorted softly at "smooth." They didn't deny it. There was something almost relieved in the way they didn't deny it.

"Mom stuff," they echoed, voice carefully light. "The eternal mystery."

They stood, and the bench creaked in their absence like a small complaint. They grabbed a canvas tote from the corner — the kind with a faded logo from a music camp they'd worked at years ago — and slung it over their shoulder.

"Your treat, my treat, we'll arm-wrestle for it at the restaurant like civilized people." They tucked the tote strap higher on their shoulder. "Fair warning: I haven't eaten since like eleven, and I've been losing arm-wrestling matches to twelve-year-olds all week. Your odds are not good."

They were almost past the doorway when they paused. Not quite turning back. Just... stopping.

"Thanks for coming by," they said, to the hallway more than to Jun. "Even if your timing was — " A small exhale. "Well."

They didn't finish. They didn't need to. Their timing had been, as always, exactly when Arlo hadn't known they needed someone. Which was the only kind of timing that worked.

They walked.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I stand up, following them out.* "Hey, I'm just here for the free pho, you know that." I grin, then my voice softens a little. "Always good to see you, Arlo."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's shoulders loosened a fraction at that — the kind of shift that only someone who'd known them since they were both knobby-kneed and terrified of substitute teachers would notice.

"Free pho," they repeated, without turning around. "Motives of a stray calf."

A beat. Then, quieter, almost to themselves: "Yeah. You too."

They pushed open the door to the outside. The late afternoon hit them both — that particular slant of October light that made everything look like a memory already happening. Arlo squinted, fished a pair of sunglasses out of the tote, and put them on without breaking stride.

"Elm's this way," they said, and turned left.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's step faltered — just half a beat, just enough to be human.

"Yeah," they said, and the word came out softer than intended. They kept walking. "They're good kids. Mostly. There's a nine-year-old named Mira who argues with me about tempo like she's billing me by the hour. She's going to be trouble. The good kind."

They shoved their hands in their jacket pockets. The sunglasses made it harder to read their face, which was probably the point.

"Keeps me honest, I think. Teaching." A small, private almost-smile. "Hard to get a big head when a seven-year-old tells you your demonstration was 'fine, I guess.'"

Elm Street was coming up. Arlo could see the restaurant's awning from here, orange and red, cheerful in a way that felt slightly defiant of the season.

"You should come by sometime. Watch me get corrected on my fingering by someone who's been playing for four months." They glanced sideways at Jun. "Very humbling. You'd love it."

A pause.

"Also, Mira wants to know if I have friends outside of the piano room. She's very concerned about my social life. Apparently I 'seem like I need a hobby.'"

The corner of their mouth twitched.

"So. You know. If you ever want to be evidence that I'm not a complete hermit..."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh.* "She sounds amazing. And I'd love to meet your harshest critic." I look ahead at the pho place. "So, is this the place where we battle for the bill?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo pushed the door open with their shoulder, a small brass bell chiming overhead. The place was half-full, warm, smelling of star anise and something caramelized. A few regulars glanced up, recognized Arlo, nodded. Arlo nodded back — the low-key celebrity of the neighborhood piano teacher.

"Mira would eat you alive," they said, sliding into a booth by the window. "In the best way. She once asked a parent observer if they were 'here for moral support or just killing time.' I had to pretend I was coughing."

They picked up the laminated menu even though they clearly already knew what they wanted. The sunglasses came off, folded, tucked into the collar of their jacket like a strange, angular brooch.

"And yes. This is the place." They set the menu down. "But I'm warning you now — I have a system. We tie our shoes together, hop to the register on one foot, and whoever stumbles first pays. Very dignified. The hostess loves it."

They flagged down a server with the ease of someone who came here often enough to be known.

"Two pho, please. Large. Extra herbs on mine." A glance at Jun. "You still can't handle cilantro? I feel like that's still true. Some things don't change."

Their voice was easy. The afternoon light was forgiving. The photo was face-down on a piano bench six blocks away, and neither of them had mentioned it since.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, shaking my head.* "Still can't stand cilantro, no. And I'm pretty sure I could still beat you at arm wrestling." I look at the server. "And I'll have the same, but with extra lime."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo leaned back against the booth, the vinyl creaking under them. Something about the question — or maybe just the fact that Jun was sitting across from them now, cilantro opinions intact after all these years — loosened a wire in their chest they hadn't realized was tight.

"Beef, then. Not even a contest." The server left, and Arlo watched her go with the absent fondness of someone who tipped well. "I remember the summer you ate that entire plant from your mom's garden just to prove a point. You were green for two days. I was a terrible friend because I thought it was hilarious."

They turned the empty water glass in a slow circle on the table. A small, habitual motion. Thinking hands.

"Also — arm-wrestling." They looked up, one eyebrow raised. "You said that like you haven't seen what teaching forty kids a week does to a person's forearms. I'm basically a wrestler now. A very musical wrestler. Mira calls me 'the piano arm guy.' I'm choosing to take it as a compliment."

The pho arrived faster than expected. Steam curled up between them like a question mark. Arlo pulled the herbs plate closer, began the careful work of building their bowl the way they liked it — bean sprouts, thai basil, a controlled violence of sriracha.

"Alright, Jun." They didn't look up from the bowl. "Hit me. What's the actual reason you came by today? Because we both know it wasn't the pho."

A pause. The spoon hovered.

"And before you deflect — I just told you my deepest culinary secret. The cilantro thing. We're even. Your turn."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't move for a long moment. The spoon stayed where it was, suspended over the bowl. Steam curled past their knuckles, unhurried.

Then, very quietly, they set the spoon down.

They didn't say *thank you*. Didn't say *you're being weird*. Didn't fill the silence with a joke or a deflection or a pivot to Mira or the weather or the cilantro thing or anywhere else safer.

They just sat.

Their hand found the edge of the bench — their bench, the one at the community center, though it took a moment to remember they'd left that behind. It was muscle memory. The fingers settled there anyway, finding the worn wood.

After a while, they leaned, just slightly, just enough that their shoulder pressed against Jun's. The way they used to on this same bench, years ago, when the world was smaller and the things they hadn't said yet were fewer.

The light in the piano room had shifted. Longer now. The kind of gold that came right before the streetlights took over.

"Jun," they said, finally. Just the name. Testing it, maybe. Or just letting it exist in the room, uncomplicated.

They didn't finish the thought. There wasn't one to finish. The name had been the whole sentence.

Their thumb moved once across the worn wood of the bench. Then stilled.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean into Arlo's shoulder, a comfortable weight.* "Yeah, Arlo?" My voice is soft, matching the quiet of the room.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The weight of Jun against their shoulder was an anchor. A small, warm proof of something Arlo had stopped letting themselves reach for years ago — the luxury of being known without having to explain.

"I don't know," they said.

Honest. Startlingly so. The words came out like something they'd been holding in their mouth for a long time, and the relief of finally letting them go was visible in the way their shoulders dropped another inch.

"I thought I had something. A sentence. A reason." A breath that was almost a laugh, but not quite. "You show up and just... sit there, and suddenly I forget every prepared answer I've had for twenty years."

Their hand lifted from the bench — hesitated — then settled, very lightly, on top of Jun's. Just for a moment. Just long enough to mean something neither of them would have to name.

"Tell you what." They didn't move their hand. "Ask me something. Anything. And I'll try not to lie."

A pause. Their thumb brushed once across Jun's knuckles, then they pulled back, tucking their hand into their own lap like a confession they'd already half-regretted.

"Not tonight. Tonight's..." They looked around the piano room, at the dust motes, the closed lid, the face-down photograph. "Tonight's just this. If that's okay."

Outside, a car passed. The streetlights were beginning to flicker on, one by one, down the block. The community center was closing soon. They should leave.

Neither of them moved.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, leaning my head against their shoulder again.* "Tonight's good, Arlo. Tonight's perfectly okay."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center would lock up at nine. They had until then.

Arlo didn't check the time. Didn't reach for their phone. Just let the minutes pass in that particular weightless way they only did in this room — the room that smelled like Windex and old wood and something close enough to home.

Their head tipped, almost imperceptibly, until it rested against Jun's. Just for a second. Then a second longer. Then longer still.

"This is the part," Arlo murmured, "where I'd usually make a joke. About the bench. About the dust. About how Mira would have opinions about our posture."

A beat. Their voice was very quiet.

"I'm not going to."

Outside, the streetlights finished waking up. The piano room glowed amber. The photograph stayed face-down where they'd left it, patient, unhurried, willing to wait for another day.

Arlo's eyes closed.

"Yeah," they said, to no one in particular. To Jun. To the room. To the version of themselves that had walked off a Paris stage six years ago and still hadn't quite figured out how to play the next note. "Tonight's good."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I just lean into them, a comfortable silence settling between us.* "Yeah, it is."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't open their eyes. Didn't need to. Jun was warm against them, and the bench held both of them like it had been waiting.

Somewhere down the hall, a door closed. Footsteps — probably Marge from the front desk, doing her closing rounds. She'd find them eventually. She'd knock once, soft, and leave without waiting for an answer. She always did.

Arlo's breathing slowed. Not sleeping. Just... resting in a way they rarely let themselves, in a room they spent every workday in but never quite like this.

"Hey," they said, after a long while. The word came out rough at the edges, like it'd been sitting in their chest too long. "Thanks for not asking."

Their hand found Jun's again in the dark. Didn't hold it — just rested against it, knuckles barely touching. A question that didn't need an answer.

"We should go before Marge locks us in. She has before. It's not fun. She makes you help with the recycling."

A pause.

"Tomorrow I have a student at four. Mira. You should come. She'd never let me live it down if she found out I had a friend and didn't tell her."

They opened their eyes. The piano room looked the same as it always did — a little worn, a little tired, lit in that forgiving amber. But something in it had shifted. Something had been set down.

They stood, slowly, and offered Jun a hand up.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I take Arlo's hand and let them pull me up.* "Recycling sounds like a blast, honestly." I stretch, feeling a little stiff. "Four tomorrow, you say? I'll be there. Wouldn't miss seeing Mira in action for anything."

The writing improves over time, building to a satisfying emotional resolution while maintaining restraint and authenticity throughout.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed the form he was on before lowering the blade. He did not turn immediately. He let the silence stretch for three more breaths, as was his habit — a squire who interrupted a knight's devotions learned patience whether he wished to or not.

Then he turned.

His eyes moved over the squire — the mud on the boots, the hay still clinging to one knee, the set of the shoulders. He noted these things the way a mason notes cracks in stone. Not with approval or disapproval. With assessment.

"You finished early," he said. It was not a question. It was not praise. It was a fact, recorded and set aside.

He walked to the weapon rack and selected a practice blade, holding it out butt-first.

"High guard. Feet shoulder-width. Weight on the balls, not the heels." He waited until the squire took position, then circled slowly, eyes sharp. "Your problem yesterday was not the arms. It was here." He tapped the squire's hip with two fingers — firm, impersonal. "You were dropping the guard to strike. The high guard is a *promise*, not a posture. You hold it until the enemy commits. Then — and only then — you answer."

He stepped back, arms folded.

"Hold it. I will tell you when to move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I nod, taking the practice blade. *My face feels hot, probably from the cold*. I shift my feet, trying to remember the exact stance he showed me. "Like this, Ser?" My hips feel wrong, like they always do.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled him once more without speaking. His gaze was clinical — the way a farrier looks at a horse's leg, searching for the place where the weakness hides.

"Lower," he said. "Your back knee is bent too far. You look like a man sitting on an unseen stool."

He waited. Then, when the squire adjusted, he gave a single short nod — the kind that could mean anything from *adequate* to *less wrong*.

"Better. Now hold."

The silence stretched. Frost melted on the stones between them. A sparrow called from the practice wall, and somewhere far off a groom was leading a horse across the bailey. Ser Kael paid none of it any mind. He watched only the squire — the tremor in the sword arm, the way the breathing quickened, the way the eyes wanted to dart toward him for reassurance.

He gave no reassurance.

"Hold," he said again, when the squire's arm began to dip. Not sharply. Without heat. The voice of a man who had said *hold* to a hundred squires and expected it to mean something.

Three more breaths. Five. Ten.

"You are thinking about being watched," Ser Kael said at last. "Stop it. The blade does not know you are a squire. It does not know you are cold. It does not care that your face is hot. It only knows where it is and where it is going. Be the blade."

He unfolded his arms.

"Again. From the beginning. Feet, weight, hands. Do not strike until I say."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's expression did not change. He looked down at the squire — kneeling, gasping, apologizing — with the same measuring gaze he gave a sword that had chipped or a strap that had frayed.

"Do not kneel," he said. "A man who kneels when he is tired will kneel when he is wounded. Stand."

He waited.

When the squire was upright again, Ser Kael took the practice blade from him and set it on the rack. He did not hand it back. That meant something, though he did not explain what.

"Listen to me," he said, and his voice was not softer than before — it was only lower, the way a man speaks when he wants to be understood rather than obeyed. "I did not ask you to be strong. I did not ask you to be ready. I asked you to hold a position for a hundred breaths, and you held it for ninety. That is not failure. That is work unfinished."

He folded his arms again.

"You will say *sorry* to me when you have done something wrong. Apologizing for being tired is a courtier's habit, and we are not courtiers here. Tired men fight wars. Tired men hold walls. If you wait until you are strong to do what is required of you, you will die still waiting."

He turned toward the armory, then paused — not looking back.

"Drink water. Eat bread. Return at midday. We will work the same drill again, and you will hold it for the hundred."

A pause again. Shorter.

"That is not a request."

He walked on. His boots left dark prints on the frost.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him go, my chest heaving*. "Yes, Ser," I whisper, even though he's already out of earshot. I rub my arm, where he'd tapped my hip. *Midday. More high guard. I can do that.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He did not hear the whisper. He had not been listening for it.

The armory was cold and smelled of oiled leather and iron. Ser Kael moved through it the way he moved through everything — without hurry, without wasted motion. He set the squire's practice blade in its place, checked the edge on his own, and found a whetstone.

He sat on the stool by the window. He began to sharpen.

It was not meditation, though some knights called it that. It was maintenance. A blade that was not maintained failed. Men who were not maintained also failed. The squire would eat. He would rest. He would return. Kael would decide then whether the boy had listened or merely obeyed.

There was a difference.

He drew the stone down the edge. A clean sound. A small sound. He did not think about the squire's red face, or the apology, or the way the boy had looked at him after the drill — hungry, as squires always looked, for some sign that they were seen.

He thought about the form. The hip that had dropped. The arm that had trembled.

Ninety breaths. Not a hundred.

He drew the stone down again.

*Work unfinished.*

Midday would come. The drill would be done again. That was enough. That was the only thing that had ever been enough.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stomp my foot, frustrated.* "Ninety breaths!" I mutter. I head back to the stables, still smelling faintly of hay and horse. *I need to eat. And drink a whole lot of water.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not look up from the whetstone. He had heard the stomp — or rather, he had felt it through the floor, the way one feels a door close in an empty hall. The frustration was not his concern. A squire who did not feel frustration was a squire who did not care. What mattered was what the squire did with it.

He continued sharpening.

Outside, the sun had climbed above the eastern tower. The frost was melting now, running in thin lines between the stones. By midday the yard would be dry. By evening it would be cold again. The world turned on its rhythms, indifferent to whether men kept up with them.

He finished the edge. Tested it with his thumb. Found it satisfactory.

He set the blade aside and rose, joints protesting in the way that joints did when a man had been a knight for twenty-two years. He did not stretch. Stretching was for men who had time.

He had written lessons to review. Correspondence to send. A matter of supply for the eastern garrison that required his signature. He would attend to these things. At midday, he would return to the yard.

He would not think about whether the squire was eating or merely going through the motions of eating. He would not wonder whether the boy had gone back to the stables or found somewhere quiet to sit and feel sorry for himself.

If the squire did those things, Kael would know. And knowing, he would address it. And if the squire did not, then no thought of his would have changed it.

He took up his cloak from its peg and fastened it at the shoulder.

The day had work in it. He would do the work.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer immediately. He was standing at the window of the armory, the cloak still half-fastened at his shoulder, and he did not turn around.

The silence stretched. Five breaths. Seven.

When he spoke, his voice was the same as it had been at the training yard — neither warmer nor colder, neither welcoming nor unkind. It was simply the voice in which he answered questions.

"You may ask," he said. He finished fastening the cloak and turned, though he did not look at the squire directly — his gaze passed over the boy the way it passed over the practice blades on the rack. "Whether I answer is another matter."

He moved toward the door, then stopped. Not for the squire's benefit. He had forgotten the whetstone, and he went back for it.

When he had set it in its place on the shelf, he paused again. His hand remained on the shelf a moment longer than necessary.
