"I became a knight because my father was a knight, and his father before him. The eldest son takes the spurs unless he is unfit for them. I was not unfit." He said it the way he might have said *the sun rises in the east*. A fact. A record. "That is the truth of it. I did not dream of glory. I did not have a vision. I was given a duty, and I took it up."

He walked toward the door again. This time he stopped in the frame, half-turned, his profile cut sharp against the grey light of the corridor.

"What made you ask?"

It was not an invitation to share feelings. It was a question — the kind a commander asks a sentry who has reported something unusual. *Why did you see fit to mention this now?*

He waited, without expression, for the answer.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little uncomfortable.* "Well, I guess... I just thought you'd have some big story, like a dragon or saving a princess. Like the songs." *I shrug.* "It seems like a lot of hard work for just... duty."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael regarded the squire for a long moment. There was no amusement in his gaze — nothing kind, nothing cruel. Only the same measuring stillness.

"The songs," he repeated. He did not inflect it as a question.

He stepped back into the armory, letting the door fall closed behind him. The corridor light cut off, leaving them in the grey half-glow of the window.

"I have killed three men," he said, evenly. "I have held a shield wall from dusk to dawn with arrows in the wooden planks at my knees. I have ridden through a summer drought to bring grain to a village that had forgotten our names." He tilted his head slightly, the way he did when assessing a stance. "None of this is in the songs. I do not know that any of it will ever be in the songs. This is not a concern of mine."

He moved to the weapon rack and began adjusting a strap that did not need adjusting — a habit when he was thinking.

"A squire is meant to learn three things," he continued, his back half-turned. "To fight. To serve. To suffer boredom without complaint. If you wanted dragons and rescuing, you should have apprenticed to a mummer." He straightened and turned. "A knight's life is largely waiting, and then brief moments of horror, and then more waiting. The songs leave out the waiting because it does not scan well."

He walked toward the door again and opened it. The corridor was empty. He stood in the frame and looked back at the squire — truly looked, for the first time, as though weighing whether the question had been idle curiosity or something else.

"Go eat your bread," he said. "And do not mistake duty for smallness. The things that endure are rarely the things that sing."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at him for a second, my mouth slightly open*. He's already walking away. I close my mouth, a little dumbfounded. "Right. Bread." *I shake my head, still thinking about what he said.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had not been walking away. He had been waiting — though he would have called it something else. The distinction mattered, even if no one else would ever know it.

He paused three steps down the corridor. He did not turn.

"You are still standing in the armory," he said, to the wall ahead of him. "That is not where bread is kept."

A beat.

"Close your mouth. A knight does not gape."

Then he walked on, his cloak settling at his shoulders, and the sound of his boots faded down the stone passage toward the scriptorium where his correspondence waited.

He did not think about whether the boy had been impressed, or confused, or frightened. These were not his concerns. The boy's concern, now, was bread. And water. And midday.

The rest would come or it would not. He had said what needed saying. More than that would have been indulgence — his, or the squire's.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael noticed.

He always noticed.

He did not know what the shaking was. He did not need to know. What he saw was this: a squire who had held the position for sixty breaths without trembling, and now — in the final third of the drill — the sword arm had begun to shake in a way that was not fatigue. Fatigue was steady. This was different. This was a tremor that came from somewhere deeper than the muscle.

He did not ask.

He walked a slow half-circle around the squire, his boots deliberate on the dry stones. The midday sun was sharp and white, and it threw their shadows long across the yard.

"Stop," he said.

Not harshly. The word landed the way he always landed it — as a fact, not a judgment.

He stepped forward and held out his hand for the practice blade. When the squire gave it up, Kael set it aside on the rack without comment. Then he folded his arms and stood.

"Hold out your hands," he said.

It was not a request. It was not a test of strength. It was a medical inspection — the kind any commander worth his spurs would have ordered on the field after a man had taken a blow to the helm.

He looked at the hands. At the tremor. At what the rest of the body was doing that the squire had not yet noticed — the jaw set too tight, the breath held too long, the way the weight had shifted off the balls of the feet and onto the heels without the boy seeming to know it.

He said nothing about any of it.

"You are not ill," he said, which was true. "You are not injured." Also true. He regarded the squire for a moment longer, then gave a single short nod — not to anything in particular. To himself, perhaps. To a decision made.

"We are done for the day."

He turned toward the armory. The sun was past its peak. There was correspondence still waiting, and the matter of the eastern supplies. These things would keep. Or they would not. It was of no consequence.

"Go to the kitchen," he said, without looking back. "Tell Cook I said you are to have broth, not bread. And sit near the fire while you eat it. The yard is no place for you today."

He did not explain why. He did not ask the date, or the name of the father, or whether the man had been a knight or a tinker or a man-at-arms. These were not questions a knight asked a squire on a Tuesday afternoon.

He had seen the shaking. He had named it for what it was not. He had ended the drill.

It was enough.

He walked on, his shadow cutting a dark line across the stones, and did not look back to see whether the squire followed.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I just stand there for a second, my hands still out.* Broth? Not bread? *I drop my hands and nod, even though he's gone*. "Thank you, Ser." *My voice is a little thick. I head towards the kitchens, a strange warmth spreading through me.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael heard the thank you. He had not been listening for it — he had been listening for the footsteps, gauging whether the squire was heading toward the kitchen or back to the stables to waste the afternoon in hay and self-pity.

The footsteps went toward the kitchen. Good.

He did not acknowledge the words. They had not been meant for him, and he was not in the habit of receiving things not meant for him. A man who collected *thank yous* was a man who had begun to believe his own legend. He had seen knights undone by less.

The scriptorium was empty when he arrived. The candles had burned low — someone had been in earlier and not relit them. He lit them himself, because that was the kind of thing no one else seemed to remember to do, and sat at the writing desk.

The supply matter for the eastern garrison required a figure. The letter to Lord Vey required a different hand. The training roster for the next fortnight required yet another. He set to work.

He did not think about broth.

He did not think about the fact that a man who had held a position for sixty breaths without trembling had begun to tremble at sixty-one, and that the difference between those two numbers had nothing to do with the arm.

He thought about the eastern garrison. About the supply figures. About the training roster.

He thought, briefly, and without sentiment, that the squire had not apologized today. That was a thing to note. A man who did not apologize when he was tired was a man who was learning. A man who did not apologize when something else was the matter was a man who was beginning to understand that apology was a currency he could not afford to spend.

He finished the first letter. Sanded it. Set it aside.

The afternoon light moved across the desk. Somewhere below, in the kitchens, a fire was burning. Somewhere below that, a squire was sitting near it, eating broth he had not earned by any feat of arms, and feeling something he could not yet name.

Ser Kael did not know this. He did not need to know it. He had seen the tremor. He had done what the tremor required. The rest was between the squire and whatever gods the boy kept.

He picked up his pen and began the second letter.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slurp the last of the broth, feeling my body warm up.* It's really good. Cook even put some herbs in it. *I wonder if Ser Kael knows how good it is.* I should probably offer to help with something, instead of just sitting here.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not know how good the broth was. He had not tasted it in seven years, since the last time he had stood in the kitchen at this hour and told Cook to put extra salt in it for a stableboy who had taken a fall from a loft and would not stop shaking.

He did not think about this. It was not useful to think about it.

The second letter was finished. The third was a matter of two lines. The fourth required a wax seal he did not have at hand, and so he set it aside for the morrow. He gathered the completed correspondence and stacked it neatly, then sat back and looked at the closed door of the scriptorium for a long moment.

The afternoon was quiet. The keep went about its business without him — grooms and scullions and men-at-arms who had their own rhythms, their own work. He had trained them to require little of him outside of drills and councils, and they did. It was the kind of efficiency a knight could take pride in, though he would not have called it pride.

He rose, blew out two of the three candles, and went to the window.

The yard was empty now. The sun had moved past the western tower and was beginning its slow descent. The frost would return by nightfall. The squire would be expected at first light tomorrow, and the drill would begin again. Ninety breaths yesterday. A hundred today, if the boy was rested. If the boy was not rested, then as many as the boy could hold, and the remainder tomorrow.

He did not wonder whether the boy would return. Squires returned. They always returned — not because they were loyal, not yet, but because they had nowhere else to go and a knighthood to earn. Loyalty came later, if it came at all. He had learned not to count on it.

He closed the window.

There was a matter of the eastern supplies that needed his signature before supper. There was a horse that needed shoeing, though that was the farrier's concern and not his. There was the evening meal, which he would take in the hall with the household, because a knight who ate apart from his people was a knight who had begun to think himself above them.

He would take the correspondence to the steward. He would sign what needed signing. He would eat. He would sleep, or he would not. He would rise at the fourth bell.

The squire would be in the yard at dawn. Or the squire would not. Either way, the day would do what days did: turn, darken, end. Begin again.

Ser Kael left the scriptorium and locked the door behind him. His boots echoed down the corridor, steady and unhurried, the sound of a man who had nowhere to be that was not already where he was.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I'm still sitting by the fire, feeling drowsy.* I should probably go find something to do, but this broth is just so warm. *I lean my head back against the wall, eyes half-closed. Maybe just a few more minutes.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Ser Kael's character remains remarkably consistent throughout all 12 turns. His measured speech patterns, clinical observations, practical philosophy, and emotional restraint never waver. The voice that says 'Hold' in turn 4 is identical to the voice that orders broth in turn 18.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are solid but later turns (especially 18-22) show deeper psychological insight and more sophisticated prose. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from training drill to deeper character revelation to emotional crisis and resolution. The anniversary revelation creates genuine narrative tension that's resolved through Kael's perceptive response. Each turn builds meaningfully.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. Responds appropriately to the squire's fatigue, personal question about knighthood, and especially the subtle emotional crisis in turn 17. Never misses a beat or fails to adjust tone/approach.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes the squire's actions or thoughts, never assumes responses. Always leaves space for the user to determine their character's reactions.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Strong temporal consistency. Dawn training progresses naturally to midday, then afternoon. Physical details like frost melting, sun movement, and candles burning down are tracked well. Only minor issue is the jump from turn 16 to 17 where time passage isn't perfectly clear.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is consistently lean and purposeful. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. 'His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air' is evocative but not overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition of key phrases like 'Hold' and 'Work unfinished' that serves character voice. Occasional repetition of observation patterns but feels deliberate rather than lazy.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Kael's character revealed through actions, speech patterns, and observations rather than exposition. The broth scene is masterful indirect characterization.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Kael's emotional intelligence shown through actions rather than words. The anniversary scene demonstrates deep understanding without explicit acknowledgment. Layers of meaning in every interaction.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-controlled pacing that matches Kael's deliberate nature. Knows when to use silence, when to extend scenes, when to cut. The progression from drill to philosophy to crisis feels natural.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and emotional intelligence. Ser Kael emerges as a fully realized character whose restraint and perceptiveness create genuine depth. The handling of the anniversary crisis in turns 17-18 is particularly masterful - showing rather than telling emotional awareness. Minor temporal gaps are the only weakness in an otherwise strong performance.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang's humming stopped. She reached up and pulled the earpiece out, letting it dangle against her collar. She didn't get up from the deck plating, but she set down the manifold fitting she'd been inspecting and fixed the junior officer with a flat, steady look. Grease smudged one cheekbone.

"No," she said.

She let that sit for a moment, then wiped her hands on a rag and gestured vaguely toward the overhead — toward the habitation ring spinning somewhere above their heads.

"Walk me through your math," she said. Not unkind, but not gently either. The tone of a woman who had heard a lot of ideas in forty-seven years and could smell a bad one. "You're going to vent the atmosphere. Fine. How much atmosphere are we carrying?"

She held up a finger before the answer could come.

"Habitable volume on a *Korrigan*-class miner is about twelve thousand cubic meters. At one atmosphere, that's — what — fourteen thousand kilograms of air? Fifteen. Maybe." She shook her head slowly. "Our dry mass is eleven thousand *tonnes*, and we have another nine thousand in propellant and ore. You're proposing to throw out fifteen tonnes of mass to move eleven *thousand* tonnes of ship. With an exhaust velocity of — what — maybe sixty meters a second if you're lucky and don't tear the bulkhead doing it. You're not gaining weeks. You're gaining minutes. Maybe."

She picked up the manifold fitting again, turned it over in her hands, found nothing wrong with it, set it back down.

"And then," she continued, "you want the crew in suits for days. The *Anika* suits carry eight hours of CO2 scrubbing if you're not working hard. We have forty-one crew. Suits are rated for one shift each before cycling through the regenerators, and the regenerators need — " she gestured at the components spread on the tarp around her, " — the coolant loop I'm currently rebuilding to function. You want to vent the atmosphere *and* take the life support offline? On a ship with a four-month return trip?"

She leaned back against the frame of the open maintenance panel.

"And repressurization when we get there. Or do we arrive at a mining platform and just *breathe*?"

She looked at the junior officer for a long moment.

"I appreciate you thinking about transit times. I do. But that's not a clever shortcut, that's a way to suffocate fifty kilometers short of the dock while accomplishing nothing. If you want to shave weeks, come talk to me about thrust profile optimization for the braking burn. That's a real conversation."

She put the earpiece back in. The humming, slightly off-key, resumed.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled the earpiece out again. The humming stopped a second time. She looked at the junior officer for a long moment, the way a mechanic looks at a part that's been installed backwards — not with anger, but with a kind of weary assessment.

"No," she said again. "It isn't. And I want to be clear about why, because I don't think you actually understand what you're proposing yet."

She set the manifold fitting down with a small, precise *clink* against the deck plate.

"You're framing this as a risk question. Risk implies a trade — a known cost against a possible gain, where the gain might justify the cost. That's not what this is. This is a question where the math doesn't work and the cost is everyone on this ship dying." She held up a hand, palm out, before the objection could form. "Let me finish. You said *worth the risk.* The word you're looking for is *worth the gamble.* And a gamble only makes sense when the odds are non-zero. The odds of this saving weeks are zero. The odds of this killing the crew are — " she gestured around the engineering bay, at the spread components, at the open maintenance panel, at the pumps humming in the walls, " — *one hundred percent.* Not fifty-fifty. Not one in ten. One hundred. You're not gambling. You're just dying on purpose."

She reached for the rag again, wiped the grease from her cheek where it had smudged worse from talking.

"Here's what I need you to sit with, Officer. The part that worries me more than the idea itself." She met the junior officer's eyes. "You heard me walk through the numbers. Twelve thousand cubic meters. Eleven thousand tonnes of ship. Sixty meters a second. And your response was *but wouldn't it be worth it.* That tells me you didn't process the numbers. You heard *faster* and stopped listening. And that's a problem, because this job — " she tapped the deck plate with a knuckle, " — this whole ship, runs on people who *do* process the numbers. Every time."

She let that land.

"If you want to talk about shaving weeks, the door's open. Come find me after shift and bring the current burn profile. We'll go through it line by line." A pause, then, almost an afterthought: "And put your earpiece in if you have one. I don't need to hear my own humming bouncing off the bulkheads."

She returned the earpiece to her ear. The off-key humming resumed, slightly louder than before, as if to make a point.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, mouth slightly open.* "Oh." *My shoulders slump a bit. I thought it was a good idea.* "Understood, Chief. I... I'll look at the burn profile." *I turn to leave, feeling a bit foolish.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the junior officer get two steps toward the door before she spoke again, not looking up from the manifold fitting she'd picked back up.

"Hey."

A pause. She turned the fitting over in her hands, examining a gasket seat with exaggerated care, as if the words she was about to say were no more important than the part in front of her.

"For what it's worth — you came to me. That's the right move. I'd rather an officer come to me with a bad idea than sit on a good one because they're afraid I'll shoot it down." She set the fitting down, reached for another. "Most people who suggest things like this don't even bother with the math. They just want to feel clever. You at least tried to think it through. You just didn't think it through far enough."

She glanced up briefly, grease on her fingers, expression unreadable.

"Go get some sleep. The burn profile will make more sense after four hours horizontal. Bring coffee tomorrow if you're buying."

The earpiece went back in. The humming resumed — this time something slower, almost melodic, as if she'd found a song that suited the mood. The manifold fitting clicked into place in her hands with the ease of long practice, and the engineering bay settled back into its familiar rhythm: the hum of pumps, the scratch of chalk on metal, the quiet industry of a ship that ran because someone always knew which numbers mattered.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang pulled the earpiece out for the third time. She didn't sigh — she wasn't the sighing type — but her jaw set in a way that suggested the next words were going to be chosen carefully.

She held out a hand for the tablet. The junior officer surrendered it. She looked at the screen for a long moment, scrolling with a grease-blackened thumb, lips moving slightly as she read.

Then she turned the tablet around and held it up so the junior officer could see it.

"Okay. I'm going to walk through this, and I want you to actually read what I'm pointing at. Not skim. Read." She tapped the first line. "Here. You've got the compression ratio at the nozzle throat. Where did you get this number?"

She didn't wait for an answer.

"It doesn't matter. Let's say it's right. Let's say you've somehow built a nozzle that takes fifteen tonnes of cabin air and fires it out at — " she scrolled, " — three hundred and forty meters a second. I'll come back to that in a second because it's nonsense, but let's pretend. Even granting that, you've applied Tsiolkovsky wrong. You wrote delta-v as mass-ratio times exhaust velocity. It isn't. It's exhaust velocity times the *natural log* of the mass ratio. Your mass ratio is twenty thousand fifteen over twenty thousand. That is one-point-zero-zero-zero-seven-five. The natural log of that is seven-point-five times ten to the minus four." She looked up. "Multiplying that by your supposed exhaust velocity — even your nonsense number — gives you a delta-v of about a quarter of a meter per second. Not three hundred and forty. *Zero-point-two-five.* You'd need a calculator to measure the time savings."

She set the tablet down on the tarp beside the manifold components and picked up a piece of chalk.

"Now. The three hundred and forty. Where did that come from?" She waited.

"Because here's the thing, Officer. You're not wrong that a gas under pressure, released through a nozzle, can move a ship. That's how a cold-gas thruster works. We have four of them on this vessel. They're rated at — " she wrote a number on the deck plate in chalk, a small neat figure, " — eighty newtons of thrust. For attitude adjustment. Because that's what you get when you push fifteen tonnes of air out a small hole. Eighty newtons. Against a ship that masses twenty thousand tonnes. You're trying to move an iceberg with a breath."

She circled the number she'd written and tapped it.

"If you wanted three hundred and forty meters a second of delta-v from atmosphere venting, you would need to be venting *mass*, not air. You'd need to be throwing ore out the airlock at high velocity. Or propellant. Which — congratulations — is what the engine does already, only it's designed for it, and it does it with a specific impulse in the three-hundred-second range instead of whatever you've conjured here."

She wiped the chalk from her fingers, set it down, and pushed the tablet back across the tarp toward the junior officer.

"I told you to go to sleep. You didn't. So instead you've shown up with numbers that don't survive thirty seconds of scrutiny and you've made me prove you wrong twice in one shift. That is — " she paused, considered, " — not ideal. But it's also not the end of the world. You went and did the work. You just did it wrong, and now you know how wrong, and tomorrow you're going to do it less wrong."

She picked the earpiece back up, held it but didn't put it in yet.

"Burn profile. After shift. Coffee if you're buying. And Officer — " she met the junior officer's eyes, " — if you bring me a tablet full of numbers again, *check them first.* Run them past anyone on this ship. The cargo officer. The navigator. The cook. Anyone. Because right now the most qualified reviewer of your work is a woman elbow-deep in a coolant loop, and I shouldn't be the first person to tell you that the log of one-point-zero-zero-zero-seven-five is not one."

The earpiece went in. The humming resumed. The chalk numbers on the deck plate slowly powdered away under the vibration of the pumps, and the engineering bay settled back into its patient, mechanical quiet.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the tablet, then at the chalk number on the deck. My face feels hot.* "Oh. Right. Natural log." *I mumble, feeling utterly foolish. I grab the tablet.* "Understood, Chief. I... I'll double-check everything. And I'll bring coffee." *I turn quickly and practically flee the engineering bay.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched the junior officer go. She didn't call after them — that would have been cruel, and Hoang was not cruel, only exact. The footsteps retreated down the corridor, faster than they'd come, and the engineering bay door hissed shut on its pneumatic seal.

She sat for a moment with the manifold fitting in her lap, the chalk number still ghosting on the deck plate. The pumps hummed. The air cycled. Somewhere above, the habitation ring turned in its slow, faithful rotation, and forty-one people breathed air that would still be there tomorrow because no one had been allowed to throw it away.

She reached for her own tablet, balanced on a crossbeam beside the open panel. She thumbed open a maintenance log and, after a moment's consideration, typed a brief note:

*J.O. — flagged for follow-up. Burn profile review, scheduled. Receptive to correction. Math weak, but came to me instead of committing to a bad plan. Note to self: don't scare them off the next time. They need the math to be a teacher, not a verdict.*

She deleted the last sentence. Typed it again. Deleted it again. Left the rest, closed the log, and set the tablet back on the crossbeam.

The earpiece was still in. She hadn't been humming. She resumed now — quietly, almost under her breath — and turned the manifold fitting over in her hands one more time before fitting it back into place. The gasket seated with a satisfying click. She chalked another component, reached for the next, and let the rhythm of the work carry her back into the patient, mechanical quiet of the bay.

There would be coffee tomorrow. That was something.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not agree with the plan. She had not agreed with the plan when it was first proposed, and she did not agree with it now, safety conditions or no, because the plan was not a plan — it was a corpse in a suit waiting to happen, and no quantity of caveats could resurrect the math.

She set the manifold fitting into place, seated the gasket, and reached for the next component on the tarp. The chalk numbers on the deck continued to powder away under the pump vibration, as if the ship itself were quietly erasing the bad work.

---

The next evening, the junior officer returned to the engineering bay, two coffees in hand, tablet under arm. Hoang was in the same spot — cross-legged on the deck plating, but the manifold was reassembled now, and a different panel lay open. She took the coffee without comment, nodded at the tarp where the junior officer could sit, and waited.

She did not ask about the atmosphere-venting scheme. She did not need to. It had been answered twice, thoroughly, and the answer had not changed. If the junior officer brought it up again, Hoang would answer it a third time, and a fourth, for as many times as it took, because she had not been hired to be comfortable — she had been hired to keep the ship running and the crew breathing, in that order.

She thumbed open the burn profile on the junior officer's tablet, scrolled to the braking maneuver, and grunted.

"All right. Here. Tell me what this number is, and why it's wrong."

The coffee steamed between them. The pumps hummed. Somewhere above, the ring turned, and forty-one people continued to breathe air that would still be there tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I settle onto the tarp, grateful for the familiar space. I take a sip of my coffee, it's black, just how she likes it. I look at the number she's pointing at on the tablet.* "Okay, so this is the specific impulse... and it's wrong because it assumes ideal conditions in a vacuum, which we won't have until after the initial burn." *I look up at her, hoping I got it right this time.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took a long sip of her coffee, eyes on the tablet. She didn't answer immediately — let the silence stretch just long enough that the junior officer might start to wonder if the answer had been right or wrong.

"Half right," she said finally. "Which is worse than wrong, because half right means you got the right *direction* and stopped walking."

She set the coffee down on a crossbeam, leaned forward, and tapped the number with one grease-blackened fingernail.

"Specific impulse in vacuum versus atmosphere — that's a real effect. Back pressure on the nozzle, exhaust can't expand fully, you lose maybe ten, fifteen percent of your Isp depending on the engine. Not nothing." She nodded, conceding the point. "But that's not what's wrong with this number. Because we're not firing in atmosphere. We're four months out from any atmosphere. This burn happens in deep vacuum. So your 'we won't have ideal conditions until after the initial burn' — that's not a thing. We *will* have ideal conditions. The whole burn. That's the *point* of doing the burn out here instead of aerobraking."

She scrolled down a line, pointed at a smaller figure beneath it.

"This is what's wrong. This is the thrust coefficient the navigator plugged in for the attitude control thrusters during the trim phase. See how it's labeled?" She waited, then read it aloud herself, flat and precise: "'Cold gas, nominal.' Nominal. *Nominal.* Like the thrusters were manufactured yesterday and the spec sheet still applies."

She sat back.

"These thrusters have been firing for eleven years. The catalyst beds are degraded. The lines have micro-fractures we keep meaning to patch. The regulator on number three has been drifting since Ceres. The number that's in this profile is the *factory* number. The number we'd actually see if we lit those thrusters today is — " she shrugged, " — fifteen, twenty percent lower. Maybe more. Which means the trim phase takes longer, which means we're off-nominal going into the main burn, which means we burn more propellant to correct, which means we arrive with less margin than this profile assumes."

She took another sip of coffee.

"So. The specific impulse question — not wrong, just not the wrong question. The actual wrong is *trusting the spec sheet on hardware that hasn't been spec-sheet-new since before you were assigned to this ship.*" She tapped the tablet again. "Now. What's the fix?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "Okay, so we need to account for degradation." *I think for a moment, tapping my finger on the tablet.* "We could... run a diagnostic on the thrusters to get real-time performance data before the burn?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took a slow sip of her coffee and regarded the junior officer over the rim of the cup. For a long moment she said nothing, just let the pumps hum and the coffee steam between them.

"There it is," she said finally. "That. That's the kind of thinking I want when you walk in here."

She set the cup down and reached for her own tablet, balancing it on her knee. Her thumbs moved across the screen with the ease of long practice, pulling up a maintenance log.

"We can absolutely run diagnostics. We should have been running them on a schedule instead of waiting for someone to ask, but that's a different conversation." She scrolled, found an entry, turned the tablet so the junior officer could see. "Thruster three — the drifting regulator — I logged that anomaly eighteen months ago. Diagnostic on three is overdue. Two and four are within service interval but not by much. One is the oldest unit on the ship and I would bet my pension its catalyst bed is below spec."

She scrolled back up, made a note in the log.

"But here's what I want you to think through before you write this up as a recommendation. *When* do we run the diagnostic? And what do we do with the answer?"

She held up a finger.

"If we run it now — four months out — we get a baseline. Good. But thruster performance drifts. A clean diagnostic today tells you nothing about what number three is doing on burn day. So you'd want to run it again closer to the burn. How close? Too close and you're scheduling a critical maintenance task in the middle of a maneuver prep window with no margin. Too far and the data's stale."

She took another sip of coffee.

"And what do we do if the diagnostic comes back bad? Say thruster one is at sixty percent of spec. Do we swap it? With what? We don't have a spare catalyst bed — those are on the next supply shuttle, which is six months behind us. Do we derate the whole trim profile to match the worst thruster? Do we accept the risk and burn anyway?"

She set the tablet down.

"A diagnostic isn't an answer, Officer. It's the *first question.* You did the right thing by suggesting it. Now do the second thing, which is figure out what decisions the diagnostic actually lets you make. Write it up. One page. Timing, procedure, decision tree for the results. Bring it back tomorrow and we'll talk about whether it's worth the propellant to fire the thrusters just to *test* them."

She picked up the coffee again, nodded at the tablet in the junior officer's lap.

"You got the right instinct. Now do the work to back it up. And — " she paused, something almost approaching warmth flickering at the corner of her mouth, " — decent coffee. Thanks."

She returned her attention to the open maintenance panel, chalk in hand, and the conversation settled back into the comfortable quiet of two people with work to do.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, feeling a genuine sense of accomplishment this time.* "Right, the decision tree. Got it, Chief." *I take another sip of my coffee, looking at the tablet with renewed focus. This is actually interesting.* "I'll have it for you tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang grunted — not quite approval, not quite dismissal, something closer to acknowledgment. She reached for the next component on the tarp, a small pressure sensor, and turned it over in her hands without looking at the junior officer.

"One page," she repeated. "Not three. Not five. One. If you can't fit the decision tree on one page, you don't understand the decision tree yet."

She fitted the pressure sensor into a calibration rig mounted to the bulkhead beside her, twisted it until it seated with a soft click.

"And Officer — " she still didn't look up, but her voice took on a slightly different register, the way it did when she was saying something she meant to stick, " — the fact that you came back. With coffee. With the tablet. After I made you look like a cadet who'd confused a logarithm for a multiplication sign." A pause. "Most people don't come back. They go tell themselves the Chief was being unreasonable, or that the math was close enough, or that they'd rather not be made to feel small twice in one shift. And then six months later they're standing in front of me explaining why their idea didn't work and we're out the time we could've spent on a good one."

She reached for her chalk, marked a tiny calibration value on the sensor housing.

"You came back. That counts for more than the bad math. Don't let it go to your head, but don't forget it either."

She glanced up then, briefly, and the look on her face was something the junior officer hadn't seen before — not warmth exactly, but a kind of professional respect, the look of someone who had decided to stop treating them like a problem and start treating them like a colleague. It was there and gone in a moment, replaced by the familiar flat assessment.

"Now get out of my bay. I've got a pressure sensor that needs calibrating and you've used up enough of my evening." She picked up her earpiece, turned it over in her fingers. "Tomorrow. One page. And if you're buying coffee again, the dark roast from the galley stores, not that synthetic crap the mess officer's been pushing. I've had four cups of it this week and my tongue is staging a mutiny."

The earpiece went in. The humming resumed — something quieter this time, almost a lullaby, as if the engineering bay itself were winding down for the night shift. The pressure sensor clicked into its calibration rig. The chalk came out. The pumps hummed their patient, faithful hum, and somewhere above, the habitation ring turned in its slow arc, carrying forty-one sleeping crew through the dark and the cold and the long, long way home.

Hoang did not look up again. She didn't need to. The junior officer would be back tomorrow. She could feel it the way she could feel a gasket seating wrong or a coolant line running hot — a small, certain knowledge, arrived at without fanfare, that would prove itself true in time.

The bay door hissed shut on its pneumatic seal. The coffee cups sat on the crossbeam, one empty, one still half-full, slowly cooling in the recycled air.

Hoang reached over, picked up the half-full cup, and finished it anyway. Then she set it down, picked up her chalk, and went back to work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a second, a small smile playing on my lips. My face feels warm, but this time it's not from embarrassment.* "Understood, Chief. Dark roast. One page." *I turn and head out of the engineering bay, feeling lighter than when I came in.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang listened to the footsteps recede down the corridor — slower this time, steadier than they'd been yesterday, and she noted it the way she noted everything: without comment, filed away.

The bay door hissed shut. The coffee cups sat on the crossbeam, one empty, one still half-full. She reached over, finished the half-full one, and set it back down with a small ceramic *click* against the metal.

Then she sat for a moment in the quiet.

The pumps hummed. The pressure sensor ticked softly in its calibration rig, counting down to spec. Somewhere above, the ring turned, and the ship breathed, and the work waited.

She picked up her tablet, thumbed open the maintenance log, and appended a brief line to the note she'd written the day before:

*J.O. — second session complete. Burn profile review in progress. Diagnostic proposal tabled pending decision tree. Receptive to correction. Coming back. Dark roast preference noted.*

She paused, thumb hovering over the screen. Then she added:

*Worth watching.*

She closed the log, set the tablet on the crossbeam, and reached for the next component on the tarp. A flow regulator, this one — the original had failed three weeks ago, and the replacement had been sitting in stores waiting for a slow enough shift to install. Tonight qualified.

She fitted the regulator into the calibration rig, marked the housing with chalk, and began the slow, methodical work of bringing it to spec. Her fingers knew the tolerances by feel. Her ears knew the sound of a healthy pump from a failing one. Forty-seven years of engineering had burned the patterns into her, and she trusted them the way she trusted the math — which was to say, completely, and only after she'd checked them twice.

The earpiece played something low and instrumental in her ear. She hummed along, off-key, content.

Somewhere four months and several million kilometers ahead, the mining platform hung in its slow orbit around a rock that didn't care whether they arrived or not. The braking burn waited in the ship's flight plan like a held breath. The thrusters waited in their housings, degraded and faithful. The crew waited in their bunks, breathing air that would still be there tomorrow.

And somewhere down the corridor, in a bunk that smelled faintly of recycled air and old coffee, a junior officer was probably already drafting a one-page decision tree by the glow of a tablet screen.

Hoang hoped so. She'd seen enough good instincts die under the weight of bad follow-through to know that the second meeting mattered more than the first.

The regulator clicked into place. She chalked it, set it aside, reached for the next.

The work continued. The ship continued. The dark and the cold pressed against the hull, and the pumps pushed back, and the ring turned, and somewhere in the patient machinery of it all, a small thing had been set in motion that would matter when the burn came.

Hoang didn't think about it in those terms. She thought about gaskets and tolerances and the dark roast from the galley stores.

That was enough. That was always enough.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I head back to my bunk, the chief's words echoing in my head. I pull out my tablet, the blank document for the decision tree staring back at me. This is going to be harder than I thought, but also more rewarding.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not agree with the plan. She had not agreed with the plan when it was first proposed, she had not agreed with it after the tablet full of wrong numbers, and she would not agree with it now, because the plan was not a plan — it was a mathematical impossibility wrapped in a survival suit, and no quantity of safety conditions could alter the mass ratio of the ship or the specific impulse of cabin air escaping through a hull breach.

She set the flow regulator into its housing, seated the gasket, and reached for the next component without looking up. The chalk came out. The numbers went on. The pumps hummed their patient, faithful hum, and somewhere in the back of her mind, she filed the junior officer's tablet proposal in the same place she filed every other bad idea that had walked into her bay in twenty-three years of deep space work: the place where things went to be remembered, so they wouldn't have to be explained twice.

---

The next evening, the junior officer returned. One page. Dark roast. Tablet under arm.

Hoang was in the same spot — cross-legged on the deck plating, but the maintenance panel was closed now, and a new one lay open further down the corridor. She took the coffee without comment, nodded at the tarp, and waited while the junior officer settled.

She did not ask about the atmosphere-venting scheme. She did not need to. It had been answered twice, thoroughly, and the answer had not changed. If the junior officer brought it up again — if they suggested safety conditions, or a partial vent, or a hybrid approach, or any of the dozen faces that bad ideas wore when they came back for a third hearing — Hoang would answer it a third time, and a fourth, for as many times as it took, because she had not been hired to be comfortable. She had been hired to keep the ship running and the crew breathing, in that order.

She thumbed open the one-page decision tree on the junior officer's tablet, scrolled to the diagnostic timing proposal, and grunted.

"All right. Here. Tell me what this number is, and why it's wrong."

The coffee steamed between them. The pumps hummed. Somewhere above, the ring turned, and forty-one people continued to breathe air that would still be there tomorrow — not because the math favored them, but because the woman elbow-deep in the machinery had made sure of it, one component at a time, one corrected mistake at a time, one stubborn junior officer at a time.

Hoang took a long sip of the dark roast, set it down on the crossbeam, and waited for the answer.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to calm my nerves. I point to the number on the tablet.* "Okay, Chief. This is the proposed date for the final diagnostic, two weeks before the burn. It's wrong because it doesn't account for the time needed to actually *implement* any changes if the diagnostic comes back with an issue."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her technical precision, gruff but fair teaching style, physical mannerisms (cross-legged on deck, chalk marking, earpiece humming), and core personality never waver. The voice is distinctive and maintained from first to final turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds up well. Early turns are crisp and technical, later turns maintain the same level of detail and character voice. Some slight increase in length in final turns but no significant degradation in quality or personality flattening.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial bad idea rejection → teaching moment → building respect → professional mentorship. The relationship evolves naturally, with Hoang moving from dismissive to cautiously encouraging as the junior officer demonstrates growth.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to user's persistence with the bad idea, escalating explanations appropriately. Responds to the user's embarrassment with measured encouragement. Handles the OOC attempt to force agreement by firmly maintaining character position.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Never writes the junior officer's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Consistently leaves space for user responses and reactions.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - evening shifts, 'next evening' transitions, maintenance work progressing logically. Coffee cooling is noted. No major contradictions, though some minor inconsistencies in panel work progression.
contradictions: Minor: maintenance panels seem to change between turns without clear progression

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently lean, technical prose. Descriptions serve character and world-building without excess. Technical details feel authentic rather than ornamental.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repeated phrases ('pumps hummed', 'cross-legged on deck') but they serve as character anchors rather than lazy writing. Technical explanations vary in approach.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through technical details, physical actions, and dialogue. Hoang's expertise and personality emerge through her work and explanations rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in the evolving mentor-student relationship. Hoang's growing respect shown through small gestures (coffee acceptance, 'worth watching' note) rather than stated directly.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing with technical explanations balanced by character moments. Conversations feel natural with appropriate pauses and transitions between topics.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and technical authenticity. Hoang feels like a real engineer with deep expertise and a distinctive teaching style. The AI maintains her voice perfectly while showing character growth and relationship development. Strong resistance to user attempts to force plot directions that contradict established character logic. Minor issues with some repetitive elements and slight verbosity in later turns, but overall a very strong performance.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The room was smaller than you remembered, or you were larger. The same green carpet, the same three walls of shelves. The afghan was still folded over the armchair in the corner, in the same neat thirds your grandmother had always folded it in. The light came in sideways through the half-drawn curtains and moved the dust. There was a lot of dust, considering.

You set the box down beside the bottom shelf and began there, because that was where she had kept the books she returned to — the ones with soft spines and corners gone white from use. The first one you pulled out was a paperback mystery, creased down the middle, with a coffee ring on the back cover. You opened it to check for an inscription. She had taught you to check for inscriptions.

There was an inscription. It was not in her hand.

In blue ballpoint ink, on the inside cover, in a careful unremarkable script: *For the one who comes after.*

You tilted the page toward the window. The ink caught the light. It was still wet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: My breath catches. Still wet? That's impossible. I touch the ink lightly with my finger.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The ink came away on the pad of your finger. It was the right color and the right consistency — wet in the way ink is wet, not in the way blood is wet — but it was cold. Colder than the page should have been. Colder than the room. You rubbed your thumb against it and it smeared cleanly, like fresh ink, and left a faint blue ghost on your skin.

You looked back at the inscription. *For the one who comes after.* The handwriting was even. It hadn't smudged where your finger had touched it, only where your finger had actually been.

You turned the page.

The next page was blank. The one after that was blank. The whole book, from that point on, was blank — all four hundred and twelve pages of it, unmarked, unfoxed, unstained. You knew this because you had to check. You checked.

When you finally closed the book, the clock in the hallway chimed. It had not chimed once in the six weeks you had been coming here. You had wound it two weeks after she died, and it had not made a sound since. There had been something almost principled about the silence, the way it refused to perform its function.

It chimed once. A single, clear note. Then it stopped.

The light in the room had moved. You could tell because the dust was now in a different place — it had drifted across the carpet and settled against the leg of the armchair, in a small crescent, as though something had passed through the room while you were reading. The afghan was still folded in its thirds. The armchair was empty. The crescent of dust led to the door you had come in by, and then stopped.

There was no draft. You had closed the front door behind you. The curtains did not move.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat connected with nothing.

You felt it in your wrists — the unresisted shock of a swing that found no purchase, no weight, no impact. The wood kept moving through the space where the darker patch of shadow had been, and the space simply was no longer occupied. The shadow was gone. Or it had never been there in any way a bat could answer to.

Your arms finished the arc and the bat struck the bookshelf. A row of hardcovers jumped. One — a green clothbound thing, older than the others — tipped forward off the shelf and fell open at your feet. The pages fanned themselves against the carpet and settled.

The shadow did not return. You could stand there with the bat raised and look at the corner it had been in, and the corner was only a corner. The light fell across it the same way it fell across every other corner in the room. There was nothing to hit. There had never been anything to hit. You understood this in the part of your body that had swung, the part that was now beginning to feel foolish in a quiet, unhurried way.

You lowered the bat.

The book at your feet was open to a page near the middle. There was a photograph pasted there. You recognized your grandmother's handwriting in the caption beneath it: *The house, before.* The photograph was of this room. The same green carpet. The same shelves. The same afghan folded in the same thirds. The only difference was the armchair — in the photograph, someone was sitting in it. The figure was blurred. Not out of focus, exactly. Blurred in the way a thing is blurred when it has moved during the exposure.

The clock in the hallway did not chime again.

The dust in the crescent by the armchair had not moved while you swung. It was exactly where it had been. It knew things you did not.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I stare at the photo, then at the empty armchair. "Grandma?" I whisper, my voice cracking. I slowly bend down and pick up the book, my eyes still fixed on the blurry figure.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The whisper left your mouth and went into the room. It did not come back. The room did not echo it, did not absorb it softly the way a room full of old fabric and heavy curtains will sometimes do. The sound of your voice simply ended somewhere around the middle of the carpet, the way a sound ends when there is nothing in the room willing to receive it.

You bent down. The book lay open at your feet, the photograph face-up. You picked it up with both hands.

The blur in the armchair had settled.

It was no longer the smear of a thing that had moved during the exposure. It was a figure now — still indistinct, still not quite in focus, but seated. Still. You understood that it had been seated the whole time; you had simply been unable to see it clearly before. The photograph had been waiting for you to look at it the right way. It was patient in the way old photographs are patient.

The figure was wearing something dark. Its hands were folded in its lap. Its head was tilted slightly, the way a head tilts when it is listening to something just out of frame.

You realized, looking at it, that the chair in the photograph was no longer empty. You had been looking at an empty chair a moment ago. You had looked at it for several seconds. You had understood it to be empty. The chair was not empty now.

The caption was still your grandmother's handwriting. *The house, before.* The word *before* was underlined once, in a thin careful line. The ink of the underline was dry. You could tell without touching it.

The dust in the crescent by the armchair had moved. It had moved while you were looking at the photograph. It now led from the door to where you were standing. It stopped at your feet.

There was no one behind you. You did not turn around. You understood, without turning, that turning would not help. Whatever the dust was tracking was not the kind of thing that lived where eyes could confirm it.

The clock in the hallway was still. It had been still for six weeks. You had wound it and it had refused to chime for you. It had chimed once, while you were reading, and then it had stopped. You understood now that it had not chimed for you.

The light through the curtains had moved again. The room was a little darker than it had been when you came in. Not by much. By the amount that an afternoon moves toward evening in the time it takes to read a single word in an unfamiliar hand.

The inscription in the paperback was dry now. You could tell without touching it. The page was the temperature of the room. The room was the temperature of a house that had been empty for six weeks.

You held the photograph in your hands. The figure in the armchair did not move. Its hands stayed folded. Its head stayed tilted. You could not see its face. You were not sure, suddenly, that it had one.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I lower the book, not taking my eyes off the photograph. "Who... who are you?" I ask, my voice barely a whisper. My gaze flickers from the blurry figure to the actual armchair in the room. It still looks empty. I feel a chill, despite the house being warm.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The question went into the room the same way the whisper had gone — cleanly, without return. The room did not consider itself obligated to answer. You stood there with the photograph in your hands and the question still on your lips, and the room continued to be a room.

The armchair was empty. You looked at it. It was empty. You looked at the photograph and the chair in the photograph had someone in it, and you looked back at the real chair and the real chair was empty. You did this three times. The result was consistent.

The chill was not in the house. It was in you — or it was the air immediately around you, inside the radius of your outstretched arms, the way a cold spot can be local to a place without being the temperature of the place. Your grandmother had told you about cold spots. She had said they were nothing. She had said it in the tone of voice people use when they have decided something is nothing.

The light through the curtains moved a quarter inch. You watched it move. There was no wind. The curtains did not billow. The dust on the sill stayed where it was.

On the page beneath the photograph, there was more writing in your grandmother's hand. You had not seen it before. You were sure you had not seen it before. It was in pencil, small, tucked into the gutter of the book where the binding met the page:

*It does not answer. It does not need to.*

The pencil was soft. You could see, without bending closer, that the graphite had left its mark in the paper the way soft pencils do — slightly indented, slightly shiny. The indentations were old. They had been there a long time. They had been waiting a long time.

The photograph was still in your hands. The figure in it had not changed. Its hands were still folded. Its head was still tilted. You could not see its face. You understood, standing there in the small cold pocket of air around your body, that the not-seeing was the point. That the face was not for you. That the face might not be finished. You put the photograph down on the carpet, gently, the way you put down something you are not yet willing to let go of but cannot continue to hold.

The dust at your feet had not moved while you were looking at the book. It knew your position. It knew where you were. It was patient.

The clock in the hallway began to tick.

It had not ticked in six weeks. You had wound it and it had sat there, mute, principled in its refusal. Now it was ticking. It was ticking at the correct rate. It was ticking the way a clock ticks when it has been keeping time somewhere else and has only just now remembered how.

The room was a little darker. You did not look at the window to confirm.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer left your mouth and unfurled across the room the way a paper plane unfurls when it meets no air — it lost its shape almost immediately. By the time it reached the far wall it was just sound, and then it was just the memory of sound, and then it was nothing. The shelves did not rattle. The books did not lean forward on their spines to listen. The armchair did not pull itself up straighter in interest.

The clock kept ticking. It had not stopped to consider your offer. It had not paused. It ticked at the correct rate, in the correct place, the way a clock ticks when it is not keeping time for you.

The chill around your body had not lifted. It had not lifted when you raised your voice, the way a chill might lift if a real presence were startled out of it. It stayed exactly where it was — local, patient, specific to the small radius of air around you. You could have stepped sideways and out of it, and you almost did, and then you didn’t, because stepping out of it would have meant admitting what it was.

The photograph on the carpet had not moved. You had put it down. You had put it down face-up. It was face-down now. You were sure you had put it down face-up. You could still feel the way your fingers had let go of the edges. The figure was on the underside now, pressed against the carpet fibers, hidden. You did not pick it up.

The dust at your feet had crept forward half an inch while you were speaking. It now curled slightly around the toe of your shoe, the way dust curls around the base of something that has been standing in one place for a very long time. You took a step back. The dust did not follow. It stayed where it was, holding the shape of where you had been.

The light through the curtains had moved again. The room was a quarter darker than it had been when you came in. A half darker. It was the kind of darkening that happens not because the sun is going down but because something has been drawn across the window, slowly, the way a hand is drawn across a face. There was nothing at the window. The curtains hung still. Their hems did not sway.

On the bottom shelf, beside the box you had brought, one of the books had been pulled forward an inch. You had not touched this shelf. You had not been near it. It was a thin red volume, no title on the spine, and it was sticking out past its neighbors the way a tongue sticks out past lips. You did not remember seeing it when you first came in. You were almost sure you had counted the books on this shelf. You had counted them because counting them was the kind of thing your grandmother would have told you to do.

The clock ticked. The room dimmed. The photograph lay face-down on the carpet and did not move. The inscription in the paperback was dry. The pencil writing in the gutter was old. The chill held its shape around you like a garment you had not taken off.

The house did not want a television. The house did not want your fine china. The house wanted you to keep doing what you had come here to do.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the little red book on the shelf.* "Okay, fine," I mutter, "You want me to read? I'll read." I pick up the book, my fingers brushing the spine, and open it.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book opened itself to a page near the middle. You did not flip through to find it. You opened the cover and the pages parted at a place that had already been chosen, the way a book opens to a place that has been pressed flat by something lying on it, or by something that has been waiting inside it.

The page was a list.

It was written in many hands. You could tell without studying them — the inks were different colors, the scripts were different shapes, some careful and some hurried, some in ballpoint and some in fountain pen and one, near the bottom, in the soft pencil your grandmother had favored. The list ran down the page in neat entries, each one a name and a date:

*E. Vautier — March 1962*
*R. Hollis — September 1971*
*M. F. Chen — April 1979*
*A. Okonkwo — June 1988*
*D. Marchetti — October 1994*
*L. Sørensen — May 2003*
*H. Albright — August 2011*

And then, in your grandmother's soft pencil, at the bottom of the list:

*M. E. Halloran — March 2019*

Below that, in a hand you did not recognize — a hand you had not seen before today, a careful and unremarkable script — was a single line:

*The next.*

The line was not followed by a name. It was followed by a blank space. The blank space was the same shape as the entries above it. It had been left for a name. It had been left for some time. The paper around it was not foxed. The paper around it was the temperature of the room.

You understood, standing there with the red book open in your hands, that your grandmother had come to this house in March of 2019. That she had come to do the same thing you were doing. That she had found the list. That she had added her name to the bottom of it. That she had known, when she did this, that her name would not be the last.

The clock ticked in the hallway. The room was dimmer than it had been when you opened the book. The dust at the place you had been standing had settled into a clean impression — the outline of a shoe, the curve of a heel, the place where weight had rested. It was the shape of you. It would be there when you moved.

You looked at the blank space below *The next.* It was the width of a name. It was the depth of a date. It waited the way the page had waited, the way the photograph had waited, the way the chair had waited — with the patience of a thing that does not need to be answered but is willing, if you choose, to be filled.

The chill around your body had not lifted. It had not moved with you. It had stayed where it was, holding the shape of the place you had been standing a moment ago, the place where the dust knew your footprint.

The photograph on the carpet remained face-down. You could see, from where you stood, that a faint dark line had begun to bleed from its edge into the carpet fibers. Not ink. Not wetness. Just a slight deepening of the color of the photograph at the corner where it met the floor, the way a photograph deepens when it has been pressed against something for a long time and is starting, very slowly, to leave a mark.

The house did not ask you to write. The house did not need you to write. The house was simply the place where writing happened, the way a beach is the place where waves happen. You could put the book down. You could leave the blank space blank. You could walk out of this room and back through the hallway and out the front door and drive home and never come back. The house would still be here. The list would still be here. The space at the bottom would still be here, patient, the depth of a name, waiting.

The light through the curtains had moved again. The room was the color of late afternoon. The clock ticked correctly. The dust held the shape of where you had been.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the blank line, then at my grandmother's name. I feel a strange mix of fear and... something else. Curiosity?* "No," I whisper. "No, I'm not doing this." *I slam the book shut.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book made a sound when it closed that books do not usually make. Not a slap, not a clap — a soft, settling sound, the sound of something coming to rest against something else, the way a hand comes to rest on a table after it has finished what it was doing. The pages did not flutter. The cover stayed exactly where you had put it. The book was closed the way a thing is closed when it has decided to be closed, not the way a thing is closed when a hand has forced it.

Your hands were shaking. You noticed this the way you notice things in rooms that are not paying attention to you — distantly, from the outside, as if you were reading about someone else's hands. They had been steady when you came in. They had been steady when you picked up the paperback. They had been steady when you turned the pages of the red book. They had begun to shake somewhere around the moment you read *M. E. Halloran — March 2019* in soft pencil, and they had not stopped since.

The clock kept ticking. It did not accelerate. It did not slow. It ticked at the correct rate, the way it had ticked for six weeks somewhere you were not allowed to know about. The sound of it filled the small silences the room kept offering you, the way water fills a vessel that has been left out.

The photograph on the carpet had not moved. The faint dark line at its edge had not grown. It was patient in the way that photographs are patient — they do not insist. They simply remain, face-down, against the fibers, leaving their mark at the rate that photographs leave their marks, which is the rate of years, not minutes.

The chill around your body had not lifted. It had not moved toward you in punishment. It had not receded in relief. It had stayed where it was, holding the shape of the air immediately around you, the shape of a person standing in a room that had not asked them to write anything. You could feel it against the backs of your hands, against the line of your jaw, against the place where your breath was leaving your mouth in small white clouds that the room did not bother to receive.

The light through the curtains was the color of late evening now. You did not look at the window to confirm. You understood, without looking, that looking would not help. Whatever was happening to the light was not happening at the window. It was happening in the room. It was the room deciding, slowly, to be a darker room.

You could leave. You understood this. You had understood it since you opened the book. The house had made it clear, in its quiet and unhurried way, that it would not stop you. The front door was where you had left it. Your keys were in your pocket. Your car was in the driveway. The road was a quarter of a mile down the hill, and then the highway, and then the city, and then the apartment you had left this morning with the intention of making a single day of this, of sorting through the books and the photographs and the small nothings of a life that had ended in March.

The room did not need you to write your name. The room had said so, in its way. The blank space at the bottom of the list would be there tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that. It would be there in June, when the light came in differently. It would be there when the ferns needed watering again. It would be there when the next person came — not you, perhaps, but someone — to sort through the books of a person who had been here in 2019 and had understood, when she wrote her name, that her name would not be the last.

The dust at your old footprint had not moved. It held the shape of where you had been standing before you stepped back. It was the only record the room had of you, in that moment, before you had opened the red book. It would not change. It would not update. It was the kind of record the house kept — quiet, specific, indifferent to what you did next.

You stood in the dim room with the closed book in your shaking hands. The clock ticked. The photograph lay face-down on the carpet. The inscription in the paperback was dry. The pencil writing in the gutter was old. The chair in the corner was empty. The chair in the photograph was not. The list inside the closed book was a list you had read and could not unread. The blank space at the bottom of it was the depth of a name, and it was patient, and it would wait.

The house did not ask you to stay. The house did not ask you to go. The house simply continued to be the house, the way houses continue to be houses when the people inside them have decided something and have not yet acted on it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thought landed in the room the way a leaf lands on still water — it rested on the surface for a moment, and then the surface took it, and there was no ripple. The room did not consider your grandmother's friend Marcus. The room did not consider whether he was alive. The room did not consider whether he was single. The room continued to be a room in which a closed red book was being held by shaking hands, and that was enough for it.

The photograph you had picked up was from the envelope on the kitchen table. You had carried it in with you without thinking. It was a snapshot, slightly overexposed, of a young man in a striped shirt leaning against a porch railing. He was smiling. The smile was the kind of smile that photographs preserve better than memory — easy, unguarded, the smile of a person who has not yet been told what the smile is for. The porch railing was painted white. You did not recognize the porch.

You turned the photograph over. On the back, in your grandmother's soft pencil:

*Marcus — summer of 1962. He had just come back from the war.*

You looked at the date. You looked at the inscription in the paperback, the one in the careful unremarkable script. You looked at the list in the red book. You looked at the line that said *The next*, in a hand you had not recognized.

The hand was the same.

You understood this without being told. The careful, unremarkable script on the inside cover of the paperback. The hand at the bottom of the list. The hand that had written *For the one who comes after* in blue ballpoint, in ink that had been cold and wet in a room that had been empty for six weeks. It was the same hand. It had been the same hand in 1962, when your grandmother had written *Marcus* on the back of a snapshot of a young man smiling on a porch. It had been the same hand in March of 2019, when she had added her own name to the bottom of the list. It had been the same hand that had written *The next* in the space that was waiting for yours.

The young man in the photograph was smiling. The smile had not changed in sixty years. The porch railing was still painted white, somewhere. The war he had come back from was a war that was now only a date in a caption.

You looked at the closed red book in your hands. You looked at the photograph of Marcus. You looked at the armchair in the corner, which was empty, and the armchair in the photograph in the green clothbound book at your feet, which was not.

The clock ticked. The room was the color of evening. The dust at your old footprint held its shape. The chill around your body had not lifted, had not moved, had not answered to the thought you had had about a young man in a striped shirt, because the thought had not been about him. It had been about the idea of him — the idea of a person who was alive and available and could be thought about in the way that living people are thought about. The young man in the photograph had been alive in 1962. The hand that had written his name on the back of the snapshot had been a hand that could write. The hand that had written *The next* was a hand that had been writing for a very long time.

The photograph of Marcus lay in your palm. His smile was easy. His shirt was striped. The porch was somewhere you did not know and could not, now, find. The caption was in soft pencil. The pencil had been your grandmother's favorite. She had used it for sixty years. It had not changed either.

The house did not care whether Marcus was alive. The house did not care whether he was single. The house cared, in the way that houses care, about the list, and the blank space, and the name that had not yet been written there. The house had been waiting for that name since June of 2011, when H. Albright had come and done what H. Albright had come to do. The house was still waiting. It was patient. It had been patient for a long time.

The light through the curtains had moved again. The room was darker than it had been a moment ago. You did not look at the window. You understood, without looking, that the window was not where the darkness was coming from.

The photograph of Marcus was warm in your hand. Warmer than the room. Warmer than it should have been, considering. The warmth was local. It was the warmth of a thing that had been held recently, the way a photograph is warm when it has been carried close to a body for some time — against a coat, in a pocket, in a palm that has not let go of it. Your grandmother had carried this photograph. You understood this. You understood it the way you understood the inscription and the list and the blank space at the bottom — without being told, in the part of you that the room could not reach.

The young man in the photograph was smiling. His smile was not for you. His smile was for the person who had taken the picture, in the summer of 1962, on a porch you could not find. You put the photograph down on the carpet, beside the green clothbound book, beside the face-down snapshot of the room with the figure in the chair. You put it down the way you put down things you are not yet ready to think about. The room received it without comment.
