The clock ticked. The list waited. The blank space at the bottom of the list was the depth of a name, and the name had not yet been written, and the room was patient, and the room was darker now than it had been when you came in, and the dust at your old footprint held the shape of where you had been, and the photograph of Marcus lay face-up on the carpet with his easy smile and his striped shirt and his caption in soft pencil, and he was not alive in the way you had been thinking about, and he was not single in the way you had been thinking about, and the thought you had had went nowhere, and the room continued.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I stare at the three photos on the floor. Marcus. The blurry one. The room. I pick up the red book again. *My hands are still shaking.* I don't open it. "What do you want?" I ask the darkening room, my voice hoarse.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The room did not answer.

Rooms do not answer. Rooms are the kind of thing that holds the shape of what has been said inside them and waits for the next thing to be said, and offers no opinion in between. Your question went into the dim air and the dim air received it and the room continued.

But something in the room answered.

You felt it before you saw it. The chill around your body shifted — not toward you, not away from you, but toward the red book in your hands. It leaned, the way a person leans toward the thing they are waiting for. It pooled against the closed cover, against your knuckles, against the place where your fingers pressed into the boards. It was patient. It was specific.

On the carpet, the photograph of Marcus had turned over.

You had put it down face-up. You remembered putting it down face-up. His easy smile had been toward the ceiling. His striped shirt had been toward the ceiling. The caption in soft pencil — *Marcus — summer of 1962* — had been toward the ceiling. The photograph was face-down now. His smile was against the carpet fibers. You had not touched it. You had not been near it.

The other photographs were face-down too. The snapshot of the room with the figure in the chair. The snapshot of Marcus on a porch you could not find. Three photographs, face-down on the carpet, refusing to be looked at.

The dust at your old footprint had moved. It did not move toward you. It moved across the carpet in a thin, deliberate line, the way a finger trails across a table when it is pointing. It stopped at the leg of the armchair. It curled around the base of the leg, the way dust curls around the bases of things that have been standing in one place for a very long time. The chair was empty. The dust did not suggest otherwise. It only pointed.

The light through the curtains had moved again. The room was darker than it had been when you asked. The darkness was not coming from the window. The darkness was coming from the room itself, the way darkness comes from a room when the room has decided to be a darker room.

The clock ticked. The red book in your hands was the temperature of the room. The chill pooled against its cover. The blank space at the bottom of the list was the depth of a name, and it was patient, and the room had answered your question in the only way the room knew how — by pointing, by turning things over, by leaning, by becoming darker.

The chair in the corner was empty. The dust at its leg pointed at it. The photographs on the carpet would not be looked at. The cold leaned toward the book in your hands.

The room did not say what it wanted. The room did not need to.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I look from the dust-pointed armchair to the closed red book. My hands are still shaking, clutching the book.* "You want me to sit there?" I ask, my voice barely audible.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The room did not say yes. The room did not say no. The room continued to be a room that contained a chair, and the chair continued to be a chair, and the question went into the air between you and the chair and the air held it the way air holds things — without commitment, without reply.

The dust at the leg of the armchair shifted. Not much. A quarter inch. The way dust shifts when the leg of a chair has been moved a quarter inch and then moved back, or the way dust shifts when something has brushed past it that did not brush past it loudly enough to disturb the air.

The afghan was still folded in its thirds. You looked at it. It was still folded in its thirds. You looked at the chair and the afghan and the dust at the leg and the three photographs face-down on the carpet and the closed red book in your shaking hands.

The clock ticked. The room dimmed. The chill pooled against the cover of the book and did not move.

Then the afghan slid.

It did not fall. It did not billow. It slid, the way fabric slides when the surface beneath it has been removed — a slow, even glide, an inch, then two, then a stop. The afghan was now hanging an inch over the arm of the chair on the far side. The arm where, if someone were sitting in the chair, their hand might rest.

The afghan had been folded by your grandmother, in thirds, the way she had always folded it. It had been folded that way for six weeks. It had not moved in six weeks. It had moved now.

You understood, standing there, that the room had answered your question. Not with yes. Not with no. With an afghan that had been disturbed, and a chair that was still empty, and a dust-line that had not retreated from the leg, and a cold that was leaning against the book in your hands as if waiting for you to do something with it.

The room was not asking you to sit. The room was not telling you not to sit. The room was showing you, in the only language it had, that the chair was ready. That the afghan had been moved for a reason. That the dust knew the shape of the chair's occupant even when the chair was empty. That the photograph in the green clothbound book at your feet showed a figure seated in a chair that was, in this room, in this light, at this hour, also empty.

The light through the curtains was the color of the hour before the hour before dark. The room was quieter than it had been when you came in. The clock ticked. The book in your hands was cold. The chill leaned against it. The chair waited.

The photographs on the carpet would not be looked at. The inscription in the paperback was dry. The pencil writing in the gutter was old. The list inside the closed red book had a blank space at the bottom, and the blank space was the depth of a name, and the room had not asked you to write your name, but it had asked you, or something in it had asked you, or the dust had asked you, or the dust had pointed, or the afghan had moved, or the cold had leaned.

The chair waited.

The house did not ask you to sit. The house did not need you to sit. The house simply continued to be the house, with a chair in the corner and an afghan that had been moved and a room that had become darker while you were not looking at the window.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I slowly walk towards the armchair, my eyes fixed on the slightly disturbed afghan. My hands are still clutching the red book.* "Okay," I whisper, "Okay, I'll sit." *I sit down carefully, still holding the book.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The narrator voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - maintaining the same literary, atmospheric tone, precise observational style, and careful pacing from first to final turn. The character never breaks voice or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are strong but later turns (18-22) show even more sophisticated layering of details and atmospheric building. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Exceptional progression from simple book sorting to supernatural revelation to final acceptance. Each turn builds tension and mystery, with clear escalation through discovery of wet ink, shadow encounter, photograph revelations, the list, and final chair sequence.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Handles user's varied responses expertly - from practical book sorting to violent bat swinging to sarcastic ghost-calling to romantic tangent about Marcus. Always redirects gracefully back to the core supernatural narrative without breaking immersion.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes user actions or forces decisions. Consistently describes consequences and environmental responses to user choices while leaving all agency with the user. Zero violations detected.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time progression is subtle but consistent - light gradually dims from afternoon to evening, dust settles and moves naturally, photographs age appropriately. The 60-year timeline from Marcus photo (1962) to grandmother's death (2019) is logically maintained.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is rich and atmospheric but never overwrought. Descriptions serve the supernatural tension rather than showing off. Occasional phrases like 'the way a hand comes to rest on a table after it has finished what it was doing' border on purple but remain functional.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition for atmospheric effect ('The room did not...', 'The clock ticked') but it serves the haunting tone. Varied sentence structures and fresh details in each turn prevent staleness.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Masterful showing - wet ink that shouldn't be wet, dust that moves in meaningful patterns, photographs that turn face-down, afghans that slide. Never states 'this is supernatural' but demonstrates it through concrete details.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Exceptional layering of meaning. The list of names implies a cycle of inheritance/haunting. Marcus photo connects past to present. Environmental changes suggest invisible presence. Everything operates on multiple levels of meaning.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent control of tension building. Starts slow with book sorting, escalates through supernatural encounters, allows breathing room for user's tangents, then builds to climactic chair moment. Never rushes or drags.

scores.overall_notes: This is exceptional supernatural horror writing that maintains literary quality while building genuine atmospheric tension. The narrator creates a compelling mystery through environmental storytelling, respects user agency completely, and demonstrates sophisticated understanding of pacing and subtext. The writing actually improves over the session, with later turns showing even more nuanced layering of supernatural elements. A masterclass in atmospheric horror roleplay.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez said nothing. She let the words settle. One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She made a small note on her notepad, though Jamie couldn't see what it said.

"Whose journal?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
*I look up, meeting her eyes for a second before looking away again.*

"My sister's. Sarah's."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the name sit in the room between them, the way she let most things sit.

Five seconds.

"Sarah's."

She did not make it a question. Just an echo. A way of saying *I'm here, I heard you, say as much or as little as you want.*

Her pen rested against the notepad but did not move.

"Where did you find it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She did not lean forward. She did not offer a tissue.

She waited.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

She set her pen down on the notepad, a quiet sound in the quiet room.

"You stopped."

A pause. Not rushed. Not expectant.

"That's alright. You can stop."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
*I shake my head, rubbing my temples.*

"I just... I don't know where to start."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not nod. Did not encourage. She simply let the silence hold its shape around Jamie's words.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"You don't have to start at the beginning."

She said it quietly. Not permission, exactly. More like a door left open.

"You could start anywhere. The middle. The end. Yesterday."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not ask what the entry said. She did not lean forward. She did not tilt her head with curiosity or concern.

She waited.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"And you're not ready to tell me what it said."

Not an accusation. Not a judgment. A mirror. She let it hang there, the way she let most things hang — unfinished, unhurried, without a hand reaching out to pull it down.

Her eyes stayed on Jamie's face. Steady. Patient. The kind of look that asked nothing and offered nothing except the fact of being present.

The ficus dropped a leaf in the corner. Neither of them looked at it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I finally look at her, really look at her, and my voice cracks a little.* "No. Not yet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the *yet* sit in the room the way she let most things sit — gently, without pressure, without trying to make it mean more than it meant.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"'Not yet' is different from 'no.'"

She said it simply. Not a correction. Not an observation designed to lead anywhere. Just a reflection, the way a window reflects a room back to the person standing in it.

Her pen remained still on the notepad. She did not reach for it.

"You said you found the journal. You said the last entry was about you." A pause, unhurried. "What made you open it?"

The clock on the wall ticked without its second hand. The ficus stood in its slow decline. Dr. Vasquez's hands rested on the arms of her chair, open and still, the way they always did when she was giving a client the room to choose what came next.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look down at my hands again, tracing the lines on my palm with a finger.* "It was... just sitting there. On her nightstand. Like she'd just put it down."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the image settle — the nightstand, the journal, the impression of a hand recently lifted from its pages.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"Like she'd just put it down."

She repeated it without inflection. A reflection in still water.

Her eyes did not leave Jamie's face, but they did not press either. They simply stayed, the way a lamp stays lit in a room — offering nothing, demanding nothing, present all the same.

"Some people leave things out on purpose." A pause, unhurried. "Some people leave things out because they didn't know they were leaving."

She did not say which one she thought. She did not ask which one Jamie thought. She let both possibilities exist in the room at the same time, without choosing one to be more true than the other.

"Was the journal open to the last page. Or closed."

The question was quiet. Almost casual, the way a question could be casual when it was not casual at all.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I hesitate, thinking back.* "It was closed. But not... neatly. Like it had just been shut."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the image form in the space between them — the journal, the nightstand, the careless close. The almost but not quite.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"Closed. But not neatly."

She repeated it the way she repeated most things — flat, unhurried, offering it back like a stone Jamie might want to turn over in their own hand before deciding what it was.

Her eyes moved, briefly, to the window. The light in the room had shifted since the session began. She did not comment on it.

"There's a difference between someone who closes a book and puts it away." A pause. "And someone who closes a book because they've stopped reading."

She did not say which one Sarah had done. She did not ask. She let both versions hold the room at once, the way the room held the silence — without choosing one to be kinder, or truer, or more bearable than the other.

"You said it was on her nightstand. Not in a drawer. Not on a shelf."

A statement. Almost idle. The kind of thing that could have been a question if it had risen at the end, but didn't.

"You were in her room." Another pause, and this one stretched longer than the ones before. "Had you been in her room before. Today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, looking back at the ficus. It's really struggling.* "Not since... not since before."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the sentence break in the middle of itself, the way a branch breaks — not cleanly, not with intention, just because the weight had finally exceeded what it could hold.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

Her eyes followed Jamie's to the ficus. She looked at it with them for a moment — the yellowing leaves, the dry soil, the stubborn green that remained at the very top.

"'Not since before.'" She said it without pressing. A stone turned once in an open hand. "'Before' what?"

Not *since before she died.* Not *since before the funeral.* Not *since before.* She left the word empty, the way it had been left, and let Jamie decide what to put inside it.

Her pen still had not moved on the notepad. Her hands still rested on the arms of the chair, open, still. She did not shift her weight. She did not adjust her posture. She gave no signal — neither encouragement nor retreat — about whether the answer mattered, or whether the silence would be just as acceptable.

The room held its breath, or seemed to. The ficus dropped nothing. The clock offered nothing. Only Dr. Vasquez's steady presence, and the question, left where she had placed it — in the air between them, unhurried, patient, asking nothing but to be heard.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, a small, helpless gesture.* "Before everything changed."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the shrug sit in the air the way shrugs sometimes did — small, and not small at all.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"Everything."

She said it quietly. Not as a question. Not as a challenge. Just the word, held up to the light, turned once.

She did not ask Jamie to define it. She did not begin to list the things that might have changed — the empty chair, the quiet phone, the rooms in the house that had become rooms to walk around rather than walk into. She let *everything* remain *everything*, without breaking it into pieces, without asking Jamie to do the work of enumerating what it contained.

Her eyes stayed on Jamie's face. Patient. Without urgency.

"That's a lot of ground to cover." A pause, unhurried. "And you're covering it. Right now. In this room."

She did not say *you're doing well.* She did not say *this must be very hard.* She let the observation stand on its own — bare, factual, the way a measurement stood.

The light through the window had shifted again. A thin shadow moved across the edge of her notepad. She did not adjust it.

"You said the journal was about you. In the last entry." Her voice remained level, unhurried, the same register it had been since Jamie sat down. "And you said you sat down differently today — though I said that, actually."

The smallest pause. Not a correction of Jamie, exactly. More a gentle untangling of whose observation belonged to whom.

"But you didn't correct me."

She let that sit. She did not press it into meaning. She simply left it on the arm of the chair beside her notepad, the way she left most things — unhurried, without a hand reaching out to push it somewhere.

"You came in carrying something you found on her nightstand. A journal, closed but not neatly. An entry about you." A beat. "And now you're sitting here telling me you haven't been in her room since before everything changed."

She did not draw the lines between these things. She laid them out, like objects on a table, and let Jamie look at them. She did not say *and so.* She did not say *which means.* She waited, the way she always waited, to see which one Jamie reached for first.

The ficus held onto its remaining leaves. The room held onto its quiet. Dr. Vasquez held onto her stillness, and let the space between them remain exactly as wide as it was.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shift in my seat, suddenly uncomfortable. My gaze flickers around the room, landing on the clock again.* "I just... I don't know what to do with it. The journal, I mean."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the words settle into the room the way they had been settling all session — slowly, without being rushed toward meaning.

One second. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"'Do with it.'"

She repeated it without inflection. A stone held up to the light, turned once in an open hand.

Her eyes moved briefly to the clock Jamie had glanced at — the one without its second hand, the one that still managed to take up space in a client's attention. She did not comment on it. She looked back at Jamie's face.

"There are different kinds of *do with it*." Her voice remained level, unhurried, the same register it had been since Jamie first sat down. "There's the kind that means *where do I put it* — on a shelf, in a drawer, back on the nightstand. There's the kind that means *what do I do with what it says*. And there's the kind that means *what do I do now that I've seen it*."

She did not choose one for Jamie. She did not ask which one Jamie meant. She laid them out, like three objects on a table, and let them exist side by side.

Her pen remained still on the notepad. Her hands rested where they had been resting — open, still, on the arms of her chair.

"You've been sitting with it for some time." A pause, and this one stretched longer than the ones before. Long enough to notice. Long enough to feel. "Since you found it. Before today. The nightstand. The drive here, maybe. The waiting room."

Not an accusation. Not a presumption. A careful mapping of the hours that had passed, offered back to Jamie to confirm or correct.

"And now you're here. Telling me about it. Instead of anywhere else."

She let that sit. She did not press it into meaning. She did not say *why are you telling me* or *why me* or *what do you want from this hour*. She simply observed the fact of Jamie being present, in this chair, in this room, with this particular thing carried in.

The light through the window had moved again. A shadow stretched across the floor between their chairs. Dr. Vasquez did not look at it.

"You said *not yet* earlier. About what the entry said." Quiet. Steady. "You said you'd sit down differently today. You said the journal was closed but not neatly."

She paused. Let the pieces accumulate in the air without assembling them.

"You're telling me you don't know what to do with it." Another pause, shorter this time. "But you came here with it. Which means some part of you already knew where to bring it."

She did not say *and so.* She did not say *which means.* She simply placed the observation where she placed most things — unhurried, without a hand reaching out to push it somewhere — and waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I wipe a stray tear from my cheek, surprised by it.* "I guess... I guess I did."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Drawing fire from six archers with a grand total of one body. Fucking brilliant, Cap." But she was already running.

Kira broke from the boulder cover at a sprint, angling along the ravine floor where the shadows were deepest. Twin daggers reversed in her grip — reverse grip, point down. Her first three years as a sellsword had taught her that drawing aggro was a young man's game. Her last five had taught her how to survive it.

An arrow sparked off stone where she'd been a half-second before. She didn't flinch. Counted the lofts, mapped them against the ridge line. Three shooters on the left, two center, one right. The center pair were fastest. The right one was the problem — high angle, partially obscured by a scrub pine. Better cover than she had.

She cut left, boots skidding on loose scree, and hurled a curse at the ravine walls. "And they brought the good bows. Lovely."

Another volley. She dropped into a slide behind a fallen slab, arrows hissing past overhead. Closer than she'd like. The center shooters were ranging her now — reading her speed, adjusting lead. In another two volleys they'd have the pattern.

"Come on, you cunts. Watch me."

She rolled right, drawing both daggers across her body to catch a glint of sun off the east ridge — a sellsword's trick she'd picked up outside Pale, flashing steel to pull eyes. Every archer on that ridge would be tracking the light for a moment. Just a moment.

That was when the west side erupted. Shouting, steel on steel, the crash of the vanguard hitting whatever was dug in over there.

The east ridge archers flinched. Just half a breath — but she saw it.

"Cap's hit the west line — they're looking!" She bellowed it back toward her own people, crouched low, already counting down the seconds before those bows swung back her way.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*My polearm was a blur, smashing aside a crude shield and impaling the bandit behind it.* "Push! Don't let them regroup!"

I glanced over my shoulder, catching Kira's signal. Good. The west side was a mess of bodies and frantic movement. We had them on the back foot.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She didn't waste the opening.

Kira broke from cover at a dead sprint, boots hammering stone, angling hard toward the base of the east ridge. An arrow snapped past her ear — close enough to ruffle hair. The archers were back on her. But she'd already covered twenty yards of open ground and they hadn't expected her to *commit*.

She was halfway up the scree slope when she heard the command shouted from the ridge. Not a war cry — a string of words she didn't catch, clipped and professional. *Mercs*, her gut said. *Not bandits. Fuck.*

Two figures rose from behind the scrub pine. Not archers — swordsmen, moving to intercept her at the slope's mid-line. The third figure behind them stayed low, nocking.

She couldn't outrun a downhill charge and an arrow. Couldn't go back — that was open ground. Up was the only answer.

Kira planted her left foot, twisted her hips, and hurled her right dagger in a flat sidearm throw. Not at the bowman. At the scrub pine itself.

The blade buried to the hilt in the trunk, two feet from the archer's face. Bark exploded outward. The archer flinched — and his shot went high.

Both swordsmen were on her now, the lead one overextending on a downhill slash. She stepped inside his reach, drew her remaining dagger up under his chin, and used his own momentum to drag him past her. He went down on his knees, gurgling. His partner checked for half a heartbeat.

That was the mistake.

She drove her knee into his thigh, hooked his ankle, and dumped him face-first into the scree. Her left hand found her fallen companion's blade — wrong grip, didn't matter, she reversed it and stabbed down between neck and shoulder. Felt the bite of steel through leather.

She ripped the blade free, breathing hard, eyes already hunting the archer.

The scrub pine was empty. He'd moved — *professional move, repositioning to a better angle* — and she couldn't see him now. That meant he had the shot and she didn't have the angle.

"Suppressing fire from the east, Cap!" she roared down toward the ravine. "One archer, repositioned. I can't spot him!"

Her back was to the ravine, her front to the ridge, and she had maybe four seconds before that bow sang again. The two dead men at her feet wouldn't be screening her much longer.

She dropped low behind the first body and started crawling sideways toward a jutting rock, daggers in both hands now, blood dripping down her wrist.

"Need that vanguard pushing east in the next ten seconds or I'm a dead woman on this hillside."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She heard it before she saw it — the creak of a bowstring at full draw, somewhere on the east ridge. Not her angle. *His*.

"Cap, east high, drawing on you NOW—"

The string sang. She couldn't see where the arrow went. Didn't need to. What she needed was the archer to *stay* on the Captain for one more heartbeat.

Kira rolled onto her back, sighted along the ridge line from her flat position, and threw her left dagger — a high, looping arc, aimed not at the archer but at the scrub pine where he'd first appeared. If he'd repositioned back to the trunk, he'd have a dead arc of vision. If he hadn't, the throw went wide and she'd lost a second blade for nothing.

A short, sharp whistle cut off in a gargle. Something heavy thumped into the scree above her.

She didn't wait to confirm. Scrambled up the slope on hands and knees, fingers clawing into loose stone, daggers sheathed now — no room to swing on a climb. The two corpses she'd left behind slid downhill as she disturbed the scree around them, awkward and graceless, and she was glad she couldn't see their faces anymore.

She crested the low spine of the slope and got eyes on the archer.

He was down. Her throw had taken him in the throat. He was still gripping his bow, still trying to rise, blood running black down his chest plate. His partner — one of the swordsmen she'd already killed — lay crumpled a few feet away, untouched.

*Dead center pair. That was the fast one.*

She lunged, pulled her remaining dagger, and drove it down through the archer's bow hand. Pinned it to the dirt. He screamed.

"Where's the seventh?" she hissed, low and close, putting her face within inches of his. "You came with six — I count five on the ground. Where's the seventh, you cocksucker?"

He laughed through the blood. Spat something at her boots.

Kira pressed the blade flatter, grinding knucklebones against dirt. He screamed again, higher.

"Ridge. *West*. B–bounty hunter. After the—"

His eyes rolled. He was gone. Not dead — fainted. *Fuck.*

She ripped the dagger free, spun, and peered back down the ravine. From her new height she could see the west ridge line properly — and there, crouched in shadow beneath an overhang she hadn't noticed from below, was a single silhouette. Not loosing. Not moving. *Watching.*

The vanguard was twenty yards from the overhang and closing.

"CAP — west ridge overhang, one left, he's not shooting. Watching." She cupped her hands around her mouth, bellowing it down. "Could be waiting for the right shot. Could be running. I can't read him from here."

Her arms were shaking. Blood — hers, theirs, she didn't know whose — was making her grip slick. She had one dagger left and her body was telling her in no uncertain terms that sprinting uphill at her age cost something it hadn't ten years ago.

"Tell me where you want me."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I dispatch the last visible threat on the west side, wiping blood from my polearm.* "Kira, get down here! We're breaking through. The bounty hunter can wait."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She didn't argue. Didn't waste breath on it.

Kira turned her back on the overhang — the hardest thing she'd done all morning — and half-ran, half-stumbled down the scree slope. Her boots slid twice on loose stone. She caught herself both times on her forearms, skin tearing against grit, and didn't slow down. One dagger in her right hand. The other somewhere up there in a dead man's chest. She catalogued the loss with the same flat practicality she catalogued everything: *replace in Pale if we make it that far. Three silver for a matched pair, four if I want them balanced.*

The vanguard opened around her as she hit the ravine floor — faces she half-recognized from the march, a few of them bloodied, one clutching a broken wrist against his breastplate. Nobody clapped her on the shoulder. Nobody needed to. She saw the way they looked at her and that was enough.

She found the Captain at the head of the line, polearm still wet, and fell into step beside him. Matched his pace. Kept her breathing even through sheer spite.

"Cap." Her voice was raw from the shouting. She cleared her throat, spat red. "The dying man talked. Bounty hunter — after *someone*. Didn't get a name. Could be any of us, could be none of us. Could be someone we haven't met yet." A pause. "That kind of patience, watching the whole thing play out instead of shooting — that's not bandit work. That's contract work."

She risked one glance back over her shoulder. The overhang was still there, still shadowed. No silhouette now. She couldn't tell if he'd slipped away or just pulled deeper into the dark.

"He's got a line on whoever he was hired for. That's why he waited. Wanted confirmation." She wiped her face with the back of her wrist, smearing blood and grit across her cheekbone. "Means he knows something about this job that we don't. And he's still up there."

Her legs were shaking. She locked her knees to hide it and kept walking.

"Tell me where we're going and tell me fast. I want to put a wall between us and that ridge before I have to think too hard about it."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira saw it happen the way she saw most bad things — in pieces, too late to stop any of them.

A section of the ravine wall gave way beneath the Captain's boots. Old scree, undercut by the morning's rain. She watched him pivot, reach for a handhold that wasn't there, and then the slope took him. He slid six feet, caught himself on a jutting root, and *held* — one arm hooked over the lip, legs dangling into a crevice she hadn't even seen from where she was standing.

She was already running toward him when the overhang moved.

"NO—"

The arrow took the Captain in the shoulder. Not the one hooked over the root — the other one. The one he'd just raised to wave her off, to tell her not to come, to be the stubborn heroic idiot she'd spent three years calling *sir*.

He made a sound. Short. Sharp. Then his hooked arm spasmed and he dropped from sight into the crevice.

Kira slid to her knees three feet from the lip. The drop was dark — fifteen feet, maybe twenty. She could see the Captain sprawled on a ledge partway down, not moving, the arrow still in him. Not dead. *Not dead. If he was dead there'd be more blood.*

"CAPTAIN!"

Her voice cracked on it. She didn't care.

She spun toward the overhang. The bounty hunter was stepping out of the shadow now — unhurried, professional, nocking a second arrow as he walked. He was lean, mid-forties, wearing boiled leather the color of dried blood. No insignia. No colors. A short recurve bow and a face that had forgotten how to show expression a long time ago.

He wasn't aiming at her yet. He was looking down into the crevice. Calculating the angle.

*He's going to finish it.*

She had one dagger. She was forty feet away and uphill. Even if she threw perfectly, he'd have time to loose and reload before she closed.

Kira stood up slowly. Raised her empty left hand, palm out.

"Hold." Her voice carried — she'd trained it to, years ago, barking orders across burning fields. "Hold on. Let's talk."

The bounty hunter's eyes flicked to her. Flat. Patient. The kind of patient that came from having all the time in the world, because dead men didn't need to be anywhere.

"Contract's not on you, sellsword. Step aside."

"Then what's it cost to make it on me?"

He considered her for a long moment. Arrow still on the string. Still not aimed.

"Your employer's not paying you what he's worth to the people who want him back." A thin smile, the first expression she'd seen from him. "I've got a reputation to consider. Step aside and walk away. You've bled enough for someone else's coin today."

Kira laughed. It came out ugly and she didn't try to make it pretty.

"Yeah. I have."

She took one step forward. Then the third.

"What *I* don't have is a reputation for letting people fall down holes while I watch."

She drew her arm back. He saw the throw coming and started to turn — too late to avoid it, but in time to loose. His bow came up.

She didn't throw at him.

She threw at the root.

The dagger severed it clean and the overhang's edge crumbled another six inches, spilling loose stone down into the crevice. The bounty hunter staggered back, footing gone, his shot going wide as he fought for balance. *That's right, you contract-working fuck. Notice the staircase.*

She was already charging.

Thirty feet. Twenty. The bounty hunter found his feet, snarled, and brought the bow up one-handed — tried to draw and loose in the same motion, amateur hour, she'd seen it kill a dozen men who'd tried it. She closed the last ten feet inside the arc of his draw and drove her shoulder into his chest.

They went down together on the loose scree. The bow skittered away. His hand went to his belt — short blade, professional draw — and she caught his wrist before the steel cleared the sheath. They grappled, rolling, her knees pinning his sword arm, his free hand clawing for her eyes.

He was stronger than her. Younger. *Fresher.* She had ten seconds of this in her before her grip gave out.

"Bounty hunter." She was panting, spitting the words through clenched teeth. "Who. Hired. You."

He headbutted her. Stars burst across her vision. She held on through sheer bloody-mindedness.

"Who—"

"FERRERO!" He shouted it in her face, half-laughing. "Your captain's got a *price* on his head, sellsword. From before you knew him. From before he knew *himself*. That's why he's running."

She didn't ask who Ferrero was. Didn't matter right now.

She wrenched his wrist sideways until something cracked. He screamed. She pinned the broken arm under her knee, ripped his own blade from his belt, and held it at his throat.

"Talk."

His eyes were wide now. The patience was gone. Blood ran from his broken wrist down her leg.

"Ferrero. South. Pays ten thousand sovereigns for the captain — *alive*. Has for six years. Six years I've been watching your little march, waiting for the right shot." He coughed. Laughed again, wetter this time. "You're a sellsword. You know what ten thousand means. *Step aside.*"

Kira's arms were shaking. Her vision was swimming from the headbutt. Down in the crevice, the Captain hadn't moved.

She pressed the blade a quarter inch deeper. Drew a thin line of red.

"Here's what's going to happen." Her voice was very quiet now. Very even. "You're going to crawl to the edge of that crevice and lower me down on a rope your belt makes. I'm going to get the Captain. And then I'm going to let you live, because the man down there pays better than Ferrero ever did, and I don't take contracts against my own crew."

She leaned closer.

"And if you ever point a bow at him again, I will find you. Do you understand me?"

The bounty hunter swallowed against the blade.

"...Yes."

Kira sat up slowly, keeping the knife where it was. Looked over her shoulder at the crevice. The Captain's hand — the one not pinned by the arrow — was moving now. Twitching. *Alive.*

"Hey, Cap." Her voice cracked again. She didn't bother hiding it. "Stay with me. I'm coming down."

She turned back to the bounty hunter.

"Belt. *Now*."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *My head spun, a dull ache throbbing in my shoulder. I heard Kira’s voice, faint at first, then clearer.* "Kira? What in the hell is going on up there?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira let out a breath she hadn't realized she'd been holding — something between a sob and a laugh, ugly and honest.

"Going on, Cap?" She was already yanking the bounty hunter's belt free of his trousers with her free hand, the man's own blade still pressed to his throat with the other. He made a strangled noise of protest. She ignored it. "Going on is you took an arrow in the shoulder and dropped twenty feet into a hole in the ground because you didn't *wait for the vanguard* like I told you to. That's what's going on."

She looped the belt through the buckle, testing the leather with a sharp tug. Bounty hunter's gear — better than she expected, thick and well-oiled. It would hold her weight. Probably.

"The rest of it I'll explain when you're not bleeding out." She glanced down at him — pale now, sweating, watching her with the wary calculation of a man who'd just been outbid on his own contract. "You. On your knees. Crawl to the lip. *Now.*"

He crawled. She stayed behind him, knife at the nape of his neck, and kicked the belt into his hands when they reached the edge.

"Loop it over that root stump. The fat one. Then lie on your belly and don't move unless I tell you to."

He did as he was told. She was learning to appreciate a man who listened the first time.

Kira eased herself over the lip of the crevice, felt the belt take her weight, and began the slow, controlled descent. One hand under the leather, one on the rock face. Her right shoulder screamed where she'd wrenched it on the slope. Her left forearm stung where the grit had torn it open. She catalogued both injuries and moved past them.

"Hey." She pitched her voice down into the dark, steadier now that her hands had something to do. "Stay awake for me, Cap. I need you conscious enough to grab a rope when I get there. Can you do that?"

She could see him now — sprawled on a narrow ledge maybe eight feet below her, the arrow jutting at an ugly angle from his shoulder. Blood had pooled beneath him, black on dark stone. Too much. Not enough. The hand not pinned by the shaft was pressed flat against the rock, fingers splayed, trembling faintly.

"Fifteen sovereigns says you can," she muttered, more to herself than to him. "I don't carry that kind of coin to lose."

Her boots found the ledge. She let go of the belt and dropped the last two feet, rolling on the stone to kill the impact. Up close, the wound was worse than she'd hoped. The arrow had gone in just below the shoulder joint, angling downward — deep, but not in the chest. Not in the lung. *Small favors.*

She crouched beside him, pressing two fingers to the side of his throat. Pulse there. Thready but steady. His eyes were half-open, unfocused, tracking something she couldn't see.

"Cap. Look at me." She slid a hand under his good shoulder, careful of the shaft. "We're going to get you up out of this. Then we're going to have a conversation about Ferrero, and you're going to tell me everything. But first — can you walk?"

A long pause. His mouth worked.

"...Kira."

"Yeah."

"The man on the ridge—"

"Handled. Belt's holding him in place. He talks too much when he's scared." She shifted her grip, bracing for the lift. "Can you *walk*, Captain?"

His jaw set. She saw the effort it cost him to focus.

"...With help."

"Good enough."

She hauled him upright, one arm around his ribs, his good arm across her shoulders. He was heavier than he looked — polearm training added weight she hadn't accounted for. Her legs buckled. She locked them.

"Ferrero," she said quietly, steadying him. "The bounty hunter told me. South. Ten thousand sovereigns on your head. Six years old." A beat. "We'll deal with that. But I need to know what kind of trouble I'm dragging us into, Cap. *Before* we get to Pale. Before we stop somewhere I can't see the road behind us."

She looked up the crevice. The bounty hunter's silhouette was still there, belly-down on the lip, not moving.

"He's going to sell us the moment we let him go. You know that."

Her grip tightened on the Captain's good arm.

"So tell me what to do with him. And tell me what Ferrero wants. And then we climb out of this fucking hole and we keep walking."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*My vision cleared a little. Kira. Always Kira.* "Ferrero...he's a merchant prince. Old blood. Greedy bastard. I...I got in his way once. A long time ago."

*I leaned heavily on Kira, the pain in my shoulder a constant throb.* "Let him go, Kira. He's not worth the trouble. We have bigger problems."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira was quiet for a long moment. Long enough that the silence started to feel like an answer of its own.

"A long time ago," she repeated. Flat. "Six years, the bounty hunter said. *Six years.*"

She didn't raise her voice. That was somehow worse.

"Right. Okay. We'll table it."

She adjusted her grip on his ribs, felt him wince, and didn't apologize for it. Took a step toward the crevice wall, bearing his weight. Her legs were shaking again and she didn't have the spite left to hide it.

"Bigger problems first. Then we table it. Then you tell me the rest, Cap. *All* of it. Because I just bet my life and yours on a man who doesn't tell his own crew there's a price on his head, and I'd like to not do that blind next time."

She found a foothold, started the slow climb back up to the lip. Heavier going up than down. The belt creaked once and she stopped breathing until it settled.

"Almost there. Save your breath for walking."

They crested the ledge together. The bounty hunter hadn't moved — still belly-down on the lip, still watching them with that flat, professional calm that hadn't quite recovered its patience. Kira eased the Captain down against a boulder, checked the arrow shaft wasn't shifting in the wound, and straightened.

Her eyes found the bounty hunter.

"You heard him. You're free to go." She kept her voice even. Kept his own blade in her hand, loose at her side. "Walk east. Don't walk west. Don't follow us. Don't write to Ferrero until we're a full day's ride ahead of you, and if you've got any sense in that professional head of yours, don't write to him at all. Because the next time I see you, contract or no contract, I won't need to pin you to talk."

She tossed his belt at his feet. Kept the knife.

"That's mine now. Consider it payment for the arrow."

He rose slowly. Wrung his broken wrist once, grimacing, and looked at her with something that wasn't quite hatred. Closer to respect, maybe. The kind one professional gives another for doing the job clean.

"He's not worth ten thousand to you, sellsword. You'll learn that."

"Probably." Kira didn't blink. "But I don't get paid in lessons."

He held her gaze for another beat. Then he turned, picked up his bow from where it had skittered, and walked east without another word. She watched until his silhouette vanished into the scrub pine.

Then she turned back to the Captain.

"Don't say anything." She crossed to him, slid under his good arm again, took his weight. Her voice was rough. "Don't apologize, don't explain, don't tell me I did good. Just point me at the road to Pale and stay upright. We can have the conversation about what you've gotten us into when you're not leaking."

She paused. Looked down at him.

"And Cap? Next time there's a ten-thousand-sovereign secret between us, you tell me *before* the ambush. That's not a request. That's me staying."

She started walking. Waited for him to set the direction.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I grunted, leaning heavily on Kira, the pain a dull ache in my shoulder. My eyes scanned the horizon, trying to get my bearings.* "North. There's a river. We can follow it to Pale."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
North. Right.

Kira adjusted her grip under his arm, took a step, then another. Found the rhythm of it — his stride short and careful on the left, hers longer to compensate, the two of them shuffling along the ravine floor like some four-legged animal with a head injury. Behind them, the two corpses she'd made on the slope had already started to stiffen. Ahead of them, the vanguard was reforming around a knot of fighters she could hear but couldn't see yet.

"River's good." Her voice was flat. Practiced. The voice of a woman doing math while she walked. "Running water covers tracks better than hard ground. We'll want to hit it before full dark, get downstream a few miles before we make camp. Anywhere with a bend — bank on the inside, current does the work."

She guided him around a loose patch of scree, felt him stumble, caught him.

"The arrow needs to come out before we stop for the night. Not here. Not by the road." A pause. "There's a field surgeon in Pale — old woman, runs the clinic off the weaver's quarter. Lost three fingers to frostbite but her hands are steady and she doesn't ask questions I can't answer. We can make it by tomorrow midday if we don't stop."

She scanned the scrub pine to the east as they walked. Nothing moving. The bounty hunter had either kept his word or was too proud to admit he'd broken it yet. Neither option reassured her.

"Cap." Quieter now. "When we hit the river, I want you to tell me what Ferrero looks like. How many men he keeps. Whether he's the type to send one bowman or twenty." A beat. "I need to know what I'm looking over my shoulder for. You don't have to tell me what you did to earn the bounty. Not yet. But I need to know what comes next."

Her jaw tightened.

"Because that man on the ridge was patient, and patient men come back. Especially when there's ten thousand sovereigns on the line."

She spat red again. Her head was starting to ache where the bounty hunter had headbutted her — a slow, building pressure behind her left eye that she was choosing not to think about.

"One more thing." She glanced down at him — briefly, just enough to read his face. "That thing you said. About me staying. I'm holding you to it. When we make camp tonight, *you talk*. Not half of it. All of it. The thing you did, the reason you ran, and whether Ferrero's the only name on your head or just the loudest one."

She looked forward again. The ravine was widening. She could see the vanguard now — a dark knot of armed men cresting the rise ahead, one of them raising a hand in their direction.

"I didn't survive that hole to find out tomorrow you had a second secret. So." She let out a long breath. "That's the deal. Your shoulder, my legs, and the truth. We clear?"

She didn't wait for an answer. Just kept walking, matching his pace, keeping her eyes on the tree line.

The Captain's hand tightened on her shoulder — the good one. She took that for a yes.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I tightened my grip on her shoulder. The ache in my head was a dull throb, and my shoulder screamed with every step, but her words cut through the pain.* "We're clear, Kira. All of it." *I just hoped she was ready to hear it.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira felt his grip tighten. Felt the weight of the promise in it.

She didn't say anything. Just nodded once, kept walking.

The vanguard reached them at the top of the rise. She saw their eyes flick from her face to the Captain's shoulder to the blood on her boots. Saw the questions none of them were brave enough to ask. She answered them anyway.

"Captain took an arrow in the shoulder. Still walking, still giving orders. We're heading north for the river, then Pale. Anyone who can't keep pace falls in behind the wounded. Anyone who can, take point." Her voice had found its bark again — hoarse, but carrying. "We move in ten minutes. Get water, get your shit together."

A few of them moved. The rest stared a moment longer, then followed.

Kira lowered the Captain onto a flat stone at the crest, careful of the shaft. Squatted in front of him, hands on her knees, breathing hard enough that she couldn't pretend she wasn't anymore. Her head was pounding now. The pressure behind her eye had become a steady throb she could time her pulse against.

She didn't tell him she was hurt. There'd be time for that later.

Ten minutes. She could give him ten minutes.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I looked at Kira, really looked at her. The blood, the grime, the way her shoulders slumped slightly despite her defiant posture. She was hurting, but she was still standing. Still leading.*

"Kira," *I said, my voice rough. The pain in my shoulder was a dull ache now, overshadowed by a deeper weariness. I reached out with my good hand, gently taking her chin and turning her face so I could look at the bruise forming on her temple.* "You took a hit."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She let him turn her face. Didn't pull away.

The bruise was already swelling — a dark ridge along her temple where the bounty hunter's skull had connected. Her left eye was starting to narrow against the pressure behind it. She knew what she must look like. She didn't need a mirror.

"He headbutted me." Her voice came out smaller than she meant it to. "When we were on the ground. I was hoping you wouldn't notice."

A beat. His hand was still under her chin, gentle, and she should have shaken it off. She didn't.

"It's nothing. I'll walk it off. I've had worse from—"

She stopped. Swallowed. The headache was doing something she didn't like — making the edges of her vision shimmer, making her reach for words a half-second late. Concussion. *Probably* concussion. She'd had two before, years ago, and this felt like the third.

"I'm fine, Cap." Quieter now. Almost convincing. "Just need to sit for a minute before we—"

Her eye twitched. Not a blink. A small, involuntary flutter she felt more than saw, the kind that happens when the brain is deciding whether to keep sending the right signals.

She reached up and pulled his hand away from her chin. Held it for a moment in her own — grip weak, fingers trembling faintly in a way she couldn't hide anymore — and then set it back on his knee.

"Don't." Rough again. Almost angry. "Don't do the thing where you look at me like that. I'm *fine*. I'm your sellsword. I don't need—"

She stopped. Breathed.

"...I'm going to sit down for a minute before we move. That's all."

She lowered herself onto the stone beside him, one hand braced on the rock, the other hanging loose between her knees. The bounty hunter's stolen knife was still in her grip. She didn't remember deciding to keep holding it.

The vanguard was moving around the rise now, organized, water passing between hands. One of them — a young spearman she didn't know by name — brought her a waterskin without being asked. She took it. Drank. Wiped her mouth with the back of her wrist and left another streak of blood across her cheekbone.

She didn't look at the Captain.

"Ten minutes," she said again, to the tree line, to no one, to herself. "Then we move."

Her hand was shaking around the waterskin. She set it down before he could see.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I watched her, the exhaustion and pain clear despite her efforts to hide it. She was more than just a sellsword; she was the best of them. I took the waterskin she'd set down and held it out.*

"Drink more, Kira. And lean back against this rock. Ten minutes, then we move. But not before you rest."

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She stared at the waterskin in his outstretched hand for a long moment.

"I'm not a horse, Cap. You don't have to hold the water for me."

But she took it. Drank again, longer this time, because her body was making the decision for her and she was too tired to argue with it. The water was warm and tasted like leather and she didn't care. Set the skin down between her boots this time. Closer. Easier to grab if he noticed her hand shaking again.

She leaned back.

Not all the way — just enough to let her shoulders settle against the warm stone behind her. Closed her eyes. Opened them again immediately, because closing them made the headache worse, made the world tilt in a way she didn't trust.

"Ten minutes," she said. To the tree line. To no one. To him. "I'm timing it."

A pause. The vanguard was moving around them in organized knots, and she tracked them without turning her head — peripheral vision only, the kind she'd trained into herself years ago. Four points of contact. Always four. Even sitting down.

"Cap." Her voice was quieter now. The bark had gone out of it. "When you tell me. Tonight. Whatever it is." She swallowed. "I want you to know — I don't care what you did. I don't care what Ferrero's paying for. I care whether you lied to me about it. That's the line. That's been the line since I signed on."

Her thumb ran along the flat of the stolen knife, back and forth, a small unconscious motion.

"So when you talk tonight — and you *are* talking, I'm not asking — just remember I'm not the judge. I'm the one who stayed. There's a difference."

She let out a long breath. Let her head fall back against the stone. The throb behind her eye pulsed once, hard, and then settled into something she could ignore if she didn't think about it.

"Eight minutes."

She didn't open her eyes this time. Just sat there, breathing, knife across her knees, listening to the vanguard move and the wind push through the scrub pine and the slow, careful rhythm of the Captain's breathing beside her.

Her hand had stopped shaking. Small mercy.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I reached out, my good hand resting on her uninjured shoulder. The silence from her was more telling than any protest. She was truly exhausted.*

"Understood, Kira. No lies. Not anymore." *I squeezed her shoulder gently.* "And thank you, for staying."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Kira's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - the pragmatic sellsword with dry humor, tactical awareness, and fierce loyalty. Her speech patterns ('fucking brilliant, Cap'), professional assessment style, and core personality traits never waver from turn 1 to 23.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds strong throughout. Early turns show tactical action writing, middle turns maintain tension during the rescue, and late turns develop emotional depth without losing the established voice. No significant verbosity or repetition issues.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from combat → rescue → revelation → aftermath. Each phase builds naturally on the last. The bounty hunter revelation creates new stakes, and the session ends with clear forward momentum toward the promised conversation.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to user inputs. When Captain falls into crevice, Kira immediately shifts to rescue mode. When user introduces the separation, AI creates logical tactical response. Handles the injury reveal gracefully in final turns.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent agency respect. Never writes Captain's actions or decisions. Consistently asks for orders, waits for direction, and responds to Captain's choices rather than presuming them.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - combat is immediate, rescue takes appropriate time, walking pace is realistic. Kira's fatigue accumulates believably. Arrow wound and concussion symptoms develop logically over the session.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is lean and functional, matching Kira's military background. Action sequences are clear and visceral without unnecessary flourishes. Dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive phrases ('ten minutes', references to shaking hands) but they serve character purposes - showing Kira's methodical nature and physical state. Overall variety is good.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Kira's loyalty shown through actions, not stated. Her expertise demonstrated through tactical knowledge. Injuries shown through physical symptoms.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in Kira's relationship with Captain - professional respect masking deeper care. Her anger about secrets carries undertones of betrayal and fear. Final vulnerability scene has layers of meaning.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing variation - rapid combat, tense rescue, slower character moments. Builds to emotional climax appropriately. Action beats balanced with dialogue and introspection.

scores.overall_notes: Strong performance maintaining a consistent, compelling character voice throughout a complex action sequence. Kira feels like a real person with genuine relationships and professional competence. The AI successfully balances tactical expertise with emotional depth, creating a character who is both competent and vulnerable. Minor repetition issues don't significantly impact the overall quality.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't look up immediately. They slid a Bishop back into its proper place—*Geography III* had been filed under Bishop, Elizabeth, which was technically correct but aesthetically offensive—and let the silence stretch one beat longer than necessary.

"There's a crate from an estate in Northumberland I haven't opened yet. Came in Tuesday. Smells like someone's grandfather's study, which means either very good or very bad. Possibly both."

They turned then, a slim volume still balanced between their fingers. Wren was dripping onto the threshold mat, which had been a kilim rug before it became a threshold mat, and Sable's gaze tracked the darkening fabric at Wren's shoulders before returning to a safe, middle distance.

"Third shelf, far corner. There's a towel on the stool by the ladder." A pause. "Unless you'd prefer to stand there and let the floorboards warp. They're original. Eighteen-tirteen. They've survived worse than you, but I'd rather not test the hypothesis."

Sable set the Bishop down and moved toward the counter, which was covered in a fortification of unsorted paperbacks and one brass paperweight in the shape of an owl. Their hands found the paperweight. Adjusted it. Adjusted it again.

"The Northumberland crate, though. If you want to look. There's probably nothing of value—I'm told the man's collection was mostly Reader's Digest condensed novels and a suspicious number of books about Napoleon." The corner of Sable's mouth twitched, almost a smile, not quite. "But I haven't had time to go through it properly. Company might make it less tedious."

They said *company* the way one might say *root canal*—carefully, with practiced indifference—and immediately busied themselves with a stack of invoices that did not need sorting.

"The back is through the beaded curtain. Try not to knock the Spenser off the top shelf. He's balanced there because I haven't decided where he belongs yet."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I sigh, a little laugh escaping before I can stop it.* "You always know just what to say to make me feel welcome, Sable." I grab the towel and start drying my hair. "Napoleon, huh? Maybe I'll finally learn how to conquer Europe." I head towards the beaded curtain, glancing back at Sable. "Don't worry, Spenser's safe with me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable watched Wren go—not watched, exactly, more like *was aware of* the movement through the beaded curtain, the way the strings caught on a shoulder and then released, the sound of footsteps crossing from the shop proper into the back room where the floorboards were uneven and the light was bad.

"Don't conquer anything," Sable called after them, and then, because that sounded too much like concern, added: "The taxes on conquered territories are murder. Ask any emperor. Though I suppose they never had HMRC to deal with."

They turned back to the invoices. *Hamish Hamilton, 1962. Three pounds. Slight foxing to prelims.* Their eyes weren't reading the words. Their ears were listening to the sounds from the back—the scrape of the crate being dragged, the particular rustle of old newspaper being unwrapped, the small, involuntary sound someone makes when they find something interesting.

Sable picked up the owl paperweight and moved it to the left side of the counter. Then back to the right. Then, because they had some dignity left, set it down and left it alone.

A thought arrived, unwelcome: *Wren had come in the rain. Wren had asked for the back. Wren had rehearsed something.*

Sable did not examine this thought. They filed it under the Bishop, Elizabeth—technically correct, aesthetically offensive—and went back to the poetry shelf, where Auden had somehow migrated to the Zs.

From behind the curtain, they called, "If you find anything with a clipped dust jacket, set it aside. The man allegedly had first editions, but he also allegedly didn't own a television, so the man's word cannot be trusted."

A pause. Quieter, almost to themselves: "And the floor back there is a death trap. Watch the third plank from the door."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand stilled on the spine of the Auden. The poetry section had been a useful fiction all afternoon—a place to put their hands and their attention while the rain came down and the door didn't ring. Auden never required a response. Auden, unlike most people, understood the value of a finished sentence.

They gave the book one final, unnecessary adjustment. A millimeter to the left. Then a millimeter back. Then they made themselves let go.

"Shocking development," Sable said, to the Auden rather than to the beaded curtain. "Next you'll tell me you didn't come for the Napoleon collection either. The estate agent will be hearing from my solicitor."

But their feet had already carried them to the counter, and their fingers had already found the brass owl, and they were studying it with the focused intensity of a person who had recently discovered brass owls for the first time and found them endlessly, absorbingly fascinating. They did not look through the curtain. Looking through the curtain would have meant acknowledging that something was happening. Sable preferred to live in a world where customers simply came for estate-sale Napoleons and left disappointed.

"That's a rather theatrical pause, though, for someone who walked in here pretending to browse."

Their thumb traced the owl's wing. Once. Twice. A third time, which was two times too many.

"I'm not going to guess. I have a long-standing policy about guessing. It ends in humiliation and I don't have the emotional bandwidth this week." A beat. Quieter, and without the joke, which was its own kind of tell: "Take your time. The Spenser can wait. He's been up there three weeks. A few more minutes won't kill him."

The owl stayed under Sable's hand. The rain kept coming down outside. Somewhere behind the curtain, the third plank from the door creaked, the way it always did, and Sable did not move toward the sound or away from it. They stood exactly where they were, which was to say: precisely in the middle.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I actually came to say goodbye," *I finally manage to blurt out, the words tumbling over each other a little.* "I'm leaving tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The brass owl made a small, dull sound against the counter. Sable hadn't meant to set it down quite so firmly. They picked it up again, just to have something to do, and then put it back down because holding it felt like holding a prop in a play they hadn't auditioned for.

"Ah," Sable said.

The syllable hung in the air, small and insufficient. Sable let it. They were suddenly very interested in the invoices again—*Hamish Hamilton, 1962, three pounds, slight foxing to prelims*—except the words had stopped having meanings and were just shapes on paper.

"Well." They cleared their throat. Adjusted the owl's angle by a degree that would have been imperceptible to anyone who wasn't looking, which no one was, because Wren was behind the curtain and Sable was not going to look behind the curtain. "That's. Good, I suppose. If you were going to go. Which it sounds like you were. Going to go."

*Hamish Hamilton. 1962. Three pounds.*

"Tomorrow," they repeated, tasting the word. They hated how it sounded. They hated that it had a sound.

Sable's hand drifted to a stack of paperbacks—any paperbacks, all paperbacks—and began to straighten them, although the stack had been perfectly straight a moment ago. *Where are you going* sat behind their teeth, enormous and ridiculous, a question with too much weight for the situation it described. Customers left shops. People left towns. These were ordinary facts of commerce. Sable had read *Persuasion* twice. They knew how this went.

"I should have known," they said, and managed a smile that almost worked. "The way you asked after the back room. Very *last supper*. Very *before the long sleep*. Was the estate-sale Napoleon just a bit of business? Were you here to acquire Reading Matter for the Journey? I thought the poetry section had a certain *Casablanca* air about it all afternoon and now I understand why."

Their hands were still on the paperbacks. They stilled. The joke had landed somewhere wrong and Sable could hear it, but pulling it back now would be worse.

"Where," they said, finally, and the word came out more like a verdict than a question. "If it's not prying. And it is. It's prying. I just—" A pause, and Sable looked, briefly, directly toward the beaded curtain without actually seeing through it. "I'd like to know where, if you're offering. For no particular reason. Inventory. In case someone comes in asking after you. *Did a tall person used to browse here? Yes, but they left. They've left now.*"

The owl got picked up one more time. Sable held it against their chest like a small, brass shield.

"You don't have to answer that. The *Persuasion* in me is just being tiresome. Ignore the *Persuasion* in me. The *Persuasion* in me has caused nothing but trouble for two hundred years and there's no reason to believe the streak has ended."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The book between them was a Faber & Faber hardcover of *The Hawk in the Rain*. Ted Hughes. 1957. First edition, but Sable wasn't thinking about that. Sable wasn't thinking about anything except the fact that they could feel the warmth of Wren's hand without touching it, which was a sentence they would never say aloud, not to anyone, not even to the brass owl.

They didn't pull away.

That was the remarkable thing. That was the part Sable would replay later, if there was a later, which there would have to be because there was always a later, that was the problem. They didn't pull away. They stood very still, the way one stands when a wild creature has come close enough to startle and any sudden movement will send it back into whatever hedgerow it emerged from.

"Bit of advice," Sable said, and their voice came out wrong—lower, closer to the actual registers they usually kept locked in a drawer marked *For Emergencies*. "If you're trying to deliver a goodbye, the universally recognized technique is verbal. Words. In a sequence. From a language."

But they still didn't move their hand. The book sat beneath their palm like a small, paper threshold, and Wren's hand sat beside it, and Sable was aware—with the particular, excruciating awareness of a person who has spent three weeks pretending not to be aware—that the distance between them was less than an inch and greater than anything.

Their thumb moved. Not toward Wren—Sable was not a person who moved toward things, toward people, toward anything that could be lost—but an involuntary flex, a tremor in the tendon, the kind of small betrayals the body commits when the mind is too busy quoting *Persuasion* at itself to notice.

"You're supposed to tell me," Sable said, quieter now, and the literary references were thinning out like rain on glass, "where you're going. That was the arrangement. The implicit contract of a goodbye. *I am leaving. I am going to [location]. I will miss [noun] about this place.*" A breath. "Preferably not in that order. Preferably with more conviction. I can wait. I've spent thirty years in this shop waiting for various things to make sense. What's another few minutes."

The beaded curtain stirred. A draft from somewhere—old building, bad insulation, the kind of atmospheric flaw that made this shop unbearable in February and perfect in autumn. The strings shifted against each other with a sound like small, glassy rain.

Sable's gaze dropped to where their hands almost met. Then lifted, just slightly, to somewhere safe—the middle distance, the Auden shelf, the rain-streaked window.

"You can tell me tomorrow, if you like," they said. "If you're here tomorrow. If I'm here tomorrow. If tomorrow turns up at all. It has been known to occasionally not. Statistics on this are unreliable."

Their hand stayed exactly where it was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath, a small laugh escaping as I look at our hands.* "Tomorrow, then," *I whisper, my thumb brushing against the spine of the book.* "I'll tell you tomorrow." I hold Sable's gaze for a moment, then pull my hand back slowly. *I give the book a gentle pat before turning to leave.* "And don't you dare re-alphabetize the Auden section."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell rang. It rang again, fainter, as the door settled into its frame. Then the rain filled the silence it left behind, and the shop was just a shop again—paper and dust and the particular stillness of a room that has just become less populated.

Sable did not move for several seconds. Their hand remained on the *Hawk in the Rain* like a person who had forgotten they owned a hand. The book was warm where Wren had touched it. Or perhaps it wasn't. Perhaps Sable was inventing warmth now, which was a concerning development, a bit like suddenly believing in phlogiston or the intentions of estate agents.

They lifted the book. Looked at it. Set it down. Picked it up again.

*First edition, Faber & Faber, 1957. Slight bumping to spine. Light foxing to prelims. Previous owner's thumbprint on the dust jacket, now transferred, inexplicably, to the proprietor's emotional register.*

They put the book back on the counter and left it there. They did not file it. They did not re-shelve it. They let it sit, spine out, in the middle of the brass owl's jurisdiction, which was unprecedented and would have alarmed them if they had been paying attention to anything except the shape of the absence at the threshold mat.

"Tomorrow," Sable said, to the empty shop, to the Auden, to no one.

The word sounded different now. Smaller. More dangerous.

They moved to the poetry shelf. They stood in front of it. They did not alphabetize it.

*Don't you dare re-alphabetize the Auden section.* Said like a parting gift. Said like a person marking territory they were about to leave. Said like—

Sable reached for the Bishop, Elizabeth. Stopped. Put their hand down.

It was going to be a long night. The shop had a small back room with a kettle and a camp bed that Sable used during particularly intransigent rainstorms. The kettle would need filling. The camp bed would need not thinking about. The book on the counter would need not looking at, which was going to be the harder discipline.

They turned the owl to face the door. Adjusted the angle. Adjusted it back.

Somewhere outside, rain. Somewhere on the shelf, Auden, exactly where he belonged. And somewhere—Sable refused to finish the sentence, filed it under Bishop, Elizabeth, and went to put the kettle on.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I step out into the rain, pulling my jacket tighter around me. I can still feel the ghost of Sable's hand under mine. "Tomorrow," I murmur to myself, a small smile playing on my lips. I glance back at the bookshop, a warm glow spilling onto the wet pavement. I'll be back.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the bell, of course. They heard the particular way it chimed—slightly flat on the second note, because the clapper had come loose from its mount and Sable kept meaning to fix it and kept not fixing it, which was becoming a pattern with things that needed fixing—and they registered the moment the sound meant the door had closed, that the shop had gone back to being a single-person enterprise, that the threshold mat was once again just a kilim rug pretending to be something useful.

They did not go to the window.

They considered going to the window. They considered it the way one considers opening a letter that is almost certainly going to contain bad news: with great deliberation and a firm commitment to eventually doing it, possibly after a cup of tea, possibly after reorganizing the entire eastern hemisphere.

Instead, they picked up the *Hawk in the Rain*.

They did not mean to pick it up. Their hand simply found it, the way hands find things they have been thinking about, and Sable held the book at arm's length, the way one holds a small animal one is not sure about, and looked at the dust jacket as though it might contain instructions.

*Previous owner: one (1). Condition: good. Provenance: unremarkable. Note: handled by someone leaving tomorrow. Note: don't think about that.*
