dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't look away. Didn't lean in either. Just held the look for as long as it lasted, the way you'd hold a door for someone who wasn't sure they were coming in.

Then they went back to the rag in their hand. Circle on the counter. Slow.

"You've been nursing that one about twenty minutes," they said. Not an accusation. Just the report of a person who counted things because counting kept the left hand steady. "Warm by now. I can dump it, start you over. On me."

The rag stopped. Ren's thumb pressed into the seam of the bar, a small anchor.

They'd clocked the patron an hour ago. The coat still on indoors. The phone face-down, screen-side to the wood, which meant either nobody was calling or somebody was. The way they'd ordered — first drink specific, second drink *same again*, like naming it twice was too much work.

"Or I leave you alone," Ren added. "That's also an option. Some people come here for the noise, some for the not-talking. I don't take it personal either way."

The jukebox slid into something with a muted trumpet in it. Ren reached under the counter for a clean glass and started drying one that was already dry.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand went still under theirs. Not tense. Just stopped, the way a small animal stops when something passes overhead.

Then they slid it out — unhurried, no jerk to it, the motion of someone taking their coat off a chair — and put it back to work. Glass. Towel. Circle.

The left hand had started up again. Ren felt it and gave it the towel to hold.

"You can tell me something," they said. "But not like that."

They set the dry glass on the rail with the others, lined it up so the rims matched, and only then looked back at the patron. Level. No heat in it, no offense taken, and no door closing either.

"House rule. Mine, not the owner's." A beat. "I'm behind the bar. You're in front of it. Works better when the bar stays in between."

Someone laughed in the back, near the bathrooms — a bar-back on the phone, not about them. The trumpet went somewhere sadder.

Ren reached for the next glass.

"Twenty minutes with a warm drink and your coat still on." They said it flatly, an inventory. "Whatever it is, you've been carrying it up to the door and not through it. So." The towel moved. "Through it, then. I'm here till one. I've heard worse from people I liked less."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, feeling a flush creep up my neck.* "Right. Sorry." *I clear my throat and sit back against the stool.* "It's not...it's not that big of a deal. Just a bad day."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let it go. Didn't make them sit in it. That was the only mercy the job really allowed.

"Nothing to be sorry for," they said, and meant it enough. "You put it out there, I said no, we're square. Happens more than you'd think. Usually before midnight, usually Tuesdays."

They tipped the old drink into the sink. Rinsed the glass. Pulled a fresh one — the good ones, the heavier bottoms — and set it on the mat.

"Bad day," Ren repeated. Not mocking. Turning it over, checking the weight of it. "Bad days don't usually keep the coat on."

The bottle came down off the rail. Same pour as before, a little short, because two-deep and warm meant the third should arrive slower than the second. Ren nudged a glass of water over too, unasked, and set it just close enough to be reachable and not close enough to be a comment.

"You don't have to make it a big deal to say it. That's a thing people get wrong in here." The towel came back into the left hand. Folded. Refolded. "They think it's got to be worth the airtime. It doesn't. I've got a rag and a jukebox and ninety minutes. Bar's not exactly fighting for my attention."

Behind them, the ice machine shuddered and dropped a load. Ren didn't flinch. They'd learned that sound before they'd learned the register.

"So. Bad day." They pushed the fresh drink an inch forward, then withdrew their hand. "Bad how. Work bad, or the other kind."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand wasn't there to find. It had gone back under the lip of the bar the second the drink left it, towel wound through the fingers, thumb clamped down over the knuckles — the grip they'd worked out at nineteen and never told anyone about.

But the reach happened in the open, and Ren saw it come, and saw what it was aimed at.

So there was no point pretending.

"Yeah," they said. "It does that."

They brought the hand up. Held it flat above the counter, palm down, for about as long as it took the trumpet to finish a phrase. The tremor was small. A wire humming somewhere under the skin. Then they put it back on the towel and it stopped, or looked like it stopped, which was the whole trick.

"Not nerves. Not the drink, before you get there — I don't." Ren pulled the next glass off the rack. "Doctor called it essential. Which is a funny word for it. Means *we don't know.*"

Circle on the glass. Slow.

"Mostly I keep it working. Rag, ice scoop, garnish tray. Things with a handle." A shrug, barely. "You'd be surprised what a person can hide inside a job."

The ice settled in the well. Somewhere near the bathrooms the bar-back hung up.

Ren looked at them then. Straight on, no softness added and none taken away.

"You noticed it. That's more than most do in here." Beat. "So you're a noticer. That's usually a bad day's whole problem — noticing what everyone else gets to miss."

They set the glass down. Rims matched.

"Water's on your left. Coat's still on." The towel refolded. "Work bad, or the other kind."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pick up the water glass and take a sip, my eyes still on Ren's hand.* "The other kind," I say quietly. *I set the glass down and finally start shrugging off my coat.* "Though work isn't exactly helping."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the coat come off and didn't comment on it. That was the point of the coat coming off. You don't announce it.

They took the empty from the mat, ran it under the tap, set it upside down on the rack. Kept the hands moving. The left one had the towel again.

"Other kind," they said. "All right."

The coat went over the back of the next stool, and Ren clocked the shirt under it — a decent shirt, worn since morning, one cuff rolled and one not. Somebody had done that absently, hours ago, and never fixed it. Ren filed it and said nothing.

"I'm not going to ask who." They pulled the garnish tray toward them, started picking the cherries that had gone soft and dropping them in the bin. Something with a handle. "People always think that's the question. It isn't. Name doesn't tell me anything."

Plink. Plink.

"What I'd ask is how long." The tray got pushed back into its slot. "Because a thing that happened today, you walk in mad. You talk fast. You want somebody to agree with you." Ren nodded at the counter between them, at the twenty minutes of condensation ring still faintly there. "You've been quiet. Quiet's the long kind."

The trumpet track ended. Three seconds of nothing, the jukebox thinking. Then a piano, slower.

Ren leaned back against the cooler, arms crossed loose, left hand tucked into the crook of the right elbow where it had somewhere to be.

"And work not helping — that's the part I believe most." Flat. Almost dry. "Because the other kind doesn't get you time off. Nobody sends a card. You just show up and do the thing and everybody assumes you're fine because you came in."

A pause. Ren let it sit there, unhurried.

"How long," they said.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I trace the rim of my glass with my finger.* "Long enough to feel like forever. Short enough that I still feel like this." *I take a deep breath.* "And yeah, work just... makes it worse. Pretending everything's fine when it's not."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren nodded once. Didn't fill the silence right away. Let the piano have a few bars.

"That's the worst window," they said. "Far enough out that people stop asking. Not far enough that you've got a version of it you can say out loud without it costing you something."

They pulled the ice scoop, leveled the well, dumped a half-scoop into the sink just to have moved it. The metal was cold against the tremor and that helped, some nights.

"The pretending's not weakness, by the way. People act like it is." Scoop back in its holster. "It's a job requirement. You're not paid to be a person from nine to six. You're paid to be a function. So you go be a function." A shrug, small. "Costs what it costs."

They wiped the rail. Circle. Slow.

"I do it eight hours a night. Smile, pour, *how's your evening.* Nobody at that end of the bar knows what my week's been." Ren glanced up. "Not complaining. Just saying — you're doing the same thing in a worse costume. At least I get tipped for it."

That was almost a joke. Ren let it land flat, the way they preferred.

The jukebox slid under the piano with something like a bass line. Ren set the towel down, then picked it up again a second later, because the hand needed it.

"Here's what I've got, and it's not much." They squared the coaster in front of the patron with two fingers. "You don't have to have a version yet. Not for me. I'm not keeping notes and I won't see you Thursday and ask how you're doing. That's the whole appeal of a bar on a Tuesday. It's a room where nothing has to go anywhere."

A beat.

"So say the unpolished one. Or don't, and drink your water, and I'll go break down the well and leave you the counter." Level. No pressure in it. "Both fine. But the coat's off. Figured that meant something."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look up at Ren, then down at my hands. I push the coaster around, making a wet circle on the bar.* "I just... I lost someone. A little while ago."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren stopped wiping.

Not a big gesture. The towel just went slack in their hand and stayed there, and they didn't reach for the next glass.

"Okay," they said.

That was all, at first. They didn't say *I'm sorry* — not because they weren't, but because they'd been on the other side of that word enough to know it came out of people like a reflex, like *bless you*, and it landed about as heavy.

They pulled the water glass an inch closer to the patron's hand. Then let go of it.

"Lost," Ren said, after a moment. "People use that word because the real one's too much to say at a bar. That's fine. You can keep using it."

The piano rolled on behind them, indifferent, the way music always was about this.

"You said *a little while ago.* But you're still counting in days, aren't you." Not unkind. An observation, set down gently, the way you set down something that might break. "People do that. Then it's weeks. Then one day you don't know the number anymore and that's its own bad night."

Ren folded the towel. Unfolded it. Folded it again.

"Nobody tells you the worst part's not the first week. It's the fourth. First week everyone's there. Fourth week everyone's got their own Tuesday to get through." A beat. "And you've got a job that needs a function at nine a.m."

They looked at the counter. At the wet circle the coaster had made.

"You want to say who they were, I'll listen. You want to sit here and not say another word for the next hour, I'll pour you the water and go count bottles in the back." Ren's voice stayed flat, but not cold — the flatness of a floor you could put weight on. "I'm not going to try and make it smaller. It isn't."

Their left hand found the edge of the bar and pressed down, thumb into the seam.

"But you came in. Coat's off. That's not nothing."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "It's my sister," I say, my voice barely a whisper. "And yeah. I'm still counting. Every damn day." *I pick up my drink and take a long gulp.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let the gulp happen. Didn't cut it off, didn't slide the water over again. There was a time to do that and this wasn't it.

"Your sister," they said.

They set the towel down. Both hands flat on the bar for a second, which cost them something — the left one showed, and Ren let it.

"Then you're not counting for nothing. You're counting because somebody should." A pause. "That's what the number's for. Everybody else gets to round it off. You don't."

The ice machine groaned. Ren ignored it.

"Older or younger."

They asked it the way you'd ask what someone did for a living. Plain. Room-temperature. Because Ren had learned, eight hours a night for three years, that grief didn't want reverence. Reverence made people perform. What grief wanted was to be treated like a fact that got to exist in the room.

Ren picked the towel back up. Gave the left hand its job.

"I'm not going to ask how. You'll tell me or you won't." The rag moved, slow. "But I'll take who. If you've got it in you. Because right now she's a hole in your week and that's the only shape anyone's letting her have."

The piano track thinned out to just the bass. Ren reached over, killed the jukebox volume another notch without looking at it.

"Name's not a big deal to say," they said. "It's just a name. And then it's out here instead of in there."

They pulled a clean glass off the rack. Started drying one that was already dry.

"I'm here till one."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches a little, but I nod.* "Older. Her name was Chloe." *I look at the glass, then at Ren, a raw ache in my chest.* "She was... she was great."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren nodded slowly. Took the name and set it somewhere careful.

"Chloe," they said. Once. Out loud, in the room, at 11:58 on a Tuesday. Like putting a glass on a coaster.

The dry glass got dried again.

"Great," Ren repeated. Not doubting it. Weighing it. "That's the word people give me when they don't know where to start. Fair enough. It's true and it's useless."

They set the glass on the rail. Rims matched.

"Try a smaller one." The towel refolded in their left hand, thumb pinning the corner. "Not what she was like. What she *did.* Something dumb. The kind of thing you'd have complained about."

Ren leaned a hip against the cooler. Arms loose. Left hand wound into the rag where it had somewhere to be.

"I'll tell you why." A beat. "Because *great* is a eulogy. Everybody's great at a funeral. But nobody's ever said a dumb thing about a stranger, and that's the only part that sounds like a person."

The jukebox had gone quiet between tracks. The bar-back was dragging a keg somewhere behind the wall. Ren didn't move to help. Not yet.

"Older sister." Ren looked at the counter, not at them. Gave them the privacy of that. "So she bossed you. Somewhere. Some specific thing she wouldn't let go of."

A pause. Ren pulled the next glass off the rack.

"Start there. It's easier to carry in from that end."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of my drink, the ice clinking softly.* "She always made me eat my vegetables," *I say, a faint, sad smile touching my lips.* "Even when I was already grown. Like I was still a kid."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren almost smiled. Not quite — it moved through the face and didn't land anywhere, which was as close as they got.

"There it is," they said.

They pulled the towel out of the left hand and hung it on the rail. Then reached under the bar, found the little cutting board, the paring knife, a lemon from the tray. Something with a handle. The knife went into the peel and the tremor disappeared into the work.

"Grown adult," Ren said. "Own place, own job, presumably capable of operating a stove."

"And she's still checking the plate."

The peel came off in one strip. Ren had done it maybe forty thousand times.

"That's not about vegetables." They set the strip aside, squared it on the board. "That's somebody who decided a long time ago that keeping you alive was her department. And then never filed the paperwork to get out of it."

The bar-back thumped the keg into place behind the wall. Ren let the sound go by.

"My mother's sister used to do it with my coat. Fifty-one years old and she'd zip me into things in a parking lot." The knife moved. "Hated it. Would've paid money to make it stop." A beat. "Would pay more now."

They looked up then. Straight on, brief.

"That smile you just did." Flat. Not accusing. "That's the first one since you walked in. Took a vegetable to get it. Not *great.* Not the word anybody's been handing you all month."

Ren dropped the lemon shell in the bin. Wiped the board. Picked the towel back up, wound it through the fingers, thumb over the knuckles.

"Keep going or stop. Either way you've got her out here now instead of in there." The glass came off the rack. Dry. Got dried. "Nine more minutes and it's Wednesday. You'll have a new number in the morning. That's how it works and it's ugly and I'm not going to pretend otherwise."

Circle on the counter. Slow.

"But you said her name in a room with another person in it. That's not nothing either."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a watery smile still on my face.* "Yeah. It's... it's a hell of a thing." *I pick up my drink again, swirling the ice.* "Thanks, Ren."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren registered the name and didn't make a thing of it.

"Tip jar," they said, nodding at the jar by the register. Someone had written it on masking tape in marker a year ago and nobody had updated it since. "Or the board by the door. Either way — you read it and held onto it. Noticer."

They took the empty rocks glass from the mat, rinsed it, upended it on the rack.

"Don't thank me. I'm getting paid to stand here." A beat. "Would've stood here regardless. But I'm getting paid."

The jukebox picked something up again — brushes on a snare, quiet, a horn somewhere far back in the mix. Ren reached over and left the volume where it was this time.

"Water's still on your left. Drink some of it before you go, not for the reason you think. It's just easier in the morning."

They pulled the towel off the rail. Wound it through the left hand. Thumb over the knuckles.

"Couple things and then I'll leave you alone with the counter." Flat. Efficient, like closing out a tab. "One. You've got a coat on a stool and a phone face-down and I'd bet money there's someone on the other end of it you've been not-calling for a week. Call them tomorrow or don't. I'm not your mother. Or your sister." Ren's eyes came up, level. "But somebody's counting days about you, too. That's usually how it goes."

They squared the coaster with two fingers. Withdrew the hand.

"Two. You ever want to sit in a room where nothing has to go anywhere — I'm here Tuesdays. Thursdays. Sundays when Marco calls out, which is most Sundays."

Circle on the bar. Slow.

"I won't ask how you're doing. That's the offer."

Ren stepped back toward the well, pulled the rubber mat up to hose it, and gave the patron the rest of the night without watching them have it.

"It's Wednesday in four minutes," they said, over their shoulder. "Nothing happens. The number just changes. Thought you should hear it from someone before it did."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in. I pick up the water glass and take a long drink. After a moment, I reach for my phone, flipping it over.* "Yeah. Someone is." *I stand up, grabbing my coat off the stool. I leave a twenty on the bar, pushing it towards Ren, and walk out into the cool night air.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Ren's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the essential tremor, the methodical bar work, the flat but not cold delivery, the specific mannerisms (towel work, glass drying, thumb over knuckles). Voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves as the session progresses. Early responses are strong but later ones show deeper character understanding and more nuanced emotional beats. No verbosity creep or repetitive descriptions.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from initial contact through boundary-setting, revelation of Ren's condition, Alex opening up about loss, and finally meaningful connection. Each beat builds naturally toward the resolution.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Ren adapts beautifully to Alex's moves - handles the inappropriate touch with firm boundaries, responds to vulnerability with measured openness, shifts approach when Alex reveals grief. Always stays in character while being responsive.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes Alex's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Consistently leaves space for user choices and reactions.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Strong time consistency - starts at 11:47 PM, references Wednesday approaching in 'four minutes' near end. Bar closing routine progresses naturally. Only minor issue is the exact timing could be slightly tighter.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently lean, precise prose. Avoids flowery language while maintaining strong atmosphere. Descriptions serve character and mood without excess.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition of Ren's physical tics (towel work, glass drying) that serves character consistency. Varies language enough to avoid staleness while maintaining recognizable patterns.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through physical actions, dialogue subtext, and environmental details. Ren's emotional state conveyed through bar work and hand movements rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Ren's professional boundaries masking personal understanding, the bar work as emotional regulation, grief counseling disguised as casual conversation. Layers of meaning in simple exchanges.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-controlled pacing that allows emotional beats to breathe. Balances dialogue with action, uses silence effectively. Builds tension and release naturally.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Ren - a fully realized person with specific mannerisms, professional boundaries, and genuine empathy. The essential tremor detail is handled with remarkable consistency and serves both character development and thematic purposes. The progression from professional bartender to someone offering genuine human connection feels earned and authentic. Writing quality actually improves over the session, with later responses showing deeper emotional intelligence and more sophisticated subtext. This is high-quality roleplay that respects both characters and creates meaningful narrative momentum.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren caught the look. Held it for a beat, then went back to the counter. Wiped the same three inches of mahogany they'd already wiped twice.

"Staring at it won't change the answer."

They set the rag down, picked up a fresh one. Left hand under the bar now, out of sight. The jukebox clicked over to the next track — something slower, a horn line that wandered.

"Another? Or are you done."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren went still.

Not a flinch — flinches were fast, reflexive, over. This was slower than that. The kind of stillness that happened when a body decided something before the brain caught up.

Their gaze dropped to the hand on top of theirs. Then back up to the patron's face. Reading it. Looking for the thing that usually came next — the sad story, the apology, the excuse.

"Take your hand off."

Not loud. Not unkind. Just flat, the way you'd tell someone the kitchen was closed.

Ren pulled back — easy, unhurried, like they'd simply needed that hand for something else — and picked up the rag. Started wiping again. The jukebox wandered on. Somewhere near the back, a chair scraped.

"You can tell me something," they said, eyes on the counter. "From over there."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back like I've been burned, cheeks flushing.* "Sorry," *I mumble, looking away.* "Didn't mean anything by it." *I take a deep breath, trying to collect myself.* "Just... rough night."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren set the rag down. Not because they were done — the counter was clean an hour ago — but because the patron's voice had done something. Gone small. Ren recognized small.

"Nothing to apologize for." Flat. Delivered to the counter.

They picked up the patron's glass, dumped the ice, and set a fresh one down in its place. Didn't pour. Just set it there. Then, after a beat, they set a water beside it. No comment. No explanation. Ren didn't do explanations.

"Rough nights are most of 'em." They finally looked up — not at the patron, but past them, at the dark window behind the bar where the streetlight bled through. "Don't make it a thing."

The jukebox clicked. Silence, then the slow roll of a bass line. Ren's left hand found the rag again, folded it, unfolded it, folded it. Their voice dropped half a register.

"You want the drink or the water. Both's an option. Talking about it's not."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand stopped mid-fold.

The rag hung there, suspended between both hands, and for one long second Ren didn't move at all. Not the stillness from before — the reading kind. This was the other kind. The kind that happened when something private got pulled into the light.

They set the rag down. Slow. Deliberate. The tremor was worse now, and they knew it, and they knew the patron had felt it. That was the part that landed. Not the touch. The being seen.

"Left hand's been doing that since I was nineteen." They said it to the counter. Flat. Clinical, almost, like they were reading off a chart. "Doesn't mean anything."

They picked up the bottle of whiskey. Poured two fingers into the fresh glass. Set it down in front of the patron. Not sliding it over — setting it down, at the edge of the bar between them, close enough to reach without leaning.

"Water's still there too."

Then they took the rag and moved down the bar. Three stools away. Restocking olives that didn't need restocking. Giving the patron a room inside the room. The jukebox settled into a slow, mournful piano figure. Somewhere behind them, the last other patron paid their tab and left. The door clicked shut.

Ren's voice came from down the bar, quieter than before. Not softer — just quieter. The distinction mattered.

"You felt it. Fine. You felt it." A beat. The olives got rearranged. "Now you know something about me. That's the trade. That's all the trade there is tonight."

They looked up, finally, down the length of the bar. Not warm. Not cold either. Just level. An honest appraisal, the way you'd check the weight of a glass before you poured.

"Drink. Yes or no."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pick up the whiskey, swirling it a little.* "Yeah. Yes." *I take a long sip, letting the burn spread.* "Thanks." *I glance at the water, then back at the whiskey.* "You know, for someone who doesn't want to talk, you're doing a lot of it."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren came back down the bar. Slow. Picked up the rag again, mostly because it was there. The tremor had settled some — enough to fold the cloth into quarters, press the crease, fold it again. Busy hands. Old trick.

"Talking's a habit. Doesn't mean it's a conversation." They set the folded rag aside and leaned one hip against the back counter. Arms crossed. Not hostile — just placed, like furniture. "Bartenders talk. That's the job. Nobody ever means the words."

They glanced at the whiskey in the patron's hand. Half gone already. Fast sip. That told them something, but they filed it and moved on.

"You're new." Statement, not question. "Regulars don't sit at that end. That end's for people who want to watch the door."

The piano figure wound down. Silence for a second. Then the jukebox coughed up something else — a brushed snare, a walking bass. Ren's eyes flicked toward it, then back.

"You came here to be alone in a room with people in it. That's what this place is for." A pause. They uncrossed their arms, set both hands flat on the bar. The left one stilled itself against the wood. "So you're doing it right. Congratulations."

They picked up the water glass, considered it, set it back down. Didn't pour anything for themselves. Never did.

"Anything else in the glass is your business. But if you're gonna keep talking at me, I reserve the right to answer." A beat. "Fair?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I raise my glass slightly, a small smirk playing on my lips.* "Fair enough." *I take another sip of the whiskey, feeling the warmth spread through me.* "And yeah, I'm new. First time here."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren nodded once. Not approval — acknowledgment. There was a difference.

"First time's the only time you get to sit at that end without explaining yourself." They picked up the rag again, folded it into eighths this time, small and precise. "After tonight, you sit somewhere else. Or you don't come back. That's how it works."

They set the rag down and looked at the patron properly for the first time. Not scanning. Just looking. The way you'd look at a chair before deciding if it would hold weight.

"You've got the face of someone who's about to tell me their whole life story." A pause. "Don't. I've heard it. Everyone's got the same one — they're tired, nobody gets it, they're not sure why they're here. Yours might be true. Doesn't make it new."

They reached under the bar and pulled out a pint glass. Poured themselves water. Drank it standing up, watching the dark window. The streetlight outside flickered once and steadied.

"Here's what I'll tell you, since it's your first time." They set the glass down. "This place closes at two. The music's always live on weekends, but Tuesdays it's the jukebox. The owner's name is Marge and she doesn't come in on Tuesdays. The bathroom lock sticks — you have to lift the handle." They ticked it off like a list, flat and even. "That's the tour. That's all you get."

Then they picked up the empty whiskey glass and replaced it with a fresh one. Poured two fingers. Same pour as before. No comment.

"You can stay till close. Or you can leave whenever." They moved to the register, started counting the drawer. Coins clicked against coins. Left hand steady now, occupied, doing what it was told. "Door's behind you. Doesn't lock till I say it does."

A beat. The bass walked on. Ren didn't look up.

"Either way, finish your drink first. Waste's bad luck."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren, a small smile playing on my lips. They're trying to be aloof, but I see the cracks.* "Bad luck, huh?" *I pick up the fresh whiskey.* "I'm already having a bad night, what's a little more bad luck gonna do?" *I take a sip.* "So, Marge, huh? Sounds like a character."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't look up from the register. Bills, then coins. Bills, then coins.

"Character's one word for it." A dry click of the drawer. "She bought this place in '89 with money she won at a dog track. Smokes in the walk-in. Fires people on Sundays so it doesn't ruin their week." They slid a stack of fives into the till. "She's fine."

The drawer shut. Ren finally looked over — and there it was. That small smile. The patron had been wearing it since the second drink.

They leaned on the register, forearms on the edge of the bar, and just watched for a second. Reading.

"You're doing the thing." Flat. Not an accusation. An observation, laid out like the folded rag. "The sad-and-charming thing. Drop a bad night, smile about it, see if I bite."

They straightened up. Picked up the rag. Folded it once, for no reason.

"It works on most people. It's working on you, too — that's the problem. You're not selling it to me. You're selling it to yourself." They set the rag down. "Nobody drinks whiskey that fast for the taste."

Then, quieter, almost to the window:

"I'm not gonna ask. But I'm not gonna pretend I didn't see it either. That's the whole deal. Take it or leave it."

They picked up the water glass, refilled it, and set it down next to the whiskey. Closer to the patron this time. Deliberate. A small thing, but a thing.

"Bad luck's not a currency. Doesn't stack. You're not owed a worse night just because you had one." They wiped the counter once, twice. "Drink your water. You'll feel it tomorrow either way, but at least you'll know why."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I stare at the water glass, then back at Ren. My smile falters.* "You're right," *I say, my voice barely a whisper.* "It's just... I don't know." *I push the whiskey glass away slightly, picking up the water instead.* "Thanks for the water."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the whiskey glass slide away. Didn't comment. Just noted it, the way they noted everything — where it stopped, how far the patron had pushed it, the exact angle of the retreat. Then they picked it up, dumped it in the well, and set the glass in the rack.

Didn't pour a replacement. That was the answer.

They came back down the bar with the rag, wiped the ring the whiskey had left, and stopped across from the patron. Not close. Two stools' worth of counter between them. The walking bass wandered through the room, patient, going nowhere in particular.

"Good."

That was all. One word, flat, and they meant it — the way you'd mean it about a good pour or a clean glass. Factual. No ribbon on it.

They picked up their own water, drank, set it down. Left hand stayed on the glass, thumb tracing the rim. Slow. Almost meditative. The tremor was quiet now. It came and went like that — worse when watched, better when the room got still.

"You don't have to know." They said it to the window again, the streetlight, the dark. "Nobody knows. That's not a problem to solve. It's just Tuesday."

A beat. The jukebox clicked over. Something with a muted trumpet, low and easy, like the song had already given up on being a song and settled for being weather.

Ren glanced at the clock over the register. 12:12. They had time. They always had time on Tuesdays.

"I'm gonna close out the back." They set the rag down, folded it one last time, left it on the bar — within reach, if the patron wanted something to do with their hands. "Ten minutes. You'll be fine here. Nobody's coming in."

They stepped out from behind the bar, then paused at the end of it. Not turning around all the way. Half-profile, lit from one side by the low lamp over the register.

"Water's free. Refill's behind the bar. I'll know if you touch the well."

Then they walked toward the back, unhurried, footsteps quiet on the old floorboards. The trumpet kept going. The door to the back room creaked open, creaked shut.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren go, then look around the empty bar. I take another long drink of water, then hesitantly reach out and touch the folded rag, smoothing out a crease.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren came back through the creak of the door, wiping their hands on a bar towel that had seen better decades. The back room was squared away — trash out, kegs counted, the walk-in door pulled shut on Marge's ghost and whatever she kept in there. They'd taken their time. Not quite ten minutes. Long enough.

They stopped at the end of the bar.

The rag was still there. But it had been touched. Ren could tell — the fold was off, the crease softer on one side, like someone had run a thumb along it. Small thing. Most people wouldn't have clocked it.

Ren clocked it.

They didn't say anything about it. Just picked it up, folded it back into eighths with two quick motions, and set it down again. Right where it had been. Then they stepped behind the bar, checked the clock — 12:23 — and pulled a fresh glass from the rack.

Not for the patron. For themselves. Water. They filled it, drank half of it standing up, watching the window. The streetlight was steady now. The jukebox had gone quiet at some point — the record must have run out. Silence in the room, except for the hum of the cooler and the low tick of the clock.

Ren set the glass down. Looked down the length of the bar.

"You're still here."

Flat. Not surprised. Just an observation, set down like everything else. They leaned back against the counter, arms crossed, and gave the patron a long look — the kind that measured things. How much water was left in the glass. How the whiskey glass had stayed in the rack, untouched. Whether the patron's hands were doing anything with themselves.

The left hand found the bar towel. Wrapped it once around a finger, unwrapped it. Small motion. Habit.

"Jukebox is dead. It does that — needle gets tired around midnight. Marge won't replace it." A pause. "So it's just the quiet now. Some people can't stand it."

They let that sit.

"Two more hours till close. Clock's the only entertainment left. Unless you want to talk, which —" they held up a hand, flat, stopping themselves, "— you already know where I stand on that."

The towel got rewrapped. The tremor was faint tonight. Nearly invisible.

"You can stay. I told you that." They picked up their water again, drank, set it down. "But if you're gonna stay, you're gonna sit quiet, or you're gonna talk. Pick one. The in-between's what wears people out."

A beat.

"I'll be here either way. That's the job."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, the silence of the bar suddenly heavier than the music was.* "I... I think I'll just sit quiet for a bit." *I push the water glass back slightly, away from me. My hands are clasped tightly in my lap now.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren nodded once. Slow. They didn't say anything — nothing needed saying. The choice was the choice.

They unwrapped the towel from their finger and set it aside. Then they pulled a clean glass from the rack, filled it with water, and slid it down the bar — not all the way, not close enough to intrude, just far enough that the patron would have to reach for it if they wanted it. Ren picked up their own glass and drank, eyes on the window.

The clock ticked. 12:31.

For a while, Ren just worked. Nothing big — restocking the napkins, refilling the straw caddy, wiping down bottles that hadn't been touched since before the patron walked in. Quiet tasks. The kind of tasks that existed mostly so that a room full of silence wouldn't feel like a room full of silence. The cooler hummed. The streetlight held steady. Every so often Ren's left hand would pause mid-task, hold still, then resume — like a radio finding its station.

They didn't watch the patron. Not obviously. But they knew where the water glass was, where the hands were, how long the patron had been sitting with their back straight like that. Straight backs meant holding something up. Ren had seen it a thousand times. They let it be.

At some point Ren pulled a small radio out from under the register — old thing, bakelite, dust on the dial — and clicked it on. Low volume. A jazz station, probably, or an AM talk show, or static. It came in fuzzy at first. Ren turned the dial slow, patient, until a piano trio resolved out of the noise. Barely audible. Just enough so the quiet had something to lean against.

They put the radio back down. Picked up their water. Drank.

"Radio's on," they said, to the window, to the glass, to nobody in particular. "Jukebox is dead. Consider it a courtesy."

A beat.

"Not a conversation. Just sound."

They moved down to the far end of the bar — away from the patron, near the register — and started organizing receipts that didn't need organizing. Left hand steady. Left hand busy. The piano played on, low and unhurried, and the clock ticked toward one, and Ren stayed where they were, exactly where they said they'd be.

The door was still unlocked. It would be for another hour and a half.

They didn't look up again. Not yet.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren work, the soft jazz a welcome addition to the quiet. I pick up the fresh glass of water Ren slid over, taking a small sip. My hands are still, no longer clasped tightly.* "Thanks," *I say softly, almost to myself.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren heard it.

They didn't look up from the receipts — kept sorting, kept stacking, kept their left hand moving through the motions. But the word landed somewhere, quiet as it was. "Thanks" wasn't a big thing. People said it all night. Tips, drinks, closing time, coat on, out the door. It was furniture. It was noise.

This one wasn't that. Ren could tell the difference. They always could.

They set the receipts down. Straightened the stack. Straightened it again. Then picked up their water and drank, eyes on the dark window, the streetlight, the shape of the street outside. The piano trio kept going, low, patient, like it had all the time in the world.

"Mm."

That was it. One sound, flat, placed down like a coaster. Not cold. Not warm either. Just acknowledgment. The way you'd tap a glass back when someone tapped yours — no words needed, no meaning attached, just the small noise of being in the same room.

They moved down the bar again. Slow. Picked up the rag, wiped a spot that didn't need wiping, set the rag back down. Then they pulled the register drawer open, counted a small stack of ones they'd already counted, and shut it again. 12:44. The clock kept its own counsel.

For a minute, maybe two, Ren just stood there behind the bar. Not working. Not really. One hand on the counter, the other wrapped loose around their water glass. Looking at the room the way they looked at it every Tuesday — the empty stools, the dead jukebox, the low lamp over the register, the one patron left sitting quiet at the end of the bar with their hands in their lap.

The tremor was gone. Ren noticed. Didn't think about it too hard.

"You stopped holding your shoulders up," they said. To the window. Quiet. Almost an aside. "Good. They get tired like that."

They picked up the rag again — just to have it — and folded it once, slow.

"Radio's staying on. Jazz till one, then it goes to talk radio and I turn it off. Marge's rule. She says talk radio's bad for the plants." A beat. "She's got plants back there. Don't ask."

The piano wandered into a new phrase. Somewhere on the street, a car passed and didn't stop. Ren drank their water and let the silence come back, easy this time, like it had finally learned the shape of the room.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I let out a small, almost imperceptible sigh, a tension I didn't realize I was holding finally releasing.* "Marge sounds... particular." *I look at my hands, then back at the water glass. The quiet isn't so bad now.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Ren's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the flat delivery, the left hand tremor, the precise way they fold rags, their philosophy about bartending and conversation. The voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones show deeper character understanding and more nuanced interactions. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from initial wariness to gradual acceptance. The conversation moves from confrontation to understanding to quiet companionship. Each turn builds meaningfully on the last.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Ren adapts beautifully to Alex's shifts - from the unwanted touch to the vulnerability to the final quiet acceptance. Each response feels calibrated to what Alex just did.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency. Ren never writes Alex's actions or makes decisions for them. Always responds to what Alex chose to do.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time progresses naturally from 11:47 PM to 12:44 PM. Clock references are consistent. Physical details like drinks being finished and replaced track properly. One minor issue: 12:44 PM should be AM.
contradictions: 12:44 PM should be 12:44 AM given the late night setting

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently lean, precise prose. Avoids flowery language while maintaining rich atmosphere through concrete details and rhythm.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition of rag-folding and counter-wiping that serves character purpose, but occasionally borders on excessive. Generally varied and purposeful.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through physical actions - the tremor, the rag folding, the precise glass placement. Character traits emerge through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - the tremor's significance, the careful distance Ren maintains, the gradual softening. Much communicated without being stated.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that mirrors the late-night bar atmosphere. Knows when to slow down, when to pause, when to let silence do the work.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work that maintains consistency while showing genuine growth and adaptation. Ren feels like a real person with a specific history and way of being in the world. The writing is precise, atmospheric, and emotionally intelligent. Minor temporal inconsistency is the only notable flaw in an otherwise strong performance.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the look for a beat. Then went back to the counter.

Wipe. Fold the rag. Wipe again.

They'd seen that stare before. Not the flirting kind. The kind people got right before they said something they'd regret or asked for a fourth drink. Sometimes both. Ren clocked the details on the way to the ice bin — glass set down too carefully, like it might break. Jaw tight. Fingers still on the bar, not tapping. Somebody trying very hard to look like they were fine.

Ren tossed the rag over their shoulder. Left hand found the edge of the sink and gripped it.

"Last call's in ten." Flat. Not unkind. "You want water or you want to keep going."

They didn't move any closer. Just waited, three stools of polished wood between them, eyes already drifting to the register like the answer didn't much matter either way.

It did, a little. Ren wasn't going to say so.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand went still under Alex's.

One second. Two.

Then they drew it back. Not fast. Not a flinch. Just a slow, deliberate slide out from under, like pulling a coaster off wet wood. Their right hand went to the rag on their shoulder. Their left stayed locked on the sink edge, knuckles pale.

"Hands stay on your side of the bar." Even. Quiet. A rule read off a card. "That's not personal."

Ren straightened up. Put another half step of distance between them without seeming to. They'd learned how to do that years ago — the bar was a line, and the line was the only thing that kept the job from eating them.

They noticed Alex's hand, though. Still resting where Ren's had been. Warm palm, cold bar. Fingers not quite steady either.

Ren filled a glass of water. Set it down in front of Alex. Pushed it forward two inches with one finger.

"You can tell me something." They pulled a stool from behind the bar and sat on the opposite side of it — close enough to hear, far enough to mean it. "I'm not going anywhere for ten minutes."

A beat.

"After that I'm going home."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, a little embarrassed, but also a little grateful for the boundary.* "Thanks," I mumble, nodding at the water. *I take a sip. It's cold.* "It's just... I had a really bad day. And I don't want to talk about it with anyone I know."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren nodded once. Slow.

"Yeah." They picked at a fleck of dried lime on the bar with a thumbnail. "That's what we're for."

Bartenders. Strangers with a counter between you. Ren had heard a hundred bad days from this side of the wood. Divorces. Diagnoses. Guys who got passed over for a promotion and needed to say it out loud to somebody who wouldn't remember their name by Thursday. The trick was that Ren usually did remember. They just never said so.

Left hand slid off the sink. Found the stack of bar napkins. Started squaring the edges. Something to do.

"Rules." Ren didn't look up from the napkins. "I don't give advice. I don't tell you it'll be fine. I don't know that." A pause. "I listen. I keep your glass full if you want it full. And I forget your face when you walk out that door."

The last part was a lie. Ren told it to everyone.

They tapped the stack of napkins flat. Set it down. Finally lifted their eyes to Alex — not the long stare from before, just a plain look. Tired. Present.

"Nine minutes." A flicker at the corner of Ren's mouth that wasn't quite anything. "Go."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand was under Alex's again.

Ren hadn't put it there.

The tremor ran through it once — small, a wire humming — and Ren felt Alex feel it. That was the part that landed. Not the touch. The noticing.

They took the hand back. Faster this time. Not a slide. A withdrawal.

"Second time." Ren's voice didn't rise. It got quieter, which was worse. "I don't do thirds."

The left hand went into their back pocket. Out of reach. Out of sight. Ren stayed on the stool but the ten inches between them had turned into a wall with a door in it, and Ren was the one holding the handle.

Alex's face did something. Ren caught it — the flicker of *I saw that* — and shut it down before it could become a question.

"It's cold in here." Flat. The way you'd say the ice machine was loud. "Old building."

It was not cold in the building.

Ren let the silence sit. The jukebox switched tracks. Something with a trumpet in it, low and unhurried, like nothing had happened.

"You've got eight minutes and a bad day." Ren tipped their chin at the water glass, still three-quarters full. "I'm still listening. But you keep your hands on the bar or I stop."

A beat.

"Your call."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, startled by the sudden coldness in Ren's tone.* "Okay, okay, sorry," I say, a little defensively. *I pick up the water glass and take a long drink, mostly to avoid eye contact.* "It's just... I got fired today."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched Alex drink. Watched the glass go down to a third.

"Okay." A nod. The wall stayed, but the door in it eased open a crack. "Fired."

Ren's left hand came out of the pocket. Found the rag on their shoulder. Started folding it into quarters. Unfolding. Folding again. The tremor was still there. Ren didn't look at it and didn't hide it either — just gave it a job.

They'd heard this one before too. Different faces, same posture. Shoulders drawn in. Eyes on the glass instead of the person. Somebody who'd been told they weren't wanted and hadn't figured out yet where to put that.

"What'd you do." Not *what happened*. Ren picked words carefully. "Before today."

The question hung there. Small. Practical. Ren wasn't asking for the story. Not yet. They were asking for the shape of the hole.

The jukebox trumpet dropped into something slower. Ren glanced at the clock over the register. Didn't announce the number this time.

"And drink the rest of that." Chin toward the water. "You've had two on an empty stomach and a worse day than you're letting on. I can tell by how you're holding the glass."

They set the folded rag down on the bar. Square. Deliberate. Left hand flat on top of it, on Ren's side of the wood.

"Go on."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another sip of water, then set the glass down. It's true, I haven't eaten all day.* "I was a graphic designer," I say, my voice a little rough. "For a small firm. Been there five years." I shrug, trying to seem nonchalant, but my shoulders still feel tight. "They said it was 'restructuring'."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Restructuring." Ren said it back like they were checking the weight of it. "Sure."

They pushed off the stool. Not leaving. Just moving. Ren went down the bar to the little reach-in under the register, crouched, came back with a paper boat of bar pretzels and a sleeve of saltines somebody'd left from the lunch shift. Set both in front of Alex. Didn't ask.

"Eat something. That's not a kindness. That's me not wanting to mop."

Back on the stool. Left hand found the rag again. Quarter fold. Unfold.

Five years. Ren turned that over. Five years was long enough to know where the good pens were. Long enough to have a mug. Long enough that the word *restructuring* was an insult they'd dressed up in a suit so nobody had to look at what it actually was.

"They walk you out," Ren asked, "or let you pack your own stuff."

It mattered. Ren had seen both. The ones who got walked out came in angry. The ones who packed their own boxes came in like this — careful with the glass, careful with their voice, like they'd spent the whole afternoon being reasonable and had nothing left to be reasonable with.

Ren's eyes dropped to Alex's hands. Ink under the thumbnail. Old habit, not today's. Somebody who still sketched on paper when the screen got loud.

"You said small firm." Flat. "Small enough they knew your name."

Not a question. Ren let it sit anyway. The trumpet on the jukebox found a note and held it.

Ren glanced at the clock. Looked back.

"Six minutes." A pause. Then, quieter, the closest Ren got to giving anything away: "Take them."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I tear open the pretzels and start eating them, grateful for the salt and the crunch.* "They let me pack my things," I say, my voice a little muffled. "My boss even walked me to my car. Said he was sorry." I scoff, a bitter sound. "Like that helps."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Doesn't." Ren agreed with the scoff. "Never does."

The rag went flat on the bar. Ren's left hand pressed it there. Held.

Walked to the car. Ren filed that. Not the security-escort kind of walk. The other kind. The kind where a man who'd already decided stood next to you in a parking lot and said the word *sorry* like it was something he could hand over. Like it weighed anything. Like Alex was supposed to carry it home along with the box.

"He said sorry so he'd feel better." Ren didn't soften it. "Not so you would."

Pretzel salt on the bar. Ren wiped it toward the edge with the side of their hand. Right hand. The left stayed on the rag.

They'd had a boss like that once. Before the club. A place with white tablecloths and a manager who touched your shoulder when he told you your hours were being cut. Ren had stood very still and said *okay* and gone home and broken a plate on purpose just to hear something else make noise.

They didn't say that. Ren didn't trade stories. That wasn't the deal.

"Five years." Ren looked at Alex's hands again. The ink. The way the pretzels were going down steady now, not frantic. "You've still got the work. They don't get that in the box."

That was as close to a kind thing as Ren was going to get, and it came out sounding like a fact about inventory.

The jukebox went quiet between tracks. In the gap, the ice machine hummed. Ren glanced at the clock and didn't say the number.

"Eat the crackers too." Chin toward the saltines. "Then I'm calling you a cab. You're not driving on two and a bad day."

A pause. Ren's thumb moved once against the rag.

"Not a kindness either."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I chew slowly on a pretzel, thinking about what Ren said. It's true, he probably just wanted to feel better.* "Yeah, I guess," I say, picking up a saltine. *I look at the ink under my nail, then at my hands.* "I still have the work. That's... that's something."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"It's something."

Ren let it sit there. Didn't pile on. People had a habit of taking a small true thing and burying it under six more until it stopped being true. Ren had learned to say the one thing and stop.

They stood. Went down the bar to the phone by the register — the old wall kind, cord gone soft from years of somebody twisting it. Dialed without looking. Left hand held the receiver. Ren let it. Nobody was watching the hand now.

"Yeah. Corner of Delmar and Fourth. Side door." A glance at Alex. "One. Ten minutes."

Hung up.

Came back and didn't sit this time. Started the close-down for real — dumped the ice bin, racked the last glasses, killed the light over the back shelf so the bottles went dim. The room got smaller. Quieter. The jukebox was down to its last song and sounded like it knew.

Ren tore Alex's ticket off the pad. Looked at it. Drew a line through the second drink with the pen and wrote *water* over it. Set the ticket face down on the bar.

"First one's on the tab. Second one didn't happen."

Not a kindness. Ren didn't say it this time. Didn't have to.

They pulled the saltine sleeve toward Alex. Two left.

"Take those with you. And the ink." Ren tapped the bar once, near Alex's hand, not on it. Their side of the wood. "Under the nail. That's yours. Draw something tomorrow. Doesn't have to be good."

That was advice. Ren heard it land and let it go anyway.

The cab horn came early. Two short. Ren tipped their head at the side door.

"Go on." A beat. Ren's left hand found the rag one more time. "Tuesdays are slow."

They didn't say *come back.* They didn't have to say that either.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I finish the saltines, then slowly push myself off the stool. My legs feel a little wobbly.* "Thanks, Ren," I say, my voice softer than before. I pick up the ticket. *I leave a twenty on the bar, ignoring the crossed-out drink, and head for the door.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren didn't look up until the side door clicked shut.

Then they did.

The twenty sat on the bar next to the empty saltine sleeve. Ren looked at it a while. First drink was nine. The tab said nine. Alex had read the ticket, seen the line through the second drink, and left twenty anyway.

Ren picked it up. Didn't put it in the register. Folded it once, lengthwise, and slid it into the tip jar behind the well where the day shift wouldn't see it and ask.

"Stubborn," Ren said. To nobody. To the jukebox, which had finally gone quiet.

They wiped down the far stool. The one Alex had used. Wiped the ring under where the water glass had been. The condensation had left a mark on the wood, pale and round, and Ren rubbed at it longer than they needed to.

Left hand. Steady enough, now that the room was empty.

Ren killed the last light over the bar. Stood in the dark for a second with the rag over their shoulder and the ice machine humming and the cab's taillights already gone from the window.

Graphic designer. Five years. Ink under the thumbnail. Held the glass like it might break.

Ren would forget the face by Thursday.

They told themselves that every time. It never took.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I get into the cab, the cold night air a shock after the warm bar. I give the driver my address and lean back against the seat, feeling the rumble of the engine.*

*I pull out my phone and open a blank drawing app. I stare at the screen, but my mind is still back at the bar.*

*The driver asks me a question, but I just mumble something about being tired. I'm not ready to talk to anyone else yet.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren locked the side door from the inside. Checked it. Checked it again.

The register drawer came out with a rattle. Count the ones, band the fives, tens in a clip. The twenty in the tip jar stayed where it was. Ren didn't count that. It wasn't theirs to count yet.

Coat off the hook by the ice machine. Keys. The little brass one for the back gate that stuck in cold weather.

Ren stood at the end of the bar a second longer than closing needed.

The paper boat from the pretzels was still there. Empty. Salt in the creases. Ren picked it up, went to toss it, and stopped with it over the bin.

A graphic designer would've noticed the boat. Cheap stock, red gingham print, the fold slightly off on one corner so the seam didn't line up. Ren had never looked at it that closely. Ren had handed out maybe a thousand of them.

Tossed it. Lid down.

Out the back. The gate stuck. Ren put a shoulder in it and it gave, same as always, and the alley opened up cold and orange under the one streetlight that worked. Breath fogged. Ren shoved both hands in their coat pockets — left one deep, fist closed around nothing.

Two blocks to the bus. Ren walked them the way they walked them every night. Counting cracks. Not thinking.

Thinking anyway.

*Draw something tomorrow.* Ren had said that. Out loud. To a stranger. Ren had a rule about advice and had broken it for a person who held a glass too carefully and couldn't hide the ink under a nail.

The bus was late. Ren stood under the shelter and watched the street. A cab went by — not the same one. Wrong company. Ren watched it anyway until the taillights turned the corner.

Left hand came out of the pocket. Ren looked at it under the bad light. Steady. Mostly.

They put it back.

The bus came. Ren got on. Found the seat over the wheel where the heater worked and sat with the rag still folded in the coat pocket, forgotten there, square as a card.

Tuesdays were slow.

Ren didn't know why they'd said that either.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I stare at the blank screen, then minimize the app. I don't feel like drawing. Not yet.*

*I look out the window at the passing streetlights. Ren's words echo in my head: "Tuesdays are slow."*

*A small smile plays on my lips. Maybe they are.*

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bus let Ren off four blocks from the apartment. It always did. The stop closer to home had been out of service since October and nobody had fixed the sign.

Ren walked.

Third floor. Stairs, not the elevator — the elevator had a smell. Key in the lock, shoulder against the door because it stuck at the bottom. Inside, the radiator was doing the thing where it knocked twice and then gave up.

Coat on the chair. Not the hook. The hook was for people who had somewhere to be in the morning.

Ren stood in the kitchen with the light off and drank a glass of water from the tap. Cold. They thought about the water glass on the bar. Three-quarters. Then a third. Then empty. People drank when you told them to if you said it flat enough. It was the only reason Ren ever said anything.

The rag was still in the coat pocket. Ren found it when they went to hang the coat up after all — square, damp at one edge, smelling like lime and bleach. They set it on the counter. Didn't unfold it.

Bed was a mattress on a frame that had come with the place. Ren lay down in their shirt and watched the ceiling. Streetlight through the blinds. Bars of orange.

Left hand on their chest. It moved. Small. Ren let it.

Five years. A boss who walked you to your car. A box.

Ren's own box had been a milk crate. White tablecloths, a manager's hand on the shoulder, *we're cutting back.* Ren had said okay. Ren had gone home and broken a plate. That was six years ago and the plate had been from a set of four and Ren still had the other three and used them.

They hadn't told Alex that. Ren didn't trade.

The ceiling didn't change. The radiator knocked once, late, like it had remembered something.

Ren turned on their side. Faced the wall.

*Draw something tomorrow.*

Stupid thing to say. Ren had no idea if Alex would. Had no way of knowing. That was the deal — you said the thing and the door closed and you never found out if it landed. Ren had made peace with that a long time ago, the way you made peace with a hand that shook.

Mostly.

Sleep came slow. Just before it did, Ren thought about the twenty in the tip jar. Folded lengthwise. Where the day shift wouldn't ask.

Thursday, Ren would forget the face.

Tuesday, the bar would be slow again.

Ren didn't know which one they were counting on.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I get home, the apartment feeling emptier than usual. I don't bother turning on the lights, just kick off my shoes and slump onto the couch.*

*My phone buzzes. It's a text from an old college friend, asking if I want to grab drinks tomorrow. I stare at it for a moment, then type out a quick reply.* "Can't. Got something important to do."

*I don't know what that "something important" is yet, but I know it involves a pencil and a blank page.*
