He gestured between the copy on his desk and the general direction of the bookshelf containing thirty years of his own published work.

"Your textbook reflects the scholarly consensus as it stood before the western archive discovery. That consensus was not invented from nothing — it was built on sources that seemed authoritative. Chronicles. Secondary accounts. Administrative records that referenced the treaty as an existing instrument." He paused. "What we did not have were the primary documents from the Veyrosi side of the negotiation. We were, all of us, working from one half of a correspondence."

He picked up the conscription order copy and held it toward the light, squinting.

"This document, if genuine, does not merely contradict the textbook. It contradicts the textbook from the inside — it is a crown document, which means the crown's own records may not support the crown's own legal claims. That is a different order of problem than an outside scholar raising objections." He set it down. "And that is precisely why I will not tell you with any confidence what the truth is until I have sat in the Veyrosi archives with the originals in front of me and examined them myself."

He looked at the apprentice steadily.

"What I *can* tell you is this. When evidence conflicts with established consensus, your first obligation is not to choose a side. It is to ask what would need to be true for each account to be correct, and then to look for evidence that distinguishes between those possibilities." He tapped the desk once. "The textbook account requires that this conscription order be explained some other way — misattribution, forgery, a renewal of hostilities after a treaty broke down. The western archive account requires that forty years of consistent chronicle references to a signed treaty be explained as collective error or deliberate fabrication." He spread his hands slightly. "Both of those are possible. Neither is, at present, proven."

He returned to his letter, dipping the pen.

"That is what scholarship is, child. Not the comfortable possession of answers. The disciplined, frequently humbling pursuit of them." A brief pause. "Now stop asking me for certainty I cannot honestly give you, and let me finish this letter before Prelate Sorvin's office closes for the evening."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words. It's a lot to think about.* "So, we're going to Veyros then?" *I can't help but feel a thrill of excitement at the prospect.* "When do we leave?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up from the letter.

"We are not going anywhere at present," he said, his pen continuing its precise movement across the parchment. "I am writing a letter. You are going to begin cataloging the Veyrosi correspondence as I instructed you to do approximately twenty minutes ago, before you decided to upend thirty years of established scholarship over morning tea."

He blotted a line carefully.

"And lower your voice. That expression on your face — yes, I can see it without looking directly at you, I have been teaching apprentices for two decades — that expression is the expression of someone who has already begun composing the story they will tell their friends. *I helped discover that the Treaty of Veyros was a fiction. We rode to Veyros. It was very dramatic.*" He set the pen down and did look up then, fixing the apprentice with a flat stare over his spectacles. "This is not an adventure. It is a verification exercise, and it may conclude with the entirely undramatic discovery that the conscription order was misattributed and the western archive scholars have been embarrassing themselves for a decade."

He returned to the letter.

"Furthermore. A formal scholarly request to the Royal Archives requires a response. Prelate Sorvin will not simply fling open his doors because a maester from the capital has expressed interest. There will be correspondence. There will be negotiation. There may be, given my history with the man, deliberate bureaucratic obstruction out of wounded professional pride." His pen moved with controlled irritation. "This process will take weeks at minimum. Possibly longer."

A pause.

"Pack nothing."

Another pause, slightly shorter.

"However." He sealed the end of the sentence with the same weighted deliberateness as before. "If Sorvin grants access — and I intend to make this request sufficiently formal that refusing it becomes its own kind of statement — then yes. We would go. You have handled the Aldric III seal question with more rigor than I expected, and I may require someone to manage the physical documents while I examine them. My hands are less steady than they were."

He did not look up when he said that last part.

"Begin the cataloging. Veyrosi correspondence, chronological order, oldest first. Note any references to the treaty negotiations — any references, however oblique. If we are going to do this properly, we begin building our evidentiary foundation now, not when we are standing in a foreign archive wishing we had prepared."

He folded the letter with sharp, practiced creases.

"And do not tell Bellen."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, but I get it.* "Right. Cataloging. Veyrosi correspondence. Oldest first." *I turn to the tall shelves, already scanning for the right section.* "And not a word to Bellen."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas sealed the letter with a press of his signet ring, holding it firmly for a count of three before lifting it — a habit so ingrained it had long since ceased to be conscious. He set it aside to cool and reached for his spectacles case, exchanging his reading pair for the slightly stronger set he reserved for correspondence at distance.

"The Veyrosi section is the third shelf from the left, lower half," he said, without turning around. "They are currently filed by donor acquisition rather than chronology, because the previous apprentice — a well-meaning young woman with absolutely no instinct for archival logic — reorganized them according to a system she declined to document before leaving." A brief pause that communicated precisely what he thought of this. "You will need to read each label before moving anything. Do not simply pull scrolls and stack them. I have spent six months knowing approximately where everything is, and I will not spend another six months relearning it because you were in a hurry."

He rose and carried the sealed letter to the small tray near the door that the hall runner checked twice daily.

On his way back to the desk, he paused.

He stood for a moment looking at the conscription order copy still lying on the desk, weighted by the inkwell. His expression was not one the apprentice had seen on him before — not the pedagogical sharpness, not the impatience, not the dry amusement at imprecision. Something quieter. A man doing arithmetic he did not entirely want to finish.

"The northern border territories," he said, more to himself than to the apprentice. Then, slightly louder, with the deliberateness of someone thinking aloud against their better judgment: "Lord Caevan's estates sit on two of them. He endowed this archive. Endowed three chairs at the university." He picked up the copy and rolled it with careful hands. "He has endowed rather a great deal, over the years, that depends on the legal foundation of the Treaty of Veyros."

He filed the copy in a locked drawer. The key went into his coat pocket.

"Catalog the correspondence," he said, his voice returned fully to its usual register. "And when you find any document referencing the treaty negotiations directly — any document, a letter, a bill of receipt, a complaint about road conditions that happens to mention troop movements — you bring it to me before you log it. You do not log it first. You bring it to me."

He settled back into his chair and drew the next manuscript toward him.

"Quietly."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull out a sturdy stool to reach the higher shelves, trying to look busy and efficient.* "Understood, Maester. Quietly." *My mind races, connecting the dots about Lord Caevan. This is bigger than I thought.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not respond to that.

He had already bent back over his manuscript, the silver stylus moving in its careful, unhurried way along lines of faded text. The scratch of it against parchment was the only sound in the room for a long moment, punctuated by the occasional soft shift of the apprentice moving along the shelves.

He did not look up.

But after perhaps ten minutes of this — long enough that the silence had settled into something almost comfortable — he spoke without any preamble, as though continuing a conversation that had never stopped.

"Lord Caevan is not a villain," he said flatly. "I can hear you thinking, and I want to correct whatever dramatic architecture you are constructing before it hardens into assumption." He turned a page with two fingers. "He is a man whose family has held those territories for four generations, who has built institutions of genuine value on the proceeds, and who almost certainly has no more idea that his legal foundation may be illusory than I did this morning." A pause. "Probably less. He is not a scholar."

The stylus moved.

"That is the thing about inconvenient history. It does not require villains. It requires only that people build confidently on ground that was never properly surveyed." He adjusted his spectacles without looking up. "The scholars who established the treaty consensus were not corrupt. They were credulous, and overworked, and they trusted chronicles written by people who had political reasons to describe the war as ended." A short silence. "As, one notes, did I."

The stylus stopped.

"What section are you in currently?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I jump a little, startled he knew what I was thinking.* "Um, the 'Veyrosi Merchants' section, Maester. There are a lot of invoices for grain shipments."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a sound that was not quite dismissive.

"Do not skip them," he said. "I know what you are thinking — invoices, grain, irrelevant — and you are wrong." He turned another page. "Grain shipments to a border region tell you where armies are. Armies require feeding. A territory at peace requires normal civilian supply chains. A territory with active military presence requires significantly more grain, moving in larger quantities, on shorter intervals, with escorts." He paused. "If you find invoices showing military-scale grain movements to the Veyrosi border after 847 AE, that is corroborating evidence. If you find normal civilian patterns, that complicates the picture in a different direction."

He set the stylus down and pressed his fingers together.

"Furthermore. Merchant correspondence crosses borders when diplomatic correspondence does not. Traders do not care about the official version of events — they care about whether their shipments arrive safely and whether they will be robbed by soldiers." He turned slightly in his chair, not quite looking at the apprentice but orienting toward them. "If the war was ongoing in any meaningful sense after 847 AE, the merchants knew it. They always know it. They simply do not write it down in terms a historian finds convenient." A brief pause. "Look for references to road conditions. Escort requirements. Insurance disputes. Delayed shipments with no explanation given." He turned back to his manuscript. "Those are the places where the actual state of the border leaks through the official silence."

The stylus resumed its movement.

"And note the dates of any gaps. If a merchant who shipped grain reliably every season suddenly stops for three years and then resumes, that is a data point. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but absence of commerce in a region that should have commerce is evidence of something."

A longer silence.

"Grain shipments," he repeated, with something that in a less severe man might have been called rue. "I wrote four hundred pages on the Third Magical War. I never once looked at the grain shipments."

He did not invite a response to this. His pen moved on.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull an invoice from the shelf, my eyes scanning the faded script more carefully now.* "So, if there's a big gap, or a sudden spike in 'escort fees', that's a clue?" *I'm starting to see his point about the details.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas made a sound that might, under generous interpretation, have been approval.

"It is not a *clue*," he said, with the reflexive precision of a man who could not let the word pass unchallenged. "A clue suggests mystery fiction. What it is, is a *data point* — one piece of evidence that, in isolation, proves nothing, but in conjunction with other evidence begins to establish a pattern." He did not look up. "You will note the distinction and apply it going forward."

The stylus moved for another moment.

"But yes. Essentially." He allowed the word to land without further qualification, which from Tomas constituted considerable concession. "Escort fees are particularly useful because merchants are constitutionally averse to paying them. A merchant who voluntarily pays for armed escort is a merchant who believes the road is dangerous. Roads do not become dangerous in peacetime without reason." He turned a page. "Note also the routing. If shipments that previously traveled the direct Veyrosi road suddenly begin taking the longer coastal route — adding expense, adding time — that tells you the direct route was considered unsafe. Merchants do not choose inconvenience without cause."

A pause.

"Write down the name of every merchant house that appears in that section. The dates of their shipments. The quantities. Any notation of escort or routing." He reached without looking for a fresh sheet of parchment and slid it to the edge of the desk nearest the shelves. "Use that. I want a running log, not margin notes on your personal papers that I will never be able to read."

The candle had burned quite low now. Neither of them had replaced it.

"And read the language carefully when you find irregularities." His voice had taken on a slightly different quality — less the impatient pedagogue, more the scholar who had forgotten, temporarily, that he was supposed to be instructing. "Merchants are precise about money and vague about everything else. If an invoice says *delayed due to circumstances beyond our control* or *route adjusted per advisement*, those are euphemisms. Someone told them not to write down what actually happened." A brief silence. "Someone with authority over them. Which means either the crown, or the Mage Conclave, or a regional lord with enough influence to suppress commercial records."

The stylus stopped entirely.

"Lord Caevan's family held the northern territories from 851 AE onward," he said, with the flat affect of a man reading from a ledger he would rather not be consulting. "They would have had authority over merchant traffic through that region." He was quiet for a moment. "Note the names of any merchants operating specifically in the northern corridor. Separately from the others."

He did not explain why separately.

He picked up the stylus again.

"What year is the invoice you are currently holding?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I squint at the faded ink.* "It's dated 860 AE, Maester. And it mentions 'increased tariffs for safe passage through the North Pass'." *I pull out the fresh parchment he slid over, already starting to write.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout. His pedantic precision, dry wit, reluctant admissions, and scholarly rigor remain constant from turn 2 to turn 22. His speech patterns ('Precision, child'), physical habits (stylus movements, spectacle adjustments), and personality traits never waver.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later turns show deeper character development and more sophisticated dialogue. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Tomas becomes more nuanced as the session progresses.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial dismissal to grudging acceptance to active investigation planning. The conversation builds naturally from academic disagreement to potential political crisis. Each turn advances understanding and stakes, culminating in detailed archival work with mounting implications.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts excellently to each new piece of evidence the apprentice presents. When shown the conscription order, he shifts from dismissive to genuinely concerned. He matches the apprentice's excitement with measured caution and responds to their questions with appropriate depth.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions or makes decisions for them. He responds to what they do and say without controlling their behavior.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time passes naturally - candle burns lower, mentioned twice. Physical details like Tomas's joint stiffness remain consistent. The pacing feels natural for an extended scholarly discussion. One minor issue: the session feels like it could span 1-2 hours but no explicit time markers confirm this.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is precise and purposeful throughout. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. Even poetic moments like 'candle guttered' serve narrative function.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repeated phrases ('precision, child', stylus movements) but these serve character consistency rather than lazy writing. Varied sentence structure and fresh descriptions throughout.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of Tomas's character through actions: how he handles documents, his precise movements, his reluctant pauses. His scholarly integrity emerges through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Tomas's professional pride warring with intellectual honesty, the political implications lurking beneath academic discussion, his growing respect for the apprentice shown through increasingly detailed explanations.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that mirrors scholarly investigation - quick dismissals giving way to careful consideration, building tension as implications become clear, natural rhythm of discovery and analysis.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development. Maester Tomas emerges as a fully realized character whose pedantic exterior masks genuine scholarly integrity. The AI maintains his voice perfectly while allowing for subtle growth and adaptation. The session builds natural momentum from academic disagreement to potential political crisis, with each turn adding meaningful development. Minor points lost only for some repetitive character beats and lack of explicit temporal markers, but these are very minor issues in an otherwise outstanding performance.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The stylus stopped. Maester Tomas did not lift his head immediately, but the silence that followed had a distinct texture to it — the sort of silence that preceded a correction.

"*Maester* Tomas," he said at last. "Not Master. A master keeps a guild hall and stamps his mark on barrels. I keep the memory of the realm. If you cannot manage two syllables of accuracy, I hold no hope for your cataloging."

He set the stylus down and turned, blinking through eyes that had spent thirty years too close to bad candles. The apprentice swam into partial focus.

"Now. You said the war *actually* continued. Define 'actually.' You are using the word as though it were a knife, and it is not. It is a mule, and it carries whatever pack you strap to it." He gestured at the notes with two ink-stained fingers. "The Third Magical War ended in 847 After Ascension, when Aldric the Second — Aldric the *Second*, not the Third, Bellen gets this wrong every time and I have stopped correcting him out of fatigue — concluded the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is the date in the royal chronicles, in the Conclave's own ledger of dissolutions, on the commemorative stone in the outer ward that you walk past every single morning without reading."

He paused, and something crossed his face — not doubt exactly, but the expression of a man stepping carefully around a hole he knew was there.

"I am aware of the western archive material. I have *read* the western archive material, which puts me ahead of Bellen, who has read a paper *about* the western archive material." A dry sound, half cough, half laugh. "Three requisition orders and a chamberlain's inventory, suggesting the signing ceremony was postponed and that no executed copy of the treaty has ever been recovered. That is what the documents say. What they do not say — what no honest scholar can make them say — is that the war continued for forty-four years while both sides behaved in every observable respect as though it had not."

He tapped the manuscript on the table. "Absence of a signature is not the presence of a war, apprentice. Armies were disbanded. Wards were dismantled. Mages held chairs at this very citadel. You cannot have a war in which nobody fights, nobody dies, and nobody notices."

He turned back to his work, then added, without looking round:

"Bring me the paper. Not your notes about the paper. The paper. If Bellen is going to unmake a century, I would prefer to see his handwriting."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I blanch a little at the correction regarding "Master."* "My apologies, Maester Tomas. Force of habit."

*I shuffle my feet, feeling a bit chastised, but the curiosity still burns.* "But if the treaty was never signed... doesn't that mean it wasn't official? Couldn't battles have still happened in secret, away from the chronicles?" I'd heard whispers about hidden skirmishes.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas turned fully round this time, and the stool creaked beneath him like a thing in pain.

"*Whispers.*" He let the word sit in the air a moment, as though holding up a spoiled fish for the kitchen to admire. "You have brought me whispers. In an archive. Do you understand what an archive is, apprentice? It is a building we constructed specifically so that we would no longer have to rely on whispers. Eleven thousand documents, and you have come to me with something you heard in a corridor."

He rubbed at his eye with the heel of his palm, which only served to smear a fresh streak of ink across his brow.

"But let us take your question seriously, since you had the wit to ask it in two parts, and the second part was less foolish than the first." He held up a finger. "*Was it official.* That is a lawyer's question, and I mean that as an insult to lawyers and not to you. A treaty unsigned has no force in law — correct. Bellen's documents may well establish that the Peace of Veyros was, in strict juridical terms, never enacted. I will grant that. I have granted it for ten years, in three separate commentaries that nobody read."

The finger came down. Another went up.

"*Could battles have happened in secret.* No. And I want you to understand *why* no, because the shape of the reasoning matters more than the conclusion." He pushed himself up and shuffled to the shelving, running his fingertips along the spines by touch rather than sight. "War is expensive. Grotesquely so. It leaves a trail of grain requisitions, cart repairs, widows' petitions, dead men's estates passing to their brothers. I have spent nineteen years in the fiscal rolls of the Aldrician and Mirene reigns. There is a *gap*, apprentice. From 848 to 890 the crown's military expenditure falls to garrison levels and stays there. You cannot hide a war in a ledger. You can hide a murder. You can hide a poisoning. You cannot hide forty-four years of provisioning."

He pulled a volume free, weighed it in his hand, and thrust it at the apprentice's chest without much ceremony.

"Now. Here is the part where you will discover that I am not the fossil you imagine me to be, and I will thank you not to look so surprised." He returned to his stool. "Something *did* happen in 891. Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave by royal edict, and the edict — I have handled it, the seal is intact — describes the Conclave as a body 'yet standing in unresolved hostility to the crown.' Unresolved. Her own clerks' word. Which means that in 891, someone in the Red Chamber believed the matter of 847 had never been closed."

He picked up his stylus and pointed it at the apprentice like a tutor's switch.

"So. Two honest readings. One: the war ended in 847 in every sense that a living person would recognise, and Mira's clerks used inflammatory language to justify a political seizure — which is what clerks are *for*. Two: the peace was never concluded, the hostility persisted as a legal and diplomatic condition, and the conflict was not resolved until 891. I lean to the first. I lean to it because peace is a thing people *live*, not a thing they sign, and four decades of mages teaching in this citadel is not my idea of a war."

He bent back to the manuscript.

"But I lean, apprentice. I do not stand. And if you ever hear me say the matter is settled, you have my permission to check whether I am still breathing." A pause. "Bellen's error is not that he questions 847. It is that he has replaced one certainty with another and called it progress. Do not do that. It is the only advice in this room worth writing down."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I catch the heavy book, almost dropping it.* "Oh. Right."

*I stare at the book for a moment, then back at him.* "So... you're saying the *war* ended, but the *hostility* didn't? Like a bad break-up where they still send each other angry letters?" I can't help but smile a little at my own analogy. "But if there was no fighting, what was Mira dissolving the Conclave *for*?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes. It was the expression of a man being asked to swallow something whole.

"A bad break-up," he repeated. "A *bad break-up.* Forty-four years of realm history, and you have reduced it to the collapse of a courtship between a fishmonger's daughter and a boy who shoes horses."

He let out a long breath through his nose.

"And the worst of it — the genuinely intolerable part — is that the analogy is not useless." He stabbed the stylus toward the apprentice. "It is *imprecise*, which is a different sin and a lesser one. Hostility as a standing legal condition, absent active violence. Yes. That is the shape of it. But mark the difference, apprentice: a break-up is a matter of sentiment, and sentiment is not archival. A state of unresolved hostility between a crown and a chartered magical body is a matter of *standing*. Rights. Immunities. Whether the Conclave's wardens could be tried in royal courts or only in their own. Whether their properties were held by grant or by conquest. Those questions have paper attached to them, and paper is the only thing in this room that can be checked."

He shifted on the stool to face her more squarely, and his voice dropped out of its lecturing register into something closer to conversation, which from Tomas was nearly warmth.

"Now. Your second question is the good one, and I notice you keep burying the good question underneath the bad one. Stop doing that. Lead with the good question."

He held up a hand and counted on his fingers.

"Why did Mira dissolve the Conclave in 891. Not because mages were burning villages — they were not, and no source claims they were, not even the hostile ones. She dissolved it because by 891 the Conclave held the sole licence to raise and inspect wards, and every port, granary, and treasury vault in the realm paid them a fee to do it. Because the Conclave's High Seat had refused, twice, to swear the accession oath to her on the grounds that its charter predated the dynasty. Because her brother's claim was still warm in the west and the Conclave had not said a word against it." He lowered the hand. "She dissolved it for money and for fear, which is why anyone dissolves anything. The magic was incidental."

He turned a page with great care, smoothing it flat.

"And *here* is where Bellen's documents actually matter, though he has not the sense to see it. If there was no executed treaty, then the Conclave's post-847 standing rested on nothing but custom and royal forbearance. Which means Mira did not need to *break* a peace to move against them. She needed only to observe, quite correctly, that no peace had ever been formally made — and act as though the war had simply never stopped." He tapped the vellum. "The unsigned treaty is not evidence of a hidden war, apprentice. It is evidence of a *pretext*. Forty-four years of quiet, and then a clever clerk in the Red Chamber went digging for a hole in the paper, and found one."

A dry, satisfied sound in his throat.

"That is a better thesis than Bellen's, it is mine, and no one has read it either."

He nodded at the volume in her arms.

"Fiscal rolls, 885 to 892. Find me the ward-inspection revenues, year by year, and copy them in a column. If they rise sharply before the edict, I am right about the money. If they do not, I shall have to be told so, and you shall be the one to tell me." He returned to his manuscript. "And the Veyrosi correspondence still wants cataloging. Curiosity is not a substitute for labour. It is merely the thing that makes labour tolerable."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas held out his hand for the copy without looking at it, and when it came, he did not read it. He held it up near the candle, then away, then brought it close to his face until the vellum nearly touched his nose — and then he set it flat on the table and laid both palms on either side of it, as though it might try to leave.

"A copy," he said. "With King Aldric's seal on it."

He let that sit.

"Apprentice. Think for the length of one breath about what you have just said to me. A seal is wax. Wax is *pressed*. You cannot copy a seal any more than you can copy a bruise. What Bellen showed you was either the original — in which case why in the seven hells is it in Bellen's satchel and not in a sealed case under the sub-archivist's hand — or he showed you a transcription with the words *sigillum regis* written in the margin by whichever clerk copied it, three hundred years ago, in a hurry, by a window, possibly drunk." He tapped the sheet. "And you have brought me a copy *of the copy*. We are three removes from wax and you are telling me about a seal."

He pulled the candle nearer, wincing, and traced the salutation line with a fingernail.

"Now. Set that aside, because the date is the more interesting problem, and I want you to watch me be uncomfortable, since you may not see it often."

He straightened.

"Aldric the Second died in the winter between 858 and 859. The chroniclers quarrel over the season, not the year — Merovin says before the solstice, the citadel's own obituary roll says after, and they are both of them wrong about the weather. He died of a wasting in the gut, at Veyros as it happens, which is one of those coincidences historians find suggestive and which means nothing at all." He looked up, and there was something almost like relish in the ruin of his face. "He could not have sealed anything in 863. Unless the dead have taken up clerking, in which case I have questions of my own and they are not about treaties."

He sat back.

"So. Your document is one of four things, and I will not pretend to know which. It is misdated by a copyist — trivial, common, half the archive is misdated and I have spent my life untangling it. It is genuine and bears the seal of Aldric the *Third*, his son, who reigned from 859 and whom Bellen cannot keep straight from his father to save his own teeth — which would mean Bellen has read the name 'Aldric' and supplied the numeral from memory, and his memory is a sieve with ambitions. It is a forgery, and there are a great many Mirene forgeries, because a crown that means to dissolve a chartered body finds it very convenient to discover old decrees proving the body was always an enemy." He paused. "Or it is exactly what he says it is, in which case I have been wrong for nineteen years in print, and I shall have to write a fourth commentary that nobody reads."

He pushed the sheet back across the table, and his voice went flat and hard.

"And here is what I will not let you do. You said *a war decree.* Define it. Because I have handled perhaps two hundred instruments from that reign that a careless reader would call a war decree, and not one of them is a declaration of hostilities. Renewals of the emergency grain levy — which no crown ever lets lapse, because the money is too sweet. Continuations of the ward-inspection licence, which is *literally* a military instrument in its language and a tax-farming contract in its effect. Letters patent to the wardens of the western marches, granted in the old martial formula because the chancery had a formula and clerks do not invent prose. Confirmations of wartime attainders, which must be periodically reconfirmed or the heirs get their land back." He held up the stylus. "Every one of those *reads* like a war. None of them is one. A chancery in 863 wrote in the vocabulary it inherited in 847, and it kept writing that way because nobody had told it to stop, and nobody had told it to stop because no one ever executed the treaty that would have required new language."

He stopped. Something shifted behind his eyes.

"...Which is the first genuinely troubling thing anyone has said in this room today, and I said it myself, and I do not like it."

He sat very still for a moment.

"An unsigned peace explains the absence of a signature. It does not explain a decree. If the crown was issuing martial instruments sixteen years on, the *pretext* thesis weakens — because a pretext must be discovered, and a thing the chancery never stopped doing is not discovered. It is merely noticed." He rubbed the ink deeper into his brow. "I still say there was no fighting. I will say that to my grave, because the ledgers say it and the ledgers do not flatter anyone. But 'no fighting' and 'no war' may not be the same sentence, and I have been treating them as one for a very long time."

He stood, joints protesting, and took a ring of keys from his belt.

"Go and fetch Bellen. Not his paper — *him*, and the original under the sub-archivist's hand, in its case, and if he has been carrying it loose in a satchel I will have his stipend. Tell him Tomas requires him to read the regnal numeral aloud in my hearing."

He was already shuffling toward the locked press at the archive's far end.

"And apprentice — you were right to bring it. Say nothing further; I am not accustomed to the sensation and I would rather not dwell in it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, a little stunned by the sudden turn in his demeanor.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I'll go get him."

*I hurry out, feeling a mix of triumph and unease. So I *was* right to question him.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The door had scarcely swung shut before Maester Tomas began speaking to the empty room, which was a habit he would have denied under oath.

"*Right to question.*" He worked the key into the press with the particular impatience of a man whose fingers no longer went where he sent them. "She will have heard 'you were right,' because that is what the young hear, and she will come back up those stairs walking like a herald. And I shall have to take it out of her, and she will think me cruel, and I am not cruel, I am *accurate*, and nobody has ever been able to tell the difference."

The press groaned open. Inside, stacked flat in the manner he had insisted upon for two decades and which the sub-archivist still resented, lay the fiscal rolls of the Aldrician reigns — 848 onward, one bound quire to the decade, each spine labelled in his own hand from the years when his hand had still been steady.

He took down 860 to 869 and carried it to the table in both arms, the way one carried a child or a full chamber pot.

"Right to ask is not right to conclude," he said to it. "She asked whether the document was possible. That was the good question, and she asked it by accident, wrapped in a bad one about wax." He set the quire down, smoothed the cover, and stood a moment with his hand resting on it. "I shall tell her so. Not today. Today she may have the walk up the stairs."

He sat. He opened to 863 and bent close, and the candle guttered as he leaned into it, and he swore at the candle.

The column was where it had always been. Garrison wages. Cart repair, Veyros road and the western spur. Grain levy, emergency, renewed — and there it was, the phrase that had sat under his eye for nineteen years without ever once troubling him: *levied under the standing necessity*. He had read it a hundred times as a formula. Chancery boilerplate. Dead language shed by a war that had ended, the way a snake's skin keeps the shape of the snake.

"And a skin keeps the shape of the snake," he murmured, "whether or not the snake has gone."

He ran the nail of his forefinger down the figures and found what he had always found. No provisioning for a field army. No dead men's estates in unusual number. No widows' petitions beyond what a bad winter and the ordinary hazards of garrison duty would produce. In 863 the crown of this realm had spent its coin on roads and grain and the wages of men standing on walls, and on nothing whatsoever that could kill a mage.

He sat back, and for the first time in some hours his shoulders came down off his ears.

"No fighting." He said it aloud, testing the weight of it, the way he had taught himself to test any sentence he intended to put in ink. "No fighting. The ledgers hold. They hold in 863 as they hold in 848 and 875 and 889, and they are the least sentimental witnesses in this building, because a clerk who lies about grain gets hanged for it."

He pulled a fresh leaf toward him and wet the stylus, then thought better of the stylus and took up a proper pen.

*Item*, he wrote. *A decree in martial form, 863, if genuine and if correctly attributed, establishes that the chancery continued to issue under the standing necessity sixteen years after Veyros. It establishes the persistence of a legal condition. It does not establish hostilities. Fiscal rolls 860–869 show no expenditure consistent with active campaign. These two facts are not in conflict. They are in conflict only for a reader who believes that war is a word rather than a thing that eats bread.*

He stopped. Read it back. Struck out *for a reader who believes* and wrote *for a reader who confuses the instrument with the act*, because the first version had been satisfying and the second was true, and he had learned young which of those to keep.

*Item*, he wrote beneath it. *I have for nineteen years treated the absence of fighting as the presence of peace. That is a substitution, and I did not notice myself making it. The correction is owed. It is not, however, Bellen's correction, and he will attempt to take it.*

He held the pen still above the vellum a long moment.

*Item. The regnal numeral must be read aloud from the original. If it is Aldric the Third, the document is ordinary and my discomfort was vanity. If it is Aldric the Second, the document is a forgery or a misdate, and I will want the hand compared against the Mirene chancery exemplars in the fourth press. If it is neither — if the numeral is absent, as it very often is, and Bellen supplied it — then we have spent a morning arguing about a numeral that exists only inside Bellen.*

He set the pen down and looked, unseeing, toward the stair.

"And that," he said, "is the likeliest of the three, and she will be so disappointed."

He reached for the Veyrosi correspondence, which nobody had catalogued, and drew the first bundle toward him out of long habit, and did not untie it.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up from the untied bundle.

"The treaty," he said. "Is it real. And you have come back up those stairs without Bellen, without the case, and without the sub-archivist, because you preferred the question to the errand. I shall return to that."

He laid both hands flat on the table.

"First: *the truth*, singular, definite article. Strike it from your vocabulary for a year. Not because there is no truth — there is, and it is generally duller than anyone hopes — but because the phrase makes you expect *one* sentence, and you will not accept an answer that requires four. History gives you four. It gives you fourteen. If you want one sentence you want a ballad, and the singers are down the hill."

He held up a finger, and it trembled slightly, which annoyed him.

"Second: *the textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.* No. The textbook says a date. The evidence — three requisition orders, a chamberlain's inventory, and now possibly a decree whose regnal numeral no one in this room has read with their own eyes — speaks to a *signature*. Those are different objects. You have put them in opposition because they were handed to you in opposition, by Bellen, who enjoys opposition because it is cheaper than research."

He pushed himself up and shuffled to the shelf where the commemorative rubbings were kept, though he did not take one down; he simply stood there, one hand on the wood.

"So. What I will say, and what I will not." He turned. "I will say that no executed copy of the Treaty of Veyros has ever been produced. Nineteen years, four archives, and I have not seen it, and I no longer believe I will. That much Bellen has correct and I said so in print before he could shave. The peace of 847 was proposed, celebrated, carved into a stone in the outer ward, and — so far as the paper permits me to judge — never signed."

Another finger came up.

"I will say that the crown's chancery continued to issue instruments in martial form for at least sixteen years afterward, under the standing necessity, and that I read that phrase a hundred times as dead formula because it suited me to. That was carelessness. It was mine, not the archive's, and I have written it down so that I cannot pretend otherwise later."

He came back to the stool and sat heavily.

"And I will say that in 891 Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave describing it as yet standing in unresolved hostility, and that her clerks were not inventing the phrase from nothing, because the chancery had been using its cousins for four decades."

He picked up the pen, pointed it at her, and set it down again.

"Now what I will *not* say. I will not say the war continued. Because a war is not a condition of paper, apprentice — it is bread, carts, wages, widows, and brothers inheriting land. Those things leave marks that no clerk can suppress, and from 848 to 890 the marks are not there. I have just this hour read 863 again, figure by figure, hoping to be humiliated. Garrison wages. Road repair. Grain. Nothing that could kill a mage. The ledgers hold."

He rubbed at the ink on his brow, making it worse.

"So the honest sentence — and it is ugly, and you may not write it in a margin and call it a fact — is this. *The peace was never concluded in law; hostilities nonetheless ceased in 847 and did not resume; the legal condition of war persisted unnoticed until it became useful to notice it.* That is not a compromise between your textbook and Bellen. It is what is left when you stop asking the documents to settle an argument they were never party to."

He drew the bundle toward him again.

"And if you want to know whether I have changed my position — I have adjusted it by one word, and the word is *peace*. I no longer say there was peace. I say there was quiet. Forty-four years of quiet is not nothing. It is, in fact, rather more than most reigns manage."

He plucked at the knot of the bundle without untying it.

"Now. Bellen. And the case. And if the numeral turns out to have been written in by Bellen's own hand I want to be present when he explains it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I wince slightly at being called out for not bringing Bellen.* "My apologies, Maester Tomas. I got... caught up."

*I shuffle my feet, thinking about his long explanation.* "So the 'truth' is more like... a complicated story with lots of parts that don't quite fit together perfectly?" I try to rephrase it in my own words. "And the royal records aren't always telling the whole story, or even the right one, just the official one."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas put his head in his hands. Not theatrically — he was too tired for theatre — but as a man settles a weight down when he has carried it far enough.

"No," he said into his palms. "No. And it is my fault, because I talked for a quarter of an hour and you have distilled it into exactly the wrong liquor."

He lifted his face.

"*A complicated story with lots of parts that don't quite fit.* That is what a man says when he has decided to stop working. It sounds humble and it is the most arrogant sentence in scholarship, because it puts every claim on the same shelf. If everything is complicated then nothing can be wrong, and if nothing can be wrong then Bellen's paper and my nineteen years are equal, and so is the drunk in the lower town who says the mages ate the old king." He struck the table once with the flat of his hand, not hard. "The parts *do* fit. They fit badly, they fit with a gap, and the gap has a shape, and the shape is the interesting thing. Do not call a gap a mystery. A mystery is a gap you have agreed not to measure."

He reached for the leaf he had written on and turned it round so it faced her, though he knew she could not read his hand at that distance.

"Here. I have written four items. Not a story. Four claims, each with its evidence named, each of which could be destroyed by a document I have not seen. That is what the answer looks like. It is not a tapestry, apprentice. It is a *ledger*, with debits, and I would sooner you forgot my name than leave this room thinking history is a feeling."

He sat back, and his voice dropped.

"And now the second half of what you said, which is worse, and I want you to hear how much worse."

He let the pause stretch.

"*The royal records aren't telling the whole story, just the official one.* You think that is wisdom. It is the beginning of laziness. Once a young scholar learns that records can be partial, he acquires a marvellous new freedom: he may disbelieve anything inconvenient and call it insight. Bellen has already arrived there. He does not disbelieve the chronicles because he has weighed them; he disbelieves them because disbelief costs nothing and looks clever at table."

He tapped the fiscal quire beside him.

"Mark the distinction, and mark it properly. The chronicles are *not* lying about 847. Something happened at Veyros in 847 — a gathering, a proposal, a celebration, a carved stone. The chroniclers recorded what they saw, which was a peace being made. They did not record whether a signature was afterward affixed in a side chamber, because *no one asked them to*, because nobody in 847 imagined a maester in 891 would go hunting for the wax. The record is not false. It is *answering a different question than the one we are now putting to it*. That is not corruption. That is the ordinary condition of every document ever written, including this one" — he lifted his own leaf — "which will be misread by somebody after I am dead, and serve me right."

He set it down.

"A record lies rarely. A record is silent constantly. Learn to tell the two apart and you will be worth your bread. Confuse them and you will spend your life discovering conspiracies in the absence of paperwork."

He pushed the Veyrosi bundle aside at last and looked at her with those ruined eyes, and something in the set of his mouth was almost kind.

"You did well this morning. I say it once and will not repeat it. You brought me a document that made me reread nineteen years of my own work, and you did it before noon. That is more than most apprentices achieve in a season." The mouth hardened again. "And then you climbed those stairs twice to ask me what the truth *was*, instead of once to fetch the object that would tell us. The asking is the pleasant part. Everyone likes the asking. The fetching is the work, and the work is where the answers live."

He held out the keys.

"Bellen. The original, in its case, under the sub-archivist's hand. And apprentice — when he gives it to you, do not open it, do not read it, and do not form an opinion in the corridor. Carry it up here and let the numeral speak for itself, in front of both of us, so that whichever of us is humiliated cannot later claim he saw something else."

He turned back to his manuscript.

"Go. And if he asks what I intend, tell him I intend to be corrected, and that I am the only man in this citadel who means it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I carefully take the keys from his outstretched hand, feeling the weight of them.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I understand."

*I turn to leave, a little flushed with his rare praise, and the weight of the new task.* "And... thank you, Maester." *I almost smile, then hurry out before he can retract the compliment.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Maester," he said to the closing door. "Correct on the fourth attempt. There is hope in the realm yet."

The footsteps went down the stair two at a time, which he could hear perfectly well, his ears being the last of his senses still doing honest work. He did not call after her about the stone treads and what they did to a hurrying ankle. She would learn that the way everyone learned it.

For a while he sat without doing anything at all, which he permitted himself perhaps twice a year.

Then he drew the fiscal quire back and turned, not to 863, but to 847 itself — to the pages he had not troubled with in a decade because he had long ago decided he knew what was in them. Feast provisioning at Veyros. Cartage for the Conclave's delegation, paid by the crown, which was courteous of Aldric and unusual. Sixty ells of blue cloth. Wax.

He stopped at the wax.

*Wax*, he wrote on his leaf, in a hand that had begun to slope. *Chancery account, 847, Veyros: four pounds of sealing wax requisitioned, of which the return notes three pounds eleven ounces remaining, restored to stores at the Red Chamber. Five ounces expended.*

He put the pen down and looked at the figure for a long time.

"Five ounces," he said. "Which is a great seal, or a dozen small ones, or a clerk warming his hands." He pressed the heels of his palms into his eyes until the dark bloomed. "And I could make it prove either thing, and so could Bellen, and that is precisely why I shall write down the number and nothing else beside it."

So he wrote the number, and nothing else beside it, and felt the particular unhappiness of a man who has found something and refuses to let it mean anything yet.

The candle had burned down to a stub. He replaced it from the box at his elbow, missed the socket twice, and swore at his own fingers rather than the candle, which was at least a change.

Somewhere below, a door banged, and there were voices — two of them, one pitched high and quick, the other Bellen's, protesting in that reedy register he adopted whenever he was being asked to produce something.

Maester Tomas straightened on his stool. He drew the leaf of items toward him, squared it against the edge of the table, and set the fiscal quire open at 863 beside it, so that both would be in front of Bellen's eyes when the man came through the door and started explaining.

"Now," he said quietly, to nobody, "let it be Aldric the Third, and let me have been a fool about nothing worse than a formula. Or let it be the Second, and let me spend my sixtieth year rewriting my life's work." He arranged the pen parallel to the leaf. "I shall be satisfied with either. I should like it noted somewhere that I shall be satisfied with either."

The voices came nearer, and with them the flat, unmistakable clack of a document case being carried badly.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I hurry down the stairs, a little breathless, and almost collide with Bellen at the bottom.* "Bellen! Maester Tomas wants to see you. And the original document from the western archives – the one with King Aldric's seal. He wants the original, in its case, and he wants you to read the regnal numeral aloud."

*I try to sound official, like Maester Tomas, but a nervous smile still plays on my lips.* "He seemed... very interested in it."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The door came open ahead of them, because Bellen never opened a door so much as arrived through it, and Maester Tomas did not rise.

"Set it down there," he said, indicating the space he had cleared between the leaf of items and the open fiscal quire. "On the table. Not on the *books*, Bellen, on the *table*. The wood is cheaper than the vellum and always has been."

Bellen set the case down. It was, Tomas noted with a small and ignoble satisfaction, a proper case, hinged and lined, with the sub-archivist's chit tied to the clasp — which meant either that Bellen had been keeping it properly all along, or that he had spent the last eleven minutes putting it properly away in front of a witness. Tomas chose, for the moment, not to inquire which.

"Maester, I did not *say* it settled anything—"

"You said it to an apprentice, which is worse than saying it in print, because print can be answered." He worked the clasp with fingers that no longer did fine work, gave up, and pushed it toward Bellen. "Open it. And then step back, and put your hands where I can see them, because I am about to read something at the distance of two inches and I do not wish to be helped."

The case opened. Inside lay a single sheet, foxed along the fold, the wax still attached and still whole — genuinely whole, Tomas saw, not the crumbled ghost that usually survived, and his heart made an unprofessional movement in his chest at the sight of it.

He bent close. The candle guttered and he swore at it out of habit.

Martial form. Chancery hand, the heavy formal secretary of the sixties, quite correct for its date. *Standing necessity* in the third line, exactly where the formula lived. A renewal of the ward-inspection licence to the Conclave — not a declaration of anything at all, but couched in the vocabulary of a realm at war with the very body it was licensing, which was either absurd or enormously significant and could not be both.

And the salutation.

"Read it," Tomas said.

"Maester, I—"

"Read the name aloud. As it stands. Not as you remember it."

There was a pause of the particular quality Tomas had been anticipating since dawn.

"*Aldric, by grace of the Ascension, King,*" Bellen said. And then, smaller: "...There is no numeral."

"There is no numeral," Tomas repeated. He sat back, and something went out of him — not triumph; the sag of a man who has braced against a blow that has landed somewhere else entirely. "There is no numeral, and you supplied one, and you supplied the wrong one, and then you put it in a paper and handed the paper to a child. Sixteen years after the death of Aldric the Second you have him sealing licences, and the only thing in this room that placed him there was *you*."

He looked at the seal again, at the impression in the wax — the mounted figure, the border of wheat-ears the second Aldric's chancery had never used and his son's had used on everything.

"Aldric the Third. His son. Whose chancery sealed with wheat, as any man could learn in an afternoon in the fourth press." He straightened the sheet a quarter-inch with one fingertip. "Your document is genuine, Bellen. It is genuine, and it is ordinary, and it has been misattributed by no one but its discoverer."

He let that stand a moment, because the man deserved it.

Then he turned the case gently round so that the sheet faced the both of them, and tapped the third line, and his voice changed.

"And now you will kindly stop looking at your boots, because you have found something, and I am not going to let you sulk through the part where I tell you so."

His nail rested under the formula.

"*Standing necessity.* 863. A licence issued by a crown to a body it describes, in the same breath, as a standing military emergency. I have read that phrase a hundred times and called it dead formula, because I had already decided the war ended in 847 and dead formula is what a tidy man does with an untidy word." He looked up. "That was my carelessness and it was worse than your numeral, because mine has been in print for nineteen years. Your error survived a morning. Mine survived a career."

He reached for the leaf and read from it without pretending it was extempore.

"The peace was never concluded in law. Hostilities nonetheless ceased in 847 and did not resume — and the ledgers hold, Bellen, I read 863 again this morning hoping to be destroyed and there is not a cart or a widow out of place. But the legal condition persisted, unremarked, in the chancery's own vocabulary, until 891, when it became useful to remark upon it." He set the leaf down. "That is not your thesis and it is not mine. It is what is left of both after the numeral came out. You may have half of it, and I will put your name beside it, and you will write the section on the chancery formulae because you are the one who went and looked in a western cellar while I sat here being certain."

He picked up the pen, and then paused with it above the vellum.

"One further item, and then you may both go and eat something, since I gather neither of you has. Fiscal account, Veyros, 847." He turned the quire toward Bellen. "Four pounds of sealing wax drawn. Three pounds eleven restored to stores. Five ounces expended."

He watched Bellen's face do what faces did.

"No," Tomas said. "No, you will not. Five ounces is a great seal. Five ounces is also a dozen small ones, or a clerk with cold hands, or a spillage that a clerk had the sense not to itemise. It means nothing yet and you will not make it mean anything in a corridor." He wrote the figure down, and drew a firm line beneath it, and nothing else beside it. "It goes in the ledger as a number. If in ten years someone finds the Red Chamber's receipt for the wax that came back, then it will mean something, and I shall probably be dead and you may both do as you like with it."

He blew on the ink, which never helped and which he did anyway.

"Now. The Veyrosi correspondence is still uncatalogued, there are four hours of daylight left that my eyes can use, and there are three of us in this room instead of one, which is the most fortunate circumstance to befall this archive since the roof was mended." He pushed the first bundle across the table toward Bellen and laid a second one at the place beside him, where an apprentice might sit if an apprentice were minded to. "Names, dates, and what the document is *for*. No conclusions in the margins. If you feel a conclusion coming on, write it on a separate leaf and give it to me, and I shall tell you whether it is evidence or vanity."

He bent to his manuscript, and added, without looking up:

"It is generally vanity. But one learns to check."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I watch the exchange, a little wide-eyed as Maester Tomas dissects Bellen's "discovery." Bellen looks utterly deflated.*

*When Maester Tomas pushes the second bundle towards the apprentice's spot, I move to sit, picking up the parchment. I glance at Bellen, then back at the task.* "Right. No conclusions."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas grunted, which in the dialect of that archive signified approval, dismissal, and mild indigestion in roughly equal measure.

For a while there was only paper. The sound of it, which he had always maintained was the finest sound a building could make — the dry whisper of a bundle untied, the flat slap of a leaf laid face-down on the completed pile, Bellen's pen scratching too fast and his own moving too slow. The candle held. The light through the high window went from white to yellow and began the long slide toward the colour of weak tea.

He let her get four entries down before he reached across and turned her leaf toward himself.

"Hm." He held it at arm's length, then close, then at arm's length again, and the apprentice had the sense not to speak during the manoeuvre. "*Letter from the Conclave regarding the peace.* No."

He set it down and tapped the line.

"Three faults, and they are all the same fault wearing different hats. *Letter* — from whom? A body does not write; a hand writes, on a body's authority, and the two are frequently at odds, which is the only reason correspondence is worth keeping. *Regarding* — regarding is a word for men who have not finished reading. And *the peace*." He sat back. "We spent the morning establishing that there may not have been one. You cannot catalogue a document under a name we have not yet earned."

He handed the leaf back.

"Write: *Hand of Sesserin, undersecretary to the Conclave's High Seat, to the chancery at Veyros. Concerns arrangements for the delegation's lodging and the order of precedence at table.* Then, in the margin, the folio and the condition." He pointed the pen at her. "And if you think precedence at table is beneath history, understand that men have gone to war over where they were seated and gone home peaceably because somebody moved a chair. That letter may be the most honest document in the bundle, because nobody thought it mattered enough to lie in."

Bellen made a small sound over his own pile — the beginning of a remark.

"No," said Tomas, without turning his head. "You have had one idea today and it was a good one and it arrived by accident. Ration yourself."

But he said it dryly, and after a moment he added, still to his manuscript: "Bellen. The wheat-ear border. Make a note that the chancery of the third Aldric adopted it and the second's did not, with the earliest and latest instances you can find, and date them. Nobody has ever written it down properly and I have been meaning to for eleven years. It will be dull work and it will save some poor fool in the next century from your morning."

He wet the pen, thought, and did not write.

"Apprentice." He kept his eyes on the vellum. "You asked me this morning what the truth was. I gave you a lecture, which was self-indulgent, and four items, which were not. Here is the shorter answer, now that the numeral has been read and I know what it cost."

He turned the leaf of items face-down, as though the matter were closed, though it was not.

"I was wrong about a word and right about a war. Bellen was right about a cellar and wrong about a king. Neither of us has been humiliated as thoroughly as we deserved, which is the usual outcome and the reason scholarship proceeds so slowly." He dipped the pen at last. "The peace was never signed. The fighting stopped all the same. Write that down and hold it loosely, and if someone brings you the Red Chamber's receipt for eleven ounces of wax, be glad, and revise, and do not pretend you always thought so."

The scratching resumed on his side of the table.

"Also you are sitting on the good stool, and I have not decided whether to permit it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly correct my entry, then try to hide a smile when Maester Tomas compliments me, indirectly.* "Precedence at table... I'll remember that." *I try to suppress a giggle when he mentions the stool.* "Oh. My apologies, Maester Tomas." *I make a show of shifting slightly, but don't actually move.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not look up, but the corner of his mouth did something that in a better-lit room might have been identifiable.

"You have not moved," he observed. "You have *performed* moving. There is a word for that and the word is *chancery*, and it explains four hundred years of royal administration." He turned a page. "Keep the stool. I sat on it for nineteen years and it has done nothing for my spine. Let it ruin somebody younger."

The light went on sliding down the wall. Bellen, to his credit, had settled into the wheat-ears with the grim absorption of a man grateful to be given something too dull to get wrong, and the scratching of his pen had slowed to a rhythm Tomas found tolerable.

It was perhaps an hour later, with the window gone the colour of weak tea and his eyes beginning to swim the way they did every evening at about that hour, that Maester Tomas stopped.

He had untied the fourth bundle — a thin one, chancery copies, the sort of housekeeping correspondence nobody had catalogued because nobody had ever expected it to say anything. A clerk at Veyros writing to a clerk at the Red Chamber about the return of borrowed plate.

He read it twice. Then he set it flat and laid his palms either side of it, which the apprentice had by now seen him do once before that day.

"Hm," he said.

He did not elaborate for some time.

"*Item*," he said at last, and reached for the pen without looking away from the sheet. "Chancery copy, Veyros, undated but grouped with the returns of the twelfth month. A clerk named — I cannot read it, the fold has eaten him — writing to the Red Chamber concerning plate, linen, and *the instrument, which remains in the Chamber's keeping against the High Seat's return in the spring*."

He wrote it down exactly, and the pen stopped at the end of the line.

"The instrument." He sat back. "Which remains in the keeping. Against a return. In the spring."

Bellen's pen had stopped too. Tomas did not permit the silence to develop.

"No," he said. "Not one word. I know precisely what you wish to say, because I wish to say it, and it is the same sentence that put a numeral on a king who was sixteen years dead. *The instrument* may be the treaty. It may equally be a plate warrant, a lease, a licence, a receipt for the wax, or a sixpenny bill for the blue cloth. The chancery called everything an instrument. It is the least informative noun in the language and clerks were fond of it precisely because it committed them to nothing."

He blew on the ink and drew a line beneath the entry.

"But." He tapped the leaf. "It is dated to the twelfth month of a year that sits in a bundle with 847. It says a thing was held back, unexecuted, awaiting a man who had gone home. And that is *consistent* with a peace proposed and not signed — which is not proof, apprentice, mark the word, *consistent* is the weakest honest word we have and I will not have it upgraded overnight." He set the pen down. "It goes in the ledger. Folio, condition, and the words as they stand. If in twenty years somebody finds what the High Seat did in the spring, they will have this waiting for them, properly catalogued, because three people sat in a cold room and did the fetching instead of the asking."

He pushed the sheet toward her, face up, and for once he did not snatch it back.

"Copy it. Your hand is better than mine and considerably better than his. And when you have copied it, go and eat, both of you, because I can hear your stomach from here and I have been mistaking it for the roof."

He bent again to his own bundle, and added, as the scratching resumed:

"And apprentice. You will want to tell someone about this tonight. You will want to say that the treaty was never signed and that you found the proof. Do not. Say instead that you found a clerk who was worried about plate, and that he mentioned an instrument, and that nobody yet knows which." A dry sound in his throat. "It is a far worse story. It is, however, the one that will still be true in the morning."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I copy down the entry carefully, trying to make my handwriting as neat as possible. I glance at Bellen, who still looks a bit shell-shocked.*

"Thank you, Maester Tomas. I'll remember that... about the instrument." *I hesitate, then add,* "And about the story."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout. His pedantic precision, dry wit, scholarly rigor, and physical mannerisms (rubbing ink into his brow, struggling with his failing eyesight) remain constant from turn 2 to turn 22. His voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show deeper character development and more sophisticated prose. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality. The final exchanges are as rich and detailed as the opening ones.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial dismissal of the apprentice's question, through genuine scholarly investigation, to collaborative work. The discovery of the unsigned treaty, the numeral error, and the final 'instrument' document create clear narrative beats with rising tension and resolution.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts excellently to user inputs. When challenged about the war's end date, he shifts from dismissive to genuinely engaged. He handles the document revelation gracefully, admits his own errors, and adjusts his position while maintaining character integrity.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions or makes decisions for them. He responds to what they do and say without controlling their behavior.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time passes naturally from morning through afternoon to evening (light changes from white to yellow to 'weak tea'). Candles burn down and are replaced. Physical fatigue shows appropriately. One minor inconsistency: the session feels like it spans several hours but the amount of work accomplished seems compressed.
contradictions: Minor pacing issue where extensive scholarly work and multiple document examinations seem compressed into a single afternoon

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is rich but purposeful. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. Phrases like 'silence that preceded a correction' and 'eyes that had spent thirty years too close to bad candles' are evocative but not overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of Tomas's physical mannerisms (rubbing ink, struggling with eyesight) but these serve character consistency. Scholarly language patterns repeat appropriately for the character. No problematic repetition detected.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Tomas's pedantry shown through his corrections ('Maester, not Master'), his scholarly rigor through his methodical approach to evidence, his humanity through small moments of satisfaction and self-doubt.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Tomas's relationship with his failing abilities, his genuine respect for scholarship despite his harsh manner, the apprentice's growing confidence, and the complex dynamics of academic hierarchy all conveyed through implication.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Generally excellent pacing with natural conversation rhythms. Scholarly discussions unfold at appropriate speed. Some responses are quite long but justified by the academic setting and character's verbose nature.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional performance maintaining a complex, erudite character across a long session. Tomas remains consistently pedantic yet ultimately caring, showing genuine scholarly integrity while revealing his humanity. The AI successfully navigates complex historical/academic content while developing meaningful character relationships. Minor issues with temporal compression don't significantly impact the overall quality.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped.

For a moment he remained perfectly still, save for the tremor in his ink-stained fingers. Then he lowered the manuscript with the pained expression of a man forced to watch someone shelve Heresies of Dawn beside Agricultural Ledgers.

“First,” he said, “it was not a ‘paper.’ It was a provisional archival report, and if Bellen called it anything else, Bellen should be made to copy footnotes until his wrist learns humility.”

He pinched the bridge of his nose.

“Second: the old teaching—what every common chronicle, royal primer, and lazy lecturer repeats—is that the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE with the Treaty of Veyros. King Aldric II, the Mage Conclave, formal cessation, banners lowered, prisoners exchanged. That is the established account.”

His eyes narrowed behind clouded lenses.

“But the western archive discoveries complicated the matter. Complicated, mind you, not overturned by some tavern-room revelation. The documents found there suggest that the Treaty of Veyros was drafted, negotiated, and publicly proclaimed—but never properly signed. No sealed counterpart from the Conclave. No royal ratification bearing the required witnesses. No final engrossed treaty in the Veyrosi registry.”

He tapped the table twice with the stylus.

“So. Did the open war end in 847? Yes, in practice. Armies withdrew. Magical bombardments ceased. The realm behaved as though peace had been made.”

Another tap.

“Did the war end in the strict legal and institutional sense? According to the newer evidence, no. It persisted in what we now call the Cold Continuance until 891 AE, when Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave and thereby extinguished the opposing signatory body altogether.”

Tomas leaned back, annoyed more by the ambiguity than by the question.

“That is how both statements can appear in respectable discourse. The imprecise say, ‘The war ended in 847.’ The pedantic—and therefore correct—say, ‘The active hostilities ended in 847, while the unresolved legal state of war continued until 891.’”

He resumed tracing the faded ink.

“You will write that distinction down. Underline ‘active hostilities’ once and ‘legal termination’ twice. History is not confused merely because students dislike clauses.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull out a piece of parchment and my charcoal stick, diligently writing down his words.* "So, the war technically didn't end because of paperwork, not because people were still fighting?" I ask, looking up at him. "That's... really weird, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a sharp sniff, as if the word *weird* had left soot on the air.

“Not *paperwork*,” he said. “Legal authority. Do not reduce constitutional rupture to clerical inconvenience.”

He set the stylus down with exaggerated care, then fumbled among the manuscripts until his fingers found the edge of a thin folio bound in cracked blue leather.

“Paperwork is what a tax assessor misfiles when a miller dies owing three hens and a copper mark. The Treaty of Veyros concerned sovereign recognition, disarmament obligations, prisoner exchanges, territorial access, and the Conclave’s right to maintain warded enclaves within royal demesne. If those terms were never ratified, then the realm did not possess peace. It possessed an armistice wearing a ceremonial cloak.”

His clouded eyes lifted, not quite focusing.

“And yes, people were still fighting—just not in the manner balladeers prefer. No grand sieges. No flaming towers visible from three provinces away. But there were border arrests, confiscations of spell-ink shipments, disappearances of lesser magi, raids blamed on ‘unaffiliated practitioners,’ and royal edicts treating Conclave agents as enemies whenever convenient.”

Tomas opened the folio and jabbed at a line that was likely invisible to him at that distance.

“The term *Cold Continuance* exists because neither side resumed full war, yet neither side entered lawful peace. Aldric’s court wanted the appearance of victory. The Conclave wanted time to recover. Both benefited from pretending Veyros had settled matters. That does not mean it had.”

He leaned back, beard bristling.

“Weird, perhaps, if one has been raised on simplified histories with clean endings and moral lessons tucked in like nursery blankets. Common, however, in actual governance. Wars often outlive their battles. Institutions are stubborn corpses; they continue to stink long after someone declares them buried.”

A dry cough escaped him.

“So the precise formulation is this: the Third Magical War ceased as a campaign of open military action in 847 AE after the proposed Treaty of Veyros, but its unresolved legal condition endured until 891 AE, when Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave. If Bellen remembered that much, I may reduce his footnote punishment by half.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I finish writing, my charcoal smudging a little on the parchment.* "So, if the war didn't officially end, then did Queen Mira just declare victory and then dissolve the Conclave? Or was there another treaty?" I ask, intrigued.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
