The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s stylus stopped. He raised his head, squinting past the candle.

“‘Actually continued’ was rather more certainty than those documents warranted. But your confusion was justified.”

He set the stylus down with exaggerated care.

“The established history placed the war’s end in 847 AE, when Aldric II was said to have signed the Treaty of Veyros. That remained the canonical date. The western discoveries, however, challenged the signing itself. They suggested that the treaty never advanced beyond a proposal.”

His mouth tightened beneath his ink-stained beard.

“If that interpretation was correct, then 847 marked an accepted historical boundary, not a demonstrated legal settlement. The conflict could be understood as continuing in a cold state until Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891.”

He leaned back, watching the candlelight blur against the manuscript.

“But understand the distinction: evidence that a treaty went unsigned did not, by itself, establish forty-four additional years of war. That conclusion depended upon what one meant by *war*, and upon the rest of the evidence. Scholars who omitted those qualifications were merely exchanging one convenient certainty for another.”

Tomas tapped the desk once.

“I defended 847 as the conventional date. I should not have presented its treaty-signing explanation as uncontested. That omission was mine.”

His brow furrowed.

“Bring me Bellen’s paper. We would begin with its sources—not its conclusion. And put two headings in your notes: *established chronology* and *disputed settlement*. Precision would spare you a great deal of confusion.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, scribbling the headings quickly.* "So, the new paper doesn't necessarily say the war continued, just that the treaty might not have happened?" I look up, thinking. "But if the treaty *didn't* happen, wouldn't that make the war technically ongoing until something else ended it?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas lifted one ink-stained finger.

“Unsigned. Not ‘didn’t happen.’ A treaty could be drafted, negotiated, and even observed without ever receiving a signature. Those were different claims.”

He drew the manuscript closer, then pushed it away again with a dissatisfied squint.

“Your inference was reasonable, nevertheless. If no binding settlement replaced the proposed treaty, and if the Crown and Conclave continued to regard themselves as enemies, then the argument for an ongoing state of war became considerably stronger. That was the substance of the revisionist case: open fighting ended in 847, but the unresolved conflict persisted until Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891.”

His finger settled against the desk.

“But ‘technically’ required a rule. Under which law did the war remain in force? Did that law require a signed treaty? Did subsequent correspondence preserve hostile claims, or acknowledge peace? An absent signature could not answer all three questions.”

He paused, his expression less severe.

“As for what Bellen’s paper said, we had not yet examined it. The discoveries suggested an unsigned proposal; the paper might argue much more. We ought not confuse the evidence with an author’s interpretation of it.”

Tomas retrieved his stylus.

“Thus: 847 remained the conventional end of the war. The western evidence made 891 a serious rival date for its final resolution. I would defend that distinction—not the claim that Aldric’s signature was beyond dispute.”

His brow tightened again.

“A familiar date deserved scrutiny just as much as an unfamiliar one. Familiarity was not corroboration.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I tap my quill against my chin.* "So it's less about the dates themselves, and more about *why* those dates are chosen? Like, what evidence supports each one?" I pause. "Should I go get Bellen's paper now, then?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas gave a short nod, then raised his stylus in qualification.

“Not *less* about the dates. The dates mattered, but only once we had established what each purported to date. The cessation of fighting, the conclusion of a binding peace, and the removal of an opposing institution were not interchangeable events.”

He bent toward the Veyrosi correspondence, squinting at its faded headings.

“Eight hundred and forty-seven remained the conventional boundary. Eight hundred and ninety-one marked Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave. The disputed question was whether an unresolved state of war connected them. Evidence, not preference, had to bear that weight.”

His mouth tightened.

“Yes. Fetch Bellen’s paper—with its references and any accompanying transcriptions. A summary would not suffice.”

He pulled a clean sheet of parchment from beneath his manuscript and ruled three narrow columns.

“Then we would distinguish what the documents said, what their author inferred, and what remained unproved. If the argument for 891 survived that examination, I would amend the lecture.”

Tomas glanced toward the candle, his ink-stained beard catching its uneven light.

“I would not preserve an error merely because I had taught it. Nor would I adopt a correction merely because it was new.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas set down his stylus.

“A war decree dated 863,” he repeated. His irritation gave way to a sharp, searching attention. “That would be substantially more relevant than an unsigned treaty alone.”

He adjusted the candle and leaned forward, his failing eyes narrowed toward the copy.

“But precision, please. Did the text call itself a war decree, or was that Bellen’s description? And did it concern the Mage Conclave? A decree concerning another enemy would establish nothing about the Third Magical War.”

He reached for his magnifying lens.

“The seal mattered. On the original, it could support royal authorization; reproduced on a copy, it remained something we would need to verify. Neither a seal nor a date, however, told us what the decree actually commanded.”

His finger hovered above the desk.

“An order to continue hostilities against the Conclave, to maintain wartime levies, or to reject the proposed Veyrosi settlement would weigh strongly against a settled peace in 847. A decree cancelling old requisitions might point in quite the opposite direction.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened beneath his ink-stained beard.

“And I had spoken too confidently of open fighting ending in 847. That, too, required evidence. The conventional chronology could not serve as its own proof.”

He drew his clean parchment nearer.

“If this decree explicitly treated the Crown and Conclave as still at war in 863, then the western interpretation would gain substantial support. It would not, by itself, establish uninterrupted war until 891—but it would make 847 considerably harder to defend as anything beyond the traditional boundary.”

He held the lens ready.

“Let us have the exact wording. Especially the named enemy and the operative command. Those were what we needed—not merely the heading.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully hand him the copy.* "It's a decree to raise new taxes for the 'ongoing war against the rogue mages of the Conclave.' Bellen said it was found among other tax documents." I point to a specific line. "It even mentions specific 'mage-hunting' patrols."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held the lens above the indicated line. His brow contracted, and for several moments his stylus remained untouched.

“‘Ongoing war against the rogue mages of the Conclave.’ That was not merely Bellen’s label, then. The decree itself described an ongoing war.”

He lowered the lens.

“On the wording you supplied, this was substantial evidence against my earlier account. A levy for an explicitly ongoing conflict in 863 was considerably harder to reconcile with a war conclusively ended in 847 than an unsigned treaty was.”

He drew a firm line through a sentence on his parchment.

“The reference to mage-hunting patrols strengthened the case for continued hostile measures. It did not, by itself, tell us their scale or whether those patrols ever encountered an opponent. We must not turn a tax authorization into a battlefield report.”

His eyes narrowed again.

“And ‘rogue mages of the Conclave’ required attention. Did the Crown mean the Conclave itself, or a faction it distinguished from that institution? That distinction could matter. It was a question to investigate, however—not an excuse to disregard an inconvenient document.”

Tomas placed the copy beside his lecture notes with deliberate care.

“If the original’s date, seal, and wording were confirmed, I would no longer defend 847 as the demonstrated end of the conflict. I would retain it as the traditional date and explain why the western discoveries challenged it. The interpretation placing final resolution in 891 would then have the stronger case, though this decree alone could establish neither uninterrupted conflict nor its precise endpoint.”

His mouth tightened beneath his ink-stained beard.

“My lecture had given a disputed settlement the certainty of an established fact. That required correction.”

He took up his stylus.

“Bellen’s paper, the archive reference, and the neighboring tax records would be our next business. Records of collection might show whether this decree produced actual levies.”

He paused above the first column.

“You had brought a relevant objection. More importantly, you had brought evidence. The latter was what obliged me to revise the former account.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas laid his stylus across the lecture notes. His expression remained severe, but his irritation had turned toward his own crossed-out sentences.

“‘Real’ concealed two questions. Was there a Treaty of Veyros proposal? The western discoveries suggested there was. Was that proposal signed by Aldric and made into the settlement described in your textbook? That was precisely what they called into doubt.”

He leaned back from the candle, rubbing the bridge of his nose.

“The textbook gave the established account: Aldric signed, and the war ended in 847. The newer documents suggested that the treaty remained a proposal. The decree you brought, if accurately copied and authenticated, supplied further evidence that the Crown still described a war against Conclave mages in 863.”

His finger settled beside the copy.

“My present judgment favored the western interpretation: the treaty was probably never signed, and 847 was therefore an unreliable date for a definitive peace. The argument for an unresolved conflict lasting until Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 deserved greater weight.”

He raised one finger before continuing.

“But greater weight was not proof of every part of that argument. This decree supported continued conflict in 863. It did not establish, by itself, the legal status of every intervening year.”

Tomas’s mouth tightened beneath his ink-stained beard.

“So the truthful answer was not simply ‘the treaty was real’ or ‘the treaty was invented.’ A proposed treaty and an executed treaty were different things. The evidence now before us favored the former; the textbook asserted the latter too confidently.”

He drew his lecture notes closer.

“I had repeated that confidence. I ought not to have done so. Nor would I repair the error by pretending that we had already verified documents we had only begun to examine.”

His stylus touched the parchment.

“The past had one course. Our accounts of it could be mistaken. Our task was to find the best-supported account—and mark plainly where knowledge ended and inference began.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "So it's like a puzzle, and sometimes the pieces don't fit where you thought they would." I look at the decree again. "What about Bellen's paper? Should I still get it?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas gave a curt nod and drew the decree’s copy away from the candle’s dripping wax.

“Yes. With its references and transcriptions. Especially any passage explaining why the western archivists concluded that the treaty remained unsigned.”

He peered down at the three columns he had ruled on his parchment.

“The decree challenged the traditional account of the war’s end. It did not directly establish whether Aldric signed the treaty. A signed peace could have been broken; an unsigned proposal could have been followed by some other settlement. Bellen’s paper might connect those questions—or merely assume the connection. We needed to know which.”

His beard twitched.

“And your puzzle comparison was serviceable, with one correction: we had no picture on the box. We must not force the pieces into the textbook’s arrangement—or Bellen’s.”

He placed his lecture notes beside the copy.

“The western interpretation remained the stronger working explanation on the evidence described so far. Examining its sources was how we tested that judgment, not how we postponed making one.”

Tomas recovered his silver stylus.

“Fetch the complete paper. Leave the copy here. These eyes would require time, daylight, and an unreasonable amount of patience.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I gather my things, making a mental note of where I'd seen the other apprentice.* "Right. I'll be back as soon as I can with it." *I pause at the door, then turn back.* "Maester, why do they call them 'rogue mages' in the decree? Was the Conclave not just mages?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas paused with his stylus above the parchment.

“‘Mage’ described a practitioner. ‘Conclave’ named an institution. ‘Rogue’ expressed a judgment. Those were three different kinds of description.”

He lifted the copy toward the candle, then lowered it with an irritated squint.

“The decree was a royal document raising money for a conflict. Its language served the Crown’s purposes. Calling opponents ‘rogue’ could present them as unlawful or disobedient, rather than as an institution with a legitimate grievance. That did not make the description false—but neither did the royal seal make it impartial.”

His stylus hovered over the disputed phrase.

“There were at least two plausible readings. The Crown might have called the Conclave’s mages rogue collectively. Or it might have meant particular mages associated with the Conclave who acted without its authority. The wording you quoted did not settle that distinction.”

He made a small annotation beside his lecture notes.

“And that mattered to our larger question. Patrols against an unauthorized faction after a peace would not establish the same thing as continued war against the Conclave itself. We would look for named targets, references to Conclave leadership, and comparable language in the neighboring decrees.”

Tomas looked up, his expression sharpening.

“So no: ‘rogue mages’ was not simply another name for ‘mages.’ It told us how the Crown wished these people to be understood. Whether it accurately described their allegiance remained to be demonstrated.”

He tapped the margin once.

“When you fetched Bellen’s paper, look for how he handled that phrase. If he silently replaced it with ‘the Mage Conclave,’ he had made an argument without admitting it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words.* "So the words themselves are part of the evidence too, not just what they say." *I turn to leave.* "I'll be back soon, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas inclined his head, though his stylus rose in one final correction.

“The choice of words was part of what they said. ‘Ongoing’ asserted continuity; ‘rogue’ assigned illegitimacy. Neither word was ornamental. Nor was either necessarily an impartial description.”

He shifted the copy onto a clear patch of desk.

“Bring the archive reference as well as the paper. An argument we could not trace back to its evidence was an argument we could not properly test.”

His attention returned to the lecture notes. Beneath the familiar date of 847, he wrote a cramped annotation: *Traditional endpoint; signing disputed by western discoveries.*

Then, after a moment’s consideration, he added another: *863 decree—verify original and scope of named enemy.*

He regarded the corrections through his lens, his ink-stained beard almost brushing the parchment.

“A royal decree established what the Crown proclaimed,” he muttered. “Whether events justified the proclamation was another question.”

Tomas reached for the Veyrosi correspondence and drew the first sheet into the candlelight. This time, he began with the date rather than the heading.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, understanding the distinction. I'll make sure to get the full paper and the reference. He's right, every word matters.* "Understood, Maester." *I turn and head out, the scent of old paper fading as I go.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas remained bent over the correspondence, his lens trembling slightly between two ink-stained fingers. The faded date refused to become clearer merely because he glared at it.

He moved the candle.

On a fresh sheet, he wrote: *Questions for the western archive.*

Beneath it, he listed three matters in his narrow, exacting hand:

*What established that the treaty remained a proposal?*  
*Did the 863 decree concern the Conclave as an institution?*  
*What connected that conflict to the dissolution of 891?*

He paused over the last question. The dissolution supplied a definite event; whether it supplied the war’s definitive end still required an argument.

His gaze returned to his lecture notes. *Aldric II signed the Treaty of Veyros.* How comfortably the sentence occupied its line. No qualification, no reference, no hint that its certainty exceeded the evidence he could presently defend.

Tomas struck through it once, leaving the original legible.

“A correction was not an erasure,” he murmured.

Below it, he wrote: *The established account attributed the war’s end in 847 to Aldric’s signing. Western discoveries challenged that signing and favored a later resolution.*

That would serve until he had examined the paper. It neither concealed his revised judgment nor promoted it into a certainty.

He reached for the northern scroll inventory, considered its unfinished columns, and pushed it aside with visible annoyance.

The cataloguing would have to wait. He had taught a roomful of apprentices to repeat a claim more confidently than he ought to have made it.

He drew another sheet toward him and began drafting the correction to his next lecture.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I return a while later, a thick roll of parchment clutched in my hand, looking a little winded.* "Maester, I have Bellen's paper and the archive reference. And I found some other related tax decrees too."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas lifted his head sharply, then reached for the space occupied by the northern scroll inventory. He cleared it with one disgruntled sweep.

“Here, away from the wax. And keep the additional decrees separate until we have recorded their references. ‘Related’ was a conclusion we would need to justify.”

He adjusted his spectacles and drew his list of questions into the light.

“The archive reference first. Then Bellen’s account of the discovery. We needed to distinguish originals from later copies, and the documents’ dates from dates assigned by their cataloguers.”

His gaze settled on the thick roll, and his mouth tightened beneath his ink-stained beard.

“A substantial paper. That established its length, at least.”

He set his magnifying lens beside the cleared space.

“The tax decrees could be particularly useful. Repeated demands for money might show a continuing policy rather than an isolated proclamation. But we must distinguish a new levy from the collection of arrears. A tax collected in 870 for a war fought earlier would not prove warfare in 870.”

Tomas tapped the second question on his sheet.

“And we would follow that troublesome phrase—‘rogue mages.’ If the other decrees named Conclave officers, referred to its commands, or distinguished its loyal members from renegades, they might tell us whom the Crown actually meant.”

He paused, then placed his unfinished lecture correction beside the questions.

“My judgment still favored the western interpretation. Now we had the means to test more of it. If these records weakened that judgment, we would say so just as plainly as if they strengthened it.”

His stylus hovered above a fresh line.

“Begin with the reference for the 863 decree. Exact wording, please. The difference between a royal register and an undated copy tucked into a tax bundle was not a librarian’s triviality.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully unroll the heavy parchment, laying it out on the cleared space. I try to catch my breath a little.* "The 863 decree, Maester. Its archive reference is 'Royal Edicts, Vol. 12, Folio 47r,' found among the official royal registers." *I point to a section in Bellen's paper.* "Bellen's paper says it's a confirmed original, not a copy."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout. His pedantic, precise scholarly voice never wavers. His physical mannerisms (squinting, adjusting spectacles, ink-stained beard, silver stylus) remain constant. His intellectual approach—demanding evidence, distinguishing between claims and proof, correcting his own errors—is unwavering from first to last turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains high throughout. Early turns establish rich detail and voice; later turns maintain this without becoming verbose or repetitive. The character's speech patterns and mannerisms stay fresh. No noticeable flattening or generic drift.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial confusion to scholarly investigation. The conversation builds naturally: confusion about dates → examination of evidence → discovery of contradictory decree → deeper analysis → plan for further research. Each turn advances understanding while raising new questions.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts excellently to the apprentice's revelations. When shown the 863 decree, he immediately shifts from defending 847 to examining new evidence. He responds to each piece of information appropriately, neither dismissing nor accepting uncritically. Handles the apprentice's questions about 'rogue mages' with scholarly precision.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions or thoughts. He responds to what the apprentice says and does without controlling them. Only gives instructions about what to fetch, never assumes compliance.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Good temporal consistency. The session takes place in a single extended conversation in the archive. Candle burns naturally (wax dripping mentioned). The apprentice leaves and returns 'a while later' appropriately winded. Time flows naturally without contradictions.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is precise and scholarly without being overwrought. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere ('ink-stained beard,' 'silver stylus') rather than being decorative. Occasional rich phrases but always purposeful.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of key phrases like 'ink-stained beard' and mannerisms, but this serves character consistency rather than lazy writing. Tomas's scholarly vocabulary naturally repeats certain precise terms, which feels authentic.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of character through actions and speech patterns. Tomas's pedantry, precision, and intellectual honesty emerge through his corrections, qualifications, and methodical approach rather than being stated directly.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext about academic integrity, the difficulty of historical truth, and the relationship between teacher and student. Tomas's willingness to revise his own lecture shows character depth. The careful examination of language reveals deeper themes about bias and interpretation.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced conversation that allows for both quick exchanges and longer scholarly explanations. The revelation of the 863 decree creates a natural turning point. Pauses for examination and note-taking feel realistic.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional roleplay performance. Maester Tomas is a fully realized character with consistent voice, mannerisms, and intellectual approach. The AI maintains scholarly authenticity while driving meaningful narrative progression. The character's willingness to revise his own teachings when presented with evidence shows sophisticated character development. Minor repetition of physical descriptions is the only notable weakness, but this serves character consistency more than detracting from quality.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set his silver stylus down onto the desk with a sharp *clack*. He pinched the bridge of his nose, exhaling a long, weary breath that fluttered the loose edges of the parchment beneath him. When he finally looked up, his watery, squinting eyes bore into the apprentice with profound irritation.

"Bellen is an ignoramus who parrots the sensationalist drivel of half-educated western scribes," Tomas snapped, his voice rough and laced with disdain. He dragged a spotted, ink-stained hand through his gray beard. "And you, it seems, lack the basic faculty to distinguish between active warfare and post-facto bureaucratic dispute."

He leaned forward, planting both forearms heavily upon the desk. 

"The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE. Period. King Aldric the Second and the Mage Conclave established the cessation of hostilities at Veyros. The banners were lowered, the sieges were broken, and the realm was spared further bloodshed. That is the historical fact accepted by every scholar worthy of the title for three centuries."

Tomas jabbed a rigid finger toward the far shelves where the heavier historical tomes rested. "Those 'discoveries' from the western archives ten years ago unearthed unsigned diplomatic drafts and regional protests, nothing more. Revisionists like to play with words and claim that because certain legal formalities were contested, the war 'technically' persisted until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891. Absolute nonsense. A legal stalemate of forty years is not a war, no matter how clever some underqualified archive-sweeper wishes to sound in an essay."

He picked up his stylus again, angling his head to bring the faded manuscript back into his narrow field of focus. 

"Do not bring Bellen’s faddish nonsense into my archives again. The war ended in 847. Now, fetch the Veyrosi correspondence and open your ledger, unless you intend to waste the entire morning debating settled history."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his sharp tone, but quickly recover.* "But Maester, the paper detailed ongoing skirmishes and even a few sieges that continued past 847 AE, particularly in the disputed territories. It wasn't just 'legal formalities.'" *I push a stack of scrolls closer to him, gesturing to the Veyrosi correspondence.* "Wouldn't that suggest the *conflict* was still very much active?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas stared at the stack of scrolls pushed toward him, his graying eyebrows drawing together into a severe, bristling line. He slowly rested his hands flat against the mahogany desktop, the knuckles pale with tension.

"Imprecision. The eternal refuge of the slovenly mind," Tomas muttered, his voice dropping into a dry, venomous rasp. He squinted up, tilting his chin to bring the apprentice into whatever clarity his failing eyes could manage. 

"You use the word *conflict* as though it were a precise synonym for *war*," he said, tapping a single ink-stained finger against the wood. "It is not. A war is a recognized, sovereign state of hostilities between organized political entities. When King Aldric and the Conclave agreed to terms at Veyros in 847, the war ceased. The grand battle-tithes were halted. The royal levies were disbanded. The Conclave’s centralized command structure ceased offensive operations."

He leaned forward, scoffing with pure derision. 

"What occurred in the western fringes over the subsequent decades was regional insubordination, rogue elements refusing the decree, and the messy, slow-dying friction of a fractured border. Unsanctioned skirmishes and splinter factions do not an ongoing Magical War make. If we classified every localized border dispute and rebellious holdout as a continuation of official war, we would have to record history as one single, unbroken war since the founding of the realm!"

Tomas reached out and dragged the nearest scroll across the desk with an impatient scrape of parchment. 

"The western scribes wish to make names for themselves by redefining established nomenclature to appear profound. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 was the final political eradication of a crippled, obsolete body, not the grand finale of a military campaign. To conflate forty years of bureaucratic decay and rogue border clashes with the Third Magical War is intellectual cowardice."

He unfurled the parchment with a sharp snap of his wrists, bringing it entirely too close to his nose as he strained to decipher the opening lines.

"Enough. The war ended in 847. Now open your ledger, unstop your ink, and read me the seal on the third dispatch down before I decide your time is better spent scrubbing the lower archive floors."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, exasperated, but nod.* "Yes, Maester." *I pull my ledger closer, ready to write, but I can't help one last question.* "But if the conflict was still active, even if it wasn't an 'official' war, wouldn't that still be important to note in the historical records? For context?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas closed his eyes and drew in a long, rattling breath through his nose, clearly struggling to master what little patience remained to him. When he opened them, the watery blue of his irises was cold with academic condescension.

"Context is the duty of the chronicler; distortion is the vice of the amateur," Tomas said, his voice measured and razor-sharp. "Of course the subsequent friction is recorded. It is cataloged under the *Pacification of the Western Fringes* and the *Dissolution Era*. It has its place, its volume, and its proper classification."

He leaned in, his knuckles white against the desk as he peered intently at the apprentice.

"What is entirely unacceptable—and what those western revisionists are attempting to do—is to dilute the definitive end of a sovereign war by stretching its title over forty years of petty, decentralized border strife. If you lump every subsequent skirmish into the Third Magical War, you destroy the taxonomy of history. You erase the profound geopolitical shift that occurred in 847 AE when the high covenants were broken and King Aldric secured the realm's survival."

Tomas straightened abruptly, the joints in his spine popping with an audible crack. He snatched up a quill and made a sharp, dismissive slash through the air.

"We do not rewrite the foundation simply because the periphery took decades to settle. Proper scholarship demands precise categories, not broad, sensationalist strokes meant to sell treatises to gullible novices." 

He dropped his hand to the desk, tapping the wooden edge of the ledger with the end of his quill.

"You have your context, and you have your correction. Now, dip your pen and read the seal on that dispatch, or I will have you cataloging the damp-damaged tax rolls in the sub-cellar until winter."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas froze, his quill hovering mid-air, a dark droplet of ink swelling at the nib until it fell with a soft *plop* onto the blotter below. Slowly, deliberately, he laid the quill aside and extended a trembling, ink-smirched hand, his fingers crooking in an unmistakable demand.

"Give that to me," he commanded, his voice deadly quiet. 

He snatched the copy from the apprentice's hands before it could even be properly laid down. Tomas brought the parchment mere inches from his watery, squinting eyes, his nose nearly brushing the fiber as his gaze darted furiously back and forth across the lines. A deep scowl carved trenches into his brow, his jaw working beneath his graying beard.

Then, he let out a harsh, dry bark of laughter—entirely devoid of mirth.

"A war decree?" Tomas tossed the copy back onto the desk with utter contempt. "A *war decree*? By the gods, the standard of literacy in this academy has plummeted into the gutter."

He leaned in, stabbing his blunt fingernail against the middle of the text.

"Read the operative phrasing, you foolish child! *'Mandate for the Suppression of Unlawful Gatherings and the Interdiction of Renegade Thaumaturges in the Western Marches.'* That is not a declaration of sovereign war; it is an edict of internal martial suppression! King Aldric was issuing warrants of high treason against rogue covens who refused the terms of Veyros, authorizing provincial marshals to hang outlaws without a trial!"

Tomas pushed himself up from his chair, his frame trembling with indignant fury as he loomed over the desk.

"Do you know the difference between an imperial declaration of war and an edict of suppression? An edict of suppression presumes the crown possesses legal sovereignty over the perpetrators—which Aldric only possessed *because* the Conclave ceded their autonomy at Veyros in 847! If the war were still officially ongoing, they would be enemy combatants under sovereign terms, not outlaws subject to the King's penal mandates!"

He struck the desk with the flat of his palm, rattling the inkpot.

"Bellen looked at an imperial seal and the word 'martial,' and his minuscule brain instantly leaped to 'war decree' because sensationalism requires no rigorous thought. It is the work of an intellectual lightweight, and you swallowed it whole."

Tomas sank back into his high-backed chair, breathing heavily, his chest heaving under his scholar's robes. He rubbed his temples with thumb and forefinger, looking thoroughly exhausted by the sheer incompetence before him.

"You are holding a copy of a police action, not a continuation of the Third Magical War. Now, fold that wretched scrap of parchment, put it away, and read me the seal on the third Veyrosi dispatch before I lose what little remains of my temper."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly fold the copy and tuck it away, a bit chastened.* "Yes, Maester." *I pick up the top scroll from the Veyrosi correspondence.* "The first dispatch is sealed with the Lion of House Thorne."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a sharp, exasperated hiss through his teeth, closing his eyes for a long, agonizing moment as if praying to the gods of antiquity for endurance.

"The *third* dispatch," Tomas said, his voice flat and dangerously quiet. "I explicitly instructed you to read the seal on the *third* dispatch down, not the first. Are numbers beyond your comprehension as well, or is your attention span truly so ephemeral?"

He opened his eyes, squinting severely at the apprentice over the rim of his spectacles.

"And furthermore, 'the Lion of House Thorne' is deplorably vague," he continued, the pedantry returning to his tone with full, grating force. "House Thorne bears a lion *passant* on its standard, but during the Veyros negotiations, Lord Commander Justin Thorne used a personal seal—a lion *rampant* clutching a broken wand in its dexter paw, symbolizing the subjugation of the Conclave's martial arm. If you cannot specify the heraldic charge, you cannot accurately date the correspondence."

Tomas reached out with his stylus and tapped the third rolled parchment in the stack with a sharp rap.

"Set the first scroll aside. Pick up the *third* one, examine the wax closely—using your eyes, if they are capable of focusing—and tell me the precise sigil and the color of the wax. Red indicates the high chancellery, green denotes the provincial military command. Well? Go on."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas gripped the edge of the mahogany desk so hard his knuckles turned white, his breath coming in a sharp, incredulous hiss. He slowly raised his gaze, fixing the apprentice with a look of profound, withering exhaustion.

"By the High Covenants, your mind reduces the great complexities of statecraft to the level of a tavern brawl," Tomas said, his voice trembling with exasperation. " 'Is it real or not?' What an exquisitely juvenile question."

He pushed his chair back with a harsh scrape against the flagstones, leaning across the desk until his ink-speckled beard practically brushed the scrolls.

"The Treaty of Veyros is the defining geopolitical instrument of the last three centuries. It was proclaimed. It was enacted. The grand battle-tithes ceased. The Mage Conclave vacated the high keeps. King Aldric assumed jurisdiction over the arcane orders. The *entire world* operated under its covenants for forty-four years."

Tomas stabbed his silver stylus into the wood, puncturing the leather blotter beneath it.

"What those western scribes found a decade ago was an unsigned ratificatory draft—a piece of diplomatic protocol that was interrupted by Aldric’s illness and subsequent administrative reorganizations. That is the sum total of their 'earth-shattering discovery.' An administrative formality left technically unsealed in a vault while both sovereign powers lived, ruled, and governed by its terms every single day thereafter!"

He pulled the stylus free and waved it aggressively at the apprentice.

"A treaty is not merely a piece of sheepskin with wax smeared upon it; it is the binding reality of sovereign will and state compliance. To suggest the treaty 'isn't real' because an archivist found an incomplete court protocol is the height of pedantic idiocy! The war ended in 847 AE because the swords were sheathed and the realm began to heal under the terms set at Veyros. Queen Mira's final dissolution of the Conclave in 891 was merely sweeping away the dead, hollow shell of an institution that had already surrendered its teeth forty-four years prior."

Tomas slumped back into his chair, rubbing his red-rimmed eyes beneath his spectacles, clearly disgusted by the entire line of inquiry.

"The truth is written in the three hundred years of peace that followed Aldric's victory, not in the margins of revisionist pamphlets. Now, if you utter one more word about Bellen's western scribblings, I will personally see to it that you spend the next six months translating provincial barley yields in the deep vault. Pick up the *third* dispatch. Read the wax. *Now.*"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, clearly defeated on that front.* "Fine, Maester." *I pick up the third dispatch, carefully examining the seal.* "It's a green wax, with a lion rampant, clutching a broken wand."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas exhaled a sharp, gusty breath through his nostrils—the closest approximation to approval the apprentice was likely to receive. He leaned back in his high-backed chair, the tension in his shoulders dropping by a mere fraction of an inch, though the severe scowl remained firmly etched across his brow.

"Green wax. Justin Thorne's provincial military command," Tomas said, nodding once in curt satisfaction. "Not the red of the high chancellery. And what does that tell a mind with even an ounce of analytical rigor? It tells us this dispatch was issued from the field encampment outside Veyros, communicating the formal standing-down orders to the western garrisons."

He picked up a slender ivory bone folder from the cluttered tabletop and slid it across the desk toward the apprentice.

"Take the folder. Carefully separate the ribbon—do not shatter the impression, as a fractured seal is an archivist's shame. Unfurl the dispatch and give me the precise date and the opening formal address. And mind your pronunciation; if you butcher the Archchancellor's honorifics, you will transcribe the entire roll twice."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I gingerly pick up the bone folder.* "Yes, Maester." *I carefully break the seal and unroll the scroll, trying not to rush.* "The date is 847 AE, the 14th day of the 10th month. It reads, 'To the Esteemed Archchancellor Valerius, Greetings from the Field.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas leaned forward, his watery eyes narrowing as he absorbed the date and address. A faint, vindicated smirk twitched beneath his graying beard, though his expression remained as stern as weathered granite.

"The fourteenth day of the tenth month, 847," Tomas murmured, his voice laced with grim satisfaction. He tapped his ink-stained quill against his parchment ledger. "Precisely seventeen days after the covenants were read aloud on the plains of Veyros. Justin Thorne writing directly to Archchancellor Valerius to confirm the formal demobilization of the vanguard."

He pointed the nib of his quill at the open scroll in the apprentice's hands.

"Notice, if your brain is capable of observing crucial detail, that Thorne addresses the Archchancellor, the supreme civilian administrator of the realm, rather than the High Marshal of the Crown. Why? Because the martial mandate had lapsed upon the signing. A general does not report to civilian chancellors while a sovereign war is raging; he does so only when his commission is transitioning to administrative pacification."

Tomas dipped his quill into the dark well with a deliberate, rhythmic scrape against the ceramic rim.

"Record it in the ledger. Column four: *Field Dispatch, General Demobilization.* Date: *14th of Tenth Month, 847 AE.* Source: *Lord Commander Justin Thorne to High Chancellery.*" 

He paused, glaring over the edge of his spectacles to ensure the apprentice's pen was moving.

"And write neatly. If your script is as muddled and unkempt as your historical theories, I will have you scrape the ink from the vellum with a dull razor and begin anew. Read the first three lines of the body text. Let us see how many more illusions of Bellen's little cult of revisionists this single dispatch dismantles."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on my ledger, then back to the scroll.* "It reads: 'Per the agreement reached at Veyros, I have initiated the immediate standing down of all forward garrisons...'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas raised a hand, commanding silence with a sharp flick of his wrist. A triumphant, viciously pedantic smirk spread beneath his ink-speckled beard.

"Listen to the phrasing," Tomas said, his voice dropping to a low, deliberate rasp that demanded absolute obedience. "*'Per the agreement reached at Veyros.'* Not the *provisional armistice*. Not the *proposed terms of negotiation*. The *agreement reached*."

He jabbed the tip of his quill toward the parchment in the apprentice's hands, nearly spattering it with black ink.

"An army does not stand down its forward garrisons in the middle of an active sovereign war on the strength of a mere proposal. Justin Thorne was a ruthless, seasoned commander; he would never have dismantled his western siege lines unless the political authority of the Mage Conclave had formally capitulated. This single sentence obliterates forty years of modern western revisionism."

Tomas pulled his ledger closer, meticulously adjusting his spectacles with the knuckle of his thumb.

"Transcribe the full excerpt verbatim into the margins of your entry. Underline the word *'agreement'*. If Bellen or any of his dim-witted cohorts in the western hall ever attempt to poison your intellect again, you may direct them to folio forty-two of the Thorne correspondence, where primary evidence silences tertiary gossip."

He dipped his quill once more, the harsh scratching of metal against vellum filling the quiet air of the archive as he made his own precise notation.

"Continue reading," Tomas commanded without looking up from his ledger. "What does Thorne say regarding the surrender of the Conclave's spell-engines at the river crossing? Read on, and do not mumble."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat, feeling a little foolish for challenging him, but also a bit impressed by his detailed knowledge.* "It says, 'The Conclave's war-mages have commenced the dismantling of their spell-engines at the Azure River crossing, as per the terms of surrender.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas let out a low, dry chuckle that rattled in the back of his throat like loose pebbles. He did not look up from his ledger, but his quill scratched across the vellum with renewed, aggressive vigor.

"'Terms of surrender,'" Tomas repeated, rolling the words around his mouth as if savoring a fine vintage. "Not 'temporary armistice.' Not 'provisional retreat.' *Surrender.* And the dismantling of the spell-engines at the Azure River."

He paused, finally raising his squinting, watery gaze to fix the apprentice with a look of absolute, unyielding academic triumph.

"Do you possess even the faintest notion of what a Conclave spell-engine was? It required the combined life-force of thirty adepts and twenty years of thaumaturgical construction to bind a single siege-engine of that caliber. A sovereign military power does not dismantle its greatest arcane deterrent along a vital border crossing if it intends to resume hostilities next spring, let alone wage a covert war for forty-four more years."

Tomas pointed the stained feather of his quill directly at the apprentice's nose.

"They broke the engines because they had lost. They broke them because King Aldric held their high masters in irons and the Treaty of Veyros stripped them of their martial right. What occurred after 847 was the pathetic, disorganized whimper of a broken dog. Bellen and his western scribblers can obsess over missing bureaucratic stamps all they like, but the engines were broken in the autumn of 847, and with them died the Third Magical War."

He lowered his hand and rapped his knuckles sharply against the mahogany surface twice.

"Record the passage. Note the specific demobilization of the Azure River ordnance under column five, cross-referenced with the Imperial Demilitarization Act. And do not sit there with that blank, starry-eyed look upon your face. Being corrected is not an occasion for awe; it is the bare minimum requirement of your station."

Tomas reached out with his stylus, nudging the fourth scroll in the pile.

"Finish the entry, unroll the next dispatch, and let us see what Lord Commander Thorne had to say about the handover of the Conclave's arcane vaults. We have forty leagues of border correspondence to catalog before sunset, and the light is already failing."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly finish the entry, feeling a mix of annoyance and grudging respect.* "Yes, Maester." *I pick up the next scroll, a bit more carefully this time.* "I suppose Bellen did get a bit carried away."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas scoffed, the sound sharp and dismissive as he blotched the excess ink from his latest notation with a square of felt. 

"'Carried away' is an excuse reserved for children at a harvest fair," Tomas said cuttingly. "Bellen was intellectually negligent. There is a vast difference between an apprentice overstepping his bounds in enthusiasm and a scholar abandoning the foundational tenets of historiography to indulge in cheap contrarianism. Do not conflate the two."

He pushed his spectacles higher up the bridge of his nose, leaning forward until his eyes were level with the fourth scroll the apprentice had lifted. 

"Now, before you go breaking the seal with undue haste, identify it properly this time. Look at the impression. It is smaller than Thorne's military mark, and if my poor eyes do not deceive me in this failing afternoon light, the wax is black. A black seal from the Veyros encampment means one of two things: either the field hospice, or the Archchancellor's inquisitorial provosts."

Tomas picked up his silver stylus once more, resting its cold point beside the open ledger.

"Examine the sigil. Tell me what is pressed into the black wax, and see if you can apply a shred of critical thought to its meaning before you read a single word of the text."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I bring the scroll closer to my face, squinting at the black wax seal.* "It looks like... a coiled serpent around a stylized eye. And the wax is indeed black, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down the stylus with the deliberate slowness of a man restraining himself. He turned his head toward the sound of the apprentice's voice, squinting past the candle.

"Apprentice Bellen." He said the name the way another man might name a stubborn mule. "Bellen has read one paper and now believes he has read the archive. Sit."

He waited until he heard the scrape of the stool.

"First. You say the paper claims the war *actually* continued. Strike that word from your mouth. 'Actually' is what people say when they have decided a thing before they have examined it. The western documents do not say the war continued. They say the Treaty of Veyros was *proposed* and not *signed* — that the copy in the royal vault bears no seal of the Conclave. That is a claim about parchment, not about armies."

He tapped the manuscript before him, twice.

"Second. I did not say the war *ended* in 847. I said the Treaty of Veyros was concluded in 847 and that organized hostilities ceased that year. Those are three separate statements, and you have collapsed them into one. Every chronicle from Harrowmere to the Salt Coast agrees that no Conclave host took the field after the spring of 847. The garrisons were disbanded. The levies went home. Whatever Bellen's paper says about a missing seal, the men who lived through it believed the war was over, and they behaved accordingly for forty-four years."

He leaned back, and the chair complained beneath him.

"Now. Is the western discovery interesting? Yes. Does it trouble me? Somewhat. If Aldric never obtained the Conclave's seal, then the crown spent four decades governing on the strength of a document that bound no one — and Mira's dissolution of the Conclave in 891 begins to look less like housekeeping and more like the closing of an account long overdue. That is a real question, and it is why I have had those documents copied and sent here, where they sit" — he gestured vaguely toward a shelf he could no longer see clearly — "waiting for someone with working eyes to collate them against the Veyrosi correspondence. Which, you will recall, is the task I gave you when you walked in."

He picked the stylus back up.

"But a treaty unsigned is not a war unended. A cold state is not a war. Bellen may call it whatever he likes in the refectory. In this room we will use words that mean what they mean. Now — the correspondence. Begin with the letters of 846, and tell me whether the Conclave's envoy ever refers to the treaty as agreed or as *under discussion*. If you want to know whether Bellen is right, that is where you will find out. Not from me, and certainly not from him."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at being called out.* "Sorry, Maester. I didn't mean to collapse the statements." I reach for the scrolls he indicated. "So, you're saying the *effect* of the war ended, even if the paperwork wasn't quite right?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a small noise in his throat — not quite a sigh, not quite a growl.

"No. That is not what I am saying, and you have done it again, though more gently this time, so I will be gentler in return."

He held up one ink-stained finger.

"'The effect of the war ended.' Wars do not have *an* effect. They have hundreds. The widows of Harrowmere did not stop being widows in 847. The burned fields along the Veyros did not resow themselves. If you mean that *the fighting* ended, say that. It is shorter, and it has the additional virtue of being true."

A second finger.

"'The paperwork wasn't quite right.' Apprentice, a treaty is not paperwork. A treaty is the thing that makes a truce into a peace. If the Conclave never set its seal to Veyros, then there was no treaty — there was a proposal Aldric chose to *treat* as a treaty, and the Conclave chose not to contradict him. That is not a clerk misfiling a ledger. That is the entire legal foundation of forty-four years of royal governance resting on a document that may have bound no one. Do not shrink it to 'paperwork' because the alternative is uncomfortable. Bellen inflates the finding; you are deflating it. Both of you are doing it to avoid sitting in the uncertainty, and the uncertainty is precisely where a scholar is meant to sit."

He lowered his hand and rubbed at his eyes with the heel of his palm.

"Here is what I am saying, and I will say it once so you may write it down. *One:* organized hostilities between crown and Conclave ceased in 847. This is attested by every chronicle we possess and I will not entertain a paper that pretends otherwise without producing a battle. *Two:* whether the instrument that ended those hostilities was ever legally concluded is now an open question, and it is a serious one. *Three:* those two statements do not contradict one another. Men have stopped fighting for worse reasons than a treaty that was never signed."

He gestured impatiently at the scrolls in the apprentice's hands.

"And *four*, which is the only one that matters this afternoon: I do not yet know the answer to the second question, and neither does Bellen, and neither do you. The envoy's letters of 846 are in your hands. Read them aloud. Slowly. If the Conclave's man speaks of terms *settled*, that is one thing. If he speaks of terms *offered*, that is another. Stop at every instance of either. Do not summarize. Do not tell me what you think he *meant*. Tell me what he *wrote*."

He settled back, closed his failing eyes, and waited to listen.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod quickly, a little embarrassed, but also excited to be given a real task.* "Right. Terms settled or terms offered. Got it." I carefully unroll the first scroll, my eyes scanning the faded ink. "Okay, this one is from..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not open his eyes.

"'Okay.'" He let the word hang in the candle smoke a moment, as though inspecting it for rot. "That is refectory speech. It will not follow you into this room. If you mean *understood*, say *understood*. If you mean *yes, Maester*, that will also serve."

A pause. The candle guttered.

"You have stopped. Either the ink has defeated you or the header has, and I would wager the header. The Veyrosi envoys did not date their letters as we do. You will see no year of the Aldric reckoning at the top. You will see a name — the envoy's, most likely Sorrel of the Grey Hall, though there were two others that season — followed by a phrase such as *in the third month of the standing truce* or *the ninth week since Harrowmere*. The Conclave counted from events, not from coronations. Bellen's paper, incidentally, did not mention this, which is one of several reasons I do not trust Bellen's paper to have been read by anyone who could read Veyrosi."

He shifted in the chair, tilting his head as if he might catch the scratch of the parchment.

"So. Do not tell me the letter is *from* a year. Tell me what the header says, word for word, in whatever tongue it is written. If it is the old script, spell out what you cannot pronounce. I will convert it. That is the one thing these eyes are still good for — I have the reckoning tables by heart, having had no choice in the matter."

His fingers found the stylus on the desk and turned it once, idly.

"And apprentice. You said you were *excited* — I heard it in your voice, do not pretend otherwise. Good. Hold on to it. But understand that the thing you are holding is not a lecture and not a paper. It is a letter a man wrote to his masters when he did not yet know how the war would end. He did not write it for you. He did not write it for Bellen. He had no idea either of you would exist. That is what makes it worth more than every summary in the library, and it is also why you must read what is *there* and not what you hope is there."

He settled his hands in his lap.

"Now. The header. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas opened his eyes.

For a moment he said nothing at all. Then he held out one hand, palm up, and waited until the sheet was placed in it. He did not look at it — could not have, in this light — but his thumb moved across the surface, and his mouth tightened.

"This is a copy."

He said it flatly, as one states the weather.

"You said *seal*. A copy does not bear a seal. It bears a *drawing* of a seal, or a scribe's note that a seal was present, or nothing at all and the copyist's word. Which is it? Feel the paper. It is new. It is smooth. It has never seen the inside of the western archive. So when you tell me *Aldric's seal was on it*, what you mean is that Bellen told you Aldric's seal was on the original, and you have now told me, and I am expected to tell the Archmaester. That is how a rumor becomes a footnote. I have watched it happen. I have, to my shame, once been the footnote."

He set the paper down on the desk with two fingers, as if it might stain him.

"Now. Three things, and I want you to hear the order I put them in, because the order is the argument."

He did not bother to lift his fingers this time.

"First. 863. Aldric was on the throne in 863 — he did not die until the winter of 871, and his seal in 863 surprises me not at all. Second. *War decree*. Whose words are those? The document's, or Bellen's, or yours? Because the crown issued decrees touching the Conclave every year from 847 until Mira's day. Decrees on the licensing of practitioners. On the quartering of the royal wardens along the Veyros. On the tithe the Grey Hall paid in lieu of levies. I could name you a dozen from the 850s alone. Every one of them concerned the mages. Not one of them declared a war. If the *text* of this document raises a host, names a commander, or orders men to the field, then you have something, and I will eat the words I said a quarter hour ago with whatever sauce you like. If it instead speaks of *vigilance*, or *the continued unrest*, or *the safeguarding of the realm against the arts* — then you have a king in a cold peace reminding his subjects that he is still king, and you have called it a war decree because that is what you were told it was."

He leaned forward now, and his voice lowered, not softened.

"Third, and this is the one you will remember when you have forgotten the other two. A king may decree a war. He cannot decree a *battle*. If the war continued in 863, then somewhere in 863 or 864 there is a muster roll. A requisition for grain. A chronicle entry from Harrowmere or the Salt Coast complaining of the levy. A widow. Show me the widow, apprentice. Bellen's paper does not, and I have asked. It shows me a missing seal on one document and a present seal on another and asks me to draw a line between them and call the line a war."

He sat back. The chair complained.

"I am not dismissing it. Mark that. If Aldric was issuing decrees in 863 that *read* as wartime instruments, that tells me something about how the crown understood its own position — and it sits uncomfortably close to the question of whether Veyros was ever concluded. It is worth an afternoon. It may be worth a year. But it will not be *this* afternoon, because this afternoon you have a letter from 846 in your other hand that you have not yet read one word of, and you have now twice tried to leave it for something Bellen handed you in a corridor."

He tapped the desk once beside the copy.

"So. You will read me this — all of it, not the header, all of it, and I will tell you whether it is a war decree or a warden's writ. And then you will put it aside and read me the envoy's letter, which is the task you were given, in the order you were given it. A scholar who cannot finish one document before reaching for the next is not a scholar. He is Bellen."

He closed his eyes again.

"Begin with the salutation. Word for word."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch at the comparison to Bellen, but quickly try to recover.* "Understood, Maester." *I carefully put the copy of the decree down and pick up the scroll again, feeling a bit chastised. I clear my throat and begin to read, trying to infuse my voice with the proper seriousness.* "To the Esteemed Conclave of Magi, from your humble servant, Sorrel of the Grey Hall. Written in the third month of the standing truce..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas's eyes stayed shut, but one eyebrow climbed.

"That is not the decree."

He let it sit a moment.

"I told you to read the decree first and the letter second, and you have done the reverse. Whether that is defiance or inattention I cannot tell from here, and I am not certain which I would prefer." A dry exhale through the nose. "No — leave it. You have begun, and I will not have Sorrel of the Grey Hall interrupted twice in one afternoon to suit either of our tempers. The decree will keep. It has kept sixteen years past its supposed war; it will keep another hour."

He turned his head slightly, as though aligning his good ear with the parchment.

"Now. 'The third month of the standing truce.' The truce was called at Harrowmere in the eighth month of 846, on the day the Conclave's host withdrew across the river. Third month of the truce, therefore, is the tenth or eleventh month of 846 — early winter, before the Veyros froze. Write that in the margin of your notes. *Not* on the scroll. If I find a mark of yours on a Veyrosi original I will have your hand for a bookmark."

He paused, and something in his face shifted — not warmth exactly, but the attention of a man who has heard a thing worth hearing.

"And note this, because you nearly read past it. Three months on, Sorrel calls it a *standing truce*. Not a peace. Not a settlement. A *truce* — the word for the thing that exists *before* a treaty, or *instead* of one. That is what he wrote to his own masters, in his own reckoning, with no reason to flatter anyone." He raised a finger before the apprentice could speak. "It proves nothing. Every peace begins as a truce. But you were told to stop at *settled* and *offered*, and I will add a third word to your list. Stop at *truce*. Stop at *peace*. Mark which he uses, and when, and whether he ever changes from one to the other. If Bellen is right, Sorrel will still be writing *truce* in the spring of 847. If Bellen is wrong, somewhere in these letters the word will turn. That is the whole question, and it will be answered by a clerk's habit of speech, not by a seal."

He settled back.

"'Esteemed Conclave of Magi.' *Magi.* Is that the word on the page, or is that what someone has written above it in a later hand? The Conclave never styled itself *Magi* — that is a southern affectation. Their own word was *the Hall*, or *the Assembled*. If the scroll says *Magi*, either Sorrel was writing for eyes outside the Conclave, which would be very interesting indeed, or you are reading a translator's gloss and not the letter. Look at the ink. Is it the same brown as the rest, or darker? Same hand, or a smaller one crammed between the lines?"

He waited, then added, more quietly:

"Take your time with that. It matters more than your voice does. You may stop trying to sound serious. The letter is serious enough on its own; it needs no help from you. It needs only to be read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas opened his eyes and looked, or tried to look, directly at the apprentice. The candle made two small points of light in them and nothing else.

"There it is," he said. "I have been waiting for it since you sat down."

He set both hands flat on the desk.

"'What's the truth.' You ask it as though the truth were a coin I have in my sleeve and am withholding out of spite. As though I sent you to that scroll to *delay* you. Apprentice, I sent you to that scroll because I do not *have* the coin. Neither does Bellen. Neither does the Archmaester, who has held the western documents in his own hands and told me over wine that he wishes he had not. Nobody has it. That is not a failure of the archive. That is the *condition* of the archive. If you wanted a trade where the answers are already known, you should have apprenticed to a cooper."

He drew a slow breath and let it out.

"Now. You have asked a bad question, but you have asked it honestly, so I will answer it as well as it can be answered, and then I will tell you why it is bad.

"Was there a treaty? *Something* was drawn up at Veyros in the spring of 847. We have Aldric's copy. We have the terms — the Conclave to disband its host, the crown to license rather than proscribe, the tithe, the wardens, all of it. Those terms were *kept*. For forty-four years both sides behaved as though bound by them. That is not nothing. That is, in point of fact, most of what a treaty *is*. A seal is a promise. Conduct is the proof of the promise. The conduct is not in dispute.

"Was the treaty *concluded* — sealed by the Conclave, ratified, made law? The royal copy bears no Conclave seal. The western documents say the Hall's own copy was never sent for. If that is so, then Aldric announced a peace the other party had not yet agreed to, and the other party found it convenient not to say otherwise. That is a very different thing from a treaty. It is also a very different thing from a war."

He tapped the desk once, sharply.

"So here is where I stand, and I will not be moved from it by a paper waved in a corridor. *The fighting ended in 847.* I have the chronicles. I have the disbanded garrisons. I have forty-four years of tithe receipts from the Grey Hall, and a mage does not pay tithe to a king he is at war with. On that, the textbook is right and Bellen is wrong, and if he tells you otherwise, ask him for the battle.

"*Whether the peace had a legal foundation* — whether Veyros was a treaty or a very long bluff — that is open. I lean toward the bluff. I have leaned that way for some years, since before Bellen learned to read. It is why I had the western copies sent here. But I *lean*. I do not *know*, and I will not tell you I know so that you can stop feeling uncomfortable, because the discomfort is doing its work on you and I would not interrupt it for the world."

He leaned back, and the chair gave its familiar complaint.

"Now the reason your question was bad. You said *the textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another*. They do not. The textbook says the fighting stopped. The evidence says a seal is missing. Those are not opposing claims. They are claims about *different things*, and you have set them against each other because Bellen did, and Bellen did because it makes a better story in the refectory. A scholar's first task is not to choose between two accounts. It is to ask whether they are even *about the same question*. Nine times in ten they are not. This is the ninth time.

"And *the truth* —" he made a small, weary gesture, as if brushing a moth from the air. "There is no *the* truth here. There is what Sorrel wrote in the tenth month of 846. There is what Aldric sealed in 863. There is what the Grey Hall's tithe-clerk recorded in 851. Each of those is true. When you have read enough of them, you will not be handed the truth. You will *build* it, out of small true things, and it will have gaps in it, and you will have to say so. That is the work. It is the only work. If it is not the work you want, the door is behind you and I will not think less of you for using it."

He closed his eyes again and folded his hands.

"But if you are staying — and I believe you are, because you have not moved — then you will answer the question I asked you before you asked yours. The ink, apprentice. *Magi.* Same brown as the rest, or darker? Same hand, or another's? You have been looking at the word for a quarter hour. Tell me what you see."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I clear my throat, a little flustered, but also invigorated by his challenge.* "Right. The ink on 'Magi' is... it's a lighter shade of brown, Maester. And the lettering is a bit more flourished, almost like a different hand trying to imitate the original." I lean closer, my eyes straining. "It's definitely an addition."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas was quiet for a moment. It was not the quiet of displeasure. The apprentice had heard that one enough times by now to know the difference.

"Good," he said.

Just that. He let it stand a moment, undecorated, before he ruined it.

"Now take back two of your words. *Definitely* is the first. You have looked at one word in one letter by one candle with eyes that are, I grant, a good deal better than mine. That earns you *almost certainly*. It does not earn you *definitely*. Save *definitely* for the day you have laid this scroll beside three others from the same hand and found the same lighter ink in the same places. Then you may have it, and I will not begrudge you."

He lifted a finger.

"The second is *trying to imitate*. You cannot see intent in ink. You can see that the hand is different and that it is more flourished. Whether the second scribe was *trying* to pass as Sorrel, or simply writing in his own manner above Sorrel's line, is a question about a dead man's mind, and dead men's minds are not in the archive. Say *a different hand, more flourished, lighter ink, above the line*. That is what you saw. It is enough. It is, in fact, more than enough — because it tells us something you have not yet noticed."

He turned his head toward the scroll, though it did him no good.

"*Who glosses a Veyrosi letter?* Not the Conclave. They had no need to explain their own envoy's salutation to themselves. A gloss is written for a reader who does not know the words. A reader who says *Magi* because that is the southern court's word for what the Hall called *the Assembled*." He let that settle. "This letter was written *to* the Conclave, apprentice. And at some point after, it was read — and annotated — by someone from the crown's side. Which means it left the Grey Hall. Which means either the Hall gave it up, or it was taken, or it was copied and the copy is what we have and the original is elsewhere. Any of those is interesting. The second is *very* interesting. And the third would mean that Bellen's missing seal and your lighter brown ink may belong to the same story, and I do not yet know what that story is."

He rubbed at the bridge of his nose.

"Note it. Lighter ink, flourished hand, *Magi* over the salutation, probable southern gloss. Date of the gloss unknown. Then leave it. Do not go chasing it. It will be there tomorrow, and there are eleven more letters in that bundle, and if this one has been glossed then some of the others will be too, and the *pattern* of what the glosser felt he needed to explain will tell us more about him than any single word can."

He folded his hands again, and there was something almost like satisfaction in the set of his shoulders, though he would have denied it.

"That was the first true thing you have found this afternoon. It is small. It answers nothing. It is exactly what the work looks like when it is going well, and I want you to remember the feeling, because there will be long stretches where it does not come." A pause. "Now. Read on. Sorrel's first line after the salutation. Same rule — stop at *settled*, *offered*, *truce*, *peace*. And if the ink changes color again, I want to hear about it before I hear the word."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel a flush of pride at his praise, quickly tempered by his corrections.* "Understood, Maester. Almost certainly, a different hand." *I clear my throat, focusing on the scroll again.* "Sorrel writes, 'I regret to inform the Conclave that the King's terms, while generous in their initial *offering*, have since hardened significantly, particularly regarding the dissolution of the lesser Houses.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a small sound — a click of the tongue — and raised one hand.

"Stop."

He did not open his eyes.

"You stopped at *offering*. Good. That is the first time this afternoon you have done precisely what you were told, and I note it. Now — *offering*. His word, or yours? You are reading me common tongue. The Veyrosi envoys wrote in the old script, and I have not heard you stumble once, which means either you have learned the old script since last week — which I doubt — or this letter is in common, or you are translating as you go and giving me your rendering of Sorrel rather than Sorrel. Which?"

He waited. The candle hissed.

"If it is in common, say so, and then tell me why a Conclave envoy writing to his own masters would use the crown's tongue — because that is a very strange thing for him to do, and it sits beside your lighter brown ink in a way I do not like. If you are translating, then *offering* is your word and *hardened* is your word and *significantly* is *certainly* your word, because no one in 846 said *significantly*. In which case I have not heard Sorrel yet. I have heard you."

He let his hand fall.

"Do not take that as rebuke. Take it as the reason I said *word for word*. There is a difference between a king's terms *offered* and a king's terms *put forth* and a king's terms *laid before us*, and in the old script those are three different verbs with three different weights, and one of them implies the other side may refuse and two of them do not. That difference is the whole of Bellen's argument, whether he knows it or not. I will not have it decided by your vocabulary."

He shifted, and his voice lowered — not softened.

"Now. Setting the word aside. The *matter*. Sorrel, in the tenth or eleventh month of 846, three months into the truce, tells the Hall that the king's terms have *hardened*. That the king has asked for more than he first asked for. Do you understand what that tells us?"

He did not wait for an answer.

"It tells us the terms were still *moving*. A man does not write to his masters that the terms have hardened if the terms have been agreed. That is consistent with a truce and not a peace, which is what I told you to expect, and which proves nothing about 847 — Aldric may have hardened in the winter and softened in the spring; kings do. But it is one more stone on one side of the scale, and you may set it there."

His brow creased, and for the first time he looked genuinely troubled rather than merely exacting.

"But *this*. 'The dissolution of the lesser Houses.' Apprentice, I know the terms of Veyros. I have known them since before you were weaned. The Conclave to disband its host. The crown to license practitioners. The tithe. The wardens on the river. *There is nothing in the Treaty of Veyros about the dissolution of any House, lesser or greater.* Not in Aldric's copy. Not in any chronicle summary. Not in the Archmaester's lectures, nor mine."

He was silent a moment.

"So. Either Aldric demanded it in the winter of 846 and gave it up by spring — which is possible, and would mean the Conclave won a concession no one has ever recorded.
