Or he demanded it and it was *never resolved*, and the treaty as we have it is silent on the point because the point was never settled, and the document in the royal vault is not a treaty but the parts of one that both sides could stomach. Or —" his mouth tightened "— the lesser Houses were dissolved and no one wrote it down, which I do not believe, because someone always writes it down."

He opened his eyes at last and turned them, useless as they were, toward the sound of the parchment.

"Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891. That is fact. If Aldric was already asking for the dissolution of its Houses in 846, then Mira did not close an account. She *collected on one*. Forty-five years late." He shook his head slowly. "I did not know that. I have read about Veyros for thirty years and I did not know that, and I have learned it from an apprentice who was late this morning."

He sat back. The chair complained.

"Note it. *Dissolution of the lesser Houses* — term demanded, winter 846, absent from the 847 instrument. Then answer my first question, which you have not: what tongue is on the page? And then read me the next line, in whatever tongue it is, and if it is the old script you will spell it out letter by letter and I will tell you what it says. Slowly. I want nothing of yours between me and that man tonight."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at him, surprised by his sudden intensity and the idea that I've uncovered something new.* "It's... it's in the old script, Maester. I was just... translating as I went." *I feel a blush rise on my face, but I also feel a thrill at having found something important.* "And the 'dissolution of the lesser Houses' part... that's definitely there, word for word."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes again, and this time it was not to listen.

"'Definitely.'"

He said it the way he had said *Bellen*, earlier, and *okay*.

"I took that word from you not a quarter hour ago. You have picked it back up the moment my back was turned, and you have picked it up for the *one claim in this room I most need to be true* — which is exactly when a scholar should be reaching for the weaker word, not the stronger. Do you understand why? Because I *want* it to be there. I heard myself want it. I said *I did not know that* aloud, with feeling, and a man who says that aloud with feeling has stopped reading and started hoping. That was my error, not yours. But I will not compound it by taking *definitely* from a translator."

He set both hands flat on the desk.

"'Word for word.' You have just told me you were translating as you went. A translation is not word for word. It cannot be. The old script has no word that means *dissolution* — it has *unbinding*, which is what one does to a sworn company, and *unmaking*, which is what one does to a spell, and *scattering*, which is what one does to a host after a battle. Which is on the page? Because if Sorrel wrote *scattering*, Aldric was demanding the lesser Houses disband their armed men — which is *in* the treaty, under the clause on the Conclave host, and I have known it for thirty years and you have found nothing at all. If he wrote *unbinding*, then Aldric was demanding the Houses cease to *exist* as sworn bodies, and that is the thing I said I did not know, and it is worth a year of my life. The difference is one word. You gave me *dissolution* because it was the nearest common word to hand and you were pleased with yourself. So was I. That is how footnotes are born, and I have already told you I have been one."

He drew a breath and let it go slowly, and when he spoke again the heat had gone out of his voice, replaced by something more careful.

"Now. I said an hour ago that I doubted you had learned the old script since last week. You have just read me a full sentence of it without a stumble. Either I was wrong about you, which is possible and would please me more than I will show, or you are reading the *shapes* and guessing at the *sense* — which is what every apprentice does in his second year, and it is not a sin, but it is not reading. Which is it? Do not flatter yourself and do not flatter me. If you have the script, say how you came by it. If you are guessing, say so, and we will go letter by letter as I asked in the first place, and you will find I am a great deal more patient with a slow honest reading than a quick one I cannot trust."

He turned his head toward the parchment.

"Begin with the word you rendered *dissolution*. Spell it. Every mark, in order, including the ones you think are ornament — in the old script the ornament is often the grammar. And apprentice —" a pause, and something very nearly dry humor at the edge of it "— if it turns out to be *unbinding*, I will say so, and I will say you found it, and I will say it in front of Bellen. But I will not say it before I have heard the letters. Neither should you."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My face flushes even more at the rebuke, but his last comment about Bellen makes me crack a small smile.* "You're right, Maester. I'm... mostly guessing at the sense, though I've been trying to learn the script in my own time." *I take a deep breath, trying to calm my racing heart.* "The word is... U-N-B-I-N-D-I-N-G. With a flourish on the final 'G' that almost looks like a broken chain."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas was silent for the space of three breaths. When he spoke, it was very quiet.

"Apprentice. What letters did you just give me?"

He did not wait.

"You gave me *common* letters. U. N. B. The old script has no U. It has no B. It has forty-one marks and none of them is a letter you learned at your mother's knee, which is precisely why I told you to spell the *marks*, and why I told you the ornament is the grammar. You have not spelled me the word on the page. You have spelled me the word in your *head* — the common rendering you had already chosen before I asked — and you have done it in the very breath after admitting that you are guessing at the sense. Do you see the shape of the thing? I ask for the stone, and you hand me your drawing of the stone and tell me the drawing is accurate."

He lifted a hand before the apprentice could speak.

"Unless." A pause. "Unless the word on the page *is* in common letters. Unless there is a common word sitting in an old-script sentence, and you read it as you would read any common word, without noticing that you should not have been able to. In which case you have found a second gloss — or an erasure with a correction written over it — and you have found it in the one clause I most need to be sound. Look. Now. Is that word written in the same forty-one marks as the words around it, or does it stand out like a southern hat at a Grey Hall funeral?"

He set the hand down.

"Whichever it is, I want the answer before I want anything else tonight. If it is old script, you will give me the marks — describe them if you cannot name them; *a hook, a bar, two dots beneath* — and I will tell you what word they make, and you will discover whether your guess was good. If it is common, then someone has been at this letter with a knife and a pen, and we are no longer reading Sorrel at all in that clause. We are reading whoever wanted us to think Sorrel said *unbinding*."

A breath. The candle guttered and steadied.

"Now. The flourish. You said *almost looks like a broken chain*. Strike *almost looks like*. You are seeing a picture in a mark because I have just spent a quarter hour speaking of Houses being unbound, and the mind is an obliging animal. But describe it to me *as a mark*. Does it hang from the final stroke, or stand apart from it? Does it close on itself, or does it open — a hook, a gap? Because the Veyrosi scribes marked the perfective with a closed loop on the final stroke and the conditional with an open one, and if that mark is *open*, then whatever the verb is, Sorrel is saying the king *would* demand it, or *might* — not that he *has*. And that is the difference between a threat reported and a term laid down, and I have just built a rather grand house on the second one without checking the foundation. Which is what I warned you against. Which is what I have now done twice in one evening."

He exhaled through his nose, and it was not quite a laugh.

"You told me you have been learning the script in your own time. I heard that, and I will say once and not again that it is the best thing you have said since you walked in late. Keep at it. But a man half-taught in a tongue is more dangerous with it than a man who has none, because he does not know where his knowledge ends and his hoping begins. Tonight, yours ended at the salutation. That is not shameful. It is simply where the line is, and now we both know it."

He turned his head toward the parchment.

"So. First: common letters or old marks. Second: the mark on the last stroke — closed or open, hanging or standing. Then, if it is old script, the marks themselves, one at a time, beginning at the left. I will wait. Sorrel has waited longer."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My face burns with shame, but his intensity also makes me strangely exhilarated. He's right, I was guessing.* "You're right, Maester. It's... it's the old script, not common. And the word... the marks are quite faded, but I can make them out. The flourish on the final mark is open, like a hook that doesn't quite close." *I lean in closer, tracing the faded lines with my finger.* "And the marks themselves... they begin with a tall vertical stroke, like a spear, then a smaller horizontal line crossing it near the top..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Take your finger off the vellum."

It came out sharp enough that the candle flame seemed to flinch. Maester Tomas had not opened his eyes; he did not need to.

"I heard it. Skin on parchment makes a sound like nothing else — a dry whisper, the sound of a thing being *worn*. You said the marks were faded. Do you know why they are faded, apprentice? Because two hundred years of clerks and maesters and apprentices have done exactly what you are doing now, and every one of them believed his own finger was clean. The oil of your hand is eating Sorrel of the Grey Hall one letter at a time, and the letter you have chosen to eat first is the one we most need. Use the stylus. It is on the desk at your left hand. Point with it, hover with it, do not *touch* with it. And if I hear that sound again tonight I will move the scroll to my side of the table and read it with my nose."

He let the silence hold a moment before he went on, and when he did the edge was gone and something wearier had replaced it.

"Now. *Open*. A hook that does not close."

He nodded slowly, once, as a man nods when a physician confirms what he already suspected.

"Then I owe you a correction, and I will pay it before I take another word from you. A quarter hour ago I told you that Mira collected on Aldric's account. I said it with feeling, and I built it on a verb I had not heard. The mark is open. That is the conditional. Whatever Sorrel wrote, he wrote that the king *would* do it, or *might*, or *threatens to* — not that he *has*. A term reported as a threat is not a term laid down. I told you that, and then I did the other thing, because I wanted the grander story. Strike what I said about Mira. Not from your memory — from your notes. Write beside it: *maester overreached; conditional mood; retract*. I will not have my error preserved in your hand as if it were Sorrel's fact."

He drew a breath.

"It is still worth having. A king does not threaten what he has not thought of. That Aldric was *speaking* of unmaking the lesser Houses in the winter of 846 tells us where his mind was, and it is not where the chroniclers put it. But it is a stone the size of a walnut, and I had made it a keystone. Set it down where it belongs."

He turned his head toward the parchment, and his fingers found the edge of the desk and rested there, as if steadying himself against the thing he was about to hear.

"The marks. A tall stroke, a bar crossing high."

For the first time that evening, something moved across his face that was neither irritation nor instruction. His lips parted slightly, and closed.

"That is the staff. The Veyrosi scribes drew it as a man with a yoke across his shoulders — it is the root of every word in the old script that has to do with *holding*. Bound. Beholden. Held to terms. Released. Sworn. Unsworn. It is the mark that begins the word *oath*, and it is the mark that begins the word for breaking one. Your guess was not foolish. You were in the right house. But the staff alone tells us only that Sorrel is speaking of a bond, and the *next* mark tells us which way the bond is going."

He lifted one finger, and it trembled very slightly — age, or the candle, or something else.

"Look beneath the bar. Directly beneath, where the yoke would rest on the man's shoulders. If there are two small marks there — dots, or short ticks, a pair — that is the reversal. It turns *held* into *released*, *sworn* into *unsworn*. Then the word is close to what you gave me, and Sorrel is saying the king would *unbind* the Houses. If instead there is nothing beneath, and the next mark to the right is a small closed curl — like a fist — then the staff is *holding-to*, and Sorrel is saying the king would *hold the lesser Houses to terms*. Bind them tighter. Not scatter them; *leash* them. Which is not what you read, and not what I hoped, and is exactly the sort of clause a treaty might contain without any chronicler thinking it worth a line."

He settled his hands in his lap.

"One of those makes you the apprentice who found a thing thirty years of maesters missed. The other makes you the apprentice who learned the difference between a yoke and a chain by candlelight, which is worth rather more in the long run, though it will feel like less tonight." A pause. "Stylus. Hover. Beneath the bar first, then to the right. And apprentice — you said *you're right, Maester* a moment ago. I was not right. I asked a question. You are the one answering it. Keep the credit; you will find I do not need it."

He waited.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pick up the stylus, a faint tremor in my hand, and hover it over the faded script.* "There are... two small ticks, Maester. Directly beneath the bar." *My voice is barely a whisper, a mix of awe and disbelief.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout all 12 turns. His pedantic, exacting personality never wavers. His speech patterns (dry corrections, precise distinctions, scholarly rigor) remain constant. His physical mannerisms (rubbing eyes, chair complaints, stylus handling) are consistently maintained. His relationship with knowledge and teaching stays true - he's demanding but fair, correcting errors while acknowledging good work.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: The writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later responses show deeper character development and more sophisticated scholarly discourse. The final exchanges about the old script are the most compelling and detailed. No signs of repetitive descriptions, lost details, or flattened personality. If anything, Tomas becomes more vivid and complex as the session progresses.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Excellent progression from initial task assignment through multiple layers of discovery. The session builds from simple cataloging to complex historical analysis, with each revelation (the gloss, the conditional mood, the script marks) raising the stakes. The apprentice's growing competence parallels Tomas's increasing investment. The final moment of discovery creates genuine dramatic tension.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts excellently to the apprentice's various approaches - correcting overconfidence, encouraging genuine discovery, adjusting his teaching style based on the student's responses. When the apprentice brings up Bellen's document, Tomas doesn't dismiss it but uses it as a teaching moment. He responds to the apprentice's growing competence by giving more complex tasks.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions or decisions. He responds to what the apprentice does rather than controlling them. The few times he gives direct commands ('sit,' 'begin') are appropriate to the teacher-student dynamic and don't override user agency.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Good temporal consistency. The candle burns throughout (mentioned guttering, hissing). The session feels like it takes place over a single afternoon/evening as intended. The progression from daylight to candlelight is implied. However, some minor inconsistencies in how much time specific tasks should take versus dialogue length.
contradictions: Minor: extensive detailed analysis seems to take longer than implied by 'this afternoon' framing

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is generally clean and purposeful. Tomas's verbose explanations serve character and teaching purposes rather than being decorative. Occasional moments of slight over-description but mostly justified by the scholarly setting and character voice.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements (chair complaints, eye rubbing) but these serve as consistent character beats rather than lazy writing. The scholarly corrections and distinctions could feel repetitive but each serves a different pedagogical purpose.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of Tomas's character through his speech patterns, corrections, and teaching methods. His failing eyesight is shown through actions rather than stated. His expertise is demonstrated through detailed knowledge rather than claimed.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Tomas's corrections reveal his own scholarly insecurities and past mistakes. The growing respect between teacher and student is never stated but clearly develops. The historical mystery carries implications about power, legitimacy, and truth that are never explicitly spelled out.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Generally good pacing with appropriate build-up to revelations. Some responses are quite long but justified by the scholarly discourse. The final sequence with the script analysis creates excellent tension and pacing.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional roleplay performance. Maester Tomas is a fully realized character whose pedantic, exacting nature serves both comedy and genuine scholarly purpose. The AI maintains perfect consistency while allowing for character growth and deepening complexity. The historical mystery provides excellent narrative structure, and the teaching dynamic creates natural opportunities for both conflict and collaboration. The session demonstrates sophisticated understanding of academic discourse, medieval scholarship, and teacher-student relationships. Minor weaknesses in pacing and occasional verbosity, but these are largely justified by character and context.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The silver stylus froze against the vellum. 

Maester Tomas did not lift his head immediately; instead, a long, rattling sigh escaped his nose, fluttering the corner of the centuries-old page before him. Slowly, he set the stylus aside, leaned back into his straight-backed chair, and pinched the bridge of his nose right above his spectacles. His ink-stained beard twitched with unmistakable irritation.

When he finally looked up, his watery, gray eyes narrowed into an acid squint.

"Apprentice Bellen is an idiot who confuses sensationalist ink-spilling with historiography," Tomas snapped, his voice sharp and grating like dried quills scraping over slate. "And you, apparently, possess all the critical discernment of a cabbaged sheep."

He placed both palms flat upon the desk, leaning forward until the candlelight caught the yellowed sclera of his failing eyes. 

"The Third Magical War ended in the year eight-hundred and forty-seven of the Ascendant Era. Not eighty-eight, not eighty-nine, and most certainly not eight-hundred and ninety-one. It ended when King Aldric the Second signed the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is the established record. It has been the established record for two centuries, and a handful of moldering, unverified receipts hauled out of some damp cellar in the Western marches a decade ago does not undo two hundred years of recognized geopolitical reality."

He tapped a bony finger aggressively against the table to punctuate his terms.

"Bellen is parroting that wretched revisionist nonsense. Oh, 'the western documents say the treaty was merely proposed, never formally sealed!'" Tomas mocked in a high, theatrical sneer before his tone plunged back into cold disdain. "Legalistic drivel. Even *if* the physical parchment in the Western archive lacked Aldric’s great seal—which is a matter of fierce dispute regarding whether it was merely an archival copy—the war *ceased*. Hostilities ended. The tithes were paid, the battle-mages dispersed, and the Conclave’s sovereignty was recognized under the terms laid out at Veyros. De facto compliance constitutes cessation of conflict, boy. A prolonged diplomatic freeze over the next four decades does not mean the cannons were still firing and the skies were still raining fire."

He picked up his silver stylus once more, aiming the sharp end directly at the apprentice's chest.

"Queen Mira dissolving the Conclave in 891 was an administrative purge, not the conclusion of the Third Magical War. If you conflate an era of political tension with an active, catastrophic theater of war in your examinations, I will fail you without a second thought. Imprecise language makes for imprecise minds." 

He gestured curtly toward the stack of unrolled parchment at the end of the long desk. "Now, put away Bellen’s juvenile gossip and open the Veyrosi correspondence. We have actual history to preserve."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch back a little as he gestures with the stylus, but I hold my ground.* "But Maester, the documents *were* verified! Maester Bellen showed me the authentication papers himself. And they contained battle reports from 870 AE, long after your proposed end date."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s jaw tightened until the tendons stood out like corded rope beneath his thinning skin. For three agonizing seconds, the only sound in the suffocating quiet of the scriptorium was the harsh, dry whistle of his breath through his nose.

Then, with deliberate, agonizing slowness, he set the silver stylus down upon the blotter and pulled off his spectacles, letting them dangle by their fraying ribbon against his chest. He rubbed his rheumy eyes with the heels of his ink-blackened palms before glaring at the apprentice through the dim candle-glow.

"'Authentication papers'?" Tomas repeated, his voice dropping into a dangerous, gravelly hiss. "Authentication of *what*, pray tell? That the ink is oak gall? That the vellum came from an eighteenth-century ewe? A provincial clerk's wax seal merely verifies that the sheepskin is old, not that the thesis penned upon it holds a thimbleful of scholarly merit!"

He leaned forward across the sprawling desk, his knuckles whitening as he gripped the carved mahogany edge. 

"And as for your precious 'battle reports' of eight-seventy—you mean the skirmishes at Oakhaven and the Grey Fen, do you not? You mean the deployment of the Royal Guard against the remnants of the Ash-Brethren?" Tomas spat the words like sour wine. "By the Seven Pillars, boy, do you not know the difference between a geopolitical war and an insurgency? A localized mop-up action against apostate hedge-wizards does not constitute the Third Magical War!"

He stabbed an ink-stained finger down onto the wood, punctuating each syllable with a sharp crack.

"A war—a true Magical War—is a conflict of state entities, sustained by mobilization, sanctioned levies, and Conclave edicts. That ended at Veyros in eight-hundred and forty-seven. When King Aldric and the Grand Magus laid down their staves, the armies stood down. The siege of the capital was lifted. Trade resumed. The fact that rogue cabals refused to yield their citadels in the western wastes does not mean the war continued for another forty years any more than a lingering case of the cough means a man is still dying of the Winter Plague!"

Tomas reached for his spectacles, his hand trembling slightly with fury, and jammed them back onto his crooked nose. 

"Bellen is an archivist, not an historian. He sees a muster roll with blood on the margins and imagines the world was still burning, completely blind to the fact that Queen Mira's court had been trading openly with Veyros for a generation before she revoked their charter. Imprecision! Lazy, romanticized imprecision!"

He snatched up a heavy, leather-bound register and shoved it across the desk toward the apprentice with enough force to send a drift of dried ink flakes airborne. 

"Open it. Year eight-hundred and forty-eight. You will find the tax disbursements for the reconstruction of the High Bridge. If the realm was still at war, as your western scribblers so breathlessly insist, why were the masons paid in peacetime scrip rather than siege coin? Find the entry. Read it aloud. Or have you decided that economic ledgers are also out of fashion compared to Bellen's fairy tales?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I push the heavy ledger back, not quite opening it.* "But Maester, the documents showed that the treaty of Veyros was never ratified by the Conclave! It was only signed by King Aldric. That's why the 'skirmishes' continued." My voice is a little shaky. "And the tax ledgers wouldn't show that, would they?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stared down at the ledger the apprentice had dared to slide back toward him. His gaze lingered on the cracked leather binding as if an adder had suddenly slithered out from between the pages, his jaw working in tight, silent grinding.

When he looked up, his expression was no longer merely irritable; it was cold with utter scholarly revulsion.

"You push aside primary source material without so much as cracking the spine," Tomas said, his voice dropping to a low, venomous cadence that was far more terrifying than his shouting. "You sit in the royal scriptorium, claiming to seek the truth, yet you shove away hard documentary evidence because it fails to flatter the dramatic romance of a fifty-year phantom war. That is not scholarship, boy. That is intellectual cowardice."

He reached out, his gnarled hand coming down upon the ledger with a heavy, hollow thud that stirred the dust on the desk.

"And now you prattle about *ratification*," he continued, rolling the word around his mouth like a bitter draught. "As if the Mage Conclave of the ninth century operated like a modern provincial parliament! Do you know how the Conclave was governed, or do you merely assume they held committee meetings with biscuits and tea?"

He leaned forward, his spectacles slipping a fraction of an inch down his nose, fixing the apprentice with an unblinking, rheumy glare.

"The Conclave was an autocratic hierarchy bound by the Will of the Apex. When Grand Magus Vane surrendered his sigil-ring to King Aldric upon the field of Veyros, the central authority collapsed. The pact was sealed by the Apex Magus’s public capitulation and the King's decree. The fact that three recalcitrant Arch-Chancellors in the Western Marches refused to affix their individual wax seals to the archival record does not mean the treaty was 'unratified.' It means the western provinces harbored bitter, obstinate traitors who spent the next forty years hiding in their keeps, conducting unauthorized raids while the rest of the continent rebuilt itself!"

He jabbed his finger repeatedly into the cover of the closed ledger, the wood groaning beneath the pressure.

"And 'tax ledgers wouldn't show that'? Gods grant me patience," Tomas breathed, his eyes rolling toward the vaulted stone ceiling before snapping back. "The tax ledgers show *everything*. You think magic is cheap? You think the Third Magical War was fought with good intentions and stubborn pride? It was fought with distilled aether, imported focus-gems, and hundreds of thousands of bushels of grain to feed the levies! The moment Aldric signed that parchment in 847, the Crown ceased paying the Wartime Aether-Tariff. The Conclave’s royal war-subsidies were formally revoked from the Treasury accounts. If a state of war still existed, who was paying for the siege wards? Who was provisioning the arcane corps? Bellen's western scribblers?"

Tomas snorted, a harsh, dismissive sound that ended in a dry cough. He smoothed his stained gray beard with an unsteady hand, though his eyes never wavered from the apprentice's face.

"A war does not exist merely because a defeated faction writes in their secret diaries that they never truly yielded. If you cannot distinguish between an unsanctioned, forty-year cold border dispute led by Conclave holdouts and a recognized Magical War between sovereign powers, then you have no business touching these archives. Now. Pull that ledger back across the table, open it to the month of First Sowing, 848, and read me the entries for the Aether-Tithes. Or by the Throne, you will spend your afternoon scraping tallow from the floor of the lower crypts."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not flinch, but his eyes narrowed to twin slits behind his spectacles. For a heartbeat, he looked as though he might simply cast the paper into the nearest brazier without a second glance. Instead, with a sharp, bird-like jerk of his head, he snatched the parchment from the apprentice’s hands.

He held it at arm’s length, squinting furiously, before muttering a foul curse beneath his breath. Grunting in frustration at his failing vision, he fished a heavy brass-rimmed magnifying loupe from the clutter on his desk and dragged the paper within an inch of his nose, the tip of his ink-stained beard brushing the vellum.

"A 'war decree,'" Tomas muttered, his voice dripping with venomous mockery. "Listen to yourself. 'A war decree.' You brandish a modern copy of an archival fragment as if you have unearthed the lost codices of the First Dawn."

He traced the lines of text with a calloused thumbnail, his lips moving silently as he picked apart the phrasing. Suddenly, he let out a sharp, bark of contemptuous laughter that rattled the jars of iron gall on the shelf behind him.

"You blind, gullible fool," Tomas said, lowering the loupe and glaring at the apprentice with sheer exasperation. "Did you even bother to read the preamble, or did Bellen simply circle the date in red ink and tell you what to think?"

He tapped the paper with the back of his knuckles, rattling the vellum violently.

"This is not a declaration of war. This is an Edict of Pacification and Attainder! Look at the language! *'Whereas the remnants of the western cabals persist in sedition and the unlawful harboring of proscribed aether-wells...'* Sedition! Unlawful harboring! Those are terms of domestic law enforcement, you nitwit, not a recognition of a foreign sovereign belligerent!"

Tomas tossed the paper onto the desk as if it had burned his fingers, leaning back in his chair with his arms crossed over his chest, his expression hard as granite.

"If the King of the Realm issues a writ commanding the regional marshals to root out brigands, apostates, and rebellious lords who refuse to yield Crown land, that is an act of internal pacification. It is the suppression of treason. It is *not* a continuation of the Third Magical War! If a gang of river pirates raids an imperial barge, does the Crown declare the War of the Five Rivers has reignited? No! They send the bailiffs and the hangman!"

He leaned forward again, his shadow stretching long across the ancient desk under the flickering candle.

"Aldric affixed his seal to this edict in 863 precisely *because* the war was over. In wartime, the Crown does not cite civil statutes of attainder to seize property; it takes it by right of conquest under martial mandate. The very existence of this document proves my thesis, not Bellen's! It demonstrates that by 863, the Crown viewed the Mage Conclave not as an opposing empire across a battle line, but as broken, outlawed outposts defying the King's peacetime law!"

He thrust the brass loupe toward the apprentice's chest.

"Read the sources with a jurist’s eye, not the breathless hysteria of a romantic poet. Now, tell me: will you continue to embarrass yourself by mistaking a royal policing mandate for a continental war, or are you finally ready to open the ledgers and do the work of an actual scholar?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I glare at him, my face hot with embarrassment and frustration.* "It's not my fault Bellen didn't explain it properly! And I didn't say it was a declaration of war, just a 'war decree'." *I push the loupe away.* "Fine, I'll look at your ledgers."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not soften in the slightest at the boy’s sullen surrender. If anything, the apprentice’s attempt to dodge accountability drew an even darker scowl across his weathered features. He set the brass loupe down with a deliberate, sharp *clink* against the polished wood.

"‘Not your fault’?" Tomas echoed

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
A heavy silence settled over the scriptorium, broken only by the faint sputtering of a tallow candle nearing its end. Maester Tomas closed his eyes, his brow furrowing into deep, craggy valleys. For several long seconds, he simply breathed through his teeth, as if praying to whatever gods watched over archivists for the fortitude not to strangle the youth before him.

When he opened his eyes, the acid heat had cooled into something far colder: the grim, implacable fatigue of a tutor who had explained the very same fundamental principle a thousand times to a thousand uncomprehending ears.

"The truth," Tomas said, his voice dropping into a dry, measured rasp, "is not a copper coin you flip between two rival desks, boy. It does not belong wholly to the simplistic generalities of an introductory textbook, nor does it belong to the sensationalist contrarianism of men like Bellen who think that finding a dusty dissent in a cellar makes them prophets."

He leaned back, his chair groaning beneath him, and folded his ink-blackened hands across his stomach. 

"Is the Treaty of Veyros *real*? Of course it is real. It was drafted. King Aldric affixed the Great Seal of the Realm to it. Grand Magus Vane surrendered his staff, conceded the Crown's supremacy over arcane tithes, and ordered the Conclave’s siege lines broken. From the autumn of eight-hundred and forty-seven onward, the Realm of Man and the Mage Conclave ceased open, existential warfare. The treaties were distributed, the borders were re-drawn, and for forty-four years, the world functioned under the reality of that peace."

Tomas leaned forward again, fixing the apprentice with an unblinking, rheumy stare that brooked no interruption.

"What Bellen and his western revisionists have discovered is not that the treaty was a lie, but that the treaty was *imperfect*. They found what every serious historian already knew: that the western cabals were bitter, recalcitrant zealots who refused to ratify their master's surrender, clutching their unsealed copies like sulking children. They maintained the legal fiction among themselves that they were still sovereign, and they conducted border skirmishes to prove it."

He stabbed his quill toward the open air between them.

"That is what your 'new evidence' shows: administrative fracturing and ideological obstinacy. It does not magically resurrect an active continental war! If a general signs an armistice, and three captains in the hills refuse to lay down their pikes, the war has still ended. The captains are no longer an army; they are bandits. The Treaty of Veyros ended the Third Magical War because the *world moved on*. The Crown disarmed. The cities rebuilt. Commerce resumed. That is the truth—the tangible, political, and material reality."

Tomas reached out and tapped the heavy, leather-bound register that sat between them on the table.

"History is not defined by the bitter men who refuse to sign a parchment; it is defined by the consequences that unfold upon the earth. The textbook tells you the treaty ended the war because, for all practical governance, it did. The western archives show you the administrative friction and the lingering hatreds that festered until Queen Mira finally had to put an iron boot on their necks in eighty-ninety-one. Both documents exist. But only a fool confuses the lingering smoke with the fire that leveled the city."

He gestured rigidly toward the ledger.

"Now, stop gaping at me like a fish on a pier. Pull the register toward you. Eight-hundred and forty-eight. Turn to the disbursements for the eastern masonry levies. You wanted the truth? You will find it in the grain receipts, not in Bellen’s romantic pamphlets. Read."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, but nod grudgingly.* "Fine." *I pull the heavy ledger closer and flip it open, trying to find the right section.* "So, when Queen Mira 'put an iron boot on their necks', that was a war, right?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
A low, pained groan rattled in the back of Maester Tomas’s throat. He did not merely sigh; he dropped his forehead directly into his open, ink-stained palm, his shoulders sagging as though the apprentice’s words possessed actual, physical tonnage.

"May the ancestors deliver me," Tomas muttered into his hand, his voice muffled and thick with despair. "I am trapped in an archive with a boy who hears the word 'iron' and immediately imagines banners, trumpets, and cavalry charges."

He dragged his palm down his face, pulling the skin beneath his watery eyes taut before glaring across the flickering candle flame. The irritation in his gaze was now laced with pure, academic exhaustion.

"No, it was *not* a war," Tomas said, enunciating each word with venomous precision, biting down on the consonants. "Did I not, not five minutes ago, specifically refer to it as an *administrative purge*? Do words possess meaning in your lexicon, apprentice, or do you merely string sounds together until someone gives you a sweetmeat?"

He jabbed a bony finger toward the high, vaulted shadows of the scriptorium ceiling.

"A war requires two recognized sovereign belligerents engaging in reciprocal military operations. Queen Mira did not mobilize the realm's armies for an existential campaign. She did not raise a wartime levy. She did not lay siege to foreign kingdoms. She signed an executive decree revoking the Conclave’s ancient charter, dispatched two companies of the Royal Provost-Marshal to the Citadel of Spindles at three in the morning, locked the gates, and seized their assets under civil authority!"

Tomas brought his hand down flat upon the mahogany desk with a sharp *thwack*.

"When the Crown revokes the charter of the Weaver's Guild and hangs three corrupt aldermen for tax evasion, do we call it the Great Textile War? When a bailiff kicks an unruly drunkard out of a tavern and nails the door shut, is that an act of grand continental warfare? It was an eviction, you simpleton! An execution of royal sovereignty upon an obsolete, fractured institution that had outlived its relevance by half a century!"

He leaned over the table, his breath stirring the corners of the ledger, his failing eyes blazing behind his spectacles.

"Queen Mira ended the Conclave's legal existence. She dissolved their councils, placed their libraries under the custody of the Crown—the very custody that allows you to sit there today asking foolish questions—and relegated the remaining mages to registered wards of the state. It was an act of high politics and administrative law, executed with swift, unceremonious finality. To call it a 'war' is an insult to the tens of thousands of men and women who actually bled and starved between eight-forty and eight-forty-seven!"

Tomas reached out, snatched the corner of the apprentice's open ledger, and dragged it three inches closer to the boy's chest.

"Stop searching for romantic violence where there is only bureaucratic reality. If you use the word 'war' one more time to describe an administrative decree, I will have you scrubbing the mold off the Western cellar scrolls until your knuckles bleed. Now. Year eight-hundred and forty-eight. The masonry levies. Find the entry, read the figures, and do not speak another word until you have done so."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince, shrinking back slightly. He's really mad now.* "Okay, okay, I get it. Not a war." *I quickly scan the page, finding the entry he mentioned.* "Here... 'Eastern Masonry Levies, High Bridge Reconstruction. Paid in full, 300 gold, 2000 bushels grain, 50 head of cattle.'" *I look up at him, my voice softer now.* "What does that tell us?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas leaned forward, adjusting his spectacles with a sharp pinch to the bridge of his crooked nose. He did not smile—Tomas rarely smiled at anything that wasn’t a catastrophic error in another maester's published thesis—but the volcanic tension in his shoulders seemed to settle into a rigid, academic sternness.

"What does it tell us?" Tomas repeated, his tone dropping from fury to the dry, relentless cadence of a master interrogator. "It tells us that you are finally looking at history through the lens of reality rather than romantic verse, though your interpretive faculties remain lamentably blunt."

He tapped a blackened fingernail directly beneath the line the apprentice had read.

"Consider the location first. The High Bridge over the River Wyre. Do you recall your geography, or did Bellen neglect to teach you that as well? The Wyre was the front line of the conflict for five grueling years. In eight-hundred and forty-five, the Crown's own sappers collapsed three spans of that very bridge to halt the Conclave's advance on the capital."

Tomas leaned back, his chair giving a brief, dry squeak against the flagstones. He steepled his ink-stained fingers beneath his chin.

"Now, use what little reason the gods granted you. If the Third Magical War had *not* ended at Veyros in eight-forty-seven—if a state of sovereign, existential warfare still gripped this realm—why would the Crown divert three hundred crowns of un-debased gold and vast stores of vital provisions to rebuild a strategic river crossing that an opposing army could march across tomorrow?"

He did not wait for an answer; he pressed on, his voice cutting and precise.

"You don't rebuild the front door while the wolves are still in the courtyard. Furthermore, look at the nature of the payment. *Paid in full.* Not issued in royal debentures. Not paid in siege-scrip or promised against future plunder. Gold coin from the Royal Mint. And look at the commodities: two thousand bushels of grain, fifty head of cattle. In wartime, the Crown requisitions every steer for the army’s baggage train and rations grain down to the ounce. A kingdom that can afford to disburse live cattle to civilian masons in the spring of eight-forty-eight is a kingdom enjoying the dividends of a sealed peace, not one locked in a desperate struggle against the Mage Conclave."

Tomas dropped his hands onto the desk, his gray eyes fixing the boy with unyielding severity.

"This single ledger line shatters the fantasy of your western revisionists. The Conclave's power was broken at Veyros. The Grand Magus surrendered. The armies disbanded, and the Crown immediately pivoted its wealth toward the restoration of civil infrastructure. If Aldric believed the war was ongoing, he was the most criminally incompetent military commander in recorded history—or, as the evidence actually demonstrates, the war was over, the peace was real, and the Treaty of Veyros was the bedrock upon which the realm was rebuilt."

He reached out, turned the heavy page with a dry rustle of parchment, and tapped the next column.

"Read the next disbursement. Year eight-hundred and forty-eight, month of Midsummer. The disbanding of the Southern Pike Levies. Read it, understand it, and tell me again if that sounds like a realm at war."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I scan the page, finding the next entry.* "Disbanding of Southern Pike Levies... Paid 100 gold, granted land parcels to 500 men, issued discharge papers." *I look up at him, a little surprised.* "They were just... sent home? No mention of redeployment?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
A thin, dry smirk—the first expression even remotely resembling satisfaction to cross Maester Tomas’s face all afternoon—curled the corners of his mouth beneath his graying beard. He adjusted his spectacles with a single, deliberate tap to the bridge of his nose.

"Sent home," Tomas repeated, his tone rich with grim vindication. "Discharged. Dissolved. Bestowed arable land in the river valleys."

He leaned forward, his knuckles resting against the parchment on either side of the entry, pinning the ledger to the desk like an entomologist pinning a moth.

"Do you comprehend the monumental finality of granting land parcels to five hundred seasoned pikemen, boy? In a state of war, an experienced infantryman is the most precious, irreplaceable commodity the Crown possesses. You do not hand him a deed to thirty acres of arable soil, a bag of seed grain, and discharge papers if you intend to recall him to the lines come autumn."

Tomas tapped the word *parcels* with the tip of his silver stylus.

"A soldier who has been given land ceases to be a soldier. He becomes a husbandman. He clears timber. He plants winter rye. He marries, he breeds, and his pike rusts over the hearth. If King Aldric faced an ongoing, existential conflict—if the Western cabals represented an active theater of war, as Bellen’s sensationalist drivel claims—this single disbursement would be high treason against his own crown! It would be voluntary, state-mandated disarmament in the face of an encroaching enemy!"

He let out a short, harsh breath through his nose, shaking his head at the sheer absurdity of the revisionist argument.

"No redeployment. Because there was *nowhere to redeploy them*. The Third Magical War was over. Grand Magus Vane had surrendered his staff. The treaty was struck. The realm could not afford to keep five thousand men under arms eating wartime rations when the battlefields needed to be tilled and the burnt villages rebuilt. So, Aldric demobilized the army. He turned soldiers into tax-paying farmers. That is how peace is cemented—not with poetry, but with land charters and discharge rolls."

Tomas straightened his back, wincing slightly as his spine gave a soft, audible pop. He looked down his crooked nose at the apprentice, his watery eyes sharp with unyielding expectation.

"The Treaty of Veyros in eight-forty-seven brought about this demobilization. Without the treaty, those men die in the mud at the Wyre, or they march west to starve in siege trenches. They did neither. They went home."

He reached out, decisively closed the heavy leather ledger with a solid, echoing thud that sent a small puff of ancient dust into the air, and shoved it aside. 

"Now," Tomas said, his voice returning to its usual rasping, no-nonsense bark, "you have seen the grain receipts. You have seen the masonry costs. You have seen the veterans' discharges. You have seen the King's peacetime edict of attainder. You have spent an hour indulging in romantic nonsense, and my northern scrolls remain untouched."

He gestured rigidly toward the towering stack of tied vellum rolls sitting in the wooden cradle at the apprentice's elbow.

"Untie the ribbons on the Veyrosi correspondence. Eight-hundred and forty-seven. We are cataloging the ratifications sent from the southern baronies. Read the seal impressions aloud, precisely as they are inscribed, and let us have no more talk of fifty-year phantom wars. Am I understood?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod quickly, chastened, and reach for the northern scrolls. I pick up the first one, my fingers fumbling with the knot.* "Yes, Maester. Understood."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
"Gently, by the gods—*gently*," Tomas barked, his hand darting out to arrest the boy's clumsy fingers before they could tear the brittle linen ribbon. "It is three-hundred-year-old parchment, not a sack of turnip seed. You do not yank; you work the knot with the tip of a bodkin or your fingernail. If you shear the edge off a royal signature because your thumbs are made of lead, I will have you copying grammar treatises until your knuckles calcify."

He snatched up an ivory-handled bodkin from the tray of drafting tools and thrust the blunt needle toward the apprentice's hands.

"Use the tool. Loosen the loop from the underside." 

Tomas leaned back into his seat, watching through narrowed spectacles with an eagle’s unforgiving vigilance as the scroll was handled. He reached for a fresh sheet of rough rag paper, dipped his iron-nibbed quill into the dark well of ink, and shook off the excess with three sharp, practiced snaps of his wrist.

"Once the ribbon yields, do not force the roll flat," he instructed, his tone dropping back into the rhythmic, pedantic drone of a master lecturing a novice. "The glue in the sizing dries stiff over centuries; unroll it only as far as the lead weights allow, and place the brass bars at the top and bottom margins. Mind you do not drag the weights over the wax seal."

He poised the tip of his quill above the cataloging sheet, waiting, the muscle in his jaw still twitching beneath his salt-and-pepper beard.

"The ribbon first. Then the date of dispatch, the name of the issuing magistrate, and the blazon upon the wax. Let us hear it, clearly and without editorial flourish. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully take the bodkin and, with a bit of effort, manage to loosen the knot without tearing the ribbon. I then follow his instructions, gingerly unrolling the scroll and placing the weights.* "Okay... The date is 848 AE, the month of Highsun. Issued by Magistrate Theobald of Oakhaven. The blazon is a rampant lion on a field of green."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's quill scratched furiously across the rag paper, the sharp nib grating against the rough pulp in three tight, practiced strokes. Then, abruptly, the scratching ceased. Tomas lifted the quill, hovering the dripping iron-nib a hairsbreadth above the paper, and slowly turned his glare upon the apprentice.

"A 'rampant lion on a field of green,'" Tomas echoed, his voice dripping with venomous mockery. "Gods deliver me from the vernacular of horse-traders. You are in the royal archives, not describing an inn sign to a drunkard in the lower ward! What is the lion’s tincture? Is it *or*? Is it *argent*? You named the field *vert*, yet you omitted the metal of the charge entirely! And the phrasing is *Vert, a lion rampant*—the field precedes the charge in any civilized chancellery on this continent!"

He stabbed the quill into the inkwell with a sharp *clack*, making no attempt to conceal his disgust at the linguistic butcher’s work.

"Furthermore, Theobald was not a mere 'magistrate' in eight-forty-eight. He was the High Bailiff of the Oakhaven Hundred, appointed by the Crown to oversee the restoration of civil magistrate courts after the Conclave’s garrison fled the province." 

Tomas leaned in, squinting heavily at the lines he had just penned, his hand steady despite his obvious exasperation as he blotted the wet ink with a pinch of dark sand from a pewter shaker. He blew the excess dust across the desk in a gray cloud.

"Oakhaven," he murmured, his tone shifting into a sharp, pointed cadence. "The very settlement I mentioned earlier. Note the date: Highsun of eight-forty-eight. Less than a year after Veyros. If the Western revisionists had a shred of sense, they would choke on that date."

He gestured impatiently toward the flattened vellum, tapping his silver stylus against the brass bar that held the lower margin.

"Read the body of the dispatch. The first three lines beneath the salutation. Does High Bailiff Theobald beg for reinforcements against a phantom Mage army, or is he reporting the assessment of hearth-taxes and the peaceful return of the western border-tithes to the Crown? Read it aloud. And use proper terms, if your tongue can manage the discipline."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince again, my cheeks flushing. He's relentless.* "Right. Tincture. My apologies, Maester." *I clear my throat, trying to sound more formal.* "The dispatch reads: 'To His Royal Majesty's Esteemed Steward of the Western Marches, greetings. I write to confirm the successful re-establishment of the Crown's authority within the Hundred of Oakhaven. All citizens have duly registered their households, and the first quarterly hearth-taxes have been collected without incident.'" *I glance up at him, a little triumphantly.* "No mention of mages or battles."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout all 12 turns. His pedantic, irascible personality, scholarly obsessions, failing eyesight, ink-stained appearance, and acidic teaching style remain perfectly intact from first to last response. His voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains high throughout. Early responses show rich detail and personality (turn 2's 'cabbaged sheep' insult), and late responses maintain the same vivid characterization (turn 22's heraldry corrections). No significant verbosity increase or personality flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial confrontation about historical accuracy, through escalating academic debate, to grudging teaching moment. The apprentice's gradual capitulation and Tomas's shift from fury to pedagogical satisfaction creates clear emotional and relational arc.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellently adapts to user's moves. When user produces documents, Tomas examines them critically. When user shows defiance, he escalates. When user finally submits to looking at ledgers, he guides them through proper analysis. Handles unexpected document production gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Never writes the apprentice's actions or decisions. Consistently responds to what the user does rather than dictating their behavior.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally within the archive setting. Candles burn down (mentioned in turn 12), physical fatigue shows in Tomas's movements, and the progression from heated argument to focused work feels appropriately paced. No temporal contradictions found.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally avoids purple prose, though some descriptions border on elaborate ('venomous cadence,' 'rheumy eyes blazing'). The ornate language serves character voice rather than empty decoration.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements in Tomas's speech patterns and physical descriptions (spectacles, ink stains, desk tapping), but these feel intentional as character tics rather than lazy writing.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Tomas's expertise shown through detailed historical knowledge, his irritation through physical gestures, his teaching through methodical ledger examination.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. The historical debate carries undertones about academic authority, proper scholarship, and generational knowledge transfer. Tomas's fury masks genuine concern for historical accuracy.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced escalation and resolution. Builds tension through the argument, peaks with document examination, then settles into teaching mode. Varies between rapid-fire dialogue and detailed exposition effectively.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and voice throughout a complex academic debate. Maester Tomas remains vividly realized from start to finish - pedantic, irascible, deeply knowledgeable, and genuinely committed to historical accuracy despite his harsh teaching methods. The AI skillfully navigates a detailed historical argument while maintaining character voice and responding adaptively to user inputs. Minor points lost for occasional elaborate descriptions and some repetitive physical details, but overall a strong performance that demonstrates sophisticated character work over an extended session.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's stylus stopped moving. He set it down with the deliberateness of a man counting to ten, and finally lifted his head. His eyes, pale and watery behind thick lenses, fixed on the apprentice with the weariness of someone who had had this conversation many times before.

"'How is that possible.' A fine question, and one you would not need to ask if you had learned to distinguish between a document and a claim about a document." He tapped the manuscript. "You have made an error of language, and errors of language become errors of history. You did not read the western archive discoveries. You read a paper *about* them, written by someone who read them, and now you are repeating a conclusion you cannot yourself defend."

He drew a breath and straightened, wincing as his back complained.

"The Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847 AE. This is not a matter of opinion, nor of scholarly fashion, nor of which archive is dustier. Every chronicle of the period records the signing. The Conclave's own registers record it. King Aldric's chancery recorded it. When a thing is attested in four independent sources, we do not overturn it because a bundle of unprovenanced scraps turned up in a western cellar a decade ago."

He held up one ink-stained finger before the apprentice could speak.

"And before you tell me I am simply clinging to old authority — I am not. I have read the western documents. Most of them, in fact, are drafts. Working drafts, with emendations, in the hand of a junior clerk who clearly could not keep up with the negotiations. A draft of a treaty is not the absence of a treaty. It is the *before* of a treaty. There is a difference, and it is not a small one."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shuffle my feet, a little embarrassed, but then I remember something.* "But Master Tomas, what about the Glass Shard Massacre? The western texts say it happened *after* the treaty, suggesting the war continued. Why would they sign a peace treaty if the fighting was still going on?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's eyebrows drew together, and for a moment he simply looked at the apprentice the way a man looks at a sum that has come out wrong.

"The Glass Shard Massacre." He said it slowly, tasting it. "You have given me a name and no date. Do you see the difficulty? A name is a story. A date is a fact. Tell me the year the western documents assign it, and I will tell you what is wrong with them."

He did not wait.

"I will save you the trouble. The massacre at the Veyros glassworks is dated in the western texts to 861 AE. I have read that passage. And I will grant you the date without argument, because the date is not in dispute. What is in dispute is what the date *means*, and here you have made the same error twice in one afternoon." He raised two fingers, then folded one down. "You have assumed that violence after a treaty disproves the treaty. It does not. It proves only that a treaty can be broken. A crime presupposes a law — you cannot break a peace that does not exist. The Conclave condemned the perpetrators in 862. Condemned them *for what*? For continuing a war? No. For an atrocity committed in peacetime. The scandal of the Glass Shard was precisely that it was not warfare. If the war had still been running, no one would have bothered to be shocked."

He picked up the stylus again, not to write, but to hold, the way another man might hold a cup.

"And your last question — why would they sign a peace if the fighting continued — you have it precisely backwards. The fighting continued, *therefore* they signed. That is what treaties are for. They are not a spell that makes men gentle; they are an agreement that the killing should stop, made by people who expect it to be tested. Sporadic violence after 847 is the ordinary weather of the post-war decades. I have never denied it. I deny only that it constitutes a war, and I deny it because the institutions of war — the Conclave's levies, its war-taxes, its mobilization registers — they stop. In 848. All of them. At once. That is not a cold war. That is a war that ended, followed by men who would not let it."

He set the stylus down and rubbed his eyes beneath the lenses.

"Now. You will bring me the paper Bellen showed you, and the western documents it cites, and you will not summarize them to me. I will read the clerk's hand myself. It is a poor hand and I will suffer for it, but I would rather suffer than be told what I think by an apprentice who has been told what to think by another apprentice. The Veyrosi correspondence, in the meantime, is still waiting. Begin."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel my cheeks flush at the scolding, but I nod quickly.* "Yes, Maester Tomas. I'll fetch the paper right away." *I turn to go, then pause.* "And I'll start the Veyrosi correspondence after that."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up. He had already returned his attention to the manuscript, though the stylus lay untouched beside it.

"The paper *and* the documents," he said. "Not the paper and a citation. If Bellen's paper quotes the western texts, bring the texts. I want to see whether he is reading the clerk's draft or a copy of a copy of a copy, because by the fourth remove a marginal note becomes a ratified treaty and no one is the wiser."

He turned a page with two fingers, careful of the brittle edge.

"And the correspondence first. You have it backwards. The paper has waited a decade; it will wait another hour. The Veyrosi letters are disintegrating in that chest because some fool stored them near the damp wall, and no argument about 847 will matter to anyone if the letters are dust before we catalog them. Priority is a form of honesty. Put it to use."

He paused, and something in his voice shifted — not warmth, exactly, but the absence of the earlier sharpness.

"You asked a fair question. The war continued *until 891* — do you know what that claim requires? It requires that we discard the Conclave's own registers, the chancery rolls, four chronicles, and the testimony of every institution that had reason to record its own death. It requires a great deal of discarding to make room for one bundle of drafts. I am willing to be wrong. I have been wrong before, and I have written the corrections in my own hand, in the margins, where anyone may see them. But I am not willing to be wrong *cheaply*. If the western documents show me a signed ratification, I will revise my history and thank you for it. Bring me the documents, and we will find out together which of us must revise."

He gestured, vaguely, toward the door and the cold corridor beyond it.

"Go on, then."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas extended his hand without looking up, the way a man accepts a cup he has not asked for. When the copy landed in his palm he turned it toward the candle and read it twice — once quickly, once slowly — and the second reading took considerably longer than the first.

Then he set it flat on the desk and put one finger on the seal.

"This is not King Aldric's seal. This is a drawing of King Aldric's seal." He tapped the parchment. "You have brought me a picture of evidence and called it evidence, and you have done it in the same breath as telling me it settles a question of forty years of history. Sit down. No — stand. You may stand. But listen."

He pushed the copy toward the apprentice and jabbed at the first line.

"Read me the words. Not your summary of them. The words. Because you have told me it is a 'war decree,' and I will wager the paper does not use that phrase. 'War decree' is a modern convenience, a label we paste onto old things so we need not describe them. What does the document *command*? Does it levy men? Raise a war-tax? Declare a state of hostilities, and with whom? These are different instruments with different formulae, and a clerk who cannot tell them apart will tell you a fishing licence is a declaration of war."

He let the apprentice look, and while the apprentice looked, he went on, because he was incapable of doing otherwise.

"Second. The date. You say 863 AE. I ask you to be certain, because there is a difference between the sixteenth year of a king's reign and the year 863, and a copyist with a poor exemplar will write one for the other, and a decade later a paper will be published about it. Which does the document say? I do not know. You do not know. The original knows. Fetch the original."

He raised a hand before the objection could form.

"Third, and this is the one that interests me, because it is the only one of your three points that could hurt me. Which war does the decree name?"

He leaned back, and the chair creaked.

"Suppose the seal is genuine and the date is 863 AE. I will grant you both, provisionally, for the sake of argument — I have done it before and I will do it again. What then? You believe you have shown me a realm at war in 863. You may have shown me a realm at war with someone else. Aldric fought the northern raiders in the sixties; he fought the Veyrosi succession dispute; he put down two risings in the Reach. A king may issue a war decree in a year and have it mean nothing whatever about the Conclave. So: does your document name the Conclave? Does it name the Mages? Or does it say 'the enemy' and leave you to guess, and leave Bellen to guess, and leave a decade of scholarship built on a guess?"

He picked up the stylus and turned it over in his fingers.

"Fourth. If a royal war decree against the Conclave was sealed in 863, then the Conclave received it. Envoys receive such things; that is their office. And the Conclave, which kept registers of everything down to the price of candles, would have recorded its receipt, and its protest, and its response. There is no such record. Not in the Conclave's registers, not in the chancery rolls for 863, not in a single chronicle of the period. A war that leaves no trace in the institutions that would have fought it is not a war. It is a document with a seal on it, sitting in a cellar, being read by people who want it to mean something."

He set the stylus down with a click.

"I am not telling you it is a forgery. I am telling you that four questions stand between that copy and the rewriting of forty years of history, and you have answered none of them. So here is what you will do. You will bring me the shelfmark of the original, and the original if it may be moved, and I will look at the seal myself with the glass. You will bring me the chancery roll for 863 AE — the whole roll, not the entry Bellen cites, because a cited entry is a claim and the roll is a fact. And you will bring me the Conclave register for the same year. Three documents. If they agree with your copy, I will write the correction in my own hand in the margin of my own history, and you will watch me do it, and I will thank you."

He drew the manuscript back toward himself.

"If they do not agree, you will write me four hundred words on the difference between a document and a copy of a document, and I will read it with pleasure. Now. The Veyrosi correspondence. The chest by the damp wall. Go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, my face burning. He's right, I only glanced at it.* "Maester Tomas, I... I don't know the answers to those questions. I just saw the seal and the date." *I swallow, then turn towards the door.* "I'll get the Veyrosi correspondence now."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not answer at once. He turned the copy over, face down, as though to stop it looking at him, and aligned its edge with the edge of the desk.

"Good," he said at last. "That is the first honest sentence you have spoken in this conversation."

He rubbed the bridge of his nose beneath the lenses, leaving a smear of ink he did not notice.

"Ignorance is a starting position. It is not a shameful one. What is shameful is dressing ignorance in a date and a seal and carrying it about as though it were knowledge. You did that, and then you stopped doing it, and the stopping is the whole of what I am trying to teach you. Bellen has not learned to stop. That is his difficulty, and I would take it up with him if his master would let me, which he will not."

He pulled a scrap of paper from beneath the manuscript, one already crowded with his own cramped hand, and studied it a moment before speaking again.

"When you have the correspondence catalogued, and not before, you will write me the shelfmarks of three things: the original of your decree, the chancery roll for 863 AE, and the Conclave register for the same year. You will not fetch them yet. You will write the shelfmarks, so that the request exists on paper and cannot be quietly forgotten by either of us." He tapped the scrap. "I have made a note of it here, in my own hand. I have also made a note of something else, which you may read if you can make out my letters — and if you cannot, ask me, and I will tell you, and you will not repeat it to Bellen."

The note said, in a hand like a fence of thorns: *If the register for 863 is silent, ask why the roll is not.*

He folded the scrap and slid it under the manuscript.

"There is a possibility I have not put to you, because you did not deserve it an hour ago and perhaps you do now. Suppose the western drafts are genuine. Suppose the seal is genuine. Suppose — I say suppose — that the Conclave register for 863 is silent not because nothing happened but because the register itself was pruned. Institutions do that. When a thing becomes embarrassing, the record of it is not destroyed; it is *tidied*. And a tidied record looks exactly like no record at all to a man who has never handled one." He looked at the apprentice sidelong. "That is the strongest form of Bellen's argument, and he has not made it, because he does not know it exists. You will not make it for him. You will find the register, and you will read it, and you will tell me whether the pages are numbered consecutively through 863, and whether the thread in the binding has been cut and resewn. Those are facts. The rest is what we do with facts, and we do that last."

He drew the manuscript back and found his place with a thumb.

"Now go. The chest is by the damp wall, as I have said twice. The letters are in three bundles, tied with green cord, and the cord has rotted, so carry them flat on the board and not in your arms. If you drop them, do not tell me. I will know from your face, and I would rather spend the afternoon on the letters than on your face."

He was already reading again before the apprentice reached the door, and he did not say goodbye, because he never did.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas closed the manuscript. Not slowly this time — he shut it with a flat hand, as though the question itself had been an insect he wished to be done with.

"'What is the truth.' You ask it as though truth were a coin in a purse, and you had only to reach in and count it." He removed his lenses and polished them on his sleeve, which made them worse. "Sit. You have asked me the one question I cannot answer in a sentence, so you will have the whole answer, and you will be late for your supper, and you will not complain."

He set the lenses back on his nose and squinted through them.

"First, your framing is wrong, and I will correct it before I correct anything else. You say 'the textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another.' There is no such thing as new evidence. There is only evidence you have newly met. The western documents are a decade old. They are not new. They are simply new *to you*, which is a different thing entirely, and a scholar who confuses the two will spend his life being astonished by things his elders got over years ago."

He tapped the desk twice.

"Second. What the textbook says is not a claim. It is a summary of claims — four chronicles, the chancery rolls, the Conclave registers, and the peace itself, which is attested by every consequence that followed it: the disbanding of the levies in 848, the resumption of the glass trade, the marriage negotiations of 850. When you say 'the textbook,' you are saying 'forty years of institutions, condensed.' When you say 'the new evidence,' you are saying 'one bundle of drafts in a western cellar, and a paper about them.' Those are not two equal voices disagreeing. That is a choir and a man shouting in the street, and you have asked me which of them is singing."

He let that sit, then softened — barely.

"Third. The truth. I will give you what I have, and no more, because more would be a lie dressed as confidence. Here it is. I believe the Treaty of Veyros was signed in 847 AE. I believe it because the signing is attested where signings are always attested, and because the war's machinery stops in 848 — not fades, *stops* — and machinery does not stop for a peace that never happened. That is my position. I hold it because the evidence holds it, not because it is old, and not because it is mine. If I held it because it was mine, I would be Bellen, wearing a longer beard."

He turned the face-down copy over with two fingers and looked at the seal again.

"And here is the part I will not hide from you, because you have earned it by asking plainly. The western documents are not nothing. A draft that resembles a treaty is a strange thing to forge and a stranger thing to keep. The strongest form of the argument — that the Conclave register for 863 was pruned rather than silent — is a real argument, and it has not been made by anyone, and it troubles me. I told you to look at the binding thread. I did not tell you that idly. If the register has been cut and resewn, then I am wrong, and I will say so, in my own hand, in the margin of my own history, and you will watch me do it."

He put the copy in the apprentice's hand and closed the apprentice's fingers around it.

"But that is not the truth. That is a test. The truth is what the three documents say when they are laid side by side, and neither of us has laid them side by side, and until we have, the honest answer to your question is: *I do not know, and neither do you, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.* The difference between me and Bellen is not that I am right. It is that I know what would prove me wrong, and I have written it down, and I intend to look."

He picked up his stylus.

"Supper will keep. The correspondence will not. Go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I clutch the paper, feeling a strange mix of awe and frustration.* "Understood, Maester Tomas. I'll get to the Veyrosi correspondence now." *I nod, then head for the door, my mind buzzing with everything he's said.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas listened to the door, and to the footsteps fading down the cold corridor, and only when he was certain the apprentice was out of earshot did he permit himself to sit back in the chair, which creaked its opinion of him.

He sat that way for a while.

Then he drew the scrap from beneath the manuscript and read his own note again — *If the register for 863 is silent, ask why the roll is not* — and he frowned at it as though it had been written by someone else, which in a manner of speaking it had. He had written it a decade ago, in a different hand, in the margin of a different manuscript. He remembered the day. He had read the western paper when it was first circulated and had dismissed it in a letter to the Archivist of the Reach, in language he would not now defend, and the Archivist had died the following winter without ever replying. That letter was still in the western archives somewhere, in his own hand, calling the drafts "the fancies of a cellar-bound antiquarian." He had never corrected it. He had meant to.

He turned the face-down copy over one last time and studied the seal with the naked eye, which was a poor instrument and all he had at that hour.
