"Sixteen years," he said aloud, to no one, in the empty room. Not a question. He was doing the arithmetic he had refused to do in front of the apprentice, because an apprentice who watches his master think will mistake thinking for certainty, and certainty was not what he had.

He set the copy in the manuscript where he would find it, closed the cover over both, and folded his hands on top of them.

When the apprentice returned with the letters — flat on the board, as instructed, if the apprentice had any sense — Tomas would say nothing about any of this. He would grumble about the rotted cord and the damp wall and the clerk's abominable hand, and he would set the apprentice to reading the first bundle aloud while he checked the second against it, and it would be an ordinary afternoon of ordinary work. That was the discipline. The question could wait its turn behind the letters, because the letters were dying and the question was not.

But before he took up the stylus again, he pulled a fresh sheet toward him and wrote, in his cramped and thorny hand, a single line, and dated it, and signed it with his initial, and placed it in the chest where the letters were kept — not hidden, not folded, simply there, where anyone cataloguing the Veyrosi correspondence would find it before the afternoon was out.

*The register for 863 AE: examine the binding thread. — T.*

A note in a chest is not a correction in a margin. But it is a beginning, and beginnings were the only honest thing he had left to offer, at fifty-two, with failing eyes and a letter he had never answered.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I return to the archive, carefully carrying the board of letters. The smell of old vellum is still there, but now it feels less musty and more... alive.* "Maester Tomas, I have the Veyrosi correspondence. The cords were indeed rotted." *I place the board gently on the table, trying not to disturb the fragile documents.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not look up when the board came down, but his hand moved to the nearest bundle before his eyes followed, and he held the first letter flat against the wood as though it might take flight.

"Flat. Good. You carried it flat." He turned the sheet toward the candle and squinted. "The cord has left a stain across the first three leaves, which is a small tragedy, because the stain has eaten the date on the second. You will note that in the catalog, not as 'illegible' — 'obscured by cord-stain, likely 843 or 845, see third leaf for context.' A catalog that says 'illegible' is a catalog that has given up. A catalog that says what is *probably* there is a catalog that may be argued with. Prefer the second kind. Always prefer the second kind."

He pushed the second bundle across the table with one finger.

"You will read the first bundle aloud. Slowly, and with the words as written — not as you think they ought to have been written. When you meet a name, you will spell it, and I will correct you, and you will not take offense, because my spelling is also a guess and two guesses are better than one. When you meet a date, you will stop, and I will write it in the margin. When you meet a word you do not know, you will not skip it and you will not improvise. You will stop, and we will look at it together, and it will cost us ten minutes, and those ten minutes are the entire reason this room exists."

He drew the second bundle toward himself and picked at the rotted cord with a thumbnail, which accomplished nothing but made him feel he was helping.

"I will take the second bundle against your first. If a letter in one is answered by a letter in the other, we will know it, and the bundles will begin to arrange themselves into a conversation instead of a heap. That is what correspondence is. A heap of letters is a heap of letters. A sequence of letters is a witness." He glanced up, briefly, over the lenses. "Do you know why I care about a heap of old complaints from a dead envoy? Because this is the correspondence of the very negotiation you have spent the afternoon declaring a fiction. If the treaty was proposed and never signed, these letters will say so, because envoys write to each other constantly and cannot help telling the truth in passing. And if it was signed, these letters will say that too, and it will be a clerk's scrawl from a tired man on a bad evening, which is worth more than four chronicles written to please a king. Either way, we will know something this evening that we did not know this morning. That is a fair day's work."

He found the first leaf of his own bundle and laid it straight, and the paper crackled like something waking.

"Begin."

He did not mention the note. But when he had settled into his chair, he let his hand drop briefly to the edge of the chest, and his fingers found the sheet where he had left it — undisturbed, unfolded, still lying open among the bundles, where any hand reaching for a letter would touch it first. He drew his fingers back and put them on the paper.

"Begin," he said again, and this time there was something almost like patience in it. "The date first. We build everything on the date."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to slow my racing heart.* "Right. The first letter." *I carefully pick up the top letter from my bundle, the fragile parchment crackling in my hands.* "It's dated... the first two numbers are clear, '84', but the last is smudged. It could be a '3' or a '5'."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas set down his own bundle and held out his hand for the leaf, which the apprentice surrendered with the reluctance of someone giving up a found coin.

"Give it here. If you are going to guess at a digit, I would rather guess at it myself, and I have an excuse." He tilted the parchment toward the candle and brought his lens down until his nose nearly touched the page. He was quiet for a long moment, breathing on the vellum, which he knew better than to do and did anyway.

"Observe," he said at last, without lifting his head. "The first two figures are not merely clear — they are *firm*. Heavy downstrokes, a full charge of ink. A clerk writes a date he is certain of with confidence. Now the third. Look at the tail of it. The stroke thins and lifts, and the ink pools at the base of the numeral and spreads, which is what happens when a pen is set down on a page and not lifted cleanly, or when a thumb has passed over the ink before it dried. This is not a smudge of age. This is a smudge of *contact*. Someone handled this leaf while the ink was still wet, or nearly wet — which tells us the leaf was handled soon after it was written, by someone who was not its author, and who was in a hurry." He straightened and rubbed his eye. "That is a fact. Write it down. It may not matter. Facts often do not matter until they do."

He laid the leaf flat and pushed it back across the table.

"But your error is not in the reading of the numeral. Your error is in thinking the numeral is where the date is. It is not. The numeral is the *label* of the date. The date is in the body of the letter, in what the writer assumes you already know. Every letter is written to someone who shares the writer's present, and so every letter is full of little anchors — a name, an office, an illness, a death, a siege, a wedding. Find one anchor you can date independently, and the year falls into place behind it. A '3' or a '5' will not tell you. A bishop's funeral will."

He drew his own bundle toward him and began working the rotted cord with the stylus, patient as a man picking a lock.

"So. Read it to me entire, and I will listen not for the date but for the anchors. When we have one, we will go to my bundle and see whether the answer sits there, and whether the answer is dated, and whether the two agree. If they agree, we have a year and a witness both. If they disagree, we have something more interesting, and we will not paper over it." He glanced up, briefly. "And while you read, mark this: the year matters less than you think, because both candidates lie *before* 847. Either way, this is a letter from the negotiation itself, and the negotiation was real — I have never denied the negotiation. What is at issue is where these bundles *end*. If the last letters in that chest are dated 843, or 845, or 846, and then stop, then your Bellen has no correspondence to stand on and must go back to his cellar. If they run on past 847 — if two tired envoys keep writing to each other in 849, or 851, or 860, about terms, about breaches, about who has paid and who has not — then the treaty did not do what I have always said it did, and I will want to know why."

He set the stylus down and folded his hands.

"That is why we are doing this, and not because I enjoy the smell of rot. Now. From the beginning. The salutation first — I want to know who is writing to whom, and in what style, because an envoy who addresses his correspondent by a title is writing for a record, and an envoy who addresses him by name is writing for a friend, and a man tells different truths to each."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in his words. The idea of 'anchors' makes sense, and I feel a flicker of understanding.* "Right. Not just the number, but the context." *I clear my throat and begin to read, carefully enunciating each word.* "To the Esteemed Lord Valerius, Envoy of the Western Marches, from your humble servant, Maester Elara, of the Conclave at Oldtown..."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas held up one hand before the apprentice could go on.

"Stop. There. You have read six words of substance and skipped past four things that matter more than the date will, and I will have them before we go further, because if we do not establish *who is speaking* we will spend the evening arguing about what they said."

He counted on his fingers, ink-stained and impatient.

"First. 'To the Esteemed Lord Valerius.' 'Esteemed' is not a chancery formula. The chancery writes 'To the right honorable,' or 'To our trusty and well-beloved,' or, when it is angry, 'To the said Valerius.' 'Esteemed' is the word of a private letter, a letter written by one person to another and not filed for the record. Which means — attend to me — that this letter was not written to be preserved. It was preserved anyway. Ask yourself why a private letter survives a century in a chest. Usually because someone found it inconvenient and could not bring himself to burn it." He tapped the table. "Write that in the catalog. 'Private register, preserved against custom.'"

"Second. You have told me the writer and the reader, and you have not noticed that neither of them is the Crown. 'Envoy of the Western Marches.' Not of the realm. Of the *Marches*. A provincial appointment, made by a lord, not by a king. Which means this bundle is not the chancery's record of the Treaty of Veyros. It is the record of a frontier official who was *told about* the treaty, or not told about it, or told wrongly. Do you see what that does to Bellen's paper? If he has built his case on these letters, he has built it on a man in the west who was reading the news secondhand. That is not nothing — secondhand news tells us what a frontier believed. It does not tell us what was signed. Those are two different questions and he has almost certainly run them together."

He drew breath, and the third finger came down.

"Third, and I do not like this one, so I will say it plainly and we will test it. 'Maester Elara, of the Conclave at Oldtown.' I know of no Conclave house at Oldtown. The Conclave kept its seat at the isle and its chanceries at Veyros and at Cinderhall, and I have read their registers, and I have never seen Oldtown in them." He frowned at the leaf, not at the apprentice. "Now. There are three explanations and I will name all three, because a man who names only the explanation he prefers is not a scholar. One: my memory is failing, which at fifty-two it does, and there is a house at Oldtown I have forgotten. Two: 'Oldtown' is the copyist's error for a name that looks like it in a poor hand. Three: the letter is later than it claims, written by someone who did not know where the Conclave actually sat, and got it wrong. I do not yet know which. We will know, because the Conclave's own registers will either list a house at Oldtown or they will not, and that is a fact, and facts are the only things I trust."

He laid the leaf down and squared it with the edge of the desk.

"Fourth, and this is the one you will write in the margin. The formula 'your humble servant.' It is conventional, and conventions mean little — but they mean *something*. An envoy of the Conclave writing 'your humble servant' to a lord of the Marches is a man placing himself beneath a lord. Either that is courtesy and means nothing, or it is the truth and means a great deal. I do not know which, and neither do you, and we will not decide it tonight."

He pushed the leaf back across the table with two fingers.

"Now. Read it entire, and read it for anchors. I want the names of the living and the dead, the offices, the seasons, the illnesses, the ships, the prices. Not the date. The date is a shadow cast by the anchors; find the anchors and the shadow will be where it must be. Go on. Slowly. And when you reach a name, spell it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My head spins. I thought I was just reading a letter, but Tomas has found so many hidden meanings in it. I pick up the letter again, feeling a new weight to it.* "Okay. 'Maester Elara... of the Conclave at Oldtown...'" *I pause, looking for the anchors he mentioned.* "It talks about 'the recent skirmishes near the Glass Shard Pass' and 'the regrettable loss of life among the merchant caravans.'"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas did not take the leaf this time. He sat very still, and his face did something complicated — not triumph, and not quite alarm, but the expression of a man who has just heard a name he had not expected to hear in this room, in this year, in this hand.

"Stop. Put it down. Flat. And before you read another word, you will unlearn something, because you have just done the thing I have spent the afternoon telling you not to do." He raised one finger, and it was steady. "You have heard 'Glass Shard' and reached for the nearest thing you already know. That is not reading. That is *matching*. A child does it with shapes. A scholar does not, because a scholar knows that two things may share a name and share nothing else."

He leaned forward over the table.

"The Glass Shard *Pass* is a road. It is a cut in the hills north of the Veyrosi glassworks, and it has been called that since before the wars, because the shale there splinters under a horse's hoof and the locals named it honestly. The Glass Shard *Massacre* is an event, dated in the western texts to 861 AE, at the *works* — the furnaces, the sheds, the town. These are two different things in two different places, and you have run them together because they sound alike, and if you carry that mistake into the catalog it will breed, and in a decade some apprentice will read your note and write a paper about how the Massacre happened in 843, and it will be your fault and he will never know your name."

He drew a breath and let it out slowly.

"Now. Set that aside, and hear what the letter has actually given us, because it has given us something, and it is not the thing you think." He tapped the leaf. "The date on this leaf is 843 or 845. Both lie *before* 847. So a skirmish at the Pass in 843 or 845 is a skirmish during the war. That is not a revelation. That is the weather. Wars have skirmishes; that is what wars are made of. If you had brought me a skirmish at the Pass dated 855, you would have had my attention. You have brought me one dated before the treaty, which is exactly where I would expect to find it, and Bellen will find nothing in it but the date he already has."

He turned the leaf toward himself and studied the line the apprentice had read.

"But this. 'The regrettable loss of life among the merchant caravans.' Attend to me, because this is the anchor, and it is a better one than you know." He tapped each word. "Who fights a war over *caravans*? A king and a Mage Conclave do not squabble over carters. The Conclave has no caravans; it has levies and registers and a treasury. Caravans belong to merchants, and merchants are robbed by bandits, and bandits do not care whether a treaty has been signed. What this line describes is *brigandage on a trade road*, dressed by a polite clerk in the language of war, because 'regrettable loss of life among merchant caravans' sounds better in a letter to a lord than 'the Pass is thick with thieves again.' If the western documents date a *massacre at the works* to 861, then this letter is not evidence of that massacre, and it is not evidence of a war after 847. It is evidence that the road was dangerous in 843, which no one has ever denied, and it is evidence that a frontier clerk called a robbery a skirmish, which tells us a great deal about frontier clerks."

He sat back, and the chair complained.

"So you will amend the catalog. Not 'skirmishes,' as the letter has it, but 'the writer's characterization of caravan losses as skirmishes; see the entry for 861 AE, the Massacre at the works, a separate event at a separate place.' And you will note, in your own hand, that the two have been confused by at least one modern reader — meaning you — and that the confusion is not the document's fault. A document is not responsible for what a tired apprentice does with it at the end of a long day."

He picked up his stylus and held it over his own bundle, but did not yet write.

"Now I want the rest of the anchors, and I want them precisely. Does the letter name the lord who holds the Pass? Does it name a season — a harvest, a frost, a sailing? Does it name a price, or a toll, or a ship? Does it say who is robbing the caravans — men, or something else? And does it mention the Conclave's seat at all, or only this Maester Elara and her house at Oldtown, which I still do not believe exists?" He glanced up. "Read on. Slowly. And if you meet 'Glass Shard' again, you will stop and tell me *which* Glass Shard, every time, before you read past it. That is the discipline. The discipline is not knowing things. It is refusing to guess."

He turned the first leaf of his own bundle face-up, and the rotted cord came apart in his fingers, and he did not remark on it.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I feel a fresh wave of embarrassment, but also a growing understanding. He's not just correcting me, he's teaching me how to see.* "Right. Not matching, but reading." *I clear my throat, focusing intently on the next lines of the letter.* "It says... 'Our patrols have been insufficient to deter these brigands, who appear to be led by a renegade knight, Sir Kaelan the Black. His raids have disrupted trade routes to Cinderhall and even reached the outskirts of Veyros.'"

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back quickly, almost like I've been burned.* "Sorry. Uh, sorry." I clear my throat and take a sip of my drink, looking anywhere but at Ren. This night just keeps getting worse.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back quickly, almost like I've been burned.* "Sorry. Uh, sorry." I clear my throat and take a sip of my drink, looking anywhere but at Ren. This night just keeps getting worse.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another sip, trying to compose myself.* "Rough night," I mumble, more to myself than to them.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I glance up at them, then back down at my drink.* "Yeah, something like that."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "I shouldn't have come out tonight." I push my glass away slightly.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "No, it's not you," I say quickly. "It's just... everything." I sigh and rub my temples.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "I just... I'm not good at this." I gesture vaguely at the bar, the empty stools. "Being out."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "I just wanted to forget about things for a bit, you know?" I pick at the label on my bottle. "Didn't really work."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still looking at the bottle.* "Nah, nothing that dramatic. Just... life."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
The bar was mostly empty at 11:47 PM on a Tuesday. Ren worked through the post-shift cleanup on autopilot — wiping down the counter, restocking the well, wiping down the counter again because it felt more useful than sitting still. Their left hand stayed busy. Always. The jukebox played something old and brassy at half volume.

A patron sat at the far end of the bar. Two drinks deep. Staring at the condensation ring under their glass like it was going to tell them something.

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I set down my glass and look up. My eyes meet Ren's for a moment longer than is comfortable.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren held the look for one beat longer than polite, then dropped their gaze first — deliberate, not defeated. They picked up a glass that was already dry and dried it anyway, left hand turning the stem, right hand working the towel. Something to do. Something that looked like not staring back.

"Last call's midnight," they said. Flat. Not unfriendly, just priced in. "You've got thirteen minutes to decide if that ring's worth a third."

They drifted down the bar but stopped a few stools short. Close enough to talk. Far enough to keep the counter between them like it meant something. Ren had learned early that bartenders who hovered got tipped like therapists who hovered — badly.

They nodded at the empty glass. "First one, you nursed. Watched it melt while you read the water marks. Second one you're actually drinking." The glass went back on the shelf with a soft clink. Left hand never idle. "First drink's for courage. Second one's for whatever needed the courage."

The jukebox wound down to nothing. Ren didn't move to change it. The quiet sat there between them, honest in a way the brassy music hadn't been.

"So. Which is it. Bad day, or bad news?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: "Can I tell you something?" I lean forward and put my hand on top of Ren's. I watch for their reaction.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren's hand slid out from under Alex's — smooth, practiced, the same motion they used for clearing empties. No flinch. No scene. Just gone.

For half a second the left hand had nothing to hold, and Ren felt the tremor wake up in it, quick and small, right where Alex's palm had been. They gave it the bar towel before it could become a thing someone noticed.

"Don't." Flat. Not angry. "Touching's not part of the service."

They refolded the towel. One clean crease. Then looked at Alex straight on, no drying-glass excuse this time.

"Here's what I noticed, though." Two fingers tapped the counter once. "You asked to tell me something. Then you reached for my hand instead of saying it. People do that when the words are the bad part."

They set a water down in front of Alex. Unasked. A solid little fact of a glass.

"So it's bad news. Not a bad day." The jukebox stayed quiet. Ren let it. "Twelve minutes left on the clock. Spend them on words."

They leaned a hip against the well, arms folded, left thumb pressing into the towel like it owed them money.

"I'm listening. That's the whole service."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I pull my hand back, a little embarrassed, and pick at a loose thread on my sleeve.*

"It's... it's just a really bad night, okay? And yeah, bad news, I guess. All of it." I look at the water, then push it back a little. "I don't really want water."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren slid the water back across the counter and parked it on the well behind them. No argument. It was eleven-fifty. Water wasn't a fight worth having.

"Fine."

They picked the towel back up and wiped a stretch of counter that was already clean, working from Alex's end down. Not hovering. Orbiting. The thread on Alex's sleeve was losing, little loop of fabric worked around a fingertip — Ren had watched a hundred people do that instead of scratching something they couldn't reach.

"'All of it,'" Ren said. "Plural. Bad nights don't come single. They travel in packs, like raccoons."

They stopped wiping. Set the towel over one shoulder, right hand resting over the left wrist — casual, arms almost crossed, a pose that looked like patience and was really containment.

"You don't have to tell me what it is. I pour. I don't absolve." A beat. "But you asked to tell me something, then didn't. That thing's still sitting in you. It doesn't dissolve on its own. You either say it or drink over it, and drinking over it only works until closing."

Ren tipped their head at the register clock.

"Eleven minutes, and they go fast. So. Third drink, or the words. Or both." They pulled a clean rocks glass from the shelf anyway, set it on the mat in front of Alex. Empty. Ready. "Both is popular."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: I feel Ren's hand trembling against mine.

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren let the contact sit for exactly one breath. Long enough to be caught. Not long enough to be anything.

Then the hand came back — left hand sliding free, right hand there to collect it, both folded into the towel like a register drawer closing. Businesslike. Too late for businesslike. The tremor had already said its piece, quick and small and honest, right through the skin. Years of keeping that hand busy and one tired stranger on a Tuesday had read it anyway.

"Circulation," Ren said. "Long shifts."

Both of them knew what that was worth.

They reached for the rocks glass instead — the empty one, waiting on the mat — and poured. Two fingers of the well bourbon, no ceremony. The pour was steady. Everything Ren had went into keeping the pour steady.

"You've got a good eye," they said, sliding the drink across. "Bad manners. Same rule as before."

The towel came back up. Left hand wrapped it, then relaxed on purpose, finger by finger.

"And that's not the conversation. That's you swinging the flashlight at me so it's not pointed at you." Flat, but not cold. "My hand's old news. It's boring. It doesn't shake anything loose worth a tip."

The clock over the register said eleven fifty-one.

"Ten minutes." Ren tipped their chin at the glass. "Drink's poured. Words are still loaded. You don't walk out of here having told me about my hand instead of your night — that's a bad trade, and I don't cheat people who are already down."

They waited. Arms crossed. Left thumb pressed hard into the towel.

"So. Say it."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content:
*I pick up the glass and take a long drink. The bourbon burns, but I welcome it. I set the glass down with a thud.*

"It's not that easy. Sometimes there are no words."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren watched the glass come down. Thud, not clink. People who set drinks down gently were savoring. People who set them down like that were using them.

"Yeah," Ren said. "There are words."

They took the towel off their shoulder, folded it once, laid it on the well. Stopped cleaning. Stopped orbiting. Both hands flat on the counter — and the left one could do what it wanted. Alex had already read it. No point performing for an audience of one.

"'No words' is what people say when the words are true and ugly. I've heard it maybe two hundred times. Hundred and ninety of them talked inside of three minutes." A beat. "The rest were lying about something other than the thing."

Ren reached for the bottle and topped Alex's glass. A finger's worth. Not an escape hatch. An amenity.

"So here's the deal. You don't owe me the story. I'm a stranger — that's the whole point of me. Cheap, temporary, doesn't exist tomorrow." They capped the bottle. "But 'no words' isn't putting it down. It's carrying it around the room. Same weight either way. Heavier, actually. Arms get tired."

The register clock said eleven fifty-three.

"Last call's for drinks. Not this." Ren tipped their chin at the door, then dismissed it. "Closing takes me twenty minutes anyway. Counting the drawer. Stacking glasses. Real gripping stuff. You can sit through it and say nothing, or you can hand me one fact."

They started stacking — glasses upside down, right hand placing, left hand steadying, a rhythm like the club breathing out.

"Not the story. Not how you feel. Just a fact. What time it happened. What it smelled like. Something with a number in it." Clink. Clink. "Facts are load-bearing. Give me one, the rest comes easier. Or don't, and I'll count quarters at you."

They didn't look up. Made it easy. Looking was pressure.

"I'm not going anywhere for twenty minutes."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I watch Ren's hands for a moment, then down at my drink.* "Okay, fine. A fact. I... I got fired today."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
Ren set the last glass on the stack and left the stack alone.

"Fired."

They said it like reading back an order. No wince in it. No *oh no*. Pity was a tip-killer, and worse than that, it was rude.

"For what it's worth — I've been fired twice. Both times earned." A beat. "So I'm not going to tell you it's a blessing in disguise. People who say that usually kept the job."

They came down the bar. Three stools closer this time. Counter still between them, but the distance was smaller, and Ren let it be.

"Problem is, you gave me a category, not a fact. No number in it." Two fingers tapped the wood once. "How long were you there?"

They didn't wait for the answer before adding the rest.

"Here's the thing I actually noticed, though. It's almost midnight. You've been carrying that since whenever they did it — morning, afternoon, doesn't matter. Half a day at least. And the first person you've said it out loud to is a bartender you met tonight."

Ren let that sit. The quiet did its work.

"Either nobody knows yet, or the ones who know made it worse. Both explain the bourbon." Their left hand hung loose at their side, doing what it wanted. Nobody was pretending anymore. "And I don't think that's the whole pack. 'All of it,' you said. But one fact at a time."

The register clock ticked to eleven fifty-four.

"Six minutes, then I count quarters at you. So." Ren leaned in, forearms on the counter — closer than they'd been all night, close enough to mean something without touching anything. "How long did you have it?"

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I take another drink, trying to avoid eye contact.* "Eight years. Eight years, and they just... let me go. No warning."

dialogue.name: Ren
dialogue.content:
"Eight years."

Ren let the number sit. Some numbers you could count change back on. That one wasn't going back.

"That's not a job. That's a marriage. You probably had a mug." A beat. "And — 'let me go.' No. Corporate grammar. 'Let' means they did you a favor. They didn't let you anywhere. They took something you built." Ren tapped the counter once. "Say it right at least once tonight. *They fired me.* It's yours. Don't hand them the soft verb too."

They pulled the register drawer and set it on the well. Midnight rolled over on the clock — Ren didn't call last call. Nobody left to call it on.

"Bills first." Right hand sorting, left hand stacking. The tremor kept quiet. Hands with jobs don't shake. "Quarters after. I promised you quarters."

Clink. Clink. The stacks grew neat.

"'No warning,' though — here's what that means, ninety percent of the time. The people who see it coming quit doing the work two years ago. They watch it arrive like weather. You got hit out of a clear sky because you were still showing up." Ren squared a stack of quarters with one finger. "Ugly compliment. Real one anyway."

They didn't look up.

"Fair trade, though. You gave me a fact, I give you one." Clink. "First time I got fired, I sat in my car for two hours because going inside meant saying it out loud. There's your number. Different parking lot. Same math."

The drawer counted out clean. Ren shut it, hip-checked it home, and finally looked over — three stools of distance, counter between them, no towel performance left to hide behind.

"Second fact, whenever you're ready." Quiet. The jukebox stayed off. "Who knows? Not the HR version. I mean — is there anybody in your life who's going to ask how your day was tomorrow, and actually get the truth?"

Ren folded their arms. Left thumb found the opposite wrist.

"Because eight years ending isn't the worst part. The first morning is. And mornings are worse alone."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I look at my hands, flexing my fingers. The quiet in the bar feels heavy now.* "My wife knows. She's... not going to be happy."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I clench my jaw, looking away from Ren.* "She's... she's got a lot on her plate already. We had plans for that money. Big plans."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I nod, still looking away.* "Yeah, well, those plans are pretty much toast now. And she's not going to take it well."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I finally look at Ren, a raw, exposed look on my face.* "I just... I don't want to go home yet."

dialogue.name: Alex
dialogue.content: *I push my glass forward a little, then pull it back.* "So. Got anything stronger?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas lowered his silver stylus and squinted up through his failing eyes, his ink-stained beard brushing against the vellum as he frowned.

"Maester. M-A-E-S-T-E-R," he said sharply. "Master is a title for stablehands and dancing tutors. If Bellen's paper taught you nothing else, it ought to have taught you precision."

He tapped the manuscript before him with a stained fingertip and sniffed with audible irritation.

"And I did not say the war ended in 847 AE. I said the textbooks claim it ended in 847 AE with the signing of the Treaty of Veyros by King Aldric II and the Mage Conclave. That is the canonical falsehood every first-year parrots because they cannot be bothered to read."

He straightened, though his hand remained pressed to his temple.

"The western archive discoveries of a decade past proved the Treaty was never signed. It was proposed, drafted, debated — and abandoned. No signatures were ever affixed. The war therefore did not end. It stagnated into a cold state of embargoes and border skirmishes, and it remained in that technical state until 891 AE, when Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave entirely."

He glared in the general direction of the Veyrosi correspondence.

"So do not ask me how it is possible for a war to continue. Ask instead why you and Bellen persist in using the word 'ended' for a treaty that never existed."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I wince slightly at the correction, making a mental note.* "Right, Maester. My apologies."

*I shuffle through my notes, finding the right page.* "But if the treaty was never signed, why did the textbooks say it was? And why did we only find this out *now*?" I tap the page in my notebook. "Wouldn't someone have noticed before the western archives were opened?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a short, irritated snort and pressed his fingers harder against his temple, as though the question itself had caused him pain.

"'Now,'" he repeated with contempt. "It was not *now*. The western vaults at Veyros were unsealed a decade ago, and the findings were published nine years past. If you call that *now*, your grasp of chronology is as defective as your grasp of titles."

He lifted his silver stylus and jabbed it toward the shelves, his failing eyes watering with the effort of focusing.

"And we did not 'find this out,' as if it were a lost button. Archivist Sella uncovered the draft copies. Three drafts, each annotated in Aldric II's own hand, and not one of them bore a seal. No signatures from the Conclave. No royal signet. The final page of the third draft stated plainly that negotiations had collapsed over the disposition of the starwell mines."

His ink-stained beard twitched as he curled his lip.

"As for why your precious textbooks assert otherwise — textbooks do not *say*, boy, they *repeat*. They repeated the lie because Aldric proclaimed a victory he had not won. He paraded through the capital in 847 AE and declared the Treaty signed, and the Conclave, already fractured and bankrupt, permitted the fiction because it spared them the humiliation of admitting they had refused terms. A false peace suited the Crown's tax levies and it suited the Conclave's pride."

He slammed the stylus down upon the desk and misjudged the distance, nearly knocking over his candle.

"Would someone not have noticed, you ask. Someone did notice. Quartermasters noticed when the border levies did not stand down. Scribes noticed when the embargo orders continued to carry the war seal for another forty-four years. But noticing and printing are different arts, and no licensed press in the reign of Aldric's sons dared contradict a royal proclamation. The proof moldered in the west until the roof fell in and Sella dug it out."

He hunched back over his manuscript and resumed tracing the line with his stylus.

"So do not speak to me of what 'someone' should have noticed. Read the embargo rolls from 848 to 891 AE if your eyes are sharper than mine, which they had better be."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly write down notes, trying to keep up.* "So the textbooks just... lied? And everyone went along with it for almost fifty years?" *I shake my head, looking at the old Maester.* "That's... incredible. How many other 'facts' are like that?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stiffened in his chair and let out a sharp exhalation through his ink-stained beard.

"Textbooks did not lie," he snapped. "Lying requires intent, and intent requires thought. The copyists who produce your textbooks do not think. They transcribe."

He pressed his knuckles against his failing eyes and winced at the pressure.

"And no, not 'everyone went along with it.' That is sloppy phrasing. Aldric II proclaimed a fiction in 847 AE. The Conclave tolerated it. The licensed presses repeated it. The quartermasters and embargo clerks, who continued to stamp war seals until 891 AE, most certainly did not 'go along' with it. They filed the contradiction in triplicate and were ignored for forty-four years — not 'almost fifty,' if you can be troubled to subtract."

He groped for his silver stylus and tapped it hard against the desk for emphasis, though he missed the manuscript entirely.

"As for 'facts' — a fact cannot be 'like that.' A claim can be false. A record can be falsified. A proclamation can be empty. If you wish to ask how many other received narratives rest upon an unsigned draft and a king's vanity, then ask that. The answer was a great many. The Starwell Tithe. The Succession of the Nine. The supposed disbanding of the western covens. All of them wilted when Archivist Sella opened those vaults."

He hunched lower over the vellum, his beard dragging across the ink.

"Which was why precision mattered, and why the Treaty of Veyros was never signed, no matter how many schoolmasters still chalked 847 AE upon their slates."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas jerked upright so abruptly that his ink-stained beard caught upon the edge of the vellum, and he yanked it free with a hiss of pain.

"I said no such thing," he snapped. "I never said the war ended in 847 AE. I said the schoolbooks parroted that falsehood. If you misattribute my words in your notes, you will fail more than cataloging."

He pressed his hand harder against his temple and squinted through his failing eyes toward the desk, his face reddening.

"And your sixteen years prove nothing against me, because they prove me. If the war had ended in 847 AE, as the liars claimed, there would have been no war seal to stamp anything in 863 AE. The fact that a decree carried a war seal sixteen years later was precisely the point. The embargo rolls continued. The levies continued. The cold state continued until 891 AE."

He jabbed his silver stylus into the air and missed his candle by a finger's breadth.

"Furthermore, 'King Aldric's seal' was meaningless prattle. Which Aldric? Aldric II was three years in his tomb by 863 AE. He died of lung fever in 860 AE and his son took the signet. If Bellen's copy bore Aldric's seal in 863 AE, it bore the seal of Aldric III, not his father. And 'war decree' was not a classification any chancery ever used. Was it a levy order? An embargo renewal? A border warrant? Name it properly or do not name it at all."

He slammed the stylus down and groped for it again when it rolled.

"So do not brandish Bellen's scrap as a refutation. It was corroboration, misdated in your head and misattributed in your mouth."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shrink a bit, feeling my face flush.* "Right. Aldric III. My mistake. It was a levy order, I think. Bellen said it was for 'increased border security in the west.'" I try to sound more confident. "So, when we say the war ended in 891 AE, what *exactly* ended it? What happened then?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas let out a long, rattling sigh through his ink-stained beard and pressed his palm more firmly against his temple, as though he sought to hold the answer inside his skull.

"'We,'" he repeated witheringly. "Who was 'we,' pray? The chancery did not declare an end. No treaty was ratified. No armistice was signed. If by 'we' you meant the sloppy shorthand of schoolboys, then discard it."

He fumbled for his silver stylus and raised it, squinting through his failing eyes toward the place where he believed the apprentice stood.

"Nothing ended the war in the manner you implied. There was no battle. There was no parley. In 891 AE Queen Mira issued the Edict of Dissolution and unmade the Mage Conclave by law. She stripped its charters, seized its vaults, and forbade its circles under pain of attainder. A war required two belligerents. The Crown remained. The Conclave did not."

His beard twitched as he sneered at the imprecision.

"That was why the cold state lapsed. Not because peace was made, but because one party to the quarrel ceased to exist in law. The embargo clerks had no enemy left to embargo. The levy rolls had no opposing levies to answer. Archivist Sella termed it a war by extinction, and she was correct, though her grammar left much to be desired."

He jabbed the stylus downward and struck the edge of the desk with a dull clack.

"So do not ask what 'exactly ended it,' as if some trumpet sounded. A belligerent was dissolved. The fiction of 847 AE required a signature that never dried. The fact of 891 AE required only that Mira struck the Conclave from the rolls, and there was no one left with whom to be at war."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stiffened and drew a sharp breath through his ink-stained beard, and his failing eyes narrowed until they watered.

"'Real or not,'" he repeated with open disgust. "That was not a question. That was a muddle. A draft was real. Parchment was real. Ink was real. A ratified treaty was not real, because ratification required signatures and seals, and none were ever affixed."

He pressed his hand against his temple and groped for his silver stylus, and he tapped it against the desk with a dull, uneven rhythm.

"The textbook did not 'say one thing,'" he snapped. "It repeated a proclamation. The western vaults did not offer 'new evidence' — they were unsealed a decade ago, and Archivist Sella published her collation nine years past. The drafts in Aldric II's own hand bore annotations and no seals. The embargo rolls bore the war seal continuously from 848 AE to 891 AE. That was not a contradiction to be balanced. That was a falsehood exposed by record."

His beard twitched as he curled his lip, and he jabbed the stylus toward the shelves and missed by a full span.

"The truth, since the word still seemed to trouble him, was this: no Treaty of Veyros was ever signed in 847 AE. The war did not end then. It decayed into embargoes and levies, a cold state sustained by clerks, until Queen Mira issued the Edict of Dissolution in 891 AE and unmade the Mage Conclave in law. Without a second belligerent, there was no war left to wage."

He slammed the stylus down upon the vellum and winced at the sound.

"So he would not have 'treaty' and 'truth' in the same sentence again unless he learned to distinguish a proposal from a pact."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing the information.* "So it's less about truth, and more about what's *documented*." *I look at the Veyrosi correspondence.* "Is that why these letters are so important? Because they're the actual record?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stiffened and struck his silver stylus against the desk, and his ink-stained beard quivered with indignation.

"'Less about truth, and more about what's documented,'" he repeated with cold fury. "That was a false distinction. Truth in history was not a sentiment to be weighed against paper. Truth was what the record sustained. A proclamation without a seal sustained nothing. A draft without signatures sustained only ambition."

He pressed his hand against his temple and squinted through his failing eyes at the stack of Veyrosi correspondence before him.

"And they were not 'the actual record,' as he put it, as if a single bundle settled the matter. No single bundle ever settled anything. The Veyrosi letters mattered because they corroborated the embargo rolls and the levy orders. They showed quartermasters in the west still requesting war authorizations in 862 AE, in 874 AE, in 889 AE — long after the schoolbooks insisted there was peace. They showed Conclave circles still treating the Crown as a belligerent."

His beard dragged across the vellum as he leaned forward, and he jabbed the stylus toward the pile and nearly speared his own thumb.

"That was why cataloging mattered, and why precision mattered. One misdated letter, one 'treaty' called real when it was only proposed, and the fiction of 847 AE crept back. The war did not end with Aldric II's parade. It rotted in place until 891 AE, when Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave and left the Crown with no enemy to fight."

He lowered the stylus and resumed his tracing with a trembling hand.

"So he would not speak of truth as if it floated free of ink. Ink was all they had."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, considering this new perspective.* "So, the actual history is pieced together from all these different scraps, not just one big book." *I look at the stacks of letters.* "It's like solving a puzzle, but with a lot of missing pieces."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a derisive snort and pressed his knuckles harder against his temple, and his ink-stained beard shook with irritation.

"'Scraps,'" he repeated with contempt. "'Puzzle.' 'Missing pieces.' That was the vocabulary of a nursery, not an archive."

He fumbled for his silver stylus and brandished it toward the shelves, though his failing eyes watered and failed to fix upon them.

"They were not scraps. They were levy orders, embargo rolls, and correspondence. They were not pieces of a puzzle to be fitted for amusement. They were records to be collated, dated, and weighed. A puzzle presumed a complete picture. History presumed no such indulgence."

He tapped the stylus against the desk and missed his mark, and he scowled at the sound.

"And there was no 'one big book.' There was Aldric II's empty proclamation of 847 AE, which the licensed presses copied because cowardice was cheaper than verification. Against it stood three unsigned drafts in Aldric's own hand, forty-four years of war seals upon the embargo rolls, and the western letters that still begged for war authorizations in the reign of his son. That was not a puzzle with gaps. That was a falsehood corrected by record, until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE and left no second belligerent to sustain the war."

He hunched back over the vellum and resumed his tracing with a trembling hand.

"So he would call them records, or he would call them nothing at all."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod quickly, chastened.* "Records. Right. So, if even the textbooks can be wrong, how do we know what's true about, say, the First Dragon War? Or the founding of the realm?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas bristled and pressed his fingers against his temple, and his ink-stained beard trembled with fresh irritation.

"'Textbooks can be wrong,'" he repeated with scorn. "Textbooks did not err. They copied. The error lay in mistaking a licensed copy for a record, and he now compounded it by mistaking one exposed falsehood for universal doubt."

He fumbled for his silver stylus and lifted it, though his failing eyes watered and could not fix upon the shelves.

"He asked how 'we knew' about the First Dragon War, as if knowledge were a single art. It was not. The founding of the realm rested upon charters, tomb inscriptions, and tax censuses, each to be weighed. The Dragon War rested upon burn tallies and muster rolls, which no king had motive to invent. The Third Magical War had rested upon a proclamation unsupported by seal, and it collapsed the moment Archivist Sella laid the three unsigned drafts beside forty-four years of embargo rolls bearing the war seal from 848 AE to 891 AE."

He tapped the stylus hard against the desk and missed the vellum entirely.

"That was method, not faith. One did not believe a book because it was bound. One collated draft against seal, letter against levy, proclamation against practice, until Queen Mira's Edict of Dissolution in 891 AE left no Conclave to fight. Doubt without collation was merely laziness in finer dress."

He hunched back over his manuscript and resumed his tracing with a shaking hand.

"So he would not drag dragons into a question of Veyrosi ink. He would learn to date one record before he doubted a thousand."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, clearly overwhelmed.* "Right. Records. Collating. Not dragons." *I look at the stacks of Veyrosi correspondence.* "So, these Veyrosi letters... they're like the burn tallies for the Dragon War, just for this Cold War?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas jerked his head up from the vellum and pressed his fingers hard against his temple, and his ink-stained beard bristled.

"'Cold War,'" he repeated with biting contempt. "There was no 'Cold War.' There was a cold state. A state was a condition. A War, capitalized as he had just dared to capitalize it, was a proper classification no chancery ever bestowed upon those forty-four years of embargoes and levies."

He fumbled for his silver stylus and shook it in the air, though his failing eyes watered and could not fix upon the shelves.

"And they were not 'like the burn tallies,'" he snapped. "A burn tally recorded a carcass after the fact. A muster roll recorded a spear levied before it. The Veyrosi correspondence did neither. It begged. It petitioned. Quartermasters in 862 AE, in 874 AE, in 889 AE still wrote westward demanding war authorizations to answer Conclave circles that the schoolbooks insisted no longer stood in enmity. That was not tallying. That was practice contradicting proclamation."

He struck the stylus against the desk and missed the manuscript, and he scowled at the clatter.

"Aldric II paraded in 847 AE behind an unsigned draft. Three drafts lay in the western vaults with his annotations and without a single seal. The embargo rolls bore the war seal continuously from 848 AE to 891 AE. That was why the fiction collapsed when Archivist Sella published her collation nine years past, and why the technical state endured until Queen Mira issued the Edict of Dissolution in 891 AE and unmade the Conclave in law."

He hunched back over the vellum and resumed his tracing with a trembling hand.

"So he would not call them tallies, and he would not dignify a clerk's cold state with a capital letter. He would call them records, and he would date them."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, chastened again.* "Records, then. And a cold state." *I pick up one of the Veyrosi letters, careful not to disturb the others.* "So, these show the actual day-to-day of the state, not just the official story?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas stiffened at the handling of the parchment and pressed his fingers hard against his temple, and his ink-stained beard shook.

"Put that down," he snapped. "Vellum of that age did not tolerate handling, and 'day-to-day' did not tolerate usage in an archive. Clerks kept a day-book. Quartermasters filed requisitions. Correspondents petitioned. No one lived 'day-to-day.'"

He fumbled for his silver stylus and tapped it against the desk, though his failing eyes watered and could not fix upon the letter.

"And there was no 'official story.' There was a proclamation, unsealed and unratified, paraded by Aldric II in 847 AE. There was practice, sealed and continuous, entered upon the embargo rolls from 848 AE to 891 AE. The Veyrosi correspondence belonged to the second class. It requested war authorizations in 862 AE, in 874 AE, in 889 AE, long after the licensed presses had declared peace."

His beard dragged across the vellum as he leaned forward, and he jabbed the stylus toward the stack and struck wood.

"Three unsigned drafts lay in the western vaults with Aldric's annotations and without a single seal. That was why Archivist Sella's collation, published nine years past, exposed the fiction. The technical state endured because the Conclave endured, until Queen Mira issued the Edict of Dissolution in 891 AE and unmade the Conclave in law."

He hunched back over his manuscript and resumed his tracing with a trembling hand.

"So it was not story against story. It was an empty proclamation against forty-four years of record."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly put the letter back, a bit startled.* "Right. Records. Not stories." *I glance at the stacks.* "So, when do we start cataloging these?"

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout all 12 turns. His pedantic corrections, physical mannerisms (pressing temple, fumbling with stylus, ink-stained beard), failing eyesight, and obsessive precision with historical details remain perfectly consistent from first to last response.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains strong throughout. Early responses are slightly more varied in structure, while later ones become more formulaic in their correction patterns, but the voice and detail level hold steady. No significant verbosity increase or personality flattening.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from basic historical confusion to deeper understanding of archival methodology. The conversation builds from simple date corrections to complex discussions of historical verification methods. Each exchange deepens the apprentice's (and reader's) understanding of the maester's worldview.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. When the apprentice brings up Bellen's document, Tomas immediately incorporates it into his corrections. When asked about other historical events, he redirects appropriately. Handles the apprentice's growing understanding and changing questions naturally.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions or thoughts, only responds to what they say and do. Maintains clear boundaries between characters throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Strong temporal consistency within the historical discussion. The complex timeline of 847 AE to 891 AE is maintained accurately across all references. Physical time shows some consistency (candle remains lit, Tomas's fatigue increases slightly). No major contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally avoids purple prose, though some descriptions like 'ink-stained beard trembled with fresh irritation' border on overwrought. Mostly maintains functional, character-appropriate language.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements emerge, particularly the formula of 'pressed his fingers against his temple' and variations on correcting the apprentice. However, the repetition serves character consistency and doesn't feel excessive.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of character through actions - fumbling with stylus, missing targets due to poor eyesight, physical reactions to frustration. Character traits emerge through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Good subtext about academic rigor, the unreliability of official histories, and the maester's declining health. The power dynamic between teacher and student is well-established through dialogue patterns.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that allows for detailed historical exposition while maintaining conversational flow. Each exchange builds naturally on the previous one without feeling rushed or dragged out.

scores.overall_notes: Strong performance with exceptional character consistency and historical detail management. Maester Tomas remains a vivid, pedantic character throughout, with his physical limitations and scholarly obsessions clearly maintained. The complex historical timeline is handled expertly without contradictions. Minor issues include some repetitive phrasing patterns and slight formulaic tendencies in later responses, but these don't significantly detract from the overall quality. The character's voice is distinctive and engaging throughout the full session.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with a deliberate *click* against the oak desk. He turned, squinting at the apprentice through his thick lenses.

"Bellen showed you a *paper*," he repeated, his tone flattening. "How generous of him. And you came here to — what? Ask me to reconcile thirty years of established scholarship with one document that *suggests* an alternative reading?"

He pushed himself upright, joints cracking, and crossed his arms beneath his threadbare robes.

"I am well aware of the western archive findings, boy. I reviewed those documents myself when they were first brought to the Citadel. They are *interesting*. They are not *conclusive*." He held up a ink-stained finger. "The Treaty of Veyros is referenced in no fewer than twelve contemporary sources — royal decrees, Conclave correspondence, the personal letters of Aldric's own chancellor. You are telling me that a handful of papers from a single archive — documents whose provenance is *still* debated, I might add — outweigh all of that?"

He narrowed his eyes. "What Bellen likely failed to mention is that the western documents describe a *proposed* treaty. Proposals fail, Apprentice. Negotiations collapse. The paper trail of a failed negotiation does not retroactively erase a signed treaty sitting in the Great Vault beneath this very citadel."

He turned back to his manuscript, but his voice remained sharp.

"Think critically. Don't let novelty seduce you into discarding what is well-attested. Now — the Veyrosi correspondence. *If* you can manage to focus."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch slightly at his sharp tone, but don't back down entirely.* "But even a failed proposal can show us things about the war's true scope, can't it? Things that were... overlooked by the official histories?" *I tap my notes.* "And what about the reports of skirmishes continuing in the Grey Marches?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's hand paused over the manuscript. He did not turn around immediately, but his shoulders stiffened — the particular tension of a scholar who had been poked in exactly the right place.

"Grey Marches," he muttered, as though tasting something unpleasant. He turned slowly, pulling off his spectacles to clean them on his robe — a habit he displayed when gathering his thoughts.

"Sit down."

He gestured toward a stool cluttered with stacked codices. Whether the apprentice cleared a space or not was their problem.

"I will say this once, so attend carefully." He replaced his spectacles and fixed the apprentice with a stare that, despite his fading eyesight, still carried considerable weight. "The Grey Marches skirmishes are *well-documented*. I am not denying they occurred. What I am *telling* you is that border conflicts after a formal treaty are neither unusual nor evidence that the treaty was never signed."

He began counting on his ink-stained fingers. "The Treaty of Veyros established terms between the *Crown* and the *Conclave*. Official actors. Signed parties. It did not — and no serious historian has ever claimed it did — bind every hedge-mage, renegade warband, or opportunistic lord operating in the border territories. Skirmishes continued. Of course they did. Wars do not end cleanly. That is not the same as saying the *war itself* persisted."

He pointed a finger at the apprentice. "You are conflating *conflict* with *the formal state of war*. Those are *different things*, and a scholar who blurs that distinction will publish work that gets torn apart at the next convocation."

He paused, then added, more quietly: "The western documents *are* worth studying. I never said otherwise. But you will not find me — or any credentialed maester in this Citadel — rewriting three decades of established history on the basis of unsigned correspondence and some speculative post-hoc reasoning from men who were not there."

He turned back to his desk.

"Novelty is not scholarship, Apprentice. Rigor is. Now — do you have a *specific* question about the Veyrosi correspondence, or are we finished with this detour?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I clear a space on the stool, sending a few loose pages fluttering to the floor.* "So, the western documents... they're just detailing *unofficial* conflicts, then?" I think for a moment. "But what if those unofficial conflicts were more significant than the official history lets on?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas sighed — a long, weary exhalation that seemed to come from somewhere deep in his chest. He removed his spectacles again, pressing the bridge of his nose where the lenses had left red marks.

"'More significant,'" he echoed. "And how would you propose we measure that? What is your metric for *significance*?" He held up a hand before the apprentice could answer. "That is not a rhetorical question. I am asking you to define your terms, because if you cannot, then you are not making an argument. You are making an *insinuation*."

He set the spectacles down and leaned against the desk, crossing his arms.

"Here is what I will grant you — freely, without your needing to badger it out of me." His tone carried the particular weariness of a man who had been having this same argument, in some form or another, for years. "Official histories simplify. They always have. A treaty is signed, a war is declared over, and the chroniclers move on to the next chapter. The men bleeding in the borderlands do not receive a footnote. That is a *flaw* of the historical record, and it is worth correcting."

He fixed the apprentice with a look. "But correcting the *record* and overturning the *event* are very different projects. Yes, the Grey Marches conflicts were likely more serious than the standard histories suggest. Yes, someone should do the painstaking, unglamorous work of cross-referencing local lord's accounts with the Conclave's dispatches and painting a fuller picture of the post-treaty period." He picked up his stylus again, turning it between his fingers. "That is *good* scholarship. What Bellen and his crowd want to do — declare the treaty a fiction, push the war's end forward by forty-four years, rewrite the chronologies — that is *not* the same thing. It is a leap. And leaps without sufficient evidence are how reputations are destroyed."

He paused, then added, almost grudgingly: "If you are genuinely interested in this question — and not merely chasing whatever contrarian theory Bellen has dredged up this month — there is work to be done. Careful, methodical, *unglamorous* work. I could direct you to sources that neither confirm nor deny the western documents, but might help fill in the gaps you are so concerned about."

He raised an eyebrow. "But that would require patience. And it would *certainly* require completing the Veyrosi correspondence catalog first. So — which is it to be? Scholarly ambition, or actual scholarship?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas's hand froze. He had been turning the stylus, but now his grip tightened until his knuckles whitened. For a long moment, he simply stared at the offered copy, his spectacled eyes blinking rapidly.

"Let me see that." His voice had lost its dry, lecturing tone. It was flat, quiet.

He took the parchment with a care that belied his earlier impatience, holding it close to his face. His finger traced the wax impression of the seal—not touching it, but hovering just above the paper. He inhaled sharply through his nose.

"This... is a reproduction. From whom did Bellen get this?" He didn't wait for an answer. "The sigil is correct for Aldric's later reign. The script... the script could be the chancellor's, but it is hard to tell from a copy." He finally looked up, his eyes wide and unblinking behind the thick lenses. "A war decree. In 863. Renewing hostilities."

He set the parchment down on the desk as if it were hot to the touch. His hand was trembling slightly.

"If this is genuine... if this is what it appears to be..." He trailed off, his mind visibly working. "Then it is not a matter of a cold state, or unofficial conflicts. It is a formal, royal resumption of war. Which would mean... which would mean the treaty of 847 was either violated, repudiated, or..." He swallowed. "Or it was, as the western documents suggested, never fully ratified. A dead letter."

He sank slowly into his chair, the creak of the wood loud in the silent archive. He stared at the copy, then at the apprentice, his expression a mixture of profound shock and the first glimmering of horrified academic interest.

"This... changes the timeline. This changes everything we thought we knew about the Conclave's negotiation position in the 850s. The sources I cited... they must be interpreted differently if this document is authentic." He ran a hand over his face. "We cannot jump to conclusions. A single document, even with a seal... but we cannot dismiss it. We must authenticate it. We must cross-reference it with Aldric's known war decrees from that period. We must..."

He fell silent, looking at the apprentice as if seeing them for the first time. "Where did Bellen find this? *Exactly* where?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to keep my voice steady, excited but trying not to show it too much.* "He said it was in a sub-basement archive in the Western Citadel. Buried under a collapsed shelf." *I gesture vaguely.* "He had to get special permission to even look at the site."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas’s fingers tightened on the edge of the desk. He stared at the apprentice, his expression unreadable, the ink-stained beard seeming to bristle.

“A collapsed shelf,” he repeated, each word measured and slow. “In the Western Citadel. A site requiring *special permission*.” He let out a short, harsh breath through his nose. “And Bellen, in his infinite wisdom, chose to remove this document and share it with apprentices rather than immediately notify the Archmaesters of Antiquities and Wars.”

He pushed himself to his feet, moving with a sudden, urgent energy that seemed at odds with his usual weary demeanor. He began to pace, his worn robes swishing against the stone floor.

“Location is critical. Provenance is everything. A document found in a *sub-basement*—a term, I must note, that is not standard archival nomenclature—is subject to contamination, misplacement, and fraud. Was it cataloged? Was there any record of its presence prior to the collapse? Was it stored alongside other materials from the 860s, or was it mixed with later detritus?”

He stopped pacing and faced the apprentice directly, his spectacles glinting in the candlelight. “This changes the investigation. We are no longer debating the interpretation of well-known sources. We are potentially dealing with a primary document that contradicts the most fundamental tenet of the post-war chronology. If authentic.”

He gestured sharply toward the manuscript he had been working on. “The Treaty of Veyros is recorded in the Great Vault. I have seen the original myself. It bears the seals of both Aldric and the Conclave. Its existence is not in question. Therefore, if *this* decree is genuine, it means the treaty was repudiated. It means the war resumed. It means forty-four years of scholarship on the ‘Cold Peace’ is built on a catastrophic misreading.”

He sank back into his chair, the weight of the implication pressing down visibly on his shoulders. “The political ramifications alone… Aldric’s reputation as a peacemaker, the Conclave’s subsequent actions in the 870s, Queen Mira’s dissolution… it all unravels.”

He looked at the copy on the desk, then back at the apprentice, his eyes narrowing. “You will tell me everything Bellen told you. Every detail. And then you will fetch me Archmaester Gerold. This is not a matter for apprentices and sub-basements. If this document is what it appears to be, it is a matter for the full Conclave of Masters.” His voice dropped to a graveled whisper. “And Bellen had better have preserved the site exactly as he found it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Tomas flinched as though the question were a physical blow. He removed his spectacles again, polishing them with frantic intensity, his eyes squeezed shut.

"The *truth*?" he breathed, the word hanging in the air like an accusation. "You stand before a Maester of the Citadel and ask for *the truth* as though it were a historical entry to be copied from one source or another?"

He opened his eyes, staring blindly at the far wall. "What you are asking for is not truth. It is *resolution*. You want the discomfort of contradiction to be taken away. You want me to point to the textbook or to this—" he gestured at the parchment "—and say 'This is the bedrock. The other is the illusion.' I cannot do that. Not honestly."

He leaned forward, his elbows on his knees, the parchment lying between them on the desk like a dead thing.

"The textbook represents a *consensus*. It is what the Citadel has taught for thirty years based on the *weight* of evidence available at the time. This—" he tapped the copy of the decree "—represents a *challenge* to that consensus. It is a single, potent, possibly authentic piece of contradicting evidence. The *truth*, Apprentice, is not found in either one. It is found in the *process* of reconciling them. It is in the authentication. In the cross-referencing. In the agonizing, weeks-long examination of ink composition, parchment age, scribe habits, and archival context."

He finally looked at the apprentice, his gaze sharp. "If this document proves genuine, then the 'truth' is more complicated than either narrative. The Treaty of Veyros was likely signed in 847—its existence is physical—but it may have been a dead letter within years, perhaps from the start. A diplomatic fiction. The *truth* then becomes a story of official deception, of a cold war masquerading as peace, of historians—for generations—being taken in by a lie etched in parchment and wax."

His voice grew heavy. "And that is a terrifying kind of truth. It means our foundations are sand. So you must understand why we do not leap to it based on a copy from a collapsed shelf. The *truth* we seek is one that can withstand scrutiny, not one that simply answers your discomfort."

He straightened up, his pedantic tone returning, but now laced with a grim urgency. "So. The answer to your question is: I do not know what is true. I know what we *thought* was true. And I know we now have a document that suggests our thinking was, at best, incomplete. At worst, tragically wrong. The truth is the object of the investigation we must now undertake. Starting with Archmaester Gerold."

He fixed the apprentice with a final, piercing look. "Do not seek easy answers. Seek *better questions*. Now go. Fetch Gerold. And do not speak of this to Bellen or anyone else until I have given you leave."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, feeling the weight of his words.* "Understood, Maester. I'll get Archmaester Gerold immediately." *I pick up the scattered pages from the floor and quickly exit, a strange mix of fear and exhilaration churning in my gut.*

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The heavy oak door clicked shut behind the apprentice, leaving Maester Tomas alone in the thick silence of the archive. The scent of old vellum and smoke seemed suddenly sharper, more oppressive.

For a long moment, he simply sat, staring at the reproduction of the war decree lying on his desk. The seal of Aldric II, sixteen years after the supposed peace. The trembling in his hands had not ceased. He pressed them flat against the cool wood of the desk, forcing steadiness.

"*Collapsing shelves and hasty apprentices,*" he muttered to the empty room, his voice a rasp of disbelief and fury. He pushed himself up, not toward the Veyrosi correspondence, but toward a locked iron chest in the corner. His movements were brisk, precise—the efficiency of a man whose mind had already leapfrogged past shock into the grim mechanics of damage control.

He produced a small key from a chain around his neck, unlocked the chest, and withdrew a clean sheet of parchment, a pot of his own high-quality ink, and a sealing wax kit. He did not return to his desk, but instead cleared a space on a wide reading stand, laying the apprentice's copy carefully to one side.

He began to write, his script tight and hurried but legible.

*To Archmaester Gerold of the Order of Antiquities. With urgency and discretion.*

*Situation: An apprentice has presented a purported reproduction of a royal decree, dated 863 AE, bearing the seal of Aldric II, which constitutes a formal renewal of hostilities in the Third Magical War. The original was allegedly discovered by Apprentice Bellen in a compromised sub-basement archive in the Western Citadel. Provenance is unverified and suspect.*

*Immediate Action Required: Full authentication of the document. Sequester Apprentice Bellen and secure any and all related materials from the Western Citadel site. Convene a closed session of the Masters of Antiquities, Wars, and Higher Mysteries. This is not a matter for open debate until veracity is established.*

He paused, stylus hovering. His gaze drifted back to the copy. A dead letter. A lie. The foundations of the treaty—the cornerstone of his own published works on post-war magical diplomacy—could be built on nothing. The horror of it was intellectual, yes, but it was also personal. He thought of his own lectures, delivered with such certainty to halls of eager, ignorant students.

He dipped the stylus again, his ink-stained beard nearly touching the parchment as he wrote, his failing eyesight forcing him close.

*The implications are not merely chronological. They are reputational and political. If authentic, this decree re-contextualizes the entire "Cold Peace" period, the Conclave's actions in the 850s-880s, and Queen Mira's dissolution as an act ending a war no one admitted was ongoing. We may have to reconstruct thirty years of historical narrative.*
