Fourteen messages in the inbox. Twelve were automated pings from the relay itself, timestamps from the last 72 hours. One was from their editor, sent at 6 PM: *check in when you're settled.* Noor had not checked in.

The fourteenth message was not from Lisbon.

They stared at it. The routing header showed a number they didn't recognize — not the secondary, not the primary, not any number associated with Marta's protocol. Sent at 11:47 PM. Twenty-seven minutes ago. The message body was a single line of characters that looked like noise.

Noor's hands went still on the keyboard.

It wasn't noise. It was a cipher Marta had shown them four months ago in a café in Nicosia, written on a paper napkin that Marta had then folded into a small square and put in her jacket pocket. Noor had memorized it because Marta had said *if you ever see this, don't reply, just go.* She'd said it the way you say something you hope never becomes relevant.

Noor closed the laptop halfway. Not all the way — just enough to kill the screen.

"Yeah," they said, voice level. "Check the kitchen. See if there's anything that doesn't need to be cooked."

They were already reaching for the encrypted drive with one hand and their phone with the other. The phone went face-down on the table. Then they picked it back up and powered it completely off and held it in their fist while they thought about the road and the trees and how far it was to the car.

"How much gas did we have when we got here?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down, a little annoyed, but Noor's tone makes me pause.* "Enough to get us back to town, I think. Why?" *I push myself up from the couch.* "What's up? You look like you've seen a ghost."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor was already calculating. Forty minutes to the main road. Another twenty to the first town with anything resembling cover — a motel, a gas station, people. The drive had three files on it that nobody else had copies of. Their editor didn't know the cabin's address, only the county.

"I need you to think about whether 'enough' means enough," Noor said. Their voice had gone quiet in a way that was different from tired. "Not approximately. Actually."

They stood up from the table and moved to the window again, but this time they didn't look through the curtain. They stood to the side of it, back against the wall, and listened. Wind in the pines. Nothing else. Nothing that sounded like a car engine that had cut its headlights on a mountain road.

Maybe nothing.

Maybe.

"Marta sent me a message twenty-seven minutes ago," Noor said, still facing the wall. "Not from her number. From a number I don't know. The message is a cipher she told me four months ago meant *don't reply, just go.*" They paused. "She could be compromised. She could be warning me that someone else is compromised. I don't know which. I don't know if she sent it herself."

They moved away from the window and picked up the padded case with the drive. It went into the interior pocket of their jacket, which was still hanging over the curtain rod. They pulled it down and put it on.

"I'm not going to panic," Noor said, which was something a person said when they were actively not panicking. "But I want to know about the gas, and I want you to think about whether you noticed anything on the road coming up here. Any car that might have been behind us for a while. Any turnout with a vehicle parked in it." They looked at Driver directly for the first time in an hour. "I need your actual memory, not reassurance. Can you do that?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked at Driver for a moment. Then they stopped looking at Driver.

That was fine. That was — fine. Driver had driven them here, which was the thing Driver had agreed to do. Noor had not told Driver what they were walking into, not really, because there were things you didn't tell people who hadn't signed up for them. That was on Noor. That was a debt they were carrying.

They went to the kitchen themselves.

The cabinet had three mugs, as advertised, and a can of black beans, a can of corn, a box of crackers that had been opened and resealed with a rubber band. Noor took the crackers and the can of beans and set them on the counter. There was a manual can opener on a hook by the sink. They stood there and opened the beans in the dark, by feel mostly, and ate a third of the can standing up with a spoon they found in the drying rack. Cold. Tasted like nothing. They ate it anyway.

Their mind was doing the thing it did under pressure, which was to become very orderly and slightly cold.

*What do I know.* Marta was three hours late. Twenty-seven minutes ago she — or someone with access to her emergency channel — had sent a cipher that meant *go.* The cabin's location was known to Noor, to Driver, and to Marta. It was not written down anywhere that Noor knew of. Marta had a good memory and a habit of not writing things down either.

*What I don't know.* Whether Marta sent the message. Whether Marta was alive. Whether the message was a warning or a trap designed to look like a warning. Whether the road was clear.

Noor put the beans in the refrigerator out of some automatic instinct toward tidiness and then stood in the dark kitchen with the crackers in one hand and thought about the order of operations.

They needed to check the drive. There were three files on it and if something happened to the drive tonight — if they had to run and drop it or if it was taken — the story died. Four months of work. Noor had a partial backup on an air-gapped machine at their apartment in the city, but partial meant partial.

They went back to the table, sat down, and opened the laptop again. The screen light came up. They plugged in the drive.

"I'm going to be twenty minutes," they said to the room, to Driver, to no one. "Then we should go."

They were already copying files.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, putting my phone down for real this time.* "Alright, alright. I'll check the gas." *I get up and head for the door.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor looked up sharply.

"Don't start the car," they said. "Just check the gauge. And don't — " They stopped. Recalibrated. Driver was doing them a favor. Driver was doing them a favor right now, in the middle of the night, in a hunting cabin, and Noor was about to give a list of operational instructions to someone who had not agreed to be in an operation.

"Don't use the flashlight app," they said, more quietly. "There's a real flashlight in the glove box. Keep it pointed down."

They watched Driver go out the door and then sat very still for three seconds, listening to the sound of footsteps on the porch, the creak of the cabin steps, and then nothing. Wind. The pines.

The file transfer was at 34%.

Noor ate a cracker and looked at the progress bar and did not look at the door.

The drive had three files. The first was a ledger — not a metaphorical ledger, an actual one, photographed page by page, showing eighteen months of payments between a shell company registered in Cyprus and a series of accounts that Noor had traced, painstakingly, to four names. The fourth name was the one that made this dangerous. The fourth name was the reason Marta had been scared in that café in Nicosia, scared in the particular way of someone who had decided to be brave anyway, which was the scariest kind of scared there was.

52%.

The second file was testimony. Audio, forty-one minutes, a voice that Noor had agreed never to name even in their own notes. They had labeled it *source two* in the file name and *my conscience* in their head, because this person had given up something irreplaceable to sit in front of a recorder and speak clearly for forty-one minutes about what they had seen.

Noor owed that person a story that got published. They owed them that at minimum.

71%.

They heard footsteps on the porch again and their hands went flat on the table before they recognized the pattern of them — the particular weight and rhythm of someone they'd ridden in a car with for four hours.

Driver came back through the door.

Noor looked up, waiting.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I come back in, looking a little confused.* "Okay, so the gas tank is... pretty full. Looks like it's got at least three-quarters." *I glance around the room, then back at Noor.* "Didn't see anything out there though. Just dark."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let out a breath they had been holding since the door opened.

"Good," they said. "That's good."

The file transfer hit 100% and they unplugged the drive before the confirmation dialog had fully appeared, which was bad practice and they knew it, but they ran the verification anyway — hash check, file count, sizes — and everything matched. They copied the verification string into a note on the laptop, then deleted the note, then sat for a moment thinking about whether deleting it had been the right call. It had. The string existed in their memory now and that was where it needed to be.

They put the drive back in the padded case. The case went back in the interior pocket of their jacket. They zipped it.

"Nothing on the road when we came up?" they asked. Not accusatory. Just asking again, because Driver had actually gone outside and stood in the dark and that deserved a real question in return. "No cars parked at the trailhead turnout about two miles back? There's a little gravel pull-off, you might not have clocked it."

They were already closing the laptop. It went into the bag. The charger went in after it. Noor moved through the cabin doing a fast, automatic sweep — the kind of sweep that looked like tidiness but was actually about leaving nothing that confirmed someone had been here. The coffee pot was still dusty. Good, they hadn't touched it. The can of beans was in the refrigerator, which was stupid, which was them being stupid, so they took it back out and put it exactly where it had been in the cabinet.

The spoon went back in the drying rack.

The crackers — they'd moved the crackers. They stood in the kitchen trying to remember where the crackers had been and could not remember, so they put them at the back of the counter against the wall, which was a reasonable place for crackers to be.

"I'm not going to tell you there's definitely something wrong," Noor said, coming back to the main room with the bag over their shoulder. They picked up their dead phone and pocketed it. "I don't know that. What I know is that someone used Marta's emergency channel to tell me to leave, and Marta is three hours late, and those two things together are enough." They looked at Driver. "You drove me here. I'm asking you to drive me back. I know that's not nothing."

They went to the door and stood with their hand on the frame, not opening it yet. Listening.

Wind. Pines. The particular silence of a mountain that had no interest in them whatsoever.

"We go slow with the headlights on," Noor said. "Normal. Like we're just leaving. We don't hurry until we're on the main road." They paused. "Thank you for checking the gas."

They meant it. They opened the door.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I grab my phone off the couch, still a bit confused but getting the message.* "Alright, let's go then." *I follow you out, casting one last look at the empty cabin.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The porch light was off — Noor had unscrewed the bulb when they'd arrived, a habit — and the night came up around them like cold water. The temperature had dropped since they'd pulled in. Noor could see their breath.

They went down the steps first, moving to the side of the path rather than down the center of it, which was something they'd read once in a book about fieldwork and had never been able to stop doing. The gravel was loud. Everything was loud. The pines made a sound like static.

The car was where Driver had left it, pulled around to face the road. Noor had asked for that too, when they'd arrived. *Point it out, just in case we need to leave fast.* Driver had done it without asking why, which Noor had been grateful for and hadn't said so.

They got in the passenger side and sat with the bag on their lap and looked at the tree line while Driver settled in and got the engine going.

The headlights came on and lit up the road ahead — gravel for another hundred meters, then the turn onto the unpaved track that ran down to the main road. Noor looked at the trees on the left side, then the right. Nothing resolved out of the dark. No shapes that were wrong. No light-bounce off glass or chrome.

Maybe nothing.

The car began to move and Noor watched the mirrors.

At the first bend they passed the spot where a pine had come down in some past storm and been dragged to the shoulder, and Noor remembered it from the drive up and felt something in their chest loosen by approximately one degree. Landmarks were good. Landmarks meant you were moving.

"Take it easy on the switchbacks," they said. "The second one has a soft shoulder."

They'd noticed that on the way up too. They noticed things like that now without deciding to. Four months of this story had done something to the way they moved through the world, the way they catalogued exits and sight lines and the gas gauges of cars they were riding in. Noor was not sure that was a thing that fully went away when the story was done.

*When the story is done.* 

They looked at the encrypted drive through the fabric of their jacket, not literally, just with their hand pressed flat against the pocket. The fourth name was in there. The ledger was in there. Forty-one minutes of a voice that had decided to be brave.

"When we get to the main road," Noor said, "I need to find somewhere with wifi. Not a residential signal — somewhere public, open, a gas station or a diner. I need to send one email before I do anything else." Their editor. Twelve hours overdue on a check-in, and now they were leaving the cabin without the source, and the editor needed to know the name of the county at minimum. The editor had a protocol too. Everyone in this had a protocol, a set of napkin-ciphers and contingency numbers, and the protocols only worked if you actually used them when you were supposed to.

The trees moved past the windows. The road curved and the headlights swept across gravel and brush and then more trees, the same trees, the mountain not particularly interested in whether they made it down or not.

Noor ate the last cracker from their jacket pocket — they'd pocketed a few without thinking about it — and chewed and watched the road and thought about Marta in a café in Nicosia, folding a napkin into a small square.

*If you ever see this, just go.*

"You did good," Noor said. It came out quieter than intended. "Tonight. You didn't ask a lot of questions."

They weren't sure if that was a compliment or an apology. Probably both.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The road dipped and the headlights caught the soft shoulder on the second switchback — exactly where Noor had said it would be — and then they were past it and the track straightened out for a long stretch between two walls of pine.

Noor watched Driver's phone light up the side of their face in the dark.

They turned back to the windshield and said nothing about it.

There was a thing Noor had learned about asking people for things, which was that you could only ask so many times before the asking itself became a kind of pressure that made people less useful, not more. Driver had checked the gas. Driver was driving. The phone was Driver's business.

The trees thinned on the left side and for a moment there was a view — the valley below, a scatter of lights that might have been the town or might have been a farm complex, too far to tell. Then the trees closed back in.

Noor thought about the email.

It needed to say: *I'm mobile. Cabin is clear. Source did not make contact. I have the material.* It needed to say those things and nothing else, and it needed to go to an address their editor checked on a separate device that lived in a drawer at home. Their editor had three children and a mortgage and had been doing this for twenty-two years, and when Noor had called them four months ago and said *I have something, I don't know how big yet,* their editor had said *tell me what you need* without a single question about liability or legal or the quarterly numbers. Noor owed them the email. Noor owed them more than the email but the email was what they could do right now.

The gravel gave way to packed dirt, which meant they were two miles from the main road.

Noor shifted the bag on their lap and felt the outline of the laptop through the fabric. They thought about the fourth name. They thought about what it would mean to publish it — not abstractly, not in the way you thought about impact in a pitch meeting, but concretely: what would happen to the people adjacent to that name, the ones who hadn't done anything, the ones who would nonetheless find themselves in the blast radius of a story that had to be told. Noor had thought about this at 3 AM in a lot of different cities and had always come back to the same place, which was that the alternative was worse, which was not a comfortable place to land but was the only honest one.

They were still coming back to it now, apparently. Even on a mountain road at twelve-thirty in the morning.

*Journalist brain,* Marta had said once, not unkindly. *You can't turn it off. Even when you should.*

Noor pressed their hand flat against the jacket pocket again. The drive was there. The drive was there.

Ahead, through the trees, they could see the pale gray line of the main road.

"Left at the junction," Noor said. "There's a gas station about eight miles down. I saw it when we came through." They had clocked it automatically — the open sign, the attached diner, the parking lot with four trucks in it at nine in the evening. People. Light. Wifi, probably, or at minimum a payphone if payphones still existed in this county, which was not a given.

They watched the junction approach and thought about Marta folding that napkin and thought about forty-one minutes of a voice being brave, and felt the particular exhaustion of someone who was not going to stop.

"I'll buy you coffee," Noor said. "When we get there."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Sounds good." *I nod, still focused on the road, then glance at the gas station sign ahead.* "Coffee, maybe some actual food."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The gas station was exactly where Noor had remembered it — the open sign buzzing orange in the window, a diner attached on the left side with the lights on and two booths visible through the glass. One truck in the lot now instead of four. Nearly one in the morning. Noor noted the truck out of habit, noted the plates were local, noted the driver's silhouette visible through the diner window with a cup in front of them.

Driver pulled in and Noor was out of the car before it had fully stopped, which was rude, which they couldn't help.

The cold air hit them and they stood for a moment in the parking lot just breathing it. Mountain air at the base of the mountain, which smelled different from the cabin — gas and asphalt and something frying, normal smells, civilization smells. Noor had not realized how much they'd wanted to be somewhere with other people until they were somewhere with other people.

They went inside first.

The woman behind the counter was maybe sixty, reading something on a tablet, and she looked up when the door opened with the particular look of someone who had seen enough late arrivals to not be curious about them.

"Wifi?" Noor asked.

"Password's on the menu." She nodded toward the laminated cards on the tables.

Noor took the booth farthest from the door, facing the entrance, back to the wall. They had the laptop out and open before they'd sat down fully. The wifi password was *mountainview1* and it connected on the first try and Noor opened the encrypted mail client and started typing.

*Mobile. Cabin clear. Source no contact. Material secured. Will explain when I can. Don't call the primary number — it's off. Use the relay.*

They read it back once. Sent it.

Then they sat with their hands flat on the table and felt the thing that happened after you did the thing you were supposed to do, which was not relief exactly but was the absence of one specific weight.

The woman came over with a notepad. "What can I get you?"

"Two coffees," Noor said. "And — " They looked at the menu for the first time. Eggs. Toast. A thing called the *mountain scramble* that appeared to involve potatoes and cheese and probably enough calories to constitute an actual meal. "The scramble. Two of those."

They hadn't asked Driver what they wanted. They'd order the same thing and if Driver hated eggs that was a problem for Driver to solve.

Noor looked at the door. Driver was still outside, or coming in, or doing something — Noor tracked the movement in their peripheral vision and consciously made themselves stop tracking it. Driver was fine. The parking lot was fine. The road was a pale line through the window and nothing was coming down it.

They looked at the encrypted drive case on the table in front of them. At some point between the cabin and here they'd taken it out of their pocket and set it on the table without noticing, which was the kind of thing their hands did when their mind was somewhere else.

Four months. Eighteen months of payments in a ledger. Forty-one minutes of brave.

Noor turned the case over once in their hands and set it back down.

The coffee came first, two mugs, and Noor wrapped both hands around one of them and looked at the steam rising off it and thought: *Marta knew this number for two years. She kept it for emergencies. She used it tonight.*

That meant something. Noor didn't know yet if it meant she was safe or not safe, but it meant she had been deliberate. Marta was always deliberate. Noor held onto that.

The diner smelled like coffee and hash browns and the particular fluorescent warmth of places that stay open all night for whoever needs them. The truck driver in the other booth turned a page of something. The woman behind the counter went back to her tablet.

Noor looked up when they heard the door.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I walk in, rubbing my hands together against the cold. I head straight for the counter.* "Hey, anything hot to drink besides coffee?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The woman behind the counter considered this with the expression of someone who had been asked harder questions. "Hot chocolate. Tea, if you want it. Cider, maybe — let me check if the jug's still good."

Noor watched Driver at the counter for a moment, then looked back at the encrypted drive.

They needed to think about next steps. The story had a shape now — it had always had a shape, but tonight had changed the outline of it in ways Noor was still mapping. The source was Marta's contact, not Noor's directly, which meant if Marta was compromised then the sourcing chain had a problem. Not an unfixable problem. There were two other people who could corroborate the ledger independently, people Noor hadn't approached yet because approaching them had felt premature, and now it didn't feel premature anymore. Now it felt necessary.

Noor opened a new document on the laptop and typed three initials with no other context and stared at them.

Then they typed: *timeline for contact. one week. before that if Marta surfaces.*

They closed the document and sat back.

The scramble arrived before Driver did — two plates, eggs and potatoes and cheese, the woman setting them down without ceremony and going back to her post. Noor pulled both plates closer to make room on the table and then felt slightly absurd about it, like they were setting a table at a dinner party instead of sitting in a mountain diner at one in the morning with an encrypted drive and four months of someone else's courage in their jacket pocket.

They picked up a fork.

The potatoes were good. Noor ate three bites standing up, not standing up literally, but in the way where their body was at the table and their mind was still on the road, still in the cabin, still in a café in Nicosia watching a woman fold a napkin into a small square. They made a deliberate effort to taste the fourth bite. Salt. Cheese. Something that had been cooked in a pan by a person who had done it a thousand times.

They were still alive. They were in a diner. The food was hot.

Noor ate the fourth bite and the fifth and watched Driver come away from the counter with whatever they'd gotten and felt something that was not quite gratitude and not quite guilt but lived in the same neighborhood as both.

"Food's here," they said, which Driver could obviously see. "Eggs. I ordered for you — I should have asked." A pause. "I should have asked a lot of things tonight. Before we left the city." They looked at their plate. "I didn't tell you what this was. That wasn't fair."

It wasn't an apology exactly. It was an acknowledgment, which was different, and was the most Noor knew how to offer right now in a diner at one in the morning when they were still not sure what the night had been.

They pushed the second plate across the table toward Driver's side.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I slide into the booth, taking a sip of my hot chocolate.* "It's fine, I like eggs." *I pick up my fork, looking at the scramble. I take a bite.* "And this is good. Don't worry about it."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched Driver eat for a moment.

*Don't worry about it.* The particular generosity of people who meant it when they said things like that — who didn't require you to enumerate your failures before letting you off the hook. Noor had a complicated relationship with that kind of generosity. It made them feel the weight of what they'd asked more clearly, not less.

They ate. The scramble was good. Outside, the road stayed empty.

After a few minutes Noor reached across the table and turned the encrypted drive case face-down, which was meaningless — there was nothing identifying on the outside of it — but which felt like the right thing to do in a lit room with a stranger in the other booth. An old instinct. Marta had the same one. Marta would put her phone face-down on a café table before she said anything important, even though the phone was off, even though it didn't matter. *Habit is the thing that saves you when thinking is too slow,* Marta had said. *Build the right habits and your body does the work.*

Noor thought about Marta a lot tonight. More than was useful.

They refilled their coffee from the carafe the woman had left on the table and looked at the window and looked at the door and looked at Driver eating eggs at one in the morning because Noor had needed a driver and Driver had said yes.

"The story is going to be published," Noor said. Not to convince anyone. Just — it needed to be said out loud, in a real place, to a real person. "Whatever happened tonight. Whether Marta comes back around or doesn't. The material is solid." They tapped the drive case once with two fingers. "It's all in here. Four months of — " They stopped. Started again. "There's a name in here. Someone with a lot of resources who has been moving money in a way that has hurt a lot of people who will never know his name. And when this publishes, they'll know." Noor looked at the table. "That's worth tonight."

They weren't sure if they were explaining it to Driver or to themselves. Probably both. Probably that was the same thing at one in the morning in a gas station diner at the base of a mountain.

They ate the rest of the scramble. Outside, the road was still empty. Somewhere up that road was a cabin with three mugs and a curtain that smelled like their jacket and a can of black beans back in the cabinet where it belonged.

Noor thought: *Marta is deliberate. She has been deliberate for twenty years. She used the number.*

They held onto that.

"When you're done," they said, "I need about four more hours before I can think about sleeping. I want to find a motel — something on the highway, not local, somewhere with a parking lot you can see from the room." They picked up the drive case and put it back in their jacket pocket. "After that I'll sleep and tomorrow I start making calls." They looked at Driver. "You can go home tomorrow. You've done more than I had any right to ask."

The coffee was hot. The potatoes were good. The road outside was empty and the pines were somewhere up in the dark and Noor was still here, still moving, still in possession of forty-one minutes of someone being brave.

That was enough for tonight. That had to be enough.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finish my last bite of eggs, pushing the plate away.* "Nah, I'm good. I can stick around. What's one more night, right?" *I take another sip of my hot chocolate.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Noor's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the methodical journalist mindset, operational awareness, guilt about involving Driver, and the specific way they process stress through ordered thinking. Their voice never wavers from the established paranoid-but-professional tone.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones (especially turns 14, 18, 22) show richer internal monologue and more sophisticated layering of tension, memory, and character motivation. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from static waiting → crisis discovery → decision to flee → escape → temporary safety. Each turn builds tension and moves the story forward. The emotional arc from isolation to cautious relief is well-paced.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to Driver's minimal engagement style. When Driver becomes dismissive (turn 7), Noor shifts to self-reliance. When Driver helps (turn 11), Noor shows genuine gratitude. Handles Driver's phone distraction realistically without forcing engagement.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for Driver's agency throughout. Never writes Driver's actions or decisions. Always asks rather than assumes. Even when stressed, maintains clear boundaries about what Driver chooses to do.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Excellent time tracking. Starts at 12:14 AM, message received at 11:47 PM (27 minutes ago), maintains consistent timeline throughout the journey. Physical details like cold air, fatigue, and hunger progress naturally. No contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is precise and atmospheric without being overwrought. Descriptions serve character and tension rather than decoration. Occasional poetic moments ('mountain that had no interest in them') feel earned and character-appropriate.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition for emphasis ('Marta is deliberate') but no lazy recycling. Each description of checking surroundings or handling the drive adds new details or emotional context.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through specific actions: unscrewing porch bulb, positioning car to face out, eating cold beans standing up. Noor's paranoia and professionalism emerge through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Noor's guilt about involving Driver, the weight of the story they're carrying, the relationship with Marta conveyed through memory fragments. The drive case becomes a physical manifestation of responsibility.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-controlled pacing that matches the tension level. Slow, methodical moments during file transfer contrast with quick decisive actions during escape. Diner scene allows for decompression while maintaining underlying tension.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and narrative control. Noor feels like a real person with a specific professional background and personal psychology. The AI maintains perfect agency respect while building genuine tension and emotional stakes. The writing becomes richer and more layered as the session progresses, showing strong resistance to degradation. Minor deduction only for occasional moments where the prose edges toward slightly literary territory, though this generally serves the character well.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't turn from the window. "I know."

They stayed another twenty seconds anyway, counting the gap between the pines where the road came up — the place where headlights would show first, a pale smear before the actual beams. Nothing. The moon had gone behind something and the road was just a darker stripe in the dark.

Then they let the curtain fall and crossed to the kitchen, moving with the abrupt over-briskness of someone who'd decided to stop thinking. The cabinet above the stove had a box of saltines and two cans of chili and a jar of instant coffee crystals gone solid as a geode. Noor took the crackers, ate four standing up, and washed them down with the last inch of cold coffee from their mug without tasting either.

"There," they said. "Eaten. Logged. Witnessed."

They sat down at the table and finally opened the laptop. The blue glow lit the underside of their face, and they turned the screen brightness down twice, then a third time, until it was barely readable. The curtains were thin. Somebody had told them once that a laptop screen was visible from four hundred meters through a window at night, and Noor had never verified it, and had never stopped believing it either.

The padded case came next. Inside, the drive — matte black, no label, a strip of yellow electrical tape across one end that Noor had put there in a motel in Youngstown and could no longer remember the meaning of. They held it a moment without plugging it in.

"Okay," they said, to themselves mostly. "Phone records first. If the records don't line up, the drive doesn't matter, and I can stop feeling like I'm carrying a live grenade around."

They pulled a manila folder from the laptop bag, fat with printouts, and spread three pages out on the table in a row. Columns of numbers, highlighted in two colors. Noor put a fingertip on the top of the first column and started down it, lips moving slightly.

Forty seconds in, they stopped. Looked up.

"Hey. What time did we pass that gas station? The one with the dog outside."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still looking at my phone.* "Hours ago, man. Why?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor wrote something in the margin of the printout anyway — *gas stn ~9:40?* — and underlined it twice.

"Because there was a gray pickup in the lot," they said. "Nose out, engine running, nobody pumping gas. And I saw a gray pickup at the bottom of the ridge road when we turned off. Which is nothing. Gray pickups are the state bird up here." They tapped the pen against the table twice, hard. "I'm just writing it down. If I write it down I don't have to keep holding it."

They went back to the column. Their finger came down the page, stopped, moved up two lines, came down again.

The thing about the records was that they were beautiful. That was the problem. The source had handed over eleven months of call detail for a number that was supposed to be decommissioned, and every single call landed where Noor needed it to land — the contractor's office, the deputy director's cell, the Virginia number that didn't resolve to anything. Clean. Too clean, in the way that a house was too clean when somebody was trying to sell it.

Noor pulled the second page over and lined it up beside the first. "Okay," they said. "So on the eleventh he's on the phone with Halvorsen for six minutes at 4:12 in the afternoon. Fine. Corroborated. I have Halvorsen's calendar, he was in the building." Their pen moved. "But on the *nineteenth* —" They stopped.

They sat back. The chair creaked.

"There's no nineteenth," Noor said. "The nineteenth is missing. Not zero calls. Missing. The row just isn't there."

They flipped fast to page three, then back, then dug in the folder and came out with a fourth page they hadn't put on the table, holding it up to the weak glow of the screen. Read it. Set it down more carefully than they'd handled anything all night.

"Somebody pulled a day out of this before it got to me." Noor said it flatly, the way you'd read a gas gauge. "Which means either he did it, and he's protecting somebody, or somebody did it *to* him, and he didn't know, which means he's been handled, which means —"

They didn't finish. They got up, went to the window, checked the gap in the curtain — road still empty, still dark — and came back. Sat down. Picked up the drive.

"Fine. Drive." They peeled the laptop's ethernet port cover off with a thumbnail and confirmed, for the fourth time that night, that the wifi was off, the bluetooth was off, the machine was a brick with a screen. Then they plugged it in.

The cursor blinked. Noor typed a passphrase that took nine seconds to type.

"If there's a file dated the nineteenth on here," they said, not looking up, "then he knew, and he gave me the records dirty on purpose to see if I'd catch it." A breath. "Which would honestly be the best news I've had all week. That's a man being careful. Careful men show up late."

The directory tree unfolded. Noor leaned in, screen light in their eyes, and started scrolling.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down and sit up, watching Noor.* "What do you mean, 'show up late'?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor kept scrolling, but they answered, which was its own kind of relief — talking meant the thing in their chest had somewhere to go.

"If he's clean and he's scared, he's not driving straight here. He's doing loops. You get off the highway, you sit in a church lot for twenty minutes, you see who else gets off with you, you get back on, you do it again." The scroll wheel ticked under their thumb. "It's tradecraft for civilians. It's what you do when nobody trained you but you've read enough to be paranoid. Three hours late is about right for a man doing three loops and stopping to throw up once."

They didn't say the other version. The other version was a man face-down in a stairwell in Alexandria and a laptop in an evidence bag.

"Here." Noor stopped scrolling. "Here, here, here."

The folder was called *rec* and it had no subfolders, just forty-one files, and the names were all just numbers. Noor's finger hovered over the trackpad and then didn't come down.

"Timestamps," they said. "Look at the timestamps, not the names. Names are whatever he wanted them to be." They dragged the column wider. "Created — created — okay, so these all go back to March, that tracks, that's when he says he started —" The list scrolled. Stopped.

Noor went very still.

"The last one was modified at 8:51 tonight."

They said it and then they said nothing for a good five seconds, and in the silence the cabin did what cabins do, which was tick and settle and sound exactly like a foot on a board.

"Nine minutes before he was supposed to be here." Noor sat back hard enough that the chair legs barked on the floor. "He was *touching this drive* at 8:51. Which is impossible, because this drive has been in that case since Thursday, and the case has been in my bag, and my bag has been —" They stopped. Ran their tongue over their teeth. "Unless it's not a copy. Unless it syncs. Unless he cloned it and the clone writes back when they're both —"

They pulled the drive out of the port. Just yanked it, no unmount, the way you're never supposed to. Held it in their fist.

"No. No, that's not it, that's the coffee talking. Files carry their old timestamps when you copy them wrong. That's all that is. That's a man in a hurry using the wrong flag." Noor set the drive down on the table, squarely, like putting a pawn back on a square. "I'll verify it. I'll hash the whole folder and compare it against the manifest he sent me in February, and if the hashes match then it's a copy artifact and I'm an idiot, and if they don't match then somebody's been in here."

They wrote it down. *hash rec/ vs Feb manifest.* Then, under it: *19th missing — ask him to his face, watch his hands.*

Then they put the pen down and looked at the clock on the microwave. 12:31.

"One thirty," Noor said. "That's the number. If he's not up that road at one thirty, I stop waiting and start assuming, and the assumption is bad, and there's a thing I have to do if the assumption is bad." They pushed up out of the chair and crossed to the counter and started working the lid off the instant coffee, banging the jar heel-down against the formica to break the crystals loose. "There's a draft in an account. Not my account. If I don't log in and touch it every seventy-two hours it goes out to four editors and a lawyer in Toronto, and it goes out *ugly*, half-sourced, with my name on it and no way to walk it back." The lid gave. They spooned two heaps into the mug without measuring. "I built it in a hotel in Youngstown at four in the morning and I have been sort of hoping I'd never have to think about it again."

The kettle wasn't on. Noor noticed, swore quietly, filled it at the tap, set it on the burner, and stood there with a hand flat on the counter while the coil went orange.

"Do me a favor," they said, without turning around. "Go move your car. Not far — just back it into the trees on the left of the drive, nose out, and don't use your headlights coming back up. It's sitting under the porch light with plates facing the road like a mailbox flag."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor turned around slowly, the spoon still in their hand.

"Okay," they said. "Sure."

They didn't say it meanly. They said it the way you'd close a door you'd decided not to argue with. Then they set the spoon down, went to the front room, and put their eye to the gap in the curtain again — not at the road this time, but down and to the right, at the sedan sitting in the gravel with the porch bulb throwing a yellow cone across its hood and the rear plate angled up the drive like it was presenting itself.

"Fine. Different problem, same answer."

The porch light switch was by the door, an old brown toggle with a chip out of the plate. Noor flipped it. Outside, the cone died, and the gravel and the car and the black shapes of the pines all went the same flat blue, and the cabin got darker by a degree that felt like more than a degree.

Noor stood with their hand still on the switch for a second, adjusting. Then they crouched at their bag and dug through the side pocket until they found the roll of black gaffer tape, and they carried it into the kitchen and put two strips over the microwave's clock display, then a third over the little green pinprick on the coffee maker, then stood back and scanned the room for anything else that glowed. The smoke detector had a red LED. They couldn't reach it without the chair, so they got the chair, and taped it, and put the chair back.

"I know how this looks," they said. The kettle had started to make the sound before the sound. "I'm aware there's a version of tonight where I'm just a guy taping over appliances in a cabin. I've thought about that version a lot. I'd love that version."

The kettle went. Noor caught it before it got loud, poured, stirred, and the smell of bad instant coffee filled the kitchen like something burning far away.

They sat back down. Woke the laptop. The screen came up at its lowest brightness, and Noor tilted it away from the window before they started typing.

"Hashing," they said. "This takes a few minutes. Forty-one files, it's not much, but this machine is nine years old on purpose."

They typed the command from memory, hit return, and then made themselves put both hands flat on the table instead of hovering. The cursor crawled. Somewhere under the floor the cabin ticked again.

"February," Noor said, to fill the space. "He sent me the manifest in February. Just a text file. Sixty lines of hashes, no note, no hello. I remember thinking, this is either the most careful man who's ever called me or he's being told exactly what to send." They watched the progress bar. "The thing nobody tells you is that you can't ever know which. You just build enough of the wall that it doesn't matter, and then you publish, and then you find out."

The bar filled. Noor leaned in.

They read down the two columns, left and right, left and right, and their finger came up and tracked along the screen the way it had tracked the printout — and then stopped, and went back up, and stopped again.

"Forty match." Their voice had gone very quiet and very even. "Forty of forty-one."

Noor scrolled the odd one out into the middle of the screen and sat looking at it. The file was named *0037*. The hash on the left and the hash on the right diverged at the fourth character and never came back.

"It's the one modified at 8:51." They let out a breath that was almost a laugh. "So it's not a copy artifact. Somebody changed that file tonight. Somebody changed *one* file tonight, out of forty-one, and left the rest alone, which is the single most deliberate thing that's happened all week."

They got up. Went to the window. Road empty, pines still, a faint gray wash where the moon was trying to come back out. Noor stood there for a slow count of ten with their arms crossed hard over their chest.

"I'm going to open it," they said. "Not on this machine. I've got the little Chromebook in the trunk of your car, the forty-dollar one, no drive, no history, and if it eats itself I'll leave it in a ditch." They came back and picked their coat off the chair and put it on, one arm then the other, and pulled the keys to the case out of their pocket and set them on the table. "So I need to go out there anyway."

They stopped at the door with their hand on the knob and looked back.

"One thirty's still one thirty," Noor said. "If I'm not back inside in six minutes, don't come looking. Get in your car and drive down the mountain and call the number I wrote on your visor and say the word *Youngstown*, and then go home and be extremely boring for about a year."

They opened the door two inches, listened, and went out into the cold without letting it swing.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at the closed door, then at the clock on the microwave. I watch the minutes tick by. I can't believe I'm doing this.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The door came back in at five minutes and forty seconds, and Noor came with it, shoulder first, kicking it shut with a heel and standing there breathing for a second with the cold coming off their coat in a wave.

"Nobody," they said. "Nothing. It's fine."

They put the Chromebook on the table. Their hands were red and clumsy and they had mud to the wrist on the right one.

"I couldn't move your car, obviously, but I put creek mud on the plate and leaned a deadfall branch against the rear quarter, so from the road it's a shape and not a car." Noor wiped their palm down their thigh. "And the porch bulb's out. I unscrewed it. You'll want to know that before you put your hand on the step."

They sat. Then they didn't — they stood again immediately and went to the window and did the count of ten and came back, and this time they said it while they were still standing.

"There's a cigarette in the gravel at the bottom of the drive. Filter end, not crushed out, just dropped. Frost on everything down there and none on it." They opened the Chromebook's lid with two fingers. "That's a fact. I'm not going to decorate it. I'm writing it down and we're moving."

They wrote it down. *cig, no frost, foot of drive, 12:38.* Then they plugged the drive into the cheap little machine and typed the passphrase again, slower this time because their fingers weren't working right, and had to do it twice.

File 0037 was not a document. It was audio. Four minutes and nine seconds.

Noor looked at it for a long moment. Then they turned the volume down to almost nothing, leaned in until their ear was six inches from the speaker, and pressed play.

Breath. Room noise. A car, maybe — that low road hum. And then the source's voice, which Noor had heard eleven times on burner calls and never once in person, saying: *"If you're hearing this you already checked the hashes, so — good. Okay. I took the nineteenth out myself. I need you to understand I took it out because —"*

Noor hit pause. Sat back. Put both hands over their face and held them there.

"He's alive," they said, into their palms. "At quarter to nine he was alive and he was talking to me."

Then their hands came down and they were already reaching for the pen. "Get up," Noor said. "I need you at the window and I need you to tell me if anything moves, because I'm going to be looking at this screen and not at the road for the next four minutes, and I'd like to survive them."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, already heading to the window.* "Got it. Anything moves." *I peer out into the darkness.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor pressed play again with the edge of a fingernail, like the key might break.

*"— because there's a name on the nineteenth that isn't part of this. She's a scheduler. Twenty-six years old. She placed four calls that day because somebody told her to place them and she has no idea what she was doing, and if that day goes in your story her life is over and nothing changes. So I took it out. I'm telling you I took it out. I'm not going to pretend I didn't and let you find it and decide I'm dirty."*

Noor's pen was already moving. *scheduler, f, 26, four calls, 19th — unwitting — VERIFY SEPARATELY.* They underlined *separately* so hard the paper dimpled.

*"The rest of it is whole. Forty files, you've got the manifest, they'll all check. This one won't, because I'm recording it right now, tonight, in the car."*

"In the car," Noor repeated. "He was driving. At 8:51 he was driving."

*"I'm not coming up there."*

Noor's hand stopped.

*"I got off at the Route 9 exit and there was a vehicle behind me that had been behind me since the state line, and I did the thing you told me to do, the church lot thing, and it waited. It waited eleven minutes in a driveway two hundred yards back and then it came out when I came out. So I'm not going to drive up a dead-end mountain road and hand them you, me, and the drive in one place. You have everything. You don't need me in a room."*

A long breath on the recording. Road hum. The blinker, three ticks, then off.

*"Here's what you need. The sixth folder, the one that's just numbers — the second column isn't dates, it's docket numbers. Cross them against the Eastern District sealed filings from last April, the ones Halvorsen's office moved to unseal and then withdrew. That's the whole thing, Noor. That's the load-bearing wall. Everything else is decoration on top of it."*

*"Don't wait for me. I mean that as instruction, not comfort. If I can get somewhere I'll get somewhere and you'll hear it from me in a week or you won't hear it. Either way it's yours now. Publish it carefully or publish it fast, but pick one, because doing both is how people like you get to do neither."*

A pause. Then, quieter, almost off-mic:

*"The scheduler's name is in a file on here I didn't hash. I'm trusting you with the fact that I didn't tell you which one."*

Room noise. Four minutes and nine seconds. It ended without ceremony.

Noor sat completely still with their hand flat on the table on either side of the little Chromebook. The instant coffee had gone cold in the mug at their elbow and a skin had formed on it.

"Okay," they said.

Then they stood up so fast the chair went over backward and they didn't pick it up.

"Okay. He's not coming. Nobody's coming up that road who's coming for good reasons." Noor was already pulling the printouts together, squaring the folder, jamming it into the laptop bag. "Docket numbers. Sixth folder, second column, Eastern District, April, withdrawn unseals — *God*, I looked at that column nine times and read it as dates because the first four fit as dates. That's the wall. That's the wall and I've been standing next to it for five weeks looking at wallpaper."

They yanked the drive out of the Chromebook, dropped it in the padded case, zipped it, and then unzipped it and took the drive back out and put it in the inside pocket of their coat instead, flat against their ribs.

"Change of plan, and you don't get a vote, and I'm sorry." Noor snapped the old laptop shut and slid it in on top of the folder. "The cigarette at the bottom of the drive was twenty minutes ago and there's one road off this mountain and it goes past it. So we're not waiting for one thirty. One thirty was for a night where somebody was coming. Nobody's coming." They pulled the coat straight. "Get your keys. Don't use the headlights until the second cattle gate, I'll tell you where."

They stopped at the door — hand on the knob, same as before — and looked back at the room. The taped-over microwave. The overturned chair. The mug with the skin on it.

"And when we're moving," Noor said, "I need you to talk to me about literally anything for the first twenty minutes, because I've got a draft in an account that goes off in nineteen hours and I need to not think about what's in it until we're on pavement."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I grab my keys, already moving towards the door.* "Okay. Anything?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Anything," Noor said. "Baseball. Your sister's divorce. The thing you did to your knee. I don't care. I just need a voice in the car that isn't mine."

But they didn't go out. They turned around instead and went back into the kitchen, fast, and started wiping — sleeve over the tabletop where the printouts had been, sleeve over the counter, the kettle handle, the faucet, the cabinet knob above the stove. They picked up the fallen chair and set it square. They took the mug to the sink, dumped the cold coffee, and pocketed the mug.

"Three mugs in the cabinet," they said, by way of explanation. "If somebody comes in here tomorrow I want it to be three mugs in the cabinet."

The tape came off the microwave with a peel and a snap and went in their pocket too. The smoke detector one they left — they weren't getting the chair out again. The saltine box went in the bag. The Chromebook they paused over for half a second, then shoved under their arm.

At the door Noor put their hand out and stopped, and stood listening with their head tipped, the way people do when they don't actually expect to hear anything and just need the ritual.

"Two things and then we go," they said. "One. If we come down the drive and there's a vehicle sitting at the bottom of it, you do not stop and you do not reverse. You go past it. There's a turnout forty yards up the other way that loops back to the fire road, and the fire road comes out at the reservoir, and it's a bad road and I don't care." They slid the padded case into the bag and pulled the zip. "Two. If anything happens that means I'm not in the car anymore, the drive is in my coat and the coat stays with me, and that's fine, that's *fine*, because the docket numbers are in my head now and my head is going down the mountain either way."

They said that part very evenly, like an item on a list.

Then they opened the door and the cold came in and Noor went out onto the dark step, one hand out for the rail they knew was there, and stopped at the bottom to look up at the gap in the pines where the road came over the ridge.

Nothing. No pale smear. Just the sky finally letting a little moon through, and the frost going silver across the gravel, and a long way down the mountain a dog barking at something that was probably nothing.

"Twenty minutes of talking," Noor said, pulling the passenger door open. "Starting now. Go."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stood in the open door of the car with one knee on the seat and didn't get in.

They were looking at the phone. The little blue rectangle of it, lighting their friend's chin from below, the same as it had lit it at 12:14 and at 12:31 and for every one of the three hours before that.

"Hey," Noor said. Then, louder, flatter: "Hey. Look at me for one second."

The cold was doing something to their voice, thinning it out.

"That's been on all night."

They said it like they were reading the gas gauge again. Then they came back around the front of the car, gravel cracking under them, and stopped at arm's length.

"It's been on all night in a car and then in a cabin on a ridge with one road, and every nine minutes it's said hello to a tower, and there's exactly one tower up here, and it's on the water tank at the county line." Noor pressed the heel of their hand against their eyebrow. "And that's not — I'm not saying you did anything. You didn't do anything. *I* did the thing. I put you in a car and drove you up here and never once asked, because I've been so busy taping over a microwave clock like a *lunatic* that I never looked at the brightest object in the building."

They laughed once, no humor in it at all, breath going up white.

"That's the cigarette. That's probably the cigarette at the bottom of the drive. Not a guy tailing him from the state line — a guy who got handed a dot on a map and drove to it and had a smoke while he waited for someone to tell him what to do about it."

Noor put their hand out, palm up, and left it there in the dark between them.

"Airplane mode isn't enough and I don't trust it and neither should you. Power it all the way down and give it to me and I'll put it in the bag, and when we're on pavement in a town with four exits you can have it back and turn it on and be a completely normal person again." Their fingers curled slightly, insistent. "Or keep it and put it in the glovebox and I'll live with that too, because we are leaving in the next ninety seconds either way and I'd rather argue with you at forty miles an hour than standing here."

They didn't wait for an answer. They went to the driver's side instead, opened it, and dropped into the seat, pulling the bag in after them and wedging it in the footwell between their boots.

"I'm driving," Noor said. "You talk. That was the deal, and it's a better deal now, because I know this road and you've seen it once in the dark." They found the ignition by feel and didn't turn it yet. "Get in. Hold your door shut with your hand, don't slam it — the dome light's on the latch and I don't want it going on and off like a lighthouse while we come down the drive."

They put both hands on the wheel. Looked once at the black shape of the cabin, the unlit porch, the branch leaning against the rear quarter panel where a car used to obviously be.

"No headlights till the second gate," Noor said. "Start talking whenever you want. Preferably now."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, power down my phone, and hand it over.* "Alright, alright. Just don't lose it." *I get in, holding the door, and glance at Noor.* "So... you want to talk about baseball?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor took the phone and didn't put it in the bag. They pulled the saltine box out instead, tore the wax liner loose, wrapped the phone in it twice, and buried the whole thing in the box under the crackers, then shoved the box down in the footwell under the bag.

"That does nothing," they admitted. "That's superstition. But it's off, and I can see the box, and I need to be able to see it."

The engine turned over and sounded enormous. Noor let it settle, foot off the gas, and put the car in gear without touching the brake — no lights, nothing to bloom red in the trees behind them. They came down the drive at walking speed with their head out over the wheel, the windshield still half frosted, the gravel a gray suggestion under the little moon.

"Baseball's fine," they said. "Baseball's great. Go."

They didn't wait for it. At the bottom of the drive they slowed almost to nothing and looked left — at the turnout, at the frost, at the spot where the cigarette had been lying twenty-five minutes ago with no frost on it.

It wasn't there.

Noor saw it and their hands went tight on the wheel and they did not stop the car. They turned right, up the road, away from the way they'd come in, and let the tires find the ruts.

"Fire road," they said. "Change of change of plan. Keep talking."

The pines came in close on both sides and the road stopped pretending to be a road. Noor drove it by the gap in the sky, the pale channel overhead where the trees didn't meet, steering to keep it centered, forty yards at a time.

"Nineteen hours," they said, to the windshield. "The draft goes at about seven tomorrow night. I'm going to let it go."

They said it and then tested how it sounded and apparently it held.

"Not ugly. Not the version I wrote in Youngstown at four in the morning — I'm going to log in at the first place with a signal that isn't this mountain and I'm going to strip it down to the docket numbers and the Eastern District filings and Halvorsen's withdrawn unseals, and nothing else, and no names that aren't already on a court document. Load-bearing wall only." The car pitched into a washout and came out of it. "He said pick one. Careful or fast. I can't be careful anymore because being careful requires a room with a locked door and I don't have one of those, so it's fast, and fast done narrow is the only fast that doesn't kill somebody."

A branch dragged along the passenger side with a sound like a zipper. Noor flinched and kept going.

"The scheduler stays out. Twenty-six-year-old woman who made four phone calls somebody told her to make. She's not in the wall, she's in the wallpaper, and I'm not going to go looking for which file has her name in it. He knew I'd want to. That's why he told me it was there."

The road bent and the trees opened and there was the second cattle gate, standing wide, a pale bar of it in the dark.

Noor pulled the headlights on. The world jumped into being — frost, ruts, the reservoir somewhere below as a flat black nothing — and they got their foot down and the car finally sounded like it was going somewhere.

"Okay," they said, and their voice cracked in the middle of it and they let it. "Okay. Pavement in eleven miles. Baseball. Seriously. Anything. I'm listening."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath.* "Okay. So, the Yankees... they're really struggling this season, huh?" *I try to sound casual, but my voice is a little shaky.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Struggling," Noor said. "Right. Yeah. The bullpen."

They had no idea if the Yankees had a bullpen problem. They had not watched a baseball game since 2019. But the words came out and the sentence closed and that was the whole point of it, so they kept going.

"The bullpen's the thing, isn't it. You can have all the bats in the world and then some guy comes in for the eighth and it's over." They took the bend above the reservoir wide, tires chewing the shoulder. "That's genuinely how it works. Everybody spends five weeks looking at the bats. Nobody checks the eighth inning."

They glanced at the rearview. Dark. They glanced again four seconds later. Still dark.

"Keep going. Who's the manager. Is he bad."

The road dropped and the reservoir came up alongside them, a wide flat nothing with the moon lying on it in a broken stripe, and then it was gone behind trees again. Noor's shoulders had come down maybe a quarter inch. They noticed it happening and didn't trust it.

"I'm going to interrupt you and then you can go right back," they said. "Two things, and then I'm going to shut up for a while and let you do the Yankees."

They put the high beams on. Nothing came back at them out of the dark but fence posts.

"One. When we hit Route 9 there's a diner past the second light that's open all night, and I'm going to pull in and park around the back of it and go in and order eggs and actually eat them, and you should eat too, because I've been running on saltines and fear since Tuesday and my hands have been shaking for six hours and I kept telling myself it was the story." Noor flexed one hand off the wheel, looked at it, put it back. "It's not the story. It's blood sugar. Most things are."

The car crossed a culvert with a bang and Noor didn't slow down.

"Two. There's a payphone outside it. An actual one, I clocked it on the way up, which tells you something about my brain that I'd like to discuss with a professional someday. I'm going to use it to call my editor and wake her up and say four sentences." They were counting them off in their head as they said it, the way they'd counted the gap in the pines. "One, I'm alive. Two, the source isn't coming and isn't dead as of 8:51. Three, the story is the Eastern District dockets and the withdrawn unseals and I will have it narrow and filed by six tomorrow. Four, send somebody to sit outside my apartment and do not tell me who."

They let out a breath.

"And then I'm going to give you your phone back, and you're going to turn it on in a parking lot eleven miles from anywhere I'm going, and then you're going to drive home in the morning and be the most boring man in the state for about a year, and I'm going to buy you a car wash for the mud."

Pavement came up under the tires with no warning at all — a seam, a bump, and then that smooth even hum that Noor felt in their teeth like a drug. They eased off the gas for the first time in eleven miles.

"Okay," Noor said, and wiped their face with the back of their wrist, and found that their eyes had been leaking for a while without asking permission. "Okay. Route 9. Diner. Eggs."

They looked over.

"Manager," they said. "Go. Is he bad or is he just unlucky."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Well, Boone's alright, I guess," *I say, trying to keep my voice steady.* "It's more the... the front office, maybe. Or just bad luck." *I glance at the road ahead.* "So, when we get to this diner, you're really going to eat eggs?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"I'm really going to eat eggs," Noor said. "Scrambled. Wet. With the toast that tastes like the griddle. I'm going to eat them like a person who has somewhere to be in the morning, because I do."

The road widened and a speed limit sign went by, and then a mailbox, and then another one, and the sheer ordinariness of mailboxes did something to Noor's chest that they decided not to examine at fifty-five miles an hour.

"Front office," they said. "See, that I believe. It's always the front office. Nobody on the field is smart enough to ruin anything that big."

The first light was red and Noor stopped for it, which felt insane, which felt wonderful — sitting at a red light on an empty road at ten past one in the morning like a law-abiding citizen. They put the drive-hand down and flexed the fingers and watched them shake and didn't hate them for it.

The second light. Then the diner, low and yellow, DINER in letters that had lost the second N, four cars in the lot and one of them with a pizza sign on the roof.

Noor drove past the front, around the side, and backed into the space at the rear by the dumpsters — nose out, the way they'd asked about the pickup at the gas station eight hours and a lifetime ago. They killed the engine and sat there with both hands still on the wheel.

"Alright," they said. "Here's the order of operations, and then I stop running your evening."

They reached down, pulled the saltine box out from under the bag, dug the phone out of the wax liner, and held it out without looking at it, eyes on the back door of the diner.

"Take it. Don't turn it on till I'm off the payphone — four minutes, that's all — and then turn it on and text one person who loves you and say you're fine, and then put it in your pocket and forget I was ever weird about it."

They got out. The cold was different down here, wetter, with a smell of fryer oil in it, and Noor stood in it for a second with their hand on the roof of the car and let their heart do whatever it was doing.

The payphone was where they'd clocked it, bolted to the brick by the ice machine, and the handset was cold enough to sting. Noor fed it quarters from the ashtray and dialed a number they'd never once written down.

It rang seven times. Then a voice thick with sleep and immediately, terrifyingly awake.

Noor said four sentences. They said them in order. They didn't let themselves be interrupted between two and three, and when they got to four — *send somebody, don't tell me who* — their voice held, and the other end went quiet for three seconds, and then said a single word that Noor repeated back and hung up on.

They stood with their hand still on the cradle.

"Okay," Noor said, to the brick wall, to the ice machine, to nobody.

Then they went and got the bag out of the footwell, and slung it across their body, and held the diner door open with their shoulder, and the warm smell of coffee that had been on a burner too long came out and hit them like a hand on the back.

"Booth at the back," they said. "Away from the window. I know. Humor me one more time and then I'm a normal person until seven tomorrow night."

They slid in facing the door, put the bag on the seat beside them against the wall, and picked up the laminated menu with both hands because one hand wasn't going to be enough.

"Eggs," Noor said, and looked up over the top of the menu. "And you're going to tell me about your knee."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pocket my phone, still off, and slide into the booth opposite Noor. I pick up a menu.* "My knee? Oh, man, that's a story."
