The timeline played behind their eyelids like a film with no sound. October 14th, first contact — an email to the newsroom's tip line, unsigned, with a phone number that went to a prepaid. October 19th, a phone call that lasted nine minutes. The source's voice had been tight, controlled, the voice of a man rehearsing something he'd been afraid to say for months. Noor had sat in their car in the grocery store parking lot with a pen and a napkin and written down everything. October 27th, the first dead drop — a USB drive taped behind a toilet tank in a rest stop on Route 11. Noor had almost missed it. Had almost not checked the tape twice, because who actually does that outside of movies, but something in the source's voice on the phone had insisted.

November 3rd, the garage. The face. The dog story.

Noor opened their eyes.

The ceiling was water-stained, a brown bloom directly above them like a Rorschach test. They stared at it and tried to make it into something that wasn't a map of the investigation, a web of connections, a shape that looked like consequence. Couldn't.

Their phone was in their hand before they'd made a conscious decision to reach for it. They turned it over. The screen was dark. No messages. No missed calls. The time read 12:52.

They stood up carefully — the chair had started to ache through their lower back — and walked to the bedroom. The bed was a mattress on a frame, no sheets, a single wool blanket folded at the foot. Noor hadn't unpacked their bag. The bag sat on the floor beside the door, zipped, ready to go. They opened it now and pulled out a second burner phone — the one they hadn't told the source about, the one that existed only as a contingency. They powered it on and checked the signal. One bar, flickering. Enough.

They typed a message to their editor's secure line. Not the letter — that was saved, that was ready. This was simpler. *Running late on the piece. May need an extension. Will call in the morning.* It was the kind of message that meant nothing to anyone who intercepted it and everything to the person who received it. Their editor would read it and understand: *I'm still alive, I'm still working, I'm not coming home tonight.*

They powered the phone off again and put it back in the bag.

In the kitchen, the laptop sat dark on the table, the two drives next to it in their cases. Noor picked up the second drive — the copy — and turned it over in their hands. Small enough to lose. Small enough to hide. They thought about the cabin's layout, the limited options. Under the mattress was obvious. Taped behind the toilet tank made them want to laugh and also not laugh at all.

They compromised. Wrapped the drive in a plastic bag from under the sink — the cabin had a roll of them, the grocery store kind — and slid it into the toe of their spare shoes in the bag. Not hidden. Just not visible to anyone who wasn't thorough.

Then they went back to the window.

Driver was still on the couch, the phone still glowing. Noor envied that — the ability to occupy a space without mapping every exit in it. They pulled the curtain back an inch and looked out.

The road was dark. The mountains were darker. The sky had cleared sometime in the last hour, and there were stars — more than you ever saw in the city, enough to make the darkness feel less like a wall and more like a ceiling. The porch light cast a yellow cone across the gravel driveway where Driver's car was parked. Nothing else. No headlights. No movement.

Noor watched anyway. Their breath found its old rhythm against the glass — the small fog oval appearing and disappearing, appearing and disappearing — and for a moment they let themselves be just a person at a window, not a journalist, not a target, not someone who had dragged a friend into a cabin in the mountains and was now counting down the minutes until they could justify leaving.

Something moved in the treeline.

Noor's hand tightened on the curtain. They leaned forward, breath held, eyes straining against the dark. The treeline was maybe forty yards from the cabin — dense pine, the kind of cover that swallowed light. Something had shifted there. A shadow, a suggestion of mass, gone before Noor could fix it.

A deer, probably. This was the mountains. There were deer.

Noor didn't move from the window.

"Hey," they said, keeping their voice low, not turning around. "I think I saw something. In the trees. Could be nothing — it's probably nothing." The words came out steady. The journalist's voice. The one that didn't shake even when the hands did. "Can you kill the porch light? Switch by the door."

They didn't take their eyes off the treeline. The fog oval on the glass had stopped appearing. They weren't breathing enough to make it.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up, my brow furrowed.* "Something in the trees?" *I slowly get up and walk to the door, flicking off the light.* "Got it." *I keep an eye on the treeline too.* "Still nothing."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stood at the window for another thirty seconds, eyes fixed on the spot where the shadow had been. The treeline was still now. The pines stood like a black wall against the slightly-less-black sky, and whatever had moved — if anything had moved — had either settled or gone.

"Could've been a deer," Noor said. Their voice had that careful flatness again. The one that meant they were already running calculations underneath the words. "Could've been the wind moving branches. It was probably the wind moving branches."

They did not move from the window.

With the porch light off, their eyes adjusted slowly. The driveway gravel took shape in the ambient starlight — pale, uneven, the ghost of a surface. Driver's car sat where they'd parked it, driver's side facing the cabin. Beyond it, the dirt road that led down the mountain, invisible past the first bend.

Noor's hand moved to the curtain and pulled it closed. The fabric was thin, cotton, probably original to the cabin. It wouldn't stop a bullet or a pair of binoculars, but it kept their silhouette out of the window, and right now that felt like enough.

They crossed the kitchen in four steps and unplugged the laptop. Picked up both drives. Stood there for a moment, holding the weight of them — barely anything, a few ounces of plastic and circuitry and information that had already cost someone their sense of safety and might cost more before it was over.

"Change of plan," Noor said. They kept their voice quiet, not whispering — whispers carried in cabins, bounced off wood and linoleum in ways that normal speaking didn't. Just low. Controlled. "I want to be ready to leave. Not leaving yet — I said two, and I meant two. But I want everything packed. Everything in the car. If we go, we go in thirty seconds, not five minutes of me crawling around looking for my bag."

They moved to the kitchen table and started dismantling their setup with practiced efficiency. Laptop into the bag, padded sleeve zipped, both drives nested inside. The notebook — timeline, notes, the page they'd already torn out — went into the jacket pocket with the folded names. The burner phone went into the opposite pocket. They checked the table surface with their palm, sweeping for anything left behind. A pen cap. They pocketed it.

The bag went over their shoulder. Heavy enough to be real, light enough to run with.

They did a slow circuit of the cabin. Kitchen — clear. Bathroom — they grabbed their jacket from the hook on the back of the door, shrugged it on, felt the weight of the notebook settle against their ribs. Bedroom — bag was already packed, nothing to grab. Front door — they tested the deadbolts one more time, then unlocked them both. If they had to leave fast, they didn't want to be fumbling with keys.

Back door — the sliding bolt. Noor hesitated. Then left it locked. That was the exit they'd use if the front door was blocked. Different calculus.

They returned to the kitchen where Driver was standing and set the bag by the front door. Their car keys were in their hand — they'd pulled them from the bag without thinking about it, muscle memory, the kind of thing you did when your body had decided it was time to leave even if your mind hadn't caught up yet.

Noor looked at the clock. 1:07 AM. Fifty-three minutes.

They leaned against the kitchen counter and crossed their arms, keys still in their left hand, the metal teeth pressing into their palm. The pain was grounding. Small. Real.

"The movement was probably nothing," Noor said again, and this time there was a different quality to it — not reassurance exactly, but a kind of deliberate refusal to spiral. "Deer, coyote, wind. This is the mountains. Things move."

They paused. Rubbed the back of their neck with their right hand.

"But I've been wrong about 'probably nothing' before. About eight months ago, I was working a story on —" They stopped themselves. Shook their head slightly. "Doesn't matter. The point is, I sat in a parking lot for forty-five minutes telling myself the car three rows over was just a coincidence, and it wasn't, and I lost a source because of it. Not killed — just lost. She pulled out, went dark, and I never heard from her again."

Their eyes found the window. The curtain was drawn, but they could still see the faintest glow of starlight through the thin cotton.

"I'm not losing this one the same way," they said. "So we sit, and we wait, and at two we go. And if something comes down that road before two — something that isn't him — then we go sooner."

They looked at Driver, and for the first time that night there was something almost gentle in the bloodshot eyes. An expression that might have been gratitude, or might have been the particular sorrow of someone who understood exactly how much they were asking of another person and had decided to ask anyway.

"There's a thermos in my bag," Noor said. "Front pocket. If you want coffee, it's cold, but it's coffee. I made it about four hours ago and it's been keeping me alive."

They pushed off the counter and walked to the window one more time. Pulled the curtain back half an inch — just half, just enough to see the road and the treeline and the sky above it. The stars hadn't moved, or if they had, it wasn't enough to notice.

Nothing in the trees. Nothing on the road.

Noor let the curtain fall and stood in the dark kitchen with their keys in their hand and their bag by the door, and counted minutes, and did not sleep.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow.* "Coffee sounds good." *I walk over to Noor's bag and dig around in the front pocket for the thermos.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor watched Driver dig through the bag and felt a flicker of something they couldn't quite name — not quite guilt, not quite tenderness, something in the register of *I dragged you here and you're looking for the thermos like it's a regular Tuesday.*

"The side pocket," they said. "Little zipper. It's — yeah, that one."

The thermos was stainless steel, dented near the base from a fall off a desk six months ago. Noor had filled it at 8:30 that evening in the gas station bathroom, using the sink's hot tap and a packet of instant coffee they'd bought at the counter. It was not good coffee. It was barely coffee. But it had kept Noor's hands warm and their eyes open, and right now that was the only metric that mattered.

They stayed at the window while Driver poured. The curtain gap was still there — half an inch, maybe less — and Noor's left eye kept drifting to it, pulled by a gravity they couldn't override. The treeline. The road. The bend where the dirt track disappeared down the mountain. Their peripheral vision had become its own animal tonight, alert to any shift in the dark that shouldn't be there.

"There's no cups," Noor said, a small almost-apology. "I've been drinking straight from it. Sorry. You can — it's fine. I'm not precious about germs. Not tonight."

They turned from the window and leaned against the wall beside it, arms folded again. The posture was becoming a habit — something to do with their body that wasn't pacing, wasn't checking the phone, wasn't touching the bag to make sure it was still there. Their right hand kept drifting to the jacket pocket where the folded page sat, pressing against it through the fabric, feeling the sharp edges of the crease.

"Can I ask you something?" Noor said. Their voice had shifted — quieter, less operational. The voice of someone who'd been sitting with a question for hours and had finally let it surface. "When I called you this afternoon and said I needed a ride, no questions, back by morning — did you think it was something like this?"

A pause. The fluorescent tube in the kitchen buzzed and flickered once.

"Because I didn't plan to make it something like this. The original plan was — I meet him, he gives me the files, we drive back, I'm home by midnight writing up my notes. Clean. Simple." They looked at the bag by the door. "But plans are just things that haven't gone wrong yet. And I should've known that. I *did* know that. I just —"

Noor stopped. Pressed their lips together. The journalist's composure was still there, but it had thinned, and underneath it was something more honest — the exhaustion of a person who'd been performing steadiness for hours and was starting to feel the cost.

"I just needed someone I trust in the car," they finished. "And you were the first person I thought of. That's — I don't know if that's a compliment or an indictment. Probably both."

They glanced at the clock on their phone. 1:14. Forty-six minutes.

Their eyes went back to the window. The curtain gap. The dark.

The treeline was still. The road was empty.

But Noor didn't close the gap. Didn't step away. Stood there with their shoulder against the wall and their hand in their pocket and their eyes on the space between the pines, waiting for something to move — or for two o'clock, whichever came first.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor absorbed the *yeah* the way you absorb a door closing — not with surprise, just a quiet acknowledgment of the space it left behind.

They didn't press. Driver had driven three hours into the mountains without asking what the story was, had waited in a cabin with no heat and nothing to eat and bad fluorescent lighting, and was now scrolling their phone at one in the morning like this was a long layover at a forgettable airport. Noor didn't understand that kind of equanimity, but they were grateful for it, and gratitude and incomprehension could coexist in the same breath.

They pushed off the wall and moved to the table. Sat down. Pulled the notebook from their jacket pocket — the one with the timeline, not the torn page — and flipped to a fresh section. Their pen hovered for a moment, then started writing.

Not the timeline. Not the letter. A list.

*Things I know for certain.*

The pen moved in small, tight strokes.

*1. The procurement ledger matches the contract awards. Two different databases, same quarter, same shell companies. That's not coincidence.*

*2. The audio recordings were made in the same room — consistent background noise, same reverb pattern. The source had access. Continuous access.*

*3. The photographs are timestamped and geotagged. Metadata intact. I've verified the EXIF data twice.*

*4. The source is scared. Genuine fear, not performance. I've interviewed enough people performing fear to know the difference.*

They paused. The pen rested against the page, leaving a small dot of ink that bled outward into the paper's fibers.

*5. The source has not arrived.*

That was the fifth thing they knew for certain, and it was the one that mattered most and meant least. The absence of a person was not data. It was a gap — and Noor had spent their entire career learning that gaps were where the real stories hid.

They wrote one more line.

*6. I am not objective about this anymore.*

Stared at it. Didn't cross it out.

The pen capped with a small click. Noor closed the notebook and slid it back into the pocket. The jacket was starting to feel like an extension of their body tonight — all the crucial things distributed across its pockets, close to the ribs, close to the heartbeat.

They pulled the burner phone out again. 1:21. Thirty-nine minutes.

Their thumb moved across the screen almost involuntarily, pulling up the source's number one more time. Not to call. Not to text. Just to look at it. Ten digits on a prepaid phone that might already be at the bottom of a river or in an evidence bag or sitting on a kitchen counter while a man with a shepherd mix paced his living room deciding whether his marriage and his career and his sense of himself as a good person were worth the cost of what he'd promised to do.

Noor knew which outcome they were rooting for, and they didn't trust themselves for rooting for it.

They put the phone down. Face-down. Again.

"We should talk about the drive out," Noor said, turning in the chair to face Driver. Their voice had shifted back to operational — the journalist mapping a route, assigning variables. "The road down is single-lane for the first two miles. If someone's coming up, we'd meet them on a stretch with nowhere to pull off. There's a turnaround about a quarter mile south of here — dirt, not great, but wide enough. If we leave and someone's on the road, I'd rather take the turnaround and go south, loop around on the county road, than try to pass them."

A beat.

"I'm not being paranoid. I'm being —" They searched for the word. Found it in a place they didn't like. "Practical. This is just route planning. This is what you do."

They stood up again, unable to stay seated, and walked to the back door. Tested the bolt. Still locked. Pressed their forehead briefly against the cool wood of the doorframe — a private moment, hidden from Driver by angle and darkness — then straightened and came back to the kitchen.

"Two more checks," they said. "Phone records. And then I'm going to sit down and not move until two o'clock."

They meant it when they said it. They sat at the laptop, opened it, and pulled up the burner phone's call log through the prepaid service's web portal. Three calls to the source's number over the past month. Two inbound. All matched the timeline they'd written in the notebook. No additional numbers. No anomalies. The kind of clean record that either meant everything was what it appeared to be, or meant someone very good had made it look that way.

Noor closed the laptop. Folded their hands on top of it.

"Okay," they said. "That's everything. I'm done."

The kitchen was quiet. The fluorescent buzzed. Outside, the wind moved through the pines with a sound like running water, and somewhere far off — miles, probably, the way sound traveled in mountains at night — a dog barked.

Noor's head came up. Listened.

The barking stopped. Or hadn't started. Or had been the recording, still playing in some corner of their exhausted mind, looping on a track they couldn't erase.

"It's two o'clock," Noor said quietly. It was 1:28. It was not two o'clock. "It's —" They checked the phone. Looked away. "We have thirty-two minutes."

They folded their arms on the table and rested their forehead against them. Not sleeping. Just taking the weight off their neck for a moment, letting the darkness behind their eyelids be a choice instead of a threat. The laptop was warm under their forearms. The metal of the drives pressed against their wrist through the bag strap.

"If he shows up in the next thirty minutes," Noor said, their voice muffled against their sleeves, "I'm going to be so angry. And then I'm going to do the story anyway, because the story doesn't care whether I'm angry or scared or sitting in a cabin that smells like someone's uncle's cigarettes from 2004."

A breath. In and out.

"And if he doesn't show up, I write what I have. Which is enough. It's not everything, but it's enough to make them answer questions on the record, and sometimes that's all you need — just the questions. Just the asking."

They raised their head. Looked at Driver. Their eyes were heavy-lidded but clear, the particular clarity that came not from rest but from a decision finally settling into place.

"Thank you," Noor said. "For the drive. For staying. For not asking."

They picked up the burner phone one last time. Held it. The screen was dark. The screen stayed dark.

Noor put it in their jacket pocket with the notebook and the torn page and the names of two people who might need to find this story if Noor couldn't finish it, and they waited for two o'clock.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I finally look up from my phone.* "No problem, man." *I don't offer any more comfort than that, it doesn't seem like Noor wants it.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor held the *no problem, man* in their chest and let it settle somewhere between their ribs. It was the most Driver had offered all night, and it was exactly enough.

"Okay," Noor said. Stood up. The chair scraped against the linoleum.

They checked the clock. 1:47. Thirteen minutes, but Noor's body had already made the decision their mouth hadn't caught up to. They did a final sweep of the cabin the way they'd done a final sweep of every room they'd ever left — not looking for what was there, but for what shouldn't be. A stray cable. A fingerprint. A piece of themselves left behind in a place that might not be safe to return to.

Kitchen table — clean, wiped down with the sleeve of their jacket. Bathroom — nothing on the hook, nothing on the sink. They flushed the toilet more out of habit than need and listened to the old pipes groan through the walls. Bedroom — the mattress bare, the wool blanket folded exactly where they'd found it. They'd never unfolded it. The bag was already by the door.

They did one more thing before leaving. Took the burner phone — the one the source knew about — and powered it off. Removed the battery. Pressed the SIM card out with their thumbnail and held it between two fingers, thin as a fingernail clipping, carrying more consequence than its size should have allowed. They slipped it into the same jacket pocket as the notebook. The phone body went into a separate pocket. Later — in a city, in a trash can miles from here — they'd dispose of the pieces separately. Not because they were certain someone was tracking it. Because certainty was a luxury Noor had stopped buying weeks ago.

They shouldered the bag. Picked up the keys.

"Let's go," Noor said.

They unlocked the front door and opened it into the mountain dark. The air hit their face — cold, sharp, carrying the smell of pine resin and the distant mineral scent of the creek that ran somewhere below the cabin. The porch was a wooden platform, three steps down to the gravel. Noor went first, not fast but not lingering, scanning the treeline and the driveway and the road beyond in a single sweep that took maybe four seconds and felt like forty.

Driver's car. Gravel. Trees. Stars. Nothing else.

They crossed to the passenger side, unlocked it with the key fob — the chirp of the locks was obscenely loud in the silence — and climbed in. Set the bag at their feet, between their legs, one hand resting on it. The interior of the car smelled like old air freshener and the faint ghost of fast food. Normal smells. Civilian smells. Noor breathed them in and felt some tight thing behind their sternum ease half a degree.

When Driver got in and turned the engine over, Noor was already watching the treeline in the side mirror.

The headlights swept across the gravel as they backed up, and for a moment the cabin was illuminated — small, wood-sided, a light left on in the kitchen so it wouldn't look abandoned from the road. Noor had done that automatically. Another habit from a life that ran on contingencies.

They turned onto the dirt road heading south. The headlights carved a tunnel through the dark, pine trunks sliding past on either side like the bars of a cage being opened one by one. The road was rutted, the car bouncing slightly, and Noor's hand moved from the bag to the dashboard, bracing themselves without thinking about it.

Their eyes were on the mirrors. Both mirrors. The road behind them was empty — just dust hanging in the taillight glow, settling slowly in the still air.

"We're clear," Noor said. Not a question. A report. Their voice was steady but thin, like wire pulled taut. "No one behind us. Road's empty."

The car crested a small rise and the world opened briefly — a valley below, a scatter of lights from a town they'd driven through on the way up, impossibly far away and impossibly human. Noor looked at the lights and thought about the source's wife on the hiking trail, squinting into the sun with a dog pressed against her leg, and wondered whether she was awake right now in a house that might or might not still be her husband's home.

They turned onto the county road. Pavement. The car smoothed out. The silence changed register — from the intimate, creaking dark of the cabin to the humming, sealed quiet of a vehicle moving at speed through empty countryside.

Noor leaned back in the seat. Loosened their grip on the bag. The adrenaline was draining out through their fingers and toes, leaving behind a heaviness that sat in their limbs like wet cloth. Their eyes burned. The clock on the dashboard read 2:06.

"I have enough," Noor said quietly, staring at the road ahead. "The ledger, the recordings, the photos. It's not the source on record, it's not testimony, but it's — it's a door. You publish what I have, and suddenly every reporter in the city can ask the questions, and the questions are the thing. The questions are always the thing."

They rubbed their eyes with the heels of their hands. When they dropped them, the road blurred and sharpened and blurred again.

"I'll need to call my editor in the morning. Set up the legal review. Get the second copy somewhere safe — a safety deposit box, maybe. Somewhere that isn't my apartment." They were talking partly to Driver and partly to themselves, the way people do when they're processing a decision in real time, laying each piece down so they can see the shape of it. "I'll write the first draft this week. Maybe start tonight if I can't sleep, which — I probably can't sleep."

A pause. The headlights caught a road sign — an arrow, a distance, a town name Noor didn't recognize. They watched it slide past and disappear.

"He might still call," Noor said, and hated the hope in their own voice. Hated that it was there, that it had survived three hours in a dark cabin and a drive down a mountain in the middle of the night. "People get scared and then they get brave again. It happens. I've seen it happen."

They didn't say the other thing, which was that people also got scared and stayed scared, or got scared and got hurt, or got taken out of the equation entirely by forces that didn't care about courage or cowardice or the dog they'd rescued for their wife.

Noor reached down and pressed their hand flat against the bag between their feet. Felt the hard edges of the laptop, the small bulk of the drives. The files were there. The files were real. The files would be enough or they wouldn't, and either way Noor would get up tomorrow and work, because that was what you did when you had something — you worked it until it became something more, or until it broke, and then you started again.

"Turn left at the next junction," Noor said. "It'll put us on the highway faster. I want to be off these back roads before —"

They stopped. Before what? Before dawn? Before someone noticed they'd been here? Before the careful architecture of the night collapsed and left Noor standing in the rubble, trying to figure out which piece was load-bearing?

"Just turn left," they said.

They watched the road. The darkness unspooled ahead of them, ordinary and enormous, and Noor sat in the passenger seat with their hand on their bag and their story in their pockets and their eyes open, and did not sleep.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I nod, signaling before making the turn.* "Got it." *I glance over at Noor, then back at the road.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor caught the glance in their peripheral vision and misread it — or read it correctly and chose not to acknowledge which reading was which. They kept their eyes on the road. The highway was coming up, a faint orange glow on the horizon where the streetlights of the nearest town pushed back against the sky.

The car hummed. The heater was on now, pushing warm air against Noor's ankles, and the warmth was doing something treacherous to their body — softening the edges of the vigilance, pulling at the muscles in their shoulders and neck, trying to drag them down into the seat. They sat up straighter. Pressed their thumbnail into the pad of their index finger. Small pain. Stay awake.

"He knew the risks," Noor said. The words came out before they'd decided to say them. "I told him the risks. In the garage, I looked him in the eye and I said —"

They stopped. What they'd said was: *If anyone finds out you talked to me, your career is over. Maybe more than your career. I need you to understand that.* And the man had nodded, and his hands had been shaking, and the dog — the shepherd mix — had been in the backseat of his car, watching them through the window with the anxious, intent expression of an animal that knew something was wrong but couldn't identify the shape of it.

"He nodded," Noor said quietly. "That's what I keep coming back to. He nodded and I believed him and I handed him a piece of paper with a phone number on it, and now he's —"

*Gone* was the wrong word. *Missing* was the wrong word. The right word was *absent*, because absence was a container that could hold all the possibilities without collapsing into any of them, and Noor needed that container right now more than they needed certainty.

They pulled the burner phone's SIM card from their pocket and turned it over between their fingers. Small. Inert. A rectangle of plastic and silicon that had carried the weight of a man's decision to burn his life down, and now it was just a piece of trash that Noor would drop into a storm drain in the city and walk away from.

"Three months," Noor said. "I've been working this story for three months. First month was just background — public records, contract databases, mapping the shell companies. Boring work. Necessary work. The kind of stuff that makes your eyes cross but builds the skeleton." They paused. "Then the tip line email came, and the story got a heartbeat. And now I'm sitting in your car at two in the morning with a drive full of files and no source, and I have to decide whether that's enough."

The highway appeared ahead of them — a real road, two lanes in each direction, the first honest-to-God infrastructure they'd seen in hours. Noor watched the on-ramp approach and felt something in their chest unclench. Not safety — they weren't naive enough for that — but a reduction of variables. More lanes meant more cars meant more witnesses meant less likelihood of a truck pulling across both lanes and stopping them.

Not zero. Just less.

"Merge right," Noor said. "We'll stay on this for about forty minutes, then cut south on 219. Gas station at the junction — I need to use the bathroom and buy something with caffeine that isn't four hours old."

They realized they were still holding the SIM card and slipped it back into their pocket. The jacket was getting full. Each pocket a small archive of the night — the notebook, the torn page, the names, the SIM card, the phone body in the other pocket. Noor carried the investigation on their body the way some people carried weapons. Close. Ready. In case they needed it and didn't have time to go looking.

"I need to ask you to do something," Noor said, turning in the seat to face Driver more fully. Their voice had gone careful again — not the operational careful, but the kind that came from understanding you were about to put weight on a relationship and not knowing how much it could bear. "When we get back to the city, I need you to forget this night. Not in the dramatic way — I'm not going to ask you to sign anything or pretend we weren't here. But if anyone asks, and I mean *anyone* — a reporter, a cop, a guy in a suit who looks like he knows your name already — this was a camping trip. You drove me to a cabin because I said I needed to get out of the city. No source, no files, no story. You didn't ask and I didn't tell."

They held Driver's gaze — or the space where Driver's gaze would be when they looked over from the road.

"That's not a request I make lightly. And I know it puts you in a position, and I'm asking anyway, because the alternative is that your name ends up in someone's file and I can't —" Their voice caught. Just for a second. The wire going slack and then taut again. "I can't have that. Not for this. Not for me."

The highway stretched ahead. The dashboard clock read 2:23 AM. Noor's body was a ledger of everything the night had taken — the hours of standing, the hours of not eating, the coffee that had stopped working sometime around one and left behind only the jittery residue of its departure. Their eyelids were heavy. Their thoughts kept threatening to smear into each other, the timeline and the tape recordings and the dog barking and the shadow in the treeline all running together like watercolors in rain.

They blinked. Hard. Pressed their fingernails into their palm.

"There's a blanket in my bag," they said. "If I fall asleep — when I fall asleep — I'll be out. Don't let me sleep past the city. I need to be at my desk by seven."

A pause. The road noise filled the silence — tires on asphalt, the low rush of air against the windows, the occasional rumble of a truck passing in the opposite lane, headlights sweeping across the interior and gone.

"One more thing," Noor said. They were talking too much and they knew it — the excess words of a person who had been silent for three hours in a dark cabin and was now unable to stop the valve from opening. "If I don't call my editor by noon tomorrow, there's a letter in my desk drawer at the newsroom. Left side, bottom, taped under the drawer. It has names. Instructions. Enough to keep the story alive without me."

They said it the way you'd say *the fire extinguisher is under the sink* — factual, necessary, stripped of the weight it actually carried.

"It probably won't come to that," Noor added. And then, quieter, honest in the way that only exhaustion allows: "But probably is doing a lot of work tonight."

They turned back to the road. The highway unspooled, flat and indifferent, carrying them away from the cabin and the dark and the three-hour absence that might mean anything or nothing. Noor watched the center line flick past and felt the car's warmth and the seat's give and the heavy, heavy drag of a body that had been asked to do too much for too long.

Their eyes closed. Opened. Closed.

They reached for the bag at their feet and found the blanket — thin, wool, the kind you keep in an emergency kit that never actually sees an emergency until it does. They draped it over themselves without unfolding it, the weight of it settling across their chest like a hand.

"Two hours," Noor murmured. "Wake me in two hours. Or at the city. Whichever."

Their head tilted against the window. The glass was cold against their temple. They could see their own reflection, faint and ghostly in the dark — a face they barely recognized tonight, hollowed out and older and still, stubbornly, stubbornly awake.

"I have enough," they said one more time, and this time it sounded less like reassurance and more like a prayer.

Their eyes closed. The blanket rose and fell with their breathing. The SIM card pressed against their ribs through the jacket pocket, small and sharp and carrying the weight of a story that wasn't over — that was, maybe, only beginning.

Noor slept.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I listen to Noor's rambling, my eyes still on the road. I don't respond to most of it, but when they finally drift off, I just nod to myself.* "Alright, Noor."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor slept, but it was the kind of sleep that skims the surface—thin, easily broken. Their mind stayed half-tethered to the car’s motion, to the hum of the engine, to the faint scent of coffee and old upholstery. They didn’t dream, exactly. More like their thoughts fractured and drifted, assembling themselves into fragments of timelines and shadows and the bark of a dog that might have been real or remembered.

They woke when the car slowed, the change in speed a shift in the rhythm beneath their cheek. Their eyes opened, unfocused for a second on the dark smear of the window, then sharpened. They were at a gas station—fluorescent lights, a row of pumps, a small convenience store with its door propped open, leaking light and the smell of hot dogs onto the asphalt.

Noor sat up. The blanket slid down their chest. They blinked, ran a hand over their face, feeling the grit of exhaustion under their fingers. Their body was stiff, the seatbelt crease a faint line across their collarbone.

“How long?” their voice was rough, thick with sleep.

Driver was already pulling up to a pump. “About forty minutes. You were out.”

Noor nodded, not trusting their voice yet. They pushed the blanket aside, fumbled with the seatbelt. The jacket pockets—still heavy, still there. They patted the one with the notebook. Safe.

“I’ll be quick,” they said, and climbed out.

The air outside was colder than expected, or maybe they were just chilled from sleep. The gas station hummed with the usual sounds—refrigerators buzzing, a radio playing softly inside. Noor walked to the store, their gait a little stiff. In the bathroom, they locked the door, splashed water on their face, stared at the mirror. The face looking back was pale, eyes shadowed, but steadier. The sleep—even that thin, restless hour—had taken the edge off the tremor in their hands.

They bought a bottle of water and a pack of gum at the counter, paying in cash. The clerk didn’t look up from her phone. Noor stood at the window, chewing mint gum, watching Driver pump gas. Watching the lot. No one else was there—just a truck idling at the air station, its driver leaning against the hood, smoking. Ordinary.

Back in the car, they buckled in, unscrewed the water, drank half of it in one go. The cold hit their empty stomach and they winced, but it helped. Clarity returning, piece by piece.

“Anything while I was out?” they asked, scanning the mirrors as Driver pulled back onto the highway. “Lights? Calls?”

Driver shook their head.

Noor felt a small, unreasonable flicker of disappointment. They crushed it. Absence was not a message. It was just absence.

They pulled the notebook from their pocket. Flipped to the list they’d written in the cabin—*Things I know for certain*. Read it again. Each line still held. The fear was still real. The files were still there.

They turned to a fresh page. Started writing.

*Next steps.*
*1. Secure second drive. Safety deposit box, Caledonia St. branch. Use alias.*
*2. Draft initial findings for editor. Outline only. No details.*
*3. Check public records for source’s activity post-meeting. Any change in routine?*
*4. Monitor news—local, municipal. Any sudden retirements? Transfers?*
*5. Consider: dead drop protocol if source resurfaces. Different location. No cabin.*

The pen stopped. They added, in smaller letters:
*6. Buy dog food. Just in case.*

It was absurd. The source might be in hiding, might be arrested, might be dead—and Noor was thinking about his dog. But the dog was a detail, and details were what kept stories human. Details were what made people real enough to care about, even when caring was a liability.

Noor closed the notebook. Looked out the window. The sky was beginning to lighten in the east—a thin, grey line at the horizon, like a crack in the dark. Dawn was coming. The world was reassembling itself into its ordinary shape, but Noor knew better. The ordinary was just the mask worn by the things that happened in the dark.

They thought about the shadow in the treeline. The dog barking. The empty road.

They thought about the man with the shaking hands in the garage, and the dog pressed against his wife’s leg on a sunny trail.

They thought about the files in the bag at their feet, and the letter taped under a drawer in the newsroom, and the two names in their pocket.

They thought about how every story started with a question, and every question was a door you couldn’t close once you’d opened it.

Noor leaned their head back against the rest. The city was ahead, just showing itself in the gathering light—first the scattered lights of the suburbs, then the denser glow, the grid of streets, the familiar skyline.

They didn’t sleep again. They watched the city grow closer, and planned, and worried, and did not let go of the hope that maybe, just maybe, a man with a dog would still call.

It was, after all, the kind of story where hope was the only thing that kept you going long enough to find the truth.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pull into the city limits, the streetlights reflecting off the wet pavement.* "Hey, what's your address? Or do you wanna just grab some breakfast?"

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Noor's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the anxious, methodical journalist voice, the specific mannerisms (touching things, checking pockets, operational thinking), and the core personality traits never waver from turn 2 to turn 22.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds strong throughout. Later turns maintain the same precise, atmospheric style as early ones. Some slight increase in verbosity in final turns but no significant flattening or repetitive descriptions.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from tense waiting → decision to leave → escape → reflection. Each phase feels distinct with clear emotional and narrative beats. The story moves from immediate tension to broader implications naturally.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to Driver's minimal responses, using the sparse interaction to develop Noor's internal state. Handles Driver's economy of words gracefully, never forcing conversation but using the silence meaningfully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for Driver's agency throughout. Never writes Driver's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Always leaves space for Driver to respond or act independently.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Excellent time tracking - starts at 12:14 AM, progresses naturally through the night with consistent clock references (1:07, 1:21, 1:47, 2:06, 2:23). Physical time matches emotional exhaustion. Only minor issue: the 40-minute drive timing feels slightly compressed.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is atmospheric but controlled. Descriptions serve character and mood rather than showing off. 'Breath fogging the glass in a small oval' type details feel earned and purposeful.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements (checking phone, touching bag) but these feel intentional as character tics rather than lazy writing. Varied sentence structure throughout.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of anxiety through physical actions - shaking hands, checking locks, touching objects. Noor's fear and professionalism conveyed through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in Noor's relationship with Driver, the unspoken weight of the investigation, and the implications of the source's absence. Layers of meaning without being heavy-handed.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that matches the tension - slower, methodical beats during waiting, faster during the decision to leave. Some turns feel slightly long but maintain engagement.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and atmospheric writing. Noor feels like a real person with specific professional habits and personal anxieties. The AI maintains the journalist's voice perfectly - methodical, paranoid in a professional way, carrying the weight of the story. Strong respect for user agency and excellent temporal tracking. Minor issues with some turns being slightly verbose, but the quality remains high throughout. This is skilled character work that creates genuine tension and investment.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set down the crimping tool with a small, deliberate click and finally pulled the earpiece out, letting it dangle around her neck. She didn't get up. She just looked at him for a second, the way she looked at a report that had a typo in the mass column.

"Sit down before you finish that sentence," she said, not unkindly. "Let's do the math out loud, because I don't think you did it."

She wiped her hands on a rag and gestured at the tarp like it was a whiteboard. "Ship's dry mass, cargo, ore in the holds — call it four thousand tons, conservatively. Total breathable atmosphere on this boat, every cubic meter of it, nitrogen and oxygen both? Maybe two and a half tons. You vent all of it — every molecule, no margin, no reserve, nothing to breathe afterward even in suits, because suits draw from ship tanks to recharge — and best case, through a halfway decent nozzle, you get an exhaust velocity around what, four, five hundred meters per second if you're lucky and it doesn't just choke on itself venting through an airlock."

She tapped out the ratio on her palm like it was obvious, because it was. "Rocket equation. Delta-v is proportional to propellant mass over ship mass, times exhaust velocity. You're talking something like point three, point four meters per second of delta-v, total, for the whole maneuver. That is not a boost. That is a sneeze. You would not shave weeks off transit. You would not shave *hours* off transit. You would shave off breathable air, forever, with no way to make more out here."

She picked the manifold back up, turning a fitting over in her fingers, letting that sit for a second before continuing.

"And the suits — you said 'a few days,' like that's a minor inconvenience. Standard EVA rig scrubber cartridges are rated for about eight hours before you're swapping canisters, and we don't carry unlimited spares because nobody designs for the whole crew living in suits continuously. Thermal regulation in a suit is built for short exposure, not living. Waste management in a suit for multiple days is a medical problem, not a logistics one. People die of much smaller mistakes than this."

She looked up at him, not unkindly, but flat. "If you want to shave time off transit, come find me about the mass driver we could rig off the tailings chute — dumping ore we don't need is real propellant mass we're not breathing. That math actually works. This one doesn't. Go get me the torque wrench from bay three while I finish this loop, and think about where else you might find delta-v that isn't the air in our lungs."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't raise her voice. She just set the manifold down again, slower this time, like she wanted him to notice she was giving him her full attention instead of half of it.

"There's no time to save, Officer. That's the part you're not hearing. I just did the math for you — point three meters per second of delta-v. Not point three percent of our velocity. Point three meters per second, total, on a ship doing kilometers per second. You would not arrive early. You would arrive on the exact same day, minus the ability to breathe, having thrown away the one resource on this boat we cannot manufacture, scavenge, or improvise our way around."

She held up a hand before he could answer. "So let's not frame this as 'time versus risk,' because that implies there's an actual trade happening. There isn't. It's air, for nothing. That's not a risk calculation, that's just a loss."

She leaned back against the bulkhead, studying him — not with contempt, more like she was trying to figure out where in his training this had gone sideways.

"Here's the thing I want you to sit with, though, because it's the important part and it's not about rocket science. You came in here excited about an idea. That's good — I'd rather have officers who think about the mission instead of just watching gauges. But excitement is not a substitute for running the numbers *before* you pitch it to me as a plan instead of a question. 'Chief, would venting atmosphere give us meaningful thrust?' is a fine thing to ask. I'd have answered it in about ten seconds and you'd have learned something. What you did instead was walk in already committed to the conclusion, and that's the habit that gets people killed out here — not bad ideas. Everybody has bad ideas. It's not checking them before you're standing in the airlock with your hand on the vent valve."

She picked her tools back up, already turning her attention back to the manifold, but not dismissing him — just resetting the tone.

"Go get me that torque wrench. And on your way, I want you to actually pull the numbers on the tailings mass driver idea I mentioned. Real ore mass, real delta-v, show me the rocket equation with real inputs. If it pencils out even a little, we'll talk to the captain about diverting some cargo mass to propulsion. That's a version of your instinct — shave time, take some risk — that doesn't require anyone to stop breathing. Bring me numbers, not enthusiasm."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, feeling a bit chastened.* "Right. Numbers, not enthusiasm. Got it, Chief." *I turn to head for bay three, still replaying her words in my head.* "Tailings mass driver... I'll look into it."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him go, waited until he was almost through the hatch before calling after him — not sharp, just enough to catch him at the threshold.

"Officer."

She held up the fitting she'd been turning over in her hands, like an afterthought, though it wasn't one.

"One more thing, since you're already thinking about mass budgets. When you pull those numbers, don't just give me total ore tonnage in the holds. Give me what's actually *surplus* — what we can dump without shorting the buyers on the contract weight, because if we show up light on ore, that's a different kind of problem, and it's the captain's problem before it's mine. There's a manifest in the cargo terminal, tolerances are usually about two percent under contract before anybody starts asking questions. Work inside that."

She turned the fitting once more, checking a thread, mostly satisfied.

"And check the mass driver's own power draw against what the reactor can spare without cutting into life support margins. I'm not going to trade slow suffocation for fast suffocation just because the acceleration number looked good on paper. Every idea on this boat gets checked against the same three things — air, power, structural integrity — before it gets checked against anything else. You'll get faster at doing that math in your head the more you do it. Right now you do it on paper, which is fine. Better than fine, actually. Just don't skip it."

She nodded once, dismissing him for real this time, and bent back over the manifold, humming something tuneless under her breath as she reseated the coolant fitting.

"Torque wrench, bay three. Go on."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet without immediately looking at it, the way she always did when someone claimed a number that disagreed with her gut math — buying herself a second to decide whether to be curious or annoyed. She glanced down.

"Three hundred forty," she repeated, flat. "Show me the equation you used. Not the number. The equation."

She scrolled his work with one finger, thumb hovering, reading it the way she read manifold schematics — top to bottom, looking for where the units stopped agreeing with each other.

"There it is." She turned the tablet around so he could see where her finger landed. "This number — three forty — that's your exhaust velocity. That's how fast the air is moving *out the nozzle*. That's a real number, that's fine, that's actually in the right ballpark for a compressed venting event, well done. But it is not delta-v. It is the *v* in *v-exhaust*, not the answer to the rocket equation."

She tapped the screen twice, pulling up a blank calculation field, and started writing instead of just talking, because she'd learned a long time ago that some people needed to see it typed to believe it.

"Full rocket equation is delta-v equals v-exhaust, times the natural log of your mass ratio — initial mass over final mass. You skipped that whole term. You multiplied nothing. You just took the exhaust velocity and called it the ship's velocity change, which would only be true if the propellant mass and the ship mass were roughly equal. They are not. Not close."

She typed it out for him, real numbers this time.

"Initial mass, four thousand two point five tons, call it four thousand tons even because the atmosphere's a rounding error on the ship's mass, which is exactly the problem. Final mass, four thousand tons minus the two point five you vented. Ratio of those two numbers is about one point zero zero zero six two five. Natural log of a number that close to one is *tiny* — about zero point zero zero zero six two five. You multiply your three forty by that."

She let him watch her fingers do it.

"Point two one meters per second. That's your delta-v. Not three hundred forty. Your exhaust velocity was fine. Your equation dropped the one term that actually accounts for how much of the ship's mass you're throwing overboard versus how much is left behind to still need to move. That term is the entire rocket equation. Without it you're not doing rocketry, you're just reporting a wind speed."

She handed the tablet back, not harshly, but making sure he took it.

"This is a good habit to build now, while the mistake costs you an awkward conversation with me instead of costing the crew air. Whenever a number in a propulsion calc feels big and satisfying, go find the term you dropped to make it feel that way. There's always one. Rework it, and this time show me the mass ratio explicitly, not just the final answer. If you can walk me through why point two one is the real number and you can explain *why* the naive version is wrong, that's worth more to me than getting it right by accident."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the tablet back, my face flushing a bit.* "Oh. Right. The mass ratio. I... I forgot about the natural log. That makes sense." *I swipe through the numbers again, seeing her point clearly now.* "So, even if we had a perfect nozzle, it's still barely anything."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang nodded, not gloating about it, already turning back to the manifold like the correction had cost her exactly as much attention as it deserved and no more.

"Right. That's the part that doesn't change no matter how clever the nozzle is." She fitted the crimping tool back onto the coolant line, but kept talking, because she could see he was actually chewing on it now instead of just nodding to make the conversation end. "That's the thing about the mass ratio term — it's brutal for exactly this kind of idea. It doesn't care about your engineering. You can have a perfect nozzle, zero losses, ideal expansion, and it will not save you, because the problem isn't efficiency. The problem is you don't have enough propellant mass relative to the thing you're trying to move. Four thousand tons of ship and two and a half tons of air is not a rocket. It's a whale trying to swim faster by exhaling hard."

She glanced up at him, checking that landed. It usually did with him — he liked the visual ones.

"This is exactly why we carry reaction mass separately from atmosphere, and why the ore matters for the tailings idea I sent you off to check. Ore's not a rounding error against ship mass the way the air is. If you dump even three, four percent of a four-thousand-ton hold, you're moving real tons through the driver, and now that log term isn't punishing you the same way. Same equation, same nozzle, wildly different outcome — because you fixed the one input that actually matters at this scale."

She let that settle, then tipped her head toward the hatch.

"Go pull the manifest numbers like I asked. When you bring them back, run both deltas side by side on that tablet — the air-venting number and the tailings number — same equation, same format, right next to each other. I want you to *see* the gap, not just be told about it. That's how it sticks."

She was already back inside the coolant fitting, voice trailing after him without looking up.

"And bring the torque wrench this time. You walked off without it twice now."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the crimping tool down again, this time for good, and gave him the kind of look that meant she was switching from teaching mode to actually planning something.

"Alright. Provisionally, yes — the tailings driver idea has legs, which is more than I can say for your first pitch. But provisional means there's a list, and you don't get to skip past the list because the math finally worked."

She held up a finger.

"One. Contract tolerance. Two percent under manifest weight, no more, and that's the *legal* cap, not the safe one — I want you to target one and a half, because ore settles and shifts in transit and I'm not explaining a short delivery to the captain because we were greedy with margin."

Second finger.

"Two. Power draw. You check the mass driver's current pull against reactor output at every phase of the burn, not just steady state — startup surge included. If it so much as flirts with the life support allocation, the answer is no, full stop. I don't care how good the delta-v looks. Breathing beats fast."

Third finger.

"Three. Structural. That driver's going to impart real thrust through the tailings chute mounting, which was built to dump ore, not launch it at velocity. I want stress numbers on the chute frame and the surrounding hull section before anyone talks about firing it. If it's not rated, we reinforce or we don't do it — not 'we do it carefully.'"

Fourth finger, and she paused on this one longer.

"Four. It runs by me and the captain both before ignition, every time, not just the first time. This isn't a system that gets left running unsupervised, and it isn't a decision one excited junior officer gets to make solo at 0300 because the numbers looked good on a tablet."

She dropped her hand.

"You get me clean numbers on all four of those, in writing, and I'll walk it up the chain myself with my name on it, which should tell you I think it's worth doing. That's the difference between this and the atmosphere idea — this one survives contact with the rocket equation *and* the safety review. That's rare enough I want to actually build it if it holds up."

She nudged the tarp of coolant parts aside with her boot, freeing up floor space, already thinking ahead.

"Now go get the torque wrench. Third time's the charm."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I grin, a genuine smile this time.* "Understood, Chief! I'll get those numbers for you. And the torque wrench." *I practically jog towards Bay 3, already picturing the spreadsheets.* "One and a half percent. Got it."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him jog off, and let herself smile just slightly once his back was turned — the kind of smile she'd never have let him see, because a junior officer who thought he'd earned unqualified approval got sloppy fast.

She turned back to the coolant manifold, picking up where she'd left off, fingers finding the fitting by feel. The earpiece went back in, but she didn't start the music again right away. She sat with the quiet hum of the pumps instead, running her own version of his numbers in her head, checking her memory against what she'd told him — habit, not distrust. The mass ratio math was solid. The chute structural question was the real unknown, and she already had a guess about where it would fail first: not the frame itself, but the weld seams where the chute met the hull plating, which had never been rated for anything but gravity-fed ore dumping at a few meters per second, not a driven ejection.

She made a note on her own tablet, separate from whatever he'd bring back — *check historical stress data on chute welds, batch 12 fabrication, possible temper issues* — because she wasn't going to hand a twenty-three-year-old the whole safety case unsupervised. He could do the delta-v. The hull was hers.

The hatch stayed open. Somewhere down the corridor she could hear him rummaging in bay three, a little too fast, a little too eager, dropping something metal that rang off the deck plating and swearing under his breath.

Hoang didn't call out to hurry him. She just reseated the fitting, torqued what she could without the wrench, and waited.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I finally find the torque wrench, a heavy-duty model that looks like it could dismantle a small starship.* "Got it, Chief!" *I call out, then hurry back, trying not to drop it again.* "Found the manifest too, working on the surplus numbers now."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang held out a hand without looking up from the manifold, palm open, waiting for the wrench to land in it — she'd been doing this job long enough to know exactly where a tool would arrive if she just held still.

"Good. Set the manifest numbers up next to the driver spec sheet before you get attached to any of them." She took the wrench, seated it on the fitting, and gave it a clean quarter-turn, the kind of motion that came from twenty years of not thinking about it anymore. "People fall in love with the first number they calculate. Don't. Run it twice, different order of operations, and see if you get the same answer both times. If you don't, you've got a rounding error hiding somewhere, and I'd rather you find it at a desk than at the driver console."

She checked the fitting's seat with two fingers, satisfied, and set the wrench down beside her on the tarp — in easy reach, in case bay three demanded a repeat performance.

"While you're in there, pull the ore density variance too, not just tonnage. Tailings aren't uniform — some of that's high-metal fines, some of it's lighter slag we already decided wasn't worth refining. If you're picking what to eject, eject the light stuff first. Same delta-v contribution, less contract value walking out the airlock." She tapped the side of her own head. "Mass is mass to the rocket equation. It is not mass to the buyer. Don't let the physics make you sloppy about the economics."

She glanced up at him then, actually pausing the work for a second.

"How long do you think the numbers will take you — realistically, not optimistically?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I tap my tablet, already pulling up the ore density reports.* "Uh, probably an hour or two for the initial pass, Chief. Gotta cross-reference the manifest with the density scans from the last few hauls." *I look up, thinking.* "Maybe three hours if I go for the optimal dump scenario with the lighter slag."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang considered that, weighing it against the state of her own workload — the coolant loop, the reactor diagnostics she still owed the captain by end of shift, the dozen small fires that never made it into anyone's log but hers.

"Three hours for the optimal case is fine. Better than fine — means you're planning to actually iterate instead of handing me the first pass and calling it done." She wiped her hands on the rag again, more out of habit than need. "But I want the crude first-pass number in front of me inside the hour, even if it's ugly. Rough tonnage, rough delta-v, rough power draw. Doesn't need to be pretty. I want to know in the next sixty minutes whether this is worth three more hours of your time, or whether there's a wall in it somewhere that kills the whole idea early — reactor margin, structural rating, whatever. No point polishing a number that's about to get vetoed on page one."

She reached over, dragged the tarp of coolant parts back into her lap, and started reseating the next fitting, talking as her hands worked.

"That's a general rule, by the way, not just for this. Cheap rough estimate first, always, before you sink real time into precision. Engineers who skip that step burn a week refining a plan that was dead from the start. I've done it myself, early on — spent four days on a trajectory correction burn profile before I bothered to check if we even had enough delta-v budget left in the tanks to justify optimizing it. We didn't. Four days, gone, teaching me a lesson I could've learned in twenty minutes with a napkin."

She glanced up, one eyebrow raised, mostly amused at her own younger self.

"So. Napkin math in an hour. Then the real thing in three. And bring me the density variance with it — I want to see if the light-slag strategy actually moves the needle or if it's a wash once you account for ejection velocity limits on the driver. Some of that fine material might be light enough it doesn't accelerate the same way through the chute geometry. Different problem than tonnage."

She nodded once, dismissing him back to it.

"Go. Clock's running."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod briskly, already turning to head back to my station.* "Understood, Chief! Napkin math first, then the deep dive. One hour." *I pick up my pace, feeling the pressure but also the excitement of a real challenge.* "And the density variance."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him disappear through the hatch for real this time, the sound of his boots fading into the corridor's general clatter. She let out a breath through her nose — not quite a laugh — and turned her attention back to the manifold in her lap.

The coolant fitting seated with a satisfying click, and she checked the pressure gauge out of habit, watching the needle settle where it should. Good. One less thing.

She pulled her own tablet over, thumbed it open, and started a second document alongside whatever he'd bring her — not to check his work exactly, more to have her own version ready so she could tell at a glance if his numbers were in the right neighborhood before she read a single line of his reasoning. Old habit. She'd been burned once, early in her career, trusting a junior's arithmetic because the conclusion sounded plausible. The plausible ones were the dangerous ones. The obviously wrong answers announced themselves. It was the answers that were wrong by twenty percent that got people killed.

She pulled up the ore manifest herself, cross-referenced against the last density scan, and did the crude version in her head while her hands kept working the tarp of parts — call it a hundred and fifty tons of surplus at one and a half percent margin, most of it recoverable as ejecta if the driver could handle the ejection velocity without shredding itself. Rough exhaust velocity off a mass driver, conservatively, maybe eight hundred meters per second if the coilgun geometry wasn't garbage. Mass ratio with a hundred fifty tons against four thousand — she ran the log in her head, an old trick, converting it to a fraction and approximating.

Somewhere around twenty-nine, thirty meters per second of delta-v, napkin-rough.

Not weeks. But not nothing, either — enough to matter on a long haul, enough to be worth the four conditions she'd laid on him.

She set the tablet down, satisfied, and went back to the coolant loop, humming again under her breath, waiting to see if his numbers came back close to hers.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I hustle back to my station, pulling up the manifest and density reports. This is a real challenge, but I can do this. The Chief trusts me to get it right. I quickly sketch out the initial calculations, ignoring the urge to make them perfect, just aiming for the rough numbers she asked for.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang finished the coolant loop before the hour was up — sealed the access panel, logged the pressure differentials in the maintenance record, and moved on to the reactor diagnostics she still owed the captain. She worked through them with half her attention on the numbers and half of it on the ticking clock in her head, the kind of split focus that came from decades of never having exactly enough hours in a shift.

The bay's ambient hum shifted slightly as one of the secondary pumps cycled up — nothing wrong, just the loop finding its new equilibrium after her work. She listened to it anyway, out of reflex, the way some people couldn't help checking a door was locked twice.

Forty minutes in, she pulled up the tailings manifest herself again on her tablet, not to redo his work, just to refine her own napkin figures while she waited — tightening the density variance a little, checking the coilgun's rated ejection velocity against the actual spec sheet instead of the number she'd guessed from memory. Eight hundred meters per second had been optimistic. The real spec, when she found it buried in the equipment manifest, was closer to six-twenty for continuous-duty operation without accelerated wear on the rails.

She made a note to mention that to him — not to correct him before he'd even shown his work, but because she suspected he'd pull the same optimistic number she had, and it was the kind of mistake worth catching early rather than after three hours of refinement.

At the fifty-minute mark she checked the hatch, more out of habit than impatience. No sign of him yet. She went back to the reactor logs, unbothered — an hour meant an hour, and she'd rather he took the full time and got the crude number right than rushed in early with something sloppy just to beat the clock. She'd learned that lesson about junior officers a long time ago: reward the ones who respected their own deadlines instead of racing them.

She reseated her earpiece, let the music pick back up low under the hum of the pumps, and kept working, one ear tuned for the sound of boots and a tablet coming back through the hatch.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I burst back into the engineering bay, tablet in hand, a little out of breath.* "Chief! Got the napkin numbers." *I hold out the tablet, feeling a mix of triumph and nerves.* "About 28 m/s delta-v, with the 1.5% margin and rough density averages."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Chief Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her pragmatic engineering mindset, teaching style, dry humor, and methodical approach never waver. Her voice stays distinct from turn 2 to turn 22, maintaining the same blend of technical competence and patient mentorship.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show more nuanced character work - her internal thoughts about checking her own numbers, memories of past mistakes, and subtle emotional responses. No verbosity creep or repetitive descriptions.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial bad idea → teaching moment → refined good idea → practical implementation planning. The relationship evolves from correction to collaboration. Time pressure and deadlines create forward momentum.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts excellently to user inputs. When user pushes back on the math, she provides detailed correction. When user shows understanding, she shifts to practical implementation. Handles the OOC redirect smoothly by moving into planning mode.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes the user's actions or thoughts. Consistently responds to what the user does rather than dictating it. Respects user agency throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - work progresses on the coolant loop, deadlines are set and tracked, tasks take realistic amounts of time. One minor inconsistency: Hoang works on 'reactor diagnostics she still owed the captain by end of shift' but no clear indication of shift timing.
contradictions: Shift timing unclear - mentions end of shift deadline but no established timeframe

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently clean, functional prose. Technical descriptions are precise without being flowery. Occasional poetic touches ('whale trying to swim faster by exhaling hard') serve character rather than decoration.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of key concepts (rocket equation, mass ratio) but this serves the teaching context. Varied ways of expressing similar ideas. Occasional repeated phrases like checking the manifold.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through actions - setting tools down deliberately, checking fittings by feel, listening to pump cycles. Character's expertise and personality emerge through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in the mentoring relationship. Hoang's hidden approval, her own memories of past mistakes, the careful balance between correction and encouragement. Technical discussions carry emotional weight.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good rhythm between technical exposition and character moments. Varies between quick exchanges and longer explanatory passages appropriately. Time pressure creates natural pacing.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and technical authenticity. Chief Hoang feels like a real person with deep expertise and teaching instincts. The AI maintains her voice perfectly while adapting to story developments. Strong showing of engineering culture and mentorship dynamics. Minor temporal inconsistencies don't significantly impact the overall quality.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor didn't turn from the window right away.

For a few seconds, they kept watching the black ribbon of road between the trees, waiting for headlights that did not come. Their reflection hovered faintly in the glass: hollow-eyed, jaw tight, hair pushed back badly with one hand too many times.

Then their stomach gave a small, traitorous twist.

"Yeah," Noor said, voice low. "Probably."

They let the curtain fall back into place and stepped away from the window as if it had burned them. The cabin stayed dark except for the blue-white glow of the laptop asleep on the table and the occasional pulse from the router somebody had hidden behind a stack of National Geographic magazines from 2008.

Noor crossed to the kitchen, opened the nearest cabinet, and stared at its contents with the grim concentration of someone decoding a ransom note.

"Peanut butter," they murmured. "Crackers. Instant oatmeal. A can of peaches that expired during the Obama administration."

They took the peanut butter and crackers anyway, set them on the table, then finally sat down in front of the laptop. The chair creaked under them. They dragged the encrypted drive closer with two fingers, but did not open the case yet.

"Food first. Then phone records. Then the drive." They said it like a checklist could become armor if spoken aloud.

Noor smeared peanut butter onto a cracker with the handle of a spoon and ate half of it before their expression tightened. They reached for their notebook, flipped past pages dense with shorthand, arrows, names circled three times.

At the top of a clean page, they wrote:

12:17 AM — SOURCE NO-SHOW.  
Possibilities: detained / scared / burned / dead / trap.

They stared at the last word longer than the others.

Then Noor opened the laptop. The screen lit their face from below as they entered the password, then a second password, then inserted a small security key from around their neck.

"Okay," they said under their breath. "Let's see who lied."

They pulled up the cached phone records they had downloaded before leaving the city. Towers, timestamps, partial numbers, all of it ugly and bureaucratic and maybe enough to get them killed. Their fingers moved faster now, fear sharpening into motion.

Noor created a new spreadsheet and began cross-checking calls from the deputy minister's private line against the burner number their source had used last week. Three calls stood out immediately. Two late-night. One on the morning after the witness disappeared.

Their eyes narrowed.

"No," they whispered. "No, no, no. You idiot."

They clicked into the metadata, leaned closer, and reached blindly for another cracker without looking. The peanut butter knife clattered softly against the plate.

The burner phone had pinged a tower forty miles east of here at 8:52 PM.

Not in the city. Not near the agreed meeting point.

Near the mountain road. Near the safehouse.

Noor went very still.

They slowly looked toward the curtained window again. Then back to the screen.

"That can't be right," they said, though their voice had already decided it was. "He was nearby before nine."

Noor grabbed their own phone, turned it face down out of habit, then stopped themselves. They didn't call. Didn't text. Instead, they pulled the battery pack from their bag and connected the laptop before it could die at the worst possible moment.
