Then they opened the padded case containing the encrypted drive.

"If he came up here and didn't make it to the door," Noor said quietly, "then either he ran, or somebody got to him first."

They slid the drive into the port.

A password prompt appeared.

Noor flexed their fingers once, wiped their palms on their jeans, and began typing.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm still on my phone, half-listening to Noor's monologue. I look up when they say "somebody got to him first."* "Wait, what?" *My phone screen goes dark as I lower it.* "Got to who?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor did not answer immediately.

Their fingers froze over the keyboard, one letter short of completing the passphrase. They listened.

Not to the question. Past it.

To the cabin.

The refrigerator's tired hum. The tick of cooling pipes in the wall. Wind dragging pine branches against the roof with a dry, fingernail scrape.

No engine. No tires on gravel. No footsteps.

Still, Noor lowered their voice.

"My source," they said. "The one we came here to meet."

They finished typing the passphrase and hit enter.

The encrypted drive took three seconds to mount. Three seconds too long. Noor watched the progress bar crawl across the screen while their jaw worked once, hard.

"He was supposed to approach from the south road after nine. No phone. No car headlights until the last half-mile. That was the plan." Their eyes flicked to the cached phone records again. "But his burner pinged a tower east of us at 8:52. Close enough that he was already in the mountains before the meeting time."

The drive opened.

A folder appeared with no title. Inside it: six files.

Noor's fear changed shape.

Not lessened. Focused.

They copied the full contents to the laptop first, then to a hidden partition they had set up earlier and not mentioned. Only after the transfer began did they click the first file.

Audio.

Noor plugged in their earbuds, then stopped, thought better of it, and pulled one bud free so they could still hear the room. They scrubbed ten seconds into the recording.

A man's voice came through, tinny and compressed.

"...not a procurement issue. It's a disposal issue. You understand me? The money is the least of it now."

Noor's face went slack for half a second.

Then they grabbed the notebook and wrote fast.

DISPOSAL ISSUE — male voice.  
Confirm identity.  
Not just bribery. Cleanup.

They clicked the next file. A scanned document loaded sideways. Noor rotated it, zoomed in, and their mouth went dry.

It was a transfer order.

Names. Dates. A detention facility listed under a false logistics code. A signature block at the bottom with a ministerial seal.

Noor let out a breath that was almost a laugh and almost not human.

"Jesus," they whispered. "He got it."

They looked toward the curtained window again, but this time their attention did not linger there. They stood abruptly, chair legs scraping the floor, and crossed to the kitchen counter where their go-bag sat open.

Noor pulled out a compact camera, two memory cards taped together, and an old prepaid phone wrapped in foil.

"We're not waiting blind anymore," they said. "If he's near here, there's a reason he didn't knock. If someone followed him, there's a reason they haven't knocked either."

They moved quickly now.

First, they turned the laptop brightness all the way down. Then they started duplicating the drive contents onto one of the memory cards. A progress bar appeared: eight minutes.

Too long.

Noor stared at it as if they could intimidate it into speed.

"Okay," they said, more to themselves than anyone else. "Eight minutes. In eight minutes, one copy goes on me, one gets hidden here, one gets out if the network still behaves."

They crossed to the router behind the magazines and crouched beside it. The blinking green lights reflected in their eyes. They did not like what they saw, but they did not unplug it yet.

"No outgoing messages from my main phone," they murmured. "If they have his burner, they may have mine. If they have mine, they may have watched us leave the city."

Noor returned to the table and opened a terminal window. Their fingers flew. They checked the VPN tunnel, then a dead-drop upload script they had prepared weeks earlier and hoped never to use.

The connection stuttered.

Noor's shoulders tightened.

"Come on," they breathed. "Come on."

The first packet went out.

Then the second.

Then the upload failed.

Noor stared at the error message.

AUTHENTICATION INTERRUPTED.

They leaned back very slowly.

That was not normal.

For the first time all night, they looked genuinely cold.

"That's bad," Noor said.

They reached for the prepaid phone, unwrapped it from the foil, and powered it on. While it booted, they went to the drawer nearest the stove and began opening it with efficient, sharp movements.

Junk drawer. Matches. Batteries. Twine. A rusted bottle opener. Two screwdrivers.

Noor took the screwdrivers.

Then they opened the cabinet under the sink and found a roll of black trash bags, a flashlight, and a half-empty bottle of bleach. They took the flashlight and clicked it once against their palm to test the weight, not the beam.

The prepaid phone lit up.

No bars.

Noor gave it a look of pure contempt.

"Of course."

They returned to the laptop. The memory card copy still had five minutes left.

Five minutes was suddenly an entire country.

Noor opened the third file from the drive.

A photo appeared.

Dark. Grainy. Taken through a windshield or from behind glass. A roadside pullout. Two vehicles. One man standing near an open trunk.

Noor zoomed in.

Their breathing changed.

The man by the trunk was their source.

Alive, at least when the photo had been taken.

There was a timestamp embedded in the file name.

20:57.

Five minutes after the burner ping.

Noor zoomed in further, past the source's blurred profile, past the reflective strip on the side of one vehicle, to the second car's plate.

Only three characters were visible.

Noor wrote them down.

Then they opened the fourth file.

A text document.

One line.

IF I AM LATE, DO NOT LOOK FOR ME ON THE ROAD. LOOK UNDER THE FLOOR.

Noor did not move.

Their eyes lifted from the screen to the cabin around them.

The floorboards were old pine, warped and uneven, with dark seams between them. A braided rug sat beneath the table. Another in front of the cold fireplace. Dust gathered thick in the corners where no one had swept properly in months.

Noor swallowed.

"Under the floor," they said.

They stood, slower this time, and picked up one of the screwdrivers.

The copy had four minutes remaining.

Noor looked at the table. The laptop. The drive. The window. The door.

Then they walked to the braided rug beneath the table and hooked the screwdriver under its edge. They dragged it back with a soft hiss across the boards.

Beneath it, one floorboard near the wall had newer screws than the others.

Noor crouched.

Their voice dropped to almost nothing.

"He was here before us."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I'm sitting up now, watching Noor with wide eyes. My phone is forgotten on the couch cushion.* "He was *here*? What are you talking about?" *I look at the floorboard they're pointing at, then back at Noor.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor's eyes stayed on the newer screws.

"He made a dead drop," they said. "Or he tried to."

Their voice had gone thin, stripped down to function. Panic was still there, but it had been shoved behind the work.

Noor glanced back at the laptop.

Three minutes, twelve seconds.

"Come on," they muttered.

They drove the screwdriver into the first screw and twisted. The metal squealed softly in the wood. Too loud. Everything was too loud now — the scrape of the tool, the creak of Noor's knees against the floorboards, the blood beating in their ears.

The first screw came loose.

Noor set it carefully on the rug instead of letting it roll.

Second screw.

Their hand slipped once. They hissed through their teeth, tightened their grip, and kept going.

"He wouldn't have told me to look here unless he knew he might not make contact," Noor said. "Which means he either came inside before we arrived, or someone brought him close enough to stash something. Either way, he knew this cabin."

The second screw came free.

Noor paused and looked toward the window again.

Nothing moved behind the curtain.

That did not comfort them.

They worked the screwdriver under the board and pried upward. For one sick second it did not budge. Then the old pine gave a dry crack, and the board lifted half an inch.

Noor froze.

Not from the sound.

From the smell.

Damp earth. Cold rot. Oil. Something metallic underneath it.

They set the screwdriver down and used both hands to lift the board carefully aside.

A narrow cavity opened beneath the floor.

Inside was a black plastic document tube, the kind architects used for plans, wrapped in two layers of trash bag and sealed with silver tape. Beside it sat a smaller object: a cheap GPS tracker, its casing cracked, one red light dead and dark.

Noor stared at the tracker.

"Oh, you clever bastard," they whispered.

They reached in and lifted it out first, holding it between thumb and forefinger like it might bite.

The battery compartment had been smashed. Deliberately. Recently. A smear of dried mud marked one side.

Noor turned it over.

A strip of tape on the back had three handwritten numbers.

857.

The partial plate from the photograph.

Noor's face hardened.

"Not a coincidence."

They set the tracker on the table, then pulled the document tube from the cavity. It was heavier than it should have been.

The laptop gave a soft chime.

Noor's head snapped up.

Copy complete.

For half a second, relief passed over their face so quickly it almost did not count.

They moved.

Noor crossed to the laptop, ejected the memory card properly because even terror did not excuse corrupting evidence, then slid it into the tiny case taped beneath their watch strap. The motion was practiced. Automatic. One copy on them.

They took the second memory card and started another copy from the drive.

Estimated time: seven minutes.

"Fine," Noor said. "Fine, fine."

They returned to the document tube and cut through the tape with the edge of the screwdriver. The plastic resisted, then split.

Inside were three things.

A folded map.

A stack of printed photographs.

And a small notebook sealed in a freezer bag.

Noor took out the map first and spread it on the floorboards. It showed the mountain roads around the cabin, but someone had marked it heavily in red grease pencil.

The south road.

The east tower.

A logging track half a mile behind the cabin.

And a point marked with an X near a dry creek bed.

Noor pressed two fingers to the X.

"That's not far," they said quietly. "Ten minutes on foot. Less if you know the trail."

They opened the photographs next.

The first showed the same roadside pullout as the digital image, but clearer. Their source stood beside the trunk of a gray sedan, one hand raised defensively. Another man faced him.

Noor knew the second man.

Not personally. Not well enough for him to know Noor's coffee order or what fear did to their hands.

But well enough.

They had his face in a folder labeled CIVIL SERVICE / PROCUREMENT / INTERMEDIARIES.

Noor sat back on their heels.

"Marek Voss," they said. "Of course it was you."

They flipped to the next photograph.

Voss handing over a satchel.

Next.

The source looking toward the trees, startled.

Next.

A third figure emerging from the dark behind him.

Noor stopped breathing for one beat.

The third figure wore a sheriff's department jacket.

The face was turned away.

But the build, the hairline, the watch on the left wrist—

Noor's hand curled around the edge of the photo hard enough to bend it.

"Deputy Harlan," they said.

The name tasted like rust.

They looked at the map again, then at the floor cavity, then at the door.

"He didn't run," Noor said. "He was intercepted."

The prepaid phone still had no signal. The router lights blinked their useless little heartbeat from behind the magazines.

Noor grabbed the notebook in the freezer bag and held it up to the laptop glow. The first page was visible through the plastic.

A list of names.

Some crossed out.

Some circled.

At the bottom, written harder than the rest:

IF NOOR GETS THIS, PUBLISH THE CHAIN, NOT THE STORY. THE STORY CAN BE DENIED. THE CHAIN CAN'T.

Noor's mouth tightened.

For a moment, exhaustion broke through. It showed in the slackness around their eyes, in the way their shoulders lowered as if some invisible hand had pressed them down.

Then it was gone.

They stood and began packing with sudden precision.

"New plan," Noor said. "We don't stay until morning."

They moved to the laptop and checked the second copy.

Six minutes.

Too long again.

Noor swore under their breath, then began dividing materials.

The original encrypted drive went back into its padded case. The printed photos went into a large envelope from their bag. The map they folded into quarters and slid into the inside pocket of their jacket. The notebook stayed sealed in plastic.

They took one photograph of every item with the compact camera, angling the screen away from the window.

Click.

Click.

Click.

A chain of custody, improvised on a kitchen floor.

Noor opened their notebook to a clean page and wrote fast:

12:31 AM — FLOOR CACHE RECOVERED.  
Contents: tracker 857 / map w X creek bed / photos Voss + Harlan / notebook list.  
Source anticipated failure to arrive.  
Likely compromised route east approach.  
Possible active surveillance.

They tore the page out, folded it twice, and tucked it beneath the insole of their boot.

Then Noor stood very still.

A sound had come from outside.

Not wind.

Not branch scrape.

A single faint pop, far off through the trees.

A gunshot, maybe.

Or a car backfiring.

Noor's face gave no sign they believed in backfires anymore.

They crossed to the window but did not touch the curtain. Instead, they lowered themselves beside it and looked through the tiny gap near the sill.

The road was black.

The trees were blacker.

Nothing visible.

That was not the same as nothing there.

Noor backed away from the window and went to the cabin's rear door. They checked the lock. Then the hinges. Then the floor in front of it for disturbed dust.

Noor crouched.

A smear of mud crossed the threshold.

Old? New?

They touched it lightly.

Still damp.

Their pulse changed again.

"He used the back," Noor murmured. "Before we got here."

They looked toward the kitchen table.

Five minutes on the copy.

"No. No more waiting for machines."

Noor pulled the second memory card before the transfer completed, grimacing as the laptop protested. Partial copy was better than none. They wrapped it in a scrap of paper towel, crossed to the fireplace, and reached up into the cold chimney.

Soot blackened their fingers as they wedged the card behind a loose brick.

"Hidden copy," they said. "Maybe readable. Maybe enough."

They returned to the laptop, closed the files, and shut it down without ceremony. The screen went dark, taking the cabin's only clean light with it.

For a second, Noor was only a shape in the dark kitchen.

Then they clicked on the flashlight, covering most of the beam with their fingers so only a red sliver escaped.

They gathered the drive, the notebook, the photos, the compact camera, the prepaid phone, and the tracker. All of it went into the go-bag except the map in their jacket and the memory card on their wrist.

Noor took one cracker from the plate, shoved it into their mouth, chewed twice, and seemed to remember only then that their body existed.

"Food," they said flatly. "Done."

They lifted the floorboard back into place but did not replace the screws. The rug went over it again, slightly crooked.

Then Noor went to the front door and stood beside it rather than in front of it.

They listened.

The cabin held its breath with them.

After several seconds, Noor spoke softly, eyes fixed on the dark line beneath the door.

"If he's alive, he's not on the road. The note said don't look there. It said under the floor because he needed me to find the chain. But the map gives us the creek bed."

Their hand tightened around the screwdriver.

"That could be where he hid. It could be where they took him. It could be where he wanted me to find the last piece."

Noor looked back once, face pale and set.

"And if Harlan is involved, calling local police gets us killed faster."

They crossed to the table, took the old foil from the prepaid phone, and wrapped their main phone in it too. Then they shoved both into separate pockets.

Noor picked up the flashlight, the screwdriver, and the go-bag.

Their voice dropped again.

"We leave through the back. No lights. No talking once we're outside unless we have to."

A pause.

Then Noor added, almost to themselves, "And if there are headlights on that road, we go into the trees."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor stared for one long second.

Something in their face closed.

Not anger, exactly. There was no room for anger. Anger took oxygen. Anger made noise.

Noor turned away.

"Fine," they said quietly. "Then I do this alone."

They did not say it dramatically. They said it like another item on the checklist.

They tightened the strap of the go-bag across their chest, then moved through the cabin with fast, controlled purpose. At the kitchen counter, they swept the peanut butter, crackers, and spoon into the sink to make the table look less recently used. They wiped the laptop’s outline from the dust with their sleeve, then reconsidered, dragged two fingers back through it, and made the disturbance look older, messier.

At the router, Noor crouched and watched the lights blink.

Then they unplugged it.

The green points died.

The cabin became darker than before.

Noor waited three seconds.

No shout outside. No sudden beam through the window. No engine turning over in the distance.

Good, or bad in a quieter way.

They crossed to the back door and eased the bolt open millimeter by millimeter. The metal gave a soft scrape. Noor stopped. Counted silently to ten. Then finished the motion.

The rear door opened onto black trees and cold mountain air.

Noor crouched before stepping out, sweeping the covered flashlight beam low across the threshold. The mud smear continued outside in broken marks, half-dried along the porch boards. A boot tread. Narrow heel. Deep pressure on the left side.

Someone had come in limping.

Or carrying weight.

Noor’s mouth went flat.

They slipped outside and left the door open only wide enough to pass through. The cold hit them instantly, sharp through denim and jacket, smelling of pine sap, wet leaves, and distant rain.

The back of the cabin faced uphill. Beyond the sagging porch, a thin path disappeared between trees. Not an official trail. Not something a vacationing uncle would use to get firewood. Too narrow. Too direct.

Noor pulled the folded map from their jacket and opened it just enough to orient themselves. Their thumb found the cabin, then the marked logging track, then the red X by the dry creek bed.

Half a mile.

Maybe less.

They put the map away.

"No lights," they murmured to themselves.

The flashlight went off.

For a few seconds, blindness swallowed them whole.

Then the forest separated into degrees of black. Tree trunks. Underbrush. Pale stones. The faint suggestion of sky between branches.

Noor moved.

They kept low, one hand out, boots landing on pine needles where possible instead of leaves. Every few steps, they stopped and listened.

Wind.

Branches.

An owl somewhere down the slope.

No cars.

No voices.

No help.

After twenty yards, the cabin behind them became only a darker block among trees. Noor did not look back again.

The trail climbed first, then cut sharply east. Whoever had used it knew the terrain. Noor found more mud on a stone, then a broken fern stem, then a scuff where someone had slipped and caught themselves against a birch trunk. The mark on the bark was fresh, pale wood showing beneath scraped skin.

Noor touched it with two fingers.

Still damp.

They kept going.

The go-bag knocked once against their hip. Noor stopped, adjusted it tighter, then took the screwdriver from their pocket and held it reversed against their palm. A pathetic weapon. Better than empty hands.

The path bent around a cluster of boulders.

There, under the shadow of a pine, Noor found the first blood.

Not much.

Three dark spots on a flat stone. Nearly black in the night, but wrong enough that their eyes caught on it.

Noor crouched.

Their breath came shallowly now, not from the climb.

They took out the compact camera, covered the tiny screen with their jacket to block the glow, and photographed the blood, the stone, the trail direction. Then they marked the location in their notebook by feel, writing badly in the dark.

12:46 — blood trace on rear trail, approx 90m from cabin.

They hesitated, then added:

Likely source injured before/after cache.

The word likely disgusted them. Too soft. Too careful.

They moved on.

The trail descended toward the dry creek bed. The air changed before Noor saw it. Colder. Wetter. The ground dipped, and the pine needles gave way to loose shale that shifted underfoot.

Noor heard water.

Not much. Just a thin trickle where the map had said dry.

They stopped at the edge of the creek bed and lowered themselves behind a fallen log.

Below, the shallow gully cut through the trees like a scar. Pale stones lined the bottom. A narrow stream threaded between them, catching what little moonlight reached through the branches.

And near the far bank, partly hidden beneath a tarp weighted with rocks, was something rectangular.

Not a body.

Noor’s first thought was not relief.

Their first thought was trap.

They stayed behind the log and watched the tarp for a full minute. Nothing moved. No visible wire. No blinking device. No breath steaming in the cold.

Then, from farther downstream, came a faint metallic click.

Noor went still.

Not natural.

Not animal.

A lighter? A gun part? A carabiner against a belt?

They lowered themselves completely behind the log, cheek nearly against wet moss. Their heart punched hard enough to hurt.

A beam of light appeared between trees downstream.

Not aimed high. Not searching broadly. Hooded, careful, kept low to the ground.

Someone else was in the creek bed.

Noor did not move.

The light swept over stones, paused near a boot print, then shifted away. Whoever held it was moving slowly upstream, toward the tarp.

Toward Noor.

Noor’s fingers tightened around the screwdriver until their knuckles ached.

They could retreat.

They could let whoever it was reach the tarp first.

They could survive and maybe lose the last piece.

Noor closed their eyes for half a second.

Publish the chain, not the story.

They opened them.

Then they did the only thing that made sense and terrified them at the same time.

They took the cracked GPS tracker from the go-bag, thumbed the dead casing, and threw it hard downslope to their left.

It struck rock with a plastic clatter, bounced once, and skidded through leaves.

The flashlight beam snapped toward the sound.

A man’s silhouette turned sharply downstream.

Noor moved.

They slid over the log, keeping low, boots skidding in shale as they crossed the creek bed at an angle. Cold water splashed over one ankle. They did not stop. The tarp was six yards away. Four. Two.

Behind them, the beam swung back.

Noor dropped beside the tarp and shoved the weighted rocks away with both hands. One crushed their finger. Pain flashed white and immediate, but they bit it down.

Under the tarp was not a body.

It was a metal lockbox, green military surplus, mud-smeared and dented. A strip of duct tape ran across the top.

Written on it in black marker:

N — IF YOU’RE HERE, HARLAN WAS TOO CLOSE.

Noor’s blood turned to ice.

A voice downstream called out, low and male.

"Don’t move."

Noor moved.

They grabbed the lockbox by its handle. It was heavier than expected, and the weight nearly pulled it from their grip. They did not try to open it. Opening things was for people with time.

The flashlight beam caught the edge of their shoulder.

Noor threw themselves sideways into the creek bed as something cracked through the trees.

A gunshot this time.

No maybe.

Stone chipped near their left hand.

Noor scrambled on elbows and knees, dragging the lockbox, shale tearing at their palms. Another shot split the night, louder, closer, the sound punching through the gully and rolling up into the trees.

They reached the far bank and crawled behind a boulder just as the flashlight beam cut over where they had been.

Their breath came in small, ugly bursts.

Noor pressed their back to the cold rock and forced themselves to think.

Shooter downstream. Unknown distance. Light source moving. Maybe one person, maybe more. Noor had the box. Cabin behind and uphill. Logging track east. Road south compromised. Harlan too close.

They touched the memory card under their watch strap.

Still there.

They touched the map in their jacket.

Still there.

They touched the envelope of photos in the go-bag.

Still there.

Good.

Alive and carrying the chain.

That counted.

For now.

The beam swept the creek again.

Noor looked up the far bank. Steep. Root-tangled. Possible.

They shoved the screwdriver through the lockbox handle to keep it from swinging, then looped the go-bag strap around it and hauled. The added weight dragged brutally at their shoulder.

Noor climbed.

Dirt broke under their boots. Roots tore free in their hands. Once, they slipped back almost a full body length and swallowed a cry as their shin struck stone.

Below, the man cursed.

Closer now.

Noor reached the top of the bank and rolled into wet leaves. For half a second, they lay there staring at the black lattice of branches overhead.

Then they heard movement below.

They got up.

Noor ran east, not back toward the cabin.

Not toward comfort. Not toward the road. Toward the old logging track marked on the map.

Branches whipped their face. The lockbox slammed against their thigh with every step. Their lungs burned. Their injured finger throbbed hot and stupid in the cold.

Behind them, the flashlight beam appeared and vanished through the trees.

The man was following.

Noor cut right around a stand of firs, then dropped abruptly behind a rotting stump. They clamped one hand over their mouth and forced their breathing down.

The pursuer crashed past ten yards away.

Too fast. Too confident.

Local, Noor thought.

Or law enforcement.

Or both.

They waited until the footsteps moved ahead, then backed silently away in the opposite direction, one step at a time, placing each boot with care.

Their body wanted speed.

Their brain chose quiet.

After thirty feet, they turned north and found the logging track by accident more than sight. The ground widened, flattened. Old tire ruts lay under grass and pine duff. No vehicles had come this way recently, but it gave Noor a direction.

They checked the map again under the smallest possible sliver of flashlight.

The logging track curved behind the cabin, then met an old fire road two miles north.

Two miles.

Noor almost laughed.

Instead, they knelt in the mud and set the lockbox down.

No time to carry dead weight without knowing why.

They wedged the screwdriver under the latch and pried. The latch held. Noor tried again, harder. Metal bent with a sharp pop that sounded much too loud.

They froze.

No movement nearby.

Again.

The latch snapped.

Inside the lockbox were three items packed in oilcloth:

A second burner phone.

A flash drive sealed in wax.

And a pistol.

Noor stared at the gun.

They hated guns. Hated how quickly a room changed around one. Hated the false authority of them. Hated that fear made them look like answers.

They picked it up anyway.

It was compact, matte black, heavier than expected. A note was wrapped around the grip with a rubber band.

Noor unfolded it.

Noor,  
Phone has one number preloaded. Not police. Not press. Use only if you have the notebook and photos.  
Drive has full chain. Names, payments, transfer logs, disposal orders.  
If Harlan finds this first, I am dead.  
If you find it first, I might still not be.  
— S.

At the bottom, in rushed handwriting:

They took me toward the quarry.

Noor read the last line twice.

The quarry.

They pulled out the map.

There it was, barely marked in gray beyond the fire road. An abandoned granite quarry north of the creek bed.

Three miles from the cabin.

Noor looked back through the trees in the direction of the safehouse. The cabin was invisible from here, swallowed by forest and dark.

Then they looked north.

Fear said leave.

The story said publish.

The note said might still not be.

Noor packed the flash drive and phone into separate pockets. The gun they checked with clumsy but careful hands, remembering an afternoon years ago at a range with a photographer who had insisted every conflict reporter should know the basics. Magazine seated. Safety. Finger away from trigger. Always.

They did not feel safer.

They felt implicated.

Noor shut the broken lockbox and shoved it under a pile of brush beside the track. Too heavy to take. The essentials were already on them.

Then they started moving north.

Not running now.

Hunting pace.

A journalist’s pace, if journalism had teeth: observe, record, survive, decide.

At 1:03 AM, Noor stopped beneath a dead cedar, took out the second burner phone, and powered it on.

One bar appeared.

Then vanished.

Then returned.

Noor held their breath.

The contacts list contained one entry.

CHAIN.

They selected it.

Their thumb hovered over call.

For once, Noor did not hesitate long.

They pressed it and lifted the phone to their ear, eyes fixed on the black road of trees ahead.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, grab my phone, and open a game. I can't believe Noor is still going on about this.* "Whatever," *I mumble, not really paying attention.* "Just wake me up when you're done."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor held the burner phone so tightly the plastic creaked.

For three rings, there was nothing but dead air and the faint hiss of bad signal.

On the fourth, someone answered.

No greeting.

No name.

Just a woman’s voice, low and alert. “Chain.”

Noor closed their eyes for half a second.

“S sent me,” Noor said. “I have the notebook and photos.”

A pause.

Then, “Proof.”

Noor looked into the trees ahead, then down at the mud-dark track beneath their boots.

“Marek Voss at the roadside pullout,” Noor said. “Deputy Harlan in a sheriff’s department jacket. Partial plate eight-five-seven. Cache under the cabin floor. Second cache near the creek. Note says they took him toward the quarry.”

Silence.

Not doubt.

Recognition.

The woman exhaled once, sharply. “Where are you?”

“North of the cabin. Old logging track. Moving toward the fire road.”

“Is Harlan with you?”

“No.”

“Is anyone with you?”

Noor glanced back into the dark behind them. Their throat tightened.

“No,” they said. “Not anymore.”

Another pause. Then the woman said, “Listen carefully. Do not go to the quarry.”

Noor’s jaw set.

“That’s where they took him.”

“That’s where they want the rest of the evidence to go missing.”

“He wrote it after the rest of the note. Different pressure. Different angle. He was rushed.”

“You’re a journalist, not a rescue team.”

Noor almost laughed, but there was no humor left in them.

“I’m the only person with the chain.”

“Exactly. Which means you are not expendable.”

Noor kept walking, slower now, phone pressed to their ear, pistol heavy and alien in their jacket pocket. The flash drive felt like a live coal in the other.

“What’s your name?” Noor asked.

“No.”

“Then what do I call you?”

“Relay.”

That fit. Anonymous. Functional. Someone S trusted enough to preload but not enough to identify.

Noor stepped over a fallen branch and crouched beside an old stump when the track opened too wide ahead. They watched the tree line for movement before continuing.

“Relay,” Noor said, “the upload failed at the cabin. Authentication interrupted. Was that on your end?”

“No. If you attempted the dead drop and it failed that way, someone was in the channel.”

Noor’s stomach sank.

“They were watching the route.”

“They may have been watching more than that.”

Noor stopped moving.

Above the trees, clouds dragged across a thin moon. The logging track ahead silvered for two seconds, just enough to show tire ruts, wet stones, and the dark wall of forest beyond.

No headlights.

No voices.

But somewhere far behind them, a dog barked once.

Then again.

Noor turned their head slowly.

Relay heard the silence change.

“What was that?”

“Dog,” Noor said.

“How far?”

“Hard to tell. South. Maybe near the cabin.”

“Then Harlan isn’t alone.”

Noor shut their eyes and breathed through their nose.

Of course he wasn’t.

One deputy with a flashlight had been too simple. Too merciful.

Relay said, “You need to get off the track.”

“I need signal.”

“You need distance first.”

Noor looked down at the mud. Their own footprints were plain in the old tire rut.

“Damn it.”

They backed into the trees, stepping on exposed roots and stone where they could. After six careful paces, they swept pine needles over the clearest prints with the side of one boot, then broke a low branch and dragged it lightly across the track behind them.

Not enough to fool a tracker for long.

Enough to buy minutes.

Maybe.

“Talk,” Noor said. “Fast.”

Relay’s voice sharpened. “The flash drive should contain a directory marked LEDGER. Is it intact?”

“I haven’t opened it.”

“Don’t, unless you’re air-gapped. It may have a beacon.”

Noor’s hand twitched toward the pocket containing the wax-sealed drive.

S had known enough to seal it physically.

Maybe not enough to make it safe.

“Notebook?” Relay asked.

“Still sealed.”

“Keep it that way. Photos?”

“With me.”

“Memory card?”

Noor touched the watch strap.

“One full copy. One partial hidden in the cabin chimney. Original encrypted drive with me.”

“Good. Better than good.” Relay’s voice softened for the first time, barely. “S chose well.”

Noor hated how much that almost broke them.

They pushed deeper through the trees, angling away from the logging track. Wet branches slapped their sleeves. Mud sucked at their boots. Every instinct wanted speed, but speed made noise.

“S may still be alive,” Noor said.

“If they took him to the quarry, they needed something from him.”

“Or they needed a place to put him.”

“Yes.”

Noor swallowed hard.

Relay did not spare them. Noor appreciated that, in a grim way.

“What’s north of the quarry?” Noor asked.

“Old service road. Locked gate. Cell coverage improves near the ridge above it. If you can reach that ridge, I can get you a secure transfer window.”

“And S?”

“If he is alive, the best thing you can do for him is make him valuable alive.”

Noor understood immediately.

Publish enough to make killing him costly.

Not everything. Not yet.

The chain, not the story.

Noor crouched behind a cluster of young firs and pulled the notebook from their bag. They did not open the freezer bag. Instead, they photographed the first visible page through the plastic with the compact camera, shielding the tiny screen under their jacket.

Click.

A list of names.

Some crossed out.

Some circled.

Their source had marked a chain of custody in human beings.

Noor zoomed in on the camera preview just long enough to confirm three names.

Voss.

Harlan.

Deputy Minister Oren Vale.

There it was.

The spine.

Noor’s mouth went dry.

“Oren Vale is in the notebook,” Noor said.

Relay went silent.

Too silent.

Noor’s pulse kicked. “You knew.”

“I suspected.”

“No. That pause was not suspicion.”

Relay said nothing.

Noor’s voice dropped. “What was S to you?”

Another silence.

Then Relay said, “My brother.”

The forest seemed to tilt slightly.

Noor pressed one hand against the fir trunk beside them.

For a moment, every file, every timestamp, every marked map point became a person again. Not a source. Not an asset. Not a key to a story.

A brother.

A man by an open trunk, hand raised defensively.

A man who had hidden evidence under a floor and still found time to warn Noor not to look on the road.

Noor closed the notebook away.

“What’s his name?” they asked.

Relay’s breath caught faintly over the line.

“You don’t know?”

“He wouldn’t tell me.”

“That was like him.”

Noor waited.

Relay said, “Samir.”

Noor repeated it silently.

Samir.

Not S.

Not source.

Samir.

Another dog bark sounded behind them, closer this time.

Noor’s head snapped up.

Relay said, “Move.”

Noor moved.

They cut northwest now, abandoning the track entirely. The map came out only twice, each time under a sliver of covered light. The ridge above the quarry rose ahead, steep and black against the clouded sky. If Noor climbed high enough, they could see down without entering the bowl.

Observe.

Record.

Survive.

Decide.

They climbed hard for seven minutes. Roots became handholds. Rock scraped their palms raw. Their crushed finger pulsed with each heartbeat. The pistol knocked against their ribs, an accusation with weight.

Below and behind, voices carried through the trees.

Not words.

Men.

At least two.

A dog gave a sharper bark, excited now.

Noor dropped flat behind a mossy outcrop and rolled into a shallow depression between stones. They pulled the go-bag tight against their chest and covered the phone with their body to muffle any glow.

The burner still showed one bar.

Barely.

Relay whispered, “Status.”

“Pursuit behind. Dogs. Two or more men. I’m climbing ridge west of quarry.”

“Can you transmit from there?”

“Maybe.”

“Do not use the flash drive yet. Send photos of the notebook page, Voss, Harlan, and the transfer order if you have it.”

Noor breathed once, twice.

“The transfer order is on the laptop copy. Laptop is with me, but powering it on here risks light.”

“Then use the camera images.”

Noor stopped.

The chain-of-custody photos.

Click. Click. Click.

They had photographed the scanned document on the laptop screen before shutting down.

Not perfect. Maybe blurry. Maybe enough.

“Good,” Noor whispered. “I have images.”

“Send them to this number. Compressed is fine. Metadata intact if possible.”

“If intercepted?”

“Then we both have a problem.”

Noor almost smiled. Almost.

They pulled the compact camera’s memory card, slotted it into a tiny reader attached to the burner phone, and waited while the device stuttered, lagged, and finally recognized storage.

The voices below grew clearer.

A man called something Noor could not make out.

The dog barked again.

Closer.

Noor selected six images.

Notebook page.

Photo of Voss.

Photo of Harlan.

Photo of plate fragment.

Photo of map with X.

Photo of transfer order on laptop screen.

Their thumb hovered over send.

The signal dropped.

No bars.

Noor stared at the dead indicator.

“No,” they breathed. “No, not now.”

Relay’s voice crackled faintly. “Noor?”

The call broke into static.

Then died.

Noor held the phone in front of their face, willing it to resurrect.

Nothing.

Below, branches snapped.

The dog had found the lower slope.

Noor shoved the phone into their pocket and climbed.

Not quietly now.

Fast.

They went straight up the ridge, using both hands, boots skidding in wet earth. Twice they nearly fell. Once a stone came loose under their foot and rattled downhill, loud enough to betray their position.

A flashlight beam speared through the trees below.

“There!”

Noor did not look back.

A shot cracked upward.

The bullet hit wood somewhere to their right with a flat, vicious thunk.

Noor climbed harder.

The ridge leveled suddenly beneath their hands. They hauled themselves over the lip and rolled onto cold grass, gasping. For three seconds they could not move.

Then the phone in their pocket buzzed.

One bar.

Noor dragged it out with shaking fingers.

The call was gone, but the message queue remained open.

Six images attached.

Not sent.

Noor raised the phone above their head.

One bar flickered to two.

They hit send.

The first image crawled forward.

Ten percent.

Twenty-three.

Below, the flashlight beams spread out at the base of the ridge.

The dog barked madly now.

Second image uploading.

Noor got to their knees and looked over the ridge.

The quarry opened below on the far side, a vast black pit cut into the mountain. Rusted equipment sat like dead insects near the rim. A gravel road curled down into the bowl. At the bottom, near an old maintenance shed, two vehicles were parked with lights off.

One gray sedan.

One sheriff’s department SUV.

Noor lifted the camera and zoomed.

There.

Beside the shed.

A man tied to a chair, head bowed.

Alive or posed to look alive.

Noor’s throat closed.

“Samir,” they whispered.

The third image sent.

Fourth.

A beam of light swung up from the quarry floor.

Someone down there had seen movement on the ridge.

Noor ducked back, heart hammering.

The fifth image stalled at sixty-eight percent.

“No,” Noor said. “Come on.”

Voices rose below from the pursuit side.

The men behind were nearly at the top.

The men in the quarry were waking.

Noor had found the center of the trap.

And, finally, the chain was leaving her hands.

Fifth image sent.

Sixth image uploading.

Twenty percent.

Thirty.

Forty.

A man’s voice came from the slope behind, close enough now to understand.

“Drop the bag, Noor.”

Harlan.

Noor went very still.

He knew their name.

Of course he knew their name.

The sixth image reached seventy-nine percent.

Noor slid the pistol from their pocket and held it low, both hands around it the way they half-remembered. Their finger stayed outside the trigger guard.

She hated that her hands knew enough to stop shaking.

Harlan stepped onto the ridge twenty yards away, flashlight angled down, pistol raised.

Noor did not stand.

Did not speak.

Did not give him the clean target he wanted.

The phone buzzed once in her other hand.

Message sent.

A second later, a new text appeared from Relay.

RECEIVED. PUBLISHING INSURANCE NOW. GET OUT IF YOU CAN.

Noor let out one breath.

Then she smiled without warmth.

Harlan’s flashlight found her face.

“Noor,” he said from the dark. “This can still end quietly.”

Noor lifted the burner phone just enough for him to see the screen glow.

“It already didn’t,” she said.

Then she threw the phone as hard as she could over the quarry edge.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *My eyes snap open. I realize I must have drifted off. I sit up, rubbing my eyes.* "What was that? Did I hear a shot?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The phone vanished over the edge, its pale screen tumbling end over end into the quarry dark.

Harlan’s flashlight followed it by reflex.

Noor moved before it hit.

They dropped flat, rolled hard across the wet grass, and fired once at the light.

The pistol cracked in their hands like the night splitting open.

The shot went wild by inches, but it was enough. Harlan flinched back, and the flashlight beam jerked skyward, slicing uselessly through the trees. His answering shot tore through the grass where Noor had been a heartbeat earlier.

Noor did not wait to see if he recovered.

They scrambled along the ridge on hands and knees, keeping low, the go-bag dragging against their ribs. The quarry opened beside them, a black drop to stone and rusted machinery below. From the pit, men shouted. One voice called Harlan’s name.

Good.

Let them know the chain had broken loose.

Let them panic.

Noor reached a cluster of boulders near the old service road and shoved themselves behind it just as another beam swept over the ridge. Their chest heaved. Their crushed finger throbbed so badly their vision pulsed around the edges.

Below, the burner phone struck rock with a bright plastic crack.

Someone shouted, “She threw something!”

Another voice: “Get it!”

For three seconds, every light in the quarry tilted downward.

Noor used them.

They rose and ran.

Not toward the cabin. Not toward Driver. Not toward the road Harlan expected.

North.

Toward the locked service gate and the ridge Relay had mentioned.

Behind them, Harlan yelled, “Noor!”

They did not look back.

The dog barked from the slope, frantic and close. Noor heard claws scrabble against stone, then a handler cursing as loose shale gave way. The ridge was steep enough to slow them. Not stop them. Nothing stopped people like Harlan for long.

Noor cut into the trees beside the service road, avoiding the pale gravel where their silhouette would show. Branches whipped their face. One tore skin near their cheekbone, warm blood slicking cold almost instantly.

Their lungs burned.

Their legs shook.

They kept going.

After fifty yards, the service road bent around a granite outcrop. Noor ducked behind it and crouched, one hand pressed to their mouth to quiet the wreckage of their breathing.

From the quarry below came the faint squawk of a radio.

Then another.

Then Harlan’s voice, closer than Noor liked.

“Find them. Bag, camera, all of it.”

Noor’s eyes narrowed.

Not kill them.

Find them.

Relay had moved fast.

The insurance had already changed the price of murder.

Noor slid the pistol back into their jacket pocket with shaking care. Then they pulled out their main phone, still wrapped in foil.

They hated using it.

They hated needing it more.

Noor unwrapped the phone, powered it on, and immediately turned the brightness all the way down. Signal flickered.

One bar.

Noor opened the secure app they had not trusted for weeks and drafted a message to three people: their editor, a lawyer in Berlin, and a colleague who owed them a favor from a massacre investigation neither of them talked about anymore.

They typed with numb thumbs.

SAMIR ALIVE AT ABANDONED QUARRY NORTH OF SAFEHOUSE.  
Harlan compromised. Voss chain confirmed. Oren Vale in notebook.  
Relay has first packet. If I miss check-in, publish everything.  
Do not contact local police.

They attached nothing yet.

Too slow.

Text first. Attachments if there was time.

They hit send.

The spinner turned.

Noor stared at it, willing the signal to hold.

Behind them, a branch snapped.

Noor killed the screen and dropped lower behind the rock.

A flashlight beam skimmed the service road.

Harlan stepped into view thirty yards away, moving carefully now, pistol raised in both hands. His face was pale in the reflected light, jaw clenched, eyes searching.

He was alone for the moment.

Noor stayed absolutely still.

Their phone vibrated once against their palm.

Message sent.

Noor closed their eyes for the briefest instant.

Then Harlan’s radio crackled.

A voice came through, thin but clear in the mountain air. “Deputy, we’ve got movement online. Vale’s office is calling. What the hell did she send?”

Harlan froze.

Noor saw the calculation happen in him.

The story was no longer in the woods.

It was outside.

It had teeth now.

Harlan turned his head slightly toward the radio.

Noor rose from behind the rock and aimed the compact camera.

Click.

The flash was off, but the tiny sound was enough.

Harlan spun.

Noor was already moving.

They ran straight across the service road, no more hiding, no more careful footprints. A bullet snapped past and struck granite ahead of them, spraying sharp dust across their neck. Noor stumbled but did not fall.

The locked gate appeared through the trees: rusted chain, sagging metal bars, a warning sign bleached nearly white.

Beyond it, the road dropped toward darker forest.

Noor did not have time to climb the gate.

They went under.

They dropped to their stomach and shoved the go-bag through first, then wriggled beneath the lowest bar. Rust scraped their jacket. Gravel tore at their palms. For one horrible second the bag strap caught.

Noor yanked.

It held.

Footsteps pounded behind them.

Noor twisted, reached back, and cut the strap free with the jagged edge of the broken screwdriver still wedged in an outer pocket. The go-bag lurched loose.

They rolled through the gap just as Harlan reached the gate.

He grabbed the bars and aimed through them.

Noor fired first.

Not at him.

At the padlock.

The shot sparked off metal and did nothing useful except make Harlan jerk back. Noor used that half-second to get up and run downhill.

Their phone vibrated again.

Then again.

Noor did not check it.

The road curved sharply, and the quarry lights vanished behind the ridge. Darkness swallowed them, thick and complete.

They ran until their legs nearly failed.

Only then did Noor leave the road, stumble into a stand of pines, and collapse behind a fallen trunk. They pressed their forehead to the wet bark and listened.

No immediate footsteps.

No dog yet.

No engine.

Noor dragged air into their lungs in silent, painful pulls. Their hands shook so violently that it took three tries to unlock the phone.

Two messages waited.

From their editor:

WHAT THE HELL IS HAPPENING. SEND LOCATION.

From Relay:

INSURANCE LIVE. SAMIR STILL MATTERS. GET TO COVER. EXTRACTION COORDS INCOMING.

Noor stared at the words until they blurred.

Samir still matters.

Alive, then.

Or alive enough to bargain over.

Noor wiped blood from their cheek with the back of their wrist and opened the camera files. The newest photo showed Harlan at the service road, gun raised, radio on his shoulder, face visible in profile.

Good.

They sent it to Relay.

Then they sent their location pin to the editor with one line:

If I disappear, publish without me.

Noor powered the screen off and pressed their back against the fallen trunk.

For the first time since leaving the cabin, they let themselves feel the cold.

It came all at once. Teeth, hands, spine. Their injured finger had swollen stiff. Their ankle was wet from the creek. Their knees felt split open beneath their jeans.

But the chain was out.

Not complete.

Not safe.

Out.

Somewhere behind them, far up the ridge, Harlan shouted orders into the dark.

Noor opened their eyes.

They still had the notebook. The photos. The memory card. The wax-sealed drive. The original encrypted drive. The pistol they hated. The story that could get them killed.

And now, maybe, enough leverage to keep Samir breathing until morning.

Noor pushed themselves up onto one knee.

They checked the map again with the faintest sliver of phone light.

Extraction coordinates would come. Harlan would adapt. Relay would publish just enough. Vale would deny everything. Voss would run. Samir was still in the quarry.

Noor folded the map and slid it back into their jacket.

“Not done,” they whispered.

Then they got moving again.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I blink, trying to shake the sleep from my head. I look at the dark cabin, then at the empty doorway. Did Noor just... leave?* "Noor? Hello?" *I call out, a little louder this time, then sit up fully, a knot forming in my stomach.*

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
By then, Noor was too far into the trees to hear anything from the cabin.

They had stopped thinking of the safehouse as shelter. It was a coordinate now. A compromised point on a map. A place where a source had bled, hidden evidence, and left warnings under pine boards.

Noor moved downhill through wet black forest, one hand out ahead of them, the other curled around the strap of the go-bag. Every few seconds, they stopped and listened.

Wind.

Branches.

Their own breath.

Far behind them, faint and intermittent, men’s voices rose from the ridge near the quarry. Once, a dog barked again, furious and confused.

Noor kept going.

The phone vibrated in their pocket.

They dropped behind a cedar stump before checking it, shielding the screen under their jacket.

Relay:

EXTRACTION NOT SAFE YET. HARLAN RADIO TRAFFIC ACTIVE.  
MOVE TO OLD FIRE LOOKOUT. GRID ATTACHED.  
HIGH GROUND. BETTER SIGNAL. 38 MIN ON FOOT IF UNINJURED.

Noor looked at their swollen finger, their scraped palms, the blood stiffening cold on their cheek.

“Optimistic,” they whispered.

A second message came through.

SAMIR CONFIRMED ALIVE 01:11. THEY KNOW INSURANCE EXISTS. THAT BUYS TIME, NOT MUCH.

Noor closed their eyes.

Alive.

The word nearly took their knees out.

They forced themselves to save the grid coordinate offline, then powered the screen down again. The lookout was northeast, above the old fire road. Higher ground. Better signal. Worse exposure.

They unfolded the map and found it by touch first, then by the smallest sliver of light.

Fire lookout.

Quarry below.

Service road curling north.

Ridge line like a broken spine.

Noor marked the route with their thumbnail. Not the road. Never the road. A drainage cut ran parallel for half a mile, then climbed through a stand of spruce toward the tower.

Harder.

Quieter.

They folded the map away.

“Okay,” Noor said under their breath. “High ground.”

They started moving again.

Five minutes later, they found the drainage cut.

It was narrow, choked with stones, half-filled with leaf rot and a thread of runoff from the night’s damp. Noor stepped into it anyway. Cold water soaked through their other boot almost immediately.

Good.

Let the dog work for it.

They followed the shallow runnel uphill, using stones where they could, letting the water break their trail where they could not. Their ankle protested with every step. Their shoulder burned from the weight of the bag. Every item inside it had become heavier now that Noor understood what each one cost.

Notebook.

Photos.

Original drive.

Wax-sealed flash drive.

Camera.

Gun.

Names enough to break ministries open if Noor lived long enough to transmit them properly.

At 1:19 AM, they stopped beneath a fallen spruce and crouched in the water, breathing through their mouth.

The forest behind them had changed.

No voices now.

No obvious pursuit.

That was worse.

Noor pulled out the compact camera and checked battery. Forty-one percent. Enough. They switched it to silent review, then photographed the notebook page again through the freezer bag, closer this time. Then the photos of Voss and Harlan. Then the handwritten note from Samir.

If Harlan finds this first, I am dead.  
If you find it first, I might still not be.

Noor stared at the line.

“Still not be,” they murmured.

Not alive.

Not safe.

Just not dead.

That was the language of someone negotiating with disaster in advance.

Noor packed the note away and opened their phone again.

One bar.

They created a new message to their editor and Relay both.

SECOND PACKET READY. CONTENTS: SAMIR NOTE, NOTEBOOK PAGE, VOSS/HARLAN PHOTOS. ORIGINALS WITH ME. FULL DRIVE NOT OPENED. POSSIBLE BEACON.

They attached four compressed images.

The first sent.

The second stalled.

Noor lifted the phone higher, arm shaking.

The second sent.

The third failed.

“Come on,” Noor breathed.

A branch cracked somewhere above the drainage cut.

Noor killed the screen instantly and lowered themselves into the mud.

A light appeared through trees on the slope above.

Not sweeping randomly.

Searching downward.

Someone had guessed the drainage.

Noor did not move.

The light paused on the water below them. It slid over stones, roots, slick leaves. It passed three feet from Noor’s boot and kept going.

A man’s voice called from farther off, muffled by trees.

Noor could not make out the words.

The light turned away.

Noor waited until the dark had been empty for a full count of thirty.

Then they backed down the drainage cut on hands and knees, slow enough that the water covered the sound. Ten feet. Twenty. Thirty.

At a bend, they slipped sideways beneath a low tangle of mountain laurel and crawled through wet leaves until the drainage vanished behind them.

Only then did they stand.

Their route to the lookout was no longer clean.

Fine.

No clean routes left.

Noor angled east, away from the searching light, climbing through thicker brush. Thorn branches caught their jacket and hair. Once, the go-bag snagged so hard it nearly pulled them backward. Noor stopped, freed it carefully, and tied the torn strap shorter across their body.

Their phone vibrated again.

They ignored it until they reached a cluster of granite slabs that gave them cover and a view downslope.

Then they checked.

Relay:

RECEIVED 2/4. SEND REST FROM LOOKOUT. DO NOT OPEN FULL DRIVE.  
VALE OFFICE REQUESTED INJUNCTION AGAINST “FABRICATED NATIONAL SECURITY MATERIAL.” THEY’RE MOVING FAST.

Noor’s mouth twisted.

“Too fast,” they said.

An innocent office did not draft injunction language before dawn.

Another message arrived from their editor.

I HAVE COUNSEL AWAKE. I HAVE TWO MIRRORS READY. SEND ANYTHING THAT MAKES THIS SURVIVE YOU.

Noor read that twice.

Anything that makes this survive you.

There was a comfort in being known by people who did not lie prettily.

Noor turned off the screen and climbed.

The fire lookout appeared twenty minutes later as a darker shape above dark trees.

It stood on four timber legs at the top of a rocky rise, old and skeletal, with a boxy cabin perched above the forest. The stairs zigzagged up one side. Half the railing was missing. A rusted sign hung from one post, creaking faintly in the wind.

Noor stopped at the tree line.

Too exposed.

Too useful.

Which meant Harlan might expect it.

They circled wide first.

Slow.

Careful.

They found old tire tracks near the base, but not fresh ones. Beer cans under a log, long rusted. A flattened place in the grass where deer had bedded down. No cigarette butts. No fresh boot prints visible in the thin moonlight.

Still, Noor did not trust it.

They took out the camera, zoomed toward the lookout windows, and scanned.

Empty.

Maybe.

They picked up a stone and threw it underhand toward the base of the stairs.

It struck wood with a dull knock.

Nothing moved.

Noor waited.

Still nothing.

They crossed the open ground in a low run and climbed the stairs as fast as the rotting boards allowed. Halfway up, one step sagged under their weight with a long, soft groan. Noor froze, gripping the rail.

No collapse.

No shout.

They continued.

At the top, the lookout door hung crooked on one hinge. Noor slipped inside and crouched immediately beneath the window line.

The small room smelled of mouse droppings, old rain, and dry wood. A broken chair lay in one corner. Someone had carved initials into the wall years ago. Glass was missing from two windows, leaving black rectangles open to the mountain air.

Noor stayed low and moved to the far side, where the wall faced away from the quarry.

Then they turned the phone on.

Two bars.

For one second, Noor simply stared.

Then they worked.

They sent the failed images again.

Samir note.

Voss photograph.

Harlan photograph.

Notebook page.

Map.

Photo of the transfer order on the laptop screen.

Harlan at the service road with gun raised.

Each upload crawled like an animal dragging itself through wire.

Noor kept the phone near the broken window, screen dimmed to almost nothing, one hand cupped around it.

Below, the forest shifted in wind.

Or movement.

Noor did not look until the sixth image sent.

Then they checked.

All delivered.

A message from Relay came immediately.

GOT THEM. INSURANCE UPDATED. VALE NAMED IN SEALED PACKAGE. PUBLIC TEASER GOES LIVE IN 4 MINUTES.

Noor exhaled, shaking.

Four minutes.

Four minutes until this became harder to bury.

Four minutes until everyone named in Samir’s chain knew Noor had not only run with the evidence but had started feeding it to the world.

Four minutes until Harlan became more dangerous or less.

Noor did not know which.

They took the wax-sealed flash drive from their pocket and held it in their palm.

Full chain.

Names, payments, transfer logs, disposal orders.

Maybe beaconed.

Maybe poisoned.

Maybe the only complete spine of the whole machine.

They did not open it.

Instead, they photographed it from all sides, including the wax seal. Then they wrapped it in a page torn from their notebook and wrote across it:

RECOVERED FROM SECOND CACHE — 01:02 AM — UNOPENED DUE POSSIBLE BEACON.

They placed it back in an inside pocket, against their ribs.

Next came the original encrypted drive. Same documentation. Same timestamp. Same chain note.

The journalist part of Noor, the old disciplined part under all the fear, kept working.

Record the object.

Record the context.

Record the risk.

Survive long enough for someone else to verify.

A glow appeared far below, through trees to the south.

Then another.

Flashlights.

Not at the base of the tower yet.

But moving.

Noor crouched lower.

The phone buzzed.

Editor:

TEASER SCHEDULED. LEGAL READY. NEED YOUR VOICE IF POSSIBLE. 30 SEC AUDIO. SAY CHAIN IS AUTHENTIC, IN YOUR POSSESSION, LOCAL LAW COMPROMISED.

Noor stared at it.

Their voice.

Not just files. Not just images. A living witness.

They pressed record.

For half a second, nothing came out.

Then Noor spoke quietly, clearly, every word placed like evidence on a table.

“This was recorded at approximately 1:47 AM. This was Noor Rahman. They had recovered documentary evidence from two caches left by Samir, a source connected to the Vale procurement investigation. Evidence included photographs linking Marek Voss and Deputy Harlan to Samir’s abduction, a notebook naming Oren Vale, and digital storage described by Samir as the full chain: payments, transfer logs, and disposal orders. Local law enforcement was compromised. If Noor Rahman disappeared, the materials already transmitted should be treated as authentic and published in full after verification.”

They stopped.

Their hand shook.

They sent the audio before they could reconsider.

Below, one flashlight angled upward.

Noor backed away from the window.

A message from Relay appeared.

PUBLIC TEASER LIVE.

Noor opened the link despite themselves.

The page loaded slowly.

Then there it was.

Noor’s publication logo.

A headline, careful but sharp enough to draw blood:

EVIDENCE LINKS SENIOR OFFICIALS TO SECRET DETENTION TRANSFERS; LOCAL DEPUTY IMPLICATED IN SOURCE ABDUCTION

No full dump.

Not yet.

Enough.

Names withheld pending verification, except Harlan’s title and Voss’s corporate connection hinted through description. Enough for lawyers. Enough for rivals. Enough for every newsroom in the capital to smell smoke.

Noor’s eyes burned.

They had wanted this story for months.

They had not wanted it like this.

A shout came from below.

Someone had seen the tower.

Noor pocketed the phone and moved to the opposite window. The lookout had a narrow emergency ladder down the rear leg, half-hidden by shadow. Rusted. Old. Better than the stairs now watched from below.

They slung the go-bag tight, checked that the notebook and drives were secure, and took the pistol out only because there was nowhere left to put fear.

Footsteps hit the first stair.

Wood creaked.

Noor climbed through the rear window.

Cold air slammed into them. The ladder was bolted to the outside of the tower, slick with moss and rain. Noor lowered one boot onto the top rung.

It shifted.

They gripped the window frame until splinters drove into their palm.

Another stair creaked inside.

A man below called, “Tower!”

Noor descended.

One rung.

Two.

Three.

The fourth snapped under their weight.

Their foot dropped into empty air.

Noor caught the side rail with both hands, shoulder wrenching so hard white pain burst behind their eyes. The pistol slipped from their pocket and vanished into the dark below without a sound Noor could track.

Fine.

Good riddance.

They found another rung with their toe and kept going.

Above them, the lookout door banged open.

A flashlight beam cut across the interior.

Noor dropped the last eight feet.

They hit the ground badly, rolled, and bit back a cry as their ankle twisted under them. For a second, the forest went bright at the edges.

Then a beam swung out over the rear side of the tower.

Noor dragged themselves behind one of the timber supports.

The light passed over empty grass.

A voice above said, “They were here.”

Noor pressed their hand over their mouth.

Their phone vibrated again.

Loud as thunder in their pocket.

The flashlight froze.

Noor did not breathe.

The vibration stopped.

A second later, from somewhere south of the tower, another phone began ringing — Harlan’s, maybe, or one of his men.

The beam jerked away.

Noor moved.

They crawled first, then forced themselves upright once the trees closed around them. Their ankle screamed. They ignored it badly, limping through ferns and deadfall, angling down the north slope away from the tower.

Only when the lookout was fully hidden behind trees did they check the message.

Relay:

EXTRACTION CHANGED. TOO HOT.  
FOLLOW NORTH SLOPE TO POWER CUT. WHITE VAN, NO LIGHTS, 12 MINUTES.  
PASSWORD: “THE CHAIN CAN’T.”  
IF MISSED, GO TO GROUND AND KEEP SIGNAL OFF.

Noor swallowed.

Twelve minutes.

Their ankle laughed at the idea.

Behind them, men shouted near the tower.

Noor put the phone away.

They broke a branch from a young ash tree, stripped the smaller twigs with shaking hands, and used it as a cane. It was ridiculous. It worked.

Step.

Pain.

Step.

Pain.

Move anyway.

At the edge of the north slope, the forest opened into a power cut: a long raw corridor beneath high transmission lines, silvered faintly by cloud-thin moonlight. The wires hummed overhead, low and constant, like the mountain itself was thinking.

At the far side, barely visible between brush and service gravel, sat a white van with no lights.

Noor stopped in the tree line.

A van was not safety.

A van was a question.

They took out the compact camera and zoomed.

No plates visible from this angle. Driver-side mirror cracked. Mud along the lower panels. No one standing outside.

The phone buzzed once.

Relay:

TWO MINUTES. MOVE OR DON’T. YOUR CALL.

Noor almost smiled.

At least someone understood consent under pressure.

They scanned the power cut again.

Behind them: Harlan, dogs, the quarry, Samir alive but captive.

Ahead: unknown van, unknown extraction, evidence still warm from Noor’s hands.

Noor touched the memory card under their watch strap.

Then the notebook.

Then the drives.

Then the spot where the pistol had been and was not.

They stepped out of the trees.

Halfway across the cut, a light flared behind them.

A shout followed.

“Noor!”

Harlan again.

Closer than he had any right to be.

Noor did not turn.

They ran the last stretch on their ruined ankle, each step tearing a sound from their throat they refused to let become a scream.

The van’s side door slid open.

Dark inside.

A figure within said, “Password.”

Noor reached the door, one hand on the frame, breath ragged, face wet with sweat and blood and cold.

“The chain can’t,” they said.

The figure moved aside.

Noor climbed in.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor climbed into the van and immediately dropped low, back against the metal wall, one hand clamped around the go-bag as if someone might still tear it away.

The side door slid shut.

Darkness folded in.

For one half-second, Noor’s body believed it had been trapped.

Then a dim red interior light clicked on, barely enough to show shapes: shelves bolted to the walls, medical kits, a plastic crate full of cables, two people in dark jackets, neither of them wearing badges.

A woman crouched opposite Noor, one hand braced against the floor as the van lurched into motion.

Relay.

Noor knew it before she spoke.

Relay looked older than her voice. Early forties, maybe. Tired in the same permanent way Samir had sounded on bad calls. Her hair was pulled back tight. Her eyes went first to Noor’s face, then their hands, then the bag.

“Do you have it?”

Noor’s breath came in torn pieces.

“Yes.”

“Notebook?”

“Yes.”

“Photos?”

“Yes.”

“Drives?”

“Yes.”

Relay’s face changed.

Not relief.

Something more dangerous than relief.

Hope.

The van bounced hard over ruts. Noor slammed a shoulder into the wall and swallowed a curse. Outside, somewhere behind them, faint shouts cut through the trees, then fell away beneath the growl of the engine.

Relay reached for Noor’s ankle.

Noor flinched violently and pulled back.

Relay stopped at once, palms open.

“Medical,” she said. “Only medical.”

Noor stared at her for another second, then forced their leg forward.

Their boot was wet, muddy, and dark around the cuff. Relay cut the laces instead of trying to untie them. Noor watched her hands. Steady. Efficient. No wasted sympathy.

Good.

Sympathy would have finished them.

The second person in the van, a narrow-faced man with a headset, leaned toward the cab partition and said, “We have pursuit lights south ridge. Two vehicles. Maybe three.”

Relay did not look up.

“Route B.”

The van turned sharply enough that Noor’s stomach dropped.

Relay peeled the boot away.

Pain flared so bright Noor nearly blacked out. They grabbed the edge of a bolted shelf and held on until the red-lit interior steadied again.

“Sprain at least,” Relay said. “Maybe fracture.”

“Later,” Noor managed.

Relay’s mouth tightened, but she nodded.

“Later.”

Noor dragged the go-bag into their lap. Their fingers fumbled on the buckles. Relay saw the tremor and did not offer to help.

Another point in her favor.

Noor opened the bag themselves.

First, the freezer-bagged notebook.

Then the envelope of photographs.

Then the original encrypted drive.

Then the wax-sealed flash drive from the lockbox.

Then the compact camera.

Then the cracked GPS tracker marked 857.

They laid each item on the van floor between them.

The red light made everything look like evidence from a crime scene because it was.

Relay stared at the notebook.

For a moment, she stopped being Relay.

She became Samir’s sister.

Her hand hovered over the plastic bag but did not touch it.

Noor said quietly, “He wrote carefully. Even at the end.”

Relay swallowed once.

“He always did.”

The van accelerated.

Branches scraped the sides with a shriek that made Noor reach automatically for the pistol that was no longer there. Their hand found only an empty pocket.

Relay noticed.

“You had a weapon?”

“Lost it at the tower.”

“Good.”

Noor looked at her.

Relay’s expression did not change. “If Harlan died tonight, they would make this about a fugitive journalist murdering a deputy. They still may try. But it will be harder.”

Noor leaned their head back against the van wall and closed their eyes.

“They shot at me first.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t. Not yet.”

Relay reached into her jacket and produced a small recorder.

Noor opened their eyes.

Relay set it on the floor between them and clicked it on.

“Then tell me.”  
“Chain of custody. Incident record. While you can still remember sequence.”

Noor almost laughed.

It came out as a broken breath.

“You really are Samir’s sister.”

Relay’s face moved slightly.

“He used to say the same thing about me when I ruined dinner by asking follow-up questions.”

The van hit another turn. The narrow-faced man braced himself and checked a tablet mounted to the wall.

“Two units behind, no lights now,” he said. “They’re trying to stay off road.”

Relay looked at Noor.

“Start at the cabin.”

So Noor did.

They spoke into the recorder with their eyes half-closed, voice rough but clear enough.

“Approximately 12:17 AM, source failed to arrive. Phone records showed burner ping east tower at 20:52. Encrypted drive mounted. Files indicated disposal orders, transfer documentation, and photographic evidence. Text instruction said to look under the floor.”

They paused and forced air into their lungs.

“Under the table rug, one floorboard had newer screws. Cache contained document tube, damaged GPS tracker marked 857, map, photographs, freezer-bagged notebook. Photographs showed Samir at roadside pullout with Marek Voss and Deputy Harlan present.”

Relay’s hand closed slowly into a fist.

Noor continued.

“Second cache located by map near dry creek bed. Pursued by armed man, later identified by voice and sight as Harlan. Lockbox contained burner phone, wax-sealed flash drive, pistol, and handwritten note stating Samir was taken toward quarry.”

The man with the headset glanced back at the mention of the quarry but said nothing.

Noor’s voice thinned.

“Visual confirmation from ridge: quarry contained gray sedan, sheriff’s department SUV, maintenance shed. A man tied to a chair was visible beside shed. Believed to be Samir. Alive status uncertain at time of observation.”

Relay’s eyes shone in the red light.

Noor did not soften the record.

“Evidence transmitted to Relay and editorial contacts from ridge and fire lookout. Public teaser went live before extraction. Harlan pursued armed. Harlan was photographed with firearm raised. Local law enforcement compromised.”

They stopped.

The recorder kept running.

The van’s engine filled the silence.

Relay clicked the recorder off.

“Good,” she said.

Noor looked at the notebook again.

“Not good.”

“No,” Relay said. “But usable.”

The narrow-faced man said, “Roadblock possible ahead. County frequency just mentioned a stolen white utility van.”

Noor’s head lifted.

Relay’s expression went flat.

“Of course they did.”

The van slowed.

Noor shifted, biting down against the pain in their ankle. “How far to wherever we’re going?”

“Too far if they keep the roads,” Relay said.

“Then don’t keep the roads.”

Relay looked at them.

Noor reached for the map with a shaking hand and unfolded it across their knees. Their finger tracked the power cut, the service road, the north spur.

“There,” Noor said. “Old maintenance access. It intersects with the rail grade.”

The headset man leaned closer. “That grade’s washed out.”

“For cars,” Noor said. “Not for foot.”

Relay’s gaze sharpened.

Noor tapped the map again. “If Harlan reports a stolen van, they’re waiting for a van. We leave it where they can find it. Make them think we bailed south toward the highway. Then we go east on the grade.”

“With your ankle?”

Noor looked up.

“With the evidence.”

Relay held their stare.

Then she turned toward the cab.

“Pull off at the next culvert. Kill lights before the bend.”

The van went dark except for the red interior glow.

Noor began repacking the evidence, but not all in one place now. The notebook went inside their jacket. The wax-sealed drive went into a medical glove, knotted twice, then into Relay’s boot. The original encrypted drive went back to Noor. The photographs were split: half with Noor, half with Relay. The memory card stayed under Noor’s watch strap.

Relay watched that last hiding place.

“Smart.”

“Paranoid.”

“Tonight, same thing.”

The van rolled to a stop.

Noor listened.

No sirens.

No immediate engines.

Just the tick of cooling metal and the high electric hum of distant transmission lines.

The side door opened onto black brush and the concrete mouth of a culvert beneath the road.

Cold air poured in.

Noor grabbed the shelf and tried to stand.

Their ankle failed.

Relay caught them under one arm before they hit the floor.

Noor hated needing it.

They accepted it anyway.

“Samir,” Noor said through clenched teeth. “If the teaser bought time, what happens next?”

Relay helped them down from the van.

“Next, Vale’s people try to discredit everything. Harlan tries to recover originals. Voss tries to leave the country. Samir stays alive only as long as he is useful.”

Noor landed on one foot in wet gravel and nearly folded.

Relay held firm.

“And us?” Noor asked.

Relay looked toward the black line of the rail grade beyond the culvert.

“We make him more useful alive than dead.”

Noor nodded once.

Rain began to fall, fine and cold, ticking softly on leaves, metal, and stone.

Behind them, the white van sat abandoned at an angle near the culvert, its door open, a decoy already becoming part of the night.

Noor adjusted the go-bag higher on their shoulder.

Their face had gone gray with pain, but their eyes stayed clear.

“Then we keep moving,” they said.

And they did.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stare at the empty doorway for a long moment, then slowly get up. I walk to the door, peering out into the darkness.* "Noor? This isn't funny." *I shiver, the cold mountain air hitting me.* "Where did you go?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor was nowhere near the cabin anymore.

They were under the old rail grade, shoulder wedged against wet stone, trying not to make a sound while headlights moved slowly across the road above.

Relay crouched beside them in the culvert, one hand gripping Noor’s jacket to keep them from slipping in the runoff. The narrow-faced man had gone ahead thirty yards to check the washout, leaving them in the dark throat of the concrete tunnel with rainwater sliding around their boots.

Above, an engine idled.

Not close enough to see.

Close enough to feel in the ribs.

Noor held their breath and counted.

One vehicle.

Maybe two.

A radio crackled faintly through the rain.

“…white van located near mile marker twelve. No visual on suspects.”

Relay’s face, barely visible in the dark, turned toward Noor.

Noor’s jaw tightened.

Suspects.

There it was.

The story changing shape in real time.

Not journalist. Not witness. Not target.

Suspect.

Noor reached slowly into their inside pocket and touched the sealed notebook beneath their jacket. Still there. Dry enough. Then the encrypted drive in the inner lining of the go-bag. Then the memory card under their watch strap.

Still there.

The headlights above swept once across the culvert mouth. Noor and Relay pressed flat against the wall.

Water soaked through Noor’s jeans. Their ankle pulsed with hot, nauseating pain. Their crushed finger had gone stiff and useless, curled half-shut against their palm.

Noor did not move.

The radio above crackled again.

“Harlan says they’re armed.”

Relay’s expression hardened.

Noor closed their eyes for one second.

Of course he had said that.

The pistol was gone in the dark under the lookout tower, but the lie had already arrived ahead of them.

Relay leaned close, mouth near Noor’s ear.

“Do not answer anything if they call out.”

Noor gave the smallest nod.

Above them, a car door opened.

Rain hissed on leaves.

Bootsteps moved across gravel.

One person. Heavy. Slow.

A flashlight beam sliced into the culvert from the far end, weak by the time it reached them, broken by the curve of concrete and the shimmer of runoff.

Noor lowered one hand into the cold water and closed their fingers around a smooth stone.

Not a weapon.

A distraction.

A last resort.

The bootsteps stopped above.

Someone spat.

Then a man said, “They didn’t go through there. Water would show tracks.”

Noor stared at the thin current running over their boots.

Relay’s hand tightened once on their sleeve.

Another voice, farther back, said, “Check it anyway.”

The flashlight beam brightened.

Noor’s heart slammed once, hard.

Relay reached into her jacket.

Noor caught her wrist.

Relay looked at them.

Noor shook their head.

No shooting. No escalation. Not unless there was no other breath left.

For one suspended moment, Relay resisted.

Then she let her hand ease away from whatever she had been reaching for.

Noor turned their head toward the culvert wall. Near their shoulder, rainwater dripped through a crack in the concrete, steady and rhythmic. Above that crack, a rusted drainage grate opened into a narrow ditch beside the road.
