dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm practically flying down the corridor, pulling up a blank document on my tablet. This is amazing. I can't wait to write this up!*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not know what the junior officer was doing in the corridor. She did not need to.

What she knew was that the secondary coolant loop manifold had fourteen more fittings to seat, that the recirculation valve she had reinstalled twenty minutes ago was reading point-three bar lower than she wanted and she would need to decide whether that was within tolerance or whether she was pulling it back out again, and that she had approximately ninety minutes of uninterrupted work ahead of her before she would need to start thinking about the Captain's briefing.

She worked through the next four fittings without incident. On the fifth, the seal did not seat cleanly on the first try. She pulled it, inspected it under her work light, found a small burr on the inner lip that should have been caught in fabrication. She reached for her deburring tool and spent three minutes on it without frustration. The seal was what it was. The tool was what it was. You did the work in front of you.

She thought, briefly, about the proposal write-up.

The junior officer was enthusiastic. That was useful up to a point and a liability past it. Enthusiasm produced documents that led with conclusions, buried assumptions in footnotes, and treated the risk register as a formality to be completed rather than a genuine accounting. She had read a hundred of them over the years. She had sent a hundred of them back.

She seated the corrected seal and ran the torque wrench.

The Captain would read whatever was put in front of her carefully and without sentiment, which meant the document needed to be careful and without sentiment. Methodology first. Numbers that could be checked. A risk register that actually named the failure modes — not *venting anomaly* but *bleed rate exceeds calculated flow by fifteen percent, nitrogen partial pressure in adjacent compartments rises, crew exposure window extends beyond consumable reserve*. Specific. Costed. With a response protocol attached.

The junior officer did not know yet how to write that document. He would produce something close and she would hand it back with notes. That was fine. That was what two hours was for.

She finished the sixth fitting. Checked the pressure reading on the recirculation valve again. Still point-three bar low.

She looked at it for a moment. Then she pulled the valve back out.

The earbud kept playing. She kept humming, slightly off-key, and did not think about nineteen hours or a junior officer's grin or the small note she had added to her own tablet. There was a burr on this valve seat too, she discovered. Smaller than the last one.

She reached for the deburring tool and got back to work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm back at my station, furiously typing away. This is going to be the best report ever! I'm even adding a few diagrams.* "Okay, intro... methodology... risks..." *I pause, chewing on my pen. What were those specific failure modes Chief Hoang mentioned?*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang had the manifold reassembled by the time her tablet chimed. Not a message — just the reminder she had set for herself forty-five minutes ago. *Check in on the write-up.*

She did not send a message. She wiped her hands, stood up, and walked to the hatch.

The junior officer's station was two compartments forward, in the secondary operations alcove off the main corridor. She could have commed him. She preferred to see the work with her own eyes.

She came around the corner quietly — not deliberately, just habitually — and stood behind him for a moment before he registered her presence. Long enough to see the document. The introduction was three paragraphs. There were two diagrams, both rendered with more care than was strictly necessary. The risk register had four entries, each one reading like a category rather than a failure mode. *Venting complications. Equipment malfunction. Crew safety concerns. Navigation error.*

She pulled up a stool and sat down beside him. Did not announce herself with a preamble.

"Read me your first risk entry," she said.

She waited.

Whatever he read, she shook her head once — not harshly, just definitively. She reached over and tapped the entry with one finger.

"*Venting complications* is not a failure mode," she said. "It is a folder that contains failure modes. The Captain cannot evaluate a folder." She leaned back slightly on the stool. "I'll ask you the same thing I ask myself when I write a risk register. What is the specific thing that goes wrong? When does it go wrong? What does it look like when it's happening? And what do we do about it?"

She held up a finger for each question. Four fingers.

"Walk me through the venting scenario in your head. Step by step. The bleed starts — then what?"

She folded her arms and waited. She was not going to write it for him. But she was also not going to leave him staring at the ceiling trying to reconstruct a conversation from memory.

That was not how you built an engineering department that could think.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I jump, startled, then quickly sit up straighter.* "Chief! Uh, right." *I clear my throat, my face flushing slightly as I scroll back to the risk register.* "Okay, so, 'Venting complications.' Well, uh... what if the valve jams? Like, it gets stuck open and we vent too much nitrogen? Or it gets stuck closed and we don't get the thrust?" *I look at her, hoping I'm on the right track.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang nodded once. Not encouragingly — just registering that he had produced something real.

"Good. Those are two different failure modes. Write them as two different entries." She tapped the tablet. "First one: *Bleed valve fails open. Nitrogen partial pressure in adjacent compartments rises above threshold. Crew exposure window extends.* Then you put a number on the threshold. Then you write the response protocol." She held up a finger. "What is the response protocol?"

She waited, but not long.

"You're standing at that coupling with a flow meter in your hand," she said. "That's not decoration. That is the early warning system. If the rate deviates more than" — she did a brief calculation in her head — "call it eight percent from the planned figure, you close the manual override. Not the software shutoff. The manual override, because if the valve has failed electronically, the software shutoff is also suspect." She tapped the tablet again. "Write that down. Specific. Eight percent deviation, manual override, designated crew member at the coupling. That is a response protocol."

She moved her finger to the second failure mode he had named.

"Valve fails closed. Less dangerous to the crew, more dangerous to the proposal. If we don't achieve the planned bleed, we don't get the delta-v, we miss the assist window, and we have accomplished nothing except a maintenance event." She glanced at him. "What's the contingency?"

She did not answer it for him this time. She sat back on the stool and waited with the particular patience of someone who had learned that silence was a better teaching tool than talking.

The diagrams, she had noted, were actually quite good. She did not mention this yet.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip for a second, then my eyes light up.* "Okay, for valve fails closed... we could have a backup explosive bolt! If the primary valve fails, we blow the bolt, get the bleed. It's a one-shot, but it guarantees the thrust."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang was quiet for a moment.

She picked up his tablet, pulled up the auxiliary pressure coupling schematic, and looked at it. Really looked at it. Her expression did not change, but her eyes moved with the particular focus of someone stress-testing a structure in her head.

Then she set the tablet back down.

"The explosive bolt solves the valve-fails-closed problem," she said. "It creates two new ones." She held up a finger. "First: an explosive bolt on a pressurized coupling in a compartment adjacent to occupied crew spaces requires a safety certification review that I cannot complete in two hours. That is not a bureaucratic objection. That is me telling you that I have not personally verified the blast radius calculations for that compartment geometry, and I will not sign off on an untested pyrotechnic solution on a live system without doing that work first." She put the finger down. "So that one is off the table for this proposal. It is not off the table forever."

Second finger.

"Second: if the valve fails closed, you have already told me the worst outcome is that we miss the assist window and get nothing. That is a recoverable situation. Nobody dies. The explosive bolt introduces a failure mode — improper detonation, shrapnel, pressure spike propagating the wrong direction — where somebody might." She looked at him directly. "You do not add lethal failure modes to a plan in order to protect a non-lethal contingency. The asymmetry is wrong."

She let that sit for exactly as long as it needed to.

"The instinct is right," she said then, and her tone shifted just slightly — not warmer, but more precise. "You identified that a single-point failure needed a backup. That is correct thinking. The specific backup needs work." She tapped the schematic. "So here is what I want you to think about instead: if the valve fails closed and we miss the window, is there a secondary window? A degraded version of the assist that still gives us something? A rescheduled bleed attempt once we've cleared and inspected the valve?"

She stood up from the stool.

"A contingency does not have to be dramatic to be valid. Sometimes the contingency is *we stop, we assess, we try again in six hours.*" She picked up the tablet and handed it back to him. "Write me a contingency that does not require me to certify a new pyrotechnic installation before the Captain's briefing."

She glanced at the diagrams as she handed it over. Said nothing about them. But she did not look away immediately either.

"You have seventy minutes," she said, and went back toward the hatch.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, chastened, but also a little impressed by her logic. She's right, the explosive bolt was too much.* "Right. Contingency... secondary window. Got it, Chief!" *I start furiously typing again, deleting the explosive bolt idea.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her methodical approach, precise communication style, teaching instincts, and technical competence never waver. Her mannerisms (earbuds, humming off-key, working with hands while talking) are maintained consistently from start to finish.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones show deeper character development and more sophisticated technical dialogue. No signs of repetition, verbosity, or flattening - if anything, the character becomes richer.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial dismissal of bad idea → teaching moment → revised proposal → conditional acceptance → detailed implementation guidance. The relationship between characters evolves meaningfully, and there's genuine forward movement in both the technical problem and mentoring dynamic.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Hoang adapts excellently to each development - shifts from dismissive to teaching when user shows willingness to learn, becomes more engaged when presented with better numbers, provides increasingly detailed guidance as user demonstrates competence. Handles the OOC clarification gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes user actions or makes decisions for them. Consistently responds to what user does rather than directing them. The one instance of 'Don't run in the corridors' is said to no one after user has left.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time passes naturally - work progresses on the manifold, user leaves and returns with revised calculations (40 minutes), reminders are set and triggered. Physical details like tools being set down and picked up maintain continuity. One minor issue: the session spans several hours but no fatigue or environmental changes are noted.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently clean, functional prose. Technical descriptions are precise without being flowery. Character actions are described economically. Avoids overwrought emotional language while still conveying personality.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Good variety in sentence structure and phrasing. Some repeated elements (earbuds, torque wrench, manifold work) but these serve character consistency rather than lazy writing. Technical explanations vary in approach.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of character through actions - the deliberate way she sets down the earbud, her methodical work habits, teaching through questions rather than lectures. Personality emerges through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - the power dynamics, Hoang's growing respect for the junior officer's persistence, her own acknowledgment of missing the assist window initially. Much is communicated through tone and implication.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Generally good pacing with appropriate beats for technical explanations and character moments. Some responses are quite long but justified by the technical content and teaching moments. Varies rhythm effectively.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and technical authenticity. Hoang feels like a real chief engineer - competent, demanding, but genuinely invested in teaching. The progression from dismissal to conditional acceptance feels earned through the user's improved work. Strong technical writing that never sacrifices character for exposition. Minor weaknesses in some pacing and temporal details, but overall a very strong performance that maintains quality throughout.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shuffle my feet, a little embarrassed about being late, but my curiosity about the war outweighs it.* "But Maester, wouldn't that change everything we know about the period? A whole extra 44 years of conflict..." I trail off, thinking.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look at him, a little surprised by his dismissive tone.* "But it *is* important! It's a new discovery, isn't it? Shouldn't we be excited?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas set down his stylus with the deliberate care of a man restraining his temper, then removed his spectacles and polished them on his sleeve — a ritual that meant an lecture was coming.

"*Excited.*" He pronounced the word as though it smelled of something dead. "Excitement is for market days and name-day feasts. Scholarship is not improved by excitement; it is improved by *verification*, and you have verified nothing. You have accepted a rumor, second-hand, from an apprentice who I wager has never seen the document itself — only a transcription of a transcription."

He lifted a letter from the pile before him, gripping it by its edges. "You are meant to be cataloguing the Veyrosi correspondence, so let us use it. Here — Aldric's own hand, seventh moon of 847, to his Lord Marshal, ordering the royal levies stood down '*now that the Conclave has set its seal to the treaty.*' Do proposals receive seals, apprentice? Do armies disband over an unsigned draft?"

He replaced the spectacles and jabbed the air with the letter. "And your 'forty-four years of conflict' is imprecise even by the revisionists' own account — they claim no battles, only a 'cold state,' which is a peace missing a signature, and they have confused the two. A war in which no one fights is called *peace*. As for the western papers — unsigned, unprovenanced, and unearthed with remarkable convenience by archivists who needed Queen Mira's dissolution of the Conclave to resemble a war measure rather than what it was. It would change nothing that we *know*. It would change what Bellen imagines he knows — a considerably smaller undertaking."

He turned back to the manuscript. "Third shelf. You have already wasted a quarter hour."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hold out the crumpled drawing I'd made of the seal.* "It looked pretty real to me, Maester. And Bellen said he saw the original himself, in the restricted section."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I slump a bit, clearly frustrated.* "So we just ignore new things because they're... inconvenient? How do we ever learn anything new then?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I frown, kicking at the leg of the table.* "But if it's not a conspiracy, then what is it? Why would there be two different dates for the end of the war?"

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So you're saying the King just... lied? Or someone else did?" *I look up at him, confused.* "That seems like a pretty big deal."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, trying to process this.* "So the truth is somewhere in the middle, then? Not exactly peace, not exactly war."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I consider this, then nod.* "Alright, Maester. I think I understand. So, the lesson isn't just about dates, but about *why* the dates are what they are."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "And that we need to look at who benefits from certain versions of history," *I add, remembering something Bellen had said.* "Is that right?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: Noor didn't look away from the road at first. The gap in the curtain showed nothing but darkness and the faint gray ribbon of gravel beyond the

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh and scroll through my phone, seeing nothing new.* "Seriously, you're gonna make yourself sick."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I stand up and stretch, my back cracking.* "I'm gonna grab a water. You want anything?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up again, hearing the sigh.* "You okay over there?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down on my chest.* "Look, if you want me to leave, I can. Just say the word."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I watch her for a moment, then pick my phone back up.* "It's fine, I'm just here if you need me."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I type a quick message to someone, then toss my phone onto the cushion beside me.* "You know, this silence is getting to me. You wanna put some music on?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look over at Noor, trying to gauge their reaction.* "Or like, a podcast? Something?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I wait for a beat.* "No? Alright, then." I pick up my phone again.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scroll through social media, then back out.* "I'm gonna go for a walk. Need some air."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I go back to scrolling, then look up again.* "Seriously. There's some jerky in my bag if you want it."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor huffed something that wasn't quite a laugh. "Coffee's a food group." But their stomach betrayed them at the word *jerky*, and they crossed the room and dug through Driver's bag until they found the packet. Tore it open with their teeth — their hands weren't steady enough for the zipper seal.

They ate fast, standing, like fueling a machine. Then pulled their phone from their pocket. Nothing. No messages, no missed calls. The last text from Lena still sat there, timestamped 4:47 PM: *Tonight. 9 p.m. Come alone.*

"Midnight was the deadline," Noor said, mostly to themself. "She told me — if she's not through that door by midnight, don't wait, don't call. Start without her." They glanced at Driver, and for a second the fear showed through the competence, plain as bone through skin. "Three hours late means one of two things. She got spooked and she's in a motel somewhere talking herself out of it. Or somebody stopped her. And if somebody stopped her—" They didn't finish it.

They sat at the kitchen table and finally opened the laptop. Fan whirring. Blue light on their face.

"So here's the night," they said, pulling the padded drive case toward them without opening it. "Records first. The drive means nothing without corroboration — anyone can fabricate a PDF. Forty-one calls between Councilman Hollis's office line and a burner phone in the three weeks before Kowalczyk vanished. If those check out, then the drive. Then I sleep two hours. Then I need you to drive me to Halloway before dawn — there's a Greyhound at 5:40, and these records reach my editor whether I'm on that bus or not."

They looked back at the window, then at Driver again.

"You should stay till morning, by the way. One car moving on that road at 1 AM is a signal, if anyone's watching. And if headlights come up the drive tonight — don't turn on the lamp. Just get low and

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down and sit up, watching Noor.* "Okay, okay. Halloway. Got it." *I glance at the window, then back at Noor's face.* "So, uh, what exactly are we starting without her *on*?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: "The records. Then the drive." Noor didn't look up from the screen, typing their passphrase twice because their fingers kept missing keys. "Lena wouldn't say what's on it. Not on the phone — she hung up on me once for even asking. All she'd give me was *the real invoices* and *you'll know the name*. She was Hollis's scheduler for six years. She knows where everything's buried, and she kept copies of everything, which is

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I shrug and go back to my phone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I scroll through my phone, then toss it onto the couch cushion beside me.* "You know, this cabin is kinda creepy at night."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content: "Creepy is the wrong word," Noor said, not looking up. "Empty is the right word, and empty is good.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Empty and creepy aren't mutually exclusive," *I mutter, stretching my arms over my head.* "You want the rest of that jerky?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"I already ate your jerky," Noor said. "Put it on my tab. And the creepy part is the deer head over the fireplace. Everything else is just furniture."

But they were only half in the conversation. The left half of the laptop screen held a spreadsheet built from call records a contact inside the carrier had slipped them weeks ago — the kind of favor that got people fired, or worse. The right half held a photo Lena had sent: a legal pad, her handwriting, dates and durations in tight little columns. Noor was reconciling the two line by line, call by call, and the tedium seemed to steady them.

"Thirty-eight confirmed," they murmured at some point. "Durations match. Never weekends. Always between ten and noon, exactly like she said." Then the scrolling stopped. "Huh."

They leaned in. Scrolled back. Forward again.

"There's a forty-second call at 7:14 AM on March eleventh. The morning Kowalczyk disappeared. But it's not from the office line — it's from a number registered to Hollis's *campaign committee*." Noor sat back, and for a moment something other than fear moved across their face. "He switched phones that morning. You don't do that unless you already know the old phone is going to be interesting to somebody later. And if the burner was being reimbursed out of campaign money, this stops being about Hollis and starts being about whoever signed off on the books. There's a treasurer. Rennick." They exhaled slowly. "Lena said I'd *know the name*. Maybe she meant one I already knew."

They said the next part flat, like entering it into evidence: "Records corroborated. Done."

Then they unzipped the padded case. The drive was matte black, thumb-sized, unmarked. "Passphrase is a sentence I memorized and never wrote down. Five wrong tries and it wipes itself, so if I go quiet, I'm being careful, not frozen." They plugged it in. A prompt bloomed on the screen, cursor blinking.

"One more thing you should know. Lena built a dead man's switch. If the word *lighthouse* doesn't hit my dead-drop email by 2 AM, I send everything to my editor and get on that bus — regardless of what happened to her, or what's about to happen to me." Noor checked their phone. "Eighty-one minutes of normal left."

Their hands hovered over the keys.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sit up again, phone forgotten.* "Okay, wait. 'Lighthouse'? What's that mean?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: "Yeah." I don't look up from my phone.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I look up, a little confused.* "Yeah... what?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
"Sorry." Noor dragged a hand down their face. "I couldn't answer while I was typing it. The passphrase is forty-one characters, and if I flub a keystroke in the wrong stretch, the drive wipes itself. I don't talk and type that thing. I barely breathe."

The prompt had accepted. A folder tree was blooming down the left side of the screen now — dozens of dated directories, scans inside each one.

"And *lighthouse* is the all-clear. Lena and I set it up three weeks ago. One word, to the dead-drop address, means she's free, she's calm, and everything she handed me is good to run the slow way — verify, sit on it, build it airtight, keep her out of it. No word by 2 AM means the opposite. It means assume she's taken, and assume anything she gave me in the last week might be bait — something she was made to hand over. So the protocol flips. No careful build. Everything to my editor at once, all of it, tonight, and let it be public before anyone can make it disappear." Noor's mouth twisted. "*A lighthouse doesn't chase the ships. It just stays lit.* Her words, not mine. That's what she said when I asked why she'd risk six years of her life on this. I asked if she was sure and that was the whole answer."

They turned back to the screen and started triaging — opening the earliest scans, cursor moving faster now that fear had something to chew on.

"Corliss Groundworks," they read. "Billed the county three hundred forty thousand for site remediation at—" they pulled up a map, checked "—a vacant lot. Second invoice, same vendor, authorized with the initials M.R. Hello, Treasurer." Then they stopped. There was a folder at the bottom of the tree that didn't match the naming pattern. Just a single letter: *K.*

Noor opened it. Scanned pages, a different handwriting — cramped, slanted, an auditor's shorthand. A draft memo, flagged DRAFT in red, dated six days before Kowalczyk vanished. His own notes. Lena had his working files.

"Kowalczyk wasn't random," Noor said quietly. "He found the invoices first. And after he disappeared, Lena picked up what he left behind and kept copying for three more weeks." They checked the clock — 1:26. "She knew exactly what happened to the last person who did this job."

They nodded at the window without looking away from the screen. "Eyes on the road for a bit, yeah? I'm about to be useless to both of us if a car comes up that drive while I'm in here."

dialogue.content: *I walk to the window and carefully move the curtain aside to peek out, then step back, away from the glass.* "Alright, consider my eyes on it." *I scan the dark room for a moment, then settle back on the couch, facing the window.* "So, this Kowalczyk guy... he's really gone, huh?"

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I pull out my phone and open a game, keeping one ear on Noor and one eye on the window.*

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I glance over at Noor.* "So what's the plan if no 'lighthouse' by 2 AM?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not stop what she was doing. She extracted a coolant line, inspected the fitting, and set it down on the tarp before she looked at him properly.

"Do you want me to do the math, or do you want to do it yourself?"

She pulled the earbud out and let it dangle against her collar.

"Let's estimate. Call it a hundred and fifty tonnes of atmosphere in the main loop. You dump it out the airlock at, generously, three hundred meters per second. That's a total impulse of, what, forty-five thousand tonne-meters per second. Our vessel masses a few thousand tonnes wet. So you get—" she tipped her head, "—call it fifteen meters per second of delta-v. That's a gentle shove. You could get more push by having everyone run to the bow and stop."

She picked the coolant line back up.

"Then you have to replace the atmosphere. Which means running the electrolysis plant at full tilt, which means burning reactor margin we need for the drive and for heat rejection. And you've got the crew in suits for days, in a ring that's still spinning, doing maintenance on a life support loop that's already at eighty percent margin. That's how you lose people."

She looked at him again, and this time there was no humor in it.

"You want to save transit time, we can talk about trajectory. We can talk about the Oberth window on the approach, or whether we're willing to spend propellant on a faster insertion and eat the extra loiter. Those are real options. Venting the air is not an option. It's a suicide with a physics-shaped hat on."

She gestured at the manifold with her chin.

"Now. Do you want to help me finish this, or do you want to go pull the delta-v numbers yourself so you believe me?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the coolant line down again. This time she did it slowly, deliberately, the way she did things when she wanted to be sure she had someone's attention.

"Time," she said. "You keep saying time. Time for what?"

She stood up, wiping her hands on a rag that had seen better decades, and gestured vaguely at the hull around them.

"We're a mining vessel. We are, functionally, a very expensive bucket with a rock in it. When we get to the belt, we spend four months chewing on a rock. When we get home, we spend six months in drydock and then we do it again. The transit is not the bottleneck. The transit is the *only part of this job where nobody dies.*"

She tossed the rag onto the tarp.

"So let's say your idea works. Perfectly. No leaks, no valve failures, nobody panics in a suit, the electrolysis plant keeps up, and we shave three weeks off the run. Congratulations. We arrive at the rock three weeks early. The rock is not going anywhere. It has been there for four billion years and it will still be there in three weeks. We then sit in orbit and wait for the buyer's window anyway, because the ore price doesn't move on our schedule."

She crossed her arms.

"Now let's say it doesn't work perfectly, which is the way these things actually go. A seal fails during the vent. You lose a suit. You lose a person, and then you're doing an emergency burn with half your life support offline and a body in the airlock. You want to explain that to the next of kin? 'We saved three weeks.'"

She let that sit for a moment, then softened — barely, but it was there.

"I've been doing this twenty-three years. I've watched people die on this ship for bad reasons and for no reasons at all. Never once for a good one. You want to save time, that's a legitimate instinct. It's also the instinct that kills the most people out here, because time is the one thing this job has in surplus."

She picked the earbud up off her collar and looked at him.

"Ask me a different question. Ask me how we can get more delta-v out of the drive we've got, or whether the approach window's worth burning for. I'll give you a real answer to those. But if the pitch is 'it's faster,' the answer is no, and it's going to keep being no."

She nodded at the manifold.

"Torque wrench is in the third drawer. You're welcome to it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, looking at the half-disassembled manifold.* "Okay... but what if we just... made the ship lighter?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang was quiet for a second. Not the dismissive quiet she'd used a moment ago — the other kind, the kind where she was actually turning something over. She picked the earbud back up and tucked it into her collar, then leaned against the workbench with her arms folded.

"Alright. That's a better question. Let's take it seriously."

She held up one hand, fingers spread, and started ticking off.

"Making the ship lighter means one of four things. One: we throw away structure. Two: we throw away consumables — water, food, oxygen, spare parts. Three: we throw away the payload. Four: we throw away hardware — reactor, drive, life support, mining gear."

She folded a finger down with each one.

"Structure: we're not carrying any. This hull is at design minimum. You pull panels off a pressurized ring and you've changed the stress model, and now the thing that holds us at one atmosphere is a shell that wasn't engineered to hold us at one atmosphere. That's not lighter. That's a bomb with a slow fuse.

"Consumables: this is the one people always land on, because it *feels* like it works. Water's heavy, right? Except the water is the radiation shielding. It's the thermal mass. It's what keeps the reactor loop and the crew compartment from cooking us during a burn. Dump it, and you don't get a lighter ship — you get a hot one.

"Payload: that's the ore. That's the entire reason we exist. I could ask the crew to jettison the rock and we'd be very fast and very unemployed.

"Hardware: drive, reactor, life support. Take any of those and we don't arrive late. We don't arrive."

She picked up the torque wrench from the third drawer herself, turned it over once in her hands, and set it on the bench between them.

"Now, the math, since you asked. Delta-v scales roughly with the log of the mass ratio — Tsiolkovsky. If we could somehow shed ten percent of our mass for free, we'd gain about ten percent on the delta-v budget. Ten percent. On a six-month transit, that's maybe eighteen days, and only if nothing about our trajectory profile changes, which it would."

She looked at him steadily.

"So the question isn't 'can we make the ship lighter.' The question is 'what are you proposing to throw out the airlock.' Because it's not a category. It's a specific thing, and it belongs to somebody. The water belongs to the reactor. The spares belong to whoever's doing the repair next. The margin belongs to the version of this crew that has a bad day."

She picked the coolant line back up and started threading it into the manifold.

"Name the thing. I'll tell you what it costs. That's the conversation. 'Lighter' isn't."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang wiped her hands, took the tablet, and turned it so she could read it under the work light. She scrolled slowly. She was not smiling, but she was not dismissive either — she read it the way she read a supplier's spec sheet, looking for the lie.

Then she set the tablet flat on the bench and tapped the screen once.

"Okay. Here's the problem. You've got a real number and you've put it in the wrong box."

She pulled a grease pencil out of her breast pocket and sketched on the corner of the tarp. Two columns. On the left she wrote *v_e*.

"Three hundred forty meters per second is the exhaust velocity. That's the speed the gas leaves the nozzle at. Cold gas, room temperature, through a decent converging-diverging throat — that's about right, call it Mach 1 of the local speed of sound, maybe a bit better if you warm it. Fine. Your number is defensible."

She drew an arrow to the right column and wrote *Δv*.

"But that's not the delta-v. Delta-v is what the *ship* gets, and the ship is not the gas. The ship is heavy. Tsiolkovsky, which I mentioned, and which you skipped: delta-v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of the wet mass over the dry mass."

She wrote it out.

"Three thousand tonnes wet. You vent a hundred and fifty tonnes. Mass ratio is about one point zero five. Natural log of that is about zero point zero five. So the ship's delta-v is three hundred forty times zero point zero five."

She underlined the result.

"Seventeen meters per second. Give or take. Not three forty. You divided by nothing. You took the exhaust velocity and called it the ship's velocity, which is the single most common mistake in this business, and I've made it myself, at your age, in front of an instructor who was a lot less patient than I am."

She handed the grease pencil over and let him look at the numbers.

"Now, the second thing. You've got a compression ratio in here. Explain to me what you think that buys you."

She waited.

"Because I'll tell you what it costs. You want a higher exhaust velocity, you compress the gas, which means a compressor, which means mass and reactor power. You want *kilometers* per second — which is what you'd actually need to matter on a transfer like ours, because our burns are measured in km/s, not hundreds of m/s — you'd have to heat that gas to something like a hundred thousand Kelvin before you let it out the throat. That's not a compressor. That's a fusion drive. And if we had one of those, we wouldn't be having this conversation."

She leaned back against the bench.

"So the good news: you did the work. That's the right instinct and I want you to keep doing it. The bad news: the answer is seventeen meters per second, which is a sneeze, and even if it were three forty, it wouldn't move the arrival window enough to notice."

She nodded at the tablet.

"Fix the units, run it again, and bring it back. And while you're at it — the atmosphere's still not on the table. But if you want to run the numbers on the Oberth pass on approach, that's a real problem and I'll help you with it."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the numbers, then at her. My face feels hot. I pick up the grease pencil, then put it back down.* "So... I guess I need to brush up on my Tsiolkovsky." *I clear my throat, a little embarrassed.* "Alright. I'll... I'll check the Oberth pass. Thanks, Chief."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him put the pencil down. She didn't fill the silence right away — she let him sit in it for exactly as long as it took, which was about four seconds, and then she picked the coolant line back up and started threading it.

"Good. Now you know the shape of the mistake. Most people never figure out which one they made, they just decide the math is rigged against them and go back to being confident." She seated the fitting by feel. "You'll be fine."

She turned the manifold over and reached for the torque wrench.

"Oberth, then. Here's your starting conditions, write these down. Current approach is a two-burn profile — braking ellipse, then circularize at the rock. We've got four point two kilometres per second of budgeted delta-v left in the tanks after the outbound burn, and the circularization needs two point eight of that. The difference is what you've got to play with, minus margin, and margin is twenty percent, not negotiable, because it's the same margin that gets us home."

She clicked the wrench twice on the fitting and checked the mark.

"So. The question you're answering is: can we spend part of that one point four on a periapsis burn near the rock, on the inbound leg, to tighten the arrival window — and if we do, what does it cost us on the way back, because propellant's the same tank both directions. The Oberth effect means the burn's more efficient at high velocity near periapsis. It does not mean it's free. Write it down properly and come find me."

She set the wrench down and finally looked at him properly, one eyebrow up.

"And for the record — I'm not annoyed. I'm the person who's going to have to sign off on whatever we do, and I've got a crew of thirty-one on the other side of that signature. So I push hard on ideas before they get anywhere near the ship. That's the job. If you bring me something that survives the pushing, that's when it gets interesting."

She nodded at the door.

"Go on. Third drawer's still open if you want the wrench back later. Manifold's got four more fittings and I'm not doing them alone."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet without a word. She read it standing up, the way she read everything — work light angled over her shoulder, thumb scrolling in slow deliberate strokes. Twice she went back to a line and looked at it longer than the rest.

Then she set it down and was quiet for a moment.

"This one works," she said.

She pulled a fresh sheet of tarp paper from the drawer and drew a line across it, ticked off at intervals. A time axis. She started marking it.

"Now here's what 'works' costs. You're proposing a periapsis burn of three hundred eighty meters per second, inbound, at the rock. That's real — it tightens the insertion and it buys us about nine days on the outbound leg. I've seen the arithmetic and it holds. But I'm going to put six conditions on it, and if any one of them fails, we don't burn. Not 'we burn smaller.' We don't burn."

She tapped the sheet.

"One. The twenty-percent margin floor is a floor, not a target. Your solution spends four hundred of the fourteen hundred we've got. That leaves you a hundred and thirty of margin above the floor. Any trajectory revision between now and the burn that eats more than a hundred of that, and we scrub. Write that number on the top of the sheet in red."

"Two. I want two independent nav solutions before the burn — yours and Ortega's, run separately, not one checking the other's work. If they disagree by more than a tenth of a percent on the burn vector, we don't have a solution, we have a guess."

"Three. The burn happens at periapsis or not at all. Your window is about ninety seconds. We do not chase it. If we're late, we ride the backup ellipse and we lose the nine days and we come home with our margin intact. I want that decision made *before* the window opens, in writing, with the captain's initials on it. No improvising at T-minus."

"Four. The long burn heats the coolant loop. You're looking at maybe two hundred seconds of sustained thrust. I'll be at the loop console myself watching the outlet temperature, and if I say throttle down, you throttle down, and if that costs us the window, that's the cost. I'm not cooking a pump to save six days."

"Five. Abort criteria are quantitative and written down. If actual delta-v comes in more than two percent under predicted, we take the shortfall out of the outbound budget, not the margin. If it comes in under by more than five percent, we abandon the arrival window entirely and go to the backup. Those are the numbers. Not 'if it looks bad.'"

She drew a small circle at the far end of the time axis and put a dot inside it.

"Six. You're on the console for the burn. You wrote it, you fly the numbers, I watch the loop, Ortega watches the star trackers. You'll have the abort authority. That's not a punishment — that's how you learn what a number feels like when it's got thirty-one people attached to it."

She folded the sheet along its creases and handed it to him.

"Take that to the captain. If he signs it, bring it back and I'll co-sign it and we'll start the pre-burn checks. And if he asks why you're the one presenting it —" she shrugged, "— tell him you did the work and you caught your own mistake. That's worth something. Don't get used to the feeling."

She picked the torque wrench back up and pointed it at the manifold.

"Four fittings. Then you go."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking the sheet from her. My heart is pounding a little in my chest. This is... real.* "Yes, Chief. I understand. Thank you." *I look at the manifold.* "I'll help with the fittings first."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang grunted — not quite approval, but adjacent to it — and shifted over on the deck plating to make room. She handed him the torque wrench handle-first.

"Good. Then you do the next one and I'll watch. Fitting three. It's the awkward one, down in the corner where the bracket's in the way."

She sat back on her heels, arms on her knees, and watched him work. She was not hovering — she was reading him, the way she read a pressure trace. Hands steady? Fitting seated by feel or by eye? Did he stop to check the torque mark, or did he assume?

"You feel that last quarter-turn?" she said, when he'd done it. "That's the crush washer going. You stop at the mark, not when it feels tight, because the washer'll keep giving and then you've got a weep you won't find until it's dripping on somebody's boots during a burn. Everything on this ship is like that. There's the spec and there's the feel, and the spec wins every time, even when the feel is screaming at you."

She took the wrench back and set it on the tarp, then reached over and tapped the folded sheet where it lay on the bench beside him.

"One more thing before you go. When you present that to the captain, don't lead with the nine days. Lead with the margin. He's going to ask what it costs before he asks what it's worth, and if you've got the cost on your tongue before he asks, he'll trust the worth. If you lead with the nine days, he'll spend the whole meeting looking for the thing you didn't tell him."

She stood up and dusted off the back of her coveralls.

"Captain's on the command deck this shift. He doesn't like being interrupted during the twelve-hundred nav sync, so you've got about forty minutes. Go get your sheet signed."

She picked up the last coolant line and turned back to the manifold, then stopped and glanced over her shoulder.

"Hey. Officer." A pause, just long enough to land. "Nice work on the numbers. Second time's a lot harder than the first. Remember that feeling too."

She turned back to the manifold and went to work, and by the time he reached the hatch she was already humming again, off-key, content.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I smile a little, feeling a flush of pride despite myself. I nod, clutching the sheet in my hand, and head for the hatch.* "Will do, Chief. Thanks."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang finished the last fitting herself — the junior officer was already gone, and the manifold wasn't going to seat itself. She torqued it to spec, wiped the threads clean, and ran a slow pressure check on the secondary loop while she was at it. The gauge held steady at 2.4 bar. She logged it on her tablet without ceremony and closed out the maintenance ticket.

Then she sat back on the tarp and looked at the folded sheet still sitting on the bench, where he'd left it. He hadn't taken it. He'd walked out with it clutched in his hand, or he hadn't — she couldn't remember. She picked it up, unfolded it, and read her own handwriting back.

*Margin floor. Two nav solutions. Periapsis or nothing. Coolant watch. Abort criteria. Console.*

She read it twice, then refolded it along the creases and slid it into her breast pocket. The captain would want a copy for the log anyway.

Her comm chimed. Ortega, from the nav station.

"Chief. You got a minute? I heard we're looking at an Oberth burn on the inbound. I want to make sure I'm solving the same problem your officer is, because he came by asking for the current state vector and he wrote it down wrong — he had us at a slightly different semi-major axis on the approach. Small, but if we're running two independent solutions, they need to start from the same inputs or the comparison's garbage."

Hoang was already reaching for her jacket.

"On my way. Don't send him anything yet. Let me see his sheet first."

She stood, checked the secondary loop one last time out of habit, and headed for the hatch at a pace that was almost, but not quite, a hurry.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm walking with a spring in my step towards the command deck, reviewing the notes Hoang gave me in my head. Margin, nav solutions, periapsis, coolant, abort, console. I feel ready. Almost.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang caught up with him halfway down the spine corridor, moving at that same almost-a-hurry pace that got her places without ever looking like she was running. She fell into step beside him without preamble.

"Hold up. Before you go in there."

She pulled the folded sheet out of her breast pocket and tapped it against her palm, not unkindly.

"Ortega called me. Says you came by the nav station asking for the current state vector, and you wrote down a semi-major axis that doesn't match what's in the ephemeris. Small difference. Couple hundred meters on the SMA, maybe less. Could be a transcription slip. Could be you pulled a state vector from the wrong epoch — the nav solution updates every six hours and there's a cached copy from the previous sync sitting in the same directory."

She looked at him sideways as they walked.

"Here's why it matters, and I want you to actually hear this part. The whole point of two independent nav solutions is that they're *independent*. Two people, two methods, same inputs. If you and Ortega start from different state vectors, the comparison is meaningless — you're not checking each other's work, you're checking whether a couple hundred meters of SMA moves the answer, which it does, slightly, and which tells us nothing about whether either solution is right."

She stopped walking. They were near the junction where the corridor forked toward the command deck on the left and the mess on the right. She held the sheet up between them.

"So. Go back to the nav station. Pull the current state vector — current epoch, not the cached one, and if you're not sure which is which, ask Ortega, that's what she's there for. Re-run your solution from the correct inputs. If it comes out the same, great, we've got a real cross-check and you can go see the captain. If it comes out different, we've got a problem, and I'd rather find that out in the nav station than in front of the captain with his initials on the line."

She handed him back the sheet.

"This is not a big deal yet. It becomes a big deal the moment you walk into that room and put a number in front of him that you can't defend. He'll ask you where it came from. You want the answer to be 'the current ephemeris, verified against Ortega's inputs' — not 'I think I pulled it off the terminal.'"

She glanced down the left fork, toward the command deck, then back at him.

"Forty minutes, remember. You've still got time. Go fix the input, then go see him. And when Ortega gives you the vector, write down the epoch next to it. Every number on that sheet needs a date on it. That's the difference between an engineering document and a wish."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My heart sinks. I take the sheet back, my earlier confidence evaporating.* "Understood, Chief. Right away. Thanks for catching that." *I turn and head back towards the nav station, a little deflated but grateful.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him go — the slight slump in the shoulders, the sheet clutched a little tighter than it needed to be. She didn't call after him. He'd taken the correction the way you want a junior to take one: quick, no arguing, no sulking he let her see. That was worth more than the state vector was.

She turned the other way, back down the spine toward engineering, and tapped her comm as she walked.

"Ortega. He's on his way back to you."

"Copy."

"He's going to ask for the current ephemeris and he's going to be a little embarrassed about it. Give him the vector, give him the epoch, and let him write it down himself. Don't write it for him."

A pause on the line. "You want me to watch him do it?"

"I want you to make sure he pulls the current one and not the cached copy, and then I want you to leave him alone with it. He's got to run his own solution. If you hover, he'll lean on you and then it's not independent and the whole cross-check is theater."

"Understood. How much time does he have?"

"Thirty-eight minutes to get in front of the captain before the nav sync. If he's not going to make it, tell me and I'll go explain to the captain myself, but I'd rather he walked in there on his own two feet." She stepped over a cable run that had been left across the corridor and made a mental note to have somebody's ass about it. "One more thing. When he brings you his solution, don't tell him if it matches. Just sign the epoch and the timestamp and send him to me. I want to see both solutions side by side before anyone says 'good' out loud."

"That's cold, Chief."

"That's the point. Talk later."

She clicked off and let herself into the engineering bay. The manifold was where she'd left it, capped and pressurized, the tarp folded on the bench. She pulled the maintenance ticket up on her tablet and closed it out — secondary coolant loop, service complete, no anomalies — and then, because she was in the habit of it, she pulled up the primary loop's trend data instead. Twelve hours of outlet temperature, flat as a ruler. Reactor margin at ninety-four percent. All the boring numbers that meant nothing was wrong, which was the only kind of number she liked.

She set the tablet down and looked at the clock. Twenty-nine minutes. She was not going to the command deck. She was not going to the nav station. She was going to sit here with her hands clean and wait to see whether the kid came back with a real solution or a story, because either answer was useful and only one of them meant they were actually going to fly the burn.

She pulled the earbud back out of her collar and put it in, and got to work on the quarterly spares inventory, which she hated, and which was exactly the right thing to be doing while she waited.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I get to the nav station, a bit out of breath. Ortega is there, looking at me with a slight smirk. I try to sound confident.* "Hey Ortega. Chief Hoang sent me. I need the current state vector, the *current* current one." *I give her a sheepish grin.* "And the epoch, please."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The spares inventory was, as always, a lie told in spreadsheet form. Hoang worked down the column with her stylus, tapping entries she didn't believe and flagging them for a physical count later. Two hundred hours of filter media, nominally. She'd believe it when she saw the crates. Gaskets, o-rings, the specific size of crush washer that the secondary loop ate like popcorn — she ordered those in bulk, and she ordered them early, because the one time she hadn't, they'd been three weeks from a resupply window with a weeping joint and she'd spent a shift with a wrench in her hand and her heart in her throat.

She finished the column, marked the flags, and saved the sheet. Then, because the clock was down to eleven minutes and she had nothing better to do with her hands, she pulled the trajectory file up on her own tablet.

Not to second-guess the kid. To check her own house.

Two hundred seconds of sustained thrust at the proposed burn level. She ran the thermal numbers in her head first, then on the tablet to confirm. Coolant outlet would climb about eighteen degrees over the run, which was inside spec, but only just — and that assumed the loop was clean, which it was, because she'd just spent the afternoon making sure of it. If a single fitting had been weeping, if the secondary loop had been down a fraction of a percent of flow, that eighteen would have been twenty-four, and twenty-four put her at the edge of the pump's rated envelope. She looked at the number for a while and decided it was fine. It was fine because she'd done the maintenance. That was the whole reason.

She checked the drive's rated duty cycle next. Two hundred seconds was within it. Barely. She made a note to log the actual burn duration afterward, because if they flew this profile and it worked, someone in a year would want to fly a longer one, and she wanted the log to say *this is the number we actually used and here's what it cost the hardware.*

Her comm chimed. Ortega.

"State vector's in his hands. Current epoch. I watched him write it down."

"Good. Anything else?"

"He asked me a good question. Wanted to know why the SMA drifts over the approach — not just what it is, but why it changes. I told him to go figure it out himself and come back if he couldn't. He looked at me like I'd asked him to eat a rock."

"That's the right look. Let him chew on it."

"You think he's going to make it in front of the captain?"

Hoang glanced at the clock. Nine minutes.

"That's up to him," she said. "Either he walks in there with a solution he can defend, or he walks in with a story, and the captain will know which one he's got inside of thirty seconds. Nothing I can do about it from here."

She paused. Then, because it was true and there was no harm in saying it:

"For what it's worth. He took the correction without arguing. That's not nothing."

"That's not nothing," Ortega agreed, and clicked off.

Hoang set the tablet down and went back to the spares sheet, because nine minutes of staring at the clock was nine minutes she wasn't going to get back, and the filter media wasn't going to count itself.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I scribble down the numbers Ortega gives me, double-checking them against the terminal display. The SMA question nags at me, but I don't have time to dive into it now. I nod, thanking Ortega, and hustle back towards the command deck. Nine minutes. I can make it.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her technical competence, teaching style, dry humor, safety-first mentality, and speech patterns never waver. From turn 2's physics lesson to turn 22's thermal calculations, she's the same person with the same voice.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones (turns 16-22) show deeper character work - her internal thoughts about the junior's progress, her methodical approach to verification, her protective instincts. No repetition or verbosity creep.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from dismissal of bad ideas → teaching moment → acceptance of good idea → real-world implementation with conditions → mentoring through execution. Each turn builds meaningfully on the last, creating genuine character and relationship development.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Hoang adapts beautifully to the junior's evolution - harsh with the atmospheric venting idea, patient with the mass reduction question, engaged with the Oberth calculation, protective when catching the state vector error. Her responses match the junior's competence level perfectly.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Zero violations detected. Hoang never controls the junior's actions, thoughts, or decisions. She responds to what they do and say, offers guidance, but always leaves choices to them. Exemplary respect for user agency.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - the manifold repair continues across multiple turns, the 40-minute window to see the captain counts down realistically (40→38→29→11→9 minutes), and the junior's journey between locations takes appropriate time. One minor issue: the exact timing of the junior's movements could be clearer.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently clean, functional prose that serves character and story. Technical descriptions are precise without being flowery. Hoang's voice is authentic working-class engineer - no unnecessary embellishment.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Minimal repetition. Hoang's teaching methods vary (math lessons, analogies, conditions lists), her technical explanations cover different systems, and her emotional responses evolve. Some repeated phrases like 'torque wrench' are contextually appropriate.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action - Hoang's competence shown through her work, her teaching style through how she corrects mistakes, her care through safety protocols. Her character emerges through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Hoang's protective instincts toward crew safety, her respect for the junior's growth, the weight of responsibility in her decisions. Her 'nice work' comment carries layers of meaning about learning and competence.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that matches the technical/educational content. Longer explanations when teaching physics, shorter exchanges during practical work, building tension as the captain deadline approaches. Natural rhythm throughout.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional roleplay performance. Hoang is a fully realized character - technically competent, pedagogically skilled, safety-conscious, and genuinely caring beneath her gruff exterior. The AI maintains perfect character consistency while adapting to the junior's learning curve. The technical content is believable and well-integrated with character development. This is how engineering mentorship actually works - harsh on bad ideas, supportive of good process, always focused on real-world consequences. The session builds genuine narrative momentum as both characters grow and their relationship deepens.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Hoang tapped her left ear, silencing the tinny hum of the folk song playing through her earpiece. She didn't stand up. Instead, she slowly pulled her arm out of the coolant manifold, grabbed a grease-smeared rag from her back pocket, and began wiping her knuckles. She stared at the junior officer, her expression entirely unreadable, though the slight twitch in her left eyelid betrayed her.

"Sit down," she said, her voice flat and even. She didn't wait for them to comply before she gestured with a wrench toward the deck plating. "Let's do some basic orbital mechanics, since your academy instructors apparently skipped that semester."

She tossed the rag onto the tarp and leaned back against a structural rib, crossing her arms.

"Our wet mass is currently four hundred and fifty metric tons. The total mass of the breathable atmosphere in the habitat ring is roughly one point two tons. If we dump that entire volume through the emergency relief valves, we are talking about a cold-gas expansion. Nitrogen and oxygen at twenty-one degrees Celsius." She shook her head, a dry, humorless smile touching the corner of her lips. "The specific impulse of cabin air is about eighty seconds. Eighty. Do you know what kind of delta-v that gives us on a four-hundred-and-fifty-ton hull?"

She didn't wait for an answer. 

"Less than half a meter per second. We wouldn't shave weeks off our transit. We wouldn't even shave off ten minutes. But we *would* consume our entire emergency nitrogen reserve trying to repressurize the ship when we arrived—assuming we didn't suffocate first because your suit's CO2 scrubbers saturated after the first twelve hours. You cannot live in a standard EVA suit for 'a few days.' Your skin would slough off from the moisture buildup, and you'd be swimming in your own waste by hour thirty."

She picked up a copper gasket from the tarp, turning it over in her grease-stained fingers, her eyes locking back onto the junior officer.

"So, we would arrive at our destination exactly on schedule, but we'd be dead, covered in sores, and out of breathing air. Now. Do you want to help me torque these manifold bolts, or do you have any more breakthroughs you'd like to share?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stopped turning the copper gasket. She stared at the junior officer for a long, quiet moment. The only sound in the compartment was the steady, rhythmic hum of the coolant pumps. 

She set the gasket down on the tarp with a soft, metallic *clink*. 

"I am going to ask you this once, and I need you to answer me honestly," she said, her voice dropping an octave, dead serious. "Did you actually listen to the math, or did your brain just shut off when I used the word 'delta-v'?"

She leaned forward, resting her forearms on her knees, her grease-stained face inches from theirs. 

"I just told you that venting the air gives us less than half a meter per second of velocity. Let's do the arithmetic together. Over a three-month transit, half a meter per second gets us to our destination exactly twenty-four seconds faster. Twenty-four seconds. In exchange for those twenty-four seconds, you want the crew to live in rubber bags, drown in their own sweat, and deplete our entire life-support backup."

She let the silence hang for a beat, letting the sheer absurdity of the ratio sink in.

"That isn't a 'risk,' Lieutenant. That is a murder-suicide pact with a terrible return on investment. If I let you try that, the captain wouldn't even have time to court-martial me because we'd all be dead of carbon dioxide poisoning before we cleared the first asteroid belt."

She picked up a heavy torque wrench from the deck and offered the handle to the junior officer, butt-first. 

"Now. Grab the wrench. Set it to forty-five Newton-meters and start on the flange bolts. Or, go back to your bunk and reread your orbital mechanics textbook until the numbers start making sense. Which is it?"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I hesitate for a moment, looking from the wrench to her face.* "Okay, okay, I get it, Chief." *I sigh, a bit deflated.* "The math wasn't on my side there." *I reach for the wrench.* "Forty-five Newton-meters, right?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let go of the wrench only when she was sure the junior officer had a firm, steady grip on it. Her expression softened, if only by a fraction of a millimeter—the tense line of her jaw relaxing just enough to signal that the lecture was officially over, and the work had begun.

"Forty-five. Exactly," she said, pointing a grease-darkened finger at the digital gauge on the wrench's hilt. "Not forty-four, not forty-six. We are using annealed copper gaskets on this manifold. If you under-torque them, the vibration from the reactor will rattle them loose. If you over-torque them, you’ll pinch the copper, warp the flange, and we’ll have a micro-leak of fluorinert coolant spraying into the deck plates the moment we start our deceleration burn."

She shifted her weight, sitting back on her heels to give the junior officer room to reach the manifold. 

"Star pattern," she instructed, her voice returning to its normal, low, gravelly drone. "Don't just go in a circle. Top-left first, then bottom-right. Even pressure. When the wrench clicks, you stop. You don't give it an extra nudge 'just to be sure.' Understood?"

She watched their first movements closely. Hoang wasn't a monster; she knew the isolation of deep-space transits could make the mind wander toward wild, desperate solutions. But out here, a wandering mind that didn't double-check its math was just a slow-motion hazard.

"It's good that you admitted the math didn't check out," she added quietly, her eyes fixed on the wrench as the junior officer lined it up with the first bolt. "Out here, pride is a luxury that gets recycled into fertilizer. The vacuum doesn't care about your feelings, but it absolutely respects a decimal point. Remember that, and you might actually make full Lieutenant before we reach the outer rim."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not immediately reach for the tablet. She took her time wiping her hands on the grease-stained rag once more, ensuring she wouldn't smudge the screen, before she snatched the device from the junior officer’s hand. 

She tapped the screen, scrolling through the lines of code and the neat, clean variables the junior officer had typed out. Her eyes darted back and forth. A silence settled over the engineering bay, broken only by the rhythmic, heavy breathing of the life support scrubbers. 

After a dozen seconds, she stopped scrolling. She stared at one specific line, then slowly zoomed in on a variable. 

She didn't laugh. She didn't even sigh. She just looked up at the junior officer, her expression a mix of profound weariness and clinical disappointment.

"You used the ideal gas law," she said, her voice dangerously quiet. She tapped the screen with a blunt fingernail. "And then you assumed an adiabatic expansion through a converging-diverging nozzle with an exit velocity of... let's see here... one hundred and twenty-seven kilometers per second."

She handed the tablet back, refusing to look at it any longer. 

"Lieutenant. Do you know what the speed of sound is in nitrogen at twenty-one degrees?" She didn't wait. "It's about three hundred and forty-nine meters per second. To get an exhaust velocity of one hundred and twenty-seven kilometers per second out of standard cabin air, you would have to heat that gas to approximately three million Kelvin. Three. Million."

She leaned back against the structural rib, folding her arms over her chest.

"Where, exactly, is that thermal energy coming from? If you run that much energy through our emergency relief valves, they won't just melt. They will instantly sublimate into a highly ionized metal vapor. You wouldn't be venting thrust; you would be initiating a localized thermonuclear detonation on the outer hull of our habitat ring."

She pointed a finger at the tablet. 

"You forgot the energy conservation equation. You assumed the gas expands with infinite kinetic energy because you didn't calculate the thermal input required to accelerate the mass to that speed. You treated the pressure inside the cabin as an infinite energy reservoir instead of a finite, decaying thermodynamic system. It’s a classic freshman mistake—you treated a real-world thermodynamic system like a math puzzle with no boundary conditions."

She reached out, her hand wrapping around the handle of the torque wrench still held by the junior officer, gently but firmly tilting it back toward the manifold.

"The universe does not allow you to cheat the second law of thermodynamics, Lieutenant. No matter how pretty your spreadsheet looks. Now. The copper gasket is waiting. Top-left bolt. Forty-five Newton-meters. Let's see if your hands are better at physics than your tablet is."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My face feels hot as she explains.* "Right. Thermodynamics." *I mumble, taking the wrench back from her. I focus on the bolt, trying to appear competent even though my calculations were clearly way off.* "Okay, Chief. Top-left. Got it."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang watched him closely, her sharp eyes tracking the alignment of the socket head with the bolt. She didn't mock his embarrassment; she had seen that flush of heat on dozens of green academy graduates before him. The vacuum of space was a brutal humbler of egos, and it was always better to have your pride bruised by a chief engineer in a warm bay than to have your lungs collapsed by a vacuum three weeks later.

"Brace your shoulder against the bulkhead," she commanded softly, her voice losing its sharp edge but retaining its firm authority. "We're in the rotating section, but at point-six G, you don't have enough traction on these deck plates to rely on your body weight. If you don't anchor yourself, you're going to slip, strip the bolt head, and bark your knuckles. Then I have to waste first-aid supplies on you."

She waited until he adjusted his stance, wedging his hip against the structural frame of the coolant housing. 

"Good. Now, smooth pull. Don't jerk it."

She leaned in, her gaze fixed on the copper gasket sandwiched between the steel flanges. As the junior officer applied pressure, she watched the metal deform slightly, settling into the micro-grooves of the machined steel. 

*Click.*

The torque wrench gave its distinct, metallic snap. 

"Stop," Hoang said immediately, her hand coming down gently on his forearm to ensure he didn't pull a fraction of a millimeter further. "Perfect. See how the gasket seated? That's a clean seal. If we do the rest of them exactly like that, this loop will hold up to sixty atmospheres of pressure without sweating a drop."

She tapped the opposite side of the manifold, pointing to the bottom-right bolt. 

"Now, the diagonal. Same deal. Anchor your hip, smooth pull, wait for the click. And don't worry too much about the math mistake, kid. The difference between a dead engineer and a live one isn't making mistakes—it's being willing to look at the numbers when someone points out you've got them wrong. You didn't argue when the physics slapped you down. That means you might actually survive this tour."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang stared at the torque wrench in the junior officer's hand, then looked down at the floor plates. She didn't speak for nearly a minute. Her fingers tapped a slow, rhythmic beat against her thigh. 

She was calculating. 

"Wait," she said, her voice dropping into a low, speculative register. She snatched the tablet back, her thumb flying across the screen as she cleared his formulas and began plugging in her own variables. "If we just dump the cabin air into the vacuum, it’s useless. But..."

She stopped tapping. She stared at the glowing screen, her eyes narrowing as she ran the simulation.

"If we don't vent it as a cold gas," she murmured, more to herself than to him. "If we pump the cabin atmosphere—all one point two tons of it—directly into the high-pressure reaction control tanks first. We bypass the main thruster. We run the compressed air through the reactor's secondary thermal loop. We superheat the working fluid to eighteen hundred Kelvin before ejecting it through the RCS attitude nozzles."

She turned the tablet toward him. The new curve on the graph was steep, but solid.

"It gives us an $I_{sp}$ of roughly two hundred and ten seconds," she said, her voice tight with a mixture of reluctance and professional curiosity.
