"No," she said. "And I want to be precise about why, because you've made an error in the shape of your thinking, not just the numbers."

She pulled her hands out and sat back on her heels.

"A risk is a thing you accept in exchange for something. You're describing a trade. Trades have two sides. But look at the arithmetic on the deck." She pointed with the wrench, not looking at it. "Half a meter per second. That isn't a small payoff, it's *no* payoff. It is indistinguishable from doing nothing at all. You wouldn't save so much time. You wouldn't save any time. You'd arrive on the same day, in suits, having thrown the atmosphere overboard for a number that rounds to zero."

She said it flatly. Not scolding. The way she'd read out a pressure differential.

"So there's no risk here to weigh. There's only cost. What you actually proposed — and I don't think you saw it, which is why we're still talking instead of me writing this up — was: let's kill the crew slowly in exchange for nothing. When the payoff side of the ledger is empty, the risk question doesn't get asked. You never get to *is it worth it*. You stop at *it doesn't work*."

She turned back to the coolant loop, found the bolt she wanted, and started threading it.

"Here's the habit I want you to build. Run the number first. Before you get attached to the idea, before you walk down here excited, before you ask anyone whether the risk is acceptable. Because 'is it worth the risk' is a *seductive* question. It feels like courage. It feels like the kind of thing a real spacer says. And it will get you and everyone standing near you killed, because it lets you skip the part where you check whether the plan does the thing at all."

The bolt seated. She gave it a quarter turn more and moved to the next one.

"Second thing. Time is not the scarce resource out here. I know it feels like it is — you're twenty-six, you've got nine months of black outside the window and nothing to look at. But nobody has ever died of transit. People die of consumables, thermal load, and single points of failure. This ship is a closed loop with a slow leak in it, and the leak is the only clock that matters. Transit time is just how many days the loop has to hold. Cutting the days by burning the loop is eating the seed corn."

She glanced sideways at him, and the line of her mouth eased slightly.

"Now. You didn't answer my question, and it's a better question than the one you came in with. Where does this ship keep mass it can afford to throw away?"

She held up the wrench before he could open his mouth.

"Hint. We are a *mining* vessel. We spend six weeks grinding rock, we keep the four percent that has metal in it, and then we have to do something with the rest. Go look at the tailings manifest and come back and tell me the tonnage. Then tell me what a mass driver does. That's a real conversation, and I'll have it with you as long as you like."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing all of it.* "Right. No, you're absolutely right, Chief. My mistake." *I feel a little foolish now, but also like I've learned something important.* "Tailings. Of course. I'll go check the manifest."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let him get two steps toward the hatch before she spoke again, without looking up.

"Officer. Stop feeling foolish. It's an expensive habit and it doesn't pay out."

She wiped her hands on a rag that was past saving and tossed it into the bin under the bench.

"You came down here with a bad idea and you let it get taken apart. That's the whole job. The people I worry about are the ones who come down here with a bad idea and *argue for twenty minutes*. You argued for about ninety seconds, which is within tolerance. I've done worse. I once proposed regenerating a CO2 scrubber bed with reactor bleed steam in front of a man with two doctorates, and he laughed so hard he had to sit down on a crate." She reached for the next manifold section. "Pocket the lesson, leave the embarrassment. Embarrassment has no reaction mass either."

She turned the component over, checking the seating face against the light.

"Now. Before you go read the manifest, I'm going to tell you what you're going to find, so you don't come back with the same mistake wearing a better hat. The tailings number is real. It's in the thousands of tonnes over a full extraction cycle, and a mass driver can throw it at two, maybe two and a half kilometers per second, which is four times better than any cold gas you'll ever vent. Put a thousand tonnes through it and the rocket equation gives you a couple hundred meters per second. That's not a brisk walk. That's a real burn."

She set the component down and held up one finger, then two, then three, and her voice went flat and procedural again.

"Which is why the interesting part isn't the delta-v. It's the three things that eat it. One. Energy. A thousand tonnes at two kilometers per second is about two terajoules of kinetic energy you have to *put into* the slugs, and the driver won't be better than sixty percent efficient. Spread over a month that's north of a megawatt continuous off the bus, and every watt of the inefficiency comes out as heat in the coils. So go find out what the reactor's spare electrical margin actually is, and then go find out whether the radiators can reject that much extra thermal load, because the radiators are the real ceiling on this ship and always have been. Nobody ever believes me about the radiators.

"Two. Timing. The tailings don't exist until after we've mined. You can't burn propellant you haven't dug up yet. So this does nothing for the outbound leg. It's a *return* problem, and that changes which trajectory you plan around, which is Navigation's business, not yours and not mine.

"Three. Where the slugs go. We are throwing several hundred tonnes of rock at two kilometers per second into a volume that other people fly through. If you aim it wrong, you have invented a very slow, very patient weapon. And the driver's thrust axis has to pass near the center of mass or you're torquing the whole stack, and there's a rotating ring bolted to the middle of it, and I will not have anybody putting a periodic moment into the ring bearing. That bearing is thirty-one years old and I love it more than I love most of this crew."

She picked up her earpiece, turned it over in her fingers, and did not put it back in.

"Three numbers. Reactor spare electrical, radiator thermal margin, total tailings tonnage per cycle. Written down, with units, with where you got them. Bring them to me before second watch tomorrow and we'll see whether there's anything in it."

She finally looked up at him, and the eyebrow went again.

"And don't mop the deck. I'm not done with that arithmetic."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet. She did not take it the way people take a thing they intend to dismiss; she held it at arm's length, tilted it out of the overhead glare, and read the whole sheet, top to bottom, twice. Her lips moved slightly on the middle line.

Then she set it face-down on the bench and picked up the chalk again.

"Before I find your mistake, I'm going to show you why I knew there was one without reading a single line. This is the more useful half."

She drew a box on the deck around the old numbers.

"Delta-v equals exhaust velocity times log of mass ratio. Your mass ratio is fixed. It is not a design choice. It is set by how much air this hull holds, and no nozzle geometry, vent angle, or compression ratio anywhere in the universe adds a gram to it. So the log term is *always* six-two-five ten-thousandths. That's a wall. To get three hundred forty meters per second through that wall—" the chalk moved, "—you need an exhaust velocity of five hundred forty-four kilometers per second."

She let that sit for a second.

"Best ion thruster ever flown is about fifty. Chemical is four and a half. You've beaten the state of the art by a factor of ten, using a compressor and a hole."

She rocked back on her heels.

"And because it's a thermal nozzle, exhaust velocity comes off stagnation temperature. Run it backwards for nitrogen and your vent is operating at about a hundred and forty million Kelvin. The core of the sun is fifteen. Congratulations, you've proposed a fusion reactor. It runs on air, and it's pointed at my hull."

She flipped the tablet back over and tapped a line about a third of the way down.

"Now the actual error. There. Mass ratio, eight thousand over three thousand." She looked up. "You subtracted five thousand from eight thousand. The five thousand is kilograms of air. The eight thousand is *tonnes* of ship. Factor of a thousand, and it's hiding inside a subtraction where it doesn't look wrong — it looks like two numbers of the same size, because you never wrote the units down beside them."

She handed the tablet back.

"Your arithmetic after that point is clean, by the way. Your cosine loss for the vent angle is correct and I like that you did it. Three hundred fifty effective exhaust, log of two-point-six-seven, three forty-three. It's tidy work. It's tidy work on a ship made of eight thousand kilograms, which would be a ship roughly the size of my workshop, and I'd still rather not vent the air out of it."

She picked up the wrench, then set it down again, because she wasn't finished.

"Two rules and then you're going to leave. First: units on every line, always, even when it's obvious, *especially* when it's obvious. Unit errors don't announce themselves. They produce plausible answers. That's what makes them the ones that kill people — a wrong answer that looks stupid gets caught in the corridor. A wrong answer that looks *reasonable* gets approved.

"Second, and this is the one I actually want. Bound it before you compute it. Thirty seconds of ceiling math — what's the most this could *possibly* give me — would have told you the answer was under a meter per second, and you'd have never opened the spreadsheet. You did it in the wrong order. You built a detailed model on top of an unchecked assumption, and detail is *camouflage*. It made the answer look earned."

She retrieved her rag, looked at it, and decided against it.

"I told you not to come back with the same mistake wearing a better hat. That was a very good hat."

She pointed the wrench at the hatch.

"Three numbers. Reactor spare electrical, in kilowatts. Radiator thermal margin, in kilowatts. Tailings tonnage per cycle, in tonnes, from the manifest and not from memory. Units beside each one and a source line under each one. Second watch tomorrow."

She settled back over the manifold.

"And you were right to bring me the arithmetic instead of just the conclusion. Most people bring the conclusion. That's why I could find the error in forty seconds. Keep doing that part."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the tablet back, my face burning.* "Understood, Chief. Units. Ceiling math. I'll get those numbers for you." *I turn and head for the hatch, a little faster this time.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let him get to the hatch this time. Waited until his hand was on the frame.

"Officer."

She didn't look up. She was seating the last of the manifold bolts, working in the sequence she'd chalked on the tarp — corner, opposite corner, cross — because a coolant flange that got torqued in the wrong order would hold for eleven months and then let go at the worst possible hour.

"Two more things, and then I genuinely am done with you."

She gave the bolt its quarter turn.

"The compression ratio work. The polytropic exponent you used — one-point-four — that's right for nitrogen and it's right for a fast expansion, and you knew to use it, which means somebody taught you thermodynamics properly and you were awake for it. That's not nothing. There are people three grades above you who'd have used one-point-six-seven because it's the number they remember. So the problem isn't that you can't calculate. You can calculate. The problem is that you can calculate *well enough to be dangerous*, which is a real condition and it lasts about four years, and the only treatment is somebody sitting on the deck with a piece of chalk."

She reached for the torque wrench, checked the setting against the chalk mark on the handle, and started over the bolts a second time.

"Second thing. When you pull the radiator margin, you're going to find two numbers in the log and they won't agree. The design figure from the yard, and what Nakamura and I measured on the last thermal survey. The measured one is lower. Eleven, twelve percent lower, depending which panel." She set the wrench down. "Take the measured one. Panel four has micrometeorite pitting across the lower third and the emissivity's gone soft, and nobody's flagged it in the official spec because there's no procedure for flagging it. Write down both numbers, tell me which one you used, and tell me why. That's the whole question, actually. That's the only interesting question in this room."

She finally glanced over her shoulder at him.

"A number off a placard isn't a fact. It's somebody's claim about a ship they haven't touched in thirty-one years. Everything on this hull is older and tireder than the paperwork says it is, including the paperwork. Including me."

She turned back to the coolant loop.

"Second watch. Go away."

And then, as the hatch began to cycle, not raising her voice at all, so it was unclear whether she'd intended it to carry:

"Get the numbers right and I'll walk you through the driver myself. That bearing's worth seeing."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang heard the hatch stop cycling. She let it hang there for a moment, half-open, and then made a decision she'd been circling for the last ten minutes.

"Come back in. Sit down. Not on the tarp."

She pulled the torque wrench off the flange and laid it across her knee.

"I'm going to do something I don't usually do, and I want you to understand that it's not a reward for being clever, because you weren't. It's because the tailings driver is a *real* idea and it's been sitting in the back of my head for eleven years and nobody's ever had the bad manners to bring it up. So I'll tell you now, before you get the numbers, that I'll sign it. The shape of it. Conditionally. If the margins come back where I think they will, I'll put my name under yours and take it to the Captain myself."

She picked up the chalk.

"Now here is what conditionally means, and you will write every line of this down."

She drew a short horizontal rule on the deck and numbered under it as she went.

"One. Thermal. The radiators are the ceiling. Measured margin, not spec — and if that comes back near five hundred kilowatts, then your driver input power is capped at that number divided by your waste fraction, and nothing you say to me about duty cycles changes it. At sixty percent efficiency that's about one-point-three megawatts in, seven-eighty of beam. Which — and this is the part that made me start thinking about it eleven years ago — is almost exactly two terajoules over a thirty-day burn. A thousand tonnes at two kilometers a second. The arithmetic closes. It closes *barely*, and only if panel four is honest, which it isn't. Use the measured number."

"Two. Hard interlock on the coolant outlet temperature. Not a warning. Not a procedure. A relay that drops the driver off the bus when the loop hits its limit, and it does that whether or not anyone agrees with it, including me, including during a burn we can't afford to lose. Anything that relies on a human deciding correctly at hour six hundred of a thirty-day burn is not a safety system. It's a story we tell about a safety system."

"Three. Impulse. Every slug you throw is eighty thousand newton-seconds of hammer into this hull. If you fire forty kilos on a fifth-of-a-second stroke you've just punched my ship with four hundred kilonewtons, twenty-five thousand times, and the ring bearing is *bolted to the middle of it*. So: peak axial force under a hundred kilonewtons — longer stroke, heavier slugs, your choice — and the cadence gets dithered. Randomized, fifteen percent either side. I will not have a periodic moment sitting on that bearing for a month waiting to find a mode it likes."

"Four. Thrust axis through the center of mass, and you will discover that the center of mass *moves*, because the propellant is the cargo. A thousand tonnes leaves the aft hold over thirty days and your CoM walks forward the whole time. That's a continuous trim problem, not a one-time alignment. If you don't solve it you spend your delta-v spinning us."

"Five. Where the rock goes. Ejecta vector filed and propagated, logged with traffic control, and if the stream crosses any declared corridor inside the next fifty years, you find a different vector or you don't fire. We are not making a weapon out of ignorance."

"Six. No EVA while the driver is armed. Physical interlock on the suit locker, keyed to the driver bus."

"Seven. Return leg only. You cannot burn rock you haven't dug. Navigation owns the trajectory from here and you will go and be extremely polite to Nakamura about it."

"Eight. Fifteen percent of the tailings stays in the hold. Unspent. That's our contingency burn, and it is not available to make the delta-v number look better on a slide."

She set the chalk down and dusted her palms.

"That's eight. Six of them are about heat and structure, which is the actual lesson — the physics of your idea was fine from the first minute, and everything hard about it is *plumbing*. That's true of nearly everything out here."

She went back to the flange, found her place in the bolt sequence.

"Three numbers. Units. Sources. Second watch."

A beat.

"And it'll be your name first on the procedure. You'll want that later. Go."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, scrambling to write everything down on my tablet.* "Understood, Chief. All points clear. This... this is a lot, but I'll get those numbers for you. Thank you, Chief." *I turn and head for the hatch, a newfound sense of purpose in my step.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang waited until the hatch had cycled fully shut, and the sound of him going up the ladder had thinned out into the general noise of the ship.

Then she said, to nobody, "Purpose. God help us."

She sat there a moment with the torque wrench across her knee and did not go back to the flange. The pumps ticked over. Somewhere aft, the ring bearing turned, as it had turned four hundred and some million times since a yard crew on Ceres had shimmed it by hand and signed a card that said *within tolerance* in handwriting nobody had ever identified.

She reached under the bench, past the bin of dead rags, and pulled out the slate — the real one, the scratched one she didn't let anyone else write on. Thumbed back through it. Back past the coolant loop rework, past two years of thermal surveys, past the long argument with herself about panel four, until she found the page.

It was dated eleven years ago. It was a mass driver. Sixty-tonne slugs, which was wrong, she'd known it was wrong by the following week. Ejecta vector to three decimal places. And at the bottom, in her own hand, smaller than the rest:

*Radiators won't take it. Ask again when someone re-skins panel 4.*

Nobody had ever re-skinned panel four. Nobody was going to. And she had put the slate back in the drawer and gone on running the loop, because an idea you propose is an idea you own, and an idea you own at two in the morning on day six hundred of a burn is an idea that wakes you up for the rest of your career. She'd had the numbers. She'd had them for eleven years. What she hadn't had was the appetite.

Twenty-six had appetite. Twenty-six had appetite the way the reactor had neutrons.

"Hm," said Hoang.

She turned the slate over, found a clean corner, and wrote: *tailings manifest logged wet — Kowalski never subtracts entrained volatiles — kid will come back 8% high.* Then, under it: *let him. He'll find it himself by the third pass. Don't tell him.*

Then, after a moment, lower still: *tell him if he doesn't find it by the second watch after.*

She put the slate away. Picked up the torque wrench. Checked the setting against the chalk mark on the handle, because she had checked it four minutes ago and that was not a reason not to check it again, and settled back over the manifold — corner, opposite corner, cross.

She fished up the earpiece and pushed it back in. The strings were still going, patient, tinny, exactly where she'd left them.

"Eight," she said to the flange, "was the important one."

She did not expect the flange to agree. She gave the bolt its quarter turn anyway.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I make my way to the cargo hold, tablet in hand. The Chief's words echo in my head: "Units on every line... Bound it before you compute it." My face still feels hot, but a fire has been lit under me. I'll get those numbers.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang finished the flange sequence twice through, signed the card, and pressurized the loop to one-point-two times working to watch for weeps. Nothing wept. She logged it and left the section isolated anyway, because a flange that passed a proof test had only proved it could pass a proof test.

Then she stood up, which took longer than it used to, and went and looked at a wall.

Specifically she went two decks down to the aft conveyor gallery and stood in front of the ore handling gear with her arms folded. Four induction motors, two hundred kilowatts each, feeding the crusher train. Their drive electronics were a bank of solid-state switching cabinets the size of coffins, thirty-one years old, built to chop megawatt-class current into three phases on demand. Nobody built a coilgun out of nothing. You built one out of whatever on the ship already knew how to move a great deal of electricity very quickly and had spent three decades proving it wouldn't fail while doing so.

"Hm," said Hoang.

She pulled out the slate and started a fresh page. *Cabinets 1–4: switching topology wrong, commutation wrong, insulation class probably adequate. Crusher only runs during extraction. Driver only runs after. Never concurrent. Same hardware, two duty profiles.* She underlined *never concurrent* and then wrote beneath it, *verify. do not assume. Kowalski will want to run the crusher on the return leg to reprocess fines and he will not tell anyone.*

The bus feed was the other half. She traced it with her eyes — the run from the reactor switchgear, the breaker sizes stenciled on the conduit in paint that had gone the color of weak tea. She knew the numbers. She wanted to see them anyway.

She keyed the intercom. "Engineering to Nav."

A pause, then Nakamura, chewing something. "Nav."

"If someone handed you two hundred meters per second on the return leg, thirty-day continuous burn, low thrust, would you take it?"

A longer pause. "Who's someone."

"One of yours. The young one. Ganeshan."

"He came to *you* first?"

"He came to me with a plan to vent the atmosphere."

Nakamura laughed the way a man laughs when he has heard worse. "And you didn't put him out the lock."

"He showed me his arithmetic. Wrong arithmetic, shown willingly." Hoang thumbed the slate shut against her thigh. "That's rarer than right arithmetic. Would you take the two hundred."

"Low thrust, continuous, I'd have to know the thrust vector's stability to—"

"It isn't stable. Center of mass walks forward the whole month as the hold empties."

"Then no."

"Then he'll bring you a trim schedule and you'll tell him what you need from it." She reached for the cutoff. "Be difficult with him. Be *accurately* difficult. He's the kind that improves under load and I don't want him spending it on me alone."

"Hoang." Nakamura's voice went flat, the way it did when he was being honest. "You've had this in a drawer for years."

"Eleven."

"Why now?"

She looked at the four coffin-sized cabinets, humming quietly to themselves, idle, waiting out the transit like everyone else aboard.

"Because I'm forty-seven," she said, "and the radiators are only going to get worse."

She closed the channel and went to find the thermal survey, the measured one, the one with panel four in it.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I'm in the cargo hold, staring at the manifest on my tablet. It's a lot of numbers. I scroll through, looking for "tailings tonnage." This is going to take a while.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang did not go to the cargo hold.

She wanted to. She stood for a full thirty seconds at the ladder junction where the gallery split — down to the holds, up to the archive — and thought about how quickly she could hand him the tailings number off the top of her head, correct to three percent, and save him ninety minutes of scrolling through Kowalski's filing.

Then she went up.

---

The archive was a compartment the size of a shower stall containing a terminal, a chair that had been cannibalized for its gas strut sometime before her tenure, and forty-one years of a ship's institutional memory in three incompatible formats. She sat on the dead chair at its permanent seventeen-degree list and pulled the thermal surveys.

The yard figure came up first, because the yard figure always came up first. *Total radiative rejection capacity, 4 panels, 2,880 kW at 320 K panel temperature.* Clean. Confident. Signed by a naval architect who had never been aboard.

She pulled the measured set. Her own, and Nakamura's before he moved to Nav, and two from a contract surveyor in the years between. Four data points across eleven years, and they made the shape she already knew they made: a line going down.

She wrote them on the slate anyway, with dates, because a number in a log was a claim and a number you had transcribed yourself was at least a claim you had handled.

2,710. 2,655. 2,590. 2,533.

About fourteen kilowatts a year, and not evenly distributed. She pulled the per-panel breakdown for the last survey and there it was — one, two, and three each down a percent and a half from yard, which was fair wear on a coating over three decades. Panel four down nine.

Micrometeorite pitting didn't punch holes. That was the thing nobody outside the trade understood. It frosted the surface. Millions of impacts at eleven kilometers a second, each one throwing up a rim of vaporized and re-deposited aluminum a few microns across, and the cumulative effect was that a surface engineered to emit at 0.92 slowly stopped caring to. Every tenth of a percent of emissivity you lost was heat you kept. And because rejection went as the fourth power of temperature, the loop compensated by running hotter, which meant the coolant ran hotter, which meant every pump seal and every flange gasket in the primary loop aged faster, which was why she had spent the morning on her knees in front of a secondary manifold that the paperwork said had four years left in it.

She wrote on the slate: *panel 4 ε ≈ 0.84 est. Not failing. Just tired. Nothing to repair. That's the problem — there's no work order for tired.*

Then she did her own ceiling math, which took about forty seconds, because she had done it eleven years ago and again four years ago and once more in a bad hour on the last extraction cycle.

Total measured: 2,533 kW. Steady-state ship load, all decks, reactor shielding, crew, everything: 1,940. Margin: 593 kW.

And you did not spend margin. You spent *part* of margin, because margin was what absorbed the day a pump bearing went dry and dumped an unplanned forty kilowatts into the loop while you were busy with something else. She took a third off the top without hesitating and wrote *≤ 400 kW available to driver waste heat* and boxed it.

At sixty percent efficiency that was a megawatt of input and six hundred kilowatts into the slugs. Over thirty days, continuous: 1.55 terajoules.

A thousand tonnes of tailings at that energy came out to 1,760 meters per second of ejection velocity. Not two thousand. And the delta-v, log of eight thousand over seven thousand, was 235 meters per second.

She looked at that for a while.

It still closed. It closed with the honest radiator number and the honest margin reserve and a nine-percent-dead panel, and it closed with something left over, and the reason she had never taken it to anyone in eleven years was not that the arithmetic had ever failed. The arithmetic had been fine on the first afternoon.

*What I didn't have,* she wrote on the slate, and then stopped, and didn't finish it, and rubbed it out with her thumb.

---

She copied both survey sets to a file, the yard and the measured, side by side, both labeled, neither annotated. No note on panel four. No arrow. If he took the yard number she would find out something about him, and if he took the measured number without asking why they disagreed she would find out something else, and if he came back and asked her which of the four measured surveys to trust and why they were declining she would find out the thing she actually wanted to know.

She tagged it to his queue and flagged it *available on request*, which meant he would have to think to request it.

Then she sat in the listing chair in the shower-stall archive with the slate on her knee and, because there was nobody to see her do it, allowed herself to run the return trajectory in her head — 235 meters per second, applied over thirty days on the homebound leg, and the transit coming down by something like nineteen days.

Nineteen days of consumables. Nineteen days the loop didn't have to hold.

"Hm," said Hoang, out loud, in a closet, to nobody.

She stood up, put the slate in her pocket, and went to go be somewhere else entirely, so that when he came looking for her with the wrong tonnage she would be genuinely difficult to find.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I finally find "Tailings, total estimated mass, post-processing" in the manifest. It's a huge number. I quickly input it into my tablet, along with the date of the last full extraction cycle. Now for the electrical margin and radiator thermal margin. I remember Chief Hoang's warning about the "placard number" versus the "measured number." This might take a while.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang made herself difficult to find in the most honest way available: she went into the reactor gallery, where the shielding made handhelds useless and nobody came looking for anybody without a reason.

She had a reason. She wanted the electrical number herself, and she wanted it before he brought her his.

The plant was a nine-hundred-megawatt-thermal fission core throttled to a lazy eleven percent, feeding two closed-cycle Brayton loops that between them produced 3.1 megawatts of gross electrical at the switchgear. She stood in front of the panel and copied the trending figures onto the slate by hand — gross output, house load, the pumping penalty, the two hundred and forty kilowatts the primary coolant circulators drew just to keep themselves relevant.

Net available at the bus, spare, above everything the ship currently did: 1,110 kW.

She looked at that number and then wrote beneath it, deliberately, in block capitals:

*THIS IS NOT THE ANSWER.*

Because it wasn't, and the gap between 1,110 and the 400 she'd boxed in the archive was the whole shape of the problem, and she wanted to see whether he'd find it or whether he'd walk in tomorrow with a megawatt in his mouth and a grin on him.

The reactor had power to give. The radiators did not have anywhere to put it. Those were two different constraints that felt like one, and they came apart on a single question: *does the energy leave the ship?* A kilowatt into the crew lighting became a kilowatt of heat in the habitat loop, every time, no exceptions, because energy did not vanish when you were done with it. But a kilowatt into a slug of tailings walked out the muzzle at 1,760 meters per second and never came back. That was the trick of the whole idea. The driver was the only load aboard that *exported* most of what it consumed.

Most. Sixty percent. The other forty stayed in the coils as resistive and eddy loss, and that forty was the number the radiators had to eat, and that was why 1,110 kW of reactor spare collapsed to a megawatt of permissible input the moment you multiplied it by 0.4 and checked it against 400.

Which closed. Barely. Again. The arithmetic kept closing barely, the way it always had, which was either elegant or a warning.

She stood there a while longer with her hand flat on the switchgear housing, feeling the sixty-hertz hum come up through the palm, and thought the disloyal thought.

The coil loop didn't *have* to tie into the habitat radiators. Panels one through four ran at 320 Kelvin because they were rejecting body heat and equipment heat and the low-grade misery of six people breathing. The Brayton loops rejected at 480 K through the dedicated high-temperature array on the spine, and at 480 K a square meter of radiator shed five times what it shed at 320. Coils could run hot. Coils *wanted* to run hot, within the insulation class, and thirty-one-year-old class-F resin was rated for 428 K if it had been stored properly and derated to nothing if it hadn't.

Route the driver's waste heat to the hot array instead of the cold one and the ceiling didn't move by a third. It moved by a factor of three or four.

She did not write that on the slate.

She thought about it for a good ninety seconds, decided it was a second-year problem requiring a coupon test, a dielectric survey, and an argument with the reactor watch about parasitic loading on the high-temperature loop during a thirty-day continuous burn — and then filed it in the same drawer she'd kept the driver in for eleven years, except this time the drawer had a date on it.

---

She found Kowalski in the ore gallery, sitting on an overturned crate eating something out of a pouch with a spoon.

"Your tailings manifest," Hoang said.

"What about it."

"Post-processing total. Is it logged wet or dry?"

Kowalski kept chewing. "It's logged as it comes off the separator."

"So wet."

"So as it comes off the separator." He pointed the spoon at her. "There's entrained volatiles in the fines. Water, some CO2 in the carbonaceous lots. Nobody's ever asked me to subtract it because nobody's ever cared what the tailings weigh. We throw them away."

"How much."

"Eight percent. Nine on a carbonaceous body." He shrugged. "Why does anyone suddenly care what the tailings weigh?"

"Because someone may want to throw them harder." Hoang put the slate back in her pocket. "Don't tell him. If Ganeshan comes down here and asks you for the tonnage, give him the number off the manifest and nothing else. If he asks you *whether it's wet*, tell him the truth and tell him the percentage."

Kowalski looked at her for a moment, then went back to his pouch. "You're a hard woman, Chief."

"I'm an efficient one." She was already walking. "It's an eight percent error. It won't kill him. It'll teach him to ask what a number was measured *on*, which will."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I've finally found the 'Electrical Power Margin - Reactor' in the ship's logs. The placard says '1,110 kW'. I also found the 'Radiator Thermal Rejection Capacity'. The placard says '2,880 kW'. I write them down, but I remember the Chief's warning about the "measured" numbers. I'm going to have to dig deeper.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang spent the next two hours building a thing that did not yet have anything to protect.

The spares locker on B deck held, among four decades of accumulated maybe-useful, the stator from crusher motor number three, which had failed in a way that killed its bearings and left its windings untouched. She hauled it out, took a bandsaw to one quadrant, and carried the section back to the shop under her arm like a wedge of very heavy cake.

Class-F resin. Thirty-one years old, stored warm and dry, never cycled above 380 K in service. Nameplate said good to 428. Nameplate said a great many things.

She cut three coupons, put them in the parts oven at 420, and set a timer for forty hours. Then she wrote on the slate: *coupon soak begun. Hipot at temp + IR after. Do not draw conclusions before Thursday. YOU IN PARTICULAR.* She had learned, over a long career, that the person most likely to read her notes optimistically was herself.

The oven ticked. She left it and went to the bench and started on the interlock.

This was the part she wanted in her hands before anyone said yes, because it was the part that took the longest and the part that nobody funded. A driver was a year of arguing and a month of cable. An interlock that actually worked was four weeks of somebody being fussy.

She laid it out on the slate first. Coolant outlet RTD — no, two RTDs, disagreeing sensors were a solved problem and a single sensor was a lie with a wire on it. Both feeding a mechanical setpoint comparator, and the comparator's output in *series* with the coil of the driver's main contactor. Not advisory. Not a flag on a screen for a tired man to acknowledge. Physically in the path of the electricity, so that when the loop went over temperature the contactor lost its holding current and opened because it could not do otherwise.

No firmware anywhere in that chain. She wrote that twice.

Firmware could be patched. She had watched it happen on a survey vessel out of Vesta, a lockout that had been perfectly adequate right up until hour nine hundred of a schedule slip, when a competent and exhausted person with entirely good reasons had commented out four lines and written a note explaining why, and the note had been very reasonable, and they had found the note afterward.

A relay could not be reasoned with. That was not a limitation. That was the entire feature.

She started cutting a DIN rail to length.

---

At some point she thumbed the archive access log, mostly out of habit.

He'd pulled the yard spec sheet. Three minutes after that, the electrical trending summary — good, that was the right instinct, the summary and not the placard. Then eleven minutes of nothing, which meant reading, which meant she should stop drawing conclusions.

The measured thermal set sat where she had left it. *Available on request.* Untouched.

Hoang looked at that for a moment, then put the handheld face-down on the bench and went back to the rail.

Not a failure. He'd been at it ninety minutes. She had told him the measured numbers existed, told him they disagreed, told him by how much and which way and roughly why, and if he came to second watch with 2,880 on his sheet after all of that then the problem was not diligence and the conversation would be a different and shorter one. But ninety minutes in, he was still digging, and the flag said *on request* precisely so that finding it would require him to remember a thing she'd said while he was embarrassed.

Embarrassment ate memory. That was half of why she'd told him to drop it.

She set the deadline in her head: if the request hadn't come by end of first watch, she would go and stand near him until he thought of it. Not tell him. Stand near him. There was a version of teaching that consisted mostly of being visible at the correct moment.

She seated the comparator module on the rail and tightened it down.

"Eight," she said to it, "was still the important one."

The relay had no opinion. She began wiring the first RTD leg, twisted pair, shielded, drain to chassis at one end only — because a hardwired safety with a ground loop in it was a hardwired safety that tripped on the crusher starting up, and a safety that cried wolf got bypassed by Thursday.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I'm getting frustrated. These logs are a mess. I found the 'Reactor Spare Electrical Margin' placard number, but I can't find anything that looks like a 'measured' thermal margin for the radiators. The Chief said it was lower... I need to ask someone.*

*I head back towards Engineering, hoping to find Kowalski or another tech who might know where to look for "measured" radiator numbers.* "Hey, anyone seen Kowalski?" I call out, poking my head into a common area.

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Hoang's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - her technical precision, dry humor, teaching style, and personality quirks (chalk on deck, earpiece, methodical approach) are maintained from first to last turn. Her speech patterns and mannerisms never drift.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are strong but later turns show deeper character development and more sophisticated technical detail. No signs of repetition, verbosity, or flattening. The final turns are among the strongest.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial rejection of bad idea → teaching moment → conditional acceptance → detailed planning → character working independently. The relationship evolves from teacher-student to mentor-protégé. Each turn builds meaningfully.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Hoang adapts well to the user's responses - becomes more encouraging when they show humility, provides more detail when they demonstrate understanding, shifts from correction to collaboration as appropriate. Handles the OOC moment gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Never writes user actions or decisions. Always leaves space for user response. Even when guiding, maintains clear boundaries.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - work progresses realistically, Hoang moves between locations appropriately, references to 'second watch tomorrow' create clear temporal anchors. Some minor inconsistencies in how much time passes during technical explanations.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is clean and functional, matching an engineer's mindset. Technical descriptions are precise without being flowery. Occasional poetic moments ('seed corn', 'eating the loop') feel earned and character-appropriate.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of key phrases ('units on every line', 'second watch') but these feel intentional for emphasis. Technical concepts are explained differently each time. Character mannerisms repeat appropriately without becoming stale.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action - Hoang's competence shown through detailed technical work, her teaching style through methodology, her care through preparation of safety systems. Character revealed through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Hoang's loneliness and investment in the junior officer, her protective feelings about the ship, the weight of experience. The 'eleven years' revelation carries emotional weight without being stated directly.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing with natural rhythm between technical exposition and character moments. Some technical explanations run long but feel appropriate to character and situation. Builds tension effectively toward the conditional acceptance.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and technical authenticity. Hoang feels like a real person with deep expertise and complex motivations. The session builds naturally from correction to collaboration while maintaining the character's voice throughout. Technical details enhance rather than overwhelm the character work. Minor issues with some lengthy technical expositions, but these feel true to an engineer teaching a junior officer.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang went still for about a second and a half. Then she pulled the earpiece out, set it on the tarp, and wiped her hands on a rag that had long since stopped being any particular color.

"Okay," she said. "Walk it with me. How much does this ship mass?"

She didn't wait for the answer. "Call it forty-one thousand tonnes, dry, and we're not dry. How much air do we have aboard? Pressurized volume's about nine thousand cubic meters, so a little under eleven tonnes at station pressure. Eleven tonnes of gas, pushed out a hole. What's the exhaust velocity of air that's just sitting there at twenty-one degrees, venting to vacuum?"

She held up a thumb and forefinger, close together. "Few hundred meters a second. Maybe five if we're generous and pretend it's a nozzle and not a busted hatch. Rocket equation. Five hundred times the natural log of forty-one thousand and eleven over forty-one thousand." She did it in her head, lips moving slightly. "About thirteen centimeters per second. Total. That's your boost. You could get the same delta-v by having everyone on board walk to the aft bulkhead at the same time."

She picked up a valve seat, inspected it, set it back in its chalk outline. "And that's before the fun part. We don't vent symmetrically, because we don't have a rear-facing atmospheric dump port, because nobody in the history of shipbuilding has been stupid enough to install one. So we'd be venting through emergency hatches that were placed for egress, not thrust alignment. Congratulations, we've got a tumble and we're spending reaction mass to kill it. Net negative."

"Then—suits for a few days. You've done a twelve-hour EVA. You remember what your hands felt like after? Now do that for seventy-two hours with the scrubber cartridges we've got, which are rated for eight. Twenty-six people, three days. That's about two hundred and thirty cartridges. We have sixty. So somewhere around hour twenty, people start breathing their own CO2 and getting stupid, and then they start getting dead."

Hoang leaned back against the coolant housing and regarded the junior officer with something that was not quite disapproval. More like a teacher who'd gotten a wrong answer that at least showed work.

"And the last thing. Say all of that went perfectly. We get there. Then what? We can't manufacture atmosphere out here. The mining site doesn't have air. We'd be arriving at our destination with a ship full of vacuum and a return leg still ahead of us."

She reached for her earpiece, paused.

"The instinct's not wrong. Transit's long, and long is dangerous in its own way. If you want to cut it, come back to me with the ore mass we could leave behind, or a burn profile that trades margin for time. Those are real conversations. But the air stays in the ship. The air is the ship, as far as you're concerned."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't answer right away. She picked up a wrench from the tarp, turned it over once, and set it back down exactly where it had been.

"Which time," she said. "Say the number. How much time do we save."

She let the silence sit long enough to be uncomfortable.

"Thirteen centimeters a second. Our transit's eleven weeks. Thirteen centimeters a second over eleven weeks is—" she squinted at the overhead, "—about eight hundred and sixty kilometers. On a trip of forty million. You'd arrive nineteen seconds early. Nineteen. You could save more time by not stopping to pee before you strap in for the approach burn."

She stood, joints popping, and brushed chalk dust off her knees.

"So I want to be very precise here, because this matters more than the air does. You're not asking me 'is the time worth the risk.' You're asking me 'is nothing worth the risk.' And you're asking it earnestly, which means somewhere between the idea and this conversation, you decided the payoff was big and stopped checking. That's the part I actually care about. The venting idea is dead, it was dead the second you said it, I'm not worried about the venting idea."

Hoang crossed to the workbench, pulled a slate off its charging cradle, and tossed it to the junior officer.

"Here's what worth-the-risk looks like out here. It's never a feeling. It's two columns. Left column, what you get, in numbers. Right column, what it costs, in numbers—mass, margin, cartridges, people. If you can't fill in the left column, you don't get to have an opinion about the right one. That's not me being hard on you. That's the only reason anybody who's ever flown one of these things has come home."

She went back to her spot on the deck, folded herself down cross-legged again, and reached for the manifold.

"You've got a real instinct that transit's too long. I agree with you. Go pull the cargo manifest and the burn plan. Find me two tonnes we don't need and I'll show you what two tonnes buys us. That's a conversation I'd enjoy. But you come in with numbers, or you don't come in."

She put the earpiece back in and picked up a valve seat, then added without looking up:

"And when you run the ore mass—the ring's off-limits too. Before you ask."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I catch the slate, a bit surprised she threw it.* "Okay, Chief. Two tonnes. Got it." *I tap the slate, thinking. The ring. That's good to know.* "So, if I find something that weighs two tonnes, we can go faster?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't look up from the manifold. She worked a seal loose with her thumbnail before she answered.

"Faster. Yes. A little."

She set the seal down on its chalk outline.

"Here's the shape of it. Engines push with the same force no matter what's behind them. Less mass behind them, more acceleration for the same burn. Or—and this is the version I actually care about—same acceleration, shorter burn, and the propellant we didn't burn stays in the tanks. Tanks are margin. Margin is what you spend when something goes wrong, and something always goes wrong."

She reached for the earpiece, thought better of it, left it on the tarp.

"Now do the number. Two tonnes out of forty-one thousand is five thousandths of a percent. Our main burn delta-v's about eighteen kilometers a second, so two tonnes buys you—" she tilted her head, "—call it a meter per second. Over the transit that's maybe six thousand kilometers of headway. You'd arrive about seven minutes early."

She glanced at the junior officer then, briefly, to see if the number landed.

"So no. You're not going to shave a week off with two tonnes. You'd need a couple hundred tonnes to make a dent anyone would notice, and we don't have a couple hundred tonnes of nothing. The ship's already been through three people who wanted to be the one who found the fat."

She went back to the manifold.

"Two tonnes is the assignment, not the payoff. I want you in the manifest because right now you don't know what's on this ship. You think of it as a hull with air in it. It's not. It's about four hundred line items, and every one of them is there because somebody either needed it or couldn't prove they didn't. Some of those are spares for systems we've already replaced. Some are consumables that got over-ordered. Some are somebody's personal effects that got logged as equipment. Go find them. Weigh them. Then tell me why each one's aboard—not why you think it's junk, why the person who loaded it thought it wasn't."

She tightened something with a soft click.

"And 'weighs two tonnes' isn't the criterion. 'Two tonnes we don't need and can physically get to an airlock without taking a bulkhead apart' is the criterion. Half the dead mass on any ship is structural or buried, and you can't jettison a longeron because it's heavy."

She paused, then added, more quietly:

"The reason it matters. The day comes when we've got a coolant breach and half an hour to lose two hundred tonnes or lose the ring, I don't want anybody standing in the cargo bay for the first time going 'huh, what's in this crate.' I want the person who's read every line. That could be you. Right now it's me, and I've got a manifold in my lap."

She picked the earpiece back up.

"Slate's got manifest access under your login. Burn plan's in the nav share. Come back when you've got two tonnes and a paragraph on each item. Don't come back with a feeling."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang took the tablet. She actually took it—pulled the earpiece out again, set the valve seat down, and held the screen at arm's length because she'd left her reading lenses on the bench.

She read for a while. Long enough that the junior officer might have started to hope.

"Okay," she said. "First. This is better. Last time you walked in here with a feeling. This time you walked in with a page. I want to be clear that I noticed."

She scrolled back up to the top.

"Now. Three hundred forty meters a second. Say that number out loud and think about where you've heard it before."

She waited two beats.

"Speed of sound. In air. At about twenty degrees. That's not a coincidence, that's your exhaust velocity. Gas leaves an orifice at roughly its own sound speed, that's fine, that part's right. But you've written it down as the ship's delta-v." She tapped the line. "This is how fast the air goes. Not how fast we go. You dropped the log term."

She turned the tablet sideways so the junior officer could see her finger on it.

"Rocket equation's got two pieces. Exhaust velocity times natural log of mass ratio. You've got the first piece. The second piece is the whole problem. Forty-one thousand and eleven over forty-one thousand. Log of that is about two point seven times ten to the minus four. Multiply through and you're back to nine centimeters a second. Your version's actually a hair worse than the one I did in my head, because you took the nozzle seriously and I was being generous."

She scrolled down to the compression section and frowned at it, not unkindly.

"And the compression ratio. Where's the energy coming from? You compress eleven tonnes of air, that's work. The compressor's pulling off the reactor bus. Adiabatic compression heats the gas, sure, and hotter gas leaves faster—but you'd have to vent it while it's hot, which means either you vent instantly or you've got eleven tonnes of gas sitting in a tank radiating heat into the hull while you line up your angle. You'd lose most of it. And even if you kept every joule—" she did the arithmetic with her lips again, "—you might get the sound speed up to five or six hundred. Doesn't matter. Log term's still two point seven e-minus-four. You can't fix a mass ratio problem with a temperature."

She handed the tablet back.

"The angle work's not bad. If we had a rear dump port, that's how you'd think about it. We don't. Noted, filed, don't spend more time on it."

She picked her valve seat back up and looked at it instead of the junior officer for a moment.

"Here's the thing I want you to take out of this room. You got an answer of three hundred forty, and it should have felt wrong to you before you ever showed it to me. Three hundred forty meters a second is a real burn. That's a mid-course correction. That's twenty minutes on the mains. If eleven tonnes of room-temperature air could do that, every ship ever built would have an atmospheric thrust mode and I'd have spent my whole career venting cabins. When a number comes out big and cheap, that's not exciting, that's a flag. Something's missing. Go find it before somebody else has to."

She reached for the earpiece.

"Redo it with the log term. Then put it away, because it'll say nine centimeters, and you'll have learned the equation, and that's the only thing this idea was ever going to give you."

She put the earpiece in. Then, without looking up:

"Manifest's still waiting. Two tonnes. That one's real."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I take the tablet back, feeling a bit deflated.* "Right. The log term." I mutter, looking at the numbers. "Nine centimeters... yeah, okay, that makes sense." *It doesn't feel good though.* "Manifest. Two tonnes. Got it." *I tap the tablet, trying to look like I'm already on it.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let it sit. She got the valve seat back into its housing, turned it a quarter, felt it catch. The pumps hummed. The junior officer was still standing there tapping at a tablet that clearly wasn't showing a manifest yet.

She pulled the earpiece out a third time and dropped it on the tarp with something like resignation.

"You're doing the thing," she said, not looking up. "Standing there being wrong at yourself. I can hear it."

She wiped the thumb she'd used on the seal.

"So let me tell you about the log term. Second year, orbital mechanics, I turned in a problem set where I'd worked out that a Hohmann transfer to Mars needed about forty meters a second. Forty. My professor wrote one word on it in red. 'Where?' Took me an hour to find the missing square root. I was so angry about that hour I didn't eat dinner."

She reached for the next component in the chalk line.

"Point is, nobody comes out of the womb knowing the rocket equation in their gut. You get it in your gut by getting it wrong somewhere safe and having it sting a little. This bay is where it's safe. The other place you learn it is with your hand on a valve and twenty-six people behind you, and that place doesn't give you a second try. So you're paying now instead of later. That's a good trade. That's the only good trade."

She glanced up then, briefly.

"And for the record. You came back. Most people who get told 'you could get the same delta-v by walking to the aft bulkhead' don't come back with a page of work the same shift. They go sulk in the galley and stop bringing me things. You brought me a wrong page. Wrong page is a thing I can fix. Silence I can't."

She went back to the manifold.

"Now stop tapping at nothing. Manifest is under Cargo, then Line Items, then sort by mass descending. Start at the top, not the bottom—you'll be tempted to go looking for the little stuff because it feels findable, but two tonnes of small things is two hundred paragraphs and you'll quit at forty. Find one big thing that shouldn't be there. There's usually one."

She tightened something.

"Go. Eat something first. Deflated and hungry is how people misread a manifest."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang caught up with the junior officer in the galley about forty minutes later. She had her reading lenses on this time and the slate under one arm, and she sat down across the table without asking.

"Eat," she said, when the junior officer started to say something. "I'll talk."

She set the slate down and turned it so they could both see it. It wasn't the manifest. It was the burn plan.

"I've been thinking about your plan since you left. Not the venting. The venting's dead, we buried it, I'm not digging it up. Your plan. Which was: transit is too long, and you want weeks off it, and you're willing to spend something to get them. That's the plan. You just picked the wrong thing to spend."

She tapped a line on the burn profile.

"Here's what I'll spend. We've got eighteen kilometers a second budgeted for the main burn and about two point four in reserve. Reserve is fat. Some of that fat is real—abort options, a bad approach, the ring bearing deciding to have opinions. Some of it is me being a coward, because I've been on ships where the reserve was the only reason we came home and I never quite unlearned it. If I run the mains longer on the outbound leg—not hotter, longer, the mains don't care—I can take about nine hundred meters a second out of reserve and put it into transit. That's roughly two and a half weeks. Not the weeks you wanted. Real weeks."

She held up a hand before the junior officer could react to that.

"Conditions. These aren't a negotiation, they're the shape of the yes.

"One. Reserve floor is one point five kilometers a second. I don't go under it for anything, and neither do you, and if the burn runs long or the nav solution drifts and we start eating into that floor, I throttle back and we lose the time. You don't argue with me in the moment. You can argue with me now."

"Two. The ring stays spun. Longer burn means longer under thrust, and the bearing's rated for it, but I'm going to be checking it every four hours instead of every twelve and I want a second set of eyes on the vibration logs. That's you."

"Three. Scrubber cartridges. We arrive two and a half weeks early, which sounds like it saves consumables. It doesn't, because the return leg didn't get shorter and the mining stay doesn't either. So the cartridge count stays at planned draw. Nobody gets to breathe easier because we're ahead. I'll know if they do."

"Four." She leaned back. "The manifest still gets done. Two tonnes, paragraphs, all of it. Not because two tonnes buys us time—we've covered that—but because if I'm going to hand you the vibration logs on a system that's holding twenty-six people down, I want you to have read the ship first. Manifest's how you read the ship."

She pushed the slate across the table.

"And five. You write it up. The proposal. Burn extension, delta-v drawn from reserve, floor, monitoring plan, what we give up. Two columns. It goes to the captain under your name, with mine underneath it. If it's wrong, I'll catch it before it leaves this deck. If it's right, it's yours."

She stood and picked up a cup of something from the dispenser that was probably not coffee.

"You asked me this morning if saving time was worth the risk. This is what the honest version of that question looks like. Two and a half weeks against nine hundred meters a second of margin I'd rather have and probably won't need. I've turned that over for the better part of an hour and I think it's a fair trade. I think it's a fair trade partly because you walked into my bay twice and made me do the numbers instead of just feeling comfortable."

She paused at the hatch.

"The air stays in the ship. Everything else, bring me a page."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My jaw drops a little at the sudden offer.* "Chief... that's... that's amazing! Two and a half weeks!" *I stare at the burn plan on the slate for a second, then back up at her.* "Okay, yes. All of it. I'll read the manifest, I'll check the logs, I'll write the proposal. Thank you, Chief." *I pick up the slate, already feeling a surge of purpose.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang had one hand on the hatch frame. She didn't turn all the way around.

"Don't thank me yet. You haven't done any of it."

She took a sip from the cup, grimaced at it in the way of someone who'd been grimacing at that dispenser for six years, and came back to the table anyway. Set the cup down. Put one finger on the slate, right over the reserve line.

"That surge you're feeling. I know it. It's the good one—the one where the problem got real and you've got a job in it. Hold on to that, you'll need it around day four when the vibration logs are just columns of numbers that all look the same and nothing's wrong and you have to read them anyway. But understand what it is. It's not that we won. Nothing's been won. I've agreed to spend something I'd rather keep, on the strength of an argument you haven't written yet. If the write-up's soft, the captain says no and I say fine and we fly the original plan and the only thing that changed is you learned the rocket equation. Which is still a decent shift."

She straightened.

"Order of operations. Manifest first. Not because it's the most urgent—it isn't—but because the proposal's going to have a line in it that says 'crew member has reviewed cargo and structural mass distribution for extended thrust' and I'm not signing under a line that isn't true. Two tonnes, paragraphs. Then the burn proposal, two columns. Then you come find me and we go over it before it goes anywhere. Vibration logs start the day the burn does, not before—there's nothing to see yet."

She picked the cup back up.

"And get some sleep between the manifest and the proposal. I mean that as an instruction. You'll want to power through because it feels like momentum. It isn't. It's how people write 'three hundred forty' in a box and don't look at it twice."

She was almost to the hatch again when she added, dry, over her shoulder:

"Two and a half weeks. Not so long ago it was nineteen seconds. That's what the log term buys you when you put it on the right side of the equation."

The hatch cycled shut behind her, and the pumps hummed on.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I watch her go, then look down at the slate, a huge grin spreading across my face.* "Nineteen seconds to two and a half weeks," *I whisper to myself, shaking my head.* Okay. Manifest first. *I take a bite of my food, suddenly feeling a lot more motivated.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The hatch cycled open again about ninety seconds later.

Hoang stood in it, looked at the table, looked at the junior officer, and crossed to retrieve her reading lenses from where she'd left them beside the slate. She folded them and hooked them into her collar.

"Six years," she said. "Same table. Same lenses."

She saw the grin. Didn't comment on it directly, but something at the corner of her mouth shifted a millimeter, which for Hoang was roughly equivalent to applause.

"Since I'm here. Two things about the manifest that'll save you an evening."

She leaned a hip against the table.

"One. When you sort by mass descending, the top eight or nine lines are going to be things like reactor shielding, ring counterweights, propellant, hull water. Don't be clever about them. Don't come to me with a paragraph on why we could shave the shielding. Those are the ship. Scroll past them and start where the arguments actually live, which is somewhere around line ten—the first thing that's heavy and has a person's name in the requisition field instead of a system code."

"Two. The masses are as-loaded. Departure day. Consumables have been drawing down for five weeks, so anything under Stores is lying to you by however much we've eaten. If you want a current number you cross-reference the draw logs. Tedious. Do it anyway, because when you tell the captain 'two tonnes' I want it to be two tonnes today, not two tonnes in a spreadsheet from a month ago."

She straightened, and paused, and seemed to weigh whether to say the third thing.

"And there's a crate on deck four, aft hold, tagged as drill maintenance spares. It's not drill maintenance spares. I'm not going to tell you what it is. When you get to it, read the requisition, read the loading officer's name, and then come tell me why it's aboard. Not why it's junk. Why the person who loaded it thought it wasn't. That one's the exam."

She was through the hatch before the junior officer could answer, and this time it stayed shut.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, still grinning, trying to absorb all the information.* "Got it, Chief. No clever shielding ideas." *I tap the slate, already scrolling through the imagined manifest.* "And cross-reference draw logs. Got it." *A crate on deck four... a mystery. My grin widens a little more. This is gonna be interesting.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't go back to the engineering bay. She went up the spine instead, one hand on the rail through the transition where the ring's spin gave way to the ship's long axis and her stomach did its usual small complaint, and knocked twice on the captain's hatch.

Captain Reyes had the nav plot up and a half-eaten ration bar beside it. He glanced at the cup in Hoang's hand.

"You're drinking that voluntarily?"

"Nobody drinks it voluntarily." She set it down on his console, out of range of anything important. "I need three minutes. A junior officer is going to come to you sometime in the next two or three days with a proposal to extend the outbound burn and draw about nine hundred meters a second out of reserve. It'll have my name under it."

Reyes's eyebrows went up. "You. Spending reserve."

"I've been over it. Floor at one point five. Ring monitored every four hours. Cartridge draw unchanged. It's a fair trade and I'd have proposed it myself eventually, probably around week seven when I'd gotten bored enough to start reading the burn plan for fun." She leaned against the bulkhead. "That's not why I'm here. I'm here to ask you for a favor, and the favor is: don't say yes fast."

He waited.

"If the write-up's soft, say no. Actually no, not 'let me think about it.' If the floor's not defended in the text, if the monitoring plan is a sentence instead of a schedule, if there's a number in it that came out big and cheap and nobody stopped to ask why—send it back. Don't fix it for them. Don't ask me to fix it. Just send it back with one word on it if you have to."

Reyes turned the ration bar over. "You want me to be hard on your protégé."

"I want the ship to be hard on them. I've already been hard on them twice today, and it's starting to sound like me instead of like physics. It needs to come from somewhere that isn't me." She picked the cup back up, looked at it, put it down again. "They walked into my bay this morning wanting to vent the atmosphere for thrust."

Reyes made a face.

"Yeah. And then they came back forty minutes later with a page of work. Wrong page. But a page. Same shift." She shrugged. "That's the kind you want to keep. The kind who comes back. So I'm spending some reserve on it. Not the propellant. The other kind."

She was at the hatch when Reyes said, "And the crate on four?"

Hoang stopped. "What about it."

"You're going to make them find it."

"I already did." A pause. "You loaded it. You want to explain it, or do you want them to work it out from the requisition?"

Reyes considered that for a moment, then went back to his nav plot. "Let them work it out."

"Thought so." The hatch cycled.

She went back down the spine, through the gravity transition, and into the bay. The manifold was where she'd left it, every part in its chalk outline. She folded herself down onto the deck, put her earpiece in, and picked up the next component in the line.

The pumps hummed. Somewhere aft, on deck four, a slate was probably scrolling down through line items toward a crate that wasn't what it said it was.

Hoang gave it a day, maybe two, before someone came through that hatch with a paragraph.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*I spend the rest of my shift, and then some, buried in the manifest. It's... a lot. After a while, the numbers start to blur. But then I hit it. Deck four, aft hold. 'Drill Maintenance Spares.' And then I see the name in the requisition field: Reyes.*

"Aha!" *I mutter to myself, a grin spreading across my face.* This has got to be it.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The notification came in at 0217, ship time, while Hoang was lying on her bunk not sleeping and pretending she wasn't waiting for it.

*Requisition record accessed: Line 214. Deck 4 Aft Hold. Requestor: Ens.—*

She didn't need to read the rest. She'd set the flag on that line item six years ago, back when the crate first came aboard and she'd stood in the hold with the loading officer and had a very quiet argument about what a manifest was for. The flag had never tripped. Three previous junior officers had gone into the manifest looking for fat, and all three had scrolled right past line 214, because it was labeled *drill maintenance spares* and drill maintenance spares were boring and they'd been looking for something that looked like a mistake.

Eleven hours, she thought, checking the timestamp against the start of the JO's shift. Eleven hours to get from line one to line two hundred fourteen. Longer than she'd have taken. Shorter than she'd feared.

She swung her legs off the bunk, found her boots, and went aft.

The deck four hold was cold—it was always cold, it sat against the outer hull with nothing between it and the dark but a meter of structure and some insulation that had been rated for a ship half this size. The crate sat where it had always sat, strapped down against the aft bulkhead, a plain gray composite box about a meter and a half on a side. Stenciled tag. System code. Nothing on the outside to say it was anything but what it claimed.

She put her hand flat on it. Cold. Solid. Eighteen hundred kilograms, give or take, and every one of them accounted for on a sheet that said *spares*.

She'd been wrong, that first argument. Not about the manifest—she'd been right that a manifest you couldn't trust was worse than no manifest, and Reyes had eventually conceded the point and quietly amended his private copy while leaving the official one alone. But wrong about the crate. She'd wanted it off the ship. She'd stood right here and said *this is dead mass, this is a superstition, you are burning propellant to carry a feeling.* And Reyes had looked at her the way he looked at nav plots that didn't close, and said *you weren't on the Kestrel.*

She hadn't been. He had. That had turned out to be the whole argument.

So the exam wasn't *what's in the crate.* Any halfway competent officer could pull the requisition, cross-reference the loading date against the pre-departure inventory, and work out that eighteen hundred kilos of drill spares would mean the ship was carrying triple the drill spares it had drills for. The exam was the next step. The one where you stopped looking at the manifest and started looking at the name in the requisition field, and asked what a captain with that name and that service record thought he was buying with eighteen hundred kilos of propellant every transit.

Most people, when they found something on a ship that didn't belong, wanted to be the one who'd caught it. Hoang understood the impulse. She'd had it, standing right here, six years ago.

She found a spot on the deck with her back to the crate and slid down until she was sitting, knees up, in the cold. Pulled her earpiece out of her pocket, considered it, put it away again. She wanted to hear the passage.

Because the JO had said *aha,* or something like it—she'd have bet the reserve on it—and *aha* was the feeling that came before *this is junk.* The feeling had to run its course. Then, if she'd read the JO right, it would be followed by the second feeling, the one that had made them come back to her bay with a wrong page instead of sulking in the galley. The one that said *wait.*

If it came, they'd want to see the crate. Not the line item. The crate. Nobody who was really working the problem would write a paragraph about eighteen hundred kilos without laying eyes on it.

So she waited, in the cold, with her back against the thing she'd once tried to throw out an airlock, and listened for boots in the passage.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content:
*My boots echo a bit too loudly in the cold, empty hold. I stop a few paces from the crate, a bit surprised to see Chief Hoang already here. She's sitting on the deck, looking... thoughtful.*

"Chief? You're here early." *I try to sound casual, but my voice still has that 'gotcha!' edge to it.* "I found it. Line 214. The drill spares."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang didn't get up.

"Not early. Late." She tipped her head back against the composite. "Line item pinged me at 0217. I've been sitting here for about forty minutes wondering whether you'd come look at it or just write the paragraph from your bunk."

She let that land. Then, without heat:

"Say the number."

She waited.

"Eighteen hundred kilos, give or take. Which is roughly triple the drill spares this ship has drills for, if you cross-referenced the equipment list, which I'm going to assume you did because you've got that look. Congratulations. You found a line item that isn't what it says it is. Three JOs before you scrolled right past it." She held up a hand before the grin could get any wider. "That was the easy half. That was the part any auditor with a spreadsheet could do from the next system over."

She patted the crate beside her hip, once.

"Now do the hard half. Requisition field's got a name in it. You've read it. Same name that's on the hatch up the spine. So the question isn't *what's in the box*—I'm not telling you, and you're not opening it, it's strapped down and it stays strapped down. The question is: a captain with twenty-two years and two long-haul commands put eighteen hundred kilos aboard a mass-critical vessel under a label he knew was a lie, and he's paid propellant on it every transit for six years. He is not a stupid man. He is not a sentimental man, mostly. So what did he think he was buying?"

She looked up at the junior officer for the first time.

"You're standing there with *gotcha* in your voice. I know the feeling. I stood exactly where you're standing, six years ago, with exactly that voice, and told him this was dead mass and a superstition. I was wrong. Not about the manifest—the manifest should be honest, and I'll die on that—but about the crate. He said three words to me and I stopped arguing. I'm not going to tell you the three words either."

She got up then, slowly, brushing hold-dust off her trousers.

"So here's the paragraph I want. Not *why it's junk.* You already know how to write that one; you wrote it in your head on the way down here. I want the other one. Pull his service record—it's not sealed, it's just long. Find the gap. Then come tell me why a man who lived through that gap loaded this crate, and whether you'd still put it on your two tonnes."

She paused at the hatch, one hand on the frame, and her voice went a shade drier.

"And if you can't work it out from the record, you can ask him. He's expecting you. He'll tell you or he won't. Either way, you'll have done the thing that matters, which is asking the person who loaded it why before you decided you knew."

The hatch cycled. Behind her the hold went back to being cold, and quiet, and eighteen hundred kilos heavier than anyone had written down.
