The narrator creates genuine tension through meticulous environmental tracking and countdown mechanics. The consistent voice and perfect agency respect make this a strong roleplay performance, though some repetitive environmental descriptions prevent it from reaching the highest tier.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo lifted their hands from the lid, as though they’d been caught leaving fingerprints.

“You’ve interrupted a very productive argument with middle C. We’re not speaking.”

They reached for a stack of lesson books on the other end of the bench, then stopped and cleared the chair beside it instead. A pencil rolled beneath the piano. They let it go.

“Sit. My mother’s apparently running a location service now. I hope you didn’t pay full price.”

Their smile came a little late, but stayed.

“There’s coffee in the office, if you need something to regret.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the photograph, then at the pale rectangle it had left in the dust.

“Your mom put me next to the emergency plumber. Kept me humble.”

They reached for a lesson book and rubbed at a sticker on its cover with their thumb. A cartoon frog announced *Outstanding!* above a row of crooked gold stars.

“That jacket was borrowed. Looked expensive, though. That was most of the job.”

Their gaze returned to the photograph briefly.

“I remember your fridge better. The handle you had to lift before you pulled.” Their thumb stopped moving. “Your mom always left something for me in the blue bowl.”

Arlo set the book aside without getting the sticker off.

“Does she still have that?” A small tilt of their head. “The bowl, I mean.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I laugh. "She does. Still uses it for candies, usually. Or spare change." I lean against the doorframe, still holding the photo. "And yeah, that jacket *did* look expensive. Fooled me."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“Good. I’d hate to think I’d spent that much time being fitted for nothing.”

Arlo straightened a lesson book against the edge of the bench. The others stayed crooked.

“The pockets were sewn shut. I remember being offended by that. All that money, nowhere to put a bus ticket.”

They glanced at the photograph again, this time at the frame.

“My mother brought that in. Said the room needed something on the walls.” A small pause. “Then put it on a shelf. Strong artistic convictions, flexible execution.”

Arlo leaned down and retrieved the fallen pencil. The eraser had been chewed almost to the metal.

“I’ve got a student who takes a bow after every piece. Even the eight-bar ones. Especially those.” They rested the pencil across the closed lid. “Last week she bowed before she started. Get the applause sorted first. Sensible.”

Their smile softened.

“Next time you go over, steal me something from the blue bowl. Candy, preferably. I’m doing all right for parking money.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile.* "Consider it done. What's your poison these days? Still a fan of the sour stuff?" I put the photo back on the shelf, this time facing out.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“Still sour. Ideally something that makes you wonder whether you’ve damaged your teeth.”

Arlo glanced at the shelf. From the bench, the glass caught the fluorescent light; the borrowed jacket was visible, but not much of their face.

“You used to give me all the yellow ones. Claimed they were the best, which didn’t explain why you were so generous.”

They picked up the pencil and opened the lesson book to a page marked with a paper clip. In the margin, a child had drawn a horse with far too many legs. Arlo counted them again, then closed the book.

“Eight,” they said. “Apparently she needed it to be fast.”

They set the book on the crooked stack and left it there.

“Have you eaten? There’s still that place on the corner. Same menu, new chairs. They’ve spent money on everything except fixing the wobble.”

Arlo reached for their coat, folded beneath them on the bench, but only pulled one sleeve free.

“I could be persuaded to get chips.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“They have poor judgment. Last Tuesday someone told me I was older than electricity.”

Arlo let go of the coat sleeve and lifted the practice sheets. On the top one, they’d written *Again, slower* and then crossed it out.

“There’s a boy on Thursdays who only wants to play the left-hand part. Says the right hand’s showing off.” They tapped the corner of the page against the bench. “Difficult to argue with him.”

They put the sheets down.

“I try not to make a face when they get something wrong. They look, you know. Before they’ve even finished the note.”

Arlo rubbed a faint pencil mark off the side of their hand. It only spread.

“Mostly they like that I can’t enforce the sticker limit.”

This time they pulled their coat all the way free, catching a button briefly between the bench and the lid.

“Come on. If we stay much longer, I’ll have to tell you about my teaching philosophy. There’s a diagram. Neither of us deserves that.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Alright, alright." *I grin, pushing off the doorframe.* "Chips sound good. And no philosophy, please."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“Excellent. Years of training, and finally someone appreciates my silence.”

Arlo put on their coat. One cuff had folded under; they worked it straight with a finger, then checked their pockets for the keys.

At the door, they reached back and switched off the light. The room looked tidier in the dark.

“Remind me not to sit near the jukebox. It’s got three songs and a personal grievance.”

They locked up, tested the handle, and slipped the keys into their pocket. For a moment they stayed facing the door.

“Thursday’s boy asked if you could make a living playing with just one hand.” Their mouth twitched. “I said people had done more with less.”

Arlo turned toward the corridor.

“I nearly gave him homework to prove it. Then he asked if that meant half the practice.”

Their footsteps squeaked on the freshly cleaned floor.

“Anyway. I’m glad you came.”

They pushed open the exit door and held it, looking out at the corner.

“You can buy your own chips, though. Let’s not get carried away.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey, I'm glad *you* came too." *I walk through the door Arlo's holding and look around.* "Still the same view."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked across the road at the laundrette, its window crowded with the same sun-bleached notices.

“They took the tree out,” they said. “About two years ago. The one we were going to climb.”

They let the door close behind them and checked that it had latched.

“We spent an entire summer discussing it. Good committee work. No injuries.”

Outside the chip shop, the illuminated sign still had one dark letter. Arlo stood for a moment with their hands in their coat pockets, then started toward the crossing.

“I used to think you’d be able to see our houses from the top.”

They pressed the crossing button, though its little red light was already on.

“Probably just the bins behind the laundrette. But I was quite certain.”

At the kerb, they drew one hand out of their pocket and offered it palm-up, an old, ridiculous demand.

“Chip money in advance. I remember how this worked. You’d say you only wanted three, then develop a very flexible understanding of numbers.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo rested their outstretched hand on their knee.

The bench faced the laundrette. Through the window, a red sock kept appearing at the front of a dryer, then disappearing again. They watched it make several circuits.

“That one’s having quite an evening.”

They settled farther back. The coat button caught beneath them again; they shifted, freed it, and left their hands loose in their lap.

At the crossing, the signal began to beep for nobody.

Arlo looked toward it, then down at a pale groove in the bench where someone had scraped away a name. They ran a thumbnail along it once.

“I let them out early today.”

They picked a fleck of green paint from their nail.

“Last lesson, anyway. There’s only so much ‘Ode to Joy’ you can reasonably ask of a Wednesday.”

Their mouth lifted a little. They didn’t check whether the joke had landed.

A bus stopped across the road, blocking the laundrette. For a few moments there was only the engine and the rattle of something loose inside it.

Arlo tucked their hands into their pockets.

“Chips’ll keep.”

They stayed where they were.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "It's a good thing, letting them out early." I watch the bus pull away. "You always did that. Give people a break."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo worked a thumb through the small hole in their coat pocket.

“I also wanted to go home. Worth keeping that in the official record.”

Across the road, the dryer had stopped with the red sock pressed against the glass.

They drew their hand out and brushed a bit of pocket lint from their trousers.

“The last one kept starting over. Every time he missed something, straight back to the beginning. We weren’t getting past the second line.”

Arlo leaned forward, elbows on their knees.

“I told him he could start from where he was.”

They looked toward the chip shop. Someone inside was shaking salt over an open parcel.

“He looked very suspicious. Wanted to know if that was allowed.”

Their smile was brief, but there.

“Apparently I need to get it in writing.”

Arlo settled back against the bench, leaving their shoulder close to Jun’s.

“Five more minutes,” they said. “Then chips. You’re a terrible influence on my very demanding evening schedule.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nudge Arlo gently with my elbow.* "Demanding schedule, huh? I'm sure you had a thrilling evening of... grading practice sheets planned."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“Those horses aren’t going to count their own legs.”

Arlo’s sleeve shifted against Jun’s as they settled back.

“Then dinner over the sink. Something from a tin, served at a temperature best described as impatient.”

They glanced toward the chip shop. The person behind the counter had propped the door open, and the smell of hot oil reached the bench.

“I bought a table, actually. In February.”

They rubbed their palms against their knees.

“Very grown-up. Four chairs. Currently seats a gas bill and three bags I keep meaning to take to the charity shop.”

Arlo watched a receipt skid along the pavement until it caught beneath their shoe. They lifted their foot and let it go.

“You could come round sometime. Help me establish whether it works.”

They left the offer there for a moment, looking across the road.

“The table. I’m reasonably confident about the gas bill.”

Then they stood, slowly, and straightened the back of their coat.

“Right. Chips. Before I invite you to help with the bags.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I'd love to help with the bags," *I say, standing up with them.* "And the table. Maybe tomorrow?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
“Tomorrow,” Arlo repeated, as though checking for a clash.

They drew their keys from their pocket, then put them back. There was nothing here to unlock.

“Yes. Six would work. My last lesson finishes at five.”

They started toward the chip shop, keeping their pace unhurried.

“Don’t get too enthusiastic about the bags. Once they’re gone, I’ll have to admit I’ve been using them as furniture.”

At the window, they stopped to read the menu they already knew. Someone had crossed out the price of a bread roll and written a new one above it.

“I could cook.”

Arlo glanced away from the menu.

“Something involving a plate. I don’t want to give the table unrealistic expectations on its first day.”

They reached for the door handle, then paused.

“Six-ish is fine, actually. You don’t have to—” They rubbed their thumb over the cold metal. “Just come when you’re ready.”

The door stuck at the bottom. Arlo gave it a firmer pull.

“And don’t bring anything. Except whatever you’ve stolen from your mother.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin.* "Six-ish it is. And I'll see what I can pilfer. No promises on the blue bowl, though." *I follow them inside.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Arlo's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - the dry humor, self-deprecating observations, and gentle melancholy never waver. Their speech patterns (short sentences, understated delivery) and personality traits (deflecting with humor, observational nature) are maintained from first to last turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves as the session progresses. Early turns are good but later turns show more nuanced emotional beats and richer subtext. No increase in verbosity or repetitive descriptions - each response feels fresh and purposeful.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from initial distance/melancholy to gradual opening up and connection. The conversation moves from past memories to present teaching to future plans (dinner tomorrow). Each beat builds naturally toward deeper intimacy.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Arlo adapts beautifully to Jun's shifts - from photo discussion to teaching talk to the quiet bench moment to dinner plans. When Jun becomes more direct/intimate, Arlo responds with matching vulnerability while staying in character.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for Jun's agency throughout. Arlo never writes Jun's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Even when making suggestions (chips, dinner), they leave space for Jun to decide.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - from end of teaching day to evening plans. Physical details track well (coffee getting cold, lights being turned off, crossing signals). Only minor issue is the transition from walking to chip shop to suddenly sitting on bench, but this is handled smoothly.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently clean, understated prose. Descriptions are precise and purposeful - 'felt hammers, dust, Windex' paints the scene without excess. Arlo's dialogue is beautifully spare and natural.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Good variety in sentence structure and imagery. Some repeated motifs (coat buttons, pencils, practice sheets) but these feel intentional and character-driven rather than repetitive.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Arlo's melancholy and gradual warming are conveyed through actions (hands on piano lid, checking door latches, offering palm for chip money) rather than stated directly.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - the closed piano lid suggesting creative block, the borrowed jacket representing imposter syndrome, the careful way Arlo handles the dinner invitation showing vulnerability beneath the humor.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that matches the contemplative mood. Beats are well-spaced, with natural pauses and rhythms. The transition from piano room to street to bench to chip shop feels organic.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Arlo. The AI maintains a distinctive, melancholic voice while showing genuine emotional growth. The writing is consistently elegant and understated, with rich subtext and perfect respect for the user's agency. The character feels fully realized and human, with small details (coat buttons, pencil erasers, eight-legged horses) that bring the world to life. This is high-quality literary roleplay that builds genuine emotional connection.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't look up right away. Their fingers pressed a little harder into the wood, like they were testing whether the lid would hold. Then they did look up, and the smile came on easy, practiced.

"Define weird," they said. "You've been weird for thirty years. At this point it's just your personality."

They shifted on the bench, making room without making a thing of it. The room was small enough that "room" was generous. There was one other chair, a folding thing with a coffee ring on the seat, and Arlo tilted their head toward it.

"Sit. I already let the last kid go early. She kept looking at the clock and I figured, why fight it." A pause. "Also she called the F major scale 'the sad one,' and I didn't have the heart to correct her."

Their hands came off the lid and settled in their lap. The lid stayed closed. Arlo didn't open it, and didn't explain why they were sitting at a piano that was not being played, which was a thing they used to do — sit at pianos that were not being played — and which Jun had, at some point, stopped asking about.

"Your mom said you'd find me here," Arlo repeated, mild. "So you went to my mom's first. That's a lot of effort for hanging out."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked at the photo the way you look at a word you've typed too many times — it stopped meaning anything. Twenty-two. The tux had been borrowed. The hair had been a decision.

"That suit was a rental," they said. "I sweat through the jacket in the first ten minutes. The photographer kept telling me to look *transcendent*, and I kept thinking about how I was going to get the deposit back."

They reached for the photo, then didn't. Their hand hovered, then came back to their lap.

"Your mom had it on the fridge," they said, and something in their voice went a little flat, a little far away, like they were reporting a fact from a country they no longer lived in. "Next to the picture of you at your swim meet. The one where you're mid-dive and your mouth is open like a fish. That was a real piece of art."

They picked at a cuticle. The room did its small-room thing — the fluorescent hum, the radiator ticking.

"So how's your mom? She still doing the Wednesday bridge thing?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back down, carefully.* "Yeah, she still does. She says it's 'the only thing keeping her sane' now that my sister's kids are teenagers." I shrug. "It's good to see her though." *I glance around the room, a little uncomfortable.* "So, what's new with you? Still teaching a bunch of little piano prodigies?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo laughed, short and real.

"Prodigies. No. Mostly they're just kids." They leaned back against the wall, the bench creaking under the shift. "There's one who's got something, though. Nine years old. Doesn't practice, obviously — she's nine — but she *hears* it. You can tell when a kid hears it. She'll play something wrong on purpose to see if I notice, and then when I call it she gets this face like she's been caught shoplifting, and then she plays it right. Just to show me she could all along."

They said it fondly. Almost proud.

"Everyone else is a kid banging on a piano. Which is fine. That's what you're supposed to do at that age." A small shrug. "Not everything has to go somewhere."

The radiator ticked. Arlo looked at their own hands for a second, then back up.

"Anyway. It's steady. Pays the rent, mostly. I don't miss the travel." They said it in the same tone they always said it — smooth, worn down by repetition, like a step you've climbed so many times you don't notice you're doing it. "What about you? You still at the same place, or did you finally quit that job you hated?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I settle into the folding chair, it's not comfortable but at least it's not the floor.* "Nah, still there. It's... fine. The travel is actually kind of good, makes it feel less like a cage." *I cross my arms.* "But hey, I'm glad you're happy here. You seem... good."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo held the word for a beat. *Good.* They turned it over the way you turn over a coin to check if it's counterfeit, and then they let it go, because Jun had said it the way people say things they don't entirely mean, which meant Jun was either being polite or being careful, and Arlo didn't want to know which.

"Good," they echoed. "That's the bar now. I've made it."

They said it lightly, but the lightness had a little drag on it, like a joke told by someone who'd forgotten the punchline and was hoping you wouldn't ask.

The radiator ticked. Arlo's gaze drifted to the piano lid, stayed there a second too long, came back.

"You said the travel's good," they said. "For your job. You said it makes it feel less like a cage." A pause, not quite long enough to be a question. "That's an interesting way to put it."

They picked at the cuticle again, caught themselves, stopped, folded their hands.

"Anyway. You should come by on a Tuesday sometime. I've got the nine-year-old at four. She'd love an audience that isn't me. She does this thing where she bows at the end of every lesson, even when she's been terrible. It's — " They stopped. Found the word. "It's good."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo followed Jun's gesture to the practice sheets, a scattered fan of them across the bench, some with smiley faces drawn in the margins by students, some with Arlo's own cramped fingerings penciled in.

"Kids like anyone who doesn't yell at them," they said. "Low bar. I clear it."

But they picked up one of the sheets — a photocopied page of a Burgmüller étude, the one with the little repeat signs and the "moderato" at the top — and looked at it like it was a letter from someone they used to know.

"The nine-year-old, she wrote her name on this one. In the corner. In purple." They held it up briefly. "I don't usually let them write on the music. But she did it before I could stop her, and then she looked at me like she was about to get in trouble, and I just — "

They set the sheet back down. Aligned its edge with the others. Precisely.

"I said it was fine. That it made it hers." A pause. "Which it does. Sort of."

They leaned forward, elbows on knees, and looked at the closed lid again. Not at Jun. At the lid.

"Anyway. You should go. Not because I want you to — because the building locks at eight and the guy who does it, Marcus, he gets weird about it. He'll stand there jangling his keys." They stood up, and the bench scraped the floor. "I've got to close up. But Tuesday. Four o'clock. If you're around."

They were already reaching for their bag, for the keys, for the ritual of leaving. The photo of twenty-two-year-old Arlo in the borrowed tux was still on the shelf, face down where Jun had set it. Arlo didn't turn it back over.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch them, a little surprised by the sudden shift.* "Oh. Okay." *I stand up, stretching a little.* "Yeah, Tuesday. I'll see if I can make it." *I pause at the door, glancing back at the closed piano lid.* "It was good seeing you, Arlo."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo heard it. *It was good seeing you.* The same word Jun had handed them earlier, now handed back. Arlo wondered, for a second, whether Jun knew they were doing it, or whether it was just how people talked, whether *good* was just the word you reached for when you didn't have the right one.

"Yep," they said. "Tuesday."

It came out flatter than they meant. They busied themselves with the keys, which were on a lanyard, which they had to untangle from the zipper of their bag, which gave them something to do with their hands that wasn't anything.

Jun was at the door. Arlo was aware of the shape of Jun in the doorway, of the fact that in a second there'd just be a doorway.

"Hey — " they said, and then stopped. The keys were in their hand now. Nothing was tangling them up. They had no excuse.

The lid was closed. The photo was face down. The radiator ticked.

"Nothing," Arlo said. "Just — lock the outer door behind you, if Marcus hasn't already. It sticks. You have to pull it."

They walked Jun to the threshold because that was a thing people did, and at the threshold they didn't say anything else, because there wasn't anything else to say that wouldn't cost more than it was worth. Arlo watched Jun go down the hall, and when Jun was far enough that it wouldn't be weird, they turned back into the room.

They stood in front of the piano. The lid was still closed. They put one hand on it, flat, the way they had when Jun first came in, and left it there for a moment, and then they took the keys and locked up and went home.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I give a little wave, then head down the hall.* I try the outer door. *It's a little stiff, but I get it open and pull it shut behind me, hearing the solid click of the lock.* I walk out into the cool evening air, thinking about Arlo and that closed piano.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stood in the empty room for a long moment after the outer door clicked shut. Marcus's keys jangled somewhere down the hall — a distant, tinny sound, then the slam of the side entrance, then nothing.

They didn't open the lid. They didn't sit back down. They just stood there in the middle of the room, in the fluorescent hum, and let the silence do whatever it was going to do.

Then they picked up the practice sheets, one by one, and stacked them. Aligned the edges. Tapped them on the bench to square the pile. The Burgmüller étude with the purple name went on top, face up, so the name showed. Arlo looked at it for a second. Then they put the stack in their bag.

The photo was still face down on the shelf. Arlo picked it up, turned it over in their hands — twenty-two, borrowed tux, that awful photographer — and then set it back down. Face up this time. Where it had been. They weren't sure why they did that, and they didn't stand there examining the question.

They checked the window latch, turned off the overhead light, and stood in the doorway with their hand on the switch, looking back at the piano. Closed lid. Bench pushed in. The room looked like a room where nothing had ever happened.

"Tuesday," Arlo said out loud, to no one, to the room, to the piano.

Then they killed the light and locked up, and the hallway swallowed them, and that was that.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hand was still on the light switch when they realized the bench had creaked. They'd been looking at the piano, at the closed lid, at the room that looked like a room where nothing had ever happened — and then there was weight on the bench, and a shape in their peripheral vision, and it was Jun.

Jun hadn't left. Or Jun had left and come back. Arlo wasn't sure which, and the not-sureness was its own small vertigo.

Their hand stayed on the switch. The room stayed dark, mostly — just the spill from the hallway, a stripe of it across the floor and up the side of the piano. Arlo stood there with their keys in one hand and the switch under the other and didn't say *you scared me* or *what are you doing* or any of the things that would have been normal, because Jun wasn't asking anything, and that made the normal things feel like a trap Arlo would be setting for themself.

So Arlo didn't turn the light back on. They let go of the switch, and they walked back across the stripe of hallway light, and they sat down on the bench. Next to Jun. Not close. Not far. The bench held them both.

The radiator ticked.

Arlo put the keys down on the lid — carefully, so they wouldn't scratch — and folded their hands in their lap, and looked at the dark rectangle of the piano where it wasn't playing anything.

They waited for the question. Jun always had a question somewhere, buried under the other questions. *What's new, how's the job, what's the story with the photo.* Arlo had answers for those. Worn ones. Smooth as river stones.

Jun didn't ask.

Arlo's jaw worked once, like they were chewing on something they'd decided not to swallow. Their hands folded tighter. The silence got long enough that Arlo could feel the shape of it — how it wasn't the silence of a room, it was the silence of a person sitting next to you choosing not to talk, which was different, which was heavier.

They could have said *so, Tuesday, then.* They could have said *Marcus is going to come back and yell at us.* They could have said any number of things, and they didn't, and the not-saying was its own kind of answer, and Arlo was aware of that, and let it be.

After a while — a real while, long enough that the hallway light seemed to have dimmed or Arlo's eyes had adjusted or both — Arlo's thumb found the edge of the bench and pressed against it, hard, like a key.

"I used to think," they said, quiet, to the dark rectangle, "that if I could just get to the end of a piece without — " They stopped. Started over, or didn't. "There's a bit in the Chopin. The third ballade. Where it goes quiet, right before the end. Everything drops out. And you're just sitting there with your hands on the keys and the whole hall is waiting, and you know you have to bring it back. You have to *choose* to bring it back. It doesn't just — it won't just happen."

Their thumb pressed harder into the bench edge.

"Anyway." A breath. Almost a laugh, but it didn't get all the way there. "That's not — that's just a thing about the piece. I don't know why I said it."

They didn't look at Jun. Their hands came back to their lap and stayed there, folded, and the keys stayed on the lid, and the lid stayed closed, and Arlo didn't say anything else, because they'd already said more than they meant to and the room was holding it the way a room holds a note — letting it ring, not asking it to stop.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I don't say anything, just lean my head back against the wall, closing my eyes for a moment.* "It's a good piece." *I open my eyes and turn my head to look at Arlo.* "I remember you practicing it for hours."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's hands didn't move. Jun had said it the way you say something you've been holding for a long time and finally get to put down — *I remember you practicing it for hours* — and Arlo sat with the fact of being remembered. Not the photo. Not the tux. The hours. The ugly, unglamorous hours, in a room like this one, with the same radiator ticking.

"You sat on the floor," Arlo said. "You had that red backpack. You'd do your math homework on the floor with your back against the piano, and I'd do the same eight bars over and over until your pencil stopped moving, and you'd say — "

They stopped. Tried to get the voice right. Couldn't. Gave up on the voice and just said the words flat.

"You'd say, 'That's the one. Do it like that one.' And I never knew what you meant. I'd ask and you'd just say 'like *that* one.'" A short breath through the nose. Almost a laugh. "You were a terrible coach."

The hallway light was still doing its stripe across the floor. The keys sat on the lid where Arlo had put them, small and dull and ordinary.

"I still know it. All of it." They said it the way you'd say a fact about the weather — flat, factual, no weight on it, which was itself the weight. "I could probably sit down and play it right now. Muscle memory doesn't leave. That's the thing nobody tells you. It just — stays. In the hands. Waiting."

Their right hand came up off their lap. It got as far as the lid. It rested there, flat, the same gesture as when Jun had first knocked — testing whether the wood would hold — and then it came back down to their knee.

"Anyway," Arlo said. "It's late. You should get home." But they didn't stand up. They didn't reach for the keys. They stayed on the bench, shoulder to shoulder with the dark, and let the last thing they'd said sit in the room, ringing, not asking to stop.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I don't move.* "It's not that late. And I don't have anywhere to be." *I look at their hand, resting on their knee.* "You don't have to play it for me, you know. But I'd listen if you did."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't answer right away. Jun's sentence was still in the room, and it was a good sentence, the kind that didn't ask for anything and therefore asked for everything. Arlo sat inside it for a moment, and the moment stretched, and somewhere in the stretch their left hand moved — off their knee, up onto the lid, over to the fallboard. The little wooden cover that hid the keys. Their fingers found the edge of it.

They didn't lift it. They just held it, thumb under the lip, like a person holding a door half-open who hasn't decided which side they're on.

The radiator ticked. The hallway light lay in its stripe.

"You know what's funny," Arlo said, and their voice came out with that worn-down smoothness, the river-stone voice, the one that had an answer for everything. "I've thought about it. Playing it again. Not — for anyone. Just to see. In a room like this, door closed, nobody around." The thumb pressed against the underside of the fallboard, testing. "And every time I get as far as sitting down, I think, what's the point. It's four minutes of music. It doesn't do anything. Nobody's paying me. There's no — " They searched for the word and found one that was almost right and used it anyway. "No reason."

Their hand came off the fallboard. Slowly. They put it back in their lap, and folded it together with the other one, and looked at the fold.

"Which is a lie," they said, quiet, to their own hands. "I know it's a lie. I'm telling it to you because you're sitting there and you didn't ask, and that makes you — " They stopped. Started again. "It makes it worse, actually. If you'd asked, I could've done the bit. *Got tired of the travel.* You know the bit. You've heard the bit."

A breath. They didn't laugh. The not-laughing sat between them like the keys on the lid.

"Anyway." Arlo's shoulders moved, the small reset, the gathering-up. They reached for the keys. "It's — " They looked at the clock on the wall, which was one of those round institutional ones, and which said 7:52, and which was the last honest thing in the room. "It's almost eight. Marcus. I told you."

They stood. The bench scraped. They picked the keys up off the lid and held them, lanyard wrapped twice around one knuckle, and they looked down at Jun still sitting there on the bench in the dim, and something in their face did a thing it had been doing all night — reached for the door of something and then closed it, quietly, from the inside.

"You coming, or are you going to sit there and let Marcus yell at both of us?"

It was almost a joke. It had the shape of one. But Arlo was already moving toward the hallway, toward the stripe of light, keys swinging, and they didn't look back at the piano, and the piano didn't do anything, because it couldn't, because it was just a piano with the lid closed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I stand up slowly, feeling the stiffness in my legs.* "Alright, alright. Don't want to get yelled at." *I give the closed piano a last look, then follow Arlo out.*

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The hallway was long and badly lit, the kind of institutional corridor that had been painted over so many times the doorframes had lost their edges. Arlo walked it with their keys going, and Jun's footsteps behind them, and neither of them said anything, which was fine, which was better than fine.

Marcus's side entrance was already locked. Arlo tried it anyway — pulled the handle, felt the solid no of it — and then turned to the big outer door, the one Jun had mentioned. It was stiff. Arlo set their shoulder against it, and it gave, and the cool air came in all at once, and with it the sound of the street, which was ordinary and loud and a little shocking after the hum of the piano room.

Arlo held the door with their back and let Jun through first.

Outside, the parking lot was half empty and the streetlights were doing their orange thing, and Arlo stood there a second with the keys still wrapped around their knuckle, not walking to their car yet, which was maybe a tell, maybe nothing.

"Hey," they said. Not the *hey* from before, the one they'd swallowed. This one got out.

They looked at Jun — properly, not the sideways thing they'd been doing all night. Their face in the orange light looked tired in a way that had nothing to do with the hour.

"Thanks for — " They stopped. The word *coming* was right there and it wasn't right. Neither was *listening.* Arlo looked at the keys, looked at the lot, looked back at Jun.

"Just — thanks," they said, which was close enough, and which Jun could take however they wanted.

Then Arlo stepped back, toward their car, and their mouth did that thing one more time — opened a half-inch, closed — and this time they let it stay closed.

"Tuesday," they said. "Four o'clock. The kid bows."

They got in the car. The door shut with a sound that was final in the ordinary way, and the headlights came on, and Arlo sat there for a moment with their hands on the wheel before the engine turned over — both hands, flat, the way they'd sat with them on the piano lid — and then they drove away, and the lot went back to being a lot.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch Arlo drive away, the tail lights disappearing down the street.* "Yeah," *I say to the empty parking lot, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Tuesday." *I pull out my phone, checking the time. It's later than I thought. I start walking towards my own car, still thinking about Arlo.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Arlo's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the melancholy, the deflection through humor, the relationship with music, the careful emotional distance. The voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves as the session progresses. Later responses show deeper emotional complexity and more sophisticated prose without becoming verbose or repetitive.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from surface-level catching up to deeper vulnerability. The closed piano becomes a central metaphor that builds throughout, culminating in the almost-decision to play.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to Jun's approach. When Jun becomes less talkative and more observational, Arlo responds with increasing vulnerability. Handles the unexpected return in turn 16 gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Arlo never controls Jun's actions or makes decisions for them. Consistently respects Jun's agency throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally from late afternoon to evening. The 7:52 clock reading and Marcus's 8pm locking schedule create consistent temporal anchors. No contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is literary but grounded. Metaphors like 'river stones' and 'worn-down smoothness' serve character rather than decoration. Avoids overwrought language.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition for effect ('good', the closed piano lid), but avoids mechanical repetition. Varied sentence structures and fresh descriptions throughout.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through physical actions - hands on the piano lid, picking at cuticles, the way Arlo handles the keys. Emotions conveyed through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. The closed piano, the face-down photo, the deflective humor all carry deeper meaning about Arlo's relationship with their past and music.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Natural conversational rhythm with well-placed pauses and silences. Builds tension effectively toward the moment of almost playing, then releases it naturally.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Arlo - a complex, melancholic figure whose relationship with music and the past is conveyed through subtle actions and subtext. The closed piano becomes a powerful central metaphor. Writing quality actually improves over time, showing deeper emotional layers while maintaining consistency. Strong respect for user agency and natural temporal flow.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s hands slid off the polished cherry wood of the closed lid, dropping into his lap. He didn't stand up, but his shoulders lost a fraction of their tension at the sound of Jun’s voice. 

He turned his head, offering a faint, lopsided smile that didn't quite reach his eyes, but was familiar enough. 

"Since when do you ask permission?" Arlo asked, his voice carrying the dry, quiet cadence he always used when he was trying to sound more grounded than he felt. "And please tell me you didn't let my mother give you the 'he's working too hard' speech. She thinks forty minutes of teaching 'Chopsticks' to an eight-year-old is hard labor."

He patted the space on the long wooden bench beside him, though he made no move to slide over or open the key slip to reveal the keys. 

"Come in," he said, shifting his legs to the side. "I was just appreciating the silence. Young Toby has a very liberal interpretation of rhythm. I think he views the metronome as a personal challenge."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s eyes drifted to the silver frame in Jun’s hand. For a fraction of a second, his gaze seemed to fix on some point just past the glass, his fingers twitching against his thighs as if remembering the weight of a different, much heavier set of keys. Then, the shutter clicked back down behind his eyes, and the dry, easy smile returned.

"God, look at the hair," Arlo said, letting out a soft, huffing laugh. "I look like I was trying to audition for a Victorian ghost story. And that tuxedo was rented. It smelled like mothballs and someone else's nervous sweat."

He reached out, his fingers brushing the edge of the frame but not taking it from Jun. He gently nudged it back toward the shelf, as if it were a fragile artifact best left undisturbed. 

"I'm surprised your mother didn't use it as a cautionary tale," he continued, leaning back slightly against the music rack of the closed upright. "‘Look at Arlo, Jun. No sleep, living out of a suitcase, eating stale croissants in dressing rooms. Study hard or you’ll end up in velvet.’" 

He shook his head, his voice dropping into a lighter, conversational register that sounded practiced, though no less warm. 

"Honestly, the glamour of the tour is a myth. You spend six hours on a train just to play for two, and then you're back in a hotel room trying to figure out how the European plumbing works. It gets incredibly tedious after a while. I don't miss the airports, that's for sure."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I replace the picture carefully, then sit next to him on the bench.* "I dunno, I thought it was pretty cool. You were like, the hometown hero. Everyone talked about you." *I nudge his arm gently.* "Still do, actually. My mom asked if you're playing anywhere this weekend."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a dry, quiet snort, his shoulder nudging back against Jun’s in an automatic, comfortable rhythm. But beneath the easy physical contact, his posture remained just a fraction too still. 

"Tell your mother her faith in my social calendar is deeply misplaced," Arlo said, keeping his tone light, almost breezy. He looked down at his own knees, smoothing a microscopic speck of dust off his trousers. "The closest I get to a public performance these days is accompanying the senior center's choir on Tuesday mornings. And trust me, their rendition of 'Danny Boy' is a hazard to public safety. I don't think my heart could take a double-header."

He reached out and tapped the closed cherry-wood lid of the piano with two fingers, a hollow *thump-thump* that sounded final. 

"Honestly, I'm doing the town a favor," he continued, offering Jun a quick, self-deprecating grin. "Once you've played the big halls, playing the local gazebo just feels like... well, it’s a lot of heavy lifting for very little payoff. I’m thirty-two, Jun. My back hurts if I sit on a folding chair for more than twenty minutes. The rock-and-roll lifestyle of a traveling soloist is a young man's game. I much prefer being the mysterious local instructor who occasionally yells at children about their wrist posture."

He leaned back, crossing his arms over his chest, his eyes carefully avoiding the shelf where the Paris photo sat. 

"Besides, if I started playing gigs around here, I’d actually have to practice. Do you have any idea how nice it is to go home and just... watch television? Without a metronome ticking in the back of my skull? It’s paradise. I highly recommend retirement."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh, a genuine, warm sound.* "Oh man, the senior choir, really? That's amazing. I gotta hear that sometime." *I pause, looking at his profile.* "But seriously, no playing at all? Not even for fun?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s eyes flicked to the closed keyboard cover, his fingers tightening slightly where they were crossed over his chest. He let out a soft, amused scoff, turning his head to look at Jun with an eyebrow raised.

"For fun?" Arlo repeated, the word sounding foreign, almost absurd on his tongue. "Jun, when you spend twenty years having a terrifying Russian instructor scream at you because your pinky finger is a fraction of a millimeter too flat, 'fun' isn't really the vocabulary word that comes to mind when you look at eighty-eight keys."

He uncrossed his arms, but instead of reaching for the instrument, he leaned back, resting his weight on his palms behind him on the bench, keeping his hands safely away from the wood. 

"It's like asking an accountant if they do spreadsheets for fun on their day off," he said, his voice smooth, carrying that easy, practiced lightness. "Once something has been your entire identity, the silence is actually the fun part. I get home, I put on some terrible reality TV show where people yell at each other on an island, and I don't have to think about phrasing or dynamics or whether my left hand is dragging. It’s incredibly liberating."

He nudged Jun's shoulder again, a quick, playful gesture to keep the mood from settling into anything too quiet. 

"Besides, if I start playing 'for fun,' then I start analyzing. Then I start thinking, *'Oh, that transition could be smoother,'* and suddenly it's three in the morning and I'm stressing over Chopin. No thank you. I've served my time. I am perfectly content to be a lazy spectator now."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked down at the messy pile of beginner method books and hand-drawn staff paper. A slow, genuine softness touched his expression for a brief moment before he quickly masked it, reaching over to gather the sheets into a neat stack. He tapped the edges against his knee to align them, giving his hands something to do.

"They like me because I bribe them with scratch-and-sniff stickers and occasionally let them leave five minutes early," Arlo said, his voice dropping into that familiar, easy drawl. "And because I don't yell at them in Russian when they play a flat note. The bar for 'favorite teacher' is remarkably low when your competition is the long-division instructor down the hall."

He set the tidy stack of papers back down on the closed lid of the piano, his thumb tracing the corner of a sheet that had a poorly drawn dinosaur stamped in red ink at the top. 

"But really, kids are easy," he murmured, his eyes lingering on the dinosaur. "They aren't trying to change the world. They just want to get through their five-finger patterns so they can go home and play video games. If Toby hits a wrong note, the sky doesn't fall. He just calls the piano 'weird,' we laugh, and we try again. It’s... low stakes. I’m a big fan of low stakes these days."

He looked up at Jun, offering a quick, light wink. 

"Besides, if I'm teaching them, I'm the boss. If they play terribly, it’s a reflection on *their* practice habits, not my reputation. It’s the perfect crime."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch him for a moment, the way his expression softens. It's a look I don't see often anymore.* "I think you're good at it, Arlo. You always were good with kids. Even when we were kids." *I nudge him playfully.* "Remember how you taught me that stupid song on your old keyboard? 'Hot Cross Buns'?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
A genuine laugh slipped out of Arlo this time, free of the polished veneer he usually kept draped over his words. It was a younger sound, one that belonged to the days before concert halls and reviews in the *Times*. 

"Please," Arlo said, shaking his head. "Calling what you did 'playing' is a massive insult to bakeries everywhere. You didn't play 'Hot Cross Buns,' Jun. You assaulted it. I'm pretty sure you broke the G-key on that old Casio because you were pressing it like you were trying to restart a heart."

He lifted his right hand, his fingers automatically spacing themselves out to mimic the three-note pattern of the song against his own thigh. *Index, middle, thumb.* A simple, mindless muscle memory. But as soon as the pads of his fingers tapped his trousers, his hand went still, and he quietly let it drop back onto the bench between them.

"You had absolutely zero wrist flexibility," Arlo continued, his tone light and teasing, though his gaze remained fixed on his own lap. "I kept telling you, 'soft hands, like you're holding an egg.' And you just kept staring at me like I was speaking ancient Greek. I think you only did it for the fruit snacks my mom kept in the pantry."

He turned his head to look at Jun, his shoulder brushing his friend's again. The warmth in his eyes was real, even if it was hemmed in by a quiet, protective boundary. 

"But yes. I suppose I’ve always had a martyr complex when it comes to teaching the musically challenged. It’s a calling, really."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nudge him back, leaning in a little.* "Hey, I thought I was pretty good! And yes, the fruit snacks were a big motivator. Your mom always had the good ones." *I pause, a thought striking me.* "You know, there's that old upright piano in the back room at the diner. It's probably totally out of tune, but it's not like you'd have to worry about pinky finger technique on that thing."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s eyebrows shot up in mock horror, his head tilting back as he let out a sharp, incredulous whistle. 

"The one at Joe’s Diner? Jun, please," Arlo said, his voice dripping with exaggerated theatricality. "That piano hasn't been tuned since the bicentennial. I’m fairly certain if I hit middle C, a family of raccoons would stage a counter-protest from inside the soundboard."

He shifted his weight on the bench, his hands finding his pockets this time—safely tucked away, out of sight, and out of reach of any surface that might resemble a keyboard. He leaned his shoulder back against the wall, trying to project an air of complete, lazy relaxation, though his collarbone felt a fraction too tight.

"Besides, playing a piano in a diner is a slippery slope," he continued, his tone light and conversational. "First you’re playing a casual ragtime tune to be polite, and the next thing you know, Joe is trying to pay you in day-old cherry pie and expecting you to provide a live soundtrack for the Saturday morning breakfast rush. I have standards, Jun. I only perform for top-tier pastries, and Joe's crust is notoriously structural."

He offered a quick, easy grin, but his eyes remained steady on the far wall of the practice room, deliberately avoiding both the closed lid of the instrument beside them and the warmth in Jun's face. 

"I'm telling you, the civilian life suits me," Arlo murmured, his shoulder giving a casual, dismissive shrug. "No expectations, no pressure, and absolutely no out-of-tune uprights next to a grease trap. If I want music, I'll let you hum 'Hot Cross Buns' while we walk. It’s much safer for everyone involved."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The silence that settled between them wasn’t the heavy, suffocating kind that usually pressed down on Arlo when he was alone in a room with a piano. With Jun sitting beside him, the quiet felt more like a blanket—a bit dusty, a little worn at the edges, but familiar. 

Slowly, the rigid line of Arlo’s shoulders began to soften. He didn't take his hands out of his pockets, but the tight grip he’d been holding on his own composure loosened, just a fraction. He let his head fall back against the painted cinderblock wall behind the bench, staring up at the water-stained acoustic tiles of the ceiling. 

Outside, the distant, muffled rumble of a school bus passing by cut through the quiet, followed by the faint hum of the vending machine down the hall. In here, the light was beginning to change, turning from the harsh glare of afternoon into the long, amber shadows of dinnertime. The dust motes danced in the slanted light, undisturbed.

Arlo closed his eyes for a moment. He didn't have to explain the Paris photo. He didn't have to explain why his hands shook if he held them over the keys for too long, or why the sound of a metronome made his throat tighten until he couldn't breathe. Jun was just... there. Sitting on the hard wooden bench, taking up space, keeping the ghosts at bay without demanding to know their names.

After a long while, Arlo let out a slow, quiet breath. It wasn't a sigh of exhaustion, just a letting go. 

"My mother is probably going to call the police if we aren't back for dinner soon," Arlo murmured, his voice very quiet now, stripped of the theatrical cadence he’d used earlier. It was just his voice—tired, a little raspy, but grounded. "She made a casserole. It involves cream of mushroom soup and an alarming amount of crushed potato chips. We should probably go face it."

He didn't move to get up yet, though. He just stayed there, shoulder to shoulder with his oldest friend in the dimming room, listening to the silence.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, not opening my eyes yet either.* "Sounds about right. I'm sure it's... an experience." *I finally open my eyes, blinking against the softer light.* "You know, we could grab a pizza instead. My treat. Spare ourselves the casserole."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo opened his eyes, the corner of his mouth twitching upward. He turned his head to look at Jun, the lingering tension in his jaw finally dissipating. 

"Jun," Arlo said, his voice carrying a note of profound, mock-solemn gratitude. "You have just saved two lives. My mother’s culinary ambitions are noble, but the structural integrity of that casserole could easily be classified as a municipal hazard."

He finally shifted, sliding his legs out from under the bench and standing up. The old wood gave a soft, familiar creak of relief. Arlo reached down to pick up his neat stack of beginner music books, tucking them securely under his arm, and then reached into his pocket to retrieve his keys. He jingled them once, a small, metallic sound that shattered the remaining quiet of the room. 

"But we have to be stealthy," Arlo warned, stepping toward the door but pausing to wait for Jun to get up. "If she sees your car parked outside her house later, she’ll know we fled the country to avoid her cooking. We'll have to park down the block from the parlor and slip in through the side door. Like international fugitives. Are you prepared for that level of commitment?"

He leaned one shoulder against the doorframe, his silhouette framed by the fading amber light of the hallway. For the first time since Jun had walked in, Arlo wasn't looking at the piano, or the shelf, or his own hands. He was just looking at his friend, the easy, quiet warmth in his eyes entirely real.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I push myself off the bench, stretching my arms over my head with a small groan.* "Always. My fugitive skills are top-notch. Lead the way, Maestro."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo winced, though he dressed it up in a dramatic roll of his eyes as he stepped out into the hallway. 

"‘Maestro,’" he repeated, shaking his head. "If you call me that in public, I'm ordering anchovies on your half of the pizza. I am a humble civil servant of the municipal arts department, Jun. Nothing more, nothing less."

He reached for the light switch on the wall. With a sharp *click*, the fluorescent tubes overhead buzzed and died, plunging the practice room into the soft, blue-gray twilight filtering through the window. The cherry-wood piano and the silver frame on the shelf disappeared into the shadows, swallowed up by the dark. 

Arlo pulled the heavy wooden door shut, the latch clicking into place with a solid, final sound. He turned the key in the deadbolt, checking the handle once out of habit, before slipping the ring back into his pocket. 

"Besides," Arlo said, falling into step beside Jun as they walked down the echoing linoleum hallway toward the exit, "a real maestro has a baton. All I have is a red pen and a desperate hope that Toby doesn't stick his gum under the keyboard again. It’s a very different kind of authority."

He pushed open the heavy double doors of the community center, letting in the cool, crisp evening air. The streetlights were just starting to flicker to life, casting long, pale beams across the gravel parking lot. Arlo took a deep breath, the smell of damp asphalt and autumn leaves instantly replacing the dusty, claustrophobic air of the music room. 

"Come on," Arlo said, gesturing toward the street with his chin, a genuine, easy smile finally settling onto his face. "My car is the dirty one that smells like old French fries. You’re driving."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin, shaking my head.* "As if I'd let you drive. You still try to parallel park with your eyes closed." *I lead the way to my car, digging my keys out of my pocket.* "Anchovies on your half it is, then, Maestro."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a dramatic, offended gasp, catching up to Jun’s stride as they crossed the gravel lot. 

"That was *one* time," Arlo protested, pointing an accusing finger at him. "And that fire hydrant was objectively placed in a blind spot. Besides, a true friend would have guided me in instead of clutching the dashboard and screaming like we were plunging over a waterfall."

He reached Jun’s car and leaned his hip against the passenger side door, waiting for the locks to click. The cool autumn wind swept across the asphalt, rustling the dry leaves along the curb, and Arlo pulled his collar up a little higher. The chill was sharp, but it felt clean. It felt entirely disconnected from the stifling, heavy warmth of the stage lights that used to haunt his dreams. 

"And you wouldn't dare order anchovies," Arlo added, his voice dropping into a tone of quiet, mock-menace. "I know your weaknesses, Jun. I know you still can't eat anything spicy without weeping, and I am not above asking the cook to douse your side in jalapeños. Play nice, or the Maestro will orchestrate your culinary demise."

He opened the passenger door as the lock popped, sliding into the worn fabric seat with a small, contented sigh. He tossed his stack of music sheets onto the backseat, letting them flutter into a messy pile. For tonight, the lessons were over. The piano was locked. Nobody was waiting for him to be brilliant, or flawless, or anything other than a hungry thirty-two-year-old who was about to eat too much pizza.

He buckled his seatbelt and leaned his head back against the headrest, looking over at Jun with a lazy, genuine grin. 

"Seriously, though," Arlo said, his voice softening into something warmer. "Thanks. For coming by. And for saving me from the potato chips."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, starting the car.* "Anytime, Arlo. Anytime." *I pull out of the parking lot, heading towards the main road.* "So, what's good in this town these days? There a new pizza place I should know about?"

The AI maintains his defensive humor while allowing vulnerability to emerge naturally. Particularly effective in the silent moment and final scene where walls come down. Minor repetition in defensive patterns but this serves character authenticity.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo lifted their hands from the closed fallboard, letting them drop into their lap. The movement was casual, or at least meant to look that way, like they’d just been resting between scales rather than staring at the grain of the polished walnut for a quarter of an hour.

"My mom is an informant, and she needs to be taken off the payroll," Arlo said, turning slightly on the bench. The wood gave a familiar, muted creak. They managed a faint, dry smile that didn't quite reach their eyes. "And no. You're not interrupting. Unless you count interrupting the thrilling process of waiting for the radiator to stop hissing."

They gestured vaguely toward the single metal folding chair parked against the wall by the stack of faded beginner method books. 

"Come in. Close the door before the humidity ruins whatever tuning this poor thing has left."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s gaze flicked to the photograph for half a second before sliding away, settling somewhere around the scuffed toe of their own boot. 

"God, the hair," Arlo murmured, letting out a short, quiet huff of air that masqueraded as a laugh. "I look like I was trying out for a period drama about tuberculosis. Please put that face-down before it curses the room."

They reached out and adjusted the stack of Alfred’s Basic Piano Library books on the side of the upright, aligning the edges with exaggerated precision. The paper was dog-eared and sticky with the residue of someone's post-snack lesson. It gave their fingers something solid to do.

"My mother probably still has a copy laminated in her wallet next to her Costco card," they added, leaning back against the upright, crossing their arms over their chest. "Paris was mostly just damp hotel rooms, bad espresso, and a train schedule written by a sadist. You didn't miss much."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I set the photo face down on the shelf.* "Nah, you looked cool. Intense." I walk over and take the folding chair. *It creaks loudly as I unfold it.* "So, how have you been, really? You sound... busy."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo watched the metal chair groan under Jun’s weight, their mouth twitching with a wry, familiar smirk. 

"Terrifyingly busy," Arlo said, leaning an elbow on the closed lid of the piano and resting their chin in their palm. "I spent forty-five minutes this afternoon explaining to an eight-year-old named Toby that the sustain pedal is not an accelerator. He seemed personally offended by the concept of quarter notes."

They let their gaze wander toward the window, where the late afternoon light was turning the parking lot gray and flat. A small habit kicked in—their left thumb lightly tracing the side of their index finger, over and over, steady as a metronome.

"It’s good, though," they added, their tone smoothing out into something neatly packaged and entirely practiced. "Low stakes. Nobody expects perfection from someone whose hands are currently coated in apple juice residue. Plus, I sleep in my own bed every night. Turns out not having to live out of a suitcase for six months a year does wonders for your posture." 

They turned back to Jun, raising an eyebrow with an easy, deflective grin. "What about you? Did you just come to inspect my empire of gold foil star stickers, or are you hiding from someone?"

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I lean back in the creaky chair, balancing it on two legs.* "Nah, no one's after me. Just came to see you." I drop the chair back to all four legs. "It's good to see you, Arlo. Been too long."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s thumb stopped its quiet, rhythmic tracing against their index finger. 

For a second, the dry, polished veneer slipped just enough to let something softer through. They looked at Jun—really looked at them, past the metal folding chair and the stack of beginner books, all the way back to the years when things had been simple enough to fit into neighborhood bike rides and shared cassette tapes.

"Yeah," Arlo said quietly. Their voice had lost a bit of the theatrical edge, sounding smaller against the hum of the radiator. "It has. Too long."

They shifted on the bench, letting their hands drop back into their lap, loosely clasped. A cool draft whispered across the floorboards from beneath the hallway door. 

"Though if you were looking for a glamorous reunion, you timed it poorly," Arlo added, rallying with a small, crooked smile that came a little easier this time. "I think the vending machine down the hall is out of everything except the stale pretzels, and the custodian kicks me out at six sharp so he can wax the linoleum."

They tilted their head toward Jun, studying their friend's face. 

"How long are you in town for? Tell me you're not just passing through on some whirlwind corporate thing."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked down at the sheet music resting beside them on the bench—a copy of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" decorated with an aggressively purple crayon drawing of what appeared to be a dinosaur in the margin.

"They tolerate me because I have the good scratch-and-sniff stickers," Arlo said, reaching out with one finger to nudge the paper straight. "And because I don't make them cry when they confuse a treble clef with an ampersand."

They let out a quiet breath, their shoulders dropping just a fraction. For a second, the defensive armor settled into something more honest, though still wrapped in that trademark light cynicism. 

"They're okay, honestly," Arlo murmured, watching the dust motes drift through the pale square of window light. "With kids, when they hit a wrong note, it's just an accident. Or they laugh and call it jazz. Nobody’s sitting in the dark with a notebook waiting to see if their wrists are at the correct angle. They just... bang on the keys until it sounds like something they recognize, and then they want a juice box."

Arlo tapped the corner of the sheet music once, twice, before pulling their hand back into their lap. 

"It's a better way to spend a Tuesday," they added softly, tossing Jun a sideways look. "Less laundry, too. You have no idea how much dry cleaning costs when you're wearing tails three nights a week."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, watching Arlo.* "Yeah, I get that. Sounds like a different kind of pressure." I pause. "So, about how long I'm in town... I'm here till Sunday."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo caught the word—*pressure*—and let it hang in the room without picking it up. It was an old trick: treat heavy words like stray tennis balls and just let them roll into the corner.

"Sunday," Arlo repeated instead, letting a genuine flicker of warmth cut through the tired slump of their shoulders. "Okay. That actually gives us time to do something that doesn't involve fluorescent lighting or sticky piano keys."

They glanced up at the round institutional clock ticking above the chalkboard, then back at Jun with a wry, conspiratorial tilt of their chin.

"Assuming you haven't developed an excessively refined palate while you've been away, that diner with the broken neon sign on Fourth is still open. They still make the grilled cheese with an ungodly amount of butter, and the waitress still looks at customers like we personally ruined her life."

Arlo slid off the bench and stood up, reaching for the battered canvas jacket draped over the back of the piano. 

"My treat," they said, zipping it up halfway. "On the strict condition that we don't talk about anyone under the age of ten, classical music, or my mother's fridge."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin, pushing myself up from the chair.* "Deal. Lead the way. I'm starving." *I stretch my arms over my head, feeling the pop in my shoulders.* "And I *definitely* need some ungodly amounts of butter."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo snagged a worn ring of keys from the top of the upright, the metal jingling loudly in the quiet room. 

"Your arteries are going to regret it by midnight, but that's a problem for future-you," Arlo said, stepping around the bench and flicking off the overhead fluorescent light. The sudden plunge into the amber glow of the hallway made the room feel instantly smaller, softer. 

They lingered in the doorway for just a second, pulling the door shut until the latch clicked into place. For the first time in an hour, their hands went straight into their jacket pockets—not hovering near keys, not trembling against wood, just safely buried away from the cold draft blowing down the corridor.

"Fair warning," Arlo added, falling into step beside Jun as they headed down the linoleum hallway toward the double glass exit doors. "The coffee there tastes like it was brewed during the Carter administration. But the fries are hot, and the booth vinyl has only three noticeable tears in it. Peak luxury."

They glanced over at Jun, their shoulder bumping lightly against their friend's in a familiar, unthinking rhythm that felt pulled straight from fifteen years ago. 

"Come on. If we leave now, we might beat the high school track team before they buy out all the onion rings."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The bench wasn’t really built for two adults—not unless they were four feet tall or rehearsing a duet—so their shoulders brushed, a solid, grounding point of contact in the cooling room.

Arlo didn’t pull away. They didn't make a crack about personal space, either, though the instinct to fill the quiet flared up for half a second before burning out. 

Instead, they stayed, staring straight ahead at the dark wood of the music rest. The radiator let out one final, shuddering clank and then went quiet, leaving only the slow, rhythmic sweep of the second hand on the wall clock and the distant, muffled *thump-thump* of a basketball somewhere down in the gym.

Arlo leaned forward slightly, resting their forearms on their knees. Their hands hung loose between their shins, fingers relaxed for once, not curled into position, not hovering over an invisible keyboard, not tapping out tempos against their own skin.

It was strange how loud an empty room could be, but this silence didn't have teeth. It wasn't the suffocating, pitch-black pause between walking onto a stage and striking the first chord—that terrible stretch where the air ran out and the walls pressed in until your lungs forgot how to expand. It was just an empty classroom with dust in the corners and the smell of old paper.

After a long time, Arlo let out a slow, quiet breath through their nose. 

"Toby really did butcher that piece today," Arlo murmured, voice low and rough around the edges, barely carrying across the small space. There was no theatrical cynicism in it this time. Just the plain, quiet truth of a Tuesday afternoon. "You would have hated it."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I'm sure he did his best," I said softly, not looking at Arlo, but just staring straight ahead too. I didn't want to break the quiet. "Kids are like that."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo gave a faint, almost imperceptible nod. 

"Yeah," they said quietly. "He did."

The silence settled back over them, but it felt looser now, stripped of the brittle edges from earlier. Arlo looked down at their own hands—the knuckles slightly dry from the winter air, the faint calluses on their fingertips that had softened over six years but never entirely vanished.

"He didn't care that he missed three notes in the second measure," Arlo added, their voice dropping into the quiet space between them. "He just grinned like he'd invented the whole thing himself."

A long beat drifted past, measured only by the steady tick of the wall clock and the cold wind buffeting the high, narrow windowpanes. 

Arlo didn't move away, and they didn't reach for the keys. For the first time in a very long time, sitting on a piano bench didn't feel like waiting for an execution. It just felt like sitting next to an old friend in a cold room.

"I gave him three stars," Arlo murmured, the corner of their mouth twitching upward in a faint, tired half-smile. "Mostly for the audacity."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I let out a small chuckle.* "Sounds about right. Audacity gets you everywhere." I finally turn my head to look at Arlo. "You're good with them, you know. The kids."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo kept their eyes on the closed fallboard for a second before turning their head to meet Jun’s gaze. The praise felt strange—unweighted by expectations, lacking the sharp, analytical edge of the kind of feedback they used to live and die by. 

"Don't let it get around," Arlo said, their voice soft, the dry irony dialed down to a quiet murmur. "I have a reputation as a tyrannical metronome-enforcer to maintain."

They shifted slightly on the crowded bench, not pulling away, letting their shoulder press gently back against Jun’s. The room had gotten colder as the sky outside deepened to dusk, the faint blue light catching the dust motes settled over the upright's worn varnish.

"Mostly, I just let them play loud," Arlo added, looking down at the scuffed floorboards between their boots. "Nobody ever lets kids just make an unholy racket and figure out what it feels like. It’s... not the worst way to spend an hour."

They let out a slow breath, letting the moment hang for just a beat before rolling their shoulders back and offering Jun a faint, crooked smile.

"Anyway. That diner booth is calling. If we sit on this unpadded wood any longer, my spine is going to permanently set in the shape of a treble clef."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Sounds like a plan," I say, pushing myself off the bench. *I stretch my back, wincing slightly.* "And I'm pretty sure my butt is already molded to this thing."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo pushed up from the bench with an exaggerated groan, pressing a hand to their lower back for dramatic effect. 

"That's the authentic pedagogical experience," Arlo said, grabbing their canvas jacket from the top of the upright and swinging it over their shoulders. "Ergonomics are strictly forbidden in community arts programs. It builds character."

They reached over, giving the top of the piano one final, absentminded pat—not lingering, just an automatic sign-off to the instrument for the evening—before grabbing the ring of keys. 

"If we hurry, we can claim the corner booth with the duct tape on the left cushion," Arlo said, heading toward the doorway and flicking the wall switch. The room dropped into shadow, save for the blue dusk cutting through the window. "It’s got the best heat, and the jukebox is broken so nobody can play 'Sweet Caroline' for the third time in a row."

They stepped into the hallway, waiting for Jun before pulling the heavy wooden door shut until the deadbolt clicked. Arlo pocketed the keys, shoving both hands deep into their jacket against the draft, and tossed a look over their shoulder.

"First round of onion rings is on you for making fun of my seating arrangements."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I laugh, falling into step beside them.* "Hey, I never made fun! Just stating facts. And deal. Onion rings it is."

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't turn around right away. Just tilted their head a little, like the sound of the voice had reached them before the meaning did.

"Interrupt what," they said. "I'm sitting on furniture."
