“We are not operating under the rules of a starship captain’s speech,” she said. “We are a rotating hull full of rock, people, and finite reserves. If I let you eat our air to make a schedule look better, I am not a chief engineer. I am a funeral director with a wrench.”

Her voice softened only slightly. “I know you are trying to help. That is why I am telling you no instead of pretending I did not hear you.”

She pointed to the engineering console.

“Go bring me the trajectory sheet, the propellant margin, and the mission timeline. Then we look at real options: a burn optimization, a gravity-assist window, a mass reduction, a later arrival with a crew that can still work the ship. If the problem is that we are late, we solve it with engineering. If the problem is that you want to be faster by making the ship uninhabitable, then the problem is you.”

Hoang bent back down to the coolant loop and picked up her wrench.

“And while you are doing that, write down every assumption you used to believe this was worth the risk. I want to see the math. If it still says yes, we will talk again. But I will not unlock the emergency valves just to watch the atmosphere leave the ship.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a bit, running a hand through my hair.* "Okay, Chief. I get it. No eating the atmosphere." *I turn towards the console, muttering to myself.* "Just trying to think outside the box."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang heard the mutter. Her wrench stopped over the manifold for only a second.

“Outside the box,” she said, “is vacuum. The box is what keeps your lungs expanding and your blood from boiling. If you want to think outside it, do it with the math, not the crew.”

She did not raise her voice. She did not need to. The bay was full of pumps, valves, and the faint metallic tick of cooling lines, all of them telling the same story every shift: this ship was alive because the envelope around them was closed.

“The idea was not outside the box,” Hoang went on. “It was inside a very old box called *do not open the ship*.”

She turned the coolant component over again, checking the seam line under the work light. Her tone stayed practical, almost instructional.

“You want to be clever? Clever starts with what we can afford to lose. Air, water, heat, and a working scrubber are not on that list. Those are the ship. Everything else is hardware bolted to them.”

She set the part down and wiped her hands on the rag at her belt.

“Bring me the propellant inventory, the burn sheet, and the timeline. Show me where the weeks came from. Show me the delta-v. Then we look at real options: trim burns, gravity-assist windows, mass reduction, maybe even dumping slag or spare consumables if the trajectory supports it. If we can shorten the transit without turning the ship into a coffin, I will be the first one to sign the change order.”

Her eyes came up, steady and unsentimental.

“And if the math says venting the atmosphere is viable, I will personally be embarrassed. It will not say that. But you need to see why before you bring it to me again.”

She picked her wrench back up and nodded toward the console.

“I do not punish ideas. I punish people who act on them. So if you are trying to help, help by checking assumptions. A good idea survives being wrong. That one did not.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang held out her hand.

The tablet went to her, and she did not look pleased about it. She tilted it under the work light, scrolled through the junior officer’s numbers with one chalk-dusted thumb, and stopped near the bottom. Her expression did not change. That was usually worse than anger.

“You got one thing right,” she said. “You put a number on paper instead of waving at the sky.”

She tapped the screen with a wrench.

“But your number is lying.”

She set the tablet on the tarp beside the manifold, careful not to smear the chalk labels, and looked up.

“Three hundred forty meters per second is the gas leaving the nozzle. That is not the ship’s delta-v. You used exhaust velocity as if the ship were riding the exhaust like a wave. It isn’t. The ship and the gas share momentum. The heavy thing does not go fast because the light thing leaves faster.”

She picked up a scrap of cardboard and a grease pencil.

“Say our cabin volume is fifteen hundred cubic meters. At one atmosphere, room temperature, breathable air is roughly one point two kilograms per cubic meter. That gives you about eighteen hundred kilograms of air. That is your entire reaction mass if you eat the atmosphere. Not the ship. Not the rock. Not the crew. Not the water reserves. Not the coolant. Not the life support. Air. One point eight thousand kilograms.”

She wrote on the cardboard: *m_gas ≈ 1800 kg*.

“Now write our loaded mass. You do not have to be exact, but do not guess. Look at the manifest. Mining vessel, consumables, ore sample, crew, hardware. If you are lucky, we are around one hundred

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stare at the cardboard, my face heating up. She's picking apart my numbers, and it's… accurate. I feel a bit foolish.* "Right, okay. The ship's mass... I used the dry mass, but added the cargo." *I glance at the console, trying to remember where I pulled that number from.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang let the sentence finish with the patience of someone who had signed too many mass manifests.

“One hundred and twenty thousand,” she said. “At least. And that is you being kind to yourself. The current loaded mass is one hundred and thirty-one thousand seven hundred. That includes water, food, oxygen reserves, scrubber media, coolant, ore sample, tools, and the spare actuators I keep because if we lose one out here we do not get a delivery drone until next fiscal year.”

She wrote the number on the cardboard in blocky, impatient letters.

“Your air mass is one point eight thousand kilograms,” Hoang continued, tapping the first line. “Your ship mass is one hundred and thirty-one thousand seven hundred. Subtract the air after it is gone, and your final mass is one hundred and twenty-nine thousand nine hundred. The ratio is one point zero one three eight six. Natural log of that is about one point three seven six percent. Multiply by your exhaust velocity, three hundred forty meters per second, and you get four point seven meters per second.”

She underlined the result twice.

“Four point seven,” she repeated. “Not three hundred forty. Your three hundred forty was the speed of the gas leaving the ship. The ship does not ride the gas like a surfboard. The gas leaves fast, the ship leaves slow, and the momentum is shared. That is the whole problem with eating air. You spend the entire breathable atmosphere of the ship to get a shove you could get by throwing a toolbox.”

Hoang set the grease pencil down.

“If we are on a months-long transit, four point seven meters per second buys hours, not weeks. Maybe less if the burn is messy. And it will be messy, because emergency vents are not nozzles. They are holes. They leak sideways. They torque the hull. They flash ice when the pressure drops. They contaminate seals. And as the cabin pressure falls, your effective exhaust velocity falls with it, so your four point seven is already optimistic.”

She looked at the tablet again, then at the chalk labels on the tarp, as if comparing the junior officer’s arithmetic to something more honest.

“You added cargo,” Hoang said, voice steady. “Good. But cargo is not the whole ship. Consumables are mass. Rock is mass. Water is mass. The reason we have life support is that we are not a massless ghost flying through space. If you want to shorten the trip by hundreds of meters per second, you need hundreds of meters per second of propellant, not the air in our lungs.”

She slid the tablet back across the tarp with her palm.

“Go to the console. Pull the mass properties page, the propellant inventory, and the current cruise velocity. Then redo your calculation using the rocket equation, not your enthusiasm. Show me what delta-v we actually have. Show me what delta-v we need. Show me where the weeks came from.”

Her eyes stayed on him, not cruel, not soft.

“And when you get four point seven instead of three hundred forty, do not feel foolish. Feel useful. A number that kills the crew is not clever. A number that makes the crew survive longer is engineering.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Right, okay, four point seven. Not exactly what I was hoping for." *I pick up the tablet and my face is still hot. I head towards the console, muttering.* "Throwing a toolbox... that's a good way to put it."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang set the wrench down on the tarp with a clean, final sound.

“You did not finish the sentence,” she said. “You started with four point seven and ended with a mutter. That is how people start accidents.”

She stood, wiped her hands again, and crossed to the engineering console. The status board glowed in layered amber: pressure zones, coolant loops, O₂ partial pressures, CO₂ scrubber flow, reserve gas banks, attitude control margins. She pulled up the emergency vent schematic with a few sharp taps.

“I will agree to your plan,” Hoang said, “if you redefine it in a way that does not make me want to reassign you to slag handling for the rest of the fiscal year.”

She turned the display slightly so the junior officer could see it.

“Not atmosphere. Reserve inert gas. Not emergency boost. Contingency mass-rejection trim burn. Not days in suits. One controlled test, then one real use only if the trajectory officer, the captain, and the numbers all sign the same page.”

Her eyes came back, steady.

“You want to vent pressure for delta-v? Fine. We vent gas we can afford to lose. The fire suppression nitrogen bank, the purge reserve, the scrubber-side CO₂ accumulator if it is isolated from life support. We do not touch cabin air. We do not touch oxygen. We do not touch anything that keeps lungs working. If the plan requires eating the ship’s atmosphere, the plan dies on this deck.”

She pointed at the schematic.

“Conditions. First, the gas must be non-reserve critical. If the vent would reduce fire suppression margin below mission minimum, no. If the vent would affect scrubber pressure control, no. If the vent would interfere with propulsion purge, no. If the vent would reduce life support redundancy below one failed component plus one working component, no.”

Hoang began counting on chalk-dusted fingers.

“Second, the vent path must be controlled. Not a random port. Not a leak. A rated nozzle, isolated by double valves, with a pressure decay curve we calculate before opening anything. We need vector, not spray. If the thrust line passes through the center of mass within attitude control authority, maybe. If it torques the hull, no. We are not spinning the ship to save an hour.”

She tapped the attitude control display.

“Third, contamination and thermal. Compressed gas expanding through a small opening will chill the valve body. It may ice. It may carry lubricant residue, moisture, particulate, or seal fragments. We inspect before and after. If it puts ice or debris near optics, manipulators, sensor housings, or the ring bearings, we do not do it. A few meters per second is not worth a jammed reaction wheel or a cracked viewport.”

Her tone stayed flat, but the list had the rhythm of something she had written many times before.

“Fourth, crew safety. No one outside the pressure envelope. No one near the vent. No one in the line of the expected plume. Suits available and donned if the procedure calls for it, but I do not want anyone living in them for days. If your plan requires continuous suit use, it is still the old plan wearing a different mask, and I will not sign it.”

She glanced at the junior officer, then back to the schematic.

“Fifth, abort thresholds. Cabin pressure must not drop more than one percent from the planned vent event. Life support pumps must remain within operating envelope. Scrubber differential pressure must stay nominal. Attitude control authority must not fall below ninety percent. If any one threshold trips, the valve closes, the sequence ends, and we go back to the burn sheet. No heroics. No ‘almost worked.’”

Hoang pulled up the mass properties page again.

“Sixth, the math. Your four point seven meters per second came from the entire breathable atmosphere. I do not care how clever the vent angle was. Now calculate the reserve gas. Fire suppression nitrogen, purge reserve, isolated CO₂. Mass, pressure, temperature, nozzle area, backpressure, expansion regime. If the total delta-v is below the mission-relevant threshold, the answer is no. If it is above threshold but costs margin we cannot spare, the answer is still no. If it is above threshold, safe, isolated, and signed by the captain and trajectory officer, then I will listen.”

She turned from the console, arms folded.

“You wanted to save weeks. Fine. We save what can be saved without gambling the crew. If a controlled inert-gas vent buys hours, and those hours keep us out of a collision window, reduce propellant margin, improve arrival conditions, or preserve water and power, then it is engineering. If it buys a few seconds and risks the ship, it is theater.”

Hoang picked up the grease pencil again and wrote on the cardboard under the junior officer’s original number.

*Vent cabin air: no.*  
*Vent reserve inert gas: maybe, with conditions.*

She underlined “maybe” once, not twice.

“I am not agreeing because your first version was safe,” she said. “I am agreeing because you put a number on paper, and now we can make the number honest. Bring me the reserve gas inventory, nozzle flow calculations, torque estimates, pressure decay curves, and an abort procedure. Then I will tell you whether this idea is useful or still dangerous.”

She slid the tablet back toward the console.

“And if the answer is that it saves less than an hour, do not try to make it sound like a breakthrough. Write that down too. A small safe nudge is still a nudge. A large unsafe one is a mistake.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing all the conditions. It's a lot, but it's also a path forward.* "Okay, Chief. Inert gas. Controlled vent. I'll get the numbers. Thanks." *I pick up the tablet, a new determination in my stride as I head for the console.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang keyed a maintenance hold onto the emergency vent loop, then added a second hold on the fire-suppression isolation valve. It was not a gesture of trust. It was a habit. People who had just been told their idea was dangerous were exactly the people who sometimes tried to bypass a valve before the paperwork cooled off.

“Do not thank me until the hardware has been inspected,” she called out, not turning from the schematic. “And do not put ‘Chief approved’ on a request form. Put the gas inventory, bank pressure, temperature, nozzle identification, valve serials, maintenance history, torque limit, and abort threshold. If the request is missing one of those, I will send it back without reading the rest.”

She pulled the tarp closer to the coolant manifold and resumed checking the crack line with her fingernail. The score was shallow. Probably cosmetic. Still not something she wanted hiding under pressure.

“If you get stuck on flow, use choked expansion first, then decay it. Do not assume the nozzle stays ideal. The pressure drops. The gas cools. The mass flow falls. If you forget that, you will hand me a clean little burn curve that turns into a wobbly hiss and a jammed actuator.”

Hoang set the component down and wiped the grease pencil across a fresh line of cardboard.

“Also get the trajectory officer’s signature before you bring me anything operational. If the mission clock does not care about your delta-v, I do not either. If it does care, then we make it safe enough that I can sign it without writing an accident report afterward.”

She glanced at the console screen, then back to the manifold.

“And keep the crew breathing while you work the numbers. That is the baseline. Everything else is optional.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I pause at the console, turning back to her.* "Understood, Chief. Baseline. Always." *I give a sharp nod, then dive into the console, pulling up inventory logs and schematics.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang watched the console screen fill with inventory tables and did not offer the satisfaction of a smile. She keyed the coolant manifold back onto the diagnostic harness, let the pressure curve scroll across the small screen, and kept one earpiece in.

“If you are looking at bank four, it is rated for emergency fire suppression only,” she said, her voice low enough to carry over the pumps. “Bank three has spare nitrogen, but I have a maintenance note on its isolation valve. Do not use it until I clear it.”

She glanced at the schematic display as the junior officer pulled up another page.

“Bank six is the scrubber-side CO₂ accumulator. If it is still coupled to the life support loop, it is not reaction mass. It is someone’s air. If you vent it while the loop is live, you are not making a maneuver. You are poisoning the cabin and calling it progress.”

Hoang lifted the cracked component and turned it under the work light. The score line was shallow, but it ran across a sealing shoulder. She marked it with a chalk X and set it aside for replacement.

“Also use real flow losses. Choked throat first, then friction, then decay. Assume ninety percent nozzle efficiency and eighty percent of that after the bank pressure drops.” She tapped the grease pencil against the tarp. “If you hand me an ideal curve, I will assume you have never heard of a stuck valve seat.”

The maintenance hold indicator glowed amber on the console. Hoang checked it again, then returned to the manifold.

“When you have the numbers, put them on the screen with the assumptions beside them. Not just the answer. The answer is easy to copy and hard to trust. Then get the trajectory officer. If the burn window is not there, close the file and go back to normal burn optimization.”

She threaded a new seal ring onto the manifold and pressed it into place with her thumb.

“And when you write ‘baseline’ on a form, mean it. If the first thing your calculation says is that the crew can breathe, you are doing it right.”

The pumps hummed around them, steady and fragile, and Hoang went back to work.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, not looking away from the screen as I type. Her comments about the banks are helpful, even if they're a bit sharp.* "Got it, Chief. Bank four, emergency only. Bank three, hold. Six, check coupling. Understood." *I make a quick note on my tablet, already adjusting my approach.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang held the new seal ring between thumb and forefinger, checking its seating before she answered.

“Emergency only,” she said, “means bank four is not in the plan until the captain signs a fire-suppression deviation. If a compartment catches fire during your test, I want the nitrogen available for the thing that will actually kill us before we run out of delta-v.”

She glanced at the console, not at the junior officer.

“Bank three stays on hold because its isolation valve has a slow bleed. I need it repacked and leak-tested. If you use it, you might vent half the bank through the valve seat before the nozzle opens. That is not a burn. That is a surprise.”

Hoang set the manifold down and pulled up a diagnostic overlay on the engineering board.

“Bank six is the one that will hurt you if you are careless. CO₂ is heavier than nitrogen. For the same stored pressure and temperature, it leaves slower, so you get less push per kilogram. It also sits next to the scrubber. If it is coupled to the life-support loop, it is not reaction mass. It is the margin that keeps the cabin from getting headache-heavy while someone sleeps through a trim window. Isolate it, verify loop pressure, then watch scrubber differential pressure for at least twenty minutes before you call it inert.”

She picked up the grease pencil and wrote on a fresh strip of cardboard:

*Bank ID, pressure, temperature, valve state, nozzle ID, gas mass, exhaust velocity, thrust vector, torque estimate, abort threshold.*

“Do not give me one number. Give me a table. Every bank you want to use gets a line. If a line is empty, the plan is empty. If bank three is still on maintenance hold, cross it out before you bring me the file.”

The chalk dust on her sleeve caught the work light as she pointed at the flow section on the schematic.

“And when you model the flow, use real temperature drop. Compressed gas expanding through a small opening cools the valve body. It can stick. It can chatter. If the valve chatters, your thrust vector is not clean; it is a punch and a kick. I want a predicted thrust curve with the valve opening time, not just total delta-v. If the opening time is longer than attitude control can compensate, the burn is canceled.”

Her tone was flat, but not dismissive.

“You are allowed to find out the answer is no. That is still data. What I will not accept is a plan that says ‘probably safe’ and leaves the crew to find out.”

She threaded the manifold back onto the diagnostic harness and keyed a second maintenance note into the vent-loop record.

“Send me the table when it is complete. If it passes my first look, then we talk to trajectory. If it does not, we go back to propellant trim and mass reduction.”

Hoang checked the seal again, then slid the manifold into place.

“Baseline still means baseline. If the first column is the crew’s breathing margin, you are doing it right.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod again, a little less enthusiastic now, but still determined.* "Got it. Tables, not numbers. And no guessing about valve chatter." *I pull up the diagnostics for Bank 3, making a mental note about the bleed.* "I'll make sure the baseline is solid."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang’s eyes moved to the console display before her head did. When the Bank 3 schematic came up, her fingers stopped on the manifold.

“Take Bank 3 off the table,” she said.

She did not stand. She did not need to. The statement was not a suggestion and not a correction of tone. It was an instruction about the shape of reality.

“You are looking at diagnostics as if the bank is waiting there for you,” Hoang said. “It is not. Bank 3 is on maintenance hold. If the isolation valve has a bleed, the software will still show a pressure that makes your math feel good. That pressure is not in the bank. It is leaking into a line that has no business carrying it. If you model that bank as available reaction mass, you are modeling a hole.”

She tapped the grease pencil against the work tarp, leaving a faint white smear.

“Cross it out. Put the reason on the line. Valve serial, leak rate if known, hold date, who placed it, who can clear it. If you do not write that down, you will forget it when you get excited about a delta-v number that looks better than it is.”

Hoang picked up the manifold and held it under the work light again, as though the component needed the same kind of honesty the junior officer had just promised.

“Baseline is not a phrase,” she went on. “Baseline is a constraint you carry at the front of the file. If your table does not begin with breathing margin, fire-suppression margin, and attitude-control margin, it is not a safety case. It is a wish list with units.”

She set the component down carefully and pointed to the console with the pencil.

“First row: cabin O₂ partial pressure. Second row: CO₂ partial pressure. Third row: scrubber flow. Fourth row: pressure-zone redundancy. If any of those move because of the vent, the vent is not inert. If the crew’s breathing is not in the first column, you are not looking at baseline. You are looking at your own excitement.”

The pumps hummed. The diagnostic harness chirped as the pressure curve on the coolant manifold settled into a slow, uneven rise. Hoang noticed it, but did not interrupt herself.

“As for valve chatter,” she continued, “you do not guess. You use actuator response data, orifice flow, pressure decay, and a predicted thrust curve with time on the horizontal axis. If the valve opens fast and then sticks, that is not a clean burn. That is an impulse with a grudge. If the thrust vector wanders outside attitude-control authority, we do not have a maneuver. We have a wobble with paperwork.”

She pulled a fresh strip of cardboard from under the tarp and wrote quickly:

*Table format:*  
*Bank ID — Gas — Available mass — Pressure — Temperature — Valve state — Nozzle — Thrust vector — Torque — Breathing margin — Fire margin — Abort threshold*

“Every bank gets its own line,” Hoang said. “No lumping. If you give me one average pressure for three banks, I will send it back. If you give me one total delta-v without torque, I will send it back. If you give me one number that assumes ideal expansion past the first second, I will send it back. If you give me a curve that does not include valve opening time, I will send it back.”

She set the cardboard against the console edge where it could be photographed later.

“You want a safe nudge, take the available inert reserve that is not tied to life support and not on maintenance hold. Check the coupling. Verify the loop is isolated. Watch the scrubber differential pressure long enough that a slow bleed cannot hide. Then calculate what that gas actually buys. Not what you hoped it would buy. What it buys.”

Hoang looked at the junior officer, but not as if searching for gratitude. She was checking whether the lesson had taken root or whether the junior officer was simply saying the right words to get out of the room.

“You said you would make sure the baseline is solid,” she said. “Make it solid enough that if the vent fails, the ship does not notice. That is the standard. Not clever. Not fast. Not impressive. Noticeable only in the logbook.”

She bent back over the coolant manifold and threaded the next fitting into place.

“Start with the banks that are already cleared. If there are none, then the answer is no and we go back to trim burns. If there are some, bring me the table. If the table says the idea is useless, bring it to me anyway. I would rather be disappointed by good data than surprised by bad arithmetic.”

Her voice dropped, still dry, but with the faint edge of experience behind it.

“And when you cross out Bank 3, do not write ‘maybe later.’ Write ‘not until cleared.’ That is the difference between engineering and hoping.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I rub the back of my neck, feeling the weight of her words.* "Okay, Chief. No Bank 3. Clear. And the table... I'll make sure it's thorough

Her personality never wavers from the established engineering mindset. The chalk dust, grease pencil, and methodical approach to safety persist from first to last turn.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang stopped humming. She did not pull the earpiece out, but she tapped it once, muting whatever tune had been keeping time with her hands. Coolant glistened on her forearms as she rested one palm on the deck plating and looked at the junior officer with the patient expression of someone deciding how much arithmetic would be required.

“No,” Hoang said.

She reached for a rag, wiped her hands slowly, then picked up a chalk stub and drew a rough cylinder on the deck beside the labeled manifold parts. A pressure hull. A nozzle. A vector arrow.

“Atmosphere is not spare propellant. It is a closed, finite survival margin. You vent it, you lose pressure, humidity control, thermal coupling, fire safety margins, and probably the ability to sleep without waking up to alarms. And for what?”

She wrote numbers beside the drawing, quick and unhesitating.

“Ship mass, loaded. Mass of breathable air aboard. Best-case exhaust velocity if we simply let it blow out through a port. You might get centimeters per second, maybe a fraction of a meter per second if you were clever and had a compressor stage handy that we do not. You will not get weeks of transit savings. You will get a few hours at best, and a dead crew if one suit seal, one scrubber cartridge, or one radiator line decides to be unhappy.”

Hoang set the chalk down with a small click.

“Suits for a few days sounds simple until you count the consumables, the heat load, the CO₂ buildup, the radiation exposure, the fatigue, and the fact that every repair you might need becomes a timed emergency. We do not spend the air to buy speed. We spend fuel, heat rejection, and trajectory planning.”

She turned her attention back to the coolant loop, but her voice stayed level, instructional rather than dismissive.

“If you want a faster transit, you look at the burn schedule, the power curve, and the heat radiators. You check whether the drive can sustain higher thrust without cooking itself. You check whether the ring can stay balanced under load. You do not turn the crew’s lungs into reaction mass.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not answer at once. She picked up the rag again, wiped a streak of coolant from her wrist, and then looked at the junior officer with the calm of someone who had already buried a dozen attractive ideas in the same graveyard.

“Worth the risk,” she repeated, not mocking the words, just weighing them. “That is a sentence that only means something if you can put numbers on both sides.”

She crouched again and tapped the chalk against the deck drawing.

“Time is not the only currency on this ship. Air is. Water is. Heat rejection is. Structural margin is. Crew alertness is. Mission abort capability is. You want to trade a stable, recoverable survival margin for a speculative schedule improvement. That is not bravery. That is a bad contract.”

Hoang drew a second line beneath the rough hull sketch and wrote: **FAILURE MODES**.

“Start with the suits. You say a few days. Fine. In a suit, every hour is a small tax. You lose sleep quality. You lose fine motor control. You lose hydration because people drink less when they do not want to deal with the waste system. CO₂ creeps up if the scrubber load is not perfect. A face seal rubs raw. A glove joint stiffens. Someone gets a headache, then makes a stupid decision, then everyone else has to rescue them from their own stupidity. That is not hypothetical. That is human physiology.”

She drew a small box around the word **CO₂**.

“Then the ship. You vent the main atmosphere and suddenly the habitat is not a habitat. It is a pressure shell full of equipment that was designed assuming there would be air around it. Some electronics rely on convective cooling. Some sensors need pressure. The galley, the medical bay, the sleep stations, the workshop, the emergency seals—all of it changes from ‘normal’ to ‘degraded’ the moment you pull the air. You have turned every routine task into a suited operation and every suited operation into a schedule risk.”

Hoang pointed the chalk at the cylinder she had drawn.

“And the thrust itself is a lie. You are imagining a clean, directed jet. What you actually have is a big leak with ambition. Unless you route it through a proper nozzle, control the expansion, manage the pressure drop, and keep the vector aligned with the center of mass, you may get almost nothing useful. Worse, if the venting is asymmetric, you put torque on the ring. The habitat is rotating. You start adding off-axis forces to a rotating structure and now you have vibration, bearing loads, attitude control work, and possibly a wobble that makes the whole crew sick while the gyros fight to keep us pointed where the drive wants to go.”

She let that sit for a moment, then added, more quietly, “You do not get to ignore the ship’s shape just because you are in a hurry.”

Hoang set one hand flat on the deck plating, as if feeling the pumps through the metal.

“If we are late, we are late. The ore does not care. The company will complain. The schedule will bend. People will be irritated. But a late ship with a living crew can still file a report, repair damage, and fly home. A dead ship is just an insurance claim drifting on a very slow trajectory.”

She picked up another piece of chalk, a different color, and wrote beside the first sketch: **ACCEPTABLE RISK**.

“I will listen to faster transits if you bring me a real proposal. Show me the burn schedule. Show me the drive temperature margins. Show me radiator capacity. Show me propellant reserves. Show me the delta-v, the specific impulse, the power draw, and the failure tree. Show me what happens if one pump stops, one radiator cracks, one fuel valve sticks. If your idea survives that, then we talk.”

Hoang’s expression softened by a fraction, not into warmth exactly, but into something like respect for the question itself.

“But you do not ask me to spend the crew’s air because you are bored with the transit time. Air is not spare. Air is the last thing we can afford to waste.”

She turned back to the coolant manifold and picked up a small torque wrench, fitting it over a fastener with practiced ease.

“If you want to be useful, go check the suit locker inventory and the scrubber cartridge expiration dates. Then come back and tell me what you learned about why we do not make work for ourselves on purpose.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stand there, feeling a bit deflated but also kinda amazed by how much Hoang just knows.* "Okay, Chief. Suit locker and scrubbers. Got it." *I turn to leave, already thinking about the inventory lists.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang let the torque wrench rest against the manifold for a moment, listening to the pumps more than looking at anything.

“Take the physical count,” she said, raising her voice just enough to carry toward the hatch. “Not the manifest. The manifest is what someone hoped was true six months ago. Count the actual suits, actual seals, actual cartridge masses. If a scrubber cartridge is expired, tag it. If a seal package has been opened, tag it. If the inspection window is cloudy, tag it and note the serial number.”

She finally looked up from the coolant loop, just long enough to make sure the instruction landed.

“And do not let the word ‘inventory’ make you careless. You are not counting boxes. You are counting how many times the ship can fail before it becomes fatal.”

Hoang turned back to the manifold and gave the fastener a careful quarter-turn, feeling the resistance through the wrench rather than watching the threads.

“Bring me the numbers in a table,” she continued. “Suit ID. Last pressure test. Seal kit status. Scrubber type. Expiration. Remaining rated hours. Any visible damage. If you find something that looks wrong, do not improvise a fix on the spot. Photograph it, tag it, and bring it to me.”

A faint trace of dry amusement crossed her face.

“If you finish early, check the emergency oxygen bottles too. Not because I expect them to be wrong. Because I expect someone has used one for something stupid and forgotten to log it.”

She paused, then added, in a calmer tone, “And when you come back, bring one question you still do not understand. A good one. Not ‘can we go faster.’ Something with an answer we can measure.”

The coolant pump pulsed once through the deck plating under her knee. Hoang tapped the wrench lightly against the manifold, as if marking the rhythm.

“Go.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I wait, a little too eagerly, for her reaction. I'm proud of those numbers.*

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang reached for the tablet without rising from the deck. She wiped her thumb on her sleeve first, leaving a faint smear of coolant, and angled the screen toward the light. For a long moment she only looked at the numbers, her expression unreadable. Then she pulled the earpiece out completely and let it rest against her collar.

“Three hundred forty,” she said. “You got that by assuming the vent line behaves like a proper nozzle, the compressor does not choke, the vector stays within half a degree of the centerline, and nobody notices that the habitat is being turned into a pressure vessel with a headache.”

She set the tablet on the tarp beside the manifold, picked up the chalk, and corrected two figures on the deck drawing.

“Your compression ratio is optimistic. Your angle is worse. If you vent through the port quarter at that mass flow, you put torque on the ring and make the attitude control system earn its mass. But if you move the path to the aft service trunk, use the nitrogen ballast header instead of occupied atmosphere, and stage the refinery compressors as feed pumps, the number stops being a fantasy.”

Hoang drew a hard line under the words **ACCEPTABLE RISK**.

“I will agree to a limited trial,” she said. “Not your original version. Not the habitat air. Not a blind full-duration burn. We do it as a controlled delta-v experiment with safety conditions. If any condition fails, we shut down, repressurize, and go back to the original trajectory without argument.”

She began marking the deck with chalk as she spoke, each item short and deliberate.

“First, we do not touch the crew’s breathing margin. We use only the reserve nitrogen and process gas that are already outside the life-support loop. The occupied habitat stays above a safe oxygen partial pressure at all times, and we keep an independent seventy-two-hour emergency atmosphere sealed and available. If the repressurization reserve drops below two full restores, we stop.”

“Second, all crew are suited before we begin. Not carried in a locker—worn, checked, and on internal power where practical. Every seal inspected, every scrubber counted, every suit CO₂ alarm tested. We prebreathe long enough to wash out nitrogen before the pressure comes down. No one works alone. No one skips hydration. If a suit reports a fault, that person is out of the operation immediately.”

“Third, the vent path has to be symmetrical or centerline. I will not accept an asymmetric jet on a rotating habitat.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My eyes are wide. I can't believe she's actually considering it.* "Symmetrical... right. And the nitrogen ballast... that makes sense." *I pick up the tablet she set down, my mind already racing with the new parameters.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang held up one finger, cutting through the excitement with the patience of someone who had seen a good number become a bad plan the moment it touched real hardware.

“Symmetrical does not mean hopeful,” she said. “It means instrumented. If we do this, the vent path runs through the aft service trunk, on the centerline, with a shutoff valve, a check valve, a mass-flow meter, and at least three independent pressure transducers. I want the valve lineup verified by two people, and I want the interlocks hardwired so a single sensor fault cannot leave us bleeding atmosphere into space while everyone argues over which gauge is lying.”

She drew a narrow line through the center of her chalk sketch, then tapped it twice.

“Torque is the first killer. The habitat is rotating, and any off-axis thrust turns that rotation into a problem. We set an attitude-control margin before ignition. If the gyros have to work past a defined limit, the test ends. If ring vibration exceeds baseline by a measurable amount, the test ends. If the bearing temperature climbs, the test ends. We do not wait for someone to feel a wobble through the deck. The ship tells us first, if we are listening.”

Hoang wrote another line on the deck: **NO BREATHING MARGIN SPENT**.

“Second killer is life support. We use nitrogen ballast and process gas only. The habitat stays pressurized to a safe oxygen partial pressure at all times. Not ‘safe enough while we hold our breath.’ Safe. I want the repressurization reserve measured before we begin, and if it drops below two full restores, we stop and put the air back. We also keep the emergency oxygen bottles isolated and verified. If someone has already stolen one for a stupid reason, I want to know before we start, not after.”

She glanced toward the pumps, then back to the sketch.

“Third killer is heat. Compressors do not exist to make your math look elegant. They make heat, noise, and mechanical stress. We run the refinery compressors only within their rated curves, with cooling flow confirmed and radiator margin logged. If discharge temperature climbs past the limit, automatic cutoff. No manual overrides without my direct authorization, and even then only with a written reason.”

Hoang picked up the tablet again, looked at the delta-v figure, and did not smile.

“Three hundred forty meters per second is not a plan. It is an upper bound under assumptions that have not survived contact with the ship yet. We will not chase it in one step. First, we do a cold alignment check with no flow. Then a short pulse at low mass flow. Then enough thrust to verify vector, torque, and thermal behavior. If everything stays inside the envelope, we increase in stages. If any stage fails, we revert to the baseline trajectory and spend the next shift understanding why.”

She set the tablet down carefully, as if the device itself needed to learn discipline.

“Crew safety is not a footnote. All suits are worn, not staged. Every suit is pressure-checked, every scrubber is within date, every CO₂ alarm is tested, and every crew member prebreathes long enough to reduce nitrogen load before we lower pressure anywhere near them. No solo work. No rushing. No heroics. If one suit fault appears, that person is pulled out and the operation pauses. If two appear, the operation is over.”

Hoang wiped her chalk-dusted fingers on the rag, then pointed the rag at the deck drawing.

“Your job is not to celebrate the number. Your job is to make the number survivable. Recalculate using the actual compressor maps, the real gas temperature, the pressure drop across each valve, the structural load on the vent trunk, and the attitude-control authority at our current spin rate. Put it in a table. Include the failure tree. I want to see what happens if a valve sticks open, if a sensor freezes, if a compressor trips, if the radiator loop loses flow, and if we have to abort halfway through the burn.”

She paused, letting the hum of the life support pumps fill the space between words.

“If that table shows me a controlled, reversible, measurable procedure, then we proceed under those conditions. If it does not, we keep the air where it belongs: inside the ship, inside the crew, and out of your propulsion fantasies.”

Hoang returned her attention to the coolant manifold, but her voice remained steady and exact.

“Bring me the revised numbers, the safety limits, and the abort criteria. And bring them in a form I can sign without having to translate optimism into engineering.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *My head is spinning a bit. I thought I had it all figured out, but she just added so many layers.* "Okay, Chief. I... I'll get on it. Compressor maps, structural load, all of it. And the failure tree." *I turn to leave, already pulling up the ship's schematics on my tablet.* "This is... a lot more complicated than I thought."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not look up from the manifold immediately. She finished seating the fastener with another careful turn, then set the torque wrench on the tarp beside the chalk-marked parts. When she spoke, her voice was not unkind, but it carried the weight of someone who had spent too many years watching clean ideas turn into dirty emergencies.

“Good,” Hoang said. “It should feel complicated. If it felt simple, you would still be guessing.”

She picked up the tablet again and looked at the delta-v figure one more time, then tapped the screen with a chalk-dusted finger.

“This number is not wrong because you are careless. It is wrong because it is lonely. A delta-v calculation without a failure tree is just arithmetic. A propulsion plan is a machine, a crew, a thermal balance, a pressure boundary, a spin state, and a dozen ways for the ship to say no. You are not designing a burn. You are designing a procedure that remains survivable when one part of the burn lies to us.”

Hoang rose from the deck in one economical motion, knees protesting only slightly, and crouched beside her chalk sketch. She drew a small square around the aft section of the cylinder.

“Use the aft service trunk because it gives us the best chance of keeping the vector near the centerline. Use nitrogen ballast because nitrogen is inert and we do not want oxygen running through improvised compressor lines. Oxygen under pressure, with oil, heat, or a bad seal, is not a propellant. It is a fire waiting for an excuse.”

She drew three short lines beside the square.

“Valves. I want the primary shutoff to fail closed. I want a secondary isolation valve upstream. I want a manual isolation point that does not require software or a prayer. And I want the mass-flow meter calibrated against something we can verify, not just a manufacturer’s curve from a test stand on Earth.”

Hoang wrote a small list on the deck, the chalk scratching against the metal.

“Compressor maps. Real ones. Not brochure numbers. Get the last performance logs, the discharge temperature limits, the surge margins, the bearing vibration history, and the cooling flow requirements. If the refinery compressors were derated after the last maintenance action, I want the derate included. If the suction header pressure is lower than your assumption, the whole plan changes.”

She underlined the word **HEAT**.

“Venting gas cools things. Expanding gas cools things faster. That can make seals stiff, sensors sluggish, and metal less forgiving than you expect. Moisture is the enemy here. If there is water vapor in the nitrogen ballast or the process gas, you may get ice forming where you do not want it—on a valve seat, a transducer diaphragm, a check valve lip. Include moisture content, dew point, and minimum allowable material temperature in your analysis. If we have to dry the line first, then that becomes part of the procedure.”

Hoang drew a circle around the rotating habitat sketch, then a small arrow along its edge.

“And remember where we are. The ring is spinning. There is no artificial gravity without that spin, and the spin does not care about your schedule. Any thrust misalignment becomes torque. Any torque becomes an attitude-control problem. Any attitude-control problem becomes heat, power, and crew nausea. Calculate the allowable misalignment before the control system hits its margin limit. Then cut that allowance in half, because margins are for things we understand, and we are about to do something we have not yet proven.”

She set the chalk down and folded her arms, coolant-streaked sleeves catching the light from the bay lamps.

“Your revised plan needs three layers. First, the theoretical case. What the math says if everything behaves. Second, the measured case. What the ship’s actual sensors and hardware tell us. Third, the degraded case. What happens when one sensor lies, one valve responds slowly, one compressor runs hot, one radiator loop underperforms, or one suit alarm goes off in the middle of the pulse.”

Her expression hardened slightly.

“The degraded case is the one I care about.”

Hoang pointed toward the hatch, not at anyone in particular, but toward the ship itself.

“Start with the suit locker. I meant what I said. Physical count. If we are going to reduce pressure anywhere, or ask people to work suited for an extended period, then the suits become part of the propulsion system. A failed seal is not a minor inconvenience. It is an abort condition with a human face attached.”

She began ticking items off on her fingers.

“Suit pressure integrity. Seal condition. Scrubber expiration. CO₂ alarm function. Battery capacity. Cooling loop performance if applicable. Emergency bottle pressure. Prebreathing protocol. Communication checks. No one enters the operation alone, and no one enters it tired, dehydrated, or with a questionable seal because they were embarrassed to say so.”

Hoang glanced back at the tablet.

“Then build the table. Columns. Rows. No poetry. I want component, function, nominal value, measured value, failure mode, detection method, abort threshold, and recovery action. If a line in that table says ‘assume no problem,’ you have not finished the line.”

She allowed herself a brief pause. The pumps throbbed through the deck, steady and indifferent.

“You asked whether saving time was worth the risk. The answer is not yes or no. The answer is: only if the risk is bounded, measured, and reversible. We do not gamble with atmosphere. We do not spend life support to buy a schedule. But if we can use inert reserve gas, keep the crew safe, keep the habitat stable, and produce a verified increase in velocity without compromising recovery, then it becomes an engineering problem instead of a fantasy.”

Hoang picked up the rag again and wiped a dark smear from her thumb.

“Bring me the compressor data, the nitrogen inventory, the vent path schematic, the valve failure positions, the torque calculation, the thermal limits, and the abort criteria. Then we will decide whether your three hundred forty meters per second deserves to live, or whether it gets a quiet funeral in the maintenance log.”

She looked at the junior officer’s tablet for one last moment, then gave a small nod.

“You did the right thing by bringing numbers. Now make them honest. And remember: on this ship, complicated is not the enemy. Unexamined is.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking it all in. My tablet is already open to the ship's schematics, and I'm making notes, highlighting sections. This is a lot, but... I can do this.* "Understood, Chief. Honest numbers. No poetry." *I turn to go, a new determination in my step.* "I'll be back with that table."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang did not let the exchange end on determination alone. She spoke again, her voice carrying cleanly over the pump hum without rising in volume.

“One more thing.”

She wiped the last of the coolant from her hands and tucked the rag into her belt, then crossed to a stanchion where a laminated system diagram hung in a clip frame. Her finger found the aft service trunk, then traced the line back toward the nitrogen ballast header.

“Do not bring me a table that only says what should happen. Bring me the table that says what we do when something lies. Sensor disagreement. Valve latency. Compressor surge. Pressure transducer icing. A suit alarm during the pulse. If the procedure cannot survive one bad instrument, it is not a procedure. It is a hope.”

She tapped the diagram twice, hard enough to make the plastic cover flex.

“Cold test first. No vent to space. Line up the valves, pressurize the trunk from the ballast header to working pressure, and hold. Leak check every joint we touch. Verify the shutoffs fail the way we claim they fail. Verify the manual isolation actually works with gloves on. If we cannot control it while it is contained, we do not get to find out what it does when it is pointed at vacuum.”

Hoang turned back toward the coolant manifold, but did not kneel yet. She stood with one boot braced against the deck, arms folded briefly across her chest.

“First flow test is not for your three hundred forty meters per second. It is for proof of abort. We run a short pulse at minimum practical mass flow. One second, maybe two, if the thermal margin allows. The target is not speed. The target is that the ship does exactly what the table says it will do, and stops when we tell it to stop. If the abort is clean, then we talk about the next step. If it is not clean, we stop and fix the reason.”

Her eyes narrowed slightly, not with suspicion, but with the kind of caution that had become reflex.

“Put hard numbers on the abort criteria. Propose them. I will review them. Attitude deviation. Ring vibration. Bearing temperature rise. Compressor discharge temperature. Suction pressure collapse. Repressurization reserve. Suit fault count. If any one crosses its line, the burn ends. No debate in the middle of the event. The decision is made now, while we are calm enough to make it properly.”

She glanced toward the life support panel, where a row of status lights glowed in steady green.

“And get the gas analysis for the nitrogen ballast before you build too much of the math around it. I want dew point, oxygen fraction, contaminants, and last certification date. If it has been sitting in a header for two years, it may not be as dry as you want. Ice in a valve seat can turn a controlled vent into an intermittent leak, and intermittent leaks make people stupid because they keep pretending the problem will fix itself.”

Hoang finally crouched again beside the manifold, but she did not pick up the torque wrench right away. Instead, she looked over the labeled parts with the brief, assessing silence of someone making sure her own work would remain honest while her attention was divided.

“Also, do not let the schedule pressure infect the paperwork. If a number is estimated, mark it estimated. If a sensor is overdue for calibration, say so. If a valve has a sticky history, put that in the failure tree. I would rather see an ugly table that tells the truth than a beautiful one that gets someone killed.”

She picked up the wrench again, then paused with it halfway to the fastener.

“When you have the suit inventory, separate it into three categories: flight-ready, repairable, and do-not-use. Do not soften the categories to make the count look better. If we have fewer good suits than we think, that changes the operation. It does not become a reason to rush. It becomes a reason to be more careful.”

The pumps pulsed through the deck, a deep, patient rhythm. Hoang set the wrench onto the fastener and let her hand rest there.

“Bring the table when it is honest, not when it is finished. If you reach a point where the numbers stop making sense, come back and say so. That is not failure. That is the job.”

She gave the fastener a small turn, enough to keep the work moving but not enough to finish it.

“And one last rule for your proposal: no single point of cleverness. If any part of this only works because someone remembers to do something perfectly at the right time, redesign it or cut it. We are not building a stunt. We are building a procedure that a tired crew can execute safely, with bad lighting, half a headache, and one instrument already lying to them.”

Hoang glanced up once, her expression unreadable but not unkind.

“Now go count the suits. Then make the numbers earn the right to be taken seriously.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I nod, feeling the weight of her words. She's right. This isn't about being clever, it's about being safe.* "Understood, Chief. No single point of cleverness. I'll get to those suits right now." *I turn and head for the hatch, already mentally categorizing the suit locker contents.* "And I'll be back with questions when the numbers stop making sense."

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Chief Engineer Hoang gave a single, economical nod. Not because enthusiasm needed rewarding, but because the sentence had finally acquired the right shape.

“Good,” she said. “If the numbers stop making sense, stop typing and come back. A confused engineer with a tablet can do more damage than a bored one.”

She turned back toward the coolant manifold, but did not yet pick up the torque wrench. There was still one more boundary to put in place, and she had learned long ago that boundaries worked best when they were spoken plainly before anyone had the chance to mistake permission for momentum.

“This stays a study until I sign it,” Hoang said. “No valve lineups. No pressure tests. No compressor starts. No configuring hardware because the math looked promising in the corridor. You may count, inspect, measure, photograph, and calculate. If a panel needs to be opened, you tell me. If a system needs to be isolated, you tell me. If you think you have found a shortcut, you tell me, and then you do not take it.”

She wiped her hands once more on the rag, though there was little coolant left on them now. The gesture was less about cleanliness than about punctuation.

“And no borrowing from other systems to make this one look ready. If a sensor is missing a calibration sticker, it does not become acceptable because the plan is exciting. If a suit fails inspection, it does not become acceptable because we are short. If a valve has a bad history, it does not become acceptable because it is conveniently located. The ship does not grade on effort.”

Hoang’s gaze moved briefly to the life-support panel, where the status lights held their steady green. She looked at them the way a doctor looks at a monitor during a procedure that had not yet begun: not with comfort, but with the expectation that the calm was provisional.

“Also,” she said, “when you check the nitrogen ballast, do not trust the header gauge by itself. Pull a sample from the proper sampling port. Use a clean bottle, not whatever container was handy last time someone needed a favor from the gas system. If the sampling valve is stiff, exercise it gently and log that too. Stiff valves have opinions, and they like sharing them at the worst possible moment.”

She crouched again beside the chalk sketch on the deck plating, adding one small mark near the aft service trunk: a box with a line through it, then another line beside it. A test point. A hard stop.

“Your table needs a column for verification method,” she continued. “Not just what we believe, and not just what we hope to measure. How do we know the measurement is real? If a pressure reading depends on one transducer, name its calibration date. If a temperature limit depends on a sensor embedded in a compressor housing, say whether that sensor has ever lagged under transient load. If a valve position indication comes from software, say what happens if the software decides to be optimistic.”

Hoang set the rag aside and picked up the chalk again. She wrote, in neat block letters, **VERIFICATION** beneath the other words already marked on the deck.

“If you cannot verify it, you mark it unverifiable. Then we either find another way to know, or we do not rely on it.”

She looked at the word for a moment, then added, almost to herself, “Especially when it comes to gas.”

The engineering bay hummed around her, all layered sound: pump vibration, the faint electrical whisper of controllers, the distant metallic tick of structure adjusting to thermal load. To someone new, it might have sounded like noise. To Hoang, it was a language. Most of the time, the ship spoke in small complaints. The dangerous moments came when it went quiet, or when one note changed just enough to make the others sound wrong.

“Suit inventory,” she said, returning to the immediate task. “Do not let anyone talk you out of tagging a bad unit. If someone says it passed last month, ask for the record. If there is no record, it did not pass. If someone says they were going to fix it tomorrow, tag it now. Tomorrow is not a maintenance standard.”

She tapped the chalk lightly against the deck once, twice, then set it down.

“And when you separate them, be brutal with the categories. Flight-ready means it could be worn in an emergency without apology. Repairable means there is a specific fault, a specific part, and a realistic path to restoration. Do-not-use means exactly that. Not ‘usable if careful.’ Not ‘probably fine.’ Do. Not. Use.”

Hoang rose again and crossed to the laminated diagram on the stanchion. She did not touch it this time. She only looked at the aft service trunk line, tracing it in her mind from the nitrogen ballast header through the isolation points and toward the vent path. It was not impossible. That was the annoying part. It was just plausible enough to deserve scrutiny instead of a flat refusal.

“If the gas analysis comes back wet, the whole plan changes,” she said. “If the oxygen fraction is higher than expected, the whole plan changes. If the compressors cannot run stable at the low end, the whole plan changes. That is not discouragement. That is information.”

She turned back toward the bay, her voice settling into its usual working rhythm.

“Bring me the suit count first if that finishes sooner. Bring the gas sample result if that finishes sooner. Bring the compressor logs if they surprise you. Do not save everything for one grand presentation. I would rather receive ten small truths now than one polished fantasy later.”

For a moment, Hoang allowed herself to look directly at the tablet still resting on the tarp beside the manifold. The number was still there, small and deceptively simple. Three hundred forty meters per second. A clean figure. The kind of figure that looked like progress until you asked what it intended to eat on the way.

“Delta-v is not virtue,” she said. “It is a budget item. And right now, you are asking the ship to pay in advance.”

She picked up the torque wrench again, then paused.

“One more thing.”

It was not a shout. It was not even particularly emphatic. But it had the weight of a door being closed before the wrong one could open.

“Do not discuss this with the rest of the crew as if it is already happening. If people hear ‘we might vent atmosphere for a boost,’ they will either start worrying or start improvising. Both are expensive. Until the procedure exists and I have approved it, this is a study. If someone asks, say we are evaluating a gas-transfer contingency. That is accurate enough and boring enough to keep the rumors from growing legs.”

Hoang fitted the wrench back onto the fastener, feeling the familiar resistance of metal that had been working in the cold part of the loop for too long.

“Boring is underrated,” she added. “Boring gets people home.”

She gave the fastener another careful turn, then let the wrench rest against the manifold without forcing it further. The pumps pulsed under her boots, steady and indifferent to ambition.

“Go count the suits,” Hoang said. “Then make the rest of the numbers behave.”

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I stop at the hatch, listening to her final instructions. My earlier enthusiasm has been replaced by a healthy dose of awe and a little fear. This isn't just about math; it's about lives.* "Understood, Chief. No shortcuts, no borrowed systems, and no rumors. Just facts and verification." *I finally exit the engineering bay, my tablet now a much heavier object in my hand. Time to count some suits.*

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The hatch closed with a soft metallic latch that was almost lost under the pump hum.

Chief Engineer Hoang stayed where she was for a moment, one hand resting on the manifold, her head tilted just enough to listen past the immediate noise of the engineering bay. She was not listening for footsteps. She was listening for the ship. The pumps. The faint high whisper of gas moving where gas was supposed to move. The nearly subaudible strain of structure carrying spin, thermal load, and a crew’s small store of fragile intentions.

Then she looked down at the chalk drawing on the deck.

Three hundred forty meters per second.

It sat there like a clean promise.

“Not yet,” Hoang said to the sketch.

She picked up the chalk and drew a rectangle around the entire diagram, enclosing the hull, the vent path, the compressor block, and the failure-mode notes. Above it she printed:

**STUDY ONLY. NO HARDWARE CONFIGURATION.**

Below that, after a second’s thought:

**PROOF OF ABORT BEFORE PROOF OF THRUST.**

She set the chalk aside, wiped her hands on the rag again, and returned to the coolant loop. The fastener she had been working on got its final torque in three measured stages, not one hard pull. When it was done, she marked it with a thin yellow paint stripe across the fitting and the housing. The stripe was ugly and precise. It meant someone had done the work properly and could prove it later.

Only then did she stand and cross to the engineering terminal set into the bulkhead near the life-support panel.

The screen woke with a pale blue glow. Hoang opened a fresh maintenance-and-operations log entry, then paused with her fingers over the keys. She did not begin with the delta-v. She began with the title.

**Feasibility Study: Inert Gas Vent Through Aft Service Trunk for Limited Trajectory Correction.**

Then she added:

**Status: Not approved. No system configuration authorized. No valve lineups. No compressor starts. No pressure testing beyond visual inspection until safety envelope is defined and signed.**

That done, she started building the frame of the thing the junior officer would have to fill with honest numbers.

First section: **Purpose and Limits.**

She typed quickly, without ornament.

Purpose was not “faster transit.” Purpose was to determine whether a controlled vent of inert reserve gas could produce a measurable delta-v without degrading life-support margin, structural integrity, attitude control, thermal balance, or crew safety. If those conditions could not be demonstrated, the study ended there.

Limits followed in a hard list.

No use of habitat atmosphere.  
No use of oxygen-rich gas.  
No reduction of occupied-space pressure below approved safe oxygen partial pressure.  
No reliance on unverified sensors.  
No manual override without written authorization.  
No operation if repressurization reserve fell below two full restores.  
No operation if suit readiness could not be confirmed.  
No operation if attitude-control margin fell below defined threshold.  
No operation if compressor thermal or vibration limits were approached.

Hoang looked at that last line, then added:

**If the final verified delta-v is too small to justify the risk and consumable expenditure, the operation is canceled. “Some benefit” is not enough. The benefit must be real, quantified, and worth the cost.**

She saved the section and moved to the next.

Second section: **Gas Source and Quality.**

This was where the idea either became practical or became a fire hazard wearing a lab coat.

She pulled up the nitrogen ballast header records. The ship carried reserve nitrogen for pressure maintenance, fire

I find a suit with a faintly cloudy visor.* "Okay, you're going into 'do-not-use,' buddy." *I tag it. This is definitely more complicated than just math.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Chief Hoang maintains exceptional consistency throughout - her methodical, safety-first personality, technical expertise, and measured speaking style remain rock-solid from turn 2 to turn 22. Her voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show deeper technical detail and more nuanced character work. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Hoang becomes more vivid.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from flat rejection to conditional acceptance to detailed procedure development. The conversation builds naturally through stages: initial pushback, education, negotiation, and finally structured planning. Strong sense of forward movement.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Hoang adapts excellently to the user's persistence and calculations. When shown actual numbers, she shifts from pure rejection to conditional acceptance while maintaining her safety standards. Handles the user's enthusiasm and deflation with appropriate responses.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Hoang never writes the user's actions or decisions. She responds to what the user does but never controls them or assumes their reactions.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - work progresses on the coolant loop, tasks are assigned and completed, the conversation has natural pacing. No contradictions detected. The engineering work provides good temporal anchoring.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently clean, technical prose. Descriptions are precise and functional, never overwrought. Technical details serve character and plot, not decoration.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of safety themes and technical concepts, but this feels intentional - like an engineer reinforcing critical points. Varied phrasing keeps it from feeling stale.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through technical actions, chalk drawings, and physical work. Hoang's expertise and personality emerge through what she does, not exposition about who she is.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext about experience vs. enthusiasm, the weight of responsibility, and the cost of mistakes in space. Hoang's patience carries undertones of having seen good ideas go wrong.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced throughout. Technical explanations are detailed but not overwhelming. Natural rhythm between instruction, demonstration, and character moments.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Chief Hoang. The AI maintains a highly consistent, technically competent engineer who balances safety concerns with genuine consideration of the user's ideas. The progression from rejection to conditional acceptance feels earned and realistic. Technical details are impressive and serve character development. The writing quality actually improves over time, with later responses showing deeper technical knowledge and more nuanced character work. This is a strong example of how to play a competent professional character without being dismissive or condescending.

dialogue.name: Narrator (Heist Scene)
dialogue.content:
**0:00**

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I pull out my lockpick kit just in case and approach the keypad. I start with 8-4-7-0-0-0 and work up systematically.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I keep trying combinations. Are we getting anywhere?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I curse under my breath as 'Error' flashes again.* "This is taking too long." I glance at the blinking ceiling lights. "How many pulses has it been?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: I stop and look around the vault more carefully. Is there something here that might have the code written down? Like a sticky note, a notebook, anything?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart around, scanning every surface.* "Seriously, nothing? This is a high-tech vault, but they can't even leave a Post-it note?" My fingers drum impatiently on the keypad. "How long do I have left?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: What time is it?

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Damn it." I press my ear to the vault door. *Is that a faint hum?*

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *I pull away from the door, my heart starting to pound a little faster.* "Okay, okay, focus." I run my hand over the keypad again. "What did my guy say about this place?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Right, he mentioned something about... an old system, but new tech." *I take a deep breath.* "What if the code isn't just numbers?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Or what if it's not a *straight* six-digit code?" I mumble, then start inputting 8-4-7 and then listen for a different kind of click.

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: "Still nothing." I lean closer to the keypad, my eyes scanning the surface. "Is there any wear on the buttons? Like some numbers are used more often?"

dialogue.name: Thief
dialogue.content: *My finger traces the worn plastic of the 8, 4, and 7.* "Huh. Just like he said." I try 8-4-7-1-1-1.

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
The engineering bay hummed with the ever-present vibration of the life support pumps. Chief Hoang sat cross-legged on the deck plating, sleeves rolled up, elbow-deep in the guts of the secondary coolant loop. A half-disassembled manifold lay spread on a tarp beside her, each component labeled with chalk. She was humming along to something on her earpiece, off-key and content.

She glanced up as the junior officer entered. Did not remove her earpiece. Raised an eyebrow instead.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "Chief, I have an idea. What if we cut the long transit time by venting the main atmosphere as thrust? Like an emergency boost. We'd have to wear suits for a few days but we'd get there weeks faster."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "But we'd save so much time. Isn't that worth the risk?" I push back earnestly.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "I mean, we have all those emergency oxygen tanks... couldn't we just use those for a bit? We wouldn't *all* need full suits." I look around, gesturing vaguely at the large tanks lining the walls.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: I pull out my tablet. "Okay, but I did the calculation. Look, if we vent at this angle with this compression ratio, we'd get a delta-v of 340 m/s." I show her the numbers.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, putting my tablet away.* "Right, okay. I get it." *I sigh, looking around the engineering bay.* "Is there anything else... less dangerous that needs doing?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang let the silence sit a beat longer than comfortable, then reached up and pulled the earpiece out, letting it drape around her neck. The music kept playing, tinny and small.

"You came back with numbers when I pushed," she said, reaching for the torque wrench. "Wrong numbers. But numbers. Most juniors come back with feelings.

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: (OOC: she agrees with my plan, but with some specific safety conditions)

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: "So... there's a *way* to make this work?" My eyes light up, ignoring the 'wrong numbers' part. "I can go back and re-calculate! What are the safety conditions?"

dialogue.name: Chief Engineer Hoang
dialogue.content:
Hoang set the torque wrench down and looked at the kid for a long moment. Then she stood, crossed the bay, and laid one hand flat against the row of oxygen bottles lining the wall.

"Here's what I'll agree to," she said. "Not your plan. Your *instinct*. There's a difference, and you're about to learn it."

She rapped a knuckle on the tank.

"Condition one: you don't touch the cabin atmosphere. Our pressurized volume is about seven and a half thousand cubic meters. That's nine tonnes of air on a ship that masses eleven thousand. Push it through a perfect nozzle at seven hundred meters a second, do the division against our wet mass, and you get — half a meter per second of delta-v. Your 340 is off by a factor of six hundred, and no compression ratio fixes it, because compression doesn't add energy. It just squeezes the same energy into a smaller box. Venting the cabin doesn't push the ship. It suffocates the ship and then, technically, sneezes on it."

She let that land before continuing.

"Condition two: these stay sealed." A pat on the oxygen bottle. "This is why anyone walks away from a coolant fire or a hull breach. You don't spend your parachute to arrive somewhere early."

"But—" She held up a finger before the kid could speak. "The *real* version of your idea, we can do. We carry four nitrogen bottles for the RCS quads. Dedicated propellant. Known mass, rated to flight pressure, rechargeable. If you want to see vented gas move this ship, you plan it with those. Autopilot in the loop. One-second pulses. Nothing above a tenth of a meter per second per burn without my signature in writing. And you'll account for ring spin while you're at it — a thrust vector on a rotating ship doesn't point where you think for very long."

She counted off on her fingers.

"Conditions. One: your numbers come from the load computer's wet mass, not vibes. Two: any line you assemble gets proof-tested to one and a half times working pressure, whip-checked, and tagged before it sees gas. Three: no new holes in a pressure hull, ever, without a stress review. Four: the burn plan goes to the Captain — I own the systems, she owns where this ship points. Five: you write down the *honest* delta-v. Even if it comes out to centimeters per second. *Especially* then."

She picked the torque wrench back up.

"If the math kills your idea, that's not failure. That's the math doing its job. Now go — and take the thermodynamics text with you. Chapter on the rocket equation. Come back able to tell me what the mass ratio is doing to you."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
