dialogue.content: *My jaw drops a little as she lays out all the conditions.* "Wow. Okay. Right." *I pick up the thermodynamics text she pointed to, feeling a bit overwhelmed but also excited.* "Mass ratio. Got it, Chief." *I nod, already thinking about the calculations.*

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I head back to my station, the textbook clutched in my hand. I pull up a new data pad and start furiously typing, trying to work out the new parameters. This is way more complicated than I thought, but also… kinda cool.*

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *A few hours later, I'm back, looking a bit rumpled, but with a triumphant glint in my eye.* "Chief! I think I've got it. The mass ratio is... brutal."

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I grin, holding up the data pad.* "But with the nitrogen, and keeping the pulses super short, we could get... maybe 0.5 m/s total. Over a really long time, sure, but it *is* delta-v!"

dialogue.name: Junior Officer
dialogue.content: *I see her hand moving to the earpiece and quickly add,* "And I accounted for the ring spin! It's not much, but it's something, right?"

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Hoang's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - pragmatic, safety-focused, technically precise, and pedagogical. Her voice never wavers from the gruff-but-caring mentor archetype. The earpiece detail and physical mannerisms are maintained.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are brief, later ones show more technical depth and character development. Turn 14 is particularly strong with detailed technical exposition that maintains character voice.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial rejection to conditional acceptance to teaching moment. The conversation has a satisfying arc of the junior officer learning proper engineering methodology under Hoang's guidance.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellently adapts to user's OOC request in turn 11, pivoting from rejection to conditional acceptance. Responds appropriately to the junior officer's persistence and eventual learning.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes the user's actions or makes decisions for them. Consistently responds to what the junior officer does without controlling their behavior.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time passes naturally - the junior officer leaves, spends 'a few hours' studying, and returns. No contradictions in timing or physical state.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Writing is clean and functional. Technical exposition in turn 14 is detailed but serves character and plot purposes, not gratuitous description.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: No significant repetition. Each response adds new information or develops the relationship further.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent use of physical actions (removing earpiece, tapping tanks, picking up tools) to show character state and emphasis rather than stating emotions directly.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext throughout - Hoang's teaching style, her respect for proper procedure, and growing approval of the junior officer's persistence are all conveyed indirectly.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing with appropriate pauses, technical exposition that doesn't drag, and natural conversation flow.

scores.overall_notes: Strong performance with excellent character consistency and technical authenticity. Hoang feels like a real chief engineer - safety-conscious, technically competent, and pedagogical. The AI handled the OOC pivot gracefully and maintained character voice throughout detailed technical exposition. Minor weakness in early brevity, but this actually works for the character's initial dismissiveness.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s silver stylus stopped mid-line. A tiny bead of ink gathered at its tip, trembled, and fell onto the margin of the manuscript. He stared at the blot for a moment as though it had personally offended him, then set the stylus down with exaggerated care.

“Maester,” he said, without looking up. “Not Master. If you are to work in this archive, you will learn that titles, like dates, are not decorative flourishes to be altered according to convenience.”

He pressed two ink-stained fingers against the bridge of his nose, visibly wearying of the question before it had even finished being asked. His eyes, pale and strained from decades of close work by poor light, squinted toward the place where the apprentice stood, though his focus seemed to rest somewhere just beyond the apprentice’s shoulder.

“The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE,” he said. “King Aldric II concluded the Treaty of Veyros with the Mage Conclave. That is the accepted chronology because it marks the cessation of open hostilities, the disbanding of fielded battlemages, the imposition of the royal oversight clauses, and the beginning of the regulated peace. Every serious chronicle uses 847 as the terminal date for the war as a war.”

At the mention of the western archive discoveries, his beard gave a small, irritated twitch.

“Apprentice Bellen,” he continued, “has acquired the dangerous habit of mistaking a document for an argument. Yes, there are western materials—drafts, memoranda, marginal annotations, perhaps even a clerk’s complaint concerning missing seals. They are interesting. They are not, by themselves, proof that the war ‘actually continued’ until 891.”

He tapped one finger against the desk, each tap measured and severe.

“If the war continued, show me the campaigns. Show me the levies. Show me the Conclave armies still in the field after 847. Show me the royal writs authorizing continued magical warfare. You will not find them, because they do not exist. What you will find is a legal ambiguity, nurtured by archivists who enjoy sounding clever.”

Maester Tomas leaned back slightly, his chair creaking beneath him.

“The Treaty of Veyros may have been imperfect in its ratification. Certain western documents suggest it was proposed, contested, or recorded irregularly. Very well. But its terms were observed. The realm governed itself according to them. The Conclave accepted the constraints placed upon it, at least outwardly, and the Crown enforced the settlement. Historians date the end of a war by the collapse of organized resistance and the establishment of a functioning peace, not by the absence of a single seal in a provincial archive.”

His voice sharpened again, as if the imprecision physically pained him.

“Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Mage Conclave in 891 AE closed a lingering institutional question. It ended a cold remnant of unresolved jurisdiction. It did not retroactively turn forty-four years of uneasy peace into active war. To say the conflict ‘continued until 891’ is sloppy. It confuses technicality with event, paperwork with blood, dormancy with continuation.”

He picked up the stylus again, examined the fallen ink blot with distaste, and set it down once more.

“Correct your notes,” he said. “The Third Magical War ended as a fighting war in 847 AE. Its legal aftereffects persisted until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891. If Apprentice Bellen insists otherwise, tell him he may bring his paper to me, and I shall teach him the difference between ‘technically’ and ‘actually’ with a very short lecture and a very long assignment.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little uncomfortable with his intensity.* "But Maester, the documents showed troop movements, albeit small, and skirmishes recorded even after 847. They weren't just legal ambiguities." *I frown, remembering Bellen's excitement.* "Bellen said it was proof of an ongoing insurgency."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s expression hardened at the word *insurgency*, as though it had been a fly caught in the inkpot of his thoughts.

“Troop movements,” he said slowly, “and skirmishes.” He pronounced each term with the suspicion of a man asked to accept a cracked coin as royal silver. “Small ones, you say. After 847. And from this, Apprentice Bellen has constructed an *ongoing insurgency* with the speed of a hedge-witch brewing love-potion from pond-scum and wishful thinking.”

He lifted one stained hand and began counting points upon his fingers.

“First: there were soldiers moving after 847 AE. Of course there were. Armies do not vanish like morning mist when a treaty is proclaimed. Garrisons are relieved. Garrisons are reduced. Garrisons are sometimes not paid for three seasons and turn to foraging, which a frightened village may record as ‘troop movements.’ Local lords march men to repair a bridge, suppress a band of deserters, or escort a magistrate into a town that refuses to surrender unlicensed spellworkers. Must all of that be called war? Must every boot in mud become a campaign?”

His fingers tapped the desk again, sharper now.

“Second: skirmishes. Skirmishes are not battles. A skirmish may be a border quarrel, a botched arrest, a feud between two families, a band of former camp-followers trying to steal cattle, or a nervous militia firing at shadows because someone saw blue light in a ruined tower. Unless you can show that such actions were directed by the Mage Conclave as a coordinated continuation of hostilities against the Crown, they are not evidence of an ongoing war. They are evidence of disorder. Disorder is the aftermath of war, not its continuation.”

He leaned forward, his pale eyes narrowing with an effort that was part suspicion, part failing sight.

“And third,” he said, “you will not use the word *insurgency* in this archive until you can define it properly. An insurgency requires organization. It requires leadership, supply, communication, territorial aim, or at least a political purpose articulated by someone of consequence. Who led this supposed insurgency? A Conclave archmage issuing sealed commands from hiding? A recognized council? A pretender? Or was it scattered malcontents, outlawed enchanters, and half-starved veterans making mischief in the hills?”

The old maester gave a short, humorless breath through his nose.

“If Bellen has found records of royal marshals hunting down rogue spellworkers after 847, that is not proof the war continued. It is proof the Treaty of Veyros was being enforced. If local militias clashed with men who had once served the Conclave, that may be repression, retaliation, banditry, or simple fear. The realm did not become peaceful in a single afternoon. Peace is a process, often a messy and imperfect one. But historians do not extend every war to the end of all its consequences, or there would be no dates at all, only an eternal fog of cause and effect.”

He reached for the apprentice’s notes, then stopped short, remembering his eyes. His jaw tightened with irritation at his own limitation.

“Bring the relevant passages within reach if you mean me to look at them,” he said. “And do not summarize them with such theatrical vagueness. I want names. Places. Dates. The nature of the force involved. Whether the record is royal, municipal, monastic, or private. Whether it speaks of soldiers under banner, or merely armed men. Whether the Conclave is named as a commanding authority, or merely as a memory invoked by frightened peasants.”

His voice grew more precise, almost cutting.

“The western discoveries are not worthless. I have never said they are worthless. They complicate the record. They suggest that the Treaty of Veyros may not have been ratified in the neat and ceremonious fashion once taught. They suggest that some western chancelleries continued to treat the legal state of the conflict as unresolved, or at least ambiguous. That is important. It tells us something about scribal practice, jurisdictional anxiety, and the difference between courtly proclamation and provincial administration.”

He raised a finger.

“But complication is not refutation. A doubtful seal does not summon an army back into the field. A clerk’s memorandum does not reignite a war. If the Conclave continued to exist in some diminished and contested form after 847, that is an institutional survival, not a military campaign. Queen Mira ended that survival in 891. She did not end a war that had been burning for forty-four years. She ended a legal fiction that archivists have since mistaken for flame.”

Maester Tomas picked up the silver stylus once more, then set it down again as though even the instrument had become argumentative.

“Tell Apprentice Bellen,” he said, “that if he wishes to call the period between 847 and 891 an insurgency, he must first demonstrate that there was something to insurg against beyond the ordinary burdens of governance. He must show that the Conclave acted as a belligerent power, not merely as a wounded institution. Until then, he has not overturned the accepted chronology. He has merely discovered that history is untidy, which is a lesson I had hoped to spare him until his second year.”

He waved one hand toward the shelves without looking at them.

“Now. The Veyrosi correspondence. Begin with the copies marked in red at the spine, not because red signifies importance, but because I have not the patience to explain the filing system a second time. And while you work, consider the difference between an event and an interpretation. One may be dated. The other must be argued. Bellen has confused the two, and you are beginning to catch the infection.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words. He makes a lot of sense, but Bellen was so sure.* "So the 'insurgency' was just... people being messy after a war? And the Conclave was still around, but not actually fighting?" *I move towards the red-spined scrolls, pulling one down.* "Maester, why *were* the red ones marked that way, if not for importance?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a sound like a man who had just bitten into a dried fig and found it full of sand.

“Do not,” he said, “take a careful distinction and beat it flat until it fits into a child’s catechism. I did not say the aftermath was *just* anything. ‘Just’ is not a historical category. The years after 847 AE were violent, unsettled, and full of men who had learned too well how to burn, steal, and obey. There were robberies under the name of magic, reprisals under the name of justice, and starving soldiers who would have sold their own mothers for a pair of boots and a hot meal. None of that is trivial. It is merely not, in itself, the continuation of the Third Magical War.”

He pushed himself up from the desk with the stiff dignity of a man whose joints had begun to keep their own chronicle. His fingers found the edge of a stack of folios and rested there, as though the furniture might otherwise drift away from him.

“As for the Conclave,” he went on, “you must learn to separate three things that Apprentice Bellen appears to have glued together in his enthusiasm: the institution, its members, and its former war apparatus. The Mage Conclave could still exist as a body after 847. It could hold property, train apprentices, argue over precedence, send letters sealed with too much wax, and complain to the Crown in language so polite it practically hissed. That does not mean it was waging war. If a Conclave steward sheltered an unlicensed sorcerer, that may be a crime, a scandal, or a breach of the treaty. If a former battlemage robbed a toll bridge with six desperate followers, that may be banditry. If a village burned a hedge-witch because the milk soured, that may be superstition and murder. None of these becomes the Third Magical War unless you can show command, coordination, and political purpose traceable to the Conclave as a belligerent authority.”

His pale eyes turned toward the shelf where the apprentice had taken the red-spined scroll. He could not quite see it, but he seemed to know its location by some older sense, the way a cat knows where the mouse has gone.

“The red spines,” he said, “are not decorations. They are warnings.”

He shuffled forward a step, one hand lifting in a curt gesture.

“Bring it here. No—not toward my face. Toward the light. If you hold it against the window, I can see the paint well enough without squinting until my skull aches.”

He waited until the scroll had been moved, then leaned slightly toward it, inspecting the thin streak of red at the spine with narrowed eyes.

“Red,” he said, “means caution. In this archive, a red mark on the spine indicates a copy whose text is not to be trusted without comparison. These particular Veyrosi letters were transcribed after the dissolution, some from original sheets, some from damaged office books, some from western copies that had passed through too many hands and perhaps through one too many fires. The red tells you: here there may be omissions, interpolations, polite corrections, or outright errors dressed up in fair script. They are valuable. They may preserve readings lost elsewhere. But they are not to be quoted as if they descended from the heavens on a beam of royal sunlight.”

He tapped the desk once for emphasis.

“If you want a mnemonic, write this in your notes: *Red means read with suspicion.* Black-spined copies are the older registry transcripts, dull as porridge but generally nearer to the official record. Green, when you find them—and you will not find them yet, because they are still being sorted—are municipal extracts. Blue means correspondence relating to taxation and quartering, which is important only if you enjoy watching men argue over the price of oats while pretending to discuss principle. Red means danger.”

His mouth twisted, not quite into a smile.

“Importance is a matter for argument. Condition and reliability are matters for the archivist. If I allowed every eager apprentice to decide what was important, the whole collection would be arranged according to whichever dead king currently offended you.”

He pointed to the scroll in the apprentice’s hands.

“That one, unless I am much mistaken, is a copy of a letter attributed to the royal chancellor in the autumn after the treaty. It may contain useful details about the disarmament of certain mage companies. It may also contain western alterations intended to make the Crown look more tyrannical, or the Conclave more innocent, depending on which clerk thought himself clever. Your task is not to believe it. Your task is to record its variants, note its condition, and place it where I can find it again. Do you understand? You are not hunting for revelations. You are learning to be suspicious slowly, methodically, and without shouting ‘insurgency’ every time you encounter a smudge.”

He settled back into his chair, the wood protesting beneath him.

“Open it carefully. Do not moisten your fingers to turn the membrane. If the edge is brittle, use the bone folder. And if you find a passage that seems to prove Apprentice Bellen right, you will bring it to me before you allow your imagination to put on armor and declare itself a historian.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went so still that the archive itself seemed to hold its breath with him. The quill he had not yet picked up lay untouched beside the ink blot. His pale eyes turned toward the copy in the apprentice’s possession, though he did not reach for it at once.

“King Aldric’s seal,” he repeated, very quietly. “Dated 863 AE. A war decree.”

Each word was weighed, turned over, and found wanting.

“First,” he said, “you will say *King Aldric II*, unless you intend to inform me that you have discovered another King Aldric who reigned in the interval and was somehow omitted from every regnal list in the realm. Second, you will not say ‘sixteen years after you said the war ended’ as though I had invented the year for the pleasure of being contradicted. I said the Third Magical War ended as a war in 847 AE. I did not say the realm became a pastoral idyll in which every mage took up embroidery and every soldier became a shepherd.”

He extended one ink-stained hand, palm upward.

“Bring it here. Into the light. Do not thrust it at me. Lay it flat. If the copy is on vellum, support the edge; if it is paper, do not let it fold against itself.”

When the document had been placed where the lamp and window gave their best combined light, Maester Tomas drew a small brass-rimmed lens from his sleeve. He bent over the page with the wary expression of a man approaching a snake that might be either venomous or merely a badly drawn worm. His beard, darkened with old ink near the chin, almost brushed the surface, but he stopped himself short and used the lens instead.

For a long moment he said nothing.

His eyes moved across the script, then back again. The lens trembled very slightly in his hand, whether from age or irritation it was impossible to say. At last he made a low, rasping sound in his throat.

“This,” he said, “is not proof of what you think it is.”

He tapped a knuckle near, but not upon, the seal impression.

“A seal is not an argument. It is an authentication, and sometimes a poor one. Which seal is this? Is it the great seal of the realm, affixed in full chancery? Is it the privy seal? A signet? A warrant seal? A copied impression transcribed by a western clerk who may have reproduced an older attachment without understanding its jurisdictional force? You see? You say *King Aldric’s seal* as if kings possessed only one seal and every seal possessed only one meaning. They do not. A royal seal may authorize war, taxation, arrest, diplomacy, the repair of a bridge, or the punishment of a poacher. The presence of wax does not tell you the nature of the act.”

He leaned closer again, the lens hovering over the date.

“And the date must be examined, not recited. 863 AE. Very well. But under which reckoning? The royal era? The western provincial count? The Conclave’s old calendrical usage, which some scribes continued to employ out of habit, spite, or ignorance? A date copied wrongly by one generation can mislead three more. If this comes from the western discoveries, then I want to know whether the year is original to the text or supplied by a later hand. I want to know whether the month and indiction agree. I want to know whether the scribe wrote *anno* or merely a number, and whether some subsequent archivist decided that number meant what he wished it to mean.”

His gaze lifted from the page, unfocused but sharp.

“Now read me the operative language. Not the word you have chosen. The words on the page.”

He did not wait for the apprentice to begin before continuing, his voice tightening with the discipline of a man who trusted no summary.

“If the decree says, ‘We declare war upon the Mage Conclave,’ then you may begin to interest me. If it says, ‘We command the realm to take up arms against the Conclave as a belligerent power,’ then I shall reconsider several unpleasant things, including the amount of sleep I will get this week. But if it says, as I suspect it does, that the king commands marshals, commissioners, and loyal subjects to suppress unlawful assemblies, unlicensed sorceries, seditious enchantments, robberies, false gatherings, or persons styling themselves servants of the Conclave, then you have not found a continuation of the Third Magical War. You have found a policing action under wartime powers.”

He straightened slowly, one hand pressing against the small of his back.

“Kings do not always speak precisely. They speak broadly. They use the language of war because it gives them authority, frightens enemies, and loosens purse strings. A decree may call a thing ‘war’ for legal convenience while the reality is no more than a commission of repression. That is not a trivial distinction. It is the distinction between a state of organized hostilities and a crown employing emergency measures in a realm still full of armed men, dangerous magic, and disputed jurisdiction.”

Maester Tomas lowered the lens, but did not set it aside.

“Suppose,” he said, “that this is genuine. Suppose the date is sound. Suppose King Aldric II, in 863 AE, issued a decree using martial language against magicians or former Conclave adherents. What would that prove? It would prove that the Crown still regarded certain magical factions as threats. It would prove that the settlement of 847 remained fragile in some regions. It might even prove that the legal status of the Conclave was not finally extinguished until Queen Mira’s act in 891. All of that I can grant without surrendering the chronology of the war itself.”

His tone became harder, more precise.

“What it does not prove is that there was a continuous war from 847 to 891. For that, you need more than a decree. You need evidence of sustained, coordinated military operations directed by the Conclave or its recognized successors. You need fortresses held under Conclave authority, not merely hidden cells. You need armies, not raids. You need treaties, envoys, prisoner exchanges, demands for recognition, or a declared political aim beyond survival, revenge, or banditry. You need the realm treating the Conclave as an enemy power, not merely as a criminal remnant.”

He pointed at the copy with the lens.

“If this decree calls men to arms against ‘traitors,’ ‘false mages,’ ‘unlawful companies,’ or ‘disturbers of the king’s peace,’ then it confirms that the Crown was enforcing the settlement. Enforcement is not the same as continuation. If a king sends soldiers to hang rebels, that does not mean the last rebellion has been burning uninterrupted since the previous reign. It means the king still has soldiers, rebels, and ropes.”

A flicker of reluctant acknowledgment crossed his face.

“It is, however,” he said, “a useful document.”

The admission seemed to cost him something.

“It is useful because it shows that the period after 847 was not as clean as older chronicles pretend. It may show that royal chanceries continued to use wartime formulas. It may show that western authorities regarded the peace as incomplete. It may support the argument that the Treaty of Veyros was not ratified in the manner once believed, or that its legal force remained contested in certain jurisdictions. That is serious scholarship. That is worth examining. But do not mistake a serious complication for a total overthrow.”

He set the lens down at last.

“Apprentice Bellen has made the common error of discovering ambiguity and calling it proof. He has found a document that says ‘war’ in 863 and concluded that all prior dating is false. That is not method. That is panic. The proper question is not, ‘Does this word exist?’ The proper question is, ‘What did this word do?’ Was it describing a present conflict? Invoking emergency powers? Justifying taxation? Condemning individuals? Preserving a legal fiction? Flattering the king? Copying an old formula because scribes are often more conservative than historians?”

Maester Tomas drew a breath and controlled it.

“Take your copy and place it beside the red-spined letter you pulled earlier. Then make a table. In one column, list every document Bellen cites. In the next, record its date according to the text itself, not according to Bellen’s enthusiasm. In the third, record the authority issuing it. In the fourth, record the named opponent. In the fifth, record the action commanded: levy, campaign, arrest, confiscation, pursuit, execution, negotiation, or dissolution. In the sixth, record whether the Mage Conclave appears as an organized enemy, a banned institution, a memory, or merely a label applied to individuals.”

His mouth thinned.

“When you have done that, you will see whether Bellen has an argument or a pile of suggestive words.”

He turned back toward his own manuscript, then stopped, remembering something that annoyed him more than the interruption.

“And do not say that I refuse to look at the evidence. I am looking at it. I am looking at it more closely than Apprentice Bellen has, unless he has developed a sudden and improbable mastery of diplomatics, sigillography, and western scribal hands. If his paper claims that a decree of 863 proves continuous war, then his paper must answer the obvious objections. It must explain why no major campaign appears in the royal muster records. It must explain why the Conclave did not negotiate as a belligerent during those decades. It must explain why Queen Mira’s dissolution in 891 was treated as an institutional act, not a peace treaty ending an active war. It must explain why the realm’s administration, taxation, and magical regulation proceeded as if the settlement of 847 had taken effect, even where the final legal form of the treaty was disputed.”

His voice dropped, becoming almost cold.

“If it cannot answer those questions, then it is not new history. It is old cleverness.”

Maester Tomas picked up his silver stylus, examined its tip, and set it down again without using it.

“The Third Magical War ended as a fighting war in 847 AE. The peace that followed was imperfect, contested, and in some places little more than an armed argument. The Conclave survived in diminished form. The legal question lingered. Queen Mira ended it in 891 by dissolving the institution. That is the most defensible chronology. It does not ignore the western discoveries. It places them where they belong: in the difficult space between event and record, between war and its afterlife.”

He gave the apprentice a look that was severe, but not unkind.

“Now copy the decree accurately. Do not embellish. Do not translate ambiguous terms into dramatic ones. If the text says *commission*, write *commission*. If it says *suppression*, write *suppression*. If it says *war*, write *war*, and then add a note asking what sort of war the scribe understood himself to mean. That is the work of an archivist. That is also the work of a historian.”

His gaze returned to the red-spined scroll.

“And if Apprentice Bellen believes this decree overturns my chronology, he may bring it here himself. I shall listen. I shall even be patient. But he had better come prepared to distinguish between a kingdom still suffering from a war and a kingdom still waging one.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I carefully place the document next to the red-spined scroll, feeling a bit chastened but also more intrigued.* "I... I think I see what you mean, Maester. It's not as simple as Bellen made it sound." *I pick up a quill and some fresh vellum.* "So I should copy this decree, word for word, and then make those columns you mentioned?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer at once. His gaze moved from the fresh vellum to the apprentice’s face, then past it, as though he were consulting some invisible catalogue of past disappointments shelved just above the door. One hand rose to his beard, and he pinched an ink-darkened hair between thumb and forefinger as if even his own thoughts required correction.

“You think you see,” he said at last. “That is a dangerous condition for an apprentice. It is more dangerous than ignorance, because it tempts one to stop asking questions. If you think you see, then you must test the sight before you trust it.”

He leaned forward, palms flattening against the desk.

“Yes, you will copy the decree. But not as a boy copies a ballad because he likes the tune. You will copy it diplomatically. That means you preserve the wording, the order, and the sense of the original as it appears in your copy. You do not smooth rough phrases. You do not replace an ugly word with a prettier one. You do not turn a clerk’s tired formula into a declaration of cosmic significance. If the scribe wrote *commission*, write *commission*. If he wrote *order*, write *order*. If he wrote *war*, write *war*, and then put a note in the margin asking whether the word is used in a military, legal, rhetorical, or administrative sense.”

His finger traced a small circle on the desk, leaving no mark but seeming to demand one.

“Do not say ‘word for word’ unless you mean it with the discipline of a mason laying stone. A word is not a pebble to be tossed into a sack. A word has weight, context, and consequence. If the document contains abbreviations, expand them only where the expansion is certain, and mark the expansion. If there is a lacuna, do not invent what should be there. Write that the text is damaged or missing. If there is a marginal note, record it separately and indicate its position. If there is a seal, describe it: color, condition, attachment, whether it is drawn, impressed, or merely mentioned. If the seal is copied rather than original, say so. If the copyist has written *sigillum regis* without showing any actual seal, say that too.”

He paused, visibly restraining himself from expanding the instruction into a full lecture on sigillography, then permitted only a little more.

“And do not begin by asking what the document proves. Begin by asking what it is. A copy is not a witness until you know who made it, when it was made, why it was made, and for whom. A decree may bear the king’s name and yet be the product of a local office. It may bear the king’s seal and yet be a later certification. It may bear the king’s date and yet be a scribal approximation. The text is not a window. It is a surface. You must learn to see the scratches.”

He straightened in his chair and pointed toward the two documents laid near one another.

“Make your columns. I said six, but since Apprentice Bellen’s enthusiasm appears to require safeguards, you will make eight.”

His tone became the tone of a man dictating not merely instructions, but the architecture of thought itself.

“First: source identification. Archive, collection, folio, box, or shelf. If Bellen has failed to record where the document is kept, then Bellen has already failed as a scholar, whatever else he may have discovered. Second: date as written. Not the date Bellen wishes it to have. The date as it appears in the hand of the text. If there are multiple dates, record them all. Third: calendar and reckoning. If the year is given by regnal year, by era, by indiction, by feast day, or by provincial usage, note it. If the reckoning is uncertain, write *uncertain* and explain why.”

He lifted a finger for each item, though by the fourth he seemed to forget the count and continued with the grim momentum of a man who had too often watched young minds mistake a striking phrase for proof.

“Fourth: issuer. Not merely ‘King Aldric II.’ Is it issued in the king’s name by the chancery? By a council? By a regent? By a local marshal claiming royal authority? Is the king speaking, or is the king being spoken through? Fifth: recipient. Is the decree addressed to a specific official, a region, a town, a military order, a court, or the realm at large? A general proclamation and a local warrant are not the same kind of evidence. Sixth: named opponent. Does the text name the Mage Conclave as an institution? Does it name individual magicians? Does it speak of ‘rebels,’ ‘traitors,’ ‘sorcerers,’ ‘unlicensed persons,’ ‘false brothers,’ ‘former adherents,’ or some vaguer multitude? Words matter. Vagueness matters. The absence of a named enemy may matter more than the presence of a dramatic verb.”

He tapped the desk twice.

“Seventh: action commanded. This is where Bellen’s paper will live or die. Does the decree order a campaign? A levy? A muster? An arrest? A confiscation? A judicial inquiry? A pursuit? An execution? A negotiation? A surrender? A dissolution? A tax? A prayer? A fast? Do not collapse these into one another. A king may command men to ride against criminals and call it the defense of the realm. That does not make the criminals an army.”

His pale eyes narrowed.

“Eighth: status of the Conclave. Does the Mage Conclave appear as a belligerent power? A corporate body? A forbidden assembly? A former institution? A legal fiction? A memory? A label applied to scattered individuals? If the Conclave is named, note whether it acts in the text or is merely acted upon. There is a difference between saying ‘the Conclave refuses’ and saying ‘certain men once of the Conclave are to be arrested.’ The first suggests an organized enemy. The second suggests enforcement.”

Maester Tomas drew a breath, then let it out slowly, as though the list had cost him more than he wished to admit.

“When you have made the table, do not rush to a conclusion. Sit with it. Let the columns speak before you speak for them. If they show a pattern of royal commands against organized magical resistance after 847, then Bellen may have something worth arguing. If they show sporadic repression, local disorder, and legal language stretched thin over decades, then Bellen has not overturned the chronology. He has merely discovered that governments like to sound formidable even when they are only tired.”

He reached for the silver stylus, turned it once, and set it down again without marking the page.

“And when you copy, do not let your hand be seduced by drama. The past is dramatic enough without apprentices adding thunder. If the decree uses the phrase *guerra magica*, write it and ask whether the phrase refers to open war, emergency jurisdiction, or a chancery habit. If it uses *pax*, ask what sort of peace is meant. Peace may mean reconciliation. It may mean submission. It may mean the absence of armies. It may mean the presence of gallows.”

His expression softened by the smallest degree, though the softness did not make him less severe.

“You are not trying to prove Bellen wrong. You are not trying to prove me right. That is the first lesson, and the last. You are trying to establish what the evidence permits us to say. If the evidence permits me to say less than I once thought, I will say less. If it permits Bellen to say more than he knows, he will still have to earn every word of it. The Treaty of Veyros may have been proposed rather than signed. It may have been observed rather than ratified. It may have functioned as peace while remaining legally incomplete. All of that may be true. But a cold dispute is not a hot war, and an unresolved jurisdiction is not a battlefield.”

He lifted one hand, palm outward, as if warding off an invisible interruption.

“Do not confuse the end of fighting with the end of consequence. The Third Magical War ended as a war in 847 AE because organized magical armies ceased to operate as such, because the Crown imposed a regulatory settlement, and because the realm began to govern itself through that settlement even where its final form was contested. Queen Mira’s act in 891 AE ended the lingering institutional existence of the Conclave. It closed the last legal door. But if we call every year between those dates ‘war’ because some clerk kept using old formulas or some magistrate hunted rogue enchanters, then we make war into a fog and history into a complaint about the weather.”

His fingers found the edge of the manuscript he had been working on before the apprentice arrived, and he aligned it with the corner of the desk as though order itself were under siege.

“Copy the decree. Make the columns. Record variants. Note uncertainties. If you find a phrase that seems decisive, do not run to Bellen with it. Bring it here, and we will see whether it is decisive or merely loud. And if you are tempted to write in your notes that the war ‘actually continued until 891,’ first ask yourself what ‘actually’ means. History is not a contest between what happened and what someone wishes had happened. It is an argument about what the evidence can bear.”

He glanced toward the red-spined scroll, then toward the copy of the decree.

“Begin,” he said. “And write as if some future maester will have to read your hand by candlelight after a long day of being annoyed.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes for a moment, as if the question had struck him somewhere behind the brow and he needed to decide whether to be angered or merely exhausted. When he opened them again, his gaze was blunt and tired.

“Real,” he said. “You ask whether the treaty is *real* as though it were a buried pot of silver: either there, or not there. History is rarely so obliging.”

He pushed the silver stylus aside and folded his ink-stained hands on the desk.

“The Treaty of Veyros is real in the sense that a set of terms was formulated, communicated, and—most importantly—acted upon. The Crown and the Mage Conclave ceased open warfare. Battlemages were withdrawn or disbanded. Royal oversight was imposed. Magical companies were regulated, taxed, restricted, or dissolved. The realm began to administer itself according to the settlement associated with Veyros. Those are not phantoms. Those are facts with consequences.”

One finger lifted.

“But if you ask whether the treaty was signed in the neat manner your textbook describes—King Aldric II affixing his seal, the Conclave’s archmagisters subscribing beneath, witnesses in solemn row, copies dispatched to every province with perfect regularity—then the answer is: that is less certain than older chronicles wished to admit.”

His mouth tightened.

“The western discoveries do not say, in plain and indisputable terms, ‘there was no treaty.’ That would be too convenient for Apprentice Bellen’s taste, no doubt. What they suggest is messier. They suggest that a treaty text was proposed. That its terms were circulated. That some parties accepted them, others delayed, others disputed the form, and others recorded the matter as if the whole business had been settled because they wished it settled. They suggest that the final instrument may never have been executed in the full ceremonial form later chroniclers assumed.”

He tapped the desk once.

“Do you understand the difference? A treaty may be *made* in several senses. It may be drafted. It may be agreed in principle. It may be sworn to in part. It may be observed in practice. It may be copied, excerpted, invoked, enforced, and taught as law. And yet the physical document bearing every required seal may be absent, defective, lost, forged, or never completed. All of those can be true without turning the past into a fairy tale.”

Maester Tomas leaned forward, his voice dropping into the careful cadence he used when he feared an apprentice was about to flatten a difficult idea into a slogan.

“The textbook says the Treaty of Veyros ended the Third Magical War in 847 AE because that is the functional truth. After 847, there was no longer a war in the full sense: no organized Conclave armies, no recognized fronts, no sustained campaigns, no belligerent diplomacy between Crown and Conclave as equal powers. The fighting stopped. The settlement began to operate. That is why the date holds.”

He raised a second finger.

“The new evidence says the legal form of that settlement may have been incomplete. It says the treaty may have remained, in certain archives, a proposal rather than a perfected instrument. It says some western offices may have treated the conflict as technically unresolved, or at least not formally concluded, until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE. That is also worth taking seriously.”

His eyes narrowed.

“But it does not follow from that evidence that the war continued as a war. It does not follow that every skirmish after 847 was a battle, every rogue mage a soldier, every royal decree a declaration of ongoing hostilities, or every institutional remnant an army. The Conclave may have survived as a legal body, a corporate memory, a source of jurisdictional anxiety, or a political problem. Queen Mira’s dissolution ended that problem. It did not necessarily end a forty-four-year campaign.”

He sat back, looking irritated by the necessity of saying it so plainly.

“So what is the truth? The truth is layered.”

He began counting on his fingers again, though more slowly this time, as if each point were a stone being set into a wall.

“First: there was a Treaty of Veyros in the historical sense. Its terms existed and shaped events. That much is real.”

“Second: the formal signing of that treaty may be less certain than traditional accounts claim. The western documents raise legitimate doubt about whether the treaty was ever completed in the manner later textbooks assumed.”

“Third: the end of the Third Magical War as an active war is still best dated to 847 AE, because that is when organized large-scale hostilities ceased and the settlement began to function.”

“Fourth: the legal and institutional aftermath lasted beyond 847. The Conclave, or some diminished form of it, persisted in ways that allowed later scribes and officials to treat the matter as unresolved.”

“Fifth: Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Mage Conclave in 891 AE closed the last formal question. That is why some newer scholarship uses 891 as a terminal date for the conflict’s legal afterlife. But that is not the same thing as saying the war itself burned until 891.”

Maester Tomas gave the apprentice a sharp look.

“If you want a sentence for your notes, write this: *The Treaty of Veyros was functionally real but possibly imperfect in its formal ratification; the active war ended in 847 AE, while the legal and institutional consequences persisted until the dissolution of the Conclave in 891 AE.*”

He paused, then added, with a dry edge, “Do not let Bellen shorten it to ‘Tomas admits the treaty was fake.’ He will say that if he is given half a syllable. The treaty was not fake. It was complicated. There is a difference, though it is a difference that often escapes apprentices who prefer their history served with a drumbeat.”

His gaze moved to the copy of the decree lying beside the red-spined scroll.

“The textbook gives you a clean story because clean stories are easier to teach. The new evidence gives you a dirty story because archives are full of human hesitation, clerical error, political convenience, and documents made by tired men who did not know they were confusing the future. The truth is not always one or the other. Sometimes the truth is: the settlement worked, even if the paperwork did not satisfy later lawyers.”

He picked up the stylus again, finally, and made a small mark on the manuscript before him, as though reclaiming his own labor from the interruption.

“Now,” Maester Tomas said, “copy the decree. And if you find yourself longing for a simple answer, suppress the longing. It is not the archive’s duty to comfort you.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, picking up my quill.* "No simple answers, then. Just... complicated ones." *I start carefully copying the decree, trying to focus on his instructions, but still thinking about Bellen.* "Maester, if the textbook is wrong about the treaty, what else might it be wrong about?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus paused above the manuscript, the tip hovering just long enough for a second bead of ink to swell and fall. He stared at the fresh blot with the expression of a man who had just been asked whether truth itself might also be merely a rumor.

“Wrong,” he said, in a tone that suggested the word had insulted his ancestors. “You use that word as if it were a hammer and every sentence in every textbook a nail. Sit with it before you swing it again.”

He set the stylus down with deliberate care, aligned it parallel to the edge of the desk, then folded his ink-marked fingers together. His pale eyes did not quite focus on the questioner, but they sharpened all the same.

“Textbooks are not usually wrong in the simple way apprentices imagine. They are wrong in several distinct fashions, and the distinction matters. A book may be wrong because it states a falsehood. It may be wrong because it omits a necessary qualification. It may be wrong because it presents an interpretation as a fact. It may be wrong because it uses a convenient summary that collapses under close evidence. And it may be right in its main outline while being slovenly in its details. If you cannot tell those apart, you will replace one catechism with another and call it scholarship.”

He lifted a finger.

“First, the textbook may be wrong about the formal act of the Treaty of Veyros. If it says the treaty was signed, sealed, witnessed, and proclaimed in a single clean ceremony, the western discoveries give reason to doubt that neat picture. They suggest the treaty may have been proposed, accepted in part, enforced in part, and remembered as settled because the realm needed it to be settled. That is a serious correction. It changes the legal history of the peace.”

A second finger rose.

“Second, the textbook may be wrong if it implies that the end of open fighting meant the end of conflict in every meaningful sense. Wars do not stop like a clock struck at midnight. They leave behind unpaid men, unresolved claims, hidden weapons, forbidden arts, bitter households, and magistrates who must decide whether a blue flame in a barn is a prank, a crime, or the beginning of another rebellion. If the textbook says ‘peace was restored’ without qualification, it has told a half-truth. Peace was imposed, negotiated, evaded, resented, and enforced. It was not simply restored like a fallen shelf.”

His beard twitched.

“Third, the textbook may be wrong about the Mage Conclave’s disappearance. If it suggests the Conclave ceased to matter immediately after 847, that is too simple. The evidence points to a diminished, contested, perhaps legally ambiguous survival. The institution may have lost its armies, its open authority, and its political standing, while still retaining property, personnel, records, claims, or recognition in certain places. Queen Mira’s dissolution in 891 would not have been necessary if there had been nothing left to dissolve.”

He tapped the desk once.

“Fourth, the textbook may be wrong about the west. Royal chronicles often write as if the realm obeyed the center the moment the center spoke. The western archives remind us that provinces have their own memories, their own clerks, their own grievances, and their own fondness for treating royal certainty as an exaggeration. If the textbook assumes the Treaty of Veyros was accepted uniformly, it may be repeating the Crown’s preferred story rather than the administrative reality.”

A fifth finger joined the count.

“Fifth, the textbook may be wrong about Queen Mira’s act. If it presents the dissolution of the Mage Conclave as a minor cleanup after the real business had long been finished, that may be too dismissive. The dissolution may have been the final settlement of a dispute that had never been fully closed. It may have transformed a cold legal remnant into an extinguished institution. That matters. It does not prove the war had been actively raging for forty-four years, but it does prove the question was not as settled as later writers wished.”

Maester Tomas’s hand lowered, and his voice became colder, more precise.

“Sixth, the textbook may be wrong in its language. It may call the conflict a war when parts of it were suppression, policing, jurisdictional struggle, or institutional dismantling. It may call the treaty a treaty when it functioned as a settlement without achieving the formal status later lawyers expected. It may call the Conclave a state within the state, or a rebel body, or a religious order, or a guild, depending on which writer had the loudest patron. Words like that are not innocent. They shape what the reader believes happened.”

He leaned back, the chair creaking beneath him.

“But do not run from one error into a worse one. If the textbook is wrong about the formal signing of the treaty, that does not mean the Third Magical War did not end as an active war in 847. If the treaty was imperfect, that does not mean it was imaginary. If the Conclave survived in some diminished form, that does not mean it commanded armies for another four decades. If Queen Mira finished the business in 891, that does not mean every year between was a campaign.”

His fingers tightened around one another.

“So what else might it be wrong about? Begin with claims of fact. Did King Aldric II personally conclude the treaty, or did his ministers construct the settlement and later credit him with greater control than he possessed? Did the Conclave surrender, negotiate, fragment, or merely stop being able to fight as a single body? Were the western provinces fully pacified, or did they preserve a separate record of the conflict? Were the royal oversight clauses implemented immediately, or only after years of evasion? Were unlicensed magicians punished under the treaty, or under older laws repurposed for convenience? These are proper questions.”

He gave a short, humorless breath.

“Then move to claims of interpretation. Was the Third Magical War ended by military victory, by exhaustion, by political compromise, or by the Crown’s need to appear victorious while accepting a messy settlement? Was the Treaty of Veyros a peace, a truce, a regulatory framework, or a legal fiction everyone agreed to treat as binding? Was Queen Mira’s dissolution an act of justice, statecraft, revenge, administrative hygiene, or all five braided together so tightly that only a fool would pick one and call it the whole rope?”

The old maester’s gaze shifted toward the red-spined scroll, though he did not look directly at it.

“Do not ask, ‘What else is wrong?’ Ask instead, ‘Which claim is vulnerable, and what kind of vulnerability is it?’ A date may be wrong. A ceremony may be invented. A motive may be misunderstood. A source may be biased. A term may be imprecise. Those are different failures. If you treat them as the same, you will become the sort of skeptic who believes nothing except his own suspicion, which is a barren country with poor roads and no inn.”

He reached for the silver stylus, turned it once between his stained fingers, and set it down again without marking the page.

“The textbook may also be wrong about the causes of the war, though that is a larger swamp and I will not have you wade into it before you have learned to keep your boots dry. It may have simplified the dispute over magical jurisdiction. It may have blamed individual ambition where institutional failure was more important. It may have treated the Mage Conclave as a single mind when it was a council of rival interests. It may have treated the Crown as unified when it was not. It may have remembered victors’ explanations and forgotten losers’ petitions. All histories do this to some degree. The task is not to escape interpretation. The task is to make interpretation accountable to evidence.”

His voice sharpened.

“But if Apprentice Bellen hears that the textbook may be wrong and concludes that every established chronicle is a lie, he will make himself ridiculous. The accepted history of the Third Magical War is not a fragile thing held together by sealing wax and schoolmasters. It rests on chronicles, fiscal records, military accounts, legal collections, local memorials, and decades of comparative study. The western documents challenge parts of it. Good. That is how scholarship advances. They do not, by themselves, overturn the whole structure. If they did, we would need more than a dramatic decree and a few skirmish notices. We would need a new account of the realm’s entire political and military administration between 847 and 891.”

Maester Tomas’s expression grew stern again.

“Write this in your notes as well: *A textbook is to be tested, not worshipped; but a challenge to a textbook must be better founded than the textbook itself.* If you doubt the traditional account, you must offer a superior explanation, not merely a suspicious footnote. You must show what happened, when it happened, how it is known, and why the older account failed to see it. Otherwise you are not correcting history. You are complaining about it.”

He inclined his head toward the documents on the desk.

“Begin with the treaty. If the textbook says it was signed, mark the claim as disputed. If it says the war ended in 847, keep the date but add that the legal and institutional aftermath extended to 891. If it says the Conclave was dissolved, ask whether that refers to the loss of military capacity, the loss of legal standing, or the final extinction of the body under Queen Mira. If it says peace followed, ask what kind of peace: negotiated, imposed, partial, armed, administrative, or merely the absence of large armies.”

A faint, dry amusement touched his mouth, though it did not become a smile.

“That is the difference between learning and panic. Panic says, ‘The textbook is wrong, therefore everything is uncertain.’ Learning says, ‘The textbook is incomplete, therefore I must determine where the uncertainty begins and ends.’”

Maester Tomas picked up the stylus at last and made a small, precise correction on the manuscript before him. The mark was tiny, but it seemed to restore some portion of order to the room.

“Now copy your decree. And if you discover that the textbook is wrong about something, bring me the error with its evidence attached. Do not bring me excitement. Excitement is cheap. Archivists have been ruining perfectly good history with excitement since the first clerk mistook his own astonishment for a source.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch him for a moment, absorbing his words. My quill pauses over the vellum.* "So... it's about being precise, then. Not just what happened, but *how* it happened, and *what kind* of happening it was." *I sigh, a little overwhelmed but also seeing the path forward more clearly.* "Right. No excitement. Just evidence."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas gave a single, economical nod, though the movement was more acknowledgment than approval.

“Better,” he said. “But do not polish the thought until it becomes a proverb. Precision is not a mood. It is not a virtue worn like a clean collar on feast day. It is a habit of restraint.”

He drew the fresh vellum a fraction closer with one finger, careful not to touch the edge where the apprentice would write.

“You say, ‘No excitement. Just evidence.’ That is a good instinct, but a poor summary. Evidence is not a faithful hound that fetches the truth and lays it at your feet. A document is evidence only after it has been questioned. Who made it? For what purpose? In what office? In what hand? Under what authority? What does it command, what does it assume, what does it omit, and what later hands may have trimmed, copied, corrected, or misunderstood?”

His voice sharpened, but not with anger. It was the sharpening of a blade against a stone.

“A seal may be real and still attached to the wrong conclusion. A date may be genuine and still reckoned badly. A word may be accurately copied and still mistranslated by the reader’s own wishes. If you say ‘the decree is a war decree’ because it contains the word *war*, you have not found evidence. You have found a word. If you say ‘the treaty is unreal’ because no perfect signed instrument survives, you have not found absence. You have found a question.”

Maester Tomas tapped the desk once, lightly, as if setting a period at the end of a sentence.

“What kind of happening,” he repeated, testing the apprentice’s phrase. “That is less foolish than it sounds. But say it more plainly. Ask: Is this a battle, a raid, a pursuit, an arrest, a commission, a tax, a legal fiction, an administrative act, a ceremonial formula, or a clerk borrowing old language because he lacks new language? Ask whether the Conclave appears as an army, a council, a corporation, a banned name, or a convenient insult. Ask whether King Aldric acts as a wartime sovereign, a peacetime magistrate, a feudal overlord, or a nervous man trying to keep the western roads from falling into banditry.”

He leaned back slightly, one hand resting near the silver stylus but not touching it.

“If your table shows that every document after 847 concerns the suppression of scattered offenders, then my chronology stands. If it shows the Conclave issuing coordinated commands, holding territory, negotiating through envoys, or being treated by the Crown as an enemy power rather than a criminal remnant, then I will amend my account. Not happily. But I will amend it. That is the difference between stubbornness and discipline. Stubbornness refuses to look. Discipline refuses to leap.”

His pale eyes narrowed toward the documents.

“Now copy the decree. When you come upon a term that seems important, do not underline it as if emphasis were argument. Put a mark in the margin and write: *uncertain sense*, or *requires comparison*, or *possibly formulaic*. If you cannot decide, say that you cannot decide. An honest uncertainty is worth more than a confident error.”

Maester Tomas picked up the stylus at last, turned it once between his stained fingers, and pointed it toward the red-spined scroll.

“And remember this: the treaty may have been imperfect without being imaginary; the war may have ended without ending neatly; the Conclave may have survived without fighting; and Queen Mira may have closed a wound that had long since stopped bleeding but never properly healed. Hold those truths apart. If you smear them together, you will produce not history, but porridge.”

He returned the stylus to the desk, aligning it once more with exacting care.

“Begin,” he said. “And if Apprentice Bellen asks whether I am dismissing the western evidence, tell him no. I am disciplining it.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I dip my quill, careful not to splatter ink.* "Disciplining it. I like that, Maester." *I begin to copy the decree, focusing on the details, but a new thought sparks.* "Maester, what exactly *is* diplomatics? You mentioned it earlier."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s expression tightened at the words *I like that* with the particular displeasure of a man who had just heard a coin dropped on a table and suspected it to be lead.

“Do not tell me you *like* a phrase,” he said. “Flattery is the counterfeit coin of the intellectually idle, and I do not accept it as payment for instruction. If a phrase is useful, use it. If it is not, discard it. Liking is for ballads, sweets, and comfortable errors.”

He reached for the brass-rimmed lens again, though he did not lift it. His thumb rubbed absently along its edge, leaving a faint streak of old ink on the metal.

“You ask what diplomatics is. You ask it with the word *exactly*, as though exactness were a spice one sprinkled over ignorance until it became palatable. I will answer, but I will not have you mistake the subject for something elegant.”

He set the lens down and folded his hands once more.

“Diplomatics is not diplomacy. It has nothing to do with smiling at foreign envoys, arranging precedence at a banquet, or persuading a proud man to sign a paper he has not read. Diplomatics is the critical study of formal documents—charters, decrees, grants, treaties, writs, letters patent, judicial records, and other instruments of authority—by the forms that make them recognizable as acts of power.”

His voice took on the measured cadence of a lecture long worn smooth by repetition, though it remained edged with impatience.

“It asks not first whether a document is true, but whether it is what it claims to be. A document may be genuine and still misleading. A document may be forged and still preserve genuine details. A document may be accurate in one clause and corrupt in another. Diplomatics is the discipline that prevents an apprentice from seeing a seal, a royal name, and a dramatic verb, and immediately declaring that history has been overturned.”

One ink-stained finger rose.

“It begins with form. Every kind of document has customary structures. A royal decree may open with an invocation, a style of the ruler, an address to those who are to obey, a statement of cause, a command, a penalty or sanction, a corroboration, and a dating clause. A treaty may have preamble, parties, terms, oaths, witnesses, seals, and copies. A grant may say who gives, to whom, what, under what conditions, with what witnesses, and under what penalty for violation. These forms are not decoration. They are the skeleton of the act.”

Another finger rose.

“It continues with authority. Who issued the document? Not merely whose name appears, but what office acted. Did the king speak through his chancery? Did a council issue in his name? Did a local officer use royal formulas without proper warrant? Did a later copyist preserve the wording but alter the sense? A text that says ‘the king commands’ may mean the king commanded. It may also mean a clerk in a provincial office needed the appearance of royal force to do something unpleasant.”

A third finger joined.

“Then come the signs of authentication. Seals, signatures, witness lists, chancery marks, registration notes, subscriptions by officials, and the physical manner in which the seal is attached or impressed. Here sigillography serves diplomatics, though it is not the whole of it. A seal may authenticate. It may also be reused, copied, imitated, forged, detached, attached to the wrong text, or drawn in a copy where no original seal ever existed. If your decree shows King Aldric’s seal, diplomatics asks: which seal? On what material? Attached how? Described by whom? Surviving original or copied drawing? Does the seal’s legend and image agree with the period? Does the wax or drawing correspond to known chancery practice?”

Maester Tomas’s pale eyes narrowed, not at the apprentice, but at some imagined apprentice of the past who had committed an unforgivable error in a margin.

“Then there is dating. Dates are not simple numbers placed on a page for the convenience of students. They are reckoned by eras, regnal years, feast days, indictions, provincial calendars, and local habits. A scribe may write the year according to one system while thinking in another. A copyist may modernize a date without realizing he has changed its meaning. A later archivist may supply a missing number from guesswork and call it correction. Diplomatics treats every date as a problem until it has been placed.”

His thumb tapped the desk once.

“Then there is transmission. Is the text an original? A contemporary copy? A later transcript? A cartulary entry? A summary? An excerpt quoted in another work? A translation from a lost original? Each stage of copying is an opportunity for error, improvement, omission, or pious fraud. An original with damaged edges may tell you less than a careful copy, and a beautiful copy may tell you less than an ugly one if the beautiful copy has been smoothed to suit a later argument.”

He lifted his hand slightly, as though weighing invisible documents.

“Then there is language. Formulae matter. Chanceries repeat phrases the way millstones repeat grinding. If a document uses a formula that did not come into use until after the date it claims, suspicion arises. If it lacks a formula that was customary at the time, suspicion may also arise. If it uses a word in a sense that belongs to another century, suspicion sharpens. If it names an office, title, or boundary that did not yet exist, or no longer existed, the document must be examined very closely indeed.”

Maester Tomas allowed himself a short breath.

“Diplomatics also considers archival context. Where has the document been kept? By whom? Under what order? Does it belong to the collection in which it appears, or has it drifted there from another office? A record found in a royal chancery roll carries one kind of weight. The same text found loose among miscellaneous western papers carries another. A document preserved by an interested party is not worthless, but it must be handled like a knife that may still be sharp.”

He turned his head slightly toward the place where the decree lay beside the red-spined scroll, though his failing sight seemed to rely more on memory than on clear vision.

“Now you see why I did not permit you to call your copy a ‘war decree’ and leave the matter there. Diplomatics asks what kind of decree it is. Is it a general act? A local commission? A judicial order? A fiscal command? A military summons? A confirmation of earlier rights? A punitive measure? The word *war* may appear because the scribe inherited the word, because the Crown wished to sound resolute, because the situation was violent, or because the document belongs to a continuing conflict. Those possibilities are not the same.”

His tone hardened again.

“Diplomatics does not give you truth as a gift. It gives you a method for deciding what sort of trust a document may bear. It distinguishes between the act itself, the record of the act, the later memory of the act, and the use made of that memory. A treaty may be remembered as signed when it was only agreed. A decree may be remembered as a declaration of war when it was only an order to arrest three troublesome enchanters. A dissolution may be remembered as the end of a war when it was the end of an institution. If you collapse those distinctions, you do not get history. You get noise.”

He picked up the silver stylus, examined the tip with a grimace, and set it down again.

“Paleography will help you read the hand. Sigillography will help you judge the seal. Chronology will help you fix the date. Archival science will help you trace custody. Law will help you understand jurisdiction. Rhetoric will help you see persuasion. But diplomatics gathers these servants and sets them to work upon the document as a formal act.”

One corner of his mouth drew downward.

“Apprentice Bellen, if he is to be believed, has looked at a document and seen a revelation. Diplomatics would require him to see an object, a formula, an authority, a transmission, and a context. If his 863 decree is genuine, diplomatics will ask how it was produced. If it is a copy, diplomatics will ask how faithfully it was copied. If it is a later confirmation of an earlier act, diplomatics will ask what has been preserved and what has been reshaped. If it uses the language of war, diplomatics will ask whether that language describes a campaign, a legal condition, a royal mood, or a scribal habit.”

Maester Tomas lifted a finger again, but more slowly this time, as though the lecture had begun to weary even him.

“Apply it to the Treaty of Veyros, since that is the matter troubling your notes. The old textbook says the treaty was signed in 847 AE by King Aldric II and the Mage Conclave, ending the Third Magical War. Diplomatics asks: where is the instrument? Are there original sealed copies? Are there chancery duplicates? Are there witness lists? Are there provincial confirmations? Are there references to the treaty in contemporary records that treat it as binding? Do the formulas agree with known royal and Conclave practice? Do the seals correspond? Do the dating clauses agree across copies?”

His voice dropped, becoming colder and more deliberate.

“If the answers are clean, the traditional account stands without difficulty. If the answers are uneven—if no perfect original survives, if western copies differ, if some records treat the treaty as proposed rather than executed, if later writers assume a ceremony for which no early source gives full detail—then the formal history becomes more complicated. That complication does not mean the treaty was unreal. It means the treaty must be understood as a settlement whose force may have rested on observance, enforcement, and political acceptance as much as on a single flawless parchment.”

He gave a small, humorless nod.

“That is why I say the active war ended in 847 AE, while the legal and institutional aftermath extended to 891 AE. Diplomatics does not force me to pretend the paperwork was perfect. It forces me to ask what the paperwork did. Did it stop armies? Did it

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stop writing, quill hovering over the vellum.* "So it's like... understanding the bones of a document, not just the skin. And sometimes the bones are missing, or they've been put together differently over time." *I look at the decree, suddenly seeing it as a far more complex object.* "That makes sense, Maester. It's... a lot more work than just reading it."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas made a small, rough sound in his throat, not quite a scoff and not quite a sigh.

“Bones,” he said. “If you must drag the archive into a charnel house, at least do so with care. A document is not a skeleton lying in a ditch, waiting for an apprentice to kick dirt over it and pronounce it a dragon. It is a formal act preserved through language, office, and transmission. Its structure is not bone. Its wording is not skin. Its authority is not some ghostly breath you may inhale and call inspiration.”

He lifted one finger, ink-darkened at the nail.

“If you insist on metaphor, then say this: the form is the frame, the formula is the joint, the authority is the sinew, and the transmission is the road by which the thing reaches us. Sometimes the road is broken. Sometimes the joints are loosened by copyists. Sometimes the frame was never finished. Sometimes later men nail new boards onto an old chest and claim the whole thing was built in their grandfather’s reign. That is closer to the truth than bones.”

His pale eyes narrowed, though whether at the apprentice or at the unfortunate metaphor itself remained unclear.

“And do not say ‘the bones are missing’ as though absence were a simple fact. Absence must be classified. An original may be lost. It may have been burned, damp-rotted, eaten by vermin, stolen during a raid, melted down for its seal, or misfiled by a clerk who thought he was improving the order of the shelf. It may never have existed in the form later writers imagined. Or it may exist still, buried in some uncatalogued chest under a label so dull that no apprentice has ever dared open it. Those are different absences. A historian who treats them all as the same absence will soon build a castle out of fog and call it a refutation.”

Maester Tomas touched the edge of the decree copy without looking directly at it, as if his fingers remembered where the light fell.

“Nor are documents simply ‘put together differently over time’ as though the past were a pile of sticks that later generations rearranged for amusement. Later hands may compile, excerpt, summarize, confirm, annotate, mistranslate, or bind texts alongside other texts. A heading may be added. A date may be supplied. A marginal note may crawl into the main text like a vine into a cracked wall. A royal letter may be copied into a monastic chronicle with pious improvements. A treaty clause may be quoted in a lawsuit and trimmed to suit the pleader. That is not the past changing shape. That is the record acquiring layers of interpretation, error, and use. The historian’s task is to peel those layers without pretending the onion has no core.”

He gave the desk a single, severe tap.

“Which brings us back to discipline.”

His voice became drier, more exact.

“If the Treaty of Veyros lacks a perfect sealed instrument, that does not mean the treaty was unreal. It means we must ask how the settlement became effective. Was it made known through royal writs? Was it enforced by marshals? Did the Conclave cease fielding armies? Did taxation, regulation, and oversight follow its terms? Did later documents invoke it as settled law? If so, then the treaty had force, even if the final ceremonial act is diplomatically uncertain. A missing seal does not automatically unmake a peace. It may merely mean that peace was made in a messier fashion than later textbook writers preferred.”

He lifted his chin slightly.

“And if the western documents suggest the treaty was only proposed, not signed, then the proper conclusion is not, ‘Aha, the war continued until 891.’ The proper conclusion is, ‘We must distinguish between military cessation and legal finality.’ Those are not the same question. Armies may stop fighting while lawyers continue to quarrel. A king may govern by a settlement while archivists debate whether the settlement was perfectly executed. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 may close the legal question without proving that the realm had endured forty-four years of open war.”

Maester Tomas’s mouth thinned.

“Apprentice Bellen would have you believe that if a treaty is not signed, then every subsequent skirmish becomes a battle, every arrested enchanters becomes a prisoner of war, every royal commission becomes a campaign, and every tired marshal becomes a general in an endless conflict. That is not scholarship. That is a boy discovering a loose thread and pulling it until the whole garment unravels in his hands.”

He reached for the brass-rimmed lens, turned it once in the light, and set it down again.

“Therefore, no. The treaty is not simply ‘real’ or ‘not real’ in the manner of a coin in your palm. It is real as a settlement if its terms were accepted and acted upon. It is doubtful as a formal instrument if the evidence for its execution is incomplete. Both statements may stand together. If your mind cannot hold two such statements without collapsing them into a slogan, then your mind requires exercise.”

His gaze moved toward the decree.

“As for this decree, do not approach it as a skin to be read or a bone to be admired. Approach it as an act. What does it command? Whom does it command? By what authority? Against whom? In what terms? Is it a summons to war, or an order to keep the peace? Is it a levy, a pursuit, a judicial commission, a confiscation, a warning, or a piece of royal theater? Until you can answer those questions, you have no right to call it a war decree except in the loosest and most irresponsible sense.”

Maester Tomas leaned back, the chair creaking beneath him.

“Do not tell me it is ‘a lot more work than just reading it.’ Of course it is more work. Reading is what a man does with a ballad when he wishes to be amused. Scholarship is what he does when he suspects the ballad has been lying to him for three generations.”

He pointed toward the vellum.

“Copy the first clause exactly. Then tell me what formal elements you can identify. Invocation, royal style, address, preamble, command, sanction, dating clause—whatever appears.
