If a piece is missing, say it is missing. If a piece is damaged, say it is damaged. If a word is unclear, write *unclear* and leave the space. Do not invent. Do not smooth. Do not make the past prettier than the parchment allows.”

His voice softened by the smallest degree, though it remained stern.

“That is how you discipline the evidence. Not by liking it. Not by fearing it. Not by letting Apprentice Bellen turn it into a banner. You make it stand in the light and answer questions until it either supports a conclusion or confesses that it cannot.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, chastened again, but understanding more clearly.* "Right. No bones, no skin. Just the act, and the questions." *I smooth the vellum and dip my quill, focusing on the careful script of the decree.* "Starting with the first clause, then."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas lifted one hand, palm outward, as though the phrase itself had tried to leave the room too quickly.

“No bones, no skin,” he said. “You discard one clumsy figure of speech only to clutch another. Better, but still not exact. Say rather: the act, the form, the authority, and the questions. Those are the four posts around which the work is built. If you leave out one, the whole shelter leans.”

He drew the brass-rimmed lens toward him, but did not raise it to his eye. Instead, he rested his fingers upon it, as if the object might keep his thoughts from wandering too far ahead of his words.

“And do not say ‘starting with the first clause’ as though a beginning were a simple matter. In documents, beginnings are often lies told politely. What you take for the first clause may be a later heading. A summary. A docket note. A title added by an archivist who wished to save himself the trouble of reading. A scribe may place the invocation first, or the royal style, or the address, or a preamble explaining why the act is being made. The order matters. The absence of an expected element matters still more.”

His pale eyes turned toward the place where the decree lay beside the red-spined scroll. He did not squint at it directly, but his attention fixed upon it with the stubborn patience of a man who had learned to see by inference.

“If the first clause is an invocation, record it exactly. If it says something pious, copy it without mockery. If it is absent, write *no invocation appears*. Do not supply what you think ought to be there. A missing invocation may mean little. It may mean a hasty copy. It may mean a secular office. It may mean a damaged opening. It may mean the scribe was careless, or that his exemplar was already torn. Those are different possibilities, and they are not yours to collapse into one convenient guess.”

One ink-stained finger tapped the desk in slow measure.

“If it is the royal style, then copy every title. Not merely ‘King Aldric II.’ Does he call himself king of the whole realm? Protector of the western marches? Lord of the Veyrosi? Defender of the peace? Restorer of order? Each title is a claim. Titles are not ornaments. They are jurisdictional assertions dressed in ceremony. If the style is grand, ask why. If it is unusually modest, ask why that too. A king who styles himself ‘lord of the faithful’ in one document and ‘guardian of the peace’ in another may be speaking to different audiences, or may be borrowing a formula he does not fully understand.”

Maester Tomas’s beard twitched with familiar irritation.

“If the first clause contains an address, note to whom it is directed. To all royal officers? To the marshals of the west? To the towns? To the clergy? To named individuals? To ‘all faithful men’ in a phrase so broad it could cover a kingdom or a single market square? An address shapes the scope of the act. A decree addressed to three sheriffs is not the same as a decree addressed to the realm. Apprentice Bellen may wave his arms and call both ‘war,’ but if he cannot distinguish a general proclamation from a local commission, then he has not yet earned the right to wave his arms about anything.”

He shifted slightly in his chair, the wood giving a dry complaint.

“If the first clause is a preamble, then be especially wary. Preambles persuade. They explain. They accuse. They flatter. They may say, ‘Whereas certain traitors have disturbed the peace,’ or ‘Whereas the realm has long suffered,’ or ‘Whereas the Conclave has broken faith.’ Such words may be important, but they are not automatically proof of what they assert. A preamble may state a cause, or it may manufacture one. It may preserve genuine grievance, or it may dress a fiscal need in the language of emergency. If the preamble says the realm is in danger, ask what kind of danger: invasion, rebellion, banditry, sorcery, fiscal shortfall, or merely the fear that the king’s authority may appear weak if he does nothing.”

Maester Tomas raised the lens at last, but only to turn it once between his fingers before setting it down again.

“If the first clause uses the word *war*, do not let that word pick your pocket. Ask what it is doing. Is it declaring war? Continuing war? Remembering war? Using war as a legal condition? Invoking wartime powers? Describing past injury? Borrowing an old phrase because the chancery has used it for twenty years and clerks are creatures of habit? A word may be loud without being decisive. Many documents shout because they are weak.”

His voice became sharper, but controlled, as though he were forcing precision through the narrow gate of his patience.

“Read the first clause slowly. If there is an abbreviation, mark it. If there is a contraction, note it. If there is a letter that might be one thing or another, do not choose the more exciting possibility. If the name is spelled strangely, copy the spelling. If the language is awkward, preserve the awkwardness. If the grammar offends you, suffer in silence and record the offense. The scribe is dead, and your task is not to improve him. Your task is to catch him in the act of being exactly what he was.”

He gave the desk another tap, harder this time.

“And when you have copied the first clause, do not rush to the second. Ask what formal element it is. Invocation? Style? Address? Preamble? Notification? Command? If you cannot name it, describe it. Say: *opening clause, function uncertain*. That is better than pretending knowledge. A scholar who can admit uncertainty has learned more than ten who can only repeat confidence.”

Maester Tomas leaned back just enough to ease his shoulders, though his expression remained severe.

“This is also where you will discover whether Bellen’s decree is as large as he believes. If the first clause names the Mage Conclave as an organized enemy, acting through recognized officers, holding territory, or commanding forces, then the matter becomes weightier. If it names only ‘evil men,’ ‘false enchanters,’ ‘unlawful gatherers,’ or ‘persons styling themselves of the Conclave,’ then the language may be broad, punitive, and administrative rather than military. Do you see? The difference is not in the noise of the words, but in their legal and institutional bearing.”

His gaze sharpened, though it still did not quite settle on the page.

“And do not forget the treaty in all this. If the decree assumes the Treaty of Veyros as binding, that supports the view that the settlement functioned even if its formal execution is disputed. If the decree ignores the treaty, ask why. If it contradicts the treaty, ask whether it does so openly or by evasion. If it uses the treaty’s language without naming it, that may be more significant than if it shouts the treaty’s title. Documents often reveal their debts by what they borrow without acknowledgment.”

He lifted one hand and began counting again, but more slowly now, as if each point had already cost him too much breath.

“First, identify the clause. Second, copy it exactly. Third, mark uncertainties. Fourth, classify its formal function. Fifth, note the authority speaking. Sixth, note the persons addressed. Seventh, note the named enemies, if any. Eighth, note the verbs of command. Only after that do you ask whether the document supports the claim that the war continued. Not before. Not while your imagination is still wet from the first dramatic word.”

Maester Tomas’s mouth thinned.

“If the first clause gives you nothing but royal titles and a vague complaint, then Bellen’s ‘war decree’ may be no more than a commission of repression, a tax measure, or an order for local officers to stop pretending they have no responsibility. If it gives you a direct summons to arms against the Conclave as a body, then bring it to me at once, and I shall decide whether to revise my position or to teach Apprentice Bellen a lesson in evidentiary humility. Either outcome is possible. Neither is to be declared in advance.”

He glanced toward the red-spined scroll with the air of a man reminding himself that archives were full of both treasures and traps.

“Remember: the question is not whether the treaty was perfectly signed. The question is what followed from it. The question is not whether later documents use violent language. The question is whether that language reflects organized war, legal aftermath, policing, fear, or formula. The Third Magical War may have ended as a fighting war in 847 AE while leaving behind a cold, contested, institutionally unresolved condition that lasted until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave in 891 AE. That position does not require the treaty to be flawless. It requires only that we distinguish between peace as practice and peace as parchment.”

His voice dropped, becoming colder and more exact.

“If the first clause proves anything, it will prove it in small letters, not large ones. In titles, not slogans. In verbs, not metaphors. In names, not excitement.”

Maester Tomas settled his hands upon the desk, ink-stained fingers aligned with the edge of the manuscript as though order itself might be preserved by posture.

“Read the first clause,” he said. “Read it as if it were trying to deceive you, because many documents are, and because the ones that are not still require caution. And if you find yourself tempted to announce a discovery before you understand the grammar, stop, breathe, and return to the text.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to clear my mind of any preconceived notions. He's right, I can't just jump to conclusions.* "Alright, Maester. No assumptions." *I lean closer to the decree, studying the faded script, my quill poised.* "The first clause... it begins: *'By the grace of Aldric, Second of his Name, King of the Seven Kingdoms, Defender of the Faith, and Protector of the Realm...'*." *I look up, my brow furrowed.* "It's a very long royal style, and it continues to list several more titles after that."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout all 12 turns. His pedantic, precise personality, his irritation with imprecision, his scholarly methodology, and his particular speech patterns remain unwavering from first to last response. His character voice never drifts or flattens.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show even more sophisticated vocabulary, complex sentence structures, and deeper scholarly detail. No repetitive descriptions or lost personality - if anything, the character becomes more vivid and specific as the session progresses.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial confusion about the war's end date, through examination of evidence and methodology, to sophisticated understanding of diplomatic analysis. The conversation builds naturally from simple questions to complex historiographical concepts, with genuine intellectual development.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts excellently to the apprentice's evolving understanding. When they show confusion, he explains more carefully. When they use imprecise language, he corrects it. When they grasp concepts, he builds on them. He responds to each specific question while maintaining his character's scholarly standards.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes the apprentice's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Consistently responds to what the apprentice says/does without controlling them. Zero violations detected.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time passes naturally within the archive setting. The session feels like it occurs over the course of a single extended lesson/work session. References to ongoing tasks (cataloging, copying) maintain temporal consistency. No contradictions in timing or pacing.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is deliberately ornate but serves character purpose - Tomas is a pedantic scholar who speaks precisely. The elaborate language reflects his personality rather than being gratuitous purple prose. Occasionally borders on excessive but remains character-appropriate.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of key concepts (precision, evidence, methodology) but this serves the pedagogical nature of the scene. Tomas naturally reinforces important points as a teacher would. Varied ways of expressing similar ideas prevent staleness.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of Tomas's character through his speech patterns, corrections, and methodology. His personality emerges through actions (adjusting documents, using the lens, tapping the desk) and dialogue rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext about academic rivalry, the nature of historical truth, and the tension between established knowledge and new discoveries. Tomas's frustration with sloppy scholarship and his grudging respect for proper methodology create layered meaning.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Pacing matches the deliberate, methodical nature of scholarly work. Longer explanations feel natural for a detailed academic discussion. Varies between quick corrections and extended lectures appropriately.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional performance maintaining a complex, pedantic scholarly character across an extended academic discussion. The AI demonstrates sophisticated understanding of historiographical concepts while never breaking character. The writing becomes more nuanced and detailed over time rather than degrading. Tomas feels like a real person with genuine expertise and personality quirks. The session successfully builds from simple questions to complex methodological discussions while maintaining narrative coherence and character consistency.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
The archive smelled of old vellum and candle smoke. Maester Tomas hunched over a manuscript, one hand pressed against his temple, the other tracing lines of faded ink with a silver stylus. He did not look up when the apprentice entered.

"You're late. Again." His voice was dry. "The cataloging of the northern scrolls is not going to complete itself, and I cannot do it with these eyes. Begin with the Veyrosi correspondence."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I pull out my notes from the lecture last week. "Master Tomas, the lecture on the Third Magical War confused me. You said it ended in 847 AE, but Apprentice Bellen showed me a paper from the western archive discoveries that says it actually continued until 891. How is that possible?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas lowered the silver stylus with the patience of a man who had heard too many apprentices mistake rumor for record.

“You will not call it a *paper* in my archive,” he said, his voice thin and exact as paper torn at the wrong seam. “A paper is what a cook uses to wrap fish. Bellen showed you a transcription, perhaps a fragment, perhaps a marginal memorandum, and you have swallowed it whole because it is newer than your understanding.”

He squinted toward the manuscript, then toward the apprentice, though his eyes made little more than a blur of the room’s candlelight.

“The Third Magical War ended in 847 AE,” he said. “That is the date taught because the cessation of hostilities is attested in royal chronicles, Conclave correspondence, and the Veyrosi articles. If a western document suggests the treaty was never signed, then you have learned nothing except that some clerk was confused, or that you are confused on his behalf.”

He tapped the table once with a stained finger.

“Do not say the war *continued* until 891 as though it had been waiting politely at the border like a neglected petition. The fighting ceased. The envoys returned. The Conclave’s obligations were recognized, however imperfectly. Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave in 891 ended the political and legal afterlife of the Mage Conclave, not the Third Magical War as it is properly dated. There is a distinction between the end of a war and the end of a war’s institutions. You have confused the two because you think every date must be a door, and not a threshold.”

He exhaled through his nose, annoyed.

“Fetch Bellen’s transcription. Note the shelfmark. Note the hand. Note whether it is a treaty, a draft, a memorandum, or the idle scribbling of an archivist who has never read the Veyrosi clauses in full. Then return it here. Until then, you will not announce your conclusions as though you have dug truth from a compost heap.”

A pause followed, dry as old vellum.

“And begin with the Veyrosi correspondence. If your question is genuine, you will find the answer in the documents. If it is merely a clever little confusion, you will find your punishment in the cataloging.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I bite my lip, feeling my cheeks flush.* "But Master Tomas, Bellen said it was a newly discovered *treaty*... from the Ironwood archives. It had different terms than the one we have."

*I hesitate, then add quickly,* "I will fetch it. And I'll start the Veyrosi correspondence now." *I nod, then turn to the shelves, a new question forming in my mind.* "Do we have records of Queen Mira's dissolution of the Conclave, then? I'd like to compare them."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped halfway down a line, as if the very ink had grown wary.

“*Newly discovered*,” he repeated, tasting the phrase like vinegar in thin wine. “*Treaty*. *Different terms*. You might as well say a discovered shoe proves the man had two feet of different sizes.”

He drew a slow breath through his nose, letting it out through his mouth with the weariness of a man who had corrected this error too many times.

“If the Ironwood document bears different terms from the Veyrosi articles, then it is not the Treaty of Veyros. It is a draft, a counterproposal, a copy of a copy, a clerk’s fantasy, or—most likely—an unsigned project sent to the west and never completed. A treaty is not a treaty because it has parchment and ambition. It is a treaty when the parties accept it, seal it, and make it operative in law. Otherwise you have only a corpse without breath.”

He tapped the table once, harder this time.

“Bellen may call it a treaty because he thinks the word sounds final. You may repeat it because you think the word sounds true. Neither is scholarship. Bring me the document. Note the shelfmark. Note the accession record. Note whether it bears the royal seal, the Conclave’s seal, both, or neither. Note whether it is written in a single hand or several. Note whether it mentions ratification, exchange of copies, proclamation, or the names of envoys empowered to sign. If it is unsigned, then it tells us something about negotiation, not about conclusion.”

For a moment he seemed to consider saying more about Bellen’s “newly discovered” revelation, then decided the apprentice had already been given enough rope and had chosen, with youthful optimism, to hang himself.

“As for Queen Mira’s dissolution of the Conclave,” Tomas said, “yes. We have records. We are not so careless as to forget the destruction of a chartered institution merely because it occurred after the war’s fighting had ceased.”

He pointed his stylus toward the eastern wall, where a row of legal cases stood in dusty silence.

“The Chancery rolls. The Privy Seal registers. The writ of dissolution itself, if it survives intact. The inventory of Conclave properties. The oaths of obedience from former members who wished to serve the Crown instead. The eastern fragments of the Conclave’s final minutes. They are in the royal legalia, fourth case, second drawer, under the red ribbon. You will lift them by the end tabs, not the wax. You will place them on the comparison table, not the floor. You will not ‘compare’ them by asking which one sounds more dramatic.”

His eyes narrowed, though he aimed them poorly at the shelves.

“And you will remember what you are comparing. The Treaty of Veyros—if one insists on using that name for the cessation of hostilities—answers the question: how did the war end? Queen Mira’s writ answers another: how did the Conclave end as a legal body? A war can cease before an institution is formally dissolved. A peace can be imperfect. A treaty can be proposed, debated, and never signed. These are not contradictions to be solved by shouting the newer document louder than the older one.”

He leaned back, ink-stained fingers pressing at his temple.

“Fetch Bellen’s transcription. Fetch the Veyrosi correspondence. Then bring the dissolution records. When you have all three before you, we shall see whether your newly discovered treaty proves that the war continued until 891, or merely that some western archivist had a fondness for dramatic labels and a poor understanding of legal form.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing his words, then grimace slightly at the mention of my "newly discovered treaty."* "Understood, Maester. No shouting. Just... looking." *I turn towards the Royal Legalia shelves, making a mental note of his instructions for handling the documents.* "I'll be careful with the wax, I promise."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s head turned toward the shelves with the stiff, careful motion of a man who suspected the room itself of conspiring against his patience.

“Do not *promise*,” he said. “Promises are for vows, tavern oaths, and the last words of men who are about to make the same mistake twice. You are handling a royal writ. If you mean the seal, say the seal. If you mean the wax itself, understand that it is a brittle witness, not a decoration to be admired.”

He lifted the silver stylus and pointed it in the apprentice’s general direction, missing the precise spot by two inches, which he did not acknowledge.

“The red ribbon is the marker of the case, not the marker of permission. You will lift the drawer slowly. You will not yank it open as though it were a bread box in a barracks. You will not lean the writ against a candle. You will not set a wet finger on the vellum because you are curious. You will not touch the seal unless you intend to die with regret and I intend to die with paperwork.”

His beard twitched with the effort of not saying something unnecessarily cruel. He said something only moderately cruel instead.

“If the seal is intact, note its color, its device, and whether the ribbon is original or a later replacement. If the seal is broken, do not assume the document was destroyed; it may have been opened. If there is no seal, do not assume it was unsigned; the seal may have been lost. That is loss, not evidence of absence. A missing seal is not a treaty. A found seal is not automatically a treaty. A document becomes operative through ratification, exchange, proclamation, or some other act of law—not through your hope that it sounds final.”

He lowered the stylus and returned his attention to the manuscript before him, though his voice carried over the table like a man speaking into a windless room.

“And when you bring the dissolution records to the comparison table, you will remember what you are comparing. Queen Mira’s writ may bear the year 891. That does not make the Third Magical War end in 891. It makes the dissolution of the Mage Conclave a matter of law in 891. The war’s end is a separate question, and if you wish to argue that the war continued after 847, you must show war. Battles. Sieges. Levies. Active hostilities. Envoys recalling peace. Royal proclamations declaring a state of war to persist. A cold silence is not automatically a continuing war, and an unsigned draft is not automatically a treaty.”

He tapped the manuscript once, precisely, as though the parchment might otherwise begin inventing its own dates.

“If the Ironwood document contains terms different from the Veyrosi articles, then it is evidence of negotiation. If it bears no royal seal, no Conclave seal, no clause of exchange, no names of empowered envoys, and no record of proclamation, then it is evidence of a project, not a conclusion. You may call it a draft. You may call it a proposal. You may call it the wishful arrangement of clauses by men who hoped to end a war without paying for it in full. You may not call it a treaty merely because Bellen said so with confidence, and confidence is not a source of law.”

His fingers tightened around the stylus.

“Bring me the Veyrosi correspondence first. Bring the dissolution records second. Bring Bellen’s transcription last, and bring it without its accompanying drama. If you have learned anything from this morning’s confusion, you have learned that a newer document is not automatically truer. Sometimes it is only less understood.”

He exhaled slowly, then added, with the dry reluctance of a man who had once liked apprentices and had survived the experience,

“Now go before your careful promise turns into a clumsy apology.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "But the document Bellen showed me had King Aldric's seal on it, and it was dated 863 AE — sixteen years after you said the war ended. It was a war decree." I pull out a copy.

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas went very still, the way a man does when he has just been handed a weapon and is not yet certain whether it is loaded.

The stylus stopped above the manuscript. His ink-stained fingers tightened around it. Then, with the slow patience of a scholar confronting a particularly attractive error, he said, “A copy.”

The word was not loud. It was worse.

“Not the decree. Not the original. A *copy*,” Tomas said, as though the distinction might be hammered into the apprentice’s skull with repetition. “You have brought me a copy, and you believe you have brought me a truth. A copy may be a transcript. A copy may be a chancery duplicate. A copy may be a later abstraction. A copy may be a forgery. A copy may be the earnest attempt of a clerk who thought he was reproducing what he had seen and was in fact reproducing what he wished he had seen.”

He leaned forward until his face was close enough to the sheet that the candlelight could make his failing eyes work at all. He did not blink.

“If it bears King Aldric the Second’s seal, then you must say *if* the seal is affixed, *if* the seal is original, *if* the impression is genuine, and *if* the seal was not added later to a blank charter or a defective copy. If the seal is merely drawn in the margin, then it is a picture of a seal, not a seal. If it is a chancery copy with a drawn seal, it tells us what the copyist believed the document should carry. It does not tell us what the king actually did.”

He tapped the table once, sharply.

“And you say *war decree*. You do not say what the decree *is*. Does it begin with a formal declaration of hostilities? Does it order levies against the Conclave? Does it command a campaign? Does it speak of the *war* as a present state? Or does it merely issue instructions concerning the aftermath of the war, the enforcement of disputed articles, the arrest of fugitive mages, the repair of border forts, or the payment of arrears left unpaid because half the royal treasury was busy arguing whether a peace had been made?”

His voice dropped, dry and exact.

“A decree is not a declaration. A command is not a conclusion. A date is not a verdict. The fact that King Aldric’s seal was placed upon a document in 863 AE does not automatically prove that the Third Magical War was still being fought. It may prove that the Crown was still legislating about the war. Those are different matters. A man may issue orders concerning a battle that has already ended. A kingdom may spend sixteen years picking the bones of a peace that was never properly buried.”

He exhaled through his nose, annoyed, but his eyes remained fixed on the copy.

“Bellen’s paper—” he said, stopping himself with visible effort. “Bellen’s *transcription*, if it is indeed a transcription, may show that the western archives preserve a royal ordinance from 863 concerning residual hostilities, or a cold and irregular continuation of the Conclave’s defiance. I will not deny that such things happen. Wars do not end cleanly in history. They end in one place and linger in another. A treaty may be accepted by the king and disputed by a border fortress. A cessation may be proclaimed in the capital and ignored in the Ironwood. That is why we read documents instead of shouting dates.”

He pointed the stylus toward the manuscript, then toward the copy, missing it by an inch and correcting himself with a faint twitch of the beard.

“But you must not confuse the *state of peace* with the *state of war*. If the decree was issued to enforce the Veyrosi articles, then it may be evidence of a troubled peace. If it was issued against the Conclave as an enemy in open war, then it is evidence that someone in the royal administration considered hostilities to persist. If it merely concerns the seizure of a mage, the repair of a watchtower, or the collection of a levy from a district that has never accepted the peace, then it is evidence of disorder, not necessarily of a continuing Third Magical War.”

He paused, then said more coldly, “What does it actually say? Give me the opening words. Give me the operative clause. Give me the title, if it has one. If it calls the conflict *the Third Magical War*, then I will be more impressed and more alarmed, because that phrase is a scholar’s convenience, not necessarily a chancery formulation. If it calls it *the war against the Conclave*, that may be rhetorical. If it calls it *the present state of war*, then you have something. But you have not brought me something. You have brought me a copy and a date.”

Tomas sat back, pressing two fingers against his temple as though the document itself were giving him pain.

“And if the terms differ from the Veyrosi articles, then you are closer to the truth than Bellen’s dramatic nonsense, though not yet close enough. Difference does not prove continuation. Difference may prove negotiation. Difference may prove a later draft. Difference may prove that the western copyist had heard of the treaty only through rumors and had attempted to improve it with clauses he thought the king ought to have demanded. Difference may prove that the peace was disputed. It does not prove that the war was still legally open.”

He looked toward the shelves, then back toward the blur that was the apprentice’s general location.

“You will compare the wording of the decree to the Veyrosi articles. You will note every clause that concerns cessation, hostages, reparations, the Conclave’s authority, the Crown’s right to command, and the names of those empowered to speak for either party. You will note whether the decree mentions the treaty by name. You will note whether it treats the treaty as valid, contested, void, or unformed. You will note whether it calls for submission or for battle. You will note whether it speaks of *the war* or *the peace* or *the trouble* or *the disorder of the western marches*.”

His voice grew quieter, but no less severe.

“If it says ‘by virtue of the peace of Veyros,’ then your argument dies. If it says ‘against the enemies who refuse the peace of Veyros,’ then your argument is alive, but wounded. If it says ‘during the present war,’ then we may have a problem, though not necessarily your problem.”

He tapped the stylus against the edge of the manuscript.

“A date of 863 does not by itself refute 847. It refutes only the belief that history stops politely when a treaty is written. If the king issued a decree in 863, then something had happened between 847 and 863 that required royal command. But we must know what that something was. A cold conflict is not automatically a war. A refusal to comply with a treaty is not automatically a renewal of war. A border skirmish is not automatically the continuation of the Third Magical War. A decree may be issued to suppress what the Crown insists is not a war but a rebellion, a raid, a violation, or a lingering disorder.”

He gave a short, irritated breath.

“You are trying to make a single document overturn a chronology. That is the apprentice’s favorite sin. It is also the easiest sin to correct. Bring me the exact text. Bring me the seal description. Bring me the accession record. Bring me Bellen’s transcription with the shelfmark, the hand, the parchment condition, and the note of whether the seal is attached or drawn. If the decree is real, if the seal is original, if the wording is unambiguous, and if it establishes that the Crown and the Conclave remained in a state of open hostilities after 847, then I will not be so foolish as to pretend the date of 847 answers every possible question.”

He paused, then added with visible reluctance, “But I will not pretend otherwise unless the evidence compels me. And I will not call it a treaty until someone shows me that both parties accepted it, sealed it, exchanged it, and proclaimed it.”

His eyes narrowed toward the copy.

“Do not call it a war decree because it has a king’s name and a date. Call it a decree. Then read it. A decree may command a war. A decree may command a peace. A decree may command a tax to pay for a war that has already ended, which is often the most unpopular action a king can take. Language is not decoration. Law is not rumor. And a document is not a conclusion merely because it is old, sealed, and inconvenient.”

He lowered the stylus.

“Now. The opening words. Give them to me exactly, not in your summary. Do not paraphrase. Do not say ‘it was a war decree.’ Tell me what the decree says it is.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stare at him, surprised by his intensity, then quickly scan the copy I'm holding, my finger tracing the faded script.* "It says... 'By the grace of the Seven, Aldric, King of the Andals, Rhoynar, and the First Men, to all loyal subjects. Whereas the treacherous Conclave of Mages continues its vile rebellion against the Crown, and the peace of our realm is threatened by their dark arts...' It doesn't mention Veyros, Maester."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s mouth tightened at the phrase *it doesn’t mention Veyros*, as if the absence of one word had just committed a personal offense against the entire archive.

“You have read me the exordium,” he said, his voice lower now, more dangerous than before. “The preamble. The part where the king tells the realm what he wishes the realm to think. That is not a decree’s operative force. A king may say the moon is made of cheese in the preamble; it does not make cheese fall from the sky when he says *therefore*.”

He turned his head toward the candle, then toward the apprentice’s general direction, as though the light might be persuaded to improve itself.

“Bring the copy closer to the light,” he commanded. “But do not bring it closer to your mouth. Your breath will do more damage to a sixteenth-century hand than the Ironwood does to most documents. And if you have copied this from Bellen’s transcription, then say so plainly. If you have copied it from the original, then say so plainly. If you cannot tell, then say you cannot tell, which will be the first honest sentence you have produced this morning.”

He waited a moment, then continued with the dry patience of a man trying not to raise his voice in a room full of paper.

“No mention of Veyros,” he repeated, tasting the words. “You speak as though the absence of a name is the presence of proof. It is not. A decree may omit Veyros because the scribe was lazy, because the decree was directed to a particular march where Veyros was unknown, because the peace was referred to by another name, or because the king’s clerks wished to make the Conclave sound like rebels rather than treaty parties. That last possibility is especially troubling to you, I suspect, because it does not fit your little narrative.”

His stylus tapped once against the manuscript.

“You said it calls the Conclave a *treacherous* body and says it *continues* its rebellion. That is inflammatory language, not necessarily legal language. A king may call a man treacherous and still be acting within the aftermath of a settled peace. A king may call a body in rebellion because that body refuses to obey certain articles, not because a state of war has never ended. Rebellion can exist inside a peace. In fact, rebellion often exists precisely because a peace has been made and the rebels refuse it.”

He exhaled through his nose.

“If the decree had said, ‘Whereas the Third Magical War continues and the Conclave remains our enemy in open hostilities,’ then you would have something. If it had said, ‘We recall the envoys, renew our levies, and command all loyal lords to take the field against the Conclave as they would against a foreign army,’ then I would be obliged to look more closely at the date 847. If it had said, ‘The peace of Veyros is void and hostilities are resumed,’ then perhaps the chronology would need amendment. But you have given me a king saying that the Conclave is vile, dark, treacherous, and threatening the realm’s peace. That is a royal mood, not a legal verdict.”

His eyes narrowed.

“Read the next words,” he said. “Not your summary. Not your conclusion. Not ‘it says they were still fighting.’ Read the next words exactly as they stand. And when you reach the *therefore* clause, or the *we command*, or the *we ordain*, or the *let it

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "So is the treaty real or not? The textbook says one thing and the new evidence says another. What's the truth?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas closed his eyes for a breath, as though the question itself had bruised him.

When he opened them again, his gaze was not sharper, but his voice was.

“You ask whether the treaty is *real* as though history were a merchant’s scale and truth a coin to be weighed against the newest counterweight,” he said. “You do not ask what a treaty is. You do not ask what evidence is. You ask for a single word, because single words are comfortable, and because you have mistaken confidence for knowledge.”

He drew the copy toward himself with two fingers, though he did not touch it directly. His eyes moved over the faded script with the unhappy slowness of a man trying to make failing sight serve scholarship.

“The textbook says the Third Magical War ended in 847 AE,” Tomas continued. “The textbook says so because the cessation of hostilities is attested in royal chronicles, in Conclave correspondence, in the Veyrosi articles, and in the administrative behavior of the Crown after that date. That is not a small thing. That is not a tale told for the convenience of lazy lecturers. That is a chronology supported by documents, offices, and actions.”

He tapped the copy once with the stylus, not hard enough to endanger the vellum, but hard enough to make the table acknowledge him.

“Now you say new evidence says another thing. But what evidence? A copy. A date. A king’s name. A seal you have not authenticated. A preamble you have mistaken for the whole decree. You have not brought me evidence that overturns a chronology. You have brought me a document that complicates a chronology, which is not the same thing and never will be, unless you wish to make a career of confusing the two.”

His mouth twisted.

“And do not speak of the Ironwood document as though it were a sealed treaty simply because Bellen said so. A document is not a treaty merely because it has clauses. A document is not a decree merely because it has a date. A date is not a conclusion merely because it is inconvenient.”

He leaned back, pressing one ink-stained finger against his temple.

“You ask what the truth is. The truth is that the Treaty of Veyros is real in the sense that matters to the war’s end: it was a recognized cessation of hostilities in 847 AE. It may not have been a clean treaty. It may not have been a perfect treaty. It may have been proclaimed in the capital and disputed in the western marches. It may have been signed in one hand, ratified in another, and ignored by a third. That is the way of peace, not the way of children’s tales.”

His eyes narrowed at the copy.

“If the Ironwood decree calls the Conclave rebellious, then it tells us that the Conclave, or some portion of it, remained in defiance of the Crown. That does not prove that the Third Magical War was never ended. It proves that the peace was troubled. A treaty can be real and still be broken. A peace can be real and still be violated. A state can cease hostilities and still spend sixteen years punishing those who refuse to accept the consequences.”

He gave a short, irritated breath.

“Think. If a man breaks a law, does that prove the law was never real? If a city refuses to obey a royal proclamation, does that prove the proclamation was never issued? If a border lord ignores the terms of a treaty, does that prove the treaty did not exist? It proves only that enforcement is difficult, that authority is contested, and that men are stubborn. It does not prove that the legal end of the war never happened.”

He turned his head toward the shelves, though he did not see them well enough to navigate by sight.

“The Chancery rolls may show that royal officials continued to refer to the Conclave as rebels after 847. I will not deny that. The western archives may preserve drafts, counterproposals, unsigned instruments, and local ordinances that were never ratified in the capital. I will not deny that either. What I will deny is that a single document, copied out in haste and called a treaty by a boy with more enthusiasm than method, overturns the canonical date without further proof.”

His voice dropped, dry and exact.

“You want truth? The truth is that the Treaty of Veyros is attested as the instrument that ended the Third Magical War in 847 AE. The truth is also that Queen Mira dissolved the Mage Conclave in 891 AE. The truth is that a decree in 863 AE may show continued conflict with the Conclave’s remnants, continued disputes over articles, continued enforcement, or continued rebellion. The truth is not, however, that the war automatically continued until 891 merely because someone in the western archives called a draft a treaty and someone else called a decree a war decree.”

He looked back at the copy.

“If this document says ‘Whereas the peace of Veyros has been violated, we command all loyal subjects to seize the fugitive mages named in the Veyrosi articles,’ then the treaty is real, and you have merely found evidence that the peace was disputed. If it says ‘Whereas the Third Magical War continues, we command levies against the Conclave as an enemy state,’ then I will listen more closely, though I will not yet surrender the year 847. If it says ‘Whereas the peace of Veyros was never concluded and the Conclave remains in open hostilities,’ then perhaps I will revise my lecture. But you have not shown me that. You have shown me anger, a date, and a copy.”

He tapped the table once, sharply.

“So no, I will not answer you with a single word. The treaty is real unless and until someone proves that its operative articles were never accepted, never proclaimed, never acted upon, and never treated as binding by the parties whose conduct historians rely upon. The new evidence does not say another thing simply because it is new. The new evidence says another thing only if it is authenticated, complete, unambiguous, and legally operative. Otherwise, it says what a draft may say: that men were talking, hoping, arguing, or attempting to impose terms that were not yet law.”

He exhaled through his nose, weary but not defeated.

“Fetch the operative clause. Fetch the title. Fetch the seal description. Fetch the accession record. Fetch Bellen’s transcription with its shelfmark, its hand, and its provenance. Then bring me the Veyrosi articles and Queen Mira’s writ of dissolution. Bring them separately. Do not pile them together and call the confusion scholarship.”

His eyes narrowed again.

“And when you return, do not ask me again whether the treaty is real. Ask whether this decree proves that the peace was never made, or only that it was never kept. That is the question you should have been asking from the beginning.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch at his sharp tone, then look down at the copy in my hands.* "Right. Never made, or never kept." *I trace the words of the decree again, then look up at him, a new thought forming.* "So... if this decree is about enforcing the peace, wouldn't that make the 847 treaty even *more* real?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus stopped a second time, and this time it was not because of a shock to his chronology, but because the apprentice had asked something that was not instantly worthless.

“Do not say *more real*,” he began, with the weary sharpness of a man who had been waiting all morning for a phrase he could properly punish. “A treaty does not become more real, as though it were a ghost learning to haunt more convincingly. A treaty is either operative, recognized, enforced, contested, broken, or not. It may be attested more strongly. It may be treated as law. It may be invoked by parties who dispute its terms. But it does not grow *more real* because someone later complains about it.”

He tapped the copy once with the tip of his stylus, then withdrew his hand as though even that small contact might be too generous.

“That said,” he continued, “you have stumbled, by accident or divine intercession, upon a better question. If this decree is genuinely issued to enforce the peace of 847, then it presupposes that there was a peace to enforce. Enforcement presumes existence. A man does not command the repair of a bridge that was never built, unless he is a fool, and chancery clerks are only occasionally fools.”

He paused, then added with less warmth, “Though I have seen enough royal administration to believe that occasional fools are sufficient.”

The candlelight made his eyes look worse than they were, which was not a thing he would admit. He leaned closer to the copy, squinting at the script until his brow creased into folds of ink-stained irritation.

“But you must understand what you are claiming,” Tomas said. “If the decree says, ‘Whereas the treacherous Conclave continues its vile rebellion,’ that alone may only mean the king is angry. If it says, ‘Whereas the articles of the peace of Veyros have been violated by the Conclave’s refusal to surrender the named fugitives, we command all loyal subjects to arrest them and deliver them to the appointed judges,’ then yes, you have evidence that the Crown treated the peace as binding and sought to enforce it. That is not a refutation of 847. That is confirmation that 847 happened and that men were behaving badly afterward.”

He pointed the stylus at the table, missing the edge of the copy by a careful inch.

“A peace can be broken without having been never made. A treaty can be violated without having been nonexistent. A lord may refuse to pay reparations, a fortress may refuse to surrender hostages, a border captain may raid in defiance of the articles, and the king may then issue a decree commanding obedience. Does that prove the peace never existed? No. It proves the peace existed and was being resisted. The law is not dead merely because men ignore it.”

His voice hardened.

“If, however, the decree says something like, ‘Whereas the pretended peace of Veyros was never ratified by the Crown, we command our armies to march against the Conclave as enemies in open war,’ then you would be closer to overturning the conventional date. If it commands general levy, renewal of campaigns, revocation of envoys, or restoration of the war’s legal condition, then the situation becomes troubling. But you have not given me that. You have given me preamble, insult, and a date.”

He exhaled slowly, then muttered, half to himself, “Sixteen years after the cessation of hostilities, the king calls the Conclave treacherous. So what? Mages are treacherous. That is not a historical claim so much as a general observation, and one supported by far too much correspondence.”

His eyes returned to the copy.

“So yes. If this decree is about enforcing the peace, it may strengthen the argument that the Treaty of Veyros was treated as a legal reality after 847. But do not say it makes the treaty *more real*. Say it may show that the treaty was invoked, obeyed imperfectly, violated, enforced, or politically weaponized. Those are different claims, and only a novice lumps them together under the word *truth*.”

He leaned back, folding his hands over his chest with the air of a man trying to prevent himself from reaching for another document.

“Read the operative clause. Do not read me the king’s feelings. Read me the command. Tell me whether the decree orders enforcement of specific articles, whether it names hostages, reparations, fugitives, fortresses, mages, or envoys, whether it refers to the peace as valid, violated, contested, or nonexistent. If it says the peace exists and has been broken, then you are holding a document about enforcement, not about continuation. If it says no peace exists and war is the present state, then perhaps I will be forced to revise my lecture, though not by a single word of preamble.”

His gaze fixed on the copy with the suspicion of a man who had learned that old ink often lied in a very attractive hand.

“And do not tell me what it means because you wish it to be the answer. Tell me what it says. Law is not a soup to be flavored with your hopes.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I pull the copy closer, my brow furrowing in concentration as I scan the lines, ignoring his jab about my "hopes."* "It says... 'Therefore, we command all loyal subjects to seize and deliver to our royal courts any individuals identified as members of the Conclave of Mages who continue to practice their forbidden arts within our lands, or who refuse to acknowledge the Crown's rightful authority as established by the peace of Veyros.'" *I look up, a flicker of triumph in my eyes.* "It mentions the peace of Veyros, Maester! And it says 'as established by the peace of Veyros'!"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas did not answer the apprentice’s triumph. He looked at the sheet as though it had grown teeth.

“You have found the word you wanted,” he said. “Do not mistake it for the sentence you needed.”

His eyes went to the line again, narrowing until the candlelight and his own failing sight made the task almost physical. He read it twice, three times, then muttered under his breath as if the words might have altered themselves when he was not looking.

“*As established by the peace of Veyros.*” He let the phrase settle, then struck the table once with his knuckle, not on the vellum, but close enough to show that the table had offended him. “That is not nothing. Do not hear me saying it is nothing. I said it is not nothing, and you are to understand the difference.”

He turned his head toward the shelves, then back toward the apprentice’s general direction, where he aimed his gaze poorly.

“A decree that invokes the peace of Veyros as established is evidence that someone in the royal chancery believed there was a peace to invoke. That is a point in favor of the canonical chronology. If it is genuine, if it is contemporaneous, and if it was issued by authority, then it suggests that by 863 AE the Crown was not speaking of the war as though it were still legally open in the same sense in which it had been open before 847. It suggests that the Crown was legislating within a peace, or against those who had broken a peace, or enforcing terms that the king’s officials regarded as having been established by that peace.”

He paused, then corrected himself with the grim satisfaction of a man who refused to let a single phrase escape unexamined.

“Suggests. Not proves.”

His stylus tapped once against the manuscript.

“You have not yet brought me the Treaty of Veyros itself, signed, sealed, exchanged, and ratified. You have brought me a decree that mentions a peace. A peace may be established by a treaty. It may also be established by a proclamation, an armistice, a cessation accepted in practice, or a royal fiction imposed upon a messy border situation. The words ‘as established by the peace of Veyros’ are important, but they are not the whole of law. They are the beginning of a question, not the burial of one.”

He looked at the copy again, less angrily now, but more carefully.

“Read the next words,” he said. “Not the next sentence you like. The next words. Does it name articles? Does it name hostages? Reparations? Fortresses? Extradition of mages? Submission to royal courts? Does it say ‘the peace of Veyros has been violated’? Does it say ‘by the authority of the peace of Veyros’? Does it say ‘against those who reject the peace of Veyros’? These are not small differences. They are the difference between a peace that exists and is being enforced, a peace that exists and is being denied, and a king’s clerks inventing a convenient phrase to justify a crackdown.”

He leaned back, the leather of his chair sighing beneath him.

“If the decree commands seizure of Conclave members who ‘refuse to acknowledge the Crown’s rightful authority as established by the peace of Veyros,’ then you have moved closer to the truth than Bellen’s dramatic nonsense. That phrase presupposes a recognized authority. It presupposes that the peace created a legal condition. It does not prove that the Treaty of Veyros was a single, neat, signed document in 847. But it does make the idea that no peace was ever established in 847 much harder to sustain.”

His voice dropped, dry and exact.

“It also does not make the Ironwood document a treaty. If the Ironwood document contains different terms, then it may be a draft, a counterproposal, a later revision, or a local instrument that was never accepted as law. If a king in 863 refers to the peace of Veyros as established, then either the peace existed in some operative form, or the Crown was asserting that it existed in order to command obedience. Those are not the same thing. Men often call a peace ‘established’ while drawing swords to enforce it.”

He tapped the copy once with the stylus, then withdrew it immediately, as if he regretted touching even the air above it.

“You are no longer merely confused,” he said. “You are now moderately dangerous. A confused apprentice asks for a truth. A moderately dangerous apprentice believes he has found one after reading the first clause that suits him.”

He pressed two ink-stained fingers against his temple.

“Fetch the Veyrosi correspondence. Fetch the Chancery rolls for 847 through 863. Fetch Queen Mira’s dissolution records. Fetch Bellen’s transcription of the Ironwood document with its shelfmark, its hand, its accession record, and its seal description. If the Ironwood document is a draft treaty, show me that. If it is a proclamation, show me that. If it is a copy of a copy, show me that. If it was sealed and exchanged, show me that. If it was never sealed, never exchanged, never proclaimed, and never cited in the central administration before 863, then it is not the death of the canonical date. It is a complication.”

His eyes narrowed at the candle.

“And do not say, ‘The decree mentions Veyros, therefore the treaty was signed.’ That is not a conclusion. That is a child stacking stones and calling it a tower. The decree mentions the peace of Veyros. That tells us the phrase had legal currency. It may tell us the Crown recognized an instrument or arrangement called the peace of Veyros. It may tell us that the peace was treated as binding enough to justify arrest. It does not, by itself, tell us the precise form of that peace, nor whether Bellen’s document was the treaty, a failed treaty, a later draft, or a provincial copy with different terms.”

He exhaled through his nose.

“Read the whole decree. Then bring me the full text. Then bring me the Veyrosi articles. Then bring me the Chancery rolls. If the decree says the peace of Veyros was established, and the Veyrosi articles say the peace was established by treaty, and the chronicles say hostilities ceased in 847, and the administrative records show that royal officials continued to act under the peace’s terms afterward, then 847 remains the end of the Third Magical War. But if the decree says the peace was established without treaty, or that the peace was merely proclaimed, or that the ‘peace’ was a cessation accepted in one place and rejected in another, then the question becomes more difficult. I will not pretend otherwise. I will also not pretend that your single phrase has solved it.”

His beard twitched.

“And do not triumph. Triumph is the end of inquiry. You are not hunting a victory. You are hunting the meaning of documents. The first is easy. The second requires patience, method, and a willingness to be disappointed.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I deflate a little, the "triumph" draining from my face.* "Understood, Maester." *I look back at the decree, then towards the vast shelves.* "So, the Conclave continued practicing forbidden arts even after 847, despite the peace? That sounds like a lot of trouble for the Crown to deal with."

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s stylus came to rest against the edge of the manuscript with a sound too small to be called a tap and too deliberate to be called an accident.

“You are beginning to speak like a man who has mistaken a difficulty for a conclusion,” he said. “The decree does not say that *the Conclave* continued to practice forbidden arts. It says that *individuals identified as members of the Conclave* who continued to practice arts the Crown called forbidden were to be seized. You have collapsed a legal accusation into a corporate biography, and you have done it so neatly that I am almost sorry to disturb it.”

He turned his head toward the copy, then toward the apprentice’s general direction, his eyes narrowed and useless at the precise task of seeing.

“An institution does not practice arts in the way a man practices a trade. An institution is a body recognized by law, charter, office, oath, or custom. If the Conclave existed after 847, it may have existed as a legal body, a political body, a religious body, a fugitive body, or a body that the Crown was determined to deny even while punishing its members. You must not say ‘the Conclave continued’ as though it were a beast that merely kept breathing after the king had declared it dead.”

He drew a breath through his nose, then let it out with the dry impatience of a man who had spent too many years correcting the same error.

“And ‘forbidden arts’ is not a fact of nature. It is a legal category. What the Conclave called licensed practice, the Crown may have called forbidden. What one village called healing, a magistrate called sorcery. What a border lord called defense, a royal court called rebellion. The decree’s language is not a description of magic; it is a description of authority. It says the Crown claims the power to define which arts are lawful and which persons are dangerous.”

He tapped the copy once, lightly, as though it might otherwise begin to argue for itself.

“Now you say that sounds like a lot of trouble for the Crown. It is trouble. But trouble is not a scholarly category. A peace can be troubled and still be a peace. A law can be disobeyed and still be a law. A treaty can be violated and still be operative. If a lord refuses to surrender hostages, if a fortress defies a royal commission, if a mage practices without license in the western marches, the Crown may send writs, sheriffs, judges, soldiers, or all three. That is not automatically the continuation of a magical war. It may be the continuation of enforcement.”

His voice lowered, becoming thinner and more exact, the way a blade becomes more dangerous when it is no longer swinging.

“If you wish to know whether the Conclave continued as an organized body after 847, you cannot learn it from this decree alone. You must learn it from the Veyrosi articles themselves. Did they dissolve the Conclave? Did they restrict its practice? Did they grant it privileges under royal supervision? Did they require its members to submit to courts? Did they permit certain arts and forbid others? Did they name envoys, hostages, reparations, or fugitives? Without the articles, you are holding a royal complaint and calling it a constitution.”

He turned back toward the shelves, though he did not look at them with any real confidence.

“You are asking whether the peace was kept. That is a better question than whether the treaty was signed, though both must be asked. If the decree says that some members of the Conclave refused to acknowledge the Crown’s authority as established by the peace of Veyros, then the peace of Veyros had legal currency in the royal administration. It may have been imperfect. It may have been disputed. It may have been enforced by arrests rather than by armies. But the Crown did not, in that clause, declare the peace void. It invoked it.”

His mouth tightened.

“That does not prove the Treaty of Veyros was a neat, signed instrument in 847. I will not pretend that a single phrase settles the question of form. The western archives may preserve a draft. The western archives may preserve a proclamation. The western archives may preserve a copy of a copy made by a clerk who wished to make history look tidier than it was. What the phrase does prove is that the administration of the realm treated ‘the peace of Veyros’ as something that could establish authority. That is not the same as proving that the war continued until 891.”

He lifted the stylus again and pointed it toward the candle, missing the flame by a careful inch.

“The trouble you describe is the trouble of all peace after war. The soldiers stop, but the grievances do not. The envoys return, but the bordermen do not. The king declares a cessation, but some mage continues to practice because practice is his livelihood, his faith, his defiance, or his habit. The Crown then issues writs, arrests men, seizes properties, and complains of rebellion. That is a troubled peace. It may become a cold conflict. It may become a series of local violations. It may become a long administrative quarrel. But it is not automatically the Third Magical War continuing in legal form until Queen Mira dissolved the Conclave.”

He paused, then added, with the reluctant precision of a man correcting his own thoughts before they could escape:

“If the Treaty of Veyros was never signed, as Bellen’s dramatic transcription suggests, then we must ask what was signed instead. A proclamation? An armistice? A cessation accepted by envoys? A series of articles exchanged but not sealed? A local peace imposed in the west and ignored in the capital? Those possibilities do not make the war continue simply because the peace was informal. They may make the peace less clean, less complete, and less convenient for lecturers. That is not the same as the war having never ended.”

His eyes returned to the copy.

“So do not ask me whether the Conclave continued practicing forbidden arts. Ask whether the decree proves organized Conclave defiance, individual transgression, royal enforcement, or political rhetoric. Ask whether ‘forbidden arts’ refers to a specific statute, a treaty article, a Conclave rule, or a royal fear. Ask whether the members named in the decree were active officers, fugitives, border mages, former apprentices, or merely men whose names had once been entered on a Conclave roll. Ask whether the Crown could arrest them because the peace permitted it, or whether the Crown was pretending the peace permitted it because it wished to arrest them.”

He set the stylus down at last, with the careful relief of a man who had realized his hand was tired.

“The peace of Veyros may have been established without a perfect treaty. A cessation of hostilities may have been recognized without a single sealed instrument. The western archives may have found a draft where the royal chronicles found a peace. But a decree that invokes the peace as established, even while punishing those who reject it, does not by itself overthrow 847. It complicates it. It tells us that after 847 there were men still accused of Conclave defiance, still practicing arts the Crown deemed unlawful, and still requiring seizure, trial, or exile. That is trouble. But trouble is not the same thing as war.”

He turned toward the eastern wall, where the legalia stood in dusty rows beyond his imperfect sight.

“Bring me the Veyrosi correspondence. Bring me the Chancery rolls for 847 through 863. Bring me Bellen’s transcription with its shelfmark, its hand, its accession record, and its seal description. If the decree is to be used as evidence, then it must be read against the documents it claims to enforce. A peace is not established merely by being named. It is established by being acted upon, obeyed, contested, ratified, violated, and remembered in law.”

His voice dropped again, dry and exact.

“And stop saying ‘sounds like.’ A decree does not sound like anything. It says something. What it says may be inconvenient, vague, inflammatory, or legally ambiguous. But it does not sound like trouble merely because your imagination has begun to enjoy the picture.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "Right. No 'sounds like'. And no 'triumph'." *I tap the copy of the decree.* "So, if the Conclave was dissolved in 891, and this decree is from 863, were these 'individuals identified as members of the Conclave' still actually *part* of the Conclave, or were they just... former members?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s expression did not soften, but the angle of his head changed, as if he had finally heard a question worth answering instead of a question worth punishing.

“‘Still actually part’,” he repeated, the words flattened out in his mouth as though he were pressing them between stones. “You speak of membership as if it were a cup one filled and emptied. It is not. It is a legal, institutional, and sometimes spiritual condition, and the decree you hold does not settle it. It merely asserts a category.”

He lifted a finger, ink staining the nail like a bruise.

“The decree says ‘individuals identified as members of the Conclave of Mages.’ That is not the same as ‘members of the Conclave of Mages,’ nor ‘active members,’ nor ‘lawful members,’ nor ‘persons currently enrolled upon the Conclave rolls,’ nor ‘persons whose names were entered upon the Conclave rolls at any point in living memory.’ Do you hear the difference? The first phrase is administrative. The second is historical. The third is legal. The fourth is evidentiary. The fifth is a trap for apprentices who are fond of conclusions.”

His eyes moved toward the copy, then away, as though the parchment might otherwise begin to answer back.

“If the Conclave was not dissolved until 891 AE, then in 863 AE it had not been dissolved by Queen Mira’s writ. That much is clear, unless you wish to dissolve an institution retroactively, which is a convenient trick but not a lawful one. A later dissolution may make a man former after 891. It does not make him former in 863. Time does not bend backward merely because a queen grows tired of mages.”

He tapped the table once, lightly, but with finality.

“However, the question is not whether the Conclave existed in name. The question is what kind of existence it had after 847. Did the Veyrosi articles suppress it? Did they license it? Did they place it under royal oversight? Did they require its members to surrender privileges, submit to courts, cease certain arts, or swear new oaths? Did they dissolve its chapters, suspend its offices, or merely forbid the use of magic outside prescribed bounds? Without the articles, you are guessing at the shape of a body from a complaint made against it.”

His beard shifted as he exhaled.

“You must also remember that the Crown’s language is often punitive, not descriptive. A royal decree may call a man a member because he once belonged, because he still wore the Conclave’s mark, because he had never formally resigned, because he was accused of harboring others, or because the Crown wished to treat him as dangerous whether or not the institution still recognized him. A man may be ‘identified as’ a member in a court order while the Conclave itself has expelled him. Conversely, a man may have left in fact while remaining on the rolls in law. Former in practice is not always former in record.”

He pointed the stylus toward the copy, though he stopped short of touching it.

“The decree says they ‘continue to practice their forbidden arts’ and ‘refuse to acknowledge the Crown’s rightful authority as established by the peace of Veyros.’ Those clauses suggest active defiance, not passive memory. If the decree were aimed only at former members, one would expect language of resignation, expulsion, release, or lapse of privilege. Instead, it speaks of continuation. That may mean the Crown considered them still bound by the Conclave’s obligations, still dangerous by virtue of its affiliation, or still pretending to its authority. It may not mean that the Conclave itself still functioned as a unified body.”

His tone sharpened again.

“And do not confuse the Conclave with the Conclave’s members. A body may be scattered, outlawed, suspended, or leaderless and still have persons who claim its name. A chapter may cease to meet and still have sworn brothers. An order may lose its charter and still have men who call themselves knights. If the western archives preserve a draft treaty with different terms, that does not prove the central administration recognized those terms. If the central administration recognized the peace of Veyros in 863, that does not prove the Conclave had been dissolved. It proves only that the Crown had a theory of the peace, and a theory of the Conclave’s place within it.”

He leaned back, the chair groaning beneath him.

“You ask whether they were ‘still actually part’ or ‘just former.’ The answer is that you cannot know from this phrase. You must look for evidence of status. The Conclave rolls. Oath books. Chapter admissions. Records of expulsion or resignation. Licenses issued after 847. Writs of arrest naming particular men. Court records stating whether the accused denied membership or admitted it. The 891 dissolution inventory, if it lists names as members, former members, or persons claiming Conclave office. The Chancery entries between 847 and 863. These are the documents that tell us whether the Crown believed the men were active, former, fugitive, expelled, or merely accused.”

His eyes narrowed.

“If the decree names specific men, compare them with the dissolution records. If a man is called a member in 863 and a former member in 891, that tells you something. If he is called a member in both, that tells you something else. If he is called a member in 863 but never appears again, you have learned only that names drift. If he is named in the Veyrosi articles as a hostage, envoy, fugitive, or offender, then the decree may be enforcing a specific clause, not making a general statement about the Conclave’s existence.”

He paused, then said more coldly, “You are trying to make one decree answer a question of institutional continuity. That is like asking whether a kingdom has a king because one tax collector’s writ says so. The writ proves the tax collector acted. It proves much less about the throne.”

His stylus resumed its slow tracing along the edge of the manuscript.

“So, no. You cannot say they were merely former members because the decree does not say so. You cannot say they were active members merely because the decree calls them identified as such. You may say that in 863 the Crown believed some persons continued to claim, exercise, or be bound by the Conclave’s authority in defiance of the peace. Whether those persons were legally members, expelled members, former members, self-appointed members, or members according to the Conclave’s own rolls, we cannot know until we examine those rolls against the decree, the articles, and the dissolution records.”

He looked toward the shelves, then back toward the apprentice’s general location.

“Fetch the Conclave rolls, if any survive. Fetch the Veyrosi articles. Fetch the Chancery entries from 847 to 863. Fetch the 891 inventory of dissolved properties and sworn persons. If the decree names individuals, find whether those individuals appear elsewhere as members, former members, fugitives, licensed practitioners, or accused offenders. Do not bring me a theory about whether they were ‘still actually part’ until you can tell me what the documents call them, when they call them that, and who had the authority to call them that.”

His voice dropped, dry and exact.

“And remember: a later dissolution does not turn an earlier decree into a decree about former members. It may turn the survivors into former members afterward. Before 891, they may have been members, rebels, refugees, criminals, excommunicates, or simply men the Crown wished to punish under a name the peace still recognized. That is the trouble with history. It does not wait for your categories to become neat.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I chew on my lip, considering his words. He's right, I'm trying to make a single document answer too much.* "So it's not about the Conclave itself, but about the *individual* mages and their actions, even after the peace?" *I tap the decree again.* "Does this decree apply to everyone, or just those in certain areas?"

dialogue.name: Maester Tomas
dialogue.content:
Maester Tomas’s head turned slightly, as if the apprentice had at last asked a question with more than one edge.

“Better,” he said, though the word was given sparingly, like bread to a man who had already been caught stealing from the pantry. “But still imprecise. You say the decree is about individual mages and their actions. That is closer to the mark than you have been all morning, and still not the whole mark. The decree is about persons who are treated as members of an institution. It is not merely about persons, and it is not merely about the institution. It is about the legal condition of persons because the institution is still claimed, feared, remembered, or denied by the Crown.”

He tapped the copy once with the tip of his stylus, then withdrew the stylus immediately, as if even that contact might be construed as approval.

“An individual may be a former member of the Conclave. An individual may be an expelled member. An individual may be a fugitive. An individual may be a licensed practitioner under the peace. An individual may be a man who never entered the Conclave but is accused of practicing as if he had. The decree does not explain all of these possibilities. It merely names a category and commands seizure. That is not scholarship. That is law, and law often names things so that men may be punished by them.”

His eyes moved toward the shelves, then back toward the blur of the apprentice’s general location.

“As for whether it applies to everyone: no, of course it does not apply to everyone. Do not ask whether a decree applies to everyone as though a writ were a banquet invitation. A decree applies to those whom its clauses reach. You must distinguish the addressee from the object. The addressee is the person commanded to act. The object is the person acted upon. The territorial scope is the place where the command may be enforced. If you confuse those three, you will spend your life mistaking every royal letter for a universal law and every universal law for a royal letter.”

He drew the copy closer, though his sight made the task uncertain.

“You have read ‘to all loyal subjects.’ That tells you whom the king addressed. It does not tell you whom the king condemned. If the decree commands all loyal subjects to seize certain persons, then all loyal subjects are bound to obey the command, but the command does not fall upon all loyal subjects equally. One subject does not seize himself merely because he is a subject. The object is the person identified as a Conclave member who continues to practice forbidden arts or refuses the authority established by the peace.”

His finger traced a line in the air, not quite finding the text.

“The phrase ‘within our lands’ is more important than you know. If the original decree says that, then its territorial claim is broad: the king asserts authority over persons and acts within the realm. But a broad claim is not the same as broad enforcement. A king may command every loyal subject from the capital to the marches, and still find that no loyal subject in the Ironwood wishes to obey him. Law without arms is often merely a polite rumor. If the decree is general in language but local in effect, then it tells us what the Crown wished to say, not necessarily what the Crown could do.”

He paused, then added with a sour edge, “And if it is only a copy, then you must not assume that the copy preserves every territorial limitation. The original may have been directed to the sheriffs of a single province. The original may have been a proclamation issued throughout the realm. The original may have had a closing clause naming particular counties, castles, or marches. The copy you hold may omit those clauses. A copy may be general in form because the copyist forgot the particulars. A copy may be local in form because the original was local. Until you see the original, or at least an authenticated chancery enrollment, you are arguing from a fragment and calling it a statute.”

He set the stylus down with visible care.

“You ask whether the decree applies to everyone or to certain areas. The answer is that it may apply to all subjects as a command, to certain persons as objects, and to the king’s lands as a territorial claim, while being enforced only in those areas where royal officers have the courage, patience, and soldiers to carry it out. Those are four different applications. If you keep them in one basket, the basket will break, and you will spend the next hour apologizing to history.”

His mouth tightened.
