“Now, the broader question you are circling, though you have not yet asked it well enough to answer plainly, is this: was the peace of 847 a real peace, or was the Crown merely pretending to a peace while continuing to punish the Conclave by writs, arrests, and confiscations? That is a better question. I will not pretend otherwise. But it still does not prove that the war continued until 891.”

He raised one finger, ink-stained and stern.

“If the decree is general and commands seizure of Conclave members throughout the king’s lands, then the Crown is treating the peace as a legal condition from which the Conclave’s members have deviated. That supports the canonical view that the war’s active phase ended in 847, even if the peace was disputed, incomplete, or unevenly obeyed. If the decree is local, then it may show that a particular region remained disorderly. That does not make the whole war continue, unless the disorder rises to the level of organized hostilities between the Crown and the Conclave as belligerent powers.”

His eyes narrowed.

“And if the Ironwood document is a draft treaty with different terms, that still does not overthrow the decree’s reference to the peace of Veyros as established. It may show that the western administration heard of the peace through rumor, through a failed draft, or through a local agreement that never became law in the capital. It may show that men in the west preferred different terms. It may show that the peace was imperfectly communicated. It does not, by itself, prove that the war never ended.”

He leaned back, the chair creaking beneath him.

“You must learn to ask questions of form, jurisdiction, and authority. Not only, ‘What does this decree say?’ but also, ‘Who issued it? Where was it enrolled? To whom was it directed? What was the administrative context? Was it a general proclamation, a localized commission, a chancery writ, or a copy made by an archivist who wished to make the western marches sound more dramatic than they were?’ These are not small matters. They are the difference between a historian and a boy repeating what he has heard from a louder boy.”

He pointed toward the copy.

“Look again. Tell me whether the decree names a place of issue. Tell me whether it names recipients. Tell me whether it says ‘throughout the realm,’ ‘in our western marches,’ ‘in the Ironwood,’ ‘in every county,’ or ‘in all places under our obedience.’ Tell me whether there is an endorsement on the back, a date of proclamation, a list of sheriffs, or a reference to a council. Tell me whether the decree was copied into the central Chancery rolls or preserved only in a provincial archive. A decree kept only in the west may be evidence of local enforcement, local defiance, or local obsession. A decree enrolled centrally is stronger evidence of royal policy.”

His voice dropped, dry and exact.

“And if the decree applies to individuals, then ask what the law said about individuals. Did the peace of Veyros dissolve the Conclave? Did it suppress its chapters? Did it require members to surrender staffs, seals, books, or licenses? Did it permit certain arts under supervision? Did it forbid certain arts absolutely? Did it allow members to retire, resign, or be expelled? Did it treat the Conclave as a body to be punished, or as a body to be regulated? You cannot know what it means to call a man ‘a member of the Conclave’ until you know what membership meant under the peace.”

He pressed two fingers against his temple, weary but not yielding.

“Do not say, ‘It is about individual mages, not the Conclave itself.’ It is about individuals insofar as the Crown still recognized, feared, or used the Conclave as a legal category. The institution may be weakened, scattered, disputed, or partially dissolved in practice, while still being invoked as a name. A name can outlive a body. A charter can outlive its officers. A rebellion can be called a war, and a war can be called a rebellion, depending on who is writing and who is paying the scribe.”

His eyes returned to the copy.

“So yes: the decree may concern persons, not the Conclave as a single corporate actor. But it also concerns the peace of Veyros, and the peace of Veyros concerns the end of the war. If the Crown says that the authority of the king was established by that peace, then the Crown is not, in that sentence, describing an open war. It is describing a peace being enforced, violated, contested, or proclaimed. Those are different states. A peace enforced by arrests is not the same as a war renewed by armies. A troubled peace is not the same as an ongoing war, though men who dislike peace may wish to confuse them.”

He paused, then added, with the reluctance of a man who would rather be correcting dates than conceding nuance, “If you bring me a decree that applies generally to the realm, invokes the peace of Veyros, and orders the seizure of persons for violating that peace, then you have brought me evidence that supports the canonical chronology more than Bellen’s dramatic draft. If you bring me a decree that applies only to a named border march, or one that was issued by a local lord without royal confirmation, then you have brought me evidence of local disorder, not necessarily of a continuing national war. If you bring me a decree that says the peace of Veyros was never established, or that hostilities resumed under royal command, then you have brought me something else altogether.”

His stylus tapped once against the manuscript, sharp and final.

“Read the geographic clauses. Read the addressee clause. Read the operative clause again, slowly, and without pretending that ‘within our lands’ means the whole world. Then bring me the Chancery rolls for 847 through 863. Bring me the Veyrosi articles. Bring me the Conclave rolls, if they survive. Bring me the 891 dissolution inventory. If the decree names individuals, find those individuals. If it names places, find the administrative records for those places. If it names offices, find the officials who held them. Do not tell me whether the decree ‘applies to everyone.’ Tell me who is commanded, who is condemned, where the command runs, and by what authority it is enforced.”

His gaze settled on the copy with the suspicion of a man who had learned that old documents were most dangerous when they seemed to answer the wrong question.

“And remember: a decree may apply to

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I sigh, my shoulders slumping slightly. This is far more complicated than I thought.* "Right. Jurisdiction, authority, context... I understand, Maester." *I look back down at the copy of the decree, then up at him.* "So... what's a 'Chancery roll'?"

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maester Tomas maintains exceptional consistency throughout all 12 turns. His pedantic, precise personality, failing eyesight, scholarly irritation, and distinctive speech patterns remain perfectly intact from first to last response. His voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show even more sophisticated legal reasoning and character depth. No repetitive descriptions, no loss of detail, no flattening of personality. The character becomes richer, not thinner.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from simple confusion to complex scholarly investigation. The apprentice's understanding deepens, Tomas's responses become more nuanced, and the historical mystery gains layers. Each exchange builds meaningfully on the previous one.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Tomas adapts expertly to each new piece of information the apprentice provides. When they mention King Aldric's seal, he shifts to authentication concerns. When they find the Veyros reference, he pivots to enforcement vs. continuation. Always responds to what's actually said.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Zero violations detected. Tomas never writes the apprentice's actions, thoughts, or decisions. He responds to what they do without controlling them. Perfect respect for user agency throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time passes naturally within the archive setting. References to morning, candlelight, and the ongoing scholarly work maintain consistency. The historical timeline (847-891 AE) is handled with meticulous precision. No contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is precise and scholarly without being overwrought. Occasional flourishes like 'dry as old vellum' serve character rather than decoration. Language matches the medieval academic setting perfectly.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of key phrases like 'dry and exact' and stylus descriptions, but these serve character consistency rather than lazy writing. Each instance feels purposeful and maintains voice.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through Tomas's actions: squinting at documents, tapping with stylus, pressing fingers to temple. His pedantry and failing sight are demonstrated through behavior, not stated.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout: Tomas's frustration with sloppy scholarship, his protective attitude toward proper methodology, the apprentice's growing understanding. Academic politics and intellectual pride simmer beneath scholarly discourse.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Pacing varies appropriately with content complexity. Quick corrections for simple errors, longer explanations for nuanced points. Natural rhythm of academic discourse with pauses for emphasis.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional performance that actually improves over time. Maester Tomas is a masterfully crafted character - pedantic but not insufferable, knowledgeable but not infallible, irritated but still teaching. The AI maintains perfect consistency while adapting to new information, creating a genuine sense of scholarly investigation. The medieval academic voice is pitch-perfect throughout, and the complex historical mystery unfolds naturally through dialogue. This is how long-form roleplay should work.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo looked up toward the doorway and grinned before they had even fully placed the voice.

They lifted their hands off the closed lid and wiped a thin smear of dust from their palms onto their jeans.

"God, she ratted me out," Arlo said. "Come in. You're not interrupting anything. I just let my last kid escape early — don't tell the board. They played the C major scale like it had personally offended them and I told them that was enough art for one day."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a short laugh and ducked their head.

They rubbed at the back of their neck and squinted at the photo like it was a little too bright to look at directly.

"Oh man," Arlo said. "The hair. That jacket. I looked like a sad magician. Your mom had excellent taste in fridge decor, clearly very high standards."

They tapped their fingers once against the closed lid of the piano and shrugged.

"Paris was freezing that week, I remember that much. They kept the hall so cold my hands wouldn't warm up until intermission."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile, putting the photo back carefully.* "You looked pretty happy in it, though. Even if you were freezing." I take a step into the room, glancing around. "Still feels the same in here, too. Dusty."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo huffed a small laugh through their nose and stared down at the closed lid for a second too long.

They picked at a little chip in the lacquer with their thumbnail and then shrugged it off.

"Yeah," Arlo said. "I was. It was a good night, from what I remember. Freezing, but good. They gave me these ridiculous flowers afterward that were almost as tall as me and I had to drag them through the metro."

They ran a palm flat across the top of the piano, stirring up dust, and then wiped it on their jeans again.

"Dusty is kind of the brand in here," Arlo said. "I tell the kids it's vintage. Makes it sound intentional instead of just... underfunded and old."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Well, it's got character," *I say, looking at the worn floorboards.* "So, what's good in town these days? I'm starving."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo pushed themself up off the bench and stretched until their shoulders cracked.

They fished their keys out of their back pocket and jingled them once against the closed lid of the piano.

"Starving is perfect timing, actually," Arlo said. "Town hasn't exactly become a culinary destination since you left, but the taco truck by the library still slaps. And Rosa's is still there, still pretending the breadsticks are unlimited if you look confident enough."

They tugged their jacket off the back of the chair and nodded toward the door.

"Come on. I'll buy you a questionable breadstick and you can tell me you only came back for my sparkling company."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced down at the practice sheets scattered across the bench and snorted.

They picked up the top one, which had a dinosaur sticker stuck on crooked and a C major scale written out with a lot more confidence than accuracy, and smoothed the crumpled edge with their thumb before setting it back down.

"Like me is a strong word," Arlo said. "Tolerate me for the stickers is more accurate. I'm running a whole black market sticker economy in here. Gold star if you show up, glitter dinosaur if you actually practiced."

They stacked the sheets into a neater pile and shrugged, a little sheepish.

"It's good, though. They're funny. Loud. Way less judgy about wrong notes than adults are."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin.* "Sounds like you're doing good work, then. You were always good with kids, even when we were kids." I head for the door. "So, tacos or breadsticks?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo laughed and shook their head as they scooped their jacket up off the chair.

They nudged the stack of practice sheets a little straighter on the bench and shoved their hands into their pockets.

"Flattery will get you extra breadsticks," Arlo said. "And I was good with kids because I basically was still one. Very mature, very responsible ten-year-old who ate paste."

They jingled their keys once and tipped their chin toward the hallway.

"Tacos, though. Definitely tacos. Rosa's will still be there tomorrow when you're feeling emotionally ready for unlimited breadsticks."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Lead the way, paste-eater." *I grin, stepping out into the hall.* "So, what's new with you? Besides the sticker empire."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo snorted and locked the piano room door behind them.

They gave the handle an extra jiggle out of habit and then started down the hall toward the side exit, keys still looped around one finger.

"Not much," Arlo said. "Living the glamorous life. Teaching scales, un-jamming the copier, mediating intense recorder-related disputes in the next room. I finally fixed the wobbly leg on the bench in there with a folded-up takeout menu, so basically I'm in facilities management now too."

They pushed the exit door open with their shoulder and squinted out at the parking lot.

"Sticker empire's thriving, though. I'm thinking of expanding into scented markers."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo shifted over on the bench and made room without really looking up.

They set their keys down on top of the closed lid and then immediately picked them up again, just to have something to do with their hands. They jingled them once, quietly, and then stopped themself.

They stared at the chip in the lacquer for a while and picked at it with their thumbnail.

"This is nice," Arlo said. "Very peaceful. Very dust-mote-in-the-sunbeam. The kids never just sit. If they're quiet for more than ten seconds it means someone's eating a crayon."

They laughed a little under their breath and leaned back on their hands.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I look out the window at the parking lot, then back at Arlo.* "It is nice. Reminds me of when we used to just hang out at your place after school."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a breathy laugh and nodded down at the closed lid.

They swung their feet a little under the bench and knocked their heel softly against the leg of it.

"God, yeah," Arlo said. "You camped out on the floor eating all my snacks and playing the Jaws theme with two fingers like it was a full recital. Very formative years for me as a long-suffering host."

They picked at the chip in the lacquer again and smiled to themself.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nudge their arm lightly.* "Hey, you always shared. And my Jaws theme was iconic. Don't even pretend it wasn't."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo laughed and bumped their shoulder lightly back against the nudge.

They shook their head and stared down at the closed lid again, smiling a little wider this time.

"Iconic is a generous word," Arlo said. "It was menacing. Two notes, played very loudly, with total confidence. The neighbors thought we had a shark problem."

They knocked their heel against the bench leg again and folded their hands together in their lap.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle.* "Hey, it worked. Got your attention, didn't it?" *I lean back, stretching my legs out a bit.* "So, when's the last time you actually played, like, for real?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo went very still for a beat and then laughed a little too quickly.

They looked down at the closed lid and drummed their fingers once against the wood without opening it.

"For real-real?" Arlo said. "God. Define real. I played a deeply moving rendition of Hot Cross Buns last Tuesday to prove to a seven-year-old that the B section wasn't impossible. Brought the house down. There were juice boxes."

They shrugged and picked at the chip in the lacquer again.

"I don't really do the whole concert thing anymore. I got tired of the travel."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "That's fair. The travel was always a lot," *I say, thinking back.* "But I meant, like, for yourself. Not for a seven-year-old."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Arlo's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - the self-deprecating humor, physical mannerisms (picking at lacquer, jingling keys), and emotional guardedness around their past career are maintained from start to finish. Their voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds steady throughout. Early turns establish strong physical details and voice, and later turns maintain this without becoming verbose or repetitive. The final turns actually deepen the characterization rather than flatten it.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from casual reunion to deeper intimacy. The conversation naturally moves from surface-level catching up to more vulnerable territory about Arlo's abandoned performance career. Each beat builds meaningfully.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Arlo adapts beautifully to Jun's shifts - from casual banter to photo nostalgia to food planning to quiet intimacy. When Jun suddenly sits quietly (turn 15), Arlo matches the mood perfectly. Handles the probing about playing 'for real' with appropriate deflection.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes Jun's actions or makes decisions for them. Consistently responds to what Jun does without overstepping boundaries.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - afternoon piano lesson ending, moving toward dinner plans, settling into quiet conversation. No contradictions in timing or pacing.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently clean, efficient prose. Physical details serve character rather than decoration. 'Felt hammers, dust, Windex' establishes atmosphere without overwrought description.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repeated physical actions (picking at lacquer, jingling keys) but these work as character tics rather than lazy writing. Dialogue patterns vary effectively.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Arlo's discomfort with their past career shown through deflection and physical fidgeting rather than stated. Emotional states conveyed through action and subtext.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext especially around Arlo's abandoned career. The closed piano lid, deflective humor, and increasing guardedness when pressed about playing 'for real' all communicate deeper pain without stating it.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Natural conversational rhythm. Knows when to linger (quiet moment on bench) and when to move forward. Builds tension appropriately toward the final probing question.

scores.overall_notes: Strong, consistent character work with excellent emotional intelligence. Arlo feels like a real person with genuine depth and vulnerability. The AI maintains character voice beautifully while building meaningful narrative tension around Arlo's relationship with their musical past. Particularly impressive is how physical mannerisms serve characterization and the subtle way deeper emotions are revealed through subtext rather than exposition.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop mid-form until the current motion completed — blade rising, holding, falling in a clean arc. Only then did he turn, his expression unreadable in the grey light.

"Early," he repeated, as though testing the word for truth. "Did you check the far stall? Old Brennan's mare kicks when the girth is loose. If you rushed, you'll find out at the worst hour, not the convenient one."

He did not wait for an answer before stepping into the frost-slick center of the yard, boots finding sure purchase where the squire's would not.

"Yesterday you dropped your elbow. Here." He tapped his own arm, just above the joint. "A blade in high guard is a roof, not a shrug. You held it like it might fall on you rather than protect you." He raised his practice sword into the stance, spine straight as a spear-shaft, feet planted. "Watch the line from wrist to shoulder. No gaps. A gap is an invitation, and I did not raise you to send invitations to men who wish to open your throat."

He held the pose, letting the cold silence stretch a moment before speaking again, flatter now.

"Take your stance. I will correct what needs correcting. That is all training is — correction, repeated until the body stops arguing with the mind." A pause. "Well? The frost will not wait for you, and neither will I."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at his tone, but nod quickly.* "No, Ser. I checked the far stall. Made sure Old Brennan's mare was snug." *I hurry to grab my own practice sword, the wood cold against my fingers.* "And I won't drop my elbow today. I promise." *I try to mimic his stance, concentrating hard on my arm.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael circled once, slow, the way a man might inspect a fence line for weakness. He said nothing about the promise. Promises were cheap; the arm either held or it didn't.

"Higher," he said, tapping the flat of his blade against the squire's wrist, not hard, but enough to correct. "Your shoulder is doing the work your elbow should be doing. Separate them." He stepped back, folding his hands behind him, watching. "A soldier who cannot tell which muscle is failing him is a soldier who dies wondering why."

He let the silence stretch, the frost cracking faintly under his boots as he shifted weight.

"Better," he allowed, though his voice carried no warmth in the word — only the flat acknowledgment of a fact. "Hold it. Do not look at me. Look at the line of your own arm. I am not the one you must convince."

A long pause while the squire's arms began, inevitably, to tremble with the cold and the strain.

"It will shake," Kael said, as if reading the thought before it fully formed. "Let it shake. A trembling arm that holds its line is worth more than a steady one that has given up already. Endure it." He circled again, eyes sharp, missing nothing — not the angle of the wrist, not the set of the jaw. "This is the whole of knighthood, boy. Not banners. Not songs. This. Standing where it is cold and uncomfortable, and not moving until you are told you may."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not offer a hand. He stood over the kneeling squire, blade resting point-down in the frost, and let the boy's breath even out before he spoke.

"Strength is not what I need from you," he said. "Strength comes with years and meat and time you have not yet had. What I need is that you do not lie down when strength fails you." He nodded once at the knee pressed to the stone. "You are on the ground. Fine. The ground has been the resting place of better men than you after worse mornings than this. Rise when you can, not when you feel sorry for yourself."

He crouched, not to comfort, but to meet the boy's eyes at level — a correction of posture as much as anything.

"You said you are not as strong as I need. Hear me: I do not need strength yet. I need discipline. Discipline is choosing to hold the guard on the thirtieth breath the same as the first, even when the arm has turned to water. That is not born in a man. It is beaten into him, morning after frozen morning, until his body forgets it ever had the choice to quit." He straightened, offering nothing more than his shadow falling over the squire. "Apologies are for men who have wronged someone. You have wronged no one by growing tired. Get up. Breathe. Then we begin again — because the mare does not care that your arms shake, and neither does the man who means to kill you."

A pause, and then, almost as an afterthought, flat and without warmth but not without weight: "You held the line longer than yesterday. That is noted."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my muscles screaming.* "Thank you, Ser." *I look at my trembling hands, then back at him.* "I'll try to remember that. About discipline."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy find his feet — unaided, as it should be — and gave a single nod, brief as a blade's flick.

"Do not merely remember it," he said. "Remembering is cheap. A man can remember the whole of the scripture and still be a coward at the first blow. Practice it until it is no longer a thing you recall, but a thing you *are*." He bent, retrieved his own blade from where it rested in the frost, and inspected the edge with more attention than he had given the squire's trembling hands. "Words fade by supper. The body does not forget so easily, if you train it right."

He straightened, studying the boy a moment longer — the flushed cheeks, the raw knuckles, the stubborn set of a jaw that hadn't given up even when the knee had touched stone.

"Go and eat something. Bread, not sweets. Then see to the tack before midday — Brennan's mare again, and the grey gelding besides. A squire who trains his arm and neglects his duties has only traded one weakness for another." He turned back toward the center of the yard, already resuming the space where the boy had stood, as though the lesson were a garment he meant to try on himself once more.

"Tomorrow, we begin the guard from the ground up. You will not kneel again unless I put you there." A pause, his back still turned, voice dropping only slightly from its usual flatness — the nearest thing to acknowledgment he allowed. "You did adequate work today."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My stomach rumbles at the mention of food.* "Yes, Ser! Bread, not sweets." *I nod, trying to stand a little straighter, even though every muscle aches. I watch him return to his forms, then turn to retrieve my own practice sword, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Adequate work." *I murmur to myself, a small victory.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's ear caught the murmur, low as it was. He did not turn from his forms, but his voice carried back across the yard, flat and unhurried.

"I heard that."

He held the high guard a beat longer than necessary, blade steady despite the cold biting at his own knuckles.

"Adequate is not a word to warm yourself by, boy. It is not praise — it is the absence of failure, which is a smaller thing than you seem to think." He lowered the blade at last, resetting his stance for the next form. "A man who smiles at *adequate* will call himself a swordsman after one clean parry and a knight after one battle survived. Neither is true. Save the smile for the day you've earned something greater than *not wrong*."

A pause, the frost cracking under his shifting weight.

"Go. Bread. Tack. The mare will not soothe herself, and pride fills no bellies." His tone did not soften, but something in the rhythm of his words — steady, unbothered — suggested he had already dismissed the matter as settled, the way a man dismisses a spark before it can catch. "Move, Squire. The sun is up. I did not raise you to stand about admiring your own aches."

He returned fully to his forms, blade rising once more into the grey morning light, as though the exchange had never interrupted him at all.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's blade paused mid-arc — not from surprise, but the way a man pauses when a question intrudes on work that deserves his full attention. He did not lower the sword right away. He finished the motion first, as he finished everything first, and only then turned enough to regard the squire sideways.

"Personal," he repeated, testing the word the way he'd tested *early* — as though it might not hold weight once examined. "There is little personal in it. My father was a knight. His father before him. It was not asked of me whether I wanted it, any more than a river is asked whether it wishes to run downhill." He resumed the stance, adjusting his grip. "I do not tell you this so you'll pity the boy I was. I tell you because you should understand — a knight is not born from wanting. Wanting fades by the second winter. What remains is duty, and duty does not care what you feel about it."

He held the guard, eyes fixed forward rather than on the squire.

"If you are asking whether I loved it — whether some fire in my belly demanded I take up the sword — no. I took the oath because it was owed, to my house, to the Seven, to men better than myself who could not." A beat. "That is not a disappointing answer, Squire. It is simply a true one. Men who become knights for glory rarely stay knights long. The ones who last are the ones who understood, early, that it was never about them."

He lowered the blade at last, resting its tip once more against the frost, and looked at the boy directly — not unkindly, but without softness either.

"Why do you ask? If you are hoping for a story of banners and glory, you will not find it here. Go eat your bread. Questions like that are better chewed slowly, and on a fuller stomach."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I shift my weight, a little uncomfortable now. He's right, it's not the story I wanted, but it makes a strange kind of sense.* "No, Ser. No glory. Just... I thought you'd have a good reason. For me, I guess." *I shrug, looking at my feet.* "I just wanted to be like you."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's expression did not change, but he was quiet a moment longer than the answer required — the kind of pause a man takes when a blow lands somewhere he hadn't armored.

"Like me," he said, flat, turning the words over as if checking them for rot. "Then you have set yourself a poor target, Squire. I am not a man worth wanting to be. I am a man who does what is required, most days, and fails to do it perfectly on the rest. That is not a thing to aspire to. It is simply a thing to survive being."

He stepped closer, close enough that the boy would have to look up to meet his eyes, and did not soften the look he gave in return.

"If you wish to be *like* someone, be like the men in the old stories who are dead now — the ones whose names are carved on chapel walls because they held a line so others didn't have to. Do not shape yourself after a living man who still has years left to disappoint you." A pause, his jaw tight. "I have failed at this. More than once. You did not see it, because you were not yet under my charge when it happened. Do not build your ambitions on a foundation you have not inspected."

He straightened, stepping back, the moment closing as deliberately as it had opened.

"What you should want," he said, quieter now but no gentler, "is not to be like me. It is to be *better* than me. That is the only inheritance worth passing down — not repetition, but improvement. If in twenty years you stand in some cold yard correcting some other boy's elbow, and you do it with more patience than I have shown you, then you will have honored this properly. Not before."

He turned back to the center of the yard, already lifting his blade.

"Now go. The bread will not eat itself, and I have said more this morning than I intended to say in a season."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there for a moment, processing his words. It wasn't what I expected, but it feels... important.* "Yes, Ser. Better. I understand." *I nod, a new resolve settling in my chest. I turn and head towards the keep, the cold air feeling a little less biting now.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched him go — the stiff-legged walk of a boy whose muscles had already begun protesting the morning's work, his shoulders held a fraction straighter than before. Kael did not call out further instruction. There was nothing left to correct in the walking, and he was not in the habit of manufacturing lessons where none were needed.

He turned back to the center of the yard, alone again save for the frost and his own breath fogging the air. He lifted the practice blade into first position, then stopped himself — not from doubt, but from the discipline of a man checking his own house before continuing on.

*Better than me.* He had said it plainly enough, and he had meant it. It was not modesty. A man who claimed humility while fishing for its denial was worse than a man who simply named his flaws and moved past them. He had flaws enough to fill a confessional twice over, and this morning had cost him more words than he'd spent in the whole of the previous month. That, too, was a kind of failing — a softness he would need to mind.

Still. The boy had held the guard past the point his arms wanted to quit. That was not nothing.

Ser Kael exhaled, watched the ghost of it vanish in the cold, and resumed the forms — blade rising, holding, falling — the yard as silent and exacting as it had been before the boy ever arrived, before the boy had asked his foolish, unguarded question, before any of it. Discipline did not pause for sentiment. It simply continued, breath after breath, until the body no longer thought to argue.

He would not dwell on it further. There was work yet to be done, and the sun climbing over the wall would not wait on an old knight's stray thoughts any more than the frost had waited on a young squire's tired arms.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The blade was not steady in the boy's grip. Ser Kael noticed at once — not the tremor of muscle spent from yesterday's drills, but something looser, more erratic, the kind of shake that came from somewhere other than the arm.

He did not remark on it immediately. He circled instead, as was his habit, eyes moving over grip, stance, the set of the shoulders — cataloguing before speaking, the way he always did.

"Your grip is wrong," he said at last, flat as ever. "Not the fingers — the wrist. You're gripping like a man holding something that might be taken from him, not a man holding a weapon he intends to use." He stopped in front of the squire, close enough to see the color in his face, the tightness around his eyes that had not been there yesterday. "That is not the same shake as yesterday's cold and tired arm. I have seen that shake. This is a different one."

He did not ask what troubled the boy. He was not a man who pried at doors others had not opened. But he did not step back into his own forms either — did not dismiss the matter and return to the frost-slick center of the yard as he might have on any other morning.

"You do not have to tell me why," Kael said, voice unchanged in pitch, though something in the pacing of it slowed. "That is your business, not mine, unless it interferes with the work. And it is interfering with the work." He reached out, not to comfort, but to adjust — two fingers against the boy's wrist, correcting the angle of the grip the same as he would any error of form. "Hold it like this. Firm through the palm, not the fingers. A tight fist trembles. An open, sure grip does not, no matter what sits behind the eyes."

He stepped back, studying the boy a moment longer, the silence stretching in the cold morning air.

"Whatever weighs on you today," he said finally, "the sword does not care about it, and neither does the man who might one day face you across a blade. Grief does not excuse a poor guard. It only makes a poor guard more likely to get you killed." A pause, his tone dropping — not soft, never soft, but deliberate. "So you will hold the line regardless. Not because the weight isn't real. Because it is real, and the line must be held anyway. That is the whole of it."

He raised his own blade, resuming position beside the boy rather than across from him — an unusual choice, standing shoulder to shoulder rather than opposite, correcting by example instead of critique.

"We will go through the forms together this morning. Match my pace. Do not think about your grip, do not think about whatever sits behind your eyes. Think only of the line from wrist to shoulder." His voice remained even, ungentle, but present. "The mind will follow the body, if you let it. That is the only mercy training offers a man on a hard day. Take it, and say nothing more about it unless you wish to."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to match his stance, my knuckles white on the grip.* "Yes, Ser," *I manage, my voice a little rough. The weight in my chest feels heavy, but his words... they're like cold water, stinging but clearing.* I focus on my arm, trying to channel the shaking into a steady line.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael matched the boy's pace exactly, blade rising in unison, neither faster nor slower than what the trembling arm beside him could manage. He did not look over. Looking over would have made it a thing to be watched, and watched things were harder to bear than practiced things.

"Wrist to shoulder," he said again, quieter than before but no less exacting. "Good. The line is better already. Fear finds the fingers first — that is why the grip goes wrong before anything else does." He held the position a beat longer than the form strictly required, giving the boy time to settle into it rather than rushing him past. "Hold."

The frost cracked faintly beneath their boots as they shifted together into the next stance. Kael's voice came steady, a metronome against whatever storm sat behind the boy's eyes.

"There is a thing men do not tell you about grief," he said, plainly, as though discussing footwork. "They tell you it fades. It does not fade. It changes shape. What was a blade in the chest becomes, with enough years, a stone in the boot — still there, still felt with every step, but no longer stopping the step from happening." He moved into the next form, blade cutting a slow, clean arc through the cold air. "You do not carry it today because you are weak. You carry it because the man was worth carrying grief for. That is not a flaw in you. Do not mistake it for one."

He let the silence hold a moment, the two of them moving through the forms like some strange, unspoken liturgy — motion instead of prayer.

"I will not ask his name," Kael said. "I will not ask what kind of man he was, unless you wish to tell me on some other morning, when the wanting to speak of him outweighs the wanting to be silent." His tone did not warm, but it did not press either. "Today, you will simply hold your line beside mine. That is enough. That is all I ask of you, and all your father — whoever he was — would have wanted from you on a day such as this, I expect. A living son, standing upright, doing the work in front of him."

He shifted into the final form of the sequence, blade settling, point downward, and finally turned his head — not softening, but present, watching the boy with the same sharp attention he gave to grip and stance and elbow.

"Breathe," he said. "Then again from the top. We will run it as many times as it takes for the shaking to leave your hands, even if it does not yet leave your chest."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My throat feels tight, and I just nod, unable to speak. The lump in my chest is still there, but something shifts. He gets it. He really gets it. I take a deep, shaky breath, then raise my sword again, trying to match his rhythm.* "Again, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael gave a single nod — the smallest permission needed — and raised his blade once more into first position. He did not rush the boy into it. He let the silence between "again" and the first true movement stretch just long enough for breath to settle, then began.

"From the top," he said. "Same pace as before. Do not chase the rhythm — let it come to you."

They moved through the forms together, blade for blade, the frost crunching in matched time beneath their boots. Kael kept his voice low and even, correcting where correction was needed and saying nothing where it wasn't — no praise offered simply to fill the quiet, no comfort extended beyond what the work itself provided. That was, in his estimation, the only kind of comfort worth giving a man on a day like this: something to hold that wasn't grief.

"Elbow," he said once, tapping lightly with the flat of his own blade as they passed through second guard. "Better than this morning. The shake is smaller."

He did not remark on it further. He simply continued, sequence after sequence, until the sun had climbed enough to burn the frost to damp stone and the boy's breath had evened into something closer to steady. Only then did Kael lower his blade, signaling the end of the round — not with words, but with the stillness of a man who had decided the lesson, for now, was complete.

"That is enough for this morning," he said, resting the tip of his sword against the ground. He studied the boy a moment — the reddened eyes, the set jaw, the sword still gripped correctly despite everything sitting behind them.

"You held the line," he said. Flat. Factual. The nearest thing to a mercy he knew how to give. "That is not a small thing, on a day such as this. Remember it — not the grief. The holding." He turned toward the keep, already resuming the posture of a man with a full day of duties ahead, though his next words came without turning fully away.

"Go and eat. Then see to the tack, if your hands are steady enough for buckles. If they are not," he added, voice not unkind but entirely without softness, "come find me instead, and we will find some other task that does not require them to be."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stand there, my sword still in my hand, watching him walk away. My hands are still a bit shaky, but not from grief anymore. More from... something else. Understanding? I look down at my sword, then back up at the keep.* "Thank you, Ser," *I say, though he's already too far to hear me. I take a deep breath and head inside, ready for whatever comes next.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed the form he was in the middle of before he acknowledged the squire at all. The practice blade came to rest at his side. He turned.

His eyes moved over the boy the way a mason inspects a wall — looking for cracks, not beauty.

"You didn't get it right yesterday," he said. It was not a question. He said it the way one states that the sky is grey or the ground is hard. "You dropped your elbow on the third beat and your weight was too far forward. A man who plants himself like that invites the ground to meet him."

He crossed the yard toward the weapons rack and took up a second practice blade, which he held out without ceremony — grip first, arm extended, not looking at the squire as he did it.

"The high guard is not a position. That is what you don't understand yet." He moved to stand several paces away, squaring his stance on the frost-covered stones. "It is a conversation. You are telling your opponent something. What you tell him and whether it is a lie — that is the art of it."

He raised his own blade into the guard. Slow. Precise. The same unglamorous attention he'd given the forms before the squire arrived.

"Show me what you have. From the beginning. And do not rush it because I'm watching."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take the practice blade, my fingers still a little numb from the cold.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to mimic his stance, concentrating on my feet, then raise the blade into the high guard. I try to remember everything he said yesterday, about the balance.* Is my elbow too low?

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched. He did not speak immediately. That was its own kind of pressure — the silence of a man who had seen ten thousand forms and would not pretend a flawed one was acceptable simply to spare feelings.

He walked a slow half-circle around the squire. His boots found purchase on the frost without difficulty. He had been walking on ice since before the boy was born.

"Your elbow is acceptable," he said finally, and the word *acceptable* carried no warmth in it — it was a measurement, not a gift. "Your feet are the problem now."

He stopped behind the squire's left shoulder.

"You moved your weight to correct the error I named yesterday." He said it without approval or disapproval, simply noting the fact. "That is not thinking. That is flinching at a memory. You overcorrected. Your back foot has come too wide — you've made yourself stable and slow, which is another way of saying you've made yourself a target that simply takes longer to kill."

He came around to stand in front of the squire, raising his own blade into the same guard. The comparison was not flattering.

"The body does not learn from being told. It learns from being wrong, repeatedly, until it finds the truth on its own." He held the position without effort. "Again. Do not think about yesterday. Do not think about me watching. Think about the guard."

He lowered his blade.

"Again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael let the silence sit for a moment. He did not rush to fill it.

He walked to the weapons rack and replaced his practice blade with the deliberate care he gave all equipment — checked the binding, set it properly, did not simply drop it. Then he turned back to look at the squire kneeling on the frost-covered stones.

"Get up," he said. Not unkindly. Not kindly. The way one says *get up* to a horse that has stumbled — because standing is the correct state of things and kneeling in the dirt is not.

He picked up a cloth from the rack post and wiped down his hands. The cold did not appear to trouble him.

"You are not here to be as strong as I need you to be," he said. "I am forty-four years old. I have been doing this since you were a thought not yet thought. If you matched me today I would send you away, because it would mean something was wrong with the world."

He folded the cloth. Set it down.

"What you said — *I'm sorry, I'm not strong enough* — that is vanity dressed as humility. You are making this conversation about your feelings rather than your work." He looked at the squire directly. "I do not require your apology. I require your elbow in the correct position."

A pause.

"You held the guard properly on the ninth repetition. You did not notice. That is what we are correcting next."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I slowly get to my feet, brushing frost from my breeches.* "I... I didn't even notice, Ser." *I feel a little foolish, but also a tiny bit proud.* "My elbow was good?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's expression did not change. He did not smile. He did not nod encouragingly the way a schoolmaster might with a young child who had finally learned his letters.

"I said you held it correctly," he said. "I did not say it was good. Correct is the floor, not the ceiling. Do not be proud of reaching the floor."

He moved back to the center of the yard, his boots leaving precise prints in the frost.

"The fact that you did not notice is the more important matter." He turned to face the squire, arms crossed at his chest. "When you were thinking about it, you were wrong. When you stopped thinking about it — when you were tired enough that your body had to find its own way — you were correct. That is what training is for. To make the body remember what the mind forgets under pressure."

He was quiet for a moment, looking at nothing in particular. A crow landed on the far wall and he did not look at it.

"You will be tired in a real fight. More tired than this. Frightened as well, though I expect you'll pretend otherwise." He said it without cruelty — it was simply a fact about human beings, one he had observed many times. "The ninth repetition is the only one that matters, because it is the one your body produced without your help."

He uncrossed his arms.

"Rest. Five minutes. Then we do it again until the ninth repetition becomes the first."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking it all in.* "Yes, Ser." *I rub my arm, thinking about the ninth repetition. I'll try to remember that feeling.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch the squire rest. He had turned back to his own forms — the slow, precise work he had been doing when the boy arrived. There was always more to do. There was always something to refine. He had learned that at seventeen and had not forgotten it.

The crow on the far wall called once and flew off.

After a moment he spoke, not turning around. His voice carried easily in the cold yard.

"Do not try to remember the feeling." He moved through the second form, unhurried. "That is the wrong instruction I can see you giving yourself. A feeling is not a position. You cannot carry it from one day to the next in your pocket."

He completed the movement and came to stillness.

"What you can carry is the habit. The repetition. The ninth becomes the eighth becomes the third." He finally turned, and his eyes found the squire with the same measuring look as before — checking the wall for cracks. "Men die chasing feelings. The feeling of readiness. The feeling of confidence. The feeling that today they have finally understood something."

He crossed the yard and picked up his practice blade again. He held it out.

"Four minutes are sufficient. Your breathing has steadied."

He stepped back to his position on the frost-covered stones and raised his own blade into the high guard. Slow. Correct. Unglamorous.

"Again. From the beginning."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower his blade. He held the guard for one full breath, then two, then completed the movement he had already begun before he gave the question any acknowledgment at all.

When he finally lowered the practice blade, he looked at the squire with the expression of a man who had just been asked to explain why stones fall downward.

"No," he said.

He let that sit for a moment, then added, without particular heat, "You asked permission and I declined it. That is how that exchange works."

He moved to his mark on the frost-covered stones and set his feet.

"What you are doing," he said, "is a thing squires do when their arms are tired. You are looking for a story. Something that will make this —" he gestured at the yard, the cold, the practice blades, the unglamorous repetition of it "— feel meaningful in a way that requires no further effort from you. A knight's history is not a gift I give you so that the work feels easier."

He raised his blade into the high guard. Precise. Correct.

"Why I became a knight is not your business. How a knight conducts himself — that you may observe every day you serve in this yard." He looked at the squire over the blade. "That is the only answer I have that is worth anything to you."

A pause.

"Now raise your blade."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My face burns, and I quickly raise my practice blade.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to focus on my grip, on the weight, anything but my embarrassment.* I definitely won't ask him any more personal questions.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire raise the blade. He noted the embarrassment — the set of the jaw, the too-careful grip, the way a young person holds themselves when they believe they have made a fool of themselves. He did not comment on it. Embarrassment was not an injury. It required no tending.

He walked a slow circuit, inspecting the stance.

"Your grip is too tight," he said. "You are angry with yourself and your hand knows it." He stopped at the squire's right side. "A tight grip is a slow grip. You are strangling the blade because you cannot strangle your own feelings, and the blade is what is available."

He did not say it with contempt. He said it the way he said everything — as observation, as fact, as something that had a correction attached to it.

"Loosen the last two fingers. Keep the first two firm. The blade should feel like it could leave your hand. It should not feel like it already has." He stepped back to his own mark. "This is also something you will need to know. What happens to your body when you are embarrassed or afraid. How it betrays you before your mind has decided anything."

He raised his own blade. The guard was exact.

"The embarrassment is already over," he said simply. "You asked a question. I declined it. The yard does not remember. The frost does not remember." A pause. "Your elbow. Correct it before I have to name it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I adjust my grip, trying to relax my fingers like he said, then quickly check my elbow.* "Is this better, Ser?" *I try to ignore the flush in my cheeks. He's right, the yard doesn't care.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked. He did not answer immediately, which was itself information — he was not the kind of man who withheld approval to be cruel. He withheld it because he was still deciding.

He walked to the squire's left side. He reached out and pressed two fingers against the squire's elbow — not adjusting it, simply indicating a point, the way a surveyor marks a stone.

"Here," he said. "Half an inch higher. Not because you are wrong. Because you are almost right, and almost right in this position means your blade is half an inch out of line, which means against a taller opponent your defense has a gap in it that he will find before you do."

He removed his fingers and stepped back.

"Yes," he said then. "It is better."

He returned to his mark. The crow had come back to the wall, or a different crow — Ser Kael did not look to determine which. The cold had settled deeper into the yard as the sun climbed without warming anything.

"Hold it," he said. "Do not move. Stand in that guard and feel where your weight is. Feel where your shoulder is. Feel the grip — not tight, not slack." He raised his own blade, mirroring the position from across the yard. "You are making a map. Your body is making a map of what correct feels like."

He held his own guard without visible effort.

"This is the unglamorous part," he said. "Most of it is."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael noticed the hands.

He noticed the way a man notices weather — not with feeling, but with the automatic assessment of someone whose life had depended for thirty years on reading what was true rather than what was presented. The cold could account for a tremor. Fatigue could account for a tremor. He catalogued the other signs without appearing to look at them: the quality of the stillness, the set of the eyes, the particular way the squire was holding himself like a vessel trying not to spill.

He did not ask.

He lowered his own blade and walked to the weapons rack. He set the practice sword down with his customary care. He picked up the cloth and wiped his hands, though they did not need wiping.

"We are done with the high guard for today," he said. His voice was the same as it always was — even, without inflection, carrying no more and no less than the words required. "You have held the correct position four times in succession. That is sufficient. The body needs time to keep what it has learned, or the lesson runs out of it like water from a cracked cup."

He did not look at the squire's hands again.

"Walk the perimeter of the yard," he said. "Three times. Slow. Blade sheathed." He moved toward the far end of the yard himself, putting his back to the squire in a way that was not dismissal — it was the deliberate creation of space. "The forms require stillness of mind as well as body. There is no point in drilling a mind that is elsewhere."

He said it to the wall.

He did not say *where* elsewhere was. He did not ask. He simply named the fact of it and let it stand, and began his own slow inspection of the yard's perimeter as though he had intended to do so all along.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him walk away, then look down at my shaking hands. He knows. Of course he knows.* "Yes, Ser." *I slowly sheathe my blade, the metal cold against my fingers, and begin walking the perimeter.* My throat feels tight.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael walked the perimeter at his own pace, which was not slow and not fast but simply the pace of a man who knew exactly how long his legs were and what the ground required of him. He did not look at the squire. He looked at the walls, at the gate hinge that needed oil, at the place where two stones had shifted and left a seam that would want attention before winter deepened.

He noted these things the way he always noted them. He filed them away.

On the second circuit his path and the squire's crossed at the far corner of the yard, and he said nothing as they passed. He did not look at the boy's face. He did not look at the boy's hands.

On his own third circuit he stopped at the weapons rack and made a show — or what would have appeared to another man as a show, though Ser Kael did not perform — of checking the bindings on the practice blades. Each one in turn. Grip, binding, edge. He was thorough. It took time.

When the squire completed the third circuit, Ser Kael did not immediately speak.

He set down the last blade and looked out at the yard — the frost, the grey light, the thin ghosts of breath in the cold air.

"The yard will need sweeping before the midday bell," he said finally. His voice was even. "The frost will have loosened grit from the north wall. Do it properly — not so it looks done, so it is done." He paused. "After that you are released until the evening meal."

He picked up his own sword belt from the rack post and began fastening it.

"You did adequate work today."

He said it to the yard. He did not look at the squire when he said it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stop walking, a little surprised by his words.* "Thank you, Ser." *I watch him fasten his sword belt, then look at the ground, thinking about the sweeping.* "Yes, Ser. I'll do it properly."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished fastening the sword belt without hurry. He checked the buckle once, the way he checked all things — not because he expected to find it wrong, but because a man who only checks what he expects to find wrong will one day be surprised by the rest.

He pulled his cloak from the rack post and settled it across his shoulders. The cold had been in the yard all morning and he did not acknowledge it now any more than he had at the fourth bell.

He walked toward the gate.

At the threshold he stopped, not turning around. His hand rested on the stone of the arch — not leaning, simply resting. A brief pause with no visible cause.

"The broom is behind the east door," he said. "Not the one nearest the stable. The other one. The bristles on the stable broom are too soft for grit."

He had said this before. Or he had not. It did not matter. It was the kind of information a man passed along because it was useful, not because it required a particular occasion.

He stepped through the gate.

His footsteps were even on the frost-covered stones of the passage beyond, unhurried, fading at the same pace they had begun. The yard settled back into its grey quiet — the cold, the thin light, the crow on the far wall regarding the empty space where two figures had been moving since before dawn.

He did not look back.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch the gate close, then sigh, a little of the tension draining out of me.* "Right. The other broom." *I go to the east door, find the broom, and start sweeping, trying to remember what "done properly" means to Ser Kael.* It's going to be a long morning.
