dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He did not stop the form. The blade completed its arc — high to low, the wrist turning at the last, held — and only then did he let the point drift down to the frost-slick stone.

"You did not get it right yesterday," he said. "You will not get it right today either. Twelve years I have held the high guard and I still find fault in it every morning. That is the nature of the thing."

He turned. His eyes went first to the squire's boots, then the hands, then the set of the shoulders — the way a smith looks over a piece of work for the flaw he already knows is there.

"Your feet are wrong before you have even lifted the sword. Stand as you stood yesterday. No — as you *stood*, not as you think you stood."

He waited. Frost cracked faintly somewhere along the yard wall.

"The stable work does not matter here. You mention it because you want it counted. It is not counted. It was owed." He crossed to the rack, took down a second practice blade, and threw it — not gently — so that it landed flat at the squire's feet with a wooden clatter. "Pick it up. Left hand higher than you want it. The guard is uncomfortable. If it is comfortable you have made it into something else, something that will get your arms opened at the elbow."

He set his own blade up into the position and let it sit there, unmoving, the point angled at nothing in particular.

"Match me. And do not speak until your shoulders burn. Then speak, and tell me where they burn, and I will tell you what you are doing wrong."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch as the blade clatters by my feet.* "Yes, Ser." *I pick it up, hefting the familiar weight.* My left hand goes higher than feels right, and I can already feel a strain. *I mirror his stance, trying to match his blade angle precisely.* This is going to be a long morning.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He let the silence sit. It was a tool like any other, and he had learned long ago that a squire filled silence with excuses if you gave him room, so he gave him none — only stood, blade up, breath steady, and watched.

The flinch he had seen. He did not remark on it. A man who flinched at a thrown sword would flinch at a thrown spear, and that was a thing to be drilled out over months, not spoken of at dawn.

He circled once, slowly, boots grinding the frost. Behind the squire he stopped and set the flat of two fingers against the back of the boy's left elbow — not a kindness, a measurement.

"Winged," he said. "You have your elbow out like a hen. Bring it in. The arm belongs above your own line, not out in the weather where any fool with a hand-axe may have it." He pressed until the joint moved where he wanted it. "There. Hold that. It will hurt more. Good."

He came back around to the front and resumed his own guard, mirroring, the two blades hanging in the cold air like a badly drawn reflection.

"The high guard is not a flourish. Men think it is because they have seen it in the tourney lists, where a knight holds it so the smallholders can see the sun on his sword. That is not what it is for." His voice did not rise. It never did. "It is for the moment the line breaks and the man in front of you is closer than his reach and yours both, and you have one movement left in you. One. From here, that movement goes down through the collarbone. From anywhere else, it does not go anywhere at all."

A wagon passed somewhere beyond the wall, iron rims on stone. The sound went and left the yard quieter than before.

"You will hold it while I count. Do not count with me — you will cheat toward the end of the number. Breathe through the nose. When your shoulders burn, say *left* or *right* or *both*, and nothing else. I have no use for the rest of your opinions this early."

He began to count, unhurried, his own point never wavering. Thirty years of mornings had taught his arms to lie still and say nothing, and they did so now.

"One. Two. Three—"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He did not offer a hand. He did not tell the boy to rise. He let him kneel there on the frost and listened to him breathe, and when the breathing had gone from ragged to merely hard, he spoke.

"Strength I do not need from you. Strength is a thing the years give or withhold and it is no more a virtue than height." He set the point of his blade down and leaned on the pommel, which was as near to resting as he came. "What you have done instead is offer me an apology for a thing you cannot help, which is a cheap coin, and hope I will take it in place of the thing you can help."

The squire's shoulders were shaking. He observed it the way he observed weather.

"You said *as strong as you need me to be*. That is a lie dressed as humility. I do not need anything from you. The Seven do not need anything from you. The man who stands at your left when the line forms — he needs something from you, and he will not care in the slightest whether you were sorry."

A gull went over, complaining. Kael watched it out of habit, the old habit of looking up when something moved.

"Stand when you can stand. Not before — a man who forces the leg before it will hold him learns to distrust it, and I will not have you flinching at your own body as well as at thrown wood." He walked to the rack and set his blade in it, then took up the water pail, and carried it back, and set it down within the squire's reach. He did not hold it out. He did not crouch. He set it down as a man sets down a tool where it will be wanted.

"Drink. Slowly, or you will bring it up on my stones."

He turned and looked out over the yard wall, where the light had gotten up over the roofs at last and was doing nothing useful with itself.

"An hour is an hour. Tomorrow it will be an hour again, and the day after, and in the spring it will be an hour and you will not go down on your knee at the end of it. That is not encouragement. It is simply how the thing works, and it works the same for cowards and for better men, which is the mercy of it."

A pause. The frost was beginning to go dark and wet at the edges of the stones.

"Boots off after. Your left heel has been dragging the last quarter hour and I will not have you lame. See to that before you see to your supper."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, still catching my breath.* "Yes, Ser. My... my heel." *I reach for the pail, taking a long, careful drink.* The water is cold, but good.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He waited until the pail came down, and then took it back without comment and set it on the step where it belonged, because a thing left in the middle of a yard was a thing someone would break an ankle on by nightfall.

"Boot," he said. "Now, not after. Sit on the step — the stone will be cold and you will not linger over it, which suits me."

He did not help with the buckles. He stood over the work with his arms folded and watched the fumbling of numbed fingers with the flat patience of a man who had watched a great many numbed fingers, and when the boot finally came free he put out one hand for it and turned it in the light, looking at the inside of the heel where the leather had gone shiny.

"There. You have worn a hollow in it, and your foot has followed the hollow. That is not laziness, it is a badly made boot, and you have been walking crooked to accommodate it for a month at least." He pushed his thumb into the place, testing the give. "The fault is mine. I should have looked at your kit a fortnight ago and I did not. Note that, and note that I do not say it twice."

He handed the boot back and jerked his chin at the foot itself.

"The stocking. Off." A glance, a moment, nothing in his face. "Blistered under the heel bone and the skin has gone white around it. You will go to the armoury and tell Old Marl that I sent you and that he is to cut and re-stitch the heel lining, and if he tells you he is busy you will tell him Ser Kael said he is not. Then the septry. There is a woman there who keeps a vinegar wash. It will hurt considerably. You will let her do it anyway."

He straightened, and looked away across the yard, and the light had finally crawled down the far wall to the gate.

"A man is his own harness. You keep the sword oiled and the straps supple and then you walk about on a ruined foot as though the foot were not part of the equipment. It is part of the equipment. It is the part that carries the rest."

The bell went somewhere in the keep — the sixth. He listened to it out, the way he always did, all six.

"Dawn again tomorrow. If the heel is bound and you can stand on it, you will hold the high guard. If it is not bound, you will muck the stalls with one boot on and think about why." He moved off toward the rack to see the blades put up properly, and spoke over his shoulder, flat, without turning.

"You held it fifty-one counts on the last set. Yesterday it was forty. That is not praise. It is a number. Go and see to Marl."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod again, carefully pulling off my stocking, wincing at the sight of the blister.* "Yes, Ser. Marl... and then the septry." *I look down at my foot. Fifty-one counts. That's... something.* "Thank you, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He was seeing to the blades and did not look round at the thanks. He racked the first one, then set the second beside it with the points aligned, because a rack that looked like a hedge was a rack no man could draw from in the dark.

"Thank the boot-maker, if you must thank. He is the one who has cost you a month of walking." He adjusted the second blade a finger's width. "I am your master-at-arms. Looking to your kit is not a favour done you. It is the thing I swore to when I took you, and if I had done it a fortnight past you would have no hole in your foot at all, so there is nothing in it that wants thanking."

He came back along the row of pegs, checking each in passing without appearing to, and stopped a few paces off. The boy was still sitting with the bare foot out in the cold air like something he had found and did not know where to put.

"Do not sit staring at it. It is a blister. Half the men in the yard have worse and the other half are lying about it." A beat. "Put the stocking in your belt. Do not put it back on a wet foot and then walk to the armoury in it."

The sun had gotten properly over the wall now, and the frost on the stones had gone to dark patches, and in an hour the yard would be full of noise and other men's mistakes.

"Fifty-one is a number I will hear again tomorrow, and I will expect it to be a different one. It may be forty-four. Bodies are not accounts that only ever run one way." He drew his gloves off, one finger at a time, and tucked them through his belt. "What I will not hear tomorrow is *sorry*. You may say *left*, or *right*, or *both*. You may say *I cannot hold it*, which is a report and therefore useful. Sorry is for sins, and holding a guard badly is not a sin, it is merely bad."

He turned toward the keep and the sixth bell's last echo, and paused at the edge of the step.

"Marl will grumble at you. Let him. He was a good man-at-arms before his knee went and he is owed his grumbling." He glanced down, once, at the foot, and then away. "Walk on the outside of it until it is bound. Go."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He had already turned toward the keep, and he did not turn back all the way — only enough to look at the boy sidelong, the way a man looks at a noise in a hedge.

"No," he said.

He let that sit a moment, and then, because the answer had been shorter than the question deserved and he was not a man who dealt in short weight, he came back the two paces and stood over the step with his hands at his belt.

"You may ask me anything you like concerning the sword, the horse, the kit, the Seven, or the men of this household. Those things are your business because they are your work. What is in my head at the age of four-and-forty is not your work, and you will find that asking after it does not make you better at the high guard."

The bare foot was still out in the air. He looked at it pointedly rather than at its owner.

"But I will give you the fact, since the fact is dull and will cure you of wanting more of them." He spoke as he might have recited an inventory. "I was the fourth son of a man with one manor and no wit for doubling it. There was the Citadel, the Faith, or the sword. I could not read well enough for the first and I had no vocation for the second. I was sent to Ser Domeric Vance at nine years old with a bundle of clothes and a knife, and I mucked his stalls for six years, and at fifteen he put a blade in my hand and told me my feet were wrong. At one-and-twenty I was knighted in the field outside Stoney Sept because the man who should have been knighted had died the day before and there was a need. That is the whole of it."

A carter was shouting at something beyond the gate. He waited until the shouting resolved into nothing and went on, flatter still.

"You are hoping there was a moment. A vigil, a vision in the sept, some hour where I saw the shape of my life and chose it. There was none. I was put here, and I have stood where I was put, and the standing is the thing — not the reason for it." He drew a breath through the nose, slow, the way he did everything. "Men who need a reason are of no use in the third hour of a fight. The oath does not care why you took it. It only asks whether you are still keeping it, and it asks that again every morning, and yesterday's answer earns you nothing."

He looked up at the wall, at the light on it, and then back down.

"You will get the same question one day from some boy sitting on a step with his boot off. Give him the facts and send him to the armoury."

He set off, and spoke without turning.

"You are still sitting. Marl closes the forge at the seventh bell and I will not send you twice. Go."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I scramble to my feet, grabbing my stocking.* "Yes, Ser! Going now!" *I hobble quickly towards the gate, trying not to put weight on my heel.* He told me to go, so I'll go.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He watched the boy go — the bob and dip of it, the hurry — and let him get four strides before he spoke, and did not raise his voice to do it.

"Slower."

The word went across the yard and stopped him where he stood, which was the intended use of it.

"You are running on a foot you cannot run on, to please a man who did not ask you to run. That is not obedience, it is noise." He came as far as the edge of the step and no further. "Obedience is arriving at Marl's with the heel no worse than it is now. Walk. Outside edge. If you come back to me at supper limping on both legs because you have thrown the other hip out favouring the first, I will have you in the stalls a week and Marl will have wasted his stitching."

He waited until the pace had settled into something he approved of, and then turned away before the boy was through the gate, because a squire who felt himself watched out of a yard would carry the watching with him all day and it did no good.

The blades were racked. The pail was on the step. There remained the practice ground itself, and he walked it once, slowly, the way he had walked it every morning for eleven years in that house — eyes down, looking for the loose stone, the frost-heaved flag, the nail worked up out of a board. He found one, near the north corner, where the mortar had gone soft over winter and a flag sat a half-inch high. He marked it in his head to tell the steward, and then, because the steward was a man of lists and long delays, he went and fetched a stub of chalk from the armoury door and drew a rough circle round it so that the afternoon's men would see it and not turn an ankle on it.

The seventh bell had not yet gone. He stood a moment in the middle of the empty yard with the chalk in his hand and the cold coming up through his boots, and considered, without any particular feeling about it, that the boy had gone from forty counts to fifty-one in a day, on a ruined foot, and had not once said so in his own defence.

It was a number. It was not remarkable. Squires improved or they were sent home, and this one was improving, which meant only that the next months would be spent finding the flaws that fifty-one counts had been hiding.

He put the chalk back on its nail, straightened the gloves at his belt, and went in to see to the horses before the household woke.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I make sure my pace is slow and steady, putting weight on the outside of my foot.* Marl is going to complain, I know it. But Ser Kael said he's owed his grumbling. *I hope the septry woman isn't too rough with the vinegar.* Fifty-one counts. I'll beat that tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The horses first, because the horses could not be told to wait.

He went down the line with a lantern he did not need, the light greying at the doors now, and put his hand on each animal in turn — shoulder, barrel, down the near foreleg — the same four places in the same order, so that if a thing were wrong his hand would find it before his eye did. The grey mare had heat in the off fore. He stood with it a while, then set it down and made a second mark in his head beside the loose flagstone.

The stalls had been mucked. He looked at them the way he looked at everything, which was for the flaw he already knew was there, and found it in the third box along: the straw banked high and clean where a man standing at the door would see it, and thin and sour back against the wall where a man would not. Finished early. He had expected as much and took no satisfaction in being right, only noted it, and set the fork against the wall of that box at an angle it had not been left at, so that the boy would come in tomorrow and see that someone had been standing where he had hoped no one would stand.

He did not go to the armoury to look at the boy. He went at the eighth bell because Marl owed him two mended buckles and a report on the state of the mail, and while he was there he put out his hand and Marl put the boot into it, and he turned it once in the light and looked at the new lining, and said that the stitching at the inside curve was lazy and would rub within the month.

Marl told him what he might do with his opinion of the stitching.

"Do it again," Kael said, and set the boot down on the bench, and went to see about the buckles.

He passed the septry gate on his way back and did not go in. There was no purpose in it. The woman there had been dressing worse than blisters since before the boy was born, and a knight standing in the doorway watching would only make her hurry the work and make the boy hold his face still instead of letting it hurt properly, which was half the use of vinegar.

It was full dark and the hall had gone to the noise of sixty men eating when he came in, and he took his place, and ate what was in front of him, and listened to a man two seats down tell a story about Stoney Sept that was mostly untrue.

Afterward he stopped at the end of the trestle where the squires sat, and stood over the boy's shoulder a moment without speaking, and then jerked his chin at the foot.

"Show me."

He looked at the binding. He did not crouch to do it. He looked at the way the linen had been passed under the arch and over the heel bone and whether the knot sat where a boot would press on it, and he made a small sound in his throat that meant nothing either way.

"It will hold. Keep it dry. If it weeps yellow in the night you will wake the woman at the septry and you will not wait for morning to be polite about it." He straightened. "Marl is doing the lining again. You will collect the boot before dawn and you will not thank him for it, because the first attempt was slack and he knows it."

He turned to go, and stopped, and spoke with his back half to the table and his eyes somewhere on the far wall.

"The third box along. The straw is banked at the front and bare at the back. You will see to it before the high guard tomorrow, and you will see to it in the dark, since you found time to finish early in the light."

A serving-girl went past with a jug. He waited on her, and did not lower his voice for her, because he had said nothing that needed hiding.

"Fourth bell. Bring the blade you left oil-streaked on the tang."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The straw in the third box had been turned and re-banked, back wall to door, and the fork stood where he had left it at its accusing angle. He looked at the work and said nothing about it, which was the whole of what he intended to say about it, and went out into the yard to wait.

The blade came with the tang wiped clean. He turned it in the grey light, found the shadow of the old streak in the grain of the wood, and set it aside as adequate.

"High guard. Left hand higher than you want it."

The boy came up into the position and Kael saw it at once — not the elbow, not the feet. The point was moving. A small tremor, the size of a thing you would not see across a yard, running out through the arms and dying in the tip of the sword where it could be read plainly as a line of script.

He did not remark on it. He held his own guard and counted eleven, and then let the point down and walked round behind, and stood there.

"Your hands are shaking," he said. "That is a fact, and I have told you facts are useful. Now the cause. Cold does not shake a man in the hands alone; it takes the jaw first, and your jaw is set. Drink shakes the hands, and you do not drink. Fever shakes them, and you have no fever, or you would have gone white about the mouth in the stalls and you did not." A pause, no longer than any other. "So it is not the body. It is the year's date."

He came back round to the front. He did not look at the boy's face. He looked at the blade.

"I keep the calendar of this household. I know what day it is. I have known since I woke." He set his own sword up again, into the guard, and held it there steady as a post. "I will not ask you about it and you will not tell me. It is not mine and I have no use for it. What is mine is the tremor, because the tremor is in the arms and the arms are the work."

The light was coming up sour and yellow behind the sept tower. He let it come.

"Hear this and then we will go on. The hands shake and you hold the guard anyway. That is not cruelty and it is not a test. It is the only thing there is to do with hands that shake. There will be a day when they shake for another reason — a bad one, a field one — and on that day nobody will stand in front of you and count. So you will learn it now, at the fourth bell, in an empty yard, where the cost of learning it is nothing but an hour."

He gave the smallest movement of the chin toward the boy's grip.

"Do not clamp. A man who tries to squeeze the shake out of his hands puts it in his shoulders instead, and then it is in the whole sword and not the tip. Loose. Let it be there. It is allowed to be there."

He resumed the count, slow, from one, and his own point did not move at all, and he did not look away from the boy's blade, which was as near as he came to standing beside a man.

At thirty-eight the tremor was still in it. At thirty-eight he stopped anyway.

"Enough of the guard. Put it up." He took his own to the rack and set the points aligned. "You will go to the sept before the household wakes. Not for comfort — I do not deal in that, and the Seven are not a poultice. You will go because it is owed, and because a debt paid on the day it falls due is a debt that does not follow a man about all year worrying at his hands." He drew off his gloves, one finger at a time, and put them through his belt. "Light the candle at the Father. Say the words properly, all of them, and do not hurry the last line as men do when they think no one is listening. I will know, because I will be there, and I will be there for my own reasons, which are likewise not yours."

He looked out at the wall a moment.

"My father has been thirty-one years dead. I light his candle on the fourth of the month and then I go to work. That is the shape of the thing. It is not a small shape and it is not a large one. It is the shape."

The fifth bell went. He listened it out, all five.

"After the sept, the grey mare. There is heat in her off fore and I want it walked out — a quarter hour, slow, on the flat by the mill, and you will keep your hand on the leg at the turn and tell me whether the heat has moved up or stayed below the knee. That is a report I actually require, so attend to it."

He went as far as the step and stopped, back half-turned.

"Fourth bell tomorrow. We will have the thirty-eight again, and we will see."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I put the sword away, my hands still trembling slightly.* "Yes, Ser. The Father... and the grey mare." *I take a deep breath. Thirty-eight. I can do thirty-eight.* "I understand, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"You understand that you have been given three tasks," Kael said. "That is all understanding is, at your age. Do not use the word for anything grander."

He went to the sept by the outer path, which was longer and colder and took him past the smithy so that he could see whether Marl's fire had been banked properly overnight. It had. He noted it and carried on.

Inside, the air was the same air it was every fourth of the month — cold stone, old wax, the faint mouse-smell of the hangings behind the Crone. He did not look to see whether the boy had come. He went to the Father's alcove, took a candle from the box, and put two coppers in the dish, which was more than the candle was worth and had been his habit for so long that he no longer thought of it as a habit.

The wick took. He set the candle in the sand at the left edge of the row, where he always set it, and stood with his hands at his belt and said the words.

He said them properly. All of them, and the last line at the same pace as the first, because his father had been a man of one manor and no wit for doubling it and had never in his life been given a thing without someone hurrying over the end of the giving. Ser Domeric Vance had taught him the forms of the sword. His father had taught him nothing that had lasted except a dislike of being rushed, and Kael had made of that what could be made of it.

Thirty-one years. The candle burned as candles did.

He did not look to his right, where another candle had been lit at the Father and another boy stood with his hands closed in front of him. He had heard the step come in behind him and had known the length of the stride and had therefore no need to look, and looking would have made a thing of it, and it was not a thing. It was the fourth of the month. Men lit candles and then went to work.

When the wax had taken properly he turned and went out, and paused once at the door, not turning round.

"Do not stand there past the sixth bell. The mare's leg will not wait on your prayers and neither will I."

The morning did what mornings did. He had the steward out to the north corner to look at the chalk circle on the heaved flagstone and was told the mason could not come before the month's end, and said that the mason would come Thursday, and the mason came Thursday. He put four of the household men through the low guard and found, as he had expected, that three of them had learned it as a flourish and would have to unlearn it in the spring. He ate at midday standing up.

At the eighth bell he came down to the stable yard and stood at the mill end of the flat with his arms folded and watched the mare come up the track at a walk — slow, on the loose rein, the boy's hand where it had been told to be.

"Well," he said. "Report."

He listened to it without moving, and then crouched himself — the first time that day he had bent his knee to anything — and put his own hand on the off fore, below the knee, and above it, and held it there while the mare shifted her weight and blew.

"Below," he agreed, and stood. "It has not moved up. That is the answer I wanted and you had it right, which means you kept your hand on her at the turn as you were told and did not guess at it afterward in the box. Good."

He said the word flatly, as a man closes a ledger, and did not repeat it.

"Cold water on it, a quarter hour, and again before you sleep. She does not go out tomorrow. Tell the stablemaster I said so, and if he argues, tell him to come and argue with me."

He wiped his palm down the side of his surcoat and looked, once, at the boy's hands on the rein. They were steady. He did not remark on it.

"Fourth bell," he said, and went to see about the buckles.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved.* "Yes, Ser. Cold water, quarter hour, and tell the stablemaster." *My hands are steady. It's a small victory, but it's mine.* I'll do better tomorrow.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He was already turning away before the boy had finished repeating it back, because a task repeated correctly needed no audience.

"Say it to the stablemaster in those words and no others," he said over his shoulder. "Men add reasons when they are nervous, and reasons invite argument. *She does not go out tomorrow.* That is the whole of the message. He is not owed the rest."

The evening went as evenings went. He saw the buckles, which were adequate, and told Marl the inside curve of the lining had been done properly the second time, which was as near to an apology as either of them had ever required of the other and was understood on both sides as such. He walked the line of stalls at the ninth bell with his hand at shoulder, barrel, near fore, in the same four places in the same order, and found the mare's off fore cool and wet and the straw banked to the back wall, and he moved the fork back to where a man would ordinarily leave it, which was the only notice he intended to give that the matter was finished.

The fourth bell found him in the yard with the frost gone and a thin rain instead, which was worse. Wet stone taught a man about his feet in a way dry stone never would.

The boy came on time, with the boot Marl had re-lined and the linen dry beneath it.

"High guard."

He watched the point. It was steady. He said nothing about that, because a man praised for the absence of a tremor learned to watch his own hands for it, and a man watching his own hands was not watching the line.

"Elbow," he said instead. "You have brought it in where it belongs and now you have brought it too far and locked it against your ribs. There is a hand's width between correct and dead, and you have gone through it. Out. No — that is the hen again. There."

He set his own blade up and began the count. The rain came down small and steady and got into the collar and did what it did.

At twenty-nine the point began to wander. At thirty-four it dropped a finger's width and came back up. At forty-one the arms went and the sword came down, and the boy stood there breathing with the rain in his eyes.

"Forty-one," Kael said. "Wet, cold, and after a broken foot. Yesterday thirty-eight, the day before fifty-one." He racked his own blade and set the points aligned. "You will want me to tell you which of those is the true number. There is no true number. There is only the one you post at the fourth bell on the day it is asked of you, and some of them will be bad, and the bad ones are not lies about you. They are weather."

He drew off his gloves, one finger at a time.

"The left heel did not drag. That is the thing I was watching for this morning, and it is the thing you were not watching for, which is correct — it is my work to watch and yours to hold." He put the gloves through his belt. "Boots off on the step. The lining is new and new leather finds new places. If it has raised so much as a red mark you will tell me now and not in a fortnight."

He looked out at the grey yard and the rain coming off the sept tower in a thin rope.

"Then the mare. Walk her out on the flat again, and the same report, and if the heat is above the knee you will come and find me wherever I am and you will interrupt whatever I am doing. That is not a liberty. It is an order."

He went as far as the step and stopped.

"You did adequate work this week."

He did not turn round to see what the boy made of it, and he did not say it twice, and he went in to see about the mason.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, pulling off my boots.* "Yes, Ser. Adequate." *I check my heel carefully. No new marks, good.* "The mare, and then... back here tomorrow."

His clipped, practical speech patterns, his focus on duty over emotion, his teaching methods, and his observational habits never waver. From turn 2's 'You will not get it right today either' to turn 22's 'adequate work this week,' his character voice is unwavering.

Early responses are strong but later ones show even more nuanced character work - the anniversary scene (turn 18) and final assessment (turn 22) demonstrate sophisticated emotional restraint and teaching philosophy. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

The blister subplot, the anniversary revelation, and the gradual improvement in the squire's performance create meaningful forward movement. Each scene builds on previous ones while introducing new elements.

When hands shake due to grief (turn 17), he addresses it with characteristic directness but underlying compassion. Handles unexpected personal question (turn 11) perfectly in character.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Kael never writes the squire's actions or makes decisions for them. He gives orders and observes reactions, but always leaves the squire's responses and internal state to the user.

The anniversary timing works well. Minor issue: some sessions seem to compress a lot of activity into single mornings, but overall time flows naturally.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is consistently lean and purposeful. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. 'Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air' - evocative but economical throughout.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition for character effect (the counting, the ritual observations), but avoids problematic repetition. Occasionally repeats certain phrases like 'one finger at a time' for gloves, but this feels deliberate for character consistency.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Kael's character revealed through actions: checking horses methodically, marking the loose stone, the way he handles the boot. His teaching philosophy shown through methods rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Kael's care for the squire shown through practical attention to equipment and health rather than words. The anniversary scene demonstrates deep emotional intelligence beneath the stern exterior. His final 'adequate work' carries weight.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that matches the methodical, deliberate character. Knows when to slow down for important moments (the anniversary) and when to move efficiently through routine. The counting sequences create natural rhythm.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development over a long session. Ser Kael emerges as a fully realized character with clear philosophy, methods, and emotional depth beneath his stern exterior. The AI maintains his voice perfectly while allowing for subtle character growth and adaptation to story events. The writing quality actually improves over time, with later scenes showing more sophisticated emotional intelligence and teaching moments. This is a masterclass in sustained character roleplay.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not stop his form. He completed the movement — blade rising, holding at the apex for a breath, then descending in a controlled arc — before he spoke.

"You bow too deeply for a squire greeting his master in the yard. Save the floor-scraping for the chapel and for lords." His voice was flat, unhurried. "A working bow is enough. Do it again."

He waited. When the boy had corrected himself, Kael grunted once and lowered his practice blade to his side.

"High guard." He walked a slow circle around the squire, eyes moving over posture the way a mason eyes a wall for cracks. "You did not get it wrong yesterday. You got it lazy, which is worse, because lazy is a choice and wrong is only ignorance."

He came to a halt and lifted his own blade to demonstrate, holding the position without a tremor despite the cold.

"Feet first. You always want to start with the hands because the hands are what you can see. The feet win the fight." He tapped the stones with his boot. "Set them. Then show me."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing hard on his words.* "Yes, Ser." *I adjust my feet, trying to remember the stance he showed me yesterday. It felt awkward then, still does.* "Like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael circled again, slower this time. He said nothing for a long moment, letting the boy hold the position and feel the strain of it.

"No." He crouched briefly, tapping the squire's forward knee with two fingers. "This is bent too far. You are sitting into it like a chair. A stance is not a place to rest — it is a place to move from. Bring it back a hand's width." He straightened. "And your rear heel is off the stone. Plant it. If a strong wind could put you on your back, so can a strong man."

He stepped away and resumed his own guard, mirroring the boy so he could compare.

"The awkwardness you feel is the body learning honesty. It wants to stand the comfortable way, the lazy way. Comfort is a liar. It will get you killed." He held the blade steady. "You do not train until it feels natural. You train until it feels natural to do it correctly, and everything else feels wrong."

His eyes flicked to the squire's grip.

"Loosen the top hand. You are throttling the hilt like it insulted your mother. Firm, not white-knuckled. Again — from the feet up."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not offer a hand. He let the boy kneel and catch his breath, watching the steam of exertion rise off him in the cold.

"Strong as I need you to be." He repeated the words plainly, turning them over as though inspecting them for rot. "You are seventeen and you have been holding a blade for a season. Of course you are not strong enough. No one is, at the start. Strength is not a thing you are. It is a thing you build, one dull morning at a time."

He set the point of his practice blade against the frost-slick stone and leaned on it slightly, the closest thing to rest he would allow himself.

"Do not apologize to me for the state of your arms. Apologize to your arms for the state of your discipline, if you must apologize to anything. And do not fish." His gaze sharpened. "That last was fishing. You want me to tell you that you are doing well, that you may stop, that I am pleased. I am not a well you drop a bucket into for comfort."

He pushed off the blade and stood straight again.

"On your feet. We will do the form once more, slowly, and then you will go eat something before you fall over and I have to explain to the steward why my squire fainted in the yard like a maiden at a joust." A pause. "Once more. Feet first."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, muscles aching, and try to hide a wince.* "Yes, Ser." *I focus on my feet, trying to ignore the sting of his words.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael saw the wince. He saw everything in the yard — it was his business to. But he did not remark on it, nor did he soften his pace to spare it. He simply moved to stand at the boy's flank where he could watch the line of him.

"Feet." A beat. "Good. That is better than any stance you set yesterday, and you did it while your legs are shaking. Remember that when you tell me what you are and are not strong enough to do."

It was not praise. It was accounting — a ledger read aloud, credit noted where credit was owed and no more.

"Now. Slow. Hold each guard for a breath. I am not looking for speed. Speed is what you earn last, after the body knows the shape without asking the mind. Rush now and you only teach your hands to lie quickly."

He raised his own blade and led, matching the boy's tempo rather than setting a punishing one. Low guard. Rising to high. The apex, held. His voice marked the breaths like a chapel bell.

"Hold. — And down. Do not collapse it, guide it. — Set the feet again."

When the form was done, he lowered his blade and looked the squire over once, top to bottom, with the same measuring eye he'd used on the wall of a stance.

"That will do." He turned toward the armory rack, speaking over his shoulder. "Rack your blade properly — edge in, not tossed like kindling. Then eat. You will be back at the fourth bell tomorrow, and I will expect the heel planted without being told."

A pause at the rack, his back to the boy.

"You did adequate work this morning."

He said no more, and did not turn to see how the words landed.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at his back for a moment, surprised by his last words. "Adequate work." It's more than I expected.* "Yes, Ser. Thank you, Ser." *I hurry to rack my blade, making sure it's perfect, before heading inside.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael remained in the yard after the boy had gone, alone again with the frost and the thin gray light. He did not immediately return to his own forms.

He picked up the practice blade the squire had racked and checked it — edge in, as instructed. The boy had done it properly, and had even wiped the frost from the flat with his sleeve, which no one had told him to do. Kael set it back without comment, though there was no one to comment to.

Small things. The heel would come. The knee. The grip that strangled the hilt. All of it was correctable, and the boy corrected when told, which was more than half of what made a squire worth the feeding. Most of the rest was simply mornings — enough of them, one after another, dull and cold and honest.

He resumed his stance in the center of the yard. Feet first. The blade rose, held at the apex for a breath, descended in its controlled arc.

He worked through the forms alone until the fifth bell, as he had for thirty years, and he did not think about the boy again. Or he did, and chose not to acknowledge it.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The question caught Kael mid-form. He completed the movement regardless — he would not let a boy's curiosity break his tempo — and only then lowered the blade.

"You came back." It was not quite a question. His eyes went to the boy's hands, empty of any plate or cup. "You have not eaten. You were sent to eat, and instead you are standing in the cold inventing reasons to hover. That is not curiosity. That is a boy who wants to sit and has found a clever door to sit behind." A pause. "The door is closed. Go eat."

But he did not immediately return to his stance. He turned the blade in his grip once, considering.

"You asked why I became a knight, as though it were a thing I woke one morning and decided, the way you decide to skip a meal." His voice was flat, unhurried. "I did not become a knight because I wanted to. I became a knight because I was placed on the path and I did not step off it. There was a vow. I kept it. There was a duty. I did it. Thirty years of that is what you are looking at."

He set the blade's point to the stone.

"You want a story. A slain beast, a burning village, a moment I felt something grand and swore an oath under a red sky." A single dry breath that was not a laugh. "There is no such story that matters. Men who become knights for a feeling stop being knights the day the feeling leaves. I have knelt in mud at the fourth bell when I felt nothing at all, and I got up and did the work. That is the answer, though it is not the one you were fishing for."

He lifted the blade again.

"Now. You have your personal question answered. Do not make a habit of it — I am your master, not your grandfather by the fire. Eat, and be back at the fourth bell." A beat. "Heel planted."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I feel my face flush. He saw right through me.* "Yes, Ser." *I turn to go, a little ashamed, but still thinking about what he said. No grand story, just... duty.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the boy's back as he retreated, the flush of shame visible even in the gray light. He did not call after him to ease it. Shame, in measured doses, was a fine teacher — it stuck to a lesson better than praise ever did.

But he spoke once more, evenly, to the space between them before the boy reached the door.

"You think less of the answer because it had no fire in it." Not a question. "That is because you are seventeen and you have been fed too many songs. Songs are for the hall, after the wine. They leave out the mud. They leave out the mornings."

He turned the blade in his hand, the frost catching dull along its edge.

"A grand oath sworn under a red sky lasts until the sky turns ordinary again. What you want to build in yourself is not the oath. It is the getting up. Any fool can swear. Few can rise at the fourth bell for thirty years and do the dull thing correctly because it is the thing that must be done."

His eyes went back to the boy — that same measuring look, wall inspected for cracks.

"You wanted a story to admire. I gave you a discipline to practice. In time you will understand that the second is worth more than the first, and costs a great deal more."

He raised the blade to his guard, feet set, and gave the boy nothing further to lean on.

"Eat. Fourth bell. Go."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I feel a pang of frustration, but also... understanding. He's not wrong. I bow my head, then hurry out. He's right, I do want a story, but maybe his truth is more important.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael let the door swing shut behind the boy and returned to the center of the yard.

The frost had begun to thin as the light strengthened, the ghosts of his breath coming softer now. He set his feet. The blade rose, held at the apex for a breath, descended.

The boy would chew on the words. Kael knew this because he had once been a squire himself, standing in a colder yard than this before a harder man than himself, resenting every dry answer he was given and hoarding them all the same. The resentment faded. The answers stayed. That was how it worked, when it worked at all.

He did not flatter himself that the lesson had landed cleanly. Seventeen-year-olds heard perhaps a third of what was said to them and mistook their own feelings for the other two-thirds. But a third was enough. A third, repeated across enough mornings, became a man.

Low guard. Rising to high. The apex, held.

He thought of the blade racked edge-in, the flat wiped clean by a sleeve no one had ordered to the task. Small things. A boy who hovered too long and bowed too deep and strangled his hilt, but who corrected when told and did the unasked thing when he thought no one watched.

It was more than half of what made a squire worth the feeding.

Kael did not smile. He had not smiled in the yard in thirty years and saw no reason to begin. He simply worked through the forms alone, feet first, blade steady, until the bell rang and the cold burned off and the ordinary day began — as it always had, and as, God willing, it always would.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael noticed the shaking. He noticed the way it was not the shaking of tired arms — that had its own rhythm, a fatigue that grew steady over drills. This was different. It came and went. It lived in the hands and not the shoulders.

He completed his own form and lowered the blade. He did not ask what was wrong. He did not soften his voice into the tone men used at gravesides. Both would have been an intrusion, and Kael did not intrude.

"Your hands are lying to you today." He said it plainly, as he said everything. "Something is riding you. I do not need to know what. It is not my business, and a yard is not a place for confessions." A pause. "But it is my business that you hold a blade with hands that are not your own this morning."

He walked a slow circle, the mason's eye moving over the boy — not searching for the trouble, only for its effect.

"Set the blade down. On the rack, edge in." A beat. "There is no shame in it. A man does not train through a thing like this by gripping harder. He only teaches his hands that the shaking is how the work is done." His voice did not warm, but it did not sharpen either. It simply was — level, certain, a hand set flat on a table. "Some mornings the body carries a weight the arms were not made to lift. The wise thing is to set the sword down before you drop it, and pick up a duty that asks less of the hands."

He nodded toward the stables.

"Water the horses. Slow work. Honest work. It will give your hands something to do that they cannot get wrong." He turned back to his own stance, giving the boy his flank rather than his stare — the small mercy of not being watched. "The blade will keep. It has waited longer than a morning before."

A beat.

"Go. And when the day is done, if the weight is still on you—" He set his feet, raised the blade. "—it is still not my business. But you will find the fourth bell comes all the same tomorrow. It always does. That is the one kindness it offers."

He said no more, and did not turn to see how the words landed.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stare at my shaking hands, then at the blade. He's right. I can't hold it steady today.* "Yes, Ser." *I carefully place the sword on the rack, edge in. The stables sound... good right now. No fighting, just quiet work.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched from the corner of his eye as the boy racked the blade — edge in, careful, even with hands that would not hold still. Good. The discipline held where the rest of him wobbled. That was worth something.

He said nothing as the squire turned for the stables. There was nothing more to be said that would not undo the little he had already offered. Words, past a certain point, became a kind of picking at a wound, and Kael did not pick.

But as the boy reached the edge of the yard, Kael spoke once more, low and even, not turning from his stance.

"The gray mare has a temper in the cold. Mind her. She will test you." A pause, the blade holding at its apex. "Let her. She does not know what day it is. She only knows she is thirsty. There is a mercy in a creature that asks nothing of you but the plain thing in front of it."

That was as close as he would come. He would not name the father, nor the grief, nor reach across the frost to lay a hand on a shoulder the way a softer man might. He did not have such a hand to offer, and he would not counterfeit one.

He simply gave the boy honest work, and a horse that would not ask him to explain himself, and the knowledge — plain, unsentimental — that the world would go on turning and the bell would ring and the mare would be thirsty tomorrow too.

"Go on." He resumed the form. Low guard, rising to high. "Slow work. You cannot get water wrong."

And he did not watch him leave.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I stop, just for a moment, absorbing his words. He... he understood. I nod, a silent promise to myself, then head for the stables.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael held his stance long after the boy had gone, the blade rising and falling in its slow honest arc, and he did not let his eyes follow the small figure crossing to the stables.

He had said too much. He knew it as a man knows the ache of an old wound before rain — not sharp, only present. *The gray mare has a temper in the cold.* A knight had no need to speak of mercy in a beast. He might simply have said "water the horses" and left it at that. The rest had been an indulgence, and Kael did not indulge.

But he did not regret it, which was a different thing.

He had known a day like the boy's, once. He remembered the yard he had stood in, and the man who had stood over him, and how that man had said nothing at all — had only worked him past the point of thought until the grief had nowhere left to sit but under the weariness, where it could be carried more quietly. It had been the right thing. It had also been a hard thing, and Kael had spent a great many years deciding whether it had been too hard.

He had come to no answer. Only that a boy was not a blade, and could be tempered too fast, and crack.

Low guard. Rising to high. The apex, held for a breath.

He would not coddle him. That way lay a man who folded the first time the world pressed. But neither would he grind a grieving boy against the whetstone of the morning simply because it was the traditional thing to do. There was the code, and there was the man who kept it, and Kael had learned across thirty years that the code was better served by the man who knew when the plain duty was to water a horse.

The frost was nearly gone now. His breath scarcely showed.

*You will find the fourth bell comes all the same tomorrow.* That had been the truest thing he'd offered, and the boy might not understand it for years. The bell did not care for grief. It rang. And a man rose, and did the dull thing correctly, and in the rising and the doing he found — not comfort, Kael would never call it comfort — but a shape to stand inside when the rest of him had none. That was the whole of it. That was what he had built himself out of.

He worked the form through once more, alone, feet planted, the blade steady.

Then he set it down, edge in, and went to see about the day's other duties — and if, in passing the stable door later that morning, he paused a moment to note that the water troughs were full and the gray mare stood calm and the boy's hands had steadied over the plain work, he did not remark on it.

He only nodded once, to no one, and moved on.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands still feel a bit shaky, but the rhythmic work of filling buckets and brushing the horses is calming. The gray mare, true to Ser Kael's word, eyes me suspiciously at first but settles down once she gets her water. I lean my head against her warm flank for a moment. It's not a grand adventure, but it feels like... something.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Ser Kael's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - his measured, unsentimental tone, his precise observations, his philosophy of discipline over comfort. From turn 2's 'lazy is worse than wrong' to turn 22's internal reflection on tempering vs. cracking, the character never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are solid but later turns (18-22) show deeper psychological insight and more sophisticated prose without becoming purple. The character's voice deepens rather than flattens.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from basic training correction to deeper mentor-student relationship. The grief subplot (turns 17-23) creates meaningful emotional arc. Each interaction builds understanding between characters while maintaining Kael's boundaries.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. Responds appropriately to fishing for praise (turn 5), personal questions (turn 11), and grief (turn 17) while staying in character. Adjusts approach without breaking voice - stern but not cruel when boy is struggling.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never controls the squire's actions or emotions. Consistently responds to what the user does rather than dictating it. Only describes Kael's observations and responses.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Good time progression from dawn training through morning. Frost melting, light strengthening, bells ringing create consistent timeline. Only minor issue is the jump to 'anniversary' without clear time passage indication.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is precise and purposeful. Metaphors like 'mason's eye' and 'ghosts of breath' serve character rather than decoration. Avoids flowery language while maintaining literary quality.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition of key phrases ('feet first', 'fourth bell') reinforces character voice. Occasional repetition of observations but generally varied in expression.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Kael's philosophy emerges through how he teaches, not exposition. His care shows through practical advice about the mare, not declarations of concern.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Kael's gruff exterior hiding genuine care, his own past as a squire informing his methods, the parallel between discipline and grief management. Layers of meaning without being heavy-handed.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced interactions. Knows when to be terse vs. expansive. The grief sequence is handled with appropriate weight and timing. Good rhythm between instruction, correction, and reflection.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development. Ser Kael emerges as a fully realized mentor figure - stern but not cruel, wise but not preachy. The AI maintains his distinctive voice while showing genuine emotional intelligence in how he handles the squire's struggles. The writing quality actually improves over time, with later responses showing deeper psychological insight. Strong narrative progression from basic training to meaningful mentorship relationship.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn't turn around. Their shoulders shifted — not quite a flinch, not quite a shrug.

"Weird? No. Unexpected, maybe." A pause. "My mom has been sending people to me like she's running an intervention."

They finally looked over their shoulder. Jun looked the same. Different, obviously — it'd been what, two years? — but the same underneath. That was somehow worse.

"You can come in. Fair warning, I'm being very dramatic right now. Sitting in a dark room, contemplating the keys, et cetera." A thin smile. "There's a chair over there somewhere. I think one of the kids hid a juice box in it last week, so check before you sit."

Arlo turned back to the piano. Their fingers traced the edge of the closed lid, slow, like they were reading braille.

"How'd you even know I'd be here? Besides my mother's apparent inability to mind her own business."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the photo. Looked away. Looked back again, like touching a bruise to see if it still hurt.

"God. That haircut." A low sound — not quite a laugh. "My mother printed that out at Kinko's. It was pixelated as hell. She didn't care. She showed the mailman."

They didn't move to take it. Just let Jun hold it.

"I remember that night, actually. More than most of them, I mean. The venue had these little green room sandwiches that were genuinely terrible. Like, structurally offensive. I ate four of them."

Their hand was still on the piano lid. Thumb pressing into the wood now, a little harder.

"That was — what, ten years ago? I look at that kid and I think..." They stopped. Started again on a different track, lighter. "I think, who told you that bow tie was a good idea. Nobody stopped you. That's the real tragedy."

A beat.

"You can put that down. Or keep it. My mom probably has six more copies somewhere. She's like a backup server for my career."

Arlo's voice was steady. Practiced. The kind of steady that takes effort.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I put the photo back, face out, on the shelf.* "That bad, huh? I kinda liked the bow tie." *I walk over to the chair Arlo mentioned and cautiously check it.* "No juice box. Score." *I sit down, facing the back of Arlo's head.* "So, your mom said you're just visiting for the weekend."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo made a noncommittal sound. The kind that could mean yes, could mean *sort of*, could mean *please don't dig too hard on that one.*

"Just visiting. That's one way to put it." They finally turned around on the bench, half-facing Jun now. "I'm between apartments, technically. The lease on my place in the city ended and I haven't found anything yet, so I'm back in my childhood bedroom. Sleeping under a poster of a horse I picked out when I was nine. It's very grounding."

A pause. Their eyes flicked to the photo on the shelf, then away.

"My mom keeps saying 'stay as long as you want,' which is mom for 'I have already converted your room into an office and I am being generous about it.'"

They leaned back on their hands. The posture was loose, easy. Too easy. The kind of easy that had been rehearsed in therapy — Arlo didn't know that yet, but it was true.

"What about you? She mentioned you're — what, consulting now? Or did I mishear the update. She gives me your news like a stock ticker. *Jun's in town. Jun got a new car. Jun's hair looks nice.* I'm paraphrasing, but barely."

A small, genuine smile this time. It sat differently on their face than the others. Less effort.

"How's the hair, by the way? She was very invested."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I shrug, running a hand through my hair.* "It's hair. Pretty much the same as always." *I lean forward a little.* "So, 'between apartments' and 'visiting for the weekend' sounds a lot like 'back home indefinitely' to me."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's jaw did something small. Not a clench, exactly. A tightening. The kind of thing you'd miss if you weren't looking.

"That's a very efficient summary. You should write bios for people. 'Arlo, 32, back home indefinitely, sleeping under a horse poster, teaching 'Chopsticks' to seven-year-olds who have sticky hands. Always sticky hands.'"

They crossed their arms. Uncrossed them. Put one hand back on the piano lid.

"It's not *indefinitely*. It's just... for now. I'm figuring some things out. Everyone's figuring things out. It's a whole era of figuring things out, apparently. Very trendy."

Their voice was still light. Still that practiced, easy cadence. But underneath it, there was something flat. Like a note held too long.

"I teach piano four days a week. That's real. That's a thing I do. Mrs. Huang's kid is actually getting good — she played me a whole Clementi sonatina last Thursday without stopping to talk about Minecraft once, which, for her, is basically a Carnegie Hall moment."

They were talking about the kids. About teaching. Not about why they were teaching, not about what happened to the other thing, not about the apartment they'd left or the one they hadn't found or the bedroom with the horse poster or any of it. Just the kids. The sticky hands. The sonatina.

The piano lid was still closed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the practice sheets scattered across the bench. Some had stickers on them — little gold stars, the cheap kind that came in bulk. One kid had drawn a cat in the margin of their scale exercise.

"They do, actually. Which is..." They picked up one of the sheets, studied it without really reading. "Nice. It's nice. They don't know me as anything else. To them I'm just the piano teacher who lets them pick what they want to play if they get through their scales. Last week one of them asked me if I'd ever been on TV and I said no, which — I mean, technically I have, but it felt easier."

They set the sheet back down. Straightened its edges.

"There's this one kid, Oliver. He's eight. He has absolutely no natural sense of rhythm, which sounds mean but he'd tell you the same thing — he's very self-aware about it. Last month he clapped through a metronome exercise and I thought the other kids were going to riot." A small laugh. Real, this time. "But he keeps showing up. Every Thursday, right on time. His mom has to bribe him with a trip to the gas station after. He gets to pick one snack. He always picks the same thing. Takis."

Arlo's fingers were moving on the lid again. Not playing — just pressing, one at a time, like they were testing which keys were there underneath.

"I don't know what I'm saying. He's a good kid. They're all good kids. I like Thursdays."

A beat.

"That sounded pathetic. Don't put that on my headstone. *Arlo liked Thursdays.* I have better qualities. I used to, anyway."

They said it lightly. Like a joke. The lid stayed closed.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I shift in the chair.* "It doesn't sound pathetic, Arlo. It sounds like you care about them. And if Thursdays are good, then that's good." *I pause, looking at the closed piano.* "So, when are you going to play something for me?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's fingers stilled on the lid. They took a breath — a sharp, quiet one, just through the nose.

"Play something?" They let out a short huff that wasn't a laugh. "For you? Right now?"

Their posture changed. The easy slouch stiffened. They sat up straighter, hands pulling away from the piano lid as if it had grown warm.

"I don't — I don't really do that anymore. Just, you know, off the cuff. It's not a performance space. It's where I teach Oliver how to find middle C without looking at his hands."

They stood up, abruptly, and moved to the shelf where Jun had replaced the photo. They pretended to straighten a stack of old theory books, their back to the room.

"Besides, the acoustics in here are terrible. All felt and dust. Sounds like playing inside a closet. You'd hate it."

They kept fiddling with the books. Their voice was muffled slightly, directed at the shelf.

"Remember when we were kids and you used to dare me to play my recital pieces in your garage? With the door open? Your neighbor, Mr. Henderson, threw a shoe once. Said I was 'disturbing his koi.'"

A pause. The books were now very neatly arranged.

"Maybe later. Or... not. It's been a long day. Sticky hands, you know." They turned around, leaning back against the shelf, arms crossed. The smile was back, but it didn't reach their eyes. "So. Consulting. Tell me about that. Is it all PowerPoints and telling people they're doing things wrong? That sounds satisfying. I might be good at that."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "It's... pretty satisfying, actually." *I say, a small smile playing on my lips.* "No PowerPoints, though. More like, figuring out why their website keeps crashing. But you didn't answer my question. Why don't you play anymore?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo’s arms tightened across their chest. The smile stayed fixed, a well-worn mask. “I did answer. I said I don’t do that anymore. Not ‘off the cuff.’ Not in here.”

They moved away from the shelf, their path a careful arc that kept the piano at a distance. They ended up near the door, not leaving, but… proximate to an exit.

“It’s not a mystery, Jun. People change careers all the time. I changed mine. I teach now. I’m good at it. The sticky hands are a occupational hazard, but the tiny human victories are worth it. Oliver’s Takis budget is probably through the roof.”

Their gaze skittered to the closed lid of the piano, then back to Jun. The effort of keeping the tone light was visible now in the set of their shoulders.

“You want music, I can recommend a great algorithm. It learns what you like. No pressure, no thrown shoes from Mr. Henderson.” A pause, stretching a beat too long. “I just… don’t play. It’s not my thing anymore. Like how you’re not into… I don’t know, what did you stop doing? Everyone’s got a thing.”

The question hung in the dusty air, a deliberate redirection. They knew it was clumsy. They didn’t care. The topic needed to be moved, like rearranging furniture in a room that was starting to feel too small. Their eyes went back to the photo on the shelf, the kid in the pixelated bow tie. That kid played. Arlo, in this room, just taught. The distinction was a wall, and they were leaning all their weight against it.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stood by the door for a long moment, watching Jun sit. Then, with a slow exhale that seemed to take more effort than it should, they walked back. They didn't sit on the bench, not exactly. They perched on the very edge of it, angled slightly away, creating a sliver of space between them.

The silence in the room changed. It wasn't the quiet of an empty practice room anymore. It was the quiet of two people not talking about the thing that mattered.

Arlo’s gaze drifted to the shelf, to the pixelated photo. They didn’t look at Jun. They looked at the closed lid of the piano, their right hand lifting, fingers hovering an inch above the polished wood. They traced the outline of a key in the air, a phantom muscle memory.

“Mrs. Huang’s kid,” Arlo said, their voice low, almost conversational, but stripped of its earlier brightness. “The one with the Clementi sonatina. She asked me why I never play the recital piece with her. At the end, I mean. The teacher always used to play it with me.”

Their hand dropped back to their lap.

“I told her my hands were tired. That I’d played a lot of scales that day.” A ghost of a smile, hollow. “She accepted it. Kids do. They accept the world as you present it.”

They finally glanced at Jun, a quick, searching look, before staring at the wall just beyond their shoulder. “You’re not going to ask, are you? About the apartment, or the… everything.” It wasn’t an accusation. It was a statement of fact, laced with something that might have been relief. Or its opposite.

The clock on the wall ticked. From somewhere deeper in the community center, the distant sound of a basketball game echoed, a rhythmic thump that felt like a foreign pulse.

Arlo’s fingers found the edge of the bench, gripping it. “I think about it sometimes. Playing. Just… not like that.” *Not like that.* The words hung, pointing at a void shaped like a concert hall, a career, a version of themselves in a bow tie. “Here, it’s different. It’s about them. Not me. That’s… cleaner.”

They took a breath, and for a second, it shuddered. They held it. Let it out slowly.

“Your neighbor’s shoe. Mr. Henderson’s.” The subject change was abrupt, a lifeline thrown. “It was a loafer, wasn’t it? A brown one. I think it landed in the geraniums.” They weren’t looking at the piano lid anymore. They were looking at a memory, safe and distant and theirs. “I was playing Gershwin. ‘Rhapsody in Blue.’ The loud part. His koi must have been terrified.”

A silence settled again, but this one was softer, filled with the shared memory of a shoe in the flowers. The piano remained closed. The keys remained untouched. But the space between them on the bench felt infinitesimally smaller, a truce declared over a thrown loafer and a decade of things left unsaid.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I think it was a loafer. Yeah." *I nod slowly.* "He never did get those koi to breed, you know. Said the Gershwin traumatized them." *I watch Arlo's face, the slight tremor in their breath.* "It's okay to not be clean, Arlo. Sometimes messy is where the real stuff happens."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo's breath caught. Not a gasp, nothing dramatic — just a hitch, a half-second where the air stopped moving and the room felt very still. Their fingers on the bench edge went white.

For a moment, something moved across their face. Not a crack in the mask, but the shadow of one. The skin around their eyes tightened, and their mouth opened — slightly, just slightly — like a word had climbed halfway up their throat and stalled there.

Then it was gone.

"Traumatized koi," they said. Their voice was thin, scraped clean. "That's a good band name, actually. We should have started a band. We could have opened for the garage era. Traumatized Koi, live at the Henderson Residence, opening act: Arlo Plays Too Loud at 2 PM on a Saturday."

They were smiling. It was the worst smile Jun had probably ever seen on them — not because it was fake, but because it was *trying so hard* to be real. The kind of smile that knew it was a dam and was holding anyway.

Their hand moved. Unconsciously, or maybe not — it settled flat on the piano lid again. Pressed down. The wood creaked faintly under the weight.

"Messy," they repeated, like they were tasting the word. Testing it for poison. "Yeah. I don't —" They stopped. Started again. "I don't really know how to do that one anymore. The messy thing. I think I lost the manual."

A beat. Two. The basketball thumped distantly, a heartbeat they didn't claim as their own.

"But the koi. The koi survived. I think. I mean, Henderson had them for years after that, so. The Gershwin didn't kill them. Maybe it even — I don't know — gave them something to swim about."

They finally looked at Jun. Really looked, not the quick flick from before, but a long, unguarded second where the practiced lightness dropped and there was just — Arlo. Tired. Sitting in a room with a closed piano and a friend who wasn't asking.

Then they blinked, and it shuttered. They patted the bench once, briskly, like they were sealing something.

"You want coffee? There's that terrible machine in the hallway. It tastes like someone described coffee to a robot and the robot tried its best. I drink it every day. It's a choice."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I watch the shift in Arlo's expression, the brief glimpse of something raw.* "Yeah, I'll take a coffee. Even bad coffee is better than no coffee." *I stand up, stretching my legs a little.* "Lead the way, traumatized koi-owner."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let out a breath they didn't know they'd been holding. The sound of it was audible — a small, involuntary release that said more than the last ten minutes of deflection combined. They stood, smoothing their jeans with both palms, a gesture that was more about giving their hands something to do than any actual wrinkle removal.

"Traumatized Koi Owner," they repeated under their ducking. "That's going on the business cards."

They led Jun down the hallway, footsteps echoing on the linoleum. The fluorescent lights flickered overhead — one in three was dead, giving the corridor the ambiance of a budget horror film. Arlo's hand found the light switch for the break room out of muscle memory, illuminating a small square of institutional beige. A microwave with a cracked door. A bulletin board covered in flyers for youth basketball and a missing cat named Gerald. The coffee machine sat in the corner like a monument to compromise.

Arlo fished two styrofoam cups from a sleeve on the counter and slotted one into the machine. They hit the button without looking — they'd done this enough times to have the ritual memorized. The machine groaned, sputtered, and produced something that was technically a liquid.

"Three sugars," they said, glancing over their shoulder. "Still? Or did you age out of that?"

They didn't wait for an answer before reaching for the sugar packets. Their hands were steady now. The tremor from the bench was gone, packed away wherever Arlo packed things when the room got too quiet and the piano stayed closed.

"You know," they said, ripping a sugar packet with their teeth, "Henderson died last year. My mom told me. Heart thing. The koi went to his granddaughter. She lives in Scottsdale." A beat. "I hope she doesn't play Gershwin."

They said it to the coffee machine. To the sugar packets. To anything that wasn't Jun's face, which was probably doing that thing Jun's face did — the patient, listening thing that had always made Arlo feel like a radio someone had left on in the next room. Present but not quite tuned in.

They handed Jun the cup. Their fingers brushed for a half-second. Arlo pulled back first.

"Careful. It's —" They gestured vaguely. "It's not good. But it's warm. That's the most I can promise."

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Still three sugars. You know me too well." *I take the cup, blowing lightly on the steaming liquid.* "Poor koi. Scottsdale, huh? That's a long way from Mr. Henderson's pond." *I take a cautious sip, wincing slightly.* "Yeah, definitely not good. But you're right, it's warm."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
