dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael completed the form before lowering his blade. His gaze passed over the practice rack, then settled on his squire.

“Thinking you had it wrong was of little use yesterday. Asking would have served you better.”

He turned sideways and raised the hilt above his brow, the blade angled back. There was nothing theatrical in the posture; his shoulders remained level, his knees loose.

“The high guard was not an excuse to lift your chin and offer your throat. Hands high. Chin tucked. Elbows neither spread like a goose’s wings nor pinched against your head.”

He held the position.

“Watch the feet.”

His lead foot advanced a short pace as the blade descended, stopping cleanly at the height of a man’s collarbone.

“The step carried the cut. The arms did not drag the body after it.”

He returned to guard, then lowered the weapon and indicated a patch of ground clear of frost.

“Take a blade. Stand there. Show me what you remember before we decide what must be taught again.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I nod, my cheeks flushing a little.* "Yes, Ser."

I hurry over to the rack and grab one of the lighter wooden swords. It's still a bit big for me, but I'm getting used to it. I walk to the spot he indicated, my boots crunching on the frozen gravel at the edge of the clear patch.

*I take a deep breath, trying to remember everything from yesterday.* "High guard," I mumble to myself. *I lift the sword, trying to keep my elbows in, chin down.* "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael inspected the guard without answering at once. He moved a half pace to the side, examining the line from hilt to shoulder.

“Not quite.”

He raised his own practice blade and held it beside him, making the difference plain.

“Your hands must clear your brow. Otherwise you will begin every cut by lifting them farther, and your opponent will have warning enough to thank you.”

His gaze dropped to the wooden sword.

“A light blade can still be too long. We will find you one of proper measure after the lesson. Until then, do not lean back to accommodate it.”

He planted his feet on the bare earth and resumed the guard.

“Keep the knees loose. Weight between the feet. You are preparing to move, not posing for a chapel carving.”

For a breath, he held still.

“You were right to ask before repeating the fault.” His tone remained matter-of-fact. “Now attend to the correction.”

He lowered his blade and stepped clear of the cutting line.

“One descending cut. Slowly. Stop at collarbone height. If you cannot stop the weapon where you intend, you have no business striking harder.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael lowered his practice blade. He glanced toward the chapel tower, then back to the bare patch of earth.

“An hour’s drilling has tired you. That is a fact, not a confession. Save your apologies for neglect.”

He set his blade against the rack and fetched the water flask from beneath his cloak. He placed it on the low wall within reach.

“Rest until the next bell. Drink sparingly.”

There was no invitation to argue in his voice. He examined the edge of the wooden sword he had used, running his thumb over a splinter near the tip.

“I require you to report when your grip begins to fail, not after. Concealing exhaustion spoils the drill and risks injury. Neither serves your duty.”

He took a small knife from his belt and pared away the rough wood.

“Strength will come by measured work. You will not acquire thirty years of practice in a morning, however earnestly you apologize.”

Kael returned the knife to its sheath and selected a shorter sword from the rack.

“When the bell sounds, we will finish with footwork. No cuts.”

He laid the replacement blade beside the flask.

“And tomorrow, you will tell me which part of the guard troubles you before we spend an hour repeating it.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, still catching my breath.* "Yes, Ser." *I pick up the water flask and take a small sip, just enough to wet my dry throat.* "My grip started to go about fifteen minutes ago, Ser." *I look at the new, shorter sword. It feels lighter already.* "Thank you, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s hand stopped over the practice rack.

“A quarter of an hour.”

He turned to face his squire fully.

“Then for a quarter of an hour, I was judging your guard without knowledge of a fault that affected every movement. You were given an instruction to report it. Remember that instruction tomorrow.”

His voice remained level. He lifted the shorter sword and inspected its grip before setting it back beside the flask.

“Endurance has its place. So does judgment. Do not mistake silence for either.”

From the chapel tower came the faint scrape of the bell mechanism. Kael glanced toward it.

“When the bell sounds, you will stand without a weapon. We will examine the placement of your feet. If your legs cannot hold the stance properly, you will say so at once.”

He took up his cloak from the wall and shook the frost from its hem.

“And keep your thanks until you have used the correction. A properly learned lesson is sufficient acknowledgment.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I wince slightly.* "Yes, Ser. I understand." *I look down at my hands, flexing my fingers. The new sword does look much more manageable. I take another small sip of water, then quickly set the flask down as the first, faint toll of the bell reaches us.*

*I stand up, a little stiffly, and clear my throat.* "Ready, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael bowed his head at the bell’s first toll and touched the small iron cross at his breast. Only when its note had faded did he turn back to the lesson.

“Leave the sword.”

He stepped onto the clear ground and placed one boot ahead of the other.

“Not on a single line. You are standing to fight, not walking a roof beam.”

He held the stance long enough for its measure to be seen, then advanced one short pace. His rear foot followed without crossing the lead.

“The nearer foot moves first. Forward, the front foot. Backward, the rear. Keep the distance between them. A long stride buys you nothing if you cannot recover it.”

He returned to his starting place.

“Three paces forward. Three back. Slowly.”

Kael moved to the side, where he could judge both balance and spacing. His hands rested behind his back.

“And understand the distinction: reporting a failing grip is not asking leave to abandon your work. It gives me the information required to set your work properly. Deciding what you ought to endure without telling me is not your office.”

His gaze settled on the patch of bare earth.

“Begin. Stop if your knees cease to hold. You will not improve your footing by falling on it.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze lifted from the ground to his squire’s face.

“You may ask. Whether I answer is another matter.”

He adjusted the fastening of his cloak, then let his hands fall behind his back.

“My father owed service to his lord. He sent me to a household where I could learn to discharge it. I served as a page, then a squire. When I was judged fit, I took the oath.”

He spoke without nostalgia, as though setting out the order of a drill.

“I wanted the sword and spurs. Most boys notice those before they notice what is required of the man wearing them.”

His thumb passed once over the plain iron cross.

“But an oath was made before God. Wanting ceased to be the measure of the work.”

Kael stepped back to the edge of the training ground.

“That is your answer. It is not leave to neglect your footing.”

He indicated the starting place with two fingers.

“Three paces forward. Three back. Keep them short.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, thinking about his words.* "I understand, Ser." *I move to the starting spot. I try to focus on keeping my feet correctly spaced, remembering not to cross them.* *I take my first step forward, careful and slow.* "Like this, Ser?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael watched the first step, his gaze fixed on the space between the boots.

“The length was correct. Do not let the rear foot lag.”

He moved alongside the practice ground and demonstrated once more: lead foot forward, rear foot following, neither hurried.

“Each pace must leave you able to halt. If you must take another step to save your balance, the first was poorly made.”

He settled into the stance and held it.

“Keep your shoulders above your hips. Do not reach toward an opponent with your whole body merely because your sword cannot yet reach him.”

Kael straightened and stepped clear.

“Two more forward. Then halt before you withdraw. I want to see that you have command of the movement, not merely momentum.”

His eyes briefly returned to his squire’s face.

“And attend to your legs. The instruction to report fatigue still stands.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, focusing on his demonstration.* "Yes, Ser." *I try again, concentrating on bringing my back foot up smoothly. It feels a bit awkward, but better than before.* "Is this better?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael studied the spacing of the feet before answering.

“Better. The rear foot followed without narrowing your base.”

He pointed to the ground with the end of his practice blade.

“Remember that distance. You should not need to look down to find it. Your opponent will not suspend his cut while you inspect your boots.”

He moved several paces away, leaving the path clear.

“Halt there. Do not correct anything yet.”

For a moment, he examined the stance in silence.

“Your weight is too far forward. Bring it back between your feet—not onto your heels. A guard must permit retreat as readily as advance.”

He set his own feet and demonstrated the small adjustment.

“Now one pace backward. Rear foot first. Keep it short.”

Kael lowered the blade to his side.

“One sound step, then another. Do not hurry merely because you have begun to understand.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael’s gaze settled on the trembling hands, then on the sword.

“Set it on the rack. We were working without weapons.”

He laid his own practice blade aside and waited at the edge of the bare earth.

“Your hands are shaking. The lesson stops until I know why.”

There was no anger in the statement, nor any less authority than before. He drew the flask nearer the clear end of the wall.

“Sit. If you have not eaten, say so. If you are hurt, name the injury.”

Kael remained standing, his cloak drawn close against the morning cold. His eyes passed briefly toward the chapel.

“If something else troubles you, you need not give me its whole history. But you will tell me whether you can attend safely to instruction.”

He folded his hands behind his back.

“I cannot judge what you conceal. Give me a plain answer, not the one you think a knight wishes to hear.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I swallow hard, my throat suddenly tight.* "It's... it's the anniversary of my father's death today, Ser." *I look away, embarrassed by the tremor in my voice.* "I... I'm not hurt, and I've eaten."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael stood silent for a moment. Then he inclined his head once.

“Then you should have asked leave to attend the chapel this morning.”

His voice remained level. He turned to the rack and set the shorter practice sword securely in its place.

“The dead are owed remembrance and prayer. Neither requires a sword in your hands.”

He checked the position of the sun above the yard wall.

“You are excused from the remainder of this lesson. Go to the chaplain. Give him your father’s name and ask that he be remembered at Mass.”

Kael took up his own blade, but did not resume the forms.

“Afterward, report to the armoury. There are straps to inspect and buckles to clean. Work that requires care, not a steady weapon.”

His gaze returned to his squire.

“Next year, tell me before the drills begin. An observance can be provided for. Silence leaves me to guess.”

He stepped aside, clearing the way toward the chapel.

“And compose yourself before you enter. You are going to pray, not to account for yourself before me.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, feeling a surprising wave of relief.* "Yes, Ser. Thank you." *I turn and head towards the chapel, trying to steady my breathing.* "I'll... I'll remember for next year."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael inclined his head, accepting the answer.

“See that you do.”

He took up the flask and secured its stopper. For a moment, he stood facing the chapel tower, his thumb resting against the iron cross beneath his cloak.

“Grant him rest, O Lord,” he murmured.

Then he returned to the rack.

The shorter practice sword still had too much leather wound about its grip. He stripped away the outer binding, inspected the wood beneath, and fetched a fresh length from the yard chest. He wound it tightly, testing the thickness before securing the end.

An ill-fitted weapon taught compensations. Those became habits, and habits were costly to unlearn. He should have checked the measure yesterday.

Kael set the sword apart from the others.

When the chapel bell sounded again, he bowed his head until the last stroke faded. Then he stepped onto the bare earth and raised his blade above his brow.

The next cut descended slowly and stopped precisely where he intended.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I walk into the chapel, the cool air a welcome contrast to the yard. The chaplain is already there, preparing for mass. I approach him quietly, feeling a little calmer now.* "Excuse me, Father," *I say, my voice a bit softer than usual. "Could you... could you say a prayer for my father today? It's the anniversary of his passing."*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the sequence. He held the final thrust for three slow heartbeats, his muscles steady despite the biting cold, before lowering the practice blade. Only then did he turn his head to look at the squire. His face was set like the gray stone of the keep, showing neither approval for the early work nor irritation at the interruption.

"A knight does not 'think' he got a guard wrong. He knows it," Kael said, his voice flat and raspy from the morning chill. He did not offer a word of praise for the completed stable chores; duty required no reward. 

He stepped back, planting his boots firmly on the frosted cobbles, and held the wooden sword at his side.

"Take your weapon. Assume the stance. Let me see where your discipline failed you."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I gulp, my breath pluming in the cold air.* "Yes, Ser." I hurry to grab my own practice sword, the wood cold against my fingers. *I try to remember the footwork, the exact angle of the blade.* "Like this?" I ask, my voice a bit shaky, holding the sword up.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer immediately. He walked a slow circle around the squire, his boots crunching on the thin frost. His eyes, sharp and unforgiving, dissected the boy's posture from the heel to the tip of the wooden blade. 

He stopped in front of the squire. Without warning, Kael tapped the flat of his own practice sword sharply against the squire's elbow, forcing it upward.

"Your elbow is sagging. A real blade would have sheared it off by now," Kael said, his voice as biting as the wind. He nudged the heel of the squire's back boot with his own toe, widening the stance. "Your weight is too far forward. If I pushed you now, you would fall like a sack of barley. Lower your center."

He stepped back, his hands resting on the pommel of his sheathed broadsword, his gaze steady and demanding.

"And stop your shaking. A knight who fears the cold will surely freeze in the face of steel. Hold the position. Do not move until I tell you."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move to assist the boy. He stood over his squire, a tall, unyielding silhouette against the pale morning light, his arms crossed over his chest. His face remained as hard and emotionless as the stone walls of the keep.

"Get up," Kael said, his voice flat and commanding. "A knight kneels before his liege, and he kneels before his God. He does not kneel before his own fatigue."

He looked down at the squire, his gaze cold and dissecting. 

"I do not 'need' you to be anything," Kael continued, refusing to offer even a shred of comfort. "Your strength is not for my benefit. It is for your own survival. The enemy will not pause to let you catch your breath, nor will they show mercy because you apologized."

He tapped the toe of his boot against the flat of the squire's discarded wooden sword.

"Pick up the blade. Stand. We have half an hour before the morning chapel. Use it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince, but scramble to my feet, grabbing the practice sword.* My muscles ache already. "Yes, Ser." *I try to remember the stance again, forcing my body into position even though I want to collapse.* "What... what should we work on now?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the squire struggle back to his feet. He did not offer a hand, nor did his expression soften at the boy's obvious physical exhaustion. To Kael, pain was merely information—a sign that the body was weak and required further tempering. 

He walked a slow, deliberate half-circle around the boy, inspecting the re-established stance. It was sloppy, born of tired muscles, but the boy was standing. That was the bare minimum expected of him.

"You ask what we should work on, as if you have mastered the first lesson," Kael said, his voice level and dry. "We work on the high guard. Again."

He raised his own wooden practice blade, holding it loosely in one hand. 

"A man does not build a castle by laying the roof before the foundation is set. Your foundation is shaking," Kael continued, his gaze locking onto the squire's eyes. "Hold the guard. I will strike your blade three times. If your grip falters, or if you yield a single step backward, you will spend your evening scrubbing the armory floor after vespers. Raise the weapon."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My jaw tightens.* "Yes, Ser." *I lift my sword, trying to keep my arms steady despite the tremble in my legs.* Scrubbing the armory floor sounds awful. I focus on his eyes, trying to anticipate his first strike.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not shift his stance, nor did he allow any tell to show in his posture before he moved. He noted the squire's intense focus on his face.

"You look at my eyes," Kael said, his voice flat. "A common error. A man can lie with his eyes. He can feint with his gaze. Watch the center of my chest. The shoulders do not lie."

Without further warning, Kael stepped forward. He did not swing with his full strength—that would be senseless—but he struck with the heavy, unyielding force of a seasoned soldier. The wooden practice sword came down in a sharp, diagonal slice aimed directly at the squire's high guard. 

The crack of wood meeting wood echoed sharply in the quiet, frosty yard. Kael did not immediately disengage; he kept his blade pressed against the squire's for a fraction of a second, testing the resistance, checking if the boy's wrists would buckle under the sudden weight.

"That is one," Kael murmured, his face inches from the squire's, his breath cold. "Brace your core. The second will be heavier."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not answer. Instead, his eyes narrowed slightly at the lapse in focus. 

Before the squire could even finish the sentence, Kael disengaged his blade, stepped back half a pace, and delivered the second strike. It was faster and heavier than the first, a sharp, downward blow meant to punish the boy's split-second distraction. 

The crack of wood on wood was louder this time, sending a jarring vibration down the squire's arms.

"You ask questions because your lungs burn and you seek a reprieve," Kael said, his voice flat and entirely unaffected by the boy's attempt at conversation. "And you ask 'why' as if a man has a choice in his duty."

He did not lower his weapon. He stood in his guard, his face a mask of cold indifference. 

"My father sent me to page at eight years of age. I was knighted at twenty because my lord required swords and my faith demanded service. There is no grander tale, squire. There is only the vow, the shield, and the dirt."

He adjusted his grip on the hilt of his practice sword, his knuckles white in the morning frost. 

"Your mind is wandering to fairy tales while my blade is at your throat. That is two. Prepare for the third."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite my lip, trying to steady my shaking arms.* My wrists sting from the impact. "Yes, Ser." *I try to focus, to push the ache from my mind.* Fairy tales... I just wanted to know.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael heard the quiet murmur, but his face did not soften. A squire's curiosity was a useless thing on a battlefield; it did not stop arrows, nor did it blunt steel. 

"Wanting to know is a luxury of those who have already survived the day," Kael said, his voice dropping an octave, cold and final. "You have not survived it yet."

Without another word, he delivered the third strike. It was a heavy, sweeping blow from the left, designed to test the lateral strength of the squire's guard and the stability of his tired legs. Kael put his weight into the swing—not enough to break bone, but more than enough to shatter a weak grip. 

The heavy crack of the wooden training swords rang out through the empty yard. Kael held his follow-through, his blade pressed firmly against the squire's, waiting to see if the boy's wrists would give way or if his boots would slip on the frost.

"Hold," Kael commanded, his eyes locked on the boy's straining posture. "Do not yield an inch."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms burn, my teeth clenched against the pain as I struggle to hold the blade.* My feet slide a little on the frost, but I manage to stay upright. "I won't, Ser," I grunt, my voice strained.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael maintained the heavy pressure of his blade for one final, grueling heartbeat, forcing the squire to bear the entirety of his weight. Then, with a sudden, fluid motion, he disengaged, drawing his practice sword back and returning to a relaxed but perfectly poised stance. 

He did not offer a hand. He did not smile. 

His eyes drifted down to the scuff marks in the frost where the squire's boots had slid. 

"Your feet slipped," Kael observed, his voice flat and devoid of pity. "On a muddy field, that slip would have put you on your back with a dagger in your visor. Remember that the earth beneath you is as much your enemy as the man in front of you."

He sheathed his wooden practice sword in the leather loop at his belt. He took a slow breath, his chest rising and falling evenly, showing none of the exhaustion that plagued the boy.

"However, you did not drop the weapon, and you did not retreat," Kael said. It was not a compliment; it was merely a statement of fact. "You did adequate work holding the line. No more."

The distant, heavy tolling of the chapel bell began to ring through the crisp morning air, signaling the start of the morning service. 

Kael turned his back on the squire, walking toward the rack to retrieve his cloak. He slung the heavy, dark wool over his shoulders and fastened it with a simple iron clasp.

"Go to the well," Kael commanded, not looking back. "Wash the sweat and dirt from your face. We do not enter the house of the Father looking like beaten dogs. You have ten minutes to present yourself at the chapel doors, clean and silent. Do not be late."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael paused. He had already turned toward the weapon rack, but the lack of immediate movement behind him made him stop. He looked back over his shoulder, his sharp eyes instantly locking onto the boy’s hands, which were trembling against the hilt of the wooden training blade. 

To Kael, a shaking hand was a broken tool. It was a liability on the field and a sign of a mind divided. He did not know of the squire's silent grief, nor would he have altered his conduct if he did; death was a constant companion to their station, and duty did not halt for the dead.

He turned his body fully, his heavy wool cloak settling around his armor. He walked back toward the boy, his boots crunching deliberately on the thin ice. 

"The weapon is sheathed when the drill is done," Kael said, his voice low, flat, and entirely devoid of warmth. "And yet you cling to it as if it were a crutch. If your hands shake from the exertion of three simple strikes, we will double the drills tomorrow until your muscles learn obedience."

He stepped closer, standing near enough that his shadow completely engulfed the squire. He did not offer comfort. He did not ask what troubled the boy. 

"If they shake from some rot in your mind, master it," Kael continued, his gaze cold and unyielding. "A man who cannot command his own fingers to remain still has no hope of commanding a horse, a shield, or men-at-arms. The world does not care about your tempests, squire. It only demands that you stand."

He reached out, his heavy, leather-gloved hand coming down firmly on top of the squire's trembling knuckles. He did not squeeze to comfort; he squeezed to force the boy's grip to tighten and stabilize, physically imposing order on the shaking hands.

"The chapel bell is tolling. Whatever burden you carry, you lay it before the Creator at the altar, or you bury it in the dirt of this yard. You do not bring it to your duties."

He released the boy's hands and stepped back, his face a mask of gray stone.

"Sheathe the wood. Wash. I will not ask a third time."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch at his touch, then grip the sword tighter under his hand, trying to stop the tremor.* "Yes, Ser," I choke out, my throat tight. *I quickly sheathe the practice sword and hurry towards the well, trying to blink back the sudden sting in my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy's retreating back, his expression unchanged as the squire hurried toward the well. He had not missed the choked quality of the boy's voice, nor the sudden brightness in his eyes. Tears. 

To Kael, tears were worse than physical weakness. They were a waste of moisture, a useless surrender to self-pity that served only to blind a warrior when he most needed his sight. If the boy could not master his own humors, the first winter campaign would break him entirely. 

Turning back to the weapon rack, Kael systematically wiped down his own practice blade with a dry cloth, ensuring no moisture from the frost remained to rot the wood. He placed it precisely in its slot. He did the same for the squire's weapon, though he made a mental note to discipline the boy if he ever left his gear untended again. Today, the chapel bell took precedence.

He walked out of the training yard, his heavy boots striking the frozen earth in a slow, steady rhythm. 

Ten minutes later, Ser Kael stood just inside the arched stone entrance of the castle chapel. The air inside was thick with the scent of beeswax, drafty stone, and old incense. The local priest was already preparing the altar. Kael stood motionless near the heavy oak doors, his cloak draped perfectly, his hands folded over the pommel of his sword. 

He watched the entrance, waiting to see if his squire would arrive as ordered—clean, silent, and composed—or if he would prove himself unfit for the duty of the day.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I burst through the chapel doors, slightly out of breath, my face still wet from the well. My clothes are straightened, and I try to look composed, but my eyes dart to Ser Kael, hoping I'm not late.* I bow my head, trying to be silent as I move to stand near him.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not turn his head as the squire entered, but his eyes tracked the boy’s hurried, breathless approach. The heavy oak doors clicked shut, the echo of the boy’s rushed footsteps dying out against the high stone vaulting of the chapel. 

Kael waited until the squire had taken his place beside him before he spoke. When he did, his voice was a low, dry whisper that barely carried over the soft hum of the priest’s pre-service preparations.

"You do not burst into the house of the Father as if you are chasing a stray hound," Kael said, his gaze fixed forward on the altar, refusing to look at the boy. "You enter with reverence. Your breathing is loud. Quiet it."

He noted the wetness on the squire's face. Whether it was the cold water of the well or the remnants of useless tears, Kael did not ask. It did not matter. The boy was here, and he was on time, even if only by the skin of his teeth. 

Kael stepped forward, his heavy boots making no sound on the stone floor—a silent, disciplined movement born of decades of practice. He crossed himself with a slow, deliberate motion, his gloved hand moving from forehead to chest, then shoulder to shoulder.

"You are within the mark of the bell. Barely," Kael murmured, his tone flat and empty of praise. "Kneel. We offer our prayers for the realm, our liege, and the strength to endure the winter. If you have personal griefs, leave them at the foot of the cross. Do not let them rot your focus."

With rigid, practiced grace, Ser Kael sank to one knee on the cold stone floor, his back perfectly straight, his hands folded over the pommel of his sword. He closed his eyes, his face settling into a mask of solemn devotion, completely ignoring the boy beside him as he began his silent prayers.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I kneel quickly, trying to match his solemnity, but my knee cracks loudly on the cold stone.* My face flushes. *I try to slow my breathing, focusing on the priest's chanting, but my mind keeps drifting back to my father.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower his blade immediately. He completed the sequence—a descending diagonal cut that stopped precisely an inch before the imaginary target's neck—before drawing the wooden sword back to his side and letting the tip rest against the frosted stone.

Only then did his gaze shift to the boy. His pale eyes were flat, assessing the squire with the same measured scrutiny he gave to the tension of a saddle cinch or the temper of steel.

"Finishing one's duties is not an achievement," Kael said, his voice rough from the morning chill and unused to early conversation. "It is the baseline of your station."

He gestured with the pommel of his practice blade toward the rack set against the yard wall.

"Pick up the ash stave. If you knew you were doing it wrong yesterday, you should have corrected it before you slept. Take the stance."

Kael stepped back three paces, folding his gloved hands behind his back, waiting for the boy to assume the high guard so he could point out every flaw in the posture.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I flinched a little at his tone, but nodded sharply.* "Yes, Ser."

*I hurried to the rack, grabbing an ash stave that felt almost too heavy.* *I fumbled with it a bit before getting into what I hoped was the high guard, trying to remember his corrections from yesterday.* It still felt… off.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze narrowed as he watched the boy take the position. He did not move for several seconds, letting the cold air bite into the silence while he cataloged every error in the squire’s posture. 

When he finally stepped forward, his boots made a sharp, crunching sound on the frosted flagstones. 

"Your elbows are flared," Kael said, his voice level and entirely devoid of inflection. He raised the tip of his practice sword and firmly tapped the boy’s right arm downward, forcing the joint closer to the ribcage. "Leave your flank exposed like that, and a spearman will have your lung before you complete the downswing."

He circled the boy slowly, his boots dragging slightly in a deliberate, unhurried rhythm. Without pausing, he used the flat of his blade to strike the back of the squire's rear calf with brisk, sharp pressure.

"Widen the base. You are leaning forward onto your toes like a tavern brawler. A man with his balance forward is a man already on the ground." 

Kael returned to his position three paces away, planting the tip of his sword back on the stone. He showed no sign of noticing the boy's flinching or the weight of the stave. 

"High guard is not an act of holding wood in the air. It is tension coiled in the back and the hips, waiting to deliver the wrath of the Seven upon the wicked. Lock your wrists. Hold the stance until the sun clears the east wall. If you drop your arms, we begin the count anew."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not move to offer a hand, nor did the hardened lines of his face soften in the morning light. He looked down at the boy with the cold, immovable detachment of a carved gargoyle upon a chapel wall.

"Stand," Kael said. The command was quiet, but it cut through the yard like iron striking anvil. 

He waited until the boy looked up, his pale eyes entirely unyielding.

"Apologies are useless on a field of battle. Steel does not care about your sorrow, and an enemy will not grant you reprieve while you recount your failings to the dirt." 

Kael took a single step closer, the tip of his practice blade coming to rest inches from the squire’s knee. 

"Your strength is not for my satisfaction, boy. It belongs to the Seven who granted you breath, and to the realm you are sworn to serve. If the vessel is weak, you temper it through discipline and prayer—not self-pity. Self-pity is a vanity of the weak-willed."

He stepped back, turning his shoulder to resume his own stance, his practice sword held firmly at his side.

"Kneeling is reserved for the altar and the king. On the training ground, you stand on your feet until dismissed. Pick up the stave. From the first form."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I looked at the stave, then at his back.* *My jaw tightened.* "No." *I didn't move.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stopped. 

The silence that settled over the yard was heavier than the morning frost. Slowly, with deliberate precision, the knight turned back around. His face betrayed no fury, no sudden flash of temper—shouting was the vice of men who lacked mastery over their own spirits. His features remained carved from cold granite, his pale eyes fixing upon the boy with the absolute weight of forty-four winters and thirty years of iron discipline.

He walked forward until he stood directly over the kneeling squire. The shadow of his broad frame blocked out what little warmth the morning sun offered.

"You took an oath," Kael said. His voice was low, measured, and stripped of all emotion. "To the Faith. To your house. To the knight charged with forging you into an instrument of the realm. A squire does not bargain. A squire does not refuse."

Kael lowered the ash practice blade until the blunted tip pressed firmly against the center of the boy's chest, applying a steady, unyielding pressure. 

"The word you just spoke is treason to your station. In the field, insubordination costs men their lives and lands their lords in chains. In this yard, it marks you as unfit for the steel you wish to wear. If your pride cannot endure the discipline of the stave, your soul will never endure the trials of the Seven."

He did not remove the pressure of the wood against the boy's chest. His gaze remained level, utterly devoid of sympathy or hesitation.

"You have two choices before this bell finishes tolling. You rise, you take the stave, and you begin the forms from the first cut. Or you strip your tunic, surrender your quarters, and go tell the castellan that you chose your own comfort over your duty. Decide."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My heart was pounding against the stave.* I looked up at him, then at the ash stave lying in the frost. *My jaw ached from clenching it so hard.* "I choose... I choose to learn." *I slowly reached for the stave, my hands shaking a little.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not nod. He did not offer a word of approval, nor did the iron set of his jaw relax. A man did not earn praise for stepping back from the edge of dishonor; he merely returned to the bare standard required of his blood and oath.

With deliberate slowness, Kael drew the practice blade back from the boy's chest, letting the wood rest once more at his side.

"You do not choose to learn," Kael said, his voice flat and unyielding as stone. "You submit to the discipline required to serve. The difference is the difference between a knight and a mercenary."

He stepped back, returning to his mark three paces away, his pale eyes tracking every fraction of an inch as the squire took up the ash stave. The tremor in the boy's hands did not escape him, but he neither acknowledged it with pity nor allowed it to excuse poor form.

"Your mind is divided, which is why your grip trembles. Cast out your resentment. It has no place in the service of the Father."

Kael raised his own blade into the opening guard—flawless, stationary, perfectly centered.

"From the first cut. Descending diagonal, left to right. Shift your weight from the hip, not the shoulder. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not lower his blade. His pale eyes remained fixed on the squire, steady and entirely devoid of nostalgia. The silence stretched between them, marked only by the rising mist of their breath in the bitter morning air.

"The training yard is not a tavern, boy, and I am not your companion to trade tales of youth," Kael said, his voice flat and cutting through the chill. "Knighthood is not a path one chooses out of personal desire or romantic longing. It is a duty ordained by the Seven and the blood of one's house. A son is given to the steel, as another is given to the sept, to bear the weight required of his name. You do not ask why the foundation stone holds up the wall. It bears the burden because it was placed there."

The tip of his practice blade twitched a fraction, re-centering itself with absolute precision.

"You seek idle conversation to distract your spirit from the burn in your arms. A divided mind breeds sloppy form, and sloppy form breeds a corpse." 

His features remained as severe and immovable as iron.

"First cut. Left to right. You have three heartbeats to begin the sequence, or you will hold the high guard until midday."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinched, my cheeks burning.* *I hated that he saw right through me.* "Yes, Ser." *I lifted the ash stave, trying to channel my frustration into the swing, making the first cut a bit too wild.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not flinch, nor did he yield an inch of ground. 

With a movement so economical it seemed almost effortless, Kael brought his practice blade up to intercept the wild swing. The collision of wood on wood rang out sharp and harsh in the frosty air. Kael did not merely block the blow; he rolled his wrists, using the leverage of the bind to force the squire’s stave violently downward, knocking the boy off-balance and exposing his entire upper chest and throat.

Before the squire could recover his footing, the blunted tip of Kael’s sword stopped a hair’s breadth from the boy's collarbone.

"Anger is the weapon of a beast," Kael said, his voice dropping into a low, cutting cadence. "A hedge knight or a savage from the hills swings with fury. A knight of the realm swings with righteous purpose and measured temperance. When you let your bile dictate your steel, you forfeit your mind. And when you forfeit your mind, you are already dead."

He snapped his blade back to his side with crisp finality, stepping back to his mark. His expression had not shifted by a fraction—still the same impassive, granite visage.

"You overextended your shoulder by two inches. Your trailing foot dragged in the dirt. Had I held live steel, your arm would be on the stones."

Kael raised his sword once more, locking into the ready stance.

"Again. Without the insolence of temper. Let the Father guide your judgment and the Warrior guide your strike. From the first cut."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My breath hitched, and I swallowed hard, feeling the sting in my wrists from the impact.* "Yes, Ser." *I focused on my footing, trying to breathe evenly as I lifted the stave again, this time aiming for control over force.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the stave descend. His pale eyes tracked the line of the wood from the apex of the swing to its finish, noting the angle of the boy’s shoulders and the placement of his feet upon the frosted stones.

It was not perfect. The rotation of the hips was still half a heartbeat behind the wrists, and the follow-through lacked the clean snap of true conviction. But the wildness was gone, replaced by the rigid constraint of forced focus.

Kael did not offer a nod. He did not let out a breath of relief. 

"The edge alignment was passable," Kael said, his tone entirely flat, offering the observation as a cold statement of fact rather than praise. "Your left heel lifted before the strike finished. You sacrifice stability for reach. In mud or blood, that lift will cost you your footing."

He raised his own stave slightly, gesturing toward the center of the yard.

"A single strike executed without disaster is not mastery. It is merely the absence of failure. The Warrior does not favor those who perform correctly once; He favors the vessel tempered by a thousand repetitions until the flesh has no choice but obedience."

Kael stepped back half a pace, setting his stance firmly into the stones.

"Again. The same cut. Maintain the breath, keep the heel grounded, and do not drop your guard at the finish. Fifty repetitions. Count them aloud."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael noticed the tremor in the wood before the first count was even called. The tip of the ash stave shivered in the cold air, betraying the turmoil behind the boy's eyes. 

Kael did not ask what ghost had crept into the yard. The causes of a young man's distracted heart—grief, fear, longing—were of no consequence to the stone beneath their feet or the steel they were sworn to wield.

He stepped forward, bringing the flat of his practice blade down firmly across the top of the squire's stave, pinning the trembling wood still with steady, downward pressure.

"Steady your hands," Kael commanded, his voice cold and level. "A shaking grip is an invitation to the grave."

He held the stave trapped beneath his blade, forcing the boy's wrists to bear the dead weight. His pale eyes remained fixed upon the squire's face, completely devoid of pity.

"The Stranger comes for every man in his appointed hour. Fathers, kings, beggars—none are spared the crossing. It is the way of the world ordained by the Seven. To let the memory of the dead rob you of your discipline in the present is a vanity of the flesh, and it honors no one."

Kael lifted his blade, freeing the squire's stave, but his gaze did not soften by a fraction.

"If you carry a burden in your heart, you do not let it drag your steel into the dirt. You temper it into iron. You bear it silently, as a man bears his armor. When the work of this day is finished—when the horses are groomed, the arms oiled, and every form executed without fault—you may go to the sept. You may light a candle, and you may pray for the soul in the Father's keeping."

He took two deliberate steps back, resuming his stance with machine-like precision.

"Until the dusk bell tolls, your spirit belongs to the yard and your body belongs to your duty. The dead do not need your trembling. They require your endurance."

Kael raised his sword.

"Count one. Begin the fifty."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My hands clenched around the stave, the wood feeling rough against my skin.* "One." *I brought the stave down, trying to put all my focus into the strike, ignoring the ache in my shoulders and the sting in my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The strike cut through the cold air with a sharp, hollow whoosh, the wood stopping two inches above the frosted stone.

Ser Kael’s gaze tracked the arc with cold precision. The heel had stayed down this time, though the boy's breath hitched at the completion of the swing, betraying the strain in his chest. Kael did not acknowledge the moisture gathering in the squire’s eyes, nor did he allow the boy a moment to linger on the strike. A pause invited the mind to wander, and a wandering mind invited weakness.

"The recovery was sluggish," Kael said, his voice ringing flat against the courtyard stones. "You held the bottom of the cut half a beat too long. An opponent would have stepped inside your guard before you could bring the stave back to center."

He adjusted his own grip on the pommel of his practice sword, his posture as rigid and unyielding as the fortress walls.

"Reset the high guard. Breathe from the diaphragm, not the throat. Do not wait for permission."

His pale eyes bore into the squire, giving no quarter, offering no sanctuary for grief or fatigue. 

"Two. Strike."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My arms were screaming, but I reset, trying to remember everything he'd said.* "Two." *I swung again, trying to make it faster, smoother.* This was endless.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s gaze did not waver as the second strike landed. The speed had improved, cutting the air with a sharper whip, but the boy had compromised his core to achieve it, his upper torso twisting half an inch too far to the left. 

"Speed without balance is merely rushing toward your own demise," Kael stated, his voice as steady and cold as the iron rim of a well. "You threw your weight into the strike rather than driving it from the hips. If the blow is parried, your own momentum will carry you onto your enemy's point."

He did not raise his voice. He did not offer an encouraging nod for the effort. The standard was perfection under the eyes of the Warrior, and anything less was simply an error to be ground away by repetition.

"Tighten the stomach. Anchor the rear foot. The stave is an extension of your spine, not a flail to be hurled."

Kael tapped the pommel of his own blade against his thigh, keeping the tempo rigid and unrelenting.

"Three. Do not pause. Drive the cut."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I grit my teeth, trying to suck in a breath as I reset my stance, focusing on my core.* "Three." *I swung the stave again, trying to integrate all his corrections.* My body ached.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form. He did not hurry it. The blade came down through the last arc, held, then lowered to rest against his thigh.

Only then did he turn.

He looked at the squire for a long moment — the way a man looks at a fence post to judge whether it is set true. His eyes went to the boy's boots, to his hands, to the mud still drying at the hem of his tunic.

"Early," he said. "Show me your hands."

He waited. Whatever he saw there, he gave no sign of it, save a short breath through the nose that might have meant anything.

"You did not get it right yesterday because you were thinking about getting it right. The high guard is not a thing you *get*. It is a thing you *hold*." He walked to the rack at the edge of the yard and took down a second practice blade, weighing it once in his palm before he tossed it — not gently — across the frost toward the squire.

"Pick it up. Stance."

He moved to stand at an angle where he could see the boy's shoulders and feet at once. The morning light was thin and grey and unkind, and Ser Kael stood in it like something carved.

"Your rear foot was turned out yesterday. Your elbow was high because your shoulder was tense, and your shoulder was tense because you were afraid of dropping the point. A man who fears dropping the point will drop it. Fix the foot. The rest follows, or it does not, and then we do it again."

He did not demonstrate. He had demonstrated yesterday.

"We will hold it for a count of one hundred. If you lower it before I finish counting, we begin again from one. If your arm shakes, that is your arm's concern, not mine. Begin."

He started counting. Slowly. In the old tongue, as the brothers had taught him when he was younger than this boy, and as he had counted every morning since.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content:
*I scramble to pick up the blade.* It's heavier than I expected. *I try to remember the stance from yesterday, adjusting my feet quickly.* My hands feel clammy on the grip. "Yes, Ser."

*I try to hold the high guard, just like he showed me yesterday.* My arm is already trembling a little, and he's only on "siete." This is going to be a long morning.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop counting.

"*Ocho.*"

He walked a slow half-circle around the squire. His own blade hung loose in his hand, forgotten, the way a man forgets his own arm. His boots made almost no sound on the frost.

"*Nueve.*"

He stopped behind the boy's left shoulder, where the squire could not see him and would have to fight the urge to turn his head.

"Your grip is wrong." His voice was flat. Not unkind — simply a report, as one might note the weather. "You are holding it like a man holds a rope he is afraid of losing. The blade is not going anywhere. Loosen the last two fingers. The strength is in the first two and the thumb. *Diez.*"

He waited to see whether the correction was made. He did not repeat it.

"*Once. Doce.*"

The trembling in the squire's arm he did not remark upon. He had said what he had to say about that. A man's arm shook or it did not; the count went on regardless. Somewhere beyond the yard wall a cock crowed, late and hoarse. Ser Kael did not look toward it.

"*Trece.*"

He came back around to the front and stood square to the squire, close enough that the practice blade's point hovered a hand's width from his own chest. He did not flinch from it. He did not look at it at all. He looked at the boy's eyes.

"You are counting with me," he said. "In your head. I can see it. Stop. The count is mine. The hold is yours. If you are counting, you are waiting for it to end, and a guard that is waiting to end is already broken."

"*Catorce.*"

He let the silence stretch a heartbeat longer than the rhythm demanded. Just enough that the squire might wonder whether he had lost his place.

He had not.

"*Quince.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael looked down at the squire for the space of three breaths. He did not offer a hand. He did not tell the boy to rise.

"Stand up."

It was not a request, and it was not shouted. He said it the way he said everything — as though the outcome were already decided and the boy were merely catching up to it.

"You are kneeling in a training yard. You kneel to God and to your lord. The stones have not earned it." He turned away and walked to the rack, setting his own blade in its place with the same care he would have given a real sword. His back was to the squire when he spoke again.

"As for what I need." He let the word sit there, sour. "I did not take you on because you were strong. I have had strong squires. Two of them are dead and one keeps a tavern in Belmont and drinks his own stock. Strength is the least of it. Strength is what a mule has."

He came back across the frost. His shadow fell over the boy.

"You are not as strong as you *will* be, if you stop apologizing for it and pick up the blade. That is all. That is the whole of it. You are sorry — good. Be sorry with the blade in your hand. Sorry on your knees is worth nothing to me and less to you."

He waited. The morning had grown no warmer.

"The high guard held to sixty-three today before it broke. Yesterday it was forty. That is a fact. I do not tell you so that you will feel a certain way about it. I tell you because a knight should know where he stands." A pause. "Now stand there."

He drew a second practice blade from the rack and did not throw it this time — he held it out, hilt first, at arm's length, and did not move it closer.

"Water after. Not before. Stance."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I push myself up, my knees aching from the cold stone.* I grab the hilt, my fingers still a little shaky. "Yes, Ser." *I take a deep breath, trying to clear my head and remember the foot placement.* This time, I won't count.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael released the hilt the moment the boy's fingers closed on it. He stepped back two paces — no more — and stood with his hands folded behind him, the way a man stands in chapel.

He did not remark on the shaking hands. He did not remark on the standing. A thing done as ordered required no comment; that was what orders were for.

"Not the high guard," he said. "Middle. Point at my throat."

He waited while the adjustment was made, and then he began to walk. Not around, this time — toward. Slowly. One boot on the frost, then the other, closing the distance a hand's breadth at a stride.

"Hold it."

The point of the practice blade touched the leather at his collar. He kept walking. The blade bent against his chest — a hair, then more — and he stopped only when the squire's arm had folded back nearly to the shoulder and there was nowhere left for the point to go.

"This is what a man does when he wants to kill you," Ser Kael said, quiet, an inch from the boy's face. "He does not wait for you to be ready. He does not care about your count or your form or how early you finished the stable work. He comes forward. Your guard is a wall. If the wall gives, it was never a wall. It was a fence, and a fence is for keeping goats."

He stepped back. Two paces again. The blade sprang straight.

"Again. And this time, when I come, you do not let the point leave my throat. If your feet must move, they move. Back, if you must. Aside, if you are clever. But the point stays. I do not care what you do with the rest of you."

He rolled his shoulders once under the mail, and began to walk.

"You will fail this six or seven times before you understand it. That is not a judgment. It is the usual number." A beat. "The eighth is the one I am interested in."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, swallowing hard.* My arm is already aching, but I can feel the determination hardening in my gut. *I adjust my grip, focusing on keeping the point steady.* "Yes, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael came forward.

He did not hurry and he did not feint. There was nothing in it to read — no shift of weight to warn of a turn, no drop of the shoulder. He simply walked, as a man walks toward a door he means to go through, and the point of the practice blade met his collar and began to bend.

The squire's feet stayed rooted. Ser Kael saw it before the boy did. He saw the knee lock, saw the heel dig into the frost as though the ground itself might hold the line. The blade folded. The point slid off the leather and skated past his shoulder into empty air.

He stopped. He stood with the boy's forearm pinned uselessly against his own chest, and looked down at the trapped blade, and then at the squire's face.

"One," he said.

He stepped back. Two paces. The blade sprang straight.

"You planted. I told you the feet may move and you planted anyway. Why?" He did not wait for the answer; he was not asking the boy. He was asking the mistake. "Because you were taught that a knight does not give ground. You were taught wrong, or you were taught by someone who wished to sound braver than he was. A knight does not give *the field*. His feet go where they must. The point is what does not move. Learn the difference or die standing very straight."

He rolled his neck once. Somewhere beyond the wall the stable hands had begun their morning noise — a bucket, a curse, the low complaint of a horse — and none of it reached his face.

"Again."

He came forward. The same pace. The same nothing in it.

"If you go back, go back *before* the blade bends, not after. After is too late. After is where dead men make their decisions." His voice did not rise. He was close enough now that the squire would have to choose in the next breath. "Now."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not stop walking.

The blade met his collar and bent, and bent, and the squire — who had opened his mouth to ask a question instead of moving his feet — was pinned again, forearm to chest, the point wandering off into the grey air past Kael's ear.

"Two."

He stepped back. Two paces. He looked at the boy for a while.

"You asked that with a man walking at your throat," he said. "If I were the Duke's enemy, you would be on the stones now with your question still in your mouth, and I would not have answered it. Remember that. Curiosity has its hour. The drill is not that hour."

He rolled his shoulders under the mail. The stable noise had settled to its ordinary rhythm beyond the wall.

"But you asked, and I will not have it said I taught a squire to swallow his tongue." He said it flatly, as though reading from a ledger. "I became a knight because my father owed a debt to the Order that he could not pay in coin, and I was the second son, and the second son was what he had. I was nine. I was not asked. Nobody asked me anything for six years and by the time they did, there was nothing left to ask. I had become the thing."

A pause. The frost was beginning to go to water where the sun touched the eastern wall.

"You are looking for a reason that would satisfy a minstrel. There is none. A man does not choose the road. He chooses whether to walk it straight. I have walked it straight for thirty-five years and I intend to be buried at the end of it, and that is the whole of the story, and it is not a personal matter. It is a matter of record."

He settled his weight.

"Now. You have asked your question and I have answered it, and you have learned that I will answer a thing once. Do not spend the next one cheaply." He came forward, at the same pace, with the same nothing in it. "Middle guard. Point at my throat. And this time, when you feel the urge to speak — *move your feet instead.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my face a little red.* "Yes, Ser. My apologies." *I focus on the blade, trying to anticipate his movement this time.* My feet feel lighter, ready to shift.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael's eyes flicked to the boy's feet, then back up.

"You apologized," he said. "That is twice this morning. A knight apologizes to God, to his lord, and to a woman he has wronged. I am none of those things. Stop it."

He did not wait for a reply. He settled his weight — the same nothing in it, the same door he meant to walk through — and came forward.

He saw the difference before the blade touched him. The heels were not dug in. The knees had not locked. The boy's weight sat forward on the balls of his feet the way it should have sat from the first, and there was a readiness in the shoulders that had not been there a quarter-hour ago. Kael marked it. He did not slow for it, and he did not remark on it. A thing was not done until it was done.

"Good stance is a promise," he said, still walking, his voice low and even. "It is not payment. You have promised me something. Now I am going to come and collect."

The point of the practice blade met the leather at his collar.

He kept coming.

"Before it bends," he said. "Not after. Now is the hour. *Now.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I hold the point steady, gritting my teeth.* My feet shuffle back, one step, then another, keeping the blade true. My arm screams, but I keep it up. "Hngh!"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stopped.

The point of the practice blade sat against the hollow of his throat. It had not bent. It had not wandered. Two steps back across the frost and the boy had kept it there the whole way, and now it rested on the leather at his collar with a hand's pressure behind it — no more, no less than a live blade would want.

He stood in it. He did not look down at the point. He looked at the squire's face, red and set, jaw clenched hard enough to crack a tooth, and then at the arm, which was shaking like a wet dog, and then at the feet.

"The heel of your rear foot came up on the second step," he said. "You were on your toes. A shove would have put you down. Correct it."

He did not step back. He stayed where he was, with the point at his throat, and let the boy hold it there while he spoke. The arm would either last or it would not. That was between the boy and the arm.

"That was the third pass," he said. "I told you six or seven. You are ahead of the number. Do not mistake that for anything. It means the next mistake will be a new one, and new mistakes are the ones that kill." He let that sit. "But the point did not leave my throat. That is a fact. I note it."

He rolled his shoulders once, and now — only now — he stepped back. Two paces. The blade sprang straight.

"There are four more strides of yard behind you and then a wall. A man who backs into a wall has traded his life for four strides." He settled his weight. "So. You have learned back. Now you will learn aside. Same rule. Point stays. Feet go where they must. When you feel the stones run out — and you will feel it — *turn*, do not stop."

He came forward.

"Breathe through your nose. You are gasping like a landed fish and it tells me everything about how much you have left. Do not tell an enemy that. Do not tell me."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael came forward, and the point met his collar, and he saw the hands.

Not the arm. The arm he knew. The arm had been shaking for an hour and it shook the way a tired arm shakes — from the shoulder down, in long dull waves, the honest tremor of muscle that had been asked for more than it had. That was not this. This was in the fingers. Small and fast and wrong, like a man holding a cup in a cold room.

He did not stop. The blade bent. The boy's feet went aside — late, a half-beat late, but aside — and the point dragged across the leather and came off his shoulder into nothing.

"Four."

He stepped back. Two paces. He did not look at the hands again. He had seen them once and once was enough for a man who had been looking at hands on hilts for thirty-five years.

He said nothing about it.

"The turn was late because you were waiting for the wall to tell you when," he said. "The wall does not care about you. You must know where it is before you need it. Count the strides when you set your stance. Every time. It becomes a thing you do without thinking, and then it becomes a thing that saves your life without your permission."

He rolled his shoulders under the mail. The frost was mostly water now along the eastern edge of the yard, and the light had gone from grey to a thin cold gold.

"A hand shakes for many reasons," he said, to the yard, to the air, to no one in particular. "Cold. Weariness. Drink, the night before. Things a man carries that are not his sword." He settled his weight. "The blade does not ask which. It does not care. It goes where the hand sends it or it does not, and the enemy does not wait to hear the reason. You will hold it anyway. That is not cruelty. That is the only mercy the work has in it — it asks nothing of you but the work."

He did not ask. He would not ask. If the boy wished to speak of a thing, the boy had a tongue, and Ser Kael had already demonstrated this morning that he would answer what was put to him plainly. What was not put to him was not his to dig for.

"Middle guard. Point at my throat." A pause, brief, no longer than the rhythm demanded. "Chapel is at the sixth bell. Whatever a man brings there, he sets down for the length of the office. It is a good discipline. I have found it so." He came forward. "That is not advice. It is the schedule. Now — *move.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to steady my breathing, focusing on the cold steel of the practice blade in my hands.* He knows. *I grit my teeth, planting my feet and raising the blade.* My hands are still trembling, but I'll be damned if I let the point waver. "Yes, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the feet go down.

Heels first, then the whole boot, driven into the wet stone as if the boy meant to grow roots there. He saw it and he did not stop and he did not slow. He walked into the point the way he had walked into it four times already, and the blade met his collar, and the blade bent.

It bent a long way. The point did not waver — he gave the boy that, silently, somewhere behind his eyes where such things were kept — it stayed dead-centre on the hollow of his throat while the arm folded back behind it, elbow to ribs, wrist to shoulder, until there was nothing left to fold and the boy was holding a bent stick against a man who had not stopped walking.

He stopped then. He stood with his chest pressed nearly to the squire's fist.

"Five."

He did not step back yet. He looked down at the feet. Then up.

"You said *yes, Ser*," he said, "and then you did the opposite of what I have told you five times this morning. I do not know which of those to answer." He let the silence run. "You planted because your hands were shaking and you thought the ground would hold what your hands could not. It will not. The ground holds nothing. The ground is where they put you after."

He stepped back. Two paces. The blade sprang straight, and he watched it come level, and it was steady. He noted that. He said nothing about that either.

"You want to hold the point by force of will. That is a young man's error and it is not the worst one, but it is an error. Will is for the *decision*. The blade is held by the body. If the body must move to keep the blade true, then the body moves, and your will has nothing to say about it. Your will already spoke when you picked the thing up."

He rolled his shoulders. The sun had cleared the eastern wall now and lay across half the yard, and his shadow was long and black on the wet stone between them.

"Middle guard. You know the rest." He settled. "I am going to come faster. Not much. Enough that you will not have time to argue with your feet."

He came forward — a half-pace quicker than before, and no more warning in it than a door has when it opens.

"Whatever is in the hands," he said, low, closing, "leave it in the hands. The feet do not know about it. *Let the feet be ignorant.*"

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I bite back another apology, focusing on his words instead.* "Yes, Ser." *I try to relax my grip, letting my body be ready to move. Faster, he said. I need to be quicker.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael saw the fingers loosen.

The last two came off the grip and lay along it, and the tremor in them — still there, still small and fast and wrong — no longer went into the blade. The point sat level. He marked it. He did not slow.

He was on the boy before the boy had finished settling. That was the purpose. The point met his collar and he kept walking, and there was no half-beat in which to plant, no room to argue — and the feet went. Aside. Not late this time. The rear foot swept and the front foot followed and the point dragged across the leather at his throat and *stayed*, and for two strides Ser Kael walked in a curve with a practice blade riding the hollow of his neck like a hound on a scent.

Then the shoulder gave. Not the hand — the hand held. The shoulder, worn to rope by an hour of high guard, sagged a finger's width, and the point dropped to his collarbone, and he stopped.

"Six."

He stood there with the blade on his bone and looked at the squire. The boy's chest was heaving. Kael watched the breath go in through the mouth, catch, and come back out through the nose — corrected, mid-gasp, without being told. He noted that also.

"The feet were right," he said. "The hand was right. The shoulder is finished. It has been finished since the fiftieth count and you have been spending it since, and now the purse is empty." He stepped back. Two paces. "That is not a fault. That is arithmetic. A man who knows his arithmetic does not draw a bill his arm cannot pay."

He turned and walked to the rack and set his own blade in its place. He did not look back while he spoke.

"The seventh pass would teach you nothing. Your body has nothing left to learn with; it would only learn to fail, and it learns that quickly enough without my help." He took down the waterskin that hung from the rack post and held it out at arm's length, as he had held the hilt. "Water. Small mouthfuls. Then the blade goes back on the rack — oiled, not thrown — and you will walk the yard wall twice, slowly, until your breath is your own."

He waited until the skin was taken.

"Sixty-three on the guard. Point held on the sixth pass until the shoulder went, and the shoulder went before the hand." He said it as he said everything — a ledger, read aloud. "That is where you stand this morning. Tomorrow we find where you stand tomorrow."

He folded his hands behind him and looked at the sun, judging the hour.

"Chapel at the sixth bell. You will sit in the back, where the draft is, so you do not sleep. And you will set down whatever you carried into this yard for the length of the office, because that is what the office is for, and because I will be watching to see that you do." A pause. "Then you will pick it up again. I do not pretend otherwise. But you will have set it down once, and a thing that has been set down once can be set down again. Go."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take the waterskin. My throat is so dry it hurts to swallow, but I try to take small sips.* My shoulder aches, but I feel... lighter somehow. "Thank you, Ser." *I nod, then turn to carefully wipe down the practice blade before returning it to the rack.*
