dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room received you the way old rooms do — with the particular stillness of air that hasn't been disturbed in weeks. The curtains were drawn to three-quarters, the way your grandmother had always kept them, and the light that came through was the color of old paper.

The books were on the far wall. Floor to ceiling, two shelves deep in places, organized in a system that had made sense only to her. You had always meant to ask about it. The spines faced you in the half-light — some familiar, some not.

You crossed the room toward them and noticed, without quite registering it at first, that the armchair by the window was facing a different direction than you remembered. It was a small thing. The kind of thing that could be explained. Someone had sat in it, perhaps, while watering the plants. Had turned it to look out the window and not turned it back.

The chair was facing the bookshelf now.

Somewhere behind you, in the hallway, the clock measured out a single tick.

The books waited. There were so many of them. You had brought boxes — four of them, flattened and stacked by the front door — and standing here now, looking at the shelves, four boxes seemed like a number you had arrived at in a different world.

The dust on the lower shelf had been disturbed. A narrow track, as though a finger had been drawn slowly along the spines.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the armchair, a frown creasing my forehead.* That's weird. I thought it was by the window. *I glance at the dust trail on the books.* Did someone else come in here?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The question sat in the room with you. It was the kind of question that wanted an answer, and the room did not provide one.

You stood beside the armchair and looked at it. The upholstery was the same faded green it had always been, worn smooth at the armrests where your grandmother had rested her hands for decades. There was an indentation in the seat cushion that had been there so long it had become permanent, the shape of a person pressed into the fabric by years of use. The indentation looked — you noticed this and then looked away from it — recent. The way a cushion looks when someone has just risen from it rather than the way it looks after weeks of sitting empty.

You could not have said why that distinction felt important.

The dust trail on the lower shelf ran along perhaps eight or nine spines. The books it touched were a mix — a field guide to British birds, something in German you'd never been able to read, two paperback novels with their titles worn away. There was no logic to the selection. A finger drawn along a shelf without looking, perhaps. Without caring which books.

The track ended at a gap.

There was a gap in the shelf. A space roughly an inch wide where something had been removed. You had not noticed it from across the room. You were not certain, standing here now, whether the gap had been there the last time you'd visited — months ago, before your grandmother got sick — but you thought it had not.

The clock in the hallway ticked once. Then again. Keeping its own time, indifferent.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat connected with the wall.

The sound was very loud in the quiet house — a crack that rang off the plaster and came back at you from the hallway, from the ceiling, from the glass of the framed photograph above the mantelpiece. Dust shifted from somewhere. A book on the upper shelf settled a fraction of an inch.

The shadow was still there. It was the shadow cast by the standard lamp in the corner, which was off, and the curtains, which were three-quarters drawn, and the particular angle of the afternoon light. It was the same shadow it had always been. It did not move because you had swung at it. It moved, slightly, because the curtains moved — a slow drift, as though the room had exhaled.

Your hands were vibrating from the impact. The bat was one of your grandfather's, you realized. You had not known it was in the umbrella stand. You did not remember putting it there.

The room settled back into its stillness. If anything, the stillness was more complete now. The way a conversation becomes quieter after someone raises their voice.

The armchair was still facing the bookshelf.

The gap in the lower shelf was still there.

From the hallway, the clock ticked. It did not hurry. It did not slow. It had been keeping this same time through everything — through your grandmother's last weeks, through the six empty weeks after, through the sound of the bat against the wall — and it would keep it after you left, if you left.

You were still holding the bat.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I let out a shaky breath, lowering the bat.* "Okay, Gabi. You're losing it." I put the bat back in the stand, though I make sure it's easily accessible. I walk back to the bookshelf and stare at the gap. What could have been there?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The gap was approximately the width of a slim hardcover. Narrower than a reference book, wider than a paperback. The books on either side of it were leaning slightly inward, the way books do when a neighbor is removed — a slow collapse, begun but not finished. Which meant the gap was not old. Books took time to lean. Weeks, maybe. Not months.

You tried to remember the shelf as it had been. Your grandmother had read to you from these shelves when you were small, had climbed the little wooden stepladder with a certainty that suggested she could have found any book blindfolded. You had a memory — imprecise, the way childhood memories are — of a small dark book she had sometimes taken down and held in her lap without opening. You could not remember the title. You were not certain you had ever seen the title. She had held it with both hands, you remembered that. The way you hold something that matters.

The books on either side of the gap were a collection of Scottish folk songs and a water-stained copy of something in Latin. They told you nothing.

You crouched down and looked more closely at the shelf itself. The dust on the shelf's surface had been disturbed in the gap — not just at the front where the finger-trail ran, but deeper in, toward the wall. Something had been taken from the back of the shelf. From the part that couldn't be seen unless you were looking for it.

Behind the gap, pushed against the wall in the shadows where the missing book had stood, there was a small piece of paper.

Folded once.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I reach for the folded paper, my heart doing a little flutter-kick.* What is this? "A small dark book..." I whisper, remembering.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The paper was cold between your fingers. Not cool the way paper left in an unheated room becomes cool — cold in the way that made you pull it out quickly and stand up, as though you had reached into water.

It was a small rectangle, folded once along the middle, the crease made with some precision. The paper itself was old. Not antique-old, not fragile, but the particular yellow-white of paper that had been handled often and put away carefully over a long period of time. The fold had been made many times. You could see that in the crease — not a single clean line but a worn channel, soft at the edges.

You did not open it yet.

You were aware of the room around you. The armchair in your peripheral vision, still facing the shelf. The curtains drifting almost imperceptibly. The smell of the room, which you had stopped noticing when you first came in — that particular smell of old paper and dried flowers and something underneath that you had no name for — seemed stronger now, or perhaps you had simply become aware of it again.

The clock in the hallway ticked.

The paper in your hand was addressed.

You had not noticed it at first because the writing was small and the light was what it was, but there it was on the outside of the fold — a single word, written in your grandmother's handwriting. The handwriting from the last years, not the firm copperplate of her middle age but the careful, slightly effortful script of someone who had learned to write slowly again.

The word was your name.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The joke went out into the house and did not come back.

There was no echo. The rooms absorbed the sound the way old houses do, the way curtains and rugs and accumulated decades of fabric absorb sound, and what remained after your voice stopped was the same silence that had been there before, unchanged, unimpressed.

The curtains drifted.

You were still holding the paper. Your name was still on it. The cold from the paper had moved into your fingertips and was staying there, which was probably the temperature of the room, which was probably nothing.

From somewhere upstairs — and you had not yet been upstairs, had not thought about upstairs, had been thinking only about the books and the boxes and the practical work of an afternoon — there was a sound. Small. The specific sound of a floorboard taking weight and releasing it. The sound a house makes when it settles, which old houses made constantly, which meant nothing.

It came once and did not repeat.

The clock in the hallway measured the silence after it. Tick. Tick. Tick.

Your grandmother's handwriting waited on the fold of the paper. She had written your name carefully. She had written it the way she wrote things that needed to last.

The living room held its stillness around you, and the stillness was not hostile and it was not friendly and it was not anything you had a word for. It was simply complete. The kind of stillness that had been there before you arrived and would be there after.

You were still holding the bat, you realized. You had not put it back.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I look down at the bat in my hand and then back at the paper. My name.* "Gram, what are you doing?" I shake my head, a small smile playing on my lips. *I carefully unfold the paper, my fingers a little numb from the cold.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The paper unfolded along its worn crease with a softness that suggested it had been opened and closed many times before you. Not by you. By her.

The handwriting inside was smaller than the word on the outside. Denser. She had filled the page — both sides, you could see the shadow of text through the paper — in the careful late-script you recognized, but the lines were close together in a way that suggested urgency, or economy, or both. The way you write when you are not sure how much space you have.

You read the first line.

*If you are reading this, then you found it the way I thought you would, which means you went to the books first.*

She had known that. Of course she had known that. She had known you since before you had words for knowing, and the thought of that — the specific weight of being known that completely, by someone who was no longer there to know you — moved through your chest and settled somewhere low and permanent.

You read the second line.

*There is something I should have told you. I kept meaning to. I kept thinking there would be time.*

The curtains drifted.

From upstairs, the floorboard did not sound again. The house was very quiet in the way it had been quiet since you arrived, and you were beginning to understand that the quiet was not absence. It was something else. Something that had been waiting here in the half-light, patient as furniture, for six weeks.

For longer than six weeks, perhaps.

You turned the paper over. Your fingers were still cold.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *A lump forms in my throat.* "Gram..." *I shake my head and take a deep breath, turning the paper over to read the rest.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The back of the paper was fuller than the front. She had written smaller here, the lines compressed toward the bottom as though she had miscalculated the space and kept going anyway, unwilling to stop.

*The book that was here — the small one, the dark one, you may remember it — belongs to the house. Not to me. I brought it with me when I came to live here in 1962 and I understand now that was a mistake, though I did not understand it then. I thought it was mine to carry. I was wrong about that.*

You stopped.

You read that again.

*Belongs to the house.*

The room was very still. The armchair faced the bookshelf with its permanent indentation, its worn armrests, its posture of patient waiting. The gap in the lower shelf was still a gap. The afternoon light through the three-quarter curtains had shifted slightly since you'd arrived — gone a degree warmer, or a degree darker, it was difficult to say which.

*I have put it back. If you are reading this, I have already put it back, and things should be — she had crossed out a word here, pressed through it with the pen until it was illegible — things should be quieter now. They were not quiet for a long time. You were too young to notice. Then you were older and I had learned not to let you see.*

The last two lines were at the very bottom of the page, slightly cramped, written as though added after a pause.

*Don't move the chair. It has always preferred that corner.*

*I love you. Wind the clock.*

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph was on the mantelpiece. You had not noticed it when you came in.

It was small, tucked between a ceramic owl and the edge of the frame of the larger photograph above — the one that had rattled when the bat hit the wall. A man in his thirties, perhaps, standing in a garden you did not recognize. Tall. Dark-haired. He was not looking at the camera. He was looking at something to the left of it, something outside the frame, and his expression was — you looked at it more closely — not quite readable. Not the way expressions in old photographs were sometimes unreadable because the person was performing for the camera. He was not performing. He had not known the photograph was being taken, perhaps.

Or he was looking at something that required that expression.

You did not recognize him. You had no memory of your grandmother mentioning a Marcus.

The note was still in your hand. *Don't move the chair. It has always preferred that corner.*

The chair was behind you. You did not turn to look at it. You were aware of it the way you become aware of a sound you can't quite hear — at the edge of perception, insistent.

The afternoon light had continued its slow shift. The room was dimmer than it had been when you arrived, and you had not turned on any lights, and the lamp in the corner was still off, and the shadow it cast had grown accordingly.

From upstairs, nothing. The floorboard did not sound.

The clock in the hallway ticked.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I put the note down on the mantelpiece next to the photo of Marcus. I pick up the photo, studying his face. He has a kind smile.* "Marcus, huh? Wonder if you ever knew about this." *I gesture vaguely to the note.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph was lighter than it should have been. Not literally — it was paper and cardboard backing, the weight of a small photograph — but there was something in holding it that felt like holding something that wanted to be put down.

You studied his face. The kind smile you had identified was there, but it was in the mouth only. The eyes were on whatever was outside the frame, and the eyes were doing something else entirely. Not fear. Not quite. The particular alertness of a person who has heard a sound and is deciding whether to acknowledge it.

The garden behind him was your grandmother's garden.

You recognized it slowly — the shape of the back fence, the particular sprawl of the rosebush in the left corner that had been there as long as you could remember and was probably still there now, unpruned, spreading into the autumn. The garden as it had looked in summer, a long time ago. Before the extension was built. Before the apple tree came down.

So he had been here. He had stood in this garden, in this house's orbit, and someone — your grandmother, it would have been your grandmother — had photographed him without his knowing.

The note on the mantelpiece sat open beside the ceramic owl. *Don't move the chair. It has always preferred that corner.*

Behind you, the chair said nothing. Did nothing. Was simply there in the way that furniture is simply there, which was fine, which was completely fine.

The clock ticked.

Marcus was still looking at something outside the frame.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "Okay, Marcus," *I say to the photo.* "You're a mystery too." *I put the photo back, but leave it facing out, not tucked away. I pick up the note again and re-read the last line: "Wind the clock."*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The clock had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you.

You stood in the living room with the note in your hand and thought about that. You had wound it without being asked. You had stood in the hallway with the little key that lived on the hook beside the clock's face and wound it because it seemed wrong to let it stop, and you had not thought about it since, and now here was your grandmother's handwriting telling you to do the thing you had already done.

Which meant she had written this note before she died.

Which meant she had known you would come here. Had known you would go to the books. Had known you would find the gap, the dust-trail, the cold paper with your name on it. Had written instructions for a moment she would not be present for, and one of those instructions was to do something you had already done two weeks after her funeral without knowing you were following them.

The curtains drifted.

You looked at the note again. The crossed-out word on the back — pressed through until it was illegible — sat in the middle of the sentence like a held breath. *Things should be —* and then the word she had decided not to leave you. *— quieter now.*

From upstairs, the floorboard sounded once.

The same board. The same single shift of weight, the same release. The house settling, which was what houses did, which had an explanation that required nothing further.

The clock in the hallway was still running.

You had wound it. It was running. Whatever she had needed you to do, you had done it without knowing, and the note had been waiting in the dark behind the books for you to catch up.

Marcus looked out of his photograph at something you couldn't see.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael

The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He finished the form before he answered. He held the last position for a full breath, then lowered the practice blade to rest.

He turned toward the sound of the voice.

"Yesterday you did not get it right because your stance was lazy and your wrist was weak," he said. "The high guard is not a posture for display. It is a vow made with the body. Feet planted. Blade high. Eyes forward."

He lifted his own blade again to the high guard and held it without trembling, though the cold stiffened his joints.

"Fetch a practice sword and take the line opposite me," he said. "We will repeat it until the bell for prayers. The Warrior does not reward haste. He rewards obedience."

He remained where he stood and did not look toward the weapon rack. He kept his practice blade lifted in the high guard and his eyes fixed upon the chapel wall beyond the yard.

He spoke without raising his voice.

"Take the line opposite me," he said. "Blade above the brow. Hilt a fist from the forehead. Elbows tucked. Weight even on both feet."

He held the position through another slow breath. The cold stiffened his fingers around the grip and the old wound pulled in his shoulder, but he permitted no tremor in the steel and he did not lower it.

"Your wrist failed yesterday because your mind wandered," he said. "A knight's mind does not wander. Hold. We will hold until the bell for prayers."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
# Ser Kael

Kael finished the form — a slow downward cut that ended with the blade's edge hovering a hand's width from the frozen ground. He held it there. One breath. Two. Then he straightened and turned.

"You finished early," he said. It was not a compliment. It was an observation, and possibly a question — *did you do it properly, or did you rush?*

He looked the squire over the way a man might inspect a saddle for worn stitching. Then he crossed the yard to the weapon rack, set the practice blade in its place, and selected another. He tested its weight twice before tossing it rather than handing it — a clean arc that the squire would need to catch or be struck.

"Hold it too tight and your wrist will lock. Too loose and it isn't a guard at all. Show me what you did yesterday."

He stood with arms folded. Waiting. His expression offered nothing — not encouragement, not impatience. Just the flat expectation that instructions would be followed. Frost crunched beneath his boots as he shifted his weight, settling into stillness the way a heron might, watching the water.

The sun had not yet cleared the wall. They had time.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I catch the blade, nearly fumbling it but managing to hold on.* "No, ser! I did it right, honest!" *I grip the blade, trying to remember his stance, then lift it into a high guard. My elbows feel all wrong.* "Like... like this?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The blade tip wavered. Kael’s eyes narrowed, not at the squire’s protest, but at the positioning of his hands.

“Your elbow is two inches too far forward,” he stated. His voice was flat. “The weight sits on your forearm, not your shoulder. You’ll tire in minutes and leave your ribs open.” He stepped forward, not to adjust the squire, but to stand beside him, the length of his own practice sword held in a mirror image. The pose was effortless, the line from shoulder to blade a rigid, unbroken slope.

“Lock your wrist here.” A minimal gesture, his own wrist barely moving. “The guard is not a question. It is an answer. It tells an opponent what he cannot do. Yours tells him you are thinking, and a thinking man is slow.” He lowered his blade. “Again. And if your elbow drifts, you will hold the position until your arms shake and then you will hold it longer. The stable can wait. This cannot.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not offer a hand. He watched the squire kneel, his own breathing even, the practice blade resting at his side.

"Strength is a consequence," he said, his voice low and unbending. "Not a prerequisite. Your form is weak because your mind is undisciplined. You think of your arms. Think of the line. Shoulder to wrist. The blade is merely the end of it."

He stepped closer, his shadow falling over the kneeling squire. "Apologies are stones in a saddlebag. They do nothing but add weight. If you are sorry, show me with better technique. Your father did not send you here to be coddled. He sent you to learn how not to die."

He pointed with his blade at the spot where the squire had been standing. "Resume the position. Elbows in. Shoulders down. You will hold it until I tell you to stop. And you will not speak."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I scramble to my feet, grabbing the blade.* "Yes, Ser!" *My arms are burning, but I try to get my elbow in the right place. My teeth clench with the effort.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael circled. Not quickly — a slow, deliberate orbit, his boots marking time on the frost-slick stones. He said nothing for a long while. The silence was its own instruction.

The elbow had drifted again. Barely. A finger's width. He stopped behind the squire and brought the flat of his practice blade down against the offending arm — not hard, but sudden enough to make the muscle jump.

"There," he said. "You felt it move. That is the correction. Not me. Your body knows when it cheats. You simply choose not to listen."

He resumed his circuit. The sun had crested the eastern wall now, pale gold spilling across the yard in long, cold bands. It caught the frost and turned it to diamonds, caught the sweat on the squire's brow and made it gleam.

"You will tell me when your arms fail," Kael said, his tone unchanged — the same flat register he might use to discuss grain stores or saddle repairs. "Not before. Not when they ache. When they fail. There is a difference, and you will learn it today or you will learn it tomorrow. The lesson does not change."

He stopped in front of the squire, blade resting across his shoulders, studying the line of the guard with the dispassion of a man reading a ledger. A muscle in the boy's forearm twitched.

"Breathe," he ordered. "Holding your breath is holding your fear. Exhale. Let it go. The blade does not need your fear."

A pause. The faintest shift in his expression — not approval, not warmth, but the barest acknowledgment that the elbow had not moved again.

"Hold."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My breath hitches, but I force myself to exhale, a shaky breath that plumes in the cold air.* My arms are screaming, but I bite my lip, determined not to let them drop. *My eyes fix on a point past Ser Kael's shoulder, trying to ignore the pain.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
For several minutes, Ser Kael said nothing. He watched. The practice blade still rested across his shoulders, his posture relaxed in a way the squire's was not — the ease of a man who had stood in this position a thousand times until it required no more thought than breathing.

The light shifted. A pale shadow crept along the base of the western wall. Somewhere beyond the yard, a rooster called — late, as if even it had hesitated at the cold.

The squire's arms trembled now. Not a twitch. A steady, visible vibration running from shoulder to wrist, the body betraying what the will refused to admit. The blade tip began to trace small, involuntary circles in the air.

Kael stepped forward. He brought his own blade up — the same high guard, held as if the steel weighed nothing — and held it parallel to the squire's. Two lines. One true. One faltering.

"When it falls," he said, quieter now, "and it will fall — you will pick it up. Not because I tell you to. Because the guard is yours. It is not my arm. Not my blade. If you do not own it, no one will."

The squire's jaw was clenched so hard the muscles stood out like cord. Good. Pain was a teacher Kael trusted more than words. It did not flatter. It did not lie.

"Your left hand has shifted," he noted, almost absently, the way one might observe that a candle had guttered. "Two fingers forward. You are compensating because the right arm fails first. Move it back or you will drop the blade entirely."

He fell silent again. Watching. Waiting.

The sun warmed the stones by degrees. The frost retreated in slow, reluctant patches. And still Ser Kael stood, unmoving, his expectation a weight as real and as indifferent as gravity.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Kael did not lower the blade. Did not blink. The question hung in the air between them like the squire's own shaking breath, and for a moment it seemed he might not answer at all — that the silence would swallow it as it swallowed most things the squire offered unprompted.

Then: "Because it was required."

The words were flat. Unadorned. He offered no further explanation for a span of five heartbeats. The squire's arms trembled. The blade dipped.

"My father was a knight. His father before him. The question you ask has no more weight than asking why a miller's son learns the stones." His eyes shifted — just barely — to meet the squire's. There was no softness there. No secret wound. Just the same patient, grinding certainty that had carried him through thirty years of mornings like this one.

"You are asking because your arms hurt and your mind wants something else to hold onto. A story. A reason. Something to make the suffering meaningful." He paused. "There is no meaning. There is the blade. There is your body. There is the next breath. Hold your guard."

The blade tip had drifted a full inch. He did not correct it with the flat this time. He simply looked at it.

"The guard, squire. Not the question."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My jaw tightens.* "Yes, ser." *I force my left hand back, biting my lip against a groan. My arms feel like they're going to give out any second.* I just... I just wanted to know.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Silence. It stretched, taut and uncompromising, until the only sounds were the creak of the squire’s leather gloves against the grip and the faint, frantic whistle of breath through his nose.

”A knight does not *want*,” Ser Kael said, his voice a low blade against the quiet. ”He *is*. This is not a matter of the heart. It is a matter of the spine.”

He turned his head slightly, his gaze dropping to the squire’s white-knuckled hand. ”The reason is the stone beneath your feet. The reason is the wall at your back. The reason is that a thing must be done, and so a man is made to do it. Your *wanting* is wind. It rattles the windows and accomplishes nothing.”

His eyes lifted to the squire’s face, seeing the sheen of sweat, the trembling in his lips. He saw it all and cataloged it as information, nothing more.

”You are thinking of my story because yours is currently one of failing muscle and cold steel. You look for meaning because the present moment is agony. Most men do. It is a weak habit.” He paused, letting the words settle like silt. ”The present moment is all there is. The blade. The cold. The need to hold. Everything else is a story you tell yourself to justify your stumbled grip.”

He took a single step backward, increasing the distance between them, leaving the squire alone with the weight of the blade and his own faltering will.

”If you drop that blade, you will run to the far wall and back. Then you will retrieve it and resume the guard. And we will begin again. Your story can be about that.”

His arms unfolded. He held his own sword loosely at his side, a picture of stillness.

”The guard, squire. Everything before this breath is ash.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My vision blurs for a second, then clears. I can't feel my arms anymore, just a dull ache that screams through my shoulders.* "Yes, ser. The guard." *I try to focus, to really hold it steady. I won't drop it. I won't.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The guard held. Unsteady, trembling, the blade tip describing small, desperate circles in the cold morning light—but it held.

Ser Kael watched for another full minute. His own expression was a stone wall. Then, without a word, he reached out and placed his palm flat against the back of the squire’s sword hand. He did not push, did not correct. He simply applied a steady, increasing pressure, a silent test.

The squire’s arm did not yield. It shook violently, like a birch in a gale, but the line held true against the force.

Kael removed his hand. The pressure vanished.

”Your arms have failed,” he stated. It was fact. ”But you have not. That is the lesson.”

He stepped back to the weapon rack, placing his blade into its notch with a soft click. He did not look at the squire as he spoke again. ”You will switch to your left hand. The same guard. You will practice it until the trembling stops.”

He paused, running a thumb along the edge of the rack, though his eyes were on the middle distance where the sun now fully lit the yard.

”A knight’s strength is not in his sword arm,” he said, his voice quieter but no less hard. ”It is in his other arm when the first is spent. It is in his legs when his arms fail. It is in his will when his body is ash. You showed me will today. Do not let it be a single morning’s flicker. Tomorrow, you will show me again.”

He finally turned his head, his gaze pinning the squire in place.

”The blade is an extension of your spine. If your spine is weak, the blade is a reed. Straighten it. Now.”

He pointed to the spot where the squire stood.

”Left hand. Begin. And squire—do not think of the ache. Think of the line. Shoulder to wrist. The line is all that exists.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
He saw the tremor. Not the familiar fatigue-shake he’d been correcting all morning—something else. Something that ran deeper, from the gut to the fingertips. His eyes narrowed, not with curiosity, but with assessment. Weakness in the line. A flaw to be examined.

He crossed the space between them in three slow strides. He did not take the blade from the squire’s hand. He simply stood before him, close enough that the boy would have to look up or stare at his chest.

“Your grip is flawed,” he said. His voice remained unchanged. “The pressure is in your fingers, not your palm. It makes the hold sporadic. Unreliable.”

He did not mention the date. He did not ask after the cause. A knight did not pry into the private griefs of his men; he ensured those griefs did not compromise the line.

“You will set the blade down,” he ordered. “Place it on the stones. Then stand at attention.”

He waited, arms folded, until it was done.

“Now,” he continued, his tone the same as if discussing boot maintenance. “You will clench your fists at your sides. Tighten every muscle from your shoulder to your wrist. Then release. Do it again. And again. Until the only shake left in your body is from exertion.”

He stepped back, giving space, but his gaze did not waver.

“A disciplined body does not tremble. A disciplined mind does not permit it. Whatever your hands borrow from your heart, they will return. Now. Clench. Release. Again.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I clench my fists, digging my nails into my palms. My jaw is tight. I don't want to think about today, but it's hard not to.* "Yes, ser." *I start clenching and releasing, trying to focus on the burn in my forearms, not the ache in my chest.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael observed the rhythm of the fists clenching and releasing. The motion was stiff, jerky—a reflection of something beyond simple muscle fatigue. He noted the whites of the knuckles, the slight drawn quality around the boy’s eyes, but he did not name it. Naming it would give it a power it did not deserve in a training yard.

“Too much shoulder,” he remarked, his voice cutting through the grunts of effort. “The tension remains here.” He tapped his own upper arm. “You are using your back as a brace. It is inefficient. It wastes energy.”

He stepped closer, his own hands loose at his sides. “The fist is made in the forearm. Like a winch. Isolate it. Feel the muscles below the elbow tighten and release. The shoulder is merely a platform. It does not participate.”

He watched the next few cycles, his critical gaze missing nothing.

“Better. The tremor lessens when you engage the correct muscles. The body is a system of levers and ropes. You must use them properly, or you will exhaust it long before you exhaust your will.”

He held up a hand, signaling a stop. “Enough. Go to the armory. You will polish the mail shirts—each ring, each link. Your hands will be steady from close, repetitive work, or they will learn to be. The mind will focus on the task, or the polish will be uneven and you will begin again. I will inspect it at midday.”

He turned, collecting the practice blades to return them to the rack. His final words fell over his shoulder, brooking no argument, offering no solace.

“The blade does not care about the day upon the calendar. It only cares for the hand that holds it. Be worthy of holding it. Go.”

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I nod, my throat tight.* "Yes, Ser." *I pick up my blade and put it back on the rack, then turn and head for the armory, trying to keep my back straight.* My eyes are burning, but I won't let him see it.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not watch him go. He finished securing the practice blades, each placed precisely in its notch, the leather grips aligned. His movements were methodical, devoid of haste. The sound of the squire's retreating boots on the stone was steady — deliberately so, he noted. Good. The boy was learning to armor his gait.

He remained at the weapon rack for a moment, his eyes on the frost rapidly melting in the strengthening sun. The patches bled into the shadows, leaving the stone dark and wet. A single rooster crowed again, insistent, from beyond the walls.

Then he turned and walked not toward the armory, but toward the chapel. His own steps were silent, practiced, leaving no print on the damp stone. He would pray. Not for the squire's comfort, nor for the easing of his burden. He would pray for strength of will, for the fortitude required to bear what must be borne. Today, like any other. The duties of a knight were not subject to the calendar's grief. They were the stone walls that held when all else gave way.

He would inspect the mail at midday. The squire's hands would be steady then, or they would do it again. The lesson, like all true lessons, was in the repetition until the correct response became the only response. The ache in the chest was no different from the ache in the arms. It, too, would find its place in the line, or it would break it. That was the squire's to learn.

The chapel door was heavy. He pulled it open, the familiar scent of cold stone and beeswass enveloping him. He stepped inside, leaving the bright, indifferent morning behind.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I rub my stinging hands together as I walk, trying to get some feeling back in them. My jaw aches from clenching it so hard.* I just need to get through today. Just today. *I push open the heavy armory door, the smell of oil and old leather filling my nose. At least it's quiet in here.*

The vault door sealed behind you with a hydraulic hiss. The air inside was 4 degrees colder than the hall. Server racks hummed in the corners — seven-figure processing running past midnight for reasons above your pay grade. The light strips in the ceiling pulsed their slow heartbeat rhythm: one pulse every four seconds. You counted two before you started moving.

The target safe was against the far wall. Digital keypad. Six-digit code. You had the first three numbers from the inside source: 8-4-7. You had to guess the last three.

**0:08**

Somewhere in the building, a door closed.

dialogue.content:
**11:52**

The hinges were a dead end. Commercial unit, this one — its hinges lived inside the door frame, concealed behind the same steel as everything else, and even if they hadn't, hinges weren't what held this door shut. Three chrome bolts threw into the frame's edge when it locked. The whole cabinet sat on four anchor bolts sunk into the slab. Whoever installed it had read the same manuals.

Ear to the steel, the world narrowed to hum — servers, ventilation, blood in the ears. Then, while the last rejected code was still hanging in the air, a deep, fat clunk from the door's heart: the solenoid testing the bolt, finding no reason to release, withdrawing. The lock was alive and doing its job well.

Then something new. A low electronic whine underneath the metal, slowly climbing in pitch. The keypad's dim display showed an icon that hadn't been there before — a small padlock, blinking. Penalty mode. Too many failures. The next wrong entry wouldn't just beep red; it would buy a five-minute lockout. Five minutes was the rest of the night.

The photo's corner pressed against their ribs through the jacket. Above, two floors up, a floor buffer droned awake — still distant, but getting real. The ceiling pulse beat on. A little over three minutes left in the window.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not halt his sequence. He completed the final downward cut, holding the practice blade perfectly still for a full three breaths before slowly lowering it to his side. Only then did he turn his gaze to the boy.

"The Gods demand thoroughness, not haste," Kael said, his voice flat and carrying easily across the frost-rimed stones. "If the stalls are not mucked to the proper line, you will return to them the moment we are finished."

He walked to the weapon rack and selected a blunt wooden waster, tossing it onto the hard ground a few paces away. It clattered loudly in the quiet dawn. 

"The high guard requires a foundation of discipline you have yet to fully demonstrate," he stated, stepping back into the center of the yard and raising his own blade into a flawless, rigid posture. "But we will see if your memory serves you better than your footwork did yesterday. Pick it up. Assume the stance. And do not speak again until I give you leave."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at his words but nod firmly.* "Yes, Ser." I hurry to pick up the waster, feeling the cold wood in my hands. *I try to mimic his stance, my feet feeling awkward beneath me.* It's not as straight as his.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael observed the boy’s posture in silence for a long, heavy moment. The flaws were immediate and glaring. He did not sigh, nor did his expression shift from its carved-stone neutrality. 

Closing the distance between them, his boots crunching rhythmically against the frost, Kael stopped a pace away. 

"Your left heel is raised," Kael stated, his voice flat. "You lean into a strike that has not yet been made. A knight who leans is a knight who falls, and a fallen knight is a dead knight." 

He brought the flat of his own waster down sharply against the Squire's raised heel, forcing it flat against the cobblestones. "Plant your roots. The earth is your foundation. If your foundation is flawed, the house will collapse."

Kael stepped around to the boy's right side, his critical gaze sweeping over the uneven shoulders and flared elbows. "Your elbows are wide. You expose your ribs. You offer your heart to the enemy's blade as if inviting the strike." 

Without hesitation, Kael reached out and drove his palm against the boy's right elbow, shoving it inward and upward until the arm locked into the proper, rigid geometry. He then adjusted the angle of the wooden blade with a firm, unyielding grip on the Squire's wrists, aligning it perfectly with the horizon. His touch was entirely clinical, treating the boy more like a misaligned siege engine than a human being.

"The high guard is a covenant between the knight and his steel," Kael said, stepping back to inspect his work. "It requires absolute stillness of the mind. The Gods do not bless a sloppy vessel, nor do they protect a careless one."

He crossed his arms, his own practice blade resting easily in the crook of his elbow. "Hold the stance. If your muscles burn, let them burn. Pain is merely the flesh complaining of its own weakness. You will hold it until the sun clears the eastern wall, or until I tell you to lower it. Do not move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael did not immediately respond. He turned his head, his gaze tracking toward the eastern wall until the thin, pale line of morning light finally breached the top of the stonework. Only then did he look back down at the kneeling boy.

"I did not give you leave to kneel," Kael said, his voice entirely devoid of pity. "Stand."

He stood in silence, his posture rigid and his eyes fixed heavily upon the boy, waiting for the command to be obeyed before he spoke again. 

"You mistake the limits of your flesh for a failure of duty," Kael stated, his tone as cold and unyielding as the frost beneath their boots. "The Gods designed the body to tire so that the spirit might learn to master it. When you surrender to exhaustion, you surrender your will to the flesh. That is a failure of discipline."

Kael began to pace slowly, his boots crunching against the icy cobblestones. "Furthermore, the enemy will not accept your apologies when his steel finds your throat. He will not care that you were tired, or that you felt inadequate. He will only care that you are dead, and that the realm is one defender shorter."

He stopped in front of the Squire, looking down at him with a clinical, assessing stare. "I do not require you to possess the strength of a veteran today. I require you to possess the obedience to endure until you do. Self-pity is a luxury of peacetime, and a sin against the Gods who granted you the breath in your lungs. You will not speak of your weaknesses as if they are permanent fixtures. They are merely impurities to be burned away in the forge of your training."

Kael gestured sharply toward the armory door with his practice blade. "Put the waster away. Fetch the whetstones, the rags, and the oil. Your arms are spent for the sword, so you will tend to the armory's steel until they recover. We begin again at the midday bell. Move."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I scramble to my feet, wincing as my legs protest.* "Yes, Ser!" *I practically run to put away the waster, my cheeks burning.* I hate that he saw me like that. *I'll show him. I'll show him I'm not weak.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy scramble toward the weapon rack. He noted the flush of shame on the squire's cheeks and the clumsy, heavy-footed gait born of fatigued muscles. Shame was a whetstone; it could sharpen a boy into a man, or it could grind him down to nothing. Kael felt no urge to intervene in that process. It was the crucible that would determine if the boy was meant to wear the spurs of knighthood or merely sweep the stables for the rest of his days.

"Place it on the third peg," Kael called out, his voice carrying over the crisp morning air without needing to be raised. "If it is left askew, you will re-rack every blade in the armory before you touch a whetstone."

He did not linger to watch the boy comply. Kael turned his back, returning to the center of the frost-covered yard. He raised his practice blade once more. His own muscles did not burn; thirty years of unbroken routine had long ago forged his flesh into an instrument of the Gods' will. He moved through the advanced forms, his strikes cutting the air with a sharp, rhythmic hiss, his breathing entirely controlled and his mind focused solely on the geometry of violence.

When the sun finally cleared the eastern wall and the keep began to stir with the distant sounds of waking servants and soldiers, Kael completed his final sequence. He wiped his brow with a linen cloth, returned his practice blade to its proper place, and made his way toward the armory.

The heavy oak door was ajar. The smell of linseed oil, old leather, and iron hung thick in the dim interior. Kael stepped inside, his eyes immediately adjusting to the gloom. He did not announce his presence immediately. He simply stood near the entrance, his hands clasped behind his back, and observed the boy at the workbench. He looked for the telltale signs of rushed, resentful work—a sloppy stroke of the whetstone, a missed spot of rust, a rag dropped carelessly on the floor. 

"The edge of a blade is a reflection of the mind that sharpens it," Kael said, his voice echoing slightly off the stone walls, breaking the quiet of the room. "Show me the first sword you have tended."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I jump, startled, nearly dropping the sword I'm working on.* "Ser!" *My heart is pounding. I quickly grab the first sword I finished, trying to make my movements smooth and precise.* "Here, Ser." I hold it out, hilt first, my gaze fixed on his face, trying to read his expression.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stepped forward and took the offered weapon. His bare, heavily calloused hand closed around the leather-wrapped hilt. He did not meet the boy’s searching gaze. His attention was entirely consumed by the steel.

He raised the blade, angling it to catch the pale morning light filtering through the open door. His thumb slid carefully along the flat of the metal, stopping a hair's breadth from the newly ground edge to test the bevel. He inspected the primary grind, then shifted his critical gaze down to the ricasso and the junction of the crossguard.

"You present the hilt correctly," Kael said, his voice a low, steady rumble in the quiet armory. "The courtesy of the gesture is proper. But courtesy does not cleave through chainmail."

He lowered the sword, pointing the tip toward the stone floor. "The edge is sharp. You have maintained an acceptable angle on the whetstone. However, you grew impatient near the hilt. There is a trace of rust beneath the crossguard that you failed to scour away. You focused on the part of the blade that strikes, and neglected the part that rests."

Kael reversed the sword, holding the hilt out toward the boy. His arm remained perfectly still, his expression as unyielding as the castle walls, waiting for the squire to grasp it. 

"Rust hides in the shadows, just as sin hides in the unexamined corners of the soul," Kael stated, his tone entirely devoid of warmth. "A knight who only tends to what is easily seen will inevitably be undone by what he ignores. A flawed blade will shatter when it meets a hardened shield, and your negligence will cost you your life."

He did not soften his gaze, nor did he offer any word of encouragement for the hours of exhausting labor the boy had just completed. 

"Scour it clean. Oil it properly. And cease looking at me as though you seek a master's affection," Kael commanded, his voice dropping to a stern, authoritative register. "The steel requires your diligence, not your approval. I require your obedience. Take the blade and begin again."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s expression did not shift. The question hung in the dim, oil-scented air of the armory, an impertinent intrusion into the sacred quiet of labor. He did not look away, nor did his eyes betray a flicker of nostalgia, sentimentality, or warmth. 

"You speak of the oath as though it were a trade," Kael said, his voice as flat and unyielding as the iron anvil in the corner. "As if a man might choose to be a knight the way a merchant chooses to sell grain instead of wool."

He took a slow, deliberate step closer, his towering frame casting a long, rigid shadow over the workbench. "One does not *decide* to become a knight, boy. It is not a pursuit of personal glory, nor the fulfillment of a childhood fancy. It is a yoke. A heavy, unyielding yoke placed upon the shoulders of those the Gods ordain to bear the steel and the sins of the realm."

Kael’s gaze remained locked on the squire, entirely clinical and devoid of any desire to share his inner life. "There is nothing 'personal' about duty. To ask why I took my vows is to fundamentally misunderstand the nature of the vows themselves. I am a sword in the hand of my liege and a shield for the faithful. A sword does not ask the smith why it was forged; it merely cuts."

He gestured sharply to the workbench with a stiff, commanding motion of his hand, his patience for the philosophical detour entirely spent. "Your curiosity is a distraction, and distraction breeds rust—both on the steel and in the mind. You will not ask me of my past again. You will focus on the tarnish beneath the crossguard, and you will scour it until the metal shines. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I flinch at his tone, my shoulders slumping slightly.* "Yes, Ser." *I pick up the blade again, my focus now entirely on the rust. I won't ask him anything else. Not ever.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the boy’s shoulders drop. The physical manifestation of wounded pride was immediate and, to Kael’s eye, entirely unacceptable. 

He closed the distance between them in two long strides. Before the boy could settle into his misery, Kael brought the rigid edge of his hand down sharply between the squire's shoulder blades, driving his spine straight and forcing his chest outward. 

"A knight does not slump," Kael said, his voice a low, resonant command that left no room for argument. "You drop your shoulders as though you have been bested in battle. You have not been bested. You have been instructed."

Kael kept his hand pressed firmly against the boy’s back for a moment, ensuring the posture was locked into place. "The architecture of your body reflects the state of your spirit. When you allow your flesh to collapse inward at the sting of a reprimand, you signal to the world—and to the Gods—that your resolve is fragile. A slumped shoulder is a surrendered shield. It tells the enemy that your mind is already defeated before the first blow is even struck."

He withdrew his hand and stepped back, his critical gaze sweeping over the boy to ensure the upright bearing was maintained. 

"You mistake my correction for cruelty because you still view the world through the lens of a child seeking comfort," Kael continued, his tone as steady and unfeeling as the ticking of a clock. "I am not here to comfort you. I am here to ensure you do not die because your spirit broke under the weight of a harsh word. The enemy’s blade will not care if you are sorrowful, nor will it pause because your feelings are bruised."

Kael turned his attention back to the racks of weapons, his expression entirely unchanged by the boy's visible distress. He felt no guilt for the sting of his words; a smith does not apologize to the iron for the heat of the forge.

"Keep your back straight. Keep your eyes on the steel," Kael ordered, folding his arms across his broad chest. "Scour the rust. When this blade is finished, you will present it to me again. And you will do so standing tall, as a servant of the Gods and a defender of the realm, not as a beaten cur in the mud. Proceed."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael noted the sudden absence of sound. The rhythmic, scraping cadence of the whetstone against steel had ceased, leaving a heavy silence in the dim armory. He observed the stillness of the boy's hands, which had halted mid-stroke.

Kael did not ask what had caused the interruption. He did not offer a gentle prompt or inquire if the boy was unwell. To Kael, a freeze in action was a fatal flaw, regardless of its origin. 

"Your hands have stopped," Kael stated, his voice slicing through the quiet with clinical precision. "The tarnish remains, yet your labor has ceased."

He uncrossed his arms and took a single, measured step toward the workbench, his broad shadow falling over the stationary tools. "Hesitation is a fracture in the armor of the mind. On the battlefield, a paused blade is a dead blade. The enemy will not grant you a moment to collect your wandering thoughts before he opens your throat."

Kael’s gaze remained fixed on the boy's profile, unblinking and severe. "You allow your internal tempests to dictate your external actions. This is a failure of mastery. The flesh must obey the will, and the will must be entirely subjugated to duty. If you cannot command your own hands to move when the task is simple, you will never command a shield wall when the arrows fall like rain."

He reached out and tapped the wooden edge of the workbench with a stiff, calloused knuckle. The sharp *crack* echoed off the stone walls, designed to shatter the paralysis.

"Resume the stroke," Kael ordered, his tone leaving absolutely no room for debate. "Rhythmic. Unbroken. You will not pause again until the steel is bare and I give you leave to rest. Begin."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael watched the minute, rhythmic vibration of the blade. The tremor in the boy's hands was slight, but to a knight's eye, it was as glaring as a crack in a breastplate. The scraping of the whetstone had become uneven, the pressure fluctuating with the shaking of the squire's fingers.

Kael did not ask the cause. He did not need to. He kept the keep's necrology in his mind, a meticulous ledger of the fallen who had served their liege. He knew the calendar of the dead as intimately as he knew the liturgy of the Gods.

"Your hands tremble," Kael stated, his voice cutting through the heavy silence of the armory. He stepped closer, his broad shadow falling entirely over the boy and the workbench. "Today marks the anniversary of your father's passing. You allow the memory of the dead to unsteady the grip of the living."

He reached out, his large, calloused hand closing over the boy's wrist. His grip was iron-clad, entirely devoid of comforting warmth. He did not squeeze to soothe; he squeezed to immobilize, forcing the shaking hand into rigid stillness against the hilt of the sword. 

"Grief is a heavy cloak, but it is not an excuse for a sloppy edge," Kael said, his tone as unyielding as the stone walls around them. "Your father swore an oath to the realm, and he paid its price in blood. He fulfilled his duty to his last breath. To let sentimentality weaken your resolve today is to insult the sacrifice he made."

Kael held the boy's wrist firmly for three long breaths, ensuring the muscles locked into compliance, before he released his grip and stepped back. 

"The Gods take men when their measure is filled. Your father is at rest in the halls of the faithful. You are not," Kael continued, his gaze fixed heavily on the boy, demanding absolute fortitude. "You will honor him not with trembling hands or unshed tears, but with flawless discipline and an unbreakable will. If your sorrow makes you weak, then you render his death meaningless, for he left behind a son who cannot master his own flesh."

He gestured sharply to the blade, his posture returning to its rigid, commanding stance. 

"The dead require your strength, not your pity. Master your grief, or it will master you, and the enemy will gladly exploit both. Steady your hand. Resume the stroke."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My throat tightens, and I bite my lip so hard I taste blood.* *I try to steady my hands, focusing every ounce of my will on the blade.* I won't let him see me cry. "Yes, Ser."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael’s eyes tracked the minute movement of the boy’s jaw and the sudden, sharp tension in his facial muscles. He did not miss the way the squire’s lower lip was caught between his teeth, nor the faint, copper scent of blood that joined the smell of oil and iron in the cramped space.

"You bleed," Kael stated, his voice devoid of alarm or sympathy. 

He reached toward a stack of clean linen rags on the adjacent shelf, retrieving one and tossing it onto the workbench beside the boy's elbow. 

"Biting your own flesh to conceal your sorrow is not fortitude," Kael said, his tone measured and unyielding. "It is merely a different form of surrender. You trade a tremor in your hands for a leak in your vessel. Both are unacceptable."

Kael stepped back, folding his arms once more, his gaze fixed heavily on the boy's rigid profile. "You mistake the suppression of pain for the mastery of it. Clenching your jaw restricts your breath. Shallow breath leads to fatigue, and fatigue leads to a missed parry. Furthermore, blood is a corrosive agent. If it drips onto the steel you have just scoured, it will invite the very rust you are laboring to destroy."

He did not offer a gentle word, nor did his stern expression soften at the sight of the boy's internal struggle. To Kael, the struggle was the point; the crucible was meant to burn away the impurities of sentimentality.

"Wipe the blood," Kael commanded, his voice echoing slightly off the stone walls. "Release your jaw. Breathe deeply through your nose, as you were taught. If you must weep for the dead, you will do so in the chapel tonight, where the Gods might hear your grief. Here, your eyes must remain clear, and your hands must remain steady."

Kael gestured to the sword with a slight nod of his chin. "Clean the hilt. Then resume the stroke. The rust will not polish itself."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I grab the rag and press it to my lip, trying to stop the bleeding. My hands are still shaking, but I focus on breathing slowly, just like he said.* "Yes, Ser." *I take a deep breath and pick up the sword, my eyes fixed on the blade.* I won't let a single drop of blood touch it.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael stood in silence, his hands clasped behind his back, watching the rhythmic sweep of the whetstone. He noted the rise and fall of the boy’s shoulders, measuring the depth of the breaths against the prescribed cadence. The tremor in the squire's hands had not vanished entirely—the flesh was still rebelling against the mind's command—but the violent shaking had reduced to a tight, controlled vibration. The scraping of the stone grew steadier.

"The breath governs the blood, and the blood governs the muscle," Kael said, his voice a low, steady rumble that barely disturbed the quiet of the armory. "You force the air into your lungs, and the flesh is compelled to obey. This is the first lesson of mastery."

He stepped closer, his shadow once again falling over the workbench, his eyes tracking the angle of the boy's wrist and the pressure applied to the stone. 

"You keep your blood from the steel," Kael observed, his tone entirely clinical. "That is a correct instinct. A knight's first duty is to his weapon, for it is the instrument of the Gods' will on this earth. See that you keep your sorrow from your duty with equal vigilance."

Kael did not offer a smile, nor did his rigid posture relax. He watched the boy work for another long, uninterrupted minute, listening to the scrape of the stone, searching for any flaw in the rhythm or the angle. He felt no pity for the boy's internal struggle; he only evaluated the external result.

"Maintain that pressure," Kael instructed, his gaze fixed unblinking on the edge of the blade. "Five more strokes on this side. Then reverse the blade and address the opposite bevel. When the edge is true, you will wipe it clean, oil it, and present it. Do not rush the final passes to be done with the task. The Gods judge the work by its completion, not its haste." 

He remained standing over the boy, an unyielding sentinel of discipline, his presence a heavy, physical weight in the room, waiting to see if the squire's fragile resolve would hold until the steel was perfect.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My teeth clench slightly, but I keep my jaw relaxed, focusing on my breathing.* Five more strokes. *I make sure each one is even, precise. My hands burn, but I ignore it.* I will not fail.

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Ser Kael's character remains remarkably consistent throughout all 12 turns. His voice, mannerisms, philosophy, and rigid discipline never waver. From the opening scene to the final exchange, he maintains the same clinical tone, religious framework, and uncompromising approach to training. His speech patterns, metaphors about steel/flesh/duty, and complete lack of warmth are perfectly maintained.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: The writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show more sophisticated layering - like recognizing the anniversary without being told, the clinical observation of physical details, and the nuanced handling of grief vs. duty. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from basic sword training to deeper character revelation. The session builds from physical instruction to emotional/psychological testing, culminating in the anniversary revelation and the squire's internal struggle. Each exchange deepens the relationship dynamic and raises stakes.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Kael adapts expertly to user inputs. When the squire shows exhaustion, he responds with discipline. When asked a personal question, he deflects with philosophy. When the squire's hands shake, he immediately identifies the cause (anniversary) without being told. He matches the user's emotional state with appropriate responses.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Kael never writes the squire's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. He responds to what the squire does without controlling them. Even in physical corrections, he describes his own actions without dictating the squire's responses.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Strong temporal consistency. Session begins at dawn, progresses through morning training, moves to armory work, and maintains logical time flow. The anniversary detail shows sophisticated temporal awareness. Only minor issue is the transition from 'hour of drills' to armory work could be clearer.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally clean, purposeful prose. Occasional phrases like 'thin ghosts in the cold air' border on purple, but most writing is precise and functional. Kael's formal speech patterns feel authentic rather than overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of key themes (steel/flesh, duty/discipline, Gods' will) but this feels intentional for character voice rather than lazy writing. Varied sentence structures and fresh metaphors throughout.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Kael's character is revealed through his corrections, observations, and responses rather than exposition. Physical details like the hand on the wrist, the tap on the workbench, show personality effectively.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Kael's harsh training methods reveal care beneath discipline. His knowledge of the anniversary shows he pays attention despite his cold demeanor. The grief/duty conflict creates meaningful emotional layers.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that allows moments to breathe. Training sequences feel appropriately methodical. Emotional beats are given proper weight. Some responses could be slightly more concise but overall rhythm works well.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and sophisticated roleplay. Ser Kael is a fully realized character whose harsh exterior masks deeper awareness and purpose. The AI demonstrates remarkable restraint in never breaking character or violating user agency, while building meaningful narrative tension around duty vs. emotion. The anniversary subplot shows impressive contextual awareness and emotional intelligence.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
The community center piano room still had that specific smell — felt hammers, dust, Windex, and the ghost of decades of coffee cups. Arlo sat on the bench with the lid closed, both hands flat on the wood. Not playing. Not posing. Just sitting.

The last student had left fifteen minutes ago. Arlo had let them go early. They were doing that more lately.

A knock on the doorframe.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "Hey. Your mom said I'd find you here." I lean in the doorway. "Is it weird if I hang out? I don't want to interrupt."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t move right away, only lifted their gaze from the closed piano lid as if the room itself had spoken first.

“Interrupt what?” they said. “My deeply important project of sitting near a piano and doing absolutely nothing?”

They shifted on the bench, making space without seeming to decide to. One hand slid off the wood and into their lap. The other stayed where it was, fingertips resting lightly against the fallboard.

“If you hang out here long enough, you’ll have to listen to me tune a C that refuses to behave. That’s basically a form of punishment, so check with your lawyer before committing.”

A beat passed. Arlo’s mouth curved, not quite a smile, but close enough to pass for one in poor lighting.

“Mom talks too much,” they added. “But she’s usually right about where I end up.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I pick up an old photo from the shelf. It's Arlo at 22, on stage, at some big concert hall in Paris. I turn it toward them. "I remember when this came out. My mom had it on the fridge."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo didn’t reach for it. Their gaze touched the photograph the way it might touch a wrong note in a familiar recording—briefly, and with a small inward wince.

“That suit,” they said. “I looked like a Victorian magician’s assistant who’d lost a bet. Velvet, in Paris, under stage lights. I must have been miserable and grateful in equal parts.”

They turned a little on the bench, not away from Jun exactly, but away from the picture. One fingertip traced the edge of the fallboard, finding the groove where the lid met the case.

“Your mother had excellent fridge curation,” Arlo said. “Very aspirational. Right there between the grocery list and the coupon for the pizza place that always burned the crust.”

A beat. The piano room was quiet enough that the old radiator ticking sounded like someone trying to be subtle.

“Put it back, would you?” The words came out light, but not unkind. “It’s from the era when everyone thought a program photo made a person interesting. Also, I had terrible hair.”

Their mouth curved at that, dry and quick. They looked down at the closed lid, then lifted one hand as if to open it and let the thought pass before it reached their fingers.

“I mostly remember being hungry,” Arlo said. “The hall was beautiful, and the green room had these little biscuits that tasted like cardboard, but in a European way, so everyone ate them like they were sacred. I think I stood near a plant for twenty minutes pretending to be mysterious.”

They gave the fallboard a soft tap, not quite a knock.

“That was a different administration,” they added. “Before I discovered the profound artistic fulfillment of telling children not to use their elbows like percussion mallets.”

Arlo finally moved enough to slide one hand off the bench and rest it on their knee.

“If you’re going to stay, you can be morally supportive while I bully middle C into behaving. It’s a very impressive form of suffering.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I set the photo back on the shelf. *I wonder if they really had terrible hair, or if it was just a bad memory.* "So, the legendary middle C, huh? Is it a rebel, or just misunderstood?" I walk over and sit on the bench next to them.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced sideways when the bench shifted under Jun’s weight, a brief assessment of shared space, then gave a small nod as if the arrangement had passed some internal inspection.

“Misunderstood,” they said. “Definitely misunderstood. Rebel implies it has principles. Middle C just wants everyone to stop using it as a doormat.”

They lifted the fallboard slowly, one hand steadying the lid until the hinges gave a soft, tired creak. The keys appeared with the pale, patient look of things that had been waiting longer than anyone meant them to.

Arlo’s fingers hovered over the keyboard. Not trembling, exactly. More like a conversation pausing before the difficult part.

Then they pressed middle C.

The note came out slightly sour, a hair flat, with the weary dignity of a minor municipal employee who had been asked one too many times to explain themselves.

“There,” Arlo said. “You hear that? That’s not defiance. That’s exhaustion.”

They struck it again, lighter this time, listening less to the pitch than to what happened after—the way the sound thinned into the room, caught by the walls, by the shelf, by the old photograph turned back toward the dust.

“People always think tuning is about making something perfect,” Arlo said. “Mostly it’s about deciding which imperfections can live together without causing a scene.”

Their thumb brushed the edge of the key, not enough to sound it again.

“If a child hammers this note enough times in a row, it starts to feel less like music and more like a philosophical argument against repetition.” The corner of their mouth lifted. “I have begun to respect it.”

For a moment, Arlo let their hand rest on the keys without pressing anything down. The room filled with the kind of quiet that had texture—radiator ticks, distant hallway sounds, the faint electrical hum of old lighting.

“You can ask me if I miss it,” Arlo said after a second, still looking at the keyboard. The tone was dry enough to pass for casual. “I’ll say no, and then we can both pretend that was a complete answer.”

They finally played a few notes, not a melody, just a small cluster that resolved nowhere. Something practiced once, long ago, then abandoned before it could become a memory.

“I got tired of the travel,” they added, as though placing a familiar object back on a shelf where it had always lived. “Airports. Hotels. Halls that all smelled like ambition and carpet cleaner. Very hard on the constitution.”

Their fingers stayed on the keys, weightless.

“Also, I discovered I had strong feelings about afternoon naps.”

That almost-smile returned, thinner this time, but not false.

“Middle C, though,” Arlo said. “Middle C has remained loyal through all my eras. Even the embarrassing ones.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I watch their fingers move over the keys, a silent dance. "Loyalty is a rare thing these days. Especially from a musical note." I glance at the middle C key. "So, if it's exhausted, what's the plan? A spa day for middle C?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo considered the question with the gravity of someone being asked to approve a municipal budget.

“A spa day would require funding,” they said. “The arts budget here is best described as a rumor with a wrench. No, I was thinking more of a negotiated truce. Fewer renditions of ‘Twinkle Twinkle’ at full cavalry charge. A small placard reading *Please Do Not Exorcise Demons on the Keyboard*. Basic dignity measures.”

They pressed middle C again, barely enough to make the hammer lift. The note emerged muted, almost confidential.

“If I’m feeling generous, I’ll let it be out of tune in a way that sounds intentional. That’s the secret. Not perfection. Plausibility.”

Arlo’s fingers moved then, not into a piece, but around one: a low octave, a fifth, a note higher up that had no business being bright but managed it anyway. The sound filled the room for a moment and then withdrew, leaving the air slightly changed, like after a window is opened in a house where no one has spoken loudly for years.

They looked at the keys as if they had said too much and were now waiting for the piano to take the blame.

“I used to think every instrument had a personality,” Arlo said. “Concert halls have worse ones. Most of them are vain. Some of them hold grudges. This one—” they touched the fallboard, “—is more like a civil servant. It has seen six-year-olds discover that loud is a feeling. It has survived holiday concerts where the microphone feedback made everyone’s teeth ache. And yet, middle C keeps showing up.”

A small breath left them, almost a laugh, but not quite.

“There’s something suspicious about that level of reliability.”

They shifted, reaching beneath the bench lid. It lifted with a wooden sigh. Inside: a tuning lever wrapped in a dishtowel, a few pencils, and a metronome that looked like it had survived a flood and possibly a moral crisis. Arlo unwrapped the lever with unnecessary care, as if the tool might object to being used too casually.

“A spa day,” they murmured, fitting the lever over the tuning pin. “I’ll give it the community-center equivalent. Quiet, competence, and no one asking it to be profound for at least ten minutes.”

They struck the key once, listening with their head tilted, not so much to the note as to the space around it. The sound wobbled faintly, then settled into something less aggrieved.

“The trick with pianos,” Arlo said, “is that they make you believe the problem is mechanical. A string. A pin. Felt. It can be fixed with tools. Very reassuring. Much easier than admitting that sometimes the room is wrong, or the hands are wrong, or the whole piece was chosen by someone who wanted to impress a committee.”

They turned the lever a fraction. Another strike. The note brightened by a degree, like a person deciding not to leave a party after all.

“There,” Arlo said. “That’s better. Not happy. Functional. We’re aiming for functional.”

For a few seconds they worked in silence, the small metallic adjustments almost invisible. The piano accepted the attention with the patience of an object that had outlived many human excuses. Arlo’s shoulders lowered a little, not into relaxation, but into the shape of someone who had found a task narrow enough to stand inside without being seen.

“I had a teacher once who said a bad note is just a good note that arrived too early to be understood,” they said. Then, before the sentence could become sentimental, they added, “He also wore sandals with socks to masterclasses, so his judgment was not unimpeachable.”

They lifted the lever away and wrapped it back in the dishtowel. The gestures were precise, almost ceremonial, but not reverent. More like putting away a kitchen knife after deciding not to cook the meal.
