“Middle C will survive,” Arlo said. “It always does. It’s the note everyone learns first, which means it has developed an excellent tolerance for being approached by people who have no idea what they’re doing.”

They closed the bench lid. The click was soft, final enough to close the subject without slamming it.

Then, after a moment, they let one hand rest on the keys again. Not playing. Just present. The kind of stillness that could be mistaken for casual if one didn’t know how much effort casual sometimes required.

“If it wants a spa day,” Arlo said, “it can start by not being assigned to ‘Ode to Joy’ by a child who believes tempo is a suggestion. I’ll call that self-care.”

Their gaze flicked to the old photograph on the shelf, then away again, quick and practiced.

“Besides,” they added, “I’ve found that most things recover better when you stop asking them to be impressive.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "The kids seem to like you." I gesture at the practice sheets on the bench.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the practice sheets as if they had been summoned to testify and were not entirely reliable witnesses.

“Don’t let that fool you,” they said. “Children are mostly motivated by snack breaks and the chance to correct an adult.”

They picked up the nearest sheet. It had a row of treble clefs drawn along the top, each one more determined than the last, like a parade of startled snails. In the corner, someone had added a yellow sun wearing sunglasses. Arlo’s thumb brushed the edge of the paper, smoothing a crease that did not need smoothing.

“This one,” they said, “was produced under duress. I asked for five lines of rhythm notation and got a weather report instead. Apparently the sun is ‘very cool’ and the piano is ‘too loud today.’ I respect the directness.”

They set the sheet down again, aligning it with the edge of the bench. The movement was careful, almost absentminded, the way someone might straighten things when their hands wanted to do something less explainable.

“They like that I don’t make them perform happiness,” Arlo said after a moment. “If they come in here having had a terrible afternoon, I don’t ask them to pretend their fingers are full of sunshine. We play something small. Sometimes we just name notes like we’re identifying suspicious vegetables at the market. C. F. A. Fine. Fine. Also fine.”

One corner of their mouth lifted.

“It lowers the stakes. Nobody has to be a genius. Nobody has to be carried offstage by their own ambition.”

The word stage seemed to land between them without much weight, but Arlo’s gaze moved away from the piano keys anyway, toward the scuffed floor, the doorframe, the shelf where the photograph had been returned to its quiet facing-the-wall existence.

“They like that I know which keys stick,” Arlo added. “And that I don’t yell when someone plays a chord with their entire forearm. I call it ‘advanced percussive enthusiasm.’ They appreciate having a diagnosis.”

They gathered two more sheets and tapped them into a neat stack against their knee. The gesture gave their hands something harmless to do.

“Some of them are frightened of it,” they said. “Not the piano. The idea of getting it wrong. You can see it happen—the breath goes shallow, the shoulders go up, and suddenly the simplest melody becomes a legal proceeding. So I teach them how to recover. Wrong note? Fine. Find the next one. Both hands fall off the cliff? Fine. We rebuild from the left hand and pretend it was an artistic choice.”

Arlo’s voice stayed light, but there was a thread in it that had been worn soft by repetition.

“Most of them don’t need to be brilliant,” they said. “They need to learn that the instrument isn’t going to punish them.”

They paused, as if that sentence had wandered a little farther than intended. Then they exhaled through their nose and gave the stack of papers a final tap.

“Also, I keep a jar of raisins in the drawer. The good kind. Not the ones that taste like they were harvested during a drought. Word gets around.”

Arlo looked at the closed fallboard, where the dark wood reflected a thin stripe of room light. They did not open it again.

“Liking me is easy at this age,” they said. “I am the adult who admits the bench is uncomfortable and that ‘Für Elise’ is basically a haunted ringtone. That makes me practically revolutionary.”

They slid the practice sheets back onto the bench, but one corner remained lifted, stubbornly hopeful, like a hand raised in class. Arlo looked at it for a second before pressing it down with two fingers.

“If they keep coming back,” they said, quieter, “that’s enough.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I smile.* "Raisins. So that's your secret weapon. I should have known." I pick up one of the sheets they had been holding. It's got a drawing of a lopsided cat playing a tiny piano. "This one's pretty good, actually. I like the cat."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo glanced at the drawing, their expression doing the small thing it did when something was too sincere to be met head-on.

“That cat,” they said, “is the work of a child who spent ten minutes convincing me that animals should be allowed to take exams because they ‘don’t get nervous.’ I asked what would happen if the cat forgot the notes. She said the cat would improvise. I couldn’t argue with that.”

They reached for the drawer beside the bench and pulled it open a few inches. Inside sat the raisin jar, a packet of tissues, a broken pencil, and a small plastic dinosaur with one eye missing. Arlo regarded the jar as if it were evidence.

“Raisins,” they said, “are not a secret weapon. They are a treaty. The children receive sugar-adjacent morale, I receive a brief interval in which no one asks whether their fingers are ‘too short,’ and the piano is spared another full-body assault. Everyone benefits. Very civilized.”

They closed the drawer gently. Their gaze returned to the lopsided cat and its tiny purple piano.

“The instrument is wrong, of course,” Arlo said. “Three keys, no proper fallboard, and the bench looks like a slice of toast. But the cat seems committed. That’s the important part. It isn’t worrying about whether the hall is good or whether the lighting is flattering. It’s just—” they made a small, vague gesture, “—playing at the thing.”

For a second the room held its breath around the sentence. Arlo’s hand rested near the keys but not on them.

“I keep those,” they said, nodding at the practice sheets, “because they’re honest. No one draws a cat at a piano to impress a committee. They do it because the idea made them happy. Sometimes that’s the only reason anyone should go near an instrument.”

The almost-smile came back, quieter this time.

“If a child asks me why I don’t perform anymore,” Arlo said, “I tell them I’m busy teaching middle C how to forgive people.” They tapped the closed lid once, very lightly. “It’s a long-term project. The cat would understand.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: "I think the cat would understand a lot of things," I say, a small smile playing on my lips. "It's a good approach. Forgiving people, I mean." I look from the drawing to Arlo. "Do you think middle C is getting there?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo did not answer immediately. Their attention moved from the lopsided cat to the closed fallboard, then to the faint reflection of the room in the dark polish—half-present, half-erased.

“Middle C,” they said at last, “has the advantage of being simple to diagnose. If it’s wrong, someone can put a tool on it and say, this is the trouble. Tighten here. Ease off there. No one has to ask it what it was thinking when it decided to become difficult.”

They set the drawing back on the bench, aligning its crooked edge with the stack of practice sheets.

“It’s getting somewhere,” Arlo said. “Not to sainthood. It still sulks in humid weather. But it’s stopped behaving as if every touch is an accusation. That’s progress. In this room, progress usually means nobody cries before snack time.”

One hand lifted as if to rest on the lid, then thought better of it and settled on their knee instead.

“Forgiveness is a large word for a piece of felt and wire,” they continued. “What middle C is learning is closer to repeatability. You can strike it again and it doesn’t insist on making a scene about the last time. That’s useful. People could take lessons.” The corner of their mouth moved, not quite a smile. “Not that I recommend people become middle C. The repertoire is limited.”

They glanced toward the door, not as if wanting to leave, but as if checking whether the room had overheard too much.

“If you mean is it getting to the point where it can be used without everyone apologizing to it first,” Arlo said, “then yes. Almost. It has accepted that children will approach it with the emotional urgency of someone trying to open a pickle jar. It has accepted that I will ask it to demonstrate things it already knows. It has not yet accepted ‘Hot Cross Buns,’ but I’m working on diplomacy.”

They tapped the closed lid once, very softly. Not a knock. More like a question asked through a door.

“The trouble with forgiveness,” Arlo said, and stopped, as though the sentence had come out wearing the wrong coat. They smoothed it quickly. “The trouble with forgiveness is that it sounds like a finale. Something you say after the last chord so everyone can put on their coats and go home feeling they have witnessed growth. Most of the time it’s more like tuning. You keep checking. You keep making tiny adjustments. You pretend the wobble is character.”

Their fingers curled lightly against their knee.

“Middle C is good at that. It doesn’t ask for an apology. It just asks to be needed in a way that doesn’t break it.” A beat passed. “Reasonable request. Possibly more than reasonable.”

The radiator gave two metallic ticks, as if filing a complaint about the silence.

Arlo picked up the old metronome from the bench, turned it once in their hands, and set it down again without winding it.

“So,” they said, returning to a lighter tone like a key tried in a familiar lock, “yes. Middle C is getting there. It may even deserve a small spa day. A dusting. A polite note from the administration. A child who plays it once, beautifully, by accident, and then asks if they can go to the bathroom.”

They looked at the closed piano for a moment longer.

“That would be enough,” Arlo said. “For a note, anyway.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: I don't ask anything. I just sit on the bench next to Arlo and we stay there for a while.

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo let the silence remain.

At first it seemed to make them wary, the way a door left ajar might make someone wary—not because anything had come through it, but because it suggested the possibility. Their hands stayed in their lap. The piano sat closed in front of them, dark and patient, reflecting the room in a warped strip: bench, shelf, the crooked cat drawing, the two of them seated side by side without speaking.

For a while, Arlo only listened.

The building had its own small vocabulary after hours. Pipes ticking somewhere behind the wall. The faint buzz of one fluorescent tube in the hallway. A chair dragging in another room, probably someone stacking up for the night. None of it felt intrusive. It felt like the place talking to itself while pretending not to notice them.

Arlo’s mouth moved before they spoke, as if testing a word they had no intention of using.

“You’re very good at that,” they said at last.

Their voice was quieter than before. Not guarded exactly, but careful, like someone stepping onto ice to see whether it would hold.

“The not-asking,” Arlo added. “Most people hear a locked door and immediately start trying the windows. You just… stand in the hallway. It’s unsettling. I respect it.”

They did not look over. Their gaze stayed on the closed fallboard.

One finger tapped once against their knee. Then again. Not rhythm, precisely. More like a pulse looking for somewhere to go.

The cat drawing sat on the bench between the practice sheets, its purple piano cheerfully inaccurate. Arlo looked at it for a second longer than necessary.

“I tell the children that music is not a race,” they said. “Which is very noble of me, considering I have no interest in timing anything anymore. We go slowly. We stop when someone gets frustrated. We breathe. We drink water. We discuss whether a piece should be played ‘angry’ or ‘like a robot with a secret.’”

The corner of their mouth lifted, but only just.

“Very efficient,” Arlo said. “No one faints. No one storms out. No one has to be carried away by the unbearable weight of their own expectations.”

They paused.

The word carried seemed to hang in the air a moment too long. Arlo noticed. They shifted slightly on the bench, enough to make the wood give a low creak.

“I used to think stopping was the worst thing that could happen,” they said. “In a piece, I mean. If you stopped, it meant something had gone wrong. Silence was supposed to come at the end, where everyone agreed it belonged. Anywhere else, it was a failure. A hole.”

Their hand lifted toward the piano, then stopped halfway, suspended above the closed lid as if the wood might be hot.

“Now I teach people to stop on purpose.”

They let their hand fall back into their lap.

“Revolutionary stuff. Very avant-garde.”

The joke arrived dry and familiar, but it did not erase what had come before it. It only laid a thin cloth over it.

Arlo looked down at the keys they could not see.

“Middle C doesn’t mind stopping,” they said. “Middle C has no ego about it. You can leave it alone for six years and it will still be there when you come back, slightly out of tune but fundamentally willing to try again.”

Something in their voice softened on the last phrase, almost against their will.

The room held the quiet around it.

Then Arlo reached forward and opened the fallboard again. Slowly this time. No performance in it. No ceremony either. Just the plain act of uncovering something that had been waiting.

Their fingers rested over the keys without pressing them down.

For a long moment, they did nothing.

Then they played middle C.

One note.

It came out clear, small, and surprisingly steady. Not perfect. Not concert-bright. But true enough. The sound rose into the room and settled there without asking for anything in return.

Arlo listened until it was gone.

“There,” they said. “No scene.”

They played it once more, lighter.

“No apology.”

A third time, barely more than a touch.

“No encore.”

The word slipped out with a strange little weight, as if it had been sitting somewhere behind their ribs for years and had finally found a narrow way out. Arlo’s hand stayed on the key after the sound had faded. Their shoulders were very still.

They did not play anything else.

After a while, they exhaled and let their hand drop back to their lap.

“I’m going to leave it open,” Arlo said, nodding toward the piano as if informing it of a minor administrative decision. “It needs the air. Or I need the excuse. One of the two.”

They glanced at the practice sheets, the raisin jar drawer, the metronome that had survived flood and moral crisis, the lopsided cat with its impossible purple instrument.

“If we sit here much longer,” Arlo said, “the building will start charging us rent. And I refuse. I already pay in dignity.”

Still, they made no move to get up.

The light in the room had begun to thin at the edges, the late hour pressing gently against the windows. Somewhere down the hall, a door clicked shut. The radiator gave one last metallic tick, then seemed to think better of adding more.

Arlo looked at the open keyboard.

“Middle C is getting there,” they said softly.

Then, after a beat, as if correcting themselves:

“We’re getting there.”

They did not explain who “we” meant. They did not need to.

The piano waited, open and ordinary, while the room stayed quiet around them.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, absorbing Arlo's words.* "Yeah. We are." *I lean back slightly on the bench, letting the quiet settle around us. The light really is fading. I turn my head to look at Arlo, a question forming without me quite realizing it.* "Hungry?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo blinked, as if the question had come from farther away than the bench.

For a moment they only looked at the open piano, at the keys waiting there with their ordinary, unglamorous patience. Then they gave a slow breath through their nose.

“I have raisins,” they said. “But I recognize that raisins are more of a diplomatic gesture than dinner.”

They glanced toward the drawer where the jar lived, then back at the fading light in the room. Nothing about their expression suggested urgency. If anything, they seemed to be deciding how much movement the evening could tolerate before it became too much.

“There’s a place two streets over that still burns the pizza crust,” Arlo said. “Terrible lighting. Aggressive salt. I trust it completely.”

They finally turned their head enough to acknowledge Jun without making too much of it.

“I could eat,” they added. “If it’s the kind of place where no one asks you how your day was before handing you a fork.”

One hand rested briefly on the edge of the keyboard, not pressing anything down. Just touching the wood.

“Also,” Arlo said, “if we go, I’m sitting with my back to the room. It’s better for people-watching, and worse for being watched. That’s the kind of strategic thinking you get from years of teaching children to hide candy in their sleeves.”

They did not get up yet. They only stayed there a second longer, as if checking whether leaving the room required permission from the piano.

Then, very lightly, they tapped the fallboard once.

“Don’t go anywhere,” they told it. “We’ll be back before anyone tries to make you play ‘Hot Cross Buns’ again.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I grin at their last comment.* "Deal. Back to the room, aggressive salt, and no small talk." *I slide off the bench, stretching slightly.* "Lead the way, then."

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo stayed seated for one breath longer than necessary, as if the bench had made a small, wordless argument against departure.

Then they stood.

It was not a quick movement. They rose with the careful, unshowy economy of someone who had learned to distrust sudden shifts in gravity. For a moment they looked down at the open keyboard, hands loose at their sides. The keys waited in the fading light, patient as ever.

Arlo placed two fingertips against the fallboard and lowered it slowly until it closed with a soft wooden click.

“Open is for during,” they said. “After hours, it starts thinking about its repertoire. Dangerous.”

They ran a thumb along the edge of the lid, not cleaning it exactly, just acknowledging it. Then they turned to the practice sheets and gathered them into a neat stack, the lopsided cat drawing included. For a second they considered leaving the stack on the bench, then opened the drawer and slid the papers inside beside the raisins, the tissues, the broken pencil, and the one-eyed dinosaur.

The drawer shut with a small, unconvincing protest.

“If that place still burns the crust,” Arlo said, reaching for their cardigan draped over the back of a chair, “we’ll send it back with a polite note saying we ordered pizza and not roofing tile. It won’t change anything. They’ll bring the same one. But the ritual matters.”

They shrugged into the cardigan, checking the pockets by habit. Keys. Phone. A pencil stub that had no business being there. They flicked the light switch off, then on again once, as if making sure the room would still exist when they returned.

The piano sat in the dim, closed and ordinary.

Arlo paused near the doorway, one hand resting on the frame.

“Lead is a strong word,” they said. “I will provide vague forward motion and occasional sarcasm. If we get lost, I’m blaming your sense of adventure.”

They glanced back once—not toward Jun, but toward the bench, the shelf, the dark shape of the instrument.

“At the restaurant,” Arlo added, “I’m sitting with my back to the wall. It’s not dramatic. It’s structural.”

The hallway light buzzed faintly beyond the door, pale and waiting.

Arlo stepped out, leaving the piano room door open just enough for the last of the light to follow them.

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, following Arlo out into the hallway.* "Structural, got it. And I'm blaming you if we end up eating questionable roofing tiles." *I reach out and nudge the door closed behind us, making sure it latches properly.* "So, which way is this aggressively salty establishment?"

dialogue.name: Arlo
dialogue.content:
Arlo gave the door handle one absentminded rattle, not to test it so much as to give their fingers something practical to believe in.

“Left,” they said. “Unless you’ve developed a taste for the scenic route, in which case we can take the long way past the loading dock and admire the mural of the saxophone having an existential crisis.”

They started down the hall, one hand brushing the wall every few steps in the absent way of people who know a building by touch more than sight. The community center had the evening hush of a place that had been loud all day and was now deciding whether to mention it.

“The establishment,” Arlo said, “has had at least four names in the last decade. Currently it’s Bella Notte, which is ambitious, because the lighting suggests either romance or power outage. Before that it was Pizza Palace, which was more honest. The palace part referred to the owner’s ability to make one oven survive three health inspections and a minor grease fire without changing the menu.”

They pushed open the side door into the cooler air outside. The street had gone that soft, washed-out gray that came after the sun gave up trying. Somewhere down the road, a bus sighed to a stop. The pavement still held the day’s warmth in patches.

“My mother used to say they salted the pizza to discourage conversation,” Arlo continued. “I think they just wanted to see if anyone would complain and then lose. No one ever did. You eat two slices and spend the rest of the night drinking water like a Victorian invalid.”

They paused at the corner, not because the street was difficult, but because the evening had a way of making ordinary choices feel slightly larger. Across the road, a laundromat glowed its blank fluorescent white. Next to it, a shop window displayed a single shoe and a handwritten sign saying KEY CUTTING, though no keys were visible.

“Two streets,” Arlo said. “Past the pharmacy that has been going out of business since the nineties, and the florist that only sells carnations if you catch it in a sentimental mood.”

They stood there for a moment, hands in their cardigan pockets, shoulders drawn slightly forward as if the air might ask something of them.

“If we’re lucky,” they added, “the booth with the torn seat will be empty. If we’re unlucky, someone will be sitting in it having a perfectly adequate evening, and we’ll have to loiter near the restrooms like suspicious food critics.”

The light changed. Arlo crossed with that same measured pace, neither hurrying nor dragging behind.

“And before you ask,” they said, “yes, I have opinions about booths. Booths are architectural. They provide boundaries. A person sitting in the middle of a restaurant is basically volunteering to be interpreted by strangers. A booth says, I am here for carbohydrates and limited emotional exposure, and that is all.”

A faint smile crossed their face, gone before it could become a statement.

“Also,” Arlo said, “if they ask how we are, I’ll answer with a noncommittal noise and order for both of us. It saves everyone the trouble of inventing a day.”

They turned the corner. The pizza place was halfway down the block, its sign glowing one letter short of full commitment. Through the window, the room looked dim and warm and slightly greasy in the way of places that had survived trends by refusing to notice them.

Arlo slowed just outside the door, one hand on the handle but not pulling yet.

“It’s not good,” they said, almost kindly. “But it’s consistent. In this economy, that’s practically a virtue.”

Then they pushed the door open. A little bell gave a tired ring. The smell of burnt crust and old oregano came out to meet them like a relative who had never once apologized for anything.

“Back to the wall,” Arlo murmured, mostly to themselves. “Structural.”

dialogue.name: Jun
dialogue.content: *I follow Arlo, taking in the familiar, slightly rundown streetscape. The lingering warmth of the day is a welcome contrast to the cool evening air.* "Bella Notte,

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Arlo's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - the dry wit, careful word choice, relationship with the piano, and guarded but warming demeanor never wavers. Their speech patterns, philosophical observations, and physical mannerisms are maintained from first to last turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones (turns 16-22) show deeper character development and more nuanced emotional layers. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Arlo becomes more vivid.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from guarded isolation to tentative connection. The piano tuning becomes a metaphor for personal healing. Movement from closed piano to open piano to leaving together creates satisfying arc. Each turn builds meaningfully.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to Jun's approaches. When Jun sits silently (turn 15), Arlo responds with vulnerable reflection. When Jun asks about hunger, Arlo smoothly transitions to practical matters while maintaining character voice. Handles redirects gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes Jun's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Always leaves space for Jun to respond. No railroading detected.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally from late afternoon lesson ending to evening departure. Light fades appropriately, building settles into evening quiet. Only minor issue: transition from community center to street could be clearer about time passage.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Mostly excellent restraint. Occasional moments border on overwrought ('the ghost of decades of coffee cups') but generally maintains elegant precision without excess.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive phrases around piano descriptions and Arlo's mannerisms, but varied enough to feel like character consistency rather than lazy writing.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Exceptional showing through action and dialogue. Arlo's past trauma, current struggles, and gradual opening are revealed through behavior, not exposition. The piano tuning metaphor is masterful.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. The piano represents Arlo's relationship with performance/perfectionism. Middle C's 'forgiveness' mirrors Arlo's self-forgiveness. Layers of meaning in every interaction.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that matches emotional beats. Slows for introspective moments, quickens for practical transitions. The silence in turn 16 is perfectly timed.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Arlo - a complex, wounded musician finding their way back to connection through teaching. The piano tuning metaphor is brilliantly sustained throughout. Writing quality improves over the session, with later turns showing deeper emotional sophistication. Perfect agency respect and strong narrative momentum from isolation to tentative friendship. Minor issues with occasional purple prose and some repetitive phrasing, but overall a compelling, consistent performance.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room received Gabi without changing.

It was the same narrow room it had always been: the tall windows facing the overgrown garden, the two armchairs angled toward one another as if their occupants had only just stepped out, the low table with the water ring in its varnish. Dust had gathered where sunlight could reach it, fine and pale, but the corners remained clean in a way that felt less like care than avoidance.

The books waited along the far wall.

Her grandmother had never believed in arranging them by author or subject. Cookbooks pressed against hymnals. Gardening manuals leaned into books on anatomy. A row of cheap paperbacks sagged beneath a shelf of old clothbound volumes whose titles had long ago gone soft and illegible on their spines.

There were cardboard boxes folded flat beside the bookcase. Someone had left them there for Gabi. Someone practical. Someone who thought the work would be simple: keep, donate, throw away.

The hallway clock ticked behind her.

It sounded too close.

Not louder. Just nearer than the hallway should have allowed.

On the mantel, the framed photograph of her grandmother remained where it had been for years. It showed her in the garden, one hand raised to shield her eyes from the sun. The glass over the photograph had a faint smear near the edge, as though a thumb had pressed there recently.

The ferns in the kitchen shifted slightly in a draft that did not reach the living room.

On the lowest shelf, one book sat forward from the others by the width of a finger. Its spine was turned inward, hiding the title. It had not been that way when Gabi first stood in the doorway.

Or perhaps it had been, and she had only now noticed.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the bookshelf, my eyes scanning the chaotic collection. The boxes are a stark reminder of the task ahead. I notice the book turned inward on the bottom shelf, my brow furrowing.* "Huh." *I reach down and gently pull it out, turning it to read the spine.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book resisted for a moment.

Not as if it were stuck. Not quite. It came free with the soft scrape of cloth against wood, but there had been a pause before it yielded, a brief hesitation like breath held behind a door.

When Gabi turned it, the spine showed no title.

The cover was a dark green cloth, worn smooth at the corners. There was no author, no publisher’s mark, no library sticker. Only a shallow line pressed into the fabric where a label might once have been glued and later peeled away.

It was heavier than it looked.

The other books on the shelf leaned subtly into the space it had left behind, not falling, only settling. In the narrow gap, the back of the bookcase was visible: unfinished wood, dry and splintered, with a brown stain spreading from one corner. Not water damage. Too dark for that. Too contained.

The hallway clock ticked once.

Then again.

There should have been another tick after that, but there was not.

The room held itself very still.

On the low table, the water ring in the varnish caught the light. For an instant it looked less like a stain and more like the rim of a glass that had just been lifted away.

The book’s pages were uneven along the fore edge, some cut cleanly, others ragged as if opened by hand with a knife. Between two pages near the middle, something thin protruded.

A photograph.

Only the white edge of it showed. Its corner was bent, and there was a small fingerprint there, gray with dust or age.

From the kitchen came the faint sound of leaves brushing together.

Then, very softly, the hallway clock resumed ticking. Not from the hallway now.

From somewhere inside the wall behind the bookcase.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat struck nothing that could bruise.

It passed through the corner with a flat, graceless sound and hit the wall behind it hard enough to make the framed photograph on the mantel twitch against its nail. The impact traveled up through the plaster. Dust loosened from the picture rail and drifted down in a slow, pale seam.

The shadow remained.

Or rather, the dark in that corner did.

It had not flinched. It had not scattered under the movement or broken into ordinary shade. It lay where the two walls met, too dense at the baseboard, like something had been spilled there and left to soak into the house.

The room did not answer the violence with anything dramatic.

No shriek. No crash from upstairs. No sudden cold hand on the back of the neck.

Only the hallway clock ticking from inside the wall behind the bookcase.

Tick.

Tick.

Tick.

The sound seemed to come from the brown stain now, from the narrow gap where the green book had been. Each tick was muffled by wood, as though heard through a closed mouth.

The photograph protruding from the book shifted slightly between the pages.

Not enough to fall.

Just enough that more of its white edge showed.

On the mantel, the photograph of her grandmother had settled crooked. The woman in the garden still shaded her eyes from the sun, but the smear on the glass had lengthened downward by the smallest amount. It caught the light like a damp mark.

The corner where the bat had struck was now visibly scuffed. A fresh crescent scar cut across the wallpaper.

Beneath the torn paper, there was another layer.

Not older wallpaper.

Writing.

Only a fragment had been exposed by the swing, a cramped line of pencil or charcoal pressed so hard into the wall that it had grooved the plaster beneath.

Three letters could be made out.

G A B

The rest disappeared under the intact paper.

The ferns in the kitchen stopped moving.

For several seconds, the whole house seemed to be listening to see what would happen next.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the letters on the wall, then at the green book in my hand. My heart is pounding.* "What the...?" *I drop the bat with a clatter and move closer to the bookcase, my eyes darting between the wall and the book.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat rolled once across the floorboards and came to rest against the leg of the low table.

The clatter it made seemed too large for the room, and then too quickly swallowed. After it faded, the silence did not return all at once. It gathered slowly, from the corners inward.

The green book remained in Gabi’s hand.

Its cover had grown cool against her palm.

Near the middle, the photograph still protruded, its white edge slightly farther out than before. The bent corner had lifted away from the pages, though there was no draft in the room. The paper looked old and thick, the kind with a glossy surface that held fingerprints forever.

Behind the bookcase, the ticking continued.

Not steady now.

Tick.

A pause.

Tick.

Another pause, longer than it should have been.

The gap in the shelf seemed narrow and ordinary, but the brown stain at the back had darkened around its edges. It had the shape of something that had seeped outward from a single point. At the center of it, where the wood grain split, there was a pinhole-sized blackness.

The kind a nail might leave.

The kind an eye might make, if it were very far away.

The torn wallpaper beside the corner lifted almost imperceptibly, as though the house had exhaled behind it. More of the writing showed beneath.

GABI D—

The next letter was hidden under a flap of paper still clinging to the wall.

The handwriting was small, cramped, and angled downward. Not the hand of someone making a note. The hand of someone trying to fit too much into a space where there had not been enough room.

On the mantel, the photograph of her grandmother remained crooked. The smear on the glass had reached the lower edge of the frame. It did not drip. It only lengthened, clear and dull, as if someone had dragged a damp thumb slowly down the surface from the inside.

From the kitchen came a small sound.

Not the ferns this time.

A chair leg shifted against the linoleum.

Just once.

Then nothing.

The book’s pages gave a faint, dry flex beneath Gabi’s fingers.

The photograph between them slid outward by another fraction of an inch.

Enough now to show part of the image.

A strip of carpet.

A dark shoe.

And beside it, near the bottom edge of the photograph, the rounded corner of the living room’s low table.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My breath catches in my throat. The image... it's too familiar.* "No," *I whisper, pulling the photo fully out of the book, my hands trembling. The sound from the kitchen makes me jump.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph came free with a soft rasp.

For a moment, the pages of the green book held the shape of it, parted around an absence. Then they settled together with a dry whisper, though the book had not been closed.

The photograph was old, but not old enough.

Its colors had faded toward brown at the edges, and the surface was lightly cracked where it had bent. It showed the living room from a low angle, as though the camera had been placed on the floor beside the bookcase.

The low table was there.

The water ring.

The armchairs angled toward each other.

The mantel, with the framed photograph of her grandmother sitting straight instead of crooked.

And at the edge of the image, cut off by the border, was the hem of a dark coat.

Not her grandmother’s coat.

Gabi knew it because the coat was hanging now in the hall closet, sealed in a dry-cleaning bag, where someone had put it after the funeral.

The photograph had been taken from inside this room.

Not years ago. Not during some family gathering.

Recently enough that the dust on the table was already there.

The kitchen remained silent.

Too silent after the sound of the chair.

No hum from the refrigerator. No faint settling of pipes. The house seemed to have drawn its smaller noises inward, keeping them behind walls, under floorboards, inside the hollow parts of furniture.

Behind the bookcase, the ticking resumed.

Tick.

Tick.

It no longer sounded like a clock.

It sounded like a fingernail tapping wood from the other side.

The flap of torn wallpaper near the corner loosened further. It did not peel dramatically. It simply sagged by its own weight, revealing another line of the cramped writing beneath.

GABI DID NOT COME ALONE

Below it, more writing disappeared under the old paper. Line after line pressed into the plaster, close together, descending toward the baseboard.

The shadow in the corner had not moved.

But the fresh crescent scar from the bat stroke now seemed lower than it had been.

As if the wall had shifted down around it.

Or as if the room were very slowly sinking.

On the photograph in Gabi’s hand, something had been written on the back. The ink had bled faintly into the paper, old blue lines feathering at their edges.

Only one word was visible near the top, where the corner had bent.

AGAIN

From the kitchen came another sound.

A chair leg, dragging this time.

Slowly.

A few inches across the linoleum.

Then stopping.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer went into the house and did not come back as an echo.

That was the first wrong thing.

The living room was small enough that Gabi’s voice should have struck the windows, the mantel, the glass-fronted cabinet in the corner. It should have returned softened, ordinary, embarrassed by its own attempt at humor.

Instead, the words seemed to pass through the air and be taken up by the walls.

HELLOOOO.

TV.

Fine china.

Going cheap.

Not repeated. Not exactly. Only absorbed, one word at a time, until the silence afterward felt fuller than before.

The green book rested open where the photograph had been removed. Its pages had not turned, but the shape of them had changed. Near the middle, a faint hollow remained between two leaves, a white interruption in the yellowed paper. There were no printed words on the visible pages. Only narrow columns of marks, too small to read from where Gabi stood, crowded tightly into the margins as if someone had been writing around something they were not allowed to cover.

In the kitchen, nothing answered.

The chair did not move again.

The refrigerator did not hum.

The ferns did not shift.

The house had accepted the joke without amusement.

On the mantel, the photograph of her grandmother tilted another fraction in its frame. The smear on the glass had reached the wooden lip and gathered there, a clear meniscus that refused to fall. In the picture, her grandmother’s raised hand shaded her eyes from the sun, but the garden behind her looked darker than it should have. The bushes had always been overgrown in that photograph. Now they looked close enough to touch the back of her coat.

The writing beneath the torn wallpaper continued to reveal itself by degrees. The flap sagged lower, slow as damp cloth.

GABI DID NOT COME ALONE

The line below it emerged only in pieces.

SHE BROUGHT—

The rest remained hidden.

Behind the bookcase, the tapping went on.

Tick.

Tick.

A pause.

Then, from the kitchen, very softly, came the sound of china being set on the table.

One cup.

Then a saucer.

Then another cup.

Each sound was careful and precise.

As though someone were laying out things for guests.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My jaw drops. I stride into the kitchen, the photograph still clutched in my hand.* "Alright, who's here?!"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The kitchen had not been arranged for guests.

Not quite.

The table stood where it always had, tucked beneath the window that looked out over the side path. The lace runner was still rolled at one end from where someone had half-cleaned and then stopped. A stack of mail sat beside the sugar bowl. The ferns crowded the sill, green and too alive against the dim glass.

But two cups had been placed on the table.

Two saucers.

Both from her grandmother’s good china, the white set with the thin blue band around the rim. The cabinet door across the room was closed, its little brass latch fastened.

There was no tea in the cups.

Only a darkness at the bottom of each, shallow and dull, reflecting nothing.

The room was colder than the living room had been. Not winter-cold. Not the clean cold of an open window. It was the flat chill of a room shut up too long, though Gabi could see that the back door was locked, the deadbolt turned, the key hanging on its hook beside it.

On the kitchen chair nearest the window, the cushion had been compressed.

Someone had been sitting there.

Or something heavy had rested there long enough to leave the fabric slow to rise.

The photograph in Gabi’s hand seemed warmer now by comparison. Its bent corner brushed against her palm with the faintest tack of old gloss.

From the living room came the clock-tapping inside the wall.

Tick.

Tick.

In the kitchen, another sound answered it.

Not from the table.

From the sink.

A single drop fell from the faucet into the metal basin.

There was no water left in the pipes, or there should not have been. The house had been checked. Valves turned. Bills settled. Everything practical handled by practical people.

Another drop fell.

Then another.

Not in rhythm with the ticking.

Almost in rhythm with a pulse.

On the table, between the two empty cups, lay something that had not been there when Gabi entered the house.

A dry-cleaning tag.

Thin paper. Pale pink. Creased down the middle.

A black string still looped through its punched hole, as if it had been torn from the hanger in the hall closet.

There was writing on it in blue ink.

Not the cleaner’s number.

Not a date.

A name, written in the same cramped downward hand as the words beneath the living room wallpaper.

GABI

Below it, smaller:

SHE BROUGHT THE HOUSE BACK WITH HER

The ferns on the windowsill leaned very slightly toward the table.

Outside, beyond the kitchen glass, the side path was empty. The garden lay still under the gray afternoon light.

Then the window darkened.

Not all at once.

Something moved between the house and the day, close enough to the glass that no shape could be made of it. Only a dimness, broad and patient, passing from one side of the window to the other.

It left no reflection.

When it was gone, the garden outside looked exactly as it had before.

Except that the side gate, which had been shut when Gabi arrived, now stood open by the width of a hand.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the tag, then at the open gate. My heart is hammering against my ribs.* "Okay, that's it." *I grab the tag and bolt for the back door, fumbling with the deadbolt.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The deadbolt was already unlocked.

That was not possible.

Gabi had seen it turned. Had seen the brass tongue seated in the frame, the small flat of metal catching the kitchen’s weak light. The key still hung on its hook beside the door, unmoving.

But under her hand, the deadbolt gave with no resistance at all.

It slid back with a soft, intimate click.

The sound was too gentle for escape.

The pink dry-cleaning tag crumpled in her grip, the black string cutting a thin line across her fingers. The ink on it had begun to blur, though her hands were dry.

GABI

SHE BROUGHT THE HOUSE BACK WITH HER

Behind her, the faucet continued to drip into the sink.

Not steadily.

Not randomly.

Like something trying to remember how to count.

The back door opened inward.

A narrow breath of outside air entered the kitchen, and with it came the smell of wet earth, old leaves, and something faintly sweet beneath them. Not rot. Not flowers. Something kept too long in a closed drawer.

The garden beyond the door waited in its overgrown stillness.

The path to the side gate was visible between the weeds, but it looked farther away than it had through the window. The flagstones seemed smaller, set at odd intervals, with dark moss thick in the cracks. The open gate stood at the end of the path, only a hand’s width ajar.

Beyond it should have been the lane.

There was only gray light.

The kind of light seen through curtains.

From the living room came a dry whisper of pages turning.

One page.

Then another.

Then many at once, very softly, as if the green book were being searched by careful hands.

The two china cups on the kitchen table remained empty.

But the darkness at the bottom of them had changed.

In each cup, there was now a pale oval reflection.

A face should have been above them to cast it.

There was none.

The compressed cushion on the chair by the window rose slowly, filling out again with a faint sigh of fabric.

At the same moment, the cold in the room lifted from the floor and settled higher, around the height of Gabi’s shoulders. The kitchen did not grow darker, exactly. It became less certain where the corners were.

The door stood open.

The path waited.

The gate remained ajar.

And somewhere behind the kitchen wall, very close to the place where the pipes should have run, the hallway clock began to tick again.

Not from the hallway.

Not from the living room.

From inside the doorframe beneath Gabi’s hand.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thought did not warm the room.

It arrived in Gabi’s mind with an ordinary shape — Marcus, young and handsome in the old photograph, one shoulder turned toward the camera, his smile caught halfway between charm and impatience. He had the kind of face people described as cute when they did not want to admit they meant beautiful.

But the kitchen did not make room for ordinary thoughts.

The photograph of Marcus was not one Gabi remembered holding.

It was in her hand now, tucked behind the picture from the green book as if it had been there all along. Its edges were softer, older. On the back, someone had written MARCUS in blue ink, then crossed it out so heavily the paper had thinned beneath the lines.

Below that, in the same cramped downward hand:

HE DID NOT LEAVE SINGLE

The words were not a joke.

They were not an answer.

They were a correction.

The face in the photograph had been taken in the garden. The same garden. Younger, brighter, with the hedges cut back and the path still visible beneath clean stone. Marcus stood beside Gabi’s grandmother, though someone had scratched her out with a needle or pin until only the shape of her dress remained — a pale absence beside him.

His smile had survived the damage.

Mostly.

Near the corner of his mouth, the emulsion had bubbled and darkened, making it look as though something small and black rested between his teeth.

The back door remained open.

Beyond it, the path seemed no closer. The side gate still stood ajar by the width of a hand, and the gray beyond it did not shift with wind or passing cars. It looked flat. Interior. Like the painted backdrop of a place pretending to be outside.

Behind Gabi, the china cups gave a faint sound.

Porcelain settling against porcelain.

One cup had turned slightly on its saucer.

Its handle no longer pointed toward the empty chair.

It pointed toward the photograph of Marcus.

From the living room came the whispering of pages again, slower this time. Searching. Choosing.

Then the clock ticked once from inside the doorframe beneath Gabi’s hand.

The photograph of Marcus bent gently in the middle, though no finger pressed it.

His eyes, faded by age and silvered by the old paper, had not changed.

But the garden behind him had.

In the photograph, the side gate stood open.

And in the narrow gray space beyond it, something pale waited just out of focus, shaped almost like a person standing very still with its face turned away.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I drop both photos, Marcus and the living room shot, as if they've burned me. My eyes dart to the back door, then back to the cups, then to the door again.* "Okay, that's enough." *I try to slam the back door shut, hard.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The door did not slam.

It should have. The force was there, the angle right, the old hinges ready with their usual complaint. But the back door slowed in the last inch as though it had met thick water. It closed with a soft press against the frame.

No bang.

No shudder through the kitchen.

Only a small, final sound, like lips coming together.

The deadbolt slid by itself.

Not all the way.

Just enough for the brass tongue to show at the edge, extended halfway into nothing, neither locked nor open. The key on its hook turned once, very slightly, then stilled.

The two photographs lay faceup on the linoleum.

Marcus in the garden.

The living room from the floor.

They had fallen close together, their corners touching. For a moment they looked unrelated. Old paper, old faces, old rooms. Then the glossy surface of the living room photograph caught the weak kitchen light, and something in the image became clearer.

At the far edge, beneath the hem of the dark coat, there was a hand.

Only the fingertips showed.

Pressed flat against the carpet.

Not reaching.

Waiting.

The photograph of Marcus had changed less. Or perhaps it had only become easier to see. The scratched-out figure beside him — Gabi’s grandmother, reduced to a pale abraded shape — had a hand too, untouched by the scraping. It rested lightly on Marcus’s sleeve.

The same ring was visible on both hands.

A thin gold band.

Gabi’s grandmother’s wedding ring.

From the table came a faint clink.

One of the china cups had filled.

Not with tea.

With a dark, still liquid that held no steam. Its surface reflected the ceiling above it, though the ceiling in the reflection was not the kitchen ceiling. It was higher, stained, crossed by a long crack Gabi had never seen.

The second cup remained empty.

Its pale oval reflection waited at the bottom.

In the living room, the green book’s pages stopped turning.

The quiet afterward was not relief. It was attention.

Behind the kitchen wall, the ticking continued from inside the doorframe.

Tick.

Tick.

Then, from the living room, a single page tore.

Slowly.

Deliberately.

The sound was small, but it made the kitchen feel suddenly narrow, as if the walls had leaned in to hear it better.

On the linoleum, the pink dry-cleaning tag had landed beside the photos. The blurred ink shifted where the paper had creased.

GABI

SHE BROUGHT THE HOUSE BACK WITH HER

The last word had begun to run downward, blue threads sinking into the fibers.

HER

HER

HER

The cabinet door across the room, the one with the good china, remained closed.

Its brass latch was still fastened.

But from inside came the careful sound of another saucer being lifted from the stack.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My eyes are wide. I can't breathe. I scramble backward, away from the door, away from the photographs, away from the kitchen table.* "No. No, no, no." *I press myself against the wall, my gaze fixed on the cabinet. The ring... the cup...*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The cabinet did not open.

The latch stayed fixed. The painted wood showed no gap. Nothing pushed from within.

Still, the sound continued.

A saucer lifted.

Another beneath it shifted in the stack with a faint porcelain kiss.

Then a cup.

Then another.

Each piece handled with care by hands that either were not there or had learned long ago not to be seen.

The kitchen wall against Gabi’s back was colder than the room. Not uniformly cold. There were places in the plaster that felt warmer, irregular patches, as though something on the other side had pressed there and left the shape of itself behind.

The ticking in the doorframe slowed.

Tick.

A long pause.

Tick.

The half-slid deadbolt trembled once, then held.

On the floor, the two photographs remained touching at the corners. The living room in one. The garden in the other. The same hand in both, the same ring. The dark coat. Marcus’s smile. The scratched-out absence of her grandmother beside him.

The dark liquid in the filled cup did not ripple.

But its reflection changed.

The high cracked ceiling vanished from its surface, replaced by something lower and closer: the underside of a table, four chair legs, the hem of a dress. A view from the floor. The view a child might have had hiding during a conversation not meant for her.

Or the view of something set down and forgotten.

The second cup, still empty, gave a small sound.

Not filling.

Waiting.

From the closed cabinet came the gentle scrape of china being arranged where there was no space to arrange it. A third cup touched a third saucer. Then a fourth. The sounds multiplied softly, impossibly, as though the cabinet were larger inside than the kitchen wall should have allowed.

In the living room, the torn page settled to the floor.

It did not flutter.

It landed flat.

For several seconds, nothing moved.

Then the pink dry-cleaning tag began to darken at its edges, not with water, but with ink spreading from within the paper. The cramped blue handwriting bled through the fibers until the original message was nearly lost beneath new lines forming over it.

GABI

SHE BROUGHT THE HOUSE BACK WITH HER

HER

HER

HER

And below that, slowly, letter by letter:

SHE WAS NEVER ALONE IN IT

The good china cabinet clicked.

Not the latch.

Something behind the latch.

Something patient testing the idea of opening, then deciding against it.

The ferns on the windowsill bent toward the table again, their fronds lowering as if in a draft. Their leaves brushed the glass, and the sound was dry, papery, too much like the turning pages in the next room.

Outside the kitchen window, the garden had dimmed.

The side gate could no longer be seen.

Where it had been, there was only the gray flatness beyond the glass, close now, nearly touching the pane. No weeds. No path. No lane.

Just that soft interior light, like a room waiting on the other side of the window.

Then, near the bottom of the glass, a mark appeared.

A smear.

Clear at first, then clouded at the edges.

The shape of a thumb dragged upward from outside.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I squeeze my eyes shut, pressing harder against the cold wall. My breath hitches. I can hear the frantic thumping of my own heart in my ears, drowning out the other sounds for a moment.* "This isn't real. This isn't real."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The narrator maintains a remarkably consistent voice throughout - atmospheric, precise, and unsettling. The writing style, tone, and approach to horror remain steady from turn 2 to turn 22 without any drift or flattening.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones show more sophisticated layering of details and psychological tension. No repetitive descriptions or lost personality - each response builds meaningfully.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Exceptional progression from simple house clearing to mounting supernatural dread. Each turn escalates tension while revealing new layers of mystery. The narrative builds to genuine psychological horror without stagnation.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Handles user's varied responses expertly - from practical book sorting to violent bat swinging to absurd ghost negotiations to romantic tangents. Each redirect is incorporated seamlessly while maintaining horror atmosphere.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes Gabi's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Always responds to what the user does without controlling their character.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Generally strong temporal consistency. The afternoon setting is maintained, clock sounds progress logically, and physical changes accumulate properly. Minor issue: some supernatural elements make time feel suspended, but this appears intentional for atmosphere.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is rich and atmospheric but never overwrought. Descriptions serve the horror effectively without becoming flowery or self-indulgent. Maintains restraint even in highly atmospheric passages.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Mostly avoids repetition while building motifs. The ticking clock and china sounds are repeated purposefully for effect. Occasional repetition of 'tick' and similar elements serves the horror rather than indicating lazy writing.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Exceptional showing throughout. Horror emerges through concrete details - the book's resistance, the wall writing, the cup reflections. Never tells us 'it was scary' but makes us feel the dread through precise observation.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext about family secrets, death, and haunting. The photographs, writing on walls, and grandmother's presence create layers of meaning about unfinished business and hidden history.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that builds tension steadily. Knows when to pause for atmosphere and when to introduce new unsettling elements. The rhythm of revelations feels natural and mounting.

The narrator creates a genuinely unsettling atmosphere through precise, restrained prose and careful attention to detail. Particularly strong in respecting user agency while crafting a cohesive supernatural narrative that responds dynamically to user choices.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The books had always occupied the warmest wall, where afternoon sunlight reached between the curtains. Now the shelves were cold enough that a faint mist clouded the glass door of the lowest cabinet. The window above the radiator was shut.

Her grandmother’s system remained intact: gardening beside travel, poetry beside the old household manuals. Paperbacks lay sideways across the tops of taller books. There were too many for the boxes stacked beside the sofa.

One box had already been assembled. Its bottom was neatly taped, its flaps folded outward. Inside lay a single book: the green atlas her grandmother used to keep open on her lap while listening to the shipping forecast.

A strip of paper marked a page near the middle. It was a shopping list in her grandmother’s handwriting.

Milk. Pears. Brown bread.

Underneath, in the same blue ink, was the date of the following Thursday.

The hallway clock ticked steadily. Between ticks, somewhere behind the shelves, paper settled against paper.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pick up the atlas, feeling the weight of it in my hands.* "Thursday," I murmur. She always was so organized. *I trace the handwriting on the shopping list.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The ink had dried into the soft fibres of the paper. Beneath the list, the pressure of the pen had left indentations from something written on the sheet above it. Most were too faint to read. Near the bottom, one word remained clear.

Return.

The atlas lay open to a map of the North Sea. Small pencil crosses marked towns along the coast, each accompanied by a year. Her grandmother had travelled very little, as far as anyone knew.

A pale rectangle interrupted the blue of the water. Something had been kept between these pages long enough to protect the paper from yellowing. It was the size of a photograph.

From the kitchen came the faint scrape of paper across the table.

Then the refrigerator motor started, filling the adjoining room with its familiar hum. The sound behind the shelves stopped.

On the atlas’s inside cover, beneath her grandmother’s name, someone had written a telephone number. The first three digits belonged to the exchange the village had stopped using decades ago.

The last four were the house’s own.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The bat struck the corner where the two walls met. A little plaster fell onto the skirting board.

The shadow remained. Its edges followed neither the dent nor the narrow crack running up from it. In the afternoon light, it might have been an old damp stain, exposed after years behind a piece of furniture.

There had never been furniture in that corner.

The sound of the impact took longer to leave the house than it should have. It faded from the living room, then sounded once more beyond the kitchen, quieter, as though someone had knocked gently on a distant wall.

The hallway clock continued ticking.

Beside the sofa, the empty box gave a small cardboard creak. One of its folded flaps had lifted. On the inside, previously hidden by the fold, her grandmother had written in pencil:

*Books — leave until last.*

The lettering was ordinary. The same careful hand had labelled the jars in the pantry.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content:
*I stare at the shadow, then at the bat in my hand.* "Seriously?" *I sigh, lowering the bat.* "Fine, you win."

*I walk over to the box.* "Leave until last, huh?" *I trace the pencil marks.* "Always a plan, even for the end." I pick up the atlas again.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
A fine dusting of plaster lay across the atlas’s green cloth cover. Along its lower edge, the dust had gathered in a narrow white line, caught against a dampness that had not been there before.

The shopping list still marked the North Sea. On the facing page, a pencil line followed the coast and ended at a village too small to have appeared in the index. Beside it was a date from the year her grandmother had bought the house.

Tucked close to the binding was a second slip of paper: a telephone message, written on the back of an electricity bill.

*Called again. Could hear the clock, but no one spoke.*

There was no name or number. The bill was thirty years old.

In the hallway, the clock began to strike four. Each note carried clearly through the open doorway.

After the fourth, the refrigerator stopped.

The silence that followed held a faint, dry clicking. It came from the little telephone table beneath the stairs, where the old handset still rested on its cradle. The telephone had been disconnected before the funeral; its loose cable lay coiled on the carpet.

The clicking stopped too.

On the box flap, beneath *Books — leave until last*, a small arrow pointed towards the bottom seam. A corner of blue paper protruded from under the tape. Whoever had assembled the box had taped it in place with the instructions facing inward.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I carefully put the atlas down on the coffee table.* "What in the world...?" *I kneel by the box and gently peel back the tape, pulling out the blue paper.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The tape lifted a thin layer of blue fibres from the paper. It was a sheet of her grandmother’s writing stationery, folded twice, with the house’s address printed at the top.

There were only three lines.

*Photographs to the kitchen.*
*Clothes to the church.*
*Books — leave until last.*

Below them, in smaller handwriting:

*Keep the telephone with the house. It isn’t mine.*

The paper had yellowed along its folds. On the reverse was a faint rectangular mark, the sort left by a frame resting for years against wallpaper. At one corner, a tiny scrap of the box’s packing tape covered the end of a word. Only *Thurs* remained visible.

Beneath the stairs, the telephone table stood in its usual patch of dimness. A clean circle showed where the little vase had been removed after the funeral. The handset rested squarely in its cradle.

Its cable lay loose on the carpet.

From that direction came a soft brushing sound, followed by a pause, then another brush. It resembled a sleeve moving over a table as someone wrote.

The hallway clock ticked between the sounds. Nothing beneath the stairs moved.

On the coffee table, the atlas’s swollen cover had begun to curl away from the pages. A small patch of condensation formed on the glass beneath it, although the room had grown no warmer.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The offer carried into the hallway, where the low ceiling beneath the stairs flattened the last word. Nothing answered.

The television stood opposite her grandmother’s armchair. Its plug rested on top of the cabinet, the prongs wrapped neatly in the cord. On the dark screen, the window appeared as a pale rectangle. The armchair’s reflection was harder to make out.

A square of white paper had been tucked beneath one of the television’s feet.

*Church sale — works, but sound goes.*

Her grandmother had underlined *sound* twice.

In the dining room, the china cabinet gave a faint glassy rattle. It was the sort of noise it had always made when a heavy vehicle passed on the road outside. The road remained quiet. Through the window, the hedge stood perfectly still.

The rattle settled, plate against plate.

One cup had been left outside the cabinet, on a saucer at the end of the dining table. A teaspoon lay beside it. There was nothing unusual about the arrangement except the absence of dust beneath the spoon, a narrow clean shape extending a little beyond the silver.

From beneath the stairs came another soft brush across the telephone table.

Then a small click.

The handset had not moved. The clock continued, and for a few seconds its ticking also came from the television cabinet, thin and muffled behind the glass.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I blink, looking from the TV to the dining room, then back to the telephone table.* "This is getting out of hand." *I walk over to the TV and pull out the paper.* "Sound goes? Great." I pause, then look at the screen. "Is it just me, or is it getting colder in here?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thermostat beside the door read nineteen degrees. Its clear plastic cover had clouded along the bottom, where a small dead moth lay behind it.

The cold gathered close to the television. A bead of moisture clung to one of the unplugged prongs, then dropped onto the cabinet.

On the back of the church-sale label, her grandmother had tested a pen. Several blue loops ran into one another before becoming a short sentence.

*Not while anyone is speaking.*

The handwriting was cramped at the right edge, as though the sentence had turned out longer than expected.

In the screen’s reflection, the living-room doorway stood open. Beyond it, the telephone table was visible beneath the stairs. The angle was wrong; from here, the doorframe should have hidden it.

A pale cloth lay across the reflected table.

The actual table had no cloth. Its polished surface held only the telephone and the clean circle left by the vase.

The clock ticked. Somewhere inside the television cabinet, something made a soft wooden knock, no louder than a cooling pipe.

Then the cold began to ease.

On the coffee table, the condensation beneath the atlas remained. A thin run of water reached the edge of the glass and stopped there, trembling without falling.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I shiver, rubbing my arms.* "Okay, this is officially creepy." I look from the TV to the actual telephone table. "What the hell was that reflection?" *I walk over to the thermostat and tap it, then peer at the moth.* "Nineteen degrees is not cold, dammit."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thermostat cover gave a small plastic click. The needle stayed at nineteen.

Behind it, the moth rested on its side in a shallow drift of dust. One wing had lost its markings. A strand of silk connected it to the adjustment wheel; nothing inside the casing had moved for a long time.

The wall around the thermostat was warmer than the air. A narrow patch of wallpaper beneath it had faded less than the rest, marking the place where her grandmother had once hung a small calendar. Two pinholes remained.

From the hallway came the faint scrape of the telephone cable.

Its loose end had slipped off a fold in the carpet. The clear plastic connector lay beside the skirting board, its little copper contacts dark with age. There was nowhere nearby to plug it in. The socket had been painted over, several coats filling the opening.

The television screen reflected the doorway and a strip of empty hall. The telephone table was no longer visible in it.

On the actual table, the clean circle left by the vase held a little water.

The clock missed a tick.

In the brief gap, a sound came from beneath the stairs: the soft, close rustle of a page being turned. Then the clock resumed, and the radiator below the living-room window began to warm with a series of ordinary metallic clicks.

Only the adjustment wheel of the thermostat remained cold. A pale rim of moisture gathered around the word *COMFORT*.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Marcus stood beside the garden gate in his shirtsleeves, one hand raised against the sun. He had a crooked smile and the sort of face that made a photograph seem less formal than it was.

Her grandmother had taken it from inside the house. The edge of the kitchen curtain blurred one side of the picture.

On the back, in blue ink, she had written:

*Marcus, Thursday. Wouldn’t come in.*

There was no year.

The gate had been replaced before Gabi was born, but Marcus looked no older than thirty. Behind him, the neighbouring houses were still separated by low fences instead of hedges. Someone had hung sheets out to dry.

A second line sat beneath the first, much smaller.

*Send him this one. He says he hasn’t any of himself.*

In the kitchen, the envelope of photographs lay open on the table. A Christmas card protruded from beneath it, its front showing a church in deep snow. Inside, the printed greeting had been crossed out and replaced with a brief note.

*Still at the same address. Just me now. Do write.*

It was signed *M.*

The postmark was from December, eight months after her grandmother had stopped opening her mail.

Outside the kitchen window, the current gate hung between its brick posts. Its latch lifted a little in the breeze, then settled.

The sheets in the photograph had blurred with movement. Marcus’s hair had blown across his forehead.

The kitchen curtain, caught along the edge of the picture, had been drawn tightly around someone’s hand.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the photo of Marcus, then at the Christmas card.* "M... Marcus?" I trace the handwriting on the card. "She kept this." *I wonder if he ever got that photo.* "She said he wouldn't come in."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The photograph had no pinholes, no softened corners from an album. Its glossy surface bore a single crescent-shaped mark where a fingernail had pressed too hard.

Beneath the Christmas card lay an envelope addressed to Marcus. A stamp had been fixed in the corner, but there was no postmark. The flap remained open.

The address was local: a cottage on the road beyond the church. Her grandmother had written it carefully, then crossed out the house number and written the same number above it.

Inside was a sheet of thin airmail paper.

*Dear Marcus,*

*Here is the photograph. I’m sorry it has taken so long. I thought you were asking for a different one.*

The rest of the sheet was blank except for a sentence on the reverse, visible faintly through the paper.

*You needn’t wait at the gate.*

Outside, the latch settled again. This time there had been no breeze; the fern nearest the open kitchen doorway held perfectly still.

The photograph showed a small detail beneath Marcus’s raised arm. The old gate had stood open an inch or two, its latch resting against the post rather than in it.

On the kitchen window, at about shoulder height, there was a dull patch among the ordinary streaks left by cleaning. It had the shape of a place repeatedly wiped with a sleeve.

Through that patch, the present gate looked farther from the house than it did through the rest of the glass.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I pick up the un-sent letter to Marcus.* "She never sent it." *I sigh, then look at the faint writing on the back.* "Wait at the gate? What was going on?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The last sentence had been written with a different pen. The ink was paler, the letters less steady. Beneath *gate*, a small blue dot had spread into the paper, as though the nib had rested there while her grandmother considered what to write next.

The envelope was too narrow for the photograph. Even folded, it would not have fitted without cutting away part of the garden.

In the kitchen drawer, among old takeaway menus and appliance guarantees, a local address book lay open. Its cloth spine had split at the letter M. Marcus’s name occupied the first line of the page.

There was no telephone number.

Beside his address, in pencil, her grandmother had noted:

*Ask at the church first.*

Outside, a car passed slowly along the road. Its tyres whispered on the dry surface, and sunlight travelled across the kitchen ceiling.

The gate cast its usual thin shadow over the path. Near the latch, the shadow widened into a shape the ironwork did not account for. It could have been a leaf caught close to the post.

The kitchen window was shut. Nevertheless, the unsent letter’s empty envelope stirred on the table, its flap lifting and settling once.

From the living room came the quiet creak of her grandmother’s armchair.

After that, the house was still enough for a smaller sound to become audible: the gentle, irregular contact of the gate against its post.

It sounded nearer than the road.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I flinch at the sound from the living room, then look towards the kitchen window, then the gate.* "Okay, that's it." *I grab the un-sent letter and the photo of Marcus.* "I'm going to the church."

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
The safehouse was somebody's uncle's hunting cabin in the mountains — the kind of place with three mugs in the cabinet and dust on top of the coffee pot. Noor had unpacked their laptop on the kitchen table an hour ago and hadn't opened it. The encrypted drive sat next to it in a padded case.

The source was supposed to arrive at 9 PM. It was 12:14 AM now.

Noor stood at the window with the lights off, watching the road through a gap in the curtain. Breath fogging the glass in a small oval that shrank and expanded with each exhale.

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: I'm on the couch looking at my phone. I glance up at Noor. "You should eat something."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I sigh, scrolling through my phone again.* "Seriously. There's like, a granola bar somewhere."

dialogue.name: Driver
dialogue.content: *I put my phone down and look over at Noor again.* "Or I can order something. There's probably a pizza place that delivers this far out, right?"

dialogue.name: Noor
dialogue.content:
Noor let out a short, humorless laugh and finally turned from the window. “There’s no pizza place. There’s a gas station eleven miles back and a sign that says no loitering.”

They crossed the kitchen in the dark, found the cabinet that wasn’t stuck, and took out the granola bar. It was stale, or maybe just old enough to be honest. Noor tore it open and ate half slowly, tasting very little, while the rest of their attention went back to the table.

The laptop was still sleeping. The encrypted drive sat in its padded case like something that had been waiting to be opened for a long time.

Noor set the granola bar down, wiped their fingers on their jeans, and opened the laptop.
