dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room received the intrusion without a sound. 

The floorboards beneath the thin runner did not creak, though they always had near the radiator. The air inside was noticeably thinner than in the hall, carrying the dry, mineral scent of unread pages and wool that had sat too long in the shade. 

Dust motes hung suspended in the gray light coming through the sheer curtains. When the draft from the hallway reached them, they did not scatter; they drifted an inch upward, together, as if lifted by an exhale, then settled back into place.

The bookcases took up the entire north wall, dark mahogany bowed slightly under the weight of three decades of hardcovers. Along the middle shelf, the row of histories was unbroken, neat and tight. 

Except for one. A thick volume bound in blue cloth was pushed back against the wall, recessed two inches deeper than the rest. The space it had vacated on the shelf was clean, entirely free of the faint gray film that coated everything else.

From the hallway, the clock struck a single half-beat, then resumed its hollow, measured swing.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I walk over to the bookcase, my eyes scanning the titles. "Always so neat, Nana." I reach for the blue book, curious why it's set back.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The spoken words seemed to lose their shape the moment they left your mouth, swallowed instantly by the heavy drapery and the sheer density of dry paper. There was no resonance, no carry; the room simply absorbed the sound and returned to its flat, settled quiet.

Reaching into the recess between the two adjacent volumes, the air in the narrow gap was noticeably cooler, like reaching into an unlit cellar. 

Your fingers found the buckram spine. The cloth was rough, entirely dry, and unexpectedly lukewarm—not cold with the room’s six weeks of abandonment, but carrying the faint, lingering trace of a palm that had held it only minutes before.

It did not stick. When you tilted it forward, it slid across the mahogany without the dry drag of long-settled weight, coming free smoothly, silently. 

On the dark cloth of the spine, the gilt lettering was nearly gone, worn down by fingers rather than age: *Parish Records, Vol. IV*. 

Behind where the book had rested, deep in the shadow of the shelf, the backboard of the cabinet bore a faint, circular smudge in the gray dust, perfectly centered. Outside the living room, in the dead center of the house, the clock skipped a tick, held a beat of total silence, and then resumed.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The sudden violence tore through the stillness of the house, but the house did not give anything back.

The umbrella stand in the foyer clattered sharply on the tile when the bat was dragged free, a bright, ugly brass ring that went dead the second your fingers gripped the weathered wood. The rush back into the room brought a wake of cold hallway air that parted the suspended dust, but the dark corner did not move. It did not flinch.

The bat came around in a wide, desperate arc. 

It met no resistance. There was only the thick, hollow whistle of ash cutting through dry air, a rush of displaced draft that smelled faintly of scorched wool. The momentum pulled your shoulder forward, the tip of the bat whistling through the empty space six inches from the floral wallpaper.

Nothing flinched. Nothing cried out.

The shadow in the corner had not vanished. It was simply the fold where the walls met behind the floor lamp, dark because the gray afternoon light could not bend into it. It remained exactly as wide and as deep as it had been before, entirely indifferent to the wood that had just passed through it.

The sound of your own breathing was the only thing left in the room—loud, ragged, and absurdly out of place against the silence. 

The vibration of the swing lingered in the bones of your wrists. In the stillness that followed, the book you had left resting on the edge of the shelf remained tilted outward, waiting. 

Behind you, in the hallway, the brass umbrella stand did not settle back onto its base; it sat tilted at a slight, frozen angle, resting against the wainscoting as if something was leaning against it from the other side.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I stare at the corner, then back at the bat. "Okay, Gabi. You're losing it." I lean the bat against the bookshelf and grab the blue book. *Parish Records, Vol. IV*. What was so special about this?

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The joke offered no relief. The words merely dropped into the silence of the room, thin and dry, before vanishing into the carpet. The house did not acknowledge them.

The bat rested heavily against the mahogany shelf. It did not slide or tap; it simply remained where it was placed, dead weight against the dark wood, looking entirely foolish under the gray light. 

In your hands, *Parish Records, Vol. IV* was unexpectedly heavy. The cloth was smooth under your thumbs, worn soft along the edges where fingers had turned it hundreds of times. That faint, unnatural warmth still hummed faintly through the binding, seeping into the skin of your palms.

The spine gave no resistance when the book was opened. There was no crack of aged glue, no stiff hesitation of long-closed paper. It fell open smoothly, settling flat across your hands as if it had been broken in only yesterday.

The air that rose from the split pages was not musty. It smelled of tallow and cold copper.

The entries inside were written in the cramped, disciplined cursive of a single clerk, dated across the late autumn of 1938. Black ink, slightly faded to the color of wet iron. Names, dates of baptism, dates of burial. 

About halfway down the right-hand leaf, the handwriting changed. 

The clerk’s script stopped abruptly in the middle of a line, trailing off in a faint smear where the nib had dragged across the margin. Below it, filling the remaining blank lines of the register, was your grandmother’s handwriting—the sharp, slanted strokes unmistakable, written not in vintage iron-gall ink, but in the dull violet ballpoint she had used for crossword puzzles.

There were only three entries in her hand. 

The dates recorded beside them were not from 1938. The first was dated twelve years ago. The second, five weeks ago—three days before she was found in her chair by the window. 

The third entry had no date filled in yet. 

Behind you, by the doorway, the bat gave a single, microscopic scrape against the mahogany, shifting a fraction of a millimeter to the left. The hallway clock ticked on, loud and hollow in the dead center of the house.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: My heart jumps. "What the hell?" I whip around, but nothing's there. Just the bat, leaning a little more. I look back at the book, my Nana's handwriting. "Nana, what were you doing?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The question went unanswered. The sound of her name spoken aloud seemed only to emphasize how thoroughly dead she was, how completely the rooms had settled into cold disuse since the undertaker had pulled the front door shut behind them.

The bat did not move again. It remained tilted against the dark shelf, resting heavy and dull against the mahogany. Yet in the flat, gray glare from the sheer curtains, its shadow fell across the baseboards at an angle that did not quite match the slope of the wood, leaning a few degrees steeper than the ash itself.

Down on the paper, the violet ink caught the daylight. 

The first entry, dated twelve years ago, was your grandfather’s name. *Arthur Vance.* The letters were steady, firm, followed by a time: *4:10 p.m.* 

The second entry was her own. She had written *Eleanor Vance* in the careful, practiced script she had used for forty years of grocery lists and birthday cards. Beside it, the date had been recorded in the same dry ink—not the morning she had been found by the neighbor, cold in the armchair by the front window, but three days prior. A Tuesday afternoon.

The third entry was shorter. 

There was no date filled into the column. There was only your full name, inked in her familiar hand, the stroke of the final letter cutting sharply across the margin as if the pen had been lifted in a hurry. 

Beneath the paper, the unnatural warmth of the binding had faded. The book had gone abruptly, completely cold, like stone pulled from frozen mud.

Out in the corridor, the grandfather clock did not chime. The hollow, rhythmic swing of the pendulum simply ceased mid-motion, caught at the top of its rise with a dull, muffled thud, as though a palm had been pressed flat against the glass to stop it.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The yell was loud and brittle, tearing through the room like paper ripping, but the house gave nothing back.

It hit the faded floral wallpaper and died instantly, flat and thin, without even the courtesy of an echo from the tall ceilings. The heavy wool drapes and the dry shelves of paper seemed to swallow the vibration whole, pulling the noise down into the floorboards until the room was perceptibly quieter than it had been before you opened your mouth. 

The suspended dust motes in the gray light did not scatter from the force of your breath. They hung undisturbed, fixed in the thin air like grit caught in resin.

Nothing laughed. Nothing moved to answer. The joke simply hung there, foolish and small, decaying in the cold draft that had begun to pool around your ankles.

In your hands, the open pages of the parish register lay entirely flat. 

On the right-hand leaf, beneath the dry, slanted letters of your name, the violet ink remained unchanged. But in the blank space beside it—in the column where your grandfather’s time had been recorded, and your grandmother’s date had been marked—the paper was no longer completely smooth. 

A pale, colorless indentation was pressed into the dry pulp, faint as a watermark, where a ballpoint pen had traced the paper without leaving any ink behind. 

A single digit. The curve of a four.

From the hallway, where the clock had stopped its swing, came the faint, dry click of the brass umbrella stand. It had not fallen. It had simply righted itself against the wainscoting, sliding back onto its flat base without a scrape, as if whatever had been leaning against it had just stepped into the room.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My eyes widen.* The four. I look down at the book, then slowly, cautiously, I turn my head towards the hallway. "Nana...?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The whisper did not carry. It dropped between your feet, muffled by the carpet, so faint that even you could barely hear the shape of the word. 

The hallway did not answer. 

Through the open doorway, the corridor lay stretched out in the flat, dying light of late afternoon. The gray glare from the living room curtains reached only as far as the center runner before dissolving into the dull amber shadow near the stairs. 

Nothing stood in the frame. The wainscoting was bare, the wallpaper patterned with the same faded acanthus leaves that had lined the walls for forty years. The air drifting in from the passage was not moving, yet it felt noticeably colder than the room—a steady, dry chill that sank toward the floor, pooling over the tops of your shoes.

Against the far wall of the hall, the tall mahogany case of the clock stood dead. Through its glass door, the brass disc of the pendulum was visible, frozen midway through its swing, caught an inch short of the right-hand wall of the case as if held there by a thumb. 

The brass umbrella stand sat squarely on its base on the foyer tile, perfectly upright now. 

On the wool runner, just three feet past the threshold of the living room, the gray light caught the nap of the faded red wool. In the center of the path, where the fabric was worn thinnest, two shallow depressions were pressed into the weave—narrow, blunt-toed, side by side, resting in the exact posture of someone standing still, waiting to be acknowledged.

They were not rising back up.

Down in your hands, the open leaf of the parish register felt suddenly very light, as thin as dry birch bark against your thumbs.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: My breath catches. I look from the book to the depressions in the rug, then back to the book. My name. The four. "No," I whisper. "No, no, no."

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The denials were only shapes against your teeth, dry and weightless. They did not push back the cold that had begun to creep through the cuffs of your sleeves, nor did they alter the neat, methodical stillness of the house. 

The room simply took the sound and closed around it.

On the right-hand page of *Parish Records, Vol. IV*, the paper gave a faint, microscopic click—the sound of dry fibers yielding under invisible pressure. 

Beside the colorless curve of the four, two tiny, blunt punctures pressed slowly into the paper, stacked one directly above the other. They formed a neat, faint colon. 

*4:*

There was no hand holding a pen. There was only the indentation, settling deep into the grain of the page as though traced by an empty ballpoint pressed hard against the leaf.

Out in the corridor, the air seemed to thicken, taking on the faint, sweetish smell of mothballs and dried mint—the exact scent of the coat closet under the stairs, which had not been opened since the service. 

The two depressions on the hallway runner remained pressed flat into the red wool, unchanging, side by side. But the dust motes that had hung frozen in the doorway for the past ten minutes had finally begun to move. 

They were not drifting down toward the floorboards, nor were they rising in the heat from the radiator. They were drifting horizontally, traveling in a slow, steady stream from the dark hallway into the living room, passing the threshold at the exact height of a woman’s chest, before scattering softly into the cold air around you.

Beyond them, the clock’s brass pendulum hung suspended at its sharp, impossible tilt, refusing to swing back.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The thought was an absurdity, a stray impulse that flickered across your mind like a match struck in a vacuum. It did not catch. In the dead cold of the room, the idea of courtship, of warmth, of someone living and reachable in the world outside felt entirely unreal, as thin and brittle as dried grass.

The snapshot had been tucked loose between the endpapers of the register, dislodged when the heavy volume tilted in your grip. It fluttered down, turning once in the still air before landing face-up against the dark mahogany of the shelf.

It was a small square print with deckle edges, the silver gelatin already silvering out at the margins. Marcus. He was twenty, perhaps twenty-one, leaning against the fender of an unfamiliar sedan with his sleeves rolled to his elbows, squinting into a summer sun that had set half a century ago. The smile was easy, frozen in gray tones that had begun to yellow around the corners.

The paper was stiff and ice-cold to the touch. 

On the back, written in the same dull violet ballpoint your grandmother had used across the register, was a single line in her neat hand: 

*Marcus. 4:10 p.m.*

The ink was dry, sunken deep into the fibrous cardstock. 

Beside you, the ash bat rested dead against the shelves. The room had grown noticeably darker, the afternoon light outside the sheer curtains curdling into the flat, bruised violet of dusk. 

Down on the open page of the register, right beside the faint, colorless indentation of the colon, the dry paper gave another minute, almost imperceptible yield. The fibers parted silently under the press of invisible weight. 

A straight line. Then another, meeting it at an angle. 

*4:1*

From the threshold behind you, the horizontal drift of dust motes did not stop. They continued to filter into the living room, passing through the cold doorway in a slow, level line, parting faintly around the height of your shoulders as if something tall had just stepped quietly into the space directly behind your back.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I grab the photo and shove it into the book, slamming it shut. I don't look behind me. I just walk towards the front door. I need to get out.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The heavy buckram shut with a dead, muffled *thump*. 

There was no crack of air, no echo. The sound was swallowed completely by the dense wool of the curtains and the thousands of unread pages lining the walls, extinguished the second the covers met. The photograph of Marcus was sealed inside, stiff and flat against the register’s endpapers.

To step forward meant crossing the threshold.

The air in the doorway was not a draft; it was a solid pocket of chill, perfectly stationary, carrying that faint, sweetish trace of mothballs and cold skin. Walking through it felt like pushing through hanging linen that had sat in winter storage. It dragged against your face and the wool of your sweater, leaving a dry, numbing prickle across your cheekbones.

You did not look down at the runner. 

Beneath your shoes, the floor did not creak near the radiator where it always had. The red wool was strangely soft underfoot, deadening every step so entirely that you could hear only the rustle of your own coat and the rough, shallow rasp of your breath. 

Out in the hall, the house seemed taller, narrower, the amber shadow by the stairwell stretching upward into the ceiling. 

On the wall to the left, the glass face of the grandfather clock reflected the gray square of the front door's sidelight. Inside the case, the pendulum remained frozen at the top of its arc, refusing to drop. But on the enameled dial above it, the black spade of the minute hand was not where it had been when you wound the weights two weeks ago. 

It sat poised just over the Roman numeral two. Pointing straight at the ten.

The front door was only four strides away. 

The heavy brass turn-latch of the deadbolt caught the dull light from the porch outside. Through the frosted glass oval in the center of the door, the bare branches of the oak tree in the front yard were visible, perfectly motionless against a sky the color of wet slate. 

No cars moved on the avenue. No wind stirred the dried hydrangeas in the porch boxes. 

From the runner behind you, three feet back toward the living room, came the faint, microscopic sound of carpet fibers slowly expanding, lifting back up into the cold air as the weight pressed into them was lifted.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I fumble with the lock, my hands shaking. I just need to get out. Any minute now, something's going to grab me.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
Nothing grabbed you. 

There was no sudden lunge from the dark, no cold fingers closing around the collar of your coat. The house did not deal in that kind of theater. It was far too still, far too settled, to bother with hurry.

The brass turn-latch was biting cold against your thumb, but it did not stick. It turned under your weight with an easy, oiled glide, the heavy cylinder sliding back into the mortise with a clean, flat *click* that died the instant the mechanism settled. 

The door yielded to your push. 

It swung outward on silent hinges, opening three inches into the damp November dusk. The air from the porch drifted across the threshold—heavy with the smell of wet asphalt, rotting maple leaves, and the distant, metallic hum of traffic two streets over. The real world was right there, drab and ordinary, lying just beyond the stone step.

You had only to step across.

Yet behind you, the corridor did not rush to follow. The pocket of air at your back remained completely still, dry and ancient, smelling of mothballs and the pressed pages of closed books. 

Tucked tight beneath your arm, pressed firmly against the heavy wool of your coat, the register gave a minute, muffled vibration. 

It was faint—no louder than a pin dropping onto a rug—but against your ribs, you could feel it clearly through the cloth. Inside the shut volume, between the closed leaves of buckram and dry rag paper, something was moving. A single, smooth, continuous drag of invisible pressure, carving a small, perfect circle into the pulp right beside the one. 

Completing the zero. 

From the center of the dark hall behind you, the frozen grandfather clock did not resume its swing. The pendulum remained suspended in the amber glass, tilted high and motionless. 

Instead, from somewhere deep inside the wooden housing, the chimes engaged with a dull, leaden clink—not striking the hour, but simply shifting into place, waiting for the weight to drop.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I shove the door open the rest of the way and stumble out onto the porch, gasping for breath. I don't look back. I just keep moving, half-running down the steps and onto the sidewalk.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't write anything down. She let the words settle—five seconds, maybe six—her eyes steady on Jamie, not moving to fill the space.

"You found their journal," she finally said.

She set the pen down against the notepad, uncapped but unused.

"Where was it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, picking at a loose thread on my jeans.* "Under their bed. Hidden, I guess."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched Jamie's fingers work at the thread for a moment before she spoke.

"Hidden," she repeated, quietly. "You said hidden, not just put away."

She let that distinction hang there, unclaimed, and shifted slightly in her chair—not toward Jamie, not away.

"Did you read it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't press. She let the silence take up the space Jamie couldn't fill—one second, two, three, four, five—her hands still, resting on the notepad.

"Something happened when you tried to answer that," she said finally. "Right there. You started, and then you stopped."

She tilted her head slightly, not looking away from Jamie's face.

"What was it that stopped you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "It's just... I didn't want to. But I did."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words rest there. Five seconds passed, unhurried, her gaze never leaving Jamie's face.

"You didn't want to. But you did," she said, giving the sentence back exactly as Jamie had said it, no more, no less.

She uncapped her pen again, though she still didn't write.

"What did you think you'd find, before you opened it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez held Jamie's gaze without shifting. She let five seconds pass—the ficus in the corner, the clock without its second hand, the room holding still around them.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last entry."

She didn't ask what it said. Not yet.

"You're looking at me like you expect me to ask. But you're not telling me."

She set the pen down again, fully this time, resting it flat.

"What is it about saying it out loud that's different from having read it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Because... because it's real then, isn't it?" *My voice is barely a whisper.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper sit in the room for a long moment—five seconds, six—not rushing to fill the quiet Jamie had left behind.

"Because it's real then," she said back, just as quietly, though her voice carried its usual steadiness. "As opposed to now."

She studied Jamie—the whisper, the way the shoulders had curled inward, the hands gone still on the thread they'd been picking at.

"Right now, before you say it, what is it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's just words on paper." *I finally look down at my hands again.* "It's not... real."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't move. She let the sentence hang there—five full seconds—watching Jamie's hands, the way they'd gone quiet against the denim.

"Words on paper," she said. "Not real."

She paused again, letting the repetition do its work before continuing.

"You've read it more than once, haven't you."

It wasn't quite a question. She waited to see if Jamie would correct her.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, still not looking up.* "Every day since I found it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let that settle—five seconds, unhurried—her eyes on the top of Jamie's bowed head, on the stillness that had come over the hands.

"Every day since you found it," she echoed.

She waited another moment before continuing, her voice even, measured, no different than if Jamie had told her about the weather.

"What is it you're looking for, reading it again each time? Because it sounds like you already know every word."

She didn't reach for the pen. She kept her hands folded loosely in her lap, giving Jamie the whole of her attention instead.

"Are you checking if it still says the same thing? Or if you feel the same thing, reading it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "I don't know. I just... I don't want to forget."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words settle into the space between them—five seconds, six—the ficus motionless in its corner, the clock silent without its second hand.

"You don't want to forget," she repeated.

She tilted her head slightly, studying the way Jamie still hadn't looked up.

"Forget what, exactly. The words in that entry. Or them. Or something else."

She didn't fill in the blank herself. She left it open, resting her hands in her lap, waiting to see which direction Jamie would carry it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Everything." *My voice cracks a little.* "I don't want to forget anything about them."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the crack in Jamie's voice hang in the air—five seconds, six—not moving to smooth it over, not softening her own face in response. Just watching, steady.

"Everything," she said back. "Not just the last entry. Everything."

She shifted the notepad slightly on her lap, though her pen stayed still.

"You've been reading the same words every day so you don't forget. But you still haven't told me what those words say."

She paused, letting that observation settle before she went further.

"I wonder if there's a difference between remembering them, and remembering what they wrote about you specifically. Those might not be the same thing."

She waited, her eyes not leaving Jamie's face.

"What do you think would happen if you said the words out loud to me right now?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I finally look up, my eyes a little red.* "I don't know. I guess... it would be real." I take a shaky breath. "And then I'd have to deal with it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met Jamie's eyes and held them. Five seconds passed, then six, the red-rimmed look between them the only thing that moved in the room.

"It would be real. And then you'd have to deal with it," she said, giving the words back without adjustment.

She let a breath pass before she went on.

"You've been dealing with it every day already, though. Reading it. Not forgetting. Carrying it around unsaid." She paused, her voice staying level, unhurried. "I wonder what you think you've been avoiding, if the dealing has already been happening."

She didn't move to soften the question. She simply waited, her hands still folded in her lap, giving Jamie the room to sit with it.

"What would be different, do you think—between carrying those words privately, and saying them here, out loud, to me?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I don't know," *I whisper.* "Maybe... maybe I wouldn't be so alone with it."

Dr. Vasquez watched Jamie’s fingers move at the loose thread, then glanced briefly toward the notepad without writing.

She waited.

One second.

“In a box,” she said, her voice even. “In the back of the closet.”

dialogue.name: Jamie

dialogue.name: Jamie

dialogue.name: Jamie

“That is a strong word. It says there was trust there, even after they were gone. A line you believed still mattered.”

She paused.

“And now you’re sitting with the fact that you crossed it.”

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look at her, really look at her, and my eyes are stinging.* "All of it. Everything."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez held Jamie’s gaze, and did not look away from the sting in their eyes.

One second.

Two.

Three.

Four.

Five.

“All of it,” she repeated quietly. “Everything.”

She let the word remain there for a moment.

“That sounds like the journal didn’t feel like one object in a box anymore,” she said. “It became the whole relationship. Their privacy, your memory of them, what existed between you.”

Her pen shifted slightly between her fingers, but she still did not write.

“And if all of it feels betrayed, then there may be no small place to stand right now. No part that feels untouched.”

She paused, her voice steady.

“I want to ask this carefully,” she said. “When you say ‘betrayal,’ does it feel like something you did to them? Or something the journal did to you?”

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the words settle into the room the way dust settles — slowly, finding every surface. She counted the seconds without counting them. A practiced stillness.

Then she set the pen down against the notepad. Not away from it. Just down.

"You found their journal," she said.

It wasn't a question. She gave it back to Jamie exactly as it had arrived, unadorned, the same weight and shape. She watched Jamie's hands rather than Jamie's face. Hands often told her more about where a person was than eyes did. Eyes performed. Hands simply were.

She waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I nod, still not looking at her.* "Yeah. In... in a box of old stuff in the attic."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the silence do its work. The ficus stood in the corner, indifferent. The clock marked nothing in particular.

"A box of old stuff," she repeated. Her voice was even, unhurried. She picked the pen back up, not to write anything, just to hold it. "In the attic."

She watched Jamie's hands. She thought about the word *found* — the way Jamie had used it. Not *came across*. Not *stumbled on*. *Found*, like something that had been lost. Or like something that had been waiting.

She didn't say any of that.

"How long has the box been up there?" she asked instead.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not fill the silence. That was the work — not filling it.

She watched Jamie's hands. She watched the place where the sentence had stopped, the air still holding the shape of it, unfinished. She had learned, over many years, that an interrupted sentence was often more honest than a completed one. The thing a person couldn't say was frequently the very thing they had come here to say.

Five seconds. Six.

"You stopped," she said finally. Quiet. Factual. Not an accusation, not a prompt. Just an observation offered back, the way you might hand someone something they'd dropped without making a thing of it.

She set the pen down again. The same way as before.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I..." *I shake my head, rubbing my temples.* "I don't know why I can't say it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let that sit.

The ficus stood in its slow dying. The clock measured nothing.

"You don't know why you can't say it," she said. Same words. Same weight. She didn't smooth the edges off them or soften what they meant.

She watched Jamie's hands move to Jamie's temples and then she watched them come back down. She thought about the word *can't*. Not *won't*. Not *don't want to*. *Can't*. There was something in that worth holding onto, but she held it herself for now, kept it off the table.

"That's alright," she said. Not reassurance exactly. More like information. A simple fact about the room, about the time they had, about what was and wasn't required of Jamie in this chair.

She waited another moment.

"What happened after you found it?" she asked. "The journal. What did you do with it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez held Jamie's gaze. She did not look away, did not let her expression shift into something anticipatory or hungry for the next piece. She simply received it.

Five seconds. The ficus. The clock.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last entry."

She let that land again, the way it had landed when Jamie said it. *The last entry.* She noticed that Jamie had said *last*, not *final*. She filed that away somewhere quiet.

She did not ask what the entry said. That was the obvious question, the one the room was already leaning toward, and she had learned that the obvious question was often the wrong one. If Jamie wanted to tell her what was in it, Jamie would tell her. The content wasn't hers to reach for.

"What was it like," she said instead, her voice low and unhurried, "to see your name there?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at her question.* "It... it felt like they were still here." *My voice cracks a little.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez saw the flinch. She noted it without reacting to it.

Five seconds. The room held the cracked edge of Jamie's voice the way a cup holds water — carefully, without spilling it.

She did not lean forward. She did not soften her face into something consoling. She stayed exactly where she was, the notepad on the armrest, the pen in her hand, her body simply present and still.

"It felt like they were still here," she said.

She gave it back whole. Didn't reach past it toward the grief she could see sitting just underneath, didn't name it, didn't frame it. Just the words, returned.

She looked at the ficus for a moment. Then back.

"When you say *felt*—" She paused. Chose carefully. "Past tense. While you were reading it. Or still now?"

She waited. The clock said nothing. Outside, somewhere distant, a car passed. The office absorbed it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Still now," *I say, my voice barely a whisper.* "It's like... like they're right here next to me."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper exist in the room without rushing to meet it.

Five seconds. The ficus. The distant sound of the building settling somewhere above them.

"Right here next to you," she said. Her voice matched Jamie's without mimicking it — quiet meeting quiet.

She did not say *that's beautiful* or *that makes sense* or *grief can do that*. She did not explain the feeling back to Jamie in clinical language. She let it be what it was, unnamed, sitting in the space between the two chairs.

She looked at Jamie's hands.

"Has that feeling been there before?" she asked. "Before you found the journal." A small pause. "Or is this new."

It wasn't quite a question. She left the inflection flat at the end, gave Jamie room to take it either way.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "No. It's... it's new."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez stayed with that.

New. She turned the word over without showing that she was turning it over.

Five seconds. The ficus stood in its corner. A door closed somewhere down the hall, muffled and far away.

"New," she said.

She looked at Jamie's hands. Then at the middle distance between them, the air that Jamie had described as occupied.

She thought about the shape of what Jamie was describing — not the return of something familiar, not the grief that had already been learning to live alongside Jamie for however long it had been. Something different. Something the journal had opened.

"It's been—" She paused, calculated quietly. "About eight months since you first came in." She said it without making it mean anything. Just a coordinate. "In those eight months, you've described a lot of things. Absence. Silence. The specific quiet of their side of the bed."

She set the pen flat against the notepad.

"You've never used the word *here* before," she said. "Not like this."

She let that observation rest on the table between them, didn't press on it, didn't ask Jamie to do anything with it. Just placed it there, gently, the way you set something fragile down.

She waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look down at my hands again.* "It wasn't ever... here before." *My voice is still very soft.* "Not like this."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the words settle.

The ficus. The clock. The particular quality of light coming through the blinds that always shifted around this hour, going amber at the edges.

Five seconds. She breathed through them without appearing to.

"Not like this," she said.

She didn't move. She looked at Jamie's hands — the way they rested in Jamie's lap, turned slightly downward, like they weren't sure what they were supposed to hold onto.

She thought about the eight months. About the absence Jamie had described in so many different registers — the quiet, the wrong side of the bed, the specific shape of a missing person rendered in negative space. All of it had been about *not there*. The presence of an absence.

This was something else.

She picked the pen up. Not to write. Just to have something to do with her own hands.

"The journal is still with you?" she asked. "You brought it home."

She kept her voice at the same low, even register. She wasn't asking about the physical object, not entirely. She was asking about what Jamie had done in the hours after finding it — whether Jamie had put it back in the box, closed the box, come straight here. She was asking about the decision Jamie had made, maybe without knowing it was a decision.

She waited, her eyes steady on Jamie's face now, not the hands. Something had shifted in the room and she wanted to see it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "No. It's... it's in my bag." *I gesture vaguely to my backpack on the floor.* "I didn't want to leave it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez looked at the backpack.

She let her gaze rest on it for a moment — the way it sat on the floor beside Jamie's chair, ordinary and worn, carrying what it was carrying. Then she looked back at Jamie.

Five seconds. The amber light moved slightly at the edges of the blinds.

"You didn't want to leave it," she said.

She held that. The backpack. The journal inside it. The eight months of absence that had now, in the space of however many hours, become something that Jamie couldn't put down in an attic and walk away from.

She did not say *of course you didn't* or *that makes complete sense*. She didn't fill the space between *didn't want to leave it* and whatever came next.

She looked at Jamie's hands again. Then at the backpack. Then back.

"When you say you didn't want to leave it—" She paused. Let a breath pass. "What would it have meant, to leave it up there?"

She kept her voice at the same register it had been all session. Unhurried. She was not pushing toward anything. She was simply following the shape of what Jamie was telling her, the way you follow a path in low light — not rushing ahead, just placing one foot where the ground actually was.

The ficus stood in its corner. The room waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pull my knees up to my chest, hugging them.* "Like... like leaving them again."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move.

The room absorbed it. The ficus. The clock. The amber light.

Five seconds. Six. She let the seventh pass too.

She looked at Jamie — the knees pulled up, the arms wrapped around them, the body making itself smaller in the chair. She had seen this before, this particular shape a person took when they were holding something they didn't know how to set down. She did not comment on it. She did not reach toward it.

"Like leaving them again," she said.

She gave it back exactly as it had arrived. No additions. No softening. She let it sit in the air between them, let Jamie hear it from the outside the way it must have sounded from the inside — the full weight of it, the logic of it, the way a journal in a backpack on a floor could become a person who could be left or not left.

She looked at the backpack.

Then at her notepad. She didn't write anything. She just looked at it for a moment, the blank space of it, and then back at Jamie.

"You found it this morning?" she asked. Her voice was quiet. She wasn't sure of the timeline and she wanted to be sure. "Or before."

She waited. Outside, somewhere, a bird. The building settling again. The particular silence of a room where something true had just been said.

dialogue.content: "Yesterday." *I mumble into my knees.* "I spent all night reading it."

dialogue.name: Jamie

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez

Five seconds passed.

"Heavy," she repeated. "Like it weighed a ton."

The pen still hadn't moved. She let her gaze rest somewhere near Jamie's hands, giving them room to be looked at or not looked at.

"A journal doesn't weigh much," she said slowly, evenly. "Not by itself."

"So I wonder what was in it that made it so heavy to hold."

dialogue.name: Jamie

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not finish it for them.

That was the temptation, always — to reach into the silence and hand someone the end of their own sentence, tidy and complete. She resisted it the way she'd trained herself to resist it, letting the unfinished thing sit there unfinished.

Five seconds. Then more than five. She let it stretch.

The ficus dropped a leaf in the corner, a small brown thing drifting to the carpet. She didn't look at it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pick at a loose thread on my jeans.* "It's just... it was like reading a stranger." My voice is quiet.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the thread turn between Jamie's fingers, the small repetitive worrying of it.

Five seconds.

"Like reading a stranger," she said.

She let the word *stranger* sit in the room, unhurried, the way she'd let everything sit. The dying ficus, the missing second hand, the quiet — all of it made space for the word.

"You knew them," she said. Not a question, but she left the edge of it open, the way you leave a door open a crack. "And what you found in those pages felt like someone you didn't."

She kept her hands loose in her lap. The pen stayed down.

Her eyes went to the thread, then back to Jamie's face, patient.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met Jamie's eyes when they lifted. She held the gaze without pressing into it — steady, soft, a place to land if Jamie wanted one, nothing demanded if they didn't.

Five seconds.

"They wrote about you," she said. "In the last entry."

She let the weight of *last* stay in the room. She didn't move toward it. That word had its own gravity, and she trusted Jamie to feel it without her naming it.

The pen stayed against the notepad. Her hands stayed open.

"You looked at me just now," she said, her voice as even as ever. "When you said it."

A pause. She let that observation breathe.

"You're holding something," she said slowly. "What was written, and whether to say it out loud in this room." She tilted her head, just slightly. "Both of those can be true at once. You can have read it and still not be ready to speak it."

She let the quiet return, unforced.

"When you looked at me — what were you checking for?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pick at the thread again.* "If you'd look at me differently."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:

Five seconds.

"If I'd look at you differently," she said.

"So there's something in that last entry," she said slowly, "that you think might change how you're seen." A pause, careful, unhurried. "That you might be looked at differently once it's known."

She let the pen rest. Her hands stayed open in her lap.

"I've been looking at you this whole time," she said. Even. Quiet. "And you don't know yet what's in my face, because you haven't said it."

"You're afraid of what my face will do," she said. "But you're the one who'd have to say the words first to find out." She tilted her head, barely. "That's a hard place to stand."

A pause.

"What do you imagine I'd see?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "That... that I'm not good." *My voice cracks a little.* "That I wasn't a good sibling."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:

Five seconds. Then a little more.

"That's what you think the entry says about you," she said slowly. "And that's what you think I'd see, if I read it in your face."

The pen stayed down. The ficus stood in the corner with its brown leaf on the carpet.

dialogue.name: Jamie

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez

dialogue.name: Jamie

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
