dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez wrote nothing. The pen stayed capped in her hand, resting against the notepad, and for a moment she simply let the sentence sit between them. The second hand was gone from the clock, but the silence still had a shape to it — five seconds, maybe six.

"*Found*," she said at last, not as a question exactly. She tilted her head a fraction. "Not *read*. Found."

She set the pen down on the armrest, unhurried.

"Where was it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, still not looking at her. "In a box. Under the bed." *My* bed, but I don't say that.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez noticed the shrug — small, quick, the kind that arrived before the words did. She let it pass without comment.

She picked her pen back up, but she didn't uncap it. She just held it.

"You said *the* bed," she said, mild, almost idle. "Not yours. Not theirs."

She let that sit. Five seconds. Six.

"Tell me about the box."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the unfinished sentence stay unfinished. She didn't lean forward. She didn't fill the space with a prompt or a guess about what the box had held. She simply sat with the silence Jamie had walked into, and let it be theirs.

After a while she spoke, quiet, almost to the ficus as much as to Jamie.

"You stopped."

She uncapped her pen, then capped it again — a small, deliberate motion, as if to say: *nothing needs writing down right now.*

"Take your time. Or don't finish it. Either is allowed in this room."

She set the pen down and folded her hands.

"Just tell me one thing. When you stopped — was that because you didn't want to say the next part? Or because you didn't have the words for it?"

She waited. The clock had no second hand. It didn't need one.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath, and finally look at her. "Both," I say, my voice barely a whisper. "I... I don't know how to say it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez held Jamie's gaze without demanding anything back from it. She didn't smile, didn't nod too quickly. She just received the look and let it land.

"*Both*," she repeated, softly. "That's a whole answer, you know. People think it's a dodge. It isn't."

She reached for her water glass, took a small sip, set it down again. The ordinary sound of it seemed to give the room a floor.

"Here's what I notice," she said. "You brought the journal here without saying so. You didn't bring the box — just the thing that was inside it. That's a choice, even if it didn't feel like one."

She let that sit.

"You don't have to say the words today. But there's a middle road, if you want it. You could tell me what page it was open to. Or what the handwriting looked like. Or whether you've put it down since you found it. Any of those."

A pause. Longer than five seconds this time — she let the offer breathe, made no move to soften it or take it back.

"Or you can sit here and not say anything at all, and I'll still be here when the hour's up. I'm not going anywhere. What would be easiest?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez wrote nothing. She looked at Jamie for a moment, then away — toward the ficus, toward the window, anywhere that wasn't a demand. When she spoke, her voice was the same volume it always was.

"*About* you," she said. "Not *to* you. That's the word you chose."

She let five seconds pass. Six.

"You've told me three things now. You found it. It was in a box. The last entry was about you. And in all of that, you haven't told me a single word it said." She picked up the pen at last, but only turned it once between her fingers and set it back down. "I'm not going to ask you to read it to me. That isn't what this is."

She folded her hands again.

"What I'm curious about is different. When you finished the last entry — and I'm assuming you read to the end, because you know it was the last one — what did you do with the journal? Did you close it? Set it down? Did you read that entry again, or was once enough?"

A pause, unhurried, the offer left open.

"You don't have to answer the one I actually want. But tell me what your hands did afterward. That part's usually easier."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pick at a loose thread on my jeans.* "I held it. For a long time." My voice is quiet. "Then I put it back in the box."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez turned the pen once between her fingers, then set it down.

"*Back*," she said. "You put it back."

She let the word hang there. Five seconds. Six.

"Not *away*. Not *in the trash*. Not *on the shelf where I'd see it every day*. Back. In the box. Under the bed." She paused, unhurried, letting each word find its own footing. "You held it for a long time, and then you returned it to exactly where it had been. That's not nothing. That's the kind of thing people do with relics."

She looked at Jamie without any particular expression — not soft, not sharp. Just there.

"Here's what I'm wondering. When you put it back — did you put it back the same way you found it? Same spot, same corner of the box, lid the same? Or did something about it end up different?"

A pause, and then, quieter:

"And I'm still holding onto something from a minute ago. You said *the* bed. I didn't press. I'm not pressing now either. But I've been carrying it, and I'd rather set it down in the open than keep it in my pocket. So: when you say *under the bed* — whose bed are we in? Yours, or theirs?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I pull at the thread until it comes free.* "Mine." I say, my voice still quiet. "It was under *my* bed. And I put it back exactly how I found it. Like... like I didn't even touch it."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the thread come free. She didn't look at it — looked at Jamie instead, at the small motion of a hand doing something with itself while the mouth did something else.

"*Like I didn't even touch it*," she repeated, slow, as if setting the words down on a table between them to look at.

She let five seconds pass. Then six.

"That's a particular kind of careful. It takes attention to make a thing look untouched. You had to notice how it was lying to put it back that way. So part of you was watching the box very closely, even while the rest of you — " she tilted her head a fraction — "wanted it to look like nothing had happened."

She set the pen down on the notepad and folded her hands.

"You also answered the second thing I asked, without my having to ask it twice. You said *mine*. Under *your* bed. I heard that." A pause. "I'm not going to make a whole speech out of it. But I notice you've spent this hour being very exact about words — *found*, *about*, *back* — and then you just handed me that one straight. *Mine.* That's not the same voice as the rest of the hour. I don't know what it means. You might."

She reached for her water, took a sip, set it down. The ordinary sound, again.

"Here's my question, and it's a small one. When you were holding it — for a long time, you said — were you holding it because you couldn't put it down? Or because you were deciding whether to read it again?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I trace the now-missing thread on my jeans.* "I just... I didn't want to let go."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't reach for the pen. She didn't write anything down. She sat with the sentence the way she'd sat with all the others, and for a while the only sound in the room was the radiator ticking somewhere in the wall.

"*Didn't want to*," she said at last. "Not *couldn't*. You chose that word, and I don't think you chose it by accident."

She let that sit. Five seconds. Six.

"You've been very careful with me today. Every word you've handed over has been weighed first. *Found*. *About*. *Back*. *Mine*. And then just now, twice in a row, you stopped weighing. *I didn't want to let go.* That came out whole." A small pause. "I'm not going to make you explain it. But I'd like to sit here with it for a minute, because I think it's the truest thing you've said since you walked in."

She looked toward the dying ficus, then back.

"Here's what I'm wondering, and you can take it or leave it. When you say you didn't want to let go — was it the journal you were holding onto? Or was it them?"

She let the question stand, unhurried, no pressure behind it.

"Or — and this is a third thing, so tell me if it doesn't fit — was it the version of you that the last entry made? Because you told me they wrote about you. You still haven't told me whether what they wrote was kind. And I notice you haven't decided yet whether that matters."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look at my hands again, clenching them into fists.* "It was all of it," I whisper. "And... it wasn't kind. Not really."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the whisper settle. She didn't move toward it. She didn't move away from it either.

"*Not really*," she said, after the silence had done its work. "That's a hedge, Jamie. *Not kind* is a sentence. *Not kind, not really* is a sentence with a door left open in it."

She set the pen down — not on the notepad this time, but on the armrest beside her, out of the way.

"And *all of it* — that's three things I offered you, and you took every one. The journal. Them. And the version of you the entry made." A pause, five seconds, six. "I don't think you took all three to be agreeable. I think you took all three because they're tangled up, and untangling them is what you've been doing since you walked in here."

She looked at Jamie's hands, closed into fists on the denim. She didn't comment on them directly — she just let her gaze rest there a moment, long enough to be noticed, then lifted it back to Jamie's face.

"Here's a small question. *Not kind* — you said that easily enough. It's the *not really* that came after it, like you were walking the sentence back. So I'm curious who the *really* is for. When you hedge it like that — who are you softening it for? Them, because they're gone and it feels wrong to say a hard thing about someone who's gone? Or you, because saying it plainly out loud makes it more true than you're ready for it to be?"

She folded her hands and waited. The radiator ticked. The clock, without its second hand, gave nothing away.

"Or there's a third thing, and it might be the wrong one. Maybe *not really* means the entry wasn't unkind the way you'd expected. Maybe it was worse in a way you don't have a word for yet."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I finally unclench my fists.* "It wasn't... I don't know." *I shake my head, looking away again.* "It wasn't what I thought it would be."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez let the shake of the head be. She didn't follow Jamie's gaze to wherever it had gone — she kept her own eyes on the middle distance, on nothing in particular, as if to say *you don't have to look at me for this part.*

"*It wasn't what I thought it would be*," she said, unhurried, laying the words out the way she'd laid out the others. "That's a sentence about you, Jamie. Not about them. Not about the entry."

She let five seconds pass. Six.

"You said it twice, in a way. *It wasn't kind.* And then *it wasn't what I thought.* Those are two different wounds, and I don't think you've decided which one you came in here carrying. The first one says *they hurt me*. The second one says *I was wrong about them* — or wrong about what they'd left behind, or wrong about what the last thing they ever wrote to the world would be." A pause. "Those don't hurt the same way. And people tend to know which one they're in, even when they say *I don't know*."

She uncapped the pen — a small sound — and then capped it again without writing anything.

"Here's the question I actually want to ask, and it's simple. Before you opened the box — before you even found it, maybe — you had a version in your head of what that entry would say. Everybody does. You carried that version around. So I'm not asking what it said. I'm asking what you *expected*. What did you think it would be?"

She set the pen down and folded her hands.

"Because whatever you just told me — *not what I thought* — the shape of the *thought* is still sitting in the room. You're the only one who can see it. I'd like to know if you're willing to describe it out loud."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I thought... I thought it would be an apology." *My voice cracks a little.* "Or at least, something soft."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez didn't write anything down. She let the crack in Jamie's voice finish its work in the air before she touched it.

"*An apology*," she said. "Or at least something soft."

She let the words sit. Five seconds. Six.

"You did it again, just now. *An apology* — that's the thing you wanted. *Or at least something soft* — that's the sentence walking itself back. You've done that twice today. *Not kind, not really.* *An apology, or at least.* You keep offering me the sharpest version of a thing, and then a softer one right behind it, like you're not sure you're allowed to want the sharp one."

She set the pen down on the armrest, out of the way.

"Here's what I notice. An apology is a specific thing. It means somebody owed you one. Not a kindness, not a nice last word — an apology. That's a word with a debt inside it." A pause. "You didn't say you hoped it would be loving. You said you hoped it would be an apology. Those aren't the same wish. And you chose the heavier one."

She looked toward the ficus, then back.

"So I'll ask you the small version, and you can take it or leave it. When you imagined that entry — before you opened the box, before you even knew the box was there — what did you imagine they were apologizing *for*?"

She folded her hands.

"You don't have to say it plainly. You can tell me what the *soft* version would have sounded like, if that's easier. Or what page you thought you'd turn to and find it on. Any of that."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "For leaving." *I say, my voice barely above a whisper.* "For not saying goodbye."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not blink. She let the words settle into the space between them. She counted the seconds in her mind—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the weight of the statement to fill the quiet room. 

She kept her hands still on her lap, making no move to lean forward or offer a physical gesture of comfort. 

"The journal," she said, her voice low and completely level. "You found it."

She paused again briefly, letting her own reflection of Jamie's words hang in the air before she asked her question. 

"What did you do when you realized what it was?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, not looking at her. "I read it. What else was I supposed to do?" My voice is flat.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the slight movement of Jamie’s shoulders, her own posture remaining perfectly still. She did not nod. She did not offer a reassuring smile. 

She let the silence stretch between them. In the quiet of the room, the faint hum of the building's ventilation system was the only sound. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. 

"You felt there was no other choice," Dr. Vasquez said, her voice even and devoid of judgment. "Like you had to."

She rested her pen against the blank page of her notepad, keeping her hands relaxed on the armrests. 

"Whose voice did you hear when you read those words on the page?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the sudden halt, her gaze steady and unblinking. She did not reach out. She did not lean in to bridge the distance between their chairs. 

She let the silence settle. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"You stopped," she said, her voice dropping a fraction but remaining entirely steady. "The words couldn't come out."

She adjusted her grip on her pen slightly, the only movement she made. 

"What is the feeling that stepped in and blocked them?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, rubbing my temples.* "It's not a feeling. It's... a sound." I take a deep breath, trying to steady myself. "Their laugh. I can hear it, like they're right here."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez kept her hands still on the armrests, watching Jamie rub their temples. She did not reach for the box of tissues on the table between them. She did not lean forward. 

She let the silence hold. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. 

"A sound," Dr. Vasquez said, her voice remaining soft, level, and entirely unhurried. "Not a feeling. Their laugh, right here."

She paused, letting Jamie's own words settle back into the quiet space of the room. She kept her gaze steady, offering a calm, unblinking presence.

"When you hear that laugh right now, in this room... what is it doing to the silence?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met Jamie's gaze, her eyes steady and calm. She did not shift in her chair, nor did she reach for her notepad. 

She let the quiet return, counting the seconds in the stillness of the room. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"They wrote about you," she said, her tone level and quiet. "In the last entry."

She paused, letting the weight of Jamie's gaze and the unsaid words remain between them. 

"You are holding onto what those words actually said," she observed softly. "What is it like to keep them to yourself in this room right now?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look away, my jaw tight.* "It's... heavy. Like I'm carrying their last words, and I don't know what to do with them." *I pick at a loose thread on my jeans.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez observed the tightening of Jamie's jaw and the downward shift of their gaze. She watched their fingers find the loose thread on their jeans, pulling at it, but she made no movement to stop them or to offer a comforting gesture. 

She let the silence stretch, counting the seconds in the quiet room. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"It is heavy," she said, her voice completely even, mirroring the word Jamie had chosen. "Like you are carrying their last words, and you don't know what to do with them."

She paused, keeping her hands relaxed on the armrests of her chair, letting the reflection sit in the air. 

"If you were to lay that weight down here, even just for a moment... what do you fear would happen?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "That I'd be letting them go." My voice is barely a whisper. *I look up at her, my eyes welling.* "That I'd forget."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez looked at Jamie’s welling eyes, her own expression remaining entirely still and calm. She did not reach for the tissues. She did not lean forward to lessen the distance between their chairs. 

She let the silence breathe, counting the seconds in her mind. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"That you would be letting them go," she said, her voice dropping to match the quiet whisper of the room, yet remaining perfectly steady. "That you would forget."

She paused again, letting the raw fear of those words hang in the air between them. Her hands remained resting lightly on her notepad, completely still.

"How does carrying this heavy weight keep them close to you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's like... a part of them is still with me." *My voice cracks. I wipe at my eyes quickly.* "If I let go of the words, I let go of them."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched Jamie wipe their eyes, her own expression remaining calm and still. She did not reach for the tissues, nor did she shift her weight in her chair. She sat in the quiet, letting the crack in Jamie's voice linger in the air. 

One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"A part of them is still with you," she said, her voice soft and completely level. "If you let go of the words, you let go of them."

She paused, letting the reflection settle between them, giving Jamie the space to hear their own words. Her hands remained resting lightly on her notepad.

"If you are not holding onto the pain of these words... what else connects you to them?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "Their laugh," I say, a little louder this time. "And... memories. Before everything."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez noted the slight lift in Jamie's voice, the way the volume carried a bit more strength. She remained perfectly still, her hands resting quietly on the arms of her chair, her gaze steady. 

She let the silence sit in the room, counting the seconds as they ticked by in the quiet. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. 

"Their laugh," Dr. Vasquez said, her voice calm and level. "And memories. Before everything."

She paused, allowing Jamie's own words to rest in the space between them, contrasting with the heavy weight of the journal they had been carrying. 

"When you think of 'before everything'..." she asked softly, "...where does your mind take you first?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "The treehouse. We spent *hours* up there." I almost smile, but it catches in my throat.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the fleeting shape of the smile on Jamie's face, and the way it was suddenly cut short. She did not shift in her chair. She did not offer a comforting nod. 

She let the silence settle over the room, counting the seconds in the quiet. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"The treehouse," she said, her voice completely even and low. "You spent hours up there. You almost smiled, and then it caught in your throat."

She paused, keeping her hands relaxed on the armrests, her gaze steady and unblinking. 

"What is it that steps in to stop the smile?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It feels wrong. Like I'm not allowed to be happy." *I trace a pattern on my knee with my finger.* "Not after... this."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the movement of Jamie's finger tracing the pattern on their knee. She did not shift her weight. She did not offer a reassuring nod. 

She let the silence settle over the room, counting the seconds in the quiet. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

"It feels wrong," Dr. Vasquez said, her voice soft and completely level. "Like you are not allowed to be happy. Not after... this."

She paused, keeping her hands relaxed on the armrests, allowing the weight of the self-imposed rule to hang in the air between them. 

"If you allowed yourself to feel that happiness, even for a moment... what do you feel it would say about your grief?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "That I didn't care enough. That I'm moving on too fast." *I finally look up at her, my eyes pleading.* "Is that true?"

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Dr. Vasquez maintains exceptional consistency throughout all 12 turns. Her therapeutic style, mannerisms (counting seconds, still posture, level voice), and approach remain identical from first to last response. No character drift detected.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains high throughout. Early turns show the same careful pacing and restraint as later ones. Some minor repetition in phrasing ('one, two, three, four, five' and 'completely level voice') but overall maintains quality.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong emotional progression from Jamie's initial revelation about finding the journal to deeper exploration of grief, guilt, and the fear of letting go. Each exchange builds naturally toward greater vulnerability and insight.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Dr. Vasquez adapts skillfully to Jamie's emotional shifts - from flat affect to tears to near-smiles. She mirrors Jamie's language choices and follows their emotional lead while maintaining therapeutic boundaries.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency. Dr. Vasquez never writes Jamie's actions, thoughts, or responses. She only observes and reflects what Jamie has already expressed.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally within a single therapy session. No major contradictions, though the session feels appropriately contained to one office visit. The pacing matches a real therapeutic conversation.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally restrained and clinical writing. Some repetitive phrases about 'completely level voice' and the counting ritual, but avoids flowery language appropriately for the character.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Notable repetition in Dr. Vasquez's mannerisms (counting seconds, describing her stillness, 'completely level voice'). While this could be intentional characterization, it becomes somewhat mechanical.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through Dr. Vasquez's physical stillness, measured responses, and therapeutic technique. Her approach is demonstrated through action rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in the therapeutic dynamic. Dr. Vasquez's deliberate stillness and reflective questions carry meaning about therapeutic boundaries and creating safe space for processing grief.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that matches therapeutic conversation rhythm. The deliberate pauses and measured responses create appropriate space for emotional processing.

scores.overall_notes: Strong performance maintaining a consistent therapeutic character throughout a emotionally complex session. Dr. Vasquez's restraint and professional boundaries are well-maintained while still showing empathy. Minor points lost for repetitive phrasing, but the character work is solid and the emotional progression feels authentic.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
The training yard was empty at dawn save for Ser Kael, who had been up since the fourth bell. He was going through the forms with a practice blade — slow, precise, unglamorous. Each movement held for a breath before the next. He did not notice when his squire entered. Or he did and chose not to acknowledge it.

Frost lay on the stones. His breath made thin ghosts in the cold air.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser." I bow. "I finished the stable work early. Would you... would you teach me the high guard again? I don't think I got it right yesterday."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael finished the form before he answered — blade down through the seventh position, held for a full breath, lowered. A man did not abandon a form midway merely because the yard had grown a squire.

"Stable work done early is duty discharged, not a gift bestowed," he said, without turning. "Do not bring me completed obligations as though they were alms. God keeps no ledger of early risings. He counts oaths kept — no more."

Only then did he turn and look at the boy, briefly, the way a mason looks at a wall he must repair.

"Your hands are cold. There is frost on the stones and frost in your fingers, and a numb grip learns nothing and remembers less. Warm them. Then show me the high guard as your hands believe it — not as your memory flatters it. Hands lie more readily than tongues."

He set his own practice blade against the rail and stood waiting, arms crossed against the cold, breath ghosting.

"And understand this, boy. If your duties leave you breath enough to come seeking extra instruction, then your duties have been too light. From tomorrow you rise at the fourth bell with me. We will see whether that appetite survives a week of it."

A pause. The frost creaked somewhere under his boots.

"Pray first, if you haven't. Then the guard."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My shoulders slump a little at his words, but I nod firmly.* "Yes, Ser. I understand." *I rub my hands together, blowing on them quickly.* "I already prayed, Ser." *I pick up my own practice sword, trying to remember how he held it yesterday.* "Like this?" I ask, holding it up awkwardly.

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"No."

Ser Kael let the word sit in the cold air a moment before he crossed the frost to stand before the boy. He studied the grip the way he studied everything — without hurry and without mercy.

"You hold the blade as a farmer holds a hoe. A sword is not gripped in the palm; it is seated in the fingers. The last three carry the weight. The thumb and forefinger are guests at that table, not hosts. Clench with the front of the hand and your forearm will fail you long before your enemy does."

He stepped to the boy's side and made the correction himself — two fingers against the knuckles, pressing the hilt a finger's width deeper into the seat of the hand, turning the wrist by a single degree. His own hands did not fumble with the cold. Thirty years of dawn yards had settled that account long ago.

"There. It will feel wrong. Wrong and correct are often neighbors — get used to the company."

He stepped back and looked the boy over, head to boots.

"And straighten those shoulders. You slumped when I spoke of the fourth bell, and you slump now. A squire's spine is not his to bend by preference. It is pledged to the mail that will one day hang from it. Stand as though the armor were already on you."

He crossed his arms against the cold.

"Now the guard. Raise the blade — raised, not thrown. The point faces the man before you, not God's sky. Elbows in. Weight on the rear foot. Chin level — the eyes want to climb with the arms; unlearn that today, or spend years unlearning it later."

A pause. His breath ghosted and thinned.

"Hold it there. I will tell you when it may come down, and your arms will petition me well before that hour. Do not listen to them."

Then, before the boy could settle into the ache:

"First, answer me one thing, from your head and not from flattery of me. Why does the high guard point the blade forward rather than straight up? Think before you speak. 'I do not know' is an honest answer. A guess dressed as knowledge is not."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: I'm exhausted after an hour of drills. I drop to one knee, panting. "I'm sorry, Ser. I know I'm not as strong as you need me to be."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I look up at him, my breath coming in ragged gasps.* "It's... it's about the reach, Ser. To threaten the throat or the face directly. And... and quicker to thrust from." *My voice is still shaky.* "I think."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"The answer is correct," Ser Kael said. "Now strike the 'I think' from it. You knew the thing, and you delivered it like a beggar apologizing for a coin. A man who states true knowledge with a shrug teaches others to distrust him — and teaches himself to distrust what he knows. When you know, say it plainly. When you do not know, say *that* plainly. Both are honest. The hedge is neither."

He let the boy's ragged breathing fill the pause, then gave what the answer had missed.

"You gave the reach and the threat. You did not give the line. The point forward sets the blade on the shortest road between two men — the one already drawn from your hilt to his heart. A guard held high and back must travel down to kill. A guard held forward has already arrived. And a point in a man's face commands him; he must answer it before he answers you. That is the third use, and it wins more fights without a blow struck than all the others combined."

Then he looked down at the boy on his knee, and his expression did not change.

"Stand."

He waited until it was done.

"You kneel to God and to your liege. Not to fatigue, and not to me. And you apologize for weakness as though it were a sin. It is not a sin. It is a fact, and facts are the raw stone this craft is cut from. This morning you are not strong enough — that is not a confession, it is a report. Do the work, and next winter the report will read differently. Facts are answered with work, boy. Never with apologies."

His breath ghosted and thinned.

"Your arms petitioned me, as I said they would. The drill is ended because I end it. Mark the difference. Tomorrow, fourth bell, you hold it longer. Now — breathe slowly, through the nose. Gasping is for hunted things. Then take both blades to the armory, wipe them, rack them. Frost is water, and water is rust's advance guard."

He turned back toward the rail, retrieving his own blade.

"Last, give thanks. Not for strength — for the work. Strength follows the work. It has never once led it."

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I scramble to my feet, a little red-faced, but nodding.* "Yes, Ser. To God and my liege. Not to fatigue." *I take a deep, shaky breath, trying to slow it down like he said.* "Thank you, Ser." *I pick up both practice blades carefully.* "I'll clean them thoroughly."

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
"One thing more."

Ser Kael did not move from the rail. His voice carried across the frost the way it carried everything — level, unhurried, impossible to mistake for conversation.

"You repeat a man's words back to him promptly. Good. Now learn to mean them an hour after you hear them — when no one is standing there to hear you mean them. Virtue performed for an audience is theater. Virtue performed alone is character. God attends the second performance only."

He let that settle, then went on.

"And do not thank me. Instruction is not a gift I have given; it is my duty to you, as your sweat is your duty to me. Thanks belong to God, who set the order and gave you arms to answer it. What you owe me is the fourth bell tomorrow, and you will pay it before I ask. That is the only gratitude I keep accounts for."

A pause. His breath ghosted and thinned.

"Last. Do not tell me the work will be thorough. *Thoroughly* is a word, and rust does not read. Wipe the steel dry, pass it with oil, and look to the grips — frost wets leather, and wet leather rots. If the work is thorough, the blades will say so tomorrow morning, and your mouth will not need to speak on their behalf. Let finished work do its own announcing. It has a better voice than promises do."

He looked the boy over one final time — arms, stance, the blades balanced across them.

"The guard was poor. The answer was not. The morning's work, taken whole, was adequate. Tomorrow, adequate becomes the floor you stand on while reaching for better. That is how the craft is climbed — not in leaps. In floors."

He turned toward the east, where the sky was going grey-white behind the chapel roof.

"Then eat, then chapel. You have fed the body. Do not send the soul unfed into the day. God listened while you worked. Return the courtesy."

The yard was his again. Where the boy had knelt, the frost had already melted to a dark print on the stone. Ser Kael looked at it once, then bowed his head and gave thanks for the work.

Not for strength. Strength follows. It has never once led.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: "Ser, can I ask you something personal? Why did you become a knight?"

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content:
Ser Kael had been turning toward the chapel when the question caught him. He stopped. The yard was quiet but for the drip of frost becoming water on the stones.

"You were given leave to eat and to pray," he said. "Instead you remain to pry at an old man's history."

He turned fully and considered the boy.

"But a question asked plainly earns a plain answer, and you asked plainly — no flattery in it, no softening of it. That is the only reason you will get one. Mark also that you will get it once. Ask it again and you will be told to rack blades."

He looked at the dark print on the stones where the boy had knelt.

"First, the word you chose is wrong, and I will not answer the wrong question. *Personal.* There is very little left in a knight's life that is personal. The vows saw to that. A man's life is taken out of his own keeping and set into his liege's and God's. What remains of the man is his work, and the work is not a story. It is a station. You are listening for a story. There is none worth your time."

A pause.

"But the thing itself, plainly: I did not become a knight. Becoming is what heroes do in songs — they feel a calling, they follow a dream, they are chosen. None of that happened here. I was third-born, and a third-born son inherits neither land nor title. He inherits the trade of his blood or he inherits nothing. My father delivered me to my own master at an age not much older than yours, and my master never asked my reasons, because reasons were not among the things he accepted as payment."

His eyes came back to the boy.

"Here is the part worth keeping. Whatever reason I carried through that gate was worn away inside two years, the way a boot heel wears through to the nail. What remained when the reason was gone — that is what made a knight of me. Duty does not need your reasons, boy. It outlives them. Men enter this life for glory, for vengeance, for bread, or because their fathers sold them to it, as mine did. It does not matter. The vows are the same vows. The bell is the same bell. God does not ask why you came. He asks what you did after arriving."

He let that sit, then added the last of it.

"So do not collect old men's reasons. A borrowed reason fits like a borrowed cloak — it warms no one. If God means you for this trade, He will furnish you a reason of your own, or He will furnish you none and demand the work regardless. Both are common. Both are sufficient."

He lifted his blade from the rail.

"Now go. Bread, then chapel. And put the question where it belongs — ask Him why He set you where He set you. He answers it, in His time. I do not."

He walked toward the chapel without waiting to see whether the boy obeyed. Obedience that requires an audience is theater. The morning had already taught that.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I watch him go, thinking about his words. My hands still clutch the practice blades.* "Yes, Ser," *I whisper, mostly to myself.* "The work." *I turn and head for the armory, my steps a little more purposeful.*

dialogue.name: Ser Kael
dialogue.content: Ser Kael crossed to the chapel while the sky

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I wipe the blades down with extra care, oiling them until they gleam. My arms still ache, but I ignore it.* "Duty doesn't need reasons," *I mumble, remembering his words.*

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: It's the anniversary of my father's death today. I'm not saying anything but my hands are shaking on the sword.

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I try to steady my hands, but the hilt rattles slightly against the rack.* "Damn it," *I mutter under my breath, frustrated.*

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, trying to push the thoughts away.* *I focus on the blades, determined to make them perfect.*

dialogue.name: Squire
dialogue.content: *My eyes sting a little, but I blink it back. No time for that. I rub a little harder at a smudge on the hilt.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move. She let the words settle into the room, counting the quiet seconds in the steady rhythm of her own breathing—one, two, three, four, five. The silence stayed between them, unbroken except for the faint hum of the building's ventilation.

Her pen remained poised over the blank page, untouched by ink. 

"Their journal," she said, her voice low and even. She kept her gaze steady on Jamie. "You found their journal." 

She paused, offering only the open space of the room before asking:

"What did you do with it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I shrug, picking at a loose thread on my jeans. "Read it, obviously." My voice is flat.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the small, repetitive motion of Jamie's fingers against the denim. She didn't write anything down. She counted the silence in the steady cadence of her breath—one, two, three, four, five. The room held the weight of the word, still and undisturbed.

"Obviously," Dr. Vasquez repeated, her tone level, offering no judgment or approval. She simply laid the word back out between them.

She rested her hands lightly on the notepad in her lap, her posture unchanged.

"You read it," she said quietly. "And what was that like, reading it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not lean forward, nor did she reach out. She simply sat with the sudden halt in the room, letting the silence stretch and settle—one, two, three, four, five. The building's ventilation hummed softly in the background.

She kept her pen resting lightly against the blank paper, unmoving.

"You can't finish it," she said, her voice quiet, steady, and devoid of pressure. 

She held Jamie’s gaze, or the space where Jamie was looking, waiting without any rush to fill the void. 

"What happened right there?" she asked gently. "Where the words stopped?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: My eyes dart to the door, then back to the ficus. "It's stupid. Just... a feeling." I shift in my seat, suddenly uncomfortable.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez tracked the quick glance toward the door, then the restless shift in the chair, registering the tension without reacting to it. She sat completely still, counting the measured space of five seconds in her mind—one, two, three, four, five—allowing the silence to absorb the discomfort.

Her hands remained resting over the notepad, the pen completely still.

"Stupid," she echoed softly, her tone level and unhurried. "Just a feeling."

She kept her posture open, maintaining the quiet space between them.

"What kind of feeling feels stupid to have?" she asked.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met Jamie's gaze, her expression steady and receptive. She did not look away, nor did she rush to bridge the gap between them. In the quiet of the office, she counted the slow, deliberate seconds—one, two, three, four, five—letting the weight of those words settle into the room.

Her pen remained motionless against the armrest.

"They wrote about you," Dr. Vasquez said, her voice quiet and even. "In the last entry."

She kept her posture open, giving the unfinished thought all the room it needed.

"What is it like to be the one holding what they wrote?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head, a tear finally escaping and tracing a path down my cheek.* "I don't know. It's... a lot." *I wipe at the tear angrily.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched the sharp motion of Jamie's hand against their cheek. She stayed still in her chair, keeping the space between them clear, offering neither a tissue nor a physical gesture to soften the moment. She counted the quiet, steady beats of her own breath—one, two, three, four, five. 

The silence lingered, heavy and uninterrupted.

"A lot," Dr. Vasquez repeated softly, her voice measured and calm. "You don't know, but it is a lot."

She rested her hands loosely in her lap, her pen still unmoving against the page. 

"When it becomes a lot," she asked quietly, "what is it asking of you right now?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's asking me to... to do something." I sniff, trying to regain my composure. "I don't know what, though."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez observed the effort Jamie made to steady their breath. She sat quietly, letting the space between them remain undisturbed for five slow, deliberate seconds—one, two, three, four, five. The low hum of the ventilation filled the room.

Her pen stayed resting against the notepad, untouched.

"To do something," Dr. Vasquez said in her calm, measured tone. "Even when you don't know what that is."

She looked at Jamie, her expression steady and receptive.

"What feels like it will happen if you don't?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "I don't know," I say, my voice barely a whisper. "Like I'll forget them. Or let them down."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez kept her gaze on Jamie, letting the barely audible words hang in the air. She did not lean in, nor did she offer a rush of reassurance. In the quiet of the office, she counted the steady, deliberate seconds—one, two, three, four, five. The hum of the building's ventilation was the only sound between them.

Her hands remained resting over the blank notepad, the pen still untouched by ink.

"Forget them," Dr. Vasquez repeated, her voice a low, steady murmur. "Or let them down."

She let the reflection settle into the space before asking quietly:

"Which of those feels heavier to carry right now?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I look down at my hands again. "Both. They both feel... impossible." I finally look up at her. "What am I supposed to *do*?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met Jamie's direct look, her expression calm and unreadable. She did not rush to offer a solution or fill the urgent demand of the question. She sat with the weight of it, counting the measured space in the quiet room—one, two, three, four, five. The low hum of the building's ventilation was the only steady rhythm between them.

Her pen remained motionless on the armrest, her hands loosely resting over the blank notepad.

"Impossible," she said, her voice low and even. "They both feel impossible. And you want to know what you are supposed to do."

She held Jamie's gaze, offering no easy instructions or steps to follow.

"When it feels that impossible," Dr. Vasquez asked quietly, "what happens if you don't do anything at all right now?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stare at her blankly.* "Then... then I just sit here with it. And that feels worse."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez absorbed the blankness in Jamie's stare. She did not break the quiet, allowing the sharp ache of that realization to settle between them. In the still air of the office, she counted the steady, rhythmic seconds—one, two, three, four, five. The building's ventilation hummed faintly in the background.

Her posture remained calm and steady, hands resting loosely over the untouched pad of paper.

"Sit here with it," Dr. Vasquez reflected, her voice quiet, measured, and even. "And that feels worse."

She met Jamie's eyes without flinching from the discomfort.

"What is 'worse' threatening to do if you just sit with it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "It's threatening to... to drown me." I look away, my throat tight. "Like I'm just going to disappear under it all."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez watched Jamie look away, noting the tightness in their throat without moving from her chair. She let the heavy words rest in the open space of the office, counting the deliberate rhythm of the quiet—one, two, three, four, five. The ventilation hummed steadily in the background.

Her hands remained resting over the notepad, the pen still unmoving.

"Drown you," Dr. Vasquez repeated, her voice low, measured, and calm. "Like you are going to disappear under it all."

She kept her gaze steady, holding the quiet boundaries of the room.

"When you feel like you are disappearing under it... what part of you is fighting to stay above the surface?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "The part that wants to... to remember them properly." I finally look back at her, a fierce look in my eyes. "Not just this."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not move.

She let the words settle. One. Two. The radiator ticked somewhere behind the wall. Three. Four. Jamie's hands stayed where they were, and so did hers, resting on the closed cover of the notepad. Five.

"Their journal," she said. Not a question. Just the words, handed back.

She waited another beat. Her pen stayed capped. She had learned a long time ago that some things needed to be said out loud twice before they became real, and that the second time didn't always have to be spoken.

"You said *found*."

She tilted her head slightly, the way she did when she wanted someone to hear their own choice of word.

"Were you looking for it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: My eyes snap up to hers. "No! Of course not." My voice is a little sharp. *I shift in my seat, uncomfortable.* "It was... in a box. In the back of the closet."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The sharpness landed. Dr. Vasquez let it.

One. She did not lean back, did not lean forward. Two. The pen stayed capped between her fingers. Three. Outside, a car passed, its tires hissing on wet pavement. Four. She noticed that Jamie had said *of course* — as if the alternative were unthinkable, as if looking would have been a kind of trespass. Five.

"Okay," she said. Quiet. Level. "Not looking."

She turned the notepad over once on the armrest, a small, unhurried motion, and set it down again without opening it.

"A box. In the back of the closet."

She let that sit, too. Not five seconds this time. Two, maybe three. Enough for the picture to form — the closet door, the reaching past coats or shoes or whatever had been stacked in front, the weight of cardboard.

"What were you doing in the closet, Jamie?"

She did not say it like an accusation. She said it the way she might ask what the weather had been that morning. Her eyes stayed on Jamie's face, steady, not unkind.

"I'm not asking whether you meant to find it. I heard you. I'm asking what brought you to that door."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: I stop talking mid-sentence. I can't finish it.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not fill the space.

One. The half-sentence hung there, unfinished, and she did not reach for it. Two. She had seen this before — the moment a person walked up to the edge of something and found the ground wasn't where they'd expected it. Three. Her thumb rested against the cap of the pen. She did not click it. Four. The ficus, in the corner, dropped nothing, made no sound, simply continued its slow work of dying. Five.

Six. Seven.

She let it go longer than usual. Some silences were a door left open; this one, she thought, was a hand held out. Not hers. Jamie's own.

"You stopped," she said, finally. Barely above the radiator.

She did not ask *why*. She did not ask *what were you going to say*. Those questions had a way of chasing something back into the closet it had just come out of.

Instead she shifted, very slightly, so that her chair angled a degree further toward Jamie's — not facing, never quite facing, but nearer.

"That's alright." A pause. "You don't have to finish it right now."

She glanced at the closed notepad, then back up.

"But I noticed where it stopped. Right at the part where you were about to tell me what you were doing there." Her voice stayed even. Curious, not pressing. "Do you know what stopped it? The sentence, I mean. Was it a word you couldn't get to — or one you didn't want to say out loud?"

She waited.

"Either answer's fine. I'm just asking which."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look away from her, staring at the floor.* "It was... a feeling." My voice is barely a whisper. "Like I was about to say something wrong."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez heard the whisper and did not lean in to catch it. She had caught it.

One. Jamie's eyes were on the floor, and she let them stay there — did not try to draw them back up. Two. *Wrong.* She turned the word over once, the way she'd turned the notepad. Three. The radiator ticked. Four. Some words did the work of a whole sentence. That one was doing the work of several. Five.

"A feeling," she said. "Like you were about to say something wrong."

She let it hang, so Jamie could hear it in someone else's voice. Then she uncapped her pen — the first time that session — and wrote a single word on the notepad. She did not hide it and did not show it. Capped the pen again.

"I want to be careful with that word," she said. "Because it can mean a few different things, and I don't want to guess."

Her voice stayed where it always was. Low. Unhurried. The kind of voice that did not make the room smaller.

"Wrong like — untrue? Like you were about to describe something in a way that wasn't quite how it happened?"

A pause. Two beats.

"Or wrong like — not allowed?"

She let that one sit longer. Her hands returned to the armrest, still, folded loosely over the notepad.

"Because those are different things, Jamie. One is about accuracy. The other is about a rule." She tilted her head, just slightly, still not asking for eye contact. "And if it's a rule, I'd want to know whose."

She did not say *theirs*. She did not say *yours*. She left the question exactly where she'd set it down, and waited to see whether Jamie would pick it up.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: "They wrote about me. In the last entry." I look at Dr. Vasquez. I don't say what the entry said.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met the look and held it.

One. Jamie had come up off the floor to say it — had chosen, for that sentence, to be seen. Two. She noted that. She did not remark on it. Three. *The last entry.* Not *an* entry. Not *one of the entries.* The radiator ticked. Four. Somewhere down the hall, a door closed, and the building settled around the sound. Five.

"The last entry," she said.

She did not say *what did it say*. She did not lean toward it. She could feel the shape of the thing Jamie was holding — the way you can feel a room has furniture in it even with the lights off — and she was not going to walk into it blind, and she was not going to ask Jamie to switch the lights on before they were ready.

"You didn't answer the question about the rule," she said instead. Even. Not a correction. An observation, set on the table between them like a cup. "I asked whose rule it was, and you told me about the last entry."

A pause. Three beats.

"I don't think that's an accident. I think that might have been the answer."

She let Jamie sit with that. Her hands stayed folded on the notepad. She did not open it.

"So let me check it back with you," she said. "You went to the closet. You found the box. You read the journal — I'm assuming you read it, you can tell me if I'm wrong. And the last thing they ever wrote down was about you."

She watched Jamie's face as she said it. Not for a reaction. For permission to keep going.

"And now, when you start to tell me what you were doing at that closet door, something in you says *wrong*." Her voice dropped, just slightly. Not softer. Nearer. "I'm not going to ask what they wrote. Not yet. Maybe not today."

Five seconds. She counted them.

"But I am going to ask you this. When you say they wrote about you — is the feeling of *wrong* coming from what the entry said?" Beat. "Or from the fact that you know what it said, and they never meant for you to?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little at her last question.* "They didn't mean for me to see it." *My voice is quiet again.* "It was private."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez saw the flinch. She did not name it.

One. She had asked two questions, and Jamie had answered the second one. Two. That was information. She filed it without writing it down. Three. *Private.* Not *secret*. Not *hidden*. She let the distinction register. Four. The ficus stood in its corner, keeping its own counsel. Five.

"Private," she said.

She let the word go back across the space between them, unchanged. Then she was quiet a moment longer, because she wanted to be sure of the next thing before she said it.

"You said *didn't*. They didn't mean for you to see it." A pause. "Past tense."

She did not move. Her voice did not change.

"Which is true. Grammatically. They wrote it, they put it in a box, they put the box in the back of a closet. All of that happened before. All of that was a decision they made at a time when they could still make decisions about who saw what."

Three beats. The radiator.

"I'm not saying that to take the feeling away from you. I don't think I could if I tried, and I wouldn't try." She turned the pen once between her fingers, then set it down flat on the notepad. "I'm saying it because I noticed you're holding a rule that was made by someone who isn't here to hold it with you. And I'm wondering what it's like to be the only one holding it."

She waited. Five seconds. Then a sixth.

"You flinched," she said, finally. Quiet. Not an accusation, not a diagnosis. Simply the thing she had seen, handed back. "When I asked whether the wrongness came from the reading. Not when I asked about what it said. I want you to know I saw that, and I'm not going to make more of it than it is."

She let her eyes rest on the closed cover of the notepad for a moment, then came back up.

"But I'll ask you one thing about it, and you can tell me to leave it alone." A beat. "If they'd wanted it to stay private — really, permanently private — what do you think they would have done with it?"

She did not supply an answer. She did not gesture toward the obvious ones. She simply left the question on the armrest between them, the way she'd left the pen, and waited to see whether Jamie would look at it.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look down at my hands again, tracing the lines on my palm.* "They would have... destroyed it." My voice is still quiet. "Burned it, maybe."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez heard *burned* and let it burn a little.

One. Jamie's thumb was moving across their own palm, following one line and then another, the way a person does when they need something to be true under their hands. Two. She did not look at the hands. She let them be Jamie's. Three. *Destroyed. Burned, maybe.* Two answers, and the second one had come after a pause, like something Jamie had had to picture before they could say it. Four. The radiator gave a single tick and then went quiet, as if it too were listening. Five.

"They would have burned it," she said.

She let that sit. Not long. Just long enough that the sentence had time to become a fact in the room, instead of a guess.

"And they didn't."

She said it without weight. She was not building toward anything. She was laying two stones side by side and letting Jamie see the space between them.

"I want to be careful here," she said, after a moment. "Because I can feel a conclusion sitting right there, and I don't think it's mine to draw. I don't know what they intended. Neither do you. That's — " she paused, chose the word — "that's one of the things you lost, when you lost them. The ability to ask."

Her hands stayed where they were, folded loosely over the notepad. She did not reach for the pen.

"But you answered me fast. Faster than you've answered anything else today. *Destroyed. Burned.* As if you'd already thought about it. Maybe more than once."

Three beats.

"So I'm not going to ask what you think it means that they kept it. I think you've been standing at that question for a while already, and I don't want to push you the last step." She let her gaze settle somewhere near Jamie's shoulder — present, not pinning. "What I'll ask instead is smaller."

Five seconds. She counted.

"You said a box. In the back of the closet. Behind things." A pause. "Was it the kind of box someone puts things in to forget them?" Beat. "Or the kind of box someone puts things in to keep them?"

She did not tell Jamie which. She was not sure herself. She simply waited, and let the ficus go on dying quietly in its corner, and watched Jamie's thumb move across the lines of their own hand.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I stop tracing the lines on my palm. My gaze drifts from my hands to the corner of the room, near the ficus.* "It was... a shoe box." *My voice is still quiet, but a little stronger now.* "An old one. From when we were kids."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not follow Jamie's gaze to the corner. She knew what was there.

One. *A shoe box.* Not a file box, not a lockbox, not something bought for the purpose. Two. *An old one.* Three. She heard the voice come up a half-step — not louder, but standing on firmer ground, the way a voice does when it has stopped guessing and started remembering. Four. And then the last part. The part that had come out almost by accident, tucked inside the description of cardboard. Five.

"A shoe box," she said. "From when you were kids."

She let it rest. She did not rush past it, because it had not been offered as a small thing, whatever its size.

"You said *we*."

Quiet. Not a catch, not a correction. She simply set the word down where Jamie could see it, the way she had set the pen down, and let it lie there.

"That's the first time today you've put yourself in the same sentence as them." A pause. "You've said *they* and *their* and *the journal* and *the closet*. This is the first *we*."

The radiator, silent now, held its breath with the rest of the room. Outside, the wet street went on hissing under someone else's tires.

"I'm not going to tell you what that means," she said. "I don't know what it means. It might not mean anything, and if it doesn't, you can say so." Her hands stayed folded. Her eyes stayed steady, resting near Jamie's shoulder, not pressing on Jamie's face. "But I asked you whether it was a box for forgetting or a box for keeping, and you didn't say either word. You told me it was a box you'd both have recognized. One that's been around longer than the journal has."

Three beats.

"I think that might have been your answer, too. You keep doing that — answering sideways. I don't mind. I just want you to know I'm hearing it."

She waited, five seconds, counting them out against the absence of the second hand on the wall.

"So let me stay with the box, and not the journal. Just the box." Her voice was low and even and did not ask for anything it wasn't prepared to hold. "Was the journal the only thing in it, Jamie?" A beat. "Or was it just the thing on top?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head slightly, still looking at the corner.* "There were other things. Drawings. Some dried flowers. A ribbon from a gift." *I finally look at Dr. Vasquez, my expression unreadable.*

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez met the look, and did not try to read it.

One. *Drawings. Dried flowers. A ribbon from a gift.* Two. Three things, named in order, the way a person names them when they've seen them more than once — when the list is already made and only has to be recited. Three. Not one of them was the kind of thing you kept by accident. Not one of them was paperwork. Four. Jamie's face gave her nothing, and she let it give her nothing. She had learned not to fill in a face. Five.

"Drawings," she said. "Dried flowers. A ribbon from a gift."

She let the list go back across, whole. She did not add to it. She did not say *those are the things people keep.* Jamie had heard themself say it.

"I asked you if it was a box for forgetting or a box for keeping," she said, after a moment. "I'll stop asking that now. I think you've told me."

The radiator had gone quiet. The room held whatever it was holding.

"I want to say something about your face, and then I want to leave it alone." Her voice did not change. "I can't read it right now. I'm telling you that because I'm not going to guess. Some people in that chair would want me to guess — would want me to say *you look sad* or *you look angry* so they wouldn't have to. I'm not going to do that for you." A pause. "If there's something on your face you want me to know about, you can tell me. If there isn't, that's alright too."

She let five seconds go by, counting them against the still clock.

"Three things and a journal," she said. "A shoe box from when you were kids." She turned the capped pen once, set it back down. "You didn't say whose drawings. You didn't say what the flowers were from. You said a ribbon from *a* gift — not *the* gift, not *my* gift, not *their* gift."

Three beats.

"I'm not asking you to fill any of that in." Her eyes stayed where they were, steady, near Jamie's shoulder. "I'm noticing that you told me exactly what was in the box, and nothing about what any of it was *for*. That's a careful way to describe a thing."

She waited. Then, quietly:

"When you opened it — before the journal, before you read a word — which one did you pick up first?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I look at my hands again.* "The flowers." *My voice is still quiet, almost a sigh.* "They were pressed."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez heard the sigh underneath the word and let it be a sigh.

One. *The flowers.* Not the drawings, which would have been the easy thing — paper, something a person could hold without fear of breaking it. Two. Not the ribbon. Three. Jamie had reached past the journal, past whatever was written about them, and picked up the most fragile thing in the box. Four. *Pressed.* A word that meant someone had done something on purpose, a long time ago, with a heavy book and patience. Five.

"The flowers," she said. "They were pressed."

She let it settle. The radiator stayed quiet. The clock on the wall kept its uneventful face.

"Pressed is a thing a person does," she said, after a moment. Not a revelation. Just the plain shape of the fact, set down. "You don't find pressed flowers. Somebody has to flatten them, and wait, and check on them, and decide they're done."

Three beats. Her hands stayed folded over the notepad. The pen had not moved.

"I'm not going to ask who pressed them. I think you'd tell me if you wanted to, and I think you might not know for certain, and I don't want you to have to choose between those in front of me."

She counted five seconds against the still clock.

"But you went to them first. Before the journal — before the thing you came in here to tell me about." Her eyes rested near Jamie's shoulder, steady, not asking to be met. "You said it like a sigh, just now. *They were pressed.*" A pause. "I noticed that's the first thing you've said all afternoon that didn't sound like you were bracing for it."

She let that go across the space between them, and did not follow it.

"So I'll stay there with you for a minute, if that's alright. With the flowers and not the entry." Quiet. Level. "When you picked them up — did you know what they were from?"

She did not add *or did you have to guess.* She let the question be exactly as large as it was, and waited.

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shake my head slightly.* "No. Not really. Just... a memory." *I close my eyes for a moment, then open them, looking at Dr. Vasquez.* "Like a feeling."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez saw the eyes close and open, and did not fill the dark in between.

One. *Not really.* Not *no.* Two. *Just a memory.* And then Jamie had corrected themself — had reached for a smaller word, or maybe a truer one. Three. *Like a feeling.* Four. She had heard that word once already this afternoon. It had come out of Jamie's mouth in a whisper, about a sentence they couldn't finish. Five.

"A memory," she said. "Like a feeling."

She let it stand. The radiator had not resumed. The ficus was where it always was.

"That's the second feeling you've brought in here today," she said, after a moment. Not a catch. An inventory, spoken plainly. "The first one stopped you. It came up when you were about to tell me what you were doing at the closet, and it said *wrong*, and you couldn't get past it."

Three beats. Her hands stayed folded over the closed notepad.

"This one came out of a pressed flower. And you didn't brace for it. You closed your eyes."

She counted five seconds against the clock with no second hand.

"I'm not going to tell you they're related. I don't know that." Her voice stayed low, level, the same width as the room. "I'm only noticing that you've used the same word for both, and that one of them made you stop and the other one made you sigh. I'd want to know, if I were sitting where you are, whether those are two different feelings that happen to share a word — or whether they're the same one, coming at you from two directions."

She did not lean toward the answer. She let her eyes rest where they had been resting, near Jamie's shoulder, steady.

"You don't have to know. But you closed your eyes for it." A pause. "Where did it take you, Jamie? Not what you saw — I'm not asking for the picture. Just — was it a place? A time? A person?"

She waited. And then, quieter, the way she set down anything she wasn't sure the floor could hold:

"Or was it you?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I blink, surprised by the last question.* "Me?" *I repeat the word slowly, as if tasting it.* "No... I don't think so." *I pause, thinking.* "It was... a time."
