dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“East ridge. Got it.”

Kira sheathed one dagger and snatched a loose stone from beside her boot. A narrow shelf cut across the eastern wall, reachable by a broken slope of scree. Not much cover between here and there.

She hurled the stone at the nearest bowman.

“Oi! Up here, you blind bastards!”

His bow swung toward her. Kira broke from the boulder, angling east rather than running straight beneath them. A bowstring snapped. An arrow struck behind her heel; another shattered against the rock ahead.

“Three tracking me!” she called.

She dropped behind a waist-high slab as two more arrows clattered overhead. Dust caught in her throat. Fuck. They had the shelf ranged already.

Kira crawled toward the slab’s far edge, keeping her head below its chipped crest. Above her, one archer stepped forward for a better angle, boots scraping grit down the slope.

She drew her second dagger again.

“Come a little closer,” she muttered.

Then she kicked loose a spray of shale and darted for the next outcrop, giving the eastern bows another moving target.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Good, Kira's drawing them out.* I see a few of our own spears already pushing up the western slope. "Keep pushing, lads! Up and over!" I bellow, gesturing with my polearm. This ground is a nightmare.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
An arrow clipped Kira’s sleeve and struck the outcrop with a sharp crack.

She threw herself behind it, shoulder first. Pain flared down her arm—not a wound, just rock meeting bone. She flexed her fingers around the dagger.

“Still here, you shits.”

Boots scraped above her. The nearest bowman had edged onto the shelf, trying to find an angle past her cover. Two others kept their bows trained on the open scree below.

Kira scooped up a fistful of grit. She had drawn their attention; now she needed to survive keeping it.

She ducked around the outcrop’s uphill side.

The bowman jerked his aim toward her. Kira flung the grit into his face and lunged inside the bow’s reach before he could loose. Her left dagger hooked the stave aside; her right drove beneath his raised arm.

She shoved him against the rock and wrenched her blade free.

“Five east!” she shouted. “One’s moving along the ridge toward your approach!”

A shadow shifted overhead. Kira caught the scrape of a blade leaving its sheath.

Not all bowmen, then.

She crouched beneath the shelf’s lip as a man with a short sword started down toward her. Behind him, another archer searched for a clear shot.

Kira backed into the narrow gap beside the outcrop, forcing the swordsman to approach between stone walls.

“Come on, then.”

She kept both daggers low and watched his feet. As long as he stood there, the bastard above couldn’t shoot through him.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
From the gap, Kira caught sight of the bowman farther along the ridge. His arrow angled west, toward the Captain.

“Cap! Archer on the ridge—he’s drawn!”

She couldn’t reach him. The swordsman blocked her way, and the bastard knew it.

He thrust into the gap. Kira twisted sideways; steel scraped stone beside her ribs. She trapped his blade against the rock with one dagger and slashed across his forearm with the other.

His grip broke. She drove her shoulder into him, forcing him back onto the shelf.

The bowman farther along still had his bow raised.

“Fuck.”

Kira shoved the swordsman toward the archer covering their fight, then snatched up a loose chunk of shale. She hurled it at the bowman aiming west.

It struck his raised elbow. His bow dipped as the string snapped forward. She lost the arrow against the opposite wall—no way to tell where it landed.

Kira dropped low as the nearer archer tried to shoot past the stumbling swordsman. The arrow struck the shelf beside her boot.

“Still four up here with bows!” she called. “Can’t hold all their eyes!”

She brought both daggers up again. The wounded swordsman had drawn a knife with his good hand, and there was barely room on the shelf to step back.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Damn, that was close.* "Fall back!" I roar, seeing the situation. No sense in getting picked off here. "Regroup at the choke point!" *We'll make them pay for every inch.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Falling back!”

Kira gave ground a half-step. The wounded swordsman followed, knife held tight against his hip. Beyond his shoulder, the nearer bowman reached for another arrow.

She had until he nocked it.

Kira kicked the swordsman’s forward knee. His leg buckled, and she shoved past him, scraping her shoulder against the ravine wall. She didn’t stop to finish him.

An arrow cracked against the shelf behind her.

“Fuck this ridge.”

She sheathed one dagger and dropped over the lip. Her free hand caught rough stone; her boots scraped for purchase before she let go of the last few feet. She landed badly on the scree, one knee striking hard enough to jar her teeth.

Still working. Good enough.

Kira scrambled downhill toward the boulders, keeping her weight low. Loose shale rattled after her. Above, someone shouted for the archers to move forward.

“They’re shifting to the edge!” she called. “They’ll have shots down the ravine!”

She ducked behind the waist-high slab as an arrow struck its crest. The choke point lay farther back, where the walls narrowed around a crooked shoulder of rock. One exposed stretch between here and there.

Kira waited for the next bowstring to snap, then ran.

Grit kicked up beside her. She reached the bend and pressed herself behind its stone shoulder, breathing hard through clenched teeth. Blood ran from her scraped palm onto the dagger hilt.

She drew her second blade and watched the way she had come.

“Ridge loses its angle here, Cap,” she called. “But there’s a goat track above this bend. If they know it, they can get over us.”

Her knee throbbed. She settled onto her good leg and waited for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira glanced across the ravine and spotted the Captain on the far side. Open ground lay between them, overlooked by the eastern bows.

“Cap! I’ve got eyes on you!”

She leaned out just far enough to check the crossing. A bowman above the shelf turned toward the movement. She pulled back before his arrow chipped the corner beside her face.

“Bastard.”

There was no crossing that. Not with her knee threatening to fold and four bows still working the ridge.

She looked along the opposite wall instead. A dark seam ran beneath an overhang, but fallen rock hid where it ended. Cover, perhaps. A dead end, perhaps. She wouldn’t sell a guess as a way out.

“Overhang along your wall!” she called. “Can’t tell if it leads through!”

Grit pattered onto her shoulder.

Kira went still, then looked up. A boot appeared on the goat track above the bend. Someone was coming down slowly, testing the loose footing. She couldn’t see his weapon yet.

Of course they knew the fucking track.

She shifted deeper beneath the stone shoulder, denying the newcomer a clear view of her. Her scraped palm burned as she tightened her grip.

“One above the choke, Cap,” she called. “I’m pinned this side. Can you reach cover?”

She kept her eyes on the track and waited for an answer.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "No, I'm pinned here too!" I shout back, pressing against the cliff face. *Damn it, this is a mess.* "Hold them there, Kira! Don't let them flank us!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Holding!”

Kira tucked herself farther beneath the shoulder of rock. Crossing was out. The goat track was hers to block.

Above her, a boot scraped closer. A man eased around the bend with a hatchet in one hand and the other braced against the cliff. The track narrowed beneath him to little more than a boot’s width.

Kira kept still. Her knee wouldn’t take a jump, and reaching too early would give him time to kick her teeth in.

A second voice came from farther up.

“What’s the hold?”

Two, then.

The hatchet man crouched, trying to peer beneath the overhang. Kira caught his ankle with her free hand and yanked it away from the wall.

His heel slipped off the track.

He dropped hard onto one knee, hatchet scraping across the stone. Kira drove her dagger into his weapon arm before he could lift it again. The hatchet fell past her shoulder and clattered down the slope.

She let go and pulled back beneath cover. His scrambling boots sent loose stones bouncing around her.

“Two on the track!” she called. “Front one’s blocking the other!”

An arrow struck the ground beyond the bend. The ridge archers still had the open approach covered. She couldn’t step out to finish the wounded man without giving them a shot.

Fine. He could stay there and bleed.

“Get back,” someone hissed overhead.

Kira bent carefully and retrieved the fallen hatchet, sheathing one dagger to make room. Her knee shook under her weight.

“Come down and fetch him,” she muttered.

Steel scraped above. The wounded man began dragging himself uphill, leaving dark smears on the rock. Behind him, a spearhead edged into view.

Kira pressed flat against the cliff as it probed beneath the lip. Longer reach. Worse angle for her.

“Fuck.”

She caught the shaft behind the head with the hatchet’s beard and hauled it downward. Wood struck the edge of the track. She held it there, dagger ready, her injured palm slick against the haft.

“Track’s blocked for now, Cap!” she shouted. “They’ve got a spear up there. I’m keeping under it!”

The shaft twisted against her grip. Kira planted her good foot against a low stone and pulled harder.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good work, Kira!" *She's a damn demon, that one.* "Hold fast! We're almost to the choke point!" I push harder, my polearm sweeping wide to keep any stray archers' heads down.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The spear shaft jerked upward, dragging the hatchet with it. Kira’s scraped palm slipped.

She let it go.

The hatchet clattered against the cliff, and the spear snapped back out of sight. Kira flattened herself beneath the lip just as its point stabbed down again. Steel scraped past her shoulder.

“Still holding!”

She drew her second dagger. No room to swing that spear properly, but its owner didn’t need much room to pin her against the rock.

Above, the wounded man cursed. His companion cursed back.

“Move your bloody leg!”

Kira glanced toward the bend. The narrow approach remained clear, but she couldn’t watch it and the spearhead together.

“Cap, stay tight to the rock coming in! They’ve still got the open ground covered!”

The spear withdrew a few inches.

She shifted toward the mouth of her shelter, deliberately letting her boot scrape.

The next thrust came hard and low.

Kira stepped aside on her good leg. The point struck gravel beside her foot. She shoved the shaft against the cliff with her forearm and slashed upward at the hand reaching below the ledge.

Her blade caught fingers. A sharp cry came from overhead.

The spear dropped.

Kira kicked its shaft behind the stone shoulder before its owner could recover it. Pain shot through her bad knee; she nearly went down with it.

“Fuck—”

She caught herself against the wall, breathing through her teeth. Above her, boots retreated a few scraping steps. Not gone. Just beyond her reach.

Kira sheathed one dagger and dragged the spear upright. Its head wavered before she braced the butt between two stones.

“Got their spear,” she called. “Track’s still denied.”

A shadow moved across the lip. She angled the point toward it, keeping her body beneath cover.

“Come on,” she muttered. “Try it without the long stick.”

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Finally, some good news.* "Alright, Kira! Hang on! We're almost there!" I see the first few of my vanguard cresting the western ridge. "Push them back, lads! Clear the high ground!" My polearm sweeps wide, knocking a loose rock down the slope to distract an archer.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Shouts broke across the western ridge. Kira caught a glimpse of spearpoints above the rocks, then movement on the eastern rim—one bowman turning away from the ravine to face the new threat.

One less watching the crossing. For now.

“East bows are looking west, Cap!”

A boot scraped directly overhead.

Kira drove the captured spear upward. Its point struck stone beside the boot, showering her with grit, but the foot jerked back. She shortened her grip before anyone could grab the shaft.

“Not through here, bastard.”

The wounded hatchet man was still on the track. She could hear him dragging himself along, breath coming in sharp little grunts. His companion stayed behind him. Neither had much room to move.

Then a stone struck the spear shaft.

Kira flinched beneath the lip. Another rock smashed against the ground where her hand had been a moment earlier.

They didn’t need to come down to hurt her.

She pulled the spear closer, keeping its point just above the ledge. Her shoulder burned. Blood from her palm had made the wood slippery.

“Two still above the bend!” she called. “Throwing rocks now. Keep clear beneath the track!”

A hand appeared over the edge, fingers curling around a fist-sized stone.

Kira jabbed toward it. The hand vanished; the stone dropped harmlessly against the cliff and bounced past her boots.

She couldn’t afford to chase either man uphill. Holding this cramped patch of shade was enough.

Kira wedged her good shoulder against the wall and adjusted her grip, leaving the spear butt braced low.

“Choke’s still held, Cap!”

She kept the point trained on the lip and listened for the next scrape of boots.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira!" *She's bought us time.* "Vanguard, secure the high ground! Push them off the ridge!" I see another of my men go down, an arrow in his leg. *This is going to cost us.* "Clear that ridge!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
A cry rose from the western slope. Kira couldn’t see its source beneath the overhang. She kept her attention on the boots above her.

One pair scraped uphill. The other stayed planted near the lip.

“Leave him,” someone said overhead. “They’re coming across.”

The wounded man swore at him.

Kira eased the spear upward, keeping the shaft close against the cliff. Her palm throbbed with every adjustment. If they pulled back, she would let them. Her orders were to hold, not chase.

A pebble bounced off her shoulder.

Then the unwounded man dropped into view.

He landed beside the spearpoint, one hand grabbing for the shaft, a knife in the other. Kira shoved the spear across him before he could turn fully toward her. Wood caught beneath his knife arm.

Her bad knee buckled under his weight.

“Fuck!”

She struck the wall hard, but kept her shoulder behind the shaft. His knife scraped across her leather sleeve. Too close to use the point. Too close to let go.

Kira slid one hand free and drew her dagger.

He tried to wrench the spear aside. She drove the blade into his thigh, then shoved him toward the open scree as his leg gave way. He fell beyond the shoulder of rock, taking the spear with him.

She stayed beneath cover.

An arrow struck its fallen shaft.

“Archers still watching the bend!” she shouted.

The man crawled toward a low boulder, knife forgotten in the gravel. Kira let him crawl. Above her, the wounded hatchet man continued dragging himself uphill.

She drew her other dagger and leaned against the cliff, taking her weight off the shaking knee.

“One off the track. Other’s backing up,” she called. “I’m still here, Cap.”

She listened beneath the shouting for fresh footsteps overhead.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira! Hold that choke point! We're breaking through on this side!" *Almost there. Just a little more.* I parry a wild swing from a desperate ambusher, my polearm ringing against his sword.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Holding, Cap!”

Kira shifted deeper beneath the overhang. Her knee had started to stiffen. She could stand on it, barely, but another scramble up the scree was out.

Above her, the wounded man’s dragging footsteps faded uphill.

She didn’t follow.

Across the ravine, steel rang against steel. An eastern bowman backed away from the rim, reaching for an arrow as shouts rose farther along the ridge. Another remained crouched behind a rock with his bow aimed down toward the bend.

“Still one covering the approach!” she called. “Low rock on the east rim!”

Gravel crunched nearby.

The man she had stabbed was no longer crawling away. From behind his boulder, he stretched a hand toward the fallen spear.

Kira watched his fingers close around the shaft.

“Don’t.”

He dragged it closer.

“Course you fucking would.”

She stayed behind the stone shoulder. Going after him meant stepping into the archer’s line. Instead, she lowered herself carefully and picked up the knife he had dropped near her cover, sheathing one dagger.

The spearhead edged around the boulder first. Then his face.

Kira threw the knife.

It struck his upper arm. He recoiled behind the rock, dropping the spear with a clatter.

She drew her dagger again and settled back beneath the lip, jaw clenched against the ache in her knee. That bought seconds, nothing more.

A bowstring snapped. An arrow skipped across the gravel beyond her shelter.

“Choke’s held,” she called. “But that bow’s waiting for anyone crossing!”

Boots scraped overhead again.

Kira looked up, both blades close to her chest. She couldn’t tell whether the wounded man had stopped retreating or someone else had reached the track.

She braced her good foot and listened.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira! Just hold on a little longer!" *That stubborn bastard.* I see a surge of movement on the western ridge. The tide is turning. "Push them back! No quarter!" I bellow, sweeping my polearm and driving a desperate fighter back into the rocks.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
“Still here!”

Kira tilted her head, listening past the fighting. The scrape came again—slow, uneven, followed by a muffled curse.

The wounded hatchet man. Probably. She wasn’t betting her throat on it.

She kept beneath the lip.

Across the ravine, figures scrambled back from the western ridge. The bowman behind the low eastern rock rose halfway, looking toward the shouting. His bow dipped.

“Covering archer’s distracted, Cap! Don’t know for how long!”

Dust spilled down her collar.

A hand reached over the ledge above her, empty and groping for a hold. Then the wounded man’s face appeared. Blood streaked his sleeve; his injured arm hung against his chest. He looked down at her daggers and stopped.

For a moment, neither moved.

“Back up,” Kira said.

He glanced uphill. A shout cracked out somewhere beyond him, followed by running feet.

“Can’t.”

Kira’s jaw tightened. There wasn’t room beneath the overhang for another body, and she couldn’t watch his hands while guarding the approach.

“Then stay exactly there.”

A stone clattered nearby.

Kira turned just enough to catch movement beyond the boulder below. The knife-wounded spearman had abandoned the shaft and was limping away along the scree, one hand pressed to his arm.

She let him go. Holding meant holding.

Above her, the man’s fingers shifted.

“Hands where I can see them,” she snapped. “Try coming down on me and you’ll land on steel.”

He flattened his good hand against the rock.

Kira eased her weight off her bad knee. It had begun shaking even when she stood still.

“One trapped above me,” she called. “Other’s pulling away. Choke’s still held!”

She kept one dagger angled toward the ledge and the other low beside her hip. The archer behind the eastern rock disappeared from view.

That didn’t mean he was gone.

Kira pressed closer to the cliff and waited.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood, Kira!" *She's a damn hero.* "All units, consolidate on the choke point! We'll make our stand there!" I signal a retreat for my vanguard, pulling them back from the ridge.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The house had been empty for six weeks. Someone had come in to water the plants — you could tell because the ferns were alive and the envelope of photographs on the kitchen table had been nudged an inch to the left. Otherwise everything was exactly as your grandmother had left it.

The clock in the hallway was still running. It had been wound two weeks after her death. That had been you. You remembered winding it and wondering at the time if you should.

You stood in the doorway of the living room and did not go in yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath and walk into the living room. I need to start on the books.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The living room was colder than the hallway, though the door had been shut.

Dust lay on the rug in a thin, even nap, except for a narrow track along the bookcase where the carpet had been pressed recently, as if someone had paced there without lifting their feet. The books waited in their shelves. Some had slipped forward a fraction, spines aligned with the edge, as though they had been taken out and put back in the wrong order.

On the side table beside the reading chair stood a glass of water. It was empty, but the inside was still faintly damp.

The silence in the room did not feel empty. It felt attentive.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the glass of water and pick it up. It's still a little cool.* "Grandma, you just left this here." *I shake my head and take it to the kitchen, rinsing it out before returning to the living room.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
When she returned, the living room had the same attentive quiet, but the shape of it seemed subtly altered, as if the furniture had been breathed around.

The track in the dust along the bookcase no longer ran only between the shelves. It curved now toward the reading chair and stopped at the side table.

The table was bare. Where the glass had stood, the wood held a pale ring, damp at the edges.

From the kitchen behind her came the faucet’s single drip, slow and patient, though it had been turned off.

On the shelf nearest the chair, one book had slipped farther forward than the others, its spine just past the edge. The clock in the hallway ticked, but the sound arrived a half-beat after the pendulum’s swing, as if the room were deciding when time should happen.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: The weird shadow in the corner — I grab a bat from the umbrella stand and swing at it, hard.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The umbrella stand had held only umbrellas a moment ago. The bat was there now, cold and familiar in the grip, as if it had been waiting for your hand.

You swung hard into the corner. The bat did not strike wall. It met something soft and unresisting, like folded cloth, and the impact made no sound until a half-second later, when the hallway clock ticked. The shadow did not scatter. It thinned only where the bat passed, then closed behind it, smooth as water.

Now the corner was ordinary, but the darkness there seemed to be facing you.

The track in the dust along the bookcase had changed again. It no longer ended at the side table. It came around the reading chair and stopped just short of where you stood.

On the shelf nearest you, the book that had slipped forward slid quietly back into line, as though someone had finished with it.

From the kitchen, the faucet dripped once.

Then it listened.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: "That's enough." *I grip the bat tighter, my knuckles white.* "What do you want?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The words did not make the room answer. They made the room listen differently.

The corner stayed ordinary, but its ordinariness felt chosen, like a face arranged after a flinch. The bat remained cold, its weight a little too precise in the hand, as if it had only just remembered what it was supposed to be.

On the shelf nearest the reading chair, the book that had slid back into line moved forward again. Not far. Only enough to be noticed. Its spine was faded, the lower corner worn soft and dark in the way of something opened often by the same fingers.

The track in the dust did not lengthen while it was watched. It was simply closer to the chair than it had been before, ending now beside the cushion, on the side where someone might sit.

From the kitchen came another drip.

Then, after a pause too exact to be accident, two more.

The hallway clock ticked. This time the sound came before the pendulum swung.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I stare at the book, then at the chair.* "No. Not yet." *I walk over to the bookshelf, ignoring the chair, and pull out a random book from a different shelf, just to assert some control.*

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: Okay this is ridiculous. I call out to the empty house, 'HELLOOOO GHOSTS, anyone want a TV? I have an extra TV. Fine china? Going cheap.'

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The book taken from the other shelf had come away too easily. Its worn lower corner showed now, though it had not been the book nearest the chair a moment before. Or it had been. The room made it difficult to keep the order of such things. The gap it had left in the shelf was pale and faintly damp-smelling, and the books on either side leaned inward, not falling, only waiting.

The call into the house did not echo. It went into the curtains, the rug, the dust, the closed doorway of the dining room, and was not returned. Nothing laughed. Nothing even stirred in a way that could be mistaken for amusement. The silence afterward had the careful quality of a room that had heard every word and chosen not to answer.

Then the china cabinet in the dining room clicked. Its latch lifted without the door opening. Behind the glass, one of the good cups had turned so that its handle pointed toward the empty space before the sideboard.

In the corner, beneath the cloth that had covered the television since the funeral, the set made no sound and gave no light. The cloth only settled closer, as if the screen had

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I sigh, running a hand through my hair.* "Fine. Be that way." *I put the book back, then head to the dining room, peering at the china cabinet.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The dining room had a stillness different from the living room’s: less attentive, more withheld. The air smelled faintly of tea leaves and cupboard dust, though no tea had been made in six weeks.

The china cabinet latch remained lifted, but the door had not opened. Behind the glass, the good cups stood in their row, all except the one that had turned. Its handle no longer pointed toward the sideboard. It pointed toward the place at the table where the dust had been disturbed in a shallow, repeated crescent, as if a plate had been shifted again and again by someone with no appetite.

The chair before that place was not quite tucked in. It stood angled just enough to suggest a body had risen from it recently, though the seat held no impression and the wood was cold.

In the cabinet glass, the room behind was reflected dimly. The reading chair faced the dining room now, or seemed to. The cloth over the television lay in folds that gathered into the shape of shoulders and a lowered head until the eye refused the suggestion and made it fabric again.

The faucet dripped in the kitchen.

The sound came back from inside the china cabinet instead, small and porcelain-bright, and when it ceased, the turned cup had a hairline crack running down its side, pale and patient as an old vein.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I walk over to the china cabinet, my hand out.* "No, no, no." *I gently push the handle of the cup back into place, as if that will fix the crack.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The handle moved, but not into its old place. It stopped a fraction too far forward, as if the cup had remembered being turned and could not quite return to what it had been. The hairline crack did not close. In the dim dining-room light it looked finer than before, and therefore deeper, a pale seam holding its own cold.

Where the porcelain had been touched, no warmth remained. The surface gave back nothing.

Inside the cabinet, the air drew very still. The other cups did not move, yet they seemed arranged around the cracked one now, faced toward it in the way people face someone who has begun to speak very quietly. The latch lowered itself another fraction, not closing, only resting near the catch.

From the living room came a soft paper sound, as though a page had settled deeper into a book no one was holding.

In the glass front of the cabinet, the reflection showed the cup with its handle pointing the other way. Seen directly, it remained as it had been placed. The crack waited in the porcelain, patient and thin, as though it had all the time in the world to decide whether it wanted to spread.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: I find an old photo of my grandmother's friend Marcus. He was so cute. Suddenly I'm thinking about whether he's still alive and single.

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
It had come from the envelope on the kitchen table, though the envelope was now on the dining sideboard, one corner exactly even with the edge of the wood. Marcus looked up from the photograph with the careful charm of someone who knew he was being seen. He was young, yes, and handsome in a way that might have invited lighter thoughts elsewhere. Here, in that room, the smile seemed to be waiting for permission. His shadow fell against the wall behind him, but it leaned a little too far toward the back of the chair.

The thought about whether he might still be alive, still single, did not become a daydream. The house took it and made it thin, the way breath becomes visible in cold air. The room stayed quiet. The quiet became more exact.

Behind the china cabinet glass, the cracked cup had turned again. Its handle now pointed toward the photograph. The hairline seam in the porcelain looked longer in the dim light, or simply more certain of where it meant to go.

From the living room came the faintest sound of paper settling, as though the books were listening with their spines closed. The track in the dust had moved again without moving. It now curved toward the dining-room doorway and stopped just beyond the threshold, where a person might stand uncertain whether to enter.

On the back of the photograph, in faded ink that had not been visible before, were three words in the same careful hand that had labeled the seed envelopes in the kitchen drawer:

M. came again.

The kitchen faucet dripped once.

The sound came from inside the china cabinet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *My eyes widen as I read the back of the photo.* "Marcus? Again? What does that even mean?" *I look from the photo to the china cabinet, then back to the photo, a chill running down my spine.*

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The question did not scatter anything. It settled instead, and the room arranged itself around the name as though the name had always been waiting there.

The photograph remained exactly as it had been, yet the smile on Marcus’s face seemed less fixed now, not changed, only less certain of being seen. Behind him, the shadow at the back of the chair leaned a little farther into the dark, as if the wall there had softened enough to receive it. On the back of the photograph, the faded ink of *M. came again* looked drier than before, and therefore older, and therefore more true.

Inside the china cabinet, the cracked cup gave a sound too fine to be called a sound. It was not breaking. It was remembering. The hairline seam darkened along one short stretch, as though something had filled it without touching the porcelain. In the glass reflection, the cup’s handle pointed toward the photograph, though the cup itself had not moved.

On the sideboard, the envelope of photographs whispered against the wood. One more picture slipped free, only halfway. It showed the dining room from the doorway, the table set for one, the chair before the crescent in the dust not empty, but occupied by a coat folded with terrible neatness. The coat was dry. The blur in the photograph gathered where a face should have been, and the longer the eye stayed there, the more the blur seemed to be breathing.

Beneath the first line on the back of the photograph, another mark became visible, faint as a watermark brought out by cold. It was not a sentence. It was only a date, written in the same careful hand, and the date was today.

The kitchen faucet stopped dripping in a way that was worse than dripping. The silence it left had weight, and shape, and patience.

From the living room came the soft sound of the reading chair accepting weight.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I gasp, dropping both photos.* "No. No, no, no." *I back away from the sideboard, my heart pounding. I glance wildly around the dining room, then at the living room doorway.* "Grandma?"

dialogue.name: Gabi (Narrator)
dialogue.content:
The name did not echo. It went into the house and was considered.

From the living room came no answer, only another small sound from the reading chair — not the creak of someone rising, but the slower settling of weight that has already been there long enough to be patient. The room beyond the doorway stayed dim and ordinary, except that the cloth over the television seemed to have drawn itself a little tighter, folding inward like hands resting in a lap.

The photographs lay where they had fallen. Marcus was facedown now, the ink on the back pale and dry in the dining-room light. The other picture remained faceup, but the folded coat in it was no longer on the chair. It lay across the table instead, sleeves arranged toward the place where the dust had been disturbed in its shallow crescent. In the room itself, the table was bare. Even so, the air above it held the faintest suggestion of warmth, as though a plate had just been removed.

Inside the china cabinet, the cracked cup stood perfectly still. Its handle pointed toward the doorway. The latch lowered another fraction and gave the smallest click, not closing, only marking the moment like a fingernail laid gently against glass.

A thread of lavender moved through the dining room — old, dry, and barely there. It did not smell like perfume. It smelled like a drawer that had been opened too often by hands no one could remember. The hallway clock ticked twice while the pendulum hung motionless at the end of its swing. Then the kitchen faucet began to drip again, slow and deliberate, one drop after another, keeping time for a room that had decided not to answer yet.

dialogue.name: Gabi
dialogue.content: *I squeeze my eyes shut, then open them again, trying to make sense of what I'm seeing.* "This isn't real. This can't be real." *I back away slowly, towards the kitchen, keeping my eyes on the dining room.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The narrator voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - maintaining the same atmospheric, literary tone, precise observational style, and supernatural logic from turn 2 to turn 22. The voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones (turns 18-22) show even more sophisticated layering of details, temporal distortions, and atmospheric building. No verbosity or repetition creep.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial unease to active supernatural manifestation. Each turn escalates tension while building a coherent mystery around Marcus and the grandmother's presence. The story moves from passive observation to active haunting.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellently adapts to user's actions. When user swings bat at shadow, narrator creates bat from thin air. When user tries to assert control by grabbing random book, it becomes the 'right' book. Handles user's sudden shift to TV joke gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes user's actions or thoughts. Always responds to what user does rather than dictating what they should do. Respects user agency completely throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Sophisticated temporal manipulation as narrative device. Time moves strangely but consistently within the supernatural logic - sounds arriving before causes, objects changing when not observed. The 'today's date' on photo is brilliant temporal anchoring.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is rich and atmospheric but never overwrought. Every descriptive element serves the supernatural tension. Avoids flowery language while maintaining literary quality.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Excellent variety in describing supernatural manifestations. Each turn introduces new unsettling details without repeating previous effects. The dust track, dripping faucet, and moving objects all evolve uniquely.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Masterful showing. Never states 'the house is haunted' but demonstrates it through concrete details: objects moving, sounds displaced in time, temperature changes, dust patterns. Pure environmental storytelling.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext about grief, memory, and unfinished business. The Marcus mystery, grandmother's presence, and the house's 'attention' all operate on multiple interpretive levels without being explicit.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent escalation from subtle wrongness to overt supernatural activity. Each response builds tension incrementally while allowing moments of uncertainty and dread to breathe.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional supernatural horror writing that maintains literary quality while building genuine atmospheric dread. The narrator creates a coherent supernatural logic where objects and time behave according to the house's mysterious intentions. Particularly strong in environmental storytelling and maintaining tension without resorting to cheap scares. The Marcus subplot adds compelling mystery depth.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't look up right away, sliding a slim volume of Neruda between two anthologies that didn't belong anywhere near each other alphabetically.

"Depends what you mean by new. I got a crate of estate sale leftovers Tuesday. Mostly moldering cookbooks and a suspicious number of Reader's Digest condensed novels." They straightened, wiping dust on their sleeve, finally glancing toward the door. "Someone's estate really loved abridged Steinbeck, apparently."

They walked to the counter, unhurried, and pulled out a battered ledger, more prop than necessity at this point. "You're soaked. There's a towel somewhere back there that isn't currently holding a stack of first editions hostage. Or you could just drip on the mystery section, it's due for some ambiance."

A pause. Sable's pen tapped once against the counter — an old, unconscious habit — before they set it down deliberately, like they'd caught themselves doing something they didn't want examined.

"You didn't come in just for cookbooks, though. You've got that look. The one where you're about to say something and instead ask about inventory."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I manage a small, watery smile.* "No cookbooks today, thankfully." *I shrug, looking around the familiar shop, taking it all in.* "Just... wanted to see if there was anything interesting before I go."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Something in the phrase caught, the way a splinter catches — small, but impossible to ignore. *Before I go.* Sable's hand found the nearest stack of index cards and began squaring their edges, a task that required exactly zero attention and gave their eyes somewhere to be that wasn't Wren's face.

"Go," they repeated, mild as anything, like the word was a title they were trying to place. "That's an interesting word to just leave lying on the counter like that. Very Hemingway. Lots of unsaid things in a short sentence."

They set the cards down, only to immediately pick up a different, entirely unrelated stack of receipts and start squaring those instead.

"Where, exactly, is *go*. Asking for — " a beat, the pen tapping again before they stilled it with two fingers, " — inventory purposes."

The shop creaked around them, radiator groaning somewhere in the back, rain still going steady against the window. Sable didn't look up yet. Just kept their eyes on the receipts, waiting, with the particular stillness of someone who'd gotten very good at appearing unaffected.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The receipts didn't need squaring anymore. Sable set them down anyway, hands going still on the counter in a way that felt more deliberate than any fidget had been.

"No," they said slowly, like tasting the word for spoiled milk. "No, I don't suppose you did."

They didn't reach for anything else to organize. That, more than anything, would have alarmed anyone who'd spent enough afternoons watching Sable's hands — the sudden, uncharacteristic idleness of them.

"You're going somewhere," Sable said, circling back to it, because it was easier than the silence Wren had left hanging. "And you didn't finish that sentence, which either means you forgot how sentences work, or you're waiting for me to fill in the blank." A pause, dry as the dust motes catching the grey window-light. "I should warn you, I'm terrible at guessing games. Spent four years failing to predict the endings of mystery novels I was literally holding in my hands."

Sable finally looked up. Really looked, in a way they usually reserved for pricing a rare edition — assessing, careful, like they might miss something if they blinked.

"So. Try again. Or don't." Their voice dropped, just slightly, losing some of its practiced ease. "But if you're going to leave a sentence like that just sitting on my counter, unfinished, I'd like to know if I'm supposed to be doing something about it."

The bell above the door stayed silent. The rain kept on. Sable didn't reorganize a single thing.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'm moving," *I say, quietly. I can feel my cheeks flush a little. It feels silly to be so nervous.* "To another city. Today."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The word *today* landed like a dropped book — flat, final, no elegant way to soften the sound of it.

Sable's hand moved toward the receipts again, an old reflex, then stopped halfway, hovering there uselessly before dropping back to the counter. For a moment they didn't say anything at all, which was, in itself, a kind of confession — Sable always had something to say. It was practically a professional requirement.

"Today," they repeated, and it came out steadier than they expected, which surprised them more than it should have. "That's — " A short laugh, more air than sound. "That's not even proper notice. You can't return a library book that fast. There are late fees for less."

They looked down at the ledger, at nothing, at the neat rows of numbers that suddenly seemed very stupid and very small.

"Where," Sable said, and this time the word came out careful, like something breakable being set down. Not *why*. They weren't going to ask *why*. That question had teeth they didn't trust themselves not to show.

The rain kept going outside, indifferent. Sable reached for the pen again, turned it over once in their fingers, didn't write anything.

"You came here to tell me in person," they said slowly, not quite a question. "Instead of just — not. That's either very kind of you, or very cruel. I haven't decided which." A beat. "Possibly both. Dickens would've had a field day with you."

They finally met Wren's eyes again, and there was something unguarded there for exactly a second and a half before the old instinct clicked back into place, papering over it with dry amusement.

"So. How long do I have you standing in my shop before the rest of your life very rudely interrupts."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The pen went still under Sable's fingers — not dropped, not gripped, just... still, like something caught mid-sentence with nowhere left to go. The warmth of Wren's hand was close enough to register without any contact at all, which was somehow worse than if they'd actually touched.

Sable didn't pull away. Didn't move closer either. They just stayed there, looking down at the small negligible distance between two hands on a countertop like it was a puzzle they'd been asked to solve without instructions.

"You're going to make me say something unbearably sincere, aren't you." Their voice had lost its usual polish, gone rougher at the edges. "Right here. In front of the Wodehouse. He'd never let me hear the end of it."

They didn't move their hand away. They also didn't move it the last half-inch it would've taken.

"I've spent eleven months," Sable said, quieter now, each word placed like they were afraid of dropping one, "cataloguing every single time you walked through that door like it wasn't the best part of my week. I had a whole system. Very organized. Dewey would've been proud." A breath. "And now you're telling me the system's obsolete in—" they glanced at the clock on the wall, absurdly, "—four hours, give or take traffic."

Their eyes lifted, and this time they didn't look away, didn't reach for the pen or the receipts or anything else to busy their hands with. Just let the quiet sit there, unbearable and unedited, the rain still ticking against the window like a clock counting something down.

"I'm not going to be the reason you're late," Sable said, and it came out almost gentle, almost a joke, entirely not one. "But I'd like it on the record that I noticed. That I've been noticing. For a while."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I look at Sable, really look at them, and my breath hitches a little.* "I noticed too." *My voice is barely a whisper.* "Every day."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
For a moment, Sable didn't trust their own voice enough to use it. The rain filled the silence generously, the radiator ticked, and somewhere in the shop a page turned itself against the draft — the kind of small, ordinary sound that suddenly felt unbearably loud.

"Every day," Sable echoed, like they were trying the phrase on for size, seeing if it fit against everything they'd told themselves for eleven months about *just being friendly, just being a good customer, nothing more.* It didn't fit. It never had. "That's — " They exhaled, short and unsteady. "That's genuinely inconvenient information to receive four hours before you leave the country. Or the state. Wherever it is you're going that I still haven't gotten out of you."

Their hand hadn't moved. Neither had Wren's. The half-inch remained, stubborn and enormous, a whole unspoken paragraph living in that small distance.

"I had this theory," Sable said, quieter, "that if I never said anything, it wouldn't be true yet. Very sound logic. Schrödinger would've approved." A pause, and something in their face went unguarded again, longer this time — not just a second and a half. "Turns out that's not how any of this works. Turns out I've just been standing very still in a burning building, congratulating myself on not noticing the smoke."

They looked down at their hands again — at the negligible, terrible distance — and this time, instead of pen or paper or receipts, Sable simply turned their hand over. Not closing the gap. Just open. An offering, not a demand.

"I'm not going to ask you to stay," they said, voice rough at the edges but steady enough to mean it. "That's not — that's not fair to either of us, and frankly, I've read enough tragic Victorian romances to know how that story ends. Someone always dies of consumption or regret." A breath. "But I'd like four hours that aren't spent pretending this is just a return trip for cookbooks."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I slide my hand over, closing the small gap. My fingers intertwine with Sable's.* "Good. Because I have a lot to say, and not a lot of time."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The contact landed somewhere Sable hadn't prepared for — not the hand itself, which was warm and real and entirely too solid to argue with, but the *certainty* of it. No hesitation. No half-inch left dangling like a question mark.

Sable's fingers curled around Wren's before they'd consciously decided to let them, and for one unguarded moment, they just stood there, looking down at their joined hands like they were reading a book they'd already memorized but never actually understood until now.

"Well," they said, and their voice cracked slightly on the single syllable, betraying them completely. "That's — " A short laugh, breathless, nothing dry about it this time. "That's not fair. I had at least three more deflections prepared. Auden. A bit of Rilke, if things got desperate."

They didn't let go. Didn't reach for the pen, the ledger, the receipts — nothing. Just stood there, hand in Wren's, the shop gone quiet around them except for rain and radiator and the sound of their own pulse doing something embarrassingly loud in their ears.

"Then talk fast," Sable said, quieter now, stepping around the counter so there was nothing left between them but air. "I'm good at listening. It's talking about myself I'm bad at — you may have noticed the pattern. Forty years of literature to hide behind and I still can't find the right page for this."

They tilted their head slightly, studying Wren's face like they were trying to catalogue every detail before the clock made it a memory instead of a moment.

"Four hours," Sable said, almost to themselves. "I've waited longer for rarer books. I can do four hours." A pause, something almost like a real smile breaking through. "Go on, then. Say the things. I promise not to alphabetize anything while you do it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I squeeze Sable's hand.* "I was hoping you'd say that." *I glance around the shop.* "So, what do you want to do for the next four hours?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable considered the question with the gravity of someone being asked to choose their own epitaph.

"Well, I could show you the back room," they said, tone dry again but softer at the edges, "where I keep the books too fragile to sell and too stubborn to throw away. Feels thematically appropriate." A beat. "Or we could sit in the reading nook, the one with the chair that's older than both of us combined, and I could read you something. Not because I think it'll say what I can't — I'm past that particular cowardice now, apparently — but because some things are better with a soundtrack."

They glanced toward the window, at the rain still coming down steady and grey, then back at Wren, unwilling to let their eyes drift far.

"Or," Sable said, quieter, "we could just stand here a while longer. Not doing anything particularly literary about it. Four hours isn't long enough to waste on being clever."

Their thumb moved once, absently, along the side of Wren's hand — small, involuntary, the kind of thing Sable would've caught and stopped a week ago.

"I don't actually care what we do," they admitted, and it cost them something to say it plainly, no Hemingway, no Dickens, no safe borrowed words. "I just don't want to spend it watching the clock. So. You choose. I'll follow. Might be the first time in my life I've said that sentence and meant it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Hmm." *I think for a moment, still holding Sable's hand.* "Let's go to the back room then. I want to see your secret treasures."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
A ghost of a smile pulled at Sable's mouth. "Secret treasures. You make it sound more exciting than it is. Mostly it's just books with broken spines and one taxidermied owl I inherited that I've never had the heart to sell or display. Long story. Involves a very eccentric great-aunt and a bet I apparently lost."

Still holding Wren's hand — deliberately now, no more hesitation about it — Sable led the way past the counter, through a narrow gap between two shelves that had been arranged, at some point, by someone with absolutely no regard for foot traffic. The bell over the front door stayed silent, and Sable, for once, didn't care if anyone else came in. Let them wait. Let the shop go untended for four hours. It had survived worse.

The back room smelled even older than the front — leather and dust and something faintly like cedar, from a drawer of pressed flowers nobody remembered opening. Shelves rose to the ceiling, crammed with things too fragile for the sales floor: a water-damaged First Folio facsimile, a box of unsent letters someone had found in a dead man's coat pocket, the owl, glass-eyed and unbothered, perched on a shelf like a disapproving landlord.

"Welcome to the graveyard of things I couldn't let go of," Sable said, gesturing vaguely at the chaos with their free hand, "which, in retrospect, might be a theme with me."

They pulled a low stool out from under a table, more out of habit than real intention to sit, then abandoned the idea entirely, turning instead to look at Wren directly, the owl and the folios and the whole ridiculous collection of hoarded things suddenly very unimportant.

"I could give you the full tour. Explain the provenance of every broken-backed novel in this room." A pause, their voice dropping slightly, losing its performance. "Or I could just say that I'm glad you're here, in this specific dusty room, instead of wherever you're supposed to be right now. And that four hours already feels like it's going too fast."

They didn't reach for a book. Didn't reorganize the shelf, even though three spines were slightly askew and it was killing them a little. Some habits, apparently, could be overridden.

"Pick your poison," Sable said instead, nodding toward the shelves. "Poetry, letters from strangers, or a taxidermied bird with better boundaries than me. I'm equally sentimental about all three."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I squeeze their hand again, my gaze lingering on the owl for a moment.* "I'm glad I'm here too, Sable." *I turn to them fully, a small smile playing on my lips.* "How about you tell me the story of the owl? And then... you can tell me what you're really thinking."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable glanced at the owl like it had just been called as a witness in a trial it hadn't agreed to testify in.

"The owl," they said, "is named Barnaby. Not by me — by my great-aunt Odette, who believed all taxidermy deserved dignity and a proper name, the same way you'd name a dog or a particularly stubborn houseplant." They reached out, not quite touching the glass case, just gesturing at it with the hand that wasn't holding Wren's. "She won him in a card game. Actual poker, actual stakes, against a man she always referred to only as 'that insufferable ornithologist.' I never learned his real name. I'm not sure she remembered it either."

Sable's mouth curved, somewhere between fondness and old grief. "When she died, everyone else got jewelry or money or, in my cousin's case, an genuinely alarming amount of taxidermied fish. I got Barnaby. And this shop, technically, though I think she saw those as a matching set — the bird and the building, both things nobody else wanted and I couldn't bring myself to let go of."

They fell quiet a moment, thumb moving once against Wren's knuckles, an anchor rather than a fidget now.

"She used to say you could tell everything about a person by what they refuse to throw away." Sable's voice had gone lower, less performance in it now, more just — them. "I've had four hours to think about that today, apparently, without meaning to."

They finally turned fully toward Wren, letting the joke about Barnaby settle and fade, no new one rushing in to fill the space it left.

"What I'm really thinking," Sable said, slower now, like each word had to be excavated from somewhere they didn't usually dig, "is that I've built this whole shop — this whole life, really — out of things I decided to keep. Old books nobody wanted. A bird nobody needed. A very stubborn refusal to change anything about how I live." A breath. "And somewhere in the last eleven months, you became one of those things. Something I was keeping. Except I never told you that, because saying it made it real, and real things can leave."

Their eyes didn't waver, even though everything in them wanted to look away, reach for a shelf, straighten something.

"I don't know how to do this part," Sable admitted, quiet and unguarded. "The part where you say the true thing and then just — stand there, without a book to hide behind. But I'd rather be terrible at it with you than good at it alone. If that's not too much, for someone who's leaving in three and a half hours."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My grip on Sable's hand tightens.* "It's not too much. Not at all." *I take a breath, my eyes searching theirs.* "I didn't want to leave without saying something. Without knowing if... if I was just imagining things."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"You weren't imagining it," Sable said, and there was no hedge in it, no literary detour, no safe quotation to hide behind. Just the plain fact of it, laid bare on the table between them like something finally taken out of storage.

"I'm fairly certain I've imagined a great many things in my life — I once convinced myself a customer was trying to steal a first edition Brontë when he was actually just looking for the bathroom — but not this. Not you." They shook their head slightly, like they were still cataloguing the evidence even now. "I noticed the way you always touched the spines of books you liked before you decided to buy them. I noticed you hummed under your breath in the poetry section, always slightly off-key, always the same three lines of some song I never asked you to name because I didn't want to know it wasn't for me."

Sable's free hand came up, hesitant, and brushed a strand of damp hair back from Wren's face — an action so uncharacteristically tender it seemed to surprise them as much as anyone, their fingers lingering a half-second longer than necessary before dropping back down.

"I don't imagine things like that," they said, quieter. "I'm too busy pretending I don't feel them at all. Turns out that's a worse habit than the hoarding."

The rain had softened outside, gentler now against the window, like even the weather had decided to give them room to breathe.

"So no," Sable said, "you weren't imagining it. You were right. About all of it. I just didn't have the nerve to be the one who said so first." A small, wry twist of their mouth. "Consider this me finally returning that particular overdue book. Sorry about the late fee."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *A small laugh escapes me.* "I'm glad you finally returned it then." *I lean my head against their shoulder, a comfortable silence settling between us.* "So, what now?"
