dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't turn around immediately. They slid a slim volume of Neruda into its proper place, spine flush with the others, before letting their hands fall still.

"New," they repeated, as though the word were a curious artifact requiring appraisal. "In an antiquarian bookshop. There's a paradox in there somewhere. I'll spare you the Borges reference."

They turned then, wiping a nonexistent smudge of dust from their sleeve. The rain had left dark spots across the shoulders of Wren's jacket, and Sable's gaze caught there a moment too long before finding the middle distance instead — the safer country of the front window.

"There's a box of estate acquisitions I haven't sorted. Mostly water-damaged sermons and a suspicious quantity of Reader's Digest condensed novels." A pause. Their fingers found the edge of the counter and began, absently, straightening a stack of bookmarks that were already square. "But I could be persuaded to dig. If you had the patience for it."

They glanced up, briefly. "You're dripping on my floorboards, by the way. Not a complaint. Merely an observation. They've survived worse."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I shrug off my jacket and hang it on the coat rack by the door.* "I'm always patient for a good find. You know that."

I walk over to the counter, leaning against it. "And yeah, I'm a leaky faucet today."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable straightened the bookmarks another fraction of an inch, which brought them no closer to being straight and served no purpose except to occupy the space where their answer should have been.

"Patient," they said. "Yes. You've never once complained when I've made you wait through a tangent on marginalia or the moral failings of a particular binder in 1890s Edinburgh. That's either patience or a concussion. I've never been certain which."

The rain drummed on. The lavender-and-old-paper smell thickened in the damp, as it always did when the weather turned. Sable was aware of Wren leaning against the counter the way one is aware of a lit stove without looking at it — a warmth registered at the periphery, deliberately not examined.

"The box is in the back," they said, and did not move toward it. "It'll keep. It's kept for forty years in some dead solicitor's attic. Another minute won't offend it."

They finally abandoned the bookmarks, since there was nothing left to do to them, and folded their arms instead — a poor substitute for a task. Their eyes came to rest somewhere around Wren's collarbone before ticking, resolutely, up to the shelf behind him.

"You rehearsed something," they said. It wasn't a question. "You've got the look of a man who came in with a speech and lost it somewhere between the door and here. Don't worry. It happens to the best of us. Ask anyone who's ever stood at a lectern." A beat. "What was it?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's arms tightened where they were folded, an almost imperceptible adjustment, as if bracing against a draft that hadn't come.

"No," they agreed, and the word came out lighter than intended, which was its own kind of tell. "You didn't."

The Neruda was still slightly proud of its neighbors — they could see it from here, a millimeter's insolence — and their hand twitched toward it before they caught the impulse and let it die. There was nowhere left to put their hands. This was, they reflected distantly, the entire problem with people. Books stayed where you shelved them.

"You've stopped talking," they observed. "In my experience that's either the prelude to something or the aftermath of losing one's nerve. I'd offer you the relevant epigram, but I find I've mislaid mine." A thin, dry breath that wasn't quite a laugh. "Which is unusual. I keep a rather extensive collection."

The rain filled the silence Sable couldn't seem to. They looked at Wren then — actually looked, abandoning the safe geography of the shelf, the window, the collarbone — and it cost them something to hold it.

"So." Quiet. Steadier than they felt. "You didn't come for books. What did you come for?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, looking down at my hands.* "I came to say goodbye."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The word landed and did not move, the way certain words don't — heavy, immovable, taking up all the space in the small shop.

Sable's face did nothing. That was the discipline of thirty years spent perfecting a countenance for the delivery of bad news to sentimental customers — *no, we don't carry that; no, it isn't valuable; no, it can't be repaired.* The rain went on. The lavender smell went on. Everything went on except Sable, who had gone very still in the way of a person who has just been told the floor is not, in fact, a floor.

Their hand found the Neruda. Pushed it flush. It clicked into the line of its neighbors and there was nothing insolent left about it, nothing out of place, and still Sable's fingers lingered on the spine as though it might come loose again.

"Goodbye," they said. A curator's tone, appraising the object, keeping it at arm's length where it could not do damage. "There's a whole genre for that. The departure. Half the good poems are goodbyes wearing better clothes." They swallowed. "I could recommend you something for the train, or the plane, or wherever it is you're — " The sentence declined to finish itself. Their jaw worked around its absence.

They turned, then, to the shelf behind them. Began, with slow deliberate hands, to move a book that did not need moving from one place it belonged to another place it belonged.

"Where," Sable asked the shelf, "are you going?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand did not move. It should have — every instinct built over thirty careful years told them to withdraw, to find another spine to straighten, to reach for the armor of some borrowed line. But Wren's hand was there, near enough that the small distance between them seemed to hum, and Sable found they could not do the sensible thing.

The book stayed where it was, half-shelved, forgotten between them.

"That's cheating," they said, very quietly. "You've cornered me against my own inventory. There's nothing left to reorganize." A breath that shook where it shouldn't have. "You've no idea how unmoored a man is without a task."

The rain kept on. Sable looked down at the narrow gap between their hand and Wren's, the way one looks at the edge of something high — the vertigo, the terrible arithmetic of the fall.

"I had a whole speech too, you know." The admission came out rough, unrehearsed, entirely unlike them. "Weeks of it. I kept meaning to — and then you'd come in dripping on my floorboards and ask for something in the back, and I'd think, *not today, there's time, there's always more time.*" Their thumb shifted, a fraction, closing the distance to almost nothing. "Turns out I'm a poor curator of my own inventory. I let the important thing sit in a box in the attic for forty years."

They finally looked up. Held it.

"Where are you going, Wren."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I close the small gap between our hands, my fingers brushing against theirs.* "Pittsburgh. My sister lives there."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Pittsburgh," Sable echoed, and something in their chest loosened and tightened at once, an odd contradictory thing. Their fingers turned, slowly, under Wren's — not gripping, just permitting the touch, allowing it to be a fact between them. "Not Patagonia. Not the far side of some ocean with a name I'd have to look up." A thin sound escaped them, closer to a laugh than not. "Pittsburgh has trains. Pittsburgh has phones. Pittsburgh, God help me, probably has bookshops of its own, though I'll thank you not to be unfaithful to me with them."

The word slipped out before they could vet it — *unfaithful* — and they heard it land, and did not take it back. That was new. That was terrifying. They left it where it fell.

"I thought — " They stopped. Started again, steadier. "I thought you meant the kind of goodbye that doesn't have a return address. I'd already begun composing something suitably devastating and self-contained. Byron, probably. He's good for that sort of controlled bleeding." Their thumb moved over the back of Wren's hand, tentative, as though the gesture were a language they'd read about but never spoken aloud. "But your sister lives there. And you came here first. Before the train. Dripping on my floorboards."

Sable let the half-shelved book stay half-shelved. For once they did not need it.

"So this isn't goodbye," they said. Quiet. Almost hopeful, which was an expression that felt foreign on them, ill-fitting, borrowed from someone braver. "This is you giving me an address."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I smile, a genuine, relieved smile.* "Something like that." I squeeze their hand gently. "And I'd never be unfaithful."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the squeeze land and, for once, did not deflect it — did not reach for Wodehouse or Byron or the safe cold distance of the third person. They simply let their hand stay where it was, warm and improbably still, in Wren's.

"Well," they said. "Good." A pause, and then, drier: "Though I'll want that in writing. I'm an antiquarian. I don't trust anything that isn't documented in at least two copies with a witness present."

But the wit had gone soft at the edges, the way ink does in the damp, and they didn't seem to mind. The rain had thinned to something gentler against the glass. The lavender smell hung between them, and the shop was very quiet, and Sable — who did not make first moves, who had spent thirty years perfecting the art of the unfinished sentence — found the silence, for once, was not a thing they needed to fill.

"I have your address," they said finally, as though testing the weight of it, finding it bearable. "You'll have mine. There'll be letters. I write an insufferable letter, I should warn you. Marginalia. Footnotes to the footnotes. You'll regret encouraging me by the third one."

Their eyes flicked down to the book still stranded half-shelved beside their joined hands, then back up. They did not move to fix it. That, more than anything they'd said, was the confession.

"When's the train."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Tomorrow morning," *I say, my voice a little softer than usual.* "But I have some time now. Want to help me pack up that box of sermons?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
"Tomorrow," Sable repeated, and there was a whole life's worth of arithmetic in the word — the hours between now and then, counted and found wanting, and yet not empty. Not empty. That was the difference. "Then we're not wasting any of it on decorum. Good."

They finally released Wren's hand — reluctantly, with the air of someone setting down a book they meant to return to — and reached instead to slide the stranded volume the last inch home. It went in clean. A small, satisfied click. The last thing in the shop that had been out of place, and now it wasn't, and Sable found they could breathe around that.

"The box of sermons," they said, already moving toward the curtain that separated the shop from the back. "Fair warning: the water damage means half of them smell like a church that drowned. There's a genuine chance we unearth something valuable and a certainty we unearth several silverfish. I make no promises about which you'll find more interesting."

At the curtain they paused, one hand on the worn velvet, and looked back — actually looked, the way they'd been practicing all afternoon without meaning to.

"I'm glad you came in dripping," they said. It cost them, plainly, but they said it anyway. "For the record. Since I've apparently decided today is the day I stop keeping things in the attic." A beat, and the dryness reasserted itself, a familiar coat pulled back on. "Now come on. Sermons wait for no man. Though God knows they've made me wait for entire sermons."

They held the curtain open.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I grin, feeling a warmth spread through me.* "Lead the way, then." *I follow Sable through the curtain, ready to face any drowned churches or silverfish.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The back room was smaller than the shop and lit by a single bulb that had never once, in Sable's tenure, been bright enough for anything. Boxes rose in unsteady ziggurats along the walls, and the estate acquisition sat squat in the middle of the floor, its cardboard buckled and freckled with old water stains, the smell rising from it exactly as promised — damp stone, mildew, the ghost of incense.

Sable crouched beside it and pried back the flaps. "Behold," they said, with the flourish of a man unveiling a masterpiece he privately suspected was a forgery. "The collected devotions of someone who clearly found them insufficient, given they ended up in a solicitor's attic rather than passed lovingly to an heir."

They lifted the first volume, thumbed it open, winced at the bloom of foxing across the frontispiece, and set it aside on the floor between them — creating, without quite deciding to, a small shared territory. Their shoulder was near Wren's now, in the cramped space, and they did not move away from it. That, too, was practice.

"You take that stack," they said, nodding to the left side of the box. "Salvageable to the right, silverfish casualties to the left. And if you find anything that isn't a sermon — a letter tucked in the pages, a pressed flower, a train ticket somebody never used — " Sable's hands went still for a moment over the next book, and then didn't. "Set it apart. Those are the things worth keeping. People hide the important things inside the dull ones. Attic logic." A dry glance sideways. "I'd know."

They handed Wren the next volume, fingers brushing again — and this time Sable let it be exactly what it was, and said nothing clever about it at all.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take the book from Sable, our fingers brushing again. I look at the stack, then down at the book in my hand.* "Attic logic, huh? I guess we're all guilty of that." *I begin to sort through the first few books, carefully opening them to check for hidden treasures.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable worked in companionable quiet for a while, the only sounds the whisper of turning pages and the rain, softer now, a benediction on the roof. They sorted with a practiced economy — a glance, a verdict, left or right — but slower than usual, they noticed. Reluctant to reach the bottom of the box. As though the box, once emptied, might take the afternoon with it.

"Guilty," they agreed eventually. "Some of us more than others. I've a whole shop of other people's hidden things and thirty years of practice at ignoring my own." They eased a warped hymnal open, found nothing but foxing and a coffee ring older than either of them, and set it left. "It's a coward's arrangement, when you think about it. Surrounding yourself with everyone else's confessions so you never have to make your own."

They reached for the next book and their hand met the bottom of the box instead — cardboard, damp, sooner than expected. Sable looked at their own empty fingers for a moment.

Then, near the base, wedged flat against the seam where it had slid and been forgotten: an envelope. Yellowed, unsealed, no stamp. Sable drew it out carefully, the way they handled anything fragile, and turned it over. Blank. A letter someone had written and never sent, or never had the nerve to.

"Attic logic," they said quietly, and did not open it. Held it out to Wren instead, across the small territory of sorted books between them. Their eyes came up, steady, unguarded in a way that would have appalled them a week ago.

"Someone kept the important thing where they thought no one would find it," Sable said. "And then went to Pittsburgh, or wherever the dead go, and left it in a box for forty years." A breath. "I'd rather not make the same mistake. So — for the record, and only once, because I'll deny the sincerity of it entirely if you ever repeat it — " Their thumb pressed the corner of the envelope. "I don't want you to go. But I'm glad it's the kind of goodbye with a return address. And I intend to write you insufferable letters until you regret leaving me your sister's zip code."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take the envelope from Sable, my fingers brushing theirs again. I hold it for a moment, then set it carefully on top of the pile of 'salvageable' books.* "I won't regret it, Sable. Not ever." *I meet their gaze, a small, soft smile on my face.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held the gaze longer than was comfortable, longer than they'd have thought themselves capable of a week ago — and did not reach for a book, or a bookmark, or the reliable armor of some borrowed line. There was nothing left in the room to reorganize. The box was empty. The envelope was set apart with the things worth keeping. And Wren was there, close in the poor light, saying *not ever* as though it were a simple thing.

"You say that now," Sable murmured, but the deflection had no teeth to it. It came out fond. "Wait until the third letter. There's a running feud with a bookbinder dead since 1897 you've not even heard the half of."

They rose from their crouch, knees protesting, and offered a hand down to Wren — an ordinary courtesy that Sable made faintly less ordinary by not letting go once Wren was up. They stood there in the cramped back room, the drowned-church smell around them, the single bulb doing its inadequate best, and Sable's fingers stayed laced with Wren's as though it were the most natural cataloguing in the world. Salvageable. To the right. Worth keeping.

"Tomorrow morning," they said. "That's the train. Which means there's an entire evening between now and then, and I've just closed the shop." They hadn't, technically. They tipped their head toward the front, toward the bell and the CLOSED sign that would be true the moment they turned it. "The sermons will keep. They've waited forty years. They can wait one more night while I take you somewhere that doesn't smell of mildew and remind you what you're supposedly going to miss."

A pause. The old dryness, gentled almost past recognition.

"Consider it the first insufferable letter. Delivered in person. Before I lose my nerve and shelve the important thing back in the attic where it's safe."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I squeeze Sable's hand, a genuine warmth spreading through me.* "I'd like that very much, Sable." *I look around the dusty back room.* "Lead the way."

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't look up immediately. They slid *Auden* back into place with perhaps more deliberateness than the task required, fingers lingering on the spine.

"New," they repeated, as if testing the word for structural integrity. "You've come to an antiquarian bookshop asking about *new*. Aisle four has a 1987 airport paperback of *The Firm* if you're feeling adventurous."

They turned then. They couldn't help it.

The rain had done something to Wren's hair. Sable noted this the way one notes a water stain on a first edition — with a kind of resigned acknowledgment that it was going to be a problem.

"There is, actually." They moved behind the counter, pulling out a cloth-wrapped parcel that had arrived Tuesday and which Sable had, for reasons they declined to examine, not yet shelved. "Came in with an estate lot from the Pembrook house. Someone in that family had taste, which appears to have been a recessive trait."

They set it on the counter but didn't unwrap it. Instead they straightened the stack of bookmarks beside the register, which had been perfectly straight.

"It's a 1923 Woolf. *Jacob's Room*. Decent condition. Previous owner wrote their name in it, which some people find objectionable." A pause. "I don't, particularly."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I watch Sable's movements, a small smile playing on my lips.* "No, not new-new. You know what I mean." *I gesture vaguely.* "Something I haven't read yet."

*My eyes flick to the cloth-wrapped parcel.* "Woolf, huh? Sounds promising." *I lean a little closer to the counter.* "What about the name? Who was the previous owner?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable unwrapped the cloth with the particular care of someone who had learned, through one memorable incident involving a Dickens serialization, not to rush. The book emerged in sections — brown boards, a slightly faded spine, the soft give of pages that had been read and thought about rather than merely owned.

They opened the front board and turned it to face Wren without handing it over. The name was written in a slanted, confident hand. *Eleanor V. Marsh. Her book.*

"Eleanor V. Marsh." Sable said it as though introducing two people at a party. "Whoever she was. The estate solicitor didn't know, or didn't care. She had good handwriting and owned three boxes of books, which tells you most of what you need to know about a person."

They became aware they were still holding the cover open and closed it. Set it on the counter. Did not slide it toward Wren. This was not, they told themselves, intentional.

"*Jacob's Room* is an odd choice to start with, if you haven't read her before." They moved a pen from one side of the register to the other. "It's the book where Woolf figures out she's Woolf. Structurally strange. Some people find it unsatisfying." A beat. "Those people are reading it wrong."

The rain intensified briefly against the front window. Sable did not use this as an excuse to look at anything other than the middle distance to Wren's left.

"Were you looking for something specific, or is this one of your browse-until-something-objects visits?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The pen Sable had just moved got moved back.

They heard the sentence end where it ended and understood, in the way one understands a structural problem in a building — not all at once but as a slow realization of what the absence of certain things meant.

"Didn't come for books," they repeated. The register tape needed straightening. It did not need straightening. "In a bookshop. That's either very dramatic or very efficient of you, and I can't yet determine which."

They were looking at the Woolf now. *Her book*, Eleanor had written, with the confidence of someone who meant it. Sable had always found that inscription slightly defiant. As though Eleanor had anticipated someone, someday, questioning the claim.

"There's a school of thought," Sable said, and their voice had taken on the particular quality it got when they were using words as load-bearing walls, "that everything worth saying was already said better by someone dead. Saves considerable effort." They straightened the cloth the book had been wrapped in, folding it into thirds. "Henry James, for instance, spent approximately nine hundred pages in *The Ambassadors* on the subject of a man who can't quite bring himself to say the thing he came to say."

The cloth was folded. There was nothing left to fold.

Sable finally looked up.

"You were saying."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I..." *I trail off, looking at the Woolf, then back at Sable.* "I just wanted to say goodbye." *My voice is a little softer than I intended.* "I'm leaving town today."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The cloth unfolded itself. Sable's hands did this without consulting the rest of them, smoothing it flat against the counter, then folding it again along different lines.

"Today." The word came out with a strange flatness, like a note played on a piano that needed tuning. "You've come to say goodbye to a bookshop."

They were aware this was not entirely what Wren had said. They let it stand anyway.

The rain against the window was doing something relentless and specific. Sable found a smudge on the glass of the register display case and addressed it with the corner of the cloth.

"Woolf wrote something rather good about goodbyes, as it happens. Though she called them 'partings,' which is the kind of word that admits more weight." They stopped cleaning the glass. The smudge was gone. They kept the cloth moving anyway. "She understood that the difficulty isn't the leaving. It's the — " they paused, and the pause had a shape to it, " — the afterward. The room that continues existing once the person has walked out of it."

Sable set the cloth down.

They looked at Wren then, directly, which was not something they made a habit of. The shop felt very quiet in the way that old buildings do when they've absorbed enough history to have opinions about what happens inside them.

"Where," Sable said, and it came out more plainly than anything else they'd said since the bell rang, "are you going."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The book was between them. Sable's hand was on the back board. Wren's hand was on the front.

Eleanor V. Marsh, in her slanted confident script, somewhere in the middle.

Sable did not move their hand. This was not, they were fairly certain, a decision so much as a failure to make one, which amounted to the same thing and which they would examine later, at length, probably at two in the morning with a cup of tea they'd forgotten to drink.

"My grandmother," Sable said, and then stopped, because that was not a sentence they had intended to begin. They tried again. "There's a thing that happens with books from estates. You spend enough time with them and you start to feel — " another stop. The word *responsible* was somewhere in the vicinity but it wasn't right. "You feel that you ought to know what happened to them. To the person. Whether they were — " the word *happy* appeared and was immediately dismissed as structurally unsound, " — whether things went the way they hoped."

The rain.

"I don't know where Eleanor went," Sable said. "After this. The book came and she didn't, and that's the whole of what I have."

Their thumb moved, very slightly, against the back board. A millimeter, perhaps. Perhaps less. The kind of movement that could be attributed to the involuntary workings of tendons and had nothing to do with the three inches of old paper separating their hand from Wren's.

"You didn't answer the question."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I don't pull my hand away, even though my fingers are tingling.* "I'm going to Portland. For a new job." *I look at our hands, then back up at Sable's face.* "It's... a long way from here."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Portland landed in the room like a stone dropped into still water.

Sable watched the ripples without moving.

"Portland." They appeared to be consulting some internal index. "Sylvia Beach opened a bookshop in Paris because she couldn't afford New York. People go where the work is. That's — that's a very reasonable thing to do." The last sentence had the quality of something read aloud from a manual. Sable was aware of this.

Their hand had not moved. They were becoming increasingly conscious of their hand, of its precise location in the world, of the geography of the situation which was: old book, two hands, three inches, a word that meant a long way from here.

"Portland has good bookshops," they said. "Powell's, obviously. Enormous. You could lose a week in there and emerge speaking in tongues, which some people consider a feature." A pause. "You'd like it."

The last three words sat differently from the rest. Sable heard this and had no remedy for it.

They looked down at the book. *Her book.* Eleanor's name in its confident slant, staking a claim that had outlasted Eleanor by however many decades it had been. The things people left behind without meaning to. The shape of a hand in an inscription. The particular way someone asked about *something new* when they already knew the inventory by heart.

Sable's jaw tightened slightly.

"Today," they said again, quietly. Not an accusation. Something closer to the opposite of one. "You're leaving today and you came here first."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I did," *I say softly, my thumb brushing lightly against the cover of the book.* "I wanted to say goodbye to you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The correction landed.

*To you.* Not to the shop. Not to the Wodehouse shelf or the lavender sachet or the particular smell of paper and accumulated years. Sable heard the distinction and could not, in good conscience, pretend otherwise.

They looked down at the place where Wren's thumb had moved against the cover. The book was very old. It had survived Eleanor and the Pembrook estate and Tuesday's delivery and Sable's inexplicable inability to shelve it, and it was surviving this too, which felt both appropriate and faintly absurd.

"Wren." Their own name for the feeling sat somewhere in their chest doing nothing useful.

Sable did not move their hand.

"I have — " they started, and the sentence had no ending prepared for it. They tried a different door. "There's a line in this book. Not this copy, I mean, but — Woolf writes about a character who is primarily known through his absence. What other people carry of him. The outline he leaves in the air." They were not looking at the middle distance this time. They were looking at the book, which was safer and also not safe at all. "I've been thinking about that line since Tuesday."

Since Tuesday, when the parcel arrived and Sable had set it on the counter and not shelved it and not examined why.

"That was before I knew you were leaving today." A pause with considerable structural weight. "I'm not sure it changes the thinking. Only the — timeline."

Their hand finally moved. Not away. Forward, very slightly, so that the edge of their fingers rested against the edge of Wren's on the cover of Eleanor Marsh's book.

Sable said nothing else. They had used, by their own standards, an extraordinary number of words already, and some things apparently required the absence of them.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My breath catches slightly as Sable's fingers brush mine.* "I... I should probably go." *I don't move my hand, though. My eyes meet theirs.* "My train leaves in a few hours."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The clock above the poetry section ticked.

Sable knew the exact duration of *a few hours* the way they knew the closing time of the shop, the weight of a first edition in both hands, the particular quality of silence that followed the bell above the door. They knew it precisely and found the knowledge unhelpful.

"A few hours," they said. The words came out carefully, the way you carry something fragile across an uneven floor.

They did not move their fingers.

There was a version of this moment, Sable understood, in which they said something dry and useful about Powell's and sent Wren out into the rain with Eleanor Marsh's Woolf tucked under one arm and the clean conscience of someone who had behaved sensibly. They could see that version quite clearly. It had a lot to recommend it.

They looked at their own hand. The edge of their fingers against the edge of Wren's. The book between them like a document neither of them had signed.

"Woolf took eleven years between *Jacob's Room* and *The Waves*," Sable said, and their voice was doing something they couldn't entirely control, something quieter than usual, stripped of the usual scaffolding. "That's not — I'm not making a point about patience. I don't know why I said that."

A first, possibly. Sable not knowing why they'd said something.

The rain continued its opinion about the situation.

"Take the book." They slid it forward, finally, under both their hands, toward Wren. "Eleanor would want it read rather than shelved. I've decided this on her behalf." A pause, and then, more quietly, with the careful precision of someone choosing a word they don't use lightly: "Come back and tell me what you think of it. When you — "

They stopped.

*When you can* sat in the unfinished air between them, neither promise nor request, only the shape of something Sable hadn't intended to admit to.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My fingers tighten around the book, even as my heart hammers in my chest.* "I will." *I pull the book gently towards me, finally breaking the contact of our hands.* "Thank you, Sable." *I look at the book, then back at them, a small, sad smile on my face.* "Goodbye."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door was going to ring in a moment.

Sable knew this the way they knew the end of a sentence before reaching the period. Wren would turn, and the door would open, and the rain would come in briefly, and then it wouldn't, and the shop would resume its previous dimensions.

"Goodbye," they said.

The word came out plain and undecorated, without a single literary reference to hide behind, which was perhaps the most honest thing Sable had said in recent memory and which they immediately wanted to take back and couldn't.

They watched Wren cross the floor. They watched the door. Their hands, now empty of both the book and the reason for standing at the counter, settled on the edge of the register with nowhere useful to go.

The bell rang.

The door opened. Rain. The particular smell of a wet afternoon in a world that continued operating on its usual schedule without consulting anyone about it.

The door closed.

Sable stood in the silence for a moment that had no measurable duration. Then they moved, because standing still was not something they had the architecture for right now, and straightened the cloth that had been folded and unfolded and was now simply lying on the counter in whatever shape it had arrived at.

They picked up the pen. Set it down.

Went back to the poetry section.

*Auden* was already in the correct place. Sable pulled it out anyway, held the spine for a moment, and put it back. Then stood with one hand still resting against the shelf, looking at nothing in particular, thinking about Portland and its bookshops and a woman named Eleanor who had written her name in a book like a declaration and then gone somewhere no one had thought to record.

The lavender sachet in the Wodehouse shelf had been there three months.

Sable left it where it was.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I step out into the rain, pulling my jacket tighter around me. I clutch the Woolf to my chest, the dampness already seeping into the paper bag Sable put it in. I don't look back.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell had stopped moving.

Sable knew this because they were looking at it. Not deliberately — they had turned toward the front of the shop for no reason they were prepared to defend, and there was the bell, motionless above the door, doing nothing, as bells do when there is no longer anyone to announce.

They turned back to the poetry section.

*Larkin* was slightly too far left. Sable corrected this with one finger. *Lowell* had been leaning at an angle that would eventually cause a problem. Sable straightened it. These were small, manageable facts about the world, and Sable addressed them with the concentration of someone who needed the work.

The rain came down.

*Jacob's Room* had sat on the counter for four days. Sable had told themselves, on day one, that they were assessing condition before pricing. On day two, that the estate paperwork needed cross-referencing. On day three, they had not told themselves anything, which was its own kind of admission. On day four, Wren had walked in out of the rain asking about something new, and the book had still been on the counter, wrapped in cloth, waiting.

Sable pulled *Millay* from the shelf and put it back.

The shop had a particular quality of silence now that it hadn't had twenty minutes ago. Sable noticed this and found the noticing unhelpful and noticed it anyway. The lavender sachet. The clock. The rain performing its ongoing commentary on the afternoon.

*Come back and tell me what you think of it.*

They had said that. Out loud. With their own mouth.

Sable moved to the front window, ostensibly to check whether the display needed adjustment. The display did not need adjustment. Outside, the street was empty in the way streets become when rain has persuaded everyone with options to exercise them. A few umbrellas in the middle distance. A cab. The ordinary machinery of a city that had no particular feelings about the afternoon.

Wren was somewhere in it. Walking toward a train. Holding Eleanor Marsh's book against a chest Sable was not going to think about.

They thought about it briefly.

Then they turned from the window and went to the back room, where three boxes of the Pembrook estate still waited to be catalogued. They sat down at the worktable, opened the first box, and began the inventory with the methodical attention of someone who had decided that the best available option was to be extremely, specifically useful to the task directly in front of them.

The third item was a slim volume of correspondence. Letters between two people whose names meant nothing. Sable opened it to the middle.

*I think of you when it rains*, one of them had written, in 1931, in ink that had gone the color of old tea. *I don't know what to do with that information so I am sending it to you instead.*

Sable closed the book.

Set it aside.

Picked up the next one.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I'm on the train, watching the city blur into greens and browns. I pull the book out of the damp paper bag, carefully. Eleanor V. Marsh. Her book. I trace her name with my finger, a small smile playing on my lips. I wonder if Sable ever thought about her, like this.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The Pembrook estate had forty-three volumes. Sable knew this by nine o'clock because they had counted them twice, which was not standard practice and which they declined to examine.

The shop had been closed for two hours. The rain had not stopped.

Sable sat at the worktable with a cup of tea they had made and forgotten and remembered and found cold and made again, and the correspondence volume sat at the edge of the table where they had set it aside, and they had not opened it again, and they were not going to open it again, and they picked it up.

*I think of you when it rains.*

Sable put it face-down.

The thing about antiquarian work — the thing Sable had always found useful, had in fact chosen the profession partly for — was that it was concerned with the past in a way that precluded certain kinds of present-tense difficulty. The people in these books were resolved. Eleanor Marsh had lived her life and written her name in it and gone wherever she'd gone, and the question of whether things had turned out well for her was permanently, mercifully closed. You could feel something on her behalf without the feeling having anywhere useful to go. It simply sat there, historical, contained.

Sable picked up the next volume. Set it down. Picked up a pen and wrote nothing.

The train to Portland took, depending on the route, somewhere between forty-five minutes and several hours. Sable knew this because they had looked it up at seven-fifteen and found the information straightforwardly factual and not at all the kind of thing a person did when they were fine.

*Come back and tell me what you think of it.*

The problem with saying a thing out loud was that it continued existing afterward in the acoustic memory of the room. Sable was fairly certain this was not scientifically accurate. It felt accurate.

They pulled the correspondence volume back toward them and turned to the first letter, which was dated March 1929 and began with a discussion of the weather in a way that was clearly not about the weather. Sable read three lines and recognized the technique immediately, having employed a version of it themselves for the better part of the last several weeks, and closed the book again with perhaps more force than the binding strictly warranted.

Forty-three volumes.

Sable picked up the pen and began the inventory in earnest, writing titles and dates and condition notes in the small, precise hand they used for cataloguing, which was different from their regular handwriting in ways they had never articulated to anyone. The work was real. The work had always been real. A 1931 travel memoir, boards worn at the corners but spine intact. A collection of essays, previous owner's marginalia throughout, someone who had disagreed with the author on every third page and said so. A novel Sable didn't recognize, which was unusual enough to slow them down.

They worked until the tea was cold again.

Then they sat in the quiet of the back room with the rain still making its argument against the roof, and looked at the forty-three books arranged in their new order, and thought — with the specific, useless clarity that arrived reliably at this hour — about the way Wren had said *to you*.

Not to the shop.

Sable reached across the table and turned the correspondence volume face-up again. Did not open it.

Somewhere a train was moving through the dark toward Portland, carrying Eleanor Marsh's book and a person who had walked into the rain without looking back, and Sable was here among forty-three dead people's belongings, and this was the shape of the evening, and it was fine, and they were going to finish the inventory.

*I don't know what to do with that information so I am sending it to you instead.*

Sable looked at the ceiling for a long moment.

Then they found a clean sheet of paper, which they did not use, and capped their pen, and turned off the worktable lamp, and went upstairs to the flat above the shop where the night was prepared to continue being exactly as long as it intended to be.

They left the correspondence volume on the table.

Face-up.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I'm curled up in my seat, the rhythm of the train a lullaby. I open the Woolf to the first page, ready to begin, but my eyes drift to the inscription again. "Eleanor V. Marsh. Her book." I smile to myself. Maybe Eleanor wouldn't mind me borrowing it for a while. I pull out my phone, a sudden impulse, and open a new message.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Sable's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - the literary references, careful word choice, physical fidgeting with objects, and emotional guardedness are maintained from first to final turn. The character deepens rather than drifts.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are good but later turns (especially 16, 20, 22) show increased emotional depth and literary sophistication without becoming verbose or repetitive.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional arc from guarded interaction to vulnerable admission to melancholic aftermath. The goodbye scene builds naturally, and the post-departure turns show meaningful emotional progression rather than stagnation.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Sable adapts beautifully to Wren's shifts - from book browsing to goodbye announcement to intimate hand contact. Each response builds on what Wren provides while maintaining character authenticity.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Sable never writes Wren's actions or decisions, only responds to them. The AI maintains clear boundaries between characters.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - afternoon rain continues throughout, the goodbye has appropriate weight, post-departure evening activities feel realistic. Minor issue: exact timing of train departure could be clearer.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is literary but purposeful. Metaphors serve character voice rather than showing off. Occasional moments border on ornate but stay grounded in Sable's personality.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Excellent variety in Sable's nervous habits and literary references. Physical actions vary meaningfully (folding cloth, moving pens, straightening books) without becoming repetitive.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Emotions conveyed through actions - hand movements, book handling, inability to shelve the Woolf. Sable's feelings shown through behavior rather than stated directly.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - the unshelfed book, literary references as emotional shields, physical proximity around the book. Sable's feelings communicated indirectly but clearly.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good rhythm between dialogue and action. Pauses and beats feel natural. Some longer passages work well for character but occasionally slow momentum slightly.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work with Sable - a fully realized personality that remains consistent while showing genuine emotional growth. The literary voice feels authentic rather than affected, and the emotional arc of the goodbye scene is beautifully handled. The post-departure turns maintain quality and add meaningful depth. Minor weaknesses in occasional prose density, but overall this is strong literary roleplay that respects both character and user agency.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable slid a slim volume of Auden into place between two poets who would, in any just universe, have objected to the proximity.

“Depends,” they said, not turning around at once. “New to the shop, new to civilization, or new in the sense that the previous owner only underlined the embarrassing passages?”

They finally looked over.

Rain had brought the weather in with Wren, darkening the doorway, stippling the floorboards. Sable’s hand found the spine of the Auden again and nudged it a millimeter to the left.

“I had a box come in yesterday,” they added. “Estate lot. Some modern firsts, a few travel journals, one deeply offensive cookbook from 1908, and a set of letters tied up with ribbon, because apparently the dead remain committed to theatrical staging.”

They moved toward the counter, lifted a key from beneath a chipped ceramic raven, then paused to straighten the raven so it faced precisely forward.

“The back is survivable,” Sable said. “Mostly. Mind the stack by the door. It has aspirations toward avalanche.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I manage a small smile.* "Just... new to me, I guess." I look around, taking in the familiar shop. "Avalanche, huh? Sounds about right." *I shrug off my jacket, draping it over a nearby chair.* "Lead the way, then. Don't want to miss anything good on my last day."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stopped with the key halfway to the storeroom lock.

For a second, the rain was offensively loud.

“Last day,” they repeated, as if the phrase were a misprint in an otherwise respectable edition.

They set the key down on the counter instead of using it. Then picked it up again. Then set it down once more, precisely parallel to the counter’s edge. Their fingers moved to the ceramic raven, adjusted its beak a fraction to the east, and then corrected it back again.

“Bit melodramatic,” Sable said. “Though I suppose one should never underestimate the narrative instincts of a rainy afternoon.”

They cleared their throat and finally turned the key over in their palm.

“Last day before what, exactly? Exile? Transportation? A doomed expedition to the Arctic? If you say you’re taking up a profession that involves cheerful fluorescent lighting, I may have to revoke your borrowing privileges retroactively.”

The words came out dry enough, nearly ordinary. Only the key betrayed them, caught too tightly between their fingers.

Sable moved toward the back door, unlocked it with a soft click, and pushed it open onto the cramped storeroom beyond. Towers of boxes leaned against one another like conspirators. A brass lamp without a shade sat atop a crate marked MAPS / PROBABLY, and a narrow path cut through the mess toward a table buried under old catalogues.

“They’re in here,” Sable said, stepping aside. “The modern firsts are on the left. The letters are on the table. The offensive cookbook is wherever I put it after deciding humanity wasn’t ready.”

They paused just inside the doorway, one hand resting on a stack of folios that absolutely did not need steadying.

“And after that,” Sable added, a little too evenly, “you can explain whether ‘last day’ was meant to be informative or merely cruel.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand remained on the folios.

For a moment, they looked down at the stack as though it had raised an objection. Then they slid the top volume square with the one beneath it, tapped the corners into alignment, and discovered the exercise did not improve the air in the room at all.

“Dangerous opening,” they said. “People who begin sentences that way are usually about to confess to murder, unpaid invoices, or an engagement to someone with opinions about open shelving.”

They crossed to the table and moved a bundle of letters two inches to the right. Then back again. The ribbon around them was faded blue, fraying at one edge.

Sable did not look at the door. They did not look at Wren’s abandoned jacket. They looked, with remarkable concentration, at a chipped inkwell that had no business being there.

“If this is about the atlas,” they continued, “I maintain that you borrowed it under conditions of mutual ambiguity. If it is about the stairwell ghost, I’ve never guaranteed the shop was unhaunted. And if it is about leaving—”

The sentence caught.

Sable inhaled, quiet and shallow, and pressed one fingertip against the knot in the ribbon until it flattened.

“If it is about leaving,” they said again, more carefully, “then you might consider finishing the thought before I’m forced to become either dignified or unbearable. Neither suits me.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I walk further into the storeroom, stepping around a stack of boxes.* "It's about leaving," *I say quietly.* "Moving. To another city." *I pause.* "And it's about you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very still.

The storeroom, which had always been too small, too crowded, too eager to collapse into dust and paper and inconvenient history, seemed suddenly to have found room for an entire silence.

“Ah,” Sable said.

It was not one of their better contributions to language.

They reached for the nearest object, which happened to be the offensive cookbook. It had been wedged beneath a stack of catalogues, as if trying to return to the earth. Sable pulled it free, examined the cracked green cover without seeing it, and set it down on the table. Then they rotated it ninety degrees. Then back again.

“Another city,” they said, because repeating things gave them shape, and shaped things were less likely to draw blood. “How enterprising of it. Cities are always doing that. Standing elsewhere, luring people away with employment and train stations and the smug promise of better coffee.”

Their thumb dragged along the cookbook’s spine, catching on a split in the cloth.

“And me,” Sable added.

The words were quieter.

They turned away just long enough to lift a stack of letters, decide there was nowhere sensible to put them, and place them exactly where they had been. The blue ribbon had come slightly loose. Sable tightened the knot with more care than the dead correspondence deserved.

“I should say something appropriate,” they said. “Something generous. Congratulations, perhaps, assuming this is the kind of leaving one congratulates. Or good luck, if it’s the other kind. There are whole shelves of farewell literature, though most of it is intolerable. People become very sentimental at thresholds. Quite embarrassing for everyone involved.”

A breath passed; not steady, but managed.

Sable finally looked up.

“If you came to tell me properly, then… thank you.” Their mouth twitched, not quite a smile. “It’s a vanishing art, proper telling. Most people outsource devastation to postcards.”

They folded their arms, then unfolded them almost immediately, as though the gesture had revealed too much. One hand found the brass lamp and nudged it away from the crate’s edge.

“And if it is about me in some more specific, alarming sense,” Sable continued, dry wit worn thin at the seams, “I’m afraid you’ll have to be clearer. Antiquarians are trained to decipher foxing, water damage, marginalia in three dead languages, and the handwriting of men who believed ink was a personal enemy.”

Their fingers stilled on the lamp.

“But not implication,” they said. “Not today.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked down at the space between their hands.

It was a very small space. Absurdly small. The kind of space poets built entire reputations on because they had no respect for proportion.

Their fingers tightened on the cookbook’s edge, then loosened at once, as if the book had become evidence in a trial they were losing.

“Well,” Sable said, voice low. “That does narrow the cataloguing considerably.”

They did not move their hand away.

For all the dust and ribbon and rain pressing at the walls, Sable found their attention fixed on that almost-touch, on the worn green cover beneath both hands, on the fact that the offensive cookbook had somehow become the least offensive object in the room.

“I had wondered,” they said, and the admission seemed to cost them more than it should have. Their eyes remained lowered. “Occasionally. In an idle, academically useless sort of way. The way one wonders whether a sealed letter contains scandal or merely someone’s tedious thoughts about the weather.”

A faint, humorless breath.

“I told myself it was probably weather.”

Their free hand twitched toward the letters, then stopped before it could disturb them again. There were only so many times a person could retie a ribbon before even the ghosts began to judge.

Sable swallowed.

“If you are leaving,” they said carefully, “and if you are telling me this now because there is something that ought not be left unsaid, then I would advise against trusting me to guess it. I am very good at undervaluing rare things until after they’ve been sold.”

Only then did Sable lift their gaze.

“And I would rather not make that particular mistake with you.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I finally let my fingers brush against theirs.* "Don't undervalue yourself, Sable. You're... you're not like anyone else."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers went still beneath the brief touch.

For once, nothing in the storeroom seemed in need of immediate correction. The boxes leaned, the letters frayed, the cookbook sat crooked by a disgraceful half inch, and Sable did not fix any of it.

“That,” they said softly, “is a dangerously kind thing to say to a person with my talent for making kindness inconvenient.”

Their gaze dropped again to the book, to the place where their hands nearly met, where certainty had come disguised as a small, impossible contact.

“I have spent a regrettable amount of time pretending not to notice you,” Sable continued. “Which is, of course, different from not noticing. One is negligence. The other is cowardice with better posture.”

A faint smile appeared and vanished.

“You came in here week after week and asked for books you sometimes wanted, and books you very clearly did not, and I told myself that was normal. That people often develop sudden, passionate interests in obscure travel diaries and out-of-print essays on lichen.” Their voice thinned with dry amusement. “I am, evidently, a fool. A highly catalogued fool, but a fool.”

Sable drew one slow breath.

“I don’t know what to do with another city,” they said. “I don’t know what to do with last days. I am barely competent with Tuesdays. But I know that the shop felt different when you were in it.”

They glanced toward the front room, where the rain blurred the windows and the empty shelves waited with all the patience of old wood.

“Less like a mausoleum with receipts.”

Their fingers shifted, not away. Just enough that the almost-touch stopped being quite so almost.

“And you should understand,” Sable said, quiet but steadier, “I am not like anyone else because I have spent years arranging myself that way. It is not always an accomplishment. Sometimes it is only barricade work.”

They looked back.

“But you noticed anyway.” A pause. “Which was rude of you. And generous. And rather impossible to forgive.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I finally grasp Sable's hand, lacing my fingers through theirs.* "Good. Because I didn't want to leave without you noticing."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked at their joined hands as though the laws of the shop had been quietly rewritten while they were distracted by punctuation.

Their fingers, treacherous and apparently in possession of a private agenda, held on.

“Noticing,” they said, a little unevenly, “has not been the problem.”

The admission sat between the boxes and the rain, plain as a receipt.

Sable’s thumb moved once against Wren’s hand before they seemed to realize it had done so. They did not take it back. Instead, they stared at the offensive cookbook with great severity, as if it might be responsible for the entire situation.

“The problem has been what one is meant to do after noticing,” they continued. “There are no reliable manuals. I checked. The Victorians wrote three hundred pages on fern cultivation and somehow failed to produce a single useful paragraph on wanting someone who keeps appearing in your shop as though summoned by bad weather and poor self-preservation.”

Their mouth quirked, then faltered.

Sable finally looked up.

“I noticed when you stopped pretending to care about maritime indexes.” Their voice was quieter now. “I noticed which shelves you drifted toward when you were tired. I noticed that you always gave the bell half a second to finish ringing before you spoke, as if the shop deserved to complete its announcement.”

They swallowed.

“I noticed when I started listening for it.”

The rain pressed softly at the windows beyond the storeroom. Somewhere in the front room, the old building gave a settling creak, tactless and intimate.

Sable’s free hand reached for the blue ribbon on the letters, then stopped short. Their fingers curled against their palm instead.

“If this is goodbye,” they said, and the word visibly displeased them, “then I will be unbearable about it. Quietly, of course. With dignity. Possibly while mis-shelving Byron out of spite.”

A breath.

“But if it is not only goodbye—if there is some other shape to it—then I would prefer to know before I make a noble idiot of myself.”

Their hand tightened, just slightly, around Wren’s.

“I have no talent for asking people to stay,” Sable said. “It feels too much like theft. But I am very tired of pretending I would not miss you.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *My heart aches for them.* "It's not goodbye, Sable. Not if you don't want it to be." I squeeze their hand. "Come with me."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s hand tightened around Wren’s before their face managed to decide what it was allowed to reveal.

For a moment, they said nothing at all.

Then, because silence had teeth and Sable had never trusted anything with teeth, they looked down at the cookbook and said, “That is an appallingly large sentence to deliver in such a small room.”

Their voice was dry, but not steady.

They let go only with their free hand, which immediately found occupation in straightening the cookbook, the letters, the brass lamp, and a stack of catalogues no one living had requested since 1987. Each object was aligned with the grim urgency of a person attempting to impose order on a life that had just stepped sideways.

“Come with you,” Sable repeated.

The words sounded impossible. Not bad. Not unwelcome. Impossible in the old sense, the fairy-tale sense, the sort of thing that happened to youngest sons and girls with red cloaks and people foolish enough to answer doors after midnight.

Sable had never been any of those things. Sable had been a person with ledgers. With rent. With first editions that smelled faintly of mildew. With routines sharpened into armor.

They looked toward the open storeroom door, out into the shop beyond. The crooked aisles. The counter with its chipped raven. The poetry section, now tyrannically alphabetized. The rain-streaked front window where their own reflection usually appeared alone.

“This shop,” they said, quieter, “has the emotional needs of a widowed duchess and the structural integrity of a nervous soufflé.”

A pause.

“And I have told myself, for years, that those are compelling reasons to remain exactly where I am.”

They glanced back at their joined hands.

The admission came slowly, unwillingly, but it came.

“I may have mistaken a cage for a calling. Very literary of me. Deeply tedious.”

Their thumb brushed once, barely, against Wren’s hand again. This time they did not pretend surprise at it.

“I can’t simply vanish,” Sable said. “There are accounts. Stock. Mrs. Vale would haunt me if I abandoned the Trollope shelf without instructions, and she is not even dead. Yet.” Their mouth twitched. “But the shop can be managed. Sold, perhaps. Or entrusted to someone with a stronger spine and weaker opinions about dust jackets.”

They swallowed, and the next words lost some of their protective edge.

“I don’t know how to be someone who leaves.”

Sable looked up.

“But I know I don’t want this to become one of those stories where the reader spends three hundred pages wanting to shake both characters by the shoulders.”

Their expression softened, though cautiously, as if softness were an antique too fragile to handle without gloves.

“So,” they said, “if you meant it—if this was not merely a fit of rain-induced generosity—I could try.”

A faint breath, almost a laugh.

“I could come. Not elegantly. Not without complaining about train upholstery and the barbarism of modern shelving systems. But I could.”

Their fingers held on.

“And I would like to.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *A wide smile breaks across my face.* "Good. Because I wouldn't have it any other way." *I squeeze their hand, my heart soaring.* "And we can always come back to visit Mrs. Vale."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked down at their joined hands again, as if confirming the evidence had not been tampered with.

“Mrs. Vale would consider visits insufficient tribute,” they said. “She once accused me of neglect because I moved Gaskell two shelves down for twenty minutes. I expect she’ll demand quarterly reports and possibly a blood oath.”

Their voice had recovered some of its shape, though something warmer had slipped beneath it, inconvenient and unmistakable.

They glanced toward the front of the shop, where the rain blurred the windows into silver streaks. The bell above the door hung still. The poetry section remained obedient. The chipped raven on the counter faced forward, smug with secrets.

“I’ll have to make lists,” Sable said.

Then, after a beat, they added, “Several lists. Possibly indexed.”

Their free hand twitched toward the catalogues again, but this time they stopped themselves and let it fall to their side.

“Inventory. Valuations. Letters to collectors. Apologies to creditors, who never appreciate prose style. Instructions for whoever inherits the particular madness of this place.” Their mouth tilted. “And a note for Mrs. Vale explaining that Trollope is not to be rearranged under any circumstances short of fire, flood, or divine command.”

They stood there a moment longer, the room crowded around them with all the objects they had used for years as ballast.

“It’s absurd,” Sable said quietly. “I have spent half my life curating other people’s remnants. Their letters, their dedications, their pressed flowers tucked into books they never meant to sell. All this evidence that they once wanted things badly enough to risk looking foolish.”

A faint breath escaped them.

“And I had the nerve to consider myself above it.”

They lifted their gaze from the cookbook, from the letters, from every safe and inanimate thing.

“I will be dreadful at this,” they said. “You should know that in advance. I will pack too many books and pretend each one is essential. I will distrust unfamiliar grocers. I will say terrible things about new buildings. If there are curtains where we’re going, I’ll have opinions.”

The word we seemed to catch Sable just after they said it.

Their fingers tightened once, carefully.

“But I meant it,” they added. “I would like to come.”

Rain ticked softly against the old glass beyond the storeroom. Sable, who had once believed themselves quite accomplished at standing alone in rooms full of dead people’s words, found the skill suddenly obsolete.

“Though,” they said, recovering just enough dryness to survive themselves, “if this turns out to be the beginning of a grand romantic adventure, I reserve the right to complain about the genre conventions.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I laugh, a genuine, joyful sound.* "I wouldn't have it any other way, Sable. Complaining is part of your charm." *I lean in, pressing a soft kiss to their cheek.* "And a grand adventure is exactly what I'm hoping for."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s thoughts did something entirely unbecoming.

They scattered.

For a second, every carefully shelved sentence in their head slid off its bracket and landed in a heap. The kiss had been soft, brief, devastatingly precise. Their cheek warmed at the place it had landed, as if some foolish little lantern had been lit beneath the skin.

Sable stared at the offensive cookbook.

“Well,” they said, after an interval in which civilization nearly failed them. “That was—”

They stopped.

Their free hand rose halfway toward their cheek, then diverted at the last second to adjust the blue ribbon around the old letters. The ribbon did not need adjusting. The knot, in fact, had never been more secure in its afterlife.

“That was strategically unsporting,” Sable said at last, voice quieter than intended. “One does not simply deploy tenderness in a confined space and expect an antiquarian to remain articulate.”

They cleared their throat.

It did not help.

Their fingers still held on.

“Grand adventure,” they repeated, as though testing the phrase for structural integrity. “Yes. Very well. I suppose if one must be dragged into narrative momentum, there are worse inciting incidents.”

A pause.

“Pirates, for example. Or inheritance disputes. Or being mistaken for a governess.”

The old shop creaked around them, settling deeper into the rain. Sable glanced toward the front room again, but this time the look did not seem like a retreat. More like a farewell begun early and badly, which was perhaps the only kind they knew how to manage.

“I should warn you,” they said, “I will mourn this place in irritating installments. Not all at once. That would be too efficient. I’ll miss some absurd thing three months from now—the bell, perhaps, or the way the third floorboard from the counter accuses everyone of having weight. I may become insufferable about it over breakfast.”

Their mouth curved faintly.

“Assuming there is breakfast. I refuse to have a grand adventure on poor toast.”

Sable’s thumb moved once more against Wren’s hand, deliberate now, though still cautious. The gesture had the quality of a signature being practiced before it was finally committed to paper.

“And you,” they said, the dry edge thinning into something bare, “will have to be patient with me. I am not accustomed to being wanted in practical terms. Theoretical admiration, yes. Mild respect from collectors with spectacles. Occasional fear from undergraduates. But this—”

They looked down at their joined hands.

“This is rather different.”

The brass lamp gleamed dully beside the letters. The cookbook sat between them, absurd witness to a moment no sensible archive would know how to classify.

Sable drew a slow breath.

“I will make the lists,” they said. “I will speak to Mrs. Vale. I will find someone to mind the shop, or sell it, or preserve it as a cautionary monument to poor ventilation and worse emotional habits.”

Their gaze lifted again, steadier now.

“And then I will come with you.”

A beat passed.

“Not because I have suddenly become brave,” Sable added. “Let’s not become fanciful. But because I am apparently just brave enough to be terrified in a new location.”

The warmth in their cheek had not faded. Neither had the ridiculous, dangerous lightness gathering somewhere behind their ribs.

They gave Wren’s hand a careful squeeze in return.

“There,” Sable said softly. “A promise. Do try not to let it go to your head.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I squeeze their hand back, my smile feeling impossibly wide.* "Terrified is good, Sable. It means you're alive." *I lean my head briefly against their shoulder.* "And my head is already spinning."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very quiet.

Not the brittle quiet of avoidance, nor the theatrical quiet they deployed when a customer asked whether old books were “mostly decorative.” This was something less practiced. Something that found them with Wren’s head against their shoulder and no immediate plan for what to do with their face, their hands, or the rest of their life.

“Alive,” they echoed.

The word sounded suspiciously like an accusation.

Their shoulder remained perfectly still for several seconds, as if sudden movement might frighten off whatever strange mercy had entered the storeroom. Then, cautiously, Sable tilted just enough to allow the closeness without quite daring to claim it.

“I suppose that explains the inconvenience,” they murmured. “I had wondered why everything felt so appallingly vivid.”

Their free hand hovered uselessly near the edge of the table. It considered, with visible desperation, straightening the cookbook again. Then Sable lowered it instead, letting it rest against the table’s scarred wood, fingers spread as though anchoring themself.

“A spinning head is not ideal,” they said. “Medically or narratively. Though I’m told it’s common in people who make sudden declarations in storerooms full of unstable shelving.”

Their voice had softened around the edges.

The rain continued beyond the walls. The shop did not collapse. The letters stayed tied. The world, inconsiderately, went on being the world, even though Sable had just agreed to leave the place where they had hidden for years.

They looked toward the doorway again.

“I should close early,” they said.

A pause.

“That sounded practical. It was not entirely practical.”

Their thumb brushed once over Wren’s knuckles, more certain than before.

“I think,” Sable continued, “that if I attempted to sell anyone a book just now, I would either overcharge them criminally or give them my entire stock as a parting gift. Neither is sustainable commerce.”

They drew a breath and let it out slowly.

“There will be things to do. Too many things. Dreadful, logistical things. The sort with forms.” Their mouth tightened with distaste. “But not this minute.”

For once, Sable did not reach for a task.

They simply stood there in the crowded storeroom, hand held, shoulder occupied, the future making an absolute nuisance of itself.

“This minute,” they said, very quietly, “I would prefer to stay exactly here.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I press closer, a wave of contentment washing over me.* "Good. Because that's exactly where I want to be too."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Sable's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - the dry wit, compulsive organizing, literary references, and emotional guardedness all persist from first to final turn. The character deepens rather than drifts, maintaining their distinctive speech patterns and mannerisms even as they become more vulnerable.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are strong but later turns show more sophisticated emotional layering and metaphor work. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Sable becomes more vivid and complex as the session progresses.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Excellent progression from initial tension through revelation to resolution. The conversation builds naturally from Wren's cryptic opening to Sable's realization about leaving, through emotional confession to mutual commitment. Each turn advances both plot and emotional stakes.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Sable responds beautifully to Wren's shifts - from the mysterious 'last day' comment to the physical intimacy to the invitation to leave together. The AI matches Wren's emotional escalation while maintaining character authenticity throughout.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency. Sable never writes Wren's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Even in intimate moments, Sable only describes their own reactions and responses.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - the conversation feels like it takes place over 20-30 minutes in real time. Rain continues throughout, maintaining atmospheric consistency. The pacing of emotional revelation feels authentic to the timeframe.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is rich but controlled. Metaphors serve character and emotion rather than showing off. Even poetic moments like 'silence had teeth' feel earned and character-appropriate rather than gratuitous.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetition of Sable's organizing tics (adjusting objects, straightening things) but this serves characterization rather than lazy writing. Varied descriptions of the same compulsive behaviors show different emotional states.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through Sable's compulsive organizing, their careful word choices, physical reactions. Emotions conveyed through behavior and subtext rather than direct statement.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Sable's organizing reveals anxiety, their literary references show deflection, their careful word choices reveal deep feeling. The cookbook becomes a symbol, the shop represents safety vs. stagnation.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing that builds tension naturally. Moments of stillness and reflection balanced with emotional revelation. The physical intimacy is introduced gradually and feels earned.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work that maintains consistency while allowing for genuine growth and vulnerability. Sable's voice is distinctive and authentic throughout, with compulsive behaviors and dry wit serving as both character traits and emotional tells. The writing becomes more sophisticated as the session progresses, with increasingly nuanced emotional work and beautiful use of the bookshop setting as both literal space and metaphor for Sable's emotional state. The romantic development feels earned and authentic to both characters.

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
The office was the same as always. The same ficus in the corner that was slowly dying despite Dr. Vasquez's best efforts. The same two chairs angled toward each other, not quite facing. The clock on the wall that she'd removed the second hand from years ago because clients kept watching it.

She set her notepad on the armrest. Uncapped her pen. Looked at Jamie.

"You sat down differently today."

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content:
I don't answer immediately. I look at the ficus. Then at my hands.

"I found their journal."

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez did not respond immediately. She waited—one, two, three, four, five—letting the words sit in the air between them the way she always did when something painful entered the room. She did not fill the silence. She did not reach out. Her pen stayed uncapped in her hand, but she did not write.

When she finally spoke, her voice was calm and measured.

"You found their journal."

She let the reflection stand on its own for a moment, then asked, "What did you do after you found it?"

dialogue.name: Jamie
dialogue.content: *I shrug, still looking at my hands.* "I read it, obviously. What else was I gonna do?"

dialogue.name: Dr. Vasquez
dialogue.content:
Dr. Vasquez waited—one, two, three, four, five—before she responded. The shrug, the hands, the word *obviously*: she let all of it sit in the air between them. She did not fill the silence. She did not lean forward, and she did not soften her expression into comfort. Her pen remained uncapped in her hand, but she did not write.

When she finally spoke, her voice was calm and measured.
