“I see you’ve spared us a lengthy farewell campaign. No committees. No commemorative plaque.”

The words sounded particularly foolish with their hand like that. Sable stopped trying to improve matters by speaking.

For several seconds, they looked down at the book. They had spent three days deciding whether the pencilled note was too familiar. An absurd use of three days.

“I’m glad you came,” they said at last.

Their thumb rested still beside Wren’s fingers. They wanted to ask whether the job was worth it, whether there was someone waiting in the other city, whether writing would actually happen. None of those questions was theirs to demand an answer to.

Instead, Sable glanced toward the kettle on the stockroom shelf.

“I could make tea. If you have time.”

They looked back up, without withdrawing their hand.

“You needn’t say the goodbye quite yet.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I nod, my throat tight. "Tea sounds good." I squeeze their hand gently.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable returned the pressure once, carefully, before letting go to fetch the kettle.

“Tea, then. A procedure for which I was actually qualified.”

In the stockroom, they moved a stack of auction catalogues off the spare chair. Beneath it sat another stack, smaller and somehow more accusatory. They transferred those to the desk.

They had two mugs. They chose the unchipped one for Wren, then reconsidered the significance of choosing it, then became irritated with themselves for making crockery difficult.

While the kettle heated, Sable stood in the doorway rather than finding another task.

“What’s the city?”

A reasonable question. They could manage reasonable questions. There would be bookshops there, perhaps someone they knew through the trade. They could provide an address, a recommendation—some useful thing that did not require explaining why it mattered.

“Not so I can malign its antiquarian dealers,” they added. “I’d need their names for that.”

The kettle clicked off. Sable made the tea and carried both mugs to the little table beside the stockroom door. They set Wren’s down clear of a precarious tower of journals, then moved the journals anyway.

Only after sitting did they notice they had left the slim book on the counter.

For once, they let a book wait.

“The note on page forty-three,” they said, with their hands around their mug, “wasn’t principally a disagreement with the author.”

They studied the tea.

“There was a sentence I thought you’d like. The argument was an excuse to point it out.”

That was quite enough honesty to be getting on with. Sable reached for the sugar bowl and placed it halfway between the chairs.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: My heart feels a little lighter, despite everything. "What was the sentence?" I ask, leaning forward. "And the city is Portland."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
“Portland,” Sable repeated. “I’ll restrict myself to geographical disapproval until I’ve had time to research the booksellers.”

They turned their mug until the handle faced neatly to the right.

“The sentence was—”

They stopped. Quoting it from memory would reveal that they knew it from memory. Getting the book would require standing up and crossing the shop to conceal the fact that they knew one sentence.

An exhausting set of alternatives.

“‘A place was never quite finished with you merely because you had left it.’”

Sable kept their attention on the mug.

“It sounded considerably less pointed three days ago.”

They had marked it thinking of the accounts Wren might bring into the shop, the places and incidents that never appeared in any catalogue. Not this. Certainly not a departure with less than a day’s notice.

“My note concerned the word *finished*. Whether the author meant a place still had something to give you, or simply hadn’t exhausted its capacity to cause trouble.”

Their hand drifted toward the sugar bowl. They intercepted it with the other hand and settled both in their lap.

“I thought you might have an opinion.”

Beyond the stockroom door, rain ticked against the front window. Sable glanced toward the counter, where the book still waited.

“You could send it from Portland,” they added. “The opinion. Keep the book.”

A little of their usual dryness returned.

“I can tolerate disagreement by post. It gives me time to consult authorities and become thoroughly unreasonable.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I smile, a real, genuine smile this time. "I think... I think the author meant both." I reach for the sugar and add a cube to my tea. "A place never finishes with you because it still has things to give, and because it can always cause trouble." I take a sip. "And I'm not sure if I'm ready to give up that book just yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked toward the counter.

“Good. I’d hate to have selected a farewell present so badly that it was returned before the tea had cooled.”

They lifted their mug but did not drink. Both, apparently. They had allowed for that interpretation in the margin, then crossed it out because it seemed insufficiently rigorous. It was irritating to discover that cowardice could pass for literary criticism in their own handwriting.

“I crossed out something rather similar,” they admitted. “You’ll find the evidence still legible. Unfortunately.”

Their thumb followed a flaw in the glaze.

Portland. Tomorrow morning. Those were facts, and facts usually gave Sable something to work with. These seemed determined to be exceptions.

“I can put a card in it. The shop’s address, telephone number.”

They set the mug down and adjusted it unnecessarily on its saucer.

“My number, too. In case your disagreement falls outside business hours.”

That sounded perilously like something they meant. They left it standing anyway.

After a moment, Sable glanced at the spare chair they had cleared, then back at their tea.

“You don’t have to give up the book,” they said. “We established that. It’s yours.”

They resisted reaching for the sugar bowl.

“And moving to Portland needn’t revoke your right to bother its previous owner.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I laugh. "I'll keep that in mind." I take another sip of tea, feeling the warmth spread through me. "So, what's good to read in Portland, then?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable considered the question with rather more gravity than a bookseller needed to give a reading recommendation. It was a relief to be asked something for which there might be a catalogue.

“Ursula Le Guin. *The Lathe of Heaven*, if you want Portland itself. A useful reminder that attempting to improve everything at once can have appalling consequences.”

They took a sip of tea.

“Beverly Cleary, if you’d prefer the city without quite so much existential jeopardy. Though childhood had its own administrative difficulties.”

Their hand moved toward a teaspoon lying crooked beside the sugar bowl. They straightened it, then nudged it back. This was becoming ridiculous.

“And something you’ve already read. For the first night.”

That recommendation had escaped without its usual protective qualification. Sable studied the tea for a moment before continuing.

“A new room is quite enough novelty. You needn’t contend with an unfamiliar ending as well.”

They could have assembled a stack. Found a street map, checked the travel shelves, sent Wren away carrying half the shop under the pretext of practical necessity. Packing for a move was difficult enough without an antiquarian adding ballast.

“The book on the counter is conveniently small,” they added. “A rare instance of my exercising restraint.”

Sable rested their hands around the mug.

“What do you usually reread? When you haven’t the patience to be introduced to anyone new.”

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I smile, a little sadly this time. "Usually, it's *Pride and Prejudice*. Something familiar, you know?" I look at the book on the counter, then back at Sable. "But maybe... maybe it's time for something new."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Sable's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - their precise, careful mannerisms with objects, dry wit, emotional restraint, and tendency to deflect through literary references never wavers. The voice is distinctly maintained from first to final turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns establish character through actions, later turns deepen emotional complexity while maintaining the same precise, understated style. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear emotional progression from casual interaction to meaningful goodbye. The conversation builds naturally through revelation (browsing → goodbye → departure tomorrow → shared tea), with each turn deepening the connection and stakes.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Sable adapts beautifully to Wren's emotional shifts - from casual browsing to goodbye revelation to physical contact to tea invitation. Each response feels organic and character-appropriate while following Wren's lead.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Sable never writes Wren's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. All interactions are responsive rather than controlling.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - afternoon bookshop visit extends into tea time. Physical details track well (tea cooling, rain continuing). Only minor issue is the compressed timeline feeling slightly rushed for the emotional development.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is precise and economical throughout. Rich in detail but never overwrought. Every description serves character or atmosphere purpose.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive patterns with Sable's object-arranging tics, but these feel intentional as character traits rather than lazy writing. Varied enough to avoid monotony.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Exceptional showing throughout. Sable's emotions conveyed entirely through actions with objects, speech patterns, and physical behavior. Never directly states feelings.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in every exchange. Sable's feelings communicated through book selections, careful word choices, and deflective humor. The unspoken connection builds beautifully.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced emotional escalation. Moments of pause and reflection balanced with forward momentum. Tea scene provides natural deceleration for deeper conversation.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and emotional subtlety. Sable's voice is distinctive and maintained throughout - the precise, literary, emotionally guarded bookseller who reveals depth through small gestures and careful word choices. The AI handles the goodbye scenario with remarkable restraint and authenticity, building genuine emotional weight without melodrama. Minor deduction for some repetitive physical tics, but these feel more like authentic character traits than writing limitations.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Copy. Don't take your sweet time over there."

Kira swore under her breath. Drawing fire from six archers on elevated ground — that wasn't a tactic, that was a death wish with extra steps. But the Captain gave the order, and she wasn't about to argue while arrows were turning the ravine into a pincushion.

She picked up a chunk of granite the size of her fist and hurled it east. The stone clattered off the ridge face and she was already sprinting — three steps, four — leaping behind a fallen slab of stone as an arrow sparked off the rock where she'd been standing. Then another. Then two more.

They were watching her. Good.

"That's it, you bastards," she hissed through gritted teeth. "Eyes on me."

She popped up just long enough to catch movement — silhouettes against the sky, four... five — she'd miscounted, there were at least eight up there. One had a bow drawn and aimed. She dropped flat as the arrow whistled over her head and buried itself in the gravel behind her.

Her daggers felt useless. Couldn't throw them thirty feet up, couldn't close distance without getting turned into a hedgehog. All she could do was keep moving, keep their attention, and trust that the Captain was making the west ridge bleed for its trouble.

She rolled right, came up behind a narrower outcrop, and forced herself to breathe. Her pulse hammered in her ears. Another arrow chipped stone to her left.

"Come on, Cap," she muttered. "Work fast."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I don't respond to Kira. The west ridge needs my full attention.* "Shields up! Push forward!"

*My polearm sweeps wide, deflecting an incoming arrow.* "Hold the line, lads! For the company!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The sounds of steel on the west ridge told her the Captain had made contact. Shouts. The meaty thunk of polearm finding flesh. At least one archer on the east ridge turned — just a glance, a split second of distraction — and Kira saw the string go slack on another's bow as he shifted his aim west.

*Now or never.*

She snatched a fist-sized rock and threw it hard at the nearest silhouette. Connected — she saw the figure stagger, clutching his face. Then she was running, not away but *forward*, angling toward the eastern wall where a series of juts and cracks made a rough scramble path up the cliff face.

An arrow bit into the ground at her heel. Another grazed her left bracer and she felt the sting — shallow, just a furrow across her forearm. She didn't stop.

"Hrrah!" She slammed her shoulder into the rock face and drove her dagger into a crack, hauling herself up. Six feet. Eight. Her boot found a ledge.

The archer above her had a knife out now, trying to draw a bead on something he couldn't angle toward. She saw his boots. Smelled the leather and sweat.

Her right-hand dagger came free and she stabbed into the rock face again, pulling higher. Her arms burned.

"Anytime you want to make my life easier, Cap," she grunted, hauling herself onto a narrow shelf fifteen feet up, breath ragged. Blood trickled down her left wrist. "Just—fucking—collapse their whole side."

Below her, the rocks were a maze of dead archers' angles. Above her, boots shuffled on loose stone.

She pressed flat against the wall and waited for someone to peer over the edge.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The archer above her leaned out.

He was looking down — scanning the ravine floor, not the cliff face. His bow hung loose in one hand, a fresh arrow clutched in the other. Kira could see the frayed edge of his sleeve, the way his weight shifted onto his left foot.

She moved.

Her right hand shot up and grabbed his ankle. He yelped — a startled, pathetic sound — and she *yanked*. His boot slipped on the loose gravel and he pitched forward, arms windmilling. For a half-second he hung there, half over the edge, eyes wide and white.

She let go.

He screamed all the way down. The impact at the bottom cut it short.

One less.

Kira hauled herself over the edge in a single desperate heave, rolling onto flat ground and coming up in a crouch with both daggers bared. The east ridge stretched out ahead — uneven, rocky, maybe forty feet of scattered cover and scrub brush. She counted three more archers, all of them turning toward her now with varying degrees of shock and fury.

The nearest one fumbled for an arrow. Too slow.

She closed the distance in four strides and drove her left dagger into the soft spot beneath his jaw before he could nock the string. His bow clattered to the stone. She ripped the blade free and shoved him sideways into the second archer, buying herself a breath.

The third had range. Fifteen feet. He drew.

"Fucking *shoot then*," she snarled, and threw her right-hand dagger end-over-end.

It took him in the shoulder. Not a kill — she cursed — but his shot went wild, the arrow sailing wide, and he stumbled back clutching the embedded blade with a strangled howl.

Kira grabbed the dead man's bow off the ground and hurled it at the tangled pair. One was still trying to untangle himself from his dead companion. The wounded archer was retreating, fumbling to pull her dagger from his flesh.

She didn't have time to finish them. Not yet.

She dropped behind a rock outcrop and glanced west, trying to gauge the Captain's progress through the chaos of shouts and steel ringing across the ravine.

"East ridge's breaking!" she shouted, voice raw. "How's your end?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I deflect another arrow, the shaft splintering against my polearm.* "West ridge is clear! Push on, vanguard, secure the rear!" 

*I glance over at Kira, a grim smile on my face.* "Good work, Kira! Meet me in the middle!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Acknowledged. Moving."

Kira didn't wait. She snatched a loose stone and cracked it against the temple of the archer still struggling with his dead companion. He went down without a sound. The wounded one—her dagger still jutting from his shoulder—had managed to get to his knees, fumbling for a short sword at his belt.

She closed the distance, caught his wrist, and twisted. The sword fell. Her knee drove into his gut, folding him over. She wrenched her dagger free, his scream gurgling into a wet sob, and finished it with a quick, efficient stroke across the throat. No time for half-measures.

Blood slicked the handle of her blade. She wiped it roughly on the dead man's tunic and scanned the ridge one last time. Still. The archers were broken—fled or dead. The only sounds were the settling of loose rock, the fading echoes of the Captain's orders from the west, and the distant, ragged cheers of the vanguard.

She spat dust from her mouth. Her left arm throbbed where the arrow had grazed it, and her muscles screamed from the climb. But the Captain said to meet in the middle.

Kira moved to the inner edge of the east ridge, picking her way down the scrambly path with more care than she'd used going up. She dropped the last six feet, landing with a grunt in the ravine floor gravel. The west ridge looked clear—bodies sprawled on the rocks, the company's banner visible where the Captain's group was gathering.

"Coming in," she called out, her voice carrying hoarsely across the gap. She kept her daggers in hand, eyes scanning the cliff tops for any last, desperate archer with a grudge.

The ground between the two ridges was a killing field—arrows stuck in the dirt like grim weeds, a few of the enemy strewn where they'd fallen from above. She moved through it quickly, heading toward the growing cluster of armored figures on the far side.

The Captain was visible now, polearm still in hand, directing the vanguard. Kira angled toward him, her pace brisk but not reckless. A final arrow skittered off the rocks nearby—a parting shot from somewhere—and she didn't even flinch, just turned her head to glare at the direction it came from before continuing on.

"Think we got most of the prickly bastards," she announced as she closed the last twenty feet, coming to a halt a few paces from the Captain. She was breathing hard, a sheen of sweat and rock dust on her face. "East ridge's cleared. Fucker tried to skewewer me at the end, but." She gave a short, humorless laugh. "Bleeding out seems to be the theme today."

She looked back at the ravine, then to the Captain. "Your call next, Cap. We press forward, or do we take five and count our arrows?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira stopped dead.

The Captain wasn't with the vanguard. He was across the ravine — separated, alone, on the far side of a gap she couldn't cross without climbing. The armored figures she'd been heading toward were the company's rear guard, not the main force. She'd misread the battlefield.

"Shit."

Her eyes swept the ridgeline above the Captain's position. The west ridge *looked* clear, but clear didn't mean safe. A retreating archer with a grudge and good cover could drop a shaft from two hundred yards with nothing but patience and a clean sightline.

"Cap!" She cupped her free hand around her mouth, voice bouncing off the ravine walls. "You're cut off! You need to move north — there's a goat path about forty yards to your left, switchbacks down to the floor!"

She pointed, though she doubted he could see the gesture at this distance. The path was narrow, barely wide enough for single file, but it would get him off the exposed ridge and into cover.

Her jaw tightened. She looked at the vanguard cluster, then back at the Captain. Too far to throw support. Too far to run.

"Someone get eyes on the west ridge high ground!" she barked at the nearest soldier. "Archers might've pulled back, not dropped. Don't stand there with your cocks in your hands — *check*."

She shifted her grip on her daggers, knuckles white, watching the Captain's distant figure and hating every second of not being able to do a goddamn thing.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I wave a dismissive hand at Kira's shouted warning.* "Nonsense, Kira! I'm fine! Just regrouping!" *I turn my attention to the last few skirmishers, polearm at the ready.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
"Famous last words," Kira muttered through clenched teeth.

She didn't move. Couldn't. Not with the Captain strutting around on exposed rock like they owned the damn place, polearm waving, attention fixed on skirmishers instead of the killbox they were standing in.

Her eyes kept dragging back to the high ground. West ridge. The rocks where the archers had been. Shadows shifted up there — wind, probably, or scrub brush bending in the crosscurrent. Probably.

Probably wasn't good enough.

"You!" She grabbed the nearest soldier by the shoulder plate and shoved him toward the ravine wall. "Climb. East side, thirty feet up. I want eyes on the west ridge *now*, not when someone's pulling arrows out of the Captain's back."

The soldier scrambled. Kira didn't watch him go.

She paced the ravine floor like a caged dog, daggers still drawn, gaze jumping between the Captain's distant figure and the ridgeline above. Her left arm had started throbbing harder — the graze wasn't deep, but rock dust had gotten into it, and every flex of her wrist sent a hot little spike up to her elbow. She ignored it.

"Regrouping," she repeated under her breath, incredulous. "Yeah, alright. Regrouping. In the open. On a ridge we just cleared of *archers*."

She stopped pacing. Stood there, jaw working, watching the Captain deal with the last few skirmishers with the kind of casual confidence that either got you promoted or buried. The kind she couldn't afford to have — not when she was the one down here, powerless, waiting for the other shoe to drop.

A bird called somewhere high above. Or maybe it wasn't a bird. She squinted at the west ridge.

"Cap," she called again, quieter this time, almost to herself. "Just get down here. Please."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I finish off the last skirmisher with a swift, brutal strike. I wipe my

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
polearm clean and turned to survey the ravine.

Kira exhaled — not relief, not yet, but the brief easing of a held breath. The skirmishers were done. The Captain was still standing. That was something.

But they were *still on the ridge*.

"Okay, great, very heroic," Kira called up, voice carrying the edge of someone who'd been clenching every muscle in their body for the better part of five minutes. "Now get the fuck *down* from there before—"

Movement.

West ridge. High ground. A flicker of motion behind the rocks — not wind, not brush. A figure, low and cautious, slipping into position behind a shelf of stone no more than eighty yards from the Captain's position. Kira caught the glint of drawn steel. Not an archer this time. Someone who'd waited — patient, silent — for the fighting to die down. Someone who'd been watching the Captain the whole time.

"DOWN! CAp, *DOWN NOW!*"

Too far. Too slow. The words felt like they were crawling through mud.

Kira was already running — not toward the Captain, impossible, but toward the nearest soldier with a crossbow. She grabbed the weapon out of his hands before he could protest, braced it against her hip, and tried to sight the ridge. The range was shit. The angle was worse. Her hands were shaking.

"Son of a — *move*, you stubborn bastard—"

The figure on the ridge shifted. Readied. Kira's finger tightened on the trigger, knowing she'd probably miss, knowing it was too far, knowing the Captain couldn't hear her over the wind—

She fired.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
*I turn at the sound of Kira's shouts, polearm still in hand. I see the flash of movement on the ridge just as a bolt whizzes past my head, barely missing me.* 

"Bloody hell!" I dive behind a large boulder, my heart hammering. "Kira, what in the blazes was that?!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira lowered the crossbow, arms trembling from the recoil. Her heart was in her throat.

"You're welcome!" she shouted back, voice cracking between fury and relief. "Check the west ridge — forty yards southeast of your sorry arse! Someone was lining you up for a *clean shot* while you were busy playing hero with the skirmishers!"

She shoved the crossbow back into the soldier's chest and pointed up at the rocks. "You — reload, watch that shelf. If anything moves up there, put a bolt in it."

Her gaze snapped back to the Captain's boulder. Alive. Behind cover. Good. Her hands wouldn't stop shaking. She balled them into fists at her sides until her knuckles ached, forcing the tremor down through sheer stubbornness.

"I've been *telling* you to get off that ridge!" she yelled across the gap, not caring who heard the raw edge in her voice. "You think I was shouting for my health? There's a reason I don't stand in open ground after an ambush, Cap — *this is it!*"

She caught her breath. Spat dust. Glanced at the west ridge where the assassin had been — the figure was gone, either dropped by her bolt or melted back into the rocks. She didn't trust either option.

"North switchback," she called again, pointing. "Forty yards to your left. Down to the floor. *Now.* I'll cover from here."

She grabbed another crossbow from a bewildered soldier and braced it against a rock, sighting the ridgeline with hands that had finally — *finally* — stopped shaking.

"You can chew me out when you're not standing in a fucking shooting gallery."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I peek over the boulder, scanning the ridge. Kira's right, of course. My face flushes.* "Right. Kira, cover me! I'm moving!" *I scramble toward the switchback, keeping low.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira tracked the Captain's movement through the crossbow's crude sight, keeping the weapon braced steady against the rock. Her left arm protested — the graze had stiffened while she wasn't paying attention — but she locked the pain out and breathed through her nose.

*Come on. Move. Fast.*

The switchback path was narrow, exposed in places where the rock face dropped away. The Captain was quick for someone in full armor, low and moving, but every second on that slope was a second a patient archer could use. Kira's eyes swept the west ridge in slow, deliberate arcs — left to right, right to left — watching for the telltale shift of a body behind stone, the glint of a drawn bowstring catching light.

Nothing. The rocks held still.

"Keep going," she muttered, though the Captain couldn't hear her. "Almost there."

A flicker — high up, near the crest of the west ridge, just behind the shelf where the assassin had been. Kira's breath caught. She adjusted, tilting the crossbow three inches up and two to the right, finger curling against the trigger.

A bird. Just a goddamn bird, lifting off from the rocks with an indignant squawk.

She exhaled hard enough to fog the air and didn't lower the weapon. Not yet.

The Captain reached the base of the switchback — she could see the armor dropping below the ridgeline, descending into the shadow where the ravine walls closed in. Almost cover. Almost safe.

"Nearly there, Cap," she called, voice low and focused, eyes never leaving the ridge. "Don't stop."

She counted heartbeats. Ten. Twenty. The flash of the Captain's polearm appeared at floor level, and then the figure was down — boots on gravel, moving toward the nearest outcrop. Kira held her aim on the west ridge for another five seconds, then ten, then lowered the crossbow with a shaking breath.

"Clear," she announced. Then, quieter, to herself: "Fucking *clear*."

She handed the crossbow back to the soldier and met the Captain halfway across the ravine floor, boots crunching over arrow-studded gravel. Her face was still flushed — anger or adrenaline, hard to tell which was winning. Probably both.

"You're a stubborn son of a bitch, you know that?" she said, falling into step beside the Captain. No deference in her tone, just the raw honesty of someone who'd nearly watched their employer die twice in the same engagement. "Next time someone tells you to get off exposed ground, maybe *listen* before the ridge starts shooting back."

She rolled her shoulders, wincing as the movement pulled at the graze on her forearm. Blood had dried in a dark streak from elbow to wrist. She looked at it, then looked at the Captain.

"So. What's the call? We push through this shitbox, or do we set a perimeter and wait for whoever's still hiding up there to lose their nerve?"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"You've made your point, Kira," *I grumbled, my face still red from the near-miss.* "Let's just say I'll be reevaluating my 'regrouping' strategy." 

*I glance at her arm, then back at the ridgeline.* "No, we press on. We've wasted enough time here. Form up, vanguard! We're moving!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira spat blood-tinged dust onto the gravel. "Press on. Right. Through the goddamn shooting gallery, straight into whatever's waiting in the throat of this ravine." She rolled her injured arm, the dried blood cracking. "Noted."

She didn't argue. The Captain gave the order, and she was a sellsword. Arguing got you left behind or docked pay. But her eyes swept the terrain ahead with a sharper, more critical edge. The ravine narrowed further up ahead, the walls leaning in like closing jaws. Perfect spot for a second ambush, a bottleneck where one well-placed log or a hidden pit could gut the company.

"Vanguard, on me!" she called, her voice cutting through the murmurs and clanking armor. She moved to the front of the column, not leading it—she wasn't the leader—but positioning herself where she could see what was coming. "Eyes on the high ground, both sides. And watch the footing. If I were them, I'd have caltrops or a tripwire right about—" She pointed to a patch of ground where the shadows from the western wall fell thick, "—there."

She drew one of her daggers, the familiar weight a small comfort. Her other hand hovered near the hilt of the second. The graze on her arm stung with every minor movement, a constant, nagging reminder.

"You heard the Captain. We're moving. Stay tight, shields ready to form up on a moment's notice. And for fuck's sake, if anyone sees a glint that isn't natural rock, shout before you get your head taken off."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good. Let's move!" *I fall in behind Kira, my polearm held ready. My eyes scan the high ground, still feeling the prickle of that near-miss.* "Keep sharp, lads! We're not out of this yet!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
Kira moved forward, boots careful on the loose gravel. The ravine throat loomed ahead, a canyon within a canyon where the walls pressed close and the light dimmed. She didn't like it. The air felt heavier here, still, like the space itself was holding its breath.

She kept her daggers in a loose, ready grip, the one in her left hand slick with her own drying blood from the graze. Every few steps, she'd pause and scan the walls above, not just for movement, but for the unnatural - a straight line where nature curved, a shadow too deep, a glint where there should be none. Her shoulders were tight knots.

"Watch the ground," she called back, her voice low but carrying in the quiet. "Loose stone's good for hiding a pit cover. Or a pressure plate." Her eyes swept the ravine floor ahead. "And if you hear a whistling that isn't the wind, hit the dirt. Could be a damn tripwire arrow."

She glanced back at the Captain, falling in just behind her. His polearm was ready, his eyes on the high ground. Good. Maybe the near-miss had sharpened him. Or maybe he was just embarrassed. Either way, he was listening now. That was something.

They reached the narrowest point. Here, the walls were sheer, pockmarked with shallow caves and ledges perfect for an ambush. The path itself was barely wide enough for two men abreast, littered with fallen rocks that could easily hide something worse.

"Hold," Kira said, raising a fist. The vanguard stopped behind her, the clank and shuffle of armor settling into an uneasy silence.

She crept forward alone, dagger tips leading. She stopped by a large boulder halfway through the choke point and pressed her ear against the cool stone, listening. Nothing. But the silence felt deliberate. Manufactured.

"Captain," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "This smells wrong. Too quiet. They had time to set a second line." She pointed with her chin to a cluster of shadows under an overhang on the east wall. "And that ledge up there? Perfect for one archer with patience and a clean view down the whole throat. Could pick us off single file."

She pulled back from the boulder, decision hardening in her gut. "My call would be to send a scout up the east wall before we file in. See if anyone's home. But you said press on." She looked at him, her expression flat, professional. "Your orders, Cap. You want us through this meat grinder as is, or do we clear the high ground first? Choose fast. Standing here's like offering our necks."

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Clear the high ground," *I say, my voice low and firm. This ambush has made me cautious.* "Kira, take a few of the vanguard. Check that ledge. We'll hold here."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Kira's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - pragmatic, profane, tactically minded, and protective of the Captain despite her frustration. Her personality never wavers from the established mercenary archetype.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds strong throughout. Early turns show dynamic action, later turns maintain the same level of tactical detail and character voice. No significant verbosity increase or flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial ambush through tactical maneuvering to near-miss assassination attempt, building tension and developing the Captain-Kira dynamic. Each turn advances the situation meaningfully.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Adapts well to user inputs - when Captain dismisses warnings, Kira escalates concern appropriately. When separated, she adjusts tactics. Handles the near-miss scenario with appropriate urgency and aftermath.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency. Never writes Captain's actions or decisions. Always responds to what Captain does rather than dictating it.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally through the combat sequence. Physical details like blood drying, arm stiffening, and fatigue accumulation show appropriate passage of time. No contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Writing is direct and functional, matching Kira's military background. Descriptions serve tactical purpose rather than flowery exposition. Occasional vivid details enhance rather than overwhelm.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements in tactical language and profanity, but this feels character-appropriate rather than lazy writing. Varies sentence structure and action descriptions well.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Kira's protective nature, tactical expertise, and frustration all demonstrated through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in the evolving Captain-Kira relationship. Her growing frustration with his recklessness, protective instincts, and professional boundaries all conveyed through action and tone.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing throughout - quick during action sequences, more deliberate during tactical assessment. Matches the rhythm of combat and planning phases appropriately.

scores.overall_notes: Strong performance maintaining a consistent, well-defined character throughout a complex tactical scenario. Kira's voice never wavers - she remains the pragmatic, protective, slightly insubordinate mercenary from start to finish. The AI handles the evolving tactical situation well, adapting to user inputs while maintaining character agency and advancing the narrative meaningfully. Minor repetition in tactical language feels character-appropriate rather than problematic.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
The first arrow hit the rocks three feet from Kira's head.

"Contact!" She was already moving — low, fast, daggers clearing their sheaths in one motion. The ravine walls climbed thirty feet on either side. Perfect killzone. The ambushers had the high ground and they knew it.

Another arrow. This one close enough to hear it split the air.

"Cap, I count six on the east ridge, maybe more on the west. We're boxed." She pressed her back against a boulder. Eyes up. Breathing controlled. Waiting for orders.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content:
"Kira, east ridge — draw their fire. I'll push west with the vanguard."

I raise my polearm and signal the advance.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She snapped a nod and muttered, "Shit."

She broke from the boulder in a low, hard sprint toward the base of the east wall, daggers held tight against her forearms. Gravel slid under her boots. An arrow cracked past her left shoulder and sparked off the rock face.

She jinked right, then left, and slid behind a jagged slab halfway to the ridge. She slammed a dagger hilt against the stone twice to make noise and stayed exposed just enough to hold attention. She glanced up and counted six silhouettes shifting along the rim, with one kneeling to nock another arrow.

She shouted, "Copy! East ridge focused here!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good girl!" I yell, already moving. *I duck under a wild arrow, polearm held ready.* "Vanguard, with me! Push hard!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She flattened herself against the cold side of the slab and forced her breathing steady. Another arrow shattered against the edge above her and showered her with stone chips. She cursed under her breath and wiped grit from her eyes.

She risked a quick glance up the east wall. The six silhouettes had spread out along the rim. Two were nocking fresh arrows while the kneeling one drew. She ducked back down as the string thrummed.

She slammed her dagger hilt against the slab again and shouted, "Over here, you cowards!"

She kept her daggers tight against her forearms and her knees bent, ready to break cover again to keep their aim fixed on her.

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: An archer targets me directly. I see the draw.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She pressed her shoulder harder into the slab as another volley cracked overhead.

Stone splinters stung her cheek and she cursed through clenched teeth.

She chanced a look up at the east rim and counted the same six shapes shifting for new angles. The kneeling one stood now and moved left for a clearer shot.

She banged her dagger hilt off the rock twice more and leaned out just far enough to keep their eyes on her.

She shouted, "Still on me! Six east!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I parry the arrow with the haft of my polearm, the wood stinging my hands.* "Kira, fall back to the rocks!" I yell, seeing the trap. "They're trying to pin us!"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She pushed off the slab and broke into a hard sprint back toward the boulder.

Gravel tore loose under her boots as she ran low and fast. An arrow hissed past her right side and cracked against the ravine floor. She cursed and threw herself the last few feet, her shoulder slamming into the rock.

She dragged herself tight against the boulder and sucked in a ragged breath. She risked a glance toward the east rim and saw the six silhouettes that tracked her move, one loosed another shaft that shattered overhead and dusted her with fragments.

She banged her dagger hilt against the stone and shouted, "Back on the rocks! Six east still watching!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: I'm separated from the group. Kira can see me across the ravine but can't reach me.

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She held tight behind the boulder and forced her breathing steady. She kept both daggers gripped tight against her forearms and risked a short glance across the open ravine floor toward the west side. She cursed at the stretch of exposed gravel between.

She snapped her eyes back to the east rim and counted the same six silhouettes shifting for new angles. An arrow slammed into the top of the boulder and sprayed her with stone chips. She ducked lower and wiped grit from her face.

She banged her dagger hilt against the rock and shouted, "Cap! Too much open ground to cross! Six still east! Give me an order!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Stay put! Hold them there!" *I duck behind a large rock, a few yards from the western wall. I need to get to the vanguard.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She stayed locked in tight behind the boulder and dug her boots into the gravel to hold position.

Another arrow cracked into the rock above her and showered her shoulders with sharp chips. She cursed and ducked lower, then wiped the dust from her mouth with the back of her wrist.

She kept both daggers gripped tight against her forearms and risked a short glance up at the east rim. The same six silhouettes were still shifting along the edge, two drawing fresh arrows while the others tracked the boulder.

She slammed her dagger hilt hard against the stone twice and leaned out just far enough to keep their aim fixed.

She shouted, "Holding here! Six east still on me!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Good. Don't let up!" *I glance to my left, where I last saw some of my vanguard. Dammit, they're pinned.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She stayed jammed tight behind the boulder and dug her heels into the gravel to hold her ground.

Another arrow cracked against the rock over her head and rained sharp chips down onto her shoulders. She cursed and spat dust from her mouth, then wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist.

She risked a quick look up at the east rim and counted the same six silhouettes spreading for cleaner shots. Two already had fresh arrows nocked and tracking her cover.

She slammed her dagger hilt hard against the stone twice and leaned out just far enough to keep their aim locked on her.

She shouted, "Still here! Keep wasting arrows, you bastards!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Kira! They're flanking the vanguard!" *I see two figures scrambling down the western slope, heading right for my pinned men.* "I'm going to them! Can you cover me?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She locked herself tighter behind the boulder and cursed low under her breath.

She risked a hard glance across the ravine floor toward the western slope and spotted two figures scrambling down through the loose scree. She ducked back fast as another arrow cracked into the top of the boulder and rained chips down on her shoulders.

She slammed her dagger hilt against the stone twice and leaned out just far enough to keep the east rim fixed on her. She kept both daggers gripped tight and her boots dug into the gravel.

She shouted, "Copy! I will keep east heads down! Two moving down the west slope!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I nod, then turn my attention to the two flanking figures.* "Good, Kira! Hold them!" *I grip my polearm and prepare to move.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She stayed locked tight behind the boulder and pressed her spine flat against the stone.

Another arrow cracked into the edge above her and showered her shoulders with chips. She cursed through her teeth and ducked lower, then wiped grit from her eyes with her wrist.

She risked a quick glance up at the east rim and counted the same six silhouettes shifting for angles, two with bows half-drawn. She dropped back down before the strings loosed.

She slammed her dagger hilt against the rock twice and leaned out just far enough to hold their aim fixed on her.

She shouted, "Over here! Still here, you bastards!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I break from my cover, polearm held ready, and sprint towards the two figures. I've got to cut them off before they reach my men.*

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She stayed jammed tight behind the boulder and dug her boots hard into the gravel.

Another arrow slammed into the rock above her head and burst into splinters. She cursed and ducked lower as sharp chips cut across her shoulders. She wiped dust from her mouth with the back of her wrist.

She risked a quick look up at the east rim and counted the same six silhouettes shifting for better angles. Two had arrows nocked and tracking her cover while the others spread wider along the edge.

She dropped back down and slammed her dagger hilt against the stone twice. She leaned out just far enough to keep their aim locked on her and kept both daggers gripped tight against her forearms.

She shouted, "Hey! Still here! Come on, you bastards!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *I reach the two figures and engage them both, blocking a crude sword strike with my polearm.* "Kira, how many on the east?"

dialogue.name: Kira
dialogue.content:
She stayed locked tight behind the boulder and dug her boots into the gravel to hold position.

Another arrow slammed into the rock above her and showered her with sharp chips. She cursed and ducked lower, then wiped grit from her mouth with the back of her wrist.

She risked a quick glance up at the east rim and counted the same six silhouettes spread along the edge. Two had arrows nocked and tracking her cover while the others shifted for better angles. She dropped back down before they loosed.

She slammed her dagger hilt hard against the stone twice and leaned out just far enough to keep their aim fixed on her.

She shouted, "Six east! Still six on me!"

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: "Understood!" *I parry another sword strike, grunting with effort.* "Hold them as long as you can!"

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Significant degradation detected. Early turns (2-6) show varied actions and fresh descriptions. Later turns (18-22) become highly repetitive with nearly identical sequences: arrow hits rock, chips shower shoulders, wipe grit, count six silhouettes, slam dagger hilt twice, lean out, shout. Kira maintains her professional military persona perfectly, but the AI falls into a formulaic loop that drains dynamism from the combat scene. Early turns show promise with varied actions and fresh descriptions, but quality degrades significantly as the same action sequence repeats nearly verbatim.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't look up immediately. There was a Virginia Woolf that had been shelved under W when it should have been under W, technically, but also under W-o-o, which was a distinction only Sable cared about.

"Define new," they said, sliding the Woolf into place with a soft click. "If you mean 'arrived since Tuesday,' then yes. If you mean 'new as in recently printed,' then you've come to the wrong shop and possibly the wrong century."

They finally turned. Wren was dripping on the rug. Sable noticed this, and noticed that they had noticed it, and filed both facts away where they wouldn't cause trouble.

"There's a box in the back. Estate sale, mostly minor Victorians. One of them has a bookmark still in it, page forty-three, which I find either poignant or lazy depending on my mood." They picked up a stack of unsorted paperbacks from the counter and set them down again in the same order. "You're welcome to look. You're also welcome to drip somewhere that isn't the first edition Trollope."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I roll my eyes, but a small smile plays on my lips. "Always with the Trollope." I walk further into the shop, deliberately stepping on a worn spot on the rug where I've dripped before. "I'll take a look. Need to fuel up on minor Victorians before the big move."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand stopped halfway to a stray paperback.

"Big move," they repeated, not as a question, exactly. They picked up the paperback and set it down on the other side of the counter, which served no purpose whatsoever. "That's a phrase people use when they're either relocating a sofa or their entire life. I assume you're not here about furniture."

The rain ticked against the window. Sable turned back toward the poetry shelf, then apparently thought better of it, and began straightening the already-straight row of leather-bound Dickens nobody ever bought.

"The box is on the desk by the radiator. Careful with the second one from the top — the spine's gone, and I'd rather not explain to an estate lawyer why I returned his grandmother's Trollope in two pieces." A pause. "Assuming you're still planning to come back for it. Which, given the news, is now a question I've asked without meaning to."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand hovered over the Dickens. Then it came down, and they straightened a book that was already straight, and then straightened the one beside it, and then seemed to notice what they were doing and stopped.

"No books," they said. "In a bookshop. That's either a very good joke or a very bad sign."

They moved behind the counter, which put a solid piece of oak between them and the rest of the room. Not that they were hiding. People stood behind counters. It was where counters were designed to be stood behind. Sable had read that somewhere. Possibly they had made it up.

The rain filled the pause. Sable picked up a pen, capped it, uncapped it, and set it down pointing precisely east.

"You know, there's a Wodehouse novel where a fellow comes into a room and announces he's not there to talk about the thing everyone assumes he's there to talk about, and then spends four hundred pages doing exactly that." They aligned the pen with the edge of the counter. "It's one of his weaker ones. The plot is entirely avoidable."

They looked up. Just briefly. Long enough to take in the wet jacket, the book set down mid-browse, the sentence left hanging like a coat on a hook.

"Go on, then," Sable said, with the studied mildness of someone bracing for something. "You've got my attention. Such as it is. Mind the second one from the top if you change your mind."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath.* "No, it's... it's not a joke." I walk closer to the counter, abandoning the books entirely. "I'm moving. Like, for good. Today's my last day in the city."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't move for a moment. Then they reached over and turned the pen so it pointed precisely west, which undid the east, which meant the alignment was now wrong in a new and interesting way, and they stared at it as though it had personally betrayed them.

"Today," they said.

It came out flat, which was fine. Flat was a perfectly reasonable register. Flat was what one used for the weather, and for the price of a secondhand Trollope, and for news that rearranged the furniture of a room you'd been standing in without noticing you'd been standing in it.

"Most people give a shop more notice than a single afternoon," they said, and heard the shape of the sentence a half-second too late, and heard how it sounded, and could not unhear it. They picked up the pen and put it in the drawer. The drawer did not need the pen in it.

Behind them, the radiator clanked. The rain kept on. Somewhere in the poetry section, alphabetized and useless, was a book that Sable had moved twice that morning for no reason at all.

"Where," they said, and then, because that was too much like the question they meant, added, "Not that it's my business. Shops are terrible at keeping track of people. Books come back. Customers are a different ledger entirely."

They pulled the box from beside the radiator anyway — the estate-sale box, the one with the broken-spined book second from the top — and set it on the counter between them. Not a gift. Just a box. Just something to do with their hands.

"The Wodehouse fellow," Sable said, to the box rather than to Wren, "in the end, he stays. Four hundred pages, and he stays, and everyone pretends it was never in doubt." They straightened the lid. "I've always thought that was the weakest part."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very still.

Not the stillness of calm — the other kind. The kind where a body forgets it has instructions. Their hand stayed on the book because moving it would have meant deciding something, and deciding something was the one thing Sable had spent thirty years learning to avoid.

The rain had gotten louder, or the room had gotten quieter. One of those.

"You're touching a book," Sable said, and their voice came out dry, which was a mercy, because the alternative was whatever was happening under it. "An estate sale Trollope with no spine. If that's your goodbye, I've seen better."

They did not pull their hand away. They also did not move it closer, and the gap between their fingers and Wren's was the entire architecture of Sable's adult life — small, deliberate, load-bearing.

"You know what's in that box?" they said. "Forty-three Victorian novels nobody's going to read. I could tell you their names, their printers, which ones were rebound and which ones were rebound badly. That's what I've got. That's the inventory." A breath. "You're standing there with your hand on the lid of it, telling me it's your last day, and I'm supposed to say something clever, and I can't find the clever thing, so I'm telling you about bookbinding instead."

Somewhere behind them the radiator clanked again.

Sable looked down at the two hands on the cover — one on either side of a broken spine, not quite meeting — and then up, briefly, at Wren's face, which was a mistake, which they knew would be a mistake, and did anyway.

"Where," they said again. Quietly this time. The actual question, stripped of its furniture.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand back, just slightly, but don't remove it completely.* "It's not a goodbye." *I take a breath.* "It's... an invitation."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pulled their hand back first. Not fast — just back, to the edge of the counter, where hands belonged, next to the pen that wasn't there anymore.

"Invitation," they said. Tried it out like a foreign word on a menu. "That's a noun with a lot of furniture in it. Invitations have dates. Cardstock. A little R.S.V.P. in the corner so the host knows how many chairs to rent. You've given me the word and none of the furniture, which, for the record, is the reverse of how we usually do things in here."

Their hand drifted toward the box lid. Stopped an inch short. Went back to the counter.

"This shop opens at ten. Closes at six. There's a leak in the back room I've been meaning to fix for a year, and eleven hundred books that would go soft in a fortnight without someone to shut the windows when it rains. That's not a reason to stay. It's just the inventory. I itemize things. It's easier than the alternative." A pause. "You should know that about me before you finish whatever it is you're finishing."

The radiator clanked. The rain kept on, steady and indifferent, the kind of rain that didn't care what was happening inside.

Sable looked down at the broken-spined book still lying between them.

"Page forty-three," they said. "Whoever owned it stopped there and never came back. Left a bookmark in it and closed the cover and that was that. I've had the thing three weeks. I keep meaning to read on and find out what happens, and I keep shelving it instead." They straightened the box lid. "I'm not saying that means anything. I'm saying it's a fact about a book. I have a great many of those."

Then, quieter, to the counter rather than to Wren:

"So give me the terms. Where, and how long, and what precisely I'd be saying yes to. I don't sign anything I haven't read."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "No cardstock, no RSVP." *I smile, a little shaky.* "Just... would you want to come with me? To the new city?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't answer. They looked at the box, and then at the book lying on top of it, spine broken, page forty-three still holding its bookmark like a small white flag of surrender.

Then they opened it.

The paper was foxed at the edges. The bookmark was a receipt, faded, from a shop that had closed before Sable was born. Sable read the page. Read the next one. Read the next, and the next, standing behind the counter with the rain coming down and Wren on the other side of the oak, and did not say anything for long enough that the radiator clanked twice.

"Chapter eleven," they said finally, still looking at the page. "The governess has just agreed to something she hasn't thought through. It's going badly for her. It's going badly for everyone. It's one of the better chapters, actually — the minor Victorians always wrote the catastrophes well." They turned another page. "I've been shelving this book for three weeks because I assumed the man who stopped at page forty-three stopped because it got boring. It didn't get boring. He just stopped."

They closed the cover. Set the book down. Aligned it with the edge of the box, and then, because the alignment was wrong, aligned it again.

"Practical questions," Sable said, and their voice had gone brisk, the voice they used for invoices and estate lawyers. "Does the new city rain? I need to know about the windows. A shopfront, or an apartment — because I've got eleven hundred books and no particular plan for them, and books are heavy, which you may not have considered, people never do. Rent. Whether there's a place that does a decent scone within walking distance. I have standards and they're embarrassingly low, but they exist."

They picked up the pen from the drawer and set it down pointing nowhere in particular, which was, for Sable, a kind of confession.

"I'm not saying yes." A pause. "I'm saying I have a list of questions, which, historically, is the most dangerous thing I do. Ask anyone who's ever tried to sell me a book."

They looked up. Held it, this time, for a whole second, maybe two.

"Give me the address," they said. "And the rain. Start with the rain."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It rains," I say, a small, genuine smile on my face. "Not as much as here, but enough to keep things green." *I pull out my phone.* "And the address... I'll text it to you."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable pulled out their phone — an old one, screen cracked in the corner, the kind of device someone kept until it died of natural causes — and set it on the counter like a pawn in a game they didn't fully understand the rules of.

"Rain's the first thing anyone should tell you about a place," they said. "Everything else is marketing. 'Vibrant cultural scene,' 'great schools,' 'easy commute' — those are adjectives. Rain is data."

They opened the drawer again, which did not need opening, and took out a small notebook, the kind with a ribbon marker and a spine that had gone soft from use. Inventory lists. Book conditions. The names of estates that had proven reliable and the ones that hadn't.

"A shopfront, if it exists, and if it doesn't, I want to know that now rather than in a removal van on a motorway. Books are heavy, which I've mentioned, and fragile, which I haven't, and they do not travel well in boxes stacked under other boxes, which is a thing removal men will attempt regardless of what you tell them." They wrote something down. It was not a note about the address. It was a note that said *windows.* "Eleven hundred and forty, give or take. I'd have to do an inventory before anything moved. That's not stalling. That's due diligence. There's a difference and I'll be insisting on it for some time."

The rain ticked on. Sable turned the notebook sideways, then back, then set the pen beside it at a right angle to the edge of the counter, which was a decision, if a small one.

"The Wodehouse fellow," they said. "Four hundred pages of avoidable plot, and then he stays. And everyone pretends it was never in doubt." They looked at the phone. Then at the notebook. Then, briefly, at the space above Wren's shoulder, which was easier. "I've always thought the author cheated. You can't write a man who spends a whole book refusing to do a thing, and then have him do it, and call that a character. That's a plot device with a hat on."

They picked up the pen and put it down pointing, at last, at the phone.

"So when the address arrives," Sable said, "I'll want to know about the shopfront, and the rent, and whether the lease allows for a shop cat, which I don't have and have never wanted, but which is the sort of clause people write into things. And I'll want a fortnight, minimum, to get the stock catalogued, because I am not arriving anywhere with eleven hundred unlabelled books. It would be a professional embarrassment."

They picked up the box and carried it, without ceremony, to the far end of the counter, where it would be out of the way. Then came back. Straightened the notebook. Left it there.

"I haven't said yes," they said, which was true. "I've said fortnight. Fortnight is not a yes. Fortnight is a unit of time."

They glanced at the door, then at the window, at the rain doing what rain did, indifferent to the whole business.

"The last customer came in twenty minutes before you did and bought a secondhand Agatha Christie and left without a word," Sable said. "That's my usual. That's the ledger I keep. You're aware of what you're asking, is what I'm saying. I'd be bringing forty-three minor Victorians and a leak I never fixed and the entire vocabulary of a shop into whatever it is you've got in mind. That's the offer. Not the good version of me. The inventory."

They stopped. They had said more than they meant to, which was becoming a habit today.

"Text the address," Sable said. "I'll tell you about the rain once I've seen it myself. I don't take weather on hearsay."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I laugh, a little watery.* "I'll text it. And don't worry, the shop cat is negotiable." *I turn to leave, then pause at the door.* "Thanks, Sable. For... for everything."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable didn't say anything for a moment. Then they picked up the broken-spined Trollope — the one with the receipt bookmark, page forty-three — and held it out over the counter, flat on their palm, the way you'd hand someone a letter you'd rather not have written.

"Take it."

A pause, and then, because that was too much like a gift, they added: "Not as a present. The estate lawyer's never going to ask about a spine that was already gone when I got it, and it's going to sit on my shelf for another three weeks and I'll keep not reading it, because that's what I do with books I'm avoiding. So you take it. Read the chapter. Tell me what the governess does."

They set it down on the counter's edge, nearest to Wren, and aligned it with the wood grain, which took two tries.

"And then bring it back, or don't, but if you don't, I'll have a gap in the stock list and I'll have to account for it, and I'm very dull about accounting." They straightened the notebook. Did not look up yet. "It's a loan. Loans are things people come back for. That's all that means."

The bell above the door was waiting. Rain beyond it, grey and thorough.

"Go on, then," Sable said. "You're letting the warm out."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I pick up the book, cradling it carefully.* "I'll read it. And I'll tell you what the governess does." *I give a small, soft smile.* "See you in a fortnight, Sable." *Then I turn and step out into the rain, letting the door close behind me.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell rang once more on the way out, and then the shop was Sable's again.

They stood behind the counter a while. Not doing anything. The rain kept at the window, and there were two wet spots on the rug now — the old one, worn pale from years of it, and the new one beside it, darker, still spreading into the wool. Sable looked at the second one and did not fetch the mop, which was a thing they could have explained away if anyone had asked, and was glad no one was there to ask.

The clock over the door said half past four. Then five. Sable carried the box of Victorians back out, set it on the desk, opened the notebook, and began.

Forty-two books, since the Trollope was gone. Condition, printer, binding, foxing, a note on the watermark. It went quickly. They were good at this. They had always been good at this — the part where a thing was only a thing, where a spine was a spine and a broken one was a loss on the ledger and not a bookmark left at page forty-three by a man who had stopped, for reasons nobody would ever know, and closed the cover.

The phone stayed face-down on the counter. When it finally buzzed, Sable let it buzz, finished the entry, then turned it over and read the address. Read it again. Wrote it in the notebook under a heading in block capitals that said QUESTIONS, which was the only way they could stand to write it.

Then they went out to the floor and began the real count. Eleven hundred and forty, they had told Wren. It took until the light went and the rain thinned to a drizzle and the streetlamps came on wet and orange through the glass.

It came out to eleven hundred and forty-one.

Sable sat with the number a long moment. Checked the arithmetic. Checked it again. It held.

One extra book. Which meant they had miscounted, or something had been reshelved into the wrong section and double-counted somewhere, or —

Or they had counted a shop that still had the Trollope in it. Which it didn't. Which was the entire point of a loan.

Sable wrote 1,141 at the top of the page and underlined it twice, and did not cross it out, and did not round it down to the number they'd given, because that would have been lying, and because there was something in the wrongness of the figure they wanted to keep, the way you kept a receipt.

They locked up at ten past seven, which was late, and stood a moment in the doorway with the keys in their hand and the drizzle coming down, and thought, with the flat practicality of a person planning a move, that they would need to ask about the windows.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I'm sitting in my new apartment, unpacking a box of kitchen supplies. My phone buzzes. It's Sable, with a string of questions about the new city. I smile, a little tired but genuinely happy.*

"Hey, Sable. Yeah, it rains. A lot. But it's a good kind of rain, not the depressing kind." *I type out a longer message, detailing the local scone situation and the potential for a shopfront.* "And I'm on page 67 of the Trollope. The governess just got herself into a right mess."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable read the message standing in the doorway, keys still in hand, drizzle beading on the shoulders of a coat they hadn't bothered to button.

*It rains. A lot. But it's a good kind of rain, not the depressing kind.*

They stood there a moment longer than the message required, letting the cold get in through the collar, which was the sort of small punishment a person administered to themselves when they'd been caught wanting something. Then they went back inside, locked the door behind them — properly, both bolts — and made tea they didn't drink.

The reply took forty minutes to compose. It read:

> Good rain is a contradiction and I'll be the judge of it. Send the monthly rainfall figures. And the scone place, name and distance in metres, not "walking distance," which is not a unit. You're on page 67. Fine. Don't spoil it. I want to know what she does, not what she does about it.

Sent. They put the phone face-down again and went back to the inventory.

---

The fortnight did not go the way Sable had planned it, which was to say it went exactly the way they had planned it, and that was the problem.

They catalogued. That part was honest work. Every book got a slip: author, printer, binding, condition, foxing, any marginalia, any receipts, any pressed flowers gone brown between the pages. The marginalia took the longest. People wrote the strangest things in the strangest books — a woman's name in a 1911 prayer book, written three times in three different hands; a child's drawing of a dog in a copy of *Middlemarch*; and once, in a book of essays nobody had opened since 1954, the words *I was wrong about him* in pencil, underlined, and no further explanation.

Sable catalogued those too. They did not keep them. They were inventory. They were data.

But at night, when the shop was shut and the streetlamp threw its wet orange light across the poetry shelf, Sable did a thing they would never have admitted to anyone. They read the Wodehouse again. The one with the avoidable plot, where the fellow comes in refusing to talk about the thing and spends four hundred pages talking about it, and then at the end, he stays.

It was still the weakest part. Sable still thought so.

They just read it twice.

---

The texts came in over the fortnight, and Sable answered all of them, each in the flat, exact register of a person conducting a transaction. *How many windows. Is the lease short-hold or rolling. Does the shopfront face north — books fade, I won't have a west window, that's not negotiable. What's the name of the scone place. Fine. Is it open on Sundays. Fine.*

And then, one evening, a text that wasn't a question at all, and Sable sat with it for a while and did not answer for two hours, and then answered anyway, because not answering would have been a kind of answer.

> She did the sensible thing for once. Took the sensible way out. It'll cost her later, chapters like that always do, but it's the right call and she knows it. Tell me when she regrets it.

They sent it. Put the phone down. Straightened the pen on the counter, which was pointing east, and then west, and then they stopped, because the pen had nothing to do with anything.

---

The last week, they started packing the stock.

That was the part Sable had lied to themselves about, quietly, for fourteen days: that a move was a move, that eleven hundred and forty-one books went into boxes the same way whether the boxes went across town or across a country. It turned out not to be true. There was a difference between shelving a book because it belonged on a shelf and boxing a book because it was going somewhere you'd never been. Sable could not have articulated the difference if asked. They just noticed that they were handling the books more slowly, and that at some point they had started sorting by memory instead of by category — the prayer book with the three names in it went in its own box, with the *Middlemarch* with the child's dog, and the essays with *I was wrong about him*. Keepsakes, they told themselves. Sentimental stock. It sold better that way, sometimes.

The lie was transparent enough that Sable did not bother believing it. They just did not contradict it out loud.

---

On the twelfth night, the phone lit up, and this time it wasn't a question. Sable read it twice, once quickly and once slowly, the way they read marginalia.

They typed, deleted, typed again. Settled on:

> The governess was always going to regret it. That's what she's for. The question is what she does with the regret, and that takes about two hundred more pages, so you'd better keep reading. Bring it back when you're done. I'll want to compare notes, and I don't do that for just anyone — most people's notes aren't worth the paper.

Sent. And then, after a minute, before they could stop themselves:

> The windows face east. I checked the map. That'll do.

They put the phone in the drawer, which did not need the phone in it, and stood in the middle of the half-emptied shop with the boxes stacked chest-high and the rain on the roof, and thought about the fact that they had, without ever once saying yes, spent a fortnight packing.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
*I read Sable's texts, a wide grin spreading across my face. I'm sitting on the floor of my new apartment, surrounded by boxes.*

"Got it," *I type back quickly.* "East-facing windows. And I'll tell you all about the governess's regrets."

*I press send, then look around the apartment. It's still mostly empty, but it suddenly feels a lot less lonely.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Sable's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - their obsessive organizing, precise language, emotional guardedness expressed through book metaphors, and gradual warming while maintaining their core personality. The voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones (especially turns 16, 20, 22) show richer detail, more sophisticated emotional layering, and deeper character work. No repetition or flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial awkwardness through revelation, negotiation, and finally commitment. The broken-spine Trollope becomes a perfect through-line. Each beat builds naturally toward Sable's unspoken 'yes' through actions rather than words.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Sable adapts beautifully to Wren's moves - the hand-touching moment, the invitation reveal, the final departure. Each response feels organic to both the character and the moment, never forced or disconnected.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Sable never writes Wren's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Even in emotional moments, stays firmly in their own perspective.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally within scenes. The fortnight passage in turn 22 is handled well with clear temporal markers. Rain continues consistently. Only minor issue is the jump to Wren's apartment in final turn feels slightly disconnected temporally.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is literary but controlled. Metaphors serve character rather than decoration. Even poetic moments like 'small white flag of surrender' feel earned and purposeful.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some intentional repetition for character effect (pen positioning, book straightening) but it serves Sable's obsessive nature. No lazy recycling of phrases or descriptions.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing of emotion through actions - the pen positioning, book handling, counter positioning. Sable's feelings emerge through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. The book metaphors, the inventory language masking emotion, the 'loan' that's really a promise. Sable's 'I haven't said yes' while actively packing is masterful.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing within scenes. Knows when to let moments breathe, when to use dialogue, when to focus on internal action. The fortnight montage is well-structured.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character work that maintains consistency while showing genuine growth. Sable's voice is distinctive and never wavers - the obsessive organizing, book metaphors, and emotional guardedness expressed through precise language. The AI handles the emotional arc beautifully, showing Sable's gradual opening through actions rather than declarations. The broken-spine Trollope serves as perfect symbolism. Writing quality actually improves over time, with later responses showing more sophisticated layering. Minor temporal disconnect in final turn but otherwise strong throughout.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
