The east ridge answered with a ragged volley. One arrow struck the ground too far right. Another punched into the cloak as she snapped it low over the stone. The third cracked past her ear close enough to make her vision flare white.

Kira dropped, rolled, and came up behind a narrower spur of rock, breath sawing through her teeth.

“Right,” she hissed. “Still dangerous.”

The recurve man was on his feet again. Blood streaked one side of his face where stone chips had bitten him, but his bow was up and his aim was shifting away from her, angling toward the gully. Toward the broken ground where the fight was turning ugly and close.

Kira’s stomach clenched.

“No, you bastard.”

She grabbed the last decent stone within reach and threw it hard. It struck the ledge in front of the recurve man’s boot and burst into grit. He staggered sideways, curse tearing out of him, and the loose went high. The arrow skipped off the ravine wall with a useless crack.

“Missed again!” Kira snarled. “Your coin’s no good here!”

One of the archers flinched at the sound of her voice. The crossbowman had reloaded, but his hands were shaking so badly the bolt rattled against the stirrup before it seated. Kira saw the fear in the set of his shoulders. Fear was useful. Fear could be spent.

She yanked the cloak free from the rock and dragged it in a sharp arc through the scree, raising a low hiss of cloth over stone. At the same time, she kicked a loose fragment against the base of the boulder. The two sounds split apart, one to the left, one to the right.

Two bows followed the cloak.

The crossbow followed the stone.

Three shots wasted in dust and echo.

Kira bared her teeth.

“That’s it,” she rasped. “Spend them. Spend them all.”

The recurve man shouted at his shooters, but his voice had gone thin and reedy. The command did not land clean. One archer looked back over his shoulder toward the gully, then toward the ravine mouth, then at the broken dust along the east wall where Kira had kicked her earlier rockslide. He did not know where the danger was. None of them did.

Good.

Kira used the confusion to move.

She crawled low along the base of the boulder, boots scraping soft in the grit, injured shoulder screaming every time she put weight against the stone. Blood from the cut on her forearm had dried stiff over her fingers. She wiped her palm on her thigh and left another dark smear there. Her ear throbbed where the stone splinter had opened it. Dust had settled into the wound, and the pain had turned hot and sharp.

She did not care. Not yet.

Her eyes found a narrow crack in the east wall a few yards farther along. Not a path. Not truly. But it was enough for fingers, maybe toes, if she was stupid enough to try.

She was stupid enough.

Kira jammed one dagger into a fissure and used it to haul herself up. The blade bit into stone. Her shoulder protested with a white flash of agony. She bit down on a curse and forced her boots to find purchase on the scree.

“Boots on the wall!” she bellowed. “East wall! East wall!”

The lie had worked before. It could work again, especially when their nerves were already frayed.

The crossbowman jerked his weapon toward the sound. One archer loosed too early, the arrow flying high and wide. The recurve man screamed at them to hold, but his own head turned toward the falling dust and the scrape of stone.

That was all Kira needed.

She climbed another half-body’s length, found a shallow shelf, and kicked a spray of loose shale down onto the ravine floor. The clatter was sharp and ugly, louder than one woman should have been able to make. Then she slapped the flat of her dagger against the wall and shouted, “Up! I’m coming up, you ugly bastards!”

The panic took them cleanly this time.

One archer backed away from the lip. The crossbowman fired at the dust, bolt cracking into stone and sending fragments whining into the air. The recurve man spun toward his own line, grabbing the nearest shooter by the shoulder and shoving him back into position.

The shove turned into a stumble. The archer shoved back.

Kira saw it and felt a savage grin split her face.

“There,” she panted. “There’s the crack.”

She could not stay on the wall. Not like this. Not with her shoulder bleeding and her grip turning slick. If she hung there much longer, one clean shot would put her off the rock and into the ravine floor with a broken neck. But she could make them pay for every second they spent looking at her.

Kira dragged herself sideways along the shelf, fingers clawing for purchase, boots scraping loose stone. The shelf narrowed. Below her, the boulders looked uglier than before. Above, the east ridge lip jutted out just enough to deny her a clean throw at the recurve

dialogue.name: Captain
dialogue.content: *Kira's a force of nature.* I see the archer stumble, then push back. "That's it! Break their line!" I yell, pushing the vanguard harder into the gully.

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Kira's voice remains remarkably consistent throughout - her crude language, tactical awareness, and fierce determination never waver. Her personality traits (resourcefulness, loyalty, dark humor) are maintained from first to final turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds up well. Early turns are tight and focused, later turns become slightly more verbose but maintain quality. No significant flattening of personality or loss of detail.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial ambush through tactical maneuvering to climactic moments. Each turn builds tension and advances the tactical situation. Clear escalation from defensive positioning to active disruption of enemy coordination.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Kira adapts well to Captain's orders and changing battlefield conditions. When Captain warns against heroics, she adjusts tactics. Responds appropriately to enemy movements and tactical shifts.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency. Never writes Captain's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Consistently responds to Captain's commands without overstepping.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally through the battle sequence. Physical details like accumulating injuries, fatigue, and ammunition depletion are tracked consistently. No major temporal contradictions.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Writing is direct and visceral without being overwrought. Combat descriptions are sharp and functional. Occasional poetic moments serve character rather than decoration.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements in combat descriptions and Kira's taunts, but this feels intentional to show the grinding nature of the fight. Varied enough to avoid monotony.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Kira's tactical awareness, injuries, and emotional state are demonstrated through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in Kira's relationship with Captain (loyalty, trust), her tactical thinking, and the psychological warfare she wages against enemies through misdirection.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that matches the intensity of combat. Alternates between quick action beats and tactical assessment moments effectively.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and tactical roleplay. Kira maintains her distinct voice, personality, and combat expertise throughout a complex battle sequence. The AI demonstrates strong understanding of military tactics, character psychology, and battlefield dynamics. Minor verbosity in later turns but no significant quality degradation. Excellent respect for user agency and adaptive responsiveness to changing conditions.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald struck his staff again — once, sharply — to signal that the Queen would respond. The sound rang off the vaulted ceiling and died.

Queen Isara did not lean forward. She did not shift her weight. She regarded you the way a cartographer regards a coastline: with precision, and without sentiment.

"Velheim sends terms," she said. Her voice carried without effort, the way voices do when rooms have been built to serve them. "The last ambassador who brought us *terms* from the north returned home considerably lighter than he arrived. His dignity did not make the journey with him."

A breath moved through the gallery. Not quite a laugh. Not quite silence.

Commander Ash's jaw tightened at the edge of your vision. He hadn't moved his hand from his pommel, but something in his posture sharpened — a blade being tested against a thumb.

"I would hear these terms," the Queen continued, "before I decide what they are worth." The pause that followed was deliberate, and measured, and long. "Choose your first word carefully, Ambassador. The court is listening."

From the gallery, Lord Daven had gone very still. His earlier nod had been encouragement. What was on his face now was something closer to warning.

In her alcove, Priestess Yuna's hands were folded. Her eyes had not left you since you entered.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, unmoved by her veiled threats.* "My Queen, Velheim seeks not to lose dignity, but to *gain* stability for our shared borders." I pause, letting her words hang in the air for a moment. "My first word, then, is 'cooperation'."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald did not strike his staff. The Queen had not yet yielded the floor.

Queen Isara let the word sit where you had placed it — *cooperation* — the way one lets a coin sit on a table before deciding whether to pocket it or sweep it to the floor.

"Cooperation," she repeated. The word sounded different in her mouth. Older. More worn. "A merchant's word. Velheim has sent us a merchant."

Commander Ash exhaled through his nose — a sound just short of contempt, and calculated to be heard.

"Your Majesty." The voice came from the gallery before the Herald could intervene. Lord Daven had stepped forward to the gallery rail, his posture impeccably correct, his tone walking the razor's edge between deference and advocacy. "If I may — the Ambassador's framing speaks to Velheim's position on the joint border surveys, which this court requested not three seasons past. Cooperation was *our* word first, as I recall."

The Queen's gaze moved to Daven. It was not a warm movement.

"You recall a great deal, Lord Daven," she said.

"I serve the court's memory, Majesty. Nothing more."

Commander Ash turned his head toward Daven then — a slow, deliberate rotation, like a siege engine finding its bearing. Whatever passed between the two men in that glance carried no warmth.

Priestess Yuna unfolded her hands. She refolded them the other way. It was the first movement she had made since you entered.

The Queen's attention returned to you. The brief skirmish in her gallery might not have occurred at all, for all her expression acknowledged it.

"Your ally speaks quickly on your behalf," she said. "I wonder whether Velheim trusted you to speak for yourself." The faintest tilt of her chin. "Continue, Ambassador. What *specifically* does Velheim's cooperation require of my crown?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald's staff struck the floor — twice, in sharp succession. A breach of address required marking.

The sound did not stop Commander Ash's expression from changing.

What had been controlled contempt became something harder and more focused. He turned from the gallery, from Lord Daven, and fixed his gaze on you with the unhurried attention of a man who had learned patience from long campaigns and longer grudges.

"The Ambassador addresses a servant of the crown without leave," the Herald said, his voice carrying the particular neutrality of a man noting a fact into a ledger. "The floor belongs to Her Majesty."

But Queen Isara raised one finger — a single, small gesture — and the Herald fell silent.

"No," she said. "Let him answer."

The permission was not a gift. It was a trap being opened with courtesy.

Commander Ash descended two steps from his position beside the throne. He did not draw his sword. He did not need to. His voice, when he spoke, was the voice of a man who had given orders in the dark and had them obeyed.

"Six weeks," he said. "Yes. By crown authority, issued in response to Velheim vessels operating within the contested boundary markers — markers your government has disputed for eleven years without resolution." He paused. "We did not blockade your merchants, Ambassador. We enforced *existing law* against ships that chose to test it." Another pause, shorter. "They made that choice. We made ours."

From the gallery, Lord Daven's knuckles had whitened against the rail.

Priestess Yuna was watching Commander Ash now. Her expression had not changed, but her attention had shifted, and that shift felt significant in a way that was difficult to name.

Queen Isara had not moved. Her finger had lowered back to the armrest.

"The Commander's account differs from yours," she said to you, her tone as even as poured water. "This is not surprising. What is surprising is that you chose to surface this particular grievance *now*, in this manner, in this room." The faintest suggestion of something — not curiosity, exactly, but its cold cousin — moved behind her eyes. "You have surrendered the initiative you arrived with, Ambassador. I am wondering whether you intended to."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The asterisk hung in the silence like a dropped coin that had not yet finished spinning.

The Herald did not strike his staff. There was nothing to announce. The court waited.

Queen Isara waited longest.

The throne room had a particular quality of silence — the kind that accumulated weight the longer it was permitted to persist. Every second you did not speak added to what would be required to break it. The marble underfoot seemed colder. The vaulted ceiling seemed higher.

Commander Ash had returned to his position beside the throne, his retreat precise and unhurried, the movement of a man who had made his point and saw no need to repeat it. His hand had found the pommel again.

Lord Daven had released the gallery rail. He stood with his hands clasped behind his back now, his expression composed into something that was not quite concern and not quite patience. He was watching you the way a man watches a fire he cannot reach.

Priestess Yuna had unfolded her hands entirely. They rested open on her knees — a posture that suggested, to those who knew her order's customs, that she was no longer merely observing. She was *recording*.

The Herald stood with his staff angled precisely, ready.

Queen Isara tilted her head by a degree. No more.

"Ambassador," she said, and her voice had changed in some subtle way — not softer, but more deliberate, the way a blade is more deliberate than a bludgeon. "The court's patience is a finite resource. You came here with terms. You have given us one word and one accusation." The pause arrived like a door closing. "Give us the rest."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, a slight smile playing on my lips. "Indeed, Majesty. My apologies for the theatrics. Sometimes, the path to cooperation requires a little... clarity."* I gesture to Commander Ash. *"His ships may have been enforcing 'law,' but they also disrupted established trade, costing Velheim considerable coin."*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald's staff struck once — a gentle correction, almost apologetic in its precision. Gesturing at crown officers without leave was a lesser breach than direct address, but a breach nonetheless. The Herald was thorough.

Queen Isara did not acknowledge the correction. Her attention had not left your face.

"Theatrics," she said. She tasted the word as you had used it — applied to yourself, offered as self-deprecation, perhaps intended to disarm. "You confess to them freely. I am not certain whether that is confidence or miscalculation."

Commander Ash had not looked at you when you gestured toward him. He stared ahead, at the middle distance, with the practiced stillness of a man who had decided you were not worth the movement of his eyes. The dismissal was architectural. Deliberate.

It was Lord Daven who spoke, carefully, from the gallery — the Herald allowing it this time without intervention, perhaps sensing the room required a valve.

"The disruption to established trade is a matter of record, Majesty," Daven said. His voice was measured, each word placed like a foot on uncertain ground. "Velheim's grievance is not without documentation. The cost figures exist. They are not trivial."

"Lord Daven." The Queen did not look at him. "You are an advocate, not an auditor. Do not read me ledgers."

Daven inclined his head and said nothing further. The rebuke had been mild. He accepted it as such.

Priestess Yuna's eyes had moved to the Queen's hands.

Queen Isara finally shifted — the first true movement since you had entered, a slight forward inclination that brought the full weight of her attention to bear in a new way.

"Considerable coin," she repeated. "Then name it. Not in metaphor, Ambassador. Not in grievance. In figures." The cold suggestion of patience thinned perceptibly. "What does Velheim believe it is owed, and what does Velheim offer in return. Those are the only two numbers that matter in this room today."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald's staff struck three times.

Three was unusual. Three meant the court had witnessed something it needed a moment to process.

The sound died in the rafters. No one moved immediately — not because the gesture had paralyzed the room, but because everyone in it was simultaneously calculating what it meant that you had done it.

Priestess Yuna looked at the documents in your outstretched hand. Then she looked at you. Her expression remained precisely what it had been — that careful blankness that was not indifference but its more disciplined cousin. She did not reach for the papers immediately. She let a breath pass. Then she accepted them with both hands, the way her order accepted offerings at the altar: without haste, without eagerness, without any signal of what the acceptance meant.

The sound of paper unfolding was very loud in the silence.

Commander Ash had gone still in a way that was different from his earlier stillness. Before, he had been a man at rest. Now he was a man arrested mid-motion by an act of will. His eyes had found the documents in Yuna's hands with an attention he could not entirely conceal, and the effort of not crossing the floor was visible in the set of his shoulders.

Lord Daven had both hands on the gallery rail again. His face had opened into something unguarded — surprise, and beneath it, something that might have been relief, or might have been the recognition that the game had just changed boards entirely.

Queen Isara had not moved. She watched Priestess Yuna read.

The Priestess turned the first page. Then the second. Her breathing was even. Her face gave nothing. When she reached the final page she did not look up immediately — she returned to the first, and read it again, more slowly.

Then she folded the documents along their original creases and held them in her lap.

"Your Majesty," Yuna said. Her voice was the first genuinely neutral sound the room had produced all morning — no performance in it, no edge, no warmth. Simply a voice carrying words. "The Ambassador has presented what appear to be operational orders. They bear a seal I recognize." A pause, brief and precise. "They are not Velheim's seal."

Commander Ash said nothing.

The Queen's gaze moved from Yuna to Ash with the slow, inevitable quality of a tide finding its direction.

"Commander," she said.

The word was not a question. It was an opening — of a door, of an inquiry, of something that had not been open a moment before. The throne room, which had been a place of performance and maneuver, had become something else.

Priestess Yuna set the documents on the small table beside her alcove and folded her hands again. She was watching Commander Ash now. So was everyone.

The Herald stood with his staff perfectly vertical, and said nothing, and waited.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Commander Ash, a small, knowing smile playing on my lips.* "It seems the 'law' was rather... expansive, wouldn't you say, Commander?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald did not strike his staff.

No one was watching the Herald.

Commander Ash turned his head toward you then — the full weight of it, the siege engine completing its rotation — and what was in his face was not guilt and not panic and not the collapse of a man exposed. It was something colder and more considered. A general reading terrain.

"The seal," he said, addressing the Queen and not you, "is a matter of operational security that I would prefer to discuss outside open court."

"I am certain you would," Queen Isara said.

The silence that followed was a different species from the silences that had preceded it. Those had been weighted with protocol and performance. This one had teeth.

Lord Daven had descended from the gallery rail and stood at its edge, his posture very straight, his expression carefully emptied of the satisfaction that was clearly pressing against the inside of it. He was a man holding a door shut against a strong wind.

Priestess Yuna had not looked away from Commander Ash. Her hands remained folded. Her order had a reputation for remembering everything it witnessed, and the quality of her attention suggested she was earning that reputation in real time.

"Expansive," Commander Ash repeated finally. He gave the word back to the room with deliberate flatness, refusing your smile its echo. His eyes moved to you for the first time since the documents had emerged — not with the contempt of before, but with the measuring regard of a man revising an estimate. "The Ambassador uses interesting language for a man who smuggled intercepted crown correspondence into a formal hearing."

The counter was clean. Not an answer, but a redirection — and competently made.

Queen Isara's finger had not risen. She let it land.

"Both observations will be addressed," she said. Her voice had acquired an edge of finality, the way a river acquires speed before a fall. "The provenance of the documents. The provenance of the orders." Her gaze moved across the room — Ash, you, Daven, and last, briefly, Yuna — with the comprehensive sweep of someone taking inventory. "This hearing has become something other than what it was announced to be."

She settled back into the throne by a fraction of an inch. The movement was the closest thing to a concession her posture had offered all morning.

"Priestess." The Queen did not look at Yuna when she spoke. "You will retain those documents under your order's seal until I call for them. You will speak to no one of their contents in the interim."

"As the Queen requires," Yuna said. Her tone was the same as it had been. It would always be the same. That was the point of her.

Commander Ash had returned his gaze to the middle distance. Whatever calculation he was running behind his eyes, he was running it quickly and without any visible indication of its outcome.

Lord Daven exhaled — a small, controlled sound that he had perhaps not entirely intended to make.

Queen Isara looked at you.

"You came with terms," she said. "You have instead given me a problem that will require considerable attention before any terms can be meaningfully discussed." The cold thing behind her eyes had shifted. It was not warmer. It was simply pointed in a different direction now. "I do not thank you for this, Ambassador. I note it." A pause, long and deliberate. "Velheim chose its envoy carefully. I am deciding whether that pleases me."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I give a small, deferential bow.* "My queen. Velheim merely seeks clarity and fair dealings. If that creates a problem, perhaps the problem was already here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald struck his staff once. Not a correction — a marker. The kind struck when something worth recording had been said.

Queen Isara did not respond immediately.

She let your words complete their journey across the throne room, let them arrive at the walls and return as echo and then as silence. Her expression had not changed. It very rarely did. But something behind it had moved — a slow, tectonic shift, the kind that precedes either the settling of ground or the opening of it.

"The problem was already here," she said at last, repeating it the way she had repeated *cooperation*, the way she had repeated *theatrics* — testing the weight of it, measuring what it was made of. "Yes. I suspect it was."

Her eyes moved to Commander Ash.

Ash was looking at the middle distance again, but the middle distance had become a more complicated place. His jaw was set. The hand on the pommel had not moved, but the quality of its stillness had changed — less statement now, more anchor.

Lord Daven said nothing. He understood, with the finely calibrated instincts of a man who had survived three changes of royal favor, that this was not a moment to spend words. He stood at the gallery rail and he watched and he saved what he had for later.

Priestess Yuna had placed one hand flat over the folded documents on the table beside her — a quiet, practiced gesture of custody. She was not looking at anyone in particular. She was looking at all of them equally, which amounted to the same thing.

The Queen rose.

It was not a dramatic motion. She did not sweep to her feet or command the room with gesture. She simply stood, and the room reorganized itself around the fact of her standing, the way water reorganizes around a stone that has shifted.

"This hearing is suspended," she said. "Not concluded. Suspended." The distinction was deliberate and everyone present understood it as such. "Commander Ash will present himself to my private council before the evening bell. Lord Daven." Now she looked at him, briefly and without warmth. "You will remain available." Her gaze returned to you, and it carried the full weight of a woman who had been underestimated before and had made productive use of every such occasion. "And you, Ambassador, will be escorted to the east receiving rooms, where you will wait, and where you will — " a pause, precise as a blade's edge, " — reflect on the considerable distance between *creating* clarity and *bringing* it."

She descended the dais steps without haste.

The Herald struck his staff four times — the formal suspension sequence — and the sound rang up through the vault and faded, and the throne room began its careful exhale.

Commander Ash moved first, turning on his heel with military precision, his departure carrying the compressed energy of a man who had a great deal to do before the evening bell and intended to do all of it.

Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery as the room began to stir. His expression had finally permitted itself something — not triumph, not relief, but the careful, private satisfaction of a man watching a long game reach an interesting turn. He gave you the smallest possible nod. The same nod as before. It meant something different now.

Priestess Yuna remained in her alcove, her hand still resting on the documents, her eyes already somewhere else — somewhere inward, recording.

Two of the Queen's attendants materialized at your flanks with the practiced unobtrusiveness of people trained to appear only when needed, and gestured, politely and without room for negotiation, toward the eastern corridor.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I return Lord Daven's nod, a faint, conspiratorial smile on my face.* "As you wish, Majesty." *I turn and follow the attendants, my head held high. No point in rushing; the game is just beginning.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The eastern corridor received you without ceremony.

It was a different architecture from the throne room — narrower, older, the stone darker where centuries of torch smoke had worked itself into the grain. The attendants walked ahead and behind with the synchronized quiet of people who had escorted difficult visitors before and expected to do so again. They neither spoke to you nor acknowledged that you might wish to speak. They were furniture that moved.

The east receiving rooms proved to be a single chamber of moderate size, furnished with the particular combination of comfort and austerity that communicated *we respect your rank* and *you are being managed* in the same breath. A fire had been laid and lit — someone had anticipated this, or someone had moved very quickly. A table held water, wine, and nothing that required a knife.

The attendants withdrew. The door did not lock. It did not need to.

You were alone for the first time since you had entered the palace that morning.

The fire cracked once, settling into itself.

Somewhere in the building's interior, beyond walls and corridors and the muffled geography of a working court, the machinery you had set in motion was already turning. Commander Ash was walking quickly toward something — a private council chamber, a trusted messenger, a decision that needed making before the evening bell. Lord Daven was choosing his next words with the care of a man who understood that the wrong ones, said to the wrong person in the next hour, could undo what the right ones had built over years.

Priestess Yuna was sitting in her alcove with her hand on documents that bore a seal that was not Velheim's.

And Queen Isara was somewhere in this palace, thinking.

That last fact was the one that mattered. You had come with terms, and you had not delivered them, and the Queen was thinking — not about the terms, not yet, but about *you*, which was a different and more valuable position than the one you had walked in with.

The fire settled again. The room was warm. The wine on the table was, by its color, considerably better than a waiting room ordinarily warranted.

Someone was sending a message of their own.

The question was whose.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I walk to the table, pour myself a glass of wine, and settle into one of the chairs. I take a slow sip, a small smirk playing on my lips.* "Well, that was certainly a productive morning."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The fire did not answer.

The wine was excellent. That fact alone was worth considering.

You turned the glass in your hand, watching the firelight move through it — that particular deep red that spoke of southern vineyards, of considerable age, of a cellar that did not surrender its better bottles without intention. Someone had authorized this. Someone had done so quickly, which meant someone had been watching the hearing closely enough to know how it would end before it ended, and had made arrangements accordingly.

The door remained closed. The corridor beyond it was quiet in the way that corridors near important rooms are quiet — not empty, but disciplined.

Outside the palace, the city would be going about its afternoon with no knowledge of what the morning had produced. Merchants would be tallying losses that had, in the last hour, acquired political weight they hadn't possessed at dawn. Ships sat in harbors under orders whose origins were now in the custody of a Priestess whose order forgot nothing. Men who had considered the northern situation settled were, in various rooms throughout this building, reconsidering.

You had arrived with terms. You had not delivered them. And yet the ground had shifted considerably in Velheim's favor — which meant the terms, when they finally came, would land on different soil than the soil you'd walked in on.

The productive part, you might have reflected, was that no one in that room had seen all of it coming.

The Queen had seen most of it. That was the complication.

*I am deciding whether that pleases me*, she had said, and she had not yet decided, and that undecided quality was either your greatest asset or your most immediate problem, and the wine, however good, was not going to resolve the question.

A small sound came from the corridor — not a knock, not a footstep, but the particular quality of silence that precedes both. Someone was standing outside the door, and had been for a few moments, and was deciding whether to knock.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I raise my glass slightly toward the door, a silent invitation.* "Come in. Don't be shy."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door opened.

Lord Daven stepped through it with the unhurried ease of a man who had every right to be where he was and intended anyone watching to believe it. He closed the door behind him — not quickly, not furtively, but with the deliberate care of someone who understood that the manner of closing a door communicated as much as the fact of it.

He looked at you. He looked at the wine. Something moved across his face that was not quite amusement and not quite relief but occupied the territory between them.

"The Crestfall Reserve," he said, nodding at the glass in your hand. "She only opens that cellar when she's impressed or when she's furious." He crossed to the table, poured a glass for himself with the familiarity of a man who had been in this room before, and settled into the chair across from yours. "I have not yet determined which this is."

He drank. He set the glass down with precision.

"The documents," he said. His voice had shed the careful gallery performance entirely. What remained was quieter and considerably more direct. "I knew you had something. I did not know what. I did not know you would give them to Yuna." A pause. "That was not the move I anticipated."

He studied you across the table with the expression of a man recalculating an estimate he had believed was accurate and was discovering had been conservative.

"Ash will spend the next two hours deciding whether to explain himself to the Queen or explain himself to whoever gave him those orders first." Daven turned his glass slowly on the table. "Those are not compatible activities. He cannot do both before the evening bell." The faintest suggestion of satisfaction moved beneath the surface of his tone, disciplined but present. "You have given me a window I did not have this morning."

He looked at you directly then — not the measured, gallery-rail look of a man performing alliance for an audience, but the unguarded attention of one who was genuinely, carefully curious.

"I would like to know," he said, "how long you have had those documents. And I would like to know what else you brought with you that you have not yet placed on any table."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I swirl the wine in my glass.* "The Crestfall Reserve, you say? Impressive." I meet his gaze. "As for the documents... let's just say Velheim has eyes and ears in interesting places. And I always come prepared for a long journey, Lord Daven."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The Narrator maintains exceptional consistency throughout. The Queen's cold precision, Commander Ash's military bearing, Lord Daven's careful political maneuvering, and Priestess Yuna's neutral recording all remain perfectly in character from first appearance to final scene. The voice and tone never waver.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are solid but later turns (especially 16-22) show richer detail, more sophisticated political maneuvering, and deeper character work. No repetition, verbosity, or flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Excellent progression from formal diplomatic hearing to political crisis to private alliance discussion. Each turn escalates stakes and reveals new layers. The session moves from protocol to accusation to evidence to suspension to private negotiation - clear narrative arc.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Handles the user's protocol breach (turn 5) expertly with Herald's staff strikes. Adapts smoothly to the document reveal (turn 11) and the user's strategic choices. When user gives incomplete response (turn 7), creates meaningful pause rather than forcing continuation.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Never writes the Ambassador's actions or decisions. Consistently describes reactions TO the Ambassador's choices without controlling them. Respects user agency throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally from morning hearing through to afternoon private meeting. References to 'evening bell' create consistent timeline. No contradictions detected. Physical details like fire settling and wine quality maintain environmental continuity.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is rich but controlled. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without becoming overwrought. 'The silence that followed was a different species' is evocative but not excessive.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Excellent variety in descriptions and character actions. Each character's reactions feel fresh and specific. No repeated phrases or formulaic responses detected.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Masterful showing through physical details: Commander Ash's hand on pommel, Priestess Yuna's folding/unfolding hands, Queen's finger movements. Political tensions conveyed through gesture and positioning rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich layers of political maneuvering, unspoken alliances, and power dynamics. The wine selection, Lord Daven's nods, the Herald's staff strikes all carry meaning beyond surface level.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent control of tension and release. Builds from formal protocol through crisis to private discussion. Uses silence and pauses effectively. Each scene has appropriate rhythm.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional political intrigue roleplay with sophisticated character work and world-building. The Narrator creates a living, breathing court with complex power dynamics and maintains perfect consistency across all characters. The writing is elegant without being purple, and the political maneuvering feels authentic and engaging. This is high-quality collaborative storytelling that respects user agency while creating a rich, immersive experience.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your bow drew a flicker of something across Queen Isara's face — approval, perhaps, or merely the satisfaction of a wager settled. She did not incline her head in return. Sovereigns rarely did.

"Patience," Queen Isara repeated, and the word arrived cold and smooth as river stone. "You presume much, Ambassador, asking for what you have not yet earned. But the court is listening. The northern routes have bled coin from three kingdoms this winter. Speak plainly, and I may find patience within me."

Before the silence had fully settled, Commander Ash's voice cut across the chamber. "Speak plainly — there's a novelty. Velheim's envoys usually arrive with more perfume than substance." His hand had not left the sword pommel. "The last time your kingdom spoke of trade routes, we buried forty men in the passes. Forgive me if I count the exits, Ambassador."

The Herald's staff struck the floor once, sharp. "The Commander speaks out of turn. The court has recognized the Ambassador."

"The court can recognize whomever it pleases," Ash returned, but he stepped back a half pace — a concession to the Herald, or to the Queen behind him.

From the gallery, Lord Daven leaned forward, his tone honeyed and quick. "Perhaps the Commander's memory serves him poorly. Those forty men fell to bandits, not to Velheim's banners — a distinction our friend across the aisle seems eager to blur." He spread his hands toward you, an invitation. "Let the Ambassador finish. Terms first, ghosts later."

In the observer's alcove, Priestess Yuna said nothing. But her pale eyes had lifted from the floor and now rested on you, patient and unreadable, weighing something the others could not see.

Queen Isara lifted two fingers, and the chamber quieted as if a lid had been set upon it. "Enough. The Ambassador holds the floor." Her gaze returned to you, narrow and expectant. "Your terms. I would hear them before the sun troubles itself to move."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, holding it as I speak.* "Indeed, Your Majesty. My terms are simple: open and safe passage for all. No tariffs on grain or lumber." *I pause, glancing briefly at Commander Ash.* "And no more 'accidental' patrols straying into Velheim territory."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara did not blink at the accusation folded into your final clause. She let it hang there a moment, as though tasting it for poison.

"No tariffs," she echoed, and now there was iron beneath the river-stone. "You ask my treasury to open its throat to Velheim's grain and expect the wound to be called generosity. Bold. The lumber I might grant — the forests rot faster than my clerks can tally them. But grain feeds armies, Ambassador, and I do not fatten men who may one day march on me."

Commander Ash made a sound that was not quite a laugh. "'Accidental patrols.'" His fingers tightened visibly on the pommel now. "Our riders keep to our borders. If your maps disagree, perhaps Velheim drew them with wishful ink. Say the word 'accidental' to me again and I'll show you where our territory ends — with my own boots."

"The Commander," the Herald began, staff rising—

"Is finished," Ash said, and let the pommel go. He folded his arms instead. "For now."

Lord Daven seized the gap like a man catching a dropped coin. "Grain for army, Your Majesty — a fine fear, but a hungry border breeds more rebellion than any fed one. Waive the grain tariff for two seasons. Test the man's honesty against the harvest. If Velheim's wagons carry bread and not blades, you've lost a pittance. If they carry blades—" he smiled, thin, toward Ash "—the Commander gets to prove his boots after all. Everyone leaves content."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna finally moved. She rose — not far, only enough to be seen — and her voice came quiet, threading through the chamber's tension without adding to it. "The Ambassador speaks of safe passage *for all*." Her pale eyes had not left you. "The gods count the pilgrims who cross those passes among the merchants. Whatever bargain is struck here, I would know it holds for the barefoot as well as the wealthy." She sat again, having asked nothing and everything.

Queen Isara's fingers drummed once against the throne's arm. "Two seasons," she said slowly, to no one, turning Daven's proposal over. Then her gaze snapped back to you, sharp as a drawn blade. "Answer the Priestess, Ambassador. And answer me — what does Velheim offer in surety, should I gamble my grain on your honesty? Words are cheap in every tongue I know."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The chamber's temperature seemed to drop. The Herald's staff hovered, uncertain whether to strike — you had spoken out of turn now, matched Ash's own breach, and the symmetry was not lost on anyone.

Commander Ash's arms unfolded slowly. "Blockade." He rolled the word around his mouth like a stone he might spit. "A strong word for a quarantine, Ambassador. Your merchants carried fever out of the southern ports — three of my harbor men are in the ground because someone in Velheim thought coin worth more than a manifest. So yes." He took a step forward, boots ringing on the marble. "I held your ships. I'll hold them again. And I did not think to trouble the *court* with the bookkeeping of a plague."

But something had shifted in the room, and Ash felt it as surely as you did — the accusation had landed sideways, and now the burden of explanation sat on his shoulders instead of yours.

Queen Isara's drumming fingers went still. "A quarantine," she said, and the word carried a question she had not been asked before. Her eyes moved — not to you now, but to her Commander. "Six weeks, Ash. You held Velheim ships for six weeks and brought it to my ear as *nothing*." It was not quite a rebuke. It was worse: the cold arithmetic of a sovereign recalculating who had cost her what.

Lord Daven did not bother to hide his delight; he only softened it into concern. "A fever, and no report to the treasury?" He spread his hands wide, appealing to the whole chamber. "Six weeks of stalled trade, Your Majesty — do we know the ledger's shape? Do we know whose coin the Commander's *quarantine* has been quietly costing?" The insinuation curled through the air, elegant and venomous. "One wonders what else keeps to our borders and forgets to send word home."

"Careful, Daven," Ash growled, turning — but he was turning between two threats now, the Queen behind and the courtier beside, and a man cannot guard both flanks at once.

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna's pale gaze had sharpened, no longer patient but attentive, as though she were watching a scale tip. "Fever is the gods' arithmetic, not a Commander's," she murmured. "If the passes carried plague, the Priestess-houses would have been told. We were not." Her eyes lifted to Ash. "That troubles me more than any tariff."

Queen Isara raised her two fingers again — but this time the gesture was slower, and it did not fall upon you. It fell upon her own Commander, freezing him mid-turn. "You will stand," she told him, quiet and absolute, "and you will not speak until I bid you." Then, at last, her gaze returned to you, and there was a new weight in it — not warmth, never that, but the recalculating regard of a player who had just watched an opponent take a piece she had assumed was buried.

"You knew this would land here," she said. It was not a question. "Very well, Ambassador. You have my attention now — and my Commander's silence. Use them before I decide you have used *me*."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I hold the Queen's gaze, a small, almost imperceptible smile playing on my lips.* "Indeed, Your Majesty. Now, regarding that grain..." *I let the implication hang in the air, a silent reminder of the shift in power.* "Velheim would offer a three-year non-aggression pact, guaranteeing safe passage not just for goods, but for your own people through the northern passes."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara's expression did not soften, but something in it recalibrated — the way a merchant's does when the scale finally balances in a direction he had not expected to profit from.

"A non-aggression pact." She let the words settle, weighing them against the grain, against the silence she had imposed on her own Commander, against the ledger Daven had so helpfully torn open. "Three years. Guaranteed passage for my people as well as your wagons." Her fingers resumed their slow drum against the throne's arm — a metronome for whatever calculation ran behind those cold eyes. "You offer surety at last. Not words. A binding."

From his frozen stance, Commander Ash said nothing — the Queen's leash held — but his jaw worked, and the look he fixed upon you promised that this was a debt he intended to collect in some other coin, on some other day.

Lord Daven exhaled, slow and satisfied, and inclined his head toward you with the air of a man watching an investment mature. "A pact honors both crowns, Your Majesty. And it costs the treasury nothing but ink." He did not glance at Ash. He did not need to. "Velheim binds itself to peace, we waive the grain for two seasons and test the harvest, and the northern passes open for pilgrim and merchant alike. The ledger closes clean." A pause, delicate as a knife laid on silk. "Cleaner than certain quarantines, at least."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna rose again — fully, this time — and the icons behind her seemed to lean into the gesture. "The gods witness pacts," she said, and her quiet voice carried the weight of something older than the throne. "If safe passage is sworn for the barefoot as for the wealthy, the Priestess-houses will hold both crowns to it. That is not a small thing, Ambassador. A pact broken before the gods is a debt no treasury can settle." Her pale eyes rested on you — not warm, but no longer merely weighing. Something in them had decided. "I would see this bound properly. In the sight of the icons, with the pilgrim-clause written first, not last."

The Herald's staff lifted, then held — awaiting the word that could only come from one seat in the chamber.

Queen Isara stopped drumming.

"Three years," she said. "The pilgrim-clause written first, as the Priestess asks — I will not have the gods counted as an afterthought in my own hall. Two seasons' grain waived, and if a single wagon carries a blade instead of bread—" now, at last, her gaze flicked to Ash, granting him a fraction of what he wanted "—my Commander will have his passes back, and his boots, and Velheim will have no ground to protest it." Her eyes returned to you, narrow and final. "Those are my terms upon your terms, Ambassador. The Herald will summon the scribes and the Priestess to witness the binding at dusk."

She leaned back against the throne, and for the first time the carved stillness of her seemed a fraction more human — the stillness of someone who had lost a small piece to gain a larger position, and knew it.

"You came asking for patience," she said. "You leave with a treaty. Do not mistake the one for a habit, Ambassador. I extend it once."

The Herald struck the floor. "The court will reconvene at dusk for the binding of the Velheim Accord. The Ambassador is dismissed with the Crown's leave."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I bow again, this time with a hint of genuine respect.* "Your Majesty, the patience you've shown today will be remembered in Velheim. We will see the terms honored." *I turn and begin my walk down the aisle, a faint, satisfied smile on my face.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your bow drew, at last, the smallest inclination of Queen Isara's head — a fraction of a degree, gone almost before it arrived, but real. In a hall where sovereigns did not bend, it was as loud as a trumpet to those who knew how to read her.

"See that it is," she said to your retreating form. "Memory is a currency, Ambassador. I intend to spend yours."

You turned and began the long walk back down the marble aisle, and the room's eyes tracked you as they had on your entrance — but the weight of them had changed. You had come in as a supplicant and left as a signatory.

Lord Daven's voice reached you low as you passed beneath the gallery, pitched for your ear alone. "Elegant," he murmured, not looking at you, a man admiring the ceiling. "You handed her a defeat wrapped in a victory, and she thanked you for the ribbon. Dusk, then. Do try to survive until dusk — the Commander has that look about him." A dry breath that might have been a laugh. "We will speak after."

Commander Ash did not speak — the Queen's leash still held him rooted — but as you drew level with his post, his eyes followed you the whole length of it, flat and cold as harbor ice. Whatever he intended to collect, he had begun keeping the account already. His silence said more than his sword ever had.

In the observer's alcove, Priestess Yuna watched you go, and as you neared the great doors she offered the only benediction she would give — a single slow nod, and words that carried across the emptying chamber without seeming to rise at all. "The icons will remember your smile too, Ambassador. Come to the binding with clean hands. The gods read those before they read the ink."

The Herald struck the floor a final time as you reached the threshold, his voice ringing formal and complete: "The Ambassador of Velheim departs with the Crown's leave. The court stands in recess until dusk."

The great doors parted before you. Behind, you heard Queen Isara's voice resume — quieter now, turning to her Commander with a question about harbor ledgers and three men in the ground, the particular chill of it promising that Ash's afternoon would be far longer and far less pleasant than yours.

Then the doors closed, and the antechamber's cooler air met you — and with it, the first clear breath since the Herald had spoken your name. You had until dusk. And already, footsteps were approaching from the corridor's shadow: a page in Daven's colors, moving fast, a folded note in his hand.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The page in Daven's colors faltered mid-stride, uncertain — you had turned back toward the chamber rather than away from it, and the note in his hand went unclaimed as you moved.

But the great doors had already closed. You stood in the antechamber, and the papers in your grip — the intercepted orders, ink and seal and all — were on the wrong side of a shut door.

For a moment there was only the choice: to knock, to demand re-entry, to spend the Crown's leave you had just been so ceremoniously granted. Protocol had a name for a dismissed envoy who forced his way back into a recessed court, and it was not a flattering one.

Yet the Priestess had not gone far. Through the narrowing gap where a side passage joined the antechamber — the observers' route, the one that did not require the Herald's staff to open — Priestess Yuna emerged, unhurried, her pale robes catching the cooler light. She had left the alcove by her own path, as the neutral so often did, belonging to no faction's exit.

Her eyes found the papers before they found your face.

"You held these through all of that," she said. Not a question. She did not reach for them at once; the gods' servants, you were learning, did not grasp. "You accused the Commander of a blockade and let him call it quarantine — when you could have shown the court his own orders." She tilted her head, and something in the gesture was almost admiration, almost wariness. "You wanted the treaty first. The binding. And now — the proof, into my hands, not the Queen's."

She extended one pale palm, upward, open.

"Give them to me, then. I will read them as the gods read — without a crown's interest and without a Commander's fear." Her fingers did not close until yours released. "But understand what you are doing, Ambassador. Once the Priestess-houses have seen these, we cannot *unsee* them. If they say what your face says they say, then the man the Queen just leashed becomes a man who defied his own crown. And a pact witnessed in the sight of the icons at dusk—" her pale eyes lifted to yours, steady and grave "—cannot be signed beside a lie left in the dark. You will have to bring these into the light too. Before the binding, or as part of it."

She drew the papers close, unopened still, and studied you over their folded edge.

"So. I will read them. And then you will tell me which you want more, Ambassador — the treaty, or the truth. Because I do not think, after dusk, you will be permitted to keep both quietly."

Down the corridor, the page in Daven's colors had stopped entirely, watching the exchange with wide eyes — and then, without delivering his note, he turned and hurried back the way he had come.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, unflinching.* "The truth, Priestess. Always the truth. But this truth needed to be heard by ears that would *listen* first." *I nod towards the corridor where the page disappeared.* "And I suspect Lord Daven will listen very carefully indeed, now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna's fingers finally closed upon the papers — a slow, deliberate motion, as though she were accepting something heavier than parchment. She unfolded them there in the antechamber's cool light, and you watched her pale eyes track down the lines: the seal at the top, the orders beneath it, the signature that no amount of naming it *quarantine* could soften into mercy.

She read once. Then, more slowly, she read again.

"Six weeks," she murmured, and the word carried a different weight in her mouth than it had in Ash's. "Signed before the fever was ever named. Dated—" her thumb pressed the margin "—before your first merchant ship fell ill." She looked up, and the last of her weighing was gone; what remained was quieter and more dangerous. "This is not a quarantine that became a blockade. This is a blockade that borrowed a plague to hide behind. The Commander did not forget to tell his Queen. He chose the day he would let her find out."

She folded the papers closed with the care of someone handling a relic.

"You are right about one thing, Ambassador." A thin, cold thread of amusement moved through her voice — the first she had shown. "Lord Daven will listen. He has been listening all afternoon. He tore open Ash's ledger before the court on a *suspicion*." She glanced toward the empty corridor where the page had fled. "Now he will have the proof carried to him by a servant in his own colors, and he will understand, very quickly, that you gave the Priestess the papers and not the courtier. That was wise. Daven with proof in his hand is a fire that decides for itself what it burns. Daven who knows the *Priestess* holds the proof—" she tucked the papers into the fold of her robe "—is a fire that must ask permission."

She began to move toward the great doors, unhurried still, but there was purpose in it now.

"I will bring these into the light. Not to the Queen in her recess — she is presently teaching her Commander the cost of quiet ledgers, and I will not spoil that lesson before it is finished. But at dusk. When the icons are lit and the scribes have their pens ready and the whole court stands to witness the binding." She paused at the threshold, half-turning, her pale robes still. "The pilgrim-clause first, as I asked. Then the pact. And then, before the wax has cooled on the seal — these. So that no man in that hall can ever say the Velheim Accord was signed beside a hidden crime."

Her eyes held yours a moment longer.

"You will have made two enemies of one Commander by then, Ambassador. The one who wanted your ships. And the one whose Queen now knows exactly what he cost her." A slow nod, the same benediction she had given across the emptying chamber. "Come with clean hands. You have them, for now. See that you keep them until dusk."

Then she was through the side passage and gone, the papers hidden in her robe, and the antechamber was quiet again — save for the distant, unmistakable sound of hurried footsteps somewhere beyond the walls, more than one set now, moving with the particular urgency of a plan being set alight before its time.

You had until dusk. And it was no longer only your own hands you would need to watch.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *A slow smile spreads across my face.* "Precisely, Priestess. Precisely." *I turn and head for the outer doors, a lightness in my step. My hands are clean, and my path, finally, clear.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The outer doors gave way before you, and the palace's grand corridor opened wide — sunlight falling in long amber bars through the high windows, the recess-hour bustle of servants and lesser courtiers moving in the choreographed hush that follows a court's dismissal. You walked into it with the ease of a man who had come to weigh less than he left with, and no one who passed could have said quite why the Ambassador of Velheim looked so unburdened.

But the corridor was not empty of interest for long.

Lord Daven stepped from a pillar's shadow as though he had grown there — perfectly placed, perfectly timed, the page in his colors nowhere in sight now, his errand delivered. Daven fell into step beside you without breaking your stride, hands clasped loosely behind his back, his voice pitched for the space between you and no further.

"So the Priestess holds it," he said, and there was a note in it you had not heard from him before — not quite pique, not quite respect, but the wary recalibration of a man who had reached for a card and found it already dealt elsewhere. "My page came back empty-handed and full of stories. You gave a plague-order to the one person in this palace who cannot be bought, bullied, or bedded into using it early." A soft breath, almost a laugh. "I confess I had a livelier evening planned for that paper. You have made it *ceremonial* instead."

He walked a few paces in silence, the amber light sliding over the fine embroidery of his coat.

"It is the better play," he admitted, and the admission cost him something, and he paid it cleanly. "Ash cannot fight the icons the way he could have fought me. And the Queen—" his eyes flicked sideways to you, sharp beneath the honey "—the Queen will not be able to pretend she was never shown. At dusk she must choose, before the gods and the whole court, whether her Commander's crime dies with the treaty or lives inside it. You have not just made two enemies of Ash, Ambassador. You have made his Queen *responsible* for him. That is a heavier thing to hand a monarch than any grain tariff."

He slowed as the corridor forked, one branch toward the guest wing that was yours, the other deeper into the palace's political marrow that was his.

"A word, then, between allies who understand each other." Daven's smile thinned to something genuine and therefore more dangerous. "Come to the binding early. Not late, not on the Herald's call — early. The hour before dusk is when men decide whether to endure a thing gracefully or to burn the hall down rather than kneel in it. And our Commander—" he inclined his head, once, in the direction of the throne room you had left behind "—does not strike me as a man with a gift for graceful endurance."

He stepped back toward his fork of the corridor, a courtier's bow already half-formed.

"Rest your clean hands, Ambassador. You will want them steady. Dusk comes quickly in this season." And then he was gone, swallowed by the deeper passage, leaving you alone in the amber light with the guest wing ahead — and the whole long, bright, dangerous afternoon still to cross before the icons were lit.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch him go, a genuine smile now.* "Indeed, Lord Daven. Indeed." *I turn towards the guest wing, eager for a moment of quiet to reflect on the morning's progress.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guest wing received you like a held breath — its corridors quieter, its light gentler, the diplomatic quarter of the palace where Velheim's small delegation had been housed with the careful courtesy afforded to those not yet decided upon as friend or foe. Two of your own attendants rose as you entered the suite, their faces a wordless question, and you gave them the small nod that meant *later* and *well enough* both at once. They withdrew.

Then, at last, quiet.

The suite's tall windows framed the palace gardens below, hedges cut into severe geometries, a fountain running its endless silver thread in the middle distance. You stood before the glass and let the morning settle into order behind your eyes — the bow that had bent a Queen a fraction of a degree, the accusation that had turned sideways and struck its own thrower, the papers passed to the one pair of hands in the palace no faction could pry open.

A supplicant had walked in. A signatory would walk to the binding.

But the afternoon stretched long and bright before that, and the quiet was not quite as complete as it seemed. On the writing table by the window sat something that had not been there when you departed for court — a small folded note, unsealed, weighted beneath a sprig of dried northern heather. The heather was Velheim's. The hand that had left it was not one of yours; your attendants would have mentioned it.

Beyond the window, in the geometric gardens, a figure in harbor-grey moved along the far hedge line — not a courtier's silk, not a priestess's pale robe. A soldier's colors. Not Ash himself; the build was wrong, too lean. But someone wearing the Commander's allegiance, walking the guest wing's gardens during the recess, with no obvious errand and a careful attention to the windows of the diplomatic quarter.

The fountain ran on. The dried heather waited beneath its note. And somewhere across the palace, the light had already begun its slow slide toward the hour Daven had warned you of — the one before dusk, when men decided whether to endure gracefully or to burn.

You had won the morning. The afternoon had not yet declared itself.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I pick up the note, ignoring the figure in the garden for now. A sprig of Velheim heather, here? Intriguing.* I unfold the paper, my eyes scanning the contents.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The note was written in a small, disciplined hand — not a courtier's flourish, not a scribe's practiced uniformity, but the cramped efficiency of someone accustomed to writing where space and time were scarce. A field hand. A soldier's hand.

The words were few.

*Ambassador —*

*The orders you carry are not the only ones. There was a second seal. The fever ships were not all fever. Three carried something the harbor men were paid to bury with them. Ash did not sign that page. Someone above him did.*

*The heather is so you know I am Velheim's before I was ever the Crown's. I cannot come to the binding. Ask the Priestess who blessed the harbor dead, and whether she counted three graves or six.*

There was no signature. Only, at the bottom, a single pressed sprig-mark where a second stem of heather had been laid against the ink while it was still wet, leaving a ghost of itself behind.

The fountain ran on beyond the glass.

Below, in the geometric gardens, the figure in harbor-grey had stopped walking. They stood now at the far hedge line, faced toward the diplomatic quarter's windows — toward yours — unmoving, making no signal, offering no greeting. Simply watching. Waiting, perhaps, to see whether the note had been read. Whether it had been believed.

The morning's clean victory had a shape to it, whole and satisfying, and this note put a crack straight through the center of it. *Someone above him did.* If it was true, then the papers now folded into Priestess Yuna's robe told only half a story — and the half they told pointed the whole court's judgment at Commander Ash while the other half stayed buried in three graves that might have been six.

You had until dusk. And the truth you had chosen so cleanly, so cleverly, had just revealed a deeper floor beneath its own foundation.

The figure in grey lifted one hand — not a wave. An open palm, held still. The same gesture Yuna had made when she asked for the papers. *Give, or do not. But decide.*

Then they turned and began, unhurried, to walk toward the garden gate that opened onto the guest wing's lower corridor — coming, it seemed, to find out your answer in person.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I quickly re-read the note, my gaze flicking to the figure in the garden. A second seal. Someone above Ash.* I pocket the note, then step to the window and give the figure a sharp, decisive nod. *I want answers.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Below in the gardens, the figure in harbor-grey caught your nod — and something in their posture eased, the coiled readiness of someone who had gambled on being received. They did not hurry now. They finished their unhurried arc toward the garden gate and vanished beneath the lower corridor's arch.

You had perhaps a minute before they reached your door.

Your attendants stirred at the sound of the outer latch, but you waved them still. Better this stayed quiet. Better the palace not learn that a soldier in the Commander's colors had come to Velheim's rooms during the recess — the wrong eyes could make a story of that as easily as any truth.

The knock came soft. Two raps, a pause, a third — the rhythm of someone who did not want to be heard by the corridor at large.

When the door opened, the figure slipped inside and shut it behind them in one motion. Up close the harbor-grey was worn at the cuffs, salt-stained at the hem — a working uniform, not a parade one. The face beneath was young, weathered early the way harbor faces were, and the eyes moved once around the room, counting exits, before settling on you.

"You read it." Not a question — they had watched you read it. Their voice stayed low, pitched beneath the fountain's murmur that carried faintly through the glass. "Good. Then you know I'm risking the rope to stand here, so I'll be quick." A breath. "My name doesn't matter and you shouldn't want it. What matters is I was harbor watch when the fever ships came in. I helped carry the dead. I counted six shrouds go into the ground and I heard the Priestess-house told three."

They took a half-step closer, and their hand went — not to a weapon — to the inside of their coat, slow, showing you the motion so you would not mistake it.

"Commander Ash signed the quarantine. That page you gave the Priestess — that's real, that's his hand, and it's ugly, but it's the *small* ugly. He held ships to hide a fever he was ashamed of, or afraid of, or ordered to hide. But the second seal—" they drew out a scrap of cloth, folded, and held it toward you without yet releasing it "—the second seal wasn't harbor business. Three of those ships carried something in the hold the fever gave good cover for. Crates. Off-loaded at night, under a seal that wasn't the Commander's and wasn't the Queen's. I only saw it once, by lamplight, before a hand heavier than mine took it away."

They unfolded the cloth. Pressed into it, in dark wax gone brittle, was the ghost of a seal — half-crushed, incomplete, but enough to show it was neither the harbor's anchor nor the Crown's crossed keys. A different sigil. A tower, perhaps, or a spire — the impression too damaged to be certain.

"I don't know whose this is," they admitted, and for the first time something like fear moved under the weathering of their face. "But I know it's above a Commander. And I know that if you walk into that binding at dusk and lay Ash's page on the table like it's the whole crime, then whoever *this* belongs to gets to stand in the same hall, wear the same clean face as you, and watch the wrong man burn for the smaller sin." Their jaw tightened. "I buried those three extra men myself, Ambassador. I'd rather not have done it for nothing."

They pressed the folded cloth into your palm and closed your fingers over it — the second gift of the afternoon, handed to you rather than to the Priestess, and heavier than the first.

"Ask Yuna about the graves," they said, already turning back toward the door. "She blessed the dead. She'll know the true count, even if her house was lied to about it. She can't lie in the icons' sight — that's why you gave her the first page, isn't it? Clever." A grim flicker that was not quite a smile. "Give her this too. But be careful *when*. The moment you reveal a second seal, every powerful person in that room starts wondering which of them you're about to name — and one of them already knows it's theirs."

Their hand was on the latch. Outside, faint, the sound of the recess-hour palace went on — but nearer now, another set of footsteps, measured and unhurried, coming down the guest-wing corridor toward your door.

The soldier froze. Their eyes met yours, wide, and their voice dropped to almost nothing.

"That's not one of mine."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *My eyes dart to the door, then back to the soldier, a silent command for them to hide.* "Under the bed. Now." *I pocket the cloth with the partial seal, then smooth my tunic, trying to appear nonchalant.*

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable’s fingers tightened on the spine of a Herrick that had been perfectly aligned thirty seconds earlier. They slid it out, then back in, as if the gap between poetry and drama were a personal failing.

“‘New

dialogue.content: *I shrug off my jacket, hanging it on the hook by the door.* "Yeah, yeah, I know. Just hoping." I walk over to the fiction section, not really looking for anything. "Slow day, huh?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Wren

dialogue.name: Wren

dialogue.name: Wren
