dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald struck the floor once more. "The Ambassador of Velheim speaks before the Crown. Let the court attend."

Queen Isara did not lean forward. She did not blink. She simply let the silence stretch until it became its own kind of question.

"Terms," she repeated, as though tasting the word for poison. "Velheim has sent terms before. They arrived wrapped in promises and left wrapped in excuses. What makes these different?"

Commander Ash shifted his weight. The leather of his gauntlet creaked against the pommel. "Your Majesty, with respect — the northern routes are a military matter. Velheim's merchants have no authority to negotiate what their soldiers have already contested."

Lord Daven's voice came smooth from the gallery. "And yet, Commander, the Crown's own treaty recognizes Velheim's right to petition. Or have we decided treaties are optional now?"

Ash turned his head just enough to show Daven his profile. "The treaty also requires advance notice of petition. I see no scroll of intent in the Ambassador's hands."

Priestess Yuna spoke for the first time, quietly, from the alcove. "He carries no scroll because he was not given one. I find that interesting."

The Queen's gaze settled back on you. "As do I."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow slightly at the Queen's pointed gaze, then turn my attention to Priestess Yuna.* "Indeed. The lack of a formal scroll was... an oversight. On your part, Your Majesty." *I let that hang in the air for a moment.* "However, my purpose remains clear."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The silence that followed had weight. It pressed on the room the way deep water presses on a diver's ears.

Priestess Yuna inclined her head a fraction — not agreement, not rebuke. Acknowledgment, perhaps, that the Ambassador had chosen to answer honesty with honesty. Then she withdrew into stillness again, and the alcove might as well have been empty.

Commander Ash did not have her restraint. His hand closed around the pommel, and this time it was not a statement. "You will address the Crown with respect, or you will address the floor when my guards remove you from it."

"Herald." Queen Isara's voice cut across him without heat, without volume. It simply was, and so it was obeyed.

The Herald struck the floor. "The Crown speaks. The court attends."

Isara regarded the Ambassador for a long moment. Whatever she had expected, it had not been that. When she spoke again, it was slowly, as if laying each word down like a card face-up.

"An oversight on my part," she said. "You accuse the throne of negligence in front of its own court. Bold. Lord Daven, you vouch for this man. Tell me why I should not take his words as an insult and his person as a hostage."

Daven stepped down from the gallery, one step, no more — the limit of what courtesy permitted him. "Because, Your Majesty, a hostage is worth what his country will pay. An honest envoy is worth considerably more. And if the oversight was ours, then the fault is ours to correct, not his to suffer for."

"Convenient," Ash said flatly. "The Lord of the Western Marches has a border with Velheim. Every concession the Crown makes, his lands grow fatter."

"And every war the Crown starts," Daven replied without turning, "his lands burn first. Which of us has more to lose, Commander?"

Priestess Yuna's voice came again from the alcove, soft and precise. "Both of you are arguing about the Ambassador's credibility. No one has yet asked him what the terms actually are."

Queen Isara's eyes did not leave the Ambassador. "Then let him speak. The court attends. But understand this — you have spent your goodwill, envoy. What you say next will be weighed without it."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash did not answer at once. That was the first thing the court noticed — the Commander, who spoke over lords and interrupted priestesses, took a full three seconds before he spoke to the Ambassador.

"Six weeks," he said at last, "of Velheim hulls running grain into the Sarrow ports and running iron back out. The blockade is lawful. The Crown authorized it. Your merchants knew the terms when they chose to sail." He turned his head, deliberate, and addressed the throne instead. "Your Majesty, the Ambassador has now accused the Crown of negligence *and* accused the Crown's own fleet of piracy in the same breath. I ask the court to note it."

"Herald," said Queen Isara. "Note it."

The Herald struck the floor. "The court notes the Ambassador's words."

Lord Daven had gone very still on the gallery step. His jaw worked once, twice. Whatever he had planned for this hearing, the Ambassador had just walked it off the map. He looked, for one unguarded instant, like a man watching his own house catch fire from a neighbor's chimney.

But he recovered. "Your Majesty," he said, choosing his words with visible care now, "the Commander speaks of lawful blockade. The Ambassador speaks of six weeks without protest lodged. If the routes were lawfully closed, why was Velheim not informed through the proper channel? The treaty requires it. Either the notice was sent and lost — or it was never sent at all."

Ash's gauntlet creaked. "The notice was sent."

"Then where is it?" Daven asked, spreading his hands.

"With the courier who carried it," Ash said. "Who has not returned."

The silence after that was different from the ones before. It had an edge to it now — a door left open, and no one certain who had left it that way.

Priestess Yuna rose from the observer's alcove. She did not step down into the court proper; the alcove's threshold was hers to keep or cross, and she kept it. "Commander," she said. "Name the courier."

Ash's mouth tightened. "That is a military matter."

"It is a matter of a missing man and a missing scroll," Yuna said, "which is precisely the kind of matter the Crown asks the temple to witness. Name him."

Queen Isara had not moved. Her hands rested on the arms of the throne, and her eyes moved from Ash to Yuna to Daven to the Ambassador, and back to Ash. When she spoke, it was to none of them in particular, and so to all of them.

"The court will recess for one hour," she said. "Commander Ash will produce the courier's name and the dispatch record. Lord Daven will produce his correspondence with Velheim. The Ambassador will remain in the palace under the Crown's hospitality" — the word was chosen, and everyone heard it — "until the court reconvenes."

The Herald struck the floor. "The Crown has spoken. The court is at recess."

Queen Isara stood. The room stood with her, a rustle of cloth and scraping chair legs, and she left by the side door without once looking back at the Ambassador she had just placed under guard.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch the Queen leave, my expression unreadable. So, under guard. Just as I suspected.* "Well, Commander," *I say, turning to Ash with a slight smirk,* "it seems our little chat has bought us some time. Pity about your courier, though."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Commander Ash turned to face you fully for the first time, and the court's remaining attendants — clerks, guards, a pair of minor lords who had lingered for the spectacle — found urgent reasons to be elsewhere.

"A pity," he repeated. He said it the way a man tests a blade against his thumb. "You think this bought you time. What it bought you is a room in the east wing with a guard on the door who answers to me." He stepped close enough that the creak of his harness was the only sound left in the hall. "The courier's name is Dallen Vesk. He is a quartermaster's son from the Sarrow coast, he has a wife and two children in the capital, and if he does not walk back through the north gate alive, I will remember who made him a topic of conversation in front of the Crown."

He did not raise his voice. He did not need to. He turned on his heel and left through the officers' door, and the sound of it closing was very final.

Lord Daven waited until the door had settled, then crossed the floor to you with a smile fixed in place and murder in his eyes. He stopped at the exact distance that made the smile plausible to anyone still watching from the far galleries.

"That was a masterwork," he said quietly. "In one breath you accused the throne of negligence and the fleet of piracy, and in the next you turned the Commander's own missing courier into a knife for the Crown to hold at his throat. Do you understand what you have done?" He glanced once at the alcove. "Half this court will spend the recess deciding whether you are a genius or a corpse who has not been informed yet. I would like to know which, before I spend my own name defending the wrong answer."

Behind him, Priestess Yuna had not left the alcove. She stood at its threshold with her hands folded, watching you the way a physician watches a wound that has not yet decided whether to close.

"You are under the Crown's hospitality," she said, and her voice carried just far enough. "That means you are fed, housed, and watched. It does not mean you are alone. The temple keeps a room in the east wing, three doors from the one they will give you." She paused. "If you wish to speak to someone who is not measuring you for a grave or a monument, the door will be unlatched."

She did not wait for an answer. She withdrew into the alcove, and the curtain fell behind her.

The Herald remained at the foot of the dais, staff planted, watching the three of you disperse with the patience of a man who had seen a hundred recesses and expected a hundred more. When the hall had emptied, he spoke to the air rather than to anyone in it.

"One hour," he said. "The court is at recess. The court is always at recess, until it is not."

A palace guard in Crown colors stepped up beside you and gestured toward the east corridor with a hand that was polite and a grip that was not.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Ash leave, then turn to Daven, my smile not quite reaching my eyes.* "I understand perfectly, Lord Daven. It seems I've bought myself an hour of... reflection. And perhaps you, a headache." *I glance towards the alcove Yuna just vacated, then back at Daven.* "As for genius or corpse, I suppose we'll find out, won't we?" I turn to the guard. "Lead the way."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guard led you through corridors that had been built to make petitioners feel small — high vaulted ceilings, portraits of dead kings, torchlight that never quite reached the corners. Your footsteps and his were the only sounds. He did not speak. Guards assigned to escort ambassadors under "hospitality" rarely did.

The east wing was older than the throne room. The stone here was rougher, the corridors narrower, and the doors set closer together than in the public halls. He stopped at the fourth door from the stairwell and opened it with a key he produced from his belt — a key, not a latch, which told you what kind of room this was before you stepped inside.

It was not a cell. It had a window, shuttered, with iron bars set discreetly behind the slats. A writing desk. A bed made up with wool blankets in Crown colors. A washbasin with water already poured, which meant someone had been told to expect you. The guard set a candle on the desk, lit it from the torch in the hall, and withdrew to the corridor.

"I'll be outside," he said, and closed the door.

Through the wall, faintly, you could hear the sound of the guards changing shift at the end of the hall. Beyond that, nothing. The palace had gone quiet the way a held breath is quiet.

You had perhaps forty minutes of the recess left when a folded slip of paper slid under the door. No knock. No footsteps retreating. Just the paper, appearing as though it had always been there.

The hand was Daven's — tight, slanting, written fast:

*Ash has already sent riders north to find Vesk's body before anyone else can. If Vesk is dead, the dispatch record dies with him, and your six weeks become slander. If he is alive, Ash controls what he says. Either way, you lose — unless the courier is found by someone the Crown cannot instruct. I can send men. They will not be Velheim men and they will not be mine. But they will not be free. Tell the guard you wish to see me, and I will come. Burn this.*

Three doors down the corridor, the temple's door was unlatched. Yuna had said so, and Yuna did not say things she did not mean. Through the bars of the shuttered window, the first bell of the hour began to toll — slow, deliberate, counting down the minutes until the court reconvened and the Queen asked her questions again.

The guard outside shifted his weight. His shadow moved across the crack beneath the door.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You did not ask the guard's permission. You simply rose, crossed the small room, and opened the door — and the guard in the corridor straightened, surprised, one hand moving to his belt out of pure reflex before he caught himself.

"The court is at recess," he said. "You are to remain in your quarters."

Three doors down, the temple's door was unlatched, exactly as Yuna had promised it would be. You walked past the guard without a word. He did not stop you — hospitality, not confinement, was the letter of the Queen's order, and he knew it as well as you did — but you heard him fall in behind you at a careful distance, and you knew that whatever happened in the next few minutes would be in Commander Ash's hands by nightfall.

The temple's room was smaller than yours and older, with a low stone shelf that served as an altar and a single lamp burning in a niche. Priestess Yuna sat on a stool beside the shelf with a ledger open on her knees. She did not look up when the door opened. She finished the line she was reading, marked her place with a strip of cloth, and closed the book.

"You came to the unlatched door," she said. "Good. Most men spend their hour deciding whether I meant it."

She looked up then, and saw what was in your hand.

Her expression did not change. It rarely did. But she set the ledger aside on the shelf with great care, as though it had suddenly become fragile, and she stood.

The guard had stopped in the doorway. He could see everything and hear everything, and he was not pretending otherwise.

Yuna crossed to him first. "Wait in the corridor," she said. "Close the door."

"My orders —"

"Come from the Commander, who serves the Crown, which has placed this man under *temple* witness." Her voice did not rise, but something in it made the guard's jaw tighten. "The temple's witness is private. Close the door."

The door closed. Yuna turned back to you and held out her hand, palm up, and said nothing at all.

You gave her the intercepted orders. She took them to the lamp — not to the desk, not to the altar, but to the light, because that was what a person did with a document they intended to read very carefully and very slowly. She read the whole of it twice. Her thumb traced the seal once, the way a blind man reads a face. Then she set the papers flat against the wall and pressed them there, holding them steady with two fingers, and read them a third time without moving her lips.

When she finally spoke, it was not to you. It was to the wall, or to the lamp, or to whatever it was she served.

"The dispatch paper is Crown stock," she said. "The hand is a clerk's hand. The countersignature is a fleet captain's mark — not the Commander's, which is why it was never entered in the record." She turned the pages over and laid them side by side. "And the date is eleven days before the blockade began."

She looked up at last, and her stillness had a new quality to it — the stillness of a scale that has finished tipping.

"That means the notice to Velheim was written *after* the order to close the routes. It was never sent to prevent anything. It was sent to make the closing lawful after the fact. The courier was not carrying a warning. He was carrying a cover story." She let the papers settle onto the altar shelf, and her hand rested over them for a moment as if over a wound. "You have not brought me evidence of a missing courier, Ambassador. You have brought me evidence of a crime."

The first bell had finished tolling. Outside the door, the guard's shadow shifted along the corridor floor, and somewhere beyond him, at the far end of the east wing, a second set of footsteps — heavier, booted, unhurried — began to approach.

Yuna heard them too. She did not look at the door. She looked at you.

"When the court reconvenes, I will be asked what the temple witnessed during the recess," she said quietly. "I can testify to this. I can also choose not to. But if I testify, I do so as the temple, and the temple does not take sides — which means I will tell the Queen the truth about these papers, and the truth about how they came into your hands, and the truth about who walked you to my door and watched you do it." Her eyes flicked toward the corridor, where the footsteps had grown close enough to count. "So before that door opens, Ambassador — tell me plainly. Where did you get these, and who else knows you have them?"

The footsteps stopped. On the other side of the temple's door, someone knocked twice — flat, commanding, the knock of a man who did not expect to be kept waiting.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze evenly.* "These were... acquired through unconventional means. No one else knows I have them, and no one else knows I'm here. This is between us, Priestess."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Priestess Yuna held your gaze for the space of one breath — long enough to weigh the answer, not long enough to believe it.

"No one else knows," she repeated, without inflection. She tilted her head a fraction toward the door, toward the corridor, toward the guard standing ten feet away with his ear to the wood and Commander Ash's orders in his belt. "Then we have already lost the argument, Ambassador. That man heard every word you said to me. He will repeat it before the second bell."

The knock came again. Twice, flat, harder this time — and then a voice through the wood, unhurried and cold.

"Priestess. Open the door."

Yuna did not move. She looked down at the papers on the altar shelf, and something crossed her face that you had not seen there before — not fear, not anger, but the particular stillness of a woman who has decided something and does not intend to explain it. She picked up the dispatch pages, squared them with two fingers, and held them out to you.

"Take them," she said. "The temple witnesses. The temple does not carry. If I keep these, the Crown can call me a conspirator and my testimony becomes worthless to you. If you keep them, they are evidence in your hands, and the temple can speak about them without owning them." Her eyes did not leave yours. "That is the only way this survives the next hour. Decide now."

You had taken them — into a sleeve, into a fold of your coat, wherever a document could vanish — when the knock came a third time, and the door did not wait for permission. It opened.

Commander Ash filled the doorway. He was not wearing his helm, and the effect was worse without it — a face that had been to war and had not been improved by it. Two of his men stood behind him in the corridor, and between them, at a respectful distance, stood the guard who had escorted you from your room. The guard would not meet your eyes.

Ash looked at Yuna. He looked at the empty altar shelf. He looked at you, standing three paces from the priestess in a room you had no business being in, with your hands loose at your sides and your sleeves very slightly too full.

"Priestess," he said. "The Ambassador was ordered to remain in his quarters."

"He was placed under the Crown's hospitality," Yuna said. "Which the Crown defined as fed, housed, and watched. It did not define him as confined. If the Crown meant a cell, the Crown should have said so." She folded her hands. "This is a temple room. You may stand in the doorway, Commander. You may not enter it. Those are the laws your own oath binds you to."

Ash's jaw worked once. He did not cross the threshold. He had not crossed it in twenty years, and both of them knew it.

Instead he spoke past her, to you, and his voice was quiet in a way that made the corridor behind him go still.

"The second bell tolls in ten minutes," he said. "When the court reconvenes, the Queen will ask you what you did during the recess. You will answer her. And when you do, I want you to remember that whatever is in your sleeve right now — the Crown will see it before the day is out. One way, or another." He stepped back. "Escort him to the chamber. Gently. He is, after all, a guest."

The two guards came forward. Yuna watched them take their places at your shoulders, and when they turned you toward the corridor she spoke once more — quietly, so that only you and the walls could hear.

"The door stays unlatched," she said. "It always does."

Down the corridor, faint and unhurried, the second bell began to toll. The Herald's voice echoed from somewhere far off in the throne room, carrying through the stone the way sound carries over water.

"The court reconvenes."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I slide the papers out of my sleeve and hold them up, letting Ash see them for a brief moment before tucking them back away.* "I believe the Queen will find these... illuminating." *I follow the guards, a small smile playing on my lips. Yuna's words echo in my mind.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The guards did not walk you quickly. That was the first thing you noticed — they walked you at the pace of a procession, one on each shoulder, through the east wing and back into the public corridors where the portraits of dead kings watched you pass a second time. Word had gone ahead of you. Clerks stood in doorways with their ledgers half-closed. A pair of minor lords who had lingered at the recess found sudden reason to be in the corridor precisely where you would walk. By the time the throne room doors opened before you, half the court already knew that the Ambassador of Velheim had left his quarters during a Crown recess and been returned under escort.

The Herald struck the floor as you crossed the threshold.

"The court is reconvened. The Ambassador of Velheim is returned to the Crown's attention."

Queen Isara was already seated. She had returned by the side door, as she had left by it, and her hands rested on the arms of the throne in the same position they had held an hour ago, as though she had not moved at all and the hour had simply happened to everyone else.

Commander Ash stood at his post to her right. His hand was on his sword pommel again, but his knuckles were pale now, and he did not look at you. He looked at the Queen, and he spoke before anyone else could.

"Your Majesty," he said. "During the recess, the Ambassador left the quarters assigned to him, entered a temple room uninvited, and was found there in private conference with Priestess Yuna. I have reason to believe he attempted to suborn the temple's witness before this court could hear her testimony. I ask that the Crown take possession of any documents found on his person, and that the temple's account be heard with that in mind."

Lord Daven was on his feet before the last word landed. "The Crown's hospitality was defined as fed, housed, and watched — not confined. The Ambassador broke no order. And as for the temple's witness, Commander, you are asking the Crown to distrust a priestess before she has said a single word. That is not a legal argument. That is a confession that you are afraid of what she will say."

"I am afraid of nothing," Ash said. "I am *reporting*."

"Herald," said the Queen.

The Herald struck the floor. "The Crown speaks. The court attends."

Isara's eyes found you, and there was something in them now that had not been there during the first session — not warmth, precisely, but attention. The hour had changed the shape of the room, and she knew it as well as you did.

"The Commander has made an accusation," she said. "Priestess Yuna, you keep the temple's witness. You were in that room. Before I hear the Ambassador, I will hear you."

The curtain of the alcove drew back. Priestess Yuna stepped to its threshold — not past it, never past it — and folded her hands. She had come straight from the temple room, and the lamp was still in her eyes, and she did not look at Ash, or at Daven, or at you. She looked at the Queen.

"Your Majesty," she said. "During the recess I was shown a document. I read it three times. I will testify to its contents, because the temple's witness does not belong to me to withhold — and I will testify to how it came into my hands, because a witness who edits her own account is no witness at all." She paused, and in the pause the whole court leaned forward without moving. "The document is a dispatch order bearing Crown paper, a clerk's hand, and a fleet captain's countersignature, dated eleven days before the northern blockade began. It directs that notice of closure be sent to Velheim *after* the routes were already closed."

The silence broke into pieces. Someone in the gallery — not Daven — drew breath sharply. A clerk dropped a stylus and did not stoop to pick it up. Commander Ash did not move at all, and that was somehow worse than if he had.

"It is not a warning," Yuna said. "It is a cover story. And I will add, for the court's record, that the Ambassador did not tell me where he obtained it. He refused to. I asked him plainly, and he refused." Her eyes came to you at last, level and unreadable. "Make of that what you will."

Queen Isara let the silence sit. Then she turned her gaze on you, and it had the weight of a door closing.

"The court has heard the temple's witness," she said. "The court now requires the document itself. You will produce it, Ambassador, and it will be examined — by the temple, by the Crown's own clerks, and by the Commander, whose name is not on it but whose fleet's mark is. You will answer, here, before this court, where it came from. And you will do so now, because I will not recess again."

Commander Ash's hand had come off his sword pommel. Both hands hung at his sides now, loose and open, and his eyes were fixed on the Ambassador's sleeve with an intensity that had nothing left of the parade-ground in it.

The Herald raised his staff. "The Ambassador of Velheim is called. The court attends."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, then glance at Ash.* "As Your Majesty wishes." *I pull the papers from my sleeve once more, but before handing them over, I address the court.* "These came from a source who believes in fair play, even when their own Crown does not."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald took the papers from your hand with both of his, the way a man takes something that may be a relic or may be a weapon, and carried them to the dais. He laid them flat on the low table before the throne and stepped back. Queen Isara did not touch them. She gestured, and two clerks emerged from the shadow of the dais with a lamp between them and began to read — one aloud, one following with a finger, the two of them checking each other the way clerks did when they expected to be asked to swear to it later.

The room listened to the whole of it. The clerk's voice was flat and gave nothing away, and that was somehow worse — a room full of courtiers hearing their own Crown's fleet mark read out in a monotone, dated eleven days before the fact.

When he finished, Queen Isara said only, "Commander."

Ash had not moved. His hands were still open at his sides. When he spoke, it was with the control of a man who had decided, somewhere in the last two minutes, that the fight was no longer about denying the document.

"The paper is Crown stock," he said. "That proves nothing. Any clerk in the capital can steal a ream. The countersignature is a captain's — Captain Rennick, I would guess, whose ship was on the northern station at that date, and who is dead these two months of fever at Sarrow." He looked at you directly for the first time since the recess. "Convenient, Ambassador. A dead man's mark on a living man's accusation. You have produced a document that could have been written by anyone, signed by a man who cannot deny it, and delivered by a source you will not name. I have seen forgeries built with more care and less luck."

Lord Daven had gone very still. He was watching the papers on the dais, not Ash, and his face had the particular blankness of a man doing arithmetic he did not like. Whatever he had offered you in the note under the door — men, riders, a courier found by hands the Crown could not instruct — you had not taken it. You had gone three doors down instead, and shown the papers to the temple, and now the temple had read them into the record and named every hole in them in the same breath.

"Your Majesty," Daven said at last, carefully, "the Commander's objection is well-taken in part. A document without provenance is half a document. But the Commander's objection also proves too much. If the paper is Crown stock and the hand is a clerk's hand, then the Crown has the means to trace it — every ream is inventoried, every clerk is on the rolls, every countersignature is logged in the fleet registry at Sarrow. The court does not need the Ambassador's source. The court needs the *ledger*." He spread his hands. "Call for the dispatch records of the northern station, sealed or unsealed, and we will know in an afternoon whether this is a forgery or a confession."

Ash turned his head slowly. "The dispatch records of the northern station are military records."

"And the Crown is the military's sovereign," Daven said. "Or has that changed since I last sat in this room?"

Priestess Yuna spoke from her threshold, quietly, and the room turned to her. "There is one more thing the court should weigh, Your Majesty. The Ambassador refused to name his source when I asked him, and he refuses again now. That is his right. But a witness who will not name a source is a witness the court cannot test — and this court has already watched a courier vanish carrying a document nobody will claim." She paused. "I do not say the Ambassador lies. I say the Crown should not decide this on his word alone, any more than it should decide it on the Commander's."

Queen Isara let the silence settle the way she always did — until it was heavy enough that whatever came next would have to be true to carry it. Then she spoke to you.

"You have heard the court," she said. "The Commander says the document is a forgery. The Lord of the Western Marches says the ledgers will settle it. The temple says your source must be named before your evidence can be weighed. Three roads, Ambassador, and all three of them run through the same door — the door you will not open." She leaned forward by exactly the width of one finger. "So I will ask you once. Not for your source's name. I will ask you what your source *is* — a person, a faction, a foreign power, or a lie. Answer that, and this court can proceed. Refuse, and I will order the dispatch ledgers sealed to this hearing, your document struck from the record as unproven, and you remanded to the east wing until Velheim sends someone with a scroll and a signature."

Commander Ash watched you. Lord Daven watched you. Priestess Yuna watched you, and her face gave away nothing at all. And on the dais, the two clerks stood with their hands folded over the papers, waiting for the Crown's word to carry them away or call for the ledger that would make them real.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's intense gaze, then let my eyes drift to Daven, then Ash, before returning to her. A small, knowing smile touches my lips.* "My source, Your Majesty, is a person. A loyal subject of Velheim, who believes in justice, even when it is inconvenient."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara did not blink. She had been given a person and a loyalty and a virtue, which was to say she had been given nothing, and both of them knew it. She sat back — one finger's width, returning to the throne's exact posture — and let the answer stand in the room long enough for everyone to measure it.

"A loyal subject of Velheim," she repeated. "Who believes in justice. Commander Ash, how many loyal subjects of Velheim do you suppose believe in justice?"

"All of them, Your Majesty," Ash said. "When it is convenient."

"Then the Ambassador has told us his source is Velheim itself, and his evidence is therefore an accusation by one crown against another, delivered by a man who will not sign it." She turned to the clerks. "Unseal the northern dispatch ledgers. Not the abstracts — the ledgers. Every ream issued to the northern station for the last two years, every clerk who drew one, and every countersignature logged by Captain Rennick's hand before he died. The court will not weigh this document until it has weighed the paper it was written on."

The clerks bowed and left by the side door at a pace that stopped just short of running. The Herald struck the floor. "The Crown has ordered the northern ledgers produced. The court stands at recess until they arrive."

He had not said *one hour* this time. He had said *until they arrive*, which was a different kind of clock, and everyone in the room understood the difference. The galleries did not empty. No one stood. This was not a recess for refreshment and quiet negotiation; it was a recess the way a drawn blade is a pause.

Lord Daven crossed to you before the Queen had finished rising. He did it smoothly, as though he had intended to inspect the tapestries and you merely happened to be standing beneath them, but his voice when it came was pitched for your ear alone.

"You did not take my men," he said. "You went to the temple instead. I am not certain yet whether that was courage or arithmetic, and I would very much like to be certain before the ledgers arrive." He glanced once at the dais, where the Herald stood guard over two documents that had just been promoted from evidence to liability. "If the ledgers are clean — if every ream is accounted for and no clerk drew Crown stock on that date — then the Commander is right and you are finished. If they are *not* clean, then the Crown has just ordered its own dispatch office to indict itself in front of a foreign envoy, and the Commander will spend the afternoon deciding whose fault that is. Which of those two outcomes do you expect, Ambassador? Because I am standing beside you either way, and I would like to know how loudly to do it."

Behind him, Priestess Yuna had not returned to her alcove. She stood at its threshold with her hands folded, watching the clerks' door through which the ledgers would come, and her expression had settled into something the court rarely saw on her — patience that had a direction, like water finding a crack. Commander Ash stood at his post to the right of the throne, and he had not moved since the Queen's order, and his hand had not returned to his sword. He was staring at the dais table where the dispatch pages lay under the Herald's watch, and his mouth was a flat line, and whatever he was thinking, he was not thinking it at the Ambassador.

The far doors opened. A clerk came back at a half-run, and behind him two porters carried between them a wooden chest bound in iron, the kind of chest that held a ledger's worth of a station's entire paper history, and it hit the floor between the dais and the court with a sound that made the gallery sit up.

The Herald struck the floor. "The northern dispatch ledgers are produced. The court attends."

Queen Isara had not sat back down. She stood above the chest with one hand resting on the arm of the throne, and she looked at the Ambassador the way she had looked at him at the very start of the day — except that at the start of the day, there had been nothing at stake but protocol.

"The chest is opened in open court," she said. "The Ambassador will observe. The Commander will observe. The temple will observe. Whatever the ledgers say, the whole court will hear it at once, and no one will have the chance to be surprised by it privately." She gestured to the clerks. "Open it."

The two clerks knelt on either side of the chest. The iron bands came loose. The lid lifted, and the smell of old paper and lamp oil rose up out of it, and every eye in the throne room leaned toward the ledgers inside as though the answer to the whole afternoon were printed on the first page.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I give Daven a tight smile.* "I expect the truth, Lord Daven. And the truth, like justice, is rarely convenient." *I turn my gaze to the chest, a flicker of anticipation in my eyes.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The first clerk lifted the top ledger out of the chest and set it on the dais table, and the second clerk opened it to the front, where the station's index was bound. They worked without ceremony, the way men worked when the Crown was watching and the room was silent. Every page turned with a sound like a held breath released.

"The northern station," the first clerk read, "drew Crown stock against the following reams and dates." He began at the top of the index and moved down it, and the room listened to a year and a half of paper go by — names of clerks, dates, reams issued for patrol reports, supply manifests, weather logs, the ordinary gray business of a fleet station on the far coast.

Then he reached the date on the dispatch.

He stopped. He looked at the page. He looked at his fellow clerk, who looked back. Then he looked at the Queen, and his voice, when it came again, had changed.

"Your Majesty. The entry for the date in question has been excised."

The gallery made a sound like a wave hitting a breakwater. Queen Isara did not move. "Show the court."

The clerk turned the ledger around and held it up, and the two clerks carried it to the foot of the dais so the nearest lords could see. There was a gap in the index — a neat rectangle of missing paper, cut close to the binding with a blade, the stub of the page still furred along the inner edge. The entry before it was dated thirteen days before the blockade. The entry after it was dated nine days after. The date itself was gone.

Commander Ash spoke before anyone else could, and his voice had the flatness of a man who had already seen this coming and had decided to say it first rather than be accused of it later.

"There," he said. "The court has its answer. The page is gone. Anyone could have removed it. Anyone could have drawn the ream and cut the record. The Ambassador's document is unproven, exactly as I said, and the ledger proves only that someone wanted the record hidden — which proves nothing about who."

Lord Daven's face had gone the color of old wax. He was staring at the excised page, and whatever arithmetic he had been doing all afternoon had just produced a number he did not want to read aloud. "Your Majesty," he said, and his voice came out thinner than he intended, "a cut page is not an absence of evidence. It is evidence of tampering. Someone removed this entry *after* the fact. The question is not whether the Ambassador's document is real — the question is who in the Crown's own service cut this page to hide it."

"And the answer to that question," Ash said, "is not the Ambassador's to demand."

The second clerk, who had been reading the ledger's duplicate log while the first clerk held the index open, cleared his throat — quietly, the way a man clears his throat when he is about to say something that will change the shape of the room. He had been forgotten in the argument, and now every eye in the throne room turned to him at once.

"Your Majesty," he said. "The index is cut. But the station kept a duplicate abstract, bound at the back of the same volume, for the fleet registry at Sarrow." He turned the ledger to its rear pages and laid his finger on a line. "The abstract is intact. It records the ream drawn on the missing date. It records the clerk who drew it. And it records the countersignature."

Queen Isara said, "Read it."

The clerk read it. The name of the clerk was one no one in the court recognized — a junior station hand, long since transferred. But the countersignature was not a name. It was a mark, and the clerk read it the way clerks read marks, by the registry number, and the registry number was logged in the fleet rolls, and the fleet rolls named the man who held that number on that date.

The name was Captain Rennick's. The dead man. Exactly as Commander Ash had predicted.

For one heartbeat the room belonged to Ash again. He drew breath to speak.

Then the second clerk went on, because he had not finished, and because a clerk who stops reading in the middle of an entry is a clerk who has been bribed.

"Your Majesty," he said, "the abstract also carries a second countersignature. A countersignature above the captain's — the mark of the officer who authorized the draw." He looked up, and his eyes went not to the Queen, not to the Commander, but to the paper in his own hands, as though he did not trust them to look anywhere else. "The mark is the fleet command seal of the northern station."

The northern station's command seal belonged to one man. It had belonged to one man for eleven years. And that man was standing to the right of the throne with both hands at his sides and a face that had gone entirely still.

Commander Ash did not deny it. He did not reach for his sword. He looked at the clerk, and then at the ledger, and then — slowly, deliberately — at the Ambassador, and when he spoke, his voice was quiet enough that only the front of the room heard him.

"The seal is a stamp," he said. "A stamp sits in a drawer. A drawer has a key. A key is carried by a duty officer, and a duty officer changes every four hours." He turned to the throne. "Your Majesty, I did not sign that order. I did not see that order. If my seal was used, it was used by someone in my command — and I will find who, and I will bring him to this court myself, because I am the only man in this room who can."

Queen Isara looked at him for a long moment. Then she looked at the Ambassador, and her face gave away nothing at all — not gratitude, not suspicion, not the least acknowledgment that the afternoon had turned. When she spoke, it was to the Herald.

"The court has heard the ledgers," she said. "The dispatch document is entered into the record as corroborated. The northern station's command is placed under Crown inquiry as of this hour. Commander Ash will surrender his seal to the Crown's clerks and will answer the inquiry in person." She paused. "And the Ambassador of Velheim will remain in the palace, under the Crown's hospitality, until Velheim sends a scroll and a signature — because a corroborated document is still a document without a treaty behind it, and I do not negotiate with evidence. I negotiate with envoys."

The Herald struck the floor. "The Crown has spoken. The court stands adjourned."

The room came apart into motion — clerks closing the chest, lords rising, the gallery emptying in a murmur that would be all over the capital by supper. Daven did not move from your side. He was looking at Ash, and there was something in his expression that had not been there this morning: not satisfaction, not triumph, but the careful stillness of a man who has just watched the board change under his feet.

"Congratulations, Ambassador," he said quietly. "You have broken the Commander in open court and made the Crown investigate itself in front of a foreign witness. I hope you understand that this is not a victory. This is the moment the Crown stops deciding whether you are a genius or a corpse, and starts deciding which of the two it can *use*."

Across the emptying hall, Priestess Yuna had returned to her alcove threshold and stood watching you, her hands folded, her face unreadable. And at the foot of the dais, Commander Ash had not left his post. He was handing his seal to the Crown's clerk with the slow care of a man surrendering something he intended to take back, and his eyes were on you the whole time.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Ash. Our eyes meet, and I give him a slow, deliberate nod of acknowledgment, perhaps even respect.* "Lord Daven, it seems the truth found its way out, regardless. As for being used... I prefer to think of it as leverage." *I offer him a genuine smile for the first time.* "Perhaps now we can truly negotiate."

Each character's voice remains distinct - Queen Isara's measured authority, Ash's military directness, Daven's political calculation, Yuna's quiet precision. The formal court atmosphere and political tension never wavers from turn 1 to 23.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains strong throughout. Early turns establish rich atmosphere and character dynamics. Later turns maintain this quality while building tension. No significant verbosity increase or repetitive descriptions. The final turns actually intensify rather than flatten.

Each turn escalates stakes: protocol violations → accusations → evidence → investigation → consequences. The story builds to a satisfying climax with the ledger revelation and doesn't stagnate.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Writing is rich but controlled. Descriptions serve atmosphere and character without becoming overwrought. Phrases like 'silence that had weight' and 'the way deep water presses on a diver's ears' are evocative but not excessive.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Character emotions and motivations revealed through actions, dialogue, and physical details. Ash's 'knuckles were pale' and Daven's 'face had gone the color of old wax' show tension without stating it.

The AI maintains the formal court setting while building genuine tension and delivering a compelling revelation. The writing quality actually improves as stakes escalate, showing good session-level craft.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A heavy silence settled over the polished stone beneath your boots. 

Queen Isara did not blink. Her ringed fingers rested flat against the carved armrests of the throne, unyielding as granite. "Patience is a commodity, Ambassador," she said, her voice carrying across the vast chamber without the slightest strain. "One that Velheim has spent rather freely of late."

Commander Ash did not wait for formal leave to speak. He shifted his weight, his leather scabbard groaning under the sudden motion. "Patience won't feed the garrisons along the Pass, Your Majesty," Ash barked, his scowl locked firmly upon you. "Every caravan Velheim delays costs our soldiers rations. If they come seeking concessions on tariffs after choking our supply lines, they should be escorted to the border, not the dais."

"A soldier sees a battlefield in every ledger, Commander," Lord Daven interjected smoothly from the gallery rail. He leaned forward, smiling with a polished poise that betrayed his sharp ambition. "Trade requires recalibration, not saber-rattling. If Velheim has prepared terms, it implies they wish to balance the scales, not tip them. We would be wise to listen before we reach for our hilts."

In the shadow of the alcove, Priestess Yuna tilted her head slightly. Her prayer beads clicked like dry bones as she turned them between her fingers, her serene gaze fixed upon the floor between you and the throne. "The gods abhor a false weight," she murmured softly, her tone entirely devoid of warmth or malice. "Let the word be weighed alongside the deed. Truth bears scrutiny; falsehood invites ruin."

The Herald struck the floor with the butt of his staff, the sharp crack cutting through the court's sudden tension. "Decorum before the throne," he intoned flatly, his eyes fixed straight ahead.

Queen Isara raised a single hand, and the hall fell utterly mute. Her gaze remained pinned upon you, measured and chillingly deliberate. 

"Present your terms, Ambassador," the Queen commanded. "Let us see what Velheim values more: our patience, or our peace."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, unflinching.* "Velheim values both, Your Majesty. And I assure you, these terms will reflect that." *I produce a rolled parchment from my tunic, holding it out for a nearby attendant to take to the Queen.* "The document outlines our proposal for a new trade agreement."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A liveried page stepped forward with measured, hurried strides, took the scroll from your outstretched fingers with a low bow, and carried it up the dais. 

Commander Ash’s eyes tracked the parchment as though it were a drawn dagger. "Ink and promises," Ash muttered, the leather of his gauntlet creaking as his grip tightened on his pommel. "Easily drafted in the warmth of a palace, and even more easily broken once the snows choke the high passes. If there is no mention of compensating the border garrisons, Your Majesty, this parchment isn't worth the sheep it was scraped from."

"Then let us see what it is worth before we consign it to the hearth, Commander," Lord Daven said smoothly, leaning his forearms against the velvet cushion of the gallery railing. A faint, calculating smile touched the corner of his lips as he glanced toward you, then back to the throne. "A kingdom that rejects a treaty before breaking the seal advertises its fear, not its strength. Surely the crown can spare three minutes to weigh an advantage."

"Parchment burns as swiftly as autumn wheat," Priestess Yuna murmured from the shadows of her alcove. Her silver prayer beads clicked together in an unbroken, rhythmic cadence. "Yet words, once uttered before witnesses and the heavens, carve grooves that cannot be smoothed away. Take care what you bind yourself to, Daughter of the Sun."

The Herald stepped forward half a pace, his voice cutting clean and sharp through the murmurs rising in the lower gallery. "The Queen considers the petition of Velheim. Silence in the presence."

Queen Isara took the scroll from the kneeling page. Her thumb cracked the wax seal bearing the sigil of your homeland with a decisive snap that echoed against the marble walls. She unfurled the vellum, her pale eyes scanning the dense lines of script. Not a single muscle in her face shifted; neither outrage nor satisfaction broke the porcelain stillness of her expression. 

After a long, suffocating silence, the Queen allowed the parchment to curl partially shut in her lap. Her gaze lifted from the text and locked onto you, piercing and devoid of warmth.

"A reduction in the salt levy," Isara said, each syllable measured and chillingly deliberate. "In exchange for shared patrol rights along the Whispering Crag. A bold stroke, Ambassador. Or a remarkably brazen one." She leaned back against the carved stone of her throne. "Velheim asks us to welcome your soldiers onto our soil to protect the very merchants your crown has been stalling for three months. Tell me—should I call that an alliance, or an occupation under contract?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A sharp intake of breath echoed through the gallery as you bypassed the throne to level your challenge directly at the realm's military head. 

The Herald’s staff struck the stone floor with a thunderous *crack*, the sound reverberating off the high vaulted ceiling. "Insolence!" the Herald shouted, his face reddening above his high collar. "Protocol dictates the envoy addresses the Crown, and the Crown alone! Hold your tongue, Ambassador!"

Commander Ash took a fierce step forward, his gauntleted hand clattering against the basket hilt of his broadsword. His weathered face darkened with crimson fury. "You dare speak of blockades in this hall, dog?" Ash snarled, his voice rasping with barely suppressed violence. "Those were naval interdictions against unflagged smuggler craft crawling out of your estuaries! If your merchants choke on our patrols, it is because your guilds refuse inspection and smuggle black-market iron across the sound. Call it what it is—lawful enforcement of sovereign waters!"

"Enforcement that conveniently slipped past the maritime ledgers presented to the High Council," Lord Daven observed, his voice cutting across Ash’s fury like a silk ribbon. Daven leaned forward over the gallery railing, resting his chin on a ringed hand, his eyes gleaming with calculating delight. "Fascinating, Commander. A six-week interdiction of foreign vessels is an act of war, not a customs check. One would think such an enterprise required the seal of the Crown—unless, of course, the fleet now answers to the garrison rather than the throne."

"Mind your tongue, Daven!" Ash snapped, whirling partially toward the gallery. "You know nothing of the northern waters or the filth Velheim floats past our watchtowers!"

From the shadow of her alcove, Priestess Yuna did not flinch, though the steady click of her beads ceased. Her calm, fathomless eyes drifted from Ash toward you. "The water keeps no secrets from the deep," she spoke softly, her serene voice somehow carrying beneath the rising anger in the chamber. "A net cast in shadows still catches the light when pulled to the surface. Concealment is merely debt owed to the truth, and the gods always collect."

"Enough."

Queen Isara’s voice did not rise in volume, yet the single word silenced the room instantly. The courtiers in the galleries held their breath. 

The Queen did not look at Ash. Her gaze remained pinned entirely upon you, cold, unblinking, and dangerously still. The parchment rested forgotten beneath her fingers. 

"You forget yourself, Ambassador," Isara said, her tone smooth as polished ice. "You stand in my hall. You speak under my sufferance. Bypassing the dais to interrogate my councilors is an affront that has seen envoys stripped of their credentials and cast beyond the city gates before nightfall." 

A terrible pause hung in the air. Then, the Queen’s eyes slowly cut toward Commander Ash. 

"However," Isara continued, her voice dropping into a register that made the seasoned soldier stiffen to absolute stillness, "my commander’s memory appears to require refreshing as urgently as your manners do. An undeclared blockade is an expensive endeavor to hide from one's sovereign." 

Her gaze shifted back to you, piercing and analytical. "You have played a dangerous card to force my hand, Velheim. Now make your point. If my ships sit in your waters, what is it your prince truly wants? Redress... or an excuse?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "My Prince wants peace, Your Majesty." *I keep my voice level, despite the Queen's veiled threat.* "But not at the cost of our sovereignty. These terms address both."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The quiet that followed your words was thin and brittle, stretched tight across the breadth of the throne room. You had held your ground before a sovereign accustomed to seeing knees buckle at her displeasure. 

Commander Ash’s knuckles went white against the brass of his scabbard, his jaw clenched so hard a muscle twitched beneath his scar. "Sovereignty," Ash spat under his breath, though the word carried clearly enough to draw wary glances from the surrounding guards. "They call a naval cordon an attack on their sovereignty, yet they demand our blood and steel to patrol the Whispering Crag. If we yield the high ridges to Velheim's spears under the guise of an 'accord,' we hand them the keys to our valley gates."

"Only if one presumes our garrisons are incapable of holding their own ground alongside an ally, Commander," Lord Daven countered smoothly. He adjusted the fur trim of his mantle, looking down from the gallery with an air of amused condescension. "The treasury bleeds every day the northern pass remains contested, and your ships do not sail on good intentions alone. Velheim offers an end to the bleeding. If sovereignty can be preserved through coin and shared watchtowers rather than pyres, only a fool insists on the fire."

"Fire purifies what words corrupt," Priestess Yuna said, her soft voice sliding between their arguments like oil over troubled water. She let the silver beads slip through her pale fingers, one by one. Her hooded gaze remained fixed on you, cold and searching. "A boundary drawn in blood endures only until the rain falls; a boundary drawn by treaty endures only until ambition hungers. Peace is not an absence of war, Ambassador. It is a debt paid daily. The question is whose sons will pay the interest."

The Herald raised his staff, though he did not strike the floor, his posture rigid as a spear. "The court will hear the judgment of the Crown," he proclaimed, his clear, ritual baritone cutting off Ash’s muttered retort before it could ignite.

Queen Isara leaned forward, the carved stone lions of her throne framing her silhouette. Her fingers drummed a slow, deliberate cadence against the armrest as her eyes bored into yours.

"Sovereignty is a luxury bought with leverage, Ambassador," Isara said, her voice dropping into a lethal, measured calm. "You come to my court, brandish the indiscretions of my admiralty, and ask me to split the watch over our shared border. You claim your prince desires peace, yet you corner my councilors in the presence of my peers."

She paused, lifting the parchment slightly before letting it fall back onto her knee. 

"Velheim will have its trade routes cleared," the Queen decreed, each word falling like an iron weight. "The blockade will lift by the turn of the moon. But I will not cede the Whispering Crag to foreign steel. If you wish to protect your merchants, your prince will pay the garrison tax to fund *my* patrols, or your caravans will take the southern sea route through the storms."

Isara tilted her head slightly, the faint shadow of a challenge in her gaze. "Tell me, Velheim. Does your prince's love for peace extend to his coffers, or does his desire for sovereignty only apply when the coin flows toward his treasury?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I allow a small, almost imperceptible smile to play on my lips.* "Your Majesty, my Prince understands that peace has a price. But he also understands that a shared burden strengthens alliances, rather than weakening them."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your faint smile did not go unnoticed; it rippled through the gallery like a pebble cast into frozen water.

Commander Ash let out a harsh, guttural bark of laughter that carried no humor whatsoever. "A shared burden?" Ash took half a step toward the dais, gesturing aggressively toward you with a gloved hand. "He calls it a shared burden, Your Majesty! In plain tongue, he means our men bleed holding the ramparts while Velheim's inspectors count the wagons and second-guess our captains. An alliance is forged by blood and loyalty, not by foreign accountants clutching ledgers in our frontier outposts!"

"An alliance without ledgers, Commander, is merely a very expensive funeral waiting to happen," Lord Daven remarked smoothly from above. He folded his hands atop the gallery rail, casting an amused glance down at Ash before fixing his gaze respectfully upon the throne. "The Ambassador makes a fair point, Your Majesty. If Velheim pays the full garrison tax without shared oversight, they are not our allies—they are our tributaries. And tributaries inevitably rebel. A joint logistics council on the Crag would bind Velheim's coin to our defenses without yielding a single crenel to their infantry."

In her shadowed alcove, Priestess Yuna shifted, the pale silk of her vestments whispering against stone. Her prayer beads slipped between her fingertips with a slow, dry rasp. "Two oxen hitched to an unequal yoke break the furrow," Yuna intoned, her vacant gaze drifting toward the vaulted rafters. "If one pulls and the other merely watches, the cart overturns. Burdens shared in deceit yield harvest in ashes. Choose carefully which yoke you fashion beneath the eyes of the righteous."

The court broke into a subdued, anxious rustle until the Herald struck the floor once more. *Crack.* The sound rang like an iron bell. "Silence for the Crown!" the Herald bellowed, his voice stiff with rehearsed indignation as he surveyed the whispering nobles.

Queen Isara remained motionless, but her eyes narrowed just enough to betray the sharp machinery turning behind them. She did not raise her voice; she did not need to.

"A shared burden implies shared risk, Ambassador," Isara said, her tone smooth and cutting as a glass blade. "Yet Velheim risks only parchment and surplus coin, while my soldiers stake their lives against the northern hill tribes. If your prince wishes to call this an alliance of equals, he must offer collateral equal to our blood."

The Queen leaned forward, resting her chin upon a curled hand, pinning you beneath a predatory stare.

"The blockade ends as promised," she declared, her decree echoing off the high stone walls. "The Whispering Crag will see joint patrols, but under a garrison commander of *my* choosing. And until the first year's treaty concludes without incident, Velheim will surrender its maritime tariffs on our southern grain fleet."

Isara let the words settle over the court like an executioner’s shadow.

"A shared burden, Ambassador," the Queen murmured, a ghost of a challenge in her pale eyes. "Tell me: does your prince possess the stomach for that kind of equality?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The sudden departure from the dais sent an audible tremor of shock through the court. You turned your back on the throne, crossed the distance toward the shadowed alcove, and held the folded missive out to the neutral custody of the cloth.

The Herald took two frantic strides forward, his staff slamming against the flagstones in rapid, panicked succession. "Halt! Stand down, envoy!" the Herald bellowed, his voice cracking with outrage. "The sacred alcove is inviolable! To present unsanctioned script to the clergy before the Crown inspects it is high sacrilege!"

Commander Ash’s steel cleared its scabbard by three ringing inches. "Guards! Seize that cur!" Ash roared, his face draining of color before flushing into a murderous purple. "Those are military ciphers! He brandishes stolen intelligence in the sovereign's presence—cut him down where he stands!"

"Stay your blade, Ash, unless you wish to join him on the executioner’s block," Lord Daven’s voice lashed out from the gallery, sharp and commanding as a whip. Daven leaned far over the railing, his eyes gleaming with triumphant malice as he watched the commander unravel. "A soldier who screams treason at the sight of a letter only proves he fears what was written. Let the Temple read it. Or do you fear the judgment of the gods even more than the Queen's justice?"

Priestess Yuna did not flinch, nor did she recoil from your outstretched hand. Her silver beads fell silent, draped motionless across her knuckles as she reached out with pale, steady fingers and accepted the parchment. 

The chamber plunged into a suffocating, breathless hush. 

Yuna broke the wax without hesitation. Her dark, fathomless eyes tracked the lines of handwriting, absorbing the ink with an unnerving, deliberate slowness. For several agonizing seconds, only the rustle of the vellum broke the silence. 

"The wax bears the seal of the Admiralty of the Northern Reach," Yuna said softly, her calm, melodic voice carrying effortlessly into every corner of the vast hall. "The script commands the immediate seizure of all Velheim merchantmen bearing timber and ore, under pain of insubordination, dated three weeks prior to the Crown's formal tariff dispute." She lifted her serene gaze, not toward you, but straight into Commander Ash’s stricken face. "A lie spoken in daylight casts a long shadow. A lie written in secret rots the marrow of the state."

"They are forgeries!" Ash snarled desperately, though his hand trembled violently against the grip of his sword. He turned toward the dais, dropping to one knee with a heavy clatter of armor. "Your Majesty—it is Velheim trickery, designed to fracture the council on the eve of negotiations!"

"Silence, Ash."

Queen Isara did not shout. The command was spoken with the lethal, crystalline calm of a winter frost, yet it instantly strangled every breath in the room. 

The Queen did not glance at her kneeling commander. Her pale eyes drifted from the priestess back to you, cold, calculating, and dangerously sharp. Every trace of the court's earlier mockery had evaporated, replaced by the lethal stillness of an apex predator recalculating its hunt.

"The Temple has borne witness," Isara said, each word falling like an executioner's stone upon the silence. "The neutral word is given."

She rose from the throne. Tall, regal, and terrifyingly composed, the Queen stood at the edge of the dais, looking down from her height upon the shattered equilibrium of her court.

"It seems the Whispering Crag is not the only ground requiring inspection, Ambassador," Isara murmured, her gaze locking onto yours with an intensity that promised blood. "You brought an accusation to my feet, and now you have laid out the corpse. Speak plainly, Velheim. Do you ask for Ash’s head as the price of your treaty... or do you intend to use this leverage to demand even more?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "Your Majesty, I ask only for a fair and equitable treaty." *I meet her gaze, unflinching.* "And for all parties to be held accountable for their actions."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The restraint in your voice rang louder than a demand for blood would have. By refusing to call openly for execution, you left the blade hanging squarely in the Queen's own hands—and stripped Commander Ash of any martyr’s mantle he might have claimed.

Commander Ash remained on one knee before the dais, his knuckles white against the stones. His breath came in ragged, uneven gasps as the silence stretched, the weight of his own treachery dragging him down under the court's stares. "Your Majesty..." he rasped, his voice cracking, devoid of the thunder it carried only moments before. "The safety of the borders... I acted to protect the realm from northern encroachment. If I overstepped, it was out of duty—"

"Duty wears the Crown's colors, Commander, not the cloak of a private cabal," Lord Daven interrupted, descending the sweeping staircase from the gallery with slow, graceful steps. He stopped a respectful distance behind you, his hands clasped behind his back, his eyes alight with triumph. "To wage an unauthorized war while the treasury starves is not duty. It is insubordination. Perhaps worse. A fair treaty requires partners who answer to their sovereign, Your Majesty, not captains who write their own warrants in the dark."

Priestess Yuna stepped from the alcove, her vestments sweeping soundlessly over the marble. She extended her pale hands, offering the intercepted missive back toward the dais where a trembling page scurried to receive it. "The scales tip toward judgment," Yuna spoke, her tone cool and clear as winter water. "When the shepherd leads the flock into the wolf's path for his own sport, he forfeits the crook. Accountability is not vengeance, Daughter of the Sun; it is the restoration of holy balance."

The Herald stood frozen for a half-beat before remembering his office. He raised his gilded staff, striking the flagstones with a single, sharp report that sent a shudder through the silent hall. "Hear the word of the Sovereign!" the Herald proclaimed, his voice solemn and rigid. "Let no tongue wag while the Crown deliberates!"

Queen Isara remained standing atop the dais, looking down at the kneeling commander. Her expression did not waver; there was no fury in her eyes, only the glacial, terrible detachment of a monarch severing a diseased limb.

"Relinquish your sword, Ash," Isara commanded.

The hall held its breath. Ash flinched as though struck across the face. For a terrifying second, his hand drifted toward the weapon’s hilt, but the Queen’s unblinking gaze pinned him to the floor. Trembling, the commander unclasped the leather baldric, laid the heavy blade upon the marble with a dull, hollow clatter, and bowed his forehead until it brushed the stone.

"You will await my pleasure in the western tower," Isara said, her tone utterly flat. "The Ministry of Justice will examine every ledger, every dispatch, and every ship manifest bearing your seal. If another lie is unearthed, the block will be the least of your concerns." 

Two imperial guards stepped forward, hauling the disgraced commander to his feet and escorting him from the throne room. The heavy iron doors thudded shut behind them, sealing his fate.

The Queen turned her gaze slowly back to you. The cold precision in her eyes had not softened, but the calculus had shifted entirely. 

"Accountability has been served, Ambassador," Isara said, descending one step down the dais, closing the distance between you. "And with it, your leverage has done its work. The blockade ends today. Velheim's ships will move without hindrance, and the salt levy will be halved."

She paused, folding her hands before her, her voice dropping into a measured, lethal whisper that carried across the hushed assembly.

"In return, you will have your shared patrols along the Whispering Crag. But you will assign no more than three hundred men, and their stationing will be overseen by a marshal appointed by Lord Daven." She cast a fleeting, piercing look toward Daven before returning her focus entirely to you. "You wanted equity. You have extracted your terms, and you have humbled my council. Tell me, Ambassador—will Velheim sign this peace, or does your prince harbor yet another revelation beneath his sleeve?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, a hint of satisfaction on my face.* "My Prince will sign, Your Majesty. This is a fair path forward for both our kingdoms." *I hold her gaze, a silent challenge in my eyes.* "Provided, of course, that all parties uphold their end of the agreement."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The quiet challenge in your parting words hung in the air like frost, a parting parry delivered in the lion’s own den. 

Lord Daven stepped smoothly into the space Commander Ash had vacated, his velvet cloak sweeping the marble where the disgraced soldier’s sword had lain only moments before. A wolfish satisfaction gleamed in Daven’s dark eyes, though his posture remained flawlessly deferential as he bowed toward the dais. "The Crown’s wisdom is unmatched, Your Majesty," Daven murmured, his voice rich with polished charm. "Velheim will find that an accord forged in the light of day leaves no shadows for treason to fester. I shall personally see to it that the marshal appointed to the Crag understands the delicate nature of this fraternity. Our borders will be secured, our grain will move, and our treasuries will mend."

From the edge of the dais, Priestess Yuna turned her serene, unreadable face toward you. The silver beads in her hands resumed their slow, measured rhythm, clicking softly in the vast stillness. "An oath spoken beneath the vaulted sky is witnessed by more than kings and councils," Yuna whispered, her cool voice carrying an ancient, detached weight. "A pledge upheld brings rain to the fields and quiet to the cradle. A pledge broken calls the carrion birds to banquet. The scales are balanced for this hour, Ambassador. Walk carefully, lest your own footfall disturb the dust."

The Herald raised his golden staff high above his head and struck the stone floor three times in rapid, measured succession. *Crack. Crack. Crack.* The sharp clatter banished the lingering ghosts of Ash’s fury and sealed the formal proceedings. "Let the scribes inscribe the terms!" the Herald proclaimed, his voice echoing grandly off the vaulted ceiling. "The petition of Velheim is accepted. The word of the Sovereign is spoken. Let no man dispute what the Crown has decreed!"

Queen Isara took one final, deliberate step down the dais, descending to the level of the court until she stood barely an arm’s length from you. Up close, her pale eyes were as unforgiving as glacial ice, devoid of both grievance and forgiveness.

"You need not remind me of my own obligations, Ambassador," Isara said, her voice dropping into a lethal, quiet register meant for you alone. "My house has held this throne for four centuries not by the charity of our neighbors, but by knowing precisely which debts to collect, and when."

The Queen signaled with a flick of two ringed fingers, and the page scurried forward to present the parchment containing the terms, along with a newly brought wax candle and the royal signet ring. 

"The scribes will draft the formal charters before twilight," Isara concluded, holding your gaze with terrifying stillness. "You and Lord Daven will ratify the specifics before the High Council on the morrow. You have won your day, Velheim. You have saved your merchant fleets and clipped the wings of my hawks." 

A razor-thin, dangerous smile touched the corner of the Queen’s lips before vanishing into granite calm. 

"Go to your embassy and rest upon your triumph," she murmured. "And pray your prince proves as formidable at keeping a peace as you are at demanding one."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I offer a slight, respectful bow.* "My Prince understands the weight of his word, Your Majesty. I assure you, Velheim will hold to this peace." *I take the parchment from the page, my gaze lingering on the Queen's for a moment longer.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The heavy parchment settled into your grasp, its weight tangible evidence of the concession you had wrested from the Crown. 

Queen Isara did not blink beneath your lingering gaze. For a heartbeat, the silence between you was taut enough to snap, the cold calculation in her eyes measuring the exact depth of your resolve. Then, with a faint, imperceptible incline of her chin, the Queen turned her back to the assembly and ascended the steps of the dais, the train of her gown sweeping over the stone with the hiss of dry grass.

"We shall see what the dawn brings, Velheim," Isara said, seating herself upon the throne once more, her posture unyielding. "Words are easily pledged in the light; it is the night that tests their fidelity."

To her left, the space where Commander Ash had stood remained conspicuously vacant, marked only by the scuff of armor and the absence of his brash hostility. The silent void was a stark reminder to every noble in the gallery of what opposing your embassy had cost the high command. 

Lord Daven retreated another half-pace, bowing low toward the throne with practiced grace before his dark eyes flicked toward you. A subtle, razor-thin smile played across his mouth—the look of a man who had backed the winning wager and already envisioned the dividends. "Until the council convenes at sunrise, Ambassador," Daven murmured just loudly enough to carry, his hands tucked elegantly into his fur-lined sleeves. "The northern border rests upon tonight's ink."

In her alcove, Priestess Yuna let her silver prayer beads drop into the folds of her vestments with a soft, final chime. Her fathomless eyes remained fixed upon you, sorrow and scrutiny mingling in her neutral gaze. "A covenant sealed in the temple of pride bears the mark of both hands," Yuna spoke, her melodic voice floating down like falling snow. "He who leaves with what he demanded must now build what he promised. May the heavens grant your prince wisdom before his victory turns to brine."

The Herald stepped forward to center aisle, bringing the iron-shod base of his gilded staff down onto the marble with a deafening *thud*.

"The audience is concluded!" the Herald proclaimed, his voice echoing from the rafters to the heavy oak doors at the hall's far end. "Let the court clear the presence! Honor to the Crown! Safe conduct to the envoy of Velheim!"

A low murmur broke out across the gallery as the assembly rose, courtiers whispering behind fans and rings of signet stone, their gazes tracking you as you turned toward the long aisle leading to the palace gates.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod to Lord Daven, then turn and walk, slowly and deliberately, down the aisle. I don't look back.* This was only the first step.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
