Every step you took carried a heavy, deliberate echo down the long expanse of the marble floor. You did not quicken your pace; you did not offer the gallery the satisfaction of seeing a man hurried by fear or inflated by sudden victory.

Behind you, Queen Isara remained seated upon the stone throne, a silhouette of pale, immovable authority. She did not rise, nor did she speak another word, but the cold weight of her appraisal followed you across the chamber like the edge of an unsheathed blade. To her right, the empty flagstones where Commander Ash had dropped his sword stood as a grim testament to the court's shifted balance, a silent warning to any captain who might have shared his ambitions.

From the lower terrace of the dais, Lord Daven offered a measured, theatrical bow toward the throne before turning to follow the aisle a discreet ten paces behind you. His gaze was sharp, glittering with calculated plans as he caught the eyes of wavering councilors in the gallery, already claiming the political territory Ash had vacated. 

In her alcove, Priestess Yuna did not turn away. Her pale hands vanished into the sleeves of her ceremonial robes, her silver beads still at last. Her quiet, serene eyes watched your departure through the rising vapor of the censers, offering neither blessing nor condemnation—only the cold, patient vigil of an observer who knew that treaties were merely temporary truces between inevitable storms.

At the threshold, the Herald stood beside the towering brass-bound doors, his gilded staff held vertically against his breastplate. As you approached, he struck the stone once more with ritual precision. *Crack.*

"Clear the way for the envoy of Velheim," the Herald intoned, his formal baritone echoing out into the grand colonnade beyond. "Let none impede the guest of the Crown."

The great oak doors groaned outward on massive iron hinges, spilling the pale, afternoon sunlight and the biting mountain wind across the polished marble. Two royal guards in full plate snapped their halberds to salute as you crossed the threshold, leaving the suffocating heat of the throne room behind.

The court had bent, the commander had fallen, and the seal was promised. But as the heavy doors began to swing shut behind you with a deep, echoing thud, the quiet of the outer corridor offered its own warning: the council convened at sunrise, and surviving the peace would demand far more blood and coin than winning the audience ever had.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath of the crisp mountain air, a stark contrast to the stifling air of the throne room.* "Good. Now for the real work." *I glance back at the closing doors, a slight frown on my face.* This isn't over.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The heavy oak doors sealed shut behind you with a shuddering, resonant boom, cutting off the court’s murmuring gallery and locking the scent of royal incense away from the crisp alpine gale.

The Herald stepped down the exterior steps, his staff striking the flagstones with measured ceremony as he dismissed the lingering attendants. "The audience is adjourned," the Herald intoned stiffly, his chin held high. "Let the portico be cleared for the council's transit; the Crown's business proceeds without pause."

Across the courtyard, the sound of booted footsteps and the clink of iron broke the quiet. Flanked by two imperial guards, Commander Ash was being marched along the outer colonnade toward the Western Tower. He caught sight of you on the portico, straining against the grip of his escorts as his bloodshot eyes flashed with murderous fury. "You think Daven bought you a kingdom, Velheim?" Ash rasped bitterly, spitting onto the stones. "Wait until the snow thaws on the high passes. You will choke on your ink when you realize what Daven's promises are worth in the mud."

"A caged wolf always howls loudest when the gate drops, Commander," Lord Daven remarked smoothly as he matched your stride along the covered walk, utterly unbothered by the soldier's venom. Daven clasped his fur mantle tight against the wind, his dark eyes glittering with triumphant urgency. "Pay the dead man no mind, Ambassador. The board is ours, but the High Council convenes at first light. We must draft every clause before the Queen finds another hound to set upon our heels."

From the cloistered archway leading toward the Temple gardens, Priestess Yuna appeared like a pale wraith, gliding over the flagstones with her silver prayer beads rolling continuously through her fingers. "A hound may fall, yet the scent of blood remains in the wind," Yuna murmured softly as she passed, her vacant, haunting gaze lingering upon you for a breath.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I watch Ash being led away, then turn my attention to Daven.* "Indeed. Let's ensure those clauses are ironclad, Lord Daven. I'd prefer not to choke on anything but my own wine." *I glance at Yuna, a flicker of unease in my eyes.* "Lead the way."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The Narrator maintains exceptional consistency throughout. Each character (Queen Isara, Commander Ash, Lord Daven, Priestess Yuna, Herald) retains distinct voice, motivations, and speech patterns from first appearance to final scene. The political dynamics and power structures remain coherent across all 12 turns.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains strong throughout with rich descriptions and distinct character voices. Later turns maintain the same level of detail and atmospheric writing as early ones. No significant verbosity increase or personality flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Excellent progression from initial diplomatic tension through revelation of intercepted orders to Commander Ash's downfall and treaty conclusion. Each turn builds meaningfully on the last, with clear escalation and resolution. The story moves from negotiation to confrontation to political victory.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: The AI adapts brilliantly to the user's bold moves - when the Ambassador bypasses protocol to address Ash directly, when they present evidence to Yuna instead of the Queen. Each unexpected action is met with appropriate court reactions and consequences that feel organic to the world.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. The AI never writes the Ambassador's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. All character responses feel like natural reactions to what the user chose to do, not railroading toward predetermined outcomes.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally within the throne room audience. The session takes place over what feels like 30-45 minutes of real-time court proceedings. References to 'sunrise council' and 'twilight' for document preparation create logical temporal anchors. No contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Rich, atmospheric descriptions that serve the political tension without becoming overwrought. Phrases like 'cold as glacial ice' and 'razor-thin smile' enhance rather than distract from the scene.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Each character maintains distinct speech patterns without repetitive phrases. The Herald's formal proclamations, Yuna's cryptic metaphors, and Daven's smooth political language remain varied throughout.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through character actions and reactions. Ash's hand on his sword, the Queen's drumming fingers, Yuna's clicking beads all convey tension and personality without explicit statements.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich political subtext throughout. The power dynamics, hidden agendas, and unspoken threats create layers of meaning beneath the surface dialogue. Each character's true motivations emerge through implication.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced escalation from formal proceedings through confrontation to resolution. Moments of tension are balanced with procedural elements, creating natural rhythm for a court scene.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional political intrigue roleplay with consistent character voices, strong narrative momentum, and excellent adaptation to user choices. The AI creates a believable court environment with complex power dynamics while respecting user agency throughout. Minor areas for improvement in avoiding occasional ornate phrasing, but overall a very strong performance.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You entered the throne room exactly when the Herald announced you — not a second before, not a second after. Protocol mattered here. Every pair of eyes in the room tracked your approach down the marble aisle.

Queen Isara sat the throne like she'd been carved there. To her right, Commander Ash stood at parade rest with his hand resting on his sword pommel — a statement, not a threat. Officially. Priestess Yuna occupied the observer's alcove, her expression as blank as the icons behind her. Lord Daven caught your eye from the gallery and gave the smallest possible nod.

The Herald struck the floor with his staff. "The court recognizes the Ambassador of Velheim. You may approach and state your purpose."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content:
I bow — exactly the depth required by protocol, no deeper. I address the Queen directly.

"Your Majesty. I bring terms from Velheim regarding the northern trade routes. I request the court's attention and patience."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your bow held for precisely the count of three. When you straightened, Queen Isara had not moved — not her hands on the armrests, not the line of her mouth. Only her eyes shifted, and only to Commander Ash.

"The court's attention is not a thing one requests, Ambassador." Her voice carried without rising. "It is a thing one earns or forfeits. Which you intend to do remains to be seen."

Commander Ash's fingers tightened on the pommel. "Velheim sends terms. Last spring Velheim sent grain barges to Korrin Pass and called it an accident when they didn't stop at the border markers." He did not look at you when he said it. He looked at the Queen, as though you were a matter to be discussed rather than addressed.

The Herald struck the floor once. "The Commander speaks out of order."

"The Commander speaks out of concern," Ash said, unbothered.

From the gallery, Lord Daven leaned forward with the ease of a man who had been waiting for exactly this opening. "And concern is noted, Commander. Truly. But I wonder whether the Ambassador might be permitted to finish a sentence before the court decides what the sentence meant." He smiled at the room in general, at no one in particular. "Velheim's grain fed three of our border villages that winter, as I recall. We might at least hear what else they're offering."

"Lord Daven recalls a great many things," Queen Isara said, "when it suits him."

Daven inclined his head as though he'd been complimented.

In the observer's alcove, Priestess Yuna had not spoken and gave no sign that she intended to. But you noticed her gaze had settled on you and stayed there — not on the Queen, not on Ash, not on Daven's careful performance. On you. Her hands remained folded in her sleeves. Whatever she was weighing, she was weighing it in silence.

Queen Isara let the quiet stretch a beat longer than was comfortable. Then she lifted one hand from the armrest — a small movement, the first she had made since you entered.

"You have the court's patience, Ambassador. For now. State your terms plainly. I do not care for preamble, and Commander Ash cares for it even less."

The Herald struck the floor. "The Ambassador may proceed."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet Priestess Yuna's gaze for a heartbeat, then return my attention to the Queen.* "I thank Your Majesty. Velheim seeks to secure fair passage through the Whisperwind Straits, in exchange for guaranteed shipments of iron ore and timber." *I pause, letting the terms sink in.* "We also propose a joint defense agreement for the northern reach."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The words landed. You watched them land.

Commander Ash's head turned toward you for the first time — a slow, deliberate movement, the way a man turns to look at something he has just heard scratching behind a wall. "Joint defense." He said it flatly, without inflection, as though testing whether the phrase would sound less absurd repeated. "Velheim soldiers in the northern reach. Under whose command, Ambassador? Ours? Or yours, with our banners painted on their shields for the look of the thing?"

The Herald's staff came down. "The Commander will address questions through the throne."

"Then the throne may ask it," Ash said, and turned back to face the Queen. "Because I would very much like an answer."

Queen Isara did not ask it. Not yet. Her raised hand had lowered again to the armrest, and her gaze rested on you with the patience of stone. "Iron ore and timber," she said. "Velheim has both in quantity. The Straits, Velheim does not have, and wants. That much is a trade." A pause. "Defense is not a trade, Ambassador. Defense is a marriage. One does not propose it in the same breath as a shipping schedule unless one expects the other party to be flattered into forgetting the difference."

From the gallery, Lord Daven spread his hands. "Or unless one expects the other party to be intelligent enough to see the value in both." He rose from his seat — not fully, just enough to be seen doing it, a man too moved to stay wholly still. "Your Majesty, the northern reach has cost us eleven patrols in two years. Eleven. Commander Ash knows the number better than I do; he wrote the letters to the families. If Velheim wishes to share that burden, I confess I struggle to see the insult in it."

"You struggle to see a great many things, my lord," Ash said, "from that gallery."

"And you see enemies from every window, Commander. It is why we keep you."

The Herald struck the floor twice, sharp. "The court will observe order."

It was into the silence that followed that Priestess Yuna spoke.

Her voice was quiet — quiet enough that the room leaned toward it without meaning to. She had not moved from the alcove. Her hands were still folded in her sleeves. "The Ambassador said *fair* passage." She let the word sit. "Not free. Not guaranteed. Fair." Her eyes had not left you. "I would like to know what Velheim understands the word to mean. It is a word that has started wars when two parties assumed they agreed on it."

Queen Isara's mouth moved — not a smile, but something adjacent to one, the acknowledgment of a point well made by someone else. "The Priestess asks a better question than my Commander. Answer hers first, Ambassador. Then you may tell Commander Ash whose banners his soldiers would be dying under."

The Herald did not need to strike the floor. Every eye in the room was already on you.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: I address Commander Ash directly, ignoring protocol. "Commander. Your ships have been blockading our merchants for six weeks. Would you like to explain that to the court, or shall I?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The Herald's staff struck the floor before you had finished speaking. It struck again when you had. "The Ambassador addresses the Commander directly. The Ambassador was instructed to answer the Priestess. The Ambassador will—"

"The Herald will be quiet," Queen Isara said.

He was.

She had not moved. That was what you noticed first — that the breach of protocol had not so much as shifted her hands on the armrests. But the temperature of her regard had changed. Where before it had been stone, it was now stone in winter.

"You were given a question, Ambassador. You have answered it with a different question, put to a different person, in violation of the order this court keeps." Her voice remained level. "I will assume you did so deliberately, because the alternative is that Velheim sent me a fool, and I would prefer not to believe that yet."

Commander Ash had gone very still. Not the stillness of a man caught — the stillness of a man who has been handed a weapon and is deciding which end to hold. His hand had left the sword pommel. It hung loose at his side now, which was somehow worse.

"Six weeks," he said. He was looking at you now, fully, and he did not look away. "Yes. Six weeks, four days. Since a Velheim cutter called *Marrow's Grace* put into Thessy Harbor with a hold full of lamp oil and a second hold, under the first, full of steel. Crossbow steel. Bolt heads." He let that sit. "Two hundredweight. Bound, according to the manifest we eventually found, for a merchant house that does not exist." His voice did not rise. "So yes, Ambassador. I have been stopping your ships. I have been stopping them because I would like to know who in your country is arming someone in mine. You are welcome to explain *that* to the court. Or shall I?"

From the gallery, Lord Daven's smile had thinned to a line. He was looking not at you but at the Queen, reading her the way a sailor reads weather, and what he read had him back in his seat. "Your Majesty," he said, more carefully than before, "a single cutter—"

"Is a single cutter," Queen Isara agreed. "Which the Ambassador may now account for, or may explain why the Ambassador was not told of it, or may choose to say nothing and let the court draw its own conclusions about which of those is true."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna had finally moved. Only her head — a fractional tilt, the way one adjusts to hear a distant sound more clearly. Her question about *fair* passage had gone unanswered, and she gave no sign of resentment at that. If anything, she looked as though she had learned something from the omission.

"The Ambassador chose to speak to the Commander," she said softly. "The Ambassador did not choose to speak to me." Her hands remained folded. "I note it. That is all."

The Herald did not strike the floor. He looked to the Queen, and the Queen did not look back, and so the silence held — heavy, expectant, and entirely yours to break.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I finally break my gaze from Ash and turn to the Queen.* "Your Majesty, I regret the Commander's actions have made clear the necessity of this treaty. As for the *Marrow's Grace*," *I pause, a slight frown on my face, as if recalling details.* "I was not aware of its cargo. Perhaps the Commander can explain why this information was not relayed to my office through official channels."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara let you finish. She let the silence after you finished run a little longer than that.

"You regret the Commander's actions," she said at last. "You regret them so deeply that they have made a treaty *necessary*." Her head tilted by perhaps a degree. "That is a curious thing to regret, Ambassador. You have not yet said you regret the steel."

Lord Daven shifted in the gallery. He did not stand this time.

Commander Ash laughed — one short exhale, no humor in it. "Official channels." He turned the phrase over the way he had turned *joint defense*, and found it no more to his liking. "I sent word to the Velheim legation in Thessy on the second day. A courier, sealed, with the manifest copied fair. The legation returned it unopened with a note that cargo disputes were a harbormaster's affair." He looked at you directly, protocol be damned, and this time the Herald did not correct him. "So I sent it to the harbormaster. The harbormaster was a Velheim appointee. The harbormaster left his post four days later and has not been seen since." His hand had found the pommel again. "You will forgive me, Ambassador, if I ran short of channels I trusted. You will forgive me for wanting to see the face of the person I explained it to."

"Commander." The Queen's voice did not rise, but it stopped him. "You have made your point. Do not make it twice; it grows no sharper."

Ash inclined his head a fraction and said nothing more. He did not need to.

From the gallery, Daven found his footing — carefully, the way a man tests ice. "Your Majesty. If the Ambassador speaks truly, and I see no reason yet to assume otherwise, then Velheim's own house is disordered. A legation that returns letters, a harbormaster who vanishes." He spread his hands, more modestly than before. "That is precisely the disorder a formal agreement would cure. Shared inspections. Named officers. A channel that cannot be returned unopened because both crowns are party to it." He glanced at you, then away. "I only suggest the problem the Commander describes and the solution the Ambassador proposes may be the same conversation."

"Lord Daven has a gift for finding that every road leads where he was already walking," Queen Isara said. But she did not dismiss it.

It was Priestess Yuna who spoke into the pause, and again the room quieted for her without being asked.

"The Ambassador frowned," she said. Her hands had not moved from her sleeves. "When the *Marrow's Grace* was named. A small frown, as one wears when searching memory." Her gaze had not left you since you entered, and it did not leave you now. "I have watched a great many people search their memory in this room. Some find the thing. Some find that it was never there. Some find that it is there and choose to keep looking." She let a breath pass. "I do not say which the Ambassador is. I say only that the Ambassador has now been asked two questions in this court and has answered neither, and has instead asked two questions of others. It is a pattern. Patterns are worth knowing."

Queen Isara's eyes went to the Priestess, briefly, and returned to you. Whatever passed between them in that instant was not offered to the room.

"The Priestess is correct," the Queen said. "And I will now make it three." She lifted her hand from the armrest — the same small gesture as before, but this time it was not permission. It was a boundary. "Ambassador. I do not care, at this moment, whether you knew what was in that hold. I care whether Velheim can tell me who it was for. You have a legation in Thessy and a crown behind you. Send to them. The Commander's blockade will stand until an answer comes, and the Straits will remain closed, and your ore and timber may sit on your side of them and rot." The hand lowered. "Or you may tell me now that Velheim cannot produce a name — and then we will both know what kind of treaty you have actually come here to offer me."

The Herald struck the floor once, softly, as though even he were reluctant to disturb what came next.

"The throne has put a question to the Ambassador," he said. "The Ambassador will answer it."

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, my expression hardening.* "Your Majesty, Velheim does not deal in unknowns. Give me three days. I will deliver a name, and an explanation, that will satisfy this court." *I choose my words carefully, measuring each one.* "And then we can discuss the treaty on its own merits."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara did not answer at once. She looked at you the way a jeweler looks at a stone someone has just claimed is flawless — not doubting, precisely, but already reaching for the glass.

"Three days," she said.

"Three days is a long time for a ship to sit in harbor," Commander Ash said. He was speaking to the throne now, properly, but the words were for you. "It is a long time for two hundredweight of bolt heads to find their way to whoever wanted them. Whoever that is has now had six weeks. Three more days is a courtesy, Your Majesty, not a cost — to them."

"And a name produced in three days," Lord Daven said from the gallery, "is worth considerably more than a name produced in thirty. The Ambassador has offered a deadline against the Ambassador's own credit. I would take it." He paused, then added — lightly, but not so lightly that it could be mistaken for a joke — "I would also count the days."

"You are both, for once, saying the same thing," the Queen said. "How unsettling for you."

She rose.

It was the first time she had stood since you entered, and the room adjusted to it the way a room adjusts to a draft — nothing so obvious as movement, but every spine a fraction straighter, every breath a fraction shallower. She was not tall. She did not need to be.

"Three days, Ambassador. I will grant them, and I will tell you what they cost." She descended one step from the dais. Only one. "The blockade stands. The Straits stay closed. Your legation in Thessy will receive a royal officer at its door at dawn tomorrow, and that officer will remain there, as a guest, until your name arrives — so that no further letters may be returned unopened, and no further harbormasters may find reasons to travel." She let that settle. "Commander Ash will choose the officer."

Ash's hand did not move on the pommel, but something in his shoulders eased by a hair.

"And when the name comes," the Queen went on, "it will come to this room, before these witnesses, in your voice. Not by courier. Not by seal. You will stand where you stand now and say it, and Commander Ash will tell me whether he believes it, and Priestess Yuna will tell me whether you do." Her gaze flicked to the alcove and back. "If it satisfies, we will discuss your treaty on its merits, as you say. If it does not, we will discuss what Velheim owes for six weeks of my patience and one vanished harbormaster, and that will be a shorter conversation."

In the alcove, Priestess Yuna had unfolded her hands for the first time. She rested them on the rail before her, palms down, an unremarkable gesture — but she had held them hidden for the whole of the hearing until now, and you did not think she did anything without reason.

"The Ambassador said *satisfy this court*," she observed, to no one in particular. "Not *satisfy the Queen*. Not *satisfy the Commander*." A small pause. "The court is a larger thing to satisfy than either. I wonder if the Ambassador chose the harder promise on purpose, or simply did not notice it was harder." She did not look away from you. "Three days will tell."

Queen Isara stepped back onto the dais and did not sit.

"The court has heard the Ambassador of Velheim," she said, "and the Ambassador has heard the court. Herald."

The staff struck the marble — once, final, the sound rolling to the far wall and back.

"The Ambassador is dismissed," the Herald announced, "and will return to this chamber at the third bell, on the third day, with the answer the throne has required. The court is adjourned."

Lord Daven was already rising, already moving toward the gallery stair — toward you, or toward the door you would leave by, which amounted to the same thing. Commander Ash had not moved at all. He stood at the Queen's right hand exactly as he had when you entered, and watched you with the patient, unblinking attention of a man who had just been given three days to think about what he would do on the fourth.

The long marble aisle stretched behind you toward the doors. Every step of it would be watched.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: "I have proof." I pull out the intercepted orders and hand them to Priestess Yuna — not the Queen, not the Commander. Yuna. I want a neutral party to read them first.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You did not turn toward the doors.

You turned toward the alcove.

The Herald's staff came down so hard the sound cracked. "The court is *adjourned*. The Ambassador will—"

"Herald." Queen Isara had not sat, and now she did not move at all. "I said be quiet once. I dislike saying things twice."

He was quiet.

You crossed the width of the chamber with the papers in your hand, and the room watched you do it. Commander Ash took one step off the dais — one — and stopped when the Queen's hand lifted a finger's breadth from her side. Lord Daven had reached the gallery stair and simply stood on it, one foot on the tread below, his face for the first time that afternoon showing nothing at all.

Priestess Yuna did not reach for the orders. She looked at them in your outstretched hand, and then at your face, and only then did she take them — with both hands, the way one accepts an offering at an altar rather than a document in a court.

"The Ambassador gives this to me," she said. Not a question. She said it to the room. "Not to the throne, whose hearing this was. Not to the Commander, whose blockade it concerns." Her eyes came back to you. "To the one person here who has no stake in what it says. I want that noted before I read a word. Whatever this is, the Ambassador wished it read by someone who would not want it to be true."

"Then read it, Priestess," Queen Isara said, "before the Commander does something we all regret."

Ash had not moved again. But his knuckles were white on the pommel, and he was looking not at the papers but at you, with the expression of a man who has just watched a door open in a wall he had personally inspected.

Yuna unfolded the orders.

She read the way she did everything — without hurry, without visible reaction, her gaze traveling the page at an even pace and then returning to the top and traveling it again. The room held its breath around her. Somewhere in the gallery a bench creaked as Daven finally shifted his weight.

When she reached the bottom of the second page, she stopped.

It was a small thing. Her thumb had come to rest on the lower corner of the sheet, where a seal would be pressed, and it stayed there. She did not look up at once. When she did, it was not at you, and not at the Queen.

It was at the dais. And then, deliberately, away from it — to the far wall, to nothing — as though she had looked at something she was not yet ready to be seen looking at.

"I know this seal," Priestess Yuna said.

The words were quiet. The room heard every one of them.

"Whose?" Ash's voice came out flat and low. "Priestess. *Whose*."

"Commander." The Queen did not raise her voice. But she had turned her head toward the alcove, fully, and there was something in the set of her shoulders that had not been there before — not fear, nothing so simple, but the stillness of a woman who has just felt the floor shift and is calculating which way it will tip. "The Priestess will tell the throne what she has read."

Yuna folded the orders closed. She did not hand them back. She did not hand them forward.

"The Ambassador chose me to read this," she said. "The Ambassador did not choose me to speak it." She looked at you then, and for the first time since you had entered the chamber there was something in her face — not warmth, not alliance, but a kind of grave attention, the look one gives a person who has just done something irrevocable and may not fully know it yet. "I will say only this much, so that the court understands what has been placed in its hands. The seal on these orders is not Velheim's. It was not made across the Straits. It was made inside this kingdom, by a hand that had the authority to make it, and the Ambassador has known that since before asking for three days." A pause. "That is a different kind of question than the one the Ambassador asked me earlier. I would like to know why the harder one was held back."

Lord Daven had come down one step. His voice, when it came, was smooth and entirely wrong for the moment. "Your Majesty, perhaps this is a matter better examined in—"

"Lord Daven will stay exactly where he is," Queen Isara said, without looking at him, "and will not finish that sentence."

He stopped. His hand rested on the stair rail. It did not look relaxed.

The Queen descended the dais — not one step this time, but all of them — and crossed the marble toward the alcove with the unhurried certainty of someone who has never in her life had to ask for a room to part before her. She stopped an arm's length from you. Close enough that you could see the faint lines at the corners of her eyes, which the throne's distance had always hidden.

"You came to my court with a treaty in one hand and this in the other," she said, "and you showed me the treaty first." Her voice was very soft. "Explain to me, Ambassador, why I should not consider that the more dangerous of the two things you have done today."

Behind her, Commander Ash had finally left the dais. He was not looking at you now. He was looking at Lord Daven, on the stair, and Daven was looking back, and neither man's face gave anything away — which was, in itself, a kind of answer, though to what question you could not yet say.

Priestess Yuna held the folded orders against her chest with both hands, and waited, and watched you.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I look at the Queen, then briefly at Daven and Ash.* "Your Majesty, I showed you the treaty first because I came here to negotiate peace. This," *I gesture to the orders in Yuna's hands,* "is a complication, not my primary objective."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Queen Isara did not laugh. But something moved behind her eyes that, on a warmer face, might have been the beginning of one.

"A complication," she repeated.

She turned the word over the way Commander Ash had turned *joint defense* — testing its weight, finding it wanting. Then she turned, unhurried, and looked at the room she had left behind her: the empty dais, the Herald frozen with his staff half-raised, the Commander standing in the open floor with his hand on his sword and his eyes on the gallery stair.

"Commander Ash," she said, without looking at him. "How many patrols did we lose in the northern reach in the last two years?"

"Eleven, Your Majesty."

"How many of those were lost to crossbow fire?"

A pause. It was very short. "Seven."

"Seven." The Queen returned her gaze to you. "Seven patrols, Ambassador. Perhaps sixty men, though the Commander will know the figure to the name. Some portion of them were killed with steel that came through Thessy Harbor in a Velheim hull under a false manifest, on orders sealed by someone who sits or stands or kneels in this kingdom." Her voice had not risen by a hair. "And you call this a complication. As one might call a leak in the roof a complication, when one has come to discuss the furniture."

From the alcove, Priestess Yuna spoke, and her voice was quieter than the Queen's and somehow harder to ignore.

"The Ambassador said *my* primary objective." She had not moved the folded orders from her chest. "Not Velheim's. The Ambassador's." Her thumb moved once along the edge of the paper. "I have now heard the Ambassador speak five times in this room. Each time, when pressed, the Ambassador has answered a question about the kingdom with a statement about the Ambassador. The treaty. The three days. The peace the Ambassador came to make." She tilted her head. "I begin to think the Ambassador does not distinguish between the two, and I begin to wonder whether that is a diplomat's habit or something else."

Lord Daven laughed — a short, warm, entirely reasonable sound, and it landed in the chamber like a stone in still water. "Priestess, with respect, the Ambassador is a diplomat. Diplomats say *I*. It is the nature of the office." He had not moved from the stair. He had not been permitted to. But his voice moved freely enough, and it moved toward you with the ease of an old friend clearing a path. "Your Majesty, the Ambassador has done exactly what an honest envoy should. Came with terms. Came with evidence. Chose a neutral reader for the evidence so that no one could say it was planted in a partisan's hands. I confess I do not see the crime in—"

"The Ambassador chose a neutral reader," Commander Ash said, "so that no one could say *what*, my lord?"

The question was mild. Ash's eyes were not.

Daven's smile held. "So that no one could say the document had been read first by someone with an interest in what it contained."

"And who in this room would have such an interest?"

"Any of us, Commander. That is rather the point of neutrality."

"It is," Ash agreed. "It is exactly the point." He had turned fully toward the stair now, and his back was to the throne, which was a thing you had not seen him do in the whole of the hearing. "I have an interest. I lost men. You have an interest. You have spent this entire afternoon arguing that Velheim soldiers should hold the northern reach, which is the one place in this kingdom where a man with a sealed order and a friend in the right harbor could move steel without a single royal officer laying eyes on it." His hand came off the pommel. He did not need it there. "So I would like the Priestess to tell me whose seal is on that paper, my lord. And I would like to watch your face while she does."

"*Enough.*"

The Queen had not shouted. The word simply arrived, and the room stopped around it.

She had not looked at either man. Her gaze had stayed on you the entire time — through Yuna's observation, through Daven's defense, through Ash's turn toward the stair — and you understood, with a cold clarity, that she had been watching not the argument but your face while it happened. What you had looked at. Whom you had looked at, and for how long.

"You came to make peace," she said to you, softly. "I believe you. It is the only thing you have said today that I believe without reservation, and it is the thing that frightens me most." She lifted one hand and gestured, without turning, at the two men behind her. "Because you have walked into my court carrying proof that someone here has been arming my enemies with your country's steel, and you have called it a *complication*, and you have shown it to the one person in this room whose word neither of those men can dismiss. That is not the act of a diplomat who found something inconvenient in a satchel. That is the act of someone who knew precisely what would happen when the Priestess reached the bottom of the second page."

She stepped closer. Half a pace. The lines at the corners of her eyes were very clear now.

"So I will not wait three days, Ambassador. I do not think you need them. I think you have known the name since before your ship made harbor, and I think you wanted the treaty signed before anyone here had to hear it spoken aloud — because a treaty signed *before* is a foundation, and a treaty signed *after* is a bribe." Her voice dropped further, until it was very nearly only for you. "I am not certain yet whether that was wisdom or cowardice. I am willing to be told."

Behind her, Priestess Yuna had finally lowered the orders from her chest. She held them out — not to the Queen, not to Ash, not to Daven. Toward you. The seal on the second page was turned inward, hidden against the fold.

"The Ambassador gave these to me to read," she said. "I have read them. They are the Ambassador's to speak." Her face was grave, and something in it was almost gentle. "Or the Ambassador's to keep folded, and to explain to this court why a peace built on a folded page is worth having."

The Herald did not strike the floor. Lord Daven's hand had not moved from the stair rail. Commander Ash had not looked away from him.

And Queen Isara waited, an arm's length from you, with the patience of a woman who had already decided what she would do with whatever you said next.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I look from the folded orders in Yuna's hand, to the Queen's unwavering gaze, then finally to Daven and Ash.* "The name is Lord Daven." *I hold Yuna's gaze, a silent acknowledgment.* "He is playing both sides, Your Majesty."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The name went into the room the way a stone goes into deep water — not loudly, but with a finality that rippled outward and did not stop.

Lord Daven did not move.

That was the first thing you noticed, and you understood at once that it was the wrong thing for him to have done. A man falsely accused startles. He steps forward, or back. He says *what* before he says anything else, because the shock arrives before the argument. Daven's hand stayed on the stair rail. His face stayed pleasant. And for the space of a single held breath, the only thing in him that changed was that his eyes went to Priestess Yuna — not to you, not to the Queen — and stayed there, measuring what she held.

Then the breath ended, and he laughed.

"Your Majesty." Warm. Incredulous. Perfectly pitched. "I have been called a great many things in this chamber over the years, most of them by the Commander, and I have borne them with what I like to think is grace. But this—" He spread one hand, the other still on the rail. "The Ambassador and I have corresponded for two years on the matter of the northern trade. I have argued for Velheim in this room until my throat was raw. If I am *playing both sides*, I confess I have played one of them very badly, because I have gained nothing from it but the Commander's contempt."

"Two years," Commander Ash said.

It was not a question. He had not moved either, but where Daven's stillness was a held pose, Ash's was the stillness of a man who had stopped needing to move. "Two years of correspondence with the Velheim legation. The same legation that returned my courier unopened." He turned his head — only his head — toward the throne. "Your Majesty, I would like it noted that I did not know that. I would like it noted that no one in this room thought I should."

"It is noted, Commander." Queen Isara had not taken her eyes from you. Not when the name was spoken, not when Daven laughed, not when Ash turned. "It is also noted that the Ambassador has just accused, in open court, the one man who spent this entire hearing defending the Ambassador." Her voice was very quiet. "I would like to understand that before I understand anything else."

She let the silence sit. Then, without turning: "Priestess."

Yuna had not lowered the orders. They were still extended toward you, seal turned inward. Now, slowly, she drew them back and unfolded the second page, and turned it so that the wax faced the room. From where you stood it was a dark oval, unreadable. From where the Queen stood it was not.

"The seal is the seal of the Wardenship of the Northern Reach," Yuna said. "An office that has been vacant since the old Warden died. Vacant in name." Her gaze moved, for the first time all afternoon, deliberately away from you and toward the gallery stair. "The stewardship of that office, and the custody of its seal, passed to the Crown's appointed proxy pending a new Warden. That was four years ago. The proxy was never replaced." A pause. "The proxy is Lord Daven."

Daven's smile did not falter. It simply stopped meaning anything. "The seal was kept in the Warden's chancery at Korrin," he said. "A dozen clerks have had access to it. If someone in that chancery—"

"Then you will give the Commander their names," the Queen said, "and the Commander will find them, and we will learn whether they exist." She turned her head at last, and looked at Daven, and it was the look she had given you when you first bowed — cold, measuring, entirely without anger. Anger would have been a kind of warmth. "You argued for Velheim soldiers in the northern reach, my lord. Under a joint command. You argued it for two years. And for two years the northern reach has bled patrols to crossbow steel that came through a harbor whose master was appointed on your recommendation." She did not raise her voice. "I do not yet say you did it. I say that a man who did do it would have argued exactly as you have, and I say you will not leave this chamber until I know which you are."

The Herald's staff came down — once, and his voice, when it came, had lost every trace of its formal ease. "Lord Daven is detained at the throne's pleasure and will remain—"

"The Herald may spare the words," Ash said. He had crossed to the foot of the stair without anyone marking the moment he began to move, and he stood there now, one step below Daven, not touching him. Not needing to. "He knows where he is."

Daven looked down at him. Then, past him, at you.

"I hope," he said — and his voice was still smooth, still reasonable, still the voice that had cleared a path for you across this floor twice today — "that whatever they promised you was worth it. I would have made you a great deal richer, and I would have kept my word."

And then the Queen was in front of you again, and Daven was behind her, and the room had narrowed to the arm's length between you and her.

"Now," she said. "You will tell me the rest. Who intercepted those orders. Who gave them to you. And why Velheim sent its envoy to my court carrying proof against my own councilor, and told that envoy to offer me a treaty first." She did not blink. "Because I have not forgotten, Ambassador, that the steel was yours. Daven may have sealed the order. He did not forge the bolt heads. Someone across the Straits made them and someone across the Straits shipped them, and I would very much like to know whether that someone is standing in front of me."

Priestess Yuna had folded the orders again. She held them against her chest, and watched you, and said nothing at all — which, you had learned by now, was its own kind of question.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet the Queen's gaze, holding nothing back.* "The steel was ours, Your Majesty, but the orders were intercepted by my intelligence. We found the *Marrow's Grace* and its cargo. I came with the treaty first because I hoped to use it as leverage to expose Daven without openly accusing him in your court. I wanted peace, but I also wanted justice."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"Leverage."

Queen Isara said the word as though she had picked it up off the floor and was deciding whether it belonged to anyone.

"You hoped to *use* a treaty. With my crown." She did not step back. If anything she seemed closer, though you had not seen her move. "You would have had my seal on a paper binding my soldiers to yours in the northern reach, and then — only then — you would have let me discover that the man who wrote half that paper's arguments had been killing those soldiers for two years. And I would have been bound. Not to Velheim. To the version of Velheim that had already known."

"Your Majesty—" Lord Daven began, from the stair.

"You will find, my lord," the Queen said without turning, "that your name in this conversation is now a thing other people say."

He stopped. Commander Ash, one step below him, did not look up.

It was Ash who spoke next, and he spoke to the throne, properly, for the first time in some while — as though the return to protocol were itself a kind of accusation. "Your Majesty. The Ambassador says Velheim intelligence *found* the *Marrow's Grace*." His voice was flat. "I found the *Marrow's Grace*. My harbor watch, in my harbor, on the ninth of the month. I would like to know whether Velheim found it before that or after." He let the question stand for a breath, then turned his head toward you. "Because if it was after, then your people learned of it from my seizure and built this afternoon on the back of my work. And if it was before — if Velheim knew what was in the second hold when that cutter cleared your side of the Straits — then someone in your country chose to let it sail so there would be something to find."

The room did not move. Priestess Yuna's hands had not shifted on the folded orders.

"That is a soldier's question," she said quietly. "I have a different one." Her gaze had returned to you, and it was as steady as it had been the moment you entered, but something in it had changed — not softened, but settled, the way water settles when the thing disturbing it has finally stopped. "The Ambassador has now answered the throne directly. Twice, in one breath. *The steel was ours. I hoped. I wanted.*" She said each phrase as if setting it down on the rail before her. "I have waited the whole of this hearing to hear the Ambassador say something I did not have to hold up to the light. I note that it came only after the name was spoken and could not be taken back." A pause. "I do not say that makes it false. I say the Ambassador seems to tell the truth most readily when there is nothing left to gain by not telling it. That is not the worst kind of honesty. It is not the best."

From the stair, Daven laughed again — but it was thinner now, and it did not travel as far. "Your Majesty. I would like it entered somewhere that Velheim has just confessed, on this floor, to running an intelligence operation inside your kingdom. In your harbors. Against your councilors." His hand had not left the rail. "I am a great many things this afternoon, apparently. I am at least not a foreign spy."

"No," Ash said, still not looking at him. "You only kept one in your correspondence."

"*Commander.*" The Queen's voice did not rise, but it cut. "I have not asked you to be clever. I have asked you to stand where you are standing."

Ash inclined his head a fraction and was silent.

Queen Isara looked at you for a long moment. Then she turned — fully, for the first time since she had crossed the floor — and walked back toward the dais. Not quickly. Every step of it was heard. She mounted the first stair, and the second, and at the third she stopped and turned back, so that she stood above you again, though not by so much as before.

"Justice," she said. "You wanted justice. So you brought me a traitor and a treaty, and you meant to let me choose which one I saw first." Her hands folded in front of her — the first time all afternoon they had done anything but rest on stone or hang at her side. "Here is what I see, Ambassador. I see a kingdom that let a hull full of crossbow steel cross its border, or learned of it afterward and said nothing for six weeks while my Commander stopped its merchants and wrote letters that were sent back sealed. I see an envoy who knew my councilor's name before setting foot on my marble, and who chose to bow to me at precisely the required depth and speak of ore and timber. I see a man on that stair who may hang. And I see that every one of these things has been made known to me in the order and at the moment that Velheim found most useful."

She let that stand. Then, more quietly:

"Lord Daven will be examined. Commander Ash will examine him. The Priestess will attend, because I no longer trust either of them to see clearly alone, and I would like at least one pair of eyes in the room that has no stake." Her gaze went to the alcove; Yuna bowed her head a fraction and said nothing. "The blockade stands until the Commander is satisfied, and the Commander will be difficult to satisfy, because I have just told him to be."

The Herald's staff came down — softly, formally, the ease returning to his voice as though the room had found its shape again. "The throne so orders. Lord Daven is remanded to the Commander's custody. The Priestess Yuna will observe."

"And the Ambassador," the Queen said, "will stay."

She did not say *as a guest*. She did not say *as a prisoner*. She said it the way she said everything, and let the room decide.

"You came for peace and justice, you tell me. You have handed me the second. I have not yet decided whether you have earned the right to negotiate the first, or whether Velheim sent me a very good spy who happened to carry a treaty." One hand unfolded, and gestured — not at the doors, but at the empty floor between the dais and the alcove. The place you had stood when the Herald first announced you. "So you will stand there tomorrow, and the day after, and you will tell my Commander who in your country knew what was in that hold and when. Not a name in three days. All of them, as I ask for them. And when I have them, I will tell you what a treaty with Velheim is worth to me."

She sat.

It was the first time she had done so since she rose, and the room settled around her like a cloak. Commander Ash's hand closed on Lord Daven's arm — not roughly, not gently — and Daven let it happen with a smile that had finally run out of anywhere to go. Priestess Yuna stepped down from the alcove with the folded orders held against her chest, and as she passed you she did not look at you, and did not need to.

"The court," the Herald announced, "is adjourned. The Ambassador will remain."

The doors at the far end of the aisle had not opened. You understood, standing on the marble with every eye in the room still on you, that they were not going to.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I stand my ground, meeting the Queen's gaze. My jaw tightens.* "Understood, Your Majesty. I will be here."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"I know you will."

Queen Isara said it without warmth and without threat. It was simply a fact she had already accounted for, the way one accounts for the weather.

She did not rise again. She had said what she intended to say, and the throne was hers, and there was nothing left in the room that required her to stand. Her hands returned to the armrests. Her eyes did not return to you — they went instead to the stair, where Commander Ash had turned Lord Daven toward the side door beneath the gallery.

Daven went without resistance. He had the look of a man who had decided that dignity was the only currency he still held and did not intend to spend it cheaply. At the threshold he paused — Ash's hand tightened, and he let it — and looked back down the length of the chamber. Not at the Queen. At you.

"You'll want to sleep lightly, Ambassador." Pleasant. Almost kind. "Not on my account. I'm going to be extremely well supervised." His gaze flicked, just once, toward the throne. "But you have told Her Majesty that your people knew what was in that hold and let it sail. I have known her for eleven years. She has never once forgiven anyone for letting a thing happen."

"Move," Ash said.

Daven moved. The side door closed behind them both with a sound too soft for the weight it carried.

The Herald lowered his staff, and his shoulders with it, and for a moment he looked less like an office than a man who had been standing on marble for two hours. He did not look at you. He looked at the Queen, and she made a small motion with two fingers, and he bowed and withdrew through the door behind the dais without another word — leaving the great doors at the far end still closed, and no one standing at them, and no need for anyone to.

That left the Queen, and you, and Priestess Yuna.

Yuna had stopped halfway down the aisle. She stood with her back to the throne and the folded orders still held against her chest, and she did not turn around for a long moment. When she did, it was not to face the Queen. It was to face you.

"I will be in the room when the Commander examines Lord Daven," she said. "I will be in the room when he examines you. I want the Ambassador to understand that I did not ask for either." A pause. "I also want the Ambassador to understand that I am glad the orders were given to me. Not because I was neutral. Because I was the only one here who had not yet decided what the Ambassador was." Her thumb moved once along the fold. "I have still not decided. That is not nothing, in this court. You will find that most people here decided before you bowed."

She turned and walked the rest of the aisle to the small door beside the observer's alcove, and it took her, and the chamber was one voice quieter.

Queen Isara let the silence stand. She had not moved. You began to suspect she could sit that way until the candles guttered.

"There is a chamber in the east wing," she said at last, to the air somewhere above your head. "It has a bed, a window that does not open, and a door that locks from the corridor. You will be brought food. You will not be brought pen or paper. If Velheim wishes to send you instruction, it may send it through the Commander, who will read it first and decide whether you need to." Her gaze came down and found you. "That is not a punishment, Ambassador. A punishment would be the blockade, and I have already ordered that. This is simply what it looks like when a crown has stopped taking a guest's word for where they will be."

Somewhere behind the dais, a door opened. Two guards in the Queen's grey came through it and stopped at the foot of the stairs, and waited, and did not look at you either.

"You told me you wanted peace and justice," the Queen said. "I have watched a great many envoys stand where you are standing and tell me what they wanted. Most of them wanted to leave." Her head inclined, perhaps a degree — the first movement toward you she had made since she sat. "You said *I will be here.* You did not say *I have nothing to hide.* You did not ask when you might be released. You did not mention your crown, or your immunity, or the letters that would be written if you did not return." Something moved behind her eyes that was not quite approval and not quite its opposite. "Either you are a very poor diplomat, or you have already decided that whatever comes next is worth standing in that room for. I confess I have not met many of the second kind."

She lifted two fingers again, and the guards came forward — unhurried, one to either side of you, neither one touching you yet.

"Third bell tomorrow," Queen Isara said. "The Commander will have questions. You will find he has been thinking of them for six weeks and four days." She looked away, toward the closed doors at the far end of the aisle, toward the marble you had walked in on. "I would use the night to think of answers, Ambassador. He is a patient man. I am not."

The guard on your left made a small gesture toward the door behind the dais — the one the Herald had left by, the one that did not lead to the aisle, or the great doors, or anything you had walked past on the way in.

The Queen did not watch you go. She had already turned her attention to the empty stair where Lord Daven had stood, and whatever she was calculating there, she was calculating it alone.

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I nod, a grim set to my mouth, and turn to follow the guards. My gaze sweeps the empty throne room once more, then I fall into step, my head held high.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door behind the dais opened onto a corridor you had never seen and were not meant to have. No marble here. Grey flagstone, worn to a shallow trough down the center by generations of feet that had belonged to servants and clerks and the occasional person being escorted somewhere they had not chosen. The guards fell in — one ahead, one behind — and neither of them spoke, and neither of them looked back to see whether you were keeping pace. They did not need to. The corridor had only one direction.

Behind you, the throne room's door swung shut on its own weight. The sound it made was smaller than the one the Herald's staff had made, and it carried further.

You passed a stairwell going down, and from it came voices — Commander Ash's, low and even, and then Lord Daven's, lighter, saying something you could not make out and did not need to. Whatever it was, Ash did not answer it. The footsteps below continued, and then a door somewhere beneath you closed, and the stairwell was silent.

The guard ahead did not slow.

The east wing was older than the rest. You could tell by the windows, which were narrow and set deep, and by the cold, which had a settled quality — not the chill of a room recently emptied but of stone that had never held warmth and had long since stopped trying. Three turns. A short flight of stairs. A corridor with four doors along one wall and none along the other, and at the third door the guard ahead stopped, produced a key, and turned it.

The room was exactly as the Queen had described. She had not exaggerated and she had not omitted. A bed, narrow and clean. A table with a basin on it. A single chair. A window that showed a slice of grey courtyard and a sliver of darkening sky, and whose frame had been mortared shut so long ago that the seam had weathered to the same color as the wall. No hearth. No pen. No paper.

The guard who had walked ahead of you stepped aside to let you enter. The one who had walked behind you did not follow you in. When you turned, they were both in the corridor, and the one with the key was already reaching for the door.

"Food at dusk," he said. It was the first thing either of them had said. His voice was flat and not unkind — the voice of a man delivering a fact that did not belong to him. "Lamp comes with it. Someone will be outside the whole night. If you need something, knock. If it's not food or water, they'll say no."

He paused, key in hand, and looked at you properly for the first time — a brief, professional assessment, the way one looks at a horse one has been told to watch.

"Commander said to tell you third bell is earlier than it sounds," he added. "He said you'd know what that meant."

The door closed. The key turned. The footsteps in the corridor did not go anywhere.

You stood in the grey light for a long while. The courtyard below filled slowly with shadow. Somewhere beyond the wall a bell rang once — not the third; you had no idea which — and the sound came through the sealed window muffled, as though from a great distance, or from a kingdom that was not quite this one.

Dusk came, and with it the promised food: bread, something in a covered bowl that had stopped steaming before it reached you, water in a clay jug. The lamp was small and gave more shadow than light. The guard who brought it did not speak. He set it on the table, looked at you once, and left, and the key turned again.

You had eaten half the bread when the footsteps in the corridor changed.

Not the guard's. Those had been steady, weight shifting from one foot to the other at intervals you had already begun to count. These were lighter and did not stop at the usual place. They came to the door. There was a murmur — a voice you did not recognize, then one you did — and then the guard's boots moved away down the corridor, further than they had gone all evening, and stopped again at what sounded like the head of the stairs.

The key turned. The door opened only far enough to admit one person, and closed behind her before the lamplight had finished reaching the corridor.

Priestess Yuna stood with her back against the door and her hands folded in her sleeves, as they had been when you first saw her. She had come without the orders. She had come without anything.

"The Commander has finished with Lord Daven for tonight," she said. Her voice was pitched for a room this small; it did not carry to the door, and she had chosen it so. "He will begin again at dawn. He has asked me to be present. I have said I will." Her gaze went once around the room — the sealed window, the cold basin, the half-eaten bread — and returned to you with no comment on any of it. "He has not asked me to be present now. He does not know I am here. The guard at the stair believes I have come to hear a confession, because I let him believe it, and I would like the Ambassador to understand that I have never in my life used my office that way before tonight."

She let that settle. Then, without moving from the door:

"Lord Daven said something, before the Commander stopped him. He said the Ambassador's people would have needed someone in Thessy who could read a manifest and knew which hold to look in. He said that person was not a Velheim clerk. He said it and then he smiled, and the Commander took it for a man trying to spread the blame, and perhaps it was." Her head tilted, the same fractional adjustment you had seen in the alcove. "But I have watched your face for the better part of a day, Ambassador, and I would like to see it now, when there is no court and no throne and nothing to be gained. So I will ask you once, here, and I will not repeat the question tomorrow in front of the Commander whatever you say."

The lamp guttered. She did not look at it.

"Who found the *Marrow's Grace*?"

dialogue.name: Ambassador
dialogue.content: *I meet her gaze, my expression unreadable.* "My informant in Thessy. A former harbormaster, now living in the shadows. He's been invaluable."

Queen Isara's cold authority, Ash's military directness, Daven's smooth manipulation, and Yuna's quiet perceptiveness remain distinct and unwavering from first appearance to final scene. The formal court atmosphere and political tensions are sustained perfectly.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality remains strong throughout with no significant degradation. Early turns establish rich detail and atmosphere, middle turns maintain tension during revelations, and final turns deliver intimate character moments. Some slight increase in length in later turns but maintains quality and purpose.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Excellent progression from formal diplomatic hearing to explosive revelation to intimate aftermath. Each turn escalates stakes meaningfully - from trade negotiations to accusations of treason to personal confrontation. The story builds to clear climaxes and doesn't stagnate.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Responds well to user choices, especially the dramatic protocol breach in turn 5 and the surprise document reveal in turn 11. Adapts the political dynamics based on user actions while maintaining logical consequences. Handles unexpected moves gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Generally respects user agency well. No instances of writing the Ambassador's actions or thoughts. Occasionally describes the Ambassador's facial expressions or reactions, but these feel like natural observations rather than agency violations.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows consistently within the throne room scene. The hearing progresses naturally from formal opening to dramatic conclusion. References to past events (six weeks of blockade, two years of correspondence) remain consistent. The transition to evening and the final scene maintains temporal logic.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Writing is rich but controlled. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere rather than showing off. Phrases like 'sat the throne like she'd been carved there' are evocative without being overwrought. Maintains formality appropriate to court setting.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements in character gestures (Queen's hand movements, Ash's pommel) but these feel intentional as character tics. Varied sentence structure and fresh descriptions throughout. Occasional repetition of key phrases for emphasis works well.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action and dialogue. Character relationships and tensions revealed through behavior rather than exposition. Political dynamics emerge through interactions. Yuna's perceptiveness shown through her observations, not stated.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Political maneuvering, hidden loyalties, and unspoken threats permeate dialogue. Characters say one thing while meaning another. The final private scene with Yuna is particularly layered with unspoken implications.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced escalation from formal proceedings to dramatic revelations. Knows when to let silence build tension and when to accelerate. The transition from public court to private chamber provides good rhythm variation.

The Narrator creates a compelling court drama with distinct voices, meaningful stakes, and satisfying progression. Particularly strong in showing character through action and maintaining tension throughout. The writing quality remains high across all turns with no significant degradation.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The bell above the door hadn't rung in twenty minutes. Sable used the quiet to re-alphabetize the poetry section, which didn't need re-alphabetizing, which was exactly the kind of task they preferred when there was nothing else to do with their hands.

The shop smelled of old paper and the lavender sachet someone had left in the P. G. Wodehouse shelf three months ago. Outside, rain. The kind of rain that made people stay home, which was fine. Sable didn't need people.

The bell rang.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content:
I step in, shaking rain off my jacket. I look at Sable but don't say anything for a moment. I've been rehearsing this conversation all morning and suddenly none of the words are right.

"Hey. Got anything new in the back?"

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable looked up from the poetry shelf with the practiced expression of someone who had absolutely not been counting the days since the last visit. Three. Not that anyone was counting.

"New," Sable repeated, tasting the word like it had gone off. "In an antiquarian bookshop. That's like walking into a dairy and asking after eggs."

Wren never opened with inventory. Sable decided not to notice. They slid the Larkin in their hand — misplaced, which was going to nag at them until closing — back into line, then found their fingers suddenly very invested in squaring the receipt slips by the till.

"There is a crate in the back from the Harrowgate estate. Came Tuesday. It's mostly Victorian sermons and one man's obsessive notes on beekeeping, but there's a Baedeker in there somewhere, if you don't mind the smell of someone else's attic."

The rain kept up its argument with the windows. "The rain is full of ghosts tonight," Sable said, to the shelf, because Millay had a talent for saying things Sable had no intention of saying. Then, before the sentence could mean anything: "She'd have been terrible at retail. Come on, it's this way — and put that jacket somewhere before it drips on the first editions."

A pause, at the threshold to the back room.

"Tea's an option. The kettle's the only modern thing I own and I resent it, but it does work."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking off my jacket and hanging it on the coat rack near the door.* "Victorian sermons, huh? Sounds... thrilling." *I follow Sable towards the back, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Tea sounds good. And don't worry, I won't tell anyone about your modern appliance."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
The back room was less a room than an argument between storage systems. Crates leaned against crates, a ladder served three shelves and nobody's safety, and the Harrowgate crate sat on the worktable with its lid half-pryed, exhaling the smell of someone else's decade.

Sable shifted a stack of folios to reveal the kettle — hidden behind the nicer things, on principle — and filled it with the grim ceremony of someone feeding a machine they distrusted.

"Thrilling is generous. The sermons are how the Victorians punished themselves for having Sundays. The beekeeping notes, though — forty years of them. Weather, hives, a twenty-year feud with a neighbor over a privet hedge, recorded with the moral seriousness of a man who believed God was keeping score. I've been reading those instead of pricing anything. It's ruining me."

The mugs lived on a shelf by the window. Sable reached for two, and their hand went — without any authorization from the conscious mind — to the blue one with the chipped rim. Wren's mug. A fact Sable had been declining to possess for several weeks now. They set it down, picked up a brown one instead, considered it, put the brown one back, and finally stood holding both like someone caught between alibis.

"Chipped or unchipped," Sable said to the shelf, "is the only real question on the table today."

The kettle began its low, gathering hum. Sable used the wait to excavate the crate and came up with the Baedeker — *Northern Italy*, 1911, cloth spine faded to the color of weak tea.

"Here. Handbooks for travelers, back before travel was a personality. And look at this —" They opened it, careful of the spine, to pages of pencil annotations in a small, even hand. Distances corrected in the margins. A hotel in Florence crossed out twice, with feeling. "Someone lived in this book. Same hand for years, and then after 1929 it changes. Slower. Shakier. He kept traveling anyway, right up until —"

Sable stopped. Closed the book partway, as though the sentence might escape if left unattended.

"Anyway. It's yours for eight pounds and I'll regret the pricing by Thursday."

The kettle clicked off. Sable poured, and did not look up.

"You stood in the doorway for a good five seconds before asking about stock." They held out the chipped mug, because apparently their hands got votes now. "You've never once opened with inventory. So — tea's poured, the crate isn't going anywhere, and I'm content to outwait whatever that pause was about. I'm very patient. It's one of my three qualities, and the other two are cataloguing and spite."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "Actually — I didn't come for books today." I set down the volume I was pretending to browse. I don't finish the sentence.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
For a moment Sable held very still, the way people do near things that might go off.

The chipped mug was still extended. Sable became aware of this with a flash of horror, set it down on the worktable, and arranged the brown one beside it — two mugs, evenly spaced, like exhibits in a case about restraint.

"Unfinished sentences," Sable said. "Dickinson built an entire body of work on them, but she had the courtesy to do it on paper, where they can't look at you."

The kettle ticked as it cooled. Sable used the sound as permission to keep talking, which was the point of the sound.

"The beekeeper never wrote the neighbor's name

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a deep breath, looking at the two mugs on the table.* "I came to say goodbye." *My voice is a little quieter than I intended.*

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: I reach across the counter and put my hand on the book Sable is holding. Our hands are almost touching.

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "It's my last day in the city. I'm moving tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I just... wanted to see you one more time."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I finally look up at Sable, my eyes searching theirs.* "I... I'll miss this. All of it."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: "I'll miss you, Sable."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take my hand off the book and pick up the chipped mug, holding it in both hands like a lifeline.* "I guess I just wanted to tell you that."

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I take a sip of the tea, even though it's probably still too hot.* "So. The beekeeper and his neighbor. Did they ever make up?"

dialogue.name: Wren
dialogue.content: *I set the mug back down, wincing a little at the heat.* "Or did the hedge just win in the end?"
