Mira pushes herself upright against the wall, face pale under the blue lights. Blood darkens the fabric around her upper thigh now. Not catastrophic yet. Not clean either.

She catches you looking.

“Later,” she says.

Ahead, the maintenance corridor splits three ways.

Left: a narrow passage marked HVAC MAIN RISER, air roaring beyond a grated turn.

Right: a descending utility ramp marked LOADING / WASTE PROCESSING, with a faint draft carrying diesel fumes.

Straight ahead: a locked mesh gate with a badge reader beside it. Beyond it, you see thicker power conduits and a yellow wall sign: SUBLEVEL ACCESS — TRANSIT SERVICE TUNNEL.

The pounding behind you stops.

A different sound replaces it.

A shaped charge being slapped against the door. Magnet clamps biting steel.

Mira looks at the mesh gate, then at the badge reader.

“I can open that,” she says. “If you buy me ten seconds.”

The charge behind you starts to whine.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The server room is not quiet.

It hums.

Racks line both walls in black, blinking columns of green and amber, throwing weak light across bundled cables and polished floor tiles. Cold air pours from vents overhead, sharp enough to raise gooseflesh beneath sweat. The room smells cleaner than the corridor—filtered air, hot plastic, dust trapped where no one bothers to look.

You get Mira down beside the nearest rack.

She braces one hand against the metal frame and keeps the other pressed high against her thigh. Blood slips between her fingers in slow, dark pulses. Her face stays controlled, but her eyes track everything: ceiling vents, cable trays, access panels, the door.

The barricade comes together fast. A rolling crash cart. A loose equipment cabinet. A heavy battery backup unit shoved against the inward-opening door. It will not stop a breaching team forever.

It might stop surprise.

Outside, the shaped charge detonates.

The corridor flashes white through the narrow security glass. The blast hits the server room door like a giant fist. The barricade jumps, metal shrieking against tile, but holds. Dust falls from the ceiling grid. Several racks chirp in protest as power briefly flickers.

Then comes shouting.

“Door inside! Secondary room!”

“Thermal?”

“Interference. Too much equipment.”

Mira exhales through clenched teeth.

“Good,” she whispers. “They don’t want to shoot blind in here.”

A red panel blinks near the ceiling: FIRE SUPPRESSION — CLEAN AGENT SYSTEM.

If they breach recklessly, they risk killing power, destroying servers, triggering suppression, or losing visibility in a sealed room full of equipment. That buys hesitation.

Not safety.

On the far wall, behind the last row of racks, a raised-floor tile sits slightly misaligned. A cable bundle disappears beneath it through a dark gap. Above it, a maintenance schematic is bolted to the wall: DATA CORE B / SUBLEVEL ROUTING / TRANSIT INFRASTRUCTURE.

Mira sees it too.

Her breathing tightens again, but this time it is not just pain.

“That floor,” she says. “Cable trench. Might connect to the tunnel route.”

Outside the door, something heavy scrapes into position.

Not a charge this time.

A ram.

The first impact hits.

The barricade lurches inward an inch. Metal groans. The server racks shiver, lights blinking faster as if afraid.

Mira grips the rack beside her and looks up at you, pale but focused.

“You want time to think,” she says. “Think fast.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Okay, trench it is." I pull my multi-tool from my belt, flipping it open to the pry bar. "Can you move at all, or am I dragging you again?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira gives the trench a hard look, then gives you one that is sharper.

“I can crawl,” she says. “Fast is optimistic.”

The ram hits again.

The door bucks against the barricade. The crash cart twists sideways, wheels shrieking across tile. One of the UPS units shifts half an inch, heavy enough to gouge the floor but not heavy enough to make you feel better.

Outside, a voice cuts through the impact noise.

“Again. Hinge side.”

Mira hears it. Her mouth tightens.

“They know what they’re doing.”

The raised tile resists at first, sealed by grime and years of chilled air pressure. The pry bar bites into the gap. Metal flexes. Somewhere below, cables thrum with hidden power, bundled thick as arteries beneath the floor.

The third hit lands.

The barricade jumps.

The door opens a fraction, then slams back against the cabinet with a brutal clang. A thin blade of corridor light appears at the edge, then vanishes.

Mira drags herself closer, leaving a dark smear across the pale tile. Her injured leg barely cooperates, but her hands are steady. She reaches the loosened panel and hooks her fingers under its lip.

“On three,” she says.

She does not wait long enough for comfort.

“One. Two.”

Another impact.

The tile pops free with a hollow metallic clatter, exposing a black trench beneath the server floor. Cold air breathes up from it, carrying dust, plastic insulation, and the deep vibration of the building’s infrastructure. Cable bundles crowd the space, but there is room—barely—for a body to squeeze through.

A schematic tag dangles from one conduit bundle:

SUBLEVEL DATA BACKBONE / TRANSIT UTILITY FEED

Mira stares into the gap.

“Could be a straight run,” she says. “Could be a dead drop.”

The ram hits again.

This time, something in the barricade gives with a crack.

The door opens two inches.

A gloved hand thrusts through the gap, grabbing for purchase. A weapon-mounted light flashes wildly into the server room, strobing across racks, Mira’s blood, the open floor trench.

“Visual! They’re going under!”

Mira lowers herself feet-first into the darkness, jaw locked so hard the muscles jump in her cheek. Her wounded leg catches on the tile edge. Pain breaks through her control for half a second, sharp and silent, all in the eyes.

Then she slips lower into the trench, one hand still gripping the floor edge.

From outside, the voice changes.

Urgent now.

“Move! Move! Move!”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I drop the multitool and slide in after her. "Move it, Mira!" I hiss, pulling her deeper into the trench, away from the light. "We don't have all day."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The multitool clatters somewhere behind you, swallowed by the trench noise.

You slide into the cable run after Mira, shoulders scraping metal brackets, knees pressing into cold dust and bundled insulation. The space is barely human-sized. Thick black data lines crowd both sides, zip-tied into rigid arteries that leave just enough room to crawl if panic does not make you broad.

Mira moves.

Not fast.

Fast enough.

She pulls herself forward on her elbows, wounded leg dragging behind her at an ugly angle. Every few feet, her boot catches on a cable tie or conduit clamp, and her whole body locks against the pain before she forces herself onward.

Behind you, the server room door gives way.

Metal crashes. Voices flood in.

“Floor opening!”

“Light it!”

A beam spears into the trench behind you, stark white against dust and cable sheathing. It finds the soles of your boots for a fraction of a second.

“Contact in the trench!”

A weapon cracks.

The shot does not enter cleanly. It punches into the raised flooring above, ricochets off something metal, and sends sparks raining into the crawlspace. One hot fleck lands against Mira’s sleeve. She keeps crawling.

Then the overhead fire suppression system triggers.

A deep mechanical cough rolls through the server room. Clean agent hisses from ceiling nozzles in a violent white flood, drowning voices, killing visibility, turning the open tile behind you into a churning rectangle of fog and flashing lights.

Mira glances back once, eyes sharp in the dim.

“Good,” she breathes. “Bad for them.”

The trench slopes downward.

The hum changes around you. Server noise fades behind. Deeper building sounds rise ahead: pumps, fans, the distant metallic thunder of transit infrastructure below the facility. The cable run bends left, then narrows so sharply that Mira has to flatten onto her stomach and pull herself under a low crossbeam.

Her injured leg catches.

This time she makes a sound—small, strangled, furious.

Ahead, a maintenance junction opens into a slightly wider crawl pocket. Three routes branch from it:

Left, a vertical ladder shaft drops into darkness, marked by a stenciled arrow: TRANSIT UTILITY — LEVEL S3.

Straight ahead, the cable trench continues under a tangle of fiber bundles toward a grated ventilation intake. Cold air blasts through it hard enough to rattle the mesh.

Right, a narrow service duct slopes upward toward a faint amber glow. Somewhere beyond it, machinery turns in slow, heavy cycles.

Behind you, someone starts feeding a probe into the trench.

A thin snake camera noses through the fog-lit opening, its tiny lens glowing red.

Mira sees the junction. Sees the camera. Sees your face.

“Ladder,” she says, voice tight. “Tunnel is below.”

The snake camera advances another foot.

A voice behind you, muffled by distance and suppression gas, calls out:

“Visual reacquired. Two targets. Crawlspace junction.”

Mira grips the lip of the ladder shaft and swings one leg over. Her bad leg refuses to follow cleanly. Blood drips from her pant leg into the darkness below, disappearing before it lands.

She looks down.

Then back at you.

“Hope you like climbing.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Hope you like tight spaces," I grunt, pushing past her good side to get to the ladder. *This is going to be fun.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You squeeze past Mira’s good side, shoulder scraping conduit, boot knocking loose dust into the shaft.

The ladder drops straight down through a concrete throat barely wide enough for one body. Rungs vanish into darkness, slick with condensation. Far below, something enormous moves through the transit level with a hollow metallic roar—train, ventilation piston, service machinery, impossible to tell from here.

Cold air rises from below.

Behind you, the snake camera angles toward the junction. Its red lens fixes on Mira.

“Camera,” she says.

She shifts her weight, reaches for the ladder, and her bad leg spasms hard enough to make her grip slip from the shaft lip. For one brutal second, she hangs half in, half out, elbows locked, teeth bared against a sound she refuses to make.

The probe behind you advances.

A voice crackles from its tiny speaker, distorted and close.

“Stay where you are. Medical assistance is available if you comply.”

Mira lets out one breath that almost becomes a laugh.

“Generous.”

A second device enters the trench behind the camera—small, wheeled, matte black. Not just surveillance. Its front casing opens like an insect’s mouth, revealing a compact taser prong assembly.

Mira sees it.

Her expression changes.

“Down,” she snaps. “Now would be ideal.”

Above and behind, boots hammer across the server room floor. Someone shouts for a cutting tool. The clean-agent fog still buys time, but not much.

Below, the ladder shaft vibrates.

A maintenance light flickers on three levels down, revealing a narrow platform and a painted arrow:

S3 TRANSIT UTILITY  
AUTHORIZED ENGINEERING ONLY

Then the black device fires.

Twin wires snap through the crawlspace toward Mira.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Shit!* I bat the wires away from Mira with my hand, sparks flying. "Go! I'm right behind you!" I push her into the shaft, then follow her down, not even looking at the probe.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The taser wires snap sideways under your strike.

Pain flashes white up your arm as one prong kisses your glove and spits sparks across the cable sheath. The charge grounds into the metal bracket beside you with a vicious crackle, filling the crawlspace with the stink of scorched insulation.

Mira drops into the shaft.

Her good hand catches the ladder. Her bad leg slams against the rung below, and her face goes bloodless for one sharp second, but she holds on.

Above, the wheeled device whirs forward, recalibrating.

“Deploy second charge,” a muffled voice orders from the trench behind you.

Mira descends fast now because gravity gives her no choice. Her boots scrape metal. One slips. She catches herself on the next rung with a gasp that tears out of her despite every bit of control she has left.

The shaft shakes around you.

Somewhere below, a train or service engine roars past behind concrete, so close the vibration rattles your teeth. Dust rains from the seams overhead. The maintenance light flickers, dies, then returns in sickly yellow pulses.

The probe reaches the lip of the shaft above.

Its red lens angles down.

A second taser assembly unfolds.

Mira reaches the S3 platform three levels below and half-falls onto the grated landing. She rolls onto one shoulder, dragging her injured leg clear just as your boots hit the last rungs above her.

The device fires again.

Twin wires streak down the shaft, bright and thin in the flickering light.

One prong strikes the ladder rung inches from your hand. The other snaps past your shoulder and vanishes into the dark. Electricity crawls across the metal ladder in jagged blue veins.

Mira sees it.

“Jump!” she shouts.

The charge builds, humming through the rungs, turning the shaft into a trap of live steel.

Below, the S3 platform waits beneath you.

Beyond it, a low concrete corridor stretches toward a heavy service door marked:

TRANSIT SERVICE TUNNEL  
EMERGENCY EXIT ROUTE — TRACKSIDE ACCESS

From somewhere on the other side of that door comes the distant rush of moving air.

And behind you, above, the hunters begin feeding a line down the shaft.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *Shit!* I let go of the ladder, dropping the last few feet. I hit the platform hard, grunting. "You okay?" I ask Mira, already looking for the next escape.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You drop the last few feet and land hard on the grated platform.

The impact booms through the shaft. Pain jolts up your legs. The ladder above crackles with blue electricity, each rung humming like a live wire. Sparks spit from the taser prongs and rain down in bright, dying flecks.

Mira lies on her side beside the platform rail, breathing through clenched teeth. Blood spreads darker across her thigh, but her eyes stay clear.

“Define okay,” she says. “Still conscious. Still moving.”

Above you, the hunters feed a black rappel line into the shaft. A gloved hand appears over the lip, then a helmet light angles down through the vertical dark.

“They’re coming,” Mira says.

The S3 platform is narrow, caged in by pipes and concrete. Warning placards cover the walls. Everything vibrates with the deep, rhythmic thunder of transit machinery nearby.

Ahead, the heavy service door bears stenciled white lettering:

TRANSIT SERVICE TUNNEL  
EMERGENCY EXIT ROUTE — TRACKSIDE ACCESS

A magnetic lock box glows red beside the handle.

To the left sits a recessed emergency cabinet with cracked glass: FIRST AID / FIRE AXE / RESPIRATOR MASKS.

To the right, a gray engineering panel hangs half-open, full of breakers, conduit labels, and a yellow manual override lever marked TUNNEL ACCESS FAILSAFE.

Beyond the service door, air rushes hard enough to whistle through the frame.

Mira sees the override lever.

“That opens it,” she says. “Or kills something important.”

Above, the first hunter starts descending the line.

The electrified ladder keeps them off the rungs, but not off the rope.

Mira plants one hand on the platform grating and drags herself toward the wall, leaving a slick red smear behind her.

“Choose fast.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "No time for important," I grunt, already moving towards the panel. *It's always something.* "Can you cover me?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira’s hand goes to the emergency cabinet.

“With optimism?” she says.

She drives her elbow into the cracked glass. It gives with a brittle pop, fragments scattering across the platform grating. Her fingers close around the fire axe handle first, then shift to a compact emergency flare clipped behind the respirator masks.

Above, the descending hunter drops another meter on the line, helmet light swinging across the shaft. The beam catches you at the engineering panel.

“Target at control box!” he shouts.

Mira twists onto her hip, plants her back against the wall, and strikes the flare cap against the platform rail.

White-red fire erupts in her hand.

The shaft floods with harsh light. The hunter recoils, visor flaring opaque with glare. Mira hurls the flare upward into the shaft, not at him, but past him.

It ricochets off concrete and lands against the rappel line.

Synthetic fiber starts to smoke.

The hunter swears and kicks away from the wall, one hand clamping above him, the other reaching for his sidearm.

You face the engineering panel.

Inside, labels crowd every breaker and conduit junction:

TRACK VENTILATION  
SIGNAL RELAY  
ACCESS MAGLOCK  
FAILSAFE OVERRIDE  
EMERGENCY DUMP

The yellow manual lever sits under a clear plastic guard secured by a red safety pin. Beside it, a warning placard reads:

FAILSAFE OVERRIDE MAY OPEN TRACKSIDE ACCESS DURING ACTIVE TRANSIT MOVEMENT.  
VERIFY PLATFORM CLEARANCE BEFORE USE.

The platform shakes again.

Beyond the service door, air pressure builds, a deep inhale from the tunnel beyond. Something fast moves somewhere out there, still distant but closing.

Mira grabs the fire axe now and drags it across her lap. Her face is slick with sweat, pale in the red flare glow.

“Whatever you’re doing,” she says, “do it mean.”

The hunter fires.

The shot cracks down the shaft and punches sparks from the wall above Mira’s shoulder. She flinches, then swings the axe up with both hands and hooks the blade around the hanging rope.

Not cutting.

Pulling.

The hunter’s line jerks sideways. He slams into the shaft wall, helmet light smashing against concrete. His second shot goes wide, shrieking into the electrified ladder with a blue-white burst.

The yellow lever in front of you hums faintly through the panel housing.

A status diode beside ACCESS MAGLOCK blinks red.

Another diode beside TRACK VENTILATION flips from green to amber.

The system is already reacting to the disturbance. Maybe to the open panel. Maybe to the nearby train. Maybe to everything going wrong at once.

Above, more voices echo down the shaft.

“Line compromised!”

“Second man, hold!”

“Cut power to ladder!”

Mira’s grip slips on the axe handle. Blood from her thigh spreads under her, turning the platform grating slick beneath her boot.

The rappel line smokes harder now where the flare burns against it. The hunter hanging from it looks down, then up, then down again. His confidence drains fast.

The service door ahead gives a heavy mechanical clunk.

Not open.

Preparing.

The maglock box remains red.

The panel gives you two obvious options:

The yellow FAILSAFE OVERRIDE lever, still pinned under the guard.

Or the breaker labeled ACCESS MAGLOCK, protected by a smaller metal latch and a warning tag that reads:

DO NOT CYCLE UNDER LOAD. LOCK FAILURE POSSIBLE.

Behind you, the rope strands start to snap one by one.

Mira looks from the hunter to you.

“Now,” she says through clenched teeth. “Any version of now works.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I yank the plastic guard off and hit the yellow lever. "Hold on, Mira!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Beyond the stairwell door, you hear the alarm flatten into a distant metallic whine. Beneath it: footsteps. Two sets, climbing fast. A third stays still, a radio hissing somewhere below.

“Hold the garage exit,” a voice says. “Let them come down.”

Through the narrow wired-glass window, you see an empty landing and the top of the descending flight. The next landing sits out of sight. Above you, a loose strip of emergency lighting flickers over the stairs toward the roof.

Mira’s weight shifts against your shoulder.

“Service tunnel needs a badge,” she whispers. “Mine still works. Maybe.”

The climbing footsteps stop.

You hear a soft scrape just below the landing, followed by the unmistakable click of a weapon’s safety.

Behind you, at the far end of the corridor, the elevator chimes.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I glance back at the elevator, then down at the stairwell.* "Roof." *I start moving Mira towards the flickering light, trying to be quick but gentle.* "Can you manage a few more steps?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“Six,” Mira whispers. “Then ask again.”

You feel her good leg take more of her weight. Her breath catches with each step, but she keeps the sound behind clenched teeth.

Below you, the stairwell door bangs open.

“Stairs. Going up.”

You hear boots strike the landing, then a sharp command stops them.

“Wait. Check the shaft.”

Above you, the flickering light reveals a narrow maintenance landing. Six steps beyond it stands the roof door: gray steel, push bar, a black reader beside the frame. Through its small window, you see rain shining against ventilation housings.

Mira holds out her badge. A split runs through the plastic, stopping just short of the chip.

“Reader first,” she says. “The bar triggers a lockdown without it.”

Your earpiece crackles.

“Roof is exposed.” Your handler’s voice comes through thin and clipped. “No aircraft. North side, window-cleaning cradle.”

Below you, the boots start again.

Beside the roof door, you notice a fresh smear of water across the otherwise dry floor. The reader glows green.

You hear the push bar ease inward from the other side.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the roof door scrape open before you reach the final step.

Through the widening gap, you see a dark rain jacket, an empty hand, then a pistol held low against a thigh. The stranger faces outward, toward the ventilation housings—not into the stairwell.

“North side is clear,” he says into a throat mic. “Bring them through.”

In your earpiece, your handler answers immediately.

“Don’t trust that.”

Mira’s fingers tighten around your sleeve. You feel her injured leg buckle, then catch against the edge of a step.

“Badge,” she whispers. “Look at his badge.”

Beneath the stranger’s open jacket, you see a white security credential with Mira’s photograph.

Below you, the pursuing boots fall silent again.

You hear a radio hiss from both directions at once.

The stranger begins to turn.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push Mira back, shielding her with my body, and draw my sidearm.* "Drop it!" I shout, aiming at the man.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You see his empty hand rise. The pistol stays low for half a second too long.

Then his fingers open.

You hear the weapon strike concrete and slide against the doorstop.

“Keep your sight on me,” he says. “Just don’t let that door shut.”

Through the gap behind him, you see a cable running from the exterior reader to a small black box clipped inside his jacket. Its indicator flashes green in time with the reader.

Against your back, you feel Mira go rigid.

“That’s my access token,” she whispers. “He’s keeping it alive.”

From below, you hear a quiet metallic rattle. Not footsteps this time. Something taps the underside of the railing.

The stranger’s raised hand trembles.

“Your handler sends you north?” he asks.

Your earpiece clicks.

“Do not engage. Take the cradle.”

Beyond the stranger’s shoulder, through the rain, you see the north parapet. A yellow window-cleaning cradle hangs just below its edge.

You also see a thin red line stretched across the roof-door opening at ankle height. One end disappears behind the frame. The other leads toward the cradle.

“Look down,” the stranger says.

Below you, a voice begins counting.

“Three.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the barricade creak under pressure from the corridor. Once. Then nothing.

Inside the server room, you have cold air, blue status lights, and the constant rush of cooling fans. No windows. One door. Through the gap beneath it, you see a shadow interrupt the corridor light.

You hear no further counting.

Beside the nearest rack, you see Mira press both hands against her injured thigh.

“Thinking is good,” she says. “Something against this wound is better.”

Within reach, you see a wall-mounted first-aid kit. Beside it, a fire evacuation diagram shows the server room adjoining a cable maintenance passage. You can make out the corresponding access panel behind the last rack: four recessed fasteners, no handle.

Your earpiece crackles.

“Confirm your location.”

At the same moment, you hear three light knocks on the door.

“The token expires in ninety seconds,” the stranger says through the steel. “After that, every reader rejects it. Including the maintenance exits.”

You see Mira shake her head.

“Readers, yes. Fire releases, no.”

On the evacuation diagram, you see a red square beside the maintenance panel.

Outside, the shadow beneath the door remains perfectly still.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I rip the first aid kit off the wall.* "Hold this on it." *I shove the kit into Mira's hands, then move to the maintenance panel.* "Help me with these fasteners."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You see four slotted fasteners recessed into the panel, each marked with a quarter-turn arrow. Beside the bottom one, a red label reads: **EQUALIZE PRESSURE BEFORE OPENING.**

“Use a coin,” Mira says. “Or the trauma shears.”

Behind you, you hear plastic packaging tear. In the panel’s brushed-metal reflection, you see her press a thick dressing against her thigh.

“I can hold pressure or crawl over there. Not both.”

The red square on the evacuation diagram corresponds to a small lever beneath a transparent cover. Above it, you see another warning: **MANUAL VENT — LOCAL ALARM.**

Your earpiece hisses.

“Do not enter the cable passage.”

Outside the door, you hear the stranger speak at almost the same instant.

“Don’t open that panel yet.”

Then you hear it through the metal: a cooling fan winding down somewhere on the other side. Beneath its fading whine comes a faint cough.

Mira’s voice drops.

“That passage is supposed to be empty.”

At the barricade, you hear the stranger lower his voice.

“Someone’s in there with you. Keep the panel shut.”

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I look at the panel, then back at Mira, then at the door. "Who's in there?" I whisper back. *I grab the trauma shears from the kit.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Through the steel door, you hear a scrape as the stranger moves closer.

“Building engineer. Gray coveralls. Ask her which way the vent draws.”

From behind the panel, you hear another cough.

“Away from you,” a woman answers. “Until the fire system reverses it. Keep that lever down.”

You see Mira lift her head.

“Sana?”

“Mira?” The voice sharpens. “How many with you?”

“One.”

“Then who’s talking outside?”

At the door, you hear nothing.

Between the server racks, you see a blue status light change to amber. Another follows. The rush of cooling air weakens against your face.

You hear Sana press something against the other side of the panel.

“Four quarter-turns. Leave the bottom fastener until last—the panel tips inward. There’s a ladder here to the loading dock.”

Your earpiece clicks twice.

“Operative. Answer.”

Beside the barricade, you see a narrow rectangle slide beneath the door: a white security credential, Mira’s photograph facing up.

“The token buys you sixty seconds,” the stranger says. “She knows the route. Take it.”

From farther down the corridor, you hear boots approach.

This time, they don’t stop.

In your hand, the trauma shears catch the amber light. Their flat tip looks narrow enough for the recessed slots.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I look at the shears, then the panel.* "Sana, can you push the panel inward once the fasteners are loose?" *I start turning the top two fasteners quickly.* "Let's move, Mira."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
“Toward me, yes,” you hear Sana say. “There’s room. Keep your feet clear.”

Under the shears, you feel the second upper fastener release with a small, sharp click. The panel’s top edge separates from its gasket. Through the slit, you smell hot dust.

Behind you, you hear Mira drag herself closer, one heel scraping the floor.

“Just get it open,” she says.

Through the door comes a hard command.

“Hands where we can see them.”

You hear the stranger answer, calm now.

“Keep your weapons down. There’s oxygen equipment in here.”

Beside you, Mira gives a tight shake of her head.

You see no oxygen cylinders among the racks.

Through the panel slit, you see a narrow flashlight beam settle on the two remaining fasteners.

“Lower left, then lower right,” Sana says. “There’s no pressure difference now. No need for the lever.”

Your earpiece crackles.

“Whoever offers you the loading dock, ask about the flood gate.”

Beyond the panel, you hear Sana draw a breath.

“The gate’s shut,” she says. “The pedestrian hatch isn’t.”

At the barricade, you hear a violent impact. The nearest rack shudders.

You see Mira brace the dressing beneath her belt, freeing one blood-slick hand.

“Two more,” she whispers.

Through the slit, you see Sana’s fingers curl around the panel’s upper edge, ready to take its weight.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push the shears into the lower-left fastener, twisting hard.* "Ready, Sana?" *I don't wait for an answer, moving the shears to the last one.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You feel resistance through the shears at the last fastener. Unlike the others, its slot sits crooked, the metal around it dented.

“Ready,” you hear Sana say. “Don’t force that one. Lift the panel a little—it binds under the weight.”

Through the upper gap, you see her fingers tighten. The panel rises a fraction. Against the shears, you feel the resistance ease.

Behind you, another impact drives the barricade across the floor. You hear a cable snap taut, then the clatter of a server sliding off its rails.

“Stop hitting the door!” the stranger shouts.

You hear a gunshot. One. Close enough to leave a thin ringing beneath the fans.

Beside your knee, you see Mira freeze.

Through the panel, Sana’s flashlight illuminates a narrow grated platform and a ladder descending into darkness. On the opposite wall, you make out a yellow depth marker. Water glints below its lowest number.

“Ankle-deep at the bottom,” you hear her say. “Stay on the grating.”

Your earpiece carries a breath, then your handler’s voice.

“Ask her why the water’s moving.”

Below the platform, you see a scrap of white plastic drift past the ladder—and accelerate.

Against the shears, the last fastener sits loose enough to turn.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Moving fast," I mutter, twisting the last fastener. "Sana, why's the water moving?" *I shove the panel inward, ignoring the door.* "Mira, *go*!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the panel strike the grating, its clang swallowing Sana’s first words.

“Drain pumps,” she repeats. “Dock side. They pull toward the flood gate.”

Through the opening, you see her brace the panel against the passage wall. Her gray coveralls shine wet below the knees. Beside her boot, a tethered tool bag slides toward the ladder until its strap catches.

“Not ankle-deep anymore,” you hear her say.

You see Mira crawl through the opening, keeping her injured leg straight. Sana catches her beneath the arms and pulls her onto the platform.

Beyond them, you see another route: a narrow ledge running above the water to a red wheel beneath an **EMERGENCY EGRESS** sign.

“That hatch?” Mira asks.

“Yes. No badge.”

Behind you, you hear the barricade scrape again—slowly this time. Through the gap beneath the server-room door, you see the white credential disappear under a spreading ribbon of blood.

Your earpiece clicks.

“Leave Mira. You cannot carry her through.”

Across the opening, you see Mira’s eyes settle on yours. You hear no protest.

Then you hear Sana turn the red wheel. A seal breaks with a hiss, and cool outside air reaches your face.

Through the widening hatch, you see wet concrete and the steady amber light of a loading-bay exit.

Behind you, the barricade shifts another inch.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I look at Mira, then at Sana.* "I'm not leaving her." *I turn and kick the barricade back against the door, buying us a precious second.* "Through the hatch, both of you. I'll cover you."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You feel the impact through your boot. Beyond the barricade, you hear a grunt and the slam of steel against the frame.

Through the maintenance opening, you see Sana duck beneath Mira’s arm and guide her along the ledge. Beneath their feet, water slaps the grating hard enough to throw spray.

“Yellow rail,” Sana says. “Nothing beyond it supports weight.”

You see Mira catch the rail with her free hand. At the hatch, her injured leg catches against the raised sill.

Behind the server-room door, you hear a radio.

“Hold fire. Defector stays alive.”

Your earpiece carries your handler’s voice.

“That order does not include you.”

Through the widening gap beside the barricade, you see the stranger’s empty hand pressed flat against the floor. His fingers move once.

“Door opens outward,” he says, barely audible. “They’re taking the hinges.”

You hear a powered tool bite into metal.

Across the passage, you see Sana haul Mira clear of the hatch. Beyond them, the loading bay remains empty beneath its amber light—but the roll-up vehicle door begins descending.

Beside the hatch, you spot a smaller personnel exit with a push bar.

You hear Sana test it.

No movement.

“Chain outside,” she calls.

Under the descending vehicle door, you see rainwater streaming across open pavement. The gap narrows to waist height.

Mira reaches back through the hatch and holds it open.

“You cover us from this side,” she says. “Come on.”

Behind you, the first hinge drops to the floor.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push the last server rack hard against the door, trying to buy more time.* "Mira, tell Sana to get out of sight. I'm coming through." *I look back at the maintenance opening.* "Sana, is there any way to lock that hatch from the outside?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You freeze with your hand on the door's push bar and listen.

For three seconds there is nothing but the alarm — that flat electronic whoop, echoing up the concrete shaft like it's coming from everywhere at once.

Then you hear it. Not footsteps. Worse. A radio squawk, two floors down, clipped and metallic: *"—south stairwell, moving up."* A pause. *"Both of them."*

Boots now. Four sets at least, disciplined, hitting the landings in rhythm. Getting louder. Getting closer.

Mira's hand tightens on your shoulder. "They know the route," she says, quiet. "That's an internal channel. That's my channel."

Below, a red emergency light strokes across the landing and vanishes. The stairwell itself is a trap now — no doors between you and them except the one you're standing at, and every landing above is a dead end once they're behind you.

To your left, the corridor runs dark past a row of shuttered offices. To your right, a narrow service alcove holds a mop sink, a breaker panel, and a ventilation grate — the kind that swallows a maintenance man but not a grown woman with a dead leg.

The boots are on the landing below. You can hear the change in the echo as they pass under the light.

Three floors. Maybe forty seconds.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content:
"Internal channel?" I hiss, pushing Mira behind me. *Damn it.*

*Forty seconds.* "Okay, new plan." I scan the offices. Locks are probably rigged. "Can you move on your own for a few steps?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
"No," Mira says. Flat. Honest. Then, before you can argue: "But I can crawl. Or I can be dragged. Choose fast."

She's already shrugging her arm off your shoulder, already dropping — a controlled collapse, one hand slapping the wall to slow it. Her dead leg drags behind her like it belongs to someone else. She gets low. She stays low. That's the plan she's offering you: cargo. Not a passenger.

Behind you, the stairwell door shudders in its frame. Not from a hand. From weight — someone leaning against it, testing. A voice on the other side, muffled but clear enough through the steel:

"Check the corridor."

You're out of time for the door. You step away from it, into the dark mouth of the office corridor, and pull Mira after you by the back of her jacket. She doesn't make a sound. She knows how to be dragged.

The first office door you try is a lever handle, unlocked, swinging inward before you've fully committed. Inside: a reception desk, dead monitors, a window that faces — you don't know what yet, you can't see. Beyond it, another window on the far wall. Adjacent building. Maybe eight feet of gap. Maybe more.

The stairwell door bangs open behind you. Light floods the corridor — swinging flashlights, boots on tile, the low chatter of men who've done this before.

"Clear left. Taking right."

They're coming down your hall.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You haul Mira backward, her boots scraping tile, and she lets you — no fight, no questions. The flashlights swing your way and miss you by the width of a doorframe.

The office. You're back inside it. Reception desk. Dead monitors. The corridor behind you fills with boots and clipped voices, and any second now someone sweeps this doorway.

But behind the desk there's a fire door. Half-hidden, wedged open a finger's width by a dead potted plant. Not on any map they're carrying.

You get it open. You drag Mira through. She gasps once — the dead leg catching on the threshold — and swallows it.

The shaft beyond is a service stair. Narrow. Unlit. No alarm light stroking the walls, just dust and the smell of old cigarettes. The steps go up and up and nowhere else.

Behind you, the office door bangs open. A flashlight beam sweeps the desk, the monitors, the fire door — and stops.

"There's a door."

You're already climbing. Mira under your arm, her good foot finding each riser, your arm carrying the rest. One flight. Two. The alarm thins out here, muffled by concrete — but so does everything else, including the radio.

It crackles. Finally. Your handler's voice, low and fast, cutting through the static: "—do you hear me? Do not take the south stair. Repeat, do *not*—"

You're not on the south stair.

"—roof access. North service shaft. Extraction in four minutes. If you can't make it, there is no second window."

The stairs end. A steel door. A narrow pane of wired glass showing black sky and the red blink of an antenna light.

Four minutes. Below you, boots on the service stairs. One flight down. Maybe less.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Four minutes," I breathe. "Can you make it that far?" I push on the door. Locked, of course. "Anything to get this open?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The handle doesn't give. Not locked — *sealed*. Somebody's engaged the mag-lock from the security panel, and the little red LED above the frame blinks a slow, patient rhythm that says it's drawing current.

Below you, boots hit a landing. Close enough that you hear the grunt of a man taking stairs two at a time.

Mira looks up at the door. Her face is grey in the dark, sweat cutting lines through the dust, but her eyes are still working. "Keypad," she says, nodding at the wall beside the frame. A nine-digit pad, no screen, just a slot for a badge. "There's a code. I know the code."

She says it like a warning.

"Every code is logged. Who entered it, when, which door. The moment I punch it in, my name goes on a timestamped record of *this* door, *this* minute. They'll know exactly where we went." She wets her lips. "And I don't have my badge anymore. I handed it to your people three days ago. So it won't be my name — it'll be a flag. *Unregistered user, restricted access.* Which is worse."

Below, a radio squawks. You can't make out the words. You don't need to.

Across the stairwell, mounted in a red case beside a fire hose reel, is a fire axe. Glass front. A small hammer on a chain. Breaking it triggers a local alarm — the kind that screams in *this* stairwell and nowhere else. Maybe.

Mira follows your eyes to the axe. Then back to the keypad. She's waiting for you to pick, and she's not going to pretend either one is good.

Two floors below, a boot scuffs concrete. Slower now. Careful. They've stopped running because they've figured out you can't run either.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You don't go through the fire door. You go sideways.

There's a door you missed in the dark — set into the stairwell's inner wall, unmarked, grey, no keypad, no LED. Just a thumb-latch worn shiny by a decade of telecom techs. It swings inward on a shallow room that isn't a room so much as a closet with ambitions: a rack of network gear bolted to the concrete, blinking amber, humming, cables in trays overhead and conduit running up through the ceiling. The building's nervous system, tucked behind a door nobody labels.

You get Mira inside. She lands on the floor against the rack and exhales like she's been holding that breath since the corridor.

The barricade is where it falls apart. You get a rolling tool cart and a fire extinguisher wedged under the latch, but the rack is bolted down and the walls are concrete and there is *nothing else*. It's a door that says *don't come in*, not a door that says *stay out*. Anyone with a shoulder and momentum is through it in two tries.

You wedge the last of it in place anyway. The cart squeals against the floor — a long, ugly metal shriek that runs down the stairwell like a struck bell.

Below you, the boots stop.

All of them. At once.

The silence that follows is worse than the running. You can hear the alarm in the main corridor now, faint through two walls. You can hear the rack fan. You can hear Mira breathing through her teeth.

Then a voice comes up the stairwell. Not a radio. A man's voice, unhurried, pitched to carry, and it is *not* shouting:

"Mira. We know you're on the north shaft. We know you're above the third floor. There are men at the roof door and men on the second landing." A pause, and something in it that's almost kind. "You've got a hurt leg and a stranger's arm. Come down and this is a medical transfer. Stay up there and it's a recovery."

Mira's eyes find yours in the dark. She doesn't answer him. She's waiting.

Above the rack, in a grey box bolted to the wall, a red LED blinks — the same patient rhythm as the roof door's mag-lock. The head-end controller. Every lock in this building answers to that box. The roof door is ten feet away through a concrete wall, and its current is running through a cable you can reach with a screwdriver.

But there's a tamper loop. You can see it — a thin wire threaded through the enclosure's screw, cheap and obvious. Break it and the panel screams to the security desk: *someone's in the closet.*

Below, the voice has stopped. The stairs have gone quiet in a different way now. The kind of quiet where men are moving without talking.

Somewhere above, four floors up, a helicopter you can't hear yet is either coming or it isn't.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Medical transfer, my ass," I mutter. I look at the control box. "Alright, Mira. Give me that code."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira recites the digits without hesitating, the way you say a thing you've said a thousand times and hoped never to say again. Nine numbers, low and even, then a tenth she adds under her breath like it's a correction. "If it's been rotated, the last digit changes. It rotates on the first. It's the fourth."

She says it all in one breath, then looks at the door.

The first shove hits the cart like a truck. The whole barricade jumps — the extinguisher skids an inch, the latch groans, and a sliver of stairwell light cuts across the concrete floor. Boots scrape. Somebody on the other side laughs, short and without humor, the laugh of a man who's done this a hundred times and is mildly bored.

Second shove doesn't come. That's the problem. The silence stretches, and in it you hear a new sound: a keycard reader chirping on the far side of the wall, once, twice, denied. Then a voice, quiet, to someone else: "Not master. It's a telecom room. Get the ram."

Mira's hand finds your sleeve. "Ram," she says. "That's a two-man job. Two minutes to bring it up. Maybe less."

Above the rack, the head-end controller blinks its patient red. The tamper wire is still threaded through the screw, thin as a hair, catching the LED's glow.

And then — in your ear, the radio, static breaking open like a wave: "—change of plan. North shaft is blown. They're stacking the roof. I'm moving extraction to the *west* face, fourth floor fire escape. Two minutes. Repeat, *two minutes*, west face. If you're not on it, we are gone."

Mira hears it too. She's close enough to your jaw that the earpiece leaks. She doesn't say anything. She just looks at the door, then at the tamper wire, then at you — and for the first time since the corridor, there's something in her face that isn't steadiness. It's arithmetic.

Two minutes. A ram coming up the stairs. A code that will flag you, a wire that will scream, and a fire escape on the wrong side of a building whose every lock answers to a box you can reach with a screwdriver.

Somewhere outside, faint, the helicopter is finally audible. Low. Getting lower.

The cart shudders again — not a shove this time. A *test*. Someone pressing a palm flat against the door, feeling for the give.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "West face, fourth floor," I repeat, looking at Mira. "Okay, new plan. Give me the code for this box. And be ready to move." *No time for subtlety.* I reach for the tamper wire.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira gives you the code fast and flat, like a phone number she's never going to forget and never wants to say again: nine digits, and then a tenth — "Four. If it's rotated. It's not, it's not the first yet."

Then, quieter, because she can hear the cart creak under someone's palm: "That's the installer code. It doesn't go to building security. It goes to the vendor's remote log, off-site, and nobody reads that queue unless a tech opens a ticket. You get four minutes of *nobody watching*. After that it's a line item with my name on it either way."

Below you, the test ends. The next sound is a count.

"Three —"

The panel cover is two screws, quarter-turn, and behind it a board of relays glowing green and a bundle of conductors zip-tied into a neat spine. The tamper wire runs through the enclosure screw to a contact, thin as a hair, waiting for the exact wrong pull.

"Two —"

You get the screwdriver onto the terminal. Mira's hand is flat on the concrete, bracing, her bad leg folded under her like something she's decided to leave behind. She's watching the door. She's not watching you. That's a kind of trust.

"One —"

The ram hits.

The cart goes over. The extinguisher rolls across the floor and knocks against the rack with a *boom* that's almost as loud as the ram itself, and the door swings inward six inches, hanging off its latch, and a flashlight beam cuts through the gap and sweeps the wall — and stops on the red LED.

"There. He's at the box."

You bridge the tamper terminal. The LED doesn't flicker. The relay under your thumb clicks once, soft as a knuckle.

And the north shaft lets go.

Every mag-lock in the stack releases at once — you hear it as a sound, a chain of heavy clunks running up and down the stairwell like dominoes, the roof door above you thudding open into the night. The corridor alarm changes key. A new klaxon joins it, deeper, the building's fire signal, and somewhere below a voice says "—that's not us, that's *not us*—" and a radio drowns in a wash of channels all talking over each other.

Then the elevators recall. Two cars, far below, ding in unison and start climbing to the lobby with their doors locked open, which means every guard in the building is now standing in a stairwell with an alarm that says *evacuate* and a panel that says *fire* and a target that the panel has just told them is in a telecom closet.

The flashlight in the doorway wavers. Pulls back.

"That's a *release*," someone says, and there's something new in his voice. Not calm anymore. "He's got the head-end."

The voice from the stairwell — the unhurried one — answers from two landings down, and now it's brisk: "Fire protocol is a building-wide unlock. West face included. He just opened his own way out." A pause. "Forget the closet. Move to the west landing. Cut him off at the escape."

Boots. Turning. Going *down* past you, fast, to beat you to the west face.

Mira looks up at you, and there's no steadiness left in her face at all, just the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is: the west fire escape door is now unlocked, four floors down and one wall over, and the men who know the building better than you do are already on their way to it, and the helicopter is loud enough now that you can feel it through the concrete in your heels.

The closet door hangs open behind you. The stairwell is dark and full of doors that are all, suddenly, unlocked.

Two minutes. West face. Fourth floor.

Mira holds up one hand. Not to be carried. To be *counted*.

"How many between us and it?"

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I grab Mira's arm, pulling her up. "Doesn't matter. We're taking the stairs down. They're going *down* the stairs, not up." *Let's go.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
She gets her good leg under her before you've finished pulling. Her hand closes on your forearm, fingernails digging in, and she comes up off the concrete in one hard, ugly motion that costs her everything she has left. She doesn't ask about the count. She already knows the count is one thing that doesn't change.

Out into the shaft.

The north stairwell is a black column with doors hanging open on every landing — mag-locks released, thumb-latches slack, the whole spine of the building standing with its mouth open. The emergency lights are still stroking red down the walls, but they're slower now, out of sync with the fire klaxon, like the building can't decide which disaster it's having.

And below you, boots. Descending. Fast. A whole column of them, radios squawking and overlapping, someone calling "west landing, west landing, on me" — and the sound is *moving down and away*, thinning out, going where the men have decided the fight is.

Mira hears it too. "They're going to the ground," she breathes, right at your ear. "West face entrance. They're going to climb the escape from below and catch us coming out."

One flight. Two. The stairwell is empty above the second landing, and the third landing — where the unhurried voice came from — is just a dark square of concrete with a spent glow-stick bleeding green on the floor. Somebody stepped on it on the way past.

At the fourth floor, a corridor door. Unlocked. You take it.

The corridor is worse than the stairs. It's carpeted and low-ceilinged and full of *noise* — the fire klaxon in here is at full volume, hammering off the drop ceiling, and the sprinkler heads along the whole run are weeping a thin mist that's already darkening the carpet in patches. Office doors, glass fronts, dead monitors behind them like rows of closed eyes. Somewhere a printer is spitting out page after page of nothing.

Mira drags. Her boot heel catches the carpet seam and she goes down to one knee, and you don't have time to be gentle, and she doesn't ask you to be. Up. Forward. The corridor runs west, and at the far end there's a red-lit sign over a door that says **FIRE EXIT — DO NOT BLOCK**, and the door is propped open a hand's width with a wet-floor cone, and through the gap you can see *sky* — black, torn, moving.

The helicopter is right there. Not visible yet, but the whole corridor is breathing with it — the ceiling tiles lifting and settling, the mist off the sprinklers blowing sideways, a stack of loose paper on a desk at the window end peeling up and scattering like startled birds.

Fifteen feet from the door, the fire escape outside rings.

*Clang. Clang-clang.* Boots. On the grating. Coming *up*, fast, and not one set of them. Below and to the left, through the misted glass, a flashlight beam sweeps up the rusted iron and paints the underside of the fire escape platform with a hard white line.

They're two landings down and climbing.

Mira's hand tightens. She's looking at the door, then at the glass beside it, then at you. The door opens onto a platform barely wide enough for two people, a drop of four floors, and a helicopter that can't land and won't hover forever — and it's the only exit in the building that doesn't have a man on it yet.

Behind you, at the far end of the corridor, the stairwell door bangs.

A voice, not far. "Corridor four. Clear it."

Mira says, very quietly, "If we go out, we're on a shelf. If we stay, we're in a box."

Outside, the boots ring again — closer. Inside, the boots are on the carpet now, and carpet doesn't echo, which is somehow worse.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Shelf it is." I push Mira toward the door, not giving her a chance to argue. *They're not expecting us to go out the window.* "Can you climb?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The door hits the stop and the night comes in.

Wind first — a wall of it, cold and hard, tearing through the doorway and stripping the mist off your face. Then sound: the fire klaxon still hammering behind you, the boot-ring of the grating, and *over* all of it the helicopter, so close now the whole platform is shaking with it, a flat chop-chop-chop you feel in your sternum.

Mira stumbles out onto the grating and drops to one knee against the rail. The platform is a shelf, exactly as she said — four feet deep, rusted, bolted to the building's west face with iron brackets older than either of you. Below it, four floors of black air and a parking lot full of sodium lights, tiny and orange. To your left, the fire escape runs up and down the face of the building like a spine. To your right, nothing but the drop.

Above, the helicopter is a black shape against torn cloud, side-on, holding fifty feet off the face. No landing. No door gunner. Just a light blinking on its belly and the downwash flattening the wet leaves of a rooftop garden four stories up.

Below you, the grating rings again — *clang, clang* — and a flashlight beam sweeps up the underside of the platform and stops dead on Mira's boot.

"Platform four!" A voice, close. One landing down. "He's on the platform!"

Then the corridor door behind you bangs, and a second voice, right at the doorway, barely ten feet back: "Corridor clear, on the — *there*—"

You're bracketed. Above, below, behind.

Mira looks up at you from the rail and answers the question you asked her outside the door. "No," she says, "I can't climb." Then she jerks her chin at the iron. "But I don't have to. The chopper's at *us*. We just have to hold the shelf."

She drags herself along the rail, one hand over hand, to a bracket at the platform's inner edge. There's a fat steel pin through it, a cotter key through the pin, and below the bracket the whole lower flight of the fire escape — the ladder down to the third-floor landing, the one the boots are climbing — hangs on a counterweight, waiting.

"Maintenance release," Mira says. Her voice is flat. "Cuts the ladder from this platform down. Drops it to the second landing. Anyone on it rides it down."

Below, the flashlight beam bobs, and a gloved hand slaps onto the platform's outer rail — six feet from Mira's foot. A man's head, a helmet, a shoulder, coming up over the edge.

The helicopter swings wide, hunting the face, its rotor wash slamming the platform hard enough that Mira's jacket snaps flat against her back.

Behind you, the corridor voice is *in the doorway*.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I grab the cotter key. "Hold on." *This is gonna be rough.* I give it a hard pull.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The key comes free.

The pin doesn't. It's painted over, seated in rust, and for one long second nothing happens at all — you're hanging off a bracket on a shaking platform with the cotter key in your fist and a man's helmeted head rising six feet to your left, and the whole escape is a stubborn piece of iron that doesn't care.

Then the counterweight shifts.

The pin shears sideways and the lower flight goes. Not falls — *goes*, all at once, like a held breath let out. The ladder tears loose from its brackets with a shriek of metal that cuts clean through the rotor noise, and the man on it doesn't have time to scream. His gloved hand claws at the platform edge, misses by inches, and then he's gone — down, riding the ladder, his flashlight tumbling free and strobing off the concrete wall all the way to the second landing, where the whole flight slams into the railing below with a crash that shakes the shelf under your feet.

The flashlight beam comes to rest pointing up, useless, at the bottom of the black.

Mira is flat against the inner wall of the platform, both hands on the bracket, her dead leg splayed behind her, and she's still here. The shelf held. She said it would.

The helicopter comes back around.

It swings in from the north, side-on, sixty feet off the face and closing, its searchlight raking down the building and then *stopping* — a white column on the platform, on you, on Mira, so bright that the rust on the grating goes white and the rain mist turns to fire. The downwash hits like a hand and pins you both to the wall. Over the rotor noise, a voice from the chopper's open door — a crewman, harnessed, one boot on the skid, a hoist cable spooling down out of the belly:

"*One at a time! Hook the line, hook the line!*"

The cable swings toward you. A steel hook on a carabiner, spinning in the wash, coming down to chest height, close enough to grab.

Behind you, the corridor door.

The second man isn't shouting anymore. He's braced in the doorway with the doorframe for cover, and in the strobing light off the chopper you can see what he's holding — not a rifle. A pistol, two hands, aimed steady at the cable, at the hook, at the space between you and the only way off this shelf. He doesn't fire. He doesn't have to. He's letting you know the line is a trap and he's the one who decides when it springs.

"Take the hook," he says, flat, over the noise, "and I take the line."

Mira sees him. She sees the hook. She's still holding the bracket, and she looks at you, and there's no arithmetic in her face anymore — just the two things she can't carry and can't drop.

The cable swings past your shoulder, back out into the wash, and starts to swing in again.

The pistol tracks it.

The chopper is holding steady, but a helicopter can't hold forever, and the crewman in the door is shouting something the wind eats.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Mira, you first." I step in front of her, shielding her from the door. *I've got an idea.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira doesn't move.

She's got both hands on the bracket and her eyes on you, and she reads the shield you just made of your body the way she read the code on the door — instantly, and without liking it.

"No," she says. "You're standing in front of the gun."

The hook swings in again. It's close now — chest height, spinning slow in the wash, a carabiner and a steel hook and a cable that disappears up into the belly of the chopper. It comes within arm's reach of the platform's outer rail and then the wash catches it and it swings back out into the black.

The crewman in the door sees it. "*Again! Next pass!*" — and the chopper is drifting, drifting west, sliding off the face because a helicopter can't hover still in a crosswind and the pilot is fighting for every inch. The searchlight column crawls across the grating, and for a second the platform is dark.

In the dark, the pistol doesn't move. It's still there, two-handed, braced on the doorframe — and now it's aimed not at the hook but at the space just left of it. At Mira. At the gap between the rail and the bracket, where a woman with a dead leg would have to be, and would have to reach, and would have to stand up.

He's not going to shoot the cable. He's going to shoot whoever grabs it, on the assumption that whoever grabs it is her, because she's the one who matters, and you're just the arm.

Mira knows it too. She's still got hold of the bracket and she hasn't let go, and she says, fast and low, over the rotor noise: "He won't fire at you. You're a nobody. The whole point of this is me alive and quiet." She swallows. "If I go, I'm not quiet. If I go, he's got a shot he'll take."

Behind the gunman, the corridor door bangs — more boots, more men, arriving. The gunman doesn't look back. He doesn't have to. He's just holding the line, and now he's got a corridor full of backup behind him and a helicopter that keeps sliding off the face and a shelf with two people on it and nowhere to go.

The searchlight sweeps back. The hook comes in a third time, lower now, swinging at hip height, close enough that you could take it without moving your feet.

The chopper's engine note changes. Pitched up. The pilot is on the radio, and the crewman in the door is looking at the instrument panel and then at you and shaking his head — *hurry, hurry, hurry* — and the helicopter starts to slide west again, slow, the cable trailing out over the drop.

Mira looks at the hook. Then at you, standing between her and the gun.

"Whatever the idea is," she says, "it's now."

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Okay, you're the distraction." I push her hard towards the inner wall, then lunge for the hook. *Gotta make this count.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The Narrator maintains exceptional consistency throughout - the tense, cinematic voice never wavers, the pacing remains tight, and the character's role as an omniscient but focused observer stays constant from first turn to last.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are strong but later turns (especially 16-22) show more sophisticated action choreography, better environmental detail, and more nuanced character moments. No verbosity creep or repetitive descriptions.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Relentless forward momentum. Each turn escalates stakes naturally - from corridor chase to stairwell trap to server room to fire escape to helicopter extraction. The tension builds consistently without repetitive beats or stagnation.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user choices. When user reverses direction (turn 5), goes to server room (turn 9), or makes tactical decisions (turns 19, 21, 23), the Narrator seamlessly incorporates these into the narrative flow while maintaining logical consequences.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Consistently respects user agency. Never writes the Operative's actions or decisions. Always presents situations and waits for user input. Mira's dialogue and actions serve the narrative without railroading.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Strong temporal consistency. The 'four minutes to extraction' countdown is tracked well, alarm progression feels natural, and physical time (Mira's injury, fatigue, helicopter approach) develops logically. Minor issue: exact timing of some sequences could be clearer.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is lean and purposeful throughout. Descriptive language serves tension and atmosphere without becoming flowery. 'Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves' is evocative but functional.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Minimal repetition. Some recurring phrases ('boots on concrete', 'flashlight beam') but used for rhythmic effect rather than lazy writing. Each description of similar elements (doors, stairs, alarms) varies meaningfully.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Mira's competence shown through her actions and knowledge, not stated. Tension conveyed through environmental details, sound, and physical sensations rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in character interactions. Mira's 'That's an internal channel' carries weight about betrayal. The gunman's tactical choices reveal professional calculation. Dialogue carries meaning beyond surface words.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Masterful pacing. Varies sentence length and structure to match action intensity. Short, clipped sentences during immediate danger, longer descriptive passages during brief respites. Never rushes or drags.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional thriller/action narrative that maintains cinematic tension throughout. The Narrator demonstrates sophisticated understanding of pacing, stakes escalation, and environmental storytelling. Particularly strong in the final act with the fire escape sequence - complex action choreography handled with clarity and mounting tension. Minor weaknesses in some temporal details, but overall a highly engaging and well-crafted session that respects user agency while driving compelling narrative momentum.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The heavy steel door cracks open an inch under your hand, letting through a draft of cool, stale air.

The concrete shaft functions like an amplifier. Beneath the muffled thrum of the facility alarm, the sound is sharp and immediate: combat boots striking steel treads, moving fast. Two floors down, maybe less. A flashlight beam cuts a frantic, geometric slice across the ceiling of the landing below, followed by the metallic clatter of a rifle sling hitting tactical gear. 

"Team two, move up! Secure the upper landing!" a voice shouts, echoing off the cinderblock walls. 

They are not sweeping methodically. They are sprinting straight up the central riser toward your floor. 

Beside you, Mira shifts her weight, her knuckles white against the doorframe as she tracks the rising noise. She looks toward the corridor behind you, then down at the stairs. 

You have less than ten seconds before the point man rounds the landing below.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Damn it!" I hiss, yanking Mira back from the door. *No time for the stairs.* I glance down the corridor we just came from, then at Mira's leg. "We're going in there." I point to a maintenance closet door a few feet away. "Can you make it?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira grinds her teeth, a sharp hiss escaping through her clenched jaw. 

"Watch me," she whispers.

She throws her weight forward, dragging the dead weight of her bad leg across the floor. You reach the maintenance closet door just as the metal latch yields under your hand. 

Inside, the air smells of pine disinfectant, damp canvas, and rust. It is suffocatingly tight—barely enough space for two bodies squeezed between wire shelving units and a rolling mop bucket. 

You pull the door shut until the catch clicks into place. 

A split second later, the stairwell fire door slams open against the concrete wall with a violent crash. 

"Clear the hall! Check the north corners!" 

Heavy tactical boots pound across the linoleum just inches from where you stand. The narrow crack beneath the closet door flickers with shadows, cut through by the frantic, pulsing red of the emergency strobes. 

Mira presses her back against the wire rack, her knuckles white as she grips the metal frame to keep herself upright. Her breathing is shallow, ragged, and far too loud in the enclosed space. She catches your eye in the gloom, her chest heaving as she fights to stay silent.

A radio squawks outside, harsh and staticky: *"Command, hallway is clear. Initiating sweep of secondary rooms."*

The footsteps slow. A pair of combat boots stops directly in front of your door. 

The brass handle jiggles.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pivot hard, abandoning the downward descent and hauling Mira upward against the grain of your escape plan. 

Mira gasps as the abrupt change in direction wrenches her injured leg, but she clamps her teeth shut against the pain and clutches your arm with a desperate, white-knuckled grip. Her good foot scrambles against the concrete steps, fighting for traction with every riser.

Below you, the stairwell erupts.

"Target on the stairs! Upper landing! Move, move, move!"

Flashlight beams lance through the vertical gap between the flights, slicing through the gloom. The sharp, concussive crack of a rifle shot echoes up the shaft, and concrete chips blast from the wall inches above your head, showering your neck and shoulders with chalky dust. 

"Rooftop," Mira wheezes, her breath rattling in her chest as she fights to keep pace. "Only way left."

The heavy fire door for the top level looms just half a flight above you—a reinforced steel hatch marked with yellow hazard stripes. At the center of the frame sits an electronic mag-lock, its indicator light glowing an unforgiving, solid red. 

Beneath you, the thudding rush of combat boots on the metal stairs closes the distance with terrifying speed.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Shit, shit, shit!" I curse under my breath. *Mag-lock, of course it's mag-locked.* I shove Mira forward. "Kick it! Anything!" I'm already pulling out my multi-tool, fumbling with the tiny picks. "Get ready to move!"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Mira slams her good shoulder against the steel door, driving the heel of her boot into the push-bar with a desperate crack. 

The heavy door shudders, but the magnetic seal does not yield. It holds rigid, bonded by hundreds of pounds of electromagnetic force. 

"It won't give!" she gasps, slumping against the frame to give you room, her breath whistling sharp between her teeth. 

You jam the thinnest blade of the multi-tool into the seam of the electronic housing mounted beside the frame. Metal screeches against metal. You lever your weight against the casing, popping the plastic faceplate free. It clatters down the steps, exposing a tight bundle of colored wiring and a blinking circuit board. 

Below you, the footfalls hit the final landing. 

"Rooftop access! Cut them off!" 

A beam of blinding white tactical light sweeps up through the stairwell grating, catching you in its glare. A red laser dot dances across your forearm, jittery and frantic. They are not waiting to clear the corners. They are surging up the last flight, three steps at a time. 

Dust and the smell of ozone sting your nostrils. You see the main power leads—blue and red, shielded in braided nylon—tucked behind the green terminal block. 

Behind you, Mira grabs a loose piece of iron conduit from a discarded cable run, bracing herself against the wall with her weapon raised, ready to swing at the first head that crests the landing.

The lead pursuer’s helmet appears below, rounding the bend just six steps away.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The blast of sub-zero air hits you the instant the door seals. 

Rows of towering black server racks hum with a deafening, mechanical roar, their internal fans cycling icy drafts across the narrow aisles. Blinking columns of blue, green, and amber LEDs cast frantic, fractured shadows against the perforated floor tiles. 

Behind you, the heavy metal frame shudders violently. 

*THUD.* 

The barricade groans under the impact. Metal screams against metal as the pursuers throw their weight against the exterior. 

"Breaching kit! Get the thermal lance up here!" a voice barks through the seam, muffled but close enough to vibrate the steel panel. 

Mira slumps against the base of a server tower, her bad leg stretched out straight before her. Her skin has a pale, waxy sheen under the stark indicator lights, sweat plastering dark hair to her temples. She clutches her thigh with trembling hands, biting down hard on her lower lip to keep from crying out. 

"The door won't hold," she gasps, her voice barely carrying over the roar of the cooling units. "They have cutting gear. We have... two minutes. Maybe ninety seconds."

A high-pitched electronic whine cuts through the hum of the servers—the unmistakable charge cycle of a shape-charge frame being set against the exterior hinges. 

Ahead of you, the aisle splits. To the left, an emergency crawlspace hatch sits flush against the floor, its yellow latch locked in place. To the right, at the far end of the rack corridor, a reinforced glass observation window looks out into the facility's central atrium, three stories above the lobby floor.

The arming tone on the door hits a rapid, steady beep.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Crawlspace," I say, already moving towards it. "It's our only shot." I drop to my knees, fumbling with the latch. "Can you move at all?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The cold steel of the floor bites through your pants as your fingers hook under the recessed yellow handle. 

It sticks. A layer of dried maintenance sealant or a seized locking pin fights you. You throw your weight into the pull, muscle straining against the frozen lever, until the mechanism snaps open with a violent, echoing *CLACK*.

Behind you, Mira does not waste breath answering. She drags herself forward on her elbows and belly, pulling her dead weight across the perforated tiles like a soldier low-crawling through wire. Her teeth are sunk so deep into her lower lip that a thin bead of dark blood wells against her chin, but her eyes remain fixed on the opening. 

"Pull the grate," she grits out, reaching out to shove at your calf to spur you on. "Just get it open!"

You haul the rectangular hatch back on its heavy hinges. It groans, opening into a dark, narrow shaft crisscrossed with thick conduits and high-voltage fiber cables—a maintenance run dropping five feet into the crawlspace below.

At your back, the rapid beeping on the server room door ceases.

Silence hangs for a single, razor-thin heartbeat.

Then the hinges detonate.

A concussive shockwave slams through the server banks, shattering the nearest indicator screens in a spray of acrylic and sparks. The reinforced door tears inward from the blast, screeching against the improvised barricade as a blinding wall of smoke and fire rolls across the ceiling.

Through the ringing in your ears, the first flash-bang grenade clatters across the linoleum, spinning straight toward the open hatch.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: "Down! Get down!" I yell, shoving Mira's head before dropping into the crawlspace myself. *That was too close*.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You drop through the opening into the subterranean gloom just as the canister detonates.

A searing white flash bleaches the rim of the hatch above. The concussive punch slams into your skull like a blunt hammer, blasting a wave of scorching air and pulverized ceiling tile down the shaft. A brutal, deafening whine instantly drowns out the hum of the facility, vibrating deep in the bone behind your ears. 

You hit the sub-floor hard on hands and knees, the impact jarring up through your wrists. Beneath you, rigid metal framing and thick bundles of shielded data cables dig into your palms. 

Beside you in the dark, Mira lies curled on her side, hands clamped over her ears, her face contorted in agony as she fights through the sensory blast. Sparks from the ruptured server bank drizzle down through the open rectangular hatch above your heads, drifting like falling embers.

Above, heavy tactical boots stomp across the shattered server room floor. Muffled by the high-pitched ringing in your head, harsh voices bark through respirators.

"Clear left! Watch the racks!"

A tactical light beam lances straight down through the open hatch, spearing the dust-choked air inches past your shoulder. The smell of scorched cordite and melting wire insulation pours into the crawlspace, thick enough to choke on. 

The low-clearance space stretches out in front of you. To your left, the cable trays run toward a vertical exhaust riser that vents to the exterior wall.
