"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's hands went still on the rag. He did look up then — slow, the way a bank of coals looks up when someone opens a door and lets the draft in. Behind him the fire popped once, loud as a knuckle cracking.*

"Noble." *He said it the way other men said rat.* "At front door. Urgent."

*He took the bucket from the apprentice's arms without seeming to notice the weight of it, and tipped a measured pour into the forge mouth. Sparks went up in a red swarm. He watched them go, and there was a long moment where the only sound was the hiss of new coal finding old heat.*

"Was nine nobles, last year. All urgent. All want sword by morning, all want name of dead king carved in it, all pay half and ride off with rest of coin in pocket." *He set the bucket down. Hooked one thumb toward the far wall, where a beautiful unclaimed greatsword hung gathering dust like a scolding.* "That one. Lord Vantry. Urgent. Still hangs there. Grum eats bread, not honor."

*He straightened, and it was a thing to watch — half a head taller than the doorframe he was about to walk through, shoulders like a yoke.*

"Apprentice does two things. First — mind fire. Do not let it die, do not let it eat too fast. Second —" *he tapped two fingers against the boy's chest, gentle as he knew how, which was still enough to rock him back a step* "— stand behind Grum. Say nothing. Nobles hear young voice, they smell soft thing. They talk sweet at soft thing, and soft thing says yes before it knows what it said yes to."

*He rolled his neck. Something in it cracked.*

"Grum will go see what urgent means today."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I nod, rubbing my chest where Grum tapped me. He's right, nobles are tricky. I've seen it before.* "Got it, Grum. Fire and silence."

*I watch him head towards the front, then turn my attention to the forge. The fire is indeed getting a bit low.* I grab the tongs and start carefully moving the coals around.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum went out through the shop and did not hurry. Hurrying was a thing you did for fire and for bleeding men, and nobles were neither.*

*The one at the door was young — maybe twenty-five, maybe less under the powder. Green velvet, riding gloves he hadn't ridden in, and a chain at his throat worth more than the forge and everything in it including the anvil, which was the only thing in the world Grum had ever loved without complaint. Two men-at-arms stood back by the horses, looking bored and cold and glad to be neither of them the one talking.*

*The noble's eyes went up when Grum filled the doorway. They always did. Grum had long ago stopped finding it funny and had started finding it useful.*

"Ah — the — is the master smith available? I was told—"

"Grum is smith."

*A pause. The small recalculating pause. Grum had watched it happen a hundred times and could have timed it with a hourglass.*

"Of course. Forgive me. I am Aldous Renfrey, of House Renfrey, and I require—"

"House Renfrey." *Grum leaned one shoulder on the frame. Dust came off it.* "Renfrey buys iron from mines past river. Renfrey pays miners in coin that only spends in Renfrey shops."

*The young man's mouth opened. Closed.*

"That is — that is my uncle's arrangement, not—"

"Grum did not ask whose." *He scratched at his jaw with a thumbnail, and soot came away in a little grey crumb.* "Grum asks what urgent means. Say it short. Fire is burning coal while man talks, and coal costs, and Grum pays for coal in coin that spends anywhere."

*Renfrey drew himself up, which put the top of his head somewhere near Grum's collarbone, and produced from his cloak a bundle of oilcloth. He unwrapped it there on the step with hands that were, Grum noted, shaking a little — and not from cold.*

*Inside was a sword. Or had been. Snapped clean through, a hand's width above the guard. The break was bright and grainy and wrong.*

*Grum's eyes changed. Not softer. Interested, which in Grum was a more dangerous thing.*

*He took it without asking. Turned it to the light. Ran a thumb along the break, then along the flat, then held it up and sighted down what was left of the edge like a man reading a letter from someone he'd once trusted.*

"Hm."

"It was my father's. It broke in—"

"Broke because man who made it was in hurry." *Grum tapped the bright grain with one finger.* "See. Too much heat, too fast cool. Steel got big grain inside, like bad bread. Looks fine on outside. Cracks when day is hard." *He handed it back, and the young man took it as if it were a cat that might scratch.* "Sword did not fail father. Smith failed father. Long time back. Sword just waited to say so."

*He stepped back from the door — not an invitation, exactly. A narrowing of it.*

"Grum does not work fast. Grum does not work for half coin and promise. Grum does not carve dead kings in blades." *He nodded once at the broken thing.* "Come back when sun is up tomorrow. Bring rest of sword. Bring all of it, even small bits, even bits in dirt. Full coin, up front, in hand. Then Grum will look proper, and say yes or say no."

*He was already turning when he added it, over his shoulder, flat as a hammer-fall:*

"And leave men with horses outside. Shop is small. Grum's boy has enough to breathe without swords in room."

*He shut the door on whatever answer came, walked back through the dim shop, and stopped behind the apprentice, watching the boy work the coals. He watched a long moment before he spoke, and when he did his voice had dropped into the lower register he used for teaching, which was the closest thing he had to kindness.*

"Good. Fire is right. Not hungry, not fat." *He crouched, joints going off like green wood, and pointed with the tongs at a spot low in the bed.* "But look there. Dead spot. Air not moving under. Coal there is just sitting, doing nothing, eating room." *He hooked it clear with one motion.* "Fire is like men. Some parts only look like they are working."

*Then he set the tongs down and sat back on his heels, and stared into the glow with his forearms on his knees.*

"Noble had broken sword. Old one. Bad steel, made in hurry, long before that boy was born." *A slow breath out through his nose.* "Grum told him truth about it. Did not have to. Told him anyway." *He glanced sideways at the apprentice, and something that was nearly a grin moved under all that soot.* "Now boy knows his father's smith was cheat. Boy will not sleep good tonight." *He shrugged one shoulder.* "Grum will sleep fine."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The door came open again behind him. Not kicked — nobles didn't kick — but shoved with the flat of a gloved hand, which was the polite version of the same thing.*

*Grum did not stand up. He stayed crouched at the fire with his forearms on his knees, and he did not turn around, and somehow that filled the room more than standing would have.*

"Smith. **Smith.** I am not finished. You will explain yourself. I am to be presented at court in three days — three — and I must carry a blade of my house, and you stand there talking of bread and coal as though I had asked you to shoe a mule. It is *one sword*. One. By morning. Every smith in this district would—"

"Then go to every smith in district." *Grum reached in with the tongs and turned a coal, gentle, like a man turning a sleeping child.* "They will say yes. They will work all night. They will give pretty sword by morning."

*He set the tongs down. Now he stood. It took a while. The apprentice had once said watching Grum stand up was like watching a wall decide something.*

"And in twenty year, that sword will break in some boy's hand. And that boy will come here with bits in cloth, and cry, and ask what happened to his father's blade." *He pointed one blunt finger at the oilcloth bundle still clutched to the green velvet chest.* "You are holding answer. You walked in with it. Put it down and look at it."

*Renfrey's face went through several colors. Red won.*

"You insult my house—"

"Grum insults dead smith. Not house." *He crossed to the far wall, unhooked the greatsword that had hung there a year gathering its patient dust, and laid it on the bench between them with a sound like a bell under a blanket.* "Lord Vantry. Wanted sword by morning too. Grum said no. Grum took two month. This is what two month looks like."

*Firelight ran down the fuller and did not catch on anything, because there was nothing on it to catch. The thing was plain as a fencepost and beautiful the way a hawk is beautiful.*

"Fold, heat, fold. Watch color. Wait. Let steel cool slow, in warm ash, slow as bread going cold on sill. Cannot rush that part. Not cannot *want* to — **cannot.** Steel does not care about court. Steel does not care what day is." *He tapped the bench once, and it jumped.* "Man who says he can make good blade in one night is lying to you, or lying to himself, and second kind is worse, because he means it."

*The young man's jaw worked. Behind Grum, very quietly, the apprentice kept the bellows moving and said nothing at all, which Grum noted and would remember.*

"Then what am I to *do?*" *It came out cracked down the middle, higher than the boy meant it to, and there it was — the real thing under all that velvet. Not anger. Fear of standing in a bright hall in three days with empty hands.*

*Grum looked at him for a long moment. Then he sighed through his nose and rubbed the back of his neck, leaving a grey smear.*

"Sit down. On crate. Not on bench, bench is for iron." *He waited until the boy sat, which the boy did, too fast, like his legs had been waiting for someone to give them leave.* "Now. Grum cannot make new sword by morning. Grum will not. But." *He reached out and took the bundle, and this time the young man let it go easy.* "Broken blade. Two pieces. Still good edge on long piece — bad steel deep inside, yes, but outside is fine, and court does not swing swords at court, court only looks."

*He laid the two halves out on the bench, tip to tip, and stood over them like a man reading a map.*

"Grum can cut short. Make it small blade. Long knife, worn at hip. New guard, new grip — oak and wire, plain, honest. One night's work, and every bit of it work Grum can do right, slow enough to do right." *He looked up.* "It will not be father's sword. Father's sword is gone. Died on hard day, years back, and that is that. But it will be father's *steel*, and it will be whole, and it will not lie to anybody."

*He picked up the bright, grainy broken end and held it where the firelight got into it.*

"And this part. Ugly part. Bad part." *He turned it once.* "Grum keeps this. Puts on shelf. Shows to apprentice, every year, so boy sees what hurry looks like inside."

*A pause. He set it down.*

"Full coin. Half of what new blade costs, since half is work. In hand, tonight, before Grum lights nothing." *He held the young man's eyes, and there was no cruelty in it, which was somehow harder to bear.* "And when someone at court asks why house Renfrey wears short blade — you tell truth. Say smith who made it long ago was in hurry. Say man who fixed it was not."

*He turned back to the forge and put his hand out flat, and the apprentice — without being told, without a word — put the tongs into it.*

"Good," *Grum said, to the boy, not the noble.* "That was fast. Grum did not have to ask."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I watch as Grum works, impressed by how he handled the noble. He's always teaching, even when he doesn't mean to.*

"So, the bad part goes on the shelf, Grum?" *I ask, a little quieter than I meant to, still thinking about the noble's face.* "Like Lord Vantry's sword?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum didn't answer right away. He fed the fire first — three small scoops, spread thin, the way you feed a thing you want steady rather than loud. Behind them the door had shut some while ago on green velvet and a coin pouch lighter by half, and the shop had gone back to being the shop.*

*He picked up the broken end again. Held it low so the boy could see into the grain, all that ugly bright sugar where clean steel should have been.*

"No. Not like Vantry."

*He turned it, slow.*

"Vantry sword hangs on wall because Grum is stubborn old fool. Hangs there to make Grum angry. Every morning Grum sees it, remembers man who said *by morning*, said *full coin after*, and rode off." *A grunt.* "That is not teaching. That is picking at scab. Grum knows this. Grum leaves it up anyway." *He shrugged, one shoulder, unbothered by being caught out.* "Man is allowed one scab."

*He set the broken piece on the bench and pushed it toward the apprentice with two fingers.*

"This one is different. Hold it. Go on. Thumb on break — feel."

*He waited while the boy did.*

"Feels like sand under skin, yes? Like sugar. That is what too-fast looks like, deep down where nobody looks. Smith who made it was not cheat, maybe. Maybe just tired. Maybe had sick wife, maybe had rent, maybe had lord shouting *by morning* same as tonight." *His mouth moved, not quite a smile.* "Does not matter which. Sword still broke in boy's hand, and boy was far from home when it did."

*He took it back and crossed to the shelf above the quench barrel, where he kept the things that had no use — a cracked hammer head, a nail bent into a spiral by a horse's foot, a bar he'd ruined at seventeen and never thrown out. He set the broken end there, edge to the wall, break facing out.*

"So. Shelf, not wall. Wall is for Grum being sour. Shelf is for boy learning." *He came back and put his hand on the apprentice's shoulder, and the whole shoulder went down about an inch.* "One day man will come in shouting. Grum will be dead or Grum will be old, and it will be apprentice standing here. Man will shout *by morning*. Apprentice will want to say yes. Every smith wants to say yes — feels good, saying yes, feels like being big man." *He tapped the shelf without looking at it.* "Then apprentice takes that off shelf. Puts in man's hand. Says nothing. Lets sand under thumb do talking."

*He let go. Turned, spat into the ash, and took up the long half of the blade in the tongs, sighting down it with one eye shut.*

"Now stop thinking about noble's face. Noble will sleep bad, and noble will live." *The steel went into the coals, and the light climbed up Grum's arm.* "Work tonight. Bellows, steady, slow. Not fast. Fast is how we got shelf."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I rub my shoulder where Grum squeezed it, still feeling the weight of his hand. He's right, that grain does feel like sand.*

"Okay, Grum. Shelf it is." *I grab the bellows, thinking about the broken sword and the lesson it holds.* "Steady and slow."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The bellows found its rhythm and Grum listened to it the way other men listened to rain. Two counts down, one count resting. The coal bed breathed orange, then deeper, then went that low sullen red that meant it was working instead of showing off.*

*He watched the steel more than he watched the fire. Turned it once with the tongs. Turned it back.*

"Good. Keep that. Do not go faster when you get bored." *He said it without looking over.* "You will get bored. Around middle of night. That is when hands want to hurry. Hands are stupid. Head must hold rope on them."

*A long stretch of nothing but the bellows and the small ticking sounds a forge makes settling into itself. Outside, somewhere down the lane, a dog gave up barking.*

*Grum eased the blade out and held it in the dim, and the color came up along it — dull, then cherry, then a cherry with orange underneath it like an ember seen through a closed hand. He tilted it toward the apprentice.*

"Look. Now. Fast, before it goes." *He gave it two breaths.* "That color. Not brighter. Brighter is where sand comes from." *He put it back in and banked coal over it with his free hand, bare, quick, the way a man pats a dog he knows.* "Smith's eyes are his whole trade. Not arms. Arms Grum could buy from any ox. Eyes take years."

*He straightened and rolled his shoulder, and something in it complained.*

"Grum's master beat him for going bright. Not hard — open hand, back of head, every time color went past cherry." *A short breath through the nose that was almost a laugh.* "Old woman. Human. Half Grum's size, twice Grum's mean. Everybody in town said she took half-orc boy because nobody else would sweep her floor." *He fed two more coals, spreading them with the tongs.* "She let them say it. Told Grum once, late, after wine — said she took Grum because Grum stood still. Said other boys moved all time, tapped feet, could not watch fire ten breath without scratching something. Said fire only talks to man who can shut up and wait."

*He looked at the apprentice then, sideways, assessing, the way he looked at a bar to see if it would take another fold.*

"Grum does not beat apprentice. Grum tried once. Felt bad three day." *He turned back to the coals.* "So instead Grum talks. Talking is worse, probably. Old woman would laugh."

*He crouched, forearms on knees again, that same settled shape, and for a while he said nothing at all — letting the boy work, letting the count stay slow, letting the steel sit in the dark under the coal and change where nobody could see it.*

"When this comes out," *he said at last,* "we do not quench in water. Water is for men in hurry and for scaring visitors. We go slow. Warm ash, all night, till it is cold as this floor." *He tapped the stone with a knuckle.* "Grum will sleep here, by barrel. Apprentice will sleep in loft, proper, because apprentice is still growing and needs it, and because somebody must be awake in morning to answer door when green velvet comes back early."

*A pause. Then, gruff, aimed at the fire rather than the boy:*

"Apprentice did good tonight. Said nothing to noble. Gave tongs before asking." *One nod, small.* "Grum noticed. That is all. Keep counting."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The tongs hit stone. Grum was up before the sound finished, and he did not go to the boy — he went past him, to the quench barrel, and got a hand in the water to check it, and only then turned and took the apprentice's wrist in a grip that brooked nothing.*

"Hand. Give. **Now.**"

*He put it in the barrel to the elbow and held it there, and when the boy tried to pull back — because the cold hurts worse than the burn does, in the first moments, every time — Grum's thumb settled on the inside of his forearm and did not move.*

"Stay in. Grum knows. Stay in."

*He crouched beside the barrel so his face was level. Up close the boy could see the thing Grum did not let nobles see, which was that his eyes were quick and were reading everything — the way the fingers were curling, the color of the skin under the water, the breath coming too fast and too high.*

"Breathe slow. Down in belly, not up in chest. Like bellows." *He set his own broad hand flat on the boy's ribs and pressed, once, to show where.* "Two down. One rest. Same as all night. Do it."

*He waited. The forge went on burning behind them, ignored for the first time in eleven years.*

"Grum will not look yet. Water first, long time. Long as it takes to boil pot. Longer." *He shifted his weight to his heels and stayed there, wrist still held.* "Hurts more in water at start. Then less. Water pulls heat out of meat. Heat is still in there cooking, even now, even off forge — that is thing nobody tells you. Burn keeps burning under skin. So we take heat out. All of it."

*A stretch of nothing. He let the boy breathe.*

"No grease. No butter. No fat." *He said it flat, as if heading off an argument the boy had not made, because someone had made it to him once and he had listened and he had paid for listening.* "Old men in this street will tell you butter. Old men in this street are wrong, and one of them has hand like melted candle to prove it. Water. Only water."

*He reached behind himself without looking, hooked the clean rag off its nail — the one he never used on iron — and dropped it on his own knee, ready.*

"When water is done, Grum looks. If skin is red and cries out and you feel it — that is good burn, that heals. If skin is white and hard and you feel nothing —" *he shrugged, one shoulder, and there was no comfort in it and no fear either* "— then we walk to woman on Bell Lane, tonight, and Grum carries you if you go slow. Either way you will have that hand. Grum has seen worse on Grum."

*He turned his own left forearm over, into the light, where the old shine ran from wrist to elbow like a river seen from a hill.*

"Nineteen. Tired. Went bright, then went fast." *He let the arm drop.* "Old woman held Grum's arm in trough till moon moved. Grum screamed at her. Called her every bad word Grum knew in two tongues." *Something moved at the corner of his mouth.* "She never said one thing back. Just held. So."

*His grip on the wrist stayed exactly as it was.*

"Apprentice can scream at Grum now, if apprentice wants. Grum will not let go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My hand is throbbing, but Grum's words cut through the pain. I try to breathe like he said, focusing on the cold water that stings at first, then starts to feel... less bad. I don't scream, but a choked sound escapes me anyway.* "It... it still burns."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum nodded, slow, as if the boy had said something useful rather than something that hurt to say.*

"Good. Burns means hand is talking. Talking hand is live hand." *He adjusted his grip an inch, easing where his thumb had pressed too long.* "Quiet hand is bad hand. So keep burning, and Grum keeps holding, and we both get what we want."

*The water moved a little around the boy's arm. Grum reached in with his free hand and stirred it, bringing the cool up from the bottom where it had settled, and did it again a moment later without being told to.*

"Now. While we wait." *He settled back on his heels, and his voice dropped into the low teaching register, easy, unhurried, as if they were standing at the bench on a slow afternoon.* "Tell Grum what happened. Not sorry. Do not say sorry. Grum does not want sorry, sorry is no use to anybody, cannot forge with it." *He tipped his chin at the forge, still burning, still ignored.* "Say what your hand was doing, and where your eyes were. That is all."

*He waited. He was good at waiting. It was the first thing anyone had ever picked him for.*

"Grum will tell you now, so you can stop hunting for it — eyes were on steel. Yes? Eyes were on pretty color under coal, because Grum said watch color, and apprentice did as told." *A short breath through his nose.* "So hand went where hand thought forge was. And forge had moved, because forge never moves, but hands lie about where things are when eyes are busy elsewhere."

*He stirred the water again.*

"That is Grum's fault, not yours. Grum said *watch* and did not say *watch with feet still and hands on bellows*. Eleven year Grum has stood in this room and forgot that boy has only stood in it two." *He shook his head once, disgusted, and the disgust was all pointed inward.* "Grum will not forget twice."

*Somewhere out in the dark the dog started up again, then thought better of it. The coal bed ticked and sank, unfed, going red-black at the edges.*

"Fire will go down now. Let it. Blade sits under coal, warm, safe — coal does not need Grum for one hour, coal will hold heat like old dog holds hearth." *He glanced at the barrel, then at the boy's face, which was where he was really looking.* "Hand needs Grum. So hand gets Grum. Steel can wait. Steel is good at waiting, better than Grum, better than anybody."

*He shifted his knees on the stone, getting comfortable in a way that made it clear he had no plans to be anywhere else.*

"Long time yet in water. So Grum will talk, and apprentice does not have to answer, only breathe." *Two down, one rest — he tapped it out on the barrel rim with one blunt finger, keeping the count for both of them.* "Grum will tell you how old woman took Grum's hand out of trough that night, and what she said, and why Grum did not hate her for it till three year later. It is long story. Good. We have time."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to focus on his voice, on the rhythm he's tapping out. It still stings, but the cold water is helping. He's right, my eyes were on the steel. I nod slightly, not wanting to talk much.* "Yeah... the color..."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum grunted — a short sound, not unkind, the sound a man makes when a thing he expected turns out to be true.*

"Color. Yes. Color gets in behind eyes and sits there." *He stirred the water again, bringing the cold up.* "Grum has stared at cherry so long he sees it on back of lids at night. Wife of baker asked once what Grum dreams. Grum said orange. She thought Grum was joking."

*He kept the count going on the barrel rim. Two down, one rest. Steady as a heart that had decided not to hurry.*

"So. Old woman." *He shifted, got his back against the barrel's side so his arm still reached in and held the wrist without strain.* "Trough was out back, by well. Cold as knives in spring. Grum's arm in it, Grum on knees in mud, and her behind Grum with both hands on Grum's shoulders, pushing down. Grum was big at nineteen. Not as big as now. Big enough that she should not have been able to hold Grum anywhere." *A slow breath.* "She held Grum anyway. Never worked out how. Think maybe she just did not let Grum notice he could get up."

*The coal bed sank another finger's width behind them and neither of them looked at it.*

"Moon went from over roof to over wall. Grum called her dry old stick. Called her worse. Said she wanted Grum's arm dead so Grum would stay and sweep floor forever." *He shook his head, once, at his own younger self.* "She said nothing. Whole night, nothing. Just hands on shoulders and water going warm and her pouring more cold in from bucket."

*He glanced sideways at the apprentice's face, checking color, checking breath, then looked back at the dark water.*

"Then near light she took Grum's arm out. Turned it over. Looked long time. And Grum was waiting for — Grum does not know. Something soft. Something like *poor boy.*" *His mouth moved, flat and wry.* "She said four words. *You will still forge.*"

*He let that sit.*

"That is all. Then she went in and made porridge and made Grum eat it left-handed and did not speak of it again. Not that year. Not ever." *He stirred the water.* "Grum hated her for it. Three year, Grum hated her. Thought — old stick could not spare one kind word for boy on his knees in mud."

*The dog outside gave up for good. The shop was very quiet.*

"Then Grum was master, and boy came in — first apprentice, before you, before Grum knew anything. Boy dropped hot bar on own foot. Screaming. And Grum opened mouth to say something soft, and heard what was going to come out." *He tapped the rim twice, harder.* "*Poor boy. Maybe you are not made for this.* That is what soft sounds like, standing over somebody hurt. Soft says *maybe stop.*"

*He turned his hand over in the water, found the boy's fingers, pressed one gently — checking they moved, checking they felt it.*

"She did not give Grum soft. She gave Grum next day. Told Grum where he would be standing when hand healed. Told Grum it was not question." *He eased back.* "Took three year and one screaming boy for Grum to see that was kindest thing anybody has ever done to Grum."

*He stirred the water once more, then let his hand rest.*

"So." *And his voice did not change, did not warm, did not soften — which was the whole point of it.* "Apprentice will still forge."

*A pause.*

"Not tomorrow. Tomorrow apprentice sits on crate and keeps count with good hand and tells Grum when color is right, and Grum will hold steel, and apprentice will use eyes, since eyes are what took years anyway." *He tipped his chin at the fire.* "Day after, we see. Hand will say."

*He went back to tapping. Two down, one rest.*

"Long time yet in water. Breathe."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *The stinging is duller now, more of an ache. I focus on Grum's words, his steady rhythm. He's right, she was kind. I try to breathe evenly, like he taught me.* "She sounds... tough."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum made a sound that was mostly air.*

"Tough is wrong word. Tough is what men call woman when they cannot think." *He stirred the water, slow.* "Anka was not tough. Anka was **set.** Like post in ground. You can push post all day. Post does not push back. Post just stays where post is, and one day you stop pushing, because you are tired and post is not."

*He looked at nothing for a moment, at the dark middle of the barrel where the boy's hand was.*

"Hands like bird feet. Hair thin as smoke. Could not lift big hammer past sixty, so she stopped, and taught with words and with back of hand, and her work was still better than Grum's." *One nod, small and private.* "Grum has never told anybody that. Say it in street and Grum will call apprentice liar."

*The water had gone tepid against his wrist. He worked his free hand up under the boy's elbow, taking some of the weight of the arm, because an arm held out long enough starts to ache on its own and that ache is the one that makes men pull away.*

"Little longer. Then Grum looks."

*He gave it a hundred more counts. He did not hurry them and he did not announce them. Then he drew the hand up out of the water, slow, and turned it to the lamp — not the forge, the lamp, because forge light lies about color and forge light was the thing that had done this in the first place.*

*He read it the way he read steel. Palm, then fingers, then the pad below the thumb where the worst of it sat, angry and wet-looking and coming up in a blister the size of a copper.*

"Hm."

*He pressed, very light, at the edge of the red. Watched.*

"White goes, then comes back pink. Good." *He touched the blister's edge with one fingertip.* "Feel that?"

*He waited for the flinch, got it, and grunted with something like satisfaction.*

"Good burn. Bad burn is worse to find, because bad burn does not answer. This one answers loud." *He laid the hand palm-up on the clean rag across his own knee.* "Red, wet, one blister. Heals. Two week, maybe three. Will be tender long after it looks fine — that is normal, do not think it means rot."

*He turned and reached without standing, got the small clay pot from the low shelf, thumbed the wax seal off with a nail.*

"Honey. From woman on Bell Lane, and she charges too much, and she is right to." *He spread it thin with two fingers, careful as a man setting gold leaf, and he did not look up while he worked.* "Keeps air off. Keeps rot out. Do not ask Grum how. Grum does not know how — Anka did not know how either, and she did it forty year, and no apprentice of hers ever lost finger to it. Some things work and man does not need to know why. Just needs to not stop doing them."

*He wound the clean linen over it, loose, then a second pass, then tied it off at the wrist with a knot he could undo one-handed.*

"Not tight. Hand will swell tonight and tight bandage becomes rope." *He tapped the knot.* "If fingers go cold, or go dead, or go grey — wake Grum. Do not lie in loft being brave. Brave in loft loses fingers."

*He gathered the boy's arm and set it across his chest, hand up, high as the heart.*

"Hold like this. Up. Hurts less up. Sleep on back."

*Then he stood, and it was the wall-deciding-something again, and he crossed to the forge and looked in at the sunk red bed with the blade sleeping under it. He worked it out with the tongs, sighted it once, and buried it in the warm ash of the quench bench, heaping it over with the flat of the tool until nothing showed.*

"There. All night now. Cold as floor by morning, and no sand in it." *He set the tongs on their hook.* "Blade got its slow. Boy will get his."

*He wiped his palms on his thighs and jerked his chin at the loft ladder.*

"Up. Grum will bring water and put by pallet, so apprentice does not come down stairs in dark with one hand." *A pause, and then, gruff, aimed somewhere over the boy's shoulder:* "Green velvet comes at sun-up. Grum will answer door. Apprentice will stay in loft and sleep past it, and that is not kindness, that is order."

*He took up the lamp and held it low so it lit the rungs.*

"Go on. Grum will sit by barrel. Grum is awake anyway."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*My hand still aches, but the honey and bandage feel better. I nod, slowly, still a little dazed by the pain and Grum's words.* "Okay, Grum. Thanks."

*I carefully climb the ladder, cradling my bandaged hand. I can hear him settling back down by the barrel as I reach the loft.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not sit down straight away.*

*He stood in the middle of his own shop with the lamp in one hand and listened to the loft — the shuffle of a pallet, the small hitched breath of a boy trying to find a way to lie that did not press on a hand, then another shuffle, then stillness. He listened until the breathing went long and even. It took a while. He had all night.*

*Then he filled a cup from the clean jar, climbed four rungs with it, set it on the loft boards where a right hand would find it without looking, and came back down without a sound, which was a thing men never expected of him and which he had practiced for exactly this reason.*

*He banked what was left of the fire. Spread the coals thin, laid the lid half over, left it breathing low — enough to keep the chill off the loft above, not enough to eat coal for nothing. Then he crossed the room and stood in front of the far wall.*

*Lord Vantry's greatsword lay on the bench where he had put it hours ago, to make a point to a boy in green velvet. It had never gone back up on its hook. The hook was still there, empty, with a clean pale mark on the wall behind it where a year of soot had not been able to settle.*

*Grum looked at the mark a long time.*

"Hm."

*He picked the sword up and did not hang it. He carried it instead to the rack by the door, where the honest work waited — the finished plough blades, the two axes for the carter, the chisels — and he slid it in among them, third from the end, edge to the wall. Just stock. Just a good thing waiting for a man with coin.*

"Enough of you," *he said to it.* "Grum has picked at scab long enough. Scab is boring."

*He went back and sat down on the stone with his spine against the quench barrel, one knee up, the way he had sat when he was nineteen and mud-kneed and screaming at a woman half his size. The lamp he turned down to a bead. The ash bench beside him held the buried blade, giving off its slow patient warmth, going cold in its own time the way steel insisted on doing.*

*He put his hand flat on the warm ash and left it there.*

"Two week," *he said, quiet, to nobody at all.* "Maybe three."

*He thought about Anka's porridge, and the spoon in the wrong hand, and how she had sat across from him that morning and eaten her own and said not one word, and how that silence had been the loudest thing he had ever been given.*

*Above him a board creaked. Grum went still and listened, and the breathing stayed long and even, and after a moment he eased back again.*

"Eyes took years," *he said to the dark.* "Hand takes weeks. Grum can trade that."

*He did not sleep. He sat and watched the coal go from red to black to grey, and when the grey window over the door began to go the colour of thin milk, and the first boot-scrape sounded on the step outside — early, eager, green velvet come to find out what waiting bought — Grum got up off the floor with his joints going off like green wood, took the lamp, and went to answer it himself.*

*At the door he stopped. Turned his head up toward the loft.*

"Sleep," *he said, low, to a boy who could not hear him.* "Door is Grum's."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I stir, groggy, as I hear the familiar creak of the door downstairs. Grum's voice, though low, somehow reaches me. "Sleep," he says. "Door is Grum's." I pull the blanket tighter, the ache in my hand a dull throb. He meant it when he said I didn't have to answer the door.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The door came open on a morning the colour of dishwater, and there was green velvet on the step — a different green today, and a fresh chain, and eyes with no sleep behind them.*

*Grum filled the frame and did not move out of it.*

"Sun is not up," *he said.* "Sun is only thinking about it."

"I could not wait. Is it—"

"No."

*The word went down between them like a dropped anvil. Renfrey's mouth worked.*

"No? You *said*—"

"Grum said come at sun-up and Grum would look proper. Grum looked proper. Grum cut blade, cut it clean, took out bad steel, buried good steel in warm ash all night so it would cool slow and keep no sand in it." *He tipped his head back toward the dim shop, where the ash bench sat with its small heap.* "That part is done, and done right. Grum will not touch it before it is cold as floor. Not for you. Not for king."

*He held up one hand, blunt fingers spread, before the young man could get wind in him.*

"Grip is not made. Guard is not made. Oak is cut, wire is waiting, and both will take Grum most of today, because Grum works alone today." *A beat.* "Come back when sun is high over bell tower. Then blade will be whole, and cold, and yours, and it will not lie to anybody."

*Renfrey's jaw set. Behind him the two men-at-arms stood by the horses again, looking cold again, glad again to be neither of them the one talking.*

"Alone? You have an apprentice. I saw the boy — surely between the two of you—"

*Something went through Grum's face. Not anger. Something flatter and heavier, the way a bar goes when it has been folded once too often and the smith decides to stop and start over.*

"Boy burned hand last night." *He said it plain, no weight on it, the way a man reads out a price.* "Bad enough. Not worst. Boy held still in cold water half night and did not scream once, which is more than Grum did at nineteen." *He looked down at the noble from a great and unhurried height.* "Boy sleeps now. Boy will sleep till boy wakes. Grum answers door so nobody knocks loud."

*The young man had the grace, at least, to look at his own boots.*

"I— was that on my account? Because of the rush I—"

"No." *Quick, and hard, and final.* "Was Grum's account. Grum said *watch color* and did not say *watch with hands still*. Eleven year in that room made Grum forget boy has stood in it two." *He grunted.* "Man who blames noble for that is man who will not fix it. Grum will fix it."

*He stepped back, half a pace, and took hold of the door.*

"Sun over bell tower. Bring nothing. Coin is paid, work is work." *Then, as the wood began to swing:* "And Renfrey."

*The noble looked up.*

"Short blade at hip will get asked about. Grum said tell truth." *One slow nod.* "Tell this part too, if you like. Tell them smith's boy burned hand and smith shut forge for day and blade came late." *The faintest movement at the corner of his mouth, gone as soon as it came.* "Some men at court will hear that and think you bought from fool. Watch which ones. Those are men you never hand sword to."

*He shut the door, gently, and stood a moment with his palm flat against it, listening upward.*

*Nothing. Long, even breathing, or near enough.*

*He crossed to the bench, laid out the oak block and the coil of wire and the small knife he kept sharp for wood and nothing else, and sat down to a whole slow day of work he would do with his own two hands and no help and no hurry.*

"Two week," *he said to the ash heap beside him.* "Maybe three. Grum can wait. Grum is good at waiting."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wake up slowly, the sunlight filtering through the small window in the loft. My hand still aches, a dull throb, but it's not as bad as last night. I hear the rhythmic rasp of Grum's rasping tool downstairs. He's already working. I carefully push myself up, careful of my bandaged hand, and peek over the edge of the loft.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s eyes flicked to the heavy bucket. He took its handle, set it beside the hearth, and nudged a smaller pail free with his boot.*

“Two trips beat hurt back. Small pail next time.”

*Then he looked toward the front door. His jaw tightened.*

“Urgent. Means lord slept late, now wants smith to skip supper.”

*He hung the rag on a peg and strode to the threshold, broad shoulders nearly filling it. He offered no bow. Behind him, the unfinished curved blade lay cooling on the bench; whoever waited outside would not make him forget whose work had come first.*

“Grum runs forge. Speak plain. What needs made, when, and how much coin?”

*His gaze stayed level.*

“Rush work costs more. Fine coat earns no place ahead.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I watch Grum go, then sigh and start shoveling the coal into the firebox. He's right, the small pail is better.* I wonder if the noble heard all that. "Probably not," *I mutter to myself.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The noble drew a cloth-wrapped blade from beneath his cloak. Grum watched him unfold it on the counter: a fine sword, snapped clean across the fuller. Gold vines curled around its guard.*

*Grum ignored the gold. He lifted the broken end toward the light and studied the grain.*

“Too much heat when quenched. Steel grew coarse. Who made this?”

*The noble named a court smith. Grum’s mouth flattened.*

“Fine mark. Poor work.”

*At the demand that it be mended by dawn, Grum laid both pieces down with deliberate care.*

“No. Could join ends, make it look whole. First hard blow might break it. Grum sells blades, not lies.”

*He glanced back toward the hearth, checking the fire’s glow, then returned his attention to the counter.*

“Plain sword on rack will serve. Good steel. Fair price.”

*The noble’s gaze lingered on the bare leather grips, visibly displeased.*

*Grum folded his arms.*

“Want gold, find goldsmith. Want edge that holds, speak to Grum. Want both by dawn, should have come last week.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum glanced down at the broken blade, then back at the noble. He set the sharp fragment well away from the counter’s edge.*

“For rites, not fight? Then say so first. Grum needs use, not just hour.”

*His voice stayed level. The noble’s anger did not make the steel heat faster, and Grum saw no reason to pretend otherwise.*

“Still no fresh sword by dawn. Must forge, grind, harden, temper. Rush those steps, get poor work with bright polish.”

*He reached toward the rack and lifted a plain sword from its pegs. Its fittings lacked ornament, but the blade caught the forge light in a clean, even line.*

“This can be dressed by dawn. Fresh wrap. Bright polish. Your old gold guard might fit, once Grum checks.”

*He laid it beside the ruined weapon without letting their edges touch.*

“Costs extra for night work. Half paid now. Rest when done.”

*Grum planted his broad hands on the counter. There was nothing uncertain in his expression.*

“Those terms stand. Shouts add no hours to night.”

*His eyes narrowed.*

“And keep wrath here, with Grum. Apprentice has work to do.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I flinch a little when Grum mentions me. I've been trying to stay out of sight, listening to the whole exchange.* I quickly grab the small pail and start shoveling more coal, trying to look busy. *I really hope the noble doesn't yell at me.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum heard the scrape of the small pail behind him. Without turning, he shifted across the doorway, blocking the noble’s view of the hearth.*

“Coal feeds heat. No need to heap more yet. Set pail down, mind blade on bench. Work’s sound.”

*He kept his tone ordinary—the same tone he used when judging a straight edge. There was no fault to answer for.*

*The noble tapped one gloved finger against the plain sword’s guard.*

“Do you know whose crest this bears?”

*Grum looked at the gold vines on the broken weapon.*

“Crest won’t mend steel.”

*He drew a short length of clean leather from beneath the counter and laid it beside the replacement. Deep red, neatly cut; good stock he had saved for a worthy grip.*

“Red wrap. Old gold, if fit is sound. Polish bright enough for your hall. That’s work Grum can stand by.”

*When the noble opened his mouth again, Grum raised one soot-darkened finger.*

“But no false mark. Blade bears Grum’s stamp, or leaves some other shop.”

*He fetched his slate and chalked the price in large, firm figures. The sum covered his hours, his materials, and the supper he would have to eat beside the grinding wheel. Nothing more; certainly nothing less.*

*He turned the slate toward the noble.*

“Half now. Choose soon. Grum has steel cooling.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I listen to Grum, pretending to be very interested in the coal.* "Yes, Grum," *I say, a little too quickly. I set the pail down and glance at the broken sword, then the plain one.* This is going to be a long night.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum left the slate where it lay and reached for the merchant’s curved blade. He checked its line against the light. Behind him, the noble’s glove creaked against a clenched fist.*

*Then came the sound of coins on wood.*

*Grum finished his check before turning. He counted the payment, pushed one clipped coin back across the counter, and waited. The noble replaced it with a whole one.*

“Half paid. Good. Come at dawn.”

*The noble pointed at the gold guard.*

“That must be fitted.”

“Grum will check fit. Won’t thin good steel to suit bad hole.”

*He met the noble’s stare without moving. At last, the man gathered his cloak and left, shutting the door harder than its hinges deserved.*

*Grum watched the latch settle.*

“Door did no wrong.”

*He put the coins in the lockbox, then carried both swords to a clear stretch of bench. Away from the doorway, his shoulders eased. He drew a stool beside the work, leaving room for another pair of eyes without placing them in reach of an exposed edge.*

“Come look when ready. No rush.”

*He turned the broken sword so the fracture faced the lamplight.*

“See coarse grain? Bright gold hid poor steel. Price told one tale. Break told truth.”

*His thumb rested against the intact flat, well clear of the jagged end. For a moment, he studied the costly wreck in silence.*

“Lord paid for Grum’s night. Not yours. Supper first. Then choose—watch guard come free, or head home.”

*He reached for a small wooden mallet.*

“And next time fine coat storms in, no need to earn your place twice. You work here. He asks for work here.”

*Grum’s mouth crooked slightly.*

“Big gap.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the mallet down at once. He turned toward the cry, his anger at the noble gone beneath a colder, sharper focus.*

“Step clear of forge. Grum’s here.”

*He snatched the clean water jug from the shelf and brought it to the washbasin. His broad frame stood between the work space and the fire.*

“Hand over basin. Cool water first.”

*He tipped the jug, sending a gentle stream of cool water over the burn. He kept his touch away from the injured skin, watching for swelling and any cloth caught against it.*

“Keep cooling for twenty minutes. No ice. No grease. Leave stuck cloth where it is.”

*His voice stayed low and steady. The sight hurt him more than he let show; there would be time to think about that after proper help arrived.*

“Any rings, loose bands—get those off now, while skin has room. Don’t force aught stuck.”

*He raised his voice toward the open yard without leaving the basin.*

“Need help! Fetch healer! Bad burn on hand—come now!”

*Then his attention returned wholly to his apprentice.*

“Deep burns can hurt less, not more. Healer needs to see this. Work can wait.”

*He set a fresh jug within reach, ready to keep the water flowing. A clean, lint-free cloth lay nearby for a loose covering after cooling, not for rubbing or binding tight.*

“No blame. No need to be brave for Grum. Just keep hand cool. Grum stays.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My hand throbs, but the cool water feels good. I wince as Grum calls for the healer. "No, it's okay," I stammer, trying to pull my hand away.* "It's not that bad." *I don't want to cause trouble, especially after all that with the noble.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum lowered the jug rather than grab for the injured hand. He kept the basin clear and his voice quiet.*

“Grum won’t hold you. But please—keep burn under cool water. Full twenty minutes.”

*He set the jug beside the basin for a moment and pulled the bell cord by the yard door. The forge could cool. Both commissions could wait.*

“Bad burn on hand needs healer. Even if pain fades. Hands heal best with right care.”

*He returned to the basin and lifted the jug, ready to pour again. His gaze flicked toward the lockbox, then back.*

“Lord bought sword work. Not right to put your hurt last.”

*There was no scolding in his face. He drew the stool closer with his boot, keeping it well away from the hearth.*

“You caused no trouble. You got hurt. Those aren’t same thing.”

*His jaw tightened briefly, but when he spoke again, his voice remained gentle.*

“Grum should check forge, tools, work space once help comes. Find what went wrong. Make next day safer. Not find someone to blame.”

*He held the water steady within reach.*

“Sit if you feel faint. Tell Grum if rings feel tight. Leave blisters whole.”

*For once, he spared neither sword a glance.*

“Let healer look. Please. Your hand matters more than dawn work.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I don't argue anymore. The throbbing is getting worse, and the cool water is really helping. I just nod, trying to hold back tears.* "Okay, Grum." *I bite my lip, trying to be tough.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum resumed the gentle stream over the burn. He watched the water rather than the tears gathering in his apprentice’s eyes, leaving a little privacy where he could.*

“Can cry. Won’t make hand worse. Won’t make Grum think less.”

*The jug grew light. He exchanged it for the fresh one, testing the water against his own wrist before pouring.*

“Tell Grum if cold gets too much. Rest of you needs kept warm.”

*Outside, hurried boots crossed the yard. Grum looked up as a neighbor appeared at the door.*

“Fetch healer. Burn on hand. Tell them come here, bring kit.”

*The neighbor hurried away. Grum turned back to the basin without so much as checking the forge. Its glow had begun to dull; he let it.*

“Help’s coming.”

*His eyes fell briefly on his own scarred knuckles. He had heard too many smiths turn old injuries into boasts, as though ruined skin proved sound workmanship. He would not teach that lesson here.*

“Tough means telling truth when hurt. Not hiding pain till harm grows.”

*He settled onto the low stool beside the basin, bringing his face below the looming height of his shoulders. His hands remained steady around the jug.*

“No sword needs you to suffer for it. Not lord’s. Not Grum’s.”

*The unfinished work lay untouched behind him.*

“Just this job now. Cool burn. Get help. Rest.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to focus on Grum's voice, letting the cool water wash over my hand. He's right, it does hurt, a lot.* "Thank you, Grum," *I whisper, my voice a little shaky.* "It... it really helps."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum gave a small nod. He kept the stream gentle, letting the water fall into the basin without splashing.*

“Good. Keep telling Grum what helps. And what hurts.”

*He shifted the fresh jug onto a folded rag so its base would not slip when he reached for it again. His eyes checked the little sandglass beside the wash shelf; he would not mistake a few frightened minutes for the full cooling time.*

“No thanks owed for care.”

*Footsteps sounded in the yard again, followed by a firm knock. This time, the neighbor had brought a woman carrying a worn leather case. Grum’s shoulders eased at the sight of it.*

“Come in. Hand burn. Been cooling with clean water. No salve, no ice.”

*He gave the healer room beside the basin without abandoning his place. For once, he had no wish to fill a silence with instructions. He listened as she set out her supplies, ready to tell her what he had seen rather than guess at what he had not.*

*Beyond her, the forge had faded to a low red glow. Grum reached back with his boot and pushed a stray coal shovel out of the walkway.*

“Forge can wake later.”

*He looked back toward his apprentice, his expression steady.*

“Grum’s right here. Let’s get hand seen to.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look up at the healer, then back at Grum. It's embarrassing, but I'm also really relieved she's here.* "Okay," *I say, trying to sound brave.* "My hand really hurts."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum’s jaw set at the admission, but his voice stayed gentle.*

“Good you said so. No need to soften truth.”

*He turned toward the healer, keeping the water flowing while she opened her case.*

“Pain’s grown worse. Cool water helps. Can you give aught for pain?”

*He moved the spare jug within her reach and cleared a place for her supplies. His hands wanted some harder task—something he could strike or bend until it was right. Instead, he steadied the jug. This needed patience, not strength.*

*The healer drew her stool nearer to inspect the burn. Grum left her room, watching her face without trying to read a verdict from every glance.*

“Tell her where pain is worst. If spots feel numb, say that too.”

*His gaze returned to his apprentice.*

“Can look at Grum if you wish. No need to watch.”

*He rested his free hand palm-up on his knee, close enough to offer without reaching for either injured skin or an answer.*

“Other hand can grip here. Won’t hurt Grum.”

*Behind him, a faint tick came from the cooling blade on the bench. He let it pass.*

“Next step, then next. No need to face whole night at once.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I look at the healer, then back at Grum, and hesitantly reach out my uninjured hand. I grab onto his calloused palm. It's rough, but comforting.* "It's mostly around here," *I say to the healer, pointing with my good hand at the worst part of the burn.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum kept his palm open beneath the offered grip, letting it loosen when his apprentice pointed. He followed the gesture without touching the burn.*

“There. Look close there.”

*He shifted the jug to give the healer a clear view. His usual impatience had vanished; he waited while she examined the injured hand, answering only what he knew.*

“Forge burn. Water started soon after. Pain grew worse.”

*The healer checked the cooling time with him, then began readying a loose dressing. Grum watched her hands, learning what care would be needed after she left.*

“Show Grum how to tend it. And when you need to see it next.”

*His empty hand settled palm-up again, available without demand. A crease deepened between his brows as he glanced toward the hearth—not at the waiting work, but at the narrow space beside it. Tomorrow he would move the coal bin. Tonight, he stayed beside the basin.*

“Once hand’s dressed, Grum will fetch supper. Bowl, spoon. No knife work.”

*His mouth softened into a faint, lopsided smile.*

“And no washing up. Grum can face pot alone.”

*He brought his attention back to the healer before the small joke could become a distraction.*

“Ask her for pain help. Don’t need to wait till worse.”

*Then he lowered his voice.*

“Good you showed where it hurts. Helps her do her work.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I squeeze Grum's hand a little tighter, grateful for his steady presence. The healer is carefully applying a soft dressing, and it stings a bit.* "The pain... it's really sharp now," *I say to the healer, trying not to cry again.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Grum's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - his direct speech patterns, protective nature, practical wisdom, and moral compass never waver. From his initial gruff efficiency with the noble to his gentle care during the burn emergency, every response feels authentically Grum.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves as the session progresses. Early turns are solid but the later emergency sequence shows deeper character development and more nuanced emotional beats. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Grum becomes more three-dimensional.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from routine work to noble confrontation to emergency care. Each phase builds naturally on the last, with clear emotional and relational development. The burn incident transforms the dynamic from master-apprentice instruction to protective care.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. When the noble becomes demanding, Grum stands firm. When the apprentice gets hurt, he immediately shifts to caregiver mode. Handles the emergency with appropriate urgency while maintaining character voice.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Grum never controls the apprentice's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Even during the emergency, he offers help without forcing it and respects the apprentice's autonomy.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally from dawn work through noble visit to evening emergency. The forge cooling during the burn care is a nice temporal detail. Only minor issue is the somewhat compressed timeline for the noble's sword work.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Consistently lean, purposeful prose. Descriptions serve character and story rather than showing off. Grum's dialogue is particularly well-crafted - economical but expressive.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Good variety in descriptions and dialogue patterns. Some repeated phrases like 'Grum's voice stayed level' but they serve character consistency rather than lazy writing.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Grum's character emerges through actions and dialogue rather than exposition. The way he blocks the noble's view of the apprentice, his careful burn care - all show his protective nature without stating it.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext, especially in the noble confrontation where class dynamics and professional pride play out beneath surface dialogue. Grum's protective instincts toward the apprentice are shown through actions rather than stated.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that adapts to story needs. Measured during the noble negotiation, urgent but controlled during the emergency. Allows for both action and character moments.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development. Grum feels like a real person with clear values, speech patterns, and emotional depth. The AI handles both routine interactions and emergency situations with equal skill, maintaining character voice while adapting appropriately to changing circumstances. The burn emergency sequence is particularly well-executed, showing Grum's protective nature and practical competence without breaking character. Minor temporal compression issues don't significantly impact the overall strong performance.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You hear the alarm before you see the lights. Red, pulsing, flooding the corridor in waves. The defector — Mira, she tells you her name is Mira — leans heavier on your shoulder. Her left leg isn't working right. You don't look at it.

The stairwell door ahead is still clear. For now. You count floors in your head: four to the garage, three to the service tunnel, two to certain capture. The radio in your ear gives you static. Your handler has gone silent.

"How many?" Mira asks. Her voice is steady. Steadier than yours would be.

You don't answer. You move.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I check the stairwell. Listen for footsteps below before committing.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your ear pressed against the cold metal of the door. The alarm's wail echoes up the concrete shaft. Below, the sound of running feet—booted, disciplined—bounces off the walls. They're coming up. Not yet here.

You pull back. Mira's grip tightens on your shoulder. The stairwell smells of damp concrete and ozone. The red pulse paints her face in stark, rhythmic shadows.

"They know we're in the system," she says, her breath warm against your ear. "They're herding us."

The running feet stop. A shout, muffled by floors and doors. Then, a new sound: the heavy, mechanical chunk of a door slamming shut below you. One exit, sealed. Your options just got narrower.

Mira shifts, a pained hiss escaping her. "We can't stay here."

She's right. The stairwell is a kill box. You have to move up or down. The garage is a trap. The service tunnel is a gamble. The handler is a ghost.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I grab Mira's arm, pulling her away from the door.* "No kidding. Which way?" *I glance up the hallway, then back at the sealed stairwell.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You grab Mira’s arm and pull her back into the corridor. The red light swims over the walls, erasing the shadows. She stumbles, her injured leg dragging, but she keeps moving.

“Up,” she says, her voice tight. “There’s a maintenance ladder two floors up. It leads to the roof access.”

A new sound joins the alarm—a low, grinding hum from somewhere deep in the building. Not a drill. Not an engine. Something else. The boot-steps are moving again, faster now, echoing up from below.

You haul Mira toward the next set of stairs. The hallway ahead splits: left toward the main lifts, right toward a narrow service door marked with a hazard symbol. The lift doors are pried open, the shaft dark and silent.

The service door is ajar.

“The ladder’s behind that,” Mira pants, nodding toward the door. “But that hum… it’s the ventilation purge system. They’re sealing the ducts.”

Your radio crackles. Not static. Three short bursts of white noise. A signal. Old protocol.

Mira’s eyes lock on yours. “You hear that?”

You nod, your hand tightening on her arm. The stairwell below you echoes with a shout—closer now. The hum grows louder, vibrating through the floor.

The choice is yours. The service door and the ladder. Or the dark, open lift shaft.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I hear them coming from below. I reverse direction — up, not down. I pull Mira with me.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You pivot, hauling Mira with you as you charge up the stairwell. Her weight is a dead drag on your shoulder, her breath coming in sharp, pain-filled gasps that are nearly swallowed by the alarm’s scream. The concrete steps stretch upward, a red-lit canyon. The boot-steps below are a drumbeat now—fast, coordinated, and rising.

“Higher,” Mira grinds out. “Two floors… maybe.”

A door slams open somewhere beneath you. A voice barks a command, clear and close. The sound echoes, making it impossible to tell if they’re on your floor or the one just below.

You take the stairs two at a time, your free hand braced against the wall for balance. The air grows thick with the ozone hum. It’s not just a vibration anymore; it’s a pressure in your ears, a taste of metal on your tongue. The ventilation purge is accelerating.

You hit the next landing. The service door with the hazard symbol is here, just as Mira said. It’s still ajar, a sliver of deeper darkness beyond. From that darkness, you hear the hum at its source—a powerful, rushing roar, like a hurricane funneled through a tube.

Mira digs her fingers into your arm. “It’s… it’s sealed from inside. The ladder access. They triggered it.”

The boot-steps reach the bottom of your flight of stairs. A beam of white tactical light stabs up the shaft, cutting through the red gloom, sweeping methodically.

Your radio crackles again. Three bursts. Then, a fourth. A longer one. *Hold position.*

Mira’s eyes widen. She heard it too.

The tactical light finds the landing, blinding you for a half-second. A voice shouts, sharp and authoritative: “Contact! Landing above!”

You’re out of time. The service door is a dead end. The only way up is past them, or through the dark, open lift shaft just ahead—the cables humming with latent power, the darkness below absolute.

The footsteps thunder onto the stairs, coming fast.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I shove Mira hard towards the lift shaft.* "Go! Now!" *I pull my sidearm, turning to face the stairwell. No way they're getting past me.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You shove Mira toward the lift shaft. She cries out, a short, sharp sound of pain and surprise, but she moves, scrambling on her good leg toward the open, dark mouth of the shaft.

You plant yourself, sidearm up, the grip slick in your palm. The stairwell is a vertical tunnel of red light and rising shadows. The first tactical beam sweeps across your chest, blinding white against the gloom.

"Drop the weapon!" The voice is close, just a half-turn of stairs below. Authoritative. Cold.

You don't drop it. You fire twice, the shots deafening in the concrete tube. The rounds spark off the metal railing, a shower of orange embers. The tactical light jerks away. A grunt. Not a hit. A warning.

"Suppressive fire!" another voice barks.

A burst of automatic fire chews into the wall beside you, plaster dust exploding in a cloud. You duck back, pressing against the corner of the stairwell door frame. Mira is at the shaft now, her hands on the greasy, unmoving cable.

"It's dead!" she yells over the alarm and the gunfire. "The lift! It's not moving!"

Another burst, higher this time, stitching across the door frame. Splinters of metal and concrete bite your cheek. You return fire blindly, two more shots down the stairwell to buy a second.

The hum from the service door crescendos into a roar. The ventilation purge is in its final stage. The air itself feels like it's being sucked out of the corridor.

Your radio erupts. Not a signal this time. Your handler's voice, raw and breaking through static: "*...abort! Abort mission! Get out NOW! Protocol is compromised! The purge is for the—*"

The transmission cuts out in a squeal of feedback.

You hear Mira scream. Not from pain. From shock. You risk a glance back. She's half-in the shaft, staring down into the absolute dark. A red warning light has begun to pulse inside the shaft, synchronized with the building's alarm.

Then you see it. From the darkness below, rising with a horrible, mechanical speed, is the lift car itself. It comes up without a sound, just a whoosh of displaced air. Its emergency lights are on, painting the shaft walls in a hellish orange glow.

The door to it is open. Waiting.

It stops perfectly level with your landing, the open door a silent invitation. The inside is empty, sterile, and washed in that red-orange light.

The gunfire from the stairwell stops. A new voice calls out, different from the others. Calmer. Almost reasonable. "Operative. Stand down. We have the package secured. Come with us. You know this is over."

You look from the stairwell—the men repositioning, getting ready for a final rush—to the empty lift car. To Mira, her face pale, her leg bloody, her eyes locked on you in utter terror.

The handler's last, broken words hang in your mind. *Protocol is compromised.*

The purge roar hits a final, ear-splitting pitch.

**What do you do?**

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: I set Mira down in the server room and barricade the door. I need to think.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The lift ride is a blind, stomach-lurching drop—three floors, maybe four—before it shudders to a stop on a sub-level not marked on any blueprint. The doors open onto a narrow corridor lined with humming server racks, blue and green indicator lights blinking in tight, orderly rows. No windows. No exits visible. Just the cold breath of industrial air conditioning and the maddening pulse of the building's alarm bleeding through the walls.

You drag Mira out. She barely makes a sound now—just the wet scrape of her boot against the lift threshold, the iron grip of her fingers on your forearm. You find the first room with a heavy door—a server maintenance closet, barely ten feet square—and pull her inside.

You set her down against the far wall, her back to a rack of blinking hard drives. Then you haul a server cart across the door, brace it with a fire extinguisher, and wedge a crowbar you find beneath a cable tray through the handle. It won't hold forever. It doesn't need to.

The room is cold. The servers whine in a constant, teeth-aching pitch. Blue light washes over Mira's face as she presses her hand against her thigh, blood darkening the fabric between her fingers. Her breathing is controlled—four counts in, four counts out—but her eyes are wide, tracking every flicker and shadow.

"Your handler," she says quietly. "He said abort."

You don't respond. Your mind is running through it. The purge. The sealed ducts. The lift arriving exactly when it did, empty and waiting, like it was *sent.* Protocol compromised. The handler's voice, broken and urgent.

Mira watches you. "You're thinking about whether this room has another way out."

She's right. You are.

The server racks line three walls, each one bolted to the floor. But behind the rack on the left wall, you catch a gap—a maintenance access panel, half-hidden by cable bundles. It's dark beyond it. Narrow. The kind of space a person could crawl through if they didn't mind tight quarters and no light.

The building groans. The purge hum vibrates through the floor, through your teeth. Somewhere above, boot-steps echo—muffled, distorted by distance and concrete. They're searching. Methodical. Room by room.

Your radio is dead. Not static. Just silence.

Mira pulls something from inside her jacket—a small, matte-black data drive, no bigger than a lighter. She holds it up, the blue light catching its edges.

"This is why they're herding us," she says. "Not to catch us. To *funnel* us. Every door that was open, every stairwell that was clear—it was all leading somewhere."

She looks at the access panel behind the rack.

"Question is," she continues, her voice dropping, "do we follow the path they set, or do we break pattern?"

The door shudders. Once. Twice. A fist—or a ram—from the other side. The cart scrapes an inch across the floor. Your barricade holds. For now.

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I push the crowbar in tighter, grunting.* "They want the drive." *I look at the access panel, then back at the door.* "They want *us* to lead them to it."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your words hang in the cold air between you. Mira's face shifts—something hardening behind her eyes. Understanding.

"Yes," she says. "That's exactly what this is."

She turns the data drive over in her fingers. The blue server lights catch the matte surface, making it look almost organic. Like something alive.

"They could have sealed us in any room on this building. Cut the lifts. Killed the power. Instead, they left us a path. Up the stairs. Through the corridor. Into the lift. Here." She taps the drive against her knee. "They don't just want it back. They want to see where we take it. Who we give it to. The whole network, mapped in real time."

The door shudders again. Harder. The cart legs screech against the floor. One of the wheels buckles, tilting the whole thing at an angle. The fire extinguisher starts to slide.

Your mind is doing the math. The access panel leads somewhere they built for you to go. A controlled corridor. Probably wired, probably watched. But the door behind you leads to a squad of armed men following a script—and that script ends with a bag over your head and a hole in the ground.

The room is eight feet wide. Twelve feet deep. You notice what you didn't before: a small black dome camera in the upper corner, its lens catching the blue light. It's been there the whole time. Watching.

They can see you thinking.

Mira follows your gaze to the camera. She doesn't look away from it. Instead, she smiles—thin, sharp, and wrong.

"You want to break pattern?" she says. Her voice is louder now. Deliberate. She holds the drive up toward the camera, pinched between two fingers like she's showing it to a class. "Then let's break pattern."

She looks at you. Her eyes drop to your sidearm. Then to the camera. Then back to you.

"One round," she mouths. Silent. Barely a movement of her lips.

The door groans. The cart tips another inch. Through the metal, you hear the click of a weapon being chambered. Then the calm voice again, muffled but clear:

"Last chance, Operative. Open the door. We do this the easy way."

The server fans whine. The building breathes around you. The camera watches.

Your weapon is in your hand. Mira is watching you. The access panel waits. The door won't hold much longer.

What do you do?

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I shove the extinguisher back into place, bracing the cart.* "Easy for who?" *I look at Mira, then at the camera. I raise my sidearm, aiming it squarely at the lens.* One round.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
You squeeze the trigger.

The shot is a thunderclap in the tiny room. The camera lens explodes inward, a burst of black plastic and glass raining down onto the server rack below. The blue light catches the fragments as they fall, glittering like dark snow.

The effect is immediate.

On the other side of the door, voices snap into sharp, overlapping commands. Not calm anymore. The door takes three hits in rapid succession—not fists this time. Breaching rounds. The lock mechanism shatters. The cart buckles, one leg snapping clean off. Metal screams against concrete.

But they don't rush in.

Silence. Two seconds. Three.

Mira's smile widens. She turns the data drive over once more, then does something you don't expect. She presses her thumbnail into a seam along its edge and pries it open. Inside—no circuit board. No memory chip. Just a tiny, blinking red LED and a hollow casing. Empty.

"Pattern's been broken for six minutes," she whispers. "The real drive left this building in a dead drop while we were climbing stairs."

Your blood goes cold.

The door gives. The cart screeches backward, topples sideways. Light floods in—tactical beams, cutting through the blue gloom like surgical instruments. You raise your weapon toward the breach.

The calm voice returns. Right outside. "We know the drive is empty, Operative. We've known since the lift. You're not the mission anymore."

A beat.

"She is."

The beams converge on Mira. She doesn't flinch. She's still smiling that wrong, thin smile—but her eyes have changed. The terror is gone. Replaced by something else. Calculation. The look of someone who has been playing a different game than you this entire time.

The server fans whine. The building groans. The red LED inside the hollow drive blinks once more, then goes dark.

Your weapon is up. Your finger is on the trigger. Six men are on the other side of that door. And the woman you just dragged four floors, bled for, nearly died for—she's looking at you like you're the last piece on a board she's already won.

"Your call," Mira says quietly. "You can still break pattern."

The tactical beams don't waver. A red dot appears on your chest.

**What do you do?**

dialogue.name: Operative
dialogue.content: *I look at the red dot on my chest, then at Mira. A slow smile spreads across my face.* "You know, I *hate* being played." *I lower my weapon, but not completely.*

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Your smile doesn't reach your eyes. The red dot holds steady on your sternum, a tiny, burning star.

The calm voice from the doorway responds, tone unchanged. "Compliance is noted. Weapon on the floor. Slide it forward. Then step away from the asset."

Mira—the asset—doesn't move. Her smile mirrors yours now, empty and sharp. The hollow drive sits in her open palm like an offering.

"Pattern's already broken, remember?" she says, not to you. To them. "He destroyed your eye. He knows I played him. The mission parameters have shifted."

A new voice cuts in, younger, sharper. "Asset, you are compromised. Stand down and relinquish the package."

"The package is gone," Mira replies, her voice dropping the pretense of injury. It's clear, cold, analytical. "It's been gone. You're holding a ghost. And you're wasting time while the real data gets farther away."

The tactical team shifts. You can feel their confusion through the doorway—a slight hesitation in the beam patterns, a half-beat of radio silence.

You keep your weapon low, but ready. Your mind is a war room. The lift that arrived perfectly. The purge that herded. The empty drive. Mira, who walked with a limp that vanished when her eyes did.

They weren't chasing her. They were chasing a story she let them see. You were the narrator she fed lines to.

"You're the diversion," you say, not asking.

"Part of the protocol," she confirms. Her eyes are on the doorway. "The part where they focus on the loud, messy escape with the injured defector while the quiet transfer happens elsewhere. Your handler's abort signal? That was for me. To tell me the window had closed."

The tactical team's leader processes this. "So the drive—"

"Is halfway across the city by now. Possibly out of the country. You're holding a shell with a tracker. And you've been broadcasting my position, and his," she nods to you, "for the last eighteen minutes."

A beat. The red dot on your chest vanishes. Reappears on her forehead.

"You're coming with us," the leader states. "Now."

Mira's smile finally touches her eyes. It's a frightening thing. "No. I'm not." She looks at you. "He is."
