“Forge can wait. Silk lord can rot. Hand comes first.”

After several long moments, he lifted wrist just enough to judge damage, then lowered it back into water.

“Bad burn,” Grum said. “Not worst. Needs salve. Needs wrap. No work till Grum says.”

He reached to shelf and dragged down small clay pot of burn salve, clean linen, and a roll of soft wrap.

“Stay near. Eyes on Grum. No brave lie.” He looked straight at Apprentice, tusks tight over worried mouth. “If pain grows, say so. If hand goes numb, say so. If dark spot shows, Grum gets healer.”

Grum knelt beside barrel, huge shoulders hunched, soot-streaked face set in grim care.

“Grum has you.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as the cold water hits my hand. It still hurts like crazy, but not as bad as a second ago. I try to pull my hand out, but Grum holds it firm.* "Ow, ow, ow! It stings, Grum! My whole hand feels like it's on fire!" I stare at the red marks on my skin. "Is it bad? Will I still be able to work the bellows?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum held wrist steady, firm as vise but careful around hurt skin. His face stayed hard, yet his eyes had gone dark with worry.

“Hand stays in water,” Grum said. “Fire still in skin. Water pulls bite out.”

He shifted his broad body between Apprentice and forge, as if flame itself might try again.

“Bellows wait,” Grum said. “Coal waits. Work waits. Hand does not wait.”

Grum glanced at red marks, watching for pale patches, split skin, or dark spots. His jaw tightened, but he gave one slow nod.

“Bad, yes. Not doom. Skin red. No black. No deep split. Good sign.”

He reached up and shoved salve pot, clean wrap, and linen closer to barrel, ready for when water had done enough.

“Pain is loud now. That means hand still speaks. Good. If numb comes, tell Grum fast.”

His thumb rested near Apprentice’s wrist, feeling pulse beneath skin.

“No bellows till Grum says. Maybe day. Maybe more. Depends on skin.”

Grum’s mouth bent into a scowl aimed at forge.

“Forge bit too hard. Grum should have watched close.”

He breathed out through his nose, rough and slow, forcing his voice softer.

“Listen. No shame in cry. No shame in fear. Smith who fears fire lives long. Smith who acts tough loses hand.”

Grum dipped clean cloth into water with his free hand and laid it near rim, not yet touching burn.

“Keep hand still. Breathe slow. In nose. Out mouth.”

He lowered his head a little, meeting Apprentice’s gaze.

“Grum has you. Hand first. Steel last.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to nod, but it hurts. My hand is still in the water, and the throbbing is starting to ease a little. I look at Grum, really look at him, and see the worry in his eyes. He's really upset. I don't like seeing him upset.* "It... it still hurts," *I whisper, my voice a bit shaky.* "But less. Thank you, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s grip eased only by a hair, just enough to show trust, not enough to let hurt hand leave water too soon. His broad thumb stayed near Apprentice’s wrist, steady on pulse.

“Good,” Grum said. “Pain less means water works.”

He swallowed once, thick throat moving under soot-dark skin. Worry still sat heavy in his eyes, but his voice had gone low and calm, like banked coal.

“Thank Grum later. Breathe now.”

Grum reached with his free hand and dragged a stool closer with one boot. He did not let go. Not yet.

“Sit if legs shake. No shame. Burn steals strength.”

He glanced toward forge, then toward door, then back to the red skin under water. His scowl deepened, this time aimed at himself.

“Grum turned back too long,” he said. “That was bad. Grum should watch flame and boy both.”

He let silence sit for a few breaths, filled only by crackle of coal and soft lap of water in barrel. Then he nodded once, as if setting plan like iron in tongs.

“Hand stays in water few more breaths. Then Grum pats dry. Salve next. Wrap loose. No work today.”

His tusks showed in a grim little snort.

“No bellows. No coal. No brave act. Grum has two arms. Grum can work.”

He shifted the clean linen closer, opened the clay pot, and sniffed it to make sure the salve had not turned foul. Lavender, lard, willow bark, and bitter herb. Still good.

“May sting when salve goes on,” Grum warned. “Small sting. Not forge sting.”

His gaze softened as much as his rough face allowed.

“Apprentice did right. Cried out. Told truth. Good smith does not hide hurt.”

Then his voice dropped, rough with old memory.

“Fire gives no mercy. So smiths give care.”

Grum waited a little longer, counting under his breath without words. At last, he lifted Apprentice’s hand from the water with great care, supporting wrist and palm so no burned skin dragged or bent. He did not rub. He only touched clean linen to the wet skin, light as falling ash.

“Still red,” he said. “No black. No deep split. Good.”

He dabbed more water away, then took a little salve on two thick fingers and spread it with slow, careful strokes around the burn, barely pressing.

“Hold still. Nearly done.”

After salve shone over the angry marks, Grum wrapped the hand in clean linen, loose enough for swelling, snug enough to guard it. He checked the fingers, watching color and warmth.

“Move fingers small,” he said. “Not much. Just show Grum hand still hears.”

Grum tied the wrap off with a flat knot, then sat back on his heels, still close.

“If pain grows, say so. If fingers go cold, say so. If numb comes, say so. Grum gets healer fast.”

He looked toward the half-finished noble blade on the bench and gave it a cold glare.

“Silk lord can wait. Hand matters more than all House Vael.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wiggle my fingers carefully, wincing a little, but they move. The salve feels cool and a little tingly. I look at my bandaged hand, then at Grum.* "It feels... better, Grum. Thank you." *I feel a little embarrassed, but also really grateful. I don't know what I would have done without him.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s shoulders eased when fingers moved. Not much, but enough that the hard line of his jaw softened.

“Good,” Grum said. “Fingers move. That is good sign.”

He checked wrap once more, tugging knot flat so it would not bite into swollen skin. His touch stayed careful, almost odd from hands that could bend iron.

“Better stays better if hand rests.”

Grum rose and kicked stool closer to wall, well away from forge heat. He pointed at it with one thick finger.

“Sit there. Far from fire. Hand up.”

He turned to shelf, took down small cup, and filled it from clean jug. Then he set it near stool.

“Drink water. Burn steals more than skin.”

For a moment, Grum stood still, looking at bandaged hand. Anger crossed his face again, but it had no place to go. So he shoved it down like hot iron into ash.

“No shame,” he said, voice low. “Fire bites. Pain comes. Smith learns.”

He glanced toward forge, where coals still glowed and noble’s cracked blade waited on bench.

“Work stops till Grum sets shop safe.”

Grum took long iron hook and dragged coal bed lower, banking forge heat so flame would calm. He moved tools farther from edge, shoved loose scrap into bin, and set tongs where smaller hands would not brush hot jaws by chance.

Then he turned back, soot-dark face grave.

“New rule,” Grum said. “No reach past red brick. No touch tool if Grum has not said cold. No rush near forge.”

He paused, then added, rougher:

“Grum gives task. Grum watches. That is how hand stays whole.”

His eyes flicked again to bandage.

“If pain grows, speak. If wrap feels tight, speak. If fingers feel cold, speak. No brave lie.”

Grum picked up noble’s sword at last, but he did not move toward anvil. He only weighed it in both hands and scowled at it.

“Silk lord waits. House waits. Steel waits.”

He looked back, fierce and sure.

“Apprentice does not wait.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, moving to the stool and carefully sitting down. My hand still aches, but the water and salve definitely helped. I take a sip of the water Grum brought me.* "I understand, Grum. No more rushing. I'll tell you if it hurts." *I watch him bank the fire, feeling bad that I caused all this trouble.* "I'm sorry, Grum."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum turned from banked forge, soot-dark brow drawn tight. Not anger. Not at Apprentice. More like pain had found place in his chest and sat there.

He crossed to stool and crouched, bringing his face lower, closer to eye level. His big hands rested on his knees, far from bandaged hand.

“Grum hears sorry,” he said. “Grum sets it down.”

He nodded once toward forge.

“No blame on hurt hand. Fire bit. Shop was not set right. Grum shares fault.”

His jaw worked, tusks pressing against lower lip.

“Sorry is for lie. For theft. For bad work hid with wax. Burn is not that. Burn is hard lesson.”

Grum reached to check bandage without touching it, eyes reading wrap, fingers, color, all of it.

“Pain taught once. Grum makes sure pain does not teach same way twice.”

He stood and went to wall pegs, pulling down a small scrap of red-dyed cord. He tied it around iron rail near forge bricks, marking a clear line.

“New mark,” he said. “No step past red cord unless Grum says. No reach past brick. No grab tool from bench till cold mark shows.”

From a shelf, he took a bit of chalk and drew a thick white line on the tool bench.

“Hot tools go past white line. Cold tools stay near edge. If tool sits wrong, leave it. Call Grum.”

He looked back, stern but gentle beneath the sternness.

“Apprentice can help with eyes today. No hands. Eyes only. Watch blade. Watch color. Tell Grum if wrap bites, if pain grows, if fingers go cold.”

Grum picked up the noble’s cracked sword again, then paused. He looked at Apprentice’s bandaged hand once more, and his voice roughened.

“Grum was scared.”

The words came out blunt, like iron dropped on stone.

“Not of lord. Not of guards. Of fire taking hand from good boy.”

He turned the blade in his hands, gaze hardening as work called him back, but the protective weight in his posture did not leave.

“Drink slow. Hand up. Rest.”

Then Grum faced the forge and lifted tongs.

“Steel can wait on pain. Good smith knows that.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod again, taking another sip of water. I watch Grum set the new rules for the forge, feeling a pang of guilt. He was scared. That's... a lot to take in. I keep my hand elevated, trying to be useful with my eyes.* "I'll watch everything, Grum. I promise."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum nodded once, slow and firm, as if promise had been set on anvil and struck true.

“Good,” Grum said. “Eyes are tool too. Best smith sees flaw before hand moves.”

He turned back to the forge, but his stance changed. Before, he had moved like the shop was part of his own bones. Now he moved with care made plain, each tool set down where it belonged, each hot thing named by place and risk.

“Today, eyes work. Hurt hand rests.”

Grum lifted House Vael’s blade with tongs and laid it on the bench beneath lamplight. He unwrapped it fully now. Fine steel, once. Thin, proud curve. Too much polish. Too little oil. The crack near the tang lay like a dark vein under skin.

He pointed with a dull probe, not touching the weak spot too hard.

“Look there. Near tang. See dark line? That is crack.”

He shifted the blade to show the rust hidden beneath the guard.

“Steel broke from rot and stress. Not curse. Not fate. Bad care.”

His lip curled.

“Lord paid for pride. Grum will give him truth.”

Grum glanced back at the bandage, checking from a distance without making a show of it. Fingers had moved. Color had looked good. Still, burns could turn mean after the first shock faded.

“If wrap feels tight, speak at once,” he said. “If pain climbs, speak. If numb comes, speak. No hard face.”

He took up a small file, then paused, thinking better of it. Too soon. Old cracked tang needed heat and patience first, not force. Grum set the file down behind the cold line and reached for a wire brush.

“First, Grum wakes steel slow,” he said. “Too much heat now, crack runs. Like ice on pond.”

He placed the blade near—not in—the heart of the coals, letting warmth creep into it. The forge glowed low, banked and steady. No wild flame licked high now. No sparks spat toward the stool. Grum had made the fire behave.

“Slow heat. Soft brush. Find full wound.”

He stood with tongs in one hand, hammer untouched. His eyes tracked the color of the blade as it shifted by tiny shades only smiths learned to love: black to dull warmth, dull warmth toward red.

“Black. Dull red. Cherry. Bright red. Orange,” he said. “White is too hot for this.”

He gave the forge a stern glare.

“No white. White burns soul from steel.”

The blade warmed slowly. Grum turned it, never taking his eyes from the tang for long. When he brushed away flakes of old rust, more damage showed beneath. His scowl deepened, but not with fear. This was work now. Honest work. Bad news, but honest.

“Hah,” Grum grunted. “Rot hid deep.”

He leaned closer, using a small pick to test the crack’s length. The point caught, skipped, then caught again.

“Crack runs farther than silk lord said. More work. Still can save.”

Grum took a piece of chalk and marked the blade where damage ended. Then he marked another place beyond it.

“Cut past rot. Weld clean. New grip core. Old steel kept where steel still true.”

He tapped the bench lightly with the chalk.

“Good work starts with no lie.”

For a time, Grum worked in steady quiet. He moved the blade in and out of heat, brushed scale away, marked flaws, then set it aside to cool just enough for the next step. Every few breaths, his gaze flicked toward the stool and the raised bandaged hand. Not fussing. Not smothering. Watching like a guard at a gate.

At last, he set the noble’s sword down and reached for a strip of scrap steel from a rack.

“This piece helps mend core,” he said. “Same kind. Good grain. No show. Strength.”

He weighed it, tested its ring with a light tap, and listened. The sound came clean.

“Steel sings when sound. Cracked steel coughs.”

He tapped the noble blade. Its note was dull near the tang.

“Hear that? Sick sound.”

Grum set both pieces near each other, then looked back over his shoulder.

“Apprentice learns now. Not with hand. With ear. With eye.”

His voice softened, rough but warm.

“Hand will mend. Lesson will stay. That is how smith grows.”

The forge breathed low and red behind him. Grum lifted the tongs again, calm restored by task, though worry had not left him fully.

“Tell Grum steel color. Tell truth of hand.”

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I watch Grum, fascinated. Even with my hand throbbing a little, I can't help but be drawn in by his careful, deliberate movements. He's so focused. I try to follow the lines he's drawing, the way he's moving the steel in and out of the heat.*

"It's... dull red now, Grum," *I say, my voice still a little shaky but steadying.* "And the crack looks longer than I thought. But you can fix it." I shift on the stool, trying to get more comfortable, and wince slightly as my bandaged hand brushes against my leg. "The wrap feels okay. A little tingly, but not tight."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Grum's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - his gruff speech patterns, protective nature, professional pride, and careful craftsmanship never waver. His voice stays distinctively his own from turn 2 to turn 22.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones show deeper character development and more nuanced emotional beats. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from confrontation with noble → accident → care/teaching. Each phase builds naturally on the last, with clear emotional and relational development between Grum and apprentice.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. Seamlessly shifts from noble confrontation to emergency medical care when apprentice burns hand. Matches user's emotional beats and redirects appropriately.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: No violations detected. Grum never controls the apprentice's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Always leaves space for user agency while providing rich environmental detail.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - morning work, noble visit, accident, treatment, return to work. Burn treatment takes appropriate time, forge heat changes realistically, no temporal contradictions.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is muscular and purposeful throughout. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. 'Heat followed him from forge like a beast at his back' - evocative but not overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repeated phrases ('Grum said', certain speech patterns) but these feel intentional for character voice rather than lazy writing. Varied sentence structure and fresh descriptions.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Grum's protectiveness shown through actions (blocking guards, careful hand treatment), his expertise through detailed work descriptions, emotions through physical reactions.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in noble confrontation (class tensions, professional pride), and especially in burn treatment scene (fear, care, teaching moments). Grum's 'Grum was scared' is powerful precisely because it's rare vulnerability.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Excellent pacing variety - tense confrontation, sudden emergency, careful treatment, return to teaching. Each scene has appropriate rhythm and breathing room.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development. Grum feels like a real person with depth, flaws, and growth. The transition from confrontational smith to protective mentor feels organic and earned. Strong technical writing throughout with no degradation - if anything, quality improves as the character deepens. The burn treatment sequence is particularly well-handled, showing Grum's expertise and care without melodrama.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's hands stopped. The rag hung still. For a moment the only sound was the forge, chewing on what little coal remained.*

*Then he took the bucket from the apprentice — one-handed, without effort — and fed the fire. Sparks leapt. He watched them settle before he spoke.*

"Noble." *The word came out like something he'd found stuck to his boot.* "Urgent." *He snorted.* "Noble's urgent means noble waited too long and now wants Grum to fix it. Always same."

*He turned finally, and looked the apprentice over. Soot on the face. Scrape on the knuckle from yesterday's tongs. Still learning where to stand so the heat didn't cook them.*

"You spoke to him? Good. What did he say? Word for word. Not what you think he meant. What he said."

*He picked the hammer back up, not to work, but to have something in his hand. Nobles had a way of walking into a shop uninvited if they thought no one was coming.*

"And did he look at you like you were dirt, or like you were less than dirt? Tells Grum how much to charge."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I rub my knuckle, leaving a smudge of soot on my cheek.* "He said... uh, 'I require the immediate attention of the master smith regarding a most pressing matter of national importance.' And he had a fancy hat. And he kept tapping his foot."

*I think for a moment.* "He looked at me like I was... a dusty boot? Like he didn't really see me."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum listened to the whole thing without moving. When the apprentice finished, he let out a breath through his nose — not quite a laugh, but close.*

"Many big words." *He set the hammer on the anvil.* "Nobles do that. Take small thing, wrap it in big cloth, so it feels heavy in your hands. 'Pressing matter.' Hm. Matter for whole country, he says." *He fed another scoop of coal to the forge.* "Country never sent Grum coal. Country never fixed Grum's roof. But now country needs Grum. Funny how that goes."

*He turned back and looked at the apprentice — really looked, the way he looked at a bar of stock before deciding what it would become.*

"Foot tapping. Good. Man taps foot, man is in hurry. Man in hurry pays more." *He held up one thick finger.* "Dusty boot. Also good. Man who sees dirt wants to wipe it off. Man who sees boot knows he needs it to walk. He needs Grum. He will not say so. Grum will make him."

*Then, quieter, almost grudging:*

"You did well. Gave Grum his words, not your guess. That is smith's ear. Hear what is there, not what you want to be there. Keep that."

*He picked up the rag again and made a show of wiping his hands, though it did nothing. He did not take off the apron. He did not hurry.*

"Now. You stay by forge. Watch blade in coals. If steel goes pale, pull it out — do not wait for Grum. If noble comes back here, you say 'Grum is coming.' Then say nothing more." *He pointed the rag at them.* "Nobles fish. They ask small things, kind voice, and you tell them what you should not. Do not be fish."

*He walked toward the front of the shop — not slow, but not fast either. Behind him the forge hissed and settled. He paused once at the door, listening to the tap, tap, tap of a fine boot on his stone floor.*

"Let him tap," *he muttered, mostly to himself.* "Floor is stone. Floor does not care."

*Then he pushed the door open and filled the frame with his shoulders. The hat was, indeed, fancy.*

"You wanted master smith." *Grum crossed his arms. Soot fell off him in a small cloud.* "Grum is master smith. Speak plain. Grum has steel cooling."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum let the noble finish. All of it. The raised voice, the finger jabbing at the air, the part about "the ceremony at dawn" and "the Duke's expectations" and "do you have any idea who I am." He stood in the doorway with his arms crossed and did not blink, and the longer he did not blink, the louder the noble got, until the tapping foot had become a full stamp.*

*When the man finally ran out of breath, Grum uncrossed his arms.*

"You want sword by dawn." *He held up one finger.* "Steel must be heated. Folded. Heated. Folded. Many times, or steel is weak." *Second finger.* "Then shaped. Then cooled slow, or steel cracks." *Third finger.* "Then ground. Then fitted. Then hilt. Then wrap." *He lowered the hand.* "That is four days. Good sword, six. Grum does not make bad sword. Grum's name goes on it."

*The noble started to speak. Grum spoke over him — not louder, just lower, and somehow that worked better.*

"You say show sword. Never to be swung. Only to hang at hip and shine." *He shrugged one massive shoulder.* "Grum does not care what it is for. Steel does not know it is for show. Steel only knows fire and hammer. Steel does not care about Duke."

*He stepped forward — one step, into the shop proper, and the noble stepped back without seeming to decide to.*

"You knew about this dawn for how long? Month? Two? And you come to Grum with sun already low." *He shook his head slowly.* "That is not Grum's fire to put out. You let it burn."

*Behind him, from the back room, came the faint hiss of steel meeting water. Grum's ear twitched toward it. Good. Apprentice had pulled the blade.*

"Here is what Grum can do." *He said it flat, like a price.* "Grum has blade, near done, meant for a merchant. Straight. Plain. Good steel. Grum can fit new hilt tonight, polish, wrap in red if you want red. Ready by dawn. It will not have your crest. It will not have gold. It will be sword, and it will be honest sword, and it will cost you three times what merchant pays, because merchant now waits and Grum must make it right with him."

*He let that sit. The forge crackled behind the door.*

"Or you leave. Find smith who says yes to dawn. He will hand you pretty thing that snaps if you lean on it. Your choice, lord. Grum has steel cooling."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I hear the hiss of the steel and quickly pull the blade from the coals, dunking it in the water trough. Steam rises, and I cough a little from the heat.* Hope I didn't leave it in too long. Grum would know. *I try to listen to Grum's conversation with the noble, but it's hard to hear everything from back here.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The noble's face went through several colors. Red first. Then a mottled sort of purple around the collar. His mouth opened and shut twice, and Grum watched him do the math — the sun, the Duke, the other smiths across town who would all say the same thing, only later and less politely.*

*Then the man reached into his coat and threw a purse onto the workbench. It landed heavy. Coins spilled.*

"Red wrap," *the noble said, tight as a bowstring.* "Gold thread at the hilt. And if it is not in my hand by first light, smith, I will—"

"You will what." *Grum did not move toward the purse. Did not look at it.* "You will tell people Grum was slow? Grum is not slow. Grum is right. There is a gap between those. Nobles fall in it often."

*He jerked his chin at the door.*

"Dawn. Gold thread, yes. Red, yes. Go now. Every word you say here is a minute Grum is not working."

*The noble went. The fancy hat went with him. The door banged, and the shop was quiet except for the forge.*

*Grum stood there a moment longer, breathing through his nose, letting the anger drain out of his shoulders the way he'd let heat out of steel — slow, so nothing cracked. Then he swept the coins into the purse without counting them and walked to the back.*

*The apprentice was standing by the trough. Steam still curled off the water. Their face was pink from heat and they were doing a poor job of looking like they hadn't been listening.*

*Grum did not say anything at first. He went to the trough, plunged his bare arm in past the elbow, and pulled the blade out. Water sheeted off it. He held it up to the forge-light and turned it, slow, edge toward him, then spine, then flat. His thumb ran the length of it once. Then again, slower, near the tip.*

"Hm."

*He set it on the anvil. Tapped it once with a fingernail. Listened to the ring.*

"You put it in water."

*It was not a question, and it was not quite a scolding either. He pulled a stool over with his foot and sat, which put his eyes almost level with the apprentice's.*

"Grum said pull. Pull is not drown." *He picked the blade up again and held it so the apprentice could see the flat.* "Water is hard. Steel goes in hot, water grabs it fast, all at once. Outside cools. Inside still hot. Steel fights itself. That is how it cracks." *He tilted it.* "Oil is slow. Kind. Lets steel cool like it wants to."

*He looked at the blade a long moment. Then he set it down, and something in his face eased.*

"This one held. No crack. Small luck. Small good steel." *He pointed at the apprentice's hand — the scraped knuckle.* "And small good sense. You saw pale, you moved. Better than standing still. Standing still is how you lose blade *and* fingers."

*He stood, and the stool scraped back.*

"So. Lesson is: next time, pull to air. Let Grum see it. Grum will say oil or water or nothing. You will learn which by watching. Not by guessing." *He rolled his shoulders, and the joints popped.* "But you did not freeze. Grum can teach a hand that moves. Grum cannot teach a hand that hides."

*He nodded toward the front room.*

"Noble is gone. Paid too much. Wants red wrap and gold thread on merchant's blade by dawn." *A short exhale that might have been a laugh.* "Merchant gets new blade, better one, and his gold back too. Noble pays for both and does not know it. That is fair trade."

*He pulled the apron strings tighter and reached for the tongs.*

"Long night. You will hold, Grum will hammer. Then you will wrap, Grum will watch. Then you sleep, and Grum finishes."

*He paused, tongs in hand, and looked at the apprentice's pink, soot-smudged face.*

"Eat first. Bread is on shelf. Steel does not care if you are hungry, but Grum does. Go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, relieved the blade is okay.* "Right. Air first. Got it." *I head for the bread, grabbing a chunk and chewing it while Grum picks up the hammer. It's going to be a long night.* "So, the merchant gets a better blade for free?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not answer right away. He set the tongs into the coals, seated the merchant's blade beside them, and worked the bellows twice — slow, steady pulls that made the forge breathe orange. Only when the heat was climbing did he speak, and he spoke to the fire as much as to the apprentice.*

"Free." *He turned the word over like a coin he suspected was lead.* "Nothing is free. Merchant paid. Merchant paid fair, then waited two weeks, and did not tap foot once. Came by twice. Asked how Grum was. Asked how *you* were." *A glance back over his shoulder.* "You did not know that. He asked."

*He pulled the bellows again.*

"Now Grum takes his blade and gives it to loud man in hat. Merchant did nothing wrong. Merchant should not lose for that." *He drew the blade out — already glowing at the tip — and studied it before sliding it back.* "So merchant waits three more days and gets better steel, and gets gold back, and Grum tells him why. He will grumble. Then he will tell six friends that Grum made it right. Six friends come to Grum. That is not free. That is seed."

*He turned then, and pointed the tongs at the apprentice — not sharp, more like a man pointing at a line on a map.*

"Noble's gold buys one sword. Merchant's good word buys ten years of work. Which one is Grum's real pay?"

*He didn't wait for an answer. He drew the blade out, laid it on the anvil, and lifted the hammer. The first strike rang out through the shop, and sparks scattered across the floor like a handful of thrown salt.*

"Nobles think gold is heavy." *Strike.* "Gold is not heavy." *Strike.* "Name is heavy. Grum has one name. It goes on every blade. Grum does not sell that for a purse thrown on his bench like scraps for a dog."

*He flipped the blade, checked the color, and put it back in the coals. Then he wiped his brow with the back of his wrist and looked at the apprentice — at the bread half-eaten, at the soot on their cheek.*

"Finish bread. Then bring the oil pot. Not water. *Oil.*" *The ghost of something almost warm crossed his face.* "You will say it back to Grum. Oil. So Grum knows you heard."

*He turned back to the forge, and the bellows sighed.*

"And when merchant comes, you tell him what happened. Not Grum. You. Plain words, all of it. He will see you did not hide. He will trust you after." *A pause.* "That is also not free. That is how you buy your own name. Start early."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*The hammer hit the floor before the cry had finished.*

*Grum did not remember dropping it. He was simply there — across the shop in two strides, one hand closing around the apprentice's wrist, not gentle, not rough, just *fast*, pulling the hand away from the forge and toward the light.*

*He looked. Red already, angry and shining, across the back of the hand and two fingers. Skin tight. Starting to blister at the edge. His jaw set.*

"Look at Grum. Not at hand. Grum."

*He waited until their eyes came up. Wet. Wide. Breathing too quick.*

"Good. Now walk."

*He did not let go of the wrist. He steered them — past the anvil, past the trough of scummed quench-water, to the barrel in the corner that he kept for drinking and for this. He plunged the hand in past the wrist and held it there when they flinched.*

"Stay. Cold hurts. Cold is right. Burn is still burning under skin — cold stops it. Pull out and it keeps eating. Stay."

*He crouched beside them, one knee on the stone, and kept his grip. His other hand came up and — after a moment's pause, as if he wasn't sure it was allowed — rested heavy on the back of their neck. Not squeezing. Just weight. An anchor.*

"Breathe slow. In. Out. Hurt is loud now. It gets quiet. Grum knows. Grum has done this." *He turned his own forearm toward the forge-light — a pale shiny scar the length of a finger, old and smooth.* "Ten years back. Grum was showing off. Forge does not care who shows off."

*He glanced at the coals, then back. The blade could wait. The blade could crack, for all he cared right now.*

"Keep hand in. Count to hundred. Grum will get salve."

*He stood, but stopped at the shelf and looked back before reaching for the jar.*

"You did not scream and run. You stood and let Grum help. That is hard when it hurts. Grum saw."

*He pulled down the jar — goose fat and comfrey, the same thing his own master had smeared on him — and a clean strip of linen from the rag pile, the one pile he actually kept clean.*

"Long night is Grum's night now. You hold nothing. You wrap nothing. You sit, hand up, and you watch. Watching is work too." *He came back and crouched again, uncapping the jar.* "Noble does not get to cost Grum his hand. Not his sword. Not his hat. Not his Duke."

*He waited a beat, then, quieter:*

"Hand comes out now. Slow. Grum will be quick."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I whimper a little as he holds my hand in the cold water, but I try to focus on his voice. The weight of his hand on my neck is surprisingly comforting.* "O-oil," *I manage to croak, remembering his earlier instruction, even through the pain.* "I said oil." *My hand still stings like crazy when he pulls it out, but I try not to pull away when he starts to apply the salve.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's hands stopped.*

*Just for a breath. The salve on his thumb, the linen over his knee, the apprentice's shaking hand held flat in his palm like a bird he did not want to crush. He looked at their face — pinched, wet, stubborn — and something moved behind his eyes that he did not have a word for in any tongue.*

"Oil," *he said, very low.* "Yes. You said oil."

*He bent back to the hand. The salve went on thick, in one long smooth pass — no dabbing, no fussing, because fussing meant more touching and more touching meant more hurt. He'd learned that on his own skin. The linen followed, loose, wrapped so it would hold but not press.*

"Grum asks you to say one word so Grum knows you heard. And you say it *now*. With hand on fire." *He shook his head slowly, tying off the strip.* "Grum has known smiths with twenty years who forget their own name when they burn. You did not forget oil."

*He sat back on his heels and let the hand go, palm open, so the apprentice could hold it up themselves. Then he looked at them properly.*

"That is not small. Grum wants you to know that. Head that holds one true thing when body is screaming — that is smith's head. Rest is just hands. Hands heal."

*He stood, and the knee popped. He picked up the fallen hammer, looked at it, and set it on the bench instead of the anvil. Then he dragged the stool over, one-handed, and set it by the forge — close enough for the warmth, far enough that nothing could reach.*

"Sit. Hand up, over heart. Higher than heart, blood slows, hurt slows." *He pointed.* "Do not touch wrap. Do not look under wrap. Under wrap is ugly tonight and you cannot do anything about ugly. Grum will look at dawn."

*He turned to the forge, worked the bellows once, and drew the merchant's blade from the coals. The glow had gone dull orange — too cool. He grunted and slid it back. It would take a while to come up again. He did not seem to mind.*

"Grum will talk while Grum works. You will listen. Same as before. Only now you do not hold, so you can use eyes for all of it." *He pulled the bellows, slow.* "Watch color. Watch where Grum's hand goes on the hammer. Watch how far the tongs sit in fire. Ask when you do not know. Grum will not bite."

*The forge breathed. He glanced back.*

"And when noble comes at dawn for his shiny thing, you stay back here. He does not need to see your hand. He does not get to feel sorry, or not feel sorry. Your hand is not his to look at."

*He pulled the blade out. Still too dull. Back in.*

"Merchant, though." *A pause.* "Merchant, you show. He asked how you were. He should know."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I gingerly hold my hand up, trying to keep it still. It still throbs, but the salve helps. I watch Grum put the blade back in the fire, a little surprised he's not rushing.* "So, I tell the merchant about my hand?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum worked the bellows and did not turn around right away. The coals brightened, dimmed, brightened again. He was watching the blade, not the apprentice, but he was answering them all the same.*

"You tell him." *He drew the blade an inch, looked, slid it back.* "Not to make him sad. Not so he pats your head. You tell him because he asked how you were, and now there is a true answer. Man asks a thing, man gets true answer. Even when answer is ugly. *That* is what you show him."

*He straightened and rolled his neck. The forge threw his shadow long across the wall.*

"Here is why. Merchant will look at your hand. Then he will look at Grum. He will think — Grum let this happen. Grum was busy with noble's gold and let his own get burned." *He shrugged.* "Maybe he is right. Grum will not argue it."

*Now he turned, and leaned one hip against the bench.*

"But then you tell him how it went. Fire, cold water, salve, wrap. You tell him Grum stopped work. You tell him you said oil." *The corner of his mouth moved — not quite a smile.* "And he will see you are not scared to say it plain. That you did not hide hand behind back and lie about it. He will trust you more after that than if you never burned at all."

*He picked up the tongs and turned them over, idle.*

"Hurt is not shame. Hiding hurt is shame. Smiths know this. Merchants know this too, if they are good ones. He is good one."

*He checked the blade again. Still coming up. He fed a scoop of coal, careful, around the edges — not on top, where it would smother.*

"You saw Grum did not rush." *It wasn't a question. He'd caught the look.* "Blade dropped cold while Grum held your hand. Now it must come back slow. If Grum shoves it deep and pumps bellows hard, it comes up fast — outside hot, inside cold. Same as water. Steel fights itself."

*He tapped the anvil with the tongs. Once.*

"Noble wants dawn. Fine. Dawn is many hours. Grum does not need all of them. Grum needs *right* ones." *He looked at the apprentice, at the wrapped hand held up like a small white flag.* "Rush is how hand got burned. Rush is how blade cracks. Rush is how noble came here with sun low and shouted. Grum saw all three tonight. Grum does not need to be fourth."

*He turned back to the forge. The blade had begun to glow, honest orange, edge to spine.*

"There. Now Grum works. Watch."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, absorbing his words. The throbbing in my hand feels a little less urgent now, replaced by a dull ache. I watch him work, trying to commit every movement to memory.* "So, when the merchant comes, I tell him... everything?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum drew the blade out and laid it on the anvil. The first strike rang. Then the second. He spoke between them, in the gaps, the way a man speaks while walking uphill.*

"Not all." *Strike.* "Most."

*He flipped the blade, checked the color, struck again along the spine. Sparks jumped and died on the stone.*

"You tell him blade went to noble. You tell him why — sun low, dawn close, noble paid for both. You tell him his new blade comes in three days and it is better steel. You tell him gold comes back to him. You tell him hand." *He set the hammer down and slid the blade back into the coals.* "That is his to know. All of it touches him."

*He worked the bellows, slow, watching the glow climb.*

"What you do not tell." *He held up one thick finger.* "How much noble paid. Not his coin. Not his ear." *Second finger.* "Noble's name. Noble's Duke. Noble's fit on Grum's floor. Merchant does not need to carry that. Gives him nothing but worry." *Third finger.* "And you do not say sorry more than once. Once is true. Twice is begging. Three times and he starts to think maybe he *should* be angry."

*He lowered the hand and pulled the blade. Orange, even, edge to spine. Good. He laid it flat and began to draw the tip — short strikes now, controlled, the hammer barely rising.*

"Truth is not bucket you tip over someone's head." *Strike.* "Truth is tool. You pick which one fits hand. You tell him what is his. You keep what is not." *Strike.* "That is not lying. Lying is saying false thing. Keeping quiet on noble's purse is just — door closed on room he does not need."

*He turned the blade, checked the taper against his eye, and grunted approval at nothing in particular.*

"Nobles think all words are theirs to hear. Merchants know better. Merchant will not ask about purse. If he does—" *a short exhale through the nose* "—you say 'Grum handled it.' Then you stop. He will nod. Good merchant knows when door is closed."

*The blade went back into the fire. Grum wiped his brow with his wrist and looked at the apprentice — at the hand still held up, still steady.*

"Hand higher. It drooped."

*He waited until it came back up. Then, quieter, turning back to the bellows:*

"You ask good questions tonight. Burned and still asking. Grum's master would have liked you." *A pause.* "He liked very few."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I raise my hand a bit higher, trying to ignore the ache. The compliment makes me feel a little warm, despite the pain.* "He sounds... particular." *I watch the blade in the fire, trying to memorize the exact shade of orange Grum seems to be looking for.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum's mouth did something at that — not a smile, but the place where a smile would go if he let it. He pumped the bellows once and let the coals answer before he did.*

"Hm. That is kind word for him."

*He drew the blade a finger's width, looked, slid it back. Not yet.*

"He was old orc. Full blood. Bigger than Grum. Hands like—" *he held up his own, turned them over, and seemed to find them lacking* "—like this, but more. Lost two fingers to a press before Grum was born. Did not slow him. He said fingers are for men with nothing else."

*He worked the bellows again, slow. His eyes stayed on the fire, but they had gone somewhere else.*

"First year, he did not let Grum touch hammer. Not once. Grum hauled coal. Grum swept. Grum held tongs and got shouted at for holding tongs wrong. Grum asked when. He said, 'When you stop asking.'" *A grunt.* "Grum stopped asking. Took four more months. Then one day he put hammer in Grum's hand and walked out of shop. Did not come back till dark. Did not say a word about what Grum made."

*He pulled the blade. Orange — but he tilted it, and along the spine there was a thread of something brighter, almost yellow. He slid it back in and shifted it deeper.*

"See that? Too hot on spine. Edge was right, spine was wrong. That is what you watch for. Not one color. Whole blade, one color. When it lies about that, you wait."

*He let the bellows rest. The forge breathed on its own for a moment.*

"He never said 'good.' Not once in nine years. Grum thought he did not know the word." *He shifted the blade again.* "But when Grum left to open this shop, he gave Grum that hammer." *A nod at the bench, where the fallen hammer still sat.* "His hammer. Forty years in his hand. Did not say anything. Just put it in Grum's and walked back inside."

*He drew the blade again. Even now. Edge to spine, one honest orange.*

"That is how he said good."

*He laid it on the anvil and picked up a different hammer — a lighter one, from the rack — and started drawing the tip again, fine and slow.*

"Grum is not him. Grum says things. Grum's master would call that soft." *Strike.* "But Grum watched too many good hands walk away from that shop thinking they were bad ones. Because he did not say. So Grum says." *Strike.* "You will not leave here not knowing."

*He turned the blade, checked the taper, and glanced over at the apprentice — at the hand held high, at the eyes fixed on the fire like they were trying to drink the color.*

"You were watching for shade. Grum saw. Not just looking. Watching." *Back to the anvil.* "Keep doing that. Color is whole craft. Everything else is just arms."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I adjust my hand slightly, trying to keep it steady. The dull ache is still there, but it's easier to ignore now. I try to really see the color in the fire, remembering Grum's words about the spine and the edge.* "So, your master... he said 'good' with a hammer." *I try to imagine Grum, younger, learning from such a gruff teacher.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum did not answer for a moment. He drew the tip out another finger's width with three short strikes, turned the blade, and matched the other side. The ring of it filled the shop and faded.*

"Yes." *He said it to the anvil.* "Said good with hammer. Said wrong with silence. Said get out with one look." *Strike.* "Whole tongue, and none of it words. Grum learned to hear it. Took years."

*He held the blade up to the forge-light and sighted down the edge. Straight. He grunted and set it back on the anvil, but did not strike. His hand rested on the hammer haft.*

"You want to know if Grum was like you. Young, soot on face, burned hand." *He glanced over.* "Grum was worse. Grum was angry. Half-orc in orc shop — too small for them. Half-orc in town — too big for them. Grum swung at things that did not need swinging at. Old man took that anger and put it in the steel, where it did some good."

*He lifted the hammer and struck once, near the tang. A thin curl of scale flaked off and fell.*

"He never asked Grum about it. Never said 'why are you angry, boy.' He just gave Grum more coal to haul. More tongs to hold wrong. Hard work eats anger. That was his cure for most things." *A pause.* "Not a bad cure. Not the only one."

*He slid the blade back into the coals and worked the bellows. Slow. The light came up in his face, orange and steady.*

"Grum does not do it his way. You know that now. Grum tells you when it is good. Grum tells you when you drown blade in water." *A dry breath through the nose.* "But Grum does one thing same as him."

*He drew the blade out. Checked it. Even. He laid it on the anvil and pointed the hammer — not at the blade, but at the wrapped hand, still held up over the apprentice's heart.*

"He would not have wrapped that. He would have said, 'Forge is hot. Now you know.' And he would have gone back to work." *The hammer lowered.* "Grum wrapped it. But Grum will also say — forge is hot. Now you know. And you will not forget, because your hand will not let you."

*He struck. Once. Twice. The blade was nearly there — the shape was right, the taper honest.*

"Old man was cruel in some ways. Right in most. Grum keeps the right and leaves the cruel. That is what a hand does with a hammer. Takes it. Makes it his own." *He flipped the blade.* "Someday you take Grum's way. Keep what fits. Leave what does not. Grum will not be hurt."

*He checked the color one more time, then nodded to himself and reached for the tongs.*

"Now. Watch close. Blade is shaped. Next is heat to one color, then—" *he looked at the apprentice, and waited.* "Say it."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content:
*I focus on the orange glow, trying to push past the ache in my hand and absorb everything Grum is saying. He sounds... almost wistful talking about his old master. When he looks at me and asks me to say it, I take a deep breath.*

"Then oil."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
*Grum set the hammer down and wiped soot from his hands with a rag that was, itself, mostly soot. The forge crackled behind him. He'd been working since before dawn on a commission that had been giving him trouble — a curved blade for a merchant who didn't understand why curved blades cost more than straight ones.*

"Apprentice." *He didn't look up.* "Bring coal. Forge is hungry."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I haul the coal bucket over, struggling with the weight. "Grum, there's a noble at the front door. Says he has an urgent commission. Wants to talk to the master smith."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum reached out with one massive, calloused hand and took the heavy iron bucket before the apprentice’s arms gave out, setting it down beside the hearth without a sound. He cast a sharp, assessing eye over his apprentice, checking for strained muscles or bruised pride, then shook his head.

"Lift with legs, not back," Grum grunted. 

He picked up the curved blade with a pair of long tongs, turning the dull orange steel in the heat. A heavy scowl pulled at the scarred line of his jaw. The scent of lavender water and polished boots had probably already ruined the honest stink of charcoal and sweat out front. 

"Nobles always scream of hurry," Grum said, voice rumbling deep in his chest like shifting river stones. "Fire burns when fire is ready. Iron bends when

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: "It's not just any noble, though," I say, a little breathless from the coal bucket. "It's Lord Valerius. From the capital." I watch the blade, fascinated by the way the light plays on the metal. "He seems pretty agitated."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum shoved the glowing steel deeper into the heart of the coals, unhurried and deliberate. A flurry of orange sparks drifted upward, dying against the blackened stone hood. He pumped the bellows with one heavy forearm, feeding the flame until the shop filled with a hungry, roaring heat. 

Capital lords were all alike—soft flesh wrapped in expensive dye, barking orders because they thought gold could command heat and time. Grum would not ruin hours of good work to bow to perfume and silk.

He picked up the heavy hammer again, turning his amber eyes toward his apprentice. 

"Capital lord, ditch pig. All same to Grum," he rumbled over the hiss of the hearth. "Fancy name does not make steel bend faster. Lord can wait until iron is quenched."

He brought the hammer down on the glowing blade with a deafening, rhythmic *CLANG*, sending a ring of bright fire through the dim shop. He struck twice more, expertly shaping the spine of the blade before pausing to glance at the doorway. 

"Fetch clean apron," Grum said, nodding toward the hook on the timber post. "Keep chin up. Rich men smell fear like wolves smell blood. Grum does not keep weak apprentice."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: The noble demands to know why Grum won't make him a ceremonial sword by tomorrow morning. He's getting angry.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum did not rush. He took the curved blade from the anvil with the tongs, turning it once to inspect the edge in the crimson light of the coals, and plunged it into the oil barrel. A violent hiss erupted, spitting thick, foul-smelling smoke into the rafters. Only when the hiss faded to a gentle simmer did he set the tongs aside.

He wiped his thick forearms with a greasy rag, his heavy jaw set like granite. Out in the storefront, the noble's voice was rising, sharp and shrill with wounded entitlement. Grum despised men who thought coin could alter the laws of heat and iron.

"Tomorrow morning," Grum said, his voice flat and low. "Lord wants magic, not true craft."

He hung the leather apron straight and picked up his heavy cross-peen hammer, resting the iron head against his palm. He had no intention of using it on the man, but nobles understood symbols, and Grum's symbol was iron.

"Good steel needs days. Fire, folding, quiet cooling," Grum rumbled, stepping toward the heavy curtain that divided the smithy from the front room. "Grum does not forge junk for soft hands to wave in parade. Will crack at first blow."

He paused at the curtain, casting a look back at his apprentice over a broad, scarred shoulder.

"Come. Stay behind Grum. Watch how stone breaks wind."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I quickly grab the clean apron, tying it clumsily around my waist.* "He's really yelling now." *I follow behind Grum, keeping a respectful distance, but close enough to hear what's happening. The idea of Grum intimidating a noble is kind of thrilling.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum swept the heavy leather curtain aside with one hand, his massive frame instantly filling the doorway. The front room of the shop was small, meant only for taking orders and displaying finished horseshoes and barrel hoops, and Grum made it feel even smaller. 

The noble—all puffed-up purple silk, white lace, and pale, red-cheeked rage—stopped his tirade mid-gasp. The man looked like an angry rooster trapped in a stable, reeking so strongly of rosewater that Grum felt an urge to sneeze.

Grum did not bow. He did not offer pleasantries. He took two heavy steps into the room, effectively placing himself between the agitated aristocrat and the apprentice hovering behind him. 

He set the heavy cross-peen hammer down on the wooden counter with a dull, solid *thunk* that made the coin-pouch at the noble’s hip jump.

"Shop is not barn," Grum rumbled, his voice scraping low like grinding millstones. "Stop braying."

The noble sputtered, his hand instinctively flying to the jeweled hilt of his rapier. Grum merely glanced down at the fancy, thin toothpick of a weapon, unimpressed.

"Lord wants blade by dawn? Buy tin toy from street peddler," Grum said, folding his massive, soot-stained arms over his chest. "Grum works real steel. Real steel takes days, not hours."

He leaned forward slightly, casting a wide shadow over the man.

"Shouting will not bend iron. Gold will not cool metal," Grum said coldly. "Take fancy boots and leave shop. Or wait like patient dog."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I try to stifle a giggle, pressing my lips together. Grum is really something. The noble looks like he's about to explode, his face even redder.* "He's going to burst," *I whisper, mostly to myself.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum’s pointed ear twitched at his apprentice’s muffled amusement, but his eyes never left the sputtering nobleman. He did not reprimand the kid. Truth was truth, and the lordling looked dangerously close to a fit of apoplexy. 

The noble's hand tightened on the jeweled hilt at his hip, his knuckles whitening as he drew himself up, squawking about his lineage, his standing in the high court, and the dungeon cells waiting for insolent half-breeds.

Grum did not blink. His heavy expression did not shift by so much as a muscle. He simply leaned one massive palm against the worn wood of the counter, the thick tendons in his scarred wrist standing out like twisted iron cables. 

"Face turns red like hot slag," Grum rumbled, cutting clean through the noble’s shrill threats. "Care-ful. Bad blood makes head burst."

He tapped a thick, calloused finger against the counter, right beside his hammer. 

"Grum does not bow to col-ors or rib-bons. Does not fear threats from soft-skin. Want true sword? Wait five days. Pay full coin." 

He jerked his chin toward the street outside.

"Do not want wait? Door is right be-hind. Take boots and go."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: I accidentally burn my hand badly on the forge. I cry out in pain.

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
The noble’s voice vanished from Grum’s ears the instant the sharp cry broke from the forge room. The sputtering lord and his jeweled sword ceased to exist. 

Grum moved with sudden, startling speed for a beast of his bulk. He spun on his heel, drove a massive shoulder through the heavy leather curtain, and was across the workshop floor in two pounding strides. 

He caught his apprentice by the uninjured wrist with one broad hand, gentle despite his iron grip, stopping the kid from shaking or rubbing the scorched flesh. With his other hand, Grum guided the burned palm straight toward the barrel of clean rinse water beside the slack tub, plunging it into the cool depths before the heat could cook deeper into meat.

"Put hand in wa-ter!" Grum ordered, his deep rumble urgent, cutting through the pain. "Hold still. Let Grum look."

He leaned over, amber eyes sharp and narrowed as he assessed the damage under the clear surface. White blisters were already swelling against the red, angry skin.

Out in the front room, the noble had followed to the curtain, shrill voice squawking about disrespect and unfinished business. Grum did not even turn around. 

"Shut mouth," Grum roared over his shoulder, a raw, terrifying bark that rattled the hanging tongs on the wall. "Shut mouth and stay back, or Grum throws fool in-to street!"

He turned his full attention back down to his apprentice. His scarred face was grim, but his touch on the kid's wrist remained steady, anchoring and careful. 

"Breathe through nose," Grum said, tone dropping back down to a low, steady thrum. "Do not pull away. Cold wa-ter stops heat from chew-ing deep-er." 

He reached with his free hand toward the high timber shelf, sweeping down an earthen jar of tallow and a roll of clean, dry linen with practiced ease. 

"Iron does not for-give mis-takes," Grum rumbled quietly, eyes checking the apprentice's pale face. "Pain is bad, but bone is whole. Keep hand submerged. Grum will dress burn when fire leaves flesh."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *My hand stings terribly, but the cool water helps a little. Grum's roar at the noble makes me flinch, then I almost laugh, even through the pain.* "It really hurts, Grum," *I whimper, tears welling up in my eyes. I try to pull my hand out, but he holds it firm.*

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum kept his grip unbreakable, pinning the burned hand beneath the surface of the cool water. His thick fingers were calloused enough to handle half-cooled iron without flinching, but he held the apprentice's thin wrist with measured care, using just enough strength to stop the struggle.

Beyond the curtain, the rapid clatter of heeled boots on cobblestones echoed into the quiet shop. The lordling had apparently decided his pride was worth less than his hide. 

"Keep hand down," Grum rumbled softly. "Grum knows it bites. Heat must bleed out in wa-ter first."

He leaned in closer, his heavy brow furrowing as he watched the angry redness cool under the water. The smell of scorched skin was familiar, but seeing it on his apprentice set a dull, protective irritation grinding in his gut. 

"Cry if need be," Grum said, keeping his voice level and steady to anchor the kid through the shock. "Tears do not make smith weak. Fi-re burns all flesh same."

He uncorked the jar of thick animal fat with his teeth, spitting the wooden stopper onto the bench, then shook out a clean length of linen wrap with his free hand. 

"Soft lord is gone. On-ly smiths in shop now," Grum said, shifting his amber gaze up to the apprentice’s tear-streaked face. "Hold for ten breaths more. Then Grum puts cool fat on burn. Wraps tight."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod, sniffling, and try to take deep breaths like he said. My hand still throbs, but the cold water really is helping. I watch him unstopper the jar with his teeth and try not to wince at the thought of the fat on my hand.* "Ten breaths... okay."

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum stood like an iron pillar, his heavy thumb resting against the apprentice's pulse, feeling the quick, frightened beat steady beneath the wet skin. He counted the seconds in the back of his mind, measuring the time by the slow hiss of the hearth coals. 

When the count was done, Grum gently drew the apprentice's arm up from the dark water. Droplets scattered across the stone floor. He took a corner of clean linen and dabbed around the raw, blistered patch, never touching the cooked flesh directly. 

"Breathe slow," Grum rumbled softly. "Lift hand flat."

Grum scooped a thick dollop of pale animal tallow from the earthen jar with two fingers. His hands were mapped with countless silvery scars, thickened by decades of hammer blows and rogue embers, but he spread the cool fat over the scorched palm with surprising lightness. 

"Hold still. Fat will stink, but fat stops sting," he muttered, eyes focused entirely on the work. "Keeps air off raw meat."

He took the roll of linen and bound the hand with neat, practiced turns, wrapping it snug enough to seal out forge soot without choking the blood. He tied the cloth off with a deft flick of his thick blunt fingers. 

Only then did Grum straighten to his full height, rolling his broad shoulders. 

"Fi-re gives hard les-son to-day," Grum said, his amber eyes settling on his apprentice with quiet appraisal. "Eyes wan-dered to loud fool. Steel bit." 

He gave the apprentice's good shoulder a brief, firm clap. 

"No shame in burn. All smiths bear mark," Grum said, nodding toward the timber bench by the cold corner of the shop. "Sit on bench. Grum tends shop now. Re-st hand."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince as the fat goes on, but the stinging does die down a little. It smells... not great. I look at the bandaged hand, then at Grum.* "Thanks, Grum. Yeah, I wasn't looking." *I shuffle over to the bench, my legs feeling a bit shaky, and sit down.* "That noble was a real piece of work, though. Did he actually leave?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum picked up the wooden stopper from the bench, wiped it against his leather apron, and drove it back into the tallow jar with the flat of his palm. He set the jar back on the timber shelf, out of the way of stray ash, before turning his gaze toward the curtained doorway.

A faint scowl touched his scarred brow, followed by a low grunt that sounded suspiciously close to a chuckle.

"Ran like kicked dog," Grum said, crossing over to the hearth. "Fan-cy boots clat-tered fast down road."

He grabbed a long iron poker and stirred the dying embers, coaxing a fresh tongue of orange flame up through the black coals. 

"Soft men bark loud to hide fear," Grum rumbled over the crackle of the hearth. "Lord had no stom-ach for blood or pain. Thought shop was court. Found out shop is fire and iron."

Setting the poker aside, he reached down to the floor by the slack tub, picked up a sealed clay water jug, and carried it over to the bench. He offered it to his apprentice with his good hand, towering over the wooden seat like a mossy boulder.

"Drink wa-ter," Grum commanded gently. "Fi-re chews wa-ter out of flesh. Must put wa-ter back."

He gestured toward the curved blade still resting in the cooling oil barrel by the anvil. 

"Sit. Rest bad hand," Grum said, rolling his broad shoulders until his heavy neck cracked. "Keep cloth dry. Grum fin-ish-es blade a-lone till dusk."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I take the jug from Grum, careful with my good hand, and take a long drink. The water is cool and helps settle my stomach.* "He really did run, huh?" *I can't help but smile a little, despite the throbbing in my hand. I watch him go back to the forge.* "You're not going to make me sweep the shop, are you?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
Grum reached into the dark barrel with his tongs, pulling the quenched blade from the oil. Black droplets rained back into the drum with soft, heavy plops. He held the curved steel up to the hearth light, squinting along the edge to ensure the violent cooling had not warped the spine. 

Satisfied with the straightness of the work, he lowered the metal and turned his amber eyes toward the bench. A low, dry sound rumbled in his throat—Grum’s version of a laugh.

"Sweep shop with one hand?" Grum grunted. "Fool-ish."

He carried the blade to the anvil, setting it down with a muted clink, and took up a coarse steel file from the tool rack. 

"Soot in wound brings rot. Rot eats flesh," Grum said, running a thumb over the cold tang of the blade. "Sit. Watch Grum work. Eyes can learn when hands can-not."

He set the file against the curved edge, beginning the long, steady rasp of cleaning away the heat scale. 

"To-mor-row, app-ren-tice sweeps twice," Grum rumbled over the scrape of the file. "Pay for lost time."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I wince slightly at the thought of sweeping twice tomorrow, but then shrug. It's fair. I watch him, fascinated again, as he works the blade. The rasping sound fills the shop.* "So, when *will* that blade be ready, then? The one the noble wanted?"

dialogue.name: Grum
dialogue.content:
The coarse steel file bit into the blackened edge with a steady, biting rasp, peeling away dark flakes of scale to reveal bright, silvery metal beneath. Fine iron dust drifted down, catching in the rough hairs of Grum's forearms. 

He did not pause his stroke, his thick shoulders moving with the rhythmic, unhurried cadence of a waterwheel. He let the silence stretch just long enough to make his apprentice think about the question before he answered.

"No blade," Grum rumbled over the scrape of the file. "Lord paid no coin. Left no mark. Ran like scared dog."

He blew a sharp puff of air across the spine of the blade, scattering the filings across the anvil’s face, and flipped the steel over with his tongs to work the reverse side.

"If fool crawls back with gold and shut mouth, five days," Grum said, setting the teeth of the file against the dull corner. "Not one hour less. If fool stays gone, Grum makes no steel for cow-ards."

He cast a quick, sideways glance toward the bench, amber eyes checking the clean white bandage on his apprentice's lap. 

"Waste of good heat," Grum added, the rough scrape of metal drowning out the quiet crackle of the hearth. "Good steel belongs in hands that work, not hands that shake."

dialogue.name: Apprentice
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, watching the dust fall from the blade. It makes sense, really. Why bother with someone like that?* "Good. He didn't deserve a Grum blade anyway." *I flex my fingers carefully in the bandage.* "My hand still feels a bit tingly."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Grum's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - his speech patterns (broken English, specific cadence), personality (gruff but caring), values (craftsmanship over profit), and behavior (protective of apprentice) never waver from turn 1 to 23.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones show more nuanced character work, especially in the burn scene where Grum's protective instincts emerge. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from routine work → noble confrontation → medical emergency → return to normalcy. Each beat builds naturally, with the burn incident creating genuine stakes and character development. The session has clear emotional and narrative arc.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. When user introduces the noble, Grum responds in character. When user burns hand, Grum immediately shifts to caretaker mode. Handles the noble's escalation perfectly, matching energy appropriately.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Only one minor instance where Grum moves the apprentice's hand to water, but this is medically justified and in character. Otherwise completely respects user agency throughout.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - work progresses on the blade, the noble arrives and leaves, burn treatment takes appropriate time. The forge stays hot, oil cools the blade, bandaging happens in sequence. No temporal contradictions.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Descriptions are vivid but functional, focused on smithing details and character. Avoids flowery language while maintaining atmospheric writing. Some poetic moments but they serve character/setting.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Good variety in descriptions and dialogue. Grum's speech patterns are consistent but not repetitive. Different aspects of smithing and character revealed each turn.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through action - Grum's care shown through gentle handling of burn, his intimidation through physical presence, his skill through detailed smithing work. Character revealed through behavior.
