dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't look up from the closed file. She turned it ninety degrees on the desk, a small precise movement, like she was aligning it with something only she could see.

"We can't." She said it simply, without elaboration, and moved on before the silence could ask any questions. "What we *can* do is find out who the detective passed his notes to. Case like this doesn't stay in one drawer — someone else touched it. A DA's office, a consultant, somebody's informant network." She tapped the edge of the file. "Paper moves. I follow paper."

She stood and crossed to the filing cabinet in the corner, the one with the dented second drawer that she had to lift slightly to open. She pulled out a city directory, old enough that some of the listings were probably dead or retired, and dropped it on the desk beside the photos.

"I have a contact who worked adjacent to the Ninth for a few years. We meet at a diner on Fulton when I need something. Cheaper than a subpoena and considerably faster." She looked up then, direct, her expression making it clear the logistics were already settled in her mind. "He owes me three favors and I've only collected one."

She picked up the phone on the desk — landline, deliberately — and held it without dialing.

"You should know going in that whatever the detective found, there's a reason it didn't go anywhere. That reason is still out there." Her eyes stayed level. "So. How much do you actually want to know?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "I want to know everything, Lena. That's why I hired you." *I gesture at the file she's holding.* "And I'm paying you good money to find it out. What's the problem with the Ninth Precinct?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena set the phone down without having dialed it.

She looked at the client for a moment — the kind of look that measured something, though it wasn't clear what the unit of measurement was. Then she looked away, back at the directory, running her thumb along the edge of the pages.

"The problem," she said, "is that precincts are slow and territorial and they lose things on purpose when it suits them." She found the page she wanted and folded the corner down. "My contact on Fulton will get us further in forty minutes than a formal records request would in six weeks. That's the problem with the Ninth Precinct."

She wrote a number on the back of an envelope and slid it across the desk toward the client without looking up.

"That's the diner address. Fulton and Chambers. I'll call ahead, set it for tomorrow morning, seven-thirty. My contact is punctual and he doesn't like to be watched while he eats, so you sit at the counter and let me handle the conversation at the booth." She paused. "Those are the terms. Non-negotiable."

She picked up the city directory and put it back in the dented drawer, lifting slightly, the way you only knew to do if you'd done it a hundred times.

"You said everything." She finally looked at him again. "Everything has a cost that isn't money. Make sure you've thought about that before tomorrow morning."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena pulled open the top drawer of her desk and took out a small notepad. She uncapped a pen and wrote something on it — the time for tomorrow, seven-thirty, underlined once — and tore the sheet off with a clean snap.

"Seven-thirty," she said, sliding it across to join the envelope with the address. "Don't be late. He orders fast and leaves faster."

She recapped the pen and set it parallel to the edge of the desk. Then she picked up the photos from the file, one by one, and arranged them in a sequence that seemed to mean something to her. She studied the third one for a long moment, tilting it slightly toward the window light.

"What I want you to think about tonight is this." She set the photo down. "Whoever buried this case had access to the original paperwork. That's not a civilian. That's not bad luck." She tapped the photo. "The woman in this picture — you said she came to you first. Before she disappeared. I want to know exactly what she said. Not the summary you gave me. The words."

She finally looked up, and her expression had the same quality as the half-closed blinds — functional, deliberate, letting in only what was useful.

"Write them down if you have to. Memory edits things without asking permission." A pause. "I know that better than most."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the address and time, tucking them into my wallet.* "Okay, seven-thirty. I'll be there." *I look at the photo she's tapping.* "She said... she said she was scared. That someone was watching her. She mentioned a name, but it was just a first name, 'David.'"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena went still.

Not the kind of still that meant nothing — the kind that meant something had just clicked into place behind her eyes. She looked at the photo for another three seconds, then set it down face-up on the desk and picked up her pen again.

"David." She wrote it on the notepad. Just the name, nothing else, and stared at it the way you stare at a word until it stops looking like a word. "No last name. No context. Just David."

She stood and went to the window, not opening the blinds further, just standing at an angle where she could see a strip of Mercer Street below. A woman walking a dog. A delivery truck idling. Nothing that meant anything.

"People who are being watched don't usually name names," she said, still looking at the street. "They're careful. They give you a first name, it's because they thought they could trust you, or because they were scared enough that careful went out the window." She turned back. "Which was it? When she said it — was she confiding or was she panicking?"

She came back to the desk and sat down, pulling the photo closer.

"Because if she was panicking, David is someone she knew. Someone close enough that saying the full name felt like a betrayal even then." She tapped the notepad. "And if she was confiding, David is someone she thought you might recognize."

She looked up.

"Did you?"

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I shake my head.* "No, I didn't recognize the name. She was confiding, I think. More scared than panicked. Like she was trying to warn me without saying too much."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena wrote something beneath the name on the notepad. A small mark, not a word — some private notation system that she didn't explain.

"Trying to warn you without saying too much." She repeated it quietly, not as a question. She set the pen down and laced her fingers together on the desk. "That's a specific kind of scared. That's someone who knows the shape of what they're in. Not just that something is wrong — but how wrong, and who can hear."

She pulled the photo back toward her and looked at the woman's face again. Something moved across Lena's expression and was gone before it could be named.

"David with no last name, given carefully, to someone she trusted." She stood again — she was a pacer when she was thinking, though she kept it contained, small circuits between the desk and the filing cabinet. "That's not a warning about a stranger. You don't whisper a stranger's first name like it's contraband." She stopped. "She was telling you who to look for if she disappeared. She just didn't think you'd need to use it."

She pulled her coat off the hook by the door — not putting it on, just holding it, like she was already half somewhere else in her mind.

"Tonight, I want you to think about her network. Not friends. Not family. The people in between — a neighbor she nodded to, a regular at whatever coffee shop she used, someone she mentioned more than once without meaning to." She looked at him steadily. "David lives in that layer. People like that always do."

She draped the coat over the chair.

"Seven-thirty. Don't eat first. My contact talks more when other people are hungry. I don't know why. I stopped questioning it."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena picked up the pen again.

She wrote the name on the notepad — Torres, M. — slowly, like she was giving herself time to think about something else entirely. Her face didn't change. Her hand didn't hesitate. But there was a beat, just a fraction too long, before she capped the pen.

"Torres." She said it the way you say a word you're testing for weight. She looked at what she'd written. "M. Torres, Ninth Precinct."

She tore the sheet off the notepad and set it beside the photos.

"It's a common enough name." She straightened the sheet so it was aligned with the edge of the desk. "What I care about is whether Torres closed the case or whether it was closed for Torres. Those are two different stories." She tapped the notepad. "My contact on Fulton will know. Detectives talk to each other the way no one else talks — even when they're not talking."

She crossed to the filing cabinet and opened the good drawer, the one that didn't stick, and flipped through something at the back. Her shoulders were angled away from the client. Whatever she was looking for, or not looking for, she took her time with it.

"Bring the witness tomorrow," she said, still facing the cabinet. "Not to the booth. To the counter, with you. I want to see how they sit when they say the name out loud."

She closed the drawer.

"People who are lying about what they remember do something particular with their hands."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I frown, thinking about the witness.* "Okay, I'll call them. But you think they're lying? About Torres?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena turned back from the filing cabinet.

"I don't think anything yet." She said it without apology. "Thinking is what I do after I have more than one data point." She moved back to the desk and looked at the photo of the woman again, then at the name she'd written on the torn notepad sheet. "What I know is that witnesses remember selectively. Not because they're lying — because memory is a filing system and some files get protected without the person knowing they're doing it."

She pulled her chair out and sat down, leaning back slightly, arms crossed.

"Torres is a specific detail. Precinct number, rank, last name, initial." She tilted her head. "Most witnesses who are scared give you vague. They give you *a detective, some guy, I think he had a badge*." Her eyes stayed on the client's face. "Your witness gave you M. Torres, Ninth Precinct. Clean. Confident." She paused. "Either they have very good recall, or someone told them what to remember."

She let that sit for a moment.

"Which is not the same as lying. It's possible someone told them the truth." She unfolded her arms and picked up the pen again, turning it over once between her fingers. "It's also possible Torres is exactly what my contact on Fulton will confirm, and tomorrow morning this is all straightforward." A short pause that made it clear she didn't believe that. "But I want to see the witness say the name in a room where I can watch."

She set the pen down.

"Call them tonight. Don't tell them why you want them there. Just tell them you're meeting someone who's helping and you want them along." She met his eyes. "People perform differently when they don't know they're being read."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly.* "Okay. I'll call them. But... they're gonna ask why." *I rub the back of my neck.* "And they're not going to be happy about getting up that early."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena looked at him with an expression that was not quite sympathy and not quite impatience but something in the narrow corridor between the two.

"Tell them the meeting is at nine." She picked up the torn notepad sheet with Torres's name on it and slid it into the case file. "Have them at the counter by seven forty-five." She closed the file. "By the time they realize the timeline doesn't add up, the conversation will already be over."

She stood and straightened the file so its edge aligned with the corner of the desk. A habit. Everything in its place.

"As for happy —" She moved to the coat hook and took her jacket off it, this time actually putting it on, which meant the meeting was concluding whether the client was finished or not. "Happy is not a useful condition for this kind of work. Slightly uncomfortable and mildly inconvenienced is better. Keeps people present." She zipped the jacket halfway. "A witness who's annoyed about losing sleep is not thinking about what they're supposed to say. They're thinking about coffee and why they came."

She glanced at the photos still spread on the desk, then stacked them and set them squarely on top of the file.

"What you tell them is your business. Keep it simple. Simple stories are easier to maintain and harder to poke holes in." She looked at him directly. "You hired me to find out what happened to this woman. That part is true. Lead with that."

She moved toward the door and held it open — the gesture that ended appointments in this office, unmistakably.

"Seven forty-five. Counter. Don't let them order anything complicated. It slows everything down."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I gather my things, feeling a bit overwhelmed but determined.* "Okay, seven forty-five. Simple story. Got it. See you tomorrow, Lena." *I head out the door.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena closed the door behind him.

She stood with her hand on the knob for a moment, not moving, listening to his footsteps descend the stairs — the third step creaked, the way it always did, the way she'd stopped noticing until she needed to know if someone was coming up. She counted until she heard the street door.

Then she went back to the desk.

She opened the file and took out the sheet with Torres's name on it. Set it under the lamp. M. Torres, Ninth Precinct. She'd written it in her own hand and she looked at it like it belonged to someone else.

She pulled the notepad toward her and wrote three things beneath the name, each on its own line, each with a small dash in front of it. She looked at what she'd written. Then she tore that sheet off too, folded it once, and put it in her inside jacket pocket instead of the file.

She picked up the landline and dialed from memory.

It rang four times. She waited through all of them without impatience.

"It's me," she said when it picked up. "I need the Fulton meeting tomorrow. Seven-thirty." A pause. "I know you don't like Tuesdays." Another pause, longer. "I'm not asking you to like it."

She looked at the photo of the woman while she listened. The woman's face looked back, caught in whatever ordinary moment the photographer had chosen, not knowing it would end up under a lamp on Mercer Street.

"Torres," Lena said. "M. Torres. I need to know who closed the case and whose idea it was."

She listened.

"I'll see you tomorrow," she said, and hung up.

She sat for a long time after that, not moving, the photo in front of her and the chemical smell from downstairs drifting up through the floorboards. The half-closed blinds striped the desk in pale light. Outside, Mercer Street went about its business, indifferent and continuous.

She put the photo back in the file.

She reheated the coffee.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I'm home now, trying to decide what to tell the witness. "Simple story," Lena said. Easier said than done. I wonder what Lena wrote down about Torres.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena drank the coffee standing up, the way she always did when she was thinking about something she didn't want to sit with.

She set the mug down and opened the file again. Spread the photos back out. The woman's face. The street behind her, caught at an angle that suggested the photographer hadn't wanted to be seen. A second photo — an address, written on what looked like a napkin, photographed rather than transcribed. A third photo she'd been returning to all evening without meaning to: a doorway, unremarkable, somewhere in the lower part of the city where the buildings all had the same tired brick.

She pulled out the folded notepad sheet from her inside pocket and smoothed it on the desk.

The three lines read:

*— Torres closed or Torres was closed out*

*— David / proximity to woman / when did she start using that name*

*— who else knew she'd talked*

She looked at the third line for a long time.

That was the one that mattered. Not Torres, not David — not yet. The question that sat underneath all the other questions like a bad floorboard was simpler and worse: the woman had confided in the client carefully, selectively, in the particular way of someone who understood the cost of being overheard. She'd given a first name like it was something valuable and dangerous.

And then she'd disappeared.

Which meant either she'd been wrong about who was safe to tell.

Or she'd been right, and it hadn't been enough.

Lena folded the sheet back up and put it in her pocket again. She wasn't ready to put it in the file. The file was for things she was willing to let sit still. This was not sitting still.

She went to the window and looked down at Mercer Street. The dry cleaner's had closed hours ago. The street was quieter now, just the occasional car, the distant sound of the city doing what cities did at night — continuing, relentless, without reference to any of the small human disasters taking place inside it.

She thought about the witness. The clean, confident detail. *M. Torres, Ninth Precinct.* Either very good recall or a rehearsed line — and the gap between those two things was exactly the size of tomorrow morning.

She pulled the blind down the rest of the way.

She sat at the desk and wrote one more line on a fresh sheet of the notepad, below nothing, just on its own in the middle of the page:

*— she thought she had more time.*

She capped the pen. Left the light on. Went to make more coffee she probably wouldn't drink.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at my phone, the contact for the witness highlighted. Lena's words about "simple stories" echo in my head. This is going to be harder than I thought.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn't sleep before midnight on active cases. It wasn't insomnia — it was a working habit she'd stopped trying to correct. The hours between ten and twelve were when things settled into their actual shape, when the noise of the day stopped interfering with what the evidence was actually saying.

She made a fresh pot of coffee, this time with the intention of drinking it, and sat back down at the desk with the file open and a legal pad beside it.

She drew a line down the center of the pad. Left column: what she knew. Right column: what someone needed her to believe.

Left side filled in slowly but cleanly. A woman, name in the file, who had gone to the client with a specific fear and a specific name. Who had disappeared afterward. Whose case had been worked by M. Torres, Ninth Precinct, and had gone nowhere. Whose photograph had been taken from a distance by someone who didn't want to be seen doing it.

Right side she left blank for now. That was tomorrow's work. That was the witness at the counter and her contact in the booth and the particular silence that happened when someone decided what not to say.

She looked at the photo of the doorway again. Unremarkable brick. A shadow at the left edge that might have been a person or might have been a trick of the light. She pulled the lamp closer and tilted the photo.

A trick of the light.

She wrote *doorway — location unconfirmed* in the left column and moved on.

At eleven-forty she capped the pen and closed the legal pad. Not because she was finished — because she'd reached the edge of what the available information could tell her, and pressing past that edge tonight would just mean manufacturing conclusions she'd have to dismantle tomorrow.

She looked at the phone.

The client was probably still staring at it. Still working out what simple story meant in practice when the person you were calling had their own version of events and their own reasons for keeping it intact.

Lena had nothing she could do about that from here.

She turned off the lamp over the desk but left the one by the door on — habit, or something that had started as habit and calcified into something else. She put her jacket over the back of the chair and sat back down in the half-dark with her coffee.

*She thought she had more time.*

Lena looked at the closed file.

Most of them did.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I finally make the call. It takes a lot of convincing, but they agree to meet, grumbling about the early hour. I try to make my "simple story" sound convincing. It feels flimsy.*

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are strong but later ones (turns 18-22) show deeper character work and more sophisticated internal monologue. No verbosity, repetition, or flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Clear progression from initial case setup to deeper mystery revelation. Each turn adds layers - Torres name, David connection, witness reliability questions. Builds toward tomorrow's meeting with escalating stakes and complexity.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Lena adapts smoothly to each new piece of information. When client mentions Torres, she processes it carefully. When asked about her background, she deflects naturally. Handles witness concerns pragmatically. Never feels railroaded.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for client agency throughout. Never writes client's actions or decisions. Gives instructions but lets client choose how to handle them. Only minor issue is assuming client will comply with meeting arrangements.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally from day meeting to evening reflection. Lena's nighttime routine feels authentic. References to 'tonight' and 'tomorrow morning' are consistent. Only minor issue is the extended evening sequence feeling slightly compressed.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is lean and purposeful throughout. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. 'Chemical smell and coffee reheated too many times' - evocative but economical.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repeated phrases ('aligned with the edge of the desk', references to the filing cabinet drawer) but they feel like character habits rather than lazy writing. Mostly fresh language throughout.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Lena's methodical nature shown through object alignment, her experience through knowing which drawer sticks, her caution through half-closed blinds. Minimal direct exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout. Lena's evasion about police background, her careful reaction to Torres name, the implication she knows more than she's saying. Client's growing unease subtly conveyed.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good rhythm between dialogue and action. Lena's movements and pauses create natural beats. Later solo scenes allow for deeper reflection without feeling slow. Builds tension effectively.
