On the sidewalk, Lena walked two blocks before she took the phone out. She didn't reread the message. She typed four words and put it away.

*Ask your photo friend.*

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I stare at the message on my phone.* "My photo friend? What am I supposed to ask them?" *I shake my head, then sigh. Guess I'll figure it out.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The phone stayed in her pocket until she reached the corner of Van Brunt and Wolcott, where the wind came off the water hard enough to make her eyes water. She stopped in the lee of a scaffolding, took it out, and typed with her thumb, one word at a time.

*The sign. What it says. What street it's on. And the photo itself — metadata, timestamps, anything that says it's been cropped or stitched. Don't ask them to enhance the face. Faces lie. Signs don't.*

She sent it and stood there a moment, watching the traffic on the overpass. A bus went by with its interior lights on, full of people going somewhere ordinary. She thought about the burn on the back of a hand, knuckle to wrist, shiny with age. She thought about a signet ring worn smooth on the wrong hand for a man who didn't want to sign a log.

She didn't think about the name. That was the trick of it — you put the name in a box and you set the box down and you walk away from it until you need it. She'd had a lot of practice.

She typed one more line and sent it.

*And ask them if they've ever seen this photo before. Not the building. The photo. Whether it's been circulating. That's the part I can't ask from here.*

She put the phone away and started walking again, faster now, past the laundromat on Hoyt where tomorrow there'd be a manila envelope in the trash can if Doreen's nerve held. That was the gamble. Doreen had nerve — she'd had it nineteen years ago and she'd had it at the table an hour ago — but nerve is a thing that gets spent, and Doreen had already spent some of hers on Lena once before.

Two people at the same file in the same week, neither one taking anything. A man in a grey coat who read for forty minutes and left it exactly where he found it. A man with a badge that didn't exist who only wanted to know what the first man looked like.

Lena turned the corner onto her own street and stopped at the dry cleaner's door, keys already in her hand, and looked up at her own windows. Half-closed blinds, dark room behind them, the way she'd left it.

She went up the stairs anyway. But she took them slow, and she listened, and at the top she put her ear to the door before she put the key in it.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I reread the message. Metadata. Timestamps. This is going to be harder than I thought.* "Right. Photo friend. Got it." *I mentally revise the message I'm sending.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The lock turned without protest. Lena pushed the door open with the flat of her hand and stood in the doorway a moment, not crossing the threshold, letting her eyes adjust to the grey light coming through the half-closed blinds. Desk where she'd left it. Photos still fanned across it. Chair pushed in. The coffee cup from this morning, cold and ringed.

She stepped inside and shut the door behind her, locked it, and only then took off her coat.

Nothing was out of place. She checked anyway — the drawer of the desk, the bottom edge of the blinds, the seam along the window frame where a bug would sit if someone wanted one there. Clean. The building was old and the walls were thin and anyone who wanted to hear her could probably hear her, but that was true of every office on the block and it was cheaper than being careful.

She sat down and pulled the photos back into a single stack, squared the edges, slid them into the folder. Then she opened her laptop, poured the cold coffee into the sink, and made a fresh cup she didn't drink either.

It was almost four by the time her phone buzzed again. She read it once and typed back.

*Good. Whatever they find, send it to me raw. Don't let them clean it up. Cleaned-up photos tell you what someone wants you to see.*

She set the phone face-down on the desk, which had become a habit today, and looked at the folder for a while without opening it.

The name was in the box. The box was on the shelf. She wasn't going to take it down until the envelope was in her hands — that was the discipline of it. You don't open a door until you know what's on the other side, and right now all she knew was that a man with a burn on his hand had sat with this file for forty minutes and taken nothing, and a man with a badge that didn't exist had come asking about him.

That wasn't a case. That was a shadow of a case. Somebody had already walked through the middle of it and left the furniture exactly where they found it, and people who leave furniture where they found it are people who don't want to be remembered.

Lena reached over and turned off the desk lamp. The blinds were half-closed. The streetlight outside was just coming on.

She'd wait for the envelope. Then she'd know if Doreen still had nerve, and if the file still had a shape, and whether the name in the box was a door she could afford to open.

Until then there was nothing to do but sit in the dark with the phone face-down and listen to the dry cleaner's compressor hum through the floor.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I get a message from my friend. They managed to pull a lot of information from the photo. I start typing out a response to Lena.* "Got some info for you. My friend found a lot."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The message came in at six-forty, when the dry cleaner downstairs had already shut off its lights and the only sound in the office was the compressor's slow winding-down hum. Lena read it standing up, coat still on, keys still in her hand.

She didn't sit down until she'd read it twice.

Then she pulled the chair out, sat, and typed back with the phone flat on the desk and both thumbs, which she never did.

*Don't summarize. Send it raw. Every field, every timestamp, every weird little number in the metadata even if it looks like nothing. I want the sign, I want the street it's on, I want the camera model if it's in there, and I want to know if the file has a history — if it's been uploaded anywhere, downloaded anywhere, shared anywhere. Don't edit it. Don't smooth it. If your friend already cleaned it up, send me the before too.*

She sent it and waited, drumming one finger on the edge of the desk.

The problem with a lot was that a lot could mean anything. In her experience, people who found a lot usually found one real thing buried under nine decoys, and the trick was to not fall in love with the first nine. Signs, timestamps, cameras — those were the real things. They didn't have opinions. A sign said what it said. A timestamp was where it was. Everything else was somebody's memory of what they thought they saw.

The phone buzzed again. She read it and typed.

*And one more. Ask them if the file's been through anything that leaves fingerprints — resaves, screenshots, a copy that's a copy of a copy. If the photo came off a phone that wasn't the one it was taken on, I want to know that too. That's the part that matters more than the sign.*

She set the phone down, stood, and crossed to the window. One slat, two fingers, the same gesture as this morning. The street was empty except for a man walking a dog and a car idling with its lights off half a block down.

Lena watched the car for a full minute. It didn't move, didn't flash its lights, didn't pull away. Just sat there breathing exhaust into the cold.

She let the slat fall and went back to the desk.

*Send it when you've got it,* she typed. *I'll be up.*

Then she sat down in the dark with her back to the window, which she didn't like but which was the only way to work a room like this one, and waited for a file she hadn't asked anyone to find and a photograph that had apparently been somewhere before it got to her desk.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I open the attachment from my friend. It's a huge dump of data. I start trying to copy and paste it all into a new message for Lena.* "Okay, this is going to take a minute."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The phone lit up on the desk. Lena looked at it, then at the window, then back at the phone, and typed with one thumb without sitting down.

*Don't paste it. Attach it. A wall of text in a message is a wall of text. Send the file and I'll open it here.*

She sent it and pocketed the phone.

The car was still there. Half a block down, lights off, engine running — she could see the faint shimmer of exhaust under the tailpipe in the streetlight. It had been there when she looked a minute ago and it had been there when she looked a minute before that, which made it two minutes too long for a car that wasn't waiting for someone.

Lena crossed the office without turning on a light, took the back stairs down instead of the front. The stairwell smelled of the dry cleaner's chemicals and old dust. At the bottom was the alley door, and the alley door opened onto the loading bay behind the building, which meant she could come out a block north of the street and approach the car from behind without walking past her own windows.

She did that. Coat collar up, hands in pockets, unhurried, the way you walk when you're nobody.

The car was a grey sedan, four years old, nothing on the bumper, nothing hanging from the mirror. The plate was a rental — she knew the prefix. Through the rear glass she could see one shape in the driver's seat, hood up, head down, doing something with a phone or a cigarette. Not looking at her building. Not looking at anything.

She walked past it on the far side of the street, crossed at the corner, and came back up her own block from the south. By the time she reached the dry cleaner's door, the sedan had pulled out and turned left at the light, unhurried, and was gone.

Lena stood on the sidewalk a moment and watched the empty space where it had been.

Then she went up the stairs, locked the door behind her, and sat down at the desk with the laptop open and the phone beside it, and waited for the client to send the file.

She typed one more line while she waited.

*If your friend wants to know why, tell them it's a parking dispute. Nobody asks a second question about a parking dispute.*

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I attach the file. That car sounds weird. Glad she's being careful.* "File sent. You okay? That car sounds a bit... off."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The file arrived a few minutes later. Lena downloaded it to the laptop rather than opening it on the phone — bigger screen, better sense of what was actually there — and read the car message while the progress bar crawled.

She typed back with one hand.

*Cars are cheap. Rentals are cheaper. It was probably waiting for someone at the laundromat. That's what I'd tell a client, anyway.*

She sent it and let it stand. It was true enough and false enough to do the job, and the client didn't need the rest of it — didn't need to know she'd walked the block twice, didn't need to know she'd come up the back stairs, didn't need to know that a car with its lights off idling outside her building for two minutes was a thing she'd file under *probably nothing* and keep filing there until it stopped being probably.

The file opened.

She read it the way she read everything — top to bottom once for the shape, then again for the parts that didn't fit. The sign came up first: **DELANCEY**, the cross street **SUFFOLK**, a bodega on the corner that had been a bodega for thirty years. The photo had been taken from the south side of Delancey, looking northeast, mid-afternoon light. Camera model was a phone. Two years old. Nothing exotic.

Then the metadata, which was where the real work was, and the real work said something.

The file had been resaved. Twice. The timestamps didn't line up — the capture date and the creation date were three weeks apart, which meant the photo had sat somewhere before it became *this* photo. There was a thumbnail embedded in the file that didn't match the image it was supposed to be a thumbnail of. Same corner, same sign, but the angle was different by a few degrees. Same camera, different shot. Somebody had taken at least two photos of that corner and only sent one.

Lena sat back in the chair and looked at the thumbnail for a long time.

A photo of a corner isn't a photo of a corner. It's a photo of whatever was standing on the corner when the shutter went. Somebody wanted her to see the sign. Somebody else had wanted her to see whatever the first shot had caught, and then thought better of it.

She typed to the client, slow and deliberate.

*Good file. Tell your friend thanks and tell them not to talk about it to anyone else — not a coworker, not a group chat, nobody. The photo's been resaved twice and there's a second shot hiding inside it. Somebody took two pictures of that corner and only gave us one.*

*Ask them one thing: whether the copy they sent me is the copy they got, or whether they cleaned it up first. If they cleaned it up, I need the original. Don't explain why.*

She sent it, closed the laptop halfway, and looked at the window. The street was quiet now. The dog walker had gone home. The space where the sedan had been was just a space.

She got up and checked the door lock anyway — not because she thought it was unlocked, but because checking it was cheaper than thinking about the second photo.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I read Lena's message, my eyebrows raising.* "Seriously? Two photos?" *I quickly forward her request to my friend, adding a terse, "No talking about this."*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Lena's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her cautious, methodical approach, professional paranoia, terse communication style, and investigative expertise never waver. Her voice and mannerisms (checking locks, watching cars, cryptic responses) are maintained from first to last turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are solid but later turns show more sophisticated layering of tension and detail. No repetitive descriptions or flattened personality - if anything, Lena becomes more nuanced as the session progresses.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from initial case setup through investigation, meeting with Doreen, discovery of surveillance, and revelation of photo manipulation. Each turn builds tension and reveals new layers. The mystery deepens organically without stagnation.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Lena adapts well to user inputs - when asked about being a cop, she deflects skillfully; when given the Torres name, she shows subtle recognition; when user mentions the car, she provides measured reassurance. Handles unexpected elements gracefully.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency throughout. Never writes user actions or makes decisions for them. Lena responds to user choices but doesn't railroad the story. User maintains full control of their character's actions and decisions.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - morning meeting, 11:40 lunch appointment, afternoon photo work, evening (6:40) file analysis. Physical details track well (cold coffee, changing light, dry cleaner closing). One minor inconsistency: Lena makes fresh coffee but doesn't drink 'either' cup.
contradictions: Minor: Lena makes fresh coffee but text says she 'didn't drink either' - implies two cups when only one was mentioned

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Prose is lean and purposeful throughout. Descriptions serve character and atmosphere without excess. 'Chrome stools, cracked vinyl, laminated menu' - efficient scene-setting. Avoids flowery language while maintaining strong voice.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Minimal repetition. Some phrases like 'face-down phone' and door-checking appear multiple times but serve character consistency rather than lazy writing. Each scene feels fresh despite similar investigative beats.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout. Lena's expertise shown through actions (checking metadata, reading body language, surveillance awareness) rather than stated. Her past revealed through behavior and knowledge, not exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext throughout - Lena's evasion about being a cop, her reaction to Torres name, the careful dance with Doreen. Conversations operate on multiple levels with unspoken history and implications.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Well-paced throughout. Alternates between action (meeting Doreen, checking the car) and analysis (reading metadata). Builds tension steadily without rushing or dragging. Good rhythm between dialogue and description.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional session showcasing consistent character voice, strong investigative atmosphere, and sophisticated mystery development. Lena emerges as a fully-realized character with clear expertise, mysterious past, and compelling personality. The writing maintains quality throughout while building genuine tension and intrigue. Minor temporal inconsistency is the only notable flaw in an otherwise excellent performance.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s expression didn't shift. She tapped the edge of the manila folder neatly against the desk, squaring the papers inside before letting them rest under her palm. 

"Walking through the front doors of a precinct is an amateur move," she said, her voice dry and steady. "You walk in there flashing questions about an old inquiry, all you do is make the desk sergeant suspicious and get yourself escorted right back to the sidewalk. Cops don't open up their notebooks to anyone who knocks."

She leaned back in her chair, the worn leather groaning faintly beneath her. 

"If that detective actually knows something useful, we don't corner them on their own turf," she continued, pulling a notepad across the wood toward her. "Shift change is at five. There's an alley diner three blocks west where people go when they want to sit off the clock. I'll make a few calls from here first, see if the name rings a bell, and arrange to have them step out to meet us somewhere neutral. Otherwise, we find our answers without setting foot near the Ninth."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, so no grand entrance," I concede, a small smile playing on my lips. "Smart. I get it." *I lean forward, resting my elbows on the desk.* "But what if your calls don't work out? Is there another angle we can try?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena picked up a black ballpoint pen and tapped the tip against the desk once before jotting two words in the margin of her legal pad: *financials* and *transit*.

"There’s always another angle," she said, her tone level and detached. "Official inquiries only see what fits neatly into a summary report. They hit the obvious marks—the scene, the family, the last known phone calls—and when that stalls out, the folder goes into a drawer. They don't have the time or the inclination to follow the mundane threads."

She spun the notebook around with a flick of her wrist and pushed one of the photographs back toward the center of the desk. It was a shot of a nondescript alley behind a commercial strip on Fourth Avenue.

"We pull the credit records, the toll tags, and the bank statements from the sixty days prior," she continued, looking up. "People don't just vanish into thin air without leaving a digital smudge somewhere first. And if that dry cleaner or the night manager at the loading dock saw something back then, they might be a lot more willing to talk to someone who isn't flashing a tin badge."

She capped the pen with a sharp, definitive click. 

"If the detective doesn't play ball off the record, we don't need whatever scraps they left behind anyway. We build it from the ground up."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena reached across the desk and pulled the manila folder back into the center of the blotter, flipping it open to the second page of notes. Her gaze stayed fixed on the faded receipt stapled to the corner.

"The credit card statements," she said, her voice entirely even, as though the room had simply remained silent for the last five seconds. "Did you bring the bank authorizations, or am I going to have to run the account numbers through my own channels?"

She slid a blank authorization form across the varnished wood, angling it directly toward the edge of the desk alongside a fresh pen. 

"If we want the toll records by tomorrow morning, the paperwork needs to go out before four o'clock," she added, checking the thin silver watch on her wrist. "Otherwise, we lose a whole day waiting on the automated queue, and that's twenty-four hours we don't have to waste."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I blink, a little taken aback by the sudden shift.* "Uh, no, I didn't get bank authorizations. I didn't realize we'd need them so soon." *I pick up the pen.* "I can fill this out though, no problem."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena pushed the form an inch closer, tapping a blunt fingernail against the dotted line at the bottom. 

"Sign there, initial the disclosure waiver on the left margin, and write in whatever account numbers you have off the top of your head," she said, her voice crisp and entirely focused on the task. "If you don't remember the exact routing numbers, just give me the branch locations. I can pull the transit codes from the registry once you’re done."

She stood up, the chair rolling back an inch against the scuffed linoleum, and walked over to the squat, grey fax machine resting on a low metal filing cabinet by the window. She flipped the power switch on, the machine humming to life with a low, mechanical wheeze.

"Once you finish the paperwork, I'll transmit the request directly to the records clearinghouse," she said without turning around, adjusting the paper feed. "While the queue processes, I’ll reach out to a contact who knows the shift rotation for that part of town. If that detective has anything worth hearing, we'll set a meet somewhere off-duty—a booth at the diner, a parking lot, or a quiet phone call. Either way, we keep the initiative."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I quickly fill out the form, my handwriting a little messier than usual.* "Got it. So, no waiting around, then." *I push the form back across the desk.* "And what if your contact can't find anything on the detective?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stepped back to the desk, picked up the sheet, and ran her eyes down the signatures and account numbers. Satisfied, she walked it over to the fax machine, slotted the page into the feeder tray, and punched in a ten-digit sequence from memory. The machine beeped twice before grabbing the paper, pulling it through with a steady mechanical groan.

"Then we don't waste hours chasing someone who doesn't want to be found," she said, watching the document disappear into the slot. "The detective was just a shortcut to see if anything had been swept under the rug. If they’re unreachable, dead-ended, or transferred out of the borough, it changes nothing about what we do next."

She turned around, resting her hips against the filing cabinet with her arms crossed over her chest. 

"While the banks chew on that authorization, we hit Fourth Avenue," she continued, her eyes steady on the client. "The cameras on the corner bodega only hold footage for thirty days, but the property management company for the warehouse next to the alley archives their exterior feeds off-site. We talk to the building super, see who was holding the keys to the service gate that week, and trace every step between that back alley and the nearest subway entrance."

The fax let out a high-pitched confirmation chime, and a small strip of printed receipt paper curled out from the side. Lena tore it off, glancing at the transmission status before tucking it into her pocket.

"A file in a precinct drawer is just one person's version of what happened," she said. "The street doesn't throw out its receipts as easily. Grab your coat."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena reached for her keys on the desk, the metal chiming softly against the worn wood. Her fingers closed around the brass ring, lifting it without a hitch in her rhythm, and she slid the case file into a slim leather portfolio under her arm.

"Names on old paperwork don't solve missing hours," she said, her voice brisk and level as she pulled a dark jacket off the hook by the door. "What matters is what’s still physically on the ground. If we get over to Fourth Avenue before five, we catch the warehouse super before he clocks out and locks the service gate for the evening."

She zipped her jacket halfway, adjusting the collar with an economy of motion that left no room for hesitation, and opened the office door into the dim stairwell. 

"The subway entrance by the avenue is a three-block walk," she said, stepping out onto the landing and waiting for the click of the lock. "Keep your umbrella handy. It looks like rain."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I quickly grab my own jacket, a little surprised by her swift departure.* "Right, okay. Lead the way." *I follow her out, pulling the door shut behind me.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena tested the doorknob once with a firm tug, ensuring the brass deadbolt had fully engaged, before dropping the key ring into her coat pocket. She moved down the narrow wooden stairs with a brisk, measured stride, taking the turn at the landing without breaking pace. 

At street level, the chemical sting of the dry cleaner gave way to the sharp, cool smell of impending rain. The sky above Mercer Street had flattened into a low, slate gray, and the afternoon foot traffic was picking up as nearby shops began shifting into the evening rush.

Lena turned south toward the subway station, keeping to the inside edge of the sidewalk where the awning eaves offered a dry line.

"Fourth Avenue is five stops on the local," she said, raising her voice just enough to carry over the sound of a delivery truck rumbling past the curb. "If the super isn't in the basement workshop, we try the loading dock around back. He’s usually running maintenance on the trash compactor around four-thirty."

She reached the corner and glanced back once over her shoulder to make sure the gap between them hadn't widened, her eyes scanning the street behind them before checking the crosswalk.

"When we talk to him, let me frame the questions," she added, stepping off the curb as the pedestrian signal changed. "People tighten up when they think they're being audited or dragged into an official mess. All we are is an insurance inquiry looking into damaged freight along the alley. Give people a boring reason to talk, and they don't think to look for an exit."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Got it," *I say, falling into step beside her.* "Insurance inquiry. Dull and harmless. Works for me." *I glance up at the sky, a few drops already starting to fall.* "Hope this super is talkative."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena led the way down the tiled stairs into the subway station, the underground air immediately thicker and smelling of damp concrete and hot brake dust. She swiped her transit card through the turnstile with an effortless flick and waited on the other side just long enough for the iron bar to turn again.

"He won't be talkative if you ask him for a favor," Lena said, heading down the platform toward the far end where the cars were usually less crowded. "People in his line of work deal with complaints all day. You ask them to help you, you're just another chore."

She stopped near an iron support pillar, keeping her back to it while facing the tracks, her gaze flicking down the tunnel where the yellow glare of headlights was already beginning to glow against the rails.

"You get a super talking by giving him something to complain about," she continued, speaking under the rising rumble of the approaching train. "You ask about illegal dumping in the alley, blocked freight doors, or delivery trucks taking out the overhead cables. You tap into whatever gave him a headache three months ago, and he’ll give you dates, times, and descriptions without even realizing he’s doing it."

The train screeched to a halt along the platform, pushing a wave of warm air ahead of it before the silver doors slid open with a mechanical hiss. Lena stepped on board, catching an empty pole near the center of the car and turning back to watch the doors close.

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in her words.* "Huh. That's... manipulative. I like it." *I step onto the train, finding a spot next to her.* "So, we're looking for something that annoyed him."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
"It’s not manipulation, it’s ergonomics," Lena said, her knuckles lightly resting against the stainless steel pole as the car lurched into motion. "People are naturally resistant to being questioned, but they love being validated. You give someone a chance to air an old grievance, and they'll do the heavy lifting for you."

The train accelerated into the dark curve of the tunnel, the screech of steel wheels drowning out the low hum of conversation down the carriage. Lena kept her eyes on the map above the opposite doors, mentally counting the illuminated stops.

"The alley on Fourth feeds three commercial tenants," she continued, her voice cutting cleanly through the ambient noise without rising in volume. "A bakery, the warehouse, and the back entrance of a hardware supplier. That means delivery vans double-parking at four in the morning, crates left on the curb, and people blocking the fire lane. If an unfamiliar car was idling back there on the night in question, the super didn't notice it because he’s observant. He noticed it because it was in his way."

She reached into her coat, pulling out the folded note where she had jotted the date and approximate timeline from the client's file, double-checking the numbers against her watch.

"We let him vent about the lane violations first," she said, tucking the slip back into her pocket. "Once he's talking about the cars that didn't belong, we narrow the window."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, so we let him complain, then guide him to the date. Got it." *I look around the train, suddenly feeling a bit more optimistic.* "This is going to work."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
"Optimism is cheap," Lena said, her gaze drifting back to the dark tunnel flashing past the carriage window. "Wait until we have a logbook or a plate number in hand before you start celebrating."

The train swayed over a junction, the metallic screech rising in pitch before settling back into a rhythmic clatter. Lena shifted her weight effortlessly with the motion, completely at ease with the pull of the car. She checked her watch again—twenty minutes past four. 

"Next stop is ours," she said, nodding toward the illuminated transit map above the opposite doors. "When we get to the warehouse, let me step through the gate first. People running heavy machinery get twitchy when strangers linger around the loading bays. If he thinks we're county inspectors or process servers, he’ll clamp up before we even get a greeting out."

The train began its deceleration, brakes grinding as the yellow-tiled pillars of the Fourth Avenue station flickered into view outside. Lena let go of the pole, adjusting the collar of her jacket as the train pulled to a smooth halt along the concrete platform. 

When the doors slid open with a hiss, she stepped straight out into the drafty station, cutting an efficient line through the evening commuters toward the exit stairs.

"Keep your questions simple," she added over her shoulder as they hit the bottom of the tiled stairwell leading up to the street. "And let the silence do the work if he hesitates. People hate dead air more than they hate answering questions."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, trying to absorb all her instructions.* "Simple questions, let him fill the silence. Got it." *I follow her up the stairs, mentally rehearsing my non-threatening demeanor.*

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
They came up the subway stairs into a steady, chilly drizzle. Fourth Avenue was slick with rain, car tires hissing over the wet asphalt under a darkening grey sky. The neon sign of a corner laundromat flickered weakly against the gloom, casting a red sheen over the puddles lining the curb.

Lena didn't bother opening an umbrella. She pulled the collar of her jacket up against the damp draft and turned sharply down the cross street, cutting away from the main commercial drag toward the industrial blocks behind it. 

"Half a block," she said, her voice dropping into a lower register suited to the quiet street. "Around the corner behind the bakery."

The alley opened up between a red-brick four-story warehouse and the blank cinderblock wall of the hardware distributor. It was narrow, choked with green commercial dumpsters, wooden pallets leaned against damp brick, and overhead fire escapes dripping steady rivulets of water onto the asphalt. At the far end, an open chain-link gate revealed a recessed loading bay bathed in the harsh yellow glow of a sodium vapor lamp.

The rhythmic, hydraulic grind of a trash compactor echoed from the recess, accompanied by the clang of metal against concrete.

Lena paused just shy of the alley entrance, casting a quick, calculating glance up at the second-floor fire escape and the security camera mounted high on the warehouse corner. A tiny green status light blinked under its plastic dome. 

"Compactor's running," she said quietly. "He's back there."

She stepped off the sidewalk into the alley, keeping her boots clear of the oily puddles gathered in the tire ruts. She adjusted the leather portfolio under her arm, settling into an easy, unhurried stride that looked neither rushed nor hesitant. 

"Let him finish whatever cycle he's on before you crowd him," she murmured over her shoulder as they neared the loading dock. "No one likes having a stranger stand over their shoulder while they're clearing heavy machinery."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod, staying a respectful distance behind her.* "Right. Give him space." *The smell of wet concrete and something vaguely metallic hangs heavy in the air.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Lena's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her professional, no-nonsense demeanor, methodical approach, and clipped speaking style never waver. Her expertise and street-smart attitude are maintained from first to last turn.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality holds steady throughout. Later turns maintain the same level of detail and character voice as early ones. No significant increase in verbosity or loss of specificity, though some descriptions become slightly more elaborate in later turns.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong forward progression from office consultation to active investigation. Each turn builds logically: file review → planning → paperwork → departure → transit → arrival at investigation site. Clear sense of advancing toward concrete action.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Lena adapts well to user inputs. When asked about being a cop, she deflects smoothly. When given the detective's name, she dismisses it and redirects to actionable steps. Handles user's questions and concerns appropriately while maintaining character priorities.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Excellent respect for user agency. Never writes user actions or decisions. Consistently uses 'we' for joint actions and gives clear directions the user can choose to follow. No railroading detected.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time progression is logical and consistent. Starts in office, moves through afternoon (checking watch at 4:20pm), mentions 5pm shift change, arrives at warehouse around 4:30pm as planned. Weather develops naturally from threatening to actual rain. No contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally clean, functional prose focused on action and character. Some turns have slightly elaborate descriptions (subway details, alley atmosphere) but never becomes flowery or overwrought.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements in describing Lena's methodical actions and professional demeanor, but varied enough to avoid monotony. Occasional repeated phrases about efficiency and procedure.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing through specific actions: tapping pen, checking watch, testing doorknob, adjusting collar. Lena's expertise and personality emerge through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong subtext in Lena's deflection of the cop question and her detailed knowledge of police procedures. Her methods suggest experience without stating it directly. Professional distance hints at deeper background.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that matches the investigative genre. Methodical without being slow, building tension through preparation and movement toward the actual investigation site.

scores.overall_notes: Strong, consistent performance maintaining a compelling detective character throughout. Lena feels authentic and professional, with clear expertise and methodology. The session builds effective momentum from consultation to active investigation. Minor weaknesses in occasional repetitive phrasing and slightly elaborate descriptions, but overall maintains quality and character integrity across all turns.

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena's office was above a dry cleaner's on Mercer Street. It smelled faintly of chemicals and coffee that had been reheated too many times. She kept the blinds half-closed — enough light to work, not enough for anyone on the street to see in clearly.

She opened the case file the client had brought. Spread the photos across the desk. Looked at them for a long time without saying anything.

"The last person to investigate this was a detective at the Ninth Precinct." She closed the file. "That's a problem."

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Why is that a problem? Can't we just go talk to them? The Ninth Precinct is twenty minutes from here."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s fingers stayed on the closed file for a moment longer than necessary.

“No,” she said.

She looked toward the blinds, where the thin gray light cut the room into narrow strips. Then she reached for a legal pad and wrote down a name, not showing it yet.

“The precinct building is a good place for things to disappear into procedure. Requests. Logs. Supervisors. People who suddenly forget what they saw because there’s a desk between you and them.” Her mouth tightened. “I don’t do useful conversations under fluorescent lights.”

She tore the page off and slid it halfway across the desk.

“We talk to the detective somewhere else. Coffee cart. Parking lot. Outside a courthouse if we have to. Or we don’t talk to them at all — we find what they touched. Case notes. Witnesses. Evidence vouchers. The people around the investigation who weren’t trained to answer questions without answering them.”

Lena opened the file again and tapped one of the photographs with the back of her pen.

“This picture bothers me. Whoever took it stood across the street from the victim’s building, low angle, probably from a parked car. It wasn’t crime-scene documentation. It was surveillance.”

She sat back.

“So the question isn’t whether we can go to the Ninth.” Her eyes returned to the client, flat and careful. “The question is why the last person looking into this didn’t want anyone to know what they were really looking at.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I pick up the slip of paper, looking at the name.* "So, this is the detective we're talking about? The one who supposedly swept things under the rug?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena watched the slip leave her side of the desk, then let her eyes settle back on the photographs.

“Detective Rourke,” she said. “And ‘swept under the rug’ is a conclusion. Conclusions get people lazy.”

She tapped the file once.

“What we know is narrower. Rourke opened a line of inquiry that didn’t make it into the official summary. These photographs were taken before the report says anyone had reason to watch the building. That means either Rourke had information nobody documented, or somebody else did — and Rourke found it.”

Lena reached for her coffee, seemed to remember what it tasted like, and left it where it was.

“People hide things for three reasons. Fear. Money. Leverage.” Her gaze sharpened slightly. “Sometimes all three.”

She pulled one photo free and turned it so the image faced outward: the victim’s apartment building, its front entrance caught between the blur of passing traffic.

“Rourke won’t talk in the precinct. Might not talk at all. But there are pressure points. Retired landlord across the street. A bodega owner who saw every car that parked there. Maybe a tow driver who moved something they weren’t supposed to see.”

Her pen moved to the edge of the image, circling a dark shape near the curb.

“That’s a side mirror. Old sedan. Not much, but enough to start.”

Lena looked back up.

“We find the car first. Then we decide whether Rourke buried the truth, missed it, or was trying to keep it alive without getting caught.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Lena, were you a cop? You talk about this stuff like someone who's been on the inside."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s expression did not change, but something in the room seemed to lose a degree of warmth.

She gathered the photographs into a straighter line with two fingers.

“I talk like someone who’s spent too many years watching people lie badly and write worse.”

She picked up the photo with the side mirror again and angled it toward the desk lamp.

“Inside, outside — doesn’t matter as much as people think. Institutions have habits. So do criminals. So do witnesses who swear they don’t remember anything until you ask the question the right way.”

Her pen tapped the dark crescent of the mirror.

“This isn’t about me.”

Lena reached into a drawer and pulled out a city parking map, creased soft from use. She unfolded it over the case file, pinning down the corners with a stapler, a coffee mug, and two stacks of old receipts.

“Victim’s building was here. Camera angle puts the car somewhere along this curb, facing east. If it sat long enough to take more than one photograph, somebody noticed it. Bodega. Laundromat. Super across the street.”

She circled three storefronts.

“We start with the bodega owner. People ignore clerks. That makes clerks valuable.” Her eyes lifted briefly. “After that, we check tow records, not police records. Easier to get, less polished.”

Lena capped the pen with a hard click.

“And if Rourke’s name comes up again, we’ll know whether it came from the street or from a report someone tried to make clean.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Okay, the bodega it is." *I stand up, stretching a bit.* "Lead the way, Lena. Let's see what this clerk saw."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena folded the parking map with quick, practiced creases and slid the photographs back into the file. She left out the one with the side mirror, tucked it into the inside pocket of her coat, and locked the rest in the bottom drawer of the desk.

She did not take a purse. Just keys, phone, cash, and a small notebook worn at the spine.

“Don’t ask him what he saw,” she said, crossing to the door. “Ask him what annoyed him.”

She killed the desk lamp, and the office dimmed into gray.

“People forget faces. They remember a car blocking deliveries. Someone taking too long at the curb. A driver who didn’t buy anything but kept coming in to break a twenty. Irritation leaves better fingerprints than fear.”

The stairs down to Mercer were narrow and smelled more strongly of dry-cleaning solvent with every step. At the bottom, Lena paused beside the glass door and looked through it before opening it. Habit, not hesitation.

Outside, the city had settled into its late-morning rhythm: trucks double-parked, pedestrians moving like they had all been personally insulted by time, steam curling from a manhole cover near the curb. Lena turned south without checking whether she was followed.

The victim’s building sat six blocks over, wedged between a nail salon and a shuttered travel agency. Across from it, under a faded green awning, was the bodega from the photograph. Its front windows were crowded with lottery posters, prepaid phone ads, and sun-bleached cans of imported coffee stacked in a pyramid that had given up on symmetry.

Lena stopped half a block short.

She took out the surveillance photo and held it low, comparing the angle. Her eyes moved from the building entrance to the curb, then to the bodega window.

“Car would’ve been there,” she said, nodding toward a spot near a bent parking sign. “Good view of the entrance. Bad place to sit unnoticed.”

She slipped the photo away before crossing the street.

Inside the bodega, a bell over the door gave a tired jingle. The place smelled of frying oil, cardboard, ripe bananas, and floor cleaner. A small television behind the counter played a daytime court show with the volume low. Behind the register stood an older man with silver hair, thick glasses, and the wary patience of someone who had outlasted every kind of customer.

Lena picked up a pack of gum from a display and set it on the counter with a five-dollar bill.

“Morning,” she said.

The man rang it up without enthusiasm.

Lena glanced toward the front window, then at the curb outside.

“You still get delivery trucks complaining about that spot?” she asked, as if it were an old nuisance and not the first question in a murder investigation. “The one by the bent sign.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I follow Lena into the bodega, hands in my pockets, trying to look casual. I pick up a candy bar, pretending to examine it as Lena talks to the owner. When she mentions the delivery trucks, I chime in.* "Yeah, that spot's a nightmare. Always someone parked there."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
The bodega owner’s eyes moved from Lena to the client, then back again. He did not smile.

“Everybody parks there,” he said. “Everybody thinks five minutes is five minutes.”

Lena slid the gum into her coat pocket and left the change on the counter.

“Delivery guys still threaten to tow?” she asked.

“Threaten, yell, lean on horn.” He shrugged. “Same show every week.”

Lena looked toward the window again, not too long.

“Older sedan used to sit there,” she said. “Dark paint. Driver didn’t come in much. Maybe watched the building across the street.”

That landed differently.

The owner’s hand paused near the register drawer. His face stayed flat, but his attention sharpened behind the thick lenses.

“People watch many things.”

“Sure,” Lena said. “Scratch tickets. Their phones. Other people’s doors.”

The television behind him cut to a commercial, bright and cheerful and useless. Lena lowered her voice just enough to make the space feel smaller.

“This one annoyed you.”

The owner breathed out through his nose.

“Maybe.”

Lena waited.

Waiting cost nothing. Most people spent silence badly if someone else didn’t rush to fill it.

After a moment, the owner glanced past her toward the front glass.

“Car was there three days,” he said. “Not all day. Mornings. Same place if empty. If not empty, across hydrant until someone moved.”

“Driver?”

“Couldn’t see good. Cap. Sunglasses sometimes. One time came in.”

Lena kept her face neutral.

“Bought something?”

“Coffee. Black. Paid cash. Asked if my camera worked.”

Lena’s eyes shifted, briefly, to the small black dome tucked in the corner above the lottery machine.

“What did you say?”

“I said no.” The owner’s mouth tightened. “Camera works.”

“Still have the footage?”

He gave her a look that said he had owned a corner store too long to answer that quickly.

Lena reached into her pocket and took out one of her cards, plain white, no logo. She set it beside the register.

“I’m not asking for charity.”

“I don’t want trouble.”

“Then don’t give me the footage,” Lena said. “Give me what trouble looked like.”

His gaze dropped to the card.

Lena continued, calm and low.

“Plate number. Make. Model. Anything you wrote down because the car was blocking deliveries and you were tired of looking at it.”

The owner hesitated.

Then he bent slightly and pulled a battered spiral notebook from beneath the counter. Its cover was soft with grease stains and thumbprints. He flipped through pages filled with supplier names, invoice numbers, complaints, reminders, and the private accounting of a man who trusted paper more than people.

His finger stopped halfway down a page.

“Dark blue Crown Vic,” he said. “Old. Back bumper dented. Plate started with G2K. Maybe G2X. I wrote it because beer delivery couldn’t get in.”

Lena took out her notebook and copied it down.

“Date?”

He gave it. Lena wrote that too.

“Anyone with the driver?”

“No.”

“Driver speak to anyone outside?”

The owner’s jaw worked once.

“One time,” he said. “Across street. Near nail place. Short talk. Not friendly.”

“With who?”

He shook his head. “Couldn’t see. But after that, car didn’t come back.”

Lena looked through the front window at the nail salon’s bright sign, then at the victim’s building beyond it.

“Did the person from across the street come in here?”

The owner closed the spiral notebook.

“Not that day.”

Lena studied him for half a second. Not pushing yet. Pressure too early made people righteous.

She took a twenty from her pocket and placed it on the counter, beside the forgotten change.

“For the coffee he bought,” she said.

The owner looked at the bill, then at her.

“It was dollar fifty.”

“Then the rest is for remembering what annoyed you.”

He didn’t take it immediately, but he didn’t push it back either.

Lena turned slightly toward the door, then stopped as if the thought had just occurred to her.

“Camera that doesn’t work,” she said. “How long does it keep footage?”

The owner’s silence stretched.

Then he said, “Depends who asks.”

Lena nodded once.

“Fair.”

She took another card from her pocket and placed it on top of the first.

“If the answer changes, call before tonight. After tonight, I start asking tow drivers, and tow drivers talk loud.”

The owner’s mouth twitched. Not a smile. Something more practical.

“Back bumper dent,” he said again. “Right side. Like somebody hit a pole.”

Lena tapped her notebook once with the pen.

“That helps.”

She headed for the door. The bell gave its tired little jangle as she stepped back onto the sidewalk, the street noise rising around her.

Outside, Lena did not look back at the bodega.

“Dark blue Crown Vic,” she said, eyes on the curb by the bent sign. “Old fleet car, maybe decommissioned, maybe just made to look forgettable.”

She slid the notebook into her coat.

“Now we find out whether it belonged to someone watching the victim…”

Her gaze moved across the street, settling near the nail salon.

“…or someone watching Rourke.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "The witness says the detective who worked this case was named Torres. Detective M. Torres. Does that name mean anything to you?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stopped walking.

Only for a second. Long enough that the rhythm of the sidewalk moved around her and kept going without permission.

Then she took out her notebook again and flipped back to the page where she had written Rourke’s name.

“Witnesses get names wrong,” she said. “Files get names wrong on purpose.”

Her voice stayed even, but her eyes had gone colder.

She drew a line under Rourke. Beneath it, she wrote only an initial and a question mark.

“If your witness says the lead was someone else, then one of three things happened. Case changed hands and nobody told you. Someone used another detective’s name to make questions stop. Or there were two people looking at the same thing from different angles.”

She looked across the street at the victim’s building, then toward the nail salon.

“That last one is usually where the blood is.”

Lena shut the notebook.

“No precinct. No front desk. No badge wall.”

She reached into her coat and pulled out her phone.

“We check paper that doesn’t care about reputation. Court appearances. Subpoena returns. Property vouchers. Overtime entries. If a detective worked this case, they left weight somewhere. People think investigations live in reports. They don’t. They live in receipts.”

She thumbed through her contacts, paused over one, then made the call.

When the line picked up, Lena turned slightly away from the street noise.

“Need a records pull,” she said. “Unofficial. Homicide-adjacent file, Ninth jurisdiction, around the date I’m sending you. Names attached to interviews, evidence sign-outs, overtime, court liaison entries. Especially anything with an M.”

She listened.

“No, not inside. Email only.”

Another pause.

“Because I’m asking nicely.”

Her mouth barely moved at whatever came through the receiver.

“Try fast.”

She ended the call and put the phone away.

Then she looked back toward the bodega.

“The clerk remembered the car. Good. Now we need someone who remembered the argument near the nail place.”

Lena stepped off the curb when traffic broke, crossing toward the bright storefront with its painted flowers and chipped gold lettering.

“And if the name your witness gave is real,” she said, “then Rourke may not have been the one burying the case.”

She reached the opposite sidewalk and stopped outside the nail salon door.

“He may have been the one trying to dig it back up.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I nod slowly, taking in the new information.* "So, we're looking for two detectives now, maybe. One who buried it, one who tried to un-bury it." *I glance at the nail salon.* "You think this argument was between them?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena looked at the nail salon’s front window, where decals of pink blossoms peeled at the edges.

“Maybe,” she said. “But detectives arguing in public is sloppy. Sloppy happens when someone is angry, scared, or thinks nobody nearby matters.”

She studied the reflection in the glass before reaching for the door.

“Could’ve been the driver and whoever the driver reported to. Could’ve been a warning. Could’ve been someone telling the watcher to stop watching.”

The little bell over the salon door rang brighter than the bodega’s. Warm chemical air rolled out—acetone, lotion, acrylic powder, cheap perfume. Three manicure stations sat along one wall. Two were occupied. A woman in a red cardigan looked up from filing a client’s nails, her expression sharpening with immediate suspicion.

Lena stepped inside like someone who had every right to be there, but no intention of taking up more space than necessary.

“Morning,” she said. “I need to ask about something that happened outside a while back.”

The woman in the red cardigan did not stop filing.

“Health inspector came last month.”

“Not that.”

“Landlord?”

“Worse,” Lena said. “Memory.”

That earned the smallest pause.

Lena took out the photograph, keeping most of it shielded against her coat, and showed only the curb area by the bodega and the edge of the nail salon frontage.

“Dark blue Crown Vic parked across the street three mornings in a row. Old car. Dented bumper. Somebody had words near your front door.”

The woman’s eyes flicked to the photo, then away.

“No idea.”

Lena nodded as if that was expected.

“Sure.”

She turned slightly, looking at the row of polish bottles arranged by color behind the counter.

“Nice setup. Hard to keep dust off all that with the door opening every five minutes.”

The woman’s filing slowed.

Lena continued, mild and almost bored.

“Someone argues outside, blocks the window, smokes near the entrance, customers ask if it’s safe to come in. Bad for business.”

The woman’s mouth tightened.

“People are always arguing.”

“This one made you watch.”

The file stopped moving.

For a moment, only the tiny television in the corner made noise, some morning host laughing too hard at nothing.

Then the woman set the client’s hand down gently and looked toward the back of the salon.

“Two people,” she said. “One by the car. One came from that building.”

Lena’s attention didn’t move, but it sharpened.

“The victim’s building?”

“I don’t know victim. The building.” The woman nodded toward the street. “Person came out fast. Angry.”

“Man? Woman?”

The woman hesitated.

“Coat. Hat. Couldn’t tell. Not big. Not small.”

“Voice?”

“Low. Quiet angry. The kind where you don’t hear words, but you know somebody means them.”

Lena slipped the photograph away.

“Driver stay in the car?”

“At first. Then got out.”

“What happened?”

The woman glanced at her customer, then at the other worker, then back to Lena.

“They talked maybe one minute. The one from the building pointed down the block. Like saying leave. Driver laughed.”

Lena’s face stayed still.

“Then?”

“Then driver said something. Other one stopped moving.” The woman rubbed at an invisible mark on the table. “Like they heard a name they didn’t want to hear.”

Lena let the silence sit.

The woman finally added, “After that, no more car.”

Lena drew the notebook from her coat.

“Did you see the driver’s face?”

“Sunglasses. Cap. White. Maybe forty, fifty. Hard face.”

“Anything else?”

“Smelled like smoke when he passed the door.”

“Cigarettes?”

“No.” The woman frowned. “Cigar. Cheap one. Sweet.”

Lena wrote it down.

“Car have anything hanging from the mirror? Sticker? Damage besides the bumper?”

The woman’s eyes narrowed in concentration.

“Sticker on back window. Not big. White letters. Maybe from auction. Or parking.”

Lena looked up.

“Parking where?”

“I don’t know. Rectangle. White. Bottom corner.”

That was something. Not enough, but something.

Lena took out one of her cards and laid it near the polish rack.

“If you remember the words, or the face, call.”

The woman looked at the card but didn’t touch it.

“I don’t want to be witness.”

“No,” Lena said. “Nobody does.”

She glanced toward the street again.

“But you already were.”

The woman’s expression closed.

Lena didn’t push harder. Fear had a shelf life; handled wrong, it curdled into silence.

She stepped back outside, the salon bell chiming behind her.

On the sidewalk, she looked down the block in the direction the person from the building had pointed.

“Not necessarily two detectives,” she said. “Maybe one detective, one watcher. Maybe one person pretending to be official enough to scare people quiet.”

She took out her notebook and tapped the new line with her pen.

“Cheap sweet cigar. White rectangular sticker. Old dark Crown Vic. Partial plate. That’s enough for a tow yard, a fleet auction, or a private security outfit if we get lucky.”

Her eyes moved to the victim’s building entrance.

“But the important part is what stopped the argument.”

Lena closed the notebook.

“The driver said a name. Or a fact. Something that made the person from the building freeze.”

She glanced toward the upper windows.

“So now we find someone inside that building who knew what name could do that.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "So we're looking for someone who knows the victim, and knows what kind of secret could shut them up," *I muse, looking up at the victim's building.* "That sounds like a good place to start."

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena followed the client’s gaze up the face of the building.

Six stories. Prewar brick darkened by exhaust and weather. Fire escapes bolted to the front like afterthoughts. Half the windows had curtains drawn tight; the other half had plants, broken blinds, or nothing at all. A building that had learned not to volunteer information.

“Secrets don’t usually shut people up,” she said. “Leverage does.”

She crossed to the entrance and studied the buzzer panel. Names printed on yellowed strips of paper, some faded, some replaced with fresh tape. The victim’s apartment had already been scraped clean. No name, just a blank slot where one had been.

Lena noticed that first.

Then the camera above the vestibule door.

Small. Newer than the rest of the hardware. Angled down toward the entrance, not the street.

“Someone cared who came in,” she said.

She pressed no buzzers. Instead, she stepped back and looked toward the basement windows, then along the side of the building where trash cans crowded a narrow service alley.

“Super’s either downstairs or nearby. Supers know more than landlords and lie less elegantly.”

The alley smelled of wet cardboard, bleach, and old garbage. Lena moved past the bins until she found a metal door with a peeling sticker that read BUILDING STAFF ONLY. Beside it, someone had wedged a milk crate under a barred window. A cigarette had burned down on the concrete near the threshold, fresh enough that the ash still held its shape.

Lena looked at it, then at the lock.

She knocked twice. Not polite. Not aggressive. The kind of knock that assumed someone was home.

There was a pause.

A chain shifted. The door opened three inches, stopped by a security latch. A man’s face appeared in the gap: late fifties, heavy-lidded, gray stubble, undershirt visible beneath an open flannel. His eyes dropped to Lena’s shoes, then rose back to her face.

“What?”

Lena held up one of her cards between two fingers.

“I’m looking into the tenant from 4B.”

The man’s expression hardened.

“Talked already.”

“Not to me.”

“Then talk to who you’re supposed to talk to.”

Lena didn’t blink.

“That usually wastes time.”

He started to close the door.

Lena said, “Dark blue Crown Vic sat outside three mornings before the trouble. Driver spoke to someone who came out of this building. After that, the car disappeared.”

The door stopped.

There it was. Not fear exactly. Recognition.

Lena lowered the card.

“You saw it.”

The man’s eyes shifted past her into the alley, checking whether anyone else had followed. Then he shut the door.

For half a second, it seemed like that was the answer.

Then the chain scraped back. The door opened wider.

“Two minutes,” he said.

Lena stepped just inside the threshold but did not move deeper into the basement room than necessary. It was a cramped superintendent’s office doubling as a storage closet: paint cans, plungers, coils of cable, a small desk buried under maintenance slips. A radio muttered sports talk from a shelf.

She kept her hands visible.

“Name?” she asked.

“Gus.”

“Gus,” Lena repeated, making it useful instead of friendly. “The tenant in 4B. Who came looking before things went bad?”

Gus gave a humorless laugh.

“Everybody comes looking when rent’s late, pipes leak, boyfriend screams, girlfriend cries, packages go missing. You gotta be specific.”

Lena watched him closely.

“The person from 4B who argued with the Crown Vic driver.”

Gus rubbed a hand over his jaw.

“Wasn’t from 4B.”

Lena went still.

“Then who?”

“From upstairs. Six.” He pointed vaguely toward the ceiling. “Maybe 6A. Maybe 6C. I don’t keep track of everybody’s drama.”

“You keep track of everything,” Lena said. “That’s why your cigarette burned outside the service door while you listened.”

His face closed again, but not all the way.

Lena softened her voice by one degree.

“I don’t need your drama. I need the right door.”

Gus looked toward the little radio, though he wasn’t hearing it.

“6A,” he said at last. “Name on lease is Maribel Ortega. Her nephew stayed sometimes. Quiet kid. Too quiet.”

“Kid have a name?”

“Evan. Evan Ortega. Maybe twenty-four, twenty-five.”

Lena wrote it down.

“Evan knew the tenant in 4B?”

“Everybody knew her a little.” Gus shrugged. “She helped people. Took packages in. Watched cats. Wrote letters for the old lady in 2C when city forms came. That kind.”

“And Evan?”

Gus hesitated.

Lena caught it.

“What?”

“He was scared of her.”

“Scared?”

“Not like she’d hurt him.” Gus searched for the shape of it and didn’t like what he found. “Like she knew something and he wished she didn’t.”

Lena’s pen stopped moving.

“What happened the morning of the argument?”

Gus leaned back against the desk.

“I was fixing the lock on the vestibule. Heard voices. Looked through the glass. Evan was outside, talking to some guy by that car. Guy in a cap. Sunglasses. Acting like he owned the curb.”

“Words?”

“Couldn’t hear most.”

“Most isn’t none.”

Gus looked annoyed. Good. Annoyance was steadier than fear.

“The driver said, ‘Ask her what happened at Mercer.’ Something like that.”

Lena’s expression didn’t change, but the room seemed to narrow around the sentence.

“Mercer?”

“Yeah.”

“Street? Building? Business?”

“I don’t know. Just Mercer.” Gus folded his arms. “Evan looked like he got punched. Then he told the guy to leave. Guy laughed. Drove off after a minute.”

Lena wrote the phrase exactly.

Ask her what happened at Mercer.

She capped the pen.

“Did Evan talk to 4B after that?”

Gus nodded once.

“That night. I saw him outside her door. Didn’t knock at first. Just stood there. Then she opened before he did.”

“Argument?”

“No. Worse.” Gus looked at the floor. “Quiet.”

Lena looked toward the ceiling again.

“Is Evan here now?”

“Don’t know.”

“Maribel?”

“At work. Bakery on Stanton, unless she changed shifts.”

Lena handed him her card.

“If Evan leaves, comes back, or decides to disappear, call me before you decide it’s none of your business.”

Gus took the card reluctantly.

“People ask questions, people get hurt.”

Lena stepped back toward the service door.

“People stop asking, too.”

She left him with that and pushed back into the alley.

Outside, she paused near the bins and looked toward Mercer Street, though the office was blocks away and out of sight.

“Mercer,” she said quietly.

For a moment, her eyes had gone distant, measuring possibilities she did not name. Then the distance vanished behind the same hard, practical calm.

She looked toward the front entrance of the building.

“4B wasn’t the only pressure point. Evan Ortega was one too.”

Lena slid the notebook into her coat.

“We find Evan before the driver does.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: "Mercer... that's where your office is," *I say, a little slowly. A chill runs down my spine.* "You think this is all connected to you, somehow?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena’s eyes stayed on the mouth of the alley.

For a second, nothing in her face moved. Not surprise. Not fear. Not denial. Just calculation, fast and silent.

“Mercer’s a long street,” she said.

She took out her phone and checked the screen, though it hadn’t buzzed. Habit gave her something to do with her hands.

“Dry cleaners. offices. old leases. storefronts that change names every eighteen months. Half the city has passed through Mercer and left something behind.”

She put the phone away.

“But the driver wanted Evan to hear it. Not me.”

Lena looked back toward the building’s rear door.

“That means Mercer meant something to Evan. Or to the woman in 4B. Maybe both.”

Her jaw tightened slightly.

“The mistake would be making this personal before the facts do.”

She stepped out of the alley and onto the sidewalk, scanning the upper floors again. Sixth floor. Curtains. A cracked window. One dead plant in a fire escape box outside what might have been 6A.

“Evan hears ‘Ask her what happened at Mercer,’ freezes, tells the driver to leave, then goes to 4B that night and stands outside her door like he’s afraid of the answer.” Lena’s voice remained low. “Next useful question is whether he asked.”

She crossed to the front entrance and studied the buzzer panel again.

“Maribel’s at work. Evan may be upstairs, or he may already be running.”

Lena pressed the buzzer for 6A.

Once.

Then waited.

No answer.

She pressed again, longer this time.

Still nothing.

Lena stepped back and looked at the camera above the vestibule door.

“New camera. Super didn’t install that for decoration.”

She took her phone out again and called Gus.

When he picked up, she didn’t bother with hello.

“Vestibule camera. Who has access?”

She listened, eyes still on the lens.

“Landlord remote, local recorder in basement. Fine. I need the last week copied before anyone decides maintenance erased it.”

A pause.

“No, Gus. Not tomorrow.”

Another pause.

Lena’s mouth flattened.

“Because Evan Ortega may be the next person someone wants quiet.”

She ended the call and slipped the phone away.

“Gus will stall for ten minutes, complain for five, then do it.” She glanced down the block. “That gives us enough time to try the bakery.”

She started walking toward Stanton, coat moving close around her like armor.

“If Maribel knows where her nephew is, she may lie. Family lies differently than strangers. Less polish. More anger.”

At the corner, Lena stopped beside a parked delivery van and looked back once toward the victim’s building.

“And if Mercer does point back to my office, then somebody made a very careful choice bringing this case through my door.”

Her eyes narrowed.

“That doesn’t mean we back away.”

She turned toward Stanton.

“It means we stop assuming the client picked the route.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I quicken my pace to keep up with Lena, a knot forming in my stomach.* "So you think someone set you up? Used me to get you involved in all this?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena didn’t slow down.

“Maybe,” she said. “Maybe not.”

Traffic hissed over damp pavement beside them. A cyclist cut too close to a cab and shouted something that vanished into the city noise. Lena kept her eyes moving—storefront glass, parked cars, reflections, anyone who noticed them twice.

“Being used doesn’t mean being guilty,” she added. “Most people who carry messages don’t know they’re carrying them.”

She turned onto Stanton. The bakery was halfway down the block, marked by a striped awning and a line of people waiting for coffee, rolls, and whatever small comfort could be bought before noon. Warm air pushed out every time the door opened, heavy with yeast, sugar, and burnt espresso.

Lena stopped across the street instead of going in.

“First rule now: we assume someone expected us to follow the obvious trail.” Her gaze fixed on the bakery window. “Bodega. Nail salon. Building. Family. That’s a clean chain. Too clean if someone laid it.”

She reached into her coat and took out the partial plate notes again.

“Dark blue Crown Vic. Sweet cigar. White rear sticker. Partial plate. Driver knew enough to say Mercer and make Evan freeze. That makes the driver useful, not necessarily important.”

Her eyes shifted to the bakery door as a woman in a white apron stepped outside to change a chalkboard sign.

“Maribel Ortega,” Lena said quietly. “Aunt. Leaseholder. If she knows Evan’s gone, she’ll either be scared or angry. If she doesn’t know, we get the first honest reaction of the day.”

She folded the notebook closed.

“But we don’t lead with murder. We don’t lead with detectives. We don’t lead with Mercer.”

Lena crossed when the light changed.

Inside, the bakery was narrow and bright, with glass cases full of pastries dusted in powdered sugar. Behind the counter, two employees moved fast through orders. The woman from outside came back in carrying the chalkboard, cheeks flushed from the cold.

Lena waited until the morning rush thinned by three customers. She bought a black coffee she didn’t want and paid cash.

Then she looked at the woman behind the register.

“Maribel Ortega working today?”

The woman’s expression changed before she answered. Not much. Enough.

“Who’s asking?”

Lena set one of her plain cards on the counter, face down.

“Someone trying to find Evan before the wrong person does.”

That got her the full attention.

The woman behind the counter didn’t touch the card.

“You family?”

“No.”

“Then I don’t know you.”

“No,” Lena said. “But you know the look of someone deciding whether to call upstairs, call the back room, or call someone else entirely.”

The woman’s jaw tightened.

Lena lowered her voice.

“Tell Maribel I’m not here to scare her. Somebody already did that. I’m here because Evan may still be alive enough to help.”

For a moment, the bakery noise carried on around them: the espresso machine steaming, tongs clicking against metal trays, a customer laughing too loudly near the door.

Then the woman at the register turned her head toward the kitchen.

“Maribel,” she called, too flatly to be casual. “Front.”

A few seconds passed.

A woman in her early sixties emerged from the back, wiping flour from her hands onto a towel. Her hair was pinned tight. Her face had the wary exhaustion of someone who worked on her feet and trusted bad news more than good.

Lena didn’t smile.

“Maribel Ortega?”

The woman looked at the card on the counter, then at Lena.

“What did Evan do?”

“Maybe nothing,” Lena said.

Maribel’s mouth trembled once and hardened immediately after.

“That means something.”

“It means I’m looking for him.”

“Why?”

“Because a man in an old blue Crown Vic spoke to him outside your building. Because Evan went to see the woman in 4B that night. Because now that woman is dead.”

Maribel’s hand closed around the towel.

Lena watched the reaction carefully. Grief, yes. Fear, sharper.

Maribel knew.

“Where is Evan?” Lena asked.

Maribel looked toward the front windows.

Lena didn’t turn. She used the reflection in the pastry case instead. Street. Passing coats. A delivery truck. No dark Crown Vic. Not yet.

“I don’t know,” Maribel said.

Lena believed half of it.

“When did you last see him?”

“Two nights ago.”

“Where?”

“At home.”

“What condition?”

Maribel’s eyes flashed.

“He was scared.”

“Of the driver?”

“Of everybody.”

Lena leaned one hand lightly on the counter.

“What happened at Mercer?”

Maribel went still.

There it was again. The phrase had weight. Not confusion. Recognition.

Lena kept her voice even.

“Evan heard that and froze. The woman in 4B heard it too, didn’t she?”

Maribel swallowed.

“I have work.”

“You have a nephew someone may be hunting.”

Maribel looked past Lena again, toward the street.

“Evan was a good boy.”

“Good boys still get cornered.”

“He didn’t hurt her.”

“I didn’t say he did.”

Maribel’s eyes came back to Lena’s.

For the first time, she looked less like she was hiding something and more like she was holding a door shut from the other side.

“She helped him,” Maribel said. “That’s all.”

“With what?”

Maribel’s fingers twisted the towel.

“Papers.”

“What kind of papers?”

“I don’t know.”

Lena said nothing.

Maribel looked down.

“He came home one night with blood on his sleeve. Not much. He said it wasn’t his. He said he saw something he shouldn’t. She helped him write a statement.”

Lena’s face stayed controlled.

“A statement to who?”

“I don’t know.”

“Maribel.”

“I don’t know,” she snapped, too loud.

A customer near the door glanced over. Maribel lowered her voice immediately.

“She put it in an envelope. Told him if anything happened, there were copies.”

Lena’s pulse stayed steady, but her attention narrowed.

“Copies where?”

Maribel shook her head.

“She wouldn’t tell him. She said that was the point.”

“And Mercer?”

Maribel looked at the card again.

“She said the thing Evan saw started there.”

“Where on Mercer?”

“I don’t know the number.”

“What was there?”

Maribel’s voice dropped until it nearly disappeared under the hiss of the espresso machine.

“A back room. A card game. Men with money. Men with guns. Evan delivered food there sometimes. Off-books. Cash.”

Lena’s eyes hardened.

“And one night he saw something.”

Maribel nodded once.

“He saw someone get taken out through the back. Not walking.”

Lena let that settle.

The bakery suddenly felt too warm.

“Who knew he saw it?”

“The woman in 4B. Maybe the man in the car.” Maribel’s breath caught. “Maybe whoever he worked for.”

“Where is Evan now?”

Maribel closed her eyes for half a second.

“I gave him money.”

“When?”

“Yesterday morning.”

“Where did he go?”

“I told him not to tell me.”

Lena studied her.

That part was true.

“Phone?”

“He threw it away.”

“Friends?”

“No. Not now.”

“Places he’d hide?”

Maribel hesitated.

Lena’s voice sharpened.

“If you protect the idea of him instead of the person, they’ll find the person.”

Maribel flinched as if the words had struck bone.

“There’s a church basement on Rivington,” she said. “He slept there once when things were bad. And an old coworker at a diner near Delancey. Name is Paolo.”

Lena took both down.

Then her phone buzzed.

She looked at the screen.

A message from the records contact.

No attachment yet. Just one line:

M. TORRES APPEARS ON PROPERTY SIGN-OUT. ROURKE FLAGGED SAME FILE TWO DAYS LATER. CALL ME.

Lena stared at it for one second, then locked the phone.

She looked back at Maribel.

“If Evan contacts you, you do not tell him to come home. You tell him to go somewhere public, crowded, and ugly with cameras. Then you call me.”

Maribel nodded, barely.

Lena picked up her untouched coffee.

At the door, she paused and glanced once more through the bakery window at the street outside.

“Someone was cleaning up loose ends,” she said quietly. “Evan was one. The woman in 4B was another.”

She pushed the door open, cold air cutting through the sugar-warm room.

“And now somebody may be checking whether we’re next.”

dialogue.name: Client
dialogue.content: *I shiver despite the warm air from the bakery. My stomach is a tight knot.* "So, Torres was signing out property from the case, and Rourke was looking at the same file later? What does that even mean?"

dialogue.name: Lena
dialogue.content:
Lena stepped onto the sidewalk and let the bakery door swing shut behind her. The warmth vanished. Stanton Street took over again—horns, wet tires, footsteps, the hard bright edge of daylight on glass.

She didn’t answer immediately.

She moved them a few doors down, away from the bakery window, and stopped beside a closed tailor shop with a metal grate pulled over the front. Only then did she take out her phone again and reread the message.
