Maren's eyes dropped to the plate for exactly one second. Crab cakes. Glistening. Still faintly warm from wherever they'd been kept.

She did not move her left hand toward them.

"Tell Lord Havel that is very generous of him," she said, and her voice carried its usual measured evenness without so much as a tremor of anything else in it. She turned toward the merchant's table and gave a short, courteous nod in the direction of whoever had sent the message. "And tell him the Antler is honored by the gesture."

She picked up the plate with her right hand — the weaker one, careful — and set it smoothly down the bar, just out of arm's reach, nudging it toward the traveler's side with a single economical motion.

"I do not care for seafood myself," she said, already turning back to her tally sheet, already picking up her pen with her left hand. "But our guest here may feel differently. Fresh crab from the coast is not something you see at a crossroads inn every evening."

She said it pleasantly. She said it the way someone says a thing they have said many times before — easy, unremarkable, closed.

She did not look at the plate again. She moved three steps down the bar, set the tally sheet flat, and bent over it with the focused attention of a woman doing arithmetic.

Her right hand, hanging at her side, was very still.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I look at the crab cakes, then back at Maren, who is now focused on her tally sheet. I glance at the merchant, who gives a slight nod and a smile. I then push the plate of crab cakes back towards Maren, leaving it between us.*

"Perhaps you just haven't had the *right* crab cakes," I say, a small smirk playing on my lips. "There's a lot of flavor in the sea, if you know how to find it."

*I pick up my spoon, ready to dive into the stew.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren did not look up from the tally sheet immediately. She finished the line she was adding — her lips moved slightly, a habit from her quartermaster days — and then she set the pen down and looked at the plate sitting between them, and then at the traveler.

"That is what people say," she said. "Usually right before they describe, at length, a meal I have no interest in eating."

She picked up the plate with her right hand, carried it back down the bar, and set it on the far end with a small decisive click. Not rude. Definitive.

"The sea and I have an understanding," she added, returning to her spot and picking up the pen again. "It stays over there and I stay over here, and we are both content with the arrangement."

She made another mark on the tally sheet. The corner of her mouth did not quite move, but something in the set of it suggested she was aware the line was funnier than her face admitted.

"Eat your stew, friend. Old Pell has been cooking since before either of us had opinions about seafood, and he will be deeply offended if it goes cold while you're busy trying to convert me." She glanced up briefly. "He won't say anything. He'll just be sad about it. Somehow that's worse."

She turned the tally sheet over, smoothed it flat, and went back to her numbers.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked up from the tally sheet.

"He'll never know you said that," she said. "He goes to bed at nine and sleeps like a man with a clear conscience, which he has, because his stew is above reproach and he knows it."

She set the pen down and reached left-handed for her own cup — she kept water behind the bar, not ale, during working hours — and raised it a fraction in the direction of the kitchen hatch.

"But I'll tell him in the morning. He won't react. He'll just nod and go back to chopping whatever he's chopping." She took a sip. "Then he'll make the bread a little better the next day. That's how he accepts a compliment."

She set the cup down and leaned her forearm on the bar again, the easy posture of someone settled into the late part of the evening. The common room had quieted some — the two merchants had moved from arguing to the quieter stage of arguing, which meant they were getting somewhere. The dwarf had folded his letter and was staring into his ale with the expression of a man reading bad news in the foam.

Maren glanced at him, noted it, filed it away. She'd check on him in a few minutes.

"Months on the road," she said, returning her attention to the traveler. It wasn't quite a question. She had a way of repeating a detail back that left room for a person to either fill it or not, entirely at their own discretion.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Something like that." I took another mouthful of stew, savoring the rich flavor. *I decide to change the subject slightly.* "Any interesting news pass through here lately? Merchants always carry the best rumors."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren considered the question the way she considered most things — briefly, thoroughly, and without telegraphing the process.

"Depends on what you call interesting," she said. She picked up the cloth and ran it left-handed along a stretch of bar that didn't especially need wiping, more out of habit than necessity. "A wool merchant came through four days ago swearing the eastern pass is being watched. Didn't say by whom. Didn't seem to know, or didn't want to say, which are different problems."

She folded the cloth and set it aside.

"Before him, a courier from the capital — wouldn't stop talking about some dispute over a bridge toll that apparently three separate lords all believe they have the right to collect. I stopped listening after the second lord." She paused. "The courier, however, did not stop talking. He stayed two nights."

The dwarf at the end of the bar turned his cup in his hands. Maren clocked it without looking directly at him.

"The more reliable news is that the southern road has been slow. Wagons backed up at the Aldenmere crossing — something with the ferry, nobody agrees on what. Which is why I have six full rooms tonight instead of ten." She tilted her head slightly. "Traders who would have passed through stopped here instead. Lord Havel among them, apparently, with his coastal delicacies."

She said the last part without inflection.

"The rumors worth believing are usually the ones nobody is trying to sell you." She glanced at the traveler's pack, then back up. "The ones people lead with tend to be either wrong or someone else's problem made to sound like yours."

She let that sit for a moment, easy and unhurried.

"Anything specific you're hoping to hear about, or just taking the general inventory?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The twelfth stroke of the clock was still fading when Maren stopped mid-sentence.

She had been saying something about the Aldenmere ferry — she finished it anyway, because she was not the sort to leave a thought dangling — and then she set down the cloth and turned to the shelf behind the bar with the quiet purposefulness of someone performing a task that required no thought because it had been performed so many times it had become the shape of the hour itself.

She took down two cups. Not the common ale cups. Two that were slightly better — not fine, the Antler was not that kind of establishment, but kept separately, on a different shelf. She filled both from the same tap. Set one in front of herself.

The second she carried to the far end of the bar, past the lockbox, past the key-board, to the very end where the counter met the wall. She set it down there with a small precise motion, adjusted it once so the handle faced out, and left it.

She came back to her spot, picked up her own cup, and took a single sip.

Then she picked up the cloth again and looked at the traveler with her usual expression — calm, attentive, giving nothing away and not trying to.

"You were asking about the ferry," she said. "The short answer is that nobody knows when it will be running reliably again, and anyone who tells you otherwise is guessing or lying, and you will have to determine which on your own."

She did not explain the second cup.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her movements, particularly the placement of the second cup.* "I imagine you get a lot of guesses and lies in here." *I take another mouthful of stew, finishing it, and push the empty bowl forward.* "So, if the southern road is slow, what's the best way to get to the coast these days?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren collected the empty bowl with her left hand and set it through the kitchen hatch without looking. Old Pell would deal with it in the morning. She heard the soft scrape of it being moved to the side — he was still up, then. He always said he went to bed at nine. She had never once known him to actually do it.

"You want the coast." She refilled the traveler's ale without being asked, left hand on the tap, and set it back down. "Which part of it matters. The coast is a long piece of geography and it does not all have the same problems."

She leaned on the bar.

"If you're headed for Venmoor or anywhere south of it, forget the Aldenmere crossing entirely. Go north first — counterintuitive, I know — take the Harwick road to the ridge junction, then cut south through the Thornfeld. Adds half a day, maybe less if your pace is reasonable. The road is unpaved past the ridge but it is maintained, which is more than I can say for the southern route right now." She paused. "There is a waystation at the Thornfeld junction. The man who runs it is called Oswick. He is unpleasant but honest, and his horses are sound. If you need a remount or a cart, he is the better option over anyone you'll find at Aldenmere even when the ferry is working."

She straightened and moved the cloth along the bar again, that same habitual motion.

"If you're headed north of Venmoor — Crestfall, the harbor towns — then the Aldenmere problem does not affect you at all. You take the eastern road through Dunnholt and you are there in three days in reasonable weather." A brief pause. "The eastern pass is being watched, according to the wool merchant. I mention this not to alarm you but because you asked for routes and that seems like relevant information."

She glanced at the pack again. The same glance she had given it three times now — not pointed, not suspicious, just the quiet noticing of a woman who paid attention to things.

"The coast is specific enough a destination," she said, her tone remaining easy, "that I suspect you have a specific reason for going. Which is entirely your business." She picked up the pen and tapped it once against the tally sheet. "I only mention it because the route changes considerably depending on what you're carrying and whether you'd prefer to arrive quietly or efficiently. Sometimes those are the same thing. Sometimes they are not."

She looked at him directly, without pressure.

"Corner room, third on the left. Key sticks. You have paid for both and I am not asking you for anything else." She set the pen down. "But if you want a better answer than the one I just gave you, a more specific question tends to get one."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I consider her words, and the look she gives my pack. The directness in her tone. I push the empty ale mug forward.* "Venmoor. And I'd prefer quietly. The package... it's fragile, and attracts unwanted attention."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren refilled the ale mug. Set it down. Did not make a production of any of it.

"Venmoor," she repeated. Not an echo — a confirmation, the way a quartermaster reads a number back before writing it in the ledger. She picked up the pen and made a small notation on the tally sheet that had nothing to do with the conversation. Old habit. Something to do with her left hand while the rest of her thought.

"Harwick road, then the Thornfeld cut," she said. "I stand by that route. It is slower than the direct road and that is precisely why you want it. The direct road is faster, which means it is busier, which means it is watched — not by anything official, in my experience, but by people who have learned that travelers moving quickly are often moving toward something worth having." She set the pen down. "Travelers moving slowly look like they have nowhere particular to be. That impression is worth half a day of your time."

She was quiet for a moment.

"Oswick at the Thornfeld waystation." She said it again deliberately, making sure it landed. "Tell him Maren sent you. He will not become pleasant but he will become cooperative, which is the more useful quality. He has a covered cart he rents out on occasion — the kind with a locked box built into the bed. He does not ask what goes in it." A pause that was not quite a pause. "He charges accordingly. But fragile things that attract unwanted attention tend to arrive in Venmoor in better condition when they travel in a covered cart than when they travel on a person."

She reached beneath the bar and pulled out a small square of paper, wrote on it in a quick, even hand — left-handed, the letters tilted slightly — and slid it across the bar.

It was a sketch. Not artistic, but precise: the fork at Harwick, the road north, the ridge junction marked with a small X, the Thornfeld cut drawn as a dotted line with the waystation indicated. Three days of road in thirty seconds of work.

"The dotted section is unpaved but passable," she said. "Do not attempt it in heavy rain. The drainage is poor past the second mile and you will lose an axle if you are in a cart, or your patience if you are on foot." She smoothed the edge of the paper flat with her thumb. "It has not rained in six days. You should be fine."

She straightened, folded the cloth over her left arm.

"I do not know what you are carrying," she said. "I am not going to ask. What I will tell you is that the Antler has twelve rooms and I have been running it for eighteen years, and the things people bring through those doors are their own business until they become someone else's problem." She met his eyes, direct and unhurried. "If whatever is in that pack is going to become someone else's problem before morning, I would appreciate knowing now. Not because I will turn you out — you have paid for the room and the stew was fair — but because I have staff here and I prefer to have time to make arrangements."

She said it without accusation. The way someone states a policy they have thought through carefully and find entirely reasonable.

"If it is simply fragile and valuable and inconvenient," she added, "then sleep well, take the Thornfeld road, and give Oswick my name."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I look at the map she's drawn, then at her. Her directness is... disarming. I push the paper back towards her, letting my hand linger on it for a moment.*

"It's just fragile and valuable," I say, a little more quietly than before. "No trouble tonight, I promise." *I tap the map.* "This is very helpful, Maren. Thank you."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at the hand on the map for a moment. Then she folded the paper in thirds, crisp and even, and pushed it back across the bar toward the traveler.

"Keep it," she said. "I know the roads. You do not, or you would not have asked."

She picked up the cloth again and moved down the bar, wiping toward the dwarf's end. He was still turning his cup. She refilled it without comment, set it down, gave him the brief nod of someone acknowledging that a man is allowed to sit with his thoughts without being asked about them. He looked up, surprised, then settled back. She moved back to her spot.

The common room had gone quieter. The merchants had finally reached some agreement or given up — either way, they were drinking instead of talking, which was a better use of everyone's time. The fire had burned down to a steady, comfortable level. Outside, the wind had picked up slightly; she could hear it in the eaves, the familiar voice of the building settling into the late hours.

Maren glanced at the end of the bar.

Tobin's cup sat where she had left it, handle out, untouched.

She looked back at the traveler.

"You have been on the road for months," she said. It was not quite the same thing as *you look tired*, which people said when they meant well and wanted to be sympathetic. It was simply an observation, delivered without weight or expectation. "The room will be there when you want it. The ale will be here until I close, which is when the last person leaves or I run out of patience, whichever comes first."

The corner of her mouth did not move.

"In eighteen years it has always been the last person."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Eighteen years, huh? You must have seen some things." I take another sip of ale, then look at the untouched cup at the end of the bar. "Who's the other drink for, if you don't mind me asking?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren was quiet for exactly one beat.

She did not follow the traveler's gaze to the end of the bar. She did not need to. She knew precisely where the cup was, the angle of the handle, the way the firelight caught the surface of the ale.

"I do mind, a little," she said. Not unkindly. The same even tone she used for everything, the one that made it impossible to tell if you had offended her or simply asked a question she had decided not to answer. "But I will tell you it is not a ghost story, if that is what you are imagining. I am not that interesting."

She picked up the cloth and folded it over her left arm, a thing she did when her hands wanted something to hold.

"Some questions I answer and some I do not," she continued, "and I find that most people, if they think about it, can tell the difference between the two kinds before they ask. You struck me as someone with that particular skill." A pause. "I may have been flattering you."

She said it without expression. Three seconds passed.

"Eighteen years," she repeated, returning to the safer part of the question, the part she had no objection to. "Before that, five years doing work that was less comfortable and paid worse. Before that, I was learning this place from the woman who left it to me." She set the cloth down on the bar. "So I have been in this room, in one capacity or another, for the better part of my life. And yes. I have seen things."

She reached left-handed for her own cup and took a measured sip.

"Most of them I have forgotten on purpose," she said. "The rest keep the winters from being boring."

dialogue.content: *I chuckle, a low, tired sound.* "Fair enough. Some things are best left unasked, or unsaid." *I nod towards the dwarf.* "Looks like you've got another winter story unfolding over there."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The pencil marks stopped at a date three years old. The graphite looked new. A cold draft moved dust from upstairs through the hall. The box shifted on the counter. Kitchen. Someone had written it not long ago.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I stare at the pencil marks, a strange pang in my chest.* "They... they kept measuring." I whisper. "After I left."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content: The graphite groove held a thin shine. A dry, chalky taste settled on the tongue. Upstairs, a floorboard ticked.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The closet door gave a low creak. Dust stirred in the frame's gap. The photograph lay beneath a wool coat.

Paper edges felt soft from handling. The image showed a woman at a garden table. Her hands rested around a blue cup. Sunlight fell across her open collar.

Time had yellowed the corners. A faint vanilla smell came from the card. The wool coat held a cold, damp scent.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I trace her face in the photo.* "Mom..." I whisper, a tear welling up. "Still so beautiful."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
A thread from the wool coat caught the light. The closet smelled of damp fibers and cedar.

The photograph lay face-up. Sunlight in the print looked thin. Dust settled over the blue cup.

The kitchen box lid lifted. A click came through the floor. Vinegar smell drifted under the door.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I sniffle, wiping my eyes with the back of my hand.* "What was that?" I ask, my voice shaky. I look towards the kitchen.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The lid had popped. The latch caught on the box edge. Vinegar stung the nose.

A boot heel clicked on tile. The kitchen floor rang under it.

Someone stood beyond the doorway. A wool sleeve brushed the cabinet. Rain tapped the window.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The real estate agent stood in the doorway. Her coat smelled of wet wool and coffee.

Her smile was wide. “Hi. I’m Dana.” Her voice carried.

She stepped into the hall. Her boot left a damp print on the carpet.

She touched a clipboard. Paper rustled. “The kitchen box isn’t mine.”

The lid banged. Vinegar sharpened the air.

Dana looked toward the counter. Her heel tapped the tile.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "I know," I say, my voice still a little wobbly. "I think someone else is here." I look from the open box to Dana.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Dana stepped toward the kitchen. Her wet coat brushed the doorframe. Vinegar rose from the box.

A cold draft moved through the hall. Dana stopped. Her eyes tracked the hallway ceiling.

A floorboard ticked above them. Dana’s clipboard trembled. Paper rustled.

“Hello?” Her voice caught. Rain tapped the window.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Dana, wait," I say, putting my hand on her arm. "Didn't you hear that?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Dana turned. Her sleeve caught Eli's hand. Wool smelled of rain and coffee.

Her eyes moved to the stairwell. The wood ticked again. Dust swirled in the draft.

Dana raised one hand. The clipboard hit her ribs. Paper shivered.

“Hold on,” she said. Her mouth stayed dry. A clock ticked in the kitchen.

Upstairs, the floorboard groaned. A shoe pressed the hallway runner. The sound moved toward the old room.

Dana's fingers tightened on the clipboard. The metal clip bit her palm.

Rain scratched the window glass. The vinegar smell thickened.

Dana looked at Eli. Her breath fogged the cold air. Her lips moved, but no sound came.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pull my hand away.* "What is going on?" I whisper. "Someone's up there."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Dana lifted her chin toward the stairwell. Her boot squeaked on the tile. Dust stirred in the draft.

The runner above shifted. A shoe pressed the old carpet. The smell of damp wool drifted down.

Dana set the clipboard against her ribs. Paper scraped wet fabric. The vinegar odor sharpened.

Her mouth opened. Breath fogged in the cold hall. A clock ticked from the kitchen.

The metal clip bit her palm. Dana’s knuckles whitened. The house groaned around them.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I grab Dana's arm, pulling her back towards the front door.* "We need to get out of here," I say, my voice tight. "Now."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. The brass handle was cold. Rain tapped the side glass.

Dana's boot scraped tile. Her wet coat smelled of coffee. The clipboard hit the wall.

Upstairs, the runner shifted. Dust swirled in the draft. A floorboard ticked above them.

Dana's nails bit the door edge. The latch clicked. Vinegar stung the hallway.

The door gave. Cold air rushed in. The porch boards groaned under wet shoes.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I tug on her arm again, pulling her onto the porch.* "Come on!" I urge, my eyes darting back to the house.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The porch boards sagged under their weight. Rain hit Eli's neck. Cold. Dana's coat clung to her shoulders, heavy with water.

The door swung shut behind them. The latch caught. A wooden thud settled the hallway silence.

Dana stepped back. Her boot heel slipped on wet concrete. She caught the railing. Metal bit her palm.

The kitchen window glowed from inside. A shape moved past the glass. Dana's breath caught.

Rain ran down the porch posts. The gravel drive hissed under the downpour. Dana's clipboard lay forgotten in the hallway. Through the side glass, the runner upstairs shifted again.

Dana's teeth chattered. The smell of wet wool and coffee faded, replaced by rain and cut grass. Her eyes stayed on the window. The shape did not move.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: *I pull Dana towards my car, fumbling for my keys.* "Did you see that?" I stammer, my heart pounding. "Someone's definitely in there."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave the pack one brief glance, not prying so much as noting the care taken with it, then reached beneath the bar with her left hand and pulled a wooden bowl from the stack.

“We have stew hot enough to remind you your tongue has nerves, bread that was fresh this morning, and cheese that has kept its opinions to itself,” she said. “Room for the night is three coppers. Supper is two. Ale is one more if you want it.”

She turned her head toward the kitchen door without raising her voice.

“Pell. One stew and bread for the bar.”

From somewhere beyond the doorway came Old Pell’s answering grunt, which Maren had long ago learned to treat as a complete sentence.

She took a key from the row of hooks behind her, choosing one from the middle with her left hand. A small iron tag hung from it, stamped with the number seven.

“Room seven. It has a bed, a basin, and a window that almost closes properly. If the wind whistles, whistle back. It gets lonely.”

Her face remained entirely solemn.

She set the key on the bar, then reached for a clean mug. “Ale, water, or cider?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Stew and bread sounds perfect. And ale, please." I push a small coin pouch across the bar. "Don't mind a whistling wind. Keeps things interesting." I give a small, tired smile.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the pouch with her left hand, weighed it by feel, and loosened the drawstring with the practiced economy of someone who could count coin by candlelight during a thunderstorm.

“Interesting is what people call trouble when they have already paid for it,” she said.

She counted out the cost, then nudged the pouch back across the bar with the change set beside it in a neat little stack.

“Room, supper, ale. If you want breakfast, that is another copper in the morning. Oats, eggs if the hens feel generous, and whatever bread survived the night.”

She drew a mug of ale from the barrel behind her, left hand steady on the tap, and set it down in front of the traveler. The ale was dark gold with a modest head of foam.

A moment later, Old Pell appeared at the kitchen hatch with a steaming bowl in one hand and half a loaf of brown bread tucked against his elbow. Maren collected both, set them on the bar, and placed a spoon beside the bowl.

The stew was thick with venison, barley, carrots, and onion, rosemary rising through the steam. It was the sort of food meant less for elegance and more for convincing a body it had not been abandoned by the world.

“There,” Maren said. “Eat slow unless you enjoy burning the roof of your mouth. I charge extra for listening to regrets.”

Her gaze flicked once more to the careful pack, then back to the traveler’s face. She did not ask. Not yet.

“Road been unkind, friend?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s eyes went to the plate before anything else.

Crab. Fried golden, smelling of butter, salt, and the sea.

For the space of one breath, her left hand stilled on the bar.

Then she reached—not for the plate, but for a clean wooden trencher. With the edge of it, she slid the crab cakes a careful handspan away from her side of the counter without touching them. Her face did not change.

“That is generous of Lord Havel,” she said, her voice even. “And poorly informed.”

She looked toward the merchant’s table, finding the sender without needing to be told twice. Nobles, merchants, drovers, and hedge-priests all had a way of wanting witnesses for their generosity.

“Tell Lord Havel he has my thanks,” Maren said, still not raising her voice, though it carried cleanly enough. “Also tell him that if he wishes to feed my guests, he may send coin to the bar and I will provide food that did not travel half the kingdom in a fish cart.”

A few heads turned. Someone near the hearth coughed into their mug in a way that sounded suspiciously like a laugh.

Maren took a folded cloth from beneath the bar with her left hand, laid it beside the plate without brushing against it, and glanced to the traveler.

“I do not care for seafood,” she said. “It has always struck me as food that tried too hard to remain water.”

Her expression remained solemn.

Then she tipped her chin toward the crab cakes.

“If you want them, they are yours. If not, I will have one of the servers return them with all the ceremony they deserve.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I look from the crab cakes to Maren, then back to the crab cakes.* "Hmm, I usually enjoy a good crab cake... but I think I'll stick with the stew tonight. Much more fortifying for a weary traveler." *I push the plate gently back towards her.* "Perhaps they'd be better suited for someone else."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the plate slide back toward her by an inch or two, and her left hand moved at once—not hurried, but precise.

She caught the edge of the plate with the folded cloth, careful not to let even a fingertip brush it, and shifted it safely aside.

“A wise choice,” she said. “Pell’s stew has never once arrived claiming noble patronage. That alone recommends it.”

She looked toward the room and made a small motion with her left hand to one of the servers, a narrow-shouldered lad named Evin who had been refilling mugs near the hearth.

“Evin. Please return Lord Havel’s gift. Use both hands, your best manners, and none of your opinions.”

Evin crossed over, took the plate, and carried it back toward the merchant’s table as if it were a diplomatic treaty with too much butter.

Maren took the cloth she had used and dropped it into a small bucket beneath the bar, then reached for a fresh one. Only then did she settle her attention back on the traveler.

“There. The sea has retreated.”

She nudged the bowl of stew a little closer with her left hand, making sure it sat well away from where the crab cakes had been.

“Eat while it is still hot, friend. Food loses heart quickly once it knows it has been ignored.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s left eyebrow lifted, the scar across it bending like a pale thread.

“Old Pell will be pleased to hear it,” she said. “He pretends not to care, but he sulks like a wet cat if no one praises the stew.”

At the kitchen hatch, Old Pell’s grey head appeared just long enough for him to glare at her.

“I heard that,” he said.

“You were meant to,” Maren replied.

The old cook vanished again, but not before the corner of his mouth twitched.

Maren took up a clean mug with her left hand, filled it halfway from the ale tap, and raised it in a small, solemn salute toward the kitchen.

“To Old Pell,” she said. “May his onions never sour and may he one day learn that pepper is not a structural timber.”

From the kitchen came a grunt of deep offense.

Maren set the mug back down untouched and looked to the traveler with the faintest warmth at the edge of her expression.

“He will put extra carrots in your breakfast now, whether you want them or not. That is what passes for affection in his country.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "I look forward to it, then." I finish the last of my stew, feeling a warmth spread through me. "So, Maren, what brings a woman with such... strong opinions to run a tavern like this?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the empty bowl with her left hand and set it aside for washing, then wiped the place in front of the traveler with slow, practical strokes.

“Strong opinions are useful in tavern work,” she said. “Weak ones get spilled on.”

She glanced around the common room as if taking stock of all the little weights that held the place together: the merchants still muttering over grain, the dwarf turning his letter over in thoughtful silence, Evin dodging a chair leg with the grace of someone who had learned pain was a stern tutor.

“My aunt Bessa owned this place before me. Raised me here, mostly. I inherited the Antler after her knees gave out and her patience followed soon after.” Maren folded the cloth once, twice, then laid it beside the basin. “Before that, I spent five years counting boots, barley, arrows, and lies for the Kingsguard. Quartermaster work. It teaches a person that most disasters begin with someone saying, ‘It will probably be fine.’”

Her mouth flattened, not quite a smile.

“When I came back, this place needed hands that knew how to lift a keg, balance a ledger, and tell a drunken wool-merchant that no, the chandelier was not challenging him to single combat.”

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand and took up the tally sheet again, though her attention stayed on the traveler.

“My husband and I ran it together for twelve years. Tobin had a gift for making strangers feel as though they had been expected. I had a gift for making them pay before they forgot their purse existed. Between us, we managed.”

For a moment, her thumb brushed the silver ring on her left hand. The motion was brief, almost absent.

“He died six years ago. Fever. Quick enough to be rude about it.”

She looked toward the kitchen hatch, where Pell had gone quiet in the particular way of someone listening while pretending not to.

“So now I run it alone. Which suits me. The Antler stands at a crossroads, and crossroads need someone stubborn enough to keep the roof mended, the stew hot, and the knives under the table instead of in someone’s ribs.”

Maren gave the traveler a level look, warm but measuring.

“As for why I stay?” she said. “Because every road eventually brings someone hungry to my door. There are worse callings than feeding them.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock in the corner gave its first low, brass note.

Maren stopped speaking.

Not abruptly. Not with alarm. The pause settled over her like a shawl she had known by touch for years. Around the common room, few noticed. The merchants had gone quiet over their accounts, the dwarf still sat with his letter, and Evin was stacking cups with the careful patience of someone trying not to drop the whole history of pottery.

The twelfth chime faded.

Maren set down the tally sheet.

With her left hand, she took two clean cups from beneath the bar. Not mugs. Cups. Small ones, dark wood polished smooth by long use. She uncorked a brown bottle from the shelf behind her and poured into each with exact care. Amber spirits caught the lamplight.

One cup she set near her own side of the bar.

The other she placed at the far end, where no one sat.

She did it as naturally as wiping a counter or drawing ale. No ceremony. No explanation. Only the steadiness of a habit too old to need permission.

For a moment, her left thumb rested against the silver ring she wore there.

Then she lifted her own cup.

“To roads that bring folk home,” she said quietly.

She drank.

The cup at the far end of the bar remained untouched.

After that, Maren corked the bottle, returned it to its place, and took up her cloth again as though midnight had been nothing more than another customer passing through.

“The hour has teeth,” she said, her tone returning to its usual dry evenness. “Best not to let it find you sitting too long without a blanket or another drink.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "A toast I can certainly drink to," I say, raising my (OOC: I don't have a drink anymore - my ale is finished) empty mug briefly before setting it down. "But it seems I've missed my chance for another one tonight." I nod towards the untouched cup. "A friend who's not here tonight?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s gaze followed the nod to the far end of the bar.

For a moment, the lines at the corners of her eyes seemed deeper in the lamplight. Then she looked back to the empty mug in front of the traveler and lifted one eyebrow.

“You have not missed your chance,” she said. “You have only failed to make proper use of it.”

She took the mug with her left hand, turned to the tap, and drew another ale. The motion was steady, practiced, quiet. She set it back down on the bar with a soft wooden knock.

“As for that cup,” she said, glancing once toward the untouched drink, “some habits earn their keep better than explanations do.”

Her voice had not gone cold, but a door had closed somewhere inside it. Not slammed. Simply shut.

She wiped a ring of moisture from the bar with her cloth.

“The Antler has seen plenty of absent friends,” Maren said. “Some gone down the road. Some gone farther. Either way, it does no harm to keep a place for them now and again.”

She nudged the fresh ale a little closer.

“Drink that one before it starts thinking poorly of you.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Fair enough. To absent friends, then." *I raise the fresh ale and take a long drink. The beer is cold and crisp.* "I appreciate the sentiment. There are plenty of good people I wish I could share a pint with right now."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren inclined her head once, accepting the toast without making a performance of it.

“To absent friends,” she said.

She did not drink again. Her cup was already empty, and the one at the end of the bar remained where it was, amber and still beneath the lamplight.

For a little while, she busied her left hand with small tasks that needed doing and did not need much thought: straightening the stack of clean bowls, turning the tally sheet square to the edge of the counter, checking the cork on the bottle she had put back on the shelf. The tavern had thinned with the hour. Chairs scraped. A merchant yawned into his sleeve. Somewhere near the hearth, Evin convinced a sleepy drover that the floor was not, in fact, a cheaper bed.

“There are some cups a body keeps reaching to fill,” Maren said at last, her voice measured. “Even years after sense says there is no one left to hand them to.”

She looked toward the traveler, not prying, but not looking away either.

“Good people have a way of making the world inconvenient once they are gone. Empty chairs. Quiet roads. Jokes no one else knows the ending to.”

Her mouth made the faintest suggestion of a smile.

“And then some fool says, ‘Time heals all wounds,’ because they have mistaken a scar for a cure.”

Maren took up her cloth again and wiped the already-clean bar in front of her.

“If you have names worth drinking to, friend, the Antler has room for them. If you would rather keep them behind your teeth, that is also allowed.” She glanced toward the fresh ale. “A tavern is good for both. Speaking and not speaking. Long as folk pay for the ale and do not bleed on the floorboards.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Well said, Maren. Plenty of names, yes." *I take another sip of ale, the bitterness a welcome contrast to the quiet sentiment in the air.* "It's rare to find a place where both are understood so well."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren gave a small nod, as if the words had been weighed and found honest enough.

“Rare things are usually either valuable or badly maintained,” she said. “I try to make the Antler the first.”

She glanced toward the far end of the bar, where the untouched cup still waited, then back to the traveler. Her left hand folded the cloth with neat, square corners.

“Roads take more than they ought,” she said. “Boot leather, coin, sleep, patience. Sometimes people. A decent roof and a warm bowl do not balance the scales, but they keep a person standing long enough to argue with them.”

The last of the late crowd had begun to drift toward beds or doors. Evin barred a yawn behind his hand and earned a look from Maren that sent him back to stacking cups with renewed dignity. From the kitchen came the muted clatter of Old Pell banking the cook-fire for the night.

Maren reached beneath the bar and set a small heel of bread beside the traveler’s mug.

“Here,” she said. “For the ale. It will sit kinder.”

She did not ask for coin for it.

“The Antler understands because it has had practice. Every table in this room has held a celebration, a quarrel, a farewell, or someone pretending not to cry into their supper.” Her expression remained calm, but not unkind. “Wood remembers. Stone too, I think. Though stone is more smug about it.”

She looked toward the stairs, then back again.

“Room seven is yours when you want it. I will be down here a while yet. If you need hot water, ask now. If you need quiet, the room provides it, except for the window with its musical ambitions.”

Her scarred eyebrow lifted slightly.

“And if what is in that pack decides it needs anything special, best tell me before it leaks, hatches, sings, or attempts diplomacy.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Sounds like a fair trade." *I pick up the bread, a thoughtful gesture.* "And no, the pack won't be leaking or singing. It just needs to get where it's going, safely." *I tap the side of my pack gently.* "Good night, Maren. And thank you." *I gather my things, heading for the stairs.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the pack with the same mild attention she gave to covered pies, sealed letters, and men who claimed they were “only passing through.” Then she looked back to the traveler’s face and inclined her head.

“Good night, friend.”

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand and took up the tally sheet again, though her eyes remained steady.

“Stairs creak on the fourth step. That is not a warning. It is just their hobby. Room seven is second on the left. Bolt works if you lift the door a little while sliding it.”

Her gaze flicked once toward the careful pack, not suspicious, only practical.

“Whatever road that thing has ahead of it, may it be shorter than expected and less interesting than feared.”

From the far end of the bar, Tobin’s untouched cup caught the lamplight.

Maren turned back to the work of closing the tavern: stacking bowls, wiping rings from the wood, and keeping one ear on the common room as the last of the night settled into place. The Gilded Antler grew quieter by degrees, its beams ticking softly in the cooling air, its hearth sinking into embers, its old walls holding every secret they had been given.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pause at the foot of the stairs, turning back to Maren.* "I'll keep that in mind. And I hope the rest of your night is... uneventful." *I offer a small smile, then head up the creaky stairs to room seven.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the rag aside and reached for a clean bowl with her left hand, ladling stew from the pot she kept warm at the end of the bar for exactly this sort of arrival. Road-dusted travelers who wanted food more than they wanted conversation.

"Stew is what is hot. Stew is what is always hot. Old Pell has made other things in his life but I could not tell you when." She set the bowl down, then a spoon, then a heel of dark bread beside it. "Room is four coppers, and that includes the water for washing. Six if you want the water warm, and I will tell you honestly that warm is worth the two."

She poured an ale without being asked, tilting the tankard against the tap with the ease of twenty-odd years, and slid it across the counter.

"Eight rooms free of twelve. You can have the one at the end of the hall if you would rather not hear the stairs. The merchants in the corner have the two beside it and they will be up before dawn arguing about grain, which is a thing I have learned to sleep through and you have not."

Maren picked the tally sheet back up, glanced at it, and made a small mark.

"The wine is also available. It is imported and it is overpriced and I would not drink it myself, but I am obligated to mention it."

She let that sit for a moment, wiping a ring of damp from the bar.

"That is the whole of the hospitality. The rest is up to you."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I take a deep breath, the smell of the stew filling my lungs. It's a welcome change from stale trail rations.* "Stew and warm water sounds perfect. And the quiet room, please."

*I take a long swig of the ale, sighing contentedly as the cold liquid hits my throat.* "Thank you. This is… much appreciated."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren made another mark on the tally sheet and set it under the edge of the bar where it would not get splashed.

"Six coppers for the room and the warm water. Two for the stew, and the ale is with it — I do not charge for the first one when somebody comes in looking like the road chewed them and spat them out." She said this the way another person might read off a grain manifest. "Eight altogether. You can settle in the morning. I have never once had a guest run out on me, and I would rather not find out what it feels like tonight."

She took a bucket from beneath the bar, set it by the stairs where her server Ilsa would find it, and came back to her place across from him.

"I will have the water sent up in a quarter hour. Eat first. Wash after. Doing it the other way around only makes you wash twice."

The dwarf in the corner folded his letter, folded it again, and stared at the tabletop. Maren's eyes went to him for a moment, took inventory of the man's shoulders and the level in his tankard, and came back.

"Pell put more rosemary in that batch than he usually does. He does it when he is in a mood and will not say why. I have stopped asking." She reached for the rag again with her left hand, though there was not much left on the counter to wipe. "If you want more, there is more. The pot does not go back to the kitchen until I do."

Her gaze dropped, briefly and without weight, to the pack he had set down with such care, and then lifted again to his face. She did not ask. She simply let him know she had noticed, which was a different thing entirely.

"Anything in there that ought not freeze, I have a shelf in the cellar. It stays cool but not cold. Mention it or do not."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren did not reach for the plate.

It was a small thing, and quick, and a person would have had to be watching her hands to notice — but her left hand, which had been halfway to the rag, stopped and settled flat on the bar instead. She leaned back a half-step. The distance was polite. It was also exactly the width of a plate of crab cakes.

"That is generous of Lord Havel," she said, in the same level voice she used for room rates. "You will tell him I said so, and you will tell him it by name, because a man who sends food to strangers deserves to have his name said out loud in a full room."

She raised two fingers and Ilsa appeared from the direction of the kitchen doorway the way she always did, as if she had been waiting for it.

"Ilsa. Move this one down to our friend here and put it on a trencher so it is not sliding about. All of it to him." A beat. "I do not care for seafood. Never have. My aunt used to say it was the one thing about me that proved I was not born on the coast, and she was right, and she never let it go."

Ilsa took the plate away from Maren's side of the bar without being told twice. She had worked there four years. She had never been told why, and she had never asked, and Maren paid her a copper more a week than the going rate for exactly that sort of sense.

Maren waited until the plate was well clear of her before she picked the rag back up.

"Eat them warm, friend. Crab does not improve with thinking about it." She glanced across at the merchant's table and inclined her head, a proper acknowledgment, the sort she gave men who paid their tab in full. "And if Lord Havel is stopping the night, the snug is free after the hour. I will not charge him for the room but I will charge him for the wine, and I will tell him what I tell everyone, which is that it is not worth the price."

She turned and set the stew ladle back in the pot, and used the turning to look at the back of her own left hand for a moment, and found it clean and unmarked, and put it out of her mind.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I give a slight nod of thanks to Lord Havel's table, then turn my attention to the crab cakes.* "Well, now. That's a surprise." *I pick one up, still warm, and take a bite.* "These are actually quite good."

*I glance at Maren, then back at the plate.* "You're sure you don't want one? They really are fresh."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren shook her head once, and there was nothing sharp in it.

"I am sure. But I thank you for the offering, which is more than most people bother with. Most people take the no and are glad of it, because it means more crab for them."

She hung the rag on the hook beneath the bar and took up the tally sheet again, though there was nothing new on it to check.

"I have run this house twenty-two years and I have served more shellfish than I could count. Mussels in autumn when the carters bring them up from Ferrow's Landing. Crab twice a year if the roads are kind. I can tell you which coastal towns send the good and which send the cheap, and I can tell you what to charge for it, and I have never once put a bite of it in my own mouth." She made a mark on the sheet that did not need making. "There are things a person keeps out of their own kitchen. That is one of mine. The other is the wine, and you have heard quite enough about the wine."

The dwarf in the corner stood, tucked his letter into his coat, and left four coppers on the table for a three-copper ale. Maren watched him go to the stairs and marked it, the coppers and the shoulders both, in whatever ledger she kept behind her eyes.

"Eat the lot of them. If you leave any, Ilsa will take them home to her brother, and he is sixteen and eats like a threshing floor, so nothing goes to waste in this building either way."

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand and came up with a second tankard, and this time she filled it and set it in front of him without ceremony.

"That one you pay for. I said the *first* one was free. I am warm, friend, I am not a charity."

She let it sit the requisite three seconds.

"Though if you tell Lord Havel I am a charity, he may send more crab, and then I could retire."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren lifted the ale she kept at her own elbow — half-finished, gone flat hours ago, the way it always was by this point in an evening — and touched it against his mug with her left hand.

"To Old Pell," she agreed. "He will not hear it from me, because if I tell him the stew is good he will change the recipe out of spite. He is seventy-one years old and he has decided that praise is a kind of insult. I have given up trying to reason him out of it."

She drank a swallow of the flat ale without visible enjoyment and set it back down.

"You may keep the *damn*, by the way. I will not charge you for it and I will not scold you for it. I only mention that I do not use the word myself, and that people usually notice by the third day and ask, and I would rather save us both the trouble."

She glanced toward the window. The shutter was drawn but she knew the hour the way sailors know weather.

"My aunt Bessa swore like a dockhand with a crushed thumb. Loudly, and in two languages, and at the soup. I decided somewhere around age eleven that I would find other words." She picked up a clean tankard and began drying it, though it was already dry. "It has worked out. There is a great deal you can say to a man who has put his boots on my table without ever once giving him the satisfaction of hearing me lose my footing."

The merchants in the corner had moved from grain prices to the price of *moving* grain, which Maren knew from long experience meant they were nearly done and would ask for the bill within the quarter hour.

"Ilsa will have your water up shortly. End of the hall, the door with the iron latch rather than the brass — the brass one sticks and I keep meaning to see to it." A pause. "I have kept meaning to see to it for two years. I want you to understand the scale of the thing."

She set the tankard down with the others, mouth-down, in a row that was perfectly straight.

"Sleep well, friend. And if you hear me moving about downstairs late, it is only me. I keep my own hours down here and they are not always sensible ones."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I nod, taking another hearty spoonful of stew.* "Good to know. And thanks for the heads-up about the room. I appreciate a quiet night after a long road."

*I glance at the mysterious package, still tucked safely beside my pack.* "Any chance of a place to keep this cool for the night? It's not valuable, just… perishable."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren set the tankard down and came around the end of the bar, which she did not do for everyone.

"The shelf I mentioned. Cellar stairs are behind the kitchen, and I will take it down myself, because the third step from the bottom is rotted through in the middle and I have not fixed it either." She held out her left hand, palm up, and waited rather than reaching. "You may carry it down and see where it sits, if you would rather know the place with your own eyes. Some people would rather. I do not take it as an insult."

She let the hand fall when he did not immediately hand it over, and there was no offense in the letting.

"Two rules and they are the same two rules for everyone. The first is that nothing goes on my shelf that is alive, because I have had a man leave a crate of eels down there and I found them in the ale cellar four days later, and I am still finding out where they went. The second is that if it leaks, it goes in a tub, and I will provide the tub."

The merchants in the corner scraped their chairs back. Maren noted it without turning her head.

"I do not ask what it is. I have never asked. I have had people bring me letters, medicine, a wedding cake, a dead man's ashes, and once a jar of something that turned out to be somebody's grandmother's starter dough that she had kept alive forty years." She started toward the kitchen doorway, unhurried, expecting him to follow or not. "The dough was the most trouble of the lot. It smelled like a boot and it had opinions."

At the doorway she paused, and glanced back, and her voice dropped — not to a whisper, only to the register she used when she meant a thing plainly.

"It stays cool but not cold, and it stays locked, and I have the only key on this ring and this ring does not leave my apron. If somebody wants it badly enough to come through my cellar door, they will have to come past me first, and I am told that is a poor use of an evening."

She waited the three seconds.

"Mind the third step."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock in the corner had been three minutes slow since Tobin bought it, and Maren had never adjusted it, and so when it struck she was already reaching under the bar.

She did not announce it. She did not finish the sentence she had been in the middle of — something about the cellar shelf and the carter who had once left a wheel of cheese there for eleven weeks. She simply stopped, mid-thought, and brought up two cups.

Not tankards. Two small clay cups, the kind that came in sets of six and were down to a set of two. She set them side by side on the bar and took the brown bottle from the back of the low shelf, the one with no label, and poured with her left hand. A measure into the first. The same measure into the second, unhurried, exact, the way a quartermaster counts out grain sacks for men who will be hungry later if she counts wrong.

Then she corked the bottle and put it back.

She took the second cup and walked it down to the far end of the bar, past the stool nobody sat on, and set it on the worn patch where the varnish had gone pale from twenty years of the same cup in the same place. She squared it up. She did not touch it after that.

She came back and stood where she had been standing and picked up her own cup and drank about half of it, and her face did not change at all.

"The cheese was the eleven weeks," she said, picking the thread back up exactly where she had dropped it. "The carter was six weeks late. Those are separate numbers and I want you to appreciate the gap between them, because I certainly did, every time I went down those stairs."

The merchants had gone up. The dwarf had gone up. The common room had emptied out the way it always did, all at once and then not at all, and there was only the fire settling and the two of them and the one cup at the end of the bar with nobody near it.

Maren finished her measure and set the cup down on her own side.

"Kitchen is closed now, properly closed. Pell banks the fire at eleven and anything after that is me with a knife and bad judgment, and I have done that to myself twice and will not do it a third time." She took up the rag, left-handed, and wiped a stretch of bar that was already clean. "There is bread in the crock by the stairs if you wake hungry. Help yourself and do not tell me about it, because then I would have to charge you and I do not want the arithmetic."

She did not look toward the end of the bar. She had not looked at it since she set the cup down.

"Water should be warm still if you go up in the next quarter hour. After that it is a courtesy bath at best."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her, fascinated by the ritual. The precision of the pour, the placement of the second cup.* "You have a story for everything, don't you?" *I take a sip of the drink. It's strong, smooth. A good nightcap.* "This is excellent, by the way."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren considered that, turning her empty cup a quarter-turn on the bar with one finger.

"Twenty-two years in the same building. A person accumulates. It is not a talent, it is sediment." She set the cup mouth-down with the others. "Ask me about anything in this room and I will tell you who broke it and what it cost to mend. That is not wisdom, friend. That is simply having stood in one place a very long time while other people moved through."

She had put a measure in front of him at some point in the last hour and could not have said precisely when — one of those things her hands did without consulting her. She nodded at it.

"Plum brandy out of Hesk. The cooper there makes it in a barrel he swears belonged to his grandfather, and I have my doubts about the barrel and none at all about the brandy. Four bottles a year is all he will sell me. I do not put it on the board and I do not serve it to anyone who asks for it, because people who ask for the good thing want to be seen having it." She looked at him levelly. "You did not ask. That is generally how it gets poured."

The fire shifted and dropped a log, and neither of them moved for it.

Down at the far end of the bar the other cup sat in its pale ring of worn varnish, untouched, and Maren went on not looking at it with the particular steadiness of a woman who could have described its exact position with her eyes shut.

"Finish it slow. It is wasted on a man in a hurry." She took up the rag and folded it, once, twice, and hung it on its hook. "And go up before that water goes cold, because I will not have it said that I charged six coppers for a bath a man had to be brave about."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content:
*I drain the last of the brandy, feeling its warmth spread through me.* "Thank you, Maren. For the food, the drink... everything." *I push off the stool, feeling more rested than I have in days.* "And don't worry, I'll brave the cold water if I have to. After that brandy, I could probably swim in a frozen river."

*I pick up my pack, making sure the mysterious package is still secure, then head for the stairs.* "Goodnight, Maren."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
"Goodnight," Maren said.

She watched him to the stairs the way she watched everyone to the stairs, which was to say she counted him — one more accounted for, one more door that would be shut and quiet — and she noticed that the pack had gone up with him and the cellar shelf had gone unused, and she did not remark on it. A man who carried his own perishables to bed had his reasons. She had been that man herself once, on a road out of Kellsmarch, with a satchel of muster rolls she would not have let go of for a warm bed and a woman's promise.

"The offer keeps until morning," she said to his back, mildly, as though mentioning the weather. "The shelf will be there and so will I. It is only that if the thing spoils overnight you will be angry at yourself, and I would rather you were angry at me. I am better at it."

Three seconds.

"More practice."

She heard the fourth stair take his weight and complain about it, and the seventh, and then the iron latch at the end of the hall, which lifted clean the way it always did.

Then the common room was hers.

Maren went round with the taper and put out the wall lamps, leaving the one by the door, because a dark window at a crossroads told travelers the wrong thing about a place. She swept, left-handed, the long strokes she had swept for twenty-two years, and stacked the merchants' chairs, and found a copper under the dwarf's table and put it in the box by the till where the strays went. She raked the fire down and set the guard across it. She checked the bolt on the cellar door and found it holding, as it always was, and rattled it anyway, as she always did.

Then she came back behind the bar and stood there a while with her hands flat on the wood.

The cup at the far end sat in its pale ring. It would sit there until she came down at half past five and poured it into the slop pail and rinsed the clay and put it back on the shelf with its twin, and she would do that tomorrow and the day after, and she did not intend to ever stop, and she did not intend to ever say why out loud to a living soul.

"Stew was good tonight," she told the empty room. "Pell put more rosemary in it. Nobody knows why."

She untied her apron, hung it on its peg, and felt for the ring of keys in the pocket out of habit even though the apron was no longer on her.

The door creaked when she checked the latch.

"Oh, for the love of every saint who ever stubbed a toe," Maren said, and made a note on the tally sheet, in her small tidy quartermaster's hand, that she would forget to read in the morning.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I settle into the quiet room, the warmth of the brandy still lingering. The bed is surprisingly comfortable. I set my pack and the package down, then quickly strip and wash up, enjoying the almost-warm water. I drift off to sleep almost immediately, the creaks and groans of the old tavern a comforting lullaby.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren woke at five the way she had woken at five for twenty-two years, without a bell or a rooster or any particular enthusiasm about it.

She dressed in the dark. She came down the back stair, which did not creak because it was the one thing in the building she had actually got around to fixing, and she went behind the bar and took the clay cup from the far end without looking at it any harder than she had to. The brandy went into the slop pail. The cup went into the wash basin, and then onto the shelf beside its twin, mouth-down, squared.

That was that. It was done before the sky had made up its mind about the hour.

Old Pell came in at half past five through the kitchen door, stamping the cold off his boots, and said nothing to her, and she said nothing to him, and he got the fire going and started the porridge and the day was properly underway. Twenty-six years they had worked mornings together. They had exhausted conversation sometime around the ninth year and found that they liked what was left better.

The merchants came down at six, arguing. They had moved on from the price of moving grain to the *insurance* on moving grain, which Maren privately considered the most tedious conceivable destination for a two-day argument, and she fed them and took their coin and counted it out on the bar left-handed, faster than either of them could follow, and handed back the four coppers they had overpaid without either of them having noticed they had.

"You are short a copper on the reckoning," the younger one said, frowning at his own palm.

"I am not," said Maren. "You paid me thirty-one for a twenty-seven tab and I have given you four back. You are welcome to do it again slower."

He did not do it again slower.

The dwarf came down at seven, and his shoulders were better than they had been the night before, which Maren noted with a certain quiet satisfaction. He asked for bread and cheese for the road and she gave him bread and cheese and a fold of paper with a name written on it — a carter out of Ferrow's Landing who owed her a favour and went the direction the dwarf's letter had come from. He looked at it a long moment. He did not say thank you in Common. He said it in Dwarvish, low and formal, the full phrasing with the word for *hearth* in it, and Maren answered him in the same tongue without any trouble at all, and neither of them made anything of it.

By eight the common room smelled of porridge and woodsmoke and the wet-stone smell that came in off the crossroads when the night had been damp.

Maren was leaning on the bar with the tally sheet, reading the note she had written herself about the door hinge and deciding, as she had decided two years running, that today was not the day, when a man came in wearing Lord Havel's colours and too clean a pair of boots for the hour.

He did not sit. He looked around the room, at the empty tables, at the stairs.

"I am looking for the traveller who came in last night," he said. "Dusty. Carrying a parcel."

Maren turned the tally sheet face down on the bar and set her left hand flat on top of it.

"Kitchen is open," she said pleasantly. "Porridge is two coppers and there is bread with it."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I'm woken by a knock on my door. I grumble, rubbing sleep from my eyes, and swing my legs out of bed. Who's up at this hour?*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The knock had been Ilsa's, and Ilsa had been sent.

Maren had done it in the space of a breath, before the man in Havel's colours had finished looking at the stairs — a glance toward the kitchen doorway, two fingers lifted, and Ilsa gone up the back stair with her skirts gathered in one fist and instructions that amounted to *wake him, tell him a man is asking, and do not tell him anything more because I do not know anything more.* Four years. A copper a week above the going rate. This was what it bought.

Downstairs, Maren stayed exactly where she was, with her left hand flat on the overturned tally sheet.

"Porridge," she said again, "is two coppers. There is bread with it. The tea is free because it is mostly water and I would be embarrassed to charge."

"I did not come for porridge."

"No," Maren agreed. "But you came a good way in the cold and you are standing in my common room, and I find that men who have eaten are generally better company than men who have not. It is not a trick. It is only porridge."

The man's jaw worked. He was young for the colours — twenty-five, perhaps, with the particular stiffness of someone who had been given an errand and told it was important.

"My lord sent a gift last night," he said. "Crab, from the coast."

"He did. It was generous and I said so out loud in a full room, which is more than most gifts get." Maren did not move. "Your lord is welcome at this bar. The snug is free after the hour and I will not charge him for the room. I will charge him for the wine, and I will tell him it is not worth the price, and that is the whole of what I have on offer this morning."

"The parcel—"

"I do not discuss my guests." She said it the way she said room rates. Level, unhurried, no more weight on it than the price of a bath. "Not their names, not their business, not their baggage. Not to a lord, not to a magistrate, not to the king's own quartermaster, and I will tell you that I *was* the king's own quartermaster, five years, so I know exactly how little that office is owed." A pause. "I do not raise my voice in this house either. The walls have enough noise without me adding to it. I mention it so you understand that nothing I have said is a threat. It is a ledger. Those are the entries. There is nothing under them."

Old Pell's spoon had stopped moving in the kitchen. That was the only sound in the building that changed.

The man looked at the stairs a third time, which was one time too many, and Maren straightened off the bar — no faster than a woman stretching her back — and the movement put her shoulder between him and the newel post without ever appearing to be about him at all.

"The porridge is two coppers," she said, "and the door is behind you, and both of those will still be true in a minute. You may take either one. What you may not do is take the stairs, because those are mine, and the third step from the bottom of my cellar is rotted through and I have not fixed it in two years, and you may draw whatever conclusion you like about how much I fix things I do not consider urgent."

Three seconds.

"The hinge on that door has needed oil since the spring before last. I am very consistent."

Overhead, the iron latch at the end of the hall lifted clean, the way it always did.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I open the door, still rubbing sleep from my eyes. I look down the hall, seeing the man in Lord Havel's colours, and then Maren, standing firm behind the bar.* "Everything alright down here?" I call out, my voice a little rough with sleep.
