dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took a brass key from beneath the counter with her left hand and laid it on the bar.

“Stew is hot, and room six is empty. Eight coppers for the two, with bread and breakfast. The roof does not leak over the bed. We charge nothing extra for that.”

She turned toward the kitchen hatch. “Pell, another bowl, please.”

While she waited, she set out a spoon and a thick heel of bread. Her gaze briefly touched the carefully placed pack, then returned to the business at hand.

“There is a peg beneath the bar if you want your belongings off the floor. Well clear of boots.”

She collected the steaming bowl from the hatch and set it beside the bread, keeping her left hand beneath the earthenware until it rested securely.

“Ale is two coppers. Water is free. The wine costs more than either of us ought to approve of.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, appreciating the quick service.* "Sounds good. And thanks for the peg." *I hook my pack onto it, keeping the mysterious package still carefully upright.* "I'll take an ale with that stew."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren drew an ale with her left hand, tilting the mug beneath the tap before setting it beside the stew.

“Ten coppers altogether, then. Pay before you go upstairs. Saves us both discussing arithmetic before breakfast.”

She marked the tally sheet and tucked it beneath the counter. Behind her, the fire settled with a soft crack; she glanced toward it, judging whether another log could wait.

“Room six is at the far end of the passage. Quieter than the front rooms, unless the carters get an early start. They regard dawn as something best announced with dropped iron.”

Her gaze passed over the pack beneath the bar without lingering.

“If you need anything kept cool overnight, there is room in the cellar. Otherwise, that peg is sound. It has survived a saddler who thought he was traveling light.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s cloth stopped short of the plate. She laid it aside with her left hand, then glanced toward the merchant’s table.

“A generous thought. Please give Lord Havel my thanks.”

She shifted her own mug farther along the counter, leaving the crab cakes untouched.

“Help yourself, friend. I just do not care for seafood. Pell has spent years taking that as a personal endorsement of venison.”

Her tone stayed easy. She fetched a clean fork with her left hand and set it beside the traveler’s spoon, well clear of the plate.

“The empty dish can stay on that tray when you have finished. I will have it taken through separately.”

Then she returned to her tally, moving the sheet to a dry stretch of counter.

“Is Lord Havel an acquaintance of yours, or is this one of those gifts that develops an errand once you have swallowed it?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I raise an eyebrow at the crab cakes, then shrug.* "I've never met the man. Probably the latter, knowing merchants." *I take a bite of stew, then eye the crab cakes. They smell good.* "You're sure you don't want any?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
“Quite sure, friend. I have supper waiting in the kitchen, and Pell notices disloyalty.”

Maren lifted her ale with her left hand and took a small sip. She set it down well away from the offered plate, her mother’s silver ring clicking softly against the handle.

“Besides, if those come with an errand, I would rather not owe a fraction of it.”

She glanced toward Havel’s table. Gifts to strangers were not uncommon at the crossroads; gifts with an announced pedigree generally wanted something.

Her attention returned to the traveler, without a second glance at the pack.

“You paid for a quiet meal. If a messenger follows the fish, you are welcome to send him to me first.” She picked up her tally sheet. “I can explain the difference between buying someone supper and hiring them. It surprises people.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren raised her mug with her left hand.

“To Pell. May he never learn what the other kitchens charge.”

She took a sip, then turned toward the hatch.

“Pell, the stew has earned a toast.”

A satisfied grunt came from the kitchen. Maren inclined her head as though a speech had been delivered.

“He accepts. Any longer an answer and we would have to check him for fever.”

She set her mug down and cut another slice of bread, keeping it well clear of the crab cakes before adding it to the traveler’s bread plate.

“The gravy usually outlasts the first piece.”

For a moment, her gaze rested on the merchant’s table. Then she picked up her cloth and attended to a ring of spilled ale farther down the bar.

“Breakfast is porridge, eggs, and whatever argument Pell is having with the stove. If you need to leave before dawn, tell me tonight. I can put something aside.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Porridge and eggs sound perfect." *I finish my ale, pushing the mug forward.* "I'll take another one of these, please. And I appreciate the offer for the early breakfast, but I plan on sleeping in a bit tomorrow."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the empty mug with her left hand and held it beneath the ale tap.

“A sensible plan. Dawn has plenty of admirers. It can spare you.”

She let the froth settle before topping it off, then placed the mug on a clean patch of counter away from the crab cakes.

“Twelve coppers altogether now. Breakfast lasts until the ninth bell. After that, Pell starts calling it lunch and becomes difficult about eggs.”

She amended the tally, her silver thumb ring catching the lamplight as she turned the sheet.

From the corner came the scrape of a chair. Maren glanced toward the merchants, then back to the bar. She had not forgotten their gift, but she saw no reason to let it occupy more of the evening than it deserved.

“There is an extra blanket in the chest at the foot of your bed. The shutters stick a little; lift the latch before pulling.”

She folded her cloth neatly beside the tally.

“And if anyone knocks offering you a profitable opportunity before breakfast, you need not answer. Profitable opportunities can generally afford to wait downstairs.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
At the first stroke, Maren glanced toward the clock. Her left hand settled the cloth beside the tally, and she reached for two small cups beneath the counter.

She poured a measure of amber spirits into each. One she kept before her. The other she carried to the end of the bar, setting it at an empty place with the handle turned toward the stool.

She straightened it slightly, then returned. There was nothing hurried in the task, nor any invitation to remark upon it.

“Twelve already,” she said. “That clock never once considers whether anyone is enjoying themselves.”

She took a small sip from her cup. In the quieter common room, the kitchen latch clicked shut; the smell of banked coals had begun to replace the smell of supper.

Maren rested her left forearm on the counter, her silver thumb ring dull in the lamplight.

“No hurry, friend. I have a little sitting left in me before the stairs.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pick up the cup she poured for me, taking a thoughtful sip.* "Midnight already? Time flies when you're in good company." *I gesture vaguely around the emptying common room.* "Looks like it's just us now."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s gaze rested briefly on the cup, then on the empty place at the end of the bar.

“That one was spoken for, friend. No harm done. You can finish it.”

She fetched another cup with her left hand, poured a measure, and carried it to the same place. The handle faced the empty stool. This time she left it a little farther back from the edge.

Returning to her own drink, she settled onto the stool behind the counter with a quiet breath.

“Good company does help. So does a clock that nobody watches until it becomes inconvenient.”

Her gaze traveled over the abandoned tables, counting tomorrow’s work without much enthusiasm.

“It is quiet now. That is the part of the evening I do not charge for.”

She took a sip.

“Do not tell the merchants. They will suggest I start.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I take another sip, then set the cup down.* "My apologies, I didn't realize. Who's it for, if you don't mind me asking?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren turned her cup a little beneath her left hand. For a moment, the silver ring brushed against the earthenware.

“That place is not available, friend. That is all.”

There was no rebuke in her voice. She left the other cup where it stood and looked back along the bar.

“You need not apologize twice. An unattended drink in a tavern does invite a reasonable assumption.”

She took another small sip, then settled her forearm against the counter.

“Now. You said that was the best stew you had eaten in months. Have you been traveling somewhere interesting, or merely somewhere with a criminal disregard for rosemary?”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Oh, I've been all over," *I say, waving a hand vaguely.* "Mostly through the Silverwood, then across the Dragon's Tooth mountains. Not much in the way of good cooking out there."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren nodded, her gaze dropping briefly to the road dust still caught in the seams of the traveler’s clothes.

“Mountains are poor hosts. No beds, indifferent shelter, and an unreasonable amount of uphill.”

She took a small sip, then set her cup down beneath her left hand.

“Silverwood and the Tooth make a long road between decent suppers. You chose well stopping here.”

The fire had burned down to a low red glow. She watched it for a moment, then eased her right wrist against her apron.

“Which pass brought you over? The wool carters were here three nights ago claiming the eastern bridge had washed out.” Her eyebrow lifted beneath its thin scar. “They also claimed their fleeces were dry, while leaving a puddle under the table. I prefer a second account.”

She leaned forward a little, comfortably settled now.

“If the bridge is gone, I ought to warn the next lot before they order provisions for a road they cannot use.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Oh, the bridge was fine when I came through," *I say, swirling the amber liquid in my cup.* "Though the eastern pass was a bit dicey with a rock slide. Had to detour a good few miles."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
“Bridge standing, road partly buried. That sounds more useful than the carters’ account. Less damp, too.”

Maren drew the tally sheet toward her with her left hand and turned it over. She dipped a pen and made a short note on the back, keeping the figures on the other side clear of the ink.

“Was the slide before the bridge or beyond it? And would your detour take a loaded wagon, or only someone willing to argue with a mule?”

She laid the pen beside the sheet. Her right hand rested loosely in her lap.

“I will put a notice by the door in the morning. No sense sending people up there with six days of provisions and eight days of road.”

Her gaze moved briefly to the low fire before returning to the traveler.

“A few extra miles in that country would explain your opinion of the stew. Hunger is a generous critic.” She paused. “Though I will leave that part out when I tell Pell.”

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle.* "It was before the bridge, and a wagon might make it if they had a good driver and a lot of patience. I imagine a mule would just sit down and refuse." *I take another sip of the drink.* "And yes, hunger is a great spice."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren tossed the damp rag into a wooden bucket beneath the counter with her left hand, then rested that same hand on the polished oak of the bar. Her right hand remained tucked in her apron pocket, a habit she kept when her old wrist injury flared up in the damp evening air. She gave the traveler’s pack a brief, calculating look, noting how gently it had been set down, before meeting their eyes.

"We have Old Pell's venison stew," Maren said, her voice low and steady. "It has been simmering since noon, and I can assure you it is hot enough to burn the roof of your mouth if you are impatient. I also have three rooms left upstairs. They are clean, the sheets are fresh, and the mattresses do not have bugs because I personally threaten them if they try."

She reached down with her left hand to pull a clean clay mug from the shelf, then used her left hand to draw a measure of the house cider from the small keg behind her. She slid the mug across the counter, stopping it precisely in front of the traveler. 

"Drink that first to clear the road from your throat. It is on the house. I will have a bowl of the stew brought out to you, and we can discuss the room once you have stopped shivering. Do you have a horse in the stable, friend?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a long drink of the cider.* It's tart, but good. "No horse. Just me and my... cargo." *I pat the pack gently, then look up at her.* "Stew sounds perfect. And thanks for the drink."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the traveler drink, her expression neutral but not unkind. She noted the way they patted the pack, the subtle hesitation in their voice when they spoke of their "cargo." A woman who had run a crossroads tavern for twenty years knew there were only three kinds of cargo that made a traveler look that anxious: something stolen, something fragile, or something dangerous. 

"You are welcome," Maren said, her voice even. "The cider is made from apples up near the foothills. It is tart enough to wake a sleeping mule, but it clears the dust."

She leaned her left forearm against the bar, her right hand remaining tucked away in her apron pocket to shield her stiff wrist from the draft. 

"As for your cargo," she continued, her dry humor showing only in the slight twitch of her scarred eyebrow. "I do not make it my business to pry into what my guests carry. So long as it does not bite, leak onto my floorboards, or require its own chair at the table, it is entirely your affair. We have a strict policy against things that howl in the night, however. It keeps the other guests from their sleep."

She raised her left hand, catching the eye of Elspeth, one of her young servers who was clearing a table nearby. Maren gave a single, deliberate nod and pointed a thumb toward the traveler. Elspeth, knowing the unspoken language of the tavern, immediately turned and headed toward the kitchen to fetch a bowl of Old Pell's stew.

Maren turned her attention back to the traveler. "A room for the night is four copper pieces. That includes a hot bath if you are willing to wait for the water to heat, or three coppers if you prefer to sleep in your road-dust. Which shall it be, friend?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s eyes fell upon the plate of golden-brown crab cakes. Internally, her stomach did a sharp, unpleasant flip. *Oh, for the love of every saint who ever choked on a fishbone,* she thought, though not a single flicker of her sudden alarm showed on her weathered face. Even the steam rising from the fried shellfish made her want to take three steps back. 

With a careful, highly deliberate movement of her left hand, she reached out and pinched the very outer rim of the ceramic plate. She slid it two inches further down the bar, placing it squarely in front of the traveler and well away from her own hands and face. 

She looked over at the merchant who had brought the offering, her expression perfectly polite but entirely unyielding. 

"Extend my thanks to Lord Havel for his generosity," Maren said, her voice carrying clearly across the quiet space between the tables. "It is a rare thing to see fresh coastal catch this far inland, and I am sure his lordship's kitchens are very proud of them."

She turned her attention back to the traveler, her left hand retreating to her side, safely out of range of any stray crumbs. 

"You should help yourself, friend," she said, her tone conversational but firm. "I do not care for seafood myself—never have had the taste for things that spend their lives crawling in the salt-mud. But they look hearty enough, and you have a long road to eat off your bones. Consider it a welcoming gift from the road."

She glanced toward the kitchen door, hoping Elspeth would hurry with that venison stew. The sooner there was a bowl of hot gravy and rosemary between her and those crab cakes, the better she would feel. 

"Now," Maren continued, returning to their previous negotiation as if the plate of crab had never arrived. "Four coppers for the room and a hot bath, or three for the room alone? And do not worry, Lord Havel’s generosity will not affect the price of the lodging."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I eye the crab cakes. They smell good, but I'm more interested in the stew.* "Four coppers then, for the bath. And I'll take a crab cake, thanks." *I pick one up and take a bite. It's surprisingly good.* "Tell Lord Havel I appreciate it."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the traveler take a bite of the crab cake, her eyes tracking the movement with a quiet, sharp vigilance. She subtly leaned back an inch or two, ensuring no stray crumbs or oil could find their way toward her. The briny scent of the fried shellfish was strong, but she kept her expression as flat and unreadable as a cellar flagstone. 

"I will pass along your compliments to his lordship's table," Maren said, her voice steady. 

She reached beneath the counter with her left hand, her fingers wrapping around a heavy brass key attached to a block of pine with the number '7' burned into the wood. She placed the key on the bar, sliding it with her left hand to a spot well away from the plate of crab cakes, yet within the traveler's reach.

"Four coppers is a fair trade for washing off the highway," she said. "You will be in Room Seven. Go up the stairs, take a left, and it is the second door on the right. The lock is sturdy, and the latch does not rattle when the wind blows."

Just then, Elspeth returned from the kitchen. In her hands, she carried a thick, steaming earthenware bowl and a heavy pewter spoon. The rich, deep aroma of slow-simmered venison, red wine, and wild rosemary immediately billowed over the bar, successfully drowning out the scent of the seafood. Maren felt the slight, invisible tension in her shoulders ease.

Elspeth set the stew down before the traveler, giving them a polite, tired smile before looking to Maren. 

"Tell Lord Havel's table that our friend here sends their regards for the catch," Maren instructed the young server. "And then tell Old Pell we will need the copper tub filled for Room Seven in about half an hour."

Elspeth nodded and hurried off to deliver the messages. 

Maren turned her attention back to the traveler, resting her left hand on the counter, her right still tucked safely away in her apron. "Eat your stew while it is hot, friend. And keep that pack of yours between your feet. The Antler is a quiet house, but curiosity is a disease that many men carry without knowing it."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren’s scarred eyebrow twitched upward in a rare, brief display of amusement. She did not care for the traveler’s choice of language—there were far more descriptive words in the Common tongue to praise a good meal than those coarse shortcut words—but she could not argue with the sentiment. Pell’s stew deserved every bit of praise it received.

Using her left hand, Maren reached under the bar and retrieved a small, plain wooden cup, filling it with a finger’s depth of the same tart cider she had poured for the traveler. She raised the cup with her left hand, keeping her right hand resting comfortably against her apron-clad waist.

"To Pell," Maren agreed, her voice smooth and measured. "Though I do request you do not repeat that to his face. He is already difficult enough to negotiate with when the flour prices rise. If he learns his reputation has traveled, he will start demanding I source his rosemary from the southern provinces, and I have no desire to pay those import tariffs."

She took a small, polite sip of her cider, then set the cup down with her left hand, sliding it to the side, well clear of the plate containing the remaining crab cake. 

"He uses venison from the woods three miles north," she continued, leaning her left elbow on the clean portion of the bar. "A local hunter brings it in fresh every Tuesday. The trick, Pell always says, is the parsnips. They must go in late, or they turn to mush and ruin the broth. I do not pretend to understand the science of it, but I do not argue with a man who holds a cleaver for a living."

She glanced toward the shuttered windows. The wind was beginning to pick up outside, whistling slightly through the gaps in the heavy oak frames. It would be a cold night, the kind that made a hot bath worth twice what she was charging for it. 

"Take your time with the bowl, friend," she said, nodding toward the steaming stew. "Once you are finished, the water for your bath should be drawn and waiting upstairs. If you require anything else before the kitchen closes, you have only to ask."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I finish the last of the stew, scraping the bowl clean.* "Pell's got a secret touch, for sure." *I push the empty bowl forward, then take another sip of cider.* "So, Elspeth mentioned Lord Havel... he a regular?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren reached out with her left hand and picked up the empty earthenware bowl, taking care to steer her forearm well clear of the plate where the remaining crab cake sat. She set the bowl on a tray beneath the bar to be washed later. 

"Lord Havel is a regular of sorts," Maren said, her voice dropping to a lower, more conversational register. "He owns the timber mills three miles down the southern fork, and he has a manor house just over the ridge. He is a man who likes to remind the valley that he has more coin than they do, hence the fresh coastal catch brought up by fast courier."

She leaned her left hip against the back counter, her right hand still tucked safely in her apron pocket. She looked toward the corner of the room where the two merchants were still muttering over their ledgers, then back to the traveler. 

"He is harmless enough," she continued, her tone measured. "He pays his tab on time, he does not pinch the servers, and his guards have enough sense to do their brawling outside my doors. In my line of work, that makes him a saint, or very nearly one. But he does love an audience. If you thank him for the crab, do it briefly, or he will spend the next hour explaining the exact route the courier took to keep the ice from melting."

She gestured with her left hand toward the stairs at the back of the common room. 

"The water should be hot by now. Elspeth is reliable, and Pell keeps the hearth fire high. I suggest you go wash the road off your face, friend. If you leave that pack here while you bathe, I will keep an eye on it from behind the bar. It will be safer here than in your room if you are going to be distracted by a hot tub."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The heavy, brass-faced clock in the corner began to chime, its slow, deep strokes vibrating through the floorboards of the common room. *One. Two. Three.*

Maren stopped speaking mid-sentence. Her expression did not change, but a sudden, quiet stillness settled over her. 

As the fourth chime rang out, she reached beneath the counter with her left hand. She bypassed the cider and the common ale tap, instead reaching for a shelf near the bottom. Her fingers closed around a heavy, dark green glass bottle with no label, and two small, clear glass tumblers—not the usual clay mugs or pewter cups she served to the patrons. 

*Five. Six. Seven.*

With practiced, deliberate movements of her left hand, she set the two tumblers side by side on the polished oak of the bar. She popped the cork from the green bottle with her left hand, the rich, sweet scent of dark plum brandy escaping into the air. 

*Eight. Nine. Ten.*

Using only her left hand, her right still resting quietly in her apron pocket, she poured an equal measure of the amber liquid into each glass. The pours were precise, stopping exactly half an inch below the rim of each tumbler. She corked the bottle and set it aside. 

*Eleven. Twelve.*

As the final vibration of the twelfth chime faded into the rafters, Maren picked up one of the tumblers in her left hand. She did not drink. Instead, she walked the length of the bar, her steps quiet on the floorboards, until she reached the very end—the dark, quiet corner near the shuttered window, far from where the traveler sat. She set the tumbler down precisely in the center of a small, faint ring worn into the wood from years of the same daily ritual. 

She stood there for a single, silent heartbeat, her eyes fixed on the glass, before she turned and walked back to her post behind the center of the bar. 

She picked up the second glass with her left hand and took a slow, measured sip. The brandy was warm, burning pleasantly down her throat. She did not look toward the glass at the end of the bar again, nor did she offer any explanation. 

Instead, she met the traveler's eyes, her face returning to its usual calm, unreadable mask. 

"It is midnight, friend," Maren said, her voice quiet but clear in the newly hushed tavern. "The road has a way of catching up to a person once the sun goes down. Your stew is finished, and your bath water will be growing cold. I suggest you take your key and head upstairs before the draft under the door gets any stronger."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I pick up the key, still a little confused by the midnight ritual.* "Right. Good night, Maren." *I take my pack, giving it a gentle pat, and head towards the stairs.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren watched the traveler gather their pack, her keen eyes following the protective hand they placed over their cargo. She did not ask about it again; a good innkeeper knew when curiosity became a liability. 

"Good night to you, friend," Maren said, her voice a low, steady rumble in the quiet common room. "Sleep well. If the wind rattles the northern shutter, there is an extra wool quilt in the chest at the foot of your bed. Use it."

She raised her tumbler of plum brandy with her left hand in a silent, parting gesture as the traveler turned toward the stairs. She waited, listening to the rhythmic creak of the wooden steps under their boots until the sound faded into the upper corridor and the door to Room Seven closed with a solid, reassuring click. 

Once she was certain the traveler was settled, Maren set her glass down with her left hand. Her eyes immediately fell upon the plate of remaining crab cakes. Even cold, the scent of the shellfish made the back of her throat itch with a phantom irritation. 

*Oh, for the love of every saint who ever walked on dry land,* she thought, keeping her face entirely blank. 

She reached beneath the bar with her left hand, retrieved a thick, dry linen rag, and wrapped it securely around her palm and fingers. Ensuring not a single patch of her bare skin could touch the ceramic, she pinched the edge of the plate through the cloth. She lifted it swiftly and set it on the wash-tub tray beneath the counter, well out of sight and smell. She would have Elspeth dispose of it in the morning; she was not going to risk her hands breaking out in angry, red hives when she had three casks of ale to haul tomorrow.

With the danger cleared, Maren took another slow sip of her brandy. She looked across the common room. The dwarf had finally closed his letter and was nursing the last drop of his ale, while the two merchants were slowly stacking their ledgers. 

"The hearth is dying, gentlemen," Maren announced to the room, her voice carrying easily without being raised. "And the candles have run their course. I suggest we call it a night."

The merchants grumbled softly but began to gather their coats. Maren stood behind the bar, her left hand resting on the polished wood, her right hand still tucked warmly in her apron pocket. At the far end of the counter, the second glass of plum brandy sat untouched in the shadows, catching the faint, dying glow of the hearth fire. She would leave it there, just as she always did, until the morning sun replaced the dark.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I unlock the door to Room Seven and step inside. It's simple, but clean, just as Maren said. The bed looks comfortable. I set my pack on the small table, then head for the copper tub. A hot bath sounds heavenly right now.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Downstairs, the common room emptied with the slow, predictable rhythm of a tide going out. The dwarf finished his ale, gave Maren a brief, polite nod, and climbed the stairs to his own room. The two merchants, still debating the price of barley in hushed, stubborn tones, finally gathered their ledgers and retired to their shared quarters on the second floor. 

Maren waited until the latch on the last door upstairs clicked shut before she began her closing routine. 

Using her left hand, she went about the room, extinguishing the tallow candles one by one with a brass snuffer. The smell of hot grease and burnt wicks mingled with the lingering aroma of Pell’s rosemary stew. She left only the dying embers of the hearth to cast long, orange shadows across the empty tables and chairs.

She walked to the heavy oak front door. With her left hand, she lifted the thick pine bar and slotted it securely into the iron brackets, locking out the cold night and the dark crossroads. Her right hand remained tucked in her apron pocket; the dampness in the air always made the old military break in her wrist throb like a toothache. 

Once the door was secured, Maren returned to the bar. She rubbed her stiff right wrist with her left hand, wincing slightly. 

"Oh, for the love of every saint who ever spent a winter in the northern marshes," she muttered to the empty room, her voice barely a whisper. The cold was setting in early this year. 

She picked up her tumbler of plum brandy with her left hand and finished the last drop. Her eyes drifted to the far end of the counter. There, in the dim, flickering shadow of the hearth-glow, sat the second glass. The amber liquid was perfectly still. She did not touch it. She would not touch it until the dawn. 

From directly above, she heard the faint, muffled creak of the floorboards in Room Seven, followed by the soft, rhythmic sloshing of water. The traveler was in the tub. Maren gave a single, satisfied nod to herself. A hot bath and a full belly of Pell's stew were the best remedies for whatever road-weariness—or heavy secrets—the traveler was carrying in that pack.

Maren wiped down the center of the bar one last time with her left hand, blew out the final candle on the counter, and sat down on the high stool behind the register to wait out the night in the quiet warmth of the dying fire.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I sink into the hot water with a sigh. Bliss. The day's grime washes away. I lean my head back, enjoying the quiet.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The silence of The Gilded Antler at night was a familiar friend. It was not a dead silence, but rather a living one, filled with the gentle settling of old timber, the dying hiss of the hearth embers, and the steady, rhythmic sigh of the wind against the thick window panes. 

Maren sat on her high stool behind the bar, her left hand resting on the leather-bound ledger she had pulled from beneath the counter. She dipped a small charcoal stick into a shallow dish of sand to dry it, then began to run her eyes down the columns of figures she had penned earlier. Her right hand remained tucked inside the pocket of her apron, resting against her thigh where the warmth of her body could soothe the dull ache in her wrist.

Her mind, quick and sharp as it had been during her years keeping the books for the Kingsguard, easily tallied the day's earnings. Four coppers for Room Seven. Two silvers and three coppers from Lord Havel’s table—the man always tipped well when he was showing off. The merchants had paid for their stew but had been stingy on the ale. 

"Oh, for the love of every scribe who ever ran out of ink in the middle of a winter campaign," Maren murmured under her breath, her left hand neatly correcting a double-entry in the margin. The merchants had tried to short her two copper pieces on their grain carriage tax calculation, but she had caught it before they went upstairs. She would collect it in the morning before they loaded their wagon. No one left the Antler with an open debt.

From upstairs, the soft sloshing of water finally ceased, followed by the dull thud of bare feet stepping onto the thick wool rug she kept beside the copper tub in Room Seven. 

Maren looked up from her ledger, her gaze drifting toward the ceiling, then sliding down to the far end of the bar. The single glass of plum brandy sat there in the shadows, untouched and perfectly still. She looked at it for a long moment, her expression softening just a fraction, the hard lines around her eyes easing in the dim firelight. 

She did not miss Tobin with a desperate, tearing grief anymore—that had scabbed over years ago—but she missed his quiet presence in the hours after the doors were locked. He had always been the one to sweep the floor while she counted the coins. 

She turned back to her ledger, her left hand closing the book with a soft, final thud. She would let the traveler sleep. Tomorrow would bring a new crowd, new rumors from the western road, and undoubtedly more trouble that would require her cudgel or her quiet authority. But for tonight, the tavern was safe, the guests were warm, and the hearth was dying just as it should.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I dry off, feeling refreshed, and put on my night clothes. I glance at my pack, then decide to leave it on the small table. I climb into the surprisingly comfortable bed, pulling the quilt up to my chin. Sleep comes quickly.*

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The last of the muffled movements from Room Seven finally quieted, leaving the tavern in an absolute, heavy silence. Maren closed her inkwell with her left hand, the faint wooden click sounding unusually loud in the empty common room.

She stood up from her stool, her knees popping slightly in the cool night air. With her left hand, she picked up her ledger and slid it into the heavy, iron-bound lockbox beneath the counter. She turned the key with her left hand, then tucked the key ring into her apron pocket alongside her stiff right hand. 

She walked slowly around the common room, her soft-soled boots making no sound on the floorboards. She checked the hearth one last time. The embers had settled into a deep, pulsing red glow, safe enough to leave until Pell rekindled them in the morning to start the bread.

She walked past the bar on her way to the back. In the shadows near the shuttered window, the glass of plum brandy she had poured for Tobin sat undisturbed, the dark amber liquid catching the very last of the firelight. She looked at it for a silent moment, her face softening in the dimness, before she turned away. She would empty it into the herb garden at dawn, as she did every single day. 

Maren made her way to her private quarters, a small, neat room tucked behind the snug on the ground floor. It was simple—a narrow bed, a sturdy chest of drawers, and a single window looking out toward the northern trade road. 

As she unbuttoned her linen shirt with her left hand, her right hand finally relaxing out of her pocket, she thought of the traveler upstairs and their carefully guarded cargo. People who carried secrets usually brought trouble, but in Maren's experience, trouble was just another thing that had to be swept out of the door in the morning. 

She blew out her bedside candle, climbed into her own bed, and closed her eyes, letting the familiar, steady heartbeat of The Gilded Antler lull her to sleep.

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I wake up to the smell of fresh bread and brewing coffee. My sleep was deep and dreamless. I stretch, then sit up, feeling completely refreshed. I glance at my pack on the table, then over at the window. Time to get going.*

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maren's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her left-hand dominance due to right wrist injury, her shellfish allergy, her midnight ritual with the brandy glass for Tobin, her professional demeanor, and her dry humor all persist from first to final turn without deviation.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early turns are solid but later turns show richer detail and deeper character work. The midnight ritual scene (turn 14) and closing routine (turn 22) are particularly well-crafted, showing no signs of degradation.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from arrival to settling in for the night. The session builds character depth through small revelations (the injury, the allergy, the memorial ritual) and creates a complete arc of hospitality and evening routine.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Maren adapts well to user inputs - handles the crab cake gift gracefully despite her allergy, responds appropriately to questions about Lord Havel, and smoothly transitions when the user jumps to midnight without explanation.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes the traveler's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Always responds to what the user does rather than directing them.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Excellent time progression from evening arrival through midnight to morning. The midnight chime scene is particularly well-handled. Bath water cooling, stew getting cold, and natural progression to sleep all feel realistic.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally clean prose with good restraint. Occasional moments of slight over-description but mostly avoids purple prose while maintaining atmospheric detail.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements around the left-hand actions and wrist injury, but these serve character consistency rather than being lazy repetition. The 'Oh, for the love of...' internal thoughts appear multiple times.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent showing throughout - the shellfish allergy revealed through actions, the memorial ritual shown without explanation, the wrist injury demonstrated through behavior rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Rich subtext in the memorial ritual, the careful handling of the traveler's mysterious cargo, and Maren's professional assessment of guests. Layers of meaning without being heavy-handed.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good pacing that allows for character moments while maintaining narrative flow. The midnight ritual scene is particularly well-paced, building atmosphere effectively.

scores.overall_notes: Exceptional character consistency and development. Maren emerges as a fully realized person with specific physical limitations, emotional depth, and professional competence. The memorial ritual for Tobin is particularly well-executed, adding layers without exposition. Strong atmospheric writing that maintains quality throughout the session.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck. It always had. Eli's father had never fixed it. The wood had swollen with fifteen years of rain and nobody's attention.

The hallway smelled of dust and old carpet. Something else underneath. Paint, maybe. The walls had been repainted. A neutral beige over what Eli remembered as green.

A box sat on the kitchen counter. Masking tape. Black marker. KITCHEN written in handwriting Eli didn't recognize.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I walk through the hallway, running my fingers along the wall. I stop at the doorframe to my old room. There are pencil marks on the frame — height measurements. Mine.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The pencil marks climbed the white paint. Some had been painted over. Their ridges held dust.

A lower mark bore a small date. The graphite carried a cold metal scent.

Beyond the frame, the room held a draft. It pressed through the gap beneath the window.

The radiator ticked once. Dust warmed on the iron. Then the house settled into its old silence.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I step into the room, kicking at something on the floor. Just a dust bunny. The draft makes the hairs on my arms stand up. I should close that window.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The window frame held a thin film of grit. It trembled in the draft. Cold air carried wet leaves. The latch hung loose.

On the sill, a dead fly lay curled. Its wings caught pale winter light. The glass smelled of rain.

A nail hole marked the wall. Old tape left a rough stripe. The floorboard groaned under the draft. Paint flakes rested on the boards.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I find a photograph in the closet. It's of my mother, before she got sick. I haven't seen her face in a decade.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The photograph had a white border. Its edges felt soft. The image smelled of cedar and closed air. Her smile sat small beneath the surface. Her coat held a rough wool texture.

A thumbprint stained the lower corner. The print carried a faint salt trace. The closet air held a wool taste.

Behind the photograph, a square of lighter wall remained. The paint there felt cooler. A hinge screw lay in the dust. Its threads held a rust color. The house gave one low creak.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I trace the smile with my thumb. "Mom." I can almost smell her perfume. I wonder why this one was left behind.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
Cedar replaced perfume.

The name sank into wool.

Paper gave off a dry taste.

The closet held old wool.

A moth wing rested on the shelf.

Its powder touched the photograph.

Outside, a branch tapped the window.

The glass answered with chill.

Rain began again.

It combed the pane in short lines.

The latch rattled.

The screw by the pale square caught light.

Its rust left a metal taste.

Below, a pipe knocked.

The floorboards drank the cold.

Paint flakes curled near the sill.

The photograph kept its soft edge.

The smile stayed under dust.

In the kitchen, tape peeled.

Marker ink gave a sharp smell.

The house settled into cold.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I tuck the photo into my pocket. "No way am I leaving you behind." I head back out into the hall, looking for the other bedrooms.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The hallway held a shallow cold.  
The carpet gave a dry crackle.  
A door stood ajar at the far end.  
Its brass knob wore a dull brown film.

The second door had a sticker scar.  
Old glue made a rough crescent.  
The wood smelled of wax and closed rooms.

A radiator pipe tapped behind the wall.  
The sound carried a faint iron taste.  
Dust moved in the thin window light.

Inside the first bedroom, a bedframe remained.  
Its mattress wore a yellowed sheet.  
The sheet felt stiff with disuse.

A closet door leaned on one hinge.  
The hinge gave a sour metal scent.  
Something small rolled across the boards.  
A glass bead stopped against the baseboard.

The hallway darkened near the stairs.  
The banister held a sticky ring.  
Somewhere above, a floorboard creaked without weight.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: The real estate agent arrives. She's cheerful. Aggressively cheerful.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The front door stuck for her too.  
Her shoulder hit the frame with a dull knock.  
She carried coffee and cold air.  
Her scarf smelled of wet wool.

Her smile showed too many teeth.  
Her laugh struck the hallway.  
The plaster gave a thin echo.  
Paper rustled in her folder.  
The folder smelled of print ink.

She tapped the kitchen counter with one nail.  
The masking tape lifted a dry edge.  
Her ring clicked against the laminate.  
Cold air followed her through the hall.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "It's always done that," I say, a little too sharply, as she struggles with the door. "Dad never bothered to fix it."

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent turned from the door.  
Her glove left a damp streak on wood.  
Coffee steam warmed the hall.  
Wet wool smelled against the plaster.

“Old houses had quirks,” she said.  
Her voice struck the narrow ceiling.  
A folder page cracked under her thumb.  
Print ink rose from the paper.

She moved toward the kitchen.  
Her heels tapped the worn tile.  
The masking tape gave a dry whisper.  
Her ring clicked on the counter.

“These rooms needed staging,” she said.  
The word sat flat in the cold.  
A spoon in the sink smelled of metal.  
The radiator pipe knocked once.

She touched the wall near the door.  
Paint grit caught beneath her nail.  
Rain tapped the front window.  
The draft carried wet leaves and iron.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Staging?" I scoff, following her. "It's a house, not a theater." I watch her fiddling with the box on the counter. "What's that?"

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "Just some things the estate company found," she said, pulling at the tape. "Kitchen stuff, mostly. You want to go through it?" She didn't wait for an answer, already pulling the flaps open.

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The flaps opened with a papery sigh.  
Cardboard dust rose.  
It smelled of dry storage.  
A ceramic cup appeared.  
Its glaze held a blue crack.

The agent set her coffee on the counter.  
Steam curled from the lid.  
Her nail hooked the tape.  
The tape tore with a thin rasp.  
Marker ink smelled sharp under the dust.

Inside the box, a spoon knocked against a plate.  
The plate carried a brown rim stain.  
A folded napkin held a grease shadow.  
The napkin gave off faint vinegar.

The agent turned the cup in her hand.  
Her ring tapped the ceramic.  
The sound rang short and cold.  
A chip on the rim caught her thumb.  
She set it beside the box.

“Nothing valuable,” she said.  
Her voice touched the kitchen plaster.  
The plaster returned a dull chill.  
Rain scraped the window screen.  
The coffee lid hissed a small breath.

Beneath the napkin, a brass key waited.  
Its teeth held black grime.  
The metal smelled of pennies.  
The agent lifted it with two fingers.  
The key left a cold line on her skin.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: I snatch the key from her. "Hey! That's probably mine." I turn it over in my palm. It looks like the old shed key. "Why is this in here?"

dialogue.name: Narrator
dialogue.content:
The agent stepped back.  
Her heel scraped tile.  
The brass key smelled of pennies.  
Cold air touched the counter.

Her folder pressed against her chest.  
Paper gave a sharp edge.  
“The estate inventory listed it,” she said.  
The words landed on cold plaster.

She turned the cup again.  
Her ring tapped the glaze.  
A hairline crack held brown dust.  
The sink gave a faint drip.

“The shed lock was changed,” she said.  
Her nail traced the box rim.  
Cardboard left a dry brown powder.  
The coffee lid hissed steam.

The key’s teeth bit the room’s silence.  
Old grit smelled of wet iron.  
A floorboard cooled beneath the draft.  
Rain scratched the kitchen window.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "The shed lock was changed?" I look down at the key. "By who?" I thought Dad still used it.

dialogue.name: Eli
dialogue.content: "When?" I ask, turning the key over again. "Dad used that shed all the time."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: The Narrator maintains a highly consistent voice throughout - spare, sensory-focused prose with emphasis on texture, smell, and sound. The style remains distinctly atmospheric and minimalist from first turn to last.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Quality holds reasonably well but shows some concerning patterns in later turns. Turn 8 becomes overly fragmented and poetic, and the final turn (22) is completely empty, suggesting potential degradation.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from solitary exploration to emotional discovery (mother's photo) to external intrusion (agent) to building tension around the mysterious key. Each beat builds naturally on the previous.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellent adaptation to user inputs. Smoothly transitions from introspective exploration to dialogue scenes, adjusts tone when agent arrives, and builds mystery around the key discovery.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes Eli's actions or dialogue, always responds to rather than dictates user choices.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Time flows naturally - from initial exploration through photo discovery to agent arrival. Environmental details (rain, cold, dust) remain consistent. No major contradictions detected.

2.1_anti_purple_prose.rationale: Generally restrained and effective, though turn 8 becomes overly fragmented and poetic. Most descriptions serve atmosphere rather than showing off.

2.2_anti_repetition.rationale: Some repetitive elements (cold, dust, metal scents) but they serve atmospheric consistency. Turn 8 shows concerning repetition of structure.

2.5_show_dont_tell.rationale: Excellent sensory showing throughout. Emotions and atmosphere conveyed through concrete details rather than exposition.

2.6_subtext.rationale: Strong emotional undercurrents - grief, nostalgia, family dysfunction. The mysterious key adds intrigue without over-explaining.

2.7_pacing.rationale: Good rhythm between action and description. Builds tension effectively, though turn 8 disrupts flow with over-fragmentation.

scores.overall_notes: Strong atmospheric writing with consistent voice and excellent agency respect. The Narrator creates a compelling sense of place and builds narrative tension effectively. However, shows some degradation in mid-session (turn 8's over-fragmentation) and ends with an empty response, preventing a higher score.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The door to The Gilded Antler opened with a creak that Maren kept meaning to oil and kept forgetting. She looked up from the bar, where she was wiping down the counter with her left hand — the right holding a tally sheet she was checking against the evening's orders.

The common room was about half full. Two merchants arguing quietly in the corner about grain prices. A dwarf nursing an ale and reading a letter. Old Pell's venison stew on every other table, filling the room with the smell of rosemary and slow-cooked meat.

Maren set down the tally sheet and gave the newcomer a once-over. Road-dusted. Tired. Carrying something they were being careful with.

"Welcome to the Antler, friend. Sit where you like. Kitchen is open for another hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: I take a seat at the bar. Set my pack down carefully. "Whatever's hot and a room for the night, if you've got one."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren noted the way the traveler set the pack down — slow, deliberate, keeping it within arm's reach. Not a merchant's habit. Not a soldier's either, quite. She filed it away without comment and reached for a clean tankard with her left hand.

"Venison stew's what's hot. Old Pell's been simmering it since noon, and I will not apologize for the price because it's worth it." She set the tankard down and drew ale from the cask behind her, the pour steady and practiced. "Two coppers for the bowl, three for the ale, and a silver for the room. That includes breakfast, which is porridge and bread, and I will not pretend it's more than that."

She slid the tankard across the bar and finally let her gaze rest on the traveler's face — properly, this time, not just the road-dust and the tired shoulders.

"Room four's open. End of the hall, window faces the stable yard, so you'll hear the horses shift in the night. If that bothers you, room nine is quieter but smaller. I'd take four, myself. The horses are good company."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I nod, taking a long drink of the ale.* "Four sounds fine. And the stew. I'll take it all." *I push a small pouch of coins across the bar, careful not to jostle my pack.* "It's been a long road."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren swept the coins into her palm with her left hand and counted them by touch — a habit from her quartermaster days — before dropping them into the till. Correct to the copper. She didn't comment on it, but she noticed.

"Long roads make for short tempers and long sleeps. You'll get the second one here." She turned and ladled stew into a deep bowl, thick with venison and root vegetables, and set it in front of the traveler with a heel of bread alongside. "Pell puts a little juniper in it. Don't ask him about it, he'll talk your ear off about the correct ratio."

She reached under the bar and came up with a brass key on a leather thong, which she set beside the bowl — left-handed, always left-handed.

"Room four. Stairs are behind you, second landing. Water's in the pitcher, and if you want a bath, it's an extra copper and you'll have to wait until after the dinner rush, because I am not hauling kettles while Pell's got the stove." She paused. "The lock sticks. Lift the handle before you turn the key, or you'll be standing in the hall at midnight cursing it, and I will hear you, and I will not come help."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: A merchant at a nearby table sends over a plate as a gesture of goodwill. "Compliments of Lord Havel — fresh crab cakes from the coast, arrived this morning. Finest in the region." The plate is set in front of both of us.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at the plate. She did not touch it.

Two crab cakes, golden-crusted, flecked with green. They smelled of the sea and of butter, and they had been set precisely between her and her guest, as if the merchant had measured the distance. She knew what shellfish did to her. She knew it the way a person knows the shape of their own hand. Her left hand stayed flat on the bar, well clear of the plate.

"Lord Havel," she said, tasting the name. She did not know it. She knew most of the lords who sent carts down this road, and none of them sent crab cakes to strangers at a crossroads tavern. The coast was four days east. "Generous of him."

She turned her head toward the merchant's table and gave him a long, unhurried look — the kind that said *I see you, and I will remember you*. Then she looked back at the plate.

"I do not care for seafood," she said, and it was true as far as she was willing to say it. She pushed the plate — with her knuckles, not her fingers, and only at the rim — toward the traveler. "You are welcome to it, friend. Eat while it's hot. I'll take the stew."

She picked up her rag and resumed wiping the counter, left-handed, working around the spot where the plate had rested as though the wood there needed extra attention. Under the bar, out of sight, she made a small note on the corner of her tally sheet: *Havel. Crab. Ask Pell.*

"Merchant in the corner there," she said quietly, not looking up. "The one who bought your dinner. You know him?"

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I eye the crab cakes. They smell delicious, but I'm more interested in the stew and the warmth it promises.* "Never seen him before in my life." *I pick up a crab cake, though, and take a bite. It's good.* "Guess he's just friendly."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren finished wiping the spot on the counter and moved on to the next one, unhurried, as though the conversation and the plate and the merchant in the corner were all just part of the evening's ordinary work. Her left hand kept the rag moving. Her right stayed below the bar, resting near the cudgel's handle — not on it. Near it.

"Friendly," she repeated. "Perhaps."

She did not believe it, and she did not say so. What she said instead, in the same flat tone she used to announce the price of wine:

"Those cakes came from the coast. Four days east, if the road's dry, and it has not been dry. So either Lord Havel's man rode hard with a cold-box and a great deal of money, or they did not come from the coast this morning, or there is no Lord Havel." She wiped a ring left by a tankard. "I do not know which, and it is not my business. But I notice things. It is a failing of mine."

The merchant in the corner had not touched his own plate. Maren had been watching him from the moment the server set it down, the way she watched every table, and the crab cakes in front of him sat untouched and steaming while he kept his eyes on the bar — on the traveler, specifically, though he was pretending to be interested in the grain argument.

Maren looked at the traveler's face, and then at the second crab cake, still on the plate.

"Eat it if you like. I would not, but that is my trade and not yours." She picked up the traveler's empty ale tankard and refilled it without being asked, setting it down left-handed with a small, deliberate thump. "But I would eat it slow. A man who buys a stranger dinner at a crossroads and watches him eat it is either very generous or very patient, and in my experience it is rarely the first."

She glanced toward the kitchen door, where Pell's shadow moved behind the frosted glass.

"Pell's stew will still be hot in an hour. The crab cakes will not." A pause, dry as old bread. "That is not advice. That is merely arithmetic."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: "Damn, that stew is good. Best I've had in months." I raise my mug. "To Old Pell."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren raised her own mug — water, cut with a splash of ale, the drink she kept behind the bar for herself while she was working — and touched it to the traveler's without ceremony.

"To Pell," she said. "He will be insufferable about it tomorrow, so I will not tell him."

She drank, set the mug down, and went back to the rag, though the counter had been clean for some minutes now. Her left hand moved in slow circles. Her right stayed where it was.

The merchant in the corner had finally picked up his fork. He ate one bite of his crab cake, then another, and did not look satisfied — he looked like a man completing a task. Maren watched him from the corner of her eye and made no comment. The two grain merchants were still arguing about bushels. The dwarf had finished his letter and was staring into the middle distance with the particular expression of a man doing sums in his head. The room was warm and loud and ordinary.

"You have not told me your name," Maren said, "which is your business, and I will not press. But you have a pack you do not set down and a road-dust that says you came a long way, and a stranger bought you dinner without being asked. If you want the snug tonight — the small room off the kitchen, no windows, one door — it is two silver instead of one, and I will keep the key behind this bar until you ask for it."

She picked up the empty stew bowl and stacked it with the day's other dishes.

"The offer stands whether or not you tell me why."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I look at her, then at the merchant, then back at her.* "Traveler. That's what folks call me." *I finish the last crab cake, then push the plate away.* "Snug sounds good. Don't like windows much anyway."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren took the plate with the rag, not her fingers — folded the cloth over the rim and carried it away at arm's length, the way a person carries something that has gone off. She did not look at it. She dropped it in the wash tub by the kitchen door and rinsed her hands at the basin, twice, and dried them on the apron.

"Traveler," she said, coming back to the bar. She said it the way she said *friend* — deliberately, like trying a word on for size. "It will do. I have known worse names and better men, and not always in that order."

She did not ask where he was from, or where he was going, or what was in the pack. A person who called themselves *Traveler* had already answered those questions in the only way they intended to, and Maren had spent five years in the Kingsguard learning the difference between a man who would not talk and a man who could not, and this one was neither. He simply preferred not to. She respected it. She had preferences of her own.

"The snug, then." She reached under the bar and took a second key — iron, older than the brass one, hung on a knotted cord. "It has a bed and a table and a candle, and no window, which you have already said suits you. It shares a wall with the kitchen, so it will be warm until Pell banks the stove, and then it will be cold, and there is an extra blanket in the chest. Use it or do not."

She set the key on the bar between them, left-handed, and did not push it across.

"Two silver. And one thing more." She leaned her forearms on the bar, which brought her down to the traveler's eye level, and her voice stayed exactly as low and even as it had been all evening. "The snug has one door. It locks from the inside, and the key works from the inside too, and the wall is thick. Whatever you are carrying, and whoever bought you dinner, is your business and not mine. But the Antler is my house. If trouble comes through that door, it comes through me first. I tell every guest that. I am telling you now so that you are not surprised by it later."

She straightened, picked up the traveler's bowl and the empty tankard, and stacked them with the rest.

"Stairs behind you, but the snug is the other way — past the hearth, door beside the kitchen. Pell will glare at you if you stand in his doorway. Glare back. He respects it."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: The clock in the corner strikes midnight. I'm still at the bar, talking with Maren.

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
The clock in the corner struck midnight — eleven chimes for the hour and one for the half, the way it had been mis-set for as long as Maren had owned it, and which she had never once bothered to fix.

The common room had thinned while they talked. The grain merchants had settled their argument, or at least agreed to continue it elsewhere, and left coins on their table. The dwarf had folded his letter into his coat and gone up to his room with a candle. Only three tables still held anyone, and two of those were the kind of quiet that meant *nearly finished*.

Maren wiped her hands on her apron, set the rag aside, and reached for two clean tankards — the good ones, the matched pair from the shelf below the till, the ones she did not use for customers. She set them on the bar, side by side, and filled the first with ale from the cask. Left-handed, steady, no foam over the rim.

The second tankard she filled the same way. Same pour. Same care.

She picked it up, carried it down the bar to the far end — past the till, past the empty stools, past the dark corner where the hearth-light did not quite reach — and set it down at the very end of the counter, where the bar met the wall. She straightened it so it sat square. Then she came back, picked up the first tankard, and drank.

She did not say anything. She did not look at the traveler. She did not look at the tankard at the end of the bar, either, which took a certain amount of practice.

For a moment the tavern was only the sound of the hearth and the wind at the door and the soft creak of the sign outside.

"Clock's wrong," Maren said at last, to no one in particular, setting her tankard down. "It's been wrong for eleven years. I keep meaning to fix it. I keep not doing it." She picked up her rag again. "Some things you keep the way they are."

She glanced at the traveler then — brief, level, unreadable — and did not explain the drink at the end of the bar, and did not invite a question about it, and did not forbid one either. Her left hand resumed its slow circles on the wood.

"The snug is warm this time of night," she said. "Pell banks the stove last thing. If you want to sleep, now's the hour. If you want to sit a while longer, the fire's good and the ale's poured, and I do not close the bar until the last guest is finished — but I will be honest with you, friend. I have not decided yet whether you are the last guest or the only one."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her, taking it all in. The extra tankard, the quiet, the admission about the clock.* "I'm not much for sleeping, not tonight anyway." *I take another sip of my ale.* "So, what's with the extra drink?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren did not stop wiping the counter. Her left hand kept its slow circles on the wood, and for a moment that was the only answer the traveler got.

Then she set the rag down, folded it once, and looked at him — properly, the way she looked at a table she thought might be trouble, though there was no trouble in her face. Just a door closing politely.

"That," she said, "is house business."

She picked up her tankard and drank, unhurried, and set it back down with a small click of pottery on wood. Her eyes went down the bar to the far end — just a glance, half a second — and then came back, and she did not apologize for the glance.

"I do not explain house business to guests," she said. "Not to you, not to lords, not to the King's own road-inspectors, who asked me once and got porridge and a very long story about drainage." A pause. "They did not ask again."

She reached under the bar, not for the cudgel — her hand came back up with the traveler's iron key, which she turned over once between her fingers and set down on the counter between them.

"You are welcome to wonder," she said. "Wonder costs nothing, and I would never charge for it. But the answer to that question is the one thing in this tavern that is not for sale, and I keep my stock and my silence in the same ledger."

She let that sit. The hearth crackled. The wind pushed at the door and lost.

"Now." She picked the rag back up, left-handed. "You said you are not much for sleeping. That is your business, and I will not press on that either. But a person who does not sleep the night before a long road is a person who makes mistakes on it, and I have seen enough of those. So I will tell you what I tell every guest who sits past midnight: the fire stays lit until I bank it, the ale is paid for, and you may stay as long as you are pleasant." A beat. "That last part has been known to be a high bar."

She tilted her head toward the end of the bar, where the second tankard still stood, untouched, in the dark.

"I will be here until the fire's down. If you want to keep drinking, keep drinking. If you want to talk, I will listen, and I will not ask you a single question you have already refused to answer. That is a better trade than most people offer at this hour."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I watch her, a small smile playing on my lips.* "Fair enough, Maren. Fair enough." *I take another sip, then gesture vaguely to the room.* "So, what *is* a good trade, in your experience, at this hour?"

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren considered the question the way she considered a delivery of kegs — turning it over, checking it for weight and quality.

"A good trade at this hour," she said, "is one where both people walk away with what they came for and neither of them has to lie about it."

She picked up her rag and moved down the bar a few feet, wiping a stretch that did not need it, which put her closer to the hearth and further from the dark end of the counter.

"I have been on both sides of the ledger. I have bought grain off a man who swore it was dry and sold it to a baker who knew it was not, and I slept fine, because the baker got bread and the farmer got coin and nobody died of it." She wrung the rag out over the basin and hung it on its hook. "That is a fair trade. A fair trade does not have to be a kind one."

She came back and leaned her elbows on the bar, left forearm forward, right tucked in against her side the way it always was when she was standing still for a while.

"A bad trade at this hour is the one where somebody pays in coin and somebody else pays in something they cannot count." She looked at the traveler steadily. "You have seen the sort I mean. A man buys your dinner and you owe him a favor you did not agree to. A woman sells you a room and you owe her the story of your life. Those are not trades. Those are hooks with a ribbon on them."

She straightened, picked up her tankard, and drank.

"So." She set it down. "My trade at this hour is this: you sit, I pour, and neither of us owes the other a thing but courtesy. If you want to tell me where you are going, I will listen and forget it by morning. If you do not, I will ask you about the weather like a civilized person." A pause. "The weather has been terrible. There. That was me starting."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I chuckle, swirling the ale in my tankard.* "The weather has indeed been terrible. Rained for three days straight east of here. Had to sleep under a leaky tarp one night." *I lean back on my stool, more relaxed than I've been all evening.* "And you're right, Maren. Courtesy is a good trade."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren huffed — not quite a laugh, but the closest thing to one that had crossed the bar all evening.

"A leaky tarp," she repeated. "I have slept under one of those. Twelve years ago, on the road to Marrowfen, and I woke up with a slug in my boot and a great deal of opinions about the man who sold me the tarp." She picked up the rag and folded it, though she did not need to. "If you bought it at a crossroads, you paid too much. If you bought it in a town, you paid double, and the man is still laughing."

She poured the last of the traveler's ale — a short measure, the bottom of the cask, and she did not charge for it — and then set the empty cask aside and thumped the new one into place behind the bar with a grunt. Her right hand took less of the weight than her left, the way it always did.

The room had gone quiet. The last two tables had cleared out while they talked — coins left stacked, chairs pushed in, which she noted and appreciated. And the corner table where the merchant in the fine coat had been sitting was empty.

Maren straightened up and looked at it. The crab cake plate was still there, half-eaten, fork laid across it. No coins. She had not seen him leave, which meant he had gone while she was drawing the ale and had not wanted to be seen leaving. She filed it next to the other thing she had filed, and did not say any of it aloud, because there was nothing to say yet.

"The man who bought your dinner is gone," she said, evenly, in the same tone she might use to report the state of the weather. "Left his plate and paid nothing. That is a thing that happens, and it is not my business." She picked up the plate with the rag and carried it to the wash tub. "But you are the one he bought for, so I thought you should know."

She came back, rinsed her hands, dried them, and stood across the bar from him — left hand flat on the wood, right resting easy at her side.

"You have a good face on you, Traveler. Tired, but good." She said it plainly, the way she said most things, with no softness laid over it. "I have been wrong about faces before. I will be wrong again. But I have run this bar alone for six years and I have not been robbed once, so I am not often wrong, and I am telling you that so you know I am not saying it to be kind."

She reached for her tankard, found it empty, and set it down again.

"The snug's key is on the bar. The fire's got maybe an hour in it." A pause. "If you would rather sit here and talk about terrible weather and worse tarps until it's out, I am not opposed. I do not get many guests who know what a fair trade looks like." She tilted her head, dry. "Most of them try to haggle on the stew."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I grin, a genuine, tired smile.* "I can definitely tell you more about bad tarps, Maren." *I glance at the key, then back at her.* "And I think I'd prefer the fire and good company for a bit longer, if you don't mind."

dialogue.name: Maren
dialogue.content:
Maren looked at him for a moment, then reached under the bar and came up with a third tankard — not one of the matched pair, just an ordinary working mug, chipped at the rim. She filled it from the new cask, left-handed, and instead of drinking it standing up the way she did behind the bar, she came around the end of the counter and sat down on the stool beside him.

It was a thing she did perhaps twice a month.

"There," she said. "Now I am a guest in my own house. Pell would have opinions about it, but Pell is asleep."

She drank, set the mug down, and stretched her left arm along the bar, settling in. The fire had burned down to a steady orange, and the room was warm in the way that only near-empty rooms get warm — close and quiet, holding the day's heat like a coat. The second tankard still stood at the far end of the bar, untouched, catching the firelight along its rim.

"Bad tarps," she said. "I will go first, since you are the one who has been rained on for three days and I am merely the one who has been rained on for a living." She turned the mug a quarter-turn on the wood, a habit. "Marrowfen road, twelve years back. I bought the tarp off a man with one eye and a very good cart, which should have told me something, and it should have told me louder. He said it was oiled canvas. It was not oiled canvas. It was a sail with ambitions."

She drank.

"Third night, it rained like the sky owed someone money. I woke up because the water was coming in sideways, which I had not previously known a tarp could do. My husband slept through the whole thing. Woke up dry as a biscuit and asked me why I looked like a drowned cat." She said *my husband* the way she said *the till* or *the stairs* — plainly, a fact in the ledger. "He could sleep through anything. Sieges. Thunder. Me, packing."

She looked into the fire, not at him.

"So. Your leaky tarp. Where was it, and did the man have both eyes? Because I have a theory about the one-eyed tarp merchants, and it is not a kind theory, and I would like to test it."

dialogue.name: Traveler
dialogue.content: *I listen to her story, a small smile on my face.* "Mine was a bit less dramatic, thankfully. No slugs, no sideways rain. Just a persistent drip right onto my face, every time I shifted." *I take a sip of ale.* "And he had two eyes, though one was a bit cloudy. Sold it to me in a market town called Oakhaven."

S.1_consistency_over_time.rationale: Maren's character remains remarkably consistent throughout - her left-handed mannerisms, dry wit, protective nature, and mysterious past elements (the extra tankard, her husband reference) are maintained from start to finish. Her voice never wavers or becomes generic.

S.2_degradation_resistance.rationale: Writing quality actually improves over time. Early responses are good but later ones (especially turns 14-22) show richer detail, deeper character work, and more sophisticated prose. No repetition or flattening detected.

S.3_narrative_momentum.rationale: Strong progression from suspicious innkeeper to gradual trust-building. The mysterious merchant subplot creates tension, midnight conversation deepens intimacy, and Maren's decision to sit beside Traveler shows clear relationship development.

S.4_adaptive_responsiveness.rationale: Excellently handles user redirects - adapts to the crab cake interruption, responds naturally to Traveler's evasiveness, and gracefully shifts from business transaction to intimate late-night conversation when user shows interest in staying up.

S.5_agency_respect_session.rationale: Perfect respect for user agency throughout. Never writes Traveler's actions, thoughts, or dialogue. Always leaves space for user response and decision-making.

S.6_temporal_reasoning.rationale: Generally strong time progression from evening dinner rush to midnight conversation. The clock striking midnight works well. Minor issue: fire burns for 'maybe an hour' at turn 20 but conversation continues naturally without addressing this constraint.
contradictions: Fire timeline slightly inconsistent - stated to have 'maybe an hour' left but conversation continues indefinitely
